shelves.title: Anti-VEGF for wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration: two drugs, equal vision — one safety signal left deliberately UNRESOLVED
shelves.question: For wet AMD, which anti-VEGF drug, on which schedule — and what should be made of the cheaper drug's serious-event excess?
shelves.mesh: Wet Macular Degeneration · Ranibizumab · Bevacizumab · Angiogenesis Inhibitors · Intravitreal Injections · Visual Acuity · Humans
shelves.balance: On vision, the question is settled twice over: bevacizumab and ranibizumab gain patients the same letters at 1 and 2 years (CATT, Cards 1–2), with IVAN (Reference 3) formally inconclusive on strict noninferiority but pointing the same way; monthly treatment protects a couple of letters that as-needed drift surrenders. On safety, this shelf follows the developer's ruling and prints the CATT finding as UNRESOLVED : serious systemic adverse events ran 24.1% vs 19.0% at year 1 and 39.9% vs 31.7% at year 2 on bevacizumab vs ranibizumab, while death, MI, stroke, and arteriothrombotic events never differed — an excess without a pattern, neither dismissed nor convicted. The diabetic macular edema comparison of the same drug family (DRCR Protocol T) has its home on Shelf #373 and is cross-linked, not duplicated, here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CATT, year 1 (Martin 2011): bevacizumab EQUALED ranibizumab on vision — and the serious-systemic-event excess (24.1% vs 19.0%) prints as UNRESOLVED
cards.summary: 1,208 patients with neovascular AMD, ranibizumab vs bevacizumab, monthly or as-needed: vision gains were equivalent drug-for-drug — monthly 8.5 vs 8.0 letters , as-needed 6.8 vs 5.9 letters (noninferiority limit 5 letters). Ranibizumab as-needed equaled ranibizumab monthly. The other result, printed at the weight the developer ruled for it — UNRESOLVED : serious systemic adverse events (primarily hospitalizations) in 24.1% on bevacizumab vs 19.0% on ranibizumab (RR 1.29 [1.01–1.66]) , spread across disease categories not previously tied to anti-VEGF therapy. Rates of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke were similar between drugs (P>0.20).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (CATT), N Engl J Med 2011 — multicenter, single-blind, noninferiority. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00593450.
cards.people: 1,208 patients with neovascular age-related macular degeneration, randomly assigned to ranibizumab or bevacizumab on a monthly schedule or as needed with monthly evaluation. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Bevacizumab administered monthly was equivalent to ranibizumab administered monthly, with 8.0 and 8.5 letters gained respectively. Bevacizumab as needed was equivalent to ranibizumab as needed, with 5.9 and 6.8 letters gained. Ranibizumab as needed was equivalent to monthly ranibizumab, although the comparison between bevacizumab as needed and monthly bevacizumab was inconclusive. The mean decrease in central retinal thickness was greater with ranibizumab monthly (196 μm) than in the other groups (152–168 μm; P=0.03). Rates of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke were similar for either drug (P>0.20). The proportion of patients with serious systemic adverse events (primarily hospitalizations) was higher with bevacizumab than ranibizumab (24.1% vs 19.0%; risk ratio 1.29 [1.01–1.66]), with excess events broadly distributed in disease categories not identified in previous studies as areas of concern.
cards.watchOut: CATT compared an approved drug against its own cheaper molecular cousin used off-label, at a fraction of the price — which is why the safety paragraph matters as much as the vision paragraph. The serious-event excess is real in the data and unexplained in pattern; CATT was not powered to resolve it, and this shelf prints it as UNRESOLVED, per the developer's ruling — neither dismissed as noise nor promoted to a proven harm.
cards.source: CATT Research Group; Martin DF et al. Ranibizumab and bevacizumab for neovascular age-related macular degeneration. N Engl J Med. 2011;364:1897–1908. PMID 21526923 · NCT00593450 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1102673

cards.headline: CATT, year 2 (Martin 2012): vision still equal; monthly beat as-needed by 2.4 letters; the serious-event gap persisted (39.9% vs 31.7%) — still UNRESOLVED
cards.summary: Among 1,107 patients followed into year 2 on the same regimen: mean vision gain differed by −1.4 letters between drugs [−3.7 to 0.8] — still equivalent territory — while monthly treatment beat as-needed by 2.4 letters [−4.8 to −0.1], and switching from monthly to as-needed after year 1 cost vision (−2.2 letters) and dryness (−19% without fluid). Death and arteriothrombotic event rates were again similar between drugs (P>0.60). The systemic serious-event excess persisted: 39.9% bevacizumab vs 31.7% ranibizumab (adjusted RR 1.30 [1.07–1.57], P=0.009) — and the authors' own sentence governs this shelf: its interpretation 'is uncertain because of the lack of specificity to conditions associated with inhibition of VEGF.'
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial, 2-year results (CATT), Ophthalmology 2012. Registry note: the trial's ClinicalTrials.gov number is NCT00593450 (from the 1-year record); this 2-year record's own databank anomalously lists ISRCTN92166560 — the IVAN trial's registration — flagged here rather than silently corrected.
cards.people: 1,107 patients followed up during year 2, among 1,185 enrolled with neovascular AMD (the record's two enrollment figures — 1,208 randomized in the 1-year report, 1,185 enrolled here — are printed as each record states them). At 1 year, patients initially on monthly treatment were re-randomized to monthly or as-needed treatment on the same drug. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Among patients following the same regimen for 2 years, mean gain in visual acuity was similar for both drugs (bevacizumab–ranibizumab difference −1.4 letters [−3.7 to 0.8]; P=0.21). Mean gain was greater for monthly than as-needed treatment (difference −2.4 letters [−4.8 to −0.1]; P=0.046). The proportion without fluid ranged from 13.9% (bevacizumab as-needed) to 45.5% (ranibizumab monthly). Switching from monthly to as-needed treatment resulted in a greater mean decrease in vision during year 2 (−2.2 letters; P=0.03). Rates of death and arteriothrombotic events were similar for both drugs (P>0.60). The proportion with 1 or more systemic serious adverse events was higher with bevacizumab (39.9% vs 31.7%; adjusted risk ratio 1.30 [1.07–1.57]; P=0.009); most excess events had not been associated previously with systemic anti-VEGF therapy.
cards.watchOut: Year 2 sharpens the practical choice rather than the drug choice: the two drugs remain interchangeable on vision, but the regimen is not — monthly dosing, or monthly review with disciplined retreatment, protects the letters that as-needed drift gives back. The safety excess, now seen at two timepoints with the same relative size, stays labeled UNRESOLVED on this shelf: consistent enough to print in bold, unspecific enough that no mechanism or causal claim is made.
cards.source: Martin DF et al.; CATT Research Group. Ranibizumab and bevacizumab for treatment of neovascular age-related macular degeneration: two-year results. Ophthalmology. 2012;119:1388–1398. PMID 22555112. DOI 10.1016/j.ophtha.2012.03.053 (registry: see Type note — the record's databank anomaly is flagged, not hidden)

cards.headline: IVAN, 2 years (Chakravarthy 2013): bevacizumab neither noninferior nor inferior (−1.37 letters, interval straddling both lines); fewer injections cost a little vision on either drug
cards.summary: 610 treated patients in the UK's 2×2 factorial trial (drug × continuous vs discontinuous dosing): bevacizumab vs ranibizumab differed by −1.37 letters [−3.75 to 1.01], P=0.26 — the interval crosses both zero and the 3.5-letter noninferiority limit, so IVAN formally proves neither noninferiority nor inferiority. Discontinuous (as-needed) treatment: −1.63 letters [−4.01 to 0.75], the same straddle. Arterial thrombotic events or heart-failure admission: 6% ranibizumab vs 4% bevacizumab (OR 1.69, NS) — no excess on bevacizumab here. Mortality was lower with continuous than discontinuous treatment (OR 0.47 [0.22–1.03], P=0.05) and did not differ by drug (OR 0.96).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (IVAN), Lancet 2013 — multicentre, 2×2 factorial, noninferiority; drug allocation masked, regimen masked to 3 months. Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN92166560.
cards.people: 628 patients aged at least 50 years with active, previously untreated neovascular AMD and best-corrected visual acuity of at least 25 letters, at 23 UK hospitals; 610 received study drugs (314 ranibizumab, 296 bevacizumab) and 525 reached the 2-year visit. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: For best-corrected visual acuity at 2 years, bevacizumab was neither non-inferior nor inferior to ranibizumab (mean difference −1.37 letters [−3.75 to 1.01]; P=0.26). Discontinuous treatment was neither non-inferior nor inferior to continuous treatment (−1.63 letters [−4.01 to 0.75]; P=0.18). Frequency of arterial thrombotic events or hospital admission for heart failure did not differ between ranibizumab (20 [6%] of 314) and bevacizumab (12 [4%] of 296; OR 1.69 [0.80–3.57]; P=0.16), or between continuous (12 [4%] of 308) and discontinuous treatment (20 [7%] of 302; OR 0.56 [0.27–1.19]; P=0.13). Mortality was lower with continuous than discontinuous treatment (OR 0.47 [0.22–1.03]; P=0.05) but did not differ by drug group (OR 0.96 [0.46–2.02]; P=0.91).
cards.watchOut: IVAN is the honest counterweight to CATT: a smaller trial whose intervals are too wide to certify equivalence, and whose prespecified safety outcome showed no bevacizumab excess. The two trials together justify this shelf's practice-facing summary — the drugs look alike on vision, as-needed dosing gives a little back, and the systemic-safety question CATT raised remains open precisely because IVAN could not close it.
cards.source: Chakravarthy U et al.; IVAN Study Investigators. PMID 23870813 · ISRCTN92166560 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(13)61501-9

shelves.title: Dupilumab for atopic dermatitis: clear or almost-clear skin for about a third of patients — sustained for a year, with conjunctivitis as the signature price
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis that topical treatment cannot control, does dupilumab clear the skin — and does the effect last?
shelves.mesh: Dermatitis, Atopic · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Interleukin-4 · Interleukin-13 · Pruritus · Quality of Life · Humans
shelves.balance: The evidence is three large placebo-controlled trials pointing one way: two 16-week monotherapy trials (SOLO 1 and 2, Card 1) put clear-or-almost-clear skin at 36–38% on dupilumab vs 8–10% on placebo, with weekly dosing adding nothing over every-other-week — and the 1-year CHRONOS trial (Reference 2) shows the benefit holding alongside topical steroids (EASI-75 64–69% vs 23%), with no accumulation of serious harm. The price is consistent and specific: injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis , the IL-4/IL-13 class's signature adverse effect, more frequent on dupilumab in every trial here. What the shelf does not claim: comparative standing against the newer oral and biologic rivals — those trials are not on this shelf, and no head-to-head claim is made. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SOLO 1 / SOLO 2 (Simpson 2016): clear or almost-clear skin in 38%/36% on dupilumab vs 10%/8% on placebo at 16 weeks; conjunctivitis the signature harm
cards.summary: Two identical phase 3 trials in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topicals (671 and 708 patients): the primary outcome (IGA 0/1 with ≥2-point improvement at week 16) occurred in 38% (SOLO 1) and 36% (SOLO 2) on dupilumab every other week — weekly dosing was the same (37%/36%) — vs 10% and 8% on placebo (P<0.001 for all comparisons). EASI-75 responses were significantly more frequent on dupilumab in both trials (P<0.001 for all comparisons; the record's abstract does not state the percentages, and this card does not borrow them from elsewhere). Pruritus, anxiety/depression symptoms, and quality of life also improved. Injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis were more frequent on dupilumab — the class's signature harm, printed here as the record states it.
cards.type: Two randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of identical design (SOLO 1 and SOLO 2), N Engl J Med 2016. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT02277743 (SOLO 1) · NCT02277769 (SOLO 2).
cards.people: 671 patients enrolled in SOLO 1 and 708 in SOLO 2 — adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topical treatment, randomized 1:1:1 to dupilumab 300 mg weekly, dupilumab 300 mg every other week, or placebo for 16 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: In SOLO 1, the primary outcome occurred in 85 patients (38%) on dupilumab every other week and 83 (37%) on weekly dupilumab, vs 23 (10%) on placebo (P<0.001 for both comparisons). In SOLO 2: 84 (36%) and 87 (36%) vs 20 (8%) (P<0.001 for both). An improvement of at least 75% on the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) was reported in significantly more patients on each dupilumab regimen than on placebo in both trials (P<0.001 for all comparisons; percentages not stated in the record's abstract). Dupilumab also improved pruritus, symptoms of anxiety or depression, and quality of life. Injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis were more frequent in the dupilumab groups.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks is a sprint for a lifelong disease: SOLO proves dupilumab works, not how it fares over years, and the weekly arm's flat equivalence to every-other-week dosing quietly halved the drug's necessary dose. The conjunctivitis signal — an eye inflammation from a skin drug, via IL-4/IL-13 blockade — is the adverse effect patients actually meet; it is carded here without an invented percentage because the record's abstract reports it qualitatively.
cards.source: Simpson EL et al. Two phase 3 trials of dupilumab versus placebo in atopic dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–2348. PMID 27690741 · NCT02277743 · NCT02277769 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1610020

cards.headline: CHRONOS (Blauvelt 2017): with topical steroids, the benefit held a full year — IGA 0/1 39% vs 12%, EASI-75 64–69% vs 23% at week 16, similar at week 52
cards.summary: 740 adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and inadequate response to topical corticosteroids, all receiving topical steroids, ± dupilumab for 1 year: at week 16, IGA 0/1 in 39% (weekly) and 39% (every-other-week) vs 12% on placebo (P<0.0001), and EASI-75 in 64% and 69% vs 23% (P<0.0001); week-52 results were similar. Adverse events: 83–88% across all groups including placebo; serious adverse events 3–4% on dupilumab vs 5% on placebo. Injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis were again more common on dupilumab. This is the shelf's long-term card: the effect is durable, and so is the eye signal.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (LIBERTY AD CHRONOS), Lancet 2017 — 1 year, 161 sites in 14 countries. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02260986.
cards.people: 740 adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and inadequate response to topical corticosteroids: 319 dupilumab 300 mg weekly + topical corticosteroids, 106 dupilumab every 2 weeks + topical corticosteroids, 315 placebo + topical corticosteroids; 623 patients were evaluable for week-52 efficacy. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At week 16, more patients on dupilumab + topical corticosteroids achieved IGA 0/1 (39% weekly [125 patients] and 39% every-2-weeks [41] vs 12% [39] on placebo; P<0.0001) and EASI-75 (64% [204] and 69% [73] vs 23% [73]; P<0.0001). Week-52 results were similar. Adverse events were reported in 261 (83%) patients on weekly dupilumab, 97 (88%) on every-2-weeks dupilumab, and 266 (84%) on placebo; serious adverse events in nine (3%), four (4%), and 16 (5%) patients respectively. No significant dupilumab-induced laboratory abnormalities were noted. Injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis were more common with dupilumab.
cards.watchOut: CHRONOS answers SOLO's open question — durability — in the affirmative, in the messier real-world frame of background topical steroids (which could be tapered, stopped, or restarted, so the comparison is dupilumab-plus-flexible-topicals vs flexible topicals alone). Serious harm did not accumulate over a year; the persistent costs are injections, injection-site reactions, and conjunctivitis surveillance.
cards.source: Blauvelt A et al. Long-term management of moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis with dupilumab and concomitant topical corticosteroids (LIBERTY AD CHRONOS): a 1-year, randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2017;389:2287–2303. PMID 28478972 · NCT02260986 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)31191-1

shelves.title: Biologics for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: a gradient — dupilumab largest, omalizumab real — as adjuncts for severe disease
shelves.question: In severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps that steroids and surgery have not controlled, do biologics shrink polyps and restore quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Nasal Polyps · Sinusitis · Rhinitis · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Omalizumab · Asthma · Quality of Life · Humans
shelves.balance: Both biologics beat placebo in severe, refractory CRSwNP, and the shelf is organized by the size of what they did: dupilumab's polyp-score effect (about −2 points vs placebo at 24 weeks, with congestion and CT opacification moving in parallel, Card 1) is the largest; omalizumab's (about −1 point, with SNOT-22 gains of 15+ points over placebo, Card 2) is roughly half — a gradient read across separate placebo-controlled programmes, not a head-to-head trial, and labeled that way. The fence is the trials' entry gate: these are adjuncts for severe disease in patients already failing intranasal steroids, many post-surgery or steroid-dependent — surgery-sparing is a hope the trials gesture at through reduced need, not an outcome either programme proved as a primary claim, and this shelf cards it no more strongly than the trials state it. Asthma comorbidity runs through both populations (SINUS stratified by it) — for the many patients carrying both diseases, one drug treating two is part of the real-world calculus. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SINUS-24 / SINUS-52 (Bachert 2019): dupilumab shrank polyps by ~2 points more than placebo (difference −2.06 / −1.80) and cleared congestion and CT opacification with them
cards.summary: 724 adults with severe CRSwNP despite intranasal steroids, prior systemic steroids, or surgery: at 24 weeks, the nasal polyp score difference vs placebo was −2.06 [−2.43 to −1.69] in SINUS-24 and −1.80 [−2.10 to −1.51] in SINUS-52 (both P<0.0001); nasal congestion improved by −0.89 and −0.87 points, and Lund-Mackay CT scores by −7.44 and −5.13 — endoscopy, symptoms, and imaging moving together. The common adverse events (nasopharyngitis, worsening polyps or asthma, headache, epistaxis, injection-site erythema) were more frequent on placebo . This is the largest biologic effect on this shelf — the top of its gradient.
cards.type: Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 and SINUS-52), Lancet 2019. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT02912468 (SINUS-24) · NCT02898454 (SINUS-52).
cards.people: 276 patients in SINUS-24 (143 dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks, 133 placebo, 24 weeks) and 448 in SINUS-52 (150 dupilumab every 2 weeks for 52 weeks, 145 dupilumab every 2 weeks then every 4 weeks, 153 placebo), at 67 and 117 centres; all were adults with severe bilateral CRSwNP and symptoms despite intranasal corticosteroids. Patients with or without comorbid asthma were included. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, the least-squares mean difference in nasal polyp score for dupilumab vs placebo was −2.06 (95% CI −2.43 to −1.69; P<0.0001) in SINUS-24 and −1.80 (−2.10 to −1.51; P<0.0001) in SINUS-52; the difference in nasal congestion/obstruction score was −0.89 (−1.07 to −0.71) and −0.87 (−1.03 to −0.71); and the difference in Lund-Mackay CT scores was −7.44 (−8.35 to −6.53) and −5.13 (−5.80 to −4.46). The most common adverse events (nasopharyngitis, worsening of nasal polyps and asthma, headache, epistaxis, and injection-site erythema) were more frequent with placebo.
cards.watchOut: Dupilumab's SINUS results are the shelf's ceiling, and their internal consistency is the point: scope scores, symptom scores, and CT scans are different instruments and they agree. The entry fence matters as much — these were severe, treatment-refractory patients, most already steroid-exposed or operated; nothing here supports biologics for ordinary sinusitis with incidental polyps. Smell and quality-of-life endpoints were part of the trials' broader programme; this card prints the outcomes the record's abstract quantifies.
cards.source: Bachert C et al. Efficacy and safety of dupilumab in patients with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 and LIBERTY NP SINUS-52): results from two multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2019;394:1638–1650. PMID 31543428 · NCT02912468 · NCT02898454 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(19)31881-1

cards.headline: POLYP 1 / POLYP 2 (Gevaert 2020): omalizumab improved polyp score by ~1 point vs placebo (−1.08 / −0.90 changes) — real, and roughly half the dupilumab gradient
cards.summary: 265 adults with severe CRSwNP and inadequate response to intranasal corticosteroids (mean polyp score >6, SNOT-22 ≈60 — genuinely burdened patients): at 24 weeks, polyp score changed by −1.08 vs +0.06 (POLYP 1, P<0.0001) and −0.90 vs −0.31 (POLYP 2, P=0.014) on omalizumab vs placebo, alongside congestion (−0.89 vs −0.35; −0.70 vs −0.20) and large SNOT-22 gains ( −24.7 vs −8.6; −21.6 vs −6.6 ). Smell test scores and sense of smell also improved significantly. Adverse events were similar between groups. A working drug, carded second because its polyp effect is about half of Card 1's — a cross-trial comparison, labeled as such.
cards.type: Two randomized phase 3 trials (POLYP 1 and POLYP 2), J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020 — 24 weeks, omalizumab or placebo plus intranasal mometasone. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 138 patients in POLYP 1 and 127 in POLYP 2 — adults with CRSwNP and inadequate response to intranasal corticosteroids, with severe disease (mean nasal polyp score above 6 and SNOT-22 score of approximately 60). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Both studies met both coprimary endpoints. At week 24, mean changes from baseline for omalizumab vs placebo were: nasal polyp score −1.08 vs +0.06 (POLYP 1; P<0.0001) and −0.90 vs −0.31 (POLYP 2; P=0.0140); nasal congestion score −0.89 vs −0.35 (P=0.0004) and −0.70 vs −0.20 (P=0.0017); and SNOT-22 score −24.7 vs −8.6 (P<0.0001) and −21.6 vs −6.6 (P<0.0001). Smell identification scores, sense of smell, postnasal drip, and runny nose also improved significantly. Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The gradient on this shelf is a cross-trial reading — POLYP and SINUS enrolled similar severity but were not randomized against each other — so it is stated as a gradient of separate placebo-controlled effects, not a head-to-head verdict. Omalizumab's own numbers need no apology: a point of polyp score and 15+ points of SNOT-22 over placebo, with placebo-level tolerability, in patients whose alternative is repeat steroids or surgery.
cards.source: Gevaert P et al. Efficacy and safety of omalizumab in nasal polyposis: 2 randomized phase 3 trials. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2020;146:595–605. PMID 32524991. DOI 10.1016/j.jaci.2020.05.032

shelves.title: Biologics for plaque psoriasis: the IL-23 and IL-17 classes clear skin the TNF era could not — PASI-90 is the new normal
shelves.question: For moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, how completely do modern biologics clear skin — and what does each class cost in safety?
shelves.mesh: Psoriasis · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Interleukin-23 Subunit p19 · Ustekinumab · Adalimumab · Severity of Illness Index · Humans
shelves.balance: A class-efficacy shelf, read against the adalimumab-era baseline: where TNF blockade cleared 90% of skin (PASI-90) in about half of patients, the IL-23 inhibitors put that figure at 73–75% at week 16 (guselkumab, Card 2; risankizumab, Card 1 — the latter also beating ustekinumab head-to-head), and dual IL-17A/F blockade with bimekizumab reached 85% (Reference 3). Safety is carded per class rather than averaged: screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B precedes starting any of these immunosuppressants ; candidiasis is the IL-17 class's signature infection (Reference 3); and IL-17 agents carry an inflammatory-bowel-disease caution the IL-23 class does not share. Trial adverse-event rates were otherwise comparable to placebo or active comparators throughout. No mortality claims are made anywhere on this shelf — these are skin-clearance trials, and the stamp grades exactly that. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: UltIMMa-1 / UltIMMa-2 (Gordon 2018): risankizumab (IL-23) — PASI-90 in 75.3%/74.8% at week 16, vs 4.9%/2.0% placebo and 42.0%/47.5% ustekinumab
cards.summary: Two replicate phase 3 trials (506 and 491 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis): at week 16, PASI-90 — at least 90% skin improvement — was achieved by 75.3% and 74.8% on risankizumab 150 mg, vs 4.9% and 2.0% on placebo and 42.0% and 47.5% on ustekinumab (P<0.0001 vs both comparators); clear-or-almost-clear (sPGA 0/1) in 87.8%/83.7% vs 7.8%/5.1% placebo and 63.0%/61.6% ustekinumab. Treatment-emergent adverse-event frequencies were similar across all groups (about 46–51% in the placebo-controlled period). This is the modern efficacy bar for the class: three of four patients nearly clear on an every-12-weeks antibody.
cards.type: Two replicate randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-comparator-controlled phase 3 trials (UltIMMa-1 and UltIMMa-2), Lancet 2018. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT02684370 (UltIMMa-1) · NCT02684357 (UltIMMa-2).
cards.people: 506 patients in UltIMMa-1 (304 risankizumab, 100 ustekinumab, 102 placebo) and 491 in UltIMMa-2 (294, 99, 98), aged 18 or older with moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis, at 139 sites. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At week 16 of UltIMMa-1, PASI 90 was achieved by 229 (75.3%) patients on risankizumab vs 5 (4.9%) on placebo (difference 70.3% [64.0–76.7]) and 42 (42.0%) on ustekinumab (difference 33.5% [22.7–44.3]; P<0.0001 vs both). In UltIMMa-2: 220 (74.8%) vs 2 (2.0%) on placebo (difference 72.5% [66.8–78.2]) and 47 (47.5%) on ustekinumab (difference 27.6% [16.7–38.5]; P<0.0001). sPGA 0 or 1 was achieved by 87.8% and 83.7% on risankizumab vs 7.8% and 5.1% on placebo and 63.0% and 61.6% on ustekinumab. The frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events was similar across treatment groups throughout both studies, with no unexpected safety signals.
cards.watchOut: UltIMMa's comparator choice is its honesty: beating placebo by 70 points is expected of a modern biologic; beating ustekinumab — itself an effective IL-12/23 drug — by 28–34 points on PASI-90 is the claim that moved risankizumab to the front of the class. Sixteen weeks remains a short window for a lifelong therapy; durability and rare-harm questions belong to registries, and this shelf makes no mortality claim of any kind.

cards.headline: VOYAGE 1 (Blauvelt 2017): guselkumab (IL-23) beat the adalimumab-era standard — PASI-90 73.3% vs 49.7% at week 16, and the gap held at week 48 (76.3% vs 47.9%)
cards.summary: 837 patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis: guselkumab vs adalimumab vs placebo. At week 16, IGA 0/1 in 85.1% vs 65.9% vs 6.9% and PASI-90 in 73.3% vs 49.7% vs 2.9% (guselkumab superior to both, P<0.001); at week 48, PASI-90 was 76.3% vs 47.9% . Patient-reported outcomes (quality of life, symptom diary) also favored guselkumab through week 48. Adverse-event rates were comparable between treatments. The comparison that dates the shelf: adalimumab, the TNF-era benchmark, is beaten by roughly 25 points — the baseline against which the IL-23 class's advance is measured.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-comparator-controlled phase III trial (VOYAGE 1), J Am Acad Dermatol 2017. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 837 patients with moderate to severe psoriasis: 329 guselkumab 100 mg (weeks 0 and 4, then every 8 weeks), 334 adalimumab (standard dosing through week 47), 174 placebo crossing to guselkumab at week 16. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Guselkumab was superior (P<0.001) to placebo at week 16 (IGA 0/1: 85.1% vs 6.9%; PASI 90: 73.3% vs 2.9%) and to adalimumab for IGA 0/1 and PASI 90 at week 16 (85.1% vs 65.9% and 73.3% vs 49.7%), week 24 (84.2% vs 61.7% and 80.2% vs 53.0%), and week 48 (80.5% vs 55.4% and 76.3% vs 47.9%). Guselkumab also significantly improved patient-reported outcomes through week 48. Adverse event rates were comparable between treatments. Analyses were limited to 48 weeks.
cards.watchOut: VOYAGE 1's durability is its contribution: the week-16 gap over adalimumab did not close by week 48, which is what 'the class moved on' means in numbers. Its stated limit — 48 weeks — applies to the whole shelf: psoriasis biologics are decade-long therapies graded here on their first year, with long-term safety carried by screening practice (see shelf balance) rather than by these trials.
cards.source: Blauvelt A et al. cards.headline: BE VIVID (Reich 2021): bimekizumab (IL-17A+F) posted the shelf's highest clearance — PASI-90 85% vs 50% ustekinumab vs 5% placebo at week 16
cards.summary: 567 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: at week 16, PASI-90 in 85% (273/321) on bimekizumab 320 mg monthly vs 50% (81/163) on ustekinumab vs 5% (4/83) on placebo (risk differences 35 [27–43] and 80 [74–86]; P<0.0001), with IGA 0/1 in 84% vs 53% vs 5%. Over 52 weeks, serious treatment-emergent adverse events ran 6% on bimekizumab vs 8% on ustekinumab . The IL-17 class's signature harm — candidiasis , the predictable cost of blocking IL-17's mucosal antifungal defense — is the adverse effect this class is screened and counseled for; the record's abstract reports the overall safety profile as consistent with previous bimekizumab studies without stating a candidiasis rate, and this card prints no invented one.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, active-comparator- and placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (BE VIVID), Lancet 2021 — 105 sites in 11 countries. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03370133.
cards.people: 567 adults aged 18 or older with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis (PASI ≥12, ≥10% body surface area, IGA ≥3): 321 bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks, 163 ustekinumab (weight-based, every 12 weeks), 83 placebo (switching to bimekizumab at week 16). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At week 16, 273 (85%) of 321 patients on bimekizumab had PASI 90 vs 81 (50%) of 163 on ustekinumab (risk difference 35 [27–43]; P<0.0001) and 4 (5%) of 83 on placebo (risk difference 80 [74–86]; P<0.0001). IGA response (0 or 1) occurred in 270 (84%) vs 87 (53%) vs 4 (5%). Over 52 weeks, serious treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 24 (6%) of 395 patients in the bimekizumab group (including placebo switchers) and 13 (8%) of 163 in the ustekinumab group. The authors conclude bimekizumab was more efficacious than ustekinumab and placebo, with a safety profile consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: Bimekizumab's numbers are the shelf's peak and its caution in one: dual IL-17A/F blockade clears skin like nothing before it, and IL-17 blockade is also the class where candidiasis clusters and where inflammatory bowel disease is a stated caution (new or flaring IBD is a reason these drugs are avoided or stopped). Efficacy rankings across separate trials are not head-to-head verdicts — BE VIVID's own randomized comparisons are against ustekinumab and placebo only.
cards.source: Reich K et al. Lancet. 2021;397:487–498. PMID 33549193 · NCT03370133 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(21)00125-2

shelves.title: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: steroids are the standard treatment — the placebo evidence is thin, the route is settled, salvage is a maybe
shelves.question: A patient loses hearing in one ear overnight. Do steroids restore it — by mouth, by injection through the eardrum, or as salvage after the first treatment fails?
shelves.mesh: Hearing Loss, Sensorineural · Hearing Loss, Sudden · Glucocorticoids · Methylprednisolone · Prednisone · Humans
shelves.balance: Card the uncertainty honestly, because this shelf's foundation is unusually weak for such a universal practice: Cochrane (Reference 1) found three small placebo-controlled trials, all at high risk of bias, two of them null — so whether primary systemic steroids beat natural history at all is genuinely unsettled, and spontaneous recovery (32% of controls improved in the one positive trial) inflates every uncontrolled series. What is solid is the route comparison: Rauch's 250-patient noninferiority trial (Reference 2) showed intratympanic methylprednisolone recovering hearing within 2 dB of oral prednisone, inside its 10 dB margin — choose the route by the patient's systemic-steroid risks, not by expected hearing. For ears that fail systemic therapy, salvage intratympanic steroids (Reference 3) point the right way in 11 studies with no serious harms, at moderate-to-very-low certainty. The stamps follow that shape exactly: POSSIBLE that steroids work, LIKELY that the routes are equivalent, POSSIBLE for salvage. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Steroids vs placebo for sudden hearing loss (Wei 2013, Cochrane): three small trials, all at high risk of bias — the benefit was never established
cards.summary: Cochrane's reviewers found only 3 randomized trials (267 participants) comparing steroids with placebo or no treatment for idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss — and all three were at high risk of bias . Two showed no effect of oral steroids on hearing recovery; the third reported improvement in 61% on steroids vs 32% of controls (a group mixing placebo-treated and untreated patients). No meta-analysis was possible. This null-and-weak picture prints first because it is the honest foundation of the shelf: steroids are the standard treatment for this condition without a large, clean placebo-controlled trial ever having established that they work .
cards.type: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2013, update of the 2006 review). The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 3 randomized trials, 267 participants with idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Only three trials satisfied the inclusion criteria and all three were at high risk of bias. One trial showed a lack of effect of oral steroids in improving hearing compared with placebo. A second showed significant improvement in 61% of patients receiving oral steroid vs 32% of the control group (placebo-treated and untreated patients combined). The third also showed a lack of effect vs placebo, with analysis limited by exclusions and poor compliance. Meta-analysis was neither possible nor appropriate given heterogeneity of populations, steroid formulations, dosages and durations. Two trials presented no clear evidence of harmful steroid side effects.
cards.watchOut: This is why the shelf's primary-treatment stamp is only POSSIBLE. The condition also recovers on its own in a substantial share of patients — the 32% control-group improvement in the one positive trial is the record's own anchor — so uncontrolled case series reporting 60–70% 'recovery on steroids' cannot distinguish drug effect from natural history. Everything else on this shelf compares one steroid strategy against another, which cannot repair this missing foundation.
cards.source: Wei BP, Stathopoulos D, O'Leary S. Steroids for idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013;(7):CD003998. PMID 23818120. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD003998.pub3

cards.headline: Rauch 2011 (JAMA): intratympanic methylprednisolone was not inferior to oral prednisone — hearing improved 28.7 dB vs 30.7 dB
cards.summary: 250 patients with unilateral sudden sensorineural hearing loss (≥50 dB pure-tone average, within 14 days of onset): oral prednisone 60 mg/day for 14 days plus taper vs 4 intratympanic methylprednisolone injections over 14 days. At 2 months, pure-tone average had improved by 30.7 dB on oral prednisone and 28.7 dB on intratympanic treatment — a 2.0 dB difference favoring oral, with the upper confidence bound (6.6 dB) inside the prespecified 10 dB noninferiority margin. Noninferiority was shown, and the per-protocol analysis confirmed it. The route question — the one this trial could answer — is settled; the whether-steroids-work question (Reference 1) is not.
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, noninferiority trial, JAMA 2011 — 16 academic otology practices. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00097448.
cards.people: 250 patients with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss presenting within 14 days of onset, pure-tone average hearing threshold ≥50 dB: 121 received oral prednisone, 129 intratympanic methylprednisolone. Follow-up was 6 months. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: In the oral prednisone group, pure-tone average improved by 30.7 dB, compared with a 28.7 dB improvement in the intratympanic group. Mean pure-tone average at 2 months was 56.0 dB (oral) vs 57.6 dB (intratympanic). Recovery of hearing on oral treatment at 2 months by intention-to-treat analysis was 2.0 dB greater than intratympanic treatment (95.21% upper confidence interval, 6.6 dB), inside the 10 dB noninferiority margin; the per-protocol analysis confirmed the result, and the hypothesis of inferiority of intratympanic treatment was rejected.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not superiority, and both arms received steroids — Rauch cannot say whether either beats doing nothing (Reference 1). What it licenses is a choice of route on other grounds: intratympanic delivery for patients in whom systemic steroids are risky (diabetes, hypertension, peptic disease), oral therapy for everyone else, without an expected hearing penalty either way. That is the claim this shelf stamps LIKELY, and it is deliberately narrower than 'steroids work'.
cards.source: Rauch SD et al. Oral vs intratympanic corticosteroid therapy for idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2011;305(20):2071–2079. PMID 21610239 · NCT00097448 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1001/jama.2011.679

cards.headline: Salvage intratympanic steroids after failed systemic therapy (2022 systematic review): more patients recover, but the certainty is moderate to very low
cards.summary: 11 studies — 4 randomized trials and 7 observational studies — of intratympanic corticosteroid given as salvage to patients whose sudden hearing loss had not responded to standard systemic treatment. Both the randomized and the observational sets showed that salvage intratympanic steroid significantly increased the number of patients displaying recovery , and no serious adverse events were identified in any included study. The reviewers' own grading is the fence: certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low (risk of bias, imprecision, heterogeneity), and they caution against extrapolating the magnitude of benefit to any individual patient. The record prints no pooled effect size, and this card prints none.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Heliyon 2022 (protocol registered in PROSPERO, CRD42019130586, as stated on the record). The record carries no MeSH terms and no registry databank entry.
cards.people: 11 studies (4 randomized trials, 7 observational studies) of patients with idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss refractory to standard systemic treatment. The record does not state a pooled patient count, mean age, or sex split.
cards.result: Both observational and randomized trials showed that salvage intratympanic corticosteroid significantly increased the number of patients displaying recovery, measured by pure-tone average improvement and recovery counts. No serious adverse events were identified in any of the included studies. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, owing to risk of bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: Salvage therapy has no clean placebo anchor either: some 'recovery' after failed systemic therapy is late spontaneous recovery, and the observational majority of this evidence base cannot separate that from drug effect. The direction is consistent and the harm signal is absent, which earns POSSIBLE — not more. Counseling should quote the uncertainty, not a number this record does not contain.

shelves.title: Allergen immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis: symptoms LIKELY controlled, the effect LIKELY outlasts treatment — asthma prevention only POSSIBLE, because GAP missed its primary
shelves.question: Does allergen immunotherapy — the SLIT tablet taken daily for years — actually change allergic disease, and can it stop hay fever from becoming asthma?
shelves.mesh: Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal · Sublingual Immunotherapy · Asthma · Desensitization, Immunologic · Humans
shelves.balance: Immunotherapy is the only hay-fever treatment whose benefit survives stopping it: three years of the grass SLIT tablet left symptom scores ~26% and medication scores ~29% relatively lower a full year after the last dose (Reference 1), an effect antihistamines and nasal steroids have never shown — LIKELY on both symptom control and sustained effect. The prevention claim is where discipline matters. GAP (Reference 2) randomized 812 asthmatic-free children for exactly this question and missed its primary endpoint : time to objectively defined asthma did not differ; only asthma symptoms and medication use favored treatment. That earns POSSIBLE, printed behind the null. Virchow (Reference 3) belongs to a different claim — treating established house-dust-mite asthma, where the tablet delayed exacerbations during steroid withdrawal (HR 0.69 relative; ~10-point absolute difference). Three claims, three grades, no borrowing between them. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Grass SLIT tablet (Durham 2010): three years of treatment cut symptom scores ~26–30% — and the benefit was still there a year after stopping
cards.summary: Adults with moderate-to-severe grass-pollen rhinoconjunctivitis inadequately controlled by symptom medication took the SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (75,000 SQ-T) daily for 3 years , then were followed untreated for a fourth year. Rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores were reduced by 26% and medication scores by 29% relative to placebo one year after treatment ended (P<.001 and P=.022) — the same level of benefit seen during the treatment years — with significantly more symptom- and medication-free days and sustained quality-of-life gains. These are relative reductions in symptom and medication scores, printed as the record states them. No safety issues were identified.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial with a 1-year post-treatment follow-up, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2010. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe grass pollen-induced rhinoconjunctivitis inadequately controlled by symptomatic medications; the analysis set comprised 257 subjects at the follow-up year. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Significant improvements were consistent across the 3 treatment years. One year after treatment, the active group showed sustained reductions in mean rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores (26%, P<.001) and medication scores (29%, P=.022) compared with placebo — a level similar to efficacy during the 3-year treatment period. Differences in percentages of symptom- and medication-free days were significant during and 1 year after treatment, quality-of-life improvements were sustained, and sustained clinical benefit was accompanied by immunologic changes (grass-specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor). No safety issues were identified.
cards.watchOut: One year of post-treatment follow-up is what this record verifies — claims of longer disease modification need the longer records, and this card makes none. The benefit is symptom control of a seasonal disease, measured in score reductions, not cure: patients still had hay fever, with roughly a quarter to a third less of it. Within those fences, a treatment whose effect survives its own discontinuation is doing something antihistamines never do, which is why the sustained-effect claim is stamped LIKELY alongside symptom control.

cards.headline: GAP trial (Valovirta 2018): the asthma-prevention primary endpoint was MISSED — time to asthma onset did not differ
cards.summary: Printed first, because it is the point: the primary endpoint failed. 812 children aged 5–12 with grass-pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and no asthma took the SQ grass SLIT tablet or placebo for 3 years, with 2 further years of follow-up. There was no difference in time to onset of asthma , defined by prespecified criteria requiring documented reversible impairment of lung function. What favored treatment was secondary: the odds of experiencing asthma symptoms or using asthma medication were lower at the end of the trial ( OR 0.66 , P<.036 — a relative measure), in the post-treatment follow-up, and across the whole 5 years; rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms were 22–30% lower and rhinitis medication use 27% relatively lower at trial end. Symptoms improved; asthma, as the trial defined and prespecified it, was not prevented .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the GAP trial) — 3 years of treatment plus 2 years of follow-up, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2018. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 812 children (5–12 years) with a clinically relevant history of grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and no medical history or signs of asthma. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: There was no difference in time to onset of asthma, defined by prespecified asthma criteria relying on documented reversible impairment of lung function (the primary endpoint). Treatment significantly reduced the risk of experiencing asthma symptoms or using asthma medication at the end of trial (odds ratio 0.66, P<.036), during the 2-year posttreatment follow-up, and during the entire 5-year trial period. Rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms were 22% to 30% reduced (P<.005 for all 5 years), end-of-trial rhinitis pharmacotherapy use was 27% relatively lower (P<.001), and total IgE, grass-specific IgE, and skin-prick reactivity were all reduced vs placebo.
cards.watchOut: This card is the library's standing warning against endpoint substitution: 'fewer asthma symptoms and less asthma medication' is not 'less asthma' when asthma onset was the prespecified, objectively defined primary and it did not move. The symptom findings are real and consistent with Card 1's symptom-control claim — but they are what earns asthma prevention only a POSSIBLE on this shelf, and a soft one. Families should be quoted the missed primary, not the favorable secondaries.
cards.source: Valovirta E et al. Results from the 5-year SQ grass sublingual immunotherapy tablet asthma prevention (GAP) trial in children with grass pollen allergy. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2018;141(2):529–538.e13. PMID 28689794. DOI 10.1016/j.jaci.2017.06.014

cards.headline: House-dust-mite SLIT in asthma (Virchow 2016, JAMA): first moderate/severe exacerbation delayed — HR 0.69 (relative), ~10-point absolute risk reduction
cards.summary: 834 adults whose house-dust-mite allergic asthma was not well controlled on inhaled corticosteroids, tested while their ICS was halved and then withdrawn: time to a first moderate or severe asthma exacerbation favored the HDM SLIT tablet at both doses — HR 0.72 [0.52–0.99] for 6 SQ-HDM and HR 0.69 [0.50–0.96] for 12 SQ-HDM vs placebo (relative effects). The absolute differences were 9 and 10 percentage points over the 6-month ICS-reduction period. Asthma control and quality-of-life questionnaires did not differ significantly. No severe systemic allergic reactions occurred; the common harms were oral itching (13–20% vs 3% on placebo), mouth edema, and throat irritation. This is an asthma- treatment card — it prevented exacerbations in people who already had asthma, not asthma itself.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, JAMA 2016 — 109 European sites. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 834 adults with HDM allergy-related asthma not well controlled by ICS or combination products, with HDM allergy-related rhinitis (mean age 33 years; 48% women); 693 completed the study. FEV1 <70% predicted and recent asthma hospitalization were exclusions.
cards.result: Both doses significantly reduced the risk of a moderate or severe asthma exacerbation vs placebo during ICS reduction (HR 0.72 [95% CI 0.52–0.99], P=.045 for 6 SQ-HDM; HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.50–0.96], P=.03 for 12 SQ-HDM), with absolute risk differences of 0.09 and 0.10. There was no significant difference between the two active doses, and no significant difference in asthma control or asthma quality-of-life questionnaire changes. No severe systemic allergic reactions were reported; the most frequent adverse events were mild-to-moderate oral pruritus (13% and 20% vs 3% on placebo), mouth edema, and throat irritation.
cards.watchOut: The benefit was demonstrated under a deliberate stress test — withdrawing the inhaled steroid — which is exactly the clinical situation (steroid sparing) where an added controller must prove itself; it is not evidence the tablet replaces ICS in stable patients. And it must not be read backward into prevention: GAP (Reference 2) asked whether immunotherapy stops asthma starting, and its primary answer was no. Treatment of established disease and prevention of new disease are different claims, and this shelf grades them separately.
cards.source: Virchow JC et al. Efficacy of a house dust mite sublingual allergen immunotherapy tablet in adults with allergic asthma: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2016;315(16):1715–1725. PMID 27115376. DOI 10.1001/jama.2016.3964

shelves.title: Topical ruxolitinib for vitiligo: the first drug that repigments — partially, slowly, and honestly short of a cure
shelves.question: Vitiligo had no approved repigmenting drug. Does the JAK-inhibitor cream change that?
shelves.mesh: Vitiligo · Janus Kinases · Skin Cream · Administration, Topical · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Two replicate phase 3 trials, one direction, one magnitude: about 30% of patients reached 75% facial repigmentation at 24 weeks against 7–11% on vehicle, with responses still deepening at a year and a harm profile of application-site acne and itch rather than systemic toxicity. That is a real first — vitiligo's first approved pharmacotherapy — and this shelf prints its limits in the same type size: most patients do not reach the endpoint, repigmentation is measured in months, the evidence covers limited (≤10% body-surface) nonsegmental disease with the face as the readout, and nothing here speaks to what happens after the cream stops. LIKELY for repigmentation as trialed; no cure is claimed anywhere on this shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TRuE-V1 / TRuE-V2 (Rosmarin 2022, NEJM): ruxolitinib cream repigmented faces — F-VASI75 in ~30% vs 7.4% and 11.4% on vehicle at week 24
cards.summary: Two phase 3 trials, 674 patients aged 12 and older with nonsegmental vitiligo covering ≤10% of body surface, applying 1.5% ruxolitinib cream or vehicle twice daily. At week 24, a ≥75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) was reached by 29.8% vs 7.4% in TRuE-V1 (relative risk 4.0 [1.9–8.4]) and 30.9% vs 11.4% in TRuE-V2 (relative risk 2.7 [1.5–4.9]) — relative risks printed beside their absolute rates. Responses deepened with continued treatment through week 52, when all patients could use the cream. Among those on ruxolitinib throughout, adverse events occurred in 54.8% and 62.3%; the commonest were application-site acne (6.3% and 6.6%) , nasopharyngitis, and application-site pruritus (~5%). Printed plainly: even on the winning arm, seven of ten patients did not reach 75% facial repigmentation at six months — this is partial, slow repigmentation, not a cure.
cards.type: Two phase 3, double-blind, vehicle-controlled randomized trials (TRuE-V1 and TRuE-V2), N Engl J Med 2022 — North America and Europe. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT04052425 (TRuE-V1) · NCT04057573 (TRuE-V2).
cards.people: 674 patients (330 in TRuE-V1, 344 in TRuE-V2), aged 12 years or older, with nonsegmental vitiligo and depigmentation covering 10% or less of total body-surface area, randomized 2:1 to ruxolitinib cream or vehicle. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: In TRuE-V1, F-VASI75 at week 24 occurred in 29.8% on ruxolitinib cream vs 7.4% on vehicle (relative risk 4.0; 95% CI 1.9–8.4; P<0.001). In TRuE-V2 the figures were 30.9% vs 11.4% (relative risk 2.7; 95% CI 1.5–4.9; P<0.001). Key secondary endpoints, including the Vitiligo Noticeability Scale, also favored ruxolitinib. Among patients applying ruxolitinib throughout 52 weeks, adverse events occurred in 54.8% (TRuE-V1) and 62.3% (TRuE-V2); the most common were application-site acne (6.3% and 6.6%), nasopharyngitis (5.4% and 6.1%), and application-site pruritus (5.4% and 5.3%).
cards.watchOut: The trials enrolled limited disease (≤10% body surface) and the headline endpoint is facial — the most responsive site; hands and feet repigment far less readily, and neither trial answers durability after stopping or outcomes beyond a year (the authors themselves call for larger, longer trials). The JAK-inhibitor class carries systemic boxed warnings for oral agents; this card claims only what a topical trial measured. Within those fences: the first pharmacotherapy ever to beat its vehicle in phase 3 vitiligo trials, twice, at LIKELY.
cards.source: Rosmarin D et al. Two phase 3, randomized, controlled trials of ruxolitinib cream for vitiligo. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(16):1445–1455. PMID 36260792 · NCT04052425 · NCT04057573 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2118828

shelves.title: Adalimumab for hidradenitis suppurativa: weekly dosing beats placebo in two phase 3 trials — response, not remission, and tunnels still belong to surgery
shelves.question: For moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa, does TNF blockade with adalimumab actually reduce lesions?
shelves.mesh: Hidradenitis Suppurativa · Adalimumab · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Two replicate phase 3 trials agree that weekly adalimumab roughly doubles the 12-week HiSCR rate over a substantial placebo response — an absolute gain of about 16 points in PIONEER I and 31 points in PIONEER II — with serious adverse events no more frequent than on placebo. The shelf's honesty is in its definitions: a response is ≥50% fewer abscesses and nodules without new abscesses or draining fistulas, which leaves established tunnels and scarring untouched; those remain surgical disease. Approved-dose nuance worth printing: the trialed regimen is 40 mg weekly — the every-other-week schedule familiar from psoriasis is not what won here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PIONEER I and II (Kimball 2016, NEJM): weekly adalimumab produced a HiSCR response in 41.8% and 58.9% vs 26.0% and 27.6% on placebo at week 12
cards.summary: 633 patients with moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa took adalimumab 40 mg weekly or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint — HiSCR, defined as at least a 50% reduction in abscess and inflammatory-nodule count with no increase in abscesses or draining fistulas — was reached by 41.8% vs 26.0% in PIONEER I (P=0.003) and 58.9% vs 27.6% in PIONEER II (P<0.001). Serious adverse events in the placebo-controlled period were low and similar (1.3% vs 1.3% in PIONEER I; 1.8% vs 3.7% in PIONEER II). The placebo response near 27% is part of the result: in a fluctuating disease, a quarter of untreated patients 'respond' by this measure in 12 weeks, so the drug's added value is the 16- and 31-point gaps, not the raw rates.
cards.type: Two similarly designed phase 3 multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (PIONEER I and PIONEER II), N Engl J Med 2016. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT01468207 (PIONEER I) · NCT01468233 (PIONEER II).
cards.people: 307 patients enrolled in PIONEER I and 326 in PIONEER II, with moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa, randomized 1:1 in the first 12-week period to adalimumab 40 mg weekly or placebo. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Clinical response rates at week 12 were significantly higher with weekly adalimumab than placebo: 41.8% vs 26.0% in PIONEER I (P=0.003) and 58.9% vs 27.6% in PIONEER II (P<0.001). Rank-ordered secondary outcomes (lesions, pain, modified Sartorius score) improved significantly more with adalimumab in PIONEER II only. Serious adverse events in period 1 (excluding worsening of the underlying disease) occurred in 1.3% vs 1.3% (PIONEER I) and 1.8% vs 3.7% (PIONEER II); in period 2 rates were 4.6% or less in all groups with no significant between-group differences.
cards.watchOut: HiSCR is a lesion-count response, not remission: it says nothing about the draining tunnels and rope-like scarring of advanced disease, which no antibody reverses — those still belong to surgery, and starting a biologic is not a reason to defer needed excision. The two trials also disagreed on the secondary outcomes (significant in PIONEER II, not I), and 12 weeks is a short read on a lifelong disease. Within the endpoint as defined, two concordant phase 3 trials earn LIKELY.
cards.source: Kimball AB et al. Two phase 3 trials of adalimumab for hidradenitis suppurativa. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(5):422–434. PMID 27518661 · NCT01468207 · NCT01468233 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1504370

shelves.title: Dupilumab for eosinophilic esophagitis: weekly injections put about 60% into histologic remission vs about 5%
shelves.question: The esophagus is inflamed and narrowing, and swallowing is failing. Does blocking IL-4/IL-13 signaling with dupilumab clear the eosinophils and the dysphagia?
shelves.mesh: Eosinophilic Esophagitis · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Deglutition Disorders · Humans
shelves.balance: LIBERTY EoE TREET (Reference 1) is a two-part phase 3 program with one consistent answer: weekly dupilumab 300 mg produced histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) in about 60% of patients vs about 5% on placebo, and — at the weekly dose — significantly improved dysphagia symptom scores in both parts. The dosing lesson is inside the same trial: every-2-week dosing matched the histology but did not significantly improve symptoms, which is why the approved EoE regimen is weekly. Serious adverse events were uncommon and split across the arms; the injection burden is weekly and indefinite. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: LIBERTY EoE TREET (Dellon 2022, NEJM): histologic remission 60% vs 5% (Part A) and 59% vs 6% (Part B) on weekly dupilumab — symptoms improved at the weekly dose in both parts
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial in patients 12 years and older with eosinophilic esophagitis. Part A (n=81): histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) at week 24 in 60% (25 of 42) on weekly dupilumab 300 mg vs 5% (2 of 39) on placebo — a difference of 55 percentage points [40 to 71]. Part B (n=240): 59% (47 of 80) weekly and 60% (49 of 81) every-2-weeks vs 6% (5 of 79) on placebo. Symptoms (Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire, 0–84, higher worse) improved significantly vs placebo at the weekly dose in both parts (Part A −12.32 [−19.11 to −5.54]; Part B −9.92 [−14.81 to −5.02]; both P<0.001) — but not on every-2-week dosing (−0.51 [−5.42 to 4.41]). Serious adverse events occurred in 9 patients across Parts A/B (7 weekly dupilumab, 1 every-2-weeks, 1 placebo).
cards.type: Three-part phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (LIBERTY EoE TREET; Dellon 2022, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03633617.
cards.people: Patients 12 years of age or older with eosinophilic esophagitis: Part A, 81 randomized (42 weekly dupilumab, 39 placebo); Part B, 240 (80 weekly dupilumab, 81 every-2-weeks, 79 placebo). Baseline DSQ scores were 33.6 ± 12.41 (Part A) and 36.7 ± 11.22 (Part B).
cards.result: In Part A, histologic remission occurred in 25 of 42 patients (60%) on weekly dupilumab and 2 of 39 (5%) on placebo (difference 55 percentage points; 95% CI 40 to 71; P<0.001). In Part B, remission occurred in 47 of 80 (59%) with weekly dupilumab, 49 of 81 (60%) with dupilumab every 2 weeks, and 5 of 79 (6%) with placebo. DSQ scores improved with weekly dupilumab vs placebo in both parts (differences −12.32 and −9.92; both P<0.001) but not with every-2-week dosing (difference −0.51; 95% CI −5.42 to 4.41). Serious adverse events occurred in 9 patients during the Part A or B treatment period.
cards.watchOut: Histology and symptoms are different claims, and this trial separates them: the microscope improves at either injection interval; the patient's swallowing improves only weekly — which is why the approved EoE regimen is weekly. The record's abstract reports serious adverse events without enumerating non-serious ones; dupilumab's signature non-serious harms — injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis — are carded on its atopic-dermatitis shelf (#374). Twenty-four weeks is the randomized window; a scarred, strictured esophagus is a decades-long disease, and this trial does not answer dilation needs or cancer-adjacent questions — it makes none.
cards.source: Dellon ES et al. Dupilumab in adults and adolescents with eosinophilic esophagitis. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(25):2317–2330. PMID 36546624 · NCT03633617 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2205982

shelves.title: Venom immunotherapy: systemic reactions to a later sting fall from about 40% to about 3% — but preventing deaths has never been proven
shelves.question: After a systemic reaction to a bee or wasp sting, does a course of venom injections protect against the next sting — and what, exactly, has been proven?
shelves.mesh: Insect Bites and Stings · Bee Venoms · Wasp Venoms · Desensitization, Immunologic · Anaphylaxis · Humans
shelves.balance: The efficacy core is old and small and consistent: in the 1978 controlled trial (Reference 1), sting challenge provoked systemic reactions in 1 of 18 venom-treated patients vs 7 of 12 on placebo — and the Cochrane pool (Reference 2) puts later systemic reactions at 2.7% on VIT vs 39.8% untreated. The fence is stated in Cochrane's own words: whether VIT prevents fatal reactions cannot be confirmed, because fatal stings are too rare for any trial to have counted them; the protection claim is about systemic reactions, full stop. Treatment itself carries risk (systemic reactions to the injections in ~9–14%), and the course runs 3–5 years; guidelines extend it indefinitely for mastocytosis or near-fatal index reactions — that extension is guideline-based, not trial-proven, and is labeled as such here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Hunt 1978 (NEJM): systemic reactions to sting challenge in 1 of 18 on venom — vs 7 of 12 on placebo and 7 of 11 on whole-body extract
cards.summary: Sixty patients with insect-sting hypersensitivity, matched for history, skin test, histamine release, and venom IgE, immunized for 6–10 weeks with venom, whole-body extract, or placebo (20 per group), then sting-challenged. Systemic reactions: 1 of 18 challenged on venom vs 7 of 12 on placebo and 7 of 11 on whole-body extract (P<0.01) — placebo and the then-standard whole-body extract performed identically, and venom beat both. The 14 patients who reacted despite placebo or extract were subsequently given venom immunotherapy; only one reacted to a later sting. This 1978 trial is why modern practice injects venom, not insect.
cards.type: Controlled trial with deliberate sting challenge (Hunt 1978, NEJM) — pre-registration era; the record carries no registry number.
cards.people: 60 patients with insect hypersensitivity in three matched groups of 20 (venom, whole-body extract, placebo), matched for history and sensitivity by venom skin test, histamine release, and IgE antibody to venom; 41 underwent sting challenge after 6–10 weeks of immunization.
cards.result: After six to 10 weeks of immunization, systemic reactions to stings occurred in seven of 12, seven of 11, and one of 18 patients treated with placebo, whole-body extract, and venom, respectively. Placebo and whole-body extract gave similar results and were significantly less effective than venom immunotherapy (P less than 0.01). The 14 patients with failure of treatment with whole-body extract and placebo were subsequently provided with venom immunotherapy; one reacted to a subsequent sting.
cards.watchOut: Deliberate sting challenge in patients with prior systemic reactions is a 1978 design no modern ethics board would wave through — the field's foundational numbers come from an experiment that cannot be repeated, in 60 patients. The post-challenge denominators (18/12/11) are small; the effect is large enough to survive that, but precision about the exact protection rate comes from the pooled review (Reference 2), not this trial. No deaths occurred or were counted: this trial, like every trial since, is silent on fatality prevention.
cards.source: Hunt KJ et al. A controlled trial of immunotherapy in insect hypersensitivity. N Engl J Med. 1978;299(4):157–161. PMID 78446. DOI 10.1056/NEJM197807272990401 (pre-registration era — no registry number.)

cards.headline: Cochrane (Boyle 2012): later systemic reactions 2.7% on VIT vs 39.8% untreated (RR 0.10, relative) — and 'unable to confirm' any effect on fatal reactions
cards.summary: Seven controlled trials, 392 participants (ant, bee, and wasp immunotherapy, mostly subcutaneous). Systemic reaction to a subsequent sting: 3 of 113 (2.7%) on VIT vs 37 of 93 (39.8%) untreated — RR 0.10 [0.03–0.28], a relative effect with its absolute rates printed here. VIT also prevented large local reactions (RR 0.41 [0.24–0.69], relative) and improved quality of life (MD 1.21 points on a 7-point scale). The reviewers' fence, quoted because it is the shelf's: 'We were unable to confirm whether VIT prevents fatal reactions to insect stings, because of the rarity of this outcome.' The treatment's own risk: systemic reactions to VIT injections in 9.3% of treated participants vs 0.7% on placebo or no treatment (RR 8.16, relative), and 14.2% in observational series of bee-venom VIT.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials, with a separate observational harms analysis (Boyle 2012, CD008838). Systematic review — no registry number applies.
cards.people: 392 participants in 6 randomized and 1 quasi-randomized controlled trials of ant, bee, or wasp immunotherapy in children or adults with previous systemic or large local reactions to a sting; harms data also from 11 observational studies.
cards.result: In the trials, 3/113 (2.7%) participants treated with VIT had a subsequent systemic allergic reaction to a sting, compared with 37/93 (39.8%) untreated participants (risk ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.28). VIT was also effective for preventing large local reactions (5 studies; RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.69) and improving quality of life (MD 1.21 points on a 7-point scale, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.67). A significant risk of systemic adverse reaction to VIT treatment itself was found: 14 of 150 (9.3%) on VIT vs 1 of 135 (0.7%) on placebo or no treatment (RR 8.16, 95% CI 1.53 to 43.46); in observational studies, systemic adverse reactions occurred in 131/921 (14.2%) on bee venom VIT. The reviewers were unable to confirm whether VIT prevents fatal reactions to insect stings, because of the rarity of this outcome.
cards.watchOut: Five of the seven trials did not blind outcome assessors, and the whole pool is 392 people — the direction is not in doubt; the exact percentages are softer than they look. The standard 3–5 year course, and its indefinite extension for mastocytosis or very severe index reactions, come from guidelines built on observational follow-up, not from randomized duration trials; this shelf prints them as guideline practice, not trial findings.
cards.source: Boyle RJ et al. Venom immunotherapy for preventing allergic reactions to insect stings. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;(10):CD008838. PMID 23076950. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD008838.pub2 (systematic review — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Omalizumab for chronic spontaneous urticaria: complete response (UAS7 = 0) in roughly a third vs under a tenth on placebo
shelves.question: Hives on most days for months, unmoved by antihistamines. Does the anti-IgE antibody omalizumab switch them off?
shelves.mesh: Urticaria · Omalizumab · Pruritus · Anti-Allergic Agents · Chronic Disease · Humans
shelves.balance: Three phase 3 trials in antihistamine-refractory patients agree: monthly omalizumab 300 mg roughly quadruples complete response (UAS7 = 0: 35.8% vs 8.8% in ASTERIA I, Card 2), cuts itch scores by about twice the placebo change (Cards 1 and 3), and works even in patients already failing combination therapy (GLACIAL, Card 3). The population fence matters — everyone here had failed H1 antihistamines, many at up to four times the licensed dose; this is not first-line evidence. Omalizumab carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis (the label puts its frequency at roughly 0.1–0.2% of patients); serious adverse events in these trials were uncommon and close to placebo. Symptoms return when treatment stops — this is control, not cure. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: ASTERIA II (Maurer 2013, NEJM): weekly itch score fell −9.8 on omalizumab 300 mg vs −5.1 on placebo at week 12
cards.summary: 323 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic spontaneous urticaria still symptomatic on licensed-dose H1 antihistamines, randomized to three monthly injections of omalizumab 75, 150, or 300 mg, or placebo. Baseline weekly itch-severity score (0–21) was ~14 in all groups. At week 12 the change from baseline was −5.1 ± 5.6 on placebo, −5.9 on 75 mg (P=0.46 — no effect), −8.1 on 150 mg (P=0.001), and −9.8 ± 6.0 on 300 mg (P<0.001) : a clean dose response with the approved dose on top. Adverse-event frequency was similar across groups; serious adverse events were low overall but ran higher at 300 mg (6%) than placebo (3%).
cards.type: Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ASTERIA II; Maurer 2013, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01292473.
cards.people: 323 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria who remained symptomatic despite H-antihistamine therapy at licensed doses; three subcutaneous injections 4 weeks apart, then a 16-week observation period.
cards.result: The baseline weekly itch-severity score was approximately 14 in all four study groups. At week 12, the mean (±SD) change from baseline was −5.1±5.6 in the placebo group, −5.9±6.5 in the 75-mg group (P=0.46), −8.1±6.4 in the 150-mg group (P=0.001), and −9.8±6.0 in the 300-mg group (P<0.001). Most prespecified secondary outcomes showed similar dose-dependent effects. The frequency of serious adverse events was low, although the rate was higher in the 300-mg group (6%) than in the placebo group (3%) or in either the 75-mg or 150-mg group (1% for each).
cards.watchOut: Only three injections and 12 weeks sit under the primary endpoint — this trial proves onset, not durability; ASTERIA I (Reference 2) dosed for 24 weeks. The 75 mg dose's failure is a useful internal control: the drug works where the dose is adequate, and asthma's weight-based dosing logic does not transfer — urticaria dosing is a flat 300 mg every 4 weeks.
cards.source: Maurer M et al. Omalizumab for the treatment of chronic idiopathic or spontaneous urticaria. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(10):924–935. PMID 23432142 · NCT01292473 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1215372

cards.headline: ASTERIA I (Saini 2015): complete response (UAS7 = 0) in 35.8% vs 8.8% — well-controlled symptoms in 51.9% vs 11.3%
cards.summary: 319 patients still symptomatic on H1 antihistamines, randomized to 24 weeks of monthly omalizumab (75/150/300 mg) or placebo. At week 12 on 300 mg: weekly itch score fell by an additional 5.80 points vs placebo [−7.49 to −4.10] , P<0.0001; well-controlled disease (UAS7 ≤6) in 51.9% vs 11.3% ; and complete response — no itch and no hives, UAS7 = 0 — in 35.8% vs 8.8% (all P<0.0001). The 300 mg arm met all nine secondary endpoints. Serious adverse events during the 24-week treatment period: 0 in the 300 mg group vs 5.0% on placebo, in this trial.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ASTERIA I; Saini 2015, J Invest Dermatol). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01287117.
cards.people: 319 patients aged 12–75 with CIU/CSU who remained symptomatic despite treatment with approved doses of H1 antihistamines (placebo n=80; omalizumab 300 mg n=81); 262 (82.1%) completed the 40-week study.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, mean weekly itch severity score was reduced from baseline to week 12 by an additional 5.80 points (95% CI −7.49 to −4.10; P<0.0001) in the omalizumab 300-mg group. The omalizumab 300-mg group met all nine secondary end points, including higher percentages of patients with well-controlled symptoms (UAS7 ≤6: 51.9% vs 11.3%; P<0.0001) and complete response (UAS7=0: 35.8% vs 8.8%; P<0.0001) versus placebo. During the 24-week treatment period, 4 (5.0%) patients in the placebo group and 0 in the omalizumab 300-mg group experienced a serious adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Complete response in a third also means two-thirds are not completely clear — partial responses fill much of the remainder, and patients should hear both numbers. These are week-12 snapshots of a relapsing disease, and the response is rented monthly: the boxed anaphylaxis warning and the indefinite injection schedule are part of the real prescription, not fine print.

cards.headline: GLACIAL (Kaplan 2013): in patients failing combination therapy — up-dosed antihistamines plus H2 blockers and/or leukotriene antagonists — itch fell −8.6 vs −4.0
cards.summary: The hardest population of the three trials: chronic urticaria patients still symptomatic despite H1 antihistamines at up to four times the approved dose, plus H2 antihistamines, leukotriene receptor antagonists, or both. Six monthly 300 mg omalizumab injections vs placebo. At week 12, mean change in weekly itch-severity score: −8.6 [−9.3 to −7.8] on omalizumab vs −4.0 [−5.3 to −2.7] on placebo (P<0.001), with benefits sustained to week 24. The trial's primary objective was safety: the overall incidence and severity of adverse events and serious adverse events were similar between omalizumab and placebo recipients, consistent with the drug's profile in allergic asthma.
cards.type: Phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GLACIAL; Kaplan 2013, JACI), with safety as the primary objective. The record carries no registry databank entry, so no registry ID is printed for this card.
cards.people: Patients with persistent CIU/CSU despite H1 antihistamines at up to 4 times the approved dose plus H2 antihistamines, leukotriene receptor antagonists, or both; 24 weeks of treatment followed by 16 weeks of observation. The record's abstract does not state the total number randomized.
cards.result: The overall incidence and severity of adverse events and serious adverse events were similar between omalizumab and placebo recipients; the safety profile was consistent with omalizumab in patients with allergic asthma. At week 12, the mean change from baseline in weekly itch severity score was −8.6 (95% CI, −9.3 to −7.8) in the omalizumab group compared with −4.0 (95% CI, −5.3 to −2.7) in the placebo group (P < .001). Significant improvements were seen for additional efficacy end points at week 12 and were sustained to week 24.
cards.watchOut: GLACIAL's job on this shelf is the fence, not the headline: it shows the ASTERIA effect survives in patients who have already failed the full conventional ladder — the exact patient for whom this drug is prescribed — with no new safety signal in that more heavily treated group.
cards.source: Kaplan A et al. Omalizumab in patients with symptomatic chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria despite standard combination therapy. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2013;132(1):101–109. PMID 23810097. DOI 10.1016/j.jaci.2013.05.013 (no registry entry on the record.)
