shelves.title: Aspirin desensitization in AERD: symptoms and quality of life improve in small trials — at a real cost in gastritis, bleeding, and a 63% real-world dropout
shelves.question: Asthma, nasal polyps, and respiratory reactions to every NSAID. Does desensitizing to aspirin — then taking it daily, indefinitely — control the disease?
shelves.mesh: Asthma, Aspirin-Induced · Desensitization, Immunologic · Aspirin · Nasal Polyps · Sinusitis · Humans
shelves.balance: The evidence shape is stated plainly because it decides the grade: five small randomized trials (233 patients in total), pooled in 2019 (Reference 1), show better sinonasal symptoms and quality of life on desensitization plus daily aspirin, with moderate-to-high certainty on those symptom outcomes — and significantly more treatment-stopping adverse events, including major bleeding and gastritis. The surgery literature (Reference 2) finds lower revision rates in patients maintained on aspirin after sinus surgery, but it is a review of uncontrolled series. And real-world follow-up (Reference 3) supplies the cold water: 63% of patients quit the daily aspirin, and those treated had no fewer revision surgeries than controls. No large trial with hard endpoints exists. That is a POSSIBLE shelf: a real option for a miserable disease, sold with its dropout rate attached. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: The randomized pool (Chu 2019): quality of life and respiratory symptoms improve — discontinuation-worthy adverse events rise too (RR 4.39, relative)
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the five randomized trials of aspirin desensitization in AERD — 233 patients in total , mean daily aspirin dose 800 mg. Versus placebo, desensitization improved quality of life (RR 2.00 [1.31–3.06] for a clinically important improvement — a relative effect; risk difference +24%; SNOT-22 mean difference −10.27 points on a 0–110 scale; moderate-certainty evidence) and respiratory symptoms (RR 2.20 [1.55–2.73]; risk difference +36%; high-certainty). The harms are in the same analysis, not a footnote: adverse events severe enough to stop treatment — major bleeding, gastritis, asthma exacerbation, or rash — RR 4.39 [1.43–13.50] (relative; risk difference +11%) , and gastritis RR 3.84 [1.12–13.19] (risk difference +9%). The two available observational studies were too confounded to inform.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials and comparative observational studies (Chu 2019, Int Forum Allergy Rhinol). Systematic review — no registry number applies.
cards.people: 233 patients with AERD across five randomized controlled trials; the observational literature contributed two studies the reviewers judged uninformative for lack of adjustment or contemporaneous controls.
cards.result: Compared to placebo, aspirin desensitization (mean daily dose 800 mg) improved quality of life (RR 2.00; 95% CI 1.31 to 3.06; risk difference +24%; SNOT-22 mean difference −10.27 [−6.39 to −14.15]; moderate-certainty) and respiratory symptoms (RR 2.20 [1.55 to 2.73], risk difference +36%; high-certainty). Aspirin desensitization increased adverse events severe enough to cause treatment discontinuation (major bleeding, gastritis, asthma exacerbation, or rash; RR 4.39 [1.43 to 13.50], RD +11%, moderate-certainty) and gastritis (RR 3.84 [1.12 to 13.19], RD +9%, low-certainty). Findings were robust to sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: 233 randomized patients is the entire world's RCT evidence for a treatment recommended to thousands — every interval here is wide, and the symptom scales are subjective in trials where aspirin's side effects can unblind. The benefit is measured in months; the commitment — daily aspirin, with desensitization lost after missed doses — is measured in decades.
cards.source: Chu DK et al. Benefits and harms of aspirin desensitization for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int Forum Allergy Rhinol. 2019;9(12):1409–1419. PMID 31518069. DOI 10.1002/alr.22428 (systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: After sinus surgery (Ryan 2020): maintained aspirin, fewer revisions — interrupted aspirin, recurrence (a review of uncontrolled series)
cards.summary: Systematic review of the six studies reporting before-and-after outcomes in AERD patients who had endoscopic sinus surgery followed by aspirin desensitization. Symptoms improved significantly after surgery, with sustained improvement following desensitization; revision surgery rates were significantly lower in patients maintained on aspirin therapy , and recurrence of polyps with worsening symptoms followed interruption of aspirin maintenance. The reviewers' conclusion is qualitative — the underlying studies are series without control arms, so no effect size is printed on this card, because the record offers none.
cards.type: Systematic review of observational surgical series (Ryan 2020, World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg). No registry number applies.
cards.people: Patients 18 years and older with AERD who underwent endoscopic sinus surgery and subsequent aspirin desensitization, in the six studies with both preoperative and postoperative data.
cards.result: The results demonstrate statistically significant improvement in symptoms following endoscopic sinus surgery, with sustained improvement following aspirin desensitization. Revision surgery rates were significantly lower in patients maintained on aspirin therapy. Recurrence of polyps and worsening symptoms requiring revision surgery occurs when aspirin maintenance therapy is interrupted.
cards.watchOut: Surgery itself improves these patients, and patients who tolerate daily aspirin for years differ from those who quit — this design cannot separate the drug's effect from the adherent patient's. Card 3 is the comparison this literature lacks, and it disagrees.
cards.source: Ryan L et al. Systematic review of outcomes for endoscopic sinus surgery and subsequent aspirin desensitization in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;6(4):220–229. PMID 33336177. DOI 10.1016/j.wjorl.2020.07.010 (systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: The real-world check (Laulajainen-Hongisto 2020): 63% quit daily aspirin — and revision surgery was NOT reduced (P=0.21)
cards.summary: Retrospective multicenter cohort: 171 patients with NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease — 102 who undertook aspirin treatment after desensitization (ATAD) and 69 controls who did not — followed a mean of 7.6 years. The ATAD discontinuation rate was 63% , usually because of side effects, independent of dose or duration. Against the untreated controls, ATAD (mean duration 2.9 years) did not reduce the revision endoscopic sinus surgery rate (P=.21) and did not reduce oral corticosteroid courses per year (P>.05). The authors' own balance: the 37% who stayed on treatment may have benefited — but as a population strategy, the therapy most patients abandon did not move the hard outcomes.
cards.type: Retrospective multicenter cohort study (Laulajainen-Hongisto 2020, JACI In Practice) — observational, labeled as such. No registry number applies.
cards.people: 171 patients with NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease seen at tertiary centers 2001–2017 (102 ATAD, 69 controls without ATAD); outcomes assessed over 2016–2019, mean follow-up 7.6 years. The ATAD group had more tissue eosinophilia, more symptoms, and more sinus surgeries before treatment than controls.
cards.result: The ATAD discontinuation rate was 63%, independent of ATAD dose or duration, usually due to side effects. Compared with the N-ERD group without ATAD, ATAD (mean duration 2.9 years) did not affect the revision endoscopic sinus surgery rate (P=.21, log-rank test) or the number of peroral corticosteroid courses per year (P>.05, Mann-Whitney U test) during follow-up, despite the dose or duration of ATAD. The remaining 37% of the ATAD group continued treatment, indicating they may have benefited.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs against ATAD here (its patients started sicker), so this null does not prove the drug useless — it proves that in ordinary practice, with ordinary adherence, the benefit seen in trials and series does not survive contact with a 63% discontinuation rate. Any clinic offering desensitization should quote the 63% beside the symptom scores.
cards.source: Laulajainen-Hongisto A et al. High discontinuation rates of peroral ASA treatment for CRSwNP: a real-world multicenter study of 171 N-ERD patients. shelves.title: Prophylaxis for hereditary angioedema: targeted drugs cut attacks by half to nearly nine-tenths
shelves.question: Swelling attacks that can close an airway, several times a month. Can long-term prophylaxis — kallikrein blockade or C1-inhibitor replacement — prevent them?
shelves.mesh: Angioedemas, Hereditary · Hereditary Angioedema Types I and II · Plasma Kallikrein · Complement C1 Inhibitor Protein · Humans
shelves.balance: Three phase 3 programs, three attacks on the same pathway, one direction. Lanadelumab (Reference 1) cut attacks from 1.97 to 0.26 per month at the every-2-week dose — an 87% relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it. Oral berotralstat (Reference 2) achieved a smaller but real reduction (1.31 vs 2.35 per month) as a once-daily pill. Subcutaneous C1 inhibitor (Reference 3) reduced attacks by 2.4–3.5 per month against placebo in a crossover design, with ~90% responders at the higher dose. None of these trials was powered on laryngeal attacks or death — the endpoints are attack counts, and no mortality claim is made on this shelf. The access line is printed once, plainly: these are orphan drugs at orphan prices, and cost decides who receives them in most of the world. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: HELP (Banerji 2018, JAMA): lanadelumab — 0.26 vs 1.97 attacks per month at 300 mg every 2 weeks (an 87% relative reduction)
cards.summary: 125 patients aged 12 and older with type I/II hereditary angioedema and at least one attack in a 4-week run-in, randomized to 26 weeks of subcutaneous lanadelumab (150 mg every 4 weeks, 300 mg every 4 weeks, or 300 mg every 2 weeks) or placebo. Mean attacks per month on placebo: 1.97 . On lanadelumab: 0.48 (150 mg q4w), 0.53 (300 mg q4w), and 0.26 (300 mg q2w) — mean differences of −1.49, −1.44, and −1.71 attacks per month (all P<0.001); the q2w figure is an 87% relative reduction, labeled relative, with the absolute rates in this sentence. Injection-site reactions were the commonest adverse event (52.4% on lanadelumab vs 34.1% on placebo); dizziness 6.0% vs 0%.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled trial (the HELP study; Banerji 2018, JAMA) at 41 sites. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02586805 (the record's abstract also carries EudraCT 2015-003943-20).
cards.people: 125 patients randomized (mean age 40.7 years [SD 14.7]; 88 women [70.4%]) with hereditary angioedema type I or II and at least one attack during the 4-week run-in (run-in rates 3.2–4.0 attacks per month); 113 (90.4%) completed the study.
cards.result: During the treatment period, the mean number of attacks per month for the placebo group was 1.97; for the lanadelumab groups, 0.48 for the every-4-week 150-mg group, 0.53 for the every-4-week 300-mg group, and 0.26 for the every-2-week 300-mg group. Compared with placebo, the mean differences were −1.49 (95% CI, −1.90 to −1.08; P<.001), −1.44 (95% CI, −1.84 to −1.04; P<.001), and −1.71 (95% CI, −2.09 to −1.33; P<.001). The most common adverse events with greater frequency on lanadelumab were injection site reactions (34.1% placebo, 52.4% lanadelumab) and dizziness (0% placebo, 6.0% lanadelumab).
cards.watchOut: A 26-week trial in a lifelong disease: long-term safety comes from extension studies, not this record. Attack counts are the endpoint — an attack's severity, and in particular the laryngeal attacks that kill, matter more than its frequency, and this trial cannot speak to mortality; no mortality claim is made on this shelf.
cards.source: Banerji A et al. Effect of lanadelumab compared with placebo on prevention of hereditary angioedema attacks: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018;320(20):2108–2121. PMID 30480729 · NCT02586805 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.16773

cards.headline: APeX-2 (Zuraw 2021): berotralstat, a once-daily pill — 1.31 vs 2.35 attacks per month at 150 mg
cards.summary: 121 patients aged 12 and older with C1-inhibitor-deficiency HAE and at least two attacks in the run-in period, randomized to 24 weeks of oral berotralstat 110 mg or 150 mg once daily, or placebo. Attack rates: 1.65 per month (110 mg, P=0.024) and 1.31 per month (150 mg, P<0.001) vs 2.35 per month on placebo — a 44% relative reduction at the approved dose, printed with its absolute rates. The most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events above placebo were gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea (plus back pain). No drug-related serious adverse events occurred. The effect is smaller than lanadelumab's (Reference 1) — the trade is a daily pill against a twice-monthly injection, and the shelf prints both numbers rather than declaring a winner without a head-to-head trial.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (APeX-2; Zuraw 2021, JACI) at 40 sites in 11 countries. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03485911.
cards.people: 121 patients randomized; 120 received at least one dose (41 on berotralstat 110 mg, 40 on 150 mg, 39 on placebo), aged 12 years or older with HAE due to C1 inhibitor deficiency and at least 2 investigator-confirmed attacks in the first 56 days of a prospective run-in.
cards.result: Berotralstat demonstrated a significant reduction in attack rate at both 110 mg (1.65 attacks per month; P=.024) and 150 mg (1.31 attacks per month; P<.001) relative to placebo (2.35 attacks per month). The most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events that occurred more with berotralstat than placebo were abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and back pain. No drug-related serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred. The most favorable benefit-to-risk profile was observed at 150 mg per day.
cards.watchOut: Cross-trial comparison with Card 1 is informal — different run-in attack rates, different designs. Berotralstat's gastrointestinal effects are dose-limiting for some patients, and 24 weeks is again short against a lifetime of prophylaxis.
cards.source: Zuraw B et al. Oral once-daily berotralstat for the prevention of hereditary angioedema attacks: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2021;148(1):164–172.e9. PMID 33098856 · NCT03485911 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/j.jaci.2020.10.015
cards.search: apex-2 (zuraw 2021): berotralstat, a once-daily pill — 1.31 vs 2.35 attacks per month at 150 mg 121 patients aged 12 and older with c1-inhibitor-deficiency hae and at least two attacks in the run-in period, randomized to 24 weeks of oral berotralstat 110 mg or 150 mg once daily, or placebo. attack rates: 1.65 per month (110 mg, p=0.024) and 1.31 per month (150 mg, p<0.001) vs 2.35 per month on placebo — a 44% relative reduction at the approved dose, printed with its absolute rates. the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events above placebo were gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea (plus back pain). no drug-related serious adverse events occurred. the effect is smaller than lanadelumab's (reference 1) — the trade is a daily pill against a twice-monthly injection, and the shelf prints both numbers rather than declaring a winner without a head-to-head

cards.headline: COMPACT (Longhurst 2017, NEJM): subcutaneous C1 inhibitor twice weekly — 2.4 to 3.5 fewer attacks per month; 90% responders at 60 IU/kg
cards.summary: 90 patients with type I/II HAE and at least four attacks in a consecutive 2-month period, in a crossover trial of self-administered subcutaneous C1 inhibitor (CSL830) at 40 or 60 IU/kg twice weekly vs placebo, 16 weeks per period. Mean attack-rate differences vs placebo: −2.42 attacks per month [−3.38 to −1.46] at 40 IU/kg and −3.51 [−4.21 to −2.81] at 60 IU/kg (both P<0.001). Responders (≥50% fewer attacks than on placebo): 76% at 40 IU/kg and 90% at 60 IU/kg . Rescue-medication use fell from 5.55 to 1.13 uses per month in the 40 IU/kg comparison and from 3.89 to 0.32 in the 60 IU/kg comparison. Adverse events — mostly mild, transient local site reactions — occurred in similar proportions on drug and placebo.
cards.type: International, phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging crossover trial (COMPACT; Longhurst 2017, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01912456 (the record also carries EudraCT 2013-000916-10).
cards.people: 90 patients with type I or type II hereditary angioedema who had had four or more attacks in a consecutive 2-month period within 3 months before screening; 79 completed the trial.
cards.result: Both doses of CSL830, compared with placebo, reduced the rate of attacks (mean difference with 40 IU, −2.42 attacks per month; 95% CI −3.38 to −1.46; and with 60 IU, −3.51 attacks per month; 95% CI −4.21 to −2.81; P<0.001 for both). Response rates were 76% (95% CI 62 to 87) in the 40-IU group and 90% (95% CI 77 to 96) in the 60-IU group. The need for rescue medication was reduced from 5.55 uses per month on placebo to 1.13 on 40 IU, and from 3.89 to 0.32 on 60 IU. Adverse events occurred in similar proportions with CSL830 and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The crossover design gives every patient both drug and placebo — statistically efficient, and the reason this card prints attack-rate differences rather than a single pooled percentage: the placebo-period rates differ between the two dose sequences, and the often-quoted ~95% median reduction does not appear in this record, so it is not carded. Twice-weekly self-injection is the burden; the drug is plasma-derived C1 inhibitor, with the supply and cost realities that implies.

shelves.title: House-dust-mite SLIT tablets: rhinitis improves modestly — asthma exacerbations fall in established disease — asthma prevention has not been shown
shelves.question: A daily tablet of house-dust-mite allergen dissolved under the tongue. What does it do for rhinitis — and what, separately, does it do for asthma?
shelves.mesh: Rhinitis, Allergic · Asthma · Sublingual Immunotherapy · Antigens, Dermatophagoides · Pyroglyphidae · Humans
shelves.balance: The rhinitis claim rests on a 992-patient phase III trial (Reference 1): the combined symptom-and-medication score fell by ~1.2 points more than on placebo over a year of daily tablets — statistically solid, clinically modest, and the reason this grades LIKELY rather than enthusiastically. The asthma claim is a treatment claim, re-carded from its home on Shelf #379 (Reference 2): in established house-dust-mite asthma, the tablet delayed exacerbations during steroid withdrawal (HR 0.69, relative; ~10-point absolute difference). The fence is printed in the shelf's title and meant: asthma prevention has not been shown for this tablet — the grass-tablet prevention trial on Shelf #379 missed its primary endpoint — and the FDA indication for the HDM tablet is rhinitis, not asthma. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: HDM SLIT tablet for rhinitis (Demoly 2016): combined symptom + medication score improved by 1.18–1.22 points vs placebo at one year
cards.summary: 992 adults with moderate-to-severe house-dust-mite allergic rhinitis despite pharmacotherapy, in 12 European countries, randomized to one year of daily SQ HDM SLIT tablet (6 or 12 SQ-HDM) or placebo. The primary endpoint — the total combined rhinitis score (symptoms plus medication) over the last ~8 weeks of treatment — improved by 1.18 points more than placebo on 6 SQ-HDM (P=0.002) and 1.22 points on 12 SQ-HDM (P=0.001) , with the treatment effect present from week 14 onward. For 12 SQ-HDM, rhinitis symptoms, medication scores, quality of life, and the combined rhinoconjunctivitis score all confirmed the result. The record describes the treatment as well tolerated without tabulating adverse-event rates in its abstract — the class's typical harms (oral itching, mouth edema, throat irritation) are quantified in Card 2's trial.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (Demoly 2016, JACI). The record carries no registry databank entry, so no registry ID is printed for this card.
cards.people: 992 adults with moderate-to-severe HDM-induced allergic rhinitis despite treatment with pharmacotherapy, randomized 1:1:1 to placebo, 6 SQ-HDM, or 12 SQ-HDM for 1 year.
cards.result: Analysis of the primary end point (observed data) demonstrated absolute reductions in total combined rhinitis score of 1.18 (P=.002) and 1.22 (P=.001) compared with placebo for 6 SQ-HDM and 12 SQ-HDM, respectively. The statistically significant treatment effect was evident from 14 weeks of treatment onward. For all key secondary end points, efficacy was confirmed for 12 SQ-HDM, with statistically significant reductions of rhinitis symptoms and medication scores, improved quality of life, and a reduced combined rhinoconjunctivitis score compared with placebo. The trial confirmed the efficacy and favorable safety profile of both doses.
cards.watchOut: A ~1.2-point average gain on a combined score is a modest effect — some patients gain much more, many gain little, and the trial cannot sort them in advance. One year of daily dosing for that gain is the honest offer. The multi-year persistence after stopping that the grass tablet showed on Shelf #379 has not been demonstrated in this record for the mite tablet, and this card does not borrow it.
cards.source: Demoly P et al. Effective treatment of house dust mite-induced allergic rhinitis with 2 doses of the SQ HDM SLIT-tablet: results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2016;137(2):444–451.e8. PMID 26292778. DOI 10.1016/j.jaci.2015.06.036 (no registry entry on the record.)

cards.headline: House-dust-mite SLIT in asthma (Virchow 2016, JAMA): first moderate/severe exacerbation delayed — HR 0.69 (relative), ~10-point absolute risk reduction [re-card — home Shelf #379]
cards.summary: Re-card: home Shelf #379, counted once there. 834 adults whose house-dust-mite allergic asthma was not well controlled on inhaled corticosteroids, tested while their ICS was halved and then withdrawn: time to a first moderate or severe asthma exacerbation favored the HDM SLIT tablet at both doses — HR 0.72 [0.52–0.99] for 6 SQ-HDM and HR 0.69 [0.50–0.96] for 12 SQ-HDM vs placebo (relative effects). The absolute differences were 9 and 10 percentage points over the 6-month ICS-reduction period. Asthma control and quality-of-life questionnaires did not differ significantly. No severe systemic allergic reactions occurred; the common harms were oral itching (13–20% vs 3% on placebo), mouth edema, and throat irritation. On this shelf the card supports a treatment claim in established asthma — it is not, and must not be read as, an asthma-prevention claim.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, JAMA 2016 — 109 European sites. Re-carded here from its home on Shelf #379, where it is counted once. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 834 adults with HDM allergy-related asthma not well controlled by ICS or combination products, with HDM allergy-related rhinitis (mean age 33 years; 48% women); 693 completed the study. FEV1 <70% predicted and recent asthma hospitalization were exclusions.
cards.result: Both doses significantly reduced the risk of a moderate or severe asthma exacerbation vs placebo during ICS reduction (HR 0.72 [95% CI 0.52–0.99], P=.045 for 6 SQ-HDM; HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.50–0.96], P=.03 for 12 SQ-HDM), with absolute risk differences of 0.09 and 0.10. There was no significant difference between the two active doses, and no significant difference in asthma control or asthma quality-of-life questionnaire changes. No severe systemic allergic reactions were reported; the most frequent adverse events were mild-to-moderate oral pruritus (13% and 20% vs 3% on placebo), mouth edema, and throat irritation.
cards.watchOut: The benefit was demonstrated under a deliberate stress test — withdrawing the inhaled steroid — which is exactly the clinical situation (steroid sparing) where an added controller must prove itself; it is not evidence the tablet replaces ICS in stable patients. And it must not be read backward into prevention: the GAP trial on Shelf #379 asked whether immunotherapy stops asthma from starting, and its primary answer was no. Treatment of established disease and prevention of new disease are different claims, graded separately on both shelves.
cards.source: Virchow JC et al. Efficacy of a house dust mite sublingual allergen immunotherapy tablet in adults with allergic asthma: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2016;315(16):1715–1725. PMID 27115376. DOI 10.1001/jama.2016.3964 (Re-card; home Shelf #379.)

shelves.title: Wisdom teeth: prophylactic removal vs watchful waiting
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with asymptomatic, disease-free impacted wisdom teeth, does prophylactic surgical removal improve health-related quality of life, dental-arch outcomes, or long-term harm to neighbouring teeth compared with retention and watchful waiting?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Asymptomatic Diseases · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Molar, Third · Prospective Studies · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tooth Extraction
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — There is almost no comparative evidence to settle this common operation: the Cochrane review found exactly one small RCT (on incisor crowding after orthodontic treatment, which found no clinically significant benefit from removal) and one prospective cohort (very low certainty, suggesting retained impacted teeth may raise periodontitis risk for the neighbouring second molar). No included study measured quality of life, costs, or the harms on either side — pericoronitis and cysts if retained, nerve injury and dry socket if removed. Removal for crowding prevention is not justified by the one RCT; beyond that, shared decision-making with regular review of retained teeth is what the evidence supports. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: two eligible studies in total, and no study measured quality of life
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020 found the whole comparative evidence base: one small RCT and one cohort (from 164 screened records). No eligible study measured health-related quality of life — the primary outcome has never been tested — and the cohort raises, at very low certainty, a periodontitis risk to the neighbouring second molar from retention.
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane) — RCTs, quasi-RCTs and long-term cohorts eligible
cards.people: The entire evidence base was one UK RCT in adolescents after orthodontic treatment (164 randomised, 77 analysed; 55% female as reported in the review) and one US prospective cohort reporting a subgroup of 416 healthy men aged 24 to 84 years; no other eligible studies were found.
cards.result: No eligible study reported the primary outcome, health-related quality of life. The cohort found very low-certainty evidence that the presence of asymptomatic disease-free impacted wisdom teeth may be associated with increased risk of periodontitis affecting the adjacent second molar over 3 to more than 25 years of follow-up, and insufficient evidence of any difference in caries risk for that tooth. The RCT found no evidence that removal had a clinically significant effect on dental-arch dimensional changes at 5 years. The included studies measured none of the other prespecified outcomes: costs, pericoronitis, root resorption, cyst or tumour formation, alveolar osteitis, nerve injury, or surgical bleeding. The reviewers concluded the evidence is insufficient to determine whether these teeth should be removed or retained.
cards.watchOut: This is a thin shelf by the evidence's own account: one high risk-of-bias RCT and one cohort at serious risk of bias are all that exist, so every number here carries low to very low certainty.
cards.source: Ghaeminia H et al (Mettes TG, senior author). Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020 May 4. PMID 32368796. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: The one RCT: removing third molars did not meaningfully prevent late incisor crowding
cards.summary: The one RCT (post-orthodontic patients): removing third molars reduced late lower-incisor crowding by 1.1 mm from a mean 2.1 mm increase with retention — p=0.15 , not significant, and judged not clinically significant by its own authors. The crowding rationale fails its only test.
cards.people: 164 patients who entered after completing orthodontic treatment and retention (recruitment from 1984); 77 (47%) returned for records at a mean of 66 months; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract (the Cochrane review reports the analysed sample as 55% female).
cards.result: Where third molars were extracted, the mean increase in lower labial segment irregularity was reduced by 1.1 mm from a mean of 2.1 mm in the retained group (P = 0.15, not statistically significant) — an absolute difference the authors also judged not clinically significant. Their stated principal conclusion: removal of third molars to reduce or prevent late incisor crowding cannot be justified.
cards.watchOut: Over half the randomised patients were lost to follow-up (77 of 164 analysed), the trial is rated high risk of bias in the Cochrane review, and it answers only the crowding question — nothing about pain, infection, nerve injury or quality of life.
cards.source: Harradine NW et al. Br J Orthod. 1998 May. PMID 9668994. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial (recruitment began 1984); no registry ID in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a very common operation resting on one small RCT and one cohort
cards.summary: A very common operation resting on one small RCT and one cohort, neither measuring quality of life: MAYBE (weak evidence) — proven neither beneficial nor harmful on patient-important outcomes.
cards.people: No new participants — synthesis of the two verified cards above.
cards.result: Stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence). Prophylactic removal is proven neither beneficial nor harmful on patient-important outcomes; the single RCT refutes the crowding rationale, and the single cohort raises — at very low certainty — a periodontitis risk to the neighbouring molar from retention. Neither pericoronitis prevented nor surgical harms incurred have ever been counted in a comparative study meeting the Cochrane criteria.
cards.watchOut: Needed evidence, as named by the Cochrane reviewers: well-designed RCTs of long-term and rare effects of removal versus retention are unlikely to be feasible, so high-quality long-term prospective cohort studies are the realistic path; in their absence, retained asymptomatic teeth should be clinically assessed at regular intervals.
cards.source: Closing synthesis of the verified cards on this shelf (PMIDs 32368796, 9668994); no new data introduced.

shelves.title: Skin abscess: antibiotics after incision and drainage add a modest cure benefit — drainage is still the treatment
shelves.question: After a skin abscess has been incised and drained, do adjunctive antibiotics improve cure and prevent new lesions, compared with drainage alone?
shelves.mesh: Abscess · Skin Diseases, Bacterial · Drainage · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Combined Modality Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large double-blind NEJM trials say yes, modestly. Talan 2016 (1,247 in the modified intention-to-treat population) found cure of 80.5% with TMP-SMX vs 73.6% with placebo after drainage — a 6.9-percentage-point gain, with fewer subsequent drainage procedures, fewer new-site infections, and fewer infections in household members. Daum 2017 (786 patients, abscesses ≤5 cm) found cure of 83.1% with clindamycin and 81.7% with TMP-SMX vs 68.9% with placebo, with the benefit restricted to patients whose abscess grew S. aureus, and more adverse events with clindamycin (21.9%) than TMP-SMX (11.1%) or placebo (12.5%). The earlier, smaller Schmitz 2010 trial missed its primary endpoint (treatment failure 17% vs 26%, P=.12) while also showing fewer new lesions on antibiotics (9% vs 28%). The benefit is consistent in direction, real, and single-digit: most drained abscesses cure without antibiotics, so the drug is an adjunct, not the therapy. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Talan 2016: TMP-SMX after drainage raised cure from 73.6% to 80.5% — and cut new infections at home
cards.summary: Talan: TMP-SMX after drainage raised cure from 73.6% to 80.5% (+6.9 points [2.1 to 11.7]) and cut subsequent drainage procedures and new-site infections.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial at five US emergency departments, N Engl J Med 2016
cards.people: Outpatients older than 12 years with an uncomplicated abscess treated with drainage, randomized to TMP-SMX (320 mg/1600 mg twice daily for 7 days) or placebo; 630 and 617 respectively in the modified intention-to-treat population. Median age 35 years (range 14–73); 45.3% had wound cultures positive for MRSA.
cards.result: Clinical cure 7–14 days after the end of treatment: 507/630 (80.5%) on TMP-SMX vs 454/617 (73.6%) on placebo (difference 6.9 percentage points; 95% CI 2.1 to 11.7; P=0.005); per-protocol cure was 92.9% vs 85.7% (difference 7.2 points). In the per-protocol population, TMP-SMX also meant fewer subsequent surgical drainage procedures (3.4% vs 8.6%), fewer skin infections at new sites (3.1% vs 10.3%), and fewer infections in household members (1.7% vs 4.1%). Gastrointestinal side effects were slightly more frequent (mostly mild); invasive infections were rare and equal (0.4% in both groups).
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain is about 7 cures per 100 patients treated — worth having in an MRSA-prevalent setting, which is the setting studied. Three of four placebo patients were cured by drainage alone; this trial does not make antibiotics the treatment, it makes them an adjunct with a measurable margin.
cards.source: Talan DA et al. Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole versus Placebo for Uncomplicated Skin Abscess. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(9):823-32. PMID 26962903 · NCT00729937.

cards.headline: Daum 2017: for smaller abscesses (≤5 cm), clindamycin and TMP-SMX both beat placebo — benefit only where S. aureus grew
cards.summary: Daum: for abscesses ≤5 cm, clindamycin ( 83.1% ) and TMP-SMX ( 81.7% ) both beat placebo ( 68.9% ) — benefit only where S. aureus grew.
cards.type: Multicenter, prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 786 outpatients — 505 adults (64.2%) and 281 children (35.8%); 448 (57.0%) male — with a skin abscess 5 cm or smaller in diameter, randomized after incision and drainage to clindamycin, TMP-SMX, or placebo for 10 days. S. aureus was isolated from 527 (67.0%), MRSA from 388 (49.4%).
cards.result: Cure 7–10 days after the end of therapy (intention-to-treat): clindamycin 221/266 (83.1%), TMP-SMX 215/263 (81.7%), placebo 177/257 (68.9%) (P<0.001 for each active drug vs placebo; clindamycin vs TMP-SMX P=0.73). The benefit was restricted to participants with S. aureus infection. Among those initially cured, new infections at 1 month were less common with clindamycin (15/221, 6.8%) than TMP-SMX (29/215, 13.5%; P=0.03) or placebo (22/177, 12.4%; P=0.06). Adverse events: clindamycin 58/265 (21.9%), TMP-SMX 29/261 (11.1%), placebo 32/255 (12.5%); all resolved without sequelae.
cards.watchOut: Where cultures grew no S. aureus, antibiotics added nothing — the drug earns its place against staphylococcal abscesses. Clindamycin's extra new-lesion prevention came with roughly double the adverse-event rate of TMP-SMX.
cards.source: Daum RS et al. A Placebo-Controlled Trial of Antibiotics for Smaller Skin Abscesses. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(26):2545-2555. PMID 28657870 · NCT00730028.

cards.headline: Schmitz 2010: the earlier, smaller trial missed its primary endpoint — failure 17% vs 26% (P=.12) — but saw fewer new lesions
cards.summary: Schmitz 2010: the smaller earlier trial missed its primary endpoint (failure 17% vs 26%, P=.12) but saw fewer new lesions (9% vs 28%).
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, Ann Emerg Med 2010
cards.people: 212 adults randomized to oral TMP-SMX or placebo after incision and drainage of an uncomplicated abscess, in patients at risk for community-associated MRSA; 190 (90%) were available for 7-day follow-up. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Treatment failure within 7 days: 15/88 (17%) on TMP-SMX vs 27/102 (26%) on placebo (difference 9%; 95% CI −2% to 21%; P=.12) — not significant. On 30-day follow-up (achieved in 69% of patients), new lesions formed in 4/46 (9%) on TMP-SMX vs 14/50 (28%) on placebo (difference 19%; 95% CI 4% to 34%; P=.02).
cards.watchOut: An underpowered null on the primary endpoint with a positive secondary endpoint on incomplete follow-up: Schmitz neither proves nor refutes — it is the reason the two NEJM trials needed to be large. Its new-lesion signal anticipated the larger trials' secondary findings.

cards.headline: Reading the abscess trials together
cards.summary: Drainage alone cures roughly 7 in 10; adding an antibiotic adds about 7–14 cures per 100 — an adjunct, not the therapy — LIKELY.
cards.people: Outpatients — adults and children — with uncomplicated, drainable skin abscesses in settings where MRSA is prevalent.
cards.result: The fence: drainage cures roughly 7 in 10 to 3 in 4 patients by itself (placebo cure 73.6% in Talan, 68.9% in Daum); adding TMP-SMX or clindamycin adds about 7–14 cures per 100, prevents subsequent drainage procedures and new lesions, and — in Daum — only helps when S. aureus is the organism. Two large blinded trials in the same direction, plus a smaller null-primary trial whose secondary endpoint agreed, support LIKELY for a modest benefit — not for a large one, and not where drainage was inadequate or the infection is complicated, populations none of these trials enrolled.
cards.watchOut: Harms are part of the balance: TMP-SMX brought slightly more gastrointestinal effects (Talan) and clindamycin the most adverse events of any arm (21.9%, Daum). For a small, well-drained abscess in a low-risk patient, the trials quantify — they do not eliminate — the case for drainage alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 26962903 (Talan 2016), PMID 28657870 (Daum 2017), and PMID 20346539 (Schmitz 2010), all carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Cellulitis: how many days? Five is probably enough when it is uncomplicated and improving — severe cellulitis remains untested
shelves.question: For cellulitis, how short can antibiotic therapy safely be — five or six days instead of ten to twelve — and in which patients has that actually been tested?
shelves.mesh: Cellulitis · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Duration of Therapy · Levofloxacin · Floxacillin · Humans
shelves.balance: This is the thinnest shelf in the slate, and it says so. The affirmative evidence is one small double-blind trial: Hepburn 2004 randomized only patients whose uncomplicated cellulitis was already improving at day 5 — 87 of 121 enrolled — and found identical 98% success on 5 vs 10 days of levofloxacin. For severe, hospitalized cellulitis, the DANCE trial (151 randomized) could neither confirm nor refute noninferiority of 6 vs 12 days (cure 49.3% vs 50.0%, with a confidence interval spanning −15.0 to +16.3 points) and raised a warning: relapse by day 90 was 24% after 6 days vs 6% after 12 days among those initially cured without relapse. A third trial (Switch, 80 patients) asked about IV duration rather than total days and was too compromised by misdiagnosis and recruitment failure to answer anything. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Hepburn 2004: in uncomplicated cellulitis already improving at day 5, stopping at 5 days tied continuing to 10 — 98% success both ways
cards.summary: Hepburn: in cellulitis already improving at day 5, stopping tied continuing to 10 days — 98% success both ways — among the day-5 improvers who were randomised.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Arch Intern Med 2004. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists on the record
cards.people: 121 subjects with uncomplicated cellulitis were enrolled and evaluated after 5 days of levofloxacin 500 mg daily; only those improving — no worsening, no persistent nidus, no abscess — were randomized: 44 to 5 more days of placebo (5 days total) and 43 to 5 more days of levofloxacin (10 days total). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Success (resolution of cellulitis at 14 days with no relapse by 28 days) was 43/44 (98%) in the 5-day group and 42/43 (98%) in the 10-day group — no significant difference at either time point, analyzed by intention to treat.
cards.watchOut: The design pre-selects winners: 34 of 121 enrolled patients were never randomized because they were not improving. The trial answers 'can responders stop at day 5?' — yes, in 87 patients — and is silent on everyone else. It is also a single small trial of one drug (levofloxacin), which is why this shelf cannot grade higher.
cards.source: Hepburn MJ et al. Comparison of short-course (5 days) and standard (10 days) treatment for uncomplicated cellulitis. Arch Intern Med. 2004;164(15):1669-74. PMID 15302637 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: DANCE 2020: 6 vs 12 days for severe hospitalized cellulitis — noninferiority neither confirmed nor refuted, and day-90 relapse ran 24% vs 6%
cards.summary: DANCE: 6 vs 12 days for severe cellulitis — cure 49.3% vs 50.0% , intervals too wide to confirm or refute noninferiority, and a day-90 relapse signal of 24% vs 6% on the short course.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial (DANCE), Clin Microbiol Infect 2020
cards.people: 248 adults hospitalized for severe cellulitis and treated with IV flucloxacillin were included; 151 who had improved and were afebrile at day 6 were randomized — 76 to 6 further days of oral flucloxacillin (12 days total) and 73 to placebo (6 days total). Mean age 62 years; 67% male; 24% diabetic.
cards.result: Cure by day 14 without relapse by day 28: 38/76 (50.0%) on 12 days vs 36/73 (49.3%) on 6 days (absolute risk reduction 0.7 percentage points; 95% CI −15.0 to 16.3) — confidence intervals too wide to confirm or refute noninferiority. With the modified cure assessment, cure was 56/76 (73.7%) vs 49/73 (67.1%) (ARR 6.6; 95% CI −8.0 to 20.8). After initial cure without relapse, day-90 relapse rates were higher in the 6-day group (24% vs 6%; p<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Two readings must coexist: the short course was not shown to be worse on the primary outcome, and it was shown to relapse more by day 90. The relapse comparison is a secondary analysis of a subset (those initially cured), so it is a warning signal, not a verdict — but it forbids stamping short-course therapy for severe cellulitis as settled. This record prints no registry ID in its databank field, so none is claimed here.
cards.source: Cranendonk DR et al. Antibiotic treatment for 6 days versus 12 days in patients with severe cellulitis: a multicentre randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, non-inferiority trial. Clin Microbiol Infect. 2020;26(5):606-612. PMID 31618678 · No registry number printed on the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Switch trial 2019: 24 hours vs ≥72 hours of IV therapy before oral step-down — a trial that could not answer its question
cards.summary: Switch trial: 24 vs ≥72 hours of IV before oral step-down — recruitment failure and misdiagnosis left it unable to answer its question .
cards.type: Randomized, controlled, open-label multicenter trial, Open Forum Infect Dis 2019; reported by its authors as inconclusive
cards.people: 80 patients with lower-limb erysipelas or cellulitis recruited over 40 months: 39 assigned to 24 hours of IV antibiotics and 41 to ≥72 hours, each followed by oral therapy to a maximum total of 7–10 days. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Mean IV duration achieved was 25.5 hours (range 17–40) vs 78 hours (41.5–210). After exclusions for withdrawal (3 in the 24-hour arm, 4 in the control arm), 6 patients (4 intervention, 2 control) did not achieve an adequate response; only 1 patient had self-limiting adverse effects. The authors conclude that the noninferiority of short-course IV therapy cannot be determined from this trial, citing resource-limited recruitment, misdiagnosis of cellulitis, withdrawals, and subjective visual outcome assessment.
cards.watchOut: Carded as a fence, not as evidence: cellulitis has no gold-standard diagnostic test and many mimics, which is why duration trials in this disease keep failing to recruit clean populations. Any future trial that could change this shelf must first solve the diagnosis problem this trial ran into.
cards.source: Clarke MC et al. Lessons Learned From a Randomized Controlled Trial of Short-Course Intravenous Antibiotic Therapy for Erysipelas and Cellulitis of the Lower Limb (Switch Trial). cards.headline: Reading the cellulitis duration trials together
cards.summary: A thin shelf: one small positive trial for uncomplicated cellulitis, one inconclusive larger trial with a relapse warning for severe disease — POSSIBLE, capped there.
cards.people: Two distinct populations that must not be merged: outpatients with uncomplicated cellulitis that is improving by day 5 (Hepburn), and patients hospitalized with severe cellulitis who have improved by day 6 (DANCE).
cards.result: The fence: for uncomplicated, improving cellulitis, one small blinded trial supports stopping at 5 days (98% vs 98%). For severe cellulitis, the one adequate attempt (DANCE) is inconclusive on cure and carries a day-90 relapse warning (24% vs 6%) for the 6-day course. This is a thin shelf — a single small positive trial plus an inconclusive larger one — so it is stamped POSSIBLE and capped there. The in-flight work that could change it: an adequately powered, double-blind duration trial in hospitalized cellulitis with relapse followed to 90 days; none was found in the 24-month sweep.
cards.watchOut: Do not import duration answers from neighboring shelves: abscess (Shelf 505) is a drained-focus disease, and gram-negative bacteremia (Shelf 503) is a bloodstream disease. Cellulitis — no focus to drain, no culture to follow — is precisely where the evidence is weakest.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 15302637 (Hepburn 2004), PMID 31618678 (DANCE/Cranendonk 2020), and PMID 31660410 (Switch/Clarke 2019), all carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Antibiotics for acute sinusitis
shelves.question: Does amoxicillin beat placebo for acute uncomplicated rhinosinusitis in primary care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Amoxicillin/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Bacterial Infections/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Drug Administration Schedule · Rhinitis/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for the null-to-small verdict): In the Garbutt randomised trial, a 10-day course of amoxicillin did not improve disease-specific quality of life at day 3 (mean difference 0.03 on a 0-3 scale, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.19) or day 10, and symptom improvement did not differ at day 3 (37% versus 34%) or day 10 (78% versus 80%); only day 7 favoured amoxicillin. The Young individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 2,547 adults in 9 trials found 15 patients must be treated for one additional cure (NNT 15, with an interval running from NNT-benefit 7 to NNT-harm 190), and no clinical sign or symptom — not even symptoms lasting longer than 7-10 days — identified a subgroup in whom antibiotics were clearly justified; purulent discharge in the pharynx lowered the NNT to 8, with an interval still crossing into harm. The honest claim is that routine antibiotics for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis buy, at most, a small average benefit most patients will not notice.

cards.headline: Garbutt 2012: amoxicillin did not improve sinus quality-of-life scores at day 3 or day 10 versus placebo
cards.summary: Garbutt 2012: amoxicillin vs placebo quality-of-life difference 0.03 [−0.12 to 0.19] at day 3 — and null again at day 10.
cards.people: 166 adults (36% male; 78% white race, as stated in the abstract) with uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis recruited from 10 community practices in Missouri (85 amoxicillin and 81 placebo); 92% concurrently used one or more symptomatic treatments. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The mean change in Sinonasal Outcome Test-16 scores did not differ significantly between groups on day 3 (decrease of 0.59 on amoxicillin and 0.54 on placebo; mean difference 0.03 [95% CI, -0.12 to 0.19]) or on day 10 (mean difference 0.01 [95% CI, -0.13 to 0.15]), but differed at day 7 favouring amoxicillin (mean difference 0.19 [95% CI, 0.024 to 0.35]). Reported symptom improvement did not differ at day 3 (37% versus 34%; P=.67) or day 10 (78% versus 80%; P=.71); at day 7 more amoxicillin participants reported improvement (74% versus 56%; P=.02). No other secondary outcome differed, and no serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: A single 166-patient trial of one antibiotic (amoxicillin 1500 mg/day for 10 days) in clinically diagnosed — not imaging- or culture-confirmed — rhinosinusitis; the isolated day-7 differences sit among many comparisons and had disappeared by day 10.
cards.source: Garbutt JM et al. Amoxicillin for acute rhinosinusitis: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012 Feb 15;307(7):685-692. PMID: 22337680. Registry ID: NCT00377403 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Young 2008 IPD meta-analysis: NNT 15 for one extra cure, and no symptom or duration subgroup in whom antibiotics were clearly justified
cards.summary: Young 2008 IPD: NNT 15 for one extra cure, with a confidence interval crossing into harm (to NNT-harm 190); no subgroup was clearly helped.
cards.people: Individual patients' data from 2,547 adults in 9 randomised trials of antibiotic versus placebo for rhinosinusitis-like complaints in primary care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 15 patients with rhinosinusitis-like complaints would have to be given antibiotics before an additional patient was cured (95% CI from NNT-benefit 7 to NNT-harm 190 — an interval that crosses into harm). Patients with purulent discharge in the pharynx took longer to cure; the NNT in that subgroup was 8 (95% CI from NNT-benefit 4 to NNT-harm 47). Patients who were older, reported symptoms for longer, or reported more severe symptoms also took longer to cure but were no more likely to benefit from antibiotics. The authors concluded that common clinical signs and symptoms cannot identify patients for whom treatment is clearly justified, and that antibiotics are not justified even if a patient reports symptoms for longer than 7-10 days.
cards.watchOut: An NNT of 15 is a ratio-scale effect well inside this library's not-solid band, and both NNT confidence intervals cross into harm; the analysis pools older trials of differing antibiotics and case definitions, all in clinically diagnosed (mostly viral) illness.
cards.source: Young J et al. Antibiotics for adults with clinically diagnosed acute rhinosinusitis: a meta-analysis of individual patient data. Lancet. 2008 Mar 15;371(9616):908-914. PMID: 18342685. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: at most a small, late, average benefit that no bedside rule can target — LIKELY the null-to-small verdict
cards.summary: At most a small, late, average benefit that no bedside rule can target — LIKELY, for the null-to-small verdict.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one placebo-controlled trial (166 adults) and one individual-patient-data meta-analysis (2,547 adults, 9 trials), both in primary-care, clinically diagnosed acute rhinosinusitis.
cards.result: The trial's primary outcome was null at days 3 and 10, and the pooled estimate is an NNT of 15 for one additional cure with an interval crossing into harm; the one apparently better subgroup (purulent discharge in the pharynx, NNT 8) still has an interval crossing into harm. Two independent designs converging on 'occasionally a little, usually nothing, and un-targetable' supports LIKELY for that null-to-small verdict. This shelf is about sinusitis in adults; otitis media in children is a different condition and lives at #253.
cards.watchOut: 'LIKELY' here stamps the smallness of the benefit, not a benefit claim; do not quote the day-7 Garbutt differences without the day-3 and day-10 nulls beside them.

shelves.title: Laser first for glaucoma: selective laser trabeculoplasty vs drops
shelves.question: In open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, is first-line selective laser trabeculoplasty as good as — or better than — starting with IOP-lowering drops?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Glaucoma, Open-Angle/therapy · Laser Therapy · Ocular Hypertension/therapy · Ophthalmic Solutions · Trabeculectomy/methods · Administration, Ophthalmic
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials frame the choice. LiGHT (718 treatment-naive patients) found selective laser trabeculoplasty gave the same health-related quality of life as drops at 3 years, with 74.2% of laser-first patients still drop-free and fewer glaucoma operations (0 vs 11). UKGTS supplies the benchmark the drops arm rests on: latanoprost preserved the visual field versus placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.44), the first placebo-controlled proof that IOP lowering protects vision. Laser-first is therefore an equal-outcome, drop-sparing first line — not a claim that laser beats a working drop on pressure.

cards.headline: LiGHT 2019: laser-first matched drops on quality of life at 3 years, with 74.2% of patients still drop-free
cards.summary: LiGHT: laser-first matched drops on quality of life (EQ-5D 0.89 vs 0.90 ), with 74.2% of laser patients still drop-free at 3 years and glaucoma surgery in 0 vs 11 patients.
cards.people: 718 treatment-naive patients with open angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension and no ocular comorbidities, recruited at six UK hospitals and randomised to initial selective laser trabeculoplasty (356) or eye drops (362); 652 (91%) returned the primary-outcome questionnaire at 36 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Average EQ-5D score at 3 years was 0.89 (SD 0.18) with laser versus 0.90 (SD 0.16) with drops (difference 0.01, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.03; p=0.23). At 36 months, 74.2% (95% CI 69.3 to 78.6) of the laser group required no drops to maintain intraocular pressure at target; eyes were within target pressure at 93.0% of visits (laser) versus 91.3% (drops), and glaucoma surgery was required in 0 laser patients versus 11 drops patients. From an ophthalmology cost perspective there was a 97% probability that laser-first was more cost-effective than drops-first at £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year.
cards.watchOut: Quality of life — not visual-field progression — was the primary outcome, and a quarter of laser-first patients still needed drops by 3 years; the trial does not show laser lowering pressure more than drops do.
cards.source: Gazzard G et al. Selective laser trabeculoplasty versus eye drops for first-line treatment of ocular hypertension and glaucoma (LiGHT): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;393(10180):1505-1516. PMID: 30862377. Registry ID: ISRCTN32038223, stated in the record's abstract (registered at controlled-trials.com); the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: UKGTS 2015: latanoprost preserved the visual field versus placebo — adjusted hazard ratio 0.44 over 24 months
cards.summary: UKGTS: latanoprost preserved the visual field vs placebo — adjusted hazard ratio 0.44 over 24 months (relative).
cards.people: 516 patients with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma at ten UK centres, randomised to latanoprost 0.005% (258) or placebo (258) drops once daily to both eyes; baseline mean intraocular pressure was 19.6 mm Hg (SD 4.6) in the latanoprost group and 20.1 mm Hg (4.8) in controls. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean intraocular pressure reduction was 3.8 mm Hg (SD 4.0) in 231 assessed latanoprost patients versus 0.9 mm Hg (3.8) in 230 placebo patients. Visual field preservation was significantly longer with latanoprost: adjusted hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.69; p=0.0003) for time to visual field deterioration — a relative measure, at or beyond the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid. There were 18 serious adverse events, none attributable to the study drug. The trial was stopped early on the Data and Safety Monitoring Committee's recommendation after an interim analysis.
cards.watchOut: A single-drug, 24-month placebo trial in newly diagnosed disease, stopped early: it benchmarks what drops can do, it does not compare drops with laser head-to-head — that comparison is LiGHT's, above.
cards.source: Garway-Heath DF et al. Latanoprost for open-angle glaucoma (UKGTS): a randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2015;385(9975):1295-304. PMID: 25533656. Registry ID: ISRCTN96423140, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: laser-first is an equal-outcome, drop-sparing first line — LIKELY
cards.summary: Laser-first is an equal-outcome, drop-sparing first line — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: LiGHT (718 patients, laser vs drops, 3 years) and UKGTS (516 patients, latanoprost vs placebo, 24 months).
cards.result: The two trials answer different halves of the question and agree: drops work (UKGTS hazard ratio 0.44 for visual-field deterioration versus placebo), and starting with laser loses nothing measurable on quality of life while sparing drops in 74.2% of patients at 3 years and avoiding 11 glaucoma operations seen in the drops arm (LiGHT). Neither trial shows laser superior on pressure or vision, so the claim carded is equivalence plus drop-sparing, not superiority.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote LiGHT as proof laser protects the visual field — its field outcome was quality of life; the field-preservation evidence on this shelf belongs to latanoprost in UKGTS.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gazzard G et al. Lancet. 2019;393(10180):1505-1516. PMID: 30862377; Garway-Heath DF et al. Lancet. 2015;385(9975):1295-304. PMID: 25533656. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.question: In chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, does eplerenone help — and does half-dose photodynamic therapy beat micropulse laser or observation?

shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — half-dose photodynamic therapy over micropulse laser · POSSIBLE — eplerenone ineffective (each on a single trial): VICI (114 patients) found eplerenone no better than placebo on visual acuity at 12 months (adjusted difference 1.73 letters, CI crossing zero), and its authors say prescribers should stop. cards.headline: VICI 2020: eplerenone was not superior to placebo for chronic central serous chorioretinopathy at 12 months
cards.summary: VICI: eplerenone was not superior to placebo at 12 months (adjusted difference 1.73 letters , non-significant) — the authors say stop prescribing it for this.
cards.people: 114 patients aged 18–60 years with treatment-naive chronic central serous chorioretinopathy for 4 months or more, at 22 UK hospitals, randomised to oral eplerenone (57; 25 mg/day for 1 week, then 50 mg/day for up to 12 months) plus usual care or placebo (57) plus usual care; the primary analysis included all 57 eplerenone patients and 54 placebo patients. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Modelled mean best-corrected visual acuity at 12 months was 80.4 letters (SD 4.6) with eplerenone versus 79.5 letters (4.5) with placebo — an adjusted mean difference of 1.73 letters (95% CI -1.12 to 4.57; p=0.24). Hyperkalaemia occurred in eight (14%) patients in each group; no serious adverse events were reported with eplerenone, versus three unrelated serious events with placebo. The authors conclude ophthalmologists who prescribe eplerenone for this condition should discontinue the practice.

cards.headline: PLACE 2018: half-dose photodynamic therapy resolved subretinal fluid in 51.2% vs 13.8% with micropulse laser at first review
cards.summary: PLACE: half-dose photodynamic therapy cleared subretinal fluid in 51.2% vs 13.8% at first review and 67.2% vs 28.8% at 7–8 months vs micropulse laser.
cards.people: 179 patients with chronic central serous chorioretinopathy confirmed on multimodal imaging, randomised to half-dose photodynamic therapy (89) or high-density subthreshold micropulse laser (90), with the same treatment repeated if subretinal fluid persisted. cards.result: Complete disappearance of subretinal fluid at the first evaluation visit (6–8 weeks) occurred in 51.2% with photodynamic therapy versus 13.8% with micropulse laser (P<0.001), and at the final visit (7–8 months) in 67.2% versus 28.8% (P<0.001). cards.watchOut: Open-label and a single trial, with retreatment allowed in both arms: the fluid-resolution gap is large, but an unmasked anatomic endpoint in one trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stop eplerenone; half-dose PDT is the leading active treatment — both halves POSSIBLE on single trials
cards.summary: Stop eplerenone; half-dose PDT leads — both halves POSSIBLE, one trial each.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VICI (114 patients, eplerenone vs placebo) and PLACE (179 patients, half-dose PDT vs micropulse laser).
cards.result: The shelf's two trials point in opposite practical directions: the drug does nothing measurable (1.73 letters, non-significant), while the procedure clears fluid in roughly two-thirds of patients by 7–8 months against under a third for micropulse laser. shelves.title: Dry eye disease: omega-3 supplements and prescription drops
shelves.question: Do omega-3 supplements improve dry eye (DREAM) — and do lifitegrast or cyclosporine drops beat vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Docosahexaenoic Acids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Eicosapentaenoic Acid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca/drug therapy · Olive Oil/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — omega-3 ineffective · POSSIBLE — lifitegrast improves dryness symptoms: DREAM was a large multicentre trial (535 randomised) and its null was complete — symptom scores, staining, tear break-up time and Schirmer results all statistically indistinguishable from olive-oil placebo at 12 months — so the null carries LIKELY under this library's large-null rule. OPUS-3 (711 participants) found lifitegrast improved the eye-dryness symptom score versus vehicle at day 84 (treatment effect 7.16 points) but showed no difference on the ocular discomfort score or any objective sign, so the symptom claim is POSSIBLE on a single carded trial. No cyclosporine trial is carded on this shelf — the drafted question's cyclosporine half has no verified anchor here and is not answered.

cards.headline: DREAM 2018: omega-3 supplements did not beat olive-oil placebo on dry-eye symptoms or signs at 12 months
cards.summary: DREAM: omega-3 did not beat olive-oil placebo (OSDI difference −1.9 points [−5.0 to 1.1]) on symptoms or any sign at 12 months.
cards.people: 535 patients with moderate-to-severe dry eye disease randomised to 3000 mg/day fish-derived n-3 fatty acids (349) or olive-oil placebo (186) for 12 months; the primary analysis included 329 and 170 patients respectively. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean change in Ocular Surface Disease Index score was -13.9 points with omega-3 versus -12.5 with placebo (mean difference in change -1.9 points; 95% CI -5.0 to 1.1; P=0.21), consistent across prespecified subgroups. There were no significant differences in conjunctival staining (difference 0.0 points), corneal staining (0.1 point), tear break-up time (0.2 seconds) or Schirmer test (0.0 mm). Adherence in the active group was 85.2% by red-cell n-3 levels, and adverse-event rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The placebo was olive oil, which some argue is not inert — but the null held across every symptom and sign endpoint, so any olive-oil effect would have to be uniformly therapeutic to rescue omega-3. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: OPUS-3 2017: lifitegrast improved eye-dryness symptoms versus vehicle at 12 weeks, with no difference in ocular discomfort score
cards.summary: OPUS-3: lifitegrast improved the eye-dryness score vs vehicle (treatment effect 7.16 at day 84) with no difference in ocular discomfort.
cards.type: Phase III, randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 711 adults (≥18 years) with dry eye disease (Schirmer 1–10 mm, corneal staining ≥2.0, eye dryness score ≥40) randomised after a 14-day placebo run-in to lifitegrast 5.0% ophthalmic solution (355) or placebo (356) twice daily for 84 days. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At day 84, lifitegrast improved the eye dryness score from baseline significantly more than placebo (treatment effect 7.16; 95% CI 3.04 to 11.28; P=0.0007), with significant differences also at day 42 (9.32) and day 14 (7.85). Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate and no serious ocular adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A symptom-score win with no objective-sign or discomfort-score win, in one 12-week industry trial: dry eye's placebo response is large, and the shelf cards no cyclosporine comparator — do not read this card as a class verdict. shelves.title: Fenofibrate to slow diabetic retinopathy progression
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does fenofibrate slow progression of diabetic retinopathy or reduce the need for laser treatment, beyond its lipid effects?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetic Retinopathy/drug therapy,etiology,surgery · Fenofibrate/therapeutic use · Hypolipidemic Agents/therapeutic use · Laser Therapy · Lipids/blood · Macular Edema/complications,surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised programmes agree. In FIELD (9,795 patients with type 2 diabetes), fenofibrate cut first laser treatment for retinopathy from 4.9% to 3.4% (hazard ratio 0.69, a relative measure). In ACCORD-Eye (2,856 participants), fenofibrate plus simvastatin cut 4-year retinopathy progression from 10.2% to 6.5% (adjusted odds ratio 0.60, relative). Both relative ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on their own; the LIKELY rests on two concordant trials with absolute differences printed beside them, and the FIELD photography substudy's overall progression endpoint was itself null (p=0.19) — the benefit is clearest for laser need and for patients with pre-existing retinopathy.

cards.headline: FIELD Eye 2007: fenofibrate cut first laser treatment for retinopathy from 4.9% to 3.4% (relative hazard ratio 0.69)
cards.summary: FIELD Eye: fenofibrate cut first laser treatment from 4.9% to 3.4% (hazard ratio 0.69, relative; absolute reduction 1.5%).
cards.type: Multinational randomised controlled trial (prespecified tertiary endpoint, masked adjudication)
cards.people: 9,795 patients aged 50–75 years with type 2 diabetes in the FIELD study, randomised to fenofibrate 200 mg/day (4,895) or placebo (4,900); a substudy of 1,012 patients had standardised retinal photography graded by ETDRS criteria. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: First laser treatment for all retinopathy was required in 164 (3.4%) fenofibrate patients versus 238 (4.9%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.84; p=0.0002 — a relative measure; absolute risk reduction 1.5%, 0.7 to 2.3). In the photography substudy, 2-step progression of retinopathy grade did not differ overall (9.6% vs 12.3%; p=0.19) or in patients without pre-existing retinopathy (11.4% vs 11.7%; p=0.87), but was significantly lower with fenofibrate in patients with pre-existing retinopathy (3.1% vs 14.6%; p=0.004). An exploratory composite (progression, macular oedema or laser) favoured fenofibrate (hazard ratio 0.66, 0.47 to 0.94; p=0.022, relative). The effect did not track plasma lipid concentrations.
cards.watchOut: Laser need was a tertiary endpoint of a cardiovascular trial, the headline hazard ratio of 0.69 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own, and the substudy's primary progression endpoint was null overall — the progression signal is concentrated in patients who already had retinopathy.
cards.source: Keech AC et al. Effect of fenofibrate on the need for laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy (FIELD study): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2007;370(9600):1687-97. PMID: 17988728. Registry ID: ISRCTN64783481, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ACCORD-Eye 2010: fenofibrate plus simvastatin cut retinopathy progression from 10.2% to 6.5% at 4 years
cards.summary: ACCORD-Eye: fenofibrate plus simvastatin cut retinopathy progression from 10.2% to 6.5% at 4 years (adjusted odds ratio 0.60, relative).
cards.type: Randomised trial subgroup (2×2 factorial programme: glycaemia, lipids, blood pressure)
cards.people: 2,856 participants with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, drawn from the 10,251-patient ACCORD trial, evaluated for retinopathy progression at 4 years by seven-field stereoscopic fundus photographs or the development of retinopathy needing laser photocoagulation or vitrectomy. shelves.title: Uveitis: fluocinolone implant vs systemic immunosuppression (MUST)
shelves.question: For non-infectious intermediate/posterior/pan-uveitis, does a sustained-release fluocinolone implant control inflammation and preserve vision as well as systemic therapy — and at what ocular price?
shelves.mesh: Drug Implants · Drug Therapy, Combination · Fluocinolone Acetonide/administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Macular Edema/drug therapy · Panuveitis/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — implant controls inflammation better at 2 years · POSSIBLE — systemic therapy gives better 7-year vision: In the MUST randomised trial (255 patients, 479 eyes), visual acuity at 24 months did not differ significantly between implant and systemic therapy (+6.0 vs +3.2 letters, P=0.16), but residual active uveitis was less common with the implant (12% vs 29%) at a steep ocular price (cataract surgery 80%, treatment for raised pressure 61%, glaucoma 17%). The non-prespecified 7-year follow-up then favoured systemic therapy on acuity by 7.2 letters — an observational extension with loss to follow-up, so both halves are POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: MUST 2011 (2-year): implant and systemic therapy tied on vision (+6.0 vs +3.2 letters); implant controlled inflammation better and cost far more eye complications
cards.summary: MUST at 2 years: vision tied ( +6.0 vs +3.2 letters ); the implant controlled inflammation better (residual activity 12% vs 29% ) at a heavy ocular price (cataract surgery 80%).
cards.type: Randomised controlled parallel superiority trial (23 centres, 3 countries; masked outcome assessors)
cards.people: 255 patients with active or recently active non-infectious intermediate, posterior or pan-uveitis (479 eyes with uveitis), randomised to systemic corticosteroids plus immunosuppression when indicated, or surgically placed fluocinolone acetonide implant (bilateral eyes implanted where both warranted treatment). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: From baseline to 24 months, visual acuity improved by +6.0 letters (implant) and +3.2 letters (systemic) (P=0.16; 95% CI for the difference -1.2 to +6.7 letters, favouring implant); vision-related quality of life improved by +11.4 versus +6.8 units (P=0.043), and residual active uveitis was present in 12% versus 29% (P=0.001). Implant eyes had higher risks of cataract surgery (80%; hazard ratio 3.3, relative), treatment for elevated intraocular pressure (61%; hazard ratio 4.2, relative) and glaucoma (17%; hazard ratio 4.2, relative), all P≤0.0008. Systemic-therapy patients had more prescription-requiring infections (0.60 vs 0.36 per person-year; P=0.034) without notable long-term consequences.
cards.watchOut: Participants and treating ophthalmologists were unmasked, and the trial was powered for the acuity difference it did not find — the inflammation and complication contrasts, not vision, are what separate the arms at 2 years.
cards.source: Multicenter Uveitis Steroid Treatment (MUST) Trial Research Group. Randomized comparison of systemic anti-inflammatory therapy versus fluocinolone acetonide implant for intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis: the multicenter uveitis steroid treatment trial. Ophthalmology. 2011;118(10):1916-26. PMID: 21840602. Registry ID: NCT00132691, from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: Of the 255 MUST patients (aged 13 years or older at enrolment), 215 consented to follow-up through at least 7 years; 7-year acuity data were obtained for 161 uveitic eyes (70% of 90 implant patients) and 167 eyes (71% of 90 systemic patients); participants were 77% female with median age at enrolment 48 years (interquartile range 36–56).

cards.watchOut: This is an extended observational follow-up, not the randomised comparison itself: about 30% of eyes lack 7-year data, treatment after the trial phase was not protocol-controlled, and the authors flag loss to follow-up as the key limitation.

shelves.title: Glaucoma drainage surgery: tube shunt vs trabeculectomy
shelves.question: In eyes with prior surgery or high failure risk, does a tube shunt give better pressure control and fewer failures than trabeculectomy with mitomycin?
shelves.mesh: Alkylating Agents/administration & dosage · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Cataract Extraction · Combined Modality Therapy · Glaucoma/physiopathology,surgery · Glaucoma Drainage Implants · Intraocular Pressure/physiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In eyes with previous surgery, tube shunt surgery beat trabeculectomy with mitomycin C on the outcome that matters — failure over 5 years was 29.8% versus 46.9% in TVT (hazard ratio 2.15 for trabeculectomy versus tube, a relative measure), with reoperation in 9% versus 29%, while achieved pressure and medication counts were similar. The second carded programme refines the tube choice itself: pooled Ahmed–Baerveldt data (514 patients) found the Baerveldt implant failed less (37% vs 49% at 5 years) and reached lower pressure on fewer medications, at a higher hypotony risk (4.5% vs 0.4%).

cards.headline: TVT 2012 (5-year): tube shunt failed less than trabeculectomy with mitomycin — 29.8% vs 46.9% cumulative failure
cards.summary: TVT at 5 years: tube shunt failed less than trabeculectomy with mitomycin — cumulative failure 29.8% vs 46.9% ; reoperation 9% vs 29% .
cards.people: 212 eyes of 212 patients aged 18–85 years with previous trabeculectomy and/or cataract extraction with intraocular lens and uncontrolled glaucoma (intraocular pressure ≥18 and ≤40 mm Hg on maximum tolerated medical therapy), randomised to a 350-mm² Baerveldt implant (107) or trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 0.4 mg/mL for 4 minutes (105). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 5 years, intraocular pressure was 14.4±6.9 mm Hg (tube) versus 12.6±5.9 mm Hg (trabeculectomy) (P=.12) on 1.4±1.3 versus 1.2±1.5 glaucoma medications (P=.23). Cumulative probability of failure over 5 years was 29.8% (tube) versus 46.9% (trabeculectomy) (P=.002; hazard ratio 2.15, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.56 — a relative measure for trabeculectomy versus tube). Reoperation for glaucoma was needed in 9% versus 29% (P=.025).
cards.watchOut: Enrolled eyes had already had surgery — the result governs the prior-surgery/high-risk population of the question, not primary trabeculectomy in virgin eyes, where the ordering may differ.
