shelves.title: Acne in adult women and adolescents: spironolactone and fixed-dose topical combinations
shelves.question: Does oral spironolactone help adult female acne (SAFA) — and do fixed adapalene–benzoyl peroxide combinations beat their components?
shelves.mesh: Spironolactone/adverse effects · Wales · Acne Vulgaris/drug therapy,complications · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Immunoglobulin A · Acne Vulgaris/drug therapy · Adapalene
shelves.balance: LIKELY: SAFA (410 women) found oral spironolactone improved acne-specific quality of life versus placebo, with the gap widening by week 24 (difference 3.45 points) and investigator-assessed treatment success of 19% versus 6% at week 12 (odds ratio 5.18, a relative measure). The fixed adapalene–benzoyl peroxide gel trial (1,670 patients) found the combination significantly more effective than either component alone and than vehicle, with differences visible from week 1. Two large double-blind trials, two different acne populations — women needing an oral option, and patients on topicals — both positive.

cards.headline: SAFA 2023: spironolactone improved acne outcomes versus placebo in adult women, more at week 24 than week 12
cards.summary: SAFA: spironolactone improved acne in adult women, more by week 24 (Acne-QoL difference 3.45 ) than week 12 ( 1.27 ); self-assessed improvement 82% vs 63% at week 24.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double-blind randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 410 women aged 18 or older in England and Wales with facial acne for at least six months judged to warrant oral antibiotics, randomised to spironolactone (201; 50 mg/day to week 6, then 100 mg/day to week 24) or matched placebo (209), with topical treatment allowed in both arms; 342 women were in the primary analysis. Baseline mean age was 29.2 years (SD 7.2); acne was 46% mild, 40% moderate and 13% severe.
cards.result: Acne-QoL symptom scores rose from 13.2 at baseline to 19.2 (spironolactone) versus 17.8 (placebo) at week 12 (difference favouring spironolactone 1.27; 95% CI 0.07 to 2.46) and to 21.2 versus 17.4 at week 24 (difference 3.45; 2.16 to 4.75). Self-assessed improvement at week 24 was 82% versus 63% (odds ratio 2.72, 1.50 to 4.93 — a relative measure), with no significant difference at week 12 (72% vs 68%; odds ratio 1.16). Investigator-assessed treatment success at week 12 was 19% (31/168) versus 6% (9/160) (odds ratio 5.18, 2.18 to 12.28, relative). Headaches were more common on spironolactone (20% vs 12%; p=0.02); no serious adverse reactions were reported.
cards.watchOut: The week-12 primary difference (1.27 points on a 0–30 scale) is small and its interval nearly touches zero — the persuasive results are the week-24 outcomes, so this is a slow treatment, and the trial enrolled women whose acne warranted oral antibiotics, not all adult female acne.
cards.source: Santer M et al. Effectiveness of spironolactone for women with acne vulgaris (SAFA) in England and Wales: pragmatic, multicentre, phase 3, double blind, randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Gollnick 2009: adapalene–benzoyl peroxide fixed gel beat both of its components and vehicle in 1,670 patients
cards.summary: Gollnick 2009: the adapalene–benzoyl peroxide fixed gel was significantly more effective than either component alone in 1,670 patients (the abstract reports no lesion-count percentages).

cards.result: The record's abstract reports the result qualitatively and prints no lesion-count percentages: adapalene–benzoyl peroxide was significantly more effective than the corresponding monotherapies, with significant differences in percentage lesion-count change observed as early as week 1, and the cutaneous tolerability profile was similar to adapalene alone. No numerical efficacy figure is carded from this record because none appears in its abstract.

shelves.title: Preventing eczema in infancy: daily emollients from birth
shelves.question: Does applying emollient daily from birth prevent atopic eczema (and food allergy) in high-risk infants?
shelves.mesh: Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Eczema/drug therapy,prevention & control · Emollients/therapeutic use · Infant, Newborn · Reference Values
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large randomised trials, one in high-risk infants and one in the general population, both found that daily emollients from birth did not prevent eczema. BEEP (1,394 newborns) found eczema at age 2 in 23% on emollient versus 25% on standard care (adjusted relative risk 0.95, CI 0.78 to 1.16), with more skin infections in the emollient group. PreventADALL (2,397 infants) likewise found no reduction by 12 months. Families should not use daily emollients to try to prevent eczema. Neither carded abstract reports a food-allergy prevention result, so that half of the drafted question is not claimed here.

cards.headline: BEEP 2020: daily emollient for the first year did not prevent eczema at age 2 (23% vs 25%) and skin infections rose
cards.summary: BEEP: daily emollient for the first year did not prevent eczema at age 2 ( 23% vs 25% ; adjusted relative risk 0.95) — and skin infections rose.
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 1,394 term newborns (at least 37 weeks' gestation) at high risk of eczema (at least one first-degree relative with doctor-diagnosed eczema, allergic rhinitis or asthma), at 12 hospitals and four primary care sites across the UK, randomised to daily emollient (Diprobase cream or DoubleBase gel) for the first year plus standard skin-care advice (693) or standard advice alone (701); adherence in the emollient group was 88% at 3 months, 82% at 6 months and 74% at 12 months.
cards.result: Eczema at age 2 years was present in 139 (23%) of 598 infants with outcome data in the emollient group versus 150 (25%) of 612 in the control group (adjusted relative risk 0.95, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.16; p=0.61 — a relative measure; adjusted risk difference -1.2%, -5.9 to 3.6). Other eczema definitions supported the primary result. Skin infections in year 1 averaged 0.23 per child on emollient versus 0.15 on control (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.55, 1.15 to 2.09, relative). The authors conclude families with atopic disease should not use daily emollients to try to prevent eczema in their newborn.
cards.watchOut: A prevention null in high-risk infants with good adherence — it does not argue against emollients as treatment for established eczema, which is a different question (dupilumab treatment of established atopic dermatitis lives on Shelf #374).

cards.summary: PreventADALL: neither early emollients nor early complementary feeding reduced atopic dermatitis by 12 months (risk differences favoured control).

shelves.title: Scabies: permethrin vs oral ivermectin, and mass drug administration
shelves.question: For ordinary scabies, is oral ivermectin as effective as permethrin cream — and does community mass drug administration control endemic scabies and impetigo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Endemic Diseases · Fiji/epidemiology · Impetigo/drug therapy,epidemiology,etiology · Insecticides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Ivermectin/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: For community control the evidence is strong: in the Fiji trial (2,051 participants), mass ivermectin administration cut scabies prevalence from 32.1% to 1.9% at 12 months (relative reduction 94%), far beyond standard care (36.6% to 18.8%) or mass permethrin (41.7% to 15.8%), and cut impetigo most as well. For individual treatment, the Cochrane synthesis of 20 small trials (2,392 people) found topical permethrin appeared more effective than oral ivermectin in the one small head-to-head trial (85 participants), so 'ivermectin is as effective as permethrin for an individual case' is NOT what this shelf claims — permethrin leads for individual treatment, ivermectin leads as a population tool.

cards.headline: Romani 2015 (Fiji): mass ivermectin cut scabies prevalence from 32.1% to 1.9% at 12 months — a 94% relative reduction
cards.summary: Romani 2015 (Fiji): mass ivermectin cut scabies prevalence from 32.1% to 1.9% at 12 months (a 94% relative reduction); mass permethrin reached 15.8%, standard care 18.8%.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial of mass drug administration (three island communities)
cards.people: 2,051 participants in three Fijian island communities assigned to standard care (permethrin for affected persons and contacts; 803), mass permethrin administration (532), or mass ivermectin administration (716), in a population with endemic scabies. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: From baseline to 12 months, scabies prevalence fell from 36.6% to 18.8% with standard care (relative reduction 49%; 95% CI 37 to 60), from 41.7% to 15.8% with mass permethrin (relative reduction 62%; 49 to 75), and from 32.1% to 1.9% with mass ivermectin (relative reduction 94%; 83 to 100) — all relative reductions, printed with their absolute prevalences. Impetigo prevalence fell from 21.4% to 14.6% (standard care), 24.6% to 11.4% (mass permethrin) and 24.6% to 8.0% (mass ivermectin; relative reduction 67%). Adverse events were mild and more frequent with ivermectin than permethrin (15.6% vs 6.8%).
cards.watchOut: Three communities, one per strategy — a community-level comparison with effectively three clusters, in an island endemic setting; it proves the mass-administration strategy there, not individual cure rates in clinic patients.
cards.source: Romani L et al. Mass Drug Administration for Scabies Control in a Population with Endemic Disease. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(24):2305-13. PMID: 26650152. Registry ID: ACTRN12613000474752, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Strong 2007 (Cochrane): topical permethrin appeared the most effective individual treatment; ivermectin an effective oral option
cards.summary: Strong 2007 (Cochrane): topical permethrin appeared the most effective individual treatment; oral ivermectin an effective oral option.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 20 small trials involving 2,392 people with scabies, searched to February 2007: one placebo-controlled, 16 comparing two or more drugs, two comparing regimens and one comparing vehicles. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Topical permethrin appeared more effective than oral ivermectin (85 participants, 1 trial), topical crotamiton (194 participants, 2 trials) and topical lindane (753 participants, 5 trials), and reduced itch persistence more than crotamiton or lindane. Oral ivermectin produced fewer treatment failures by day seven than its comparator in one small trial (55 participants). No difference in treatment failures was detected between crotamiton and lindane, lindane and sulfur, benzyl benzoate and sulfur, or benzyl benzoate and natural synergised pyrethrins. No serious adverse events were reported; skin reactions occurred with topical treatments, and headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and hypotension were occasionally reported. The review's conclusion: topical permethrin appears to be the most effective treatment for scabies, and ivermectin appears to be an effective oral treatment.
cards.watchOut: Twenty small, old trials — the permethrin-over-ivermectin judgement rests on a single 85-participant head-to-head trial, so the individual-treatment ordering is far softer than the mass-administration result carded above.
cards.source: Strong M, Johnstone P. Interventions for treating scabies. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007;(3):CD000320. PMID: 17636630. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: permethrin for the patient, ivermectin for the population — LIKELY on the split
cards.summary: Permethrin for the patient, ivermectin for the population — LIKELY, on the split.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Romani 2015 (2,051 participants, community mass administration) and Strong 2007 (20 trials, 2,392 people, individual treatment).
cards.result: The two cards answer two different units of treatment. Individual: the review's best (if thin) evidence favours permethrin cream over a single oral ivermectin dose. Population: mass ivermectin nearly eliminated scabies in its community (1.9% prevalence at 12 months) where case-based standard care left 18.8%. The stamp is LIKELY on that combined, split reading — not on any claim that the two drugs are interchangeable for an individual case.
cards.watchOut: Endemicity drives the population result; in a low-prevalence setting the logistics and benefit of mass administration do not follow from the Fiji data.

shelves.title: Common warts: cryotherapy vs salicylic acid vs waiting
shelves.question: For cutaneous warts in primary care, does cryotherapy beat topical salicylic acid — and does either beat watchful waiting by much?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Cryotherapy/adverse effects,methods · Keratolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Nitrogen/administration & dosage · Salicylic Acid/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Warts/drug therapy,therapy · Bleomycin/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — cryotherapy for common warts · MAYBE (weak evidence) — any treatment advantage for plantar warts: The one primary-care trial that tested all three strategies head-to-head (250 patients) found 13-week cure of 39% with cryotherapy, 24% with salicylic acid and 16% with waiting — but the cryotherapy advantage was confined to common warts (49% vs 15% vs 8%), with no significant difference for plantar warts. The Cochrane synthesis (85 trials, 8,815 participants) is more cautious still: salicylic acid beat placebo modestly (relative risk 1.56), cryotherapy did not beat placebo in pooled analysis, and cryotherapy did not beat salicylic acid (relative risk 1.23, interval crossing 1) — all relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, which is why neither half rises above POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Bruggink 2010: cryotherapy cured 39% vs 24% on salicylic acid and 16% on waiting at 13 weeks — the edge was in common warts only
cards.summary: Bruggink 2010: cryotherapy cured 39% vs 24% on salicylic acid and 16% on waiting at 13 weeks — the edge was in common warts only ( 49% vs 8% over waiting).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in primary care (30 practices)
cards.people: 250 consecutive patients aged 4 to 79 years with new cutaneous warts in Dutch primary care, randomised to cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen every two weeks, daily self-applied salicylic acid, or a wait-and-see approach; 240 were analysed at 13 weeks (loss to follow-up 4%), with home-visit outcome assessment at 4, 13 and 26 weeks.
cards.result: Cure (all warts gone) at 13 weeks was 39% (95% CI 29% to 51%) with cryotherapy, 24% (16% to 35%) with salicylic acid and 16% (9.5% to 25%) with waiting. Among participants with common warts (n=116) cure rates were 49% (34% to 64%), 15% (7% to 30%) and 8% (3% to 21%) respectively. Among participants with plantar warts (n=124), cure rates did not differ significantly between the three groups (the abstract prints no plantar percentages). The authors conclude cryotherapy is the most effective therapy for common warts in primary care, and that for plantar warts none of the three approaches was clinically better at 13 weeks.
cards.watchOut: One trial, unblinded by the nature of the treatments, with a 13-week primary horizon for a condition that resolves spontaneously over longer periods — waiting's 16% at 13 weeks understates eventual natural clearance.
cards.source: Bruggink SC et al. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen versus topical salicylic acid application for cutaneous warts in primary care: randomized controlled trial. CMAJ. 2010;182(15):1624-30. PMID: 20837684. Registry ID: ISRCTN42730629, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Kwok 2012 (Cochrane): salicylic acid beat placebo (relative risk 1.56); cryotherapy beat neither placebo nor salicylic acid in pooled analysis
cards.summary: Kwok 2012 (Cochrane): salicylic acid beat placebo (relative risk 1.56 , relative, in the caution band); cryotherapy beat neither placebo nor salicylic acid pooled.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane, updated to May 2011)
cards.people: 85 trials involving 8,815 randomised participants with cutaneous non-genital warts in healthy, immunocompetent adults and children; many included studies were judged at high risk of bias in one or more areas. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Salicylic acid versus placebo significantly increased clearance at all sites (risk ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.03 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band), with subgroup estimates of 2.67 for hands and 1.29 for feet. Cryotherapy versus placebo favoured neither (risk ratio 1.45, 0.65 to 3.23, relative), and cryotherapy versus salicylic acid did not differ significantly (risk ratio 1.23, 0.88 to 1.71, relative). Aggressive cryotherapy beat gentle cryotherapy (risk ratio 1.90, 1.15 to 3.15, relative) with more adverse effects; combined salicylic acid plus cryotherapy beat salicylic acid alone in two trials (risk ratio 1.24, 1.07 to 1.43, relative). The authors call the evidence for salicylic acid more consistent but only modest, and note pain, blistering and scarring are probably more common with cryotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A heterogeneous, bias-prone trial base pooled across sites and regimens — the review's pooled nulls for cryotherapy sit in visible tension with Bruggink's single-trial result, and the shelf keeps both in view rather than averaging them away.
cards.source: Kwok CS et al. Topical treatments for cutaneous warts. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;(9):CD001781. PMID: 22972052. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treat common warts with cryotherapy if treating at all; for plantar warts, waiting is defensible — split stamp
cards.summary: Cryotherapy for common warts POSSIBLE; any treatment advantage for plantar warts MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bruggink 2010 (250 primary-care patients, three arms) and Kwok 2012 (85 trials, 8,815 participants).
cards.result: Read together: the single direct three-way trial gives cryotherapy a real but site-specific lead (49% vs 8% over waiting for common warts), while the pooled literature cannot confirm cryotherapy over placebo or over salicylic acid, and confirms only a modest salicylic-acid effect (relative risk 1.56, in the caution band). That combination earns POSSIBLE for cryotherapy in common warts and only MAYBE (weak evidence) for any active-treatment advantage in plantar warts.
cards.watchOut: Percentages and pooled ratios measure different things on different horizons — do not quote the Cochrane ratios as if they refute Bruggink's absolute cure rates, or vice versa.

shelves.title: Androgenetic alopecia in men: finasteride and minoxidil
shelves.question: Do finasteride 1 mg and topical minoxidil 5% regrow or preserve hair in male pattern hair loss versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Alopecia/blood,drug therapy · Canada · Dihydrotestosterone/blood · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Finasteride/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hair/drug effects · United States
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Both drugs beat placebo in double-blind trials. Finasteride 1 mg/day (1,553 men in two 1-year trials, with blinded extensions) produced clinically significant hair-count gains over placebo at 1 and 2 years (+107 and +138 hairs in the measured vertex circle versus placebo) and slowed progression, which continued on placebo. Minoxidil 5% foam (352 men) significantly increased hair counts and subjective improvement versus placebo at 16 weeks and was well tolerated over 52 weeks of open-label follow-up. Neither carded abstract prints its placebo arm's absolute counts, so the shelf claims direction and the finasteride differences, not invented percentages.

cards.headline: Kaufman 1998: finasteride 1 mg increased hair count versus placebo at 1 and 2 years (+107 and +138 hairs) and slowed loss
cards.summary: Kaufman 1998: finasteride 1 mg increased hair count vs placebo by 107 hairs at 1 year and 138 at 2 years , and slowed loss.
cards.type: Two 1-year randomised, placebo-controlled trials with blinded extension studies
cards.people: 1,553 men aged 18 to 41 years with male pattern hair loss, given oral finasteride 1 mg/day or placebo in two 1-year trials; 1,215 men continued in blinded extensions for a second year. Hair counts were measured in a 1-inch diameter (5.1 cm²) circle of balding vertex scalp (baseline 876 hairs).
cards.result: Finasteride improved scalp hair by all evaluation techniques at 1 and 2 years (P<.001 versus placebo for all comparisons). Clinically significant increases in hair count with finasteride versus placebo were 107 hairs at 1 year and 138 hairs at 2 years (P<.001); placebo patients lost hair progressively. Patient self-assessment, investigator assessments and expert-panel photographic review all corroborated slowed loss, increased growth and improved appearance. Adverse effects were minimal.
cards.watchOut: Vertex scalp in men 18–41 with a 2-year horizon: the trials do not address frontal recession separately, older men, or what happens after stopping — and this shelf is the 1 mg hair-loss dose only; finasteride for prostate indications lives on Shelves #490/#218 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Kaufman KD et al; Finasteride Male Pattern Hair Loss Study Group. Finasteride in the treatment of men with androgenetic alopecia. J Am Acad Dermatol. 1998;39(4 Pt 1):578-89. PMID: 9777765. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1998).

cards.headline: Olsen 2007: minoxidil 5% foam significantly increased hair counts versus placebo at 16 weeks
cards.summary: Olsen 2007: minoxidil 5% foam significantly increased hair counts vs placebo at 16 weeks (the abstract prints no absolute counts, so none are carded).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial, with open-label safety extension
cards.people: 352 men aged 18 to 49 years with androgenetic alopecia, treated with 5% minoxidil topical foam or placebo for 16 weeks; 143 subjects then continued on open-label 5% foam to 52 weeks for safety collection (no efficacy data were collected beyond 16 weeks). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 16, the foam group showed a statistically significant increase in hair counts versus placebo (P<.0001) and a significantly better subjective assessment of hair-loss condition (P<.0001); the record's abstract prints no absolute hair-count values, so none are carded. The foam was well tolerated over the 52-week period.
cards.watchOut: A 16-week efficacy horizon for a lifelong condition, on a propylene-glycol-free foam vehicle — the result supports starting the foam, not its multi-year maintenance of effect, and the abstract's significance-without-magnitudes limits what can be quoted.
cards.source: Olsen EA et al. A multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial of a novel formulation of 5% minoxidil topical foam versus placebo in the treatment of androgenetic alopecia in men. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2007;57(5):767-74. PMID: 17761356. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both finasteride 1 mg and minoxidil 5% foam beat placebo — LIKELY; combination and duration questions stay open
cards.summary: Both drugs beat placebo, separately — LIKELY; no carded trial compares them or their combination.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the finasteride programme (1,553 men, 2 years) and the minoxidil foam trial (352 men, 16 weeks).
cards.result: Two independent placebo-controlled programmes in the same condition both positive: finasteride with quantified count differences sustained and growing to 2 years (+138 hairs versus placebo), minoxidil foam with significant count and subjective gains at 16 weeks. No carded trial compares the two drugs or their combination, so the shelf supports each against placebo, separately.
cards.watchOut: Hair-count gains are surrogate-scale outcomes (hairs in a 5.1 cm² circle; a 16-week count) — visible cosmetic benefit is corroborated by photographic and self-assessment for finasteride, thinner for the foam.

shelves.title: Papulopustular rosacea: ivermectin cream and comparators
shelves.question: Does ivermectin 1% cream clear inflammatory rosacea lesions better than vehicle, metronidazole, or azelaic acid?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dicarboxylic Acids/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Gels · Ivermectin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rosacea/drug therapy,pathology · Skin Cream
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A network meta-analysis of the topical rosacea trials found ivermectin 1% cream once daily more likely to succeed than azelaic acid 15% gel (relative risk 1.25) or metronidazole 0.75% cream (relative risk 1.17) at 12 weeks, with larger inflammatory-lesion reductions — but both relative risks sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on their own, and the comparison is indirect. Two 40-week extension trials found ivermectin safe and tolerable long-term with fewer related adverse events than azelaic acid gel. The underlying vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials are described inside these records but are not themselves carded, and no vehicle-comparison figures appear in the carded abstracts — hence POSSIBLE, and no vehicle claim is quantified.

cards.headline: Siddiqui 2016 (network meta-analysis): ivermectin beat azelaic acid and metronidazole on success at 12 weeks — relative risks 1.25 and 1.17
cards.summary: Siddiqui 2016 (network meta-analysis): ivermectin cream beat azelaic acid and metronidazole on 12-week success — relative risks 1.25 and 1.17 (relative, in the caution band).
cards.type: Systematic review with Bayesian network (mixed-treatment) meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 57 studies identified from January 2011 to June 2015 (earlier studies retrieved from a Cochrane rosacea review), of which 19 provided data suitable for mixed-treatment comparison, in adults with moderate-to-severe papulopustular rosacea. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, ivermectin 1% cream once daily gave a significantly greater likelihood of treatment success than azelaic acid 15% gel twice daily (relative risk 1.25, 95% credible interval 1.14 to 1.37) and metronidazole 0.75% cream twice daily (relative risk 1.17, 1.08 to 1.29) — both relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Ivermectin also reduced inflammatory lesion counts more (by -8.04 lesions, -12.69 to -3.43, versus azelaic acid; and -9.92, -13.58 to -6.35, versus metronidazole) and carried a lower risk of any adverse event (relative risk 0.83, 0.71 to 0.97, versus azelaic acid) and of treatment-related adverse events (0.47, 0.32 to 0.67).
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparisons across trials with different populations and eras, supplemented by unpublished clinical-study-report data: the success advantages (1.25, 1.17) are exactly the size this library refuses to treat as solid from ratios alone — they support, but do not prove, first-line status.
cards.source: Siddiqui K et al. The efficacy, safety, and tolerability of ivermectin compared with current topical treatments for the inflammatory lesions of rosacea: a network meta-analysis. SpringerPlus. 2016;5(1):1151. PMID: 27504249. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Stein Gold 2014: ivermectin stayed safe over 40-week extensions, with fewer related adverse events than azelaic acid gel
cards.summary: Stein Gold 2014: ivermectin stayed safe over 40-week extensions, with fewer related adverse events than azelaic acid gel.
cards.people: Subjects from two phase 3 papulopustular rosacea trials who had originally been treated with ivermectin 1% cream (continued on it) or with vehicle (switched to azelaic acid 15% gel) for the 40-week extensions — up to 52 weeks of total treatment. The abstract does not state the number of participants or mean age.
cards.result: The record's abstract reports no numerical efficacy rates: ivermectin 1% cream was safe throughout, with a lower incidence of related adverse events than azelaic acid 15% gel; no ivermectin subject discontinued either study because of a related adverse event; and the percentage of subjects scored clear or almost clear on the investigator global assessment was higher at the end of the study than at baseline. The abstract also records, as background, that the two preceding phase 3 trials had shown ivermectin significantly better than vehicle on global-assessment success and lesion reductions — those trials' figures are not printed in this record and are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Extension studies enrol phase 3 completers and switch the vehicle arm to an active comparator — there is no untreated or vehicle arm left, so these data speak to long-term safety and persistence, not to efficacy against vehicle.
cards.source: Stein Gold L et al. shelves.title: Actinic keratosis: field-directed topical therapy compared (fluorouracil, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate)
shelves.question: Among field treatments for actinic keratosis (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate), which keeps patients free from treatment failure most durably at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Aminolevulinic Acid/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Diterpenes/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Gels · Imiquimod/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Intention to Treat Analysis · Keratosis, Actinic/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (single pivotal trial): In Jansen 2019 (624 patients with five or more actinic keratosis lesions on the head), the cumulative probability of remaining free from treatment failure at 12 months was 74.7% with 5% fluorouracil cream, 53.9% with 5% imiquimod cream, 37.7% with methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy and 28.9% with ingenol mebutate gel — fluorouracil clearly first, with hazard ratios for failure of 2.03 (imiquimod), 2.73 (MAL-PDT) and 3.33 (ingenol) against it, all relative measures. Conformed to the trial it rests on: the drafted question named diclofenac, which Jansen did not test, so the shelf question names the trial's four actual arms; diclofenac is not answered here. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Jansen 2019: 5% fluorouracil kept 74.7% free from treatment failure at 12 months — ahead of imiquimod 53.9%, MAL-PDT 37.7% and ingenol mebutate 28.9%
cards.summary: Jansen 2019: 5% fluorouracil kept 74.7% free from treatment failure at 12 months — ahead of imiquimod 53.9% , MAL-PDT 37.7% and ingenol mebutate 28.9% .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (four-arm, four Dutch hospitals)
cards.people: 624 patients with a clinical diagnosis of five or more actinic keratosis lesions on the head, involving one continuous area of 25 to 100 cm², enrolled from November 2014 through March 2017 and randomised to 5% fluorouracil cream, 5% imiquimod cream, methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy (MAL-PDT), or 0.015% ingenol mebutate gel. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with a reduction of 75% or more in lesion count from baseline to 12 months after the end of treatment. At 12 months, the cumulative probability of remaining free from treatment failure was 74.7% (95% CI 66.8 to 81.0) with fluorouracil, 53.9% (45.4 to 61.6) with imiquimod, 37.7% (30.0 to 45.3) with MAL-PDT and 28.9% (21.8 to 36.3) with ingenol mebutate. Hazard ratios for treatment failure versus fluorouracil were 2.03 (1.36 to 3.04) for imiquimod, 2.73 (1.87 to 3.99) for MAL-PDT and 3.33 (2.29 to 4.85) for ingenol mebutate (P≤0.001 for all comparisons) — relative measures printed beside their absolute probabilities. No unexpected toxic effects were documented.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country's hospitals, head lesions only — and the outcome bundles lesion clearance with the trial's treatment-failure definition; the drafted diclofenac comparison is absent because Jansen never tested diclofenac.

shelves.title: Impetigo: topical vs oral antibiotics
shelves.question: For limited impetigo, are topical antibiotics (mupirocin/fusidic acid) as effective as oral antibiotics — and better than placebo or disinfection alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Administration, Topical · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Erythromycin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Fusidic Acid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Impetigo/drug therapy · Mupirocin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (on a 68-trial synthesis): The Cochrane review (68 trials, 5,578 participants) found topical antibiotics cured impetigo better than placebo (pooled relative risk 2.24, a relative measure beyond the 2.0 solidity threshold), that mupirocin and fusidic acid did not differ from each other (relative risk 1.03), and that topical mupirocin was slightly superior to oral erythromycin (relative risk 1.07, inside the caution band) with no significant difference against other oral antibiotics — so for limited impetigo, topical treatment is at least as effective as oral, with fewer side effects. There was no evidence supporting disinfectant solutions. The review could not settle extensive impetigo, where oral therapy may still be needed.

cards.headline: Koning 2012 (Cochrane): topical antibiotics beat placebo (relative risk 2.24) and matched oral antibiotics for impetigo
cards.summary: Koning 2012 (Cochrane): topical antibiotics beat placebo (pooled relative risk 2.24 , relative), mupirocin and fusidic acid tied, and topical therapy matched or edged oral antibiotics.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane update; searches to July 2010)
cards.people: 68 trials with 5,578 participants with impetigo (non-bullous, bullous, primary and secondary), reporting on 50 different treatments including placebo; most trials were in primary impetigo, and for many risk-of-bias items most studies did not provide enough information (15 studies reported blinding of participants and assessors). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Topical antibiotic treatment showed better cure rates than placebo (pooled risk ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.61 to 3.13 — a relative measure beyond the 2.0 threshold — in 6 studies with 575 participants). Mupirocin and fusidic acid did not clearly differ (risk ratio 1.03, 0.95 to 1.11; 4 studies, 440 participants, relative). Topical mupirocin was slightly superior to oral erythromycin (pooled risk ratio 1.07, 1.01 to 1.13; 10 studies, 581 participants, relative and inside the caution band), with no significant differences against other oral antibiotics. Penicillin was inferior to erythromycin (risk ratio 1.29) and to cloxacillin (risk ratio 1.59) in the oral comparisons. Topical antibiotics beat disinfecting treatments (risk ratio 1.15, 1.01 to 1.32; 2 studies, 292 participants, relative), and there was a lack of evidence for disinfectant solutions. Side effects were few and mild, and more common with oral than topical treatment, mostly gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: Many small, incompletely reported trials of an old literature, and a candid gap: with few studies in extensive impetigo, the review cannot say whether oral antibiotics beat topical there — the 'topical is enough' claim is for limited disease, as the question frames it. Resistance rates have also moved since these trials.
cards.source: Koning S et al. Interventions for impetigo. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;(1):CD003261. PMID: 22258953. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

shelves.title: Preventing recurrent leg cellulitis: prophylactic penicillin (PATCH)
shelves.question: In people with recurrent leg cellulitis, does low-dose prophylactic penicillin prevent the next episode — and for how long after stopping?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cellulitis/drug therapy,prevention & control · Health Care Costs · Health Services/economics,statistics & numerical data · Leg · Penicillins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: LIKELY: PATCH I (274 patients with two or more prior episodes) found penicillin 250 mg twice daily for 12 months cut recurrence during prophylaxis from 37% to 22% (hazard ratio 0.55, a relative measure; number needed to treat 5), with fewer repeat episodes overall (119 vs 164), and no difference once treatment stopped (27% first recurrence in both groups during follow-up) — protection lasts only while taking it. PATCH II (123 patients after a first or subsequent episode; under-recruited at 31% of target) pointed the same way over 6 months of prophylaxis (20% vs 33% recurrence; hazard ratio 0.53, relative) without reaching significance. Antibiotic duration for an acute episode is Shelf #506 — a different question, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: PATCH I 2013: penicillin prophylaxis cut recurrence from 37% to 22% while taken (relative hazard ratio 0.55; NNT 5); the effect vanished after stopping
cards.summary: PATCH I: penicillin prophylaxis cut recurrence from 37% to 22% while taken (hazard ratio 0.55, relative; NNT 5) — the effect vanished after stopping.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (28 hospitals, UK and Ireland)
cards.people: 274 patients with two or more episodes of cellulitis of the leg, randomised to penicillin 250 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months and followed for up to 3 years; the primary outcome (time to first recurrence) was tested during the prophylaxis phase because recurrence risk was not constant over the full period. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: During prophylaxis, 30 of 136 penicillin participants (22%) had a recurrence versus 51 of 138 (37%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.86; P=0.01 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates; number needed to treat 5, 95% CI 4 to 9). Median time to first recurrence was 626 days (penicillin) versus 532 days (placebo). During the no-intervention follow-up period there was no difference in first recurrence (27% in both groups). Overall, penicillin participants had fewer repeat episodes (119 vs 164; P=0.02 for trend), and adverse events did not differ significantly (37 vs 48 participants; P=0.50).
cards.watchOut: The benefit is rented, not bought: it exists only during the 12 months of prophylaxis and decays after stopping, so the trial supports continuous prophylaxis in frequent recurrers rather than a curative course.
cards.source: Thomas KS et al. Penicillin to prevent recurrent leg cellulitis. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(18):1695-703. PMID: 23635049. Registry ID: ISRCTN34716921, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PATCH II 2012: 6 months of penicillin after an episode cut recurrence from 33% to 20% — same direction, underpowered (hazard ratio 0.53, p=0.08)
cards.summary: PATCH II: 6 months of penicillin cut recurrence from 33% to 20% — same direction, underpowered (hazard ratio 0.53, p=0.08).
cards.people: 123 patients recently treated for an episode of leg cellulitis (79% had suffered one episode on entry), randomised to penicillin V or placebo for the first 6 months of up to 3 years of enrolment; recruitment reached only 31% of target because of slow enrolment. cards.headline: Synthesis: penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrences while taken — LIKELY; stopping returns the risk
cards.summary: Prophylaxis prevents recurrences while taken — LIKELY; stopping returns the risk.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PATCH I (274 recurrent-cellulitis patients, 12 months of prophylaxis) and PATCH II (123 post-episode patients, 6 months).
cards.result: Two trials, one programme, one answer with a time limit: recurrence roughly halves in relative terms while penicillin is taken (22% vs 37% absolute in the recurrent population; NNT 5), the smaller trial agrees in direction (20% vs 33%), and PATCH I's follow-up phase shows the protection does not persist after stopping (27% vs 27%). Both hazard ratios (0.55, 0.53) sit inside the caution band individually; the grade rests on their concordance plus PATCH I's absolute difference.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial answers how many years of prophylaxis are worthwhile, or whether treating predisposing factors (oedema, tinea, ulcers) can replace antibiotics — those strategies were not randomised here.

shelves.title: Plaque psoriasis, topical therapy: vitamin D–steroid combination foam/gel
shelves.question: Does fixed calcipotriol–betamethasone combination (foam or gel) clear plaque psoriasis better than either component alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Betamethasone/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Calcitriol/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Ointments
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The component question is answered directly by the 1,603-patient four-arm trial: mean PASI change at 4 weeks was -71.3% on the combination ointment versus -57.2% on betamethasone alone, -46.1% on calcipotriol alone and -22.7% on vehicle. The modern formulation evidence points the same way: in the PSO-ABLE subgroup with moderate-to-severe disease, the calcipotriol–betamethasone aerosol foam beat the same combination as a gel on mPASI75 at week 12 (57.1% vs 35.4%). Systemic biologics for moderate-to-severe psoriasis are Shelf #377 — a different treatment level, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Kaufmann 2002: combination ointment beat both components and vehicle — PASI change -71.3% vs -57.2% (betamethasone), -46.1% (calcipotriol), -22.7% (vehicle)
cards.summary: Kaufmann 2002: the calcipotriol–betamethasone combination beat both components and vehicle — PASI change −71.3% vs −57.2%, −46.1% and −22.7%.
cards.people: 1,603 patients with psoriasis vulgaris randomised to calcipotriol/betamethasone dipropionate combination ointment, betamethasone dipropionate ointment, calcipotriol ointment, or ointment vehicle, used once daily for 4 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean percentage change in PASI at the end of treatment was -71.3 (combination), -57.2 (betamethasone), -46.1 (calcipotriol) and -22.7 (vehicle): mean differences for combination minus betamethasone -14.2 (95% CI -17.6 to -10.8; p<0.001), minus calcipotriol -25.3 (-28.7 to -21.9; p<0.001) and minus vehicle -48.3 (-53.2 to -43.4; p<0.001). Local adverse reactions were reported by 6.0% (combination), 4.9% (betamethasone), 11.4% (calcipotriol) and 13.6% (vehicle). The authors conclude the once-daily combination is well tolerated and more effective than either active constituent used alone.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week ointment trial from the programme that launched the product: it proves the combination-versus-components ordering for the ointment vehicle; foam and gel performance is addressed by the PSO-ABLE card below, and longer-term steroid-sparing maintenance is a separate question.

cards.headline: PSO-ABLE subgroup 2017: calcipotriol–betamethasone foam beat the same combination as gel in moderate-to-severe psoriasis (mPASI75 57.1% vs 35.4% at week 12)
cards.summary: PSO-ABLE: the same combination as foam beat the gel in moderate-to-severe psoriasis (mPASI75 57.1% vs 35.4% at week 12).
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a phase III randomised trial (PSO-ABLE, 12 weeks)
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis (by the 'Rule of Tens': body surface area ≥10%, or modified PASI >10, or Dermatology Life-Quality Index >10) enrolled in PSO-ABLE: 77 treated with calcipotriol 50 μg/g plus betamethasone 0.5 mg/g aerosol foam and 82 with the gel. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: A greater proportion achieved mPASI75 with foam than gel at weeks 4, 8 and 12 (57.1% vs 35.4% at week 12; p=0.006 for the week-4 comparison as reported), and mPASI90 in 15.6% versus 12.2% at week 12. Overall mPASI reduction from baseline to week 12 was 64% (foam) versus 51% (gel), body-surface-area reduction 50% versus 39%, and treatment success (clear/almost clear with ≥2-grade improvement) was higher on foam at weeks 1, 2, 4, 8 (p=0.0089) and 12, with more foam patients reaching a Dermatology Life-Quality Index of 0/1 at weeks 4 (p=0.004), 8 and 12 (p=0.001).

shelves.title: Tympanostomy tubes for recurrent acute otitis media and effusion
shelves.question: In children with recurrent acute otitis media, do tympanostomy tubes reduce further episodes versus medical management — and do grommets improve hearing in persistent effusion?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Middle Ear Ventilation · Otitis Media/drug therapy,surgery
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — no reduction in otitis episodes · POSSIBLE — small, short-lived hearing gain in effusion: In the one large randomised trial of tubes versus medical management for recurrent acute otitis media (Hoberman 2021), the episode rate over two years was 1.48 versus 1.56 per child-year (P=0.66) — a null from a single trial, so POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. For effusion, the Cochrane synthesis of 10 trials (1,728 children) found hearing about 12 dB better at three months and 4 dB better at six to nine months with grommets, with no difference by 12 to 18 months and no effect on language, behaviour or cognition — a real but transient gain as effusion resolves naturally.

cards.headline: Hoberman 2021: tympanostomy tubes did not reduce acute otitis media episodes over two years (1.48 vs 1.56 per child-year, P=0.66)
cards.summary: Hoberman 2021: tubes did not reduce otitis episodes over two years ( 1.48 vs 1.56 per child-year, P=0.66).
cards.people: Children 6 to 35 months of age with recurrent acute otitis media (at least three episodes within 6 months, or at least four within 12 months with at least one in the preceding 6 months), randomly assigned to tympanostomy-tube placement or medical management with episodic antimicrobial treatment, followed for two years; the abstract does not state the total number randomised, mean age beyond the 6-to-35-month entry band, or the sex mix.
cards.result: The rate (±SE) of episodes of acute otitis media per child-year during the two-year period was 1.48±0.08 in the tympanostomy-tube group and 1.56±0.08 in the medical-management group (P=0.66) in the intention-to-treat analysis. Because 10% of the tube group did not undergo placement and 16% of the medical-management group received tubes at parental request, a per-protocol analysis gave corresponding rates of 1.47±0.08 and 1.72±0.11. Secondary outcomes were mixed: time to a first episode, several episode-related findings and treatment-failure criteria favoured tubes, while cumulative days with otorrhea favoured medical management; the frequency distribution of episodes, the percentage of severe episodes and antimicrobial resistance among respiratory isolates did not differ substantially.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and a null on its primary outcome: crossover in both directions (10% and 16%) blurs the contrast, and the per-protocol gap was not the prespecified primary analysis. The null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, on one trial.

cards.headline: Browning 2010 (Cochrane): grommets improved hearing by about 4–12 dB in the first months, with no difference by 12–18 months and no effect on language or development
cards.summary: Browning 2010 (Cochrane): grommets improved hearing by about 4–12 dB in the first months — no difference by 12–18 months , and no effect on language or development.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 10 trials, 1,728 participants — children with otitis media with effusion ('glue ear'); some trials randomised children, others randomised ears; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Grommets were mainly beneficial in the first six months, by which time natural resolution also improved hearing in non-surgically treated children. The one high-quality 'by child' trial (N=211) reported mean hearing level 12 dB better (95% CI 10 to 14 dB) with grommets at three months; meta-analyses of three high-quality trials (N=523) showed a benefit of 4 dB (95% CI 2 to 6 dB) at six to nine months, and at 12 and 18 months no differences in mean hearing levels were found. Trials randomising ears (N=230 ears) showed 10 dB better hearing in the grommet ear at four to six months (95% CI 5 to 16 dB), 6 dB at 7 to 12 months and 5 dB at 18 to 24 months. No effect was found on language or speech development, behaviour, cognitive or quality-of-life outcomes. Tympanosclerosis was seen in about a third of ears that received grommets; otorrhoea was common in infants but occurred in under 2% of grommet ears in children aged three to seven years over two years.
cards.watchOut: Searches ran to March 2010 and most included trials were small or randomised ears rather than children; no trial enrolled children with established speech, language, learning or developmental problems, so the review cannot speak for them.
cards.source: Browning GG et al. Grommets (ventilation tubes) for hearing loss associated with otitis media with effusion in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2010;(10):CD001801. PMID: 20927726. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.summary: Tubes do not prevent infections; for glue ear they buy a few decibels for a few months — split POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hoberman 2021 (children 6–35 months with recurrent acute otitis media, two years) and Browning 2010 (10 trials, 1,728 children with effusion).
cards.result: The two halves of this shelf answer differently. For recurrent acute infection, the only large head-to-head trial found essentially identical episode rates (1.48 vs 1.56 per child-year, P=0.66). For persistent effusion with hearing loss, grommets gave a hearing advantage that was largest early (12 dB at three months in the best trial; 4 dB pooled at six to nine months) and gone by 12 to 18 months, with no measured gain in language, behaviour or cognition — because effusion usually resolves on its own. This shelf tests tubes only: antibiotics for an acute ear infection live on Shelf #253 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the early decibel gains without the fade: the honest claim is a temporary hearing bridge while effusion resolves, not a developmental intervention.

shelves.title: Tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection: children and adults
shelves.question: Does tonsillectomy reduce sore-throat episodes enough to justify surgery — in severely affected children (Paradise criteria) and in adults?
shelves.mesh: Adenoidectomy/adverse effects · Evaluation Studies as Topic · Pharyngitis/epidemiology,prevention & control,therapy · Random Allocation · Recurrence · Research Design · Tonsillectomy/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, one in each age group, point the same way. In severely affected children (Paradise 1984), throat-infection incidence was significantly lower in the surgical groups in each of the first two follow-up years, though many untreated children also improved and most of their episodes were mild. In adults (NATTINA 2023, 453 randomised), immediate tonsillectomy gave a median 23 versus 30 sore-throat days over 24 months (adjusted incident rate ratio 0.53, relative) and was cost-effective — against a 19% postoperative bleeding rate. The benefit is a reduction in episode burden, not elimination, and it is bought with surgical risk.

cards.headline: Paradise 1984: in severely affected children, tonsillectomy significantly cut throat infections for two years — but many untreated children also improved
cards.summary: Paradise 1984: in severely affected children, tonsillectomy significantly cut throat infections for two years — but many untreated children also improved.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (with a parallel non-randomised preference trial)
cards.people: 187 children severely affected with recurrent throat infection: 91 assigned randomly to surgical or nonsurgical treatment and 96 assigned according to parental preference; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In both the randomised and nonrandomised trials, the effects of tonsillectomy and of tonsillectomy with adenoidectomy were similar. By various measures, the incidence of throat infection during the first two years of follow-up was significantly lower (P≤0.05) in the surgical groups than in the corresponding nonsurgical groups; third-year differences, mostly not significant, also consistently favoured the surgical groups. At the same time, in each follow-up year many subjects in the nonsurgical groups had fewer than three episodes of infection, and most episodes among them were mild. Of the 95 subjects treated with surgery, 13 (14%) had surgery-related complications, all readily managed or self-limited. The abstract reports significance levels rather than exact episode counts, so no rates are printed here beyond what it states.
cards.watchOut: A 1984 trial in children meeting stringent eligibility criteria (the 'Paradise criteria'): its result warrants surgery for children that severely affected, and the authors themselves say it equally supports individualised nonsurgical management — it does not generalise to milder recurrence.
cards.source: Paradise JL et al. Efficacy of tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in severely affected children. Results of parallel randomized and nonrandomized clinical trials. N Engl J Med. 1984;310(11):674-683. PMID: 6700642. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: NATTINA 2023: adults having immediate tonsillectomy had a median 23 vs 30 sore-throat days over two years (rate ratio 0.53, relative); 19% bled after surgery
cards.summary: NATTINA 2023: adults had a median 23 vs 30 sore-throat days over two years (rate ratio 0.53, relative); 19% bled after surgery.
cards.type: Pragmatic multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 453 adults aged 16 years or older newly referred to secondary-care otolaryngology clinics in the UK with recurrent acute tonsillitis, randomly assigned to immediate tonsillectomy (233) or conservative management (220); 429 (95%) were included in the primary intention-to-treat analysis; median age 23 years (IQR 19–30), 355 (78%) female and 97 (21%) male.
cards.result: Participants in the immediate tonsillectomy group had fewer days of sore throat during 24 months than the conservative management group (median 23 days [IQR 11–46] vs 30 days [14–65]). After adjustment for site and baseline severity, the incident rate ratio of total sore-throat days for tonsillectomy versus conservative management was 0.53 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.65; P<0.0001) — a relative reduction, with the absolute medians 23 vs 30 days beside it. There were 191 adverse events in 90 (39%) of 231 participants deemed related to tonsillectomy; the most common was bleeding (54 events in 44 [19%] participants). No deaths occurred. The authors conclude immediate tonsillectomy is clinically effective and cost-effective in adults with recurrent acute tonsillitis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a patient-reported primary outcome collected by weekly text message: expectation effects cannot be excluded, and the median gain is seven sore-throat days over two years — worthwhile to many patients, modest in absolute terms, and paid for with a one-in-five bleeding risk.
cards.source: Wilson JA et al. Conservative management versus tonsillectomy in adults with recurrent acute tonsillitis in the UK (NATTINA): a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2023;401(10393):2051-2059. PMID: 37209706. Registry ID: ISRCTN55284102, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery reduces the sore-throat burden in both age groups — LIKELY, with bleeding as the price
cards.summary: Surgery reduces the sore-throat burden in both age groups — LIKELY, with bleeding as the price.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Paradise 1984 (187 severely affected children) and NATTINA 2023 (453 adults).
cards.result: Across forty years and two age groups the direction is consistent: tonsillectomy lowers subsequent throat-infection burden — significantly fewer infections over two years in severely affected children (Paradise), and a relative rate ratio of 0.53 for sore-throat days in adults (NATTINA; absolute medians 23 vs 30 days over 24 months). Neither trial shows episodes abolished, and NATTINA quantifies the price: adverse events in 39% of operated participants, bleeding in 19%. That is why the shelf is stamped LIKELY for a burden reduction, stated two-handed, rather than as a cure. Adenotonsillectomy performed for sleep-disordered breathing rather than infection lives on Shelf #631 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled frequently and severely affected patients; extrapolating the benefit to occasional tonsillitis overstates what was tested.

shelves.title: Adenotonsillectomy for childhood sleep-disordered breathing
shelves.question: In children with obstructive sleep apnea or mild sleep-disordered breathing, does early adenotonsillectomy improve behaviour, cognition, and breathing versus watchful waiting?
shelves.mesh: Adenoidectomy · Child Behavior · Obesity/complications · Oxygen/blood · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications,psychology,surgery · Tonsillectomy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — no gain in attention or executive function · LIKELY — symptom, behaviour and breathing gains: Two large randomised trials, in established obstructive sleep apnea (CHAT 2013) and in mild sleep-disordered breathing (PATS 2023), agree closely. Neither found a significant benefit on its primary cognitive outcome — attention/executive function improved 7.1 vs 5.1 points in CHAT (P=0.16) and executive-function and attention changes were non-significant in PATS. Both found surgery better on secondary outcomes: behaviour, symptoms, quality of life and polysomnography (breathing normalised in 79% vs 46% in CHAT; progression of the apnea-hypopnea index beyond 3 events/hour in 1.3% vs 13.2% in PATS). Operate for symptoms and breathing, not for cognition.

cards.headline: CHAT 2013: early adenotonsillectomy did not improve attention or executive function (P=0.16), but breathing normalised in 79% vs 46% and behaviour, symptoms and quality of life improved more
cards.summary: CHAT 2013: early adenotonsillectomy did not improve attention or executive function (P=0.16) — but breathing normalised in 79% vs 46% and behaviour, symptoms and quality of life improved more.
cards.people: 464 children, 5 to 9 years of age, with the obstructive sleep apnea syndrome without prolonged oxyhemoglobin desaturation, randomly assigned to early adenotonsillectomy or watchful waiting with supportive care, assessed at baseline and 7 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — the attention and executive-function score on the Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment (range 50 to 150, higher better; baseline average close to the population mean of 100) — did not differ significantly between groups: mean (±SD) improvement 7.1±13.9 with early adenotonsillectomy versus 5.1±13.4 with watchful waiting (P=0.16). In contrast, there were significantly greater improvements in behavioural, quality-of-life and polysomnographic findings and a significantly greater reduction in symptoms in the early-adenotonsillectomy group, and normalisation of polysomnographic findings occurred in a larger proportion of children in that group (79% vs 46%).
cards.watchOut: Children with prolonged desaturation were excluded, follow-up was only seven months, and the baseline attention score sat near the population mean — there was little cognitive deficit to reverse, which may explain the null primary outcome.
cards.source: Marcus CL et al. A randomized trial of adenotonsillectomy for childhood sleep apnea. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(25):2366-2376. PMID: 23692173. Registry ID: NCT00560859, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PATS 2023: in mild sleep-disordered breathing, adenotonsillectomy again missed both primary cognitive outcomes but improved behaviour, symptoms, quality of life and blood pressure
cards.summary: PATS 2023: in mild disease, both primary cognitive outcomes missed again, while behaviour, symptoms, quality of life and blood pressure improved.

shelves.title: Septoplasty for nasal obstruction (NAIROS)
shelves.question: In adults with a deviated septum and nasal obstruction, does septoplasty improve symptoms more than defined medical management?
shelves.mesh: Nasal Obstruction/etiology,surgery · State Medicine · Nasal Septum/surgery · Steroids · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Nasal Obstruction/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two pragmatic randomised trials in two countries agree that septoplasty beats non-surgical management for nasal obstruction from a deviated septum. NAIROS (UK, 378 adults) found Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-22 scores 20.0 points lower (better) with septoplasty than with a defined nasal-steroid-and-saline regimen at six months, against a 9-point minimal clinically important difference. The Dutch trial (van Egmond 2019, 203 adults) found general health-related quality of life 8.3 points better at 12 months, sustained to 24 months. Harms were those of surgery: in NAIROS, 4% were readmitted with bleeding and 12% needed antibiotics for infection.

cards.headline: NAIROS 2023: septoplasty beat defined medical management by 20.0 points on the SNOT-22 at six months — more than twice the clinically important difference
cards.summary: NAIROS 2023: septoplasty beat defined medical management by 20.0 points on the SNOT-22 at six months — more than twice the 9-point clinically important difference.
cards.people: 378 adults (≥18 years, 67% men) newly referred to 17 NHS otolaryngology clinics in the UK with nasal obstruction associated with septal deviation and a Nasal Obstruction and Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) score above 30, randomised 1:1 to septoplasty (188) or defined medical management (190 — nasal steroid and saline spray for six months); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-22 (SNOT-22) scores at six months were 19.9 (95% CI 17.0 to 22.7) in the septoplasty arm and 39.5 (36.1 to 42.9) in the medical-management arm — an estimated 20.0 points lower (better) with septoplasty (95% CI 16.4 to 23.6; P<0.001), with 9 points prespecified as the minimal clinically important difference. Greater improvement was predicted by higher baseline symptom severity. Quality of life and objective nasal airflow measures (including peak nasal inspiratory flow) also improved more with septoplasty. Readmission to hospital with bleeding after septoplasty occurred in seven participants (4% of 174 who had septoplasty), and a further 20 (12%) required antibiotics for infections.
cards.watchOut: Open-label surgery versus sprays, with a patient-reported primary outcome: some of the gap may be expectation. Outcomes beyond six months were not the primary endpoint, and the trial enrolled people with at least moderate symptoms — it does not test surgery for mild obstruction.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two pragmatic trials agree septoplasty works for symptomatic septal deviation — LIKELY
cards.summary: Two pragmatic trials agree septoplasty works for symptomatic septal deviation — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: NAIROS 2023 (378 UK adults) and van Egmond 2019 (203 Dutch adults).

shelves.title: Ménière's disease: betahistine and intratympanic therapy
shelves.question: Does betahistine prevent Ménière's vertigo attacks — and for refractory disease, does intratympanic methylprednisolone match gentamicin with less hearing risk?
shelves.mesh: Betahistine/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Germany · Histamine Agonists/administration & dosage · Incidence · Meniere Disease/complications,drug therapy,psychology · Vertigo/etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — betahistine does not prevent attacks (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE — methylprednisolone matches gentamicin for vertigo control: BEMED (221 adults, double-blind, nine months, two doses) found attack rate ratios of 1.036 and 1.012 versus placebo — as tight a null as this field has, and a very large single double-blind trial may carry LIKELY for the null, stated as such. Attacks fell by about a quarter over time in every arm, placebo included. For refractory disease, one double-blind trial (Patel 2016, 60 patients) found vertigo attacks fell 87% with gentamicin and 90% with methylprednisolone over two years (difference −0.9 attacks) — a single small trial, so POSSIBLE; more steroid patients needed repeat injections (15 vs 8).

cards.headline: BEMED 2016: betahistine at either dose did not reduce Ménière's attacks versus placebo (rate ratios 1.036 and 1.012)
cards.summary: BEMED 2016: betahistine at either dose did not reduce attacks vs placebo (rate ratios 1.036 and 1.012 ) — a precise null.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-defining trial
cards.people: Adults aged 21–80 years (mean age 56 years) with definite unilateral or bilateral Ménière's disease, recruited in 14 German tertiary referral centres and randomised to placebo (74), low-dose betahistine 2 × 24 mg daily (73) or high-dose betahistine 3 × 48 mg daily (74) over nine months; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence of attacks did not differ between the three treatment groups (P=0.759). Compared with placebo, attack rate ratios were 1.036 (95% CI 0.942 to 1.140) for low-dose and 1.012 (0.919 to 1.114) for high-dose betahistine. Mean monthly attack rates over the months seven-to-nine assessment period were 2.722 on placebo, 3.204 on low-dose and 3.258 on high-dose betahistine. The overall monthly attack rate fell significantly over time by a factor of 0.758 (0.705 to 0.816; P<0.001) in all groups. Results were consistent for all secondary outcomes, and treatment was well tolerated with no unexpected safety findings. The authors conclude current evidence is limited as to whether betahistine prevents vertigo attacks compared with placebo.
cards.watchOut: There was no untreated arm, so the fall in attacks on placebo cannot be separated into placebo effect, spontaneous remission and symptom fluctuation — but that ambiguity does not rescue betahistine, whose rates were numerically above placebo at both doses.
cards.source: Adrion C et al. Efficacy and safety of betahistine treatment in patients with Meniere's disease: primary results of a long term, multicentre, double blind, randomised, placebo controlled, dose defining trial (BEMED trial). BMJ. 2016;352:h6816. PMID: 26797774. Registry IDs: EudraCT 2005-000752-32 and ISRCTN44359668, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Patel 2016: intratympanic methylprednisolone matched gentamicin for vertigo control over two years (90% vs 87% reduction), but more steroid patients needed repeat injections
cards.summary: Patel 2016: intratympanic methylprednisolone matched gentamicin for vertigo control over two years ( 90% vs 87% reduction), but more steroid patients needed repeat injections. (The abstract prints no comparative hearing outcome; the shelf claims vertigo control only.)
cards.people: 60 patients aged 18–70 years with refractory unilateral Ménière's disease, enrolled at two London/Leicester hospitals (UK) and randomly assigned to two intratympanic injections two weeks apart of methylprednisolone 62.5 mg/mL (30) or gentamicin 40 mg/mL (30), followed for two years; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the mean number of vertigo attacks in the final six months compared with the six months before the first injection fell from 19.9 (SD 16.7) to 2.5 (5.8) in the gentamicin group (87% reduction) and from 16.4 (12.5) to 1.6 (3.4) in the methylprednisolone group (90% reduction; mean difference −0.9, 95% CI −3.4 to 1.6). Non-responders could receive additional injections: eight patients in the gentamicin group versus 15 in the methylprednisolone group, and two non-responders switched from methylprednisolone to gentamicin. Both drugs were well tolerated; six patients reported one adverse event each (three per group), most commonly minor ear infections. The abstract reports vertigo outcomes and tolerability; it does not print a comparative hearing outcome, so none is claimed on this card.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, with repeat injections allowed on clinical judgement — the comparison is of two treatment strategies, not two single injections; and with no placebo arm, some of both groups' large falls may reflect the disease's natural fluctuation, as BEMED's placebo arm showed.
cards.source: Patel M et al. Intratympanic methylprednisolone versus gentamicin in patients with unilateral Ménière's disease: a randomised, double-blind, comparative effectiveness trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10061):2753-2762. PMID: 27865535. Registry ID: NCT00802529, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Betahistine is a well-tested null (LIKELY); the steroid injection matches the ablative one (POSSIBLE).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BEMED 2016 (221 adults, first-line prevention) and Patel 2016 (60 patients with refractory disease).
cards.result: The shelf separates by disease stage. For prevention, BEMED's two dose arms produced attack rate ratios of 1.036 and 1.012 versus placebo — a precise null from a large double-blind trial, which is why the null carries LIKELY under the library's large-single-null-trial reasoning, with attacks falling about 24% over time on placebo alone. cards.watchOut: The methylprednisolone claim is equivalence on vertigo counts in 60 patients, not proof of equal hearing preservation: this record's abstract prints no comparative hearing result, and the shelf does not invent one.

shelves.title: Tinnitus: cognitive behavioural therapy and sound therapy
shelves.question: Does CBT reduce tinnitus distress and severity versus waiting list or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Tinnitus/therapy · Anxiety/epidemiology,etiology,therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/instrumentation · Major Depressive Disorder/epidemiology,etiology,therapy · Internet
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, seventeen years and two delivery models apart, agree that cognitive behavioural therapy reduces tinnitus distress. Cima 2012 (492 patients) found a stepped-care CBT programme (with sound-focused retraining therapy) beat usual care on health-related quality of life (difference 0.059; effect size d=0.24), tinnitus severity (d=0.43) and tinnitus impairment (d=0.45) over 12 months. Andersson 2002 found internet-delivered CBT beat a waiting list, with significantly more treated patients achieving at least a 50% improvement on the Tinnitus Reaction Questionnaire — though only 26 of about 59 treated participants completed all stages. Effects are modest, and CBT changes the reaction to tinnitus, not the sound itself.

cards.headline: Cima 2012: stepped-care CBT improved quality of life and cut tinnitus severity and impairment versus usual care over 12 months (effect sizes 0.24–0.45)
cards.summary: Cima 2012: stepped-care CBT improved quality of life and cut tinnitus severity and impairment vs usual care over 12 months (effect sizes 0.24–0.45 ).
cards.people: 492 previously untreated adults (aged over 18 years) with a primary complaint of tinnitus, enrolled at a Dutch audiology department and randomly allocated to specialised care based on CBT with sound-focused tinnitus retraining therapy (245) or usual care (247), stratified by tinnitus severity and hearing ability; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, specialised care improved health-related quality of life over 12 months (between-group difference 0.059, 95% CI 0.025 to 0.094; effect size Cohen's d=0.24; P=0.0009) and decreased tinnitus severity (−8.062, −10.829 to −5.295; d=0.43; P<0.0001) and tinnitus impairment (−7.506, −10.661 to −4.352; d=0.45; P<0.0001). Treatment seemed effective irrespective of initial tinnitus severity, and no adverse events were noted. The authors conclude the specialised CBT-based treatment could be suitable for widespread implementation.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was a package — CBT plus sound-focused retraining therapy within stepped care — so CBT alone cannot be credited for the whole effect; effect sizes are small-to-moderate, and outcomes are self-reported distress and severity, not loudness.
cards.source: Cima RF et al. Specialised treatment based on cognitive behaviour therapy versus usual care for tinnitus: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2012;379(9830):1951-1959. PMID: 22633033. Registry ID: NCT00733044, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Andersson 2002: internet CBT reduced tinnitus distress versus waiting list — but only 26 participants completed all treatment stages (51% dropout)
cards.summary: Andersson 2002: internet CBT reduced tinnitus distress vs waiting list — with 51% dropout before completing all stages.
cards.people: 117 individuals with tinnitus of more than six months' duration, recruited through web pages and newspaper articles and randomly allocated to an internet CBT self-help manual in six modules or a waiting-list control; 26 completed all stages of treatment and 64 of the waiting-list group completed measures in the randomised phase; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Tinnitus-related distress, depression and diary ratings of annoyance decreased significantly with treatment. Immediately after the randomised phase, significantly more participants in the treatment group than the waiting-list group showed an improvement of at least 50% on the Tinnitus Reaction Questionnaire (the abstract gives the responder comparison without printing the two percentages). At the one-year follow-up, after all participants had been offered the programme, 27 (31%) of all participants had achieved a clinically significant improvement. The abstract does not print between-group effect sizes, so none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: A 51% dropout rate in the treatment arm and a waiting-list (not active) comparator: early internet-CBT evidence supports the direction of effect, not its size, and completers are a selected minority.
cards.source: Andersson G et al. Randomized controlled trial of internet-based cognitive behavior therapy for distress associated with tinnitus. Psychosom Med. 2002;64(5):810-816. PMID: 12271112. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT reliably reduces how much tinnitus bothers people — LIKELY, with modest effect sizes
cards.summary: CBT reliably reduces how much tinnitus bothers people — LIKELY, with modest effect sizes.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Cima 2012 (492 adults, clinic stepped care) and Andersson 2002 (117 adults, internet self-help).
cards.result: A large clinic-based trial (Cima: quality-of-life difference 0.059; severity d=0.43; impairment d=0.45) and an earlier internet trial (Andersson: significantly more ≥50% responders than waiting list; 31% clinically improved at one year) agree that CBT-based care reduces tinnitus distress versus usual care or waiting. Two positive randomised trials earn LIKELY; the modest effect sizes, Andersson's 51% dropout and Cima's combined CBT-plus-retraining package keep the claim worded as distress reduction, never as silencing the tinnitus. Hearing aids for cognition in hearing loss live on Shelf #350 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Patients should be told plainly: the evidence is for coping and distress, not for making the sound quieter or gone.
