shelves.title: Vestibular rehabilitation for chronic dizziness
shelves.question: Does vestibular rehabilitation — clinic-based or internet-delivered — reduce dizziness handicap in adults with chronic vestibular symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease/psychology,rehabilitation · General Practice/methods · Internet · Netherlands · Physical Therapy Modalities · Syndrome · Telemedicine/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials of internet-delivered vestibular rehabilitation versus usual care, in Dutch and English primary care, agree. Van Vugt 2019 (322 adults aged 50+) found vertigo symptom scores 4.1 points lower with stand-alone online rehabilitation and 3.5 points lower with physiotherapy-supported rehabilitation than with usual care at six months, against a 3-point clinically relevant difference. Geraghty 2017 (296 patients aged 50+) found scores 2.75 points better at three months and 2.26 points at six months, with less dizziness-related disability. Adding physiotherapy support did not obviously add benefit. No serious adverse events related to online rehabilitation occurred in either trial.

cards.headline: van Vugt 2019: stand-alone and physiotherapy-supported internet vestibular rehabilitation both beat usual care at six months (−4.1 and −3.5 points)
cards.summary: van Vugt 2019: stand-alone and supported internet vestibular rehabilitation both beat usual care at six months ( −4.1 and −3.5 points on the symptom scale).
cards.type: Pragmatic, three-arm, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 322 adults aged 50 and older with a chronic vestibular syndrome, recruited in 59 general practices in the Netherlands and randomised to stand-alone internet vestibular rehabilitation (six-week online programme, daily exercises 10–20 minutes), the same programme plus face-to-face physiotherapy home visits in weeks 1 and 3, or usual GP care; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, participants in the stand-alone and blended groups had lower Vertigo Symptom Scale–Short Form scores (range 0–60; clinically relevant difference ≥3 points) at six months than the usual-care group (adjusted mean difference −4.1 points, 95% CI −5.8 to −2.5; and −3.5 points, −5.1 to −1.9, respectively), with similar differences at three months. The rehabilitation groups also had less dizziness-related impairment, less anxiety and more subjective improvement at three and six months. No serious adverse events related to online rehabilitation occurred.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by nature (an exercise programme versus GP care) with self-reported outcomes; participants were aged 50+ with a chronic vestibular syndrome in general practice, so the result does not automatically cover acute vertigo or central causes.
cards.source: van Vugt VA et al. Internet based vestibular rehabilitation with and without physiotherapy support for adults aged 50 and older with a chronic vestibular syndrome in general practice: three armed randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2019;367:l5922. PMID: 31690561. Registry ID: NTR5712 (Netherlands Trial Register), stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Geraghty 2017: internet vestibular rehabilitation reduced dizziness at three and six months versus usual primary care (differences 2.75 and 2.26 points)
cards.summary: Geraghty 2017: internet vestibular rehabilitation reduced dizziness vs usual primary care at three and six months (differences 2.75 and 2.26 points ).
cards.people: 296 patients aged 50 years and older with current dizziness exacerbated by head movements, recruited from 54 primary care practices in southern England and randomised to an automated internet vestibular rehabilitation programme (Balance Retraining) or usual primary care; 66% were female and the median age was 67 years; outcome completion was 84% at three months and 78% at six months.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, the internet rehabilitation group had less dizziness on the Vertigo Symptom Scale–Short Form at three months (difference 2.75 points, 95% CI 1.39 to 4.12; P<0.001) and at six months (difference 2.26 points, 95% CI 0.39 to 4.12; P=0.02), where the difference is expressed as points in favour of rehabilitation. Dizziness-related disability was also lower in the rehabilitation group at three months (difference 6.15 points, 95% CI 2.81 to 9.49; P<0.001) and six months (difference 5.58 points, 95% CI 1.19 to 10.0; P=0.01). The intervention required no clinical support.

cards.headline: Synthesis: internet vestibular rehabilitation works in primary care — LIKELY, modest average gains, no support needed
cards.summary: Internet vestibular rehabilitation works in primary care — LIKELY, modest average gains.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: van Vugt 2019 (322 Dutch adults) and Geraghty 2017 (296 English patients), both aged 50+ in primary care.
cards.result: Two independent primary-care trials of essentially the same idea — structured vestibular exercises delivered online versus usual care — both found less dizziness at six months (−4.1 and −3.5 points in van Vugt; 2.26 points in Geraghty, on the same symptom scale), with less dizziness-related disability and no related serious adverse events. Physiotherapy support added nothing obvious in the three-arm trial. Two concordant randomised trials earn LIKELY; the modesty of the average differences keeps the balance worded as symptom reduction, not cure. Drug and injection treatment for Ménière's vertigo attacks specifically lives on Shelf #633 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled people 50 and older with chronic symptoms; neither tests rehabilitation for acute vestibular neuritis in the first days, where the evidence base is different.

shelves.title: Nasal saline irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent sinus symptoms
shelves.question: Does daily nasal saline irrigation improve symptoms in chronic or recurrent rhinosinusitis versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Combined Modality Therapy · Inhalation · Nasal Lavage/methods · Primary Health Care · Recurrence · Sinusitis/physiopathology,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for a modest symptomatic benefit): Two randomised trials agree in direction across twenty years. STEAM (Little 2016; 871 patients analysed in UK primary care) found nasal irrigation improved Rhinosinusitis Disability Index scores more than no irrigation at three months (adjusted mean difference −2.51) and left more patients holding a 10-point clinically important improvement at six months (44.1% vs 36.6%), with less over-the-counter medication use. Rabago 2002 (76 patients) found larger quality-of-life and symptom gains with daily hypertonic irrigation and less antibiotic use. The large pragmatic trial's own authors note the benefit was smaller than earlier evidence suggested — the stamp is for a modest benefit, not a large one. Steam inhalation, tested alongside in STEAM, did not work.

cards.headline: STEAM 2016: advice to use nasal irrigation gave a small disability-score benefit and more sustained responders (44.1% vs 36.6%); steam inhalation did not work
cards.summary: STEAM 2016: nasal irrigation gave a small disability-score benefit (adjusted difference −2.51 points ) and more sustained responders ( 44.1% vs 36.6% ); steam inhalation did not work.
cards.people: Adults aged 18–65 years from 72 UK primary care practices with chronic or recurrent sinusitis and a moderate-to-severe impact of symptoms on quality of life; 961 consented and 871 returned baseline questionnaires across four advice strategies (usual care 210, nasal irrigation 219, steam inhalation 232, combined 210); 671 (77.0%) reported outcome scores at three months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Rhinosinusitis Disability Index (RSDI) scores improved more with nasal irrigation than without it by three months (crude change −7.42 vs −5.23; estimated adjusted mean difference −2.51, 95% CI −4.65 to −0.37). By six months, significantly more patients maintained a 10-point clinically important improvement in the RSDI score with nasal irrigation (44.1% vs 36.6%); fewer used over-the-counter medications (59.4% vs 68.0%) or intended to consult a doctor in future episodes. Steam inhalation reduced headache but had no significant effect on other outcomes, and the authors conclude advice to use steam inhalation was not effective and that nasal irrigation was less effective than prior evidence suggested, but provided some symptomatic benefit. The proportion with adverse effects was the same in the intervention groups.
cards.watchOut: A pragmatic advice trial — the intervention was encouragement plus a demonstration video, not supervised irrigation — and 23% had no three-month outcome score; the measured benefit is the effect of recommending irrigation in primary care, which is exactly the clinical question, but it is small.
cards.source: Little P et al. Effectiveness of steam inhalation and nasal irrigation for chronic or recurrent sinus symptoms in primary care: a pragmatic randomized controlled trial. CMAJ. 2016;188(13):940-949. PMID: 27431306. Registry ID: ISRCTN88204146, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Rabago 2002: daily hypertonic saline irrigation improved sinus quality of life and symptoms and cut antibiotic use over six months
cards.summary: Rabago 2002: daily hypertonic saline irrigation improved sinus quality of life and symptoms and cut antibiotic use over six months.
cards.people: 76 subjects from primary care (70) and otolaryngology (6) clinics with histories of frequent sinusitis, randomised to daily hypertonic saline nasal irrigation for six months (52) or control (24); 69 (90.8%) completed the study; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compliance averaged 87%. At six months the experimental group's Rhinosinusitis Disability Index scores improved (from 58.4 ±2.0 to 72.8 ±2.2, on the paper's scoring where higher is better) compared with the control group (59.6 ±3.0 to 60.4 ±1.1; P≤0.05), and Single-Item Sinus-Symptom Severity scores improved from 3.9 ±0.1 to 2.4 ±0.1 versus 4.08 ±0.15 to 4.07 ±0.27 (P≤0.05). The number needed to treat to achieve 10% improvement on the RSDI at six months was 2.0. Experimental subjects reported fewer two-week periods with sinus-related symptoms (P<0.05), used less antibiotics (P<0.05) and less nasal spray (P=0.06); 93% reported overall improvement in sinus-related quality of life and none reported worsening (P<0.001). No statistically significant improvement was found on the SF-12 general health survey, and side effects were minor and infrequent.
cards.watchOut: A small, unblinded trial (76 subjects, uneven 52/24 allocation) from 2002 — its large effects are exactly the kind STEAM's pragmatic design later shrank; card it as the early positive, with STEAM as the governing estimate.
cards.source: Rabago D et al. Efficacy of daily hypertonic saline nasal irrigation among patients with sinusitis: a randomized controlled trial. J Fam Pract. 2002;51(12):1049-1055. PMID: 12540331. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: saline irrigation helps sinus symptoms modestly — LIKELY for a small benefit; steam does not work
cards.summary: Saline irrigation helps sinus symptoms modestly — LIKELY for a small benefit; steam does not work.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: STEAM 2016 (871 analysed, pragmatic) and Rabago 2002 (76 randomised).
cards.result: The direction is consistent and the sizes are honestly ordered: Rabago's small explanatory trial found large gains (RSDI improvement with a number needed to treat of 2.0 for 10% improvement), while STEAM's large pragmatic trial found a −2.51-point adjusted disability difference at three months and 44.1% vs 36.6% maintaining a clinically important improvement at six months. Two positive randomised trials earn LIKELY — for the modest benefit STEAM measured, not the large one Rabago suggested. Antibiotics for acute sinusitis live on Shelf #585 and biologics for nasal polyps on Shelf #375; neither is re-carded here, and saline was also the medical-management comparator inside Shelf #632's septoplasty trial.
cards.watchOut: Quote STEAM's numbers when counselling patients: irrigation is cheap and safe, but the average gain is small and about a third of STEAM's participants had no outcome data at three months.
cards.source: Synthesis of Little P et al. CMAJ. 2016;188(13):940-949. PMID: 27431306; Rabago D et al. J Fam Pract. 2002;51(12):1049-1055. PMID: 12540331. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Tecovirimat for mpox: the stockpiled drug meets its trials (PALM007, STOMP)
shelves.question: Does tecovirimat speed lesion resolution or improve outcomes in mpox — clade I in Congo (PALM007) and clade II (STOMP) — versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Benzamides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Democratic Republic of the Congo/epidemiology · Monkeypox virus/isolation & purification,genetics · Mpox, Monkeypox/diagnosis,drug therapy,mortality,virology · Infant, Newborn · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The stockpiled antiviral failed both of its placebo-controlled tests. PALM007 (597 patients with clade I mpox in the Democratic Republic of Congo) found lesion resolution at a median of 7 days on tecovirimat vs 8 days on placebo (competing-risks hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; P=0.14 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, with its absolute medians beside it), with similar PCR negativity at day 14 and no safety signal. The STOMP trial's virological analysis in clade II disease found tecovirimat did not reduce virus isolation from skin swabs (culture-positive at day 8 in 9% vs 12%), and its authors note all three phase 3 trials showed no substantial clinical benefit. Two randomised tests, two clades, one null: LIKELY. Supportive care in PALM007 held overall mortality to 1.7%, below the 4.6% case fatality reported in the DRC in 2023 — context, not a drug effect.

cards.headline: PALM007 2025: tecovirimat did not speed lesion resolution in clade I mpox — median 7 vs 8 days, hazard ratio 1.13 (P=0.14)
cards.summary: PALM007 2025: tecovirimat did not speed lesion resolution in clade I mpox — median 7 vs 8 days, hazard ratio 1.13 (P=0.14).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (all patients received supportive care)
cards.people: 597 patients in the Democratic Republic of Congo with at least one mpox skin lesion and PCR-confirmed clade I monkeypox virus, randomised to tecovirimat (295) or placebo (302), enrolled October 2022 to July 2024. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The median time from randomisation to lesion resolution (the primary end point) was 7 days with tecovirimat and 8 days with placebo (competing-risks hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; P=0.14). Results were similar for patients starting within 7 days of symptom onset (hazard ratio 1.16, 0.98 to 1.37) and after 7 days (1.00, 0.71 to 1.40). At 14 days, the percentages with blood, lesion and oropharyngeal samples negative for monkeypox virus by PCR were similar between groups. Overall mortality was 1.7% (the DRC's reported 2023 case fatality rate was 4.6%). Adverse events occurred in 72.9% (tecovirimat) and 70.5% (placebo), and serious adverse events in 5.1% and 5.0%.
cards.watchOut: A null in mostly self-limiting disease with excellent supportive care: the trial cannot exclude benefit in the severely immunocompromised patients who were not its typical enrollee — the STOMP resistance data on the next card are the cautionary evidence for exactly that group.
cards.source: PALM007 Writing Group. Tecovirimat for Clade I MPXV Infection in the Democratic Republic of Congo. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(15):1484-1496. PMID: 40239067. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05559099, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: STOMP virological analysis 2026: tecovirimat did not reduce virus isolation in clade II mpox (day-8 culture-positive 9% vs 12%); treatment-emergent resistance clustered in advanced HIV
cards.summary: STOMP virological analysis 2026: tecovirimat did not reduce virus isolation in clade II mpox (day-8 culture-positive 9% vs 12%); the card is the trial's virological substudy, labelled as such.
cards.type: Virological analysis (virus isolation and sequencing) of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, with an additional open-label arm
cards.people: Participants of the ACTG A5418-STOMP trial (clade II mpox) with day-1 culture-positive index-lesion swabs and follow-up samples: 53 in the randomised tecovirimat arm, 25 in the placebo arm and 67 in the open-label arm for the day-8 isolation analysis; longitudinal sequencing subsets of 54, 29 and 92 respectively.
cards.result: Among day-1 culture-positive participants, day-8 culture positivity was 5 of 53 (9%) on randomised tecovirimat, 3 of 25 (12%) on placebo and 8 of 67 (12%) in the open-label arm (P=0.71) — the drug did not reduce the frequency of virus isolation from skin swabs. Treatment-emergent resistance-associated mutations were rare overall (1 of 54 [2%] in the randomised tecovirimat arm, 0 of 29 on placebo, 6 of 92 [6.5%] open-label) but concentrated in advanced HIV: 5 of 23 immunocompromised participants living with HIV (22%) developed them, with markedly lower clinical resolution (1 of 5 [20%] vs 17 of 18 [94%]; P=0.0027), higher longitudinal viral loads (P=0.0014) and lower resolution by day 57 (28.6% vs 94.7%) among those with treatment-emergent resistance. Six of the seven individuals with treatment-emergent variants were living with HIV; all five with available baseline CD4 counts were below 80 cells per microlitre. The authors state that three phase 3 trials of tecovirimat showed no substantial clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: This card is STOMP's virological substudy, not its primary clinical report, and its denominators are the subsets with paired samples — small numbers (25 placebo patients in the day-8 analysis). Its resistance findings are observational within the trial and hypothesis-grade, but they are the only randomised-setting resistance data on the shelf.
cards.source: Vyshenska D et al. Tecovirimat treatment of clade II mpox: a virological analysis of a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial. Lancet Microbe. 2026;7(9):101464. PMID: 42526486. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial's ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05534984, is stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a stockpile drug with two null randomised tests — LIKELY the null for ordinary mpox
cards.summary: A stockpile drug with two null randomised tests — LIKELY the null for ordinary mpox.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PALM007 (597 patients, clade I) and STOMP's virological analysis (clade II subsets with paired samples).
cards.result: Clade I clinical endpoint: null (lesion resolution hazard ratio 1.13, P=0.14). Clade II virological endpoint: null (day-8 culture positivity 9% vs 12%, P=0.71), with the parent trial's clinical programme reported by its own investigators as showing no substantial benefit. For immunocompetent patients with mpox, tecovirimat's claim is finished unless a new trial revives it. The genuinely open question — severe disease in profound immunosuppression — is also where the only danger signal sits (treatment-emergent resistance in 22% of the immunocompromised HIV subgroup analysed), so 'no benefit shown' must not be misread as 'harmless to keep giving'.
cards.watchOut: Neither card tests tecovirimat in smallpox, its original stockpile indication, or in the severely ill hospitalised phenotype; the shelf's null is scoped to mpox as trialled.
cards.source: Synthesis of PALM007 Writing Group. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(15):1484-1496. PMID: 40239067; Vyshenska D et al. Lancet Microbe. 2026;7(9):101464. PMID: 42526486. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Single-dose lipoglycopeptides for skin infection: dalbavancin and oritavancin
shelves.question: Is one dose of dalbavancin (DISCOVER) or oritavancin (SOLO) non-inferior to a full course of vancomycin for acute bacterial skin infection?
shelves.mesh: Acetamides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Infusions, Intravenous · Linezolid · Oxazolidinones/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two drug programmes, both noninferior to vancomycin-based courses on early clinical response. Dalbavancin's twin DISCOVER trials (pooled 1,312 patients in the primary analysis) gave early response in 79.7% on two once-weekly doses vs 79.8% on vancomycin with optional oral linezolid (weighted difference −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −4.5 to 4.2), with fewer adverse events on dalbavancin. Oritavancin's SOLO trial (954 in the modified intention-to-treat population) gave the primary composite endpoint in 82.3% after a single 1200 mg dose vs 78.9% on 7–10 days of twice-daily vancomycin (difference interval −1.6 to 8.4 points, inside the 10-point margin), with clinical cure also noninferior (79.6% vs 80.0%). The claim is noninferiority and convenience — one or two infusions instead of a course — not superiority. Antibiotics after abscess drainage (Shelf #505) and cellulitis duration (Shelf #506) are different questions and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: DISCOVER 1 and 2 (2014): once-weekly dalbavancin was noninferior to vancomycin–linezolid — early response 79.7% vs 79.8%
cards.summary: DISCOVER 1 and 2 (2014): once-weekly dalbavancin was noninferior to vancomycin–linezolid — early response 79.7% vs 79.8%.
cards.type: Two identically designed noninferiority trials, reported pooled
cards.people: Patients with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection randomised to dalbavancin intravenously on days 1 and 8, or intravenous vancomycin for at least 3 days with the option to switch to oral linezolid to complete 10 to 14 days; the pooled primary-end-point analysis covered 525 of 659 dalbavancin patients and 521 of 653 vancomycin–linezolid patients with an early response assessment. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Early clinical response (cessation of spread of infection-related erythema and absence of fever at 48 to 72 hours) occurred in 525 of 659 (79.7%) on dalbavancin and 521 of 653 (79.8%) on vancomycin–linezolid (weighted difference −0.1 percentage point, 95% CI −4.5 to 4.2) — noninferior in each trial separately and pooled. Clinical status at end of therapy and investigator-assessed outcome were similar, and for Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) clinical success was 90.6% on dalbavancin vs 93.8% on vancomycin–linezolid. Adverse events, and days with an adverse event, were less frequent on dalbavancin; the most common treatment-related events in either group were nausea, diarrhoea and pruritus.
cards.watchOut: 'Once-weekly' is two doses (days 1 and 8), not one — the single-dose drug on this shelf is oritavancin. A long-half-life drug also cannot be un-given: an allergic or failed dalbavancin course persists in the body in a way a stopped vancomycin course does not.
cards.source: Boucher HW et al. Once-Weekly Dalbavancin versus Daily Conventional Therapy for Skin Infection. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(23):2169-2179. PMID: 24897082. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01339091 (DISCOVER 1) and NCT01431339 (DISCOVER 2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SOLO 2014: a single 1200 mg dose of oritavancin was noninferior to 7–10 days of vancomycin on all three efficacy endpoints
cards.summary: SOLO 2014: a single 1200 mg dose of oritavancin was noninferior to 7–10 days of vancomycin on all three efficacy endpoints.
cards.people: Adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections; the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 475 patients who received a single intravenous 1200 mg dose of oritavancin and 479 who received intravenous vancomycin twice daily for 7 to 10 days. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: All three efficacy end points met the prespecified 10-percentage-point noninferiority margin: the primary composite (cessation of spreading or reduction in lesion size, absence of fever, and no rescue antibiotic at 48 to 72 hours) was reached by 82.3% on oritavancin vs 78.9% on vancomycin (95% CI for the difference −1.6 to 8.4 points); investigator-assessed clinical cure 7 to 14 days after the end of treatment was 79.6% vs 80.0% (−5.5 to 4.7); and a reduction in lesion area of 20% or more at 48 to 72 hours occurred in 86.9% vs 82.9% (−0.5 to 8.6). Efficacy by pathogen, including MRSA, was similar between groups. Overall adverse-event frequency was similar, although nausea was more common with oritavancin.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority at a generous 10-point margin on a 48–72-hour composite dominated by lesion behaviour: the trial shows a single dose is not worse by that yardstick, not that outcomes that take weeks (recurrence, readmission) are equal — those were not the endpoints.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one visit can replace a course — LIKELY noninferior, by design nothing more
cards.summary: One visit can replace a course — LIKELY noninferior, by design nothing more.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DISCOVER 1 and 2 pooled (1,312 patients in the primary analysis) and SOLO (954 patients).
cards.result: Three randomised trials across two drugs land on the same early-response numbers as vancomycin-based therapy (79.7% vs 79.8% pooled for dalbavancin's two-dose course; 82.3% vs 78.9% for oritavancin's single dose), with tolerability equal or better. That fully supports the practical claim — selected skin infections can be treated without daily dosing, a line, or an admission for antibiotics — and nothing beyond it: both programmes were built to prove 'not worse', and neither was powered on recurrence or other late outcomes. LIKELY for noninferiority as trialled.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate current resistance and cost landscapes; the economic case (drug price vs bed-days saved) is a local calculation this shelf does not make.

shelves.title: Oral JAK inhibitors for atopic dermatitis: upadacitinib and abrocitinib
shelves.question: Do oral JAK inhibitors clear moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis versus placebo — upadacitinib in the twin Measure Up trials, abrocitinib in JADE MONO-1 — and what monitoring do they demand?
shelves.mesh: Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Janus Kinase 1 · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Administration, Oral
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of two oral JAK1 inhibitors in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis all met their coprimary endpoints. Upadacitinib achieved EASI-75 at week 16 in 60–80% across doses and trials versus 13–16% on placebo (Measure Up 1 and 2); abrocitinib achieved EASI-75 in 40% (100 mg) and 63% (200 mg) versus 12% on placebo at week 12 (JADE MONO-1), with Investigator Global Assessment responses of 24% and 44% versus 8%. These are short (12–16-week) monotherapy trials: the class's longer-term and comparative safety — the monitoring question — is not answered by these cards, and JAK-inhibitor safety in rheumatoid arthritis is a different population, home on Shelf #384. Dupilumab for the same disease is Shelf #374 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Measure Up 1 and 2 (2021): upadacitinib achieved EASI-75 in 60–80% versus 13–16% on placebo at week 16 in atopic dermatitis
cards.summary: Measure Up 1 and 2 (2021): upadacitinib achieved EASI-75 in 60–80% vs 13–16% on placebo at week 16 in atopic dermatitis.
cards.type: Two replicate multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1683 adolescents (12–17 years) and adults (18–75 years) with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (at least 10% body surface area, EASI at least 16, global assessment at least 3, worst pruritus score at least 4): Measure Up 1 randomised 847 (upadacitinib 15 mg 281, 30 mg 285, placebo 281) and Measure Up 2 randomised 836 (276, 282, 278). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: EASI-75 at week 16: Measure Up 1 — 70% (196/281) on 15 mg and 80% (227/285) on 30 mg versus 16% (46/281) on placebo (adjusted differences 53.3% and 63.4%); Measure Up 2 — 60% (166/276) and 73% (206/282) versus 13% (37/278) (differences 46.9% and 59.6%); all p<0.0001. Clear/almost-clear global responses: 48% and 62% versus 8% (Measure Up 1) and 39% and 52% versus 5% (Measure Up 2). Serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar among groups; the commonest treatment-emergent event was acne (up to 17% on 30 mg versus 2% on placebo), with upper respiratory infection, nasopharyngitis, headache and creatine phosphokinase elevation also reported.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks of monotherapy in a chronic relapsing disease: these trials establish short-term clearance, not durability, combination use, or long-term class safety.

cards.headline: JADE MONO-1 (2020): abrocitinib achieved EASI-75 in 40% (100 mg) and 63% (200 mg) versus 12% on placebo at week 12
cards.summary: JADE MONO-1 (2020): abrocitinib achieved EASI-75 in 40% (100 mg) and 63% (200 mg) vs 12% on placebo at week 12.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 387 patients aged 12 years or older with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (global assessment at least 3, EASI at least 16, at least 10% body surface area, peak pruritus score at least 4, bodyweight at least 40 kg) at 69 sites, assigned to abrocitinib 100 mg (156), abrocitinib 200 mg (154) or placebo (77) once daily for 12 weeks; all received at least one dose. shelves.title: JAK inhibitors for alopecia areata: baricitinib and ritlecitinib
shelves.question: Do baricitinib (BRAVE-AA1/-2) and ritlecitinib (ALLEGRO) regrow scalp hair in severe alopecia areata versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Alopecia Areata/drug therapy · Azetidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Purines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyrazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Sulfonamides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · COVID-19
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two JAK inhibitors regrow scalp hair in severe alopecia areata in placebo-controlled trials. Baricitinib achieved a SALT score of 20 or less (at most 20% scalp hair loss) at week 36 in 38.8% (4 mg) and 22.8% (2 mg) versus 6.2% on placebo in BRAVE-AA1, and 35.9% and 19.4% versus 3.3% in BRAVE-AA2. Ritlecitinib achieved the same threshold at week 24 in 14–31% across doses versus 2% on placebo in ALLEGRO. Even on the best arm, most patients did not reach the regrowth threshold — the honest framing of a real but partial treatment effect.

cards.headline: BRAVE-AA1 and AA2 (2022): baricitinib 4 mg achieved SALT 20 or less in 38.8% and 35.9% versus 6.2% and 3.3% on placebo at week 36
cards.summary: BRAVE-AA1 and AA2 (2022): baricitinib 4 mg achieved a SALT score of 20 or less in 38.8% and 35.9% vs 6.2% and 3.3% on placebo at week 36.
cards.type: Two randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1200 adults with severe alopecia areata (Severity of Alopecia Tool [SALT] score 50 or higher, where 0 is no scalp hair loss and 100 is complete loss): 654 enrolled in BRAVE-AA1 and 546 in BRAVE-AA2, assigned in a 3:2:2 ratio to baricitinib 4 mg, 2 mg, or placebo once daily. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The estimated percentage with a SALT score of 20 or less at week 36 was 38.8% (4 mg), 22.8% (2 mg) and 6.2% (placebo) in BRAVE-AA1, and 35.9%, 19.4% and 3.3% respectively in BRAVE-AA2. Differences versus placebo were 32.6 percentage points for 4 mg in both trials, and 16.6 and 16.1 points for 2 mg (P<0.001 for each dose versus placebo). Secondary outcomes generally favoured 4 mg but not 2 mg. Acne, elevated creatine kinase, and increased low- and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol were more common with baricitinib than placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trials' own conclusion calls for longer trials to assess efficacy and safety; at 36 weeks even the 4-mg arm left about three in five patients above the regrowth threshold.
cards.source: King B et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Baricitinib for Alopecia Areata. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(18):1687-1699. PMID: 35334197. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03570749 and NCT03899259, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ALLEGRO (2023): ritlecitinib achieved SALT 20 or less in 23% (50 mg) versus 2% on placebo at week 24
cards.summary: ALLEGRO (2023): ritlecitinib achieved a SALT score of 20 or less in 23% (50 mg) vs 2% on placebo at week 24.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 2b-3 trial with a 24-week placebo-controlled period and 24-week extension
cards.people: 718 patients aged 12 years and older with alopecia areata and at least 50% scalp hair loss, at 118 sites in 18 countries, randomly assigned across ritlecitinib dose regimens (with or without a 200 mg loading dose), a 10 mg arm, or placebo-then-switch arms; 446 (62%) were female and 272 (38%) male. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 24, a SALT score of 20 or less was achieved by 38 of 124 patients (31%) on ritlecitinib 200 mg loading dose then 50 mg, 27 of 121 (22%) on 200 mg then 30 mg, 29 of 124 (23%) on 50 mg, 17 of 119 (14%) on 30 mg, and 2 of 130 (2%) on placebo. Differences versus placebo were 29.1% (loading-dose 50 mg group), 20.8%, 21.9% and 12.8% respectively (p<0.0001 except p=0.0002 for 30 mg). Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups and there were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: A multi-arm dose-ranging design folded into a phase 2b-3 trial: the placebo comparison lasts 24 weeks, after which placebo patients switched to ritlecitinib, so longer-term controlled safety is limited.

shelves.title: Prurigo nodularis: dupilumab and nemolizumab
shelves.question: Do dupilumab (PRIME/PRIME2) and nemolizumab (OLYMPIA 1) reduce itch and clear nodules in moderate-to-severe prurigo nodularis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Prurigo/drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Injections, Subcutaneous · Pruritus/drug therapy · Chronic Disease · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Prurigo/drug therapy,diagnosis,complications
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of two biologics in moderate-to-severe prurigo nodularis all met their primary endpoints. Dupilumab produced a 4-point-or-greater itch reduction in 60.0% versus 18.4% at week 24 in PRIME and 37.2% versus 22.0% at week 12 in PRIME2; nemolizumab produced an itch response in 58.4% versus 16.7% and clear/almost-clear skin in 26.3% versus 7.3% at week 16 in OLYMPIA 1. Itch responds more strongly than nodules clear — in no trial did a majority achieve clear or almost-clear skin by the primary timepoint except on continued treatment — and the shelf states both halves.

cards.headline: PRIME and PRIME2 (2023): dupilumab produced a 4-point itch reduction in 60.0% versus 18.4% (PRIME, week 24) and 37.2% versus 22.0% (PRIME2, week 12)
cards.summary: PRIME and PRIME2 (2023): dupilumab produced a 4-point itch reduction in 60.0% vs 18.4% (PRIME, week 24) and 37.2% vs 22.0% (PRIME2, week 12).
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (LIBERTY-PN PRIME and PRIME2) reported in one paper
cards.people: 311 adults with prurigo nodularis with at least 20 nodules and severe itch uncontrolled with topical therapies (151 in PRIME, 160 in PRIME2), randomised 1:1 to dupilumab 300 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Both trials met all prespecified primary and key secondary endpoints. A reduction of at least 4 points in Worst Itch Numeric Rating Scale was achieved at week 24 by 60.0% on dupilumab versus 18.4% on placebo in PRIME (difference 95% CI 27.8 to 57.7; P<0.001) and at week 12 by 37.2% versus 22.0% in PRIME2 (CI 2.3 to 31.2; P=0.022). Key secondary endpoints included reduction in nodule number to 5 or fewer at week 24, also met. Safety was consistent with the known dupilumab safety profile.
cards.watchOut: The two trials used different primary timepoints (week 24 versus week 12), and PRIME2's itch difference is the smallest on this shelf (about 15 percentage points, CI reaching 2.3) — replication yes, uniform size no.
cards.source: Yosipovitch G et al. Dupilumab in patients with prurigo nodularis: two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. Nat Med. 2023;29(5):1180-1190. PMID: 37142763. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04183335 and NCT04202679, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: OLYMPIA 1 (2025): nemolizumab produced an itch response in 58.4% versus 16.7% and clear/almost-clear skin in 26.3% versus 7.3% at week 16
cards.summary: OLYMPIA 1 (2025): nemolizumab produced an itch response in 58.4% vs 16.7% and clear or almost-clear skin in 26.3% vs 7.3% at week 16.
cards.type: Multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 randomised clinical trial (24-week treatment)
cards.people: 286 adults with moderate-to-severe prurigo nodularis (at least 20 nodules, Investigator's Global Assessment score at least 3, Peak Pruritus score at least 7.0) at 77 centres in 10 countries, randomised 2:1 to nemolizumab 30 mg or 60 mg by weight every 4 weeks (190) or placebo (96); mean age 57.5 (SD 13.0) years; 166 (58.0%) female.
cards.result: At week 16, itch response (at least a 4-point improvement in weekly average Peak Pruritus score) was achieved by 111 of 190 (58.4%) on nemolizumab versus 16 of 96 (16.7%) on placebo (difference 40.1%, 95% CI 29.4% to 50.8%; P<.001), and Investigator's Global Assessment success (0/1 with at least a 2-grade improvement) by 50 of 190 (26.3%) versus 7 of 96 (7.3%) (difference 14.6%, 6.7% to 22.6%; P=.003). cards.watchOut: Skin clearance lags itch relief by a wide margin (26.3% clear/almost-clear versus 58.4% itch response at week 16): patients should expect itch to improve well before nodules resolve.

cards.headline: Synthesis: itch responds, nodules follow slowly — two biologics, three trials — LIKELY
cards.summary: Itch responds, nodules follow slowly — two biologics, three trials — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PRIME (151 patients) and PRIME2 (160 patients) for dupilumab, and OLYMPIA 1 (286 patients) for nemolizumab, all placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in prurigo nodularis with at least 20 nodules and severe itch.
cards.result: IL-4/13 blockade (dupilumab) and IL-31-receptor blockade (nemolizumab) both roughly tripled itch-response rates versus placebo (absolute gains of about 15–42 percentage points across trials and timepoints) and improved nodule outcomes, with the skin-clearance rates (26–31% at 16–24 weeks in OLYMPIA 1) honestly lower than the itch rates. cards.watchOut: No head-to-head trial exists between the two drugs on this shelf; cross-trial percentage comparisons are not a ranking.

shelves.title: Rituximab for pemphigus: first-line, and against mycophenolate
shelves.question: Does first-line rituximab with short-term prednisone beat prednisone alone for pemphigus (Ritux 3) — and does rituximab beat mycophenolate mofetil in pemphigus vulgaris (PEMPHIX)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pemphigus/drug therapy · Prednisolone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Rituximab/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Administration, Oral · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials against two different standard comparators both favoured rituximab decisively in pemphigus. First-line rituximab plus short-term prednisone achieved complete remission off therapy at month 24 in 89% versus 34% on prednisone alone (Ritux 3, open-label), with fewer grade 3–4 adverse events (27 events in 16 patients vs 53 in 29). Against mycophenolate, rituximab achieved sustained complete remission at week 52 in 40% versus 10% (PEMPHIX), with less cumulative glucocorticoid (3545 mg vs 5140 mg) and far fewer disease flares (6 vs 44), but more serious adverse events (22% vs 15%). The open-label design of Ritux 3 is the shelf's main caveat; the effect sizes are large in both trials.

cards.headline: Ritux 3 (2017): first-line rituximab plus short-term prednisone achieved complete remission off therapy in 89% versus 34% on prednisone alone at month 24
cards.summary: Ritux 3 (2017): first-line rituximab plus short-term prednisone achieved complete remission off therapy in 89% vs 34% on prednisone alone at month 24.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label randomised trial (3-year follow-up)
cards.people: 90 patients with newly diagnosed pemphigus aged 18–80 years, treated for the first time, at 25 dermatology departments in France, randomly assigned to prednisone alone tapered over 12 or 18 months (44 analysed) or rituximab 1000 mg on days 0 and 14 plus 500 mg at months 12 and 18 with short-term prednisone tapered over 3 or 6 months (46 analysed). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At month 24, 41 (89%) of 46 rituximab patients were in complete remission off therapy versus 15 (34%) of 44 on prednisone alone (absolute difference 55 percentage points, 95% CI 38.4 to 71.7; p<0.0001; relative risk of success 2.61, 1.71 to 3.99 — a relative measure beyond the 2.0 solidity threshold, with absolute rates printed; number needed to treat 1.82). No patient died. Grade 3–4 severe adverse events were fewer with rituximab (27 events in 16 patients; mean 0.59 [SD 1.15]) than with prednisone alone (53 events in 29 patients; mean 1.20 [1.25]; p=0.0021), the commonest being diabetes/endocrine disorder, myopathy and bone disorders.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: patients and clinicians knew the treatment, in a disease where steroid tapering decisions could be influenced by that knowledge — the remission endpoint is objective (off-therapy status), but the design caveat stands and is why two trials carry this shelf.
cards.source: Joly P et al. First-line rituximab combined with short-term prednisone versus prednisone alone for the treatment of pemphigus (Ritux 3): a prospective, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label randomised trial. Lancet. 2017;389(10083):2031-2040. PMID: 28342637. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00784589, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PEMPHIX (2021): rituximab beat mycophenolate on sustained complete remission — 40% versus 10% at week 52 — with 6 versus 44 disease flares
cards.summary: PEMPHIX (2021): rituximab beat mycophenolate on sustained complete remission — 40% vs 10% at week 52 — with 6 vs 44 disease flares.
cards.people: 135 patients with moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris randomly assigned to intravenous rituximab 1000 mg on days 1, 15, 168 and 182 (67) or oral mycophenolate mofetil 2 g per day (68), both with the same tapering oral glucocorticoid schedule; the primary outcome was assessed in 62 and 63 patients respectively; median baseline Pemphigus Disease Area Index activity scores were 22.7 (rituximab) and 18.3 (mycophenolate). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Sustained complete remission at week 52 (lesions healed, no new lesions, PDAI activity score 0 for at least 16 weeks without glucocorticoids) occurred in 25 patients (40%) on rituximab versus 6 (10%) on mycophenolate (difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 15 to 45; P<0.001). Mean cumulative glucocorticoid dose was 3545 mg versus 5140 mg (difference -1595 mg; P<0.001). Disease flares numbered 6 versus 44 (adjusted rate ratio 0.12, 0.05 to 0.29; P<0.001 — a relative measure beyond the 0.5 solidity threshold). Dermatology Life Quality Index improved more with rituximab (difference -2.87 points; P=0.001). Serious adverse events occurred in 15 of 67 (22%) on rituximab versus 10 of 68 (15%) on mycophenolate.
cards.watchOut: Rituximab won on efficacy and steroid-sparing but had more serious adverse events (22% vs 15%), and the trial says nothing beyond 52 weeks — the authors themselves call for longer comparative trials.
cards.source: Werth VP et al. Rituximab versus Mycophenolate Mofetil in Patients with Pemphigus Vulgaris. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(24):2295-2305. PMID: 34097368. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02383589, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rituximab beats both prednisone alone and mycophenolate in pemphigus — LIKELY — watch the serious-adverse-event trade in PEMPHIX
cards.summary: Rituximab beats both prednisone alone and mycophenolate in pemphigus — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ritux 3 (90 patients, newly diagnosed pemphigus, rituximab plus short prednisone versus prednisone alone) and PEMPHIX (135 patients, pemphigus vulgaris, rituximab versus mycophenolate, both with tapering glucocorticoids).
cards.result: Different comparators, different eras, same conclusion with large absolute differences (55 and 31 percentage points on remission endpoints), plus steroid-sparing in both trials. That is the LIKELY case. Rituximab for ANCA vasculitis is a different disease, home on Shelf #386, and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The harm balance flips by comparator: fewer severe events than high-dose prednisone alone (Ritux 3), more serious events than mycophenolate (PEMPHIX). Quote the comparator when quoting safety.

shelves.title: Non-steroidal topical therapy for plaque psoriasis: tapinarof and roflumilast cream
shelves.question: Do tapinarof cream (PSOARING 1/2) and roflumilast cream (DERMIS-1/-2) clear plaque psoriasis versus vehicle — steroid-free options for sensitive sites and long-term use?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Dermatitis, Contact/etiology · Headache/chemically induced · Intention to Treat Analysis · Interleukin-17/metabolism · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Psoriasis/complications,drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Four vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials of two non-steroidal creams in plaque psoriasis all met their primary endpoints. Tapinarof 1% once daily achieved a Physician's Global Assessment response in 35.4% and 40.2% versus 6.0% and 6.3% on vehicle at week 12 (PSOARING 1 and 2). Roflumilast 0.3% cream achieved Investigator Global Assessment success in 42.4% and 37.5% versus 6.1% and 6.9% on vehicle at week 8 (DERMIS-1 and -2), including strong intertriginous-site results relevant to sensitive areas. Trials are short (8–12 weeks) and vehicle-controlled only: no comparison with topical steroids or vitamin D combinations exists on this shelf.

cards.headline: PSOARING 1 and 2 (2021): tapinarof cream achieved a global-assessment response in 35.4% and 40.2% versus 6.0% and 6.3% on vehicle at week 12
cards.summary: PSOARING 1 and 2 (2021): tapinarof cream achieved a global-assessment response in 35.4% and 40.2% vs 6.0% and 6.3% on vehicle at week 12.
cards.type: Two identical phase 3 randomised, vehicle-controlled trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1025 adults with mild-to-severe plaque psoriasis (Physician's Global Assessment 2 to 4; 3–20% body surface area) enrolled across the two trials (510 in trial 1, 515 in trial 2), randomised 2:1 to tapinarof 1% cream or vehicle once daily for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A Physician's Global Assessment response (score 0 or 1 with at least a 2-point decrease) occurred in 35.4% on tapinarof versus 6.0% on vehicle in trial 1 and 40.2% versus 6.3% in trial 2 (P<0.001 for both). Secondary endpoints and patient-reported outcomes were generally in the same direction. Adverse events with tapinarof included folliculitis, nasopharyngitis, contact dermatitis, headache, upper respiratory tract infection and pruritus.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks against vehicle only, in 3–20% body-surface-area disease: the authors note larger, longer trials against existing treatments are needed — none is carded here.
cards.source: Lebwohl MG et al. Phase 3 Trials of Tapinarof Cream for Plaque Psoriasis. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(24):2219-2229. PMID: 34879448. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03956355 and NCT03983980, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DERMIS-1 and -2 (2022): roflumilast cream achieved IGA success in 42.4% and 37.5% versus 6.1% and 6.9% on vehicle at week 8, including intertriginous disease
cards.summary: DERMIS-1 and -2 (2022): roflumilast cream achieved IGA success in 42.4% and 37.5% vs 6.1% and 6.9% on vehicle at week 8.
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled multicentre trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 881 patients aged 2 years or older with plaque psoriasis involving 2–20% of body surface area, at 40 (DERMIS-1, n=439) and 39 (DERMIS-2, n=442) centres in the US and Canada, randomised 2:1 to roflumilast cream 0.3% once daily (286 and 290) or vehicle (153 and 152) for 8 weeks; mean age 47.5 years; 320 (36.3%) female.
cards.result: Investigator Global Assessment success (clear or almost clear plus at least a 2-grade improvement) at week 8 was 42.4% versus 6.1% in DERMIS-1 (difference 39.6%, 95% CI 32.3% to 46.9%) and 37.5% versus 6.9% in DERMIS-2 (difference 28.9%, 20.8% to 36.9%) (P<.001 for both). Intertriginous IGA success was 71.2% versus 13.8% and 68.1% versus 18.5%; a 75% PASI reduction occurred in 41.6% versus 7.6% and 39.0% versus 5.3%; itch success in 67.5% versus 26.8% and 69.4% versus 35.6%. Treatment-emergent adverse events were 25.2% versus 23.5% and 25.9% versus 18.4%; serious adverse events were 0.7% or fewer in every arm.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is short for a lifelong disease, and enrolment from age 2 means the population is mostly adult by mean age (47.5 years) — paediatric-specific numbers are not in the abstract.
cards.source: Lebwohl MG et al. Effect of Roflumilast Cream vs Vehicle Cream on Chronic Plaque Psoriasis: The DERMIS-1 and DERMIS-2 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2022;328(11):1073-1084. PMID: 36125472. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04211363 and NCT04211389, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: steroid-free creams clear plaque psoriasis versus vehicle in four trials — LIKELY — with no active-comparator evidence
cards.summary: Steroid-free creams clear plaque psoriasis versus vehicle in four trials — LIKELY — with no active-comparator evidence.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PSOARING 1 and 2 (1025 patients, tapinarof, 12 weeks) and DERMIS-1 and -2 (881 patients, roflumilast cream, 8 weeks), all vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials in plaque psoriasis.
cards.result: Two chemically unrelated non-steroidal mechanisms (aryl hydrocarbon receptor modulation; PDE4 inhibition) each produced absolute response gains of about 29–40 percentage points over vehicle, replicated in twin trials — the LIKELY case. The vitamin D–steroid combination foam/gel question is drafted separately (Shelf #628) and systemic biologics for moderate-to-severe disease are home on Shelf #377; neither is re-carded here, and nothing on this shelf ranks the creams against them. Roflumilast FOAM for seborrhoeic dermatitis is Shelf #829 — a different formulation and disease.
cards.watchOut: Vehicle response was only about 6–7% in all four trials, which flatters absolute differences; real-world value depends on comparison with cheap topical steroids, which these trials do not provide.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lebwohl MG et al. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(24):2219-2229. PMID: 34879448; Lebwohl MG et al. JAMA. 2022;328(11):1073-1084. PMID: 36125472. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: IL-17 blockade for hidradenitis suppurativa: bimekizumab and secukinumab
shelves.question: Do bimekizumab (BE HEARD I/II) and secukinumab (SUNSHINE/SUNRISE) improve lesion response in moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Hidradenitis Suppurativa/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Interleukin-17/antagonists & inhibitors · Hidradenitis Suppurativa/chemically induced,drug therapy · Abscess/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Four identically-designed twin phase 3 trials of two IL-17 inhibitors in moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa found higher clinical-response (HiSCR50) rates than placebo at week 16. Bimekizumab every 2 weeks achieved 48% versus 29% (BE HEARD I) and 52% versus 32% (BE HEARD II); secukinumab every 2 weeks achieved 45% versus 34% (SUNSHINE) and 42% versus 31% (SUNRISE). The odds ratios (1.6–2.4) straddle the 0.5–2.0 caution band's mirror image and the absolute gains are modest (about 11–20 percentage points against unusually high placebo responses of 29–34%) — the stamp rests on four concordant blinded trials, with the modest absolute benefit stated plainly. Adalimumab (TNF blockade) for the same disease is home on Shelf #381 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: BE HEARD I and II (2024): bimekizumab achieved HiSCR50 in 48% and 52% versus 29% and 32% on placebo at week 16
cards.summary: BE HEARD I and II (2024): bimekizumab achieved HiSCR50 in 48% and 52% vs 29% and 32% on placebo at week 16.
cards.type: Two identically designed 48-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 trials reported in one paper (placebo-controlled to week 16)
cards.people: 1014 patients aged 18 years or older with moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa (505 enrolled in BE HEARD I, 509 in BE HEARD II), randomised across bimekizumab 320 mg dosing regimens or placebo-to-bimekizumab; the primary comparison groups numbered 289 (bimekizumab every 2 weeks) versus 72 (placebo) in trial I and 291 versus 74 in trial II. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: HiSCR50 at week 16 (at least a 50% reduction in abscess and inflammatory nodule count with no increase in abscess or draining tunnel count) was met by 138 (48%) of 289 on bimekizumab every 2 weeks versus 21 (29%) of 72 on placebo in BE HEARD I (odds ratio 2.23, 97.5% CI 1.16 to 4.31; p=0.0060) and 151 (52%) of 291 versus 24 (32%) of 74 in BE HEARD II (odds ratio 2.29, 1.22 to 4.29; p=0.0032) — relative measures at or just beyond the 2.0 solidity threshold, with absolute rates printed. Every-4-week dosing also met the endpoint in BE HEARD II (54% vs 32%; odds ratio 2.42). Responses were maintained or increased to week 48. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events over 48 weeks were 8% (trial I) and 5% (trial II); the commonest events included hidradenitis itself, oral candidiasis, diarrhoea and headache. One death (congestive heart failure, in a patient with substantial cardiovascular history, judged unrelated) occurred across the two trials.
cards.watchOut: Placebo HiSCR50 rates of 29–32% are high for this disease, compressing the absolute gain to about 19–20 percentage points; the death is reported on the card face with its context, not buried.
cards.source: Kimball AB et al. Efficacy and safety of bimekizumab in patients with moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa (BE HEARD I and BE HEARD II): two 48-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2024;403(10443):2504-2519. PMID: 38795716. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04242446 and NCT04242498, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SUNSHINE and SUNRISE (2023): secukinumab every 2 weeks achieved a clinical response in 45% and 42% versus 34% and 31% on placebo at week 16
cards.summary: SUNSHINE and SUNRISE (2023): secukinumab every 2 weeks achieved a clinical response in 45% and 42% vs 34% and 31% on placebo at week 16.
cards.type: Two identical, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1084 patients aged 18 years or older with moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa (at least 5 inflammatory lesions in at least 2 anatomical areas, for at least 1 year) at 219 sites in 40 countries: SUNSHINE analysed 541 (56% women; mean age 36.1 [SD 11.7] years) and SUNRISE 543 (56% women; mean age 36.3 [11.4] years), each split across secukinumab 300 mg every 2 weeks, every 4 weeks, and placebo.
cards.result: A hidradenitis suppurativa clinical response at week 16 was achieved in SUNSHINE by 45% on secukinumab every 2 weeks versus 34% on placebo (odds ratio 1.8, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.7; p=0.0070), while every-4-week dosing did not reach significance on the trial's reported test (42% vs 34%; p=0.042 against its multiplicity threshold — reported in the abstract as no significant difference). In SUNRISE, both regimens were significant: 42% (every 2 weeks; odds ratio 1.6, 1.1 to 2.6; p=0.015) and 46% (every 4 weeks; odds ratio 1.9, 1.2 to 3.0; p=0.0022) versus 31% on placebo. All odds ratios (1.6–1.9) sit inside the range this library does not treat as solid on their own (the mirror of the 0.5–2.0 caution band); absolute differences are 8–15 percentage points. Responses were sustained to week 52. The commonest adverse event to week 16 was headache (8–12% across arms); no study-related deaths were reported to week 16.
cards.watchOut: The every-4-week regimen split its verdict across the twin trials (significant in SUNRISE, not in SUNSHINE): the shelf's secukinumab claim is for the every-2-week regimen, which was significant in both.
cards.source: Kimball AB et al. Secukinumab in moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa (SUNSHINE and SUNRISE): week 16 and week 52 results of two identical, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2023;401(10378):747-761. PMID: 36746171. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03713619 (SUNSHINE) and NCT03713632 (SUNRISE), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: IL-17 blockade works in hidradenitis suppurativa — LIKELY — with modest absolute gains over high placebo response rates
cards.summary: IL-17 blockade works in hidradenitis suppurativa — LIKELY — with modest absolute gains over high placebo response rates.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BE HEARD I and II (1014 patients, bimekizumab) and SUNSHINE and SUNRISE (1084 patients, secukinumab), all twin phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa.
cards.result: Four trials, two antibodies (dual IL-17A/F blockade and IL-17A blockade), one endpoint family (HiSCR50 at week 16): every adequately-dosed comparison favoured treatment, with absolute gains of roughly 11–20 percentage points over placebo rates of 29–34%. No head-to-head trial exists, and adalimumab's evidence stays home on Shelf #381 — this shelf neither ranks IL-17 blockade against TNF blockade nor re-cards it.
cards.watchOut: Expectation-setting matters in this disease: roughly half of treated patients did not reach HiSCR50 at week 16 in any trial, and about a third of placebo patients did.

shelves.title: Molluscum contagiosum: cantharidin drug-device and berdazimer gel
shelves.question: Do cantharidin 0.7% applied in clinic (CAMP-1/-2) and home-applied berdazimer gel (B-SIMPLE4) clear molluscum lesions versus vehicle?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two treatment programmes cleared molluscum contagiosum in vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials, in a disease with high spontaneous resolution (vehicle clearance 13–20%). Clinic-applied cantharidin 0.7% (VP-102) achieved complete clearance at day 84 in 46.3% versus 17.9% (CAMP-1) and 54.0% versus 13.4% (CAMP-2). Home-applied berdazimer gel achieved complete clearance at week 12 in 32.4% versus 19.7% (odds ratio 2.0 — at the boundary of the caution band; the absolute difference of 12.7 percentage points is the honest figure). Cantharidin's adverse events were near-universal but expected, local and mostly mild-to-moderate (application-site vesicles, pain, pruritus); berdazimer's were few, mainly application-site pain and erythema.

cards.headline: CAMP-1 and CAMP-2 (2020): cantharidin 0.7% drug-device achieved complete clearance in 46.3% and 54.0% versus 17.9% and 13.4% on vehicle at day 84
cards.summary: CAMP-1 and CAMP-2 (2020): cantharidin drug-device achieved complete clearance in 46.3% and 54.0% vs 17.9% and 13.4% on vehicle at day 84.
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials of identical design reported in one paper
cards.people: 528 individuals aged 2 years or older with molluscum contagiosum at 31 US centres (527 treated: CAMP-1 n=265, CAMP-2 n=262), randomised 3:2 to VP-102 (cantharidin 0.7% drug-device combination) or vehicle applied in clinic to all treatable lesions every 21 days until clearance or up to 4 treatments; 267 of 527 (50.7%) were male; mean ages were 7.5 (SD 5.3) and 7.4 (8.0) years in the VP-102 groups and 6.3 (4.7) and 7.3 (6.7) years in the vehicle groups.
cards.result: Complete clearance of all lesions (baseline and new) at the day-84 end-of-study visit was 46.3% with VP-102 versus 17.9% with vehicle in CAMP-1 and 54.0% versus 13.4% in CAMP-2 (P<.001 for both). Adverse events occurred in 99% (CAMP-1) and 95% (CAMP-2) of VP-102 participants versus 73% and 66% on vehicle; the commonest were application-site vesicles, pain, pruritus, erythema and scab — the expected blistering action of cantharidin — and most were mild or moderate in severity.
cards.watchOut: A paediatric population (mean age about 7 years) and a treatment whose adverse events are its mechanism: near-universal local reactions are tolerability information, not a safety surprise, and adult/sexually-transmitted disease is outside this evidence.
cards.source: Eichenfield LF et al. Safety and Efficacy of VP-102, a Proprietary, Drug-Device Combination Product Containing Cantharidin, 0.7% (w/v), in Children and Adults With Molluscum Contagiosum: Two Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA Dermatol. 2020;156(12):1315-1323. PMID: 32965495. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03377790 and NCT03377803, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: B-SIMPLE4 (2022): berdazimer gel achieved complete clearance in 32.4% versus 19.7% on vehicle at week 12 (absolute difference 12.7%)
cards.summary: B-SIMPLE4 (2022): berdazimer gel achieved complete clearance in 32.4% vs 19.7% on vehicle at week 12 (absolute difference 12.7 points).
cards.type: Multicentre, vehicle-controlled, double-blind, phase 3 randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 891 participants aged 6 months or older with 3 to 70 raised molluscum lesions at 55 US clinics, randomised to berdazimer gel 10.3% (444; mean age 6.6 years; 51.4% male) or vehicle gel (447; mean age 6.5 years), applied once daily at home to all lesions for 12 weeks; patients with sexually transmitted molluscum or periocular-only disease were excluded.
cards.result: Complete clearance of all lesions at week 12 was 32.4% (144 patients) on berdazimer versus 19.7% (88) on vehicle (absolute difference 12.7%; odds ratio 2.0, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.8; P<.001) — the odds ratio sits exactly at the 2.0 boundary of this library's solidity threshold, so the absolute difference is the figure to quote. 14.4% of the berdazimer group discontinued because of clearance versus 8.9% on vehicle. The commonest adverse events were application-site pain and erythema, mostly mild; discontinuation for adverse events was 4.1% versus 0.7%.
cards.watchOut: One in five vehicle patients cleared spontaneously in 12 weeks, and two in three berdazimer patients did not clear: the drug accelerates clearance modestly in a self-limiting disease.
cards.source: Browning JC et al. Efficacy and Safety of Topical Nitric Oxide-Releasing Berdazimer Gel in Patients With Molluscum Contagiosum: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Dermatol. 2022;158(8):871-878. PMID: 35830173. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04535531, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both clinic cantharidin and home berdazimer beat vehicle — LIKELY — against a background of spontaneous clearance
cards.summary: Both clinic cantharidin and home berdazimer beat vehicle — LIKELY — against a background of spontaneous clearance.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CAMP-1 and CAMP-2 (528 participants, clinic-applied cantharidin) and B-SIMPLE4 (891 participants, home-applied berdazimer gel), all vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials, predominantly in young children.
cards.result: Absolute clearance gains were 28–41 percentage points for cantharidin and 12.7 points for berdazimer, over vehicle clearance of 13–20% — the spontaneous-resolution backdrop that makes vehicle control essential in this disease. Common-wart treatments are a different virus and lesion, drafted at Shelf #622, and are not re-carded here. No trial compared the two treatments with each other or with watchful waiting as a strategy; the shelf claims efficacy versus vehicle only.
cards.watchOut: Do not rank cantharidin above berdazimer from these percentages: different visit schedules (day 84 versus week 12), application settings and populations separate the programmes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eichenfield LF et al. JAMA Dermatol. 2020;156(12):1315-1323. PMID: 32965495; Browning JC et al. JAMA Dermatol. 2022;158(8):871-878. PMID: 35830173. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Delgocitinib cream for chronic hand eczema
shelves.question: Does topical pan-JAK delgocitinib cream clear moderate-to-severe chronic hand eczema versus cream vehicle in the twin DELTA trials?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Eczema/drug therapy · Hand Dermatoses/drug therapy · Pyrroles/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Skin Cream
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two replicate phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials (DELTA 1, 487 patients; DELTA 2, 473 patients) of twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g in moderate-to-severe chronic hand eczema both met their primary endpoint: Investigator's Global Assessment treatment success at week 16 in 20% versus 10% (DELTA 1) and 29% versus 7% (DELTA 2). The absolute gains (about 10 and 22 percentage points) are modest — most treated patients did not reach clear/almost-clear — and adverse-event rates were similar to vehicle (45–46% versus 45–51%). LIKELY rests on twin-trial replication of a real but partial effect, in a population that had failed basic care and topical corticosteroids.

cards.headline: DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 (2024): delgocitinib cream achieved treatment success in 20% and 29% versus 10% and 7% on vehicle at week 16
cards.summary: DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 (2024): delgocitinib cream achieved treatment success in 20% and 29% vs 10% and 7% on vehicle at week 16.
cards.type: Two multicentre, randomised, controlled, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 960 adults (aged 18 years or older) with moderate-to-severe chronic hand eczema: DELTA 1 enrolled 487 (181 male, 306 female) at 53 centres in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, and DELTA 2 enrolled 473 (161 male, 312 female) at 50 centres in Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain; patients were randomised 2:1 to twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g (325 and 314) or cream vehicle (162 and 159) for 16 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Investigator's Global Assessment for Chronic Hand Eczema (IGA-CHE) treatment success at week 16 (score 0 [clear] or 1 [almost clear, barely perceptible erythema]) was achieved by 64 (20%) of 325 delgocitinib patients versus 16 (10%) of 162 on vehicle in DELTA 1, and 91 (29%) of 313 versus 11 (7%) of 159 in DELTA 2 (both trials p≤0.0055). Adverse events were reported by 45% (DELTA 1) and 46% (DELTA 2) on delgocitinib versus 51% and 45% on vehicle; the most frequent events in both groups (at least 2%) were similar and included COVID-19 and nasopharyngitis.
cards.watchOut: Success means clear or almost-clear on a strict scale, and 71–80% of treated patients did not reach it by week 16: a replicated benefit of modest absolute size in a hard-to-treat occupational disease, not a cure.
cards.source: Bissonnette R et al. Efficacy and safety of delgocitinib cream in adults with moderate to severe chronic hand eczema (DELTA 1 and DELTA 2): results from multicentre, randomised, controlled, double-blind, phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2024;404(10451):461-473. PMID: 39033766. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04871711 and NCT04872101, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: twin trials, same modest success rates, vehicle-like tolerability — LIKELY
cards.summary: Twin trials, same modest success rates, vehicle-like tolerability — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 (960 adults in total), replicate double-blind vehicle-controlled trials of delgocitinib cream in moderate-to-severe chronic hand eczema.
cards.result: Both trials separated from vehicle on the same strict endpoint (20% vs 10%; 29% vs 7%) with no tolerability penalty over 16 weeks — the twin-replication pattern behind LIKELY, with absolute size stated as modest on the face of the shelf. Generalised atopic dermatitis treatments (Shelves #374, #820) are a different distribution of disease and are not re-carded here; this shelf is chronic hand eczema that basic care and topical corticosteroids had not controlled.
cards.watchOut: Vehicle success of 7–10% and treatment success of 20–29% frame a chronic-disease expectation: improvement is likely, clearance is not the norm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bissonnette R et al. Lancet. 2024;404(10451):461-473. PMID: 39033766. Registry IDs as on the individual card.

shelves.title: Remibrutinib for chronic spontaneous urticaria
shelves.question: Does the oral BTK inhibitor remibrutinib reduce weekly urticaria activity versus placebo in chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled by antihistamines?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Agammaglobulinaemia Tyrosine Kinase/antagonists & inhibitors · Chronic Urticaria/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy · Pruritus/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two identical phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (REMIX-1, 470 patients; REMIX-2, 455 patients) of remibrutinib 25 mg twice daily in chronic spontaneous urticaria symptomatic despite second-generation H1-antihistamines both met their primary endpoint: the weekly urticaria activity score (UAS7) fell by 20.0 versus 13.8 points (REMIX-1) and 19.4 versus 11.7 points (REMIX-2) at week 12 (P<0.001 for both), sustained through week 24. Well-controlled disease (UAS7 at most 6) was achieved by 49.8% versus 24.8% and 46.8% versus 19.6%, and complete response (UAS7 of 0) by 31.1% versus 10.5% and 27.9% versus 6.5%. Petechiae were more frequent on remibrutinib (3.8% vs 0.3% combined groups) — the one adverse-event imbalance the trials report. Omalizumab for the same disease is home on Shelf #398 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: REMIX-1 and REMIX-2 (2025): remibrutinib cut the weekly urticaria activity score by 20.0 versus 13.8 and 19.4 versus 11.7 points at week 12
cards.summary: REMIX-1 and REMIX-2 (2025): remibrutinib cut the weekly urticaria activity score by 20.0 vs 13.8 and 19.4 vs 11.7 points at week 12.
cards.type: Two identical, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 925 patients with symptomatic chronic spontaneous urticaria after treatment with second-generation H1-antihistamines: REMIX-1 randomly assigned 470 (remibrutinib 313, placebo 157) and REMIX-2 randomly assigned 455 (remibrutinib 300, placebo 155), to oral remibrutinib 25 mg twice daily or placebo in a 2:1 ratio. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The change in UAS7 (itch plus hives severity over 7 days; range 0–42, higher is worse) at week 12 was -20.0±0.7 (least-squares mean ±SE) on remibrutinib versus -13.8±1.0 on placebo in REMIX-1 and -19.4±0.7 versus -11.7±0.9 in REMIX-2 (P<0.001 for both), sustained through week 24. At week 12, a UAS7 of 6 or lower was achieved by 49.8% versus 24.8% (REMIX-1) and 46.8% versus 19.6% (REMIX-2), and a UAS7 of 0 by 31.1% versus 10.5% and 27.9% versus 6.5% (all P<0.001). Any-adverse-event and serious-adverse-event percentages were similar between groups, except petechiae in 3.8% on remibrutinib versus 0.3% on placebo in the combined groups.
cards.watchOut: Placebo UAS7 falls of 11.7–13.8 points show how much spontaneous fluctuation and background antihistamine effect this endpoint carries: the drug's attributable gain is the 6–8-point difference, not the full 20-point fall.
cards.source: Metz M et al. Remibrutinib in Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(10):984-994. PMID: 40043237. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05030311 (REMIX-1) and NCT05032157 (REMIX-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: twin identical trials, same result — an oral option after antihistamines — LIKELY
cards.summary: Twin identical trials, same result — an oral option after antihistamines — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: REMIX-1 and REMIX-2 (925 patients in total), identical double-blind placebo-controlled trials of remibrutinib in antihistamine-refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria.
cards.result: Both trials produced near-identical separations on the primary score (differences of about 6.2 and 7.7 UAS7 points) and doubled-to-quadrupled the rates of well-controlled and completely controlled disease, giving the replication behind LIKELY. No trial compared remibrutinib with omalizumab (Shelf #398, injectable anti-IgE for the same disease) — the choice between an oral BTK inhibitor and an injectable biologic is not an evidence-ranked question on current data, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise.
cards.watchOut: The petechiae signal (3.8% vs 0.3%) is small but drug-specific and belongs in any counselling summary drawn from this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Metz M et al. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(10):984-994. PMID: 40043237. Registry IDs as on the individual card.

shelves.title: Roflumilast foam for seborrhoeic dermatitis
shelves.question: Does roflumilast 0.3% foam, applied once daily, clear seborrhoeic dermatitis versus vehicle — the phase 3 STRATUM trial on its phase 2a predecessor?
shelves.mesh: Dermatitis, Seborrheic · Aminopyridines/adverse effects · Immunoglobulin A · Severity of Illness Index · Benzamides · Cyclopropanes · Dermatitis, Seborrheic/drug therapy,complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 3 trial plus its phase 2a predecessor, concordant but short. In STRATUM (phase 3), roflumilast foam 0.3% once daily achieved Investigator Global Assessment success at week 8 in 79.5% versus 58.0% on vehicle (P<.001); in the phase 2a trial (226 patients), success was 73.8% versus 40.9% (P<.001), with greater itch improvement. Vehicle success rates are high (41–58%) for a foam vehicle in a fluctuating condition, and both trials lasted only 8 weeks in a chronic relapsing disease — a single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under this library's rule, however clean the result.

cards.headline: STRATUM (2024): roflumilast foam achieved IGA success in 79.5% versus 58.0% on vehicle at week 8 in seborrhoeic dermatitis
cards.summary: STRATUM (2024): roflumilast foam achieved IGA success in 79.5% vs 58.0% on vehicle at week 8 in seborrhoeic dermatitis.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blinded, vehicle-controlled trial (8 weeks)
cards.people: Patients with seborrhoeic dermatitis randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to once-daily roflumilast foam 0.3% or vehicle foam for 8 weeks. The abstract does not state the total number randomised, mean age, or sex mix.
cards.result: Investigator Global Assessment success at week 8 (IGA of 0 [clear] or 1 [almost clear] plus at least a 2-point improvement from baseline) was achieved by 79.5% on roflumilast versus 58.0% on vehicle (P<.001), with significant differences already at week 2 (43.0% vs 25.7%; P<.001) and week 4 (73.1% vs 47.1%; P<.001). Roflumilast was well tolerated with a low rate of treatment-emergent adverse events. The authors state the study limitations include the 8-week treatment period for this chronic condition, and that longer trials are needed to determine durability and safety.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports percentages without the randomised total, and the vehicle success rate (58.0%) is the highest on this slate — the attributable gain is the 21.5-percentage-point difference, and 8 weeks says nothing about relapse after stopping.
cards.source: Blauvelt A et al. Roflumilast foam 0.3% for adolescent and adult patients with seborrheic dermatitis: A randomized, double-blinded, vehicle-controlled, phase 3 trial. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2024;90(5):986-993. PMID: 38253129. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Phase 2a trial (2023): roflumilast foam achieved IGA success in 73.8% versus 40.9% on vehicle at week 8, with greater itch reduction
cards.summary: Phase 2a trial (2023): roflumilast foam achieved IGA success in 73.8% vs 40.9% on vehicle at week 8, with greater itch reduction.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 2a randomised clinical trial (8 weeks)
cards.people: 226 adult patients (aged 18 years or older) with seborrhoeic dermatitis of at least 3 months' duration, Investigator Global Assessment score of 3 or greater, affecting 20% or less of body surface area including scalp, face, trunk and/or intertriginous areas, at 24 sites in the US and Canada, randomised to roflumilast foam 0.3% (154) or vehicle foam (72); mean age 44.9 (SD 16.8) years; 116 men, 110 women.
cards.result: At week 8, 104 (73.8%) roflumilast patients achieved IGA success versus 27 (40.9%) on vehicle (P<.001), with significantly higher success from week 2, the first assessment. Mean reductions in Worst Itch Numeric Rating Scale at week 8 were 59.3% (SD 52.5%) versus 36.6% (42.2%) (P<.001). Roflumilast was well tolerated, with adverse-event rates similar to vehicle foam.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2a trial of 226 patients run by the same programme as STRATUM: supportive replication of direction, not an independent second pivotal trial — hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for the shelf.
cards.source: Zirwas MJ et al. Efficacy of Roflumilast Foam, 0.3%, in Patients With Seborrheic Dermatitis: A Double-blind, Vehicle-Controlled Phase 2a Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Dermatol. 2023;159(6):613-620. PMID: 37133856. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04091646, from the record's databank fields.
