cards.headline: Synthesis: one pivotal trial plus its own pilot, both positive at 8 weeks — POSSIBLE until durability or a second pivotal trial exists
cards.summary: One pivotal trial plus its own pilot, both positive at 8 weeks — POSSIBLE until durability or a second pivotal trial exists.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: STRATUM (phase 3, randomised total not stated in its abstract) and the phase 2a trial (226 adults), both 8-week double-blind vehicle-controlled trials of once-daily roflumilast foam 0.3% in seborrhoeic dermatitis.
cards.result: Success-rate differences were 21.5 percentage points (phase 3) and 32.9 points (phase 2a) over vehicle, with early separation by week 2 in both — a consistent short-term efficacy picture for a non-steroidal foam usable on scalp and face. Roflumilast CREAM for plaque psoriasis is Shelf #824 and oral roflumilast for COPD is Shelf #819: same molecule, three different formulations and diseases, none re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is chronic and relapsing; neither carded trial exceeds 8 weeks, so maintenance and post-treatment relapse are unknown territory, not negative findings.

shelves.title: Geographic atrophy: complement inhibition with pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol
shelves.question: Do intravitreal complement inhibitors slow the growth of geographic atrophy lesions in age-related macular degeneration — and does slowing lesion growth preserve vision?
shelves.mesh: Geographic Atrophy/drug therapy,etiology,diagnosis · Macular Degeneration/complications,drug therapy · Choroidal Neovascularization · Peptides, Cyclic · Complement Inactivating Agents/therapeutic use · Geographic Atrophy/drug therapy · Intravitreal Injections
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — slowing of lesion growth · MAYBE (weak evidence) — preserving vision: Three phase 3 sham-controlled trials across two complement inhibitors (OAKS, DERBY, GATHER2) all slowed geographic-atrophy lesion growth, by 11–22% relative depending on trial, drug and time point, with DERBY's 12-month result not reaching significance before its 24-month result did. No trial showed a difference on any key secondary visual-function endpoint at 24 months, so lesion slowing is stamped LIKELY while any claim that this preserves vision is MAYBE (weak evidence) — the anatomical effect has not yet been shown to buy sight. Both drugs raised new-onset exudative (wet) AMD rates over sham.

cards.headline: Heier 2023 (OAKS and DERBY): pegcetacoplan slowed geographic-atrophy lesion growth by 11–22% relative, with no visual-function benefit at 24 months
cards.summary: OAKS and DERBY (2023): pegcetacoplan slowed geographic-atrophy lesion growth by 11–22% relative , with no visual-function benefit at 24 months.
cards.type: Two multicentre, randomised, double-masked, sham-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1,258 patients aged 60 years or older with geographic atrophy secondary to age-related macular degeneration enrolled across OAKS (637) and DERBY (621); modified intention-to-treat populations 614 and 597; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, lesion growth was slowed relative to sham by 21% with monthly pegcetacoplan (absolute difference in least-squares mean −0.41 mm², 95% CI −0.64 to −0.18; p=0.0004) and 16% every-other-month (−0.32 mm², −0.54 to −0.09; p=0.0055) in OAKS; in DERBY the 12-month slowing was 12% (−0.23 mm², −0.47 to 0.01; p=0.062) and 11% (−0.21 mm², −0.44 to 0.03; p=0.085), not significant. At 24 months the slowing was 22% and 18% in OAKS and 19% and 16% in DERBY, all significant. There were no differences in key secondary visual-function endpoints at 24 months. New-onset exudative AMD at 24 months: OAKS 11% (monthly), 8% (every other month) vs 2% (sham); DERBY 13%, 6% vs 4%. Serious ocular treatment-emergent adverse events were 2% or fewer in every group.
cards.watchOut: The percentages are relative slowing of an imaging endpoint, not vision saved: every visual-function secondary endpoint was null at 24 months, and DERBY missed significance at its 12-month primary time point. Roughly 1 in 10 monthly-treated eyes developed wet AMD.

cards.headline: Khanani 2023 (GATHER2): avacincaptad pegol slowed geographic-atrophy growth by 14% relative over 12 months
cards.summary: GATHER2 (2023): avacincaptad pegol slowed geographic-atrophy growth by 14% relative over 12 months.
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, sham-controlled phase 3 trial (12-month results)
cards.people: 448 patients aged 50 years or older with non-centrepoint-involving geographic atrophy and best-corrected visual acuity 20/25 to 20/320, randomised to monthly avacincaptad pegol 2 mg (225) or sham (223); 68–70% female; the abstract does not state mean age.

cards.headline: Synthesis: lesion growth slows, sight does not demonstrably follow — LIKELY for slowing, MAYBE (weak evidence) for vision
cards.summary: Lesion growth slows, sight does not demonstrably follow — Split: LIKELY (slowing) · MAYBE (weak evidence) (vision). A post-hoc OAKS microperimetry analysis is fenced in the synthesis.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OAKS and DERBY (1,258 patients, pegcetacoplan, 24 months) and GATHER2 (448 patients, avacincaptad pegol, 12 months).
cards.result: Three sham-controlled phase 3 trials agree that complement inhibition slows geographic-atrophy lesion growth by roughly a seventh to a fifth in relative terms, and none shows a visual-function gain on its prespecified endpoints. The shelf therefore stamps the anatomical claim LIKELY and any vision-preservation claim MAYBE (weak evidence). The price on the face of both drugs is a several-fold rise in new wet AMD (up to 13% vs 4% at 24 months on monthly pegcetacoplan). The currency sweep found a post-hoc microperimetry analysis of OAKS reporting delayed development of absolute scotomas on pegcetacoplan (hazard ratios 0.52–0.66 — relative figures inside or beside the 0.5–2.0 caution band): it is fenced here as a pointer, not carded, because a post-hoc analysis does not overturn the prespecified secondary-endpoint nulls or lift the MAYBE (weak evidence) vision stamp. This shelf is dry-AMD atrophy only: anti-VEGF treatment of neovascular AMD lives on Shelf #372 and is not re-carded here, and the systemic pegcetacoplan programme in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (drafted #845) is a different disease and formulation, fenced, not carded.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 14–22% slowing figures without 'relative' and without the null visual-function results beside them; patients are being offered injections to slow a scan measurement.

shelves.title: Faricimab for wet AMD and diabetic macular oedema: durability against aflibercept
shelves.question: Does faricimab dosed up to every 16 weeks match aflibercept every 8 weeks on vision — in neovascular AMD and in diabetic macular oedema?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Angiopoietin-2/antagonists & inhibitors · Antibodies, Bispecific/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Intravitreal Injections · Macular Degeneration/diagnosis,drug therapy · Receptors, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Four phase 3 double-masked non-inferiority trials (TENAYA, LUCERNE, YOSEMITE, RHINE; 3,220 patients randomised in total) each found faricimab — dosed every 8 weeks or by a personalised interval extending to every 16 weeks — non-inferior to aflibercept every 8 weeks on visual-acuity change, with treatment differences of −0.2 to +1.5 letters against a 4-letter margin and comparable ocular adverse-event rates. This is a durability claim, not a superiority claim: faricimab matched aflibercept while stretching intervals, it did not beat it on vision.

cards.headline: Heier 2022 (TENAYA and LUCERNE): faricimab up to every 16 weeks was non-inferior to aflibercept every 8 weeks in neovascular AMD
cards.summary: TENAYA and LUCERNE (2022): faricimab up to every 16 weeks was non-inferior to aflibercept every 8 weeks in neovascular AMD.
cards.type: Two randomised, double-masked, phase 3 non-inferiority trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1,329 treatment-naive patients aged 50 years or older with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (TENAYA 671; LUCERNE 658), randomised to faricimab 6.0 mg up to every 16 weeks or aflibercept 2.0 mg every 8 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean best-corrected visual-acuity change averaged over weeks 40–48: TENAYA +5.8 letters (95% CI 4.6 to 7.1) on faricimab vs +5.1 (3.9 to 6.4) on aflibercept, difference +0.7 letters (−1.1 to 2.5); LUCERNE +6.6 (5.3 to 7.8) vs +6.6 (5.3 to 7.8), difference 0.0 (−1.7 to 1.8) — non-inferior against the prespecified 4-letter margin in both trials. Ocular adverse events: TENAYA 36.3% vs 38.1%; LUCERNE 40.2% vs 36.2%.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on vision is the whole claim: the gain is fewer injections, and the abstract reports the proportion reaching 16-week intervals only indirectly via the personalised regimen design.
cards.source: Heier JS et al. Efficacy, durability, and safety of intravitreal faricimab up to every 16 weeks for neovascular age-related macular degeneration (TENAYA and LUCERNE): two randomised, double-masked, phase 3, non-inferiority trials. Lancet. 2022;399(10326):729-740. PMID: 35085502. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03823287 (LUCERNE) and NCT03823300 (TENAYA), from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: YOSEMITE and RHINE (2022): faricimab every 8 weeks or by personalised interval was non-inferior to aflibercept in diabetic macular oedema.
cards.type: Two randomised, double-masked, phase 3 non-inferiority trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1,891 adults with vision loss due to centre-involving diabetic macular oedema (YOSEMITE 940; RHINE 951), randomised to faricimab every 8 weeks, faricimab by personalised treatment interval (every 4 to 16 weeks), or aflibercept every 8 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.

shelves.title: Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery vs standard phacoemulsification
shelves.question: Does femtosecond laser assistance improve vision, safety, or value over standard ultrasound phacoemulsification for cataract surgery?
shelves.mesh: Cataract · Cataract Extraction · Laser Therapy · Lasers · Phacoemulsification · United Kingdom · Cataract Extraction/adverse effects,economics,methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null: Two large randomised trials on two continents — the UK FACT non-inferiority trial (785 participants, 1 year) and the French FEMCAT superiority and cost-effectiveness trial (907 patients, 1,476 eyes) — agree that femtosecond laser assistance adds no meaningful visual, refractive or safety benefit over standard phacoemulsification, at higher cost (FEMCAT's composite success rate actually ran slightly lower with laser, 41.1% vs 43.6%). Two concordant large trials carry the null at LIKELY.

cards.headline: Day 2020 (FACT): phacoemulsification was not inferior to femtosecond laser surgery at 1 year, and laser was not cost-effective
cards.summary: FACT (2020): phacoemulsification was not inferior to femtosecond laser surgery at 1 year, and laser was not cost-effective .
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, non-inferiority trial with masked postoperative assessment
cards.people: 785 participants undergoing cataract surgery at three UK hospitals, randomised to femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (392) or phacoemulsification cataract surgery (393); 79% and 74% attended 1-year follow-up; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean uncorrected distance visual acuity at 1 year was 0.14 (SD 0.22) logMAR with laser vs 0.17 (0.25) with phacoemulsification (difference −0.03, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.01; P=.17); corrected acuity difference was likewise −0.03 logMAR (P=.11). Exactly 75% of both groups landed within ±0.5 dioptres of refractive target. The one significant secondary difference (binocular corrected acuity, −0.02 logMAR) was not clinically important. Mean cost was £167.62 per patient greater for laser, and the authors conclude laser was not cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: UK public-sector costing and one laser era: the trial rules out a meaningful average advantage, not a benefit in every complex-eye subgroup, which it was not powered to isolate.
cards.source: Day AC et al. Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery compared with phacoemulsification cataract surgery: randomized noninferiority trial with 1-year outcomes. J Cataract Refract Surg. 2020;46(10):1360-1367. PMID: 32773608. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — no databank registry entry is carried on the fetched record.

cards.headline: Schweitzer 2020 (FEMCAT): femtosecond laser was not superior to phacoemulsification and cost more
cards.summary: FEMCAT (2020): femtosecond laser was not superior to phacoemulsification (composite success 41.1% vs 43.6% ) and cost more.
cards.type: Multicentre, participant-masked, randomised superiority and cost-effectiveness trial
cards.people: 907 patients aged 22 years or older eligible for unilateral or bilateral cataract surgery at five French university hospitals (1,476 eyes); 870 patients analysed (704 laser eyes, 685 phacoemulsification eyes); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The composite surgical success rate at 3 months (no severe perioperative complication, acuity 0.0 logMAR or better, refractive error ≤0.75 dioptres, stable corneal astigmatism) was 41.1% (289 eyes) with laser vs 43.6% (299 eyes) with phacoemulsification — adjusted odds ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.12; p=0.250), a relative figure whose interval crosses 1. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was €10,703 saved per additional patient with treatment success for phacoemulsification compared with laser. No severe adverse events occurred during the laser procedure itself.
cards.watchOut: The composite bundles refractive precision with safety, so a null composite could hide small offsetting parts; the individual acuity and refractive results in FACT, carded above, show no such hidden advantage.

shelves.title: Corneal collagen cross-linking for progressive keratoconus
shelves.question: Does riboflavin–ultraviolet corneal collagen cross-linking halt progression of keratoconus versus sham or control?
shelves.mesh: Cell Count · Collagen/metabolism · Corneal Pachymetry · Corneal Stroma/metabolism · Corneal Topography · Cross-Linking Reagents · Disease Progression
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials on different continents agree on direction and mechanism: in the US multicentre sham-controlled trial (205 patients) maximum keratometry fell 1.6 dioptres by 1 year on cross-linking while control eyes progressed; in the Australian trial (100 eyes) treated eyes flattened progressively to −1.03 dioptres at 3 years while control eyes steepened +1.75 dioptres. The endpoint is corneal shape with supporting acuity gains, in a disease with no competing therapy — LIKELY for halting progression.

cards.headline: Hersh 2017: cross-linking flattened maximum keratometry by 1.6 dioptres at 1 year while sham-treated keratoconus progressed
cards.summary: Cross-linking trial (2017): flattened maximum keratometry by 1.6 dioptres at 1 year while sham-treated keratoconus progressed.
cards.people: 205 patients with progressive keratoconus in a US multicentre trial, randomised to standard cross-linking (riboflavin with epithelial removal and ultraviolet A) or sham control (riboflavin alone without epithelial removal); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Maximum keratometry decreased by 1.6 diopters (D) from baseline to 1 year in the cross-linking group, whereas keratoconus continued to progress in the control group. A fall of 2.0 D or more occurred in 28 treated eyes (31.5%) vs an increase of 2.0 D or more in 5 (5.6%). Corrected distance visual acuity improved by an average of 5.7 logMAR units (27.7% of eyes gained and 6.0% lost 10 or more units); uncorrected acuity improved 4.4 units. Corneal haze was the most frequent adverse finding; endothelial cell count did not change significantly at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: The control was riboflavin without epithelial removal rather than a full sham procedure, and the abstract reports the treated arm's change in full while describing control progression without a single headline figure — the Australian trial carded below supplies the controlled numbers.
cards.source: Hersh PS et al. United States Multicenter Clinical Trial of Corneal Collagen Crosslinking for Keratoconus Treatment. Ophthalmology. 2017;124(9):1259-1270. PMID: 28495149. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — no databank registry entry is carried on the fetched record.

shelves.title: Macular oedema after retinal vein occlusion: ranibizumab for branch and central occlusion
shelves.question: Does monthly intravitreal ranibizumab improve vision versus sham in macular oedema after branch retinal vein occlusion and after central retinal vein occlusion?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Endpoint Determination · Injections · Laser Coagulation · Macular Edema/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The twin phase 3 sham-controlled trials agree closely: in branch occlusion (BRAVO, 397 patients) ranibizumab gained 16.6–18.3 letters at 6 months vs 7.3 on sham; in central occlusion (CRUISE, 392 patients) it gained 12.7–14.9 letters vs 0.8 on sham, with ≥15-letter gains roughly doubling-to-tripling the sham rates in absolute terms (55–61% vs 29%, and 46–48% vs 17%). Large, blinded, concordant — LIKELY.

cards.headline: Campochiaro 2010 (BRAVO): ranibizumab gained 16.6–18.3 letters vs 7.3 on sham at 6 months in branch retinal vein occlusion
cards.summary: BRAVO (2010): ranibizumab gained 16.6–18.3 letters vs 7.3 on sham at 6 months in branch retinal vein occlusion.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, sham-controlled, double-masked, multicentre phase 3 trial
cards.people: 397 patients with macular edema following branch retinal vein occlusion, randomised 1:1:1 to monthly ranibizumab 0.3 mg, ranibizumab 0.5 mg, or sham injections for 6 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean best-corrected visual-acuity change at month 6 was 16.6 letters (95% CI 14.7 to 18.5) on 0.3 mg and 18.3 (16.0 to 20.6) on 0.5 mg vs 7.3 (5.1 to 9.5) on sham (P<0.0001 for each vs sham). Gains of ≥15 letters: 55.2% and 61.1% vs 28.8%. Central foveal thickness fell by 337 and 345 micrometres vs 158 on sham. Rescue grid laser was needed by 54.5% of sham patients vs 18.7% and 19.8% on ranibizumab. No new safety events were identified.
cards.watchOut: Six-month primary endpoint with monthly injections; sham patients improved substantially too (7.3 letters, with over half receiving rescue laser), so the drug's increment over good standard care is the 9–11 letters, not the full gain.

shelves.title: Adalimumab for non-infectious uveitis: active disease and flare prevention (VISUAL I and II)
shelves.question: Does adalimumab delay treatment failure in active non-infectious uveitis, and prevent flare in inactive steroid-controlled disease during steroid taper?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Treatment Failure · Uveitis/drug therapy · Vision Disorders/prevention & control · Acute Disease · Adalimumab/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 double-masked placebo-controlled trials cover the two clinical moments: VISUAL I (active disease despite prednisone) halved the treatment-failure hazard (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.70 — sitting exactly on the library's 0.5 boundary for a solid benefit ratio, and printed as such), and VISUAL II (inactive disease tapering steroids) cut flare risk with hazard ratio 0.57 (0.39 to 0.84) and absolute failure rates of 39% vs 55%. Two blinded trials, concordant — LIKELY, with the caution that VISUAL II's ratio on its own sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band and is carried by its absolute rates and by VISUAL I beside it. Adalimumab brought more adverse and serious adverse events than placebo in VISUAL I.

cards.headline: Jaffe 2016 (VISUAL I): adalimumab halved the treatment-failure hazard in active non-infectious uveitis (hazard ratio 0.50)
cards.summary: VISUAL I (2016): adalimumab halved the treatment-failure hazard in active non-infectious uveitis (hazard ratio 0.50 ).
cards.type: Multinational, double-masked, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 217 adults in the intention-to-treat population with active non-infectious intermediate, posterior or panuveitis despite prednisone for 2 or more weeks, randomised to adalimumab (80 mg loading, then 40 mg every 2 weeks) or placebo, all with a mandatory prednisone burst and 15-week taper; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to treatment failure was 24 weeks on adalimumab vs 13 weeks on placebo; the hazard ratio for treatment failure was 0.50 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.70; P<0.001) — a relative figure sitting exactly at the 0.5 boundary this library treats as the floor for a solid benefit ratio. Three ranked secondary endpoints (anterior chamber cell grade, vitreous haze grade, visual acuity) were significantly better on adalimumab. Adverse events (1052.4 vs 971.7 per 100 person-years) and serious adverse events (28.8 vs 13.6 per 100 person-years) were more frequent on adalimumab.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a composite built from inflammatory signs and acuity, not blindness avoided; the near-doubling of serious adverse events per 100 person-years is part of the bargain and belongs beside the efficacy figure.

cards.headline: Nguyen 2016 (VISUAL II): adalimumab cut flare on steroid taper — failure 39% vs 55%, hazard ratio 0.57
cards.summary: VISUAL II (2016): adalimumab cut flare on steroid taper — failure 39% vs 55% , hazard ratio 0.57.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-masked, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 229 patients aged 18 years or older with inactive non-infectious intermediate, posterior or panuveitis controlled by 10–35 mg/day prednisone (226 in the intention-to-treat population), randomised to adalimumab (115) or placebo (114) with a mandatory prednisone taper from week 2; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 45 of 115 patients (39%) on adalimumab vs 61 of 111 (55%) on placebo — an absolute difference of about 16 percentage points. Median time to treatment failure was not reached (>18 months) on adalimumab vs 8.3 months on placebo; hazard ratio 0.57 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.84; p=0.004), a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band that this library does not treat as solid on its own — the absolute rates above are the firmer ground. No opportunistic infections or (in the placebo group) malignancies occurred; one non-serious squamous cell carcinoma was reported on adalimumab. Common adverse events included arthralgia (23% vs 11%) and headache (15% each).
cards.watchOut: A flare-prevention trial in already-controlled disease: it shows adalimumab can replace steroids for maintenance, not that it induces remission — that is VISUAL I's separate question, carded above.

shelves.title: Microstents with cataract surgery for open-angle glaucoma: Hydrus and iStent inject
shelves.question: Does adding a Schlemm-canal or trabecular microstent to cataract surgery lower intraocular pressure and drop burden versus cataract surgery alone?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Aqueous Humor/physiology · Cataract/etiology,physiopathology · Glaucoma, Open-Angle/physiopathology,surgery · Gonioscopy · Intraocular Pressure/physiology · Lens Implantation, Intraocular
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, single-masked device trials with washed-out pressure endpoints agree: HORIZON (Hydrus, 556 eyes) found ≥20% unmedicated pressure reduction at 24 months in 77.3% vs 57.8% (difference 19.5 percentage points) and the iStent inject pivotal trial (505 eyes) found 75.8% vs 61.9%, with mean extra pressure lowering of about 2.3 and 1.6 mmHg over cataract surgery alone and roughly 0.4 fewer medications. Device trials cannot be double-masked, and are labelled as such; the washed-out objective endpoint and two-trial concordance carry LIKELY for a modest incremental effect.

cards.headline: Samuelson 2019 (HORIZON): Hydrus microstent plus cataract surgery beat cataract surgery alone on washed-out pressure at 24 months
cards.summary: HORIZON (2019): Hydrus microstent plus cataract surgery beat cataract surgery alone — a ≥20% pressure fall in 77.3% vs 57.8% of eyes at 24 months.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, single-masked, randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 556 eyes (369 Hydrus, 187 no stent, randomised 2:1 after phacoemulsification) in subjects with primary open-angle glaucoma, visually significant cataract, and washed-out diurnal intraocular pressure 22–34 mmHg; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 24 months, unmedicated diurnal pressure had fallen by ≥20% in 77.3% of Hydrus eyes vs 57.8% of control eyes (difference 19.5%, 95% CI 11.2% to 27.8%; P<0.001). Mean unmedicated pressure reduction was −7.6 (SD 4.1) mmHg vs −5.3 (3.9) mmHg (difference −2.3 mmHg, −3.0 to −1.6; P<0.001). Mean medications fell from 1.7 at baseline to 0.3 vs 0.7 (difference −0.4; P<0.001). No serious ocular adverse events were related to the microstent, and safety parameters did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Single-masked device trial (the surgeon knows), and cataract surgery alone does much of the work — the stent's own increment is the 2.3 mmHg and 0.4 medications, in mild-to-moderate disease only.

cards.headline: Samuelson 2019 (iStent inject pivotal): trabecular micro-bypass plus cataract surgery beat cataract surgery alone at 24 months
cards.summary: iStent inject pivotal (2019): a ≥20% unmedicated pressure reduction in 75.8% vs 61.9% at 24 months.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, single-masked, concurrently controlled, multicentre pivotal trial
cards.people: 505 eyes with mild-to-moderate primary open-angle glaucoma and cataract (387 iStent inject, 118 control, randomised 3:1 intraoperatively after cataract surgery), with medicated pressure ≤24 mmHg on 1–3 medications and unmedicated diurnal pressure 21–36 mmHg; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 24 months, ≥20% reduction in unmedicated diurnal pressure occurred in 75.8% of treated eyes vs 61.9% of controls (P=0.005); mean reduction was 7.0 (SD 4.0) mmHg vs 5.4 (3.7) mmHg (P<0.001) — an increment of about 1.6 mmHg. Medication-free pressure ≤18 mmHg at 24 months: 63.2% vs 50.0% (difference 13.2%, 95% CI 2.9 to 23.4). Among responders, 84% of treated eyes vs 67% of controls were medication-free at 23 months. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest stent increment over cataract surgery alone — LIKELY
cards.summary: A real but modest stent increment over cataract surgery alone — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HORIZON (556 eyes, Hydrus) and the iStent inject pivotal trial (505 eyes).
cards.result: Both stents, tested independently against the same control (cataract surgery alone, with medication washout), add roughly 1.6–2.3 mmHg of pressure lowering and free about two-thirds to three-quarters of eyes from drops at 2 years in responder terms. LIKELY for that modest claim. The currency sweep found a newer Swedish randomised trial comparing cataract surgery alone with cataract surgery combined with iStent inject W or a Kahook goniotomy device, plus an iStent-vs-goniotomy trial and a Hydrus cost-effectiveness analysis; all are fenced here as pointers, not carded — none displaces the two pivotal anchors for the stent-vs-no-stent question. Laser-first vs drops (drafted #609) and tube shunt vs trabeculectomy for advanced disease (drafted #617) are different rungs of the glaucoma ladder, fenced likewise.

shelves.title: Brolucizumab for wet AMD: drying power against a retinal vasculitis signal (HAWK and HARRIER)
shelves.question: Does brolucizumab match aflibercept on vision with better retinal drying — and how large is the intraocular-inflammation and retinal-vasculitis harm signal that emerged after approval?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Choroidal Neovascularization/drug therapy,physiopathology · Intravitreal Injections · Receptors, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — major harm signal): Split: LIKELY — vision non-inferiority and retinal drying · the harm signal is carried on the shelf's face, unstamped, for the developer's ruling. HAWK and HARRIER (1,817 patients) showed brolucizumab non-inferior to aflibercept on vision at week 48 with greater fluid resolution and over half of 6 mg eyes held on 12-week dosing. After approval, a case series (Baumal 2020) documented retinal vasculitis with occlusive events and severe vision loss after brolucizumab injection — a harm pattern the phase 3 papers' 'generally similar' adverse-event rates did not surface. The efficacy half is LIKELY-grade; the shelf is Tier C because the harm claim needs the developer's personal verdict, and no frequency for the vasculitis risk is asserted here — the carded series cannot supply one.

cards.headline: Dugel 2020 (HAWK and HARRIER): brolucizumab was non-inferior to aflibercept on vision, with better retinal drying and 12-week dosing in over half of eyes
cards.summary: HAWK and HARRIER (2020): brolucizumab was non-inferior to aflibercept on vision, with better retinal drying and 12-week dosing in over half of patients.
cards.type: Two phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-masked, active-controlled trials reported in one paper
cards.people: 1,817 patients with untreated active choroidal neovascularisation due to age-related macular degeneration, randomised to brolucizumab 3 mg (HAWK only) or 6 mg, or aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks after loading; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 48, best-corrected visual-acuity change was +6.6 letters (brolucizumab 6 mg) and +6.1 (3 mg) vs +6.8 (aflibercept) in HAWK, and +6.9 vs +7.6 in HARRIER — non-inferior (P<0.001 for each comparison) against the 4-letter margin. Over 50% of brolucizumab 6 mg eyes stayed on 12-week dosing through week 48 (56% HAWK, 51% HARRIER). Disease activity at week 16 was lower on brolucizumab 6 mg (24.0% vs 34.5% HAWK; 22.7% vs 32.2% HARRIER), and central subfield thickness fell further (−172.8 vs −143.7 micrometres HAWK; −193.8 vs −143.9 HARRIER). The paper reports overall adverse-event rates as generally similar between drugs.
cards.watchOut: 'Generally similar' overall adverse events is exactly the level at which a rare, specific, sight-threatening event hides: the vasculitis signal on the next card emerged only in post-marketing use and is not quantified anywhere in this abstract.

cards.headline: Baumal 2020: retinal vasculitis and intraocular inflammation after brolucizumab — 15 eyes, mean acuity fell from 20/53 to 20/191 at diagnosis
cards.summary: Case series (2020): retinal vasculitis and intraocular inflammation after brolucizumab — 15 eyes; mean acuity fell from 20/53 to 20/191 at diagnosis.
cards.people: 15 eyes from 12 patients identified at 10 US centres with retinal vasculitis and intraocular inflammation after intravitreal brolucizumab 6 mg for neovascular AMD; affected eyes had received 2–80 previous anti-VEGF injections before switching to brolucizumab.
cards.result: Vasculitis and inflammation were diagnosed a mean of 30 days after injection. Mean visual acuity fell from 0.426 logMAR (Snellen 20/53) before brolucizumab to 0.981 logMAR (20/191; range 20/25–20/1600) at diagnosis (P=0.008), and after a mean 25 days of follow-up remained reduced at 0.833 logMAR (20/136; P=0.033 vs baseline). Findings included segmental arterial sheathing and discontinuity, vascular nonperfusion, cotton-wool spots and perivenular haemorrhages; treatment was corticosteroids by various routes, and 2 eyes had vitrectomy without visual improvement.
cards.watchOut: A case series has no denominator: it establishes that the event happens and can be devastating, not how often. Any frequency claim for brolucizumab vasculitis would need registry or safety-review data beyond this card — which is why this shelf is Tier C and the harm is presented for the developer's personal verdict rather than stamped.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HAWK/HARRIER (1,817 patients, randomised) and Baumal 2020 (15 eyes, case series).
cards.result: The randomised half of this shelf is strong: non-inferior vision, better drying, longer intervals — and the currency sweep's TALON treat-and-extend results and two-year MERLIN results, fenced here as pointers, point the same way on efficacy without speaking to the vasculitis frequency. The harm half is a signal, not a rate: occlusive retinal vasculitis with severe vision loss occurred after brolucizumab in eyes that had tolerated other anti-VEGF agents, at a mean of 30 days post-injection. Weighing a LIKELY-grade convenience-and-drying advantage against an unquantified risk of catastrophic vision loss in the treated eye is a Tier C judgement, left PROPOSED for the developer. Ranibizumab vs bevacizumab for wet AMD lives on Shelf #372 and faricimab on Shelf #891 of this slate; neither is re-carded here.

shelves.title: Preventing endophthalmitis after cataract surgery: intracameral cefuroxime (ESCRS)
shelves.question: Does intracameral cefuroxime at the end of cataract surgery prevent acute postoperative endophthalmitis?
shelves.mesh: Anterior Chamber/drug effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Cefuroxime/therapeutic use · Endophthalmitis/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Eye Infections, Bacterial/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Incidence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One very large randomised factorial trial (ESCRS, 16,603 patients, 29 endophthalmitis cases) found that omitting intracameral cefuroxime carried a 4.92-fold relative increase in total postoperative endophthalmitis (95% CI 1.87 to 12.9) — equivalently, cefuroxime's relative risk is about 0.20, outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band — and the Cochrane synthesis of the prophylaxis trials reports the same comparison at risk ratio 0.21 (0.06 to 0.74). A single pivotal trial, however large, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the library's single-trial rule; the outcome is rare, so absolute rates (29 cases in 16,603 operations across all groups) must travel with the relative figure.

cards.headline: ESCRS Study Group 2007: omitting intracameral cefuroxime multiplied endophthalmitis risk 4.92-fold in 16,603 cataract operations
cards.summary: ESCRS study (2007): omitting intracameral cefuroxime multiplied endophthalmitis risk 4.92-fold in 16,603 cataract operations.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, partially masked, multicentre 2×2 factorial trial
cards.people: 16,603 patients undergoing cataract surgery at 24 ophthalmology units in nine European countries and Turkey, randomised by intracameral cefuroxime (1 mg in 0.1 mL at the end of surgery) and topical perioperative levofloxacin factors into four groups; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Twenty-nine patients developed endophthalmitis, 20 of them proven infective — an overall rate of about 0.17% across all groups. Absence of intracameral cefuroxime was associated with a 4.92-fold relative increase in risk of total postoperative endophthalmitis (95% CI 1.87 to 12.9). Other risk factors: clear corneal incisions vs scleral tunnels (5.88-fold, 1.34 to 25.9), silicone vs acrylic lens material (3.13-fold, 1.47 to 6.67), and surgical complications (4.95-fold, 1.68 to 14.6). For proven infective cases, absence of cefuroxime and silicone lens material remained significant, and men were more predisposed (odds ratio 2.70, 1.07 to 6.8). All ratios are relative measures against a rare outcome.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine events drive every ratio in this trial — the relative effect is large but the confidence intervals are wide, and surgical era (incision and lens practices of the mid-2000s) shapes the baseline risk to which the ratio applies.
cards.source: Endophthalmitis Study Group, European Society of Cataract & Refractive Surgeons (Barry P et al.). Prophylaxis of postoperative endophthalmitis following cataract surgery: results of the ESCRS multicenter study and identification of risk factors. J Cataract Refract Surg. 2007;33(6):978-988. PMID: 17531690. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial record.

cards.headline: Gower 2013 (Cochrane): injection prophylaxis beat topical-only prophylaxis across the trials — intracameral cefuroxime risk ratio 0.21
cards.summary: Cochrane review (2013): injection prophylaxis beat topical-only prophylaxis across the trials — intracameral cefuroxime risk ratio 0.21 .
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: Four randomised trials totalling 100,876 adults undergoing cataract surgery, with 131 endophthalmitis cases; searches to October 2012; the abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Heterogeneity of designs and delivery modes prevented a formal meta-analysis. The two adequately sized trials both favoured antibiotic injection during surgery over topical antibiotics alone: risk ratio 0.33 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.92) for periocular penicillin vs topical chloramphenicol-sulphadimidine, and 0.21 (0.06 to 0.74) for intracameral cefuroxime vs topical levofloxacin — relative figures against a rare outcome. Subconjunctival vs retrobulbar injection did not differ significantly (0.85, 0.55 to 1.32), and the irrigation-solution trial was underpowered. The reviewers note the ESCRS study used contemporary technique and that further trials of currently available prophylaxis are unlikely because of the sample sizes a rare outcome demands.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis of four heterogeneous trials, not a pooled estimate: the 0.21 figure is the ESCRS comparison reappearing inside the review, not independent confirmation — the shelf's two cards substantially share one trial's evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one very large trial, one concordant review, a rare outcome — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: One very large trial, one concordant review, a rare outcome — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ESCRS (16,603 patients) and the Cochrane prophylaxis review (4 trials, 100,876 adults).
cards.result: The relative protection from intracameral cefuroxime is large (relative risk about 0.20) and the Cochrane review's other adequately sized trial points the same way for injection prophylaxis generally; but the independent randomised evidence for cefuroxime itself is one trial with 29 events, so the single-trial ceiling sets POSSIBLE. shelves.title: Myopic choroidal neovascularisation: ranibizumab and aflibercept against photodynamic therapy and sham
shelves.question: Does anti-VEGF therapy improve vision in choroidal neovascularisation from pathologic myopia — ranibizumab against verteporfin photodynamic therapy, aflibercept against sham?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Choroidal Neovascularization/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology · Fluorescein Angiography · Intravitreal Injections · Myopia, Degenerative/complications,diagnosis · Photochemotherapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 double-masked trials with different drugs and different controls agree: RADIANCE (277 patients) found ranibizumab superior to verteporfin photodynamic therapy (+10.5/+10.6 vs +2.2 letters over months 1–3), and MYRROR (122 patients) found aflibercept gained 12.1 letters at week 24 while sham lost 2. Concordant, blinded, with few injections needed (median 2–4 over a year in RADIANCE) — LIKELY.

cards.headline: Wolf 2014 (RADIANCE): ranibizumab beat photodynamic therapy by about 8 letters in myopic choroidal neovascularisation
cards.summary: RADIANCE (2014): ranibizumab beat photodynamic therapy by about 8 letters in myopic choroidal neovascularisation.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-masked, multicentre, active-controlled trial
cards.people: 277 patients with visual impairment due to myopic choroidal neovascularisation, randomised to ranibizumab guided by visual-acuity stabilisation (106), ranibizumab guided by disease activity (116), or verteporfin photodynamic therapy (55, with ranibizumab or repeat photodynamic therapy allowed from month 3); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean average visual-acuity change from baseline to month 1 through month 3 (primary endpoint) was +10.5 letters (acuity-guided) and +10.6 (activity-guided) vs +2.2 on photodynamic therapy (both P<0.0001). At month 12, gains were +13.8, +14.4 and +9.3 letters — the photodynamic group's later gains came after crossover treatments were allowed. Median ranibizumab injections over 12 months were 4.0 (acuity-guided) and 2.0 (activity-guided). No deaths, endophthalmitis or myocardial infarction occurred.
cards.watchOut: The control arm could receive ranibizumab from month 3, so the 12-month comparison (+13.8/+14.4 vs +9.3) understates the drug-vs-photodynamic contrast; the clean comparison is the month 1–3 primary endpoint.
cards.source: Wolf S et al. RADIANCE: a randomized controlled study of ranibizumab in patients with choroidal neovascularization secondary to pathologic myopia. Ophthalmology. 2014;121(3):682-692.e2. PMID: 24326106. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01217944, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Ikuno 2015 (MYRROR): aflibercept gained 12.1 letters at week 24 while sham lost 2 letters in myopic choroidal neovascularisation
cards.summary: MYRROR (2015): aflibercept gained 12.1 letters at week 24 while sham lost 2 letters.
cards.type: International, phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-masked, sham-controlled trial
cards.people: 122 patients aged 18 years or older with high myopia (≤−6.0 diopters or axial length ≥26.5 mm), active myopic choroidal neovascularisation and acuity 73–35 ETDRS letters, randomised 3:1 to intravitreal aflibercept 2 mg (91) or sham (31), with sham patients crossing to mandatory aflibercept at week 24; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24 (primary endpoint), aflibercept patients gained 12.1 letters while sham patients lost 2 letters (P<0.0001) — a separation of about 14 letters. By week 48, after crossover, gains were 13.5 letters (aflibercept from baseline) and 3.9 (sham/aflibercept). Most aflibercept effect came from a median of 2 injections in the first 8 weeks, with a median of 0 injections in each later quarter. Ocular adverse events through week 48 were similar (37.4% vs 38.7%), mostly mild; no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Small sham arm (31 patients) by design, and the week-48 sham-group figure is post-crossover — the interpretable contrast is week 24. High-myopia populations in this trial were largely East Asian, a generalisability note for other settings.
cards.source: Ikuno Y et al. Intravitreal Aflibercept Injection in Patients with Myopic Choroidal Neovascularization: The MYRROR Study. Ophthalmology. 2015;122(6):1220-1227. PMID: 25745875. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the fetched record carries no databank registry entry.

shelves.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: the Epley manoeuvre against sham
shelves.question: Does the Epley canalith-repositioning manoeuvre resolve posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo versus a sham manoeuvre?
shelves.mesh: Head Movements · Otolithic Membrane/pathology · Posture · Semicircular Canals/pathology · Vertigo/therapy · Vestibular Diseases/complications,therapy · Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo/rehabilitation
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A double-blind sham-controlled trial (von Brevern 2006) found resolution at 24 hours in 80% on Epley vs 10% on sham, and the Cochrane synthesis of 11 trials (745 patients) found complete vertigo resolution rising from 21% to 56% against sham or control (odds ratio 4.42, 95% CI 2.62 to 7.44 — a relative figure well outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates) and Dix-Hallpike conversion at odds ratio 9.62. A drug-free, single-session manoeuvre with effects this size, replicated across trials — LIKELY. Recurrence is common (36% in the review).

cards.headline: von Brevern 2006: one Epley manoeuvre resolved posterior-canal BPPV at 24 hours in 80% vs 10% on sham
cards.summary: Epley vs sham (2006): one manoeuvre resolved posterior-canal BPPV at 24 hours in 80% vs 10% .
cards.people: 66 patients with posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, randomised to the Epley manoeuvre (35) or a sham procedure (31); outcome assessed 24 hours after treatment; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 24 hours, 28 of 35 patients (80%) in the Epley group had neither vertigo nor nystagmus on positional testing, compared with 3 of 31 (10%) in the sham group (p<0.001) — an absolute difference of about 70 percentage points.
cards.watchOut: A 24-hour endpoint in a condition that also remits spontaneously over weeks: this card proves rapid resolution, not durable cure — the Cochrane card below carries the recurrence figure (36%).

cards.headline: Hilton 2014 (Cochrane): across 11 trials the Epley manoeuvre raised complete vertigo resolution from 21% to 56% vs sham or control
cards.summary: Cochrane review (2014): across 11 trials the Epley manoeuvre raised complete vertigo resolution from 21% to 56% vs sham or control.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 11 randomised trials totalling 745 adults (aged 18–90; sex ratio 1:1.5 male to female) with posterior-canal BPPV, comparing Epley against sham, other repositioning manoeuvres, or control; searches to January 2014; no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: Complete resolution of vertigo occurred significantly more often with Epley than with sham or control (odds ratio 4.42, 95% CI 2.62 to 7.44; five studies, 273 participants — a relative figure, with the review's absolute proportions rising from 21% to 56%). Conversion of the Dix-Hallpike test from positive to negative also favoured Epley (odds ratio 9.62, 6.0 to 15.42; eight studies, 507 participants). Epley did not differ from the Semont or Gans manoeuvres, and beat a week of Brandt-Daroff exercises in one study (odds ratio 12.38, 4.32 to 35.47). No serious adverse effects were reported; nausea during the manoeuvre occurred in 16.7–32%. The review notes a 36% recurrence rate after treatment.
cards.watchOut: Mostly small trials with short follow-up and some unclear bias — the pooled odds ratios flatter a manoeuvre whose absolute resolution advantage (about 35 percentage points) is the honest headline; recurrence after success is part of the condition.
cards.source: Hilton MP, Pinder DK. The Epley (canalith repositioning) manoeuvre for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014;(12):CD003162. PMID: 25485940. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rapid, large, replicated resolution — LIKELY, with recurrence on the face
cards.summary: Rapid, large, replicated resolution — LIKELY, with recurrence on the face.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: von Brevern 2006 (66 patients, sham-controlled) and Hilton 2014 (11 trials, 745 patients).
cards.result: The sham-controlled trial and the pooled trials agree on a large short-term effect (80% vs 10% at 24 hours; 56% vs 21% pooled resolution), which earns LIKELY for resolving an episode of posterior-canal BPPV. Ménière's disease (drafted #633) and vestibular rehabilitation for chronic dizziness (drafted #636) are different vestibular questions, fenced, not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Resolution is not permanence: about a third recur, and the shelf's claim is about treating an episode, not preventing the next one.

shelves.title: Balloon dilation of the eustachian tube for dilatory dysfunction
shelves.question: Does balloon eustachian tuboplasty improve symptoms and tympanometry in persistent eustachian tube dilatory dysfunction versus medical management alone?
shelves.mesh: Dilatation/methods · Ear Diseases/therapy · Eustachian Tube/physiopathology · Hearing Tests · United States · Dilatation/adverse effects,methods · Eustachian Tube
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials favour balloon dilation over continued medical management — Poe 2018 (211 patients) on tympanogram normalisation at 6 weeks (51.8% vs 13.9%) and symptom-score normalisation (56.2% vs 8.5%), Meyer 2018 (60 patients) on symptom-score change (−2.9 vs −0.6) maintained to 12 months. But the procedure cannot be masked, the comparators are 'more of the medical therapy that had already failed', Meyer's controls could cross over at 6 weeks, and both trials are device-programme studies — enough for POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Poe 2018: balloon dilation normalised tympanograms at 6 weeks in 51.8% vs 13.9% on medical management alone
cards.summary: Balloon dilation trial (2018): normalised tympanograms at 6 weeks in 51.8% vs 13.9% on medical management alone.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (unmasked procedure)
cards.people: Patients aged 22 years or older with eustachian tube dilatory dysfunction refractory to medical therapy, randomised 2:1 to balloon dilation plus medical management (139 in the primary analysis) or medical management alone (72); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Tympanogram normalisation at 6 weeks was 51.8% (72/139) with balloon dilation vs 13.9% (10/72) in controls (P<.0001) — an absolute difference of about 38 percentage points; the dilation group's rate rose to 62.2% at 24 weeks. Eustachian Tube Dysfunction Questionnaire-7 score normalisation at 6 weeks was 56.2% (77/137) vs 8.5% (6/71) (P<.001). Mucosal inflammation and Valsalva manoeuvre also improved more with dilation. No device- or procedure-related serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked procedure against continued medical therapy in patients already refractory to it — expectation and regression effects cannot be separated from the device effect, and there is no sham arm in either anchor trial; a sham-controlled result is precisely what could move this shelf's stamp.
cards.source: Poe D et al. Balloon dilation of the eustachian tube for dilatory dysfunction: A randomized controlled trial. Laryngoscope. 2018;128(5):1200-1206. PMID: 28940574. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the fetched record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Meyer 2018: balloon dilation improved symptom scores by −2.9 vs −0.6 at 6 weeks, maintained to 12 months
cards.summary: Balloon dilation trial (2018): improved symptom scores by −2.9 vs −0.6 at 6 weeks, maintained to 12 months.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised, controlled trial with 1-year follow-up (unmasked procedure)
cards.people: 60 participants with medically refractory persistent eustachian tube dysfunction, randomised 1:1 to balloon dilation (31) or continued medical therapy (29), with controls offered dilation after 6 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean change in overall ETDQ-7 symptom score at 6 weeks was −2.9 (SD 1.4) with balloon dilation vs −0.6 (1.0) with control (p<0.0001). Among participants with abnormal baseline assessments, tympanogram type (p<0.006) and tympanic membrane position (p<0.001) improved significantly more with dilation. Technical success was 100% (91/91 attempts), 72% of procedures were done in the office under local anaesthesia, no complications were reported in either arm, and symptom improvement was maintained through 12 months after dilation.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, and the 12-month durability figure is within the dilation group after controls crossed over — there is no controlled comparison beyond 6 weeks in this trial.
cards.source: Meyer TA et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Balloon Dilation as a Treatment for Persistent Eustachian Tube Dysfunction With 1-Year Follow-Up. Otol Neurotol. 2018;39(7):894-902. PMID: 29912819. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the fetched record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent benefit in unmasked trials against a failed-therapy control — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Consistent benefit in unmasked trials against a failed-therapy control — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Poe 2018 (211 analysed patients) and Meyer 2018 (60 patients).
cards.result: Both trials point the same way on objective tympanometry as well as symptoms, with no procedure-related serious adverse events reported. The design ceiling — no masking, no sham, refractory-population comparators — caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The currency sweep's two records combine balloon dilation with other procedures in other middle-ear conditions and are fenced as pointers; the sham-controlled test this question still lacks was not among them. Tympanostomy tubes in children (drafted #629) are a different intervention and population, fenced likewise.
cards.watchOut: Patients in both trials had already failed medical therapy, so the comparison is 'procedure vs more of what failed' — the trials do not address first-line use.
cards.source: Synthesis of Poe D et al. Laryngoscope. 2018;128(5):1200-1206. PMID: 28940574; Meyer TA et al. Otol Neurotol. 2018;39(7):894-902. PMID: 29912819. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Persistent throat symptoms: lansoprazole and the reflux hypothesis (TOPPITS)
shelves.question: In adults with persistent unexplained throat symptoms referred to ENT, does lansoprazole beat placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cost-Benefit Analysis · Lansoprazole/therapeutic use · Secondary Health Care · Technology Assessment, Biomedical · Anti-Ulcer Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Esomeprazole/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY the null — unselected persistent throat symptoms · POSSIBLE — benefit in patients selected for laryngeal reflux signs. TOPPITS (346 randomised, double-blind, powered, pragmatic) found lansoprazole numerically worse than placebo on its primary symptom score at 16 weeks (difference +1.9 points, 95% CI −0.3 to 4.2) and at 12 months — a large definitive null, stamped LIKELY the null for the unselected referred population. The older, smaller Reichel trial, which required laryngoscopic reflux signs for entry, found significantly greater symptom and sign improvement on esomeprazole; that selected-population signal is POSSIBLE at best and does not rescue routine prescribing.

cards.headline: Wilson 2021 (TOPPITS): lansoprazole was no better than placebo for persistent throat symptoms — numerically worse at 16 weeks and 12 months
cards.summary: TOPPITS (2021): lansoprazole was no better than placebo for persistent throat symptoms — numerically worse at 16 weeks and 12 months.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised phase 3 trial (full HTA report)
cards.people: 346 participants aged 18 years or older with persistent throat symptoms and a Reflux Symptom Index score of 10 or more, recruited at eight UK ENT departments, randomised to lansoprazole 30 mg twice daily (172) or matched placebo (174) for 16 weeks; mean age 52 years (SD 13.7); 43% male.
cards.result: Mean Reflux Symptom Index at 16 weeks was 17.4 (SD 9.9) on lansoprazole vs 15.6 (9.8) on placebo — lansoprazole scores were an estimated 1.9 points higher (worse) (95% CI −0.3 to 4.2; padj=0.096). Scores in the normal range (<12) at 16 weeks: 41% vs 45%. At 12 months the gap persisted (16.0 vs 13.6; normal range 40% vs 55%). Two other symptom instruments (Comprehensive Reflux Symptom Score; Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Health-Related Quality of Life) likewise showed no benefit on any scale. The trial retained 82–89% power for its clinically relevant difference despite attrition (267 completed the primary endpoint visit).
cards.watchOut: Entry required symptoms, not proven reflux — TOPPITS rules on the prescribing habit (PPI for unexplained throat symptoms), not on PPI for objectively demonstrated laryngopharyngeal reflux, which is the narrower population on the next card.
cards.source: Wilson JA et al. Lansoprazole for persistent throat symptoms in secondary care: the TOPPITS RCT. Health Technol Assess. 2021;25(3):1-118. PMID: 33492208. Registry ID: ISRCTN38578686 and EudraCT 2013-004249-17, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Reichel 2008: in patients selected for laryngeal reflux signs, esomeprazole beat placebo on symptoms and laryngeal appearance
cards.summary: Esomeprazole trial (2008): in patients selected for laryngeal reflux signs, it beat placebo on symptoms and laryngeal appearance.
cards.people: 62 patients with a reflux finding score above 7 and a reflux symptom index above 13 (that is, selected for laryngoscopic signs as well as symptoms), randomised to esomeprazole 20 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Reductions in total reflux symptom index and reflux finding score, and in several subscores, were significantly greater on esomeprazole than placebo after 3 months (P<0.05 each), most pronounced for posterior commissure hypertrophy (P<0.01). The authors note a high placebo effect in this condition alongside the treatment difference. The abstract reports significance levels without the between-group score differences.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-two patients, one centre's selection criteria, and no effect sizes in the abstract — this is a hypothesis about a sign-selected subgroup, and TOPPITS, five times larger and unselected, is the shelf's anchor for ordinary referred patients.
cards.source: Reichel O et al. Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with esomeprazole for symptoms and signs associated with laryngopharyngeal reflux. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2008;139(3):414-420. PMID: 18722223. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stop the reflex prescription; the sign-selected question stays open — split stamp
cards.summary: Stop the reflex prescription; the sign-selected question stays open — Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TOPPITS (346 randomised, unselected throat symptoms) and Reichel 2008 (62 patients, sign-selected).
cards.result: For the patient ENT actually sees — persistent throat symptoms without demonstrated reflux — a definitive double-blind trial says a twice-daily PPI does nothing (LIKELY the null). For the narrower patient with laryngoscopic reflux signs, one small positive trial keeps a POSSIBLE benefit alive. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease shelves concern oesophageal disease and its own endpoints; this is the only throat-symptoms home.
cards.watchOut: TOPPITS's null is about lansoprazole at this dose and duration in this population; it does not rule on acid suppression where reflux is objectively proven by pH-impedance testing, which neither card required.

shelves.title: Epistaxis: topical tranexamic acid against nasal packing (NoPAC)
shelves.question: Does topical tranexamic acid reduce the need for nasal packing in emergency-department epistaxis?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Antifibrinolytic Agents/therapeutic use · Bandages · Emergency Service, Hospital · Epistaxis/drug therapy · Tranexamic Acid/therapeutic use · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE the null — packing need after first aid in ED epistaxis · MAYBE (weak evidence) — faster initial arrest versus packing. The large pragmatic double-blind NoPAC trial (496 patients, 26 UK emergency departments) found packing rates of 43.7% on topical tranexamic acid vs 41.3% on placebo (odds ratio 1.107, 95% CI 0.769 to 1.594) — a null from the trial built to answer this exact question. The earlier positive Zahed trial asked a different question (tranexamic acid vs packing itself, in anterior epistaxis, 216 patients, unblinded) and its speed-of-arrest advantage is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence): single, small, and not replicated under blinding. Systemic tranexamic acid for major bleeding lives on Shelf #138 and is not this claim.

cards.headline: Reuben 2021 (NoPAC): topical tranexamic acid did not reduce nasal packing — 43.7% vs 41.3% on placebo
cards.summary: NoPAC (2021): topical tranexamic acid did not reduce nasal packing — 43.7% vs 41.3% on placebo.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre, randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 496 adults with spontaneous epistaxis persisting after simple first aid and topical vasoconstrictor, across 26 UK emergency departments, randomised to topical tranexamic acid (254) or placebo (242) applied on a cotton-wool dental roll; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Anterior nasal packing during the index attendance was needed by 111 of 254 patients (43.7%) on tranexamic acid vs 100 of 242 (41.3%) on placebo — odds ratio 1.107 (95% CI 0.769 to 1.594; P=.59), a relative figure centred on no effect. No secondary outcome differed significantly: hospital admission, transfusion, recurrent epistaxis, or thrombotic events within 1 week.
cards.watchOut: NoPAC enrolled epistaxis that had already failed first aid and vasoconstrictor — the population in which packing is likeliest; its null does not directly test tranexamic acid as the very first intervention, which is part of what the earlier trial below did.
cards.source: Reuben A et al. The Use of Tranexamic Acid to Reduce the Need for Nasal Packing in Epistaxis (NoPAC): Randomized Controlled Trial. Ann Emerg Med. 2021;77(6):631-640. PMID: 33612282. Registry ID: ISRCTN34153772, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Zahed 2013: topical tranexamic acid arrested anterior epistaxis within 10 minutes in 71% vs 31.2% for anterior nasal packing
cards.summary: Topical tranexamic acid trial (2013): arrested anterior epistaxis within 10 minutes in 71% vs 31.2% for anterior nasal packing.
cards.people: 216 patients with anterior epistaxis presenting to an emergency department, randomised to topical injectable-form tranexamic acid (500 mg in 5 mL) or anterior nasal packing with tetracycline-ointment pledgets; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Bleeding was arrested within 10 minutes in 71% of the tranexamic acid group vs 31.2% of the packing group (odds ratio 2.28, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.09; P<.001 — a relative figure; the absolute rates are the 71% and 31.2% beside it). Discharge within 2 hours: 95.3% vs 6.4% (P<.001). Rebleeding within 24 hours was 4.7% vs 11% (P=.128, not significant). Satisfaction was higher with tranexamic acid (8.5 vs 4.4 on a 0–10 scale; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is packing itself, not placebo, and neither patients nor assessors were blinded — discharge-within-2-hours and satisfaction are near-automatic consequences of not being packed. This trial cannot answer NoPAC's question, and NoPAC's blinded null is why this card's stamp contribution is MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.source: Zahed R et al. A new and rapid method for epistaxis treatment using injectable form of tranexamic acid topically: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Emerg Med. 2013;31(9):1389-1392. PMID: 23911102. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the fetched record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the blinded trial says no packing is avoided; the unblinded trial says packing is unpleasant — split stamp
cards.summary: The blinded trial says no packing is avoided; the unblinded trial says packing is unpleasant — Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) · MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: NoPAC (496 patients, placebo-controlled) and Zahed 2013 (216 patients, vs packing).
cards.result: Read together: topical tranexamic acid does not demonstrably change whether an ED nosebleed ends up packed (NoPAC), while avoiding a pack, when bleeding stops, is plainly preferable for the patient (Zahed's satisfaction and discharge figures, heavily confounded by design). The currency sweep's single record concerns intravenous tranexamic acid in rhinoplasty surgery, a different setting and route, and is not evidence on this shelf's question. Tranexamic acid for major bleeding and trauma is Shelf #138, a systemic-haemorrhage question, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two trials into one verdict: they differ in comparator (placebo vs packing), population (post-first-aid vs all anterior epistaxis) and blinding — the discordance is the shelf.

shelves.title: Cochlear implantation for single-sided deafness: the CINGLE randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with single-sided deafness, does a cochlear implant beat a bone-conduction device or a CROS hearing aid on speech perception in noise, sound localisation, and tinnitus?
shelves.mesh: Bone Conduction · Cochlear Implantation/methods · Cochlear Implants · Hearing Aids · Hearing Loss, Unilateral/therapy · Sound Localization · Speech Perception
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised programme (CINGLE, 120 patients) reports twice — at 3–6 months and at 24 months — that cochlear implantation outperformed bone-conduction devices, CROS aids and no treatment on speech perception in noise in the configurations that matter, and was the only option to improve sound localisation and tinnitus burden. But it is a single programme, the device groups were partly self-selected after the randomised trial periods (only 28 of 120 received an implant), and masking is impossible — a single-programme ceiling of POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Peters 2021 (CINGLE, short-term): cochlear implantation beat BCD, CROS and baseline on speech in noise, localisation and tinnitus at 3–6 months
cards.summary: CINGLE, short-term (2021): cochlear implantation beat BCD, CROS and baseline on speech in noise, localisation and tinnitus at 3–6 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (three-arm, with post-trial device choice)
cards.people: 120 adults with single-sided deafness randomised to cochlear implantation, or trial periods of bone-conduction device then CROS, or CROS then bone-conduction device; after allocation the groups were implant 28, bone-conduction device 25, CROS 34, and no treatment 26 (7 patients did not receive their allocated intervention); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: With speech and noise from the front, the implant group performed significantly better than baseline and than the other groups. With speech directed to the poor ear, all treatment groups improved on baseline; with speech to the better ear and noise to the poor ear, the bone-conduction and CROS groups performed worse than baseline while the implant group improved. Only the implant group improved in sound localisation and tinnitus burden. All treatment groups improved on disease-specific quality of life vs baseline.
cards.watchOut: After the randomised trial periods, patients chose their device — so the compared groups are part-randomised, part-self-selected, and the implant arm is the smallest (28). Effect sizes are described qualitatively in this report; the 24-month report carded below carries the numbers.
cards.source: Peters JPM et al. cards.result: At 24 months, speech reception thresholds in noise favoured the implant group over the bone-conduction group (difference −4.7 dB in the speech-to-better-ear configuration, 95% CI −6.6 to −3.0; −2.2 dB, −4.6 to −1.1, speech to poor ear), over CROS (−1.3 dB, −1.7 to −0.2, speech and noise in front; −5.3 dB, −6.0 to −3.1, speech to better ear), and over no treatment (−6.3 dB, −7.5 to −4.9, speech to poor ear). shelves.title: Chronic rhinosinusitis: surgery vs clarithromycin vs placebo (MACRO)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps, does endoscopic sinus surgery beat a three-month clarithromycin course — and does either beat placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Chronic Disease · Clarithromycin/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Endoscopy/methods · Nasal Polyps/complications,surgery,drug therapy · Rhinosinusitis/complications,drug therapy,surgery
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — endoscopic sinus surgery improves disease-specific quality of life · LIKELY the null — low-dose clarithromycin vs placebo. MACRO (514 patients, three arms, all on intranasal steroids and saline) found 6-month SNOT-22 scores lower (better) after surgery by 18.13 points vs clarithromycin and 20.44 vs placebo — several times the scale's 9-point minimal important difference — while clarithromycin vs placebo differed by −3.11 (not significant). The earlier Dutch trial (238 patients, polyps only) found a smaller surgery advantage (−4.9 points, below the 9-point threshold), which tempers the size, not the direction. The clarithromycin null comes from the same large trial and is stamped LIKELY the null.

cards.headline: Philpott 2025 (MACRO): surgery beat clarithromycin and placebo by 18–20 SNOT-22 points at 6 months; clarithromycin did not beat placebo
cards.summary: MACRO (2025): surgery beat clarithromycin and placebo by 18–20 SNOT-22 points at 6 months; clarithromycin did not beat placebo.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, three-arm, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 4 trial (drug arms masked; surgery unmasked)
cards.people: 514 adults (35% female) with chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps (410) or without (104) remaining symptomatic after intranasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation and a short antibiotic course, at 20 UK sites, randomised to endoscopic sinus surgery (171), clarithromycin 250 mg twice daily for 2 weeks then once daily for 10 weeks (172), or placebo (171), all with intranasal medication; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: SNOT-22 at 6 months was significantly lower (better) in the surgery group than clarithromycin (adjusted mean difference −18.13, 98.33% CI −24.26 to −11.99; p<0.0001) and placebo (−20.44, −26.42 to −14.46; p<0.0001) — differences roughly twice the 9-point minimal clinically important difference for the scale. Clarithromycin vs placebo did not differ significantly (−3.11, −8.56 to 2.33; p=0.17). Ten serious adverse events occurred in nine participants across the groups (about 1–2% per group); none was fatal.
cards.watchOut: Surgery cannot be masked, and SNOT-22 is patient-reported — expectation effects are inseparable from the surgical effect in the surgery comparisons (the drug-vs-placebo comparison, which was masked, is the trial's internally cleanest result, and it is null). Six months is early for a chronic relapsing condition.

cards.headline: Lourijsen 2022: surgery plus medical therapy beat medical therapy alone by 4.9 SNOT-22 points — below the 9-point important difference
cards.summary: Surgery plus medical therapy (2022): beat medical therapy alone by 4.9 SNOT-22 points — below the 9-point important difference.
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, pragmatic, randomised, controlled trial
cards.people: 238 adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and an indication for surgery, at 15 Dutch centres, randomised to surgery plus medical therapy (121) or medical therapy alone (117); mean age 50.4 years (SD 12.7); 61% men; 206 analysed for the 12-month primary outcome.
cards.result: At 12 months, mean SNOT-22 was 27.9 (SD 20.2) with surgery plus medical therapy vs 31.1 (20.4) with medical therapy alone — adjusted mean difference −4.9 (95% CI −9.4 to −0.4), favouring surgery but not reaching the scale's 9.0-point minimal clinically important difference. Adverse events were similar between groups, most commonly minor epistaxis or gastrointestinal problems; there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, polyps-only, and medical therapy was at each clinician's discretion — a softer comparator than MACRO's protocolised intranasal regimen, yet it produced the smaller surgical advantage; the honest reading is that surgery helps, with the size depending on how good the medical alternative is.

shelves.title: Post-infectious smell loss: olfactory training
shelves.question: Does structured olfactory training — repeated deliberate sniffing of odour sets over months — restore smell after post-infectious olfactory loss versus no or lesser training?
shelves.mesh: Cross-Over Studies · Odorants · Olfaction Disorders/etiology,physiopathology,rehabilitation · Psychotherapeutic Processes · Recovery of Function/physiology · Respiratory Tract Infections/complications · Sensory Thresholds/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The multicentre Damm trial (144 patients, crossover) found high-concentration training improved olfactory function in 26% vs 15% on low-concentration training at 18 weeks, with a larger gap (63% vs 19%) in patients starting within 12 months of onset. But neither card has a true no-training control — Damm compares strong vs weak training, and the post-COVID Pires trial compares 4 vs 8 essences with both groups improving — so the shelf supports 'training, at proper intensity, probably helps, especially early' at POSSIBLE, not a proven margin over doing nothing.

cards.headline: Damm 2014: high-concentration olfactory training improved smell in 26% vs 15% on low-concentration training — 63% vs 19% when started within 12 months
cards.summary: Olfactory training trial (2014): high-concentration training improved smell in 26% vs 15% on low-concentration training — 63% vs 19% when started within 12 months.
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind, controlled, multicentre crossover trial
cards.people: 144 patients with persistent postinfectious olfactory dysfunction of under 24 months' duration at 12 tertiary university centres, randomised to train with high concentrations of four odours (70) or low concentrations (74) for 18 weeks, then switched for a further 18 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 18 weeks, olfactory function had improved in 18 of 70 participants (26%) in the high-concentration group vs 11 of 74 (15%) in the low-concentration group. In the subgroup with dysfunction under 12 months, improvement was 15 of 24 (63%) on high-concentration vs 6 of 31 (19%) on low-concentration training (P=.03). The authors describe training as safe and particularly useful when started within 12 months of onset.
cards.watchOut: The control is weaker training, not no training — spontaneous recovery, which is common after infection, is inside both arms, and the headline 63% vs 19% is a duration subgroup of 55 patients. Read this card as dose-and-timing evidence, not proof against natural history.

cards.headline: Pires 2022: post-COVID olfactory training improved smell on both regimens, with no advantage to doubling the essences
cards.summary: Post-COVID olfactory training (2022): improved smell on both regimens, with no advantage to doubling the essences.
cards.people: 80 patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction after COVID-19 infection of less than 3 months, randomised to olfactory training with 4 essences or 8 essences over 4 weeks; assessed subjectively and by the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Significant olfactory improvement was measured subjectively and on the smell-identification test in both groups, with no significant difference between the 4-essence and 8-essence regimens. The presence of olfactory fluctuations was associated with higher identification-test scores. The authors conclude that intensifying training by adding essences over 4 weeks is not superior to the classical method.
cards.watchOut: No untrained control group and only 4 weeks of training in very early post-COVID loss, when spontaneous recovery is fastest — this card supports 'standard training, not intensified training', and cannot on its own separate training from natural history.
