shelves.title: Allergic rhinitis: fixed azelastine–fluticasone nasal spray vs its components
shelves.question: Does the fixed intranasal azelastine–fluticasone combination relieve seasonal allergic rhinitis better than fluticasone alone, azelastine alone, or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Androstadienes/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anti-Allergic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Combinations · Fluticasone · Phthalazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal/drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A four-arm double-blind trial (779 patients) and a pooled analysis of three further double-blind trials (3,398 patients) agree: the fixed combination (MP29-02) reduced total nasal symptom scores more than either component alone and more than placebo (−5.54 vs −4.55 fluticasone, −4.54 azelastine, −3.03 placebo in the four-arm trial; −5.7 vs −5.1, −4.4 and −3.0 in the pooled analysis), with onset within 30 minutes. The margins over fluticasone alone are small (about half a point to one point on the symptom scale) — superiority is LIKELY; clinical importance is a separate, smaller claim and is stated as such.

cards.headline: Meltzer 2012: the azelastine–fluticasone combination beat both components and placebo on nasal symptoms (−5.54 vs −4.55, −4.54 and −3.03 points)
cards.summary: Azelastine–fluticasone trial (2012): the combination beat both components and placebo on nasal symptoms ( −5.54 vs −4.55, −4.54 and −3.03 points ).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial
cards.people: 779 patients with moderate-to-severe seasonal allergic rhinitis, randomised for 2 weeks to MP29-02 (azelastine/fluticasone, one spray per nostril twice daily; daily doses azelastine 548 micrograms, fluticasone 200 micrograms), fluticasone alone, azelastine alone, or placebo in the same vehicle and device; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The combination reduced the 12-hour reflective total nasal symptom score from baseline by −5.54 points, significantly more than fluticasone (−4.55; p=0.038), azelastine (−4.54; p=0.032) and placebo (−3.03; p<0.001) — the authors calculate the combination improved the score 39% beyond fluticasone's contribution (a relative characterisation of a 0.99-point absolute gap). All individual nasal symptoms contributed; onset of action was within 30 minutes; ocular symptom scores improved vs placebo; the combination was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks, one season, symptom scores only — and the margin over the steroid component alone is about one point on a multi-symptom scale, statistically solid across trials but modest for an individual patient.

cards.headline: Carr 2012: pooling three trials (3,398 patients), the combination again beat fluticasone, azelastine and placebo — from the first day
cards.summary: Pooled programme (2012): across three trials (3,398 patients), the combination again beat fluticasone, azelastine and placebo — from the first day.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of three randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trials
cards.people: 3,398 patients aged 12 years or older with moderate-to-severe seasonal allergic rhinitis across three 14-day multicentre trials (MP4002, MP4004, MP4006), each comparing MP29-02 with intranasal fluticasone, intranasal azelastine and placebo; no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: The combination reduced the summed morning-and-evening reflective total nasal symptom score by −5.7 (SD 5.3), more than fluticasone (−5.1, SD 4.9; P<.001), azelastine (−4.4, SD 4.8; P<.001) and placebo (−3.0, SD 4.2; P<.001) — absolute gaps of 0.6, 1.3 and 2.7 points respectively. cards.watchOut: A manufacturer-programme meta-analysis of its own three short trials: the replication is real but not independent, and 14-day seasonal trials cannot speak to perennial rhinitis or long-term adherence.

shelves.title: Tonsillotomy vs tonsillectomy: partial against total removal
shelves.question: In children and adults undergoing tonsil surgery for obstruction or recurrent infection, does tonsillotomy (partial, intracapsular) match tonsillectomy on symptom control with less postoperative pain and bleeding — and at what regrowth or reoperation cost?
shelves.mesh: Blood Loss, Surgical/statistics & numerical data · Postoperative Pain/epidemiology · Palatine Tonsil/surgery · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — less early postoperative morbidity · MAYBE (weak evidence) — equal long-term symptom control. The carded evidence base is paediatric (the Cochrane review covers children aged 2–16 with obstructive sleep-disordered breathing): tonsillotomy probably speeds return to normal activity by about 4 days and probably lowers first-week complications requiring medical intervention (2.6% vs 4.9% — the review prints the pair with risk ratio 1.75 for tonsillectomy vs tonsillotomy), while pain scores barely differ and every longer-term outcome — symptom control, quality of life, recurrence, reoperation — is rated very low certainty. For adults and recurrent infection, the currency sweep found one newer randomised trial (FINITE, ages 16–65, recurrent/chronic tonsillitis), fenced in the synthesis: its primary recovery-time outcome was null, so it does not lift either half of the split.

cards.headline: Blackshaw 2020 (Cochrane): tonsillotomy probably speeds recovery and cuts first-week complications, but long-term equivalence is very uncertain
cards.summary: Cochrane review (2020): tonsillotomy probably speeds recovery and cuts first-week complications (2.6% vs 4.9% needing medical intervention); long-term equivalence is very uncertain.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 22 randomised trials totalling 1,984 children aged 2–16 years with obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, comparing (adeno)tonsillotomy with (adeno)tonsillectomy; follow-up from six days to six years; most studies at unclear or high risk of bias; no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: Postoperative complications requiring medical intervention in the first week were probably lower with tonsillotomy: 2.6% vs 4.9% (risk ratio 1.75 for the tonsillectomy-vs-tonsillotomy direction, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.91; 16 studies, 1,416 children; moderate-certainty evidence) — a relative figure with its absolute rates beside it. Return to normal activity was probably about four days faster with tonsillotomy (mean difference 3.84 days, 0.23 to 7.44; 3 studies, 248 children; moderate certainty). Pain differed little or not at all at 24 hours, 2–3 days and 4–7 days (all very low certainty). Disease-specific quality of life, peri-operative blood loss, recurrence of obstructive symptoms and reoperation rates were all rated very low certainty — the reviewers state plainly that long-term comparative effectiveness cannot be determined from these data.
cards.watchOut: The review's complication risk ratio is printed against the tonsillotomy rate of 2.6% and tonsillectomy rate of 4.9% — direction matters when quoting it. Most included trials were small and at unclear or high risk of bias, and children with recurrent infection (rather than obstruction) are barely represented.

cards.headline: Borgström 2019: adenotonsillotomy vs adenotonsillectomy — less pain on two of six measures, bleeding 0% vs 5%
cards.summary: Adenotonsillotomy trial (2019): less pain on two of six measures; bleeding 0% vs 5% .
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised controlled trial (morbidity report of an obstructive sleep apnea trial)
cards.people: 79 children aged 2–6 years with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, randomised to adenotonsillectomy (40) or adenotonsillotomy (39); 63 (80%) returned the 10-day postoperative pain logbook.
cards.result: Of six pain-related outcomes, two significantly favoured adenotonsillotomy: the first day children graded themselves pain-free (p=0.021) and the first day caregivers estimated pain at 5 or less on a visual analogue scale (p=0.007); the other four (including days of analgesic use and return to normal diet) did not differ significantly. Postoperative bleeding occurred in 2 of the adenotonsillectomy cases (5%), one requiring return to theatre, and in no adenotonsillotomy cases. The parent trial's one-year report found no significant differences between the operations in nocturnal respiration or symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-nine children and a two-of-six outcome pattern: the authors themselves conclude the morbidity differences were minor and of uncertain clinical significance — this card tempers, rather than inflates, the Cochrane card's recovery advantage.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a gentler first week, an unproven decade — split stamp, children only
cards.summary: A gentler first week, an unproven decade — Split: POSSIBLE · MAYBE (weak evidence), children only. The adult FINITE tonsillectomy trial is fenced in the synthesis.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Blackshaw 2020 (22 trials, 1,984 children) and Borgström 2019 (79 children).
cards.result: Partial removal probably buys a somewhat easier first week in children (POSSIBLE) — fewer complications needing medical attention, faster return to normal activity — while whether it matches total removal on years of symptom control, regrowth and reoperation is genuinely unknown on randomised evidence (MAYBE (weak evidence)). The currency sweep found the FINITE randomised trial (179 patients aged 16–65 with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis, patient-blinded, three arms): mean recovery time was similar across extracapsular tonsillectomy and the two intracapsular techniques (12.1 vs 11.1 and 10.3 days; the predefined clinically significant difference was 3 days), although swallowing pain on postoperative days 1–10/12 was lower with the intracapsular techniques. FINITE is fenced here as a pointer, not carded: it extends the question to adults and recurrent infection, but its null primary outcome and 1-month follow-up change neither half of the split stamp. Tonsillectomy vs no surgery (drafted #630) and adenotonsillectomy vs watchful waiting (drafted #631) are the neighbouring questions, fenced, not carded here.
cards.watchOut: The carded evidence covers children with obstruction; FINITE (fenced above) is the one randomised trial in adults with recurrent tonsillitis, and its recovery-time primary outcome was null — do not extend the paediatric recovery advantage to adults on this shelf's evidence.

shelves.title: Chronic suppurative otitis media: topical antibiotics
shelves.question: Do topical quinolone antibiotics resolve discharge in chronic suppurative otitis media better than antiseptics, systemic antibiotics, or aural toilet alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bias · Chronic Disease · Otitis Media, Suppurative/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — topical quinolone beats antiseptic or placebo for discharge resolution · MAYBE (weak evidence) — quinolones vs other antibiotic classes. The 2025 Cochrane synthesis (18 studies, 1,783 participants) rates nearly everything low or very low certainty, but the direct randomised comparisons line up: topical ciprofloxacin resolved discharge in 59% vs 32% on boric-acid antiseptic in 427 Kenyan schoolchildren (relative risk 1.86), beat a framycetin–steroid combination 76.4% vs 51.8% in Aboriginal children, and the review's placebo comparison (84% vs 12%, very low certainty) and add-on-to-systemic comparison (88% vs 60%) point the same way. Whether quinolones beat other topical antibiotic classes is very uncertain (pooled relative risk 1.92 with a confidence interval reaching 1.00 and 97% heterogeneity) — MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Brennan-Jones 2025 (Cochrane): topical antibiotics probably help over placebo or as an add-on, but almost all evidence is low or very low certainty
cards.summary: Cochrane review (2025): topical antibiotics probably help over placebo or as an add-on, but almost all evidence is low or very low certainty.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane, 2025 update)
cards.people: 18 randomised studies with 1,783 participants (plus 108 ears unaccounted in participant numbers), adults and children with chronic suppurative otitis media; searches to June 2022, with one new study (100 participants) added in this update; no pooled mean age is stated.
cards.result: Topical ciprofloxacin vs placebo (both with aural toilet): resolution of discharge at 1–2 weeks 84% vs 12% (risk ratio 6.74, 95% CI 1.82 to 24.99; 35 participants; very low-certainty evidence — a relative figure on a very small base). Topical antibiotics added to systemic antibiotics vs systemic antibiotics alone: resolution 88% vs 60% (risk ratio 1.47, 1.14 to 1.88; 1 study, 100 participants; low certainty). Quinolones vs aminoglycosides for resolution at 1–2 weeks: risk ratio 1.92 (1.00 to 3.67; 7 studies, 794 participants; very low certainty, heterogeneity I²=97%). The reviewers conclude they are very uncertain about effectiveness overall, while noting some evidence of benefit vs placebo or as an add-on; harms were poorly reported.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's honest centre of gravity: one tiny placebo trial, one add-on trial, and a heterogeneous class comparison. The two primary trials carded below are inside this review's included set — they illustrate its comparisons, they do not add independent weight on top of it.

cards.headline: Macfadyen 2005: topical ciprofloxacin resolved discharge in 59% vs 32% on boric-acid antiseptic in 427 Kenyan schoolchildren
cards.summary: Topical ciprofloxacin (2005): resolved discharge in 59% vs 32% on boric-acid antiseptic in 427 Kenyan schoolchildren.
cards.people: 427 children with chronic suppurative otitis media enrolled from 141 schools in Kenya (screened from 39,841 schoolchildren), randomised to topical ciprofloxacin (216) or boric acid in alcohol (211), applied child-to-child twice daily for 2 weeks; outcome denominators 207 and 204; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 2 weeks, discharge had resolved in 123 of 207 children (59%) on ciprofloxacin vs 65 of 204 (32%) on boric acid (relative risk 1.86, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.35; P<0.0001) — a relative figure with its absolute rates beside it. The advantage persisted at 4 weeks, and ciprofloxacin was associated with better hearing at both visits. Tympanic-membrane healing did not differ. Ear pain, irritation and bleeding on mopping were significantly less frequent with ciprofloxacin than with boric acid.
cards.watchOut: A school-based paediatric trial in one setting, with treatment applied by other children — effectiveness under community conditions is its strength; it does not test ciprofloxacin against no treatment or against another antibiotic.
cards.source: Macfadyen C et al. Topical quinolone vs. antiseptic for treating chronic suppurative otitis media: a randomized controlled trial. Trop Med Int Health. 2005;10(2):190-197. PMID: 15679563. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial record.

cards.summary: Topical ciprofloxacin (2003): cured 76.4% vs 51.8% versus framycetin–gramicidin–dexamethasone drops in Aboriginal children.
cards.type: Community-based, multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial

shelves.title: Yaws: single-dose azithromycin against benzathine penicillin, and mass treatment
shelves.question: Is single-dose oral azithromycin non-inferior to benzathine benzylpenicillin injection for yaws in children — and do repeated mass rounds beat one round plus targeted treatment for eradication?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Azithromycin/administration & dosage · Injections, Intramuscular · Papua New Guinea · Penicillin G Benzathine/administration & dosage · Yaws/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Mitjà 2012 (250 children in Papua New Guinea, open-label) showed a single 30 mg/kg oral dose of azithromycin non-inferior to benzathine benzylpenicillin injection for serological cure at 6 months (96% vs 93%; difference −3.4%, 95% CI −9.3 to 2.4, within the 10% margin) — the result that made mass treatment thinkable. The 2022 cluster trial (38 wards, ~57,000 people) then found three rounds of mass azithromycin reduced active yaws prevalence further than one mass round plus targeted treatment (0.04% vs 0.16% at 18 months; adjusted relative risk 4.08 for the control strategy's higher prevalence), and latent yaws prevalence was 3.28% vs 6.54% — but three cases of macrolide-resistant yaws were found in the three-round group, the resistance shadow the topic asks about. Each claim rests on a single trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Mitjà 2012: single-dose azithromycin was non-inferior to benzathine penicillin for yaws in children — cure 96% vs 93% at 6 months
cards.summary: Mitjà 2012: single-dose azithromycin was non-inferior to benzathine penicillin for yaws (cure 96% vs 93% at 6 months).
cards.people: 250 children aged 6 months to 15 years with serologically confirmed yaws at Lihir Medical Centre, Papua New Guinea, allocated to a single oral dose of azithromycin 30 mg/kg (124) or intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg (126); the per-protocol analysis at 6 months included 110 and 113 children. Investigators were masked to group assignment.
cards.result: Cure (a fall in rapid plasma reagin titre of at least two dilutions by 6 months, plus epithelialisation of primary ulcers within 2 weeks where present) occurred in 106 of 110 children (96%) on azithromycin and 105 of 113 (93%) on penicillin — a treatment difference of −3.4% (95% CI −9.3 to 2.4), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (upper confidence limit below 10%). Drug-related adverse events (all mild or moderate) numbered 10 (8%) on azithromycin and 8 (7%) on penicillin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, per-protocol primary analysis with a serological (not clinical-eradication) endpoint and a generous 10% non-inferiority margin: it establishes 'not much worse than the injection' for individual treatment, which is what eradication programmes needed — not superiority, and not community-level effect.

cards.headline: Three-rounds trial 2022: three mass azithromycin rounds cut active yaws prevalence to 0.04% vs 0.16% with one round plus targeted treatment — and macrolide resistance appeared (3 cases)
cards.summary: Three-rounds trial 2022: three mass azithromycin rounds cut active yaws prevalence to 0.04% vs 0.16% with one round plus targeted treatment.
cards.people: 38 wards in a yaws-endemic area of Papua New Guinea: 19 wards (30,438 people) assigned to one mass round followed by two rounds of targeted treatment of active cases (control), and 19 wards (26,238 people) to three mass rounds at baseline, 6 and 12 months (experimental); 24,848 azithromycin doses were given in control wards and 59,852 in experimental wards; endpoints measured at 18 months, with latent yaws assessed in a subgroup of asymptomatic children aged 1–15 (994 control, 945 experimental).
cards.result: Active yaws prevalence fell from 0.46% at baseline to 0.16% (47 of 29,954) in the control group and from 0.43% to 0.04% (10 of 25,987) in the experimental group (relative risk adjusted for clustering 4.08, 95% CI 1.90 to 8.76, control vs experimental). Latent yaws prevalence at 18 months was 6.54% (95% CI 5.00 to 8.08) in control children and 3.28% (2.14 to 4.42) in experimental children (adjusted relative risk 2.03, 1.12 to 3.70). Three cases of yaws with macrolide resistance were found in the experimental group. The authors conclude monitoring for the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance is needed.
cards.watchOut: A single cluster trial with 38 clusters and prevalence (not incidence or eradication) endpoints at 18 months: it shows more rounds suppress more disease while rounds continue, and its own resistance finding is the strongest argument on this shelf against assuming the strategy scales indefinitely.

cards.summary: An oral non-inferior treatment and a more-is-better mass strategy, each from one trial, with resistance already visible — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Mitjà 2012 (250 children, individual treatment) and the three-rounds trial (38 wards, community eradication strategy).

shelves.title: Peanut epicutaneous immunotherapy: the Viaskin patch (PEPITES, EPITOPE)
shelves.question: Does a daily peanut patch (250 µg) raise the reaction threshold in peanut-allergic children — in school-age children (PEPITES, which missed its pre-set clinical bar) and in toddlers (EPITOPE)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Allergens/administration & dosage · Arachis/immunology · Confidence Intervals · Desensitization, Immunologic/methods · Eating/immunology · Peanut Hypersensitivity/immunology,therapy
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE in toddlers; MAYBE (weak evidence) in school-age children. EPITOPE (362 children aged 1–3 years) met its primary endpoint cleanly: a treatment response in 67.0% on the patch versus 33.5% on placebo (risk difference 33.4 percentage points, 95% CI 22.4 to 44.5; P<0.001) — one trial, so the toddler claim caps at POSSIBLE. PEPITES (356 children aged 4–11) found a responder difference of 21.7% (35.3% versus 13.6%; 95% CI 12.4% to 29.8%; P<.001) that was statistically significant but did NOT meet the trial's own prespecified lower-bound criterion (15%) for a positive result — the school-age claim is therefore MAYBE (weak evidence) as a claim of clinically meaningful benefit. Peanut oral immunotherapy lives on Shelf #376 and omalizumab for food allergy on Shelf #395; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: PEPITES 2019: the peanut patch beat placebo statistically (35.3% vs 13.6% responders) but missed its own prespecified bar for a positive trial
cards.summary: PEPITES 2019: the peanut patch beat placebo statistically (responders 35.3% vs 13.6% ) but missed its own prespecified bar for a positive trial — printed on the card, never called simply positive.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (12 months)
cards.people: 356 peanut-allergic children aged 4–11 years (median age 7 years; 61.2% male) without a history of severe anaphylaxis, reacting at an eliciting dose of 300 mg or less of peanut protein on double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge, randomised to a daily 250 µg peanut patch (238) or placebo patch (118) for 12 months; 89.9% completed the trial and mean adherence was 98.5%.
cards.result: The responder rate was 35.3% with the peanut patch versus 13.6% with placebo (difference 21.7 percentage points, 95% CI 12.4% to 29.8%; P<.001). However, the prespecified criterion for a positive trial result — a lower 95% confidence bound of 15% or more on the responder difference — was not met (lower bound 12.4%). Treatment-emergent adverse events, primarily patch-site reactions, occurred in 95.4% (active) and 89% (placebo); discontinuation for all causes was 10.5% versus 9.3%.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's central honesty point: a statistically significant result that failed the trial's own prespecified clinical bar. Any summary that calls PEPITES simply 'positive' has dropped the criterion the investigators set in advance.
cards.source: Fleischer DM et al. Effect of Epicutaneous Immunotherapy vs Placebo on Reaction to Peanut Protein Ingestion Among Children With Peanut Allergy: The PEPITES Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019;321(10):946-955. PMID: 30794314. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02636699, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: EPITOPE 2023: in toddlers, the patch produced a treatment response in 67.0% vs 33.5% on placebo — a 33.4-point difference
cards.summary: EPITOPE 2023: in toddlers, responders were 67.0% vs 33.5% — a 33.4-point difference.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (12 months)
cards.people: 362 children 1 to 3 years of age with peanut allergy confirmed by double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge (eliciting dose 300 mg or less), randomised 2:1 to daily peanut patch or placebo for 12 months; 84.8% completed the trial. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (treatment response by eliciting dose at 12 months) was observed in 67.0% on the patch versus 33.5% on placebo (risk difference 33.4 percentage points, 95% CI 22.4 to 44.5; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 100% (intervention) and 99.2% (placebo); serious adverse events in 8.6% versus 2.5%; anaphylaxis in 7.8% versus 3.4%; serious treatment-related adverse events in 0.4% versus none; treatment-related anaphylaxis in 1.6% versus none.
cards.watchOut: A single trial in 1–3-year-olds, with anaphylaxis numerically more frequent on the patch (7.8% versus 3.4%, all-cause during patch use): the desensitisation gain and the reaction risk travel together, and durability beyond 12 months is not shown on this card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: desensitisation is real in toddlers (POSSIBLE); in older children the key trial missed its own bar (MAYBE (weak evidence))
cards.summary: Desensitisation is real in toddlers (POSSIBLE); in older children the key trial missed its bar (MAYBE (weak evidence)).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PEPITES (356 children aged 4–11) and EPITOPE (362 children aged 1–3).
cards.result: The patch raises the reaction threshold in both age groups on the numbers (responder differences 21.7 and 33.4 percentage points), but the trials' own verdicts differ: EPITOPE met its primary endpoint outright, PEPITES did not meet its prespecified positivity criterion. The split stamp follows the trials, not the press releases. The endpoint throughout is desensitisation on a supervised food challenge — a raised threshold, not freedom to eat peanuts. Oral immunotherapy (#376) and omalizumab (#395) answer different versions of this question and stay home.
cards.watchOut: Never present PEPITES as an unqualified positive trial; its 15% lower-bound criterion and the observed 12.4% lower bound belong in any summary of this shelf.

shelves.title: Icatibant and C1-inhibitor for acute hereditary angioedema attacks (FAST-3, IMPACT)
shelves.question: For an acute hereditary angioedema attack, does on-demand treatment shorten time to symptom relief — icatibant, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (FAST-3), and plasma-derived C1-inhibitor concentrate (IMPACT)?
shelves.mesh: Angioedemas, Hereditary/drug therapy · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Bradykinin/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Bradykinin B2 Receptor Antagonists · Injections, Subcutaneous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Acute Disease
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of two different on-demand drugs agree that treatment shortens time to relief. FAST-3 (88 patients with cutaneous or abdominal attacks) found a median time to 50% or greater symptom-severity reduction of 2.0 hours on icatibant versus 19.8 hours on placebo (P<.001). IMPACT (125 patients) found a median time to onset of relief of 0.5 hours on C1-inhibitor concentrate 20 U/kg versus 1.5 hours on placebo (P=.0025), with the 10 U/kg dose not significantly better than placebo. Endpoints are time-to-relief in a rare disease — necessarily small trials — but the effects are large, blinded and concordant. Long-term prophylaxis of HAE lives on Shelf #400 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: FAST-3 2011: icatibant cut median time to 50% symptom reduction from 19.8 hours (placebo) to 2.0 hours
cards.summary: FAST-3 2011: icatibant cut median time to 50% symptom reduction from 19.8 hours (placebo) to 2.0 hours .
cards.type: Phase III, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: Subjects with hereditary angioedema from C1-inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction (type I/II): 43 received icatibant and 45 placebo for moderate to very severe cutaneous or abdominal attacks; small additional laryngeal-attack groups (5 randomised mild-to-moderate, 5 open-label severe) are reported separately in the abstract. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For cutaneous or abdominal attacks, icatibant significantly reduced median times versus placebo to 50% or more reduction in symptom severity (2.0 versus 19.8 hours; P<.001 — the primary endpoint), to onset of primary symptom relief (1.5 versus 18.5 hours; P<.001), to almost complete symptom relief (8.0 versus 36.0 hours; P=.012), and to initial symptom relief (0.8 versus 3.5 hours; P<.001). For laryngeal attacks, median time to 50% or more reduction was 2.5 hours (icatibant) versus 3.2 hours (placebo) in the small randomised subset. No icatibant-treated subject required rescue medication before symptom relief. Adverse events occurred in 41% (icatibant) versus 52% (placebo); all icatibant-treated subjects had injection-site reactions, with no serious adverse events reported.
cards.watchOut: A rare-disease trial of 88 randomised cutaneous/abdominal attacks, with laryngeal attacks — the most dangerous kind — represented by only a handful of patients; the laryngeal comparison (2.5 versus 3.2 hours) is descriptive, not a powered result.
cards.source: Lumry WR et al. Randomized placebo-controlled trial of the bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist icatibant for the treatment of acute attacks of hereditary angioedema: the FAST-3 trial. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 2011;107(6):529-537. PMID: 22123383. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00912093, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: IMPACT 2009: C1-inhibitor concentrate 20 U/kg halved-to-thirded time to relief — 0.5 vs 1.5 hours; the 10 U/kg dose did not beat placebo
cards.summary: IMPACT 2009: C1-inhibitor 20 U/kg sped onset of relief (0.5 vs 1.5 hours); the 10 U/kg dose did not beat placebo and is printed beside it.
cards.people: 125 patients with type I or II hereditary angioedema treated for a single acute abdominal or facial attack, randomised to intravenous C1-inhibitor concentrate 10 or 20 U/kg or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to onset of symptom relief was significantly shorter with 20 U/kg than placebo (0.5 versus 1.5 hours; P=.0025); with 10 U/kg it was only slightly shorter (1.2 versus 1.5 hours; P=.2731 — not significant). The reduction was greatest for severe attacks (0.5 versus 13.5 hours). Secondary outcomes (time to complete resolution, worsening of symptoms between 2 and 4 hours, vomiting episodes) consistently supported the 20 U/kg dose. No seroconversions for HIV, hepatitis virus or human B19 virus were observed.
cards.watchOut: The dose matters: only the 20 U/kg result is positive, and facial/abdominal attacks — not laryngeal attacks — were the studied population. A plasma-derived product, with the trial run before modern viral-safety reporting norms.
cards.source: Craig TJ et al. Efficacy of human C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate compared with placebo in acute hereditary angioedema attacks. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2009;124(4):801-808. PMID: 19767078. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in its record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: on-demand treatment shortens attacks — LIKELY, at the right dose
cards.summary: On-demand treatment shortens attacks — LIKELY, at the right dose.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FAST-3 (88 randomised patients, icatibant) and IMPACT (125 patients, C1-inhibitor concentrate).
cards.result: Both blinded trials show the same pattern — treated attacks turn the corner in a fraction of the placebo time (2.0 versus 19.8 hours to 50% reduction with icatibant; 0.5 versus 1.5 hours to onset of relief with C1-inhibitor 20 U/kg) — and both carry a dose/scope caveat (C1-inhibitor 10 U/kg null; laryngeal attacks barely studied). LIKELY for on-demand treatment of cutaneous/abdominal attacks. Prophylaxis is a different question and stays on Shelf #400.
cards.watchOut: Time-to-relief medians are not response rates: some placebo attacks also resolve, and neither trial was sized to test airway outcomes or mortality.

shelves.title: Ligelizumab for chronic spontaneous urticaria (phase 2b, PEARL 1 & 2)
shelves.question: Does the high-affinity anti-IgE antibody ligelizumab control hives better than placebo — and better than omalizumab — in chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled by antihistamines (Maurer's phase 2b dose-finding trial and the PEARL phase 3 programme)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Allergic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Anti-Idiotypic/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chronic Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Immunoglobulin E/blood,immunology
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY that ligelizumab beats placebo; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) that it does NOT beat omalizumab. The phase 2b trial (382 patients) suggested more: complete control of hives at week 12 in 51% on ligelizumab 72 mg and 42% on 240 mg versus 26% on omalizumab and 0% on placebo. The phase 3 PEARL trials (2,057 adults across two identically designed studies) confirmed superiority over placebo (week-12 UAS7 change-from-baseline differences of −8.0 to −11.1 points; p<0.0001) but found no superiority over omalizumab (differences −0.7 to +0.7 points, every confidence interval crossing zero). The phase 2 suggestion of beating omalizumab was not reproduced at phase 3 scale — the split stamp keeps both halves. Omalizumab for CSU lives on Shelf #398, remibrutinib on #828 and dupilumab for CSU on #1039; none is re-carded here.

cards.headline: Maurer phase 2b 2019: complete hive control at week 12 in 51% on ligelizumab 72 mg vs 26% on omalizumab and 0% on placebo
cards.summary: Maurer 2019 (phase 2b): complete hive control at week 12 in 51% on ligelizumab 72 mg vs 26% on omalizumab and 0% on placebo.
cards.people: 382 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled with H1-antihistamines (at approved or increased doses, alone or with H2-antihistamines or leukotriene-receptor antagonists), randomised to ligelizumab 24, 72 or 240 mg, omalizumab 300 mg, or placebo every 4 weeks for 20 weeks, or a single 120 mg ligelizumab dose. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 12, complete control of hives (weekly hives-severity score 0) was achieved by 30% (24 mg), 51% (72 mg) and 42% (240 mg) on ligelizumab, versus 26% on omalizumab and no patients (0%) on placebo; a dose-response relationship was established. Complete control of symptoms (weekly urticaria activity score 0) occurred in 30%, 44% and 40% on ligelizumab versus 26% on omalizumab and 0% on placebo. No safety concerns regarding ligelizumab or omalizumab emerged in this small, short trial.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding trial, not powered for the ligelizumab-versus-omalizumab comparison its percentages invite: the apparent edge over omalizumab (51% versus 26%) is precisely the claim the phase 3 programme then failed to confirm.
cards.source: Maurer M et al. Ligelizumab for Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(14):1321-1332. PMID: 31577874. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02477332, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PEARL 1 & 2 2024: ligelizumab beat placebo clearly (UAS7 −8.0 to −11.1 points) and omalizumab not at all (−0.7 to +0.7 points)
cards.summary: PEARL 1 & 2 2024: ligelizumab beat placebo clearly (UAS7 −8.0 to −11.1 points) and omalizumab not at all (−0.7 to +0.7 points).
cards.type: Two identically designed randomised, double-blind, active- and placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (52 weeks)
cards.people: 2,057 adult patients (of those randomised across both studies: 72 mg ligelizumab 614; 120 mg ligelizumab 616; omalizumab 300 mg 618; placebo 209) aged 12 years or older with moderate-to-severe H1-antihistamine-refractory CSU, at 347 sites in 46 countries; 1,480 (72%) were female and 577 (28%) male; mean baseline UAS7 ranged from 29.37 to 31.10 across groups. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 12, estimated differences in mean change-from-baseline UAS7 versus placebo were −8.0 (95% CI −10.6 to −5.4; PEARL-1) and −10.0 (−12.6 to −7.4; PEARL-2) for 72 mg ligelizumab, and −8.0 (−10.5 to −5.4) and −11.1 (−13.7 to −8.5) for 120 mg — both doses superior to placebo in both studies (p<0.0001). Versus omalizumab, the same differences were +0.7 (−1.2 to 2.5) and +0.4 (−1.4 to 2.2) for 72 mg, and +0.7 (−1.1 to 2.5) and −0.7 (−2.5 to 1.1) for 120 mg — not superior in either study. No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis population is described as eligible adult patients although enrolment began at age 12; and 'superior to placebo, equal to omalizumab' is the whole result — any claim of an advance over existing anti-IgE therapy is unsupported by these two trials.
cards.source: Maurer M et al. Efficacy and safety of ligelizumab in adults and adolescents with chronic spontaneous urticaria: results of two phase 3 randomised controlled trials. Lancet. 2024;403(10422):147-159. PMID: 38008109. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03580369 (PEARL-1) and NCT03580356 (PEARL-2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: better than placebo (LIKELY); better than omalizumab — no (LIKELY the null)
cards.summary: Better than placebo (LIKELY); better than omalizumab — no (LIKELY the null). The phase-2 suggestion dissolved in phase 3.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: phase 2b (382 patients) and PEARL 1 & 2 (2,057 patients randomised).
cards.result: The evidence arc is the lesson of this shelf: a phase 2 pattern suggesting superiority over omalizumab (51% versus 26% complete hive control) dissolved in two large phase 3 trials whose head-to-head differences were −0.7 to +0.7 UAS7 points, while the placebo comparison held up in both (−8.0 to −11.1 points; p<0.0001). shelves.title: Dupilumab for chronic spontaneous urticaria (LIBERTY-CSU CUPID)
shelves.question: In chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled by H1 antihistamines in anti-IgE-naive patients, does dupilumab reduce itch and hive activity versus placebo (LIBERTY-CSU CUPID-A and its replicate, CUPID-C)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Urticaria/drug therapy,immunology,diagnosis · Pruritus/drug therapy,etiology · Severity of Illness Index · Histamine H1 Antagonists/therapeutic use,administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two replicate phase 3 randomised trials with the same design (CUPID-A, 2019–2021, and CUPID-C, 2022–2024) both found dupilumab superior to placebo in anti-IgE-naive patients whose CSU was uncontrolled on H1 antihistamines. In CUPID-C (151 participants), week-24 least-squares mean changes favoured dupilumab on itch (ISS7 −8.64 versus −6.10; difference −2.54 points, 95% CI −4.65 to −0.43; P=.02) and urticaria activity (UAS7 −15.86 versus −11.21; difference −4.65 points, −8.65 to −0.65; P=.02), and the pooled CUPID-A and -C analysis (289 participants) showed the same direction. Effects are modest symptom-score differences, not complete-control rates. Dupilumab's other indications stay home — atopic dermatitis #374, nasal polyps #375, eosinophilic oesophagitis #396, asthma #1031 — and the other CSU drugs stay home too: omalizumab #398, remibrutinib #828, ligelizumab #1038. No trial from those shelves is re-carded here.

cards.headline: LIBERTY-CSU CUPID-C 2026 (with CUPID-A pooled): dupilumab improved itch by −2.54 points and urticaria activity by −4.65 points versus placebo at week 24
cards.summary: LIBERTY-CSU CUPID-C 2026 (with CUPID-A pooled): dupilumab improved itch by −2.54 points and urticaria activity by −4.65 points vs placebo at week 24.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 24-week phase 3 trial (CUPID-C), reported with its replicate trial CUPID-A
cards.people: CUPID-C analysed 151 participants (mean age 44.7 years, SD 16.9; 106 females, 70.2%) aged 6 to 80 years with CSU uncontrolled on H1 antihistamines and naive to anti-IgE therapy, in 10 countries; 51% were taking H1 antihistamines above the recommended dose and 59.6% had a baseline UAS7 of 28 or greater. The pooled CUPID-A and -C population numbered 289 participants.
cards.result: At week 24 in CUPID-C, least-squares mean changes were −8.64 (SE 1.41) on dupilumab versus −6.10 (1.40) on placebo for Itch Severity Score over 7 days (difference −2.54 points, 95% CI −4.65 to −0.43; P=.02) and −15.86 (2.66) versus −11.21 (2.65) for Urticaria Activity Score over 7 days (difference −4.65 points, −8.65 to −0.65; P=.02). shelves.title: Pilocarpine drops for presbyopia: GEMINI 1
shelves.question: Does pilocarpine 1.25% eye drops, dosed daily, improve mesopic near visual acuity without losing distance vision in presbyopia — and at what price in adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Color Vision · Pilocarpine · Presbyopia/drug therapy · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single standalone phase 3 report (GEMINI 1; 323 participants aged 40–55), pilocarpine 1.25% once daily beat vehicle on the primary endpoint — gaining ≥3 lines of mesopic near visual acuity at hour 3 on day 30 in 30.7% versus 8.1% (difference 22.5 percentage points) — with a smaller margin at hour 6 (18.4% vs 8.8%) and no participant with a near gain losing more than 5 letters of distance acuity. The twin trial, GEMINI 2, has no standalone report — only a pooled analysis exists, which the library does not card as an anchor — so this remains a single-report shelf and caps at POSSIBLE. The abstract reports an acceptable safety profile without enumerating headache or brow-ache rates, and none are printed here.

cards.headline: GEMINI 1 (2022): ≥3-line near-vision gain at hour 3 in 30.7% versus 8.1% with vehicle (difference 22.5 points)
cards.summary: GEMINI 1 (2022): ≥3-line near-vision gain at hour 3 in 30.7% vs 8.1% with vehicle (difference 22.5 points).
cards.type: Vehicle-controlled, participant- and investigator-masked, randomised, phase 3 trial (36 US sites)
cards.people: 323 individuals with presbyopia aged 40 to 55 years, randomised to pilocarpine hydrochloride 1.25% (AGN-190584) (163) or its vehicle (160), administered bilaterally once daily for 30 days; 72.8% female; mean (SD) age 49.6 (3.5) years; baseline mean mesopic near acuity 29.2 (6.3) letters.
cards.result: On day 30 at hour 3, improvement of ≥3 lines in mesopic, high-contrast, binocular distance-corrected near visual acuity occurred in 30.7% (50 of 163) with pilocarpine versus 8.1% (13 of 160) with vehicle (difference 22.5%, 95% CI 14.3% to 30.8%; adjusted P<.001); at hour 6 the figures were 18.4% versus 8.8% (difference 9.7%, 2.3% to 17.0%; P=.01). At hour 8 the ≥3-line difference was not statistically significant, though prespecified mean-change measures favoured pilocarpine. No participant with a ≥3-line near gain at hour 3 lost more than 5 letters of distance acuity. Onset was at 15 minutes. The authors report an acceptable safety and tolerability profile; the abstract does not enumerate specific adverse-event rates.
cards.watchOut: Thirty days, one formulation, ages 40–55 only — no evidence here for older presbyopes, longer use, or comparison with reading glasses, which remain the zero-drug standard. Industry trial (Allergan/AbbVie product).

shelves.title: Lotilaner for Demodex blepharitis: Saturn-1 and Saturn-2
shelves.question: Does lotilaner 0.25% ophthalmic solution eradicate Demodex mites and clear collarettes versus vehicle in Demodex blepharitis?
shelves.mesh: Ophthalmic Solutions · Blepharitis · Oxazoles · Thiophenes · Animals · Mite Infestations/drug therapy · Blepharitis/drug therapy,diagnosis
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel randomised, vehicle-controlled trials agree on large effects. Saturn-1 (421 patients): clinically meaningful collarette cure 81.3% versus 23.0%, mite eradication 67.9% versus 17.6% at day 43. Saturn-2 (412 patients): collarette cure 56.0% versus 12.5%, mite eradication 51.8% versus 14.6%. Both trials found the drops comfortable (about 91–92% rating them neutral to very comfortable) and ocular adverse events mild, chiefly instillation-site pain. Two blinded trials of the same question carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: Saturn-1 (2023): collarette cure 81.3% versus 23.0% and mite eradication 67.9% versus 17.6% at day 43
cards.summary: Saturn-1 (2023): collarette cure 81.3% vs 23.0% and mite eradication 67.9% vs 17.6% at day 43.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, vehicle-controlled, double-masked, phase 2b/3 trial
cards.people: 421 patients with Demodex blepharitis, randomised 1:1 to lotilaner 0.25% ophthalmic solution or vehicle, bilaterally twice daily for 43 days, evaluated at days 8, 15, 22 and 43. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At day 43, the lotilaner group achieved clinically meaningful collarette cure (grade 0 or 1) in 81.3% versus 23.0% (P<0.0001), complete collarette cure (grade 0) in 44.0% versus 7.4%, mite eradication (0 mites/lash) in 67.9% versus 17.6%, erythema cure in 19.1% versus 6.9%, and composite cure in 13.9% versus 1.0% — all statistically significant. Nearly 92.0% of patients rated the drop neutral to very comfortable; all ocular adverse events in the lotilaner group were mild, the most common being instillation-site pain.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks of treatment with sign-based endpoints graded on lashes and lids; erythema and composite cure rates are far lower than collarette cure — the symptom patients feel (redness) responds least. Industry programme trial.

cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-masked, vehicle-controlled, multicentre, phase 3 trial (21 US sites)

shelves.title: SMILE versus LASIK for myopia
shelves.question: Does small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) match femtosecond LASIK on visual quality and patient experience in myopia?
shelves.mesh: Corneal Stroma/surgery · Corneal Surgery, Laser · Dry Eye Syndromes/physiopathology · Glare · Intraoperative Period · Keratomileusis, Laser In Situ/methods · Lasers, Excimer/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised evidence is two small trials with equivalence-shaped results. In the paired-eye trial (70 patients, one eye SMILE and one LASIK), subjective visual symptoms did not differ at 3 months, though SMILE caused more intraoperative discomfort during tissue manipulation and more blurring at 1 month. In the parallel trial (SMILE 113 eyes, FS-LASIK 84 eyes), uncorrected acuity was worse with SMILE on day 1 but identical by 6 months, with less induced spherical aberration after SMILE. The wider SMILE literature is dominated by cohort series and meta-analyses of them, which is itself stated here: two small RCTs with short follow-up earn POSSIBLE, not more.

cards.headline: Paired-eye trial (2018): symptoms equal by 3 months; more discomfort during SMILE tissue manipulation, more blurring at 1 month
cards.summary: Paired-eye trial (2018): symptoms equal by 3 months; more discomfort during SMILE tissue manipulation, more blurring at 1 month.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, paired-eye, single-masked clinical trial (Singapore National Eye Centre)
cards.people: 70 patients with myopia, randomly treated with SMILE in one eye and femtosecond LASIK in the other, completing intraoperative questionnaires immediately after surgery and postoperative questionnaires at 1 and 3 months. Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Average discomfort was higher during tissue manipulation in SMILE (1.9 ± 0.9) than during flap lifting in LASIK (1.59 ± 0.8) (P=.020), but comparable during docking and laser application. Fear was lower in SMILE during docking (2.6 ± 1.6 vs 3.4 ± 1.9, P=.024) and similar at other stages. At 1 month, patients reported more blurring after SMILE than LASIK (2.1 ± 0.8 vs 1.8 ± 0.7, P=.025); at 3 months there were no differences in any visual symptom.
cards.watchOut: Seventy patients, subjective endpoints, single centre, 3 months — a patient-experience trial, not an acuity or safety trial; rare complications (the outcomes that decide between these operations at population scale) cannot be assessed at this size.
cards.source: Damgaard IB et al. Intraoperative Patient Experience and Postoperative Visual Quality After SMILE and LASIK in a Randomized, Paired-Eye, Controlled Study. J Refract Surg. 2018;34(2):92-99. PMID: 29425387. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this trial report's record carries no databank registry field.

cards.headline: Parallel RCT (2016): day-1 acuity favoured FS-LASIK, 6-month acuity identical; less spherical aberration after SMILE
cards.summary: Parallel RCT (2016): day-1 acuity favoured FS-LASIK, 6-month acuity identical; less spherical aberration after SMILE.

cards.result: Uncorrected distance visual acuity was better in the FS-LASIK group on postoperative day 1 (P<0.05), with no significant difference at 6 months (P=0.9). shelves.title: Antibiotics for acute infective conjunctivitis
shelves.question: Do topical antibiotics actually shorten acute infective conjunctivitis — fusidic acid versus placebo in adults, and chloramphenicol versus placebo in children — or does a self-limiting illness mostly need time?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Conjunctivitis, Bacterial/drug therapy · Fusidic Acid/therapeutic use · Survival Analysis · Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Chloramphenicol/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (antibiotics add little): Two placebo-controlled trials in primary care, one in adults and one in children, point the same way. Fusidic acid in adults: recovery at 7 days differed by an adjusted 5.3 percentage points (95% CI −11 to 18) despite bacterial eradication of 76% versus 41%. Chloramphenicol in children: clinical cure by day 7 was 86% versus 83% (risk difference 3.8%, −4.1% to 11.8%). Most acute infective conjunctivitis resolves by itself; the antibiotic reliably kills bacteria on the swab without reliably speeding the patient's recovery. Two blinded placebo trials carrying the same message earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: Rietveld 2005 (adults): fusidic acid recovery at 7 days differed by 5.3 points (CI −11 to 18) — eradication without recovery
cards.summary: Rietveld (2005, adults): fusidic acid recovery at 7 days differed by 5.3 points (CI −11 to 18) — eradication without recovery.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (25 Dutch primary-care centres)
cards.people: 181 adults presenting in primary care with a red eye and (muco)purulent discharge or glued eyelids, allocated to fusidic acid gel 1% or placebo, one drop four times daily for one week; 163 were analysed. Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At 7 days, 45 of 73 patients on fusidic acid and 53 of 90 on placebo had recovered (adjusted risk difference 5.3%, 95% CI −11 to 18), and median symptom duration did not differ. Baseline bacterial culture was positive in 32% (58 of 181). Bacterial eradication was 76% on treatment versus 41% on placebo (risk difference 35%, 9.3 to 60.4), and in culture-positive patients the recovery effect tended to be stronger (adjusted risk difference 23%, −6 to 42) without reaching significance. The authors state the findings do not support routine fusidic acid prescribing by GPs.
cards.watchOut: The interval is wide — the trial cannot exclude a moderate benefit, particularly in the culture-positive minority (only a third of presentations) — but the point estimate for unselected prescribing is small. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a self-limiting illness wearing an antibiotic habit — LIKELY that antibiotics add little.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Rietveld 2005 (181 adults) and Rose 2005 (326 children).
cards.result: The two trials isolate the habit's flaw: antibiotics clearly eradicate bacteria (76% vs 41%) yet recovery at a week barely moves (differences of about 4–5 points, both intervals including zero). shelves.title: Lebrikizumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: ADvocate 1 and 2, and ADhere
shelves.question: Does the IL-13 antibody lebrikizumab clear skin and itch versus placebo — as monotherapy in adolescents and adults (ADvocate 1 and 2), and combined with topical corticosteroids (ADhere)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,immunology,therapeutic use · Dermatitis, Atopic/complications,drug therapy,immunology · Interleukin-13/antagonists & inhibitors,immunology · Pruritus/drug therapy,etiology,immunology · Severity of Illness Index · Immunoglobulin G/immunology · Skin/drug effects,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two identically designed phase 3 monotherapy trials (ADvocate 1: 424 patients; ADvocate 2: 427) both met their primary endpoint at week 16 — clear or almost clear skin with ≥2-point improvement in 43.1% and 33.2% on lebrikizumab versus 12.7% and 10.8% on placebo, with EASI-75 in 58.8% and 52.1% versus 16.2% and 18.1%. The combination trial (ADhere, with topical corticosteroids) found the same direction (EASI-75 69.5% vs 42.2%). Conjunctivitis was the consistent excess adverse event. Two blinded trials plus a concordant combination trial carry LIKELY. Dupilumab (Shelf #374) and the oral JAK inhibitors (Shelf #820) are different mechanisms and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Deucravacitinib, the oral TYK2 inhibitor, for plaque psoriasis: POETYK PSO-1 and PSO-2
shelves.question: Does once-daily oral deucravacitinib beat placebo — and the older oral standard, apremilast — on skin clearance in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Psoriasis/diagnosis,drug therapy,chemically induced · Thalidomide/analogs & derivatives · Heterocyclic Compounds · TYK2 Kinase/antagonists & inhibitors · Dermatologic Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two replicate 52-week phase 3 trials both showed deucravacitinib superior to placebo and to apremilast at week 16. POETYK PSO-1 (666 patients): PASI 75 in 58.4% versus 12.7% (placebo) and 35.1% (apremilast). POETYK PSO-2 (1,020 patients): 53.0% versus 9.4% and 39.8%. Efficacy was maintained through week 52 in both, and adverse-event rates were similar across arms in PSO-1, with nasopharyngitis the most frequent event in PSO-2. Two blinded replicate trials carry LIKELY. The injectable biologics live on Shelf #377 and the non-steroidal topicals on Shelf #824; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: POETYK PSO-1 (Armstrong 2023): PASI 75 at week 16 in 58.4% versus 12.7% placebo and 35.1% apremilast
cards.summary: POETYK PSO-1 (2023): PASI 75 at week 16 in 58.4% vs 12.7% placebo and 35.1% apremilast.
cards.people: 666 adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, randomised 2:1:1 to deucravacitinib 6 mg daily (332), placebo (166), or apremilast 30 mg twice daily (168). Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 75 (≥75% reduction in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index) was achieved by 194 patients (58.4%) on deucravacitinib versus 21 (12.7%) on placebo and 59 (35.1%) on apremilast (P<.0001), and static Physician's Global Assessment 0 or 1 by 178 (53.6%) versus 12 (7.2%) and 54 (32.1%) (P<.0001). Efficacy improved beyond week 16 and was maintained through week 52. Adverse event rates with deucravacitinib were similar to those with placebo and apremilast. Registry ID: NCT03624127, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.
cards.watchOut: One-year duration and limited racial diversity, per the authors. The apremilast comparison is a genuine active-control win, but neither trial compares deucravacitinib with an injectable biologic, where clearance rates run higher.

shelves.title: Continuous terbinafine versus pulse itraconazole for toenail onychomycosis: the LION study
shelves.question: For toenail onychomycosis, does continuous terbinafine cure more nails than intermittent (pulse) itraconazole — and does the advantage persist at five-year blinded follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage · Foot Dermatoses/drug therapy · Itraconazole/administration & dosage · Naphthalenes/administration & dosage · Onychomycosis/drug therapy · Terbinafine · Antifungal Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the LION study (496 patients, double-blind, double-dummy), mycological cure at week 72 was 75.7–80.8% in the continuous terbinafine groups versus 38.3–49.1% in the pulse itraconazole groups (all comparisons P<0.0001). The programme's 5-year blinded follow-up (151 patients) found the gap persisted — mycological cure without second intervention in 46% versus 13%, with relapse roughly twice as common after itraconazole. One randomised programme plus its pre-planned long-term follow-up, with very large and durable differences, carries LIKELY; there were no differences in adverse events between the strategies in LION.

cards.headline: LION (Evans & Sigurgeirsson 1999): mycological cure at week 72 was 75.7–80.8% on terbinafine versus 38.3–49.1% on pulse itraconazole
cards.summary: LION (1999): mycological cure at week 72 was 75.7–80.8% on terbinafine vs 38.3–49.1% on pulse itraconazole.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, multicentre, parallel-group study (35 centres, six European countries; 72 weeks)
cards.people: 496 patients aged 18 to 75 years with clinical and mycological dermatophyte onychomycosis of the toenail, randomised to terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 or 16 weeks (T12, T16) or itraconazole 400 mg daily for 1 week in every 4, for 12 or 16 weeks (I3, I4). Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Mycological cure (negative microscopy and culture of the target toenail) at week 72: 75.7% (81 of 107) T12 and 80.8% (80 of 99) T16, versus 38.3% (41 of 107) I3 and 49.1% (53 of 108) I4 — all four terbinafine-versus-itraconazole comparisons P<0.0001, and all secondary clinical outcomes also favoured terbinafine. There were no differences in the number or type of adverse events between the terbinafine and itraconazole groups.
cards.watchOut: 1999-era trial, culture-based endpoint at 72 weeks in dermatophyte infection only — it does not cover non-dermatophyte moulds or yeast, fingernail-only disease, or patients who cannot take terbinafine. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: LION 5-year follow-up (Sigurgeirsson 2002): cure without re-treatment 46% versus 13%; relapse 23% versus 53% (mycological)
cards.summary: LION 5-year follow-up (2002): cure without re-treatment 46% vs 13% ; relapse 23% vs 53%.
cards.type: Long-term prospective blinded follow-up of the randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial (3 centres in Iceland)
cards.people: 151 patients aged 18 to 75 years with dermatophyte toenail onychomycosis from the LION programme (74 terbinafine-treated, 77 itraconazole-treated), followed for a median of 54 months; patients not cured at month 18 or who relapsed were offered an additional terbinafine course (second intervention). Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At the end of follow-up, mycological cure without second intervention was found in 34 of 74 terbinafine patients (46%) versus 10 of 77 itraconazole patients (13%) (P<.001). Mycological relapse was 23% versus 53% and clinical relapse 21% versus 48% (both significantly higher after itraconazole). Of 72 patients who received subsequent terbinafine treatment, 63 (88%) achieved mycological cure and 55 (76%) clinical cure.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up subset (151 of the original 496, from the Icelandic centres) — attrition and geography narrow it, and the second-intervention design means 'cure without re-treatment' is the honest endpoint, which is what is printed. Same programme as LION, counted once as evidence.

shelves.title: Head lice without the comb-out battle: spinosad, and ivermectin lotion
shelves.question: Do modern pediculicides clear head lice in one or two applications without nit combing — spinosad versus permethrin creme rinse, and single-application 0.5% ivermectin lotion versus vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Drug Combinations · Insecticides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Lice Infestations/drug therapy · Macrolides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Permethrin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Scalp Dermatoses/drug therapy · Administration, Topical
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two product programmes answer the same practical question. Spinosad (two phase 3 actual-use studies within one report; 1,038 participants) left 84.6% and 86.7% of primary participants lice-free without nit combing, versus 44.9% and 42.9% for permethrin with combing, most needing only one application. Ivermectin lotion (two multisite double-blind studies in one report; 765 patients completing) left 73.8% lice-free at day 15 after a single 10-minute application versus 17.6% on vehicle. Two programmes, four randomised studies in total, carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: Stough 2009: spinosad without combing left 84.6% and 86.7% lice-free versus 44.9% and 42.9% for permethrin with combing
cards.summary: Stough (2009): spinosad without combing left 84.6% and 86.7% lice-free vs 44.9% and 42.9% for permethrin with combing.
cards.type: Two phase 3, multicentre, randomised, evaluator/investigator-blinded, actual-use studies (reported together)
cards.people: 1,038 males and females aged 6 months and older with head lice, in 391 households; the youngest household member with ≥3 live lice was the primary participant, and all household members with lice received the same treatment (0.9% spinosad without nit combing, or 1% permethrin creme rinse with combing per product instructions), applied 1–2 times over 21 days.
cards.result: The proportion of lice-free primary participants 14 days after last treatment was 84.6% (study 1) and 86.7% (study 2) with spinosad versus 44.9% and 42.9% with permethrin (P<.001 for both). Most spinosad participants required 1 application, whereas most permethrin participants required 2. Adverse events were few and mild to moderate (eye irritation with permethrin; ocular hyperemia and application-site erythema/irritation with both); no laboratory measure changed significantly.
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles product with procedure (spinosad-without-combing vs permethrin-with-combing, as each is actually used) — pragmatic and fair to real life, but it cannot separate molecule from combing. Permethrin resistance in the study communities is part of the backdrop. No registry ID in the record's databank fields.

cards.type: Two multisite, randomised, double-blind studies (reported together)
cards.people: Patients 6 months of age or older with head-louse infestation; the index patient was the youngest household member with ≥3 live lice; 765 patients completed the studies. cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population, significantly more ivermectin patients were louse-free on day 2 (94.9% vs 31.3%), day 8 (85.2% vs 20.8%) and day 15 (73.8% vs 17.6%) (P<0.001 for each comparison). The frequency and severity of adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Vehicle-controlled, so this proves the lotion beats its own base — the comparative claim against older pediculicides comes from the spinosad card's permethrin data, not from this trial. The day-15 figure (73.8%) is lower than day 2 (94.9%) because reinfestation and hatching accumulate — quote day 15 for durability. A letter about this trial (PMID 23465113) is not carded.

shelves.title: An oral pill for hereditary angioedema attacks: sebetralstat (KONFIDENT)
shelves.question: Does oral sebetralstat, taken at attack onset, speed the beginning of symptom relief in hereditary angioedema attacks versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Cross-Over Studies · Hereditary Angioedema Types I and II/drug therapy · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Angioedemas, Hereditary/drug therapy,prevention & control · Plasma Kallikrein/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The phase 3 crossover trial (KONFIDENT; 110 participants treating 264 attacks) found median time to beginning of symptom relief of 1.61 hours (300 mg) and 1.79 hours (600 mg) versus 6.72 hours with placebo, with faster severity reduction and complete resolution (42.5% and 49.5% of attacks fully resolved within 24 hours versus 27.4%). The earlier two-part phase 2 crossover trial found the same direction on its primary endpoint (time to use of conventional attack treatment). A phase 2 plus phase 3 programme in the same direction carries LIKELY. Time-to-relief outcomes only; no mortality claim is made. Long-term prophylaxis lives on Shelf #400 and injectable icatibant (draft #1035) is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: KONFIDENT (2024): beginning of relief at a median 1.61 and 1.79 hours versus 6.72 hours on placebo
cards.summary: KONFIDENT (2024): beginning of relief at a median 1.61 and 1.79 hours vs 6.72 hours on placebo.
cards.people: 136 participants aged at least 12 years with type 1 or type 2 hereditary angioedema, assigned to one of six sequences of up to two oral doses of sebetralstat 300 mg, sebetralstat 600 mg, or placebo per attack; 110 participants treated 264 attacks. Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Median time to the beginning of symptom relief was 1.61 hours (IQR 0.78 to 7.04) with 300 mg and 1.79 hours (1.02 to 3.79) with 600 mg versus 6.72 hours (1.34 to >12) with placebo (P<0.001 and P=0.001). Time to reduction in attack severity and time to complete resolution were also faster with both doses. Complete resolution within 24 hours occurred in 42.5% of attacks (300 mg), 49.5% (600 mg) and 27.4% (placebo). Sebetralstat and placebo had similar safety profiles; no serious adverse events related to the trial agents were reported.
cards.watchOut: Crossover attack-level trial with patient-rated endpoints (global impression scales) — appropriate for this outcome, but the unit is attacks, not patients, and severe laryngeal attacks are not the population a self-administered oral trial can ethically enrol in numbers.
cards.source: Riedl MA et al. Oral Sebetralstat for On-Demand Treatment of Hereditary Angioedema Attacks. N Engl J Med. 2024;391(1):32-43. PMID: 38819658. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05259917, EudraCT: 2021-001226-21.

cards.headline: Phase 2 sebetralstat (2023): time to needing conventional treatment was significantly longer than with placebo in a crossover attack trial
cards.summary: Phase 2 sebetralstat (2023): time to needing conventional treatment was significantly longer than with placebo in a crossover attack trial.
cards.type: Two-part, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover phase 2 trial (25 sites, nine countries)
cards.people: 68 individuals aged 18 years or older with type 1 or 2 hereditary angioedema and at least three attacks in the past 93 days, not on prophylactic therapy; in part 2, 53 participants (78%) treated two attacks, one with sebetralstat 600 mg and one with placebo in randomised sequence. Part 1 (open-label single 600 mg dose): mean age 38.3 years (SD 13.2); 54% female.
cards.result: Time to use of conventional attack treatment within 12 hours was significantly longer with sebetralstat than placebo (at quartile 1: >12 h [95% CI 9.6 to >12] versus 8.0 h [3.8 to >12]; p=0.0010). Sebetralstat was rapidly absorbed (geometric mean plasma concentration 501 ng/mL at 15 minutes) with near-complete suppression of plasma kallikrein activity ex vivo. There were no serious adverse events or adverse-event-related discontinuations. Registry IDs in the record's databank fields include NCT04208412 (this phase 2 trial) and NCT05259917 (the phase 3 trial it led to).
cards.watchOut: A pharmacology-led phase 2 with a behavioural primary endpoint (reaching for conventional treatment) rather than a symptom endpoint — supportive, not standalone, evidence; the symptom claims rest on KONFIDENT.

shelves.title: Oral acyclovir for herpes simplex eye disease: the Herpetic Eye Disease Study
shelves.question: Does oral acyclovir help herpes simplex stromal keratitis heal when added to topical steroids — and does a year of suppressive acyclovir after an episode reduce recurrences of ocular herpes?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Administration, Oral · Administration, Topical · Drug Therapy, Combination · Keratitis, Herpetic/drug therapy,physiopathology · Patient Compliance · Prednisolone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute stromal treatment — in the HEDS stromal trial (104 patients, all on topical steroids and trifluridine), adding oral acyclovir changed nothing that mattered: median time to treatment failure 84 versus 62 days (not significant), failure by 16 weeks 75% versus 74%, resolution 18% versus 19%. POSSIBLE for recurrence prevention — in the HEDS prevention trial (703 patients), a year of oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily cut any ocular recurrence from 32% to 19% (P<0.001) and recurrent stromal keratitis from 28% to 14% (P=0.005) in those with prior stromal disease; a single trial, however definitive it became in practice, caps at POSSIBLE under the library's rules. The prevention effect is a relative reduction of about two-fifths, inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's neighbourhood, with absolute rates printed on the card.

cards.headline: HEDS stromal trial (1994): adding oral acyclovir to topical steroids did not speed failure or resolution (failure 75% versus 74% by 16 weeks)
cards.summary: HEDS stromal trial (1994): adding oral acyclovir to topical steroids did not speed failure or resolution (failure 75% vs 74% by 16 weeks).
cards.people: 104 patients with herpes simplex stromal keratitis without accompanying epithelial keratitis, randomised to oral acyclovir 400 mg five times daily for 10 weeks (51) or placebo (53), all receiving topical prednisolone phosphate and trifluridine, with examinations weekly on treatment and follow-up to 6 months. Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Median time to treatment failure was 84 days (95% CI 69 to 93) with acyclovir versus 62 days (57 to 90) with placebo — not significantly different. By 16 weeks, 38 patients (75%) on acyclovir and 39 (74%) on placebo had failed treatment, and keratitis had resolved without subsequent worsening in 9 (18%) versus 10 (19%). None of the comparisons — failure, resolution, time to resolution, or 6-month best-corrected visual acuity — was significantly different, though visual acuity improved over 6 months in significantly more patients in the acyclovir group.
cards.watchOut: Small (104 patients) and powered to detect a doubling of median time to failure — it excludes a large treatment effect, not a modest one; the lone positive (more patients with improved acuity) is a secondary signal against a field of nulls. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.
cards.source: Barron BA et al. Herpetic Eye Disease Study. A controlled trial of oral acyclovir for herpes simplex stromal keratitis. Ophthalmology. 1994;101(12):1871-82. PMID: 7997323. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pre-registration-era trial (1994).

cards.headline: HEDS prevention trial (1998): a year of acyclovir cut ocular recurrence from 32% to 19% and stromal recurrence from 28% to 14%
cards.summary: HEDS prevention trial (1998): a year of acyclovir cut ocular recurrence from 32% to 19% and stromal recurrence from 28% to 14%.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (12-month treatment, 6-month post-treatment observation)
cards.people: 703 immunocompetent patients who had had ocular herpes simplex disease within the preceding year, randomly assigned to acyclovir 400 mg orally twice daily or placebo for 12 months; 337 had a history of stromal keratitis. Mean age and sex mix are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The cumulative probability of recurrence of any ocular HSV disease during the 12-month treatment period was 19% with acyclovir versus 32% with placebo (P<0.001 — absolute rates beside the relative reduction of about two-fifths). Among patients with prior stromal keratitis, recurrent stromal keratitis occurred in 14% versus 28% (P=0.005). Nonocular (mainly orofacial) recurrence was also lower (19% vs 36%, P<0.001). There was no rebound in HSV disease rates in the six months after acyclovir was stopped.
cards.watchOut: Single trial — the reason for POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY despite its influence on practice — and its population is patients with an episode in the past year, the highest-recurrence group; indefinite-duration questions (beyond 12 months) are unanswered by design. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Fix the vein early and the leg ulcer heals: EVRA and ESCHAR
shelves.question: In venous leg ulceration, does treating the refluxing vein change healing, or only recurrence — early endovenous ablation (EVRA) against surgery added to compression (ESCHAR)?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques/adverse effects,methods · Catheter Ablation · Laser Therapy · Sclerotherapy · Varicose Ulcer/surgery,therapy · Wound Healing · Chronic Disease
shelves.balance: LIKELY, with the healing/recurrence split the two trials draw: early endovenous ablation hastened healing in EVRA (median 56 vs 82 days; hazard ratio for healing 1.38, relative, with the absolute medians and 24-week healing rates — 85.6% vs 76.3% — on the card), while ESCHAR's older open surgery did not improve healing at all (89% vs 93% healed at 3 years, P=0.73) but cut recurrence over 4 years (31% vs 56%) and increased ulcer-free time. Together: treat the vein early for healing (modern ablation), and expect the recurrence dividend over years either way. Which compression delivers the pressure while the ulcer heals is Shelf #1221; diabetic foot ulcers are Shelf #291, a different disease.

cards.headline: EVRA 2018: early ablation healed ulcers in a median 56 days versus 82 — healing at 24 weeks 85.6% vs 76.3%
cards.summary: EVRA (2018): early ablation healed ulcers in a median 56 days vs 82 — healing at 24 weeks 85.6% vs 76.3%.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (early versus deferred endovenous ablation, both with compression)
cards.people: 450 patients with venous leg ulcers at 20 UK centres, randomised to compression plus early endovenous ablation of superficial venous reflux (within 2 weeks) or compression alone with ablation deferred until healing or 6 months; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Time to ulcer healing was shorter with early intervention (hazard ratio for ulcer healing 1.38, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.68; P=0.001 — a relative measure; absolute medians: 56 days [95% CI 49 to 66] versus 82 days [69 to 92]). Healing at 24 weeks was 85.6% versus 76.3%. Median ulcer-free time in the first year was 306 versus 278 days (P=0.002). The most common procedural complications were pain and deep-vein thrombosis (no rates given in the abstract, and none printed here).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded by design, and the comparison is timing, not ablation versus none: the deferred group could receive ablation after healing or 6 months, so the trial measures the value of 'early', which is exactly the clinical question but not a test of whether ablation works at all.
cards.source: Gohel MS, Heatley F, Liu X et al. A Randomized Trial of Early Endovenous Ablation in Venous Ulceration. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(22):2105-2114. PMID: 29688123. Registry ID: ISRCTN02335796, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: ESCHAR (2007): surgery plus compression did not heal faster (93% vs 89% at 3 years) but recurrence at 4 years was 31% vs 56% .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (compression alone versus compression plus saphenous surgery), long-term follow-up
cards.people: 500 patients (500 legs) with open or recently healed leg ulcers and superficial venous reflux, in specialist nurse-led clinics at three UK vascular centres; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Ulcer healing rates at 3 years were 89% (compression) versus 93% (compression plus surgery) (P=0.73) — no healing benefit. Ulcer-free time after 3 years was greater with surgery (78% vs 71% of time; P=0.007).
cards.watchOut: Open surgical stripping in a pre-ablation era, in patients selected for superficial reflux: the healing null and recurrence benefit describe that operation and population, and the total-deep-reflux subgroup shows the recurrence benefit fading where reflux is not surgically correctable.

cards.result: The two trials are complements, not contradictions: ESCHAR's healing null came from adding an operation to compression and watching for years, while EVRA's healing gain came from doing the (less invasive) ablation within 2 weeks.
