shelves.title: Hosiery or bandages to heal the venous ulcer: VenUS IV
shelves.question: Does two-layer compression hosiery heal venous leg ulcers as fast as the four-layer bandage, and do the programme's trials — VenUS I, VenUS IV and VenUS 6 — agree on which compression system to use?
shelves.mesh: Compression Bandages/adverse effects,economics · Cost-Benefit Analysis · England · Health Care Costs/statistics & numerical data · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Northern Ireland · Quality-Adjusted Life Years
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials from one programme converge. VenUS I (2004) found the four-layer bandage more clinically and cost-effective than the short-stretch bandage after adjustment. VenUS IV (2014) found two-layer hosiery healed as fast as the four-layer bandage (median 99 vs 98 days; healed 70.9% vs 70.4%) — but more hosiery patients changed treatment (38.3% vs 27.0%), so hosiery suits many, not all. VenUS 6 (2026) found two-layer bandage non-inferior to evidence-based compression (four-layer bandage or two-layer hosiery) on its treatment-policy analysis (hazard ratio 1.01) while compression wraps healed more slowly (HR 0.78 vs evidence-based compression). The system matters less than sustained, correctly applied compression — and vein ablation timing is Shelf #1220.

cards.headline: VenUS IV 2014: hosiery healed as fast as the four-layer bandage (median 99 vs 98 days) — but 38.3% changed treatment, versus 27.0%
cards.summary: VenUS IV (2014): hosiery healed as fast as the four-layer bandage (median 99 vs 98 days ) — but 38.3% changed treatment vs 27.0%.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open, randomised controlled trial with masked photographic endpoint assessment
cards.people: 457 participants aged 18 or older with a venous leg ulcer and ankle-brachial pressure index ≥0.8, tolerant of high compression, at 34 centres in England and Northern Ireland, randomised to two-layer compression hosiery (230) or four-layer bandage (227); 453 contributed data. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to healing was 99 days (95% CI 84 to 126) on hosiery and 98 days (85 to 112) on bandage; ulcers healed in 70.9% versus 70.4%. More hosiery participants changed their allocated treatment (38.3% vs 27.0%; P=0.02). Of 895 adverse events in 300 participants, 85 (9.5%) were serious but unrelated to trial treatment. The authors conclude hosiery is a viable alternative, equally effective at healing, though the higher change rate suggests it is not suitable for all patients.
cards.watchOut: Open trial (participants and providers unmasked) with a pragmatic delivery model: 'equally effective' describes hosiery as actually worn in community care, including the third of patients who switched off it — efficacy under perfect adherence is a different number this trial does not give.

cards.headline: VenUS I 2004: the four-layer bandage beat the short-stretch bandage on adjusted healing and cost — the programme's baseline answer
cards.summary: VenUS I (2004): the four-layer bandage beat the short-stretch bandage on adjusted healing and cost — the programme's baseline answer (the BJS report of the same trial is not re-carded).
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation (HTA report)
cards.people: 387 people aged 23 to 97 years with a venous leg ulcer of at least 1 week's duration, at least 1 cm, and ankle-brachial pressure index ≥0.8, in community and hospital leg-ulcer services in England and Scotland; 82% had a reference ulcer of area ≤10 cm². The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Unadjusted Kaplan-Meier healing curves did not differ significantly between four-layer and short-stretch bandages; after adjustment (centre, ulcer area, duration, episodes, ankle mobility, weight) in a Cox model, a statistically significant treatment effect favoured the four-layer bandage — at any point, healing probability on short-stretch was significantly lower. The base-case economic analysis found the four-layer bandage dominant (greater benefit, lower cost, neither difference statistically significant), driven by fewer community nurse visits than the short-stretch arm required.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on adjustment: the unadjusted comparison was null, and the report is a 2004 HTA monograph of a bandaging era before hosiery kits and wraps existed — its durable lesson is that the elastic four-layer system, not bandaging in general, earned the standard-of-care place VenUS IV later tested hosiery against.

cards.headline: VenUS 6 2026: two-layer bandage met non-inferiority against evidence-based compression on the treatment-policy analysis (HR 1.01); wraps healed slower (HR 0.78)
cards.summary: VenUS 6 (2026): two-layer bandage met non-inferiority against evidence-based compression on the treatment-policy analysis (HR 1.01 relative) — carded from the currency sweep, analysis-dependence printed.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open, multicentre, randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 637 adults with a venous leg ulcer appropriate for compression, at 33 UK sites (2021-2024), randomised 1:1:1 to compression wraps (213), two-layer bandage (211) or evidence-based compression (213; two-layer hosiery or four-layer bandage); mean age 70.3 years (range 24.6 to 97.0); 55% male; 95% white; 633 contributed time at risk of healing.
cards.result: For the non-inferiority comparison (two-layer bandage vs evidence-based compression), the treatment-policy hazard ratio for healing was 1.01 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.28), meeting the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of 1.33; the hypothetical-strategy analysis gave HR 1.16 (0.86 to 1.58) and did NOT demonstrate non-inferiority. Healing was slower with compression wraps than with evidence-based compression (HR 0.78, 0.61 to 1.00; P=0.046) and two-layer bandage (HR 0.79, 0.61 to 1.01; P=0.056). Nine serious adverse events occurred, one potentially treatment-related (cause of death could not be ascertained). Departures from allocated treatment were common and healing events fewer than required for 80% power — both stated by the authors.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority here is analysis-dependent: it held under the treatment-policy strategy and failed under the hypothetical strategy, in an under-recruited trial with frequent treatment departures — read it as 'no clear disadvantage' for two-layer bandage, not as proven equivalence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: pick the compression the patient will actually wear, from the systems the trials cleared — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: pick the compression the patient will actually wear, from the systems the trials cleared — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VenUS I (387 patients), VenUS IV (457) and VenUS 6 (637) — three randomised trials spanning 1999-2024.
cards.result: The programme's arc is consistent: elastic four-layer bandaging set the standard (VenUS I, over short-stretch); two-layer hosiery matched it on healing while losing more patients to switching (VenUS IV); and two-layer bandage was not clearly worse than the evidence-based systems while wraps lagged (VenUS 6). No trial shows a healing difference large enough to override fit, exudate, leg shape and patient application — the adherence variables that decided VenUS IV's switch rates. Ablation timing, the other half of modern venous-ulcer care, is Shelf #1220.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are UK community-care trials in patients tolerant of high compression with adequate arterial circulation; none informs compression where arterial disease coexists beyond their entry thresholds.

shelves.title: Maggots to clean the wound: larval therapy in VenUS II
shelves.question: Do sterile larvae debride venous and mixed leg ulcers faster than hydrogel — and does faster debridement buy faster healing, or only a cleaner wound and more pain?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Bandages · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Debridement/economics,methods · Diptera · Hydrogel, Polyethylene Glycol Dimethacrylate/economics,therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — faster debridement · POSSIBLE — no faster healing. Two randomised trials agree that larvae clean the wound faster: VenUS II's hazard ratio for debridement was 2.31 (a relative measure, absolute times not stated in the abstract) and Mudge 2014 debrided 67.4% of larvae-treated ulcers within 21 days versus 26.2% on hydrogel. But VenUS II, the large trial, found no healing advantage (hazard ratio for healing 1.13, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.68) and no reduction in bacterial load — while ulcer pain was substantially higher with larvae (mean differences of 46.74 and 38.58 points on a 150 mm scale for loose and bagged larvae). The debridement effect is consistent across two trials (LIKELY); the healing null rests on the one large trial (POSSIBLE, per the single-trial ceiling). Larvae are a debridement tool with a pain cost, not a healing therapy.

cards.headline: VenUS II 2009: larvae debrided faster (HR 2.31, relative) but healed no faster (HR 1.13) — and hurt more
cards.summary: VenUS II (2009): larvae debrided faster (HR 2.31 relative) but healed no faster (HR 1.13) — and hurt more.
cards.people: 267 patients with at least one venous or mixed venous-arterial leg ulcer with ≥25% slough or necrotic tissue and ankle-brachial pressure index ≥0.6, in UK community, hospital ward and outpatient settings, randomised to loose larvae, bagged larvae or hydrogel. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Time to healing did not differ significantly between larvae (loose or bagged) and hydrogel (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.68; P=0.54 — a relative measure whose interval includes meaningful benefit and harm). Time to debridement was significantly shorter with larvae (HR 2.31, 1.65 to 3.2; P<0.001). Health-related quality of life and change in bacterial load did not differ; MRSA eradication by end of debridement was 75% (9/12) versus 50% (3/6) (P=0.34, underpowered). Mean ulcer pain scores were higher with larvae: loose versus hydrogel difference 46.74 (32.44 to 61.04) and bagged versus hydrogel 38.58 (23.46 to 53.70), both P<0.001, on a 0-150 mm scale.
cards.watchOut: A debridement trial whose primary outcome was healing: it answers both questions, and the answers point in opposite directions — quote the debridement hazard ratio only with the healing null and the pain difference beside it, as this card does.

cards.headline: Mudge 2014: BioFOAM larvae fully debrided 67.4% of ulcers within 21 days versus 26.2% on hydrogel — with more pain
cards.summary: Mudge (2014): BioFOAM larvae fully debrided 67.4% of ulcers within 21 days vs 26.2% on hydrogel — with more pain.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, open, observer-blind, parallel-group study
cards.people: 88 subjects with venous or mixed arterial/venous leg ulcers (64 completed the full study), comparing a larval therapy dressing (BioFOAM) with hydrogel (Purilon gel) on time to debridement over a 21-day intervention phase; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Among completers, 31 of 32 (96.9%) in the larvae arm debrided fully versus 11 of 32 (34.4%) on hydrogel; across all treated ulcers, 31 of 46 (67.4%) larvae-treated ulcers fully debrided within 21 days versus 11 of 42 (26.2%) on hydrogel (P=0.001). Larvae subjects needed significantly fewer dressing changes (mean 2.83 vs 5.40; P<0.001). Wound-bed and surrounding-skin condition did not differ significantly, and larvae subjects experienced more ulcer-related pain or discomfort (P<0.001). The authors note the possibility of re-sloughing should be monitored.

shelves.title: Feeding the pressure ulcer shut: arginine-enriched nutrition (Cereda; van Anholt)
shelves.question: Does a nutritional formula enriched with arginine, zinc and antioxidants heal established pressure ulcers faster than standard nutrition — in malnourished patients, and in patients who are not malnourished?
shelves.mesh: Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Arginine/therapeutic use · Food, Formulated/adverse effects · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Hospitalization · Malnutrition/complications,therapy · Pressure Ulcer/complications,therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of arginine-, zinc- and antioxidant-enriched formulas point the same way but are small and surrogate-ended. Cereda 2015 (200 malnourished patients, blinded, isocaloric/isonitrogenous control) found a greater reduction in ulcer area at 8 weeks on the enriched formula (60.9% vs 45.2%; adjusted difference 18.7%), with complete healing — the outcome patients care about — among secondary endpoints that did not differ. Van Anholt 2010 (43 non-malnourished patients, double-blind) found faster ulcer-size decrease and severity-score improvement with fewer dressings. Two small trials, one shared sponsor-era formula concept, no demonstrated complete-healing benefit: POSSIBLE. Wording note, per the library's standing rule: this shelf presents the formula as a pharmacologic-dose supplement tested as a drug; nothing here attributes ulcer healing, or any albumin change, to diet correcting a deficiency — albumin in this library reflects inflammation or injury, never diet. Pressure-injury PREVENTION (repositioning, support surfaces) is Shelf #796 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Cereda 2015: enriched formula shrank pressure ulcers more at 8 weeks (60.9% vs 45.2% area reduction) — complete healing not among the endpoints that differed
cards.summary: Cereda (2015): enriched formula shrank pressure ulcers more at 8 weeks ( 60.9% vs 45.2% area reduction) — complete healing was not among the endpoints (its odds ratio of 1.98 sits inside the developer's 0.5–2.0 observational band and is flagged as such on the card).
cards.people: 200 adult malnourished patients with stage II, III or IV pressure ulcers in long-term care or home care, randomised to an energy-dense, protein-rich formula enriched with arginine, zinc and antioxidants (400 mL/day; n=101) or an isocaloric, isonitrogenous control formula (n=99) for 8 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Ulcer area fell by 60.9% (95% CI 54.3 to 67.5) on the enriched formula versus 45.2% (38.4 to 52.0) on control (adjusted mean difference 18.7%, 5.7 to 31.8; P=0.017). A reduction in area of ≥40% at 8 weeks was more frequent on the enriched formula (odds ratio 1.98, 1.12 to 3.48; P=0.018 — a relative measure sitting just inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band, printed with its interval). No difference was found in the other secondary endpoints, which included complete healing, wound infections, number of dressings and 4-week area change.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is percentage area change at 8 weeks, not healed ulcers: a formula can win this endpoint while complete healing — listed among the endpoints that did not differ — stays unproven. Participants were all malnourished and able to drink supplements, which bounds who the result covers.

shelves.title: Irrigation of open fractures: solution and pressure (FLOW)
shelves.question: In patients with open fractures, does irrigating the wound with castile soap versus saline, or at high versus low pressure, change reoperation rates?
shelves.mesh: Fractures, Open/surgery,therapy · Therapeutic Irrigation/methods · Soaps/therapeutic use · Sodium Chloride/therapeutic use · Pressure · Reoperation · Wound Infection/prevention & control,surgery · Wound Healing · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: The definitive factorial trial (FLOW, 2,447 eligible patients at 41 centres) answers both halves. Pressure does not matter: reoperation within 12 months occurred in 13.2% with high pressure, 12.7% with low pressure and 13.7% with very low pressure (hazard ratios for the pairwise comparisons 0.92 to 1.02 relative, all confidence intervals crossing 1) — very low pressure is an acceptable, low-cost alternative. Solution does matter, against soap: reoperation occurred in 14.8% with castile soap versus 11.6% with normal saline (hazard ratio 1.32 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.66; P=0.01). One large trial settles the pressure question (LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)) and convicts soap in the same randomisation.

cards.headline: FLOW 2015: reoperation rates were identical across irrigation pressures (13.2% / 12.7% / 13.7%), and higher with castile soap than saline (14.8% vs 11.6%)
cards.summary: FLOW 2015: reoperation rates were identical across irrigation pressures (13.2% / 12.7% / 13.7%), and higher with castile soap than saline (14.8% vs 11.6%)
cards.type: Randomised trial with 2-by-3 factorial design (multicentre, single-blind outcome assessment)
cards.people: 2,551 patients with an open fracture of an extremity underwent randomization at 41 clinical centers, of whom 2,447 were deemed eligible and included in the final analyses; irrigation was by high pressure (>20 psi), low pressure (5 to 10 psi), or very low pressure (1 to 2 psi), with castile soap or normal saline, in a 2-by-3 factorial design. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Reoperation within 12 months — for promotion of wound or bone healing or treatment of a wound infection — occurred in 109 of 826 patients (13.2%) in the high-pressure group, 103 of 809 (12.7%) in the low-pressure group, and 111 of 812 (13.7%) in the very-low-pressure group. Hazard ratios for the three pairwise comparisons were: low versus high pressure, 0.92 relative (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.70 to 1.20; P=0.53); high versus very low pressure, 1.02 relative (95% CI, 0.78 to 1.33; P=0.89); and low versus very low pressure, 0.93 relative (95% CI, 0.71 to 1.23; P=0.62). Reoperation occurred in 182 of 1,229 patients (14.8%) in the soap group and in 141 of 1,218 (11.6%) in the saline group (hazard ratio, 1.32 relative; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.66; P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: A factorial trial reports each factor averaged over the other: the soap penalty (3.2 percentage points of reoperation) is the trial's most actionable finding and the one most often dropped when FLOW is cited as 'pressure doesn't matter'.
cards.source: FLOW Investigators et al. A Trial of Wound Irrigation in the Initial Management of Open Fracture Wounds. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26448371. shelves.title: Silver dressings for venous leg ulcers (VULCAN)
shelves.question: In patients with venous leg ulcers, do silver-donating antimicrobial dressings heal ulcers faster than non-adherent non-antimicrobial dressings?
shelves.mesh: Leg Ulcer/drug therapy · Anti-Infective Agents/therapeutic use · Bandages/economics,microbiology · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the PMID pinned in the topic file for this shelf (20140943) is, on verification, a comment letter about the trial with no abstract — not the trial report; the shelf is built on the trial's full report pinned from the record the topic file cross-referenced (PMID 19939335). In VULCAN (213 patients randomised), silver-donating dressings did not beat simple low-adherent dressings under compression on any endpoint: complete healing at 12 weeks was 59.6% with silver versus 56.7% with control (not significant), median time to healing did not differ (P=0.408), recurrence at 1 year was 11.6% versus 14.4%, quality-of-life measures showed no differences at any time point — and silver cost more, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £489,250 per QALY, leading the investigators to conclude the dressings were not cost-effective. A concordant null on every measured outcome, at higher cost: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: VULCAN 2009: silver dressings healed 59.6% of venous ulcers by 12 weeks versus 56.7% on plain dressings — no significant difference, at far higher cost per QALY
cards.summary: VULCAN 2009: silver dressings healed 59.6% of venous ulcers by 12 weeks versus 56.7% on plain dressings — no significant difference, at far higher cost per QALY
cards.type: Pragmatic, prospective randomised controlled trial with cost-effectiveness analysis (full HTA report of the VULCAN trial)
cards.people: 304 participants with active lower-leg ulceration present for more than 6 weeks were recruited in primary and secondary care in Sheffield and Exeter, England: 213 to the randomised trial (107 to silver-donating antimicrobial dressings, 106 to non-silver low-adherent control dressings, each applied beneath compression bandages or hosiery, with the specific product left to clinician preference) and 91 to a non-randomised observational arm. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: There were no significant differences (P>0.05) between the two groups for the primary outcome of proportion of ulcers healed at 12 weeks (59.6% for silver and 56.7% for control dressings). The overall median time to healing was also not significantly different between the two groups (P=0.408). A total of 24 patients had recurrent ulcers within 1 year; the recurrence rates of 11.6% (n=11) for the antimicrobial and 14.4% (n=13) for the control dressings were not significant. Mean utility valuations for both EQ-5D and SF-6D showed no differences for either group at 1, 3, 6 or 12 months. Compared with the control group, the antimicrobial group had an incremental cost of £97.85 and an incremental QALY gain of 0.0002, giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £489,250; modelling showed antimicrobial dressings were not cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: A class-level comparison — any silver-donating product versus any low-adherent dressing, chosen by clinicians — so the null convicts the strategy of routine silver use in non-infected venous ulcers, not every product in every wound; clinically infected ulcers were not this trial's frame.
cards.source: Michaels JA et al. shelves.title: Honey-impregnated dressings for venous leg ulcers
shelves.question: In patients with venous leg ulcers receiving compression, do honey-impregnated dressings improve healing versus usual care dressings?
shelves.mesh: Honey/adverse effects · Varicose Ulcer/economics,pathology,surgery · Wound Healing/physiology · Bandages, Hydrocolloid/adverse effects,economics · Stockings, Compression/adverse effects,economics · Quality of Life · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large trial (Jull 2008, 368 participants with venous ulcers, all receiving compression bandaging) found honey-impregnated calcium alginate dressings did not significantly improve healing: at 12 weeks, 55.6% had healed on honey versus 49.7% on usual care (absolute increase 5.9 percentage points, 95% CI −4.3 to 15.7; P=0.258), with no significant differences in time to healing, change in ulcer area, infection incidence, or quality of life — while honey was probably more expensive and was associated with more adverse events (relative risk 1.3 relative, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.6; P=0.013). The confidence interval cannot exclude a modest benefit, which is why this is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than LIKELY — and the adverse-event excess runs against honey. Honey for burns (Shelf #1271) is a different wound with positive small trials; the two must not be merged.

cards.headline: Jull 2008: honey dressings did not significantly improve venous ulcer healing at 12 weeks (55.6% vs 49.7%) and caused more adverse events
cards.summary: Jull 2008: honey dressings did not significantly improve venous ulcer healing at 12 weeks (55.6% vs 49.7%) and caused more adverse events
cards.people: 368 people with a venous leg ulcer in a community-based trial, randomised to calcium alginate dressings impregnated with manuka honey (187) or usual care (181); all participants received compression bandaging, and analysis was by intention to treat. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, 104 ulcers (55.6 per cent) in the honey-treated group and 90 (49.7 per cent) in the usual care group had healed (absolute increase 5.9 (95 per cent confidence interval −4.3 to 15.7) per cent; P=0.258). Treatment with honey was probably more expensive and associated with more adverse events (relative risk 1.3 relative (95 per cent c.i. 1.1 to 1.6); P=0.013). There were no significant differences between the groups for time to healing, change in ulcer area, incidence of infection, costs per healed ulcer, or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a patient-reported adverse-event profile (honey dressings sting and draw fluid, which may itself generate 'adverse events'): the harm signal is real but softer than the healing null, and the healing interval (−4.3 to +15.7 points) leaves a moderate benefit formally possible. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline for venous leg ulcers
shelves.question: In patients with venous leg ulcers, does oral pentoxifylline (with or without compression) increase healing versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Pentoxifylline/therapeutic use · Leg Ulcer/drug therapy · Varicose Ulcer/drug therapy,pathology · Hematologic Agents/therapeutic use · Wound Healing · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials point the same way but only one reaches significance. Colgan 1990 (80 patients, six months) found complete healing of the reference ulcer in 23 of 38 on pentoxifylline versus 12 of 42 on placebo, with life-table healing proportions at six months of 64% versus 34% (log rank P=0.03). Dale 1999 (200 patients, factorial design) found complete healing in 64% on pentoxifylline versus 53% on placebo — and its authors state plainly that the difference did NOT reach statistical significance, a qualification the topic file's one-line summary omitted; the record governs, and it is printed on the card below. Two concordant moderate signals, one significant and one not, on top of compression in both: POSSIBLE.

cards.type: Double blind, randomised, prospective, placebo controlled, parallel group study
cards.people: 80 consecutive patients with clinical evidence of venous ulceration of the leg, in whom appreciable arterial disease was excluded (ankle:brachial pressure ratio above 0.8), at four outpatient clinics in England and the Republic of Ireland; all received oxpentifylline 400 mg three times daily by mouth or matching placebo for six months (or until the reference ulcer healed), in addition to a locally standardised method of compression bandaging. cards.result: Complete healing of the reference ulcer occurred in 23 of the 38 patients treated with oxpentifylline and in 12 of the 42 patients treated with placebo. Life table analysis showed that the proportion of ulcers healed at six months was 64% in the group treated with oxpentifylline compared with 34% in the group treated with placebo (log rank test chi-squared 4.78, P=0.03), which was significant; the record also states an odds ratio of 1.81 (95% confidence interval 1.20 to 2.71).
cards.watchOut: Eighty patients from 1990, with a headline drawn from life-table estimates (64% vs 34%) that are larger than the raw healed counts (23/38 vs 12/42) suggest at a glance; the trial predates modern compression standards, though compression was used in both arms.

shelves.title: Prophylactic silicone foam dressings to prevent hospital pressure injuries
shelves.question: In high-risk hospital/aged-care patients, do prophylactic multi-layer silicone foam dressings on sacrum and heels reduce pressure-injury incidence versus standard prevention alone?
shelves.mesh: Pressure Ulcer/prevention & control · Bandages · Silicones · Sacrum · Heel · Nursing Homes · Homes for the Aged · Critical Illness/economics,therapy · Cost-Benefit Analysis/methods · Humans · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two randomised trials of the same dressing family in two high-risk settings agree. In aged care (Border III, 288 residents in 40 Australian nursing homes), pressure injuries developed in 16 residents on standard prevention versus 3 with prophylactic sacrum and heel dressings added (P=0.004) — an 80% relative risk reduction, with one injury prevented for every 12 residents treated. In critically ill hospital patients (the Border Trial, 440 patients), sacral and heel pressure-ulcer incidence was also significantly reduced with dressings (P=0.001), and the within-trial economic analysis found the intervention cost-saving overall (net AU$70.82 versus AU$144.56 per person). Concordant randomised evidence in hospital and residential care: LIKELY — with the standing caveat that a dressing trial cannot be blinded.

cards.people: 288 recently admitted residents enrolled from 40 Australian nursing homes, randomised to standard pressure-injury prevention as recommended by international guidelines (150) or the same standard care plus Mepilex Border Sacrum and Mepilex Heel dressings applied to sacrum and heels (138); participants were comparable on demographic and physiological parameters. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: More residents in the control group developed pressure injuries than in the intervention group (16 vs 3, P=0.004), and they developed more pressure injuries in total than residents in the intervention group. The authors state the results represent a relative risk reduction of 80% relative for residents treated with the dressings, and that for every 12 patients treated, one pressure injury was prevented.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen total events drive the headline: with 3 events in the intervention arm, a handful of differently judged borderline skin changes could move the result — the effect is large but its base is small, and skin assessment was unblinded.

cards.people: 440 critically ill patients in an acute care hospital, randomly allocated to prophylactic soft silicone multilayered foam dressings applied to the sacrum and heels in the emergency department and changed every 3 days in the ICU, or to standard pressure-ulcer prevention care during their ED and ICU stay; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The results showed a significant reduction of pressure-ulcer incidence rates in the intervention group (P=0.001). The intervention cost was estimated to be AU$36.61 per person based on an intention-to-treat analysis, but this was offset by lower downstream costs associated with pressure-ulcer treatment (AU$1103.52); the average net cost of the intervention was lower than that of the control (AU$70.82 versus AU$144.56). The authors conclude that prophylactic dressings in this setting result in cost savings in the acute care hospital. The record — a within-trial cost-benefit analysis of the Border Trial — reports the incidence result as a P value without the group rates, which are therefore not quoted on this card.
cards.watchOut: This card is the trial's economic companion paper: it confirms the incidence result and prices it, but an agent needing the Border Trial's primary rates must go to the primary report — and the whole programme evaluates one manufacturer's dressing family.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Border III 2018 (288 aged-care residents) and the Border Trial 2015 (440 critically ill patients).
cards.result: The prophylactic-dressing claim is one of the better-supported device claims in wound care: two randomised trials, two very different high-risk populations, the same direction, and a cost analysis that removes the usual price objection. The limits are printed on the cards — unblinded skin assessment, small event counts in aged care, single-product programme — and they hold this at LIKELY rather than beyond it. Support surfaces (Shelf #1285) and repositioning (Shelf #1286) address different layers of the same prevention stack and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from one research group studying one dressing family; independent replication with other products would strengthen the class claim.

shelves.title: Support surfaces for pressure-ulcer prevention (PRESSURE programme)
shelves.question: In patients at risk of pressure ulcers, do alternating-pressure mattresses/systems prevent ulceration better than standard or overlay surfaces?
shelves.mesh: Pressure Ulcer/epidemiology,prevention & control · Beds/adverse effects · Bedding and Linens · Patient Satisfaction · Humans · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The PRESSURE programme's two large trials are more equivocal than the topic file's summary suggests, and the records govern. PRESSURE 2 (2,029 high-risk inpatients) compared alternating-pressure mattresses with high-specification foam: at the primary 30-day post-treatment follow-up there was INSUFFICIENT evidence of a difference in time to a new category ≥2 pressure ulcer (hazard ratio 0.76 relative, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; P=0.089; absolute difference 2%); only the treatment-phase sensitivity analysis reached significance (hazard ratio 0.66 relative, 0.46 to 0.93; P=0.0176; absolute difference 2.6%). PRESSURE 1 (1,972 patients) compared alternating-pressure mattresses with alternating-pressure overlays and found no difference at all (new grade ≥2 ulcers in 10.3% versus 10.7%; difference 0.4%, −2.3 to 3.1; P=0.75). Small, time-limited advantages over foam at best: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PRESSURE 2 2019: alternating-pressure mattresses showed a small treatment-phase benefit over high-specification foam, but the primary follow-up analysis was not significant (HR 0.76; P=0.089)
cards.summary: PRESSURE 2 2019: alternating-pressure mattresses showed a small treatment-phase benefit over high-specification foam, but the primary follow-up analysis was not significant (HR 0.76; P=0.089)
cards.type: Multicentre, Phase III, open, parallel-group randomised controlled trial (full HTA report)
cards.people: 2,029 adult inpatients at high risk of pressure-ulcer development (acutely ill, bedfast/chairfast and/or with a category 1 ulcer or pain at a pressure-ulcer site), randomised at 42 UK secondary and community inpatient facilities to an alternating pressure mattress (1,016) or a high-specification foam mattress (1,013), for a maximum treatment phase of 60 days plus 30 days of post-treatment follow-up; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Of the 2,029 participants, 160 (7.9%) developed a new pressure ulcer of category 2 or worse. There was insufficient evidence of a difference between groups for time to new category ≥2 ulcer at the 30-day final follow-up (Fine and Gray model hazard ratio 0.76 relative, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; exact P=0.0890; 2% absolute difference). In the treatment-phase sensitivity analysis, 132 (6.5%) developed a new category ≥2 ulcer and the difference was statistically significant (hazard ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.93; P=0.0176; 2.6% absolute difference). There was no evidence of a difference for category ≥1 ulcers (hazard ratio 0.83 relative, 0.67 to 1.02) or category ≥3 ulcers (hazard ratio 0.81 relative, 0.40 to 1.62), or for healing of pre-existing category 2 ulcers. Health economic analysis showed alternating-pressure mattresses to be cost-effective compared with foam, with small cost differences and very small QALY gains. A lower-than-anticipated event rate limited the trial's power.
cards.watchOut: The honest headline is the primary analysis — 'insufficient evidence of a difference' — with the significant result confined to a sensitivity analysis of the treatment phase; a low event rate (7.9% overall) means even 2,029 patients left the main question imprecisely answered. The trial's journal report (PMID 31709401) is the same trial and is fenced in the synthesis, not counted twice.
cards.source: Nixon J et al. Comparing alternating pressure mattresses and high-specification foam mattresses to prevent pressure ulcers in high-risk patients: the PRESSURE 2 RCT. Health Technol Assess. 2019. PMID: 31559948. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN01151335, from the record's databank fields. The PRESSURE 2 journal report (EClinicalMedicine 2019, PMID 31709401) is the same trial as the HTA report carded above and is fenced here, not counted as separate evidence.
cards.result: Four thousand randomised patients across the programme yield a modest, carefully hedged answer: alternating-pressure mattresses may shave a couple of percentage points off ulcer incidence while the patient is on them compared with good foam, mattress and overlay formats are interchangeable, and patient comfort (fewer change requests on mattresses in PRESSURE 1) may be the most reliable difference. Prophylactic dressings (Shelf #1284) and repositioning schedules (Shelf #1286) are separate layers of prevention.
cards.watchOut: Event rates this low (8–11%) mean absolute gains from any surface are small; the trials' own conclusion points to better targeting of expensive surfaces rather than wider use.

shelves.title: Repositioning frequency for pressure-injury prevention (TEAM-UP and TURN)
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents at risk, can repositioning every 3–4 hours (on high-density foam) replace 2-hourly turning without increasing pressure injuries?
shelves.mesh: Pressure Ulcer/epidemiology,etiology,nursing · Nursing Homes · Beds/adverse effects,standards · Incidence · Risk Factors · Humans · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two large nursing-home trials on modern high-density foam mattresses found no penalty for longer intervals. TURN (942 residents at moderate or high risk, 27 nursing homes) found pressure-ulcer incidence of 2.5% with 2-hourly, 0.6% with 3-hourly and 3.1% with 4-hourly repositioning over 3 weeks — no significant difference (P=.68). TEAM-UP (992 residents analysed, nine nursing homes cluster-randomised to 2-, 3- or 4-hour protocols with sensor-cued staff) recorded ZERO pressure injuries in any arm during the 4-week intervention (versus 5.24% in the baseline period), with compliance best at 4 hours (95% vs 80% at 2 hours) — and its authors state explicitly that a causal link between interval and outcome was not established. Very low event rates throughout mean equivalence is suggested, not proven: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: TURN 2013: pressure-ulcer incidence did not differ between 2-, 3- and 4-hourly repositioning on high-density foam (2.5% / 0.6% / 3.1%)
cards.summary: TURN 2013: pressure-ulcer incidence did not differ between 2-, 3- and 4-hourly repositioning on high-density foam (2.5% / 0.6% / 3.1%)
cards.type: Multisite, randomized clinical trial (nursing homes, blinded skin assessment)
cards.people: 942 consenting residents aged 65 and older without pressure ulcers, at moderate (Braden scores 13–14) or high (scores 10–12) risk, in 20 US and 7 Canadian nursing homes using high-density foam mattresses, allocated by risk stratification to a 2-, 3- or 4-hour repositioning schedule for 3 weeks; participants were mostly female (77.6%) and Caucasian (80.5%), with mean age 85.1 ± 7.7 years; blinded assessors assessed skin weekly.
cards.result: Nineteen (2.0%) participants developed superficial pressure ulcers. There was no significant difference (Wilcoxon test for ordered categories) in pressure-ulcer incidence (P=.68) according to repositioning group (2 hour, 8 of 321, 2.5%; 3 hour, 2 of 326, 0.6%; 4 hour, 9 of 295, 3.1%), nor in incidence between high- and moderate-risk groups (P=.79), nor within high-risk (P=.90) or moderate-risk (P=.68) strata by schedule. The authors conclude there was no difference in incidence over 3 weeks between residents turned at 2-, 3- or 4-hour intervals on high-density foam mattresses when repositioned consistently and skin was monitored.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen events in 942 residents: the trial can exclude a large penalty for 4-hourly turning but not a small one, and its frame is explicit — moderate/high (not severe) risk, good foam, consistent repositioning and weekly skin checks are all part of the bargain.
cards.source: Bergstrom N et al. Turning for Ulcer ReductioN: a multisite randomized clinical trial in nursing homes. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2013. PMID: 24050454. cards.headline: TEAM-UP 2022: no pressure injuries occurred in any arm (2-, 3- or 4-hourly) during the intervention; compliance was best at 4 hours
cards.summary: TEAM-UP 2022: no pressure injuries occurred in any arm (2-, 3- or 4-hourly) during the intervention; compliance was best at 4 hours
cards.type: Embedded pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial (nine nursing homes)
cards.people: 1,100 residents in nine nursing homes fitted with wearable sensors; 992 residents formed the effective sample (mean age 78 ± 13 years; 63% women), all without current pressure injuries, with Braden scores of 10 or above (not severe risk), using viable 7-inch high-density foam mattresses; each nursing home was cluster-randomised to a single 2-, 3- or 4-hour repositioning interval as standard care for a 4-week intervention, with a wireless monitoring system cueing staff.
cards.result: The pressure-injury incidence during the intervention was 0.0% compared with 5.24% at baseline, even though intervention residents' clinical risk scores were significantly higher (P<.001). Repositioning compliance for the 4-hour interval (95%) was significantly better than for the 2-hour (80%) or 3-hour (90%) intervals (P<.001). The authors conclude that current 2-hour protocols can be relaxed for many nursing-home residents without compromising prevention — and state that a causal link was not established between repositioning interval treatments and the outcome, however, no new pressure injuries developed.
cards.watchOut: Zero events in every arm is reassuring and uninformative at once: with no injuries anywhere, the trial cannot rank the intervals, and its baseline comparison (5.24%) is historical, not randomised — the monitoring system and study attention are themselves part of what was tested.
cards.source: Yap TL et al. Effect of Varying Repositioning Frequency on Pressure Injury Prevention in Nursing Home Residents: TEAM-UP Trial Results. Adv Skin Wound Care. 2022. PMID: 35051978. shelves.question: In patients with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, does cyclical pressurised topical wound oxygen increase complete healing versus standard care with sham?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind, sham-controlled trial (TWO2) reported a large healing advantage for cyclical pressurised topical wound oxygen added to optimal standard care — complete closure at 12 weeks in 41.7% versus 13.5% (odds ratio 4.57 relative, 97.8% CI 1.19 to 17.57; P=0.010; adjusted odds ratio 6.00 relative), with 56% versus 27% still closed at 12 months (P=0.013). But the trial was STOPPED AT ITS FIRST predetermined interim analysis — after only 73 of a planned 220 patients completed the treatment phase — and trials stopped this early for benefit are known to overestimate effects; the confidence interval (odds ratios from 1.19 to 17.57 relative) is correspondingly wide. A real blinded signal at a fragile scale: POSSIBLE. Hyperbaric (systemic) oxygen is a different intervention, home on Shelf #1224.

cards.headline: TWO2 2020: topical wound oxygen closed 41.7% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers versus 13.5% on sham at 12 weeks — in a trial stopped at its first interim analysis
cards.summary: TWO2 2020: topical wound oxygen closed 41.7% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers versus 13.5% on sham at 12 weeks — in a trial stopped at its first interim analysis
cards.type: Multinational, multicenter, randomized, double-blinded, sham-controlled trial — stopped early for benefit at the first interim analysis
cards.people: Patients with diabetes and chronic diabetic foot ulcers that had failed to heal with standard care alone, randomised (double-blind) to active cyclical pressurised topical wound oxygen therapy or sham control therapy, both in addition to optimal standard care; the study used a group sequential design with predetermined analyses after 73, 146 and ultimately 220 patients completed the 12-week treatment phase, and stopped at the first analysis point. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At the first analysis point, the active arm was found superior to sham, with a closure rate of 41.7% compared with 13.5% (odds ratio (OR) 4.57 relative (97.8% CI 1.19, 17.57), P=0.010). After adjustment for University of Texas Classification ulcer grade, the OR increased to 6.00 relative (97.8% CI 1.44, 24.93), P=0.004. Cox proportional hazards modeling, also adjusted for ulcer grade, demonstrated over 4.5 times the likelihood to heal over 12 weeks compared with sham (hazard ratio 4.66 relative (97.8% CI 1.36, 15.98), P=0.004). At 12 months post-enrollment, 56% of active-arm ulcers were closed compared with 27% of sham-arm ulcers (P=0.013).
cards.watchOut: Stopping at the first of three planned looks, with roughly a third of the intended sample, is the design feature that matters most: early-stopped trials systematically exaggerate effect sizes, and an odds-ratio interval spanning 1.19 to 17.57 is the statistical shadow of that fragility. The 12-month durability figure (56% vs 27%) comes from the same small cohort.
cards.source: Frykberg RG et al. A Multinational, Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy of Cyclical Topical Wound Oxygen (TWO2) Therapy in the Treatment of Chronic Diabetic Foot Ulcers: The TWO2 Study. Diabetes Care. 2020. PMID: 31619393. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02326337, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a striking blinded result from a trial that stopped before it grew up — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a striking blinded result from a trial that stopped before it grew up — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: TWO2 2020 (stopped after 73 patients completed the treatment phase, of 220 planned).
cards.result: TWO2 is simultaneously the best-designed topical-oxygen test (multinational, double-blind, sham-controlled, hard closure endpoint) and a textbook early-stopping risk. The honest shelf reading: adjunctive cyclical topical oxygen probably improves healing of refractory diabetic foot ulcers, by an amount likely smaller than the headline odds ratio of 4.57 relative. Replication at full sample size would move this stamp; until then it sits at POSSIBLE. The sucrose octasulfate dressing trial (Shelf #1288) addresses a neighbouring ulcer population with a completed design.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this with hyperbaric oxygen evidence: systemic hyperbaric therapy and cyclical topical oxygen share a word, not a mechanism, dose, or trial base.

shelves.title: Sucrose octasulfate (TLC-NOSF) dressings for diabetic foot ulcers (Explorer)
shelves.question: In patients with neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers, does a sucrose octasulfate dressing increase wound closure versus a control dressing?
shelves.mesh: Sucrose/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Anti-Ulcer Agents/administration & dosage · Diabetic Foot/therapy · Diabetic Neuropathies/therapy · Ischemia/therapy · Bandages · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind trial (Explorer, 240 patients with non-infected neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers in five European countries) found wound closure at 20 weeks in 48% on the sucrose octasulfate dressing versus 30% on an identical dressing without it — an 18-percentage-point difference (95% CI 5 to 30; adjusted odds ratio 2.60 relative, 1.43 to 4.73; P=0.002) — with target-wound infections actually somewhat fewer on the active dressing (25 of 126 patients (20%) versus 32 of 114 (28%)), minor amputations in 1 versus 2 patients, and deaths in 3 (2%) versus 4 (4%) patients, none related to treatment. A clean, completed, blinded trial; the library's single-trial cap holds it at POSSIBLE, and the population — neuroischaemic ulcers specifically — is part of the claim.

cards.headline: Explorer 2018: sucrose octasulfate dressing closed 48% of neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers versus 30% on control at 20 weeks
cards.summary: Explorer 2018: sucrose octasulfate dressing closed 48% of neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers versus 30% on control at 20 weeks
cards.type: International, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial
cards.people: 240 inpatients or outpatients aged 18 years or older with diabetes and a non-infected neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcer greater than 1 cm², of University of Texas grade IC or IIC, at 43 hospitals with specialised diabetic foot clinics in France, Spain, Italy, Germany, and the UK, randomly assigned to a sucrose octasulfate dressing (126) or the same dressing without sucrose octasulfate (114) for 20 weeks, both with the same standard of care; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: After 20 weeks, wound closure occurred in 60 patients (48%) in the sucrose octasulfate dressing group and 34 patients (30%) in the control dressing group (18 percentage points difference, 95% CI 5–30; adjusted odds ratio 2.60 relative, 95% CI 1.43–4.73; P=0.002). In both groups, the most frequent adverse events were infections of the target wound: 33 wound infections in 25 (20%) patients of 126 in the sucrose octasulfate group and 36 in 32 (28%) patients of 114 in the control group. Minor amputations not affecting the wound site were reported in one (1%) patient in the sucrose octasulfate group and two (2%) patients in the control group. Three (2%) patients assigned to sucrose octasulfate and four (4%) assigned to control died, but none of the deaths were related to treatment, procedure, wound progression, or subsequent amputation.
cards.watchOut: The manufacturer (Laboratoires Urgo Medical) funded the trial, and the control was its own base dressing — a fair blinded comparison, but the only one; the result is specific to neuroischaemic, non-infected ulcers and does not extend to neuropathic-only or infected ulcers.
cards.source: Edmonds M et al. Sucrose octasulfate dressing versus control dressing in patients with neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers (Explorer): an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2018. PMID: 29275068. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01717183, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one completed blinded trial, an 18-point closure advantage, single-trial cap — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one completed blinded trial, an 18-point closure advantage, single-trial cap — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Explorer 2018 (240 patients with neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers).
cards.result: Explorer is among the stronger single dressing trials in this library: double-blind, multicentre, a hard closure endpoint, an absolute benefit of 18 percentage points (a number needed to treat of about 6), and no safety penalty — infections, minor amputations and deaths all at or below control rates. It earns POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY only because the library requires a second randomised trial for the higher grade. Topical oxygen for diabetic foot ulcers (Shelf #1287) is a different intervention aimed at overlapping wounds.
cards.watchOut: Quote the population with the number: '48% versus 30% closure' belongs to neuroischaemic ulcers in specialist clinics, not to diabetic foot ulcers generally.

shelves.title: Tap water versus sterile saline for wound cleansing
shelves.question: In patients with acute wounds/lacerations, does cleansing or irrigating with tap water result in infection rates no higher than sterile saline?
shelves.mesh: Fresh Water · Sodium Chloride · Lacerations/therapy · Therapeutic Irrigation/methods · Wound Infection/prevention & control · Emergency Service, Hospital · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The human randomised evidence is one multicentre trial (Moscati 2007, 715 adults enrolled with acute simple lacerations requiring sutures or staples; follow-up on 634): wound infection occurred in 12 of 300 (4%) irrigated with tap water versus 11 of 334 (3.3%) with sterile saline (relative risk 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.5 to 2.7), and the authors conclude the rates were equivalent, agreeing with previous single-institution trials. Disclosure: the second PMID pinned in the topic file for this shelf (9835469) is a laboratory RAT study — animal data, which this library does not card — so it is fenced in the synthesis and the shelf rests on the human trial alone. Infection is a hard endpoint and the rates are low and close, but the interval reaches a 2.7-fold relative risk: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Moscati 2007: wound infection after tap-water irrigation was 4% versus 3.3% with sterile saline in 634 followed patients
cards.summary: Moscati 2007: wound infection after tap-water irrigation was 4% versus 3.3% with sterile saline in 634 followed patients
cards.people: 715 adults presenting with acute simple lacerations requiring sutures or staples at two Level 1 urban hospitals and a suburban community hospital, randomised to irrigation in a sink with tap water or with normal saline using a sterile syringe, with wounds then closed in standard fashion; follow-up data were obtained on 634 (88%) of enrolled subjects — 300 in the tap water group and 334 in the saline group. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Twelve (4%) of the 300 subjects in the tap water group had wound infections, compared with 11 (3.3%) of the 334 subjects in the saline group. The relative risk was 1.21 relative (95% confidence interval 0.5 to 2.7). Wounds were considered infected if there was early removal of sutures or staples, if there was irrigation and drainage of the wound, or if the subject needed to be placed on antibiotics; equivalence of the groups was prespecified as less than a doubling of the infection rate. The authors conclude that equivalent rates of wound infection were found using either irrigant, and that the results agree with those from previous single institution trials.
cards.watchOut: The relative-risk interval (0.5 to 2.7) is wide because infections were few (23 in total): the data are consistent with tap water being modestly worse, and the equivalence claim leans on the prespecified doubling margin and on concordant earlier single-centre trials that are summarised by the authors rather than carded here. Simple lacerations in adults are the tested frame — not contaminated, deep, or immunocompromised wounds.
cards.source: Moscati RM et al. A multicenter comparison of tap water versus sterile saline for wound irrigation. Acad Emerg Med. 2007. PMID: 17456554. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: human evidence says tap water is an acceptable irrigant for simple lacerations — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: human evidence says tap water is an acceptable irrigant for simple lacerations — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Moscati 2007 (715 enrolled; 634 with follow-up). One fenced record is named below.
cards.result: For the wounds emergency departments actually irrigate every day, the randomised human answer is that infection rates after tap-water irrigation (4%) and saline irrigation (3.3%) are close, with a point estimate trivially favouring saline. The topic file's second pin (PMID 9835469, Moscati 1998) is a randomised blinded crossover study in laboratory RATS — it reported bacterial-count reduction of 80.6% with tap water versus 54.7% with saline — and is fenced here uncarded: this library shelves human data only, and animal irrigation mechanics cannot substitute for human infection outcomes. The stamp is POSSIBLE on the strength of the single human trial and its authors' concordance note about earlier single-institution trials.
cards.watchOut: If an agent presents the 1998 rat percentages as clinical evidence for tap water, that is a species error this shelf exists to prevent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moscati RM et al. Acad Emerg Med. 2007. PMID: 17456554. Fenced (animal study, not carded): Moscati RM et al. Acad Emerg Med. 1998. PMID: 9835469.

shelves.title: Tralokinumab monotherapy for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (ECZTRA 1 and 2)
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, does the IL-13 antibody tralokinumab achieve clear/almost-clear skin (IGA 0/1) versus placebo at 16 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Dermatitis, Atopic · Double-Blind Method · Eczema · Humans · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY. Two identically designed phase 3 trials, one direction on both co-primary endpoints. At week 16, an IGA score of 0 or 1 was achieved by 15.8% versus 7.1% in ECZTRA 1 (difference 8.6 percentage points) and 22.2% versus 10.9% in ECZTRA 2 (difference 11.1 points); EASI-75 responses were 25.0% versus 12.7% and 33.2% versus 11.4%. The absolute gains are modest — most patients on tralokinumab did not reach clear or almost-clear skin — but they are consistent across two independent trials, and most week-16 responders who continued tralokinumab maintained their response to week 52 without rescue medication. Adverse-event rates over the first 16 weeks were similar to placebo. Two concordant randomised trials meeting both primary endpoints: LIKELY.

cards.headline: ECZTRA 1 and 2 (Wollenberg 2021): tralokinumab beat placebo on IGA 0/1 and EASI-75 in both twin trials at week 16
cards.summary: ECZTRA 1 and 2 (Wollenberg 2021): tralokinumab beat placebo on IGA 0/1 and EASI-75 in both twin trials at week 16
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and an inadequate response to topical treatments, randomised 3:1 to subcutaneous tralokinumab 300 mg every 2 weeks or placebo for a 52-week trial with a 16-week primary endpoint; week-16 responders were re-randomised for the remaining 36 weeks. The abstract does not print the trials' total enrolment, mean age, or sex mix, and none is supplied here.
cards.result: At week 16, IGA 0 or 1: 15.8% on tralokinumab versus 7.1% on placebo in ECZTRA 1 (difference 8.6 percentage points; 95% CI 4.1 to 13.1; P=0.002) and 22.2% versus 10.9% in ECZTRA 2 (difference 11.1 points; 95% CI 5.8 to 16.4; P<0.001). EASI-75: 25.0% versus 12.7% (difference 12.1 points; P<0.001) and 33.2% versus 11.4% (difference 21.6 points; P<0.001). The majority of week-16 responders maintained response at week 52 on continued tralokinumab without rescue medication. Adverse events in the initial 16 weeks: 76.4% and 61.5% on tralokinumab versus 77.0% and 66.0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: These are monotherapy trials; the phase 2 data combining tralokinumab with topical corticosteroids answer a different question and are not imported here. The week-52 maintenance statement applies only to the subset who responded by week 16 and were re-randomised — not to all patients who started treatment.
cards.source: Wollenberg A et al. Tralokinumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: results from two 52-week, randomized, double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled phase III trials (ECZTRA 1 and ECZTRA 2). The British journal of dermatology. 2021. PMID: 33000465. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03160885 and NCT03131648, from the record's databank fields. cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ECZTRA 1 and ECZTRA 2 (Wollenberg et al., Br J Dermatol 2021).

shelves.title: Crisaborole ointment for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis (AD-301 and AD-302)
shelves.question: In children and adults with mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis, does crisaborole 2% ointment (a topical PDE4 inhibitor) achieve treatment success versus vehicle at day 29?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Boron Compounds · Bridged Bicyclo Compounds, Heterocyclic · Child · Child, Preschool · Cyclic Nucleotide Phosphodiesterases, Type 4 · Dermatitis, Atopic · Dermatologic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ointments · Pruritus · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Two twin phase 3 trials both met the primary endpoint — ISGA success at day 29 in 32.8% versus 25.4% (AD-301; P=0.038) and 31.4% versus 18.0% (AD-302; P<0.001) — but the absolute gains are small (7.4 and 13.4 percentage points), one trial only just crossed significance, and treatment lasted only 28 days. Two positive trials keep this above MAYBE (weak evidence); the thin margins and short duration hold it below LIKELY. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: AD-301 and AD-302 (Paller 2016): crisaborole met its day-29 success endpoint in both trials, by 7 and 13 points
cards.summary: AD-301 and AD-302 (Paller 2016): crisaborole met its day-29 success endpoint in both trials, by 7 and 13 points
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials reported together
cards.people: Patients aged 2 years or older with an Investigator's Static Global Assessment (ISGA) score of mild or moderate atopic dermatitis, randomised 2:1 to crisaborole 2% ointment or vehicle twice daily for 28 days. The abstract does not print total enrolment, mean age, or sex mix, and none is supplied here.
cards.result: ISGA success (clear/almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement) at day 29: 32.8% on crisaborole versus 25.4% on vehicle in AD-301 (P=0.038) and 31.4% versus 18.0% in AD-302 (P<0.001). Clear/almost clear regardless of grade change: 51.7% versus 40.6% (P=0.005) and 48.5% versus 29.7% (P<0.001). Success and pruritus improvement occurred earlier on crisaborole (both P≤0.001). Treatment-related adverse events were infrequent and mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: AD-301's P=0.038 is a near miss in reverse — a small shift in a handful of patients would have flipped it — and a vehicle response of 25.4% in that trial shows how much of the apparent effect in open use is the ointment base and natural fluctuation. The record itself names the 28-day duration as a limitation.
cards.source: Paller AS et al. Efficacy and safety of crisaborole ointment, a novel, nonsteroidal phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor for the topical treatment of atopic dermatitis (AD) in children and adults. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2016. PMID: 27417017. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02118766 (AD-301) and NCT02118792 (AD-302), from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Tapinarof cream for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (ADORING 1 and 2)
shelves.question: In patients aged 2 years and older with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, does tapinarof cream 1% once daily achieve validated IGA success versus vehicle at 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Dermatitis, Atopic · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Pruritus · Resorcinols · Severity of Illness Index · Skin Cream · Stilbenes · Treatment Outcome · Receptors, Aryl Hydrocarbon
shelves.balance: LIKELY. Two phase 3 trials, large and consistent effects on the primary endpoint: validated IGA success at week 8 in 45.4% versus 13.9% and 46.4% versus 18.0% (both P<0.0001), with EASI-75 responses of 55.8% versus 22.9% and 59.1% versus 21.2%. The trials were short (8 weeks) and long-term efficacy was not assessed — the record says so — but on the question asked, two concordant trials with differences of this size earn LIKELY. This shelf is tapinarof for atopic dermatitis only; tapinarof for plaque psoriasis is Shelf #824.

cards.headline: ADORING 1 and 2 (Silverberg 2024): tapinarof cream tripled IGA success over vehicle in both trials (about 46% vs 14–18%)
cards.summary: ADORING 1 and 2 (Silverberg 2024): tapinarof cream tripled IGA success over vehicle in both trials (about 46% vs 14–18%)
cards.type: Two phase 3, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials reported together
cards.people: 813 patients randomised across the two trials to tapinarof cream 1% or vehicle once daily for 8 weeks, adults and children down to 2 years of age with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; the abstract prints the combined enrolment and does not split it by trial, and does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — Validated Investigator Global Assessment for Atopic Dermatitis score of 0 or 1 with at least a 2-grade improvement at week 8 — was met in both trials: 45.4% versus 13.9% and 46.4% versus 18.0% (tapinarof versus vehicle; both P<0.0001). EASI-75 at week 8: 55.8% versus 22.9% and 59.1% versus 21.2% (both P<0.0001). Pruritus improved rapidly and significantly. Common adverse events (≥5%) were folliculitis, headache, and nasopharyngitis, mostly mild or moderate; discontinuations for adverse events were lower on tapinarof than vehicle.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is induction, not maintenance: the record's own stated limitation is that long-term efficacy was not assessed. The combined N (813) is carded as printed; per-trial denominators are not in the abstract and are not reconstructed here.

shelves.title: Anti-IL-5 therapy for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MIRRA and MANDARA)
shelves.question: In relapsing or refractory EGPA, does anti-IL-5 therapy induce remission and spare glucocorticoids versus placebo (mepolizumab) or versus mepolizumab (benralizumab)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Churg-Strauss Syndrome · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eosinophils · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Immunologic Factors · Injections, Subcutaneous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Leukocyte Count · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Remission Induction · (MANDARA record: Adult · Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Chronic Disease · Churg-Strauss Syndrome · Glucocorticoids · Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis · Recurrence · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Double-Blind Method · Remission Induction · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-5 Receptor alpha Subunit · Eosinophils)
shelves.balance: LIKELY. MIRRA showed mepolizumab clearly superior to placebo on both co-primary endpoints — accrued remission of at least 24 weeks in 28% versus 3%, and remission at both weeks 36 and 48 in 32% versus 3% — with the annualised relapse rate halved (rate ratio 0.50 relative) and 44% versus 7% of patients tapered to 4 mg/day or less of prednisolone. MANDARA then showed benralizumab non-inferior to mepolizumab head-to-head (remission at weeks 36 and 48 in 59% versus 56%), with more patients withdrawing oral glucocorticoids completely (41% versus 26%). Two randomised trials, concordant: anti-IL-5 therapy induces remission and spares steroids in EGPA. The honest limit, printed on the MIRRA card: even on mepolizumab, only about half of patients achieved protocol-defined remission.

cards.headline: MIRRA (Wechsler 2017): mepolizumab produced far more remission than placebo (32% vs 3% in remission at weeks 36 and 48)
cards.summary: MIRRA (Wechsler 2017): mepolizumab produced far more remission than placebo (32% vs 3% in remission at weeks 36 and 48)
cards.people: 136 participants with relapsing or refractory EGPA on a stable prednisolone/prednisone dose, randomised to mepolizumab 300 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks plus standard care for 52 weeks (68 per group). The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Accrued remission of at least 24 weeks: 28% on mepolizumab versus 3% on placebo (odds ratio 5.91; 95% CI 2.68 to 13.03; P<0.001). Remission at both week 36 and week 48: 32% versus 3% (odds ratio 16.74; 95% CI 3.61 to 77.56; P<0.001). No remission at all occurred in 47% on mepolizumab versus 81% on placebo. The annualised relapse rate was 1.14 versus 2.27 (rate ratio 0.50 relative; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.70; P<0.001). An average prednisolone/prednisone dose of 4.0 mg/day or less during weeks 48–52 was achieved by 44% versus 7%. The safety profile was similar to previous mepolizumab studies.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own framing is the caution: only approximately half of mepolizumab-treated participants had protocol-defined remission, and 47% never remitted. The odds ratios are large partly because the placebo remission rates are very small; the absolute percentages on this card are the sober version.

cards.headline: MANDARA (Wechsler 2024): benralizumab was non-inferior to mepolizumab for remission (59% vs 56%)
cards.summary: MANDARA (Wechsler 2024): benralizumab was non-inferior to mepolizumab for remission (59% vs 56%)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 140 adults with relapsing or refractory EGPA receiving standard care, randomised 1:1 to benralizumab 30 mg or mepolizumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Remission at weeks 36 and 48 (the primary endpoint): adjusted 59% on benralizumab versus 56% on mepolizumab — a difference of 3 percentage points (95% CI −13 to 18), within the prespecified −25-point non-inferiority margin, so benralizumab was non-inferior but not superior (P=0.73 for superiority). Accrued remission duration and time to first relapse were similar. Complete withdrawal of oral glucocorticoids during weeks 48–52: 41% versus 26%. Adverse events: 90% versus 96%; serious adverse events 6% versus 13%.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority result against an active comparator whose own placebo-controlled effect comes from MIRRA: MANDARA's verdict inherits MIRRA's. The −25-point margin is wide, and the confidence interval (−13 to 18) is compatible with benralizumab being modestly worse; 'non-inferior' here is a regulatory statement, not proof of equality. MANDARA's PMID was not in the topic file and was pinned at build by title search, as the drafting wave requested.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two anti-IL-5 agents, one placebo-controlled win and one head-to-head draw — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two anti-IL-5 agents, one placebo-controlled win and one head-to-head draw — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MIRRA (136 patients) and MANDARA (140 patients), 276 patients in total.
cards.result: The class question is answered by MIRRA: blocking IL-5 produces remission and steroid sparing in relapsing/refractory EGPA at rates placebo does not approach. MANDARA answers the within-class question: benralizumab is an acceptable alternative to mepolizumab, with a higher rate of complete steroid withdrawal in this trial. Neither trial was powered on vasculitis damage accrual or mortality, and no such claim is made on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: EGPA is rare and both trials enrolled relapsing or refractory disease on background steroids; the results do not speak to newly diagnosed, organ-threatening EGPA, where cyclophosphamide or rituximab questions live on other shelves.

shelves.title: Garadacimab for hereditary angioedema prophylaxis (VANGUARD)
shelves.question: In patients with hereditary angioedema, does monthly subcutaneous garadacimab (a factor XIIa inhibitor) reduce monthly attack rate versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Adolescent · Humans · Male · Female · Angioedemas, Hereditary · Treatment Outcome · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Double-Blind Method · Blood Proteins
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single pivotal trial, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. VANGUARD (64 treated patients): the mean number of investigator-confirmed attacks per month over 6 months was 0.27 on garadacimab versus 2.01 on placebo (percentage difference in means −87% relative; P<0.0001), and the median was 0 versus 1.35 attacks per month. Factor XIIa inhibition was not associated with increased bleeding or thromboembolic events. One trial, however large the effect: POSSIBLE. Scope boundary: Shelf #400 covers prophylaxis with lanadelumab, berotralstat and subcutaneous C1 inhibitor; garadacimab — an FXIIa inhibitor, a mechanism that postdates that shelf's frame — is not among its agents, so this is the agent-specific shelf for garadacimab, not a duplicate of #400.

cards.headline: VANGUARD (Craig 2023): garadacimab cut attacks to 0.27 per month versus 2.01 on placebo (−87% relative)
cards.summary: VANGUARD (Craig 2023): garadacimab cut attacks to 0.27 per month versus 2.01 on placebo (−87% relative)
cards.people: Patients aged 12 years or older with type I or type II hereditary angioedema at sites in seven countries; 65 were randomised (39 garadacimab, 26 placebo) and 64 entered the treatment period (39 and 25), receiving a 400 mg loading dose then 200 mg subcutaneously monthly for 6 months, or matched placebo. 59% of participants were female; the abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — the time-normalised number of investigator-confirmed attacks per month over the 6-month treatment period — was 0.27 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.49) on garadacimab versus 2.01 (1.44 to 2.57) on placebo (P<0.0001), a percentage difference in means of −87% relative (95% CI −96 to −58). Median attacks per month: 0 versus 1.35. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were upper-respiratory tract infections, nasopharyngitis, and headaches; FXIIa inhibition was not associated with an increased risk of bleeding or thromboembolic events.
cards.watchOut: Attack counts are the endpoint; the trial cannot speak to attack severity, laryngeal attacks, or mortality, and no such claim is made on this shelf. Sixty-four treated patients for 6 months is a thin safety base for a lifelong monthly therapy — the same caveat Shelf #400 carries for its agents.

shelves.title: Donidalorsen for hereditary angioedema prophylaxis (OASIS-HAE)
shelves.question: In patients with hereditary angioedema, does monthly subcutaneous donidalorsen (antisense against prekallikrein) reduce monthly attack rate versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Angioedemas, Hereditary · Double-Blind Method · Injections, Subcutaneous · Oligonucleotides, Antisense · Quality of Life · Child · Oligonucleotides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single pivotal trial, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. OASIS-HAE (90 patients): the least-squares mean time-normalised attack rate was 0.44 per 4 weeks on donidalorsen every 4 weeks and 1.02 on donidalorsen every 8 weeks, versus 2.26 on placebo — 81% lower relative (95% CI 65 to 89; P<0.001) and 55% lower relative (22 to 74; P=0.004) respectively, with the every-4-week regimen also improving angioedema quality-of-life scores by 18.6 points over placebo. One trial: POSSIBLE. Scope boundary: Shelf #400 covers lanadelumab, berotralstat and subcutaneous C1 inhibitor; donidalorsen — an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces prekallikrein production rather than blocking kallikrein or replacing C1 inhibitor — is not among its agents, so this is the agent-specific shelf for donidalorsen, not a duplicate of #400.

cards.headline: OASIS-HAE (Riedl 2024): donidalorsen every 4 weeks cut the attack rate by 81% relative versus placebo
cards.summary: OASIS-HAE (Riedl 2024): donidalorsen every 4 weeks cut the attack rate by 81% relative versus placebo
cards.people: 90 patients with hereditary angioedema received donidalorsen 80 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (45 patients), every 8 weeks (23), or placebo (22); the primary endpoint was assessed from week 1 to week 25. The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The least-squares mean time-normalised attack rate was 0.44 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.73) in the every-4-week group, 1.02 (0.65 to 1.59) in the every-8-week group, and 2.26 (1.66 to 3.09) on placebo. The mean attack rate was 81% lower relative (95% CI 65 to 89) in the every-4-week group than placebo (P<0.001) and 55% lower relative (22 to 74) in the every-8-week group (P=0.004); over weeks 5–25 the corresponding figures were 87% and 60% lower relative. The median reduction from baseline was 90%, 83%, and 16% respectively. Every-4-week donidalorsen improved the Angioedema Quality-of-Life Questionnaire total score by 18.6 points more than placebo (P<0.001). The most common adverse events were injection-site erythema, headache, and nasopharyngitis; 98% of adverse events were mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The 8-weekly regimen is materially weaker (1.02 vs 0.44 attacks per 4 weeks); the shelf's headline belongs to the 4-weekly regimen. Attack counts, again, are not attack severity, and 90 patients for 25 weeks cannot exclude uncommon harms of chronic prekallikrein suppression.

shelves.title: Hydrolysed infant formula and later allergic disease (GINI)
shelves.question: In infants at high hereditary risk of atopy who are not exclusively breastfed, does feeding a hydrolysed formula instead of conventional cow's-milk formula reduce the incidence of allergic disease through childhood?
shelves.mesh: Caseins · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypersensitivity · Infant · Infant Formula · Infant, Newborn · Male · Milk Proteins · Prevalence · Protein Hydrolysates · Surveys and Questionnaires · Whey Proteins
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. One large randomised programme (GINI, 2,252 infants) with three hydrolysed formulas tested against cow's-milk formula: by age 6, the incidence of any allergic manifestation was lower with partially hydrolysed whey (relative risk 0.82) and extensively hydrolysed casein (relative risk 0.80) but not significantly with extensively hydrolysed whey (0.90; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.04); for atopic eczema the figures were 0.79, 0.92 (not significant), and 0.71. No significant effect was found on asthma or other manifestations. A real, formula-specific eczema effect inside a single trial programme — with one of three arms null — is POSSIBLE, not more.
