cards.summary: GINI at 6 years (von Berg 2008): two of three hydrolysed formulas reduced allergic manifestations and eczema versus cow's-milk formula
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial programme — long-term (6-year) follow-up report carded as the anchor
cards.people: 2,252 newborns with atopic heredity, randomised at birth to partially hydrolysed whey formula, extensively hydrolysed whey formula, extensively hydrolyzed casein formula, or conventional cow's-milk formula as the milk substitute for the first 4 months whenever breastfeeding was insufficient, and followed with yearly questionnaires to age 6. The abstract does not print the sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the relative risk of a physician diagnosis of any allergic manifestation compared with cow's-milk formula was 0.82 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.96) for partially hydrolysed whey, 0.90 (0.78 to 1.04) for extensively hydrolysed whey, and 0.80 (0.69 to 0.93) for extensively hydrolysed casein. For atopic eczema: 0.79 (0.64 to 0.97), 0.92 (0.76 to 1.11), and 0.71 (0.58 to 0.88). Per-protocol effects were stronger and all significant. No significant effect on other allergic manifestations — including asthma — was found. All measures here are relative; the abstract does not print the underlying incidence rates, and none are supplied.
cards.watchOut: The effect is on eczema and the any-manifestation composite, not on asthma — a distinction the allergy-prevention literature often blurs. The extensively hydrolysed whey arm's null eczema result also warns against treating 'hydrolysed formula' as a single intervention. This record predates trial registration; the record's databank fields carry no registry ID, and none is invented.

shelves.title: Perinatal probiotics to prevent atopic eczema (Kalliomäki; Wickens)
shelves.question: In families with atopic disease, does giving Lactobacillus GG to mothers prenatally and to infants postnatally prevent atopic eczema in the first two years of life?
shelves.mesh: Child, Preschool · Chronic Disease · Dermatitis, Atopic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypersensitivity, Immediate · Immunoglobulin E · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Intestines · Lactobacillus · Pregnancy · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects · Primary Prevention · Probiotics · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Skin Tests · (Wickens record: Bifidobacterium · Breast Feeding · Child, Preschool · Dermatitis, Atopic · Double-Blind Method · Eczema · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus · Male · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third · Probiotics)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Two randomised trials of perinatal Lactobacillus rhamnosus strains agree on eczema: Kalliomäki found atopic eczema at 2 years in 23% on Lactobacillus GG versus 46% on placebo (relative risk 0.51 relative), and Wickens found L. rhamnosus HN001 reduced eczema by 2 years (hazard ratio 0.51 relative) — while Bifidobacterium animalis HN019 in the same trial did nothing (hazard ratio 0.90), and neither trial's strains prevented atopy itself. A strain-specific eczema effect replicated across two trials and two strains of the same species, with a built-in negative control strain: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kalliomäki 2001: Lactobacillus GG halved atopic eczema at 2 years (23% vs 46%)
cards.summary: Kalliomäki 2001: Lactobacillus GG halved atopic eczema at 2 years (23% vs 46%)
cards.people: Mothers with at least one first-degree relative (or partner) with atopic eczema, allergic rhinitis, or asthma received Lactobacillus GG prenatally, and their infants received it postnatally for 6 months, or placebo; 132 children were assessed at age 2. The abstract does not print mean maternal age or the children's sex mix.
cards.result: Atopic eczema was diagnosed in 46 of 132 children (35%) by age 2. Its frequency in the probiotic group was half that of the placebo group: 15 of 64 (23%) versus 31 of 68 (46%); relative risk 0.51 relative (95% CI 0.32 to 0.84); number needed to treat 4.5 (95% CI 2.6 to 15.6). Asthma was diagnosed in six of the children with eczema and allergic rhinitis in one.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (132 children assessed) with a strikingly large effect — the combination that most often shrinks on replication. The endpoint is eczema; this trial does not show prevention of asthma or rhinitis. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID (a 2001 trial), and none is invented.

cards.people: 474 infants at risk of allergic disease; pregnant women took Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001, Bifidobacterium animalis subsp lactis HN019, or placebo daily from 35 weeks' gestation until 6 months if breastfeeding, and the infants received the same treatment from birth to 2 years. cards.summary: Synthesis: strain-specific eczema prevention, replicated once — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kalliomäki 2001 (132 children) and Wickens 2008 (474 infants).
cards.result: Two L. rhamnosus strains, in two countries and two decades' designs, each halved early eczema; a bifidobacterium strain in the larger trial did not, and sensitisation/atopy was not prevented in either. shelves.title: Dilute bleach baths for atopic dermatitis (Huang)
shelves.question: In children with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and recurrent skin infection, do dilute bleach baths plus intranasal mupirocin reduce eczema severity versus water baths plus petrolatum?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Body Surface Area · Cephalexin/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Community-Acquired Infections · Dermatitis, Atopic/epidemiology,microbiology · Humans · Infant · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus/drug effects · Mupirocin/administration & dosage · Severity of Illness Index · Sodium Hypochlorite/administration & dosage · Staphylococcal Infections/epidemiology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small trial, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. Huang (31 children): the bleach-bath-plus-mupirocin group showed significantly greater mean reductions in Eczema Area and Severity Index scores than the water-bath-plus-petrolatum group at 1 and 3 months — but the abstract prints no EASI values, so no effect size can be carded, and every child in both arms also received 14 days of oral cephalexin, so the design tests a bundle on an antibiotic background, not bleach baths alone. cards.headline: Huang 2009: bleach baths plus intranasal mupirocin improved eczema severity more than water baths plus petrolatum (n=31; no effect sizes in the abstract)
cards.summary: Huang 2009: bleach baths plus intranasal mupirocin improved eczema severity more than water baths plus petrolatum (n=31; no effect sizes in the abstract)
cards.people: 31 patients aged 6 months to 17 years with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and clinical signs of secondary bacterial infection. All patients received oral cephalexin for 14 days, and were randomised to intranasal mupirocin plus sodium hypochlorite (bleach) baths or intranasal petrolatum plus plain water baths for 3 months. The abstract does not print the sex mix.
cards.result: Patients receiving both dilute bleach baths and intranasal mupirocin showed significantly greater mean reductions from baseline in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores than the placebo group at the 1-month and 3-month visits. EASI scores for the head and neck — the body sites not submerged in the baths — did not decrease in the treatment group, while scores for submerged sites did. The abstract prints no EASI values, differences, or P values, and none are supplied here. Community-acquired MRSA prevalence in this cohort was low (7.4% of S. aureus-positive skin cultures).
cards.watchOut: Three interventions are bundled — bleach baths, intranasal mupirocin, and a universal 14-day cephalexin course — so the trial cannot attribute the improvement to bleach alone; the head-and-neck internal contrast is suggestive but is not a randomised comparison. The record's databank fields carry no registry ID, and none is invented.
cards.source: Huang JT et al. Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus colonization in atopic dermatitis decreases disease severity. Pediatrics. 2009. PMID: 19403473. shelves.title: Fish-oil supplementation in pregnancy and offspring allergic disease (Palmer / DOMInO)
shelves.question: In pregnant women whose offspring are at high risk of allergy, does n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty-acid supplementation reduce infant allergic disease (eczema, food allergy) in the first year?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Breast Feeding · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Dermatitis, Atopic · Dietary Supplements · Eggs · Fatty Acids, Omega-3 · Female · Fetal Blood · Fish Oils · Food Hypersensitivity · Humans · Hypersensitivity, Immediate · Immunoglobulin E · Infant · Infant Formula · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Maternal Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Pregnancy · Regression Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). The DOMInO allergy follow-up (706 infants) found no reduction in the primary outcome: IgE-associated allergic disease at 1 year occurred in 9% on fish oil versus 13% on control oil — an unadjusted relative risk of 0.68 that did not reach significance and attenuated on adjustment (adjusted relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.09; P=0.12). Two secondary signals favoured fish oil — atopic eczema (7% versus 12%; adjusted relative risk 0.64, CI crossing 1) and egg sensitisation (9% versus 15%; adjusted relative risk 0.62) — but IgE-associated food allergy itself did not differ. A null primary with hypothesis-generating secondaries: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Palmer 2012 (DOMInO): fish oil in pregnancy did not significantly reduce IgE-associated allergic disease at 1 year (9% vs 13%; adjusted RR 0.70)
cards.summary: Palmer 2012 (DOMInO): fish oil in pregnancy did not significantly reduce IgE-associated allergic disease at 1 year (9% vs 13%; adjusted RR 0.70)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — prespecified allergy follow-up of the DOMInO trial
cards.people: 706 infants at high hereditary risk of allergic disease whose mothers participated in the DOMInO trial in Adelaide, Australia: 368 infants whose mothers took fish-oil capsules providing 900 mg of n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids daily from 21 weeks' gestation until birth, and 338 whose mothers took matched vegetable-oil capsules. The abstract does not print the infants' sex mix.
cards.result: IgE-associated allergic disease (eczema or food allergy with sensitisation) at 1 year: 32 of 368 (9%) in the n-3 group versus 43 of 338 (13%) in the control group — unadjusted relative risk 0.68 relative (95% CI 0.43 to 1.05; P=0.08); adjusted relative risk 0.70 (0.45 to 1.09; P=0.12). Atopic eczema was lower on fish oil: 7% versus 12% (unadjusted relative risk 0.61; P=0.04; adjusted 0.64, 0.40 to 1.02; P=0.06). Egg sensitisation: 9% versus 15% (adjusted relative risk 0.62; 0.41 to 0.93; P=0.02). There was no difference in IgE-associated food allergy.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion is the card's: no reduction in overall IgE-associated allergy. The eczema and egg-sensitisation signals are secondary outcomes among several, with the adjusted eczema interval crossing 1 — they justify further trials, not a recommendation. The registry ID appears in the abstract text (ACTRN12605000569606 for DOMInO; ACTRN12610000735055 for this follow-up report); the record's databank fields are empty, and the ID is noted as abstract-text only. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Tinnitus: cognitive behavioural therapy eases the distress it causes — no drug or supplement has been shown to quiet it
shelves.question: What is tinnitus, and does any treatment help it?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Depression · Humans · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tinnitus · Treatment Outcome · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: Tinnitus is the perception of sound with no external source; 10–15% of adults report it and an estimated 1–3% are severely troubled by it. No treatment has been shown to remove the sound itself. What the trial literature does support is treating the distress the sound causes. The Cochrane review of cognitive behavioural therapy (28 randomised trials, 2,733 adults with tinnitus of at least three months) found CBT reduced the impact of tinnitus on quality of life versus waiting list (standardised mean difference −0.56; 95% CI −0.83 to −0.30 — about 11 points on the 0–100 Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, against a minimal clinically important difference of 7; low-certainty evidence), probably reduced it versus audiological care (mean difference −5.65 points; moderate certainty, below that 7-point threshold), and may reduce it versus other active treatments (SMD −0.30; low certainty). Depression scores improved slightly; anxiety and general quality-of-life effects were uncertain; serious adverse effects were not increased. The American Academy of Otolaryngology—Head and Neck Surgery guideline reaches the matching practical conclusions: recommend CBT and a hearing-aid evaluation when hearing loss is documented, and recommend AGAINST antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, and other dietary supplements as routine tinnitus treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the honest offer to a patient with bothersome tinnitus is help coping measurably better — not silence, and not a pill.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020: CBT for tinnitus — 28 trials, 2,733 adults; distress reduced versus waiting list, audiological care, and other active treatments
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020: CBT for tinnitus — 28 trials, 2,733 adults; distress reduced versus waiting list, audiological care, and other active treatments
cards.people: 28 randomised controlled trials (mostly European) totalling 2,733 adults with tinnitus for at least three months (average ages 43 to 70); CBT lasted 3 to 22 weeks, delivered mostly in hospitals or online. Comparisons: no intervention/waiting list (14 studies), audiological care (3), tinnitus retraining therapy (1), and other active controls such as relaxation or information (16). Primary outcome: impact of tinnitus on disease-specific quality of life, principally the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI, 0–100; minimal clinically important difference 7 points).
cards.result: Versus waiting list, CBT reduced tinnitus impact at end of treatment (SMD −0.56; 95% CI −0.83 to −0.30; 10 studies, 537 participants; low certainty) — equivalent to about 10.91 THI points lower. Versus audiological care, CBT probably reduced THI scores (mean difference −5.65; 95% CI −9.79 to −1.50; 3 studies, 444 participants; moderate certainty). Versus other active treatments, CBT may reduce impact (SMD −0.30; 95% CI −0.55 to −0.05; 12 studies, 966 participants; low certainty), about 5.84 THI points. CBT may slightly reduce depression; effects on anxiety and general quality of life are uncertain. Serious adverse effects probably do not differ (moderate certainty).
cards.watchOut: CBT targets distress and quality of life, not tinnitus loudness — patients should be told the sound itself is not expected to change. Certainty is low to moderate throughout, and follow-up beyond end of treatment was largely absent in the trials.
cards.source: Fuller T et al. Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020. PMID: 31912887. Registry ID: none (systematic review). systematic review of randomised trials (cochrane) 28 randomised controlled trials (mostly european) totalling 2,733 adults with tinnitus for at least three months (average ages 43 to 70); cbt lasted 3 to 22 weeks, delivered mostly in hospitals or online. comparisons: no intervention/waiting list (14 studies), audiological care (3), tinnitus retraining therapy (1), and other active controls such as relaxation or information (16). primary outcome: impact of tinnitus on disease-specific quality of life, principally the tinnitus handicap inventory (thi, 0–100; minimal clinically important difference 7 points). versus waiting list, cbt reduced tinnitus impact at end of treatment (smd −0.56; 95% ci −0.83 to −0.30; 10 studies, 537 participants; low certainty) — equivalent to about 10.91 thi points lower. versus audiological care, cbt probably reduced thi scores (mean difference −5.65; 95% ci −9.79 to −1.50; 3 studies, 444 participants; moderate certainty). versus other active treatments, cbt may reduce impact (smd −0.30; 95% ci −0.55 to −0.05; 12 studies, 966 participants; low certainty), about 5.84 thi points. cbt may slightly reduce depression; effects on anxiety and general quality of life are uncertain. serious adverse effects probably do not differ (moderate certainty). cbt targets distress and quality of life, not tinnitus loudness — patients should be told the sound itself is not expected to change. certainty is low to moderate throughout, and follow-up beyond end of treatment was largely absent in the trials. fuller t et al. cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus. cochrane database syst rev. 2020. pmid: 31912887. registry id: none (systematic review). mesh: anxiety · cognitive behavioral therapy · depression · humans · quality of life · randomized controlled trials as topic · tinnitus · treatment outcome · waiting lists

cards.headline: AAO-HNS tinnitus guideline 2014: recommend CBT and hearing-aid evaluation; recommend against antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, ginkgo, melatonin, zinc, and supplements
cards.summary: AAO-HNS tinnitus guideline 2014: recommend CBT and hearing-aid evaluation; recommend against antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, ginkgo, melatonin, zinc, and supplements
cards.people: Adults (18 years and older) with primary tinnitus that is persistent (at least 6 months) and bothersome — the guideline's target population, in a condition reported by more than 50 million people in the United States (adult prevalence 10–15%). Recommendations were developed from the published evidence base for evaluation and management of persistent, bothersome tinnitus.
cards.result: The panel recommended: targeted history and examination to find treatable causes; prompt comprehensive audiologic examination for unilateral, persistent, or hearing-difficulty-associated tinnitus; education about management strategies; hearing-aid evaluation when hearing loss is documented; and cognitive behavioral therapy for persistent, bothersome tinnitus. It recommended AGAINST: antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, or intratympanic medications for routine treatment; Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements; and (strong recommendation against) routine head and neck imaging for tinnitus that is non-localising, nonpulsatile, and without focal neurology or asymmetric hearing loss.
cards.watchOut: A guideline synthesises the same trial literature as the Cochrane card — the two references are concordant, not independent. Its drug and supplement recommendations concern routine treatment of persistent primary tinnitus, not treatment of an underlying cause found on evaluation.

shelves.title: Sudafed PE doesn't work: oral phenylephrine was no better than placebo
shelves.question: In adults with nasal congestion (allergic rhinitis or the common cold), does oral phenylephrine at the sold 10 mg dose — the decongestant in 'PE' cold remedies — relieve congestion compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Phenylephrine · Nasal Decongestants · Nasal Obstruction · Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal · Common Cold · Pseudoephedrine · Humans
shelves.balance: No — at the 10 mg dose sold in 'PE' cold remedies, oral phenylephrine has not beaten placebo in any modern, adequately powered test. In the FDA-requested dose-ranging trial, 539 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis took 10, 20, 30 or 40 mg or placebo for 7 days, and no dose separated from placebo on reflective or instantaneous congestion scores (Meltzer 2015). In the Vienna Challenge Chamber, a single 12 mg dose was indistinguishable from placebo (P=.56) while pseudoephedrine 60 mg beat both (Horak 2009). The only positive signal is old and small: a meta-analysis of 8 single-dose cold trials totalling 163 subjects found an objective nasal-airway-resistance advantage of 6.0 to 16.6 percentage points over placebo between 30 and 90 minutes — below the 20% the field calls clinically meaningful (Kollar 2007). As context, in 2023 an FDA advisory committee unanimously judged oral phenylephrine ineffective as a nasal decongestant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large modern trials are null at and above the sold dose, and the one positive meta-analysis is tiny, old and below its own meaningfulness threshold.

cards.headline: Meltzer 2015: no dose of oral phenylephrine — 10, 20, 30 or 40 mg — beat placebo on congestion in 539 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis
cards.summary: Meltzer 2015: no dose of oral phenylephrine — 10, 20, 30 or 40 mg — beat placebo on congestion in 539 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis
cards.people: 539 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis (but otherwise healthy) at multiple centres, randomised to 7 days of phenylephrine hydrochloride 10, 20, 30 or 40 mg or placebo, in a phase 2 dose-ranging trial run at the FDA's request.
cards.result: None of the phenylephrine treatment groups had a statistically significant change from baseline in instantaneous or reflective nasal congestion scores compared with placebo — the primary endpoint (mean change in daily reflective nasal congestion score over the whole treatment period) and the other efficacy endpoints were null at every dose. Phenylephrine was well tolerated up to 30 mg; at least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 18.4% of participants, most commonly headache (3.0%). Registry ID: NCT01330017.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, not double-blind — participants knew what they were taking, which if anything biases toward the drug on a subjective congestion score, and the result was still null at four times the sold dose. The population had allergic rhinitis, not the common cold; the cold evidence is the older meta-analysis carded below.
cards.source: Meltzer EO et al.. Oral Phenylephrine HCl for Nasal Congestion in Seasonal Allergic Rhinitis: A Randomized, Open-label, Placebo-controlled Study. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice. 2015. PMID: 26143019. Registry ID: NCT01330017. cards.headline: Horak 2009: phenylephrine 12 mg was indistinguishable from placebo (P=.56) in the challenge chamber, while pseudoephedrine 60 mg beat both
cards.summary: Horak 2009: phenylephrine 12 mg was indistinguishable from placebo (P=.56) in the challenge chamber, while pseudoephedrine 60 mg beat both
cards.people: 39 grass-sensitive patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis exposed to grass pollen in the Vienna Challenge Chamber, in a randomised, placebo-controlled, 3-way crossover study of single doses of phenylephrine 12 mg, pseudoephedrine 60 mg (as a control) or placebo, with congestion followed for more than 6 hours.
cards.result: Phenylephrine was not significantly different from placebo on the primary endpoint, mean change in nasal congestion score at more than 6 hours (P=.56), whereas pseudoephedrine was significantly more effective than both placebo (P<.01) and phenylephrine (P=.01). Rhinomanometry and peak nasal inspiratory flow were consistent with these data; neither drug affected non-nasal symptoms, and no adverse events were reported. Registry ID: NCT00276016.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=39) and single-dose, in an artificial pollen-chamber setting. The authors note a possible carryover bias: in the first phase the phenylephrine–placebo difference looked larger, and patients' recall of the pseudoephedrine effect in a crossover may have influenced later scoring — which makes the overall null the conservative reading.
cards.source: Horak F et al.. A placebo-controlled study of the nasal decongestant effect of phenylephrine and pseudoephedrine in the Vienna Challenge Chamber. Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology. 2009. PMID: 19230461. Registry ID: NCT00276016. cards.headline: Kollar 2007: meta-analysis of 8 old single-dose trials found a small objective effect on nasal airway resistance — 6.0 to 16.6 percentage points over placebo, below the 20% called meaningful
cards.summary: Kollar 2007: meta-analysis of 8 old single-dose trials found a small objective effect on nasal airway resistance — 6.0 to 16.6 percentage points over placebo, below the 20% called meaningful
cards.people: Adults with acute nasal congestion due to the common cold in 8 single-dose, randomised, placebo-controlled trials of oral phenylephrine 10 mg as sole active ingredient, measuring nasal airway resistance: 7 crossover studies with 113 subjects in total were pooled, plus the initial phase of 1 parallel-group trial of 50 subjects reanalysed individually but not pooled.
cards.result: Phenylephrine 10 mg was significantly more effective than placebo at the primary time points (30 and 60 minutes) and at 90 minutes in both fixed-effects and random-effects meta-analyses (P≤.05), and 4 of the 8 individual studies were significant. Between 30 and 90 minutes after dosing, reductions in nasal airway resistance ranged from 6.0 percentage points higher with phenylephrine than placebo (at 30 and 45 minutes) to 16.6 percentage points higher (at 60 minutes) — against the ≥20% reduction the field prespecified as a clinically meaningful difference.
cards.watchOut: This is the best evidence ever assembled FOR phenylephrine and it is thin: 163 subjects in total, old single-dose trials drawn in part from the bibliography of the 1976 FDA monograph, an objective resistance endpoint rather than how congested people feel, and authors linked to the manufacturer of the era's phenylephrine products. A statistically detectable blip on a machine, below the meaningful threshold, is not relief a patient can feel.
cards.source: Kollar C et al.. Meta-analysis of the efficacy of a single dose of phenylephrine 10 mg compared with placebo in adults with acute nasal congestion due to the common cold. Clinical Therapeutics. 2007. PMID: 17692721. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the modern, adequately powered tests are null at and above the sold dose — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the modern, adequately powered tests are null at and above the sold dose — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Adults with nasal congestion from seasonal allergic rhinitis or the common cold across one 539-person dose-ranging trial, one 39-person crossover chamber study, and a meta-analysis of 8 small single-dose trials totalling 163 subjects.
cards.result: No phenylephrine dose from 10 to 40 mg beat placebo on congestion scores over 7 days (Meltzer 2015); a single 12 mg dose matched placebo in the chamber while pseudoephedrine separated from both (Horak 2009); the pooled older cold trials show only a 6.0–16.6 percentage-point objective resistance advantage between 30 and 90 minutes, below the 20% meaningful threshold (Kollar 2007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about oral phenylephrine at the doses sold over the counter; it says nothing about phenylephrine nasal spray (a different, direct route), and nothing against pseudoephedrine, which is sold behind the counter and did work in the chamber study.

shelves.title: Cold-sore creams work a little: about half a day to a day faster healing
shelves.question: In immunocompetent people with recurrent cold sores (herpes labialis), do antiviral creams — docosanol (Abreva), penciclovir, acyclovir, and acyclovir plus hydrocortisone — shorten healing or prevent the blister compared with vehicle or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Herpes Labialis · Antiviral Agents · Acyclovir · Fatty Alcohols · Guanine · Hydrocortisone · Recurrence · Humans
shelves.balance: Yes, a little — consistently, across four product programmes, by about half a day to a day. Docosanol 10% cream healed cold sores a median of 18 hours sooner than placebo (4.1 days; P=.008) in 737 treated patients (Sacks 2001). Penciclovir 1% cream lost classical lesions 31% faster in relative terms (hazard ratio 1.31) with pain resolution at a relative hazard ratio of 1.28, in 3,057 treated patients (Raborn 2002). Acyclovir 5% cream shortened episodes from 4.8 to 4.3 days and from 5.2 to 4.6 days in its two trials, but did not prevent classical lesions forming (Spruance 2002). The combination ME-609 (acyclovir 5% plus hydrocortisone 1%) did prevent the ulcerative lesion in 42% of episodes versus 35% on acyclovir alone and 26% on placebo, in 1,443 treated patients (Hull 2011). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): multiple large double-blind trials agree the creams work, but the absolute gain is roughly half a day to a day of a self-limiting episode, earned only with treatment started at the first sign.

cards.headline: Sacks 2001: docosanol 10% cream healed cold sores a median 18 hours sooner than placebo (4.1 days; P=.008)
cards.summary: Sacks 2001: docosanol 10% cream healed cold sores a median 18 hours sooner than placebo (4.1 days; P=.008)
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together (Sacks 2001)
cards.people: Otherwise healthy adults with documented histories of herpes simplex labialis in two identical double-blind, placebo-controlled studies at 21 sites; 737 patients treated an episode (370 docosanol 10% cream, 367 polyethylene glycol placebo), starting treatment in the prodrome or erythema stage and applying it 5 times daily until healing, with twice-daily visits.
cards.result: The median time to healing in docosanol-treated patients was 4.1 days, 18 hours shorter than in placebo-treated patients (P=.008; 95% CI 2 to 22 hours). Docosanol also shortened time to cessation of pain and all other symptoms (P=.002), complete healing of classical lesions (P=.023) and cessation of the ulcer or soft crust stage (P<.001). Aborted episodes occurred in 40% of docosanol recipients versus 34% of placebo recipients (P=.109 — not significant). Adverse experiences were mild and similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Docosanol is an over-the-counter product; the gain is real but under a day, and treatment must start at the prodrome or erythema stage, 5 times daily — late starters were not the population tested. The aborted-episode difference (40% versus 34%) was not significant.
cards.source: Sacks SL et al.. Clinical efficacy of topical docosanol 10% cream for herpes simplex labialis: A multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2001. PMID: 11464183. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Raborn 2002: penciclovir 1% cream — classical lesions lost 31% faster in relative terms (hazard ratio 1.31) and pain resolved with HR 1.28
cards.summary: Raborn 2002: penciclovir 1% cream — classical lesions lost 31% faster in relative terms (hazard ratio 1.31) and pain resolved with HR 1.28
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reported together (Raborn 2002)
cards.people: 3,057 immunocompetent people who initiated treatment (1,516 penciclovir 1% cream, 1,541 placebo) out of 4,573 enrolled with a history of recurrent herpes simplex labialis with three or more episodes a year, in two randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trials in Europe and North America; patients self-initiated treatment, applying it six times on the first day and every two hours while awake for four consecutive days.
cards.result: Combined data showed penciclovir recipients lost classical lesions 31% faster in relative terms than placebo recipients (hazard ratio 1.31; 95% CI 1.20 to 1.42; P=.0001) and experienced pain resolution with a relative hazard ratio of 1.28 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.39; P=.0001). Significant benefits were achieved whether treatment was initiated in the early stages (P=.001) or later stages (P=.0055).
cards.watchOut: The headline effects are hazard ratios — relative measures of healing speed, not days saved; the abstract reports no absolute healing times, so no day-count is claimed here. The dosing is intensive (every two hours while awake), and 1,516 of 4,573 enrolled never treated an episode and do not enter the analysis.

cards.headline: Spruance 2002: acyclovir 5% cream shortened episodes by about half a day in each of two trials (4.3 versus 4.8 days, HR 1.23; 4.6 versus 5.2 days, HR 1.24) — but did not prevent classical lesions
cards.summary: Spruance 2002: acyclovir 5% cream shortened episodes by about half a day in each of two trials (4.3 versus 4.8 days, HR 1.23; 4.6 versus 5.2 days, HR 1.24) — but did not prevent classical lesions
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials reported together (Spruance 2002)
cards.people: Healthy adults with a history of frequent herpes labialis in two independent, identical, parallel, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled multicentre trials; 686 patients treated a lesion in study 1 and 699 in study 2, self-initiating acyclovir 5% cream or vehicle five times daily for 4 days beginning within 1 hour of the onset of a recurrent episode.
cards.result: In study 1, mean episode duration was 4.3 days on acyclovir cream versus 4.8 days on vehicle (hazard ratio 1.23; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.44; P=0.007); in study 2, 4.6 versus 5.2 days (HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.44; P=0.006). Efficacy was apparent with early (prodrome or erythema) or late (papule or vesicle) initiation, and duration of lesion pain was significantly reduced in both studies. Acyclovir cream did not prevent the development of classical lesions (progression to vesicles, ulcers and/or crusts). Adverse events were mild and infrequent.
cards.watchOut: Healing is faster by roughly half a day, but a cream that does not stop the blister forming should not be sold as prevention — that distinction is exactly what the combination product below was designed to change. Treatment began within 1 hour of onset in the trial protocol.

cards.headline: Hull 2011: ME-609 (acyclovir 5% plus hydrocortisone 1%) kept 42% of episodes from becoming ulcerative lesions, versus 35% on acyclovir alone and 26% on placebo
cards.summary: Hull 2011: ME-609 (acyclovir 5% plus hydrocortisone 1%) kept 42% of episodes from becoming ulcerative lesions, versus 35% on acyclovir alone and 26% on placebo
cards.people: 1,443 patients who experienced a recurrence and initiated treatment (601 ME-609, 610 acyclovir in ME-609 vehicle, 232 placebo vehicle) out of 2,437 randomised patients with a history of herpes simplex labialis, self-initiating cream 5 times daily for 5 days at the earliest sign of a recurrence. ME-609 is the tested combination product named in the publication (acyclovir 5% plus hydrocortisone 1%).
cards.result: 42% of ME-609 patients did not develop an ulcerative lesion, compared with 35% on acyclovir alone (P=.014) and 26% on placebo (P<.0001). In patients with ulcerative lesions, healing times were reduced in both the ME-609 and acyclovir groups compared with placebo (P<.01 for both), and the cumulative lesion area for all lesions was reduced 50% with ME-609 compared with placebo (P<.0001). There were no differences among groups in positive herpes simplex virus cultures, and side-effect profiles were similar. Registry ID: NCT00361881.
cards.watchOut: The trial contained no topical-corticosteroid-alone group, so the hydrocortisone contribution cannot be isolated from the combination as tested. The placebo arm was deliberately smaller (232 treated) than the active arms, and the product is the specific tested combination, not any acyclovir cream with a separate steroid added at home.
cards.source: Hull CM et al.. Early treatment of cold sores with topical ME-609 decreases the frequency of ulcerative lesions: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, patient-initiated clinical trial. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2011. PMID: 20851499. Registry ID: NCT00361881. cards.headline: Synthesis: every antiviral cream beat its control, by about half a day to a day — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: every antiviral cream beat its control, by about half a day to a day — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Immunocompetent people with recurrent herpes labialis across eight randomised trials reported in four papers: docosanol (737 treated), penciclovir (3,057 treated), acyclovir cream (1,385 treated across two trials) and the acyclovir–hydrocortisone combination ME-609 (1,443 treated).
cards.result: Docosanol healed lesions a median 18 hours sooner (4.1 days, P=.008); acyclovir cream shortened episodes by 0.5 and 0.6 days in its two trials; penciclovir lost classical lesions 31% faster in relative terms (hazard ratio 1.31); and ME-609 prevented ulcerative lesions in 42% versus 26% on placebo. No cream is curative and acyclovir cream did not prevent lesions forming. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: All of these trials are in immunocompetent people with recurrent cold sores who start treatment at the first tingle, most with very frequent application; they do not cover first episodes, immunocompromised patients, or genital herpes, and none compares the creams against oral antivirals.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sacks SL et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2001 (PMID: 11464183); Raborn GW et al. Journal of the American Dental Association. 2002 (PMID: 11934185); Spruance SL et al. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2002 (PMID: 12069980); Hull CM et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2011 (PMID: 20851499).

shelves.title: Sweaty armpits: Botox injections and a medicated cloth both work
shelves.question: In people with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, do botulinum toxin injections (Botox) or the topical anticholinergic glycopyrronium tosylate cloth reduce sweat production compared with placebo or vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Botulinum Toxins, Type A · Hyperhidrosis · Axilla · Glycopyrrolate · Cholinergic Antagonists · Double-Blind Method · Patient Satisfaction · Humans
shelves.balance: Both treatments beat their controls in randomised, double-blind trials. In Naumann 2001, 320 people with bilateral primary axillary hyperhidrosis received botulinum toxin type A (Botox) 50 U per axilla or placebo injections: responders (at least a 50% reduction in sweat production) at week 4 were 94% on Botox versus 36% on placebo, and at week 16 the rates were still 82% versus 21%, with much higher patient satisfaction on Botox. In the pooled ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 trials, a glycopyrronium tosylate 3.75% cloth used once daily for 4 weeks produced a responder rate (at least a 4-point improvement on the Axillary Sweating Daily Diary item 2) of 59.5% versus 27.6% on vehicle — although the measured sweat reduction was modest beside vehicle: −107.6 versus −92.1 mg/5 min. The Botox effect is large and durable to 16 weeks; the cloth works on patient-reported severity but its gravimetric margin is small and the trials lasted only 4 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): each treatment has randomised placebo- or vehicle-controlled support, but the cloth's objective sweat margin is modest and neither evidence base is large or long.

cards.headline: Naumann 2001: Botox responders 94% versus 36% on placebo at week 4, and 82% versus 21% at week 16
cards.summary: Naumann 2001: Botox responders 94% versus 36% on placebo at week 4, and 82% versus 21% at week 16
cards.type: Randomised, parallel group, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
cards.people: 320 patients aged 18–75 years with bilateral primary axillary hyperhidrosis sufficient to interfere with daily living, randomised at 17 dermatology and neurology clinics in Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom (307 completed); the tested product is named in the publication: botulinum toxin type A (Botox) 50 U per axilla, given as 10–15 intradermal injections per axilla, versus placebo injections.
cards.result: Responders (patients with ≥50% reduction from baseline in spontaneous axillary sweat production) at four weeks were 94% (227) in the botulinum toxin type A group versus 36% (28) on placebo; by week 16, response rates were 82% (198) and 21% (16), respectively. Patient satisfaction was much higher on botulinum toxin type A (satisfaction score 3.3 versus 0.8, P<0.001 at 4 weeks). All other efficacy measures were significantly better in the botulinum toxin group.
cards.watchOut: Pre-registration-era trial (2001). Adverse events were reported by 27 patients (11%) in the botulinum toxin group and four (5%) in the placebo group (P>0.05). The trial covers primary axillary hyperhidrosis only — not secondary sweating or other body sites.
cards.source: Naumann M et al.. Botulinum toxin type A in treatment of bilateral primary axillary hyperhidrosis: randomised, parallel group, double blind, placebo controlled trial.. BMJ. 2001. PMID: 11557704. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 (Glaser 2019): glycopyrronium cloth responders 59.5% versus 27.6% on vehicle, but sweat-weight margin was modest
cards.summary: ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 (Glaser 2019): glycopyrronium cloth responders 59.5% versus 27.6% on vehicle, but sweat-weight margin was modest
cards.type: Pooled report of two replicate randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials
cards.people: Patients with primary axillary hyperhidrosis in ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2, two replicate randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled, 4-week phase 3 trials, randomised 2:1 to glycopyrronium tosylate 3.75% cloth or vehicle, applied once daily to each axilla for 4 weeks; results reported pooled. The publication names the compound and strength only (glycopyrronium tosylate 3.75%) — no retail brand name is given.
cards.result: Significantly more glycopyrronium-treated patients achieved an ASDD-Item 2 response (≥4-point improvement from baseline in severity of sweating) than vehicle patients (59.5% vs 27.6%), and they had reduced sweat production from baseline (−107.6 mg/5 min vs −92.1 mg/5 min) at week 4 (P < .001 for both coprimary end points). Pooled data were consistent with the individual trial results.
cards.watchOut: Short 4-week trials, and the authors themselves flag the inherent challenges in gravimetrically assessing sweat production — the objective sweat-weight difference versus vehicle is modest. Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate and infrequently led to discontinuation; the pooled report does not enumerate which specific events occurred.
cards.source: Glaser DA et al.. Topical glycopyrronium tosylate for the treatment of primary axillary hyperhidrosis: Results from the ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 phase 3 randomized controlled trials.. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2019. PMID: 30003988. Registry ID: none in this report's record. shelves.title: Athlete's foot: one week of terbinafine beat four weeks of clotrimazole
shelves.question: In people with athlete's foot (interdigital tinea pedis), does terbinafine 1% cream clear the fungus — and does one week of it beat four weeks of clotrimazole?
shelves.mesh: Terbinafine · Naphthalenes · Clotrimazole · Tinea Pedis · Antifungal Agents · Administration, Cutaneous · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Yes — and the short course beat the long one. In Evans 1994, 211 people with mycologically proven tinea pedis received terbinafine 1% cream twice daily for 1 week (followed by 3 weeks of placebo cream) or clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for 4 weeks; at week 4, mycological cure was 93.5% on terbinafine versus 73.1% on clotrimazole (p=.0001), and effective treatment (cure with no or minimal signs and symptoms) was 89.7% versus 58.7%. Against its own vehicle, terbinafine 1% cream once daily for 1 week gave a mycological cure of 91.4% versus 37.1% (p<.001), maintained 7 weeks after treatment ended (Korting 2001). One week of terbinafine therefore clears the fungus in about nine of ten patients — better than four weeks of the older azole cream and far better than vehicle. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant double-blind trials with large absolute cure differences, held at POSSIBLE because both are older industry-era trials and one lacks a stated sample size in its abstract.

cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, vehicle-controlled study
cards.people: Adult patients with interdigital tinea pedis in a prospective, randomised, double-blind, parallel group study (LAS-INT-06) of terbinafine 1% cream (Lamisil — the tested product named in the publication) applied once daily for 1 week versus its vehicle, with efficacy assessed 1 day and 1, 5 and 7 weeks after the end of treatment. shelves.title: Tea tree oil for acne: one 1990 trial found it about as good as benzoyl peroxide, slower, and gentler — and nobody has tested it properly since
shelves.question: In people with mild-to-moderate acne, does 5% tea-tree oil gel improve acne compared with standard topical treatment (benzoyl peroxide)?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris/*drug therapy/pathology · Adolescent · Adult · Benzoyl Peroxide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Child · Female · Gels · Humans · Male · Oils, Volatile/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Plant Oils/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Skin/pathology · Time Factors · *Trees
shelves.balance: Tea tree oil is the natural-remedy answer to acne, and it has exactly one randomised trial — a 1990 Australian single-blind comparison (124 patients) against 5% benzoyl peroxide lotion, the standard of the day. Both treatments significantly reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesion counts; the tea tree gel (5%) was slower to start working, and noticeably fewer patients reported side effects on it. That is the whole record: no placebo arm, no double blinding, no modern trial in the three decades since, and no named product — the publication describes a 5% tea-tree oil gel without a brand. A gentler-but-slower alternative to benzoyl peroxide is a fair reading; anything stronger is not. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf for the developer's verdict.

cards.headline: The only trial: 5% tea-tree oil gel matched 5% benzoyl peroxide on lesion counts, worked more slowly, and caused fewer side effects
cards.summary: The only trial: 5% tea-tree oil gel matched 5% benzoyl peroxide on lesion counts, worked more slowly, and caused fewer side effects
cards.people: 124 patients with mild-to-moderate acne in a single-blind randomised trial of 5% tea-tree oil gel versus 5% benzoyl peroxide lotion (Bassett 1990, Australia).
cards.result: Both treatments significantly ameliorated acne by reducing inflamed and non-inflamed lesions (open and closed comedones); the onset of action was slower with tea-tree oil, and fewer side effects were experienced on tea-tree oil than on benzoyl peroxide. The publication names no commercial product — it tested a 5% tea-tree oil gel preparation.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, no placebo group, and never replicated — the comparison shows the gel is in benzoyl peroxide's neighbourhood, not that it beats doing nothing. Essential-oil quality varies widely between modern products.
cards.source: Bassett IB et al.. A comparative study of tea-tree oil versus benzoylperoxide in the treatment of acne. The Medical Journal of Australia. 1990. PMID: 2145499. shelves.title: Aloe vera for psoriasis: one trial claims an impossible 83% cure rate; a better trial shows it roughly matching a mild steroid — believe the second
shelves.question: In people with plaque psoriasis, does topical aloe vera improve psoriasis severity compared with placebo or a topical steroid?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adolescent · Adult · *Aloe · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ointments/chemistry · Patient Compliance · Plant Extracts/*therapeutic use · *Plants, Medicinal · Psoriasis/*therapy
shelves.balance: Aloe vera for psoriasis carries one of the most implausible result patterns in the supplement literature, which is why this shelf shows its working. The placebo-controlled trial (60 patients) reported that a 0.5% aloe vera extract cream 'cured' 25 of 30 patients (83.3%) against 2 of 30 (6.6%) on placebo over a 16-week study — a cure rate no psoriasis therapy, including modern biologics, approaches in this disease. The second trial is more believable: against 0.1% triamcinolone cream in 80 patients, aloe vera reduced PASI slightly more (−7.7 versus −6.6 points over 8 weeks, p=0.0237), with quality-of-life gains identical between groups. Two positive trials say aloe cream is not inert; the first trial's numbers say its report should be read with real scepticism. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — positive twice, discounted for the implausible anchor.

cards.headline: Syed 1996: aloe cream 'cured' 25/30 patients versus 2/30 on placebo — a result too large to take at face value
cards.summary: Syed 1996: aloe cream 'cured' 25/30 patients versus 2/30 on placebo — a result too large to take at face value
cards.people: 60 patients aged 18–50 with slight-to-moderate chronic plaque psoriasis (PASI 4.8–16.7) randomised double-blind to aloe vera extract 0.5% in a hydrophilic cream or placebo cream, self-applied three times daily, in a study scheduled for 16 weeks with 12 months of follow-up.
cards.result: By the end of the study the aloe cream had 'cured' 25/30 patients (83.3%) versus 2/30 (6.6%) on placebo (p<0.001), clearing 328/396 plaques (82.8%) versus 28/366 (7.7%) and reducing mean PASI to 2.2; no adverse effects or dropouts were reported. The publication names no commercial brand for the extract cream.
cards.watchOut: Read this card as a warning label: complete cure in 83% of a chronic relapsing disease, zero dropouts and zero adverse effects is not a pattern real psoriasis trials produce. The card is kept because the trial exists and is cited — its figures are reported, not endorsed.
cards.source: Syed TA et al.. Management of psoriasis with Aloe vera extract in a hydrophilic cream: a placebo-controlled, double-blind study. Tropical Medicine & International Health. 1996. PMID: 8765459. cards.headline: Choonhakarn 2010: aloe vera reduced PASI slightly more than 0.1% triamcinolone (−7.7 versus −6.6 points; p=0.0237)
cards.summary: Choonhakarn 2010: aloe vera reduced PASI slightly more than 0.1% triamcinolone (−7.7 versus −6.6 points; p=0.0237)
cards.people: 80 patients with mild-to-moderate plaque psoriasis randomised double-blind to aloe vera cream or 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide cream for 8 weeks, assessed by PASI and the Dermatology Life Quality Index.
cards.result: Mean PASI fell from 11.6 to 3.9 (−7.7) on aloe vera and from 10.9 to 4.3 (−6.6) on triamcinolone — a small between-group advantage to aloe (p=0.0237). Quality of life improved equally (−6.1 versus −5.8; p=0.55). No follow-up beyond 8 weeks. The publication names no commercial brand for the aloe cream.
cards.watchOut: A modest, believable result — roughly matching a mild topical steroid — and the more trustworthy of the shelf's two cards. Eight weeks says nothing about a lifelong relapsing disease.
cards.source: Choonhakarn C et al.. A prospective, randomized clinical trial comparing topical aloe vera with 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide in mild to moderate plaque psoriasis. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology. 2010. PMID: 19686327. shelves.title: Ketoconazole shampoo for dandruff: 88% responded, and weekly use cut relapse from 47% to 19% — the rare OTC claim with a real trial behind it
shelves.question: In people with dandruff and scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis, does ketoconazole 2% shampoo clear the condition and prevent relapse compared with placebo shampoo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dermatitis, Seborrheic/*drug therapy/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · *Hair Preparations · Humans · Ketoconazole/*therapeutic use · Male · Scalp Dermatoses/*drug therapy/prevention & control · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo is the pharmacy-shelf treatment for dandruff and scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis, and its evidence is an old, large, well-shaped trial. In Peter 1995, 575 patients with moderate-to-severe scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff responded to twice-weekly ketoconazole shampoo in 88% of cases over 2–4 weeks; 312 responders then entered a 6-month double-blind prophylaxis phase, in which relapse struck 47% on placebo shampoo against 19% on once-weekly ketoconazole (31% on an alternating regimen) — treatment and prevention in one design. The second card is a different kind of evidence: in a 40-woman crossover, a 1% pyrithione zinc conditioning shampoo was preferred over the 2% ketoconazole shampoo by 75% of users on overall performance and scored better on combing ease, smoothness and frizz — cosmetic acceptance, not efficacy, but the thing that decides whether anyone keeps using an anti-dandruff shampoo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.summary: Peter 1995: 88% responded to 2% ketoconazole shampoo; weekly prophylaxis cut 6-month relapse to 19% versus 47% on placebo
cards.people: 575 patients with moderate-to-severe seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff of the scalp treated with 2% ketoconazole shampoo twice weekly for 2–4 weeks in a multicentre double-blind trial; 312 responders were then randomised double-blind for 6 months to once-weekly ketoconazole shampoo, an alternating active/placebo regimen, or placebo shampoo alone.
cards.result: 88% achieved an excellent response in the treatment phase. In prophylaxis, relapse occurred in 48 patients (47%) on placebo versus 23 (19%) on once-weekly ketoconazole and 31 (31%) on the alternating regimen. The medication was well tolerated in all groups. The publication names no retail brand — it tested a 2% ketoconazole shampoo preparation.
cards.watchOut: From 1995, and 'excellent response' is the trial's own global rating — but the prophylaxis phase is a genuine randomised relapse-prevention comparison, the design this question needs.

shelves.title: Bath additives for childhood eczema: a 483-child trial found no benefit on any measure — the money is better spent on the creams that stay on
shelves.question: In children with eczema, do emollient bath additives added to standard care (leave-on emollients and topical treatments) improve eczema control compared with standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: *Baths · Child · Child, Preschool · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Eczema/*therapy · Emollients/pharmacology/*therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Primary Health Care · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Skin/*drug effects · Standard of Care · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: Emollient bath additives — the oils and dispersants poured into the bath for children with eczema — cost families and health services real money, and the BATHE trial tested them the way the question deserves: 483 children aged 1–11 in 96 UK general practices, randomised to prescribed bath additives or none for 12 months, with both groups continuing ordinary leave-on emollients and standard care. The answer was no. Weekly POEM eczema scores over the first 16 weeks did not differ significantly; the adjusted difference was 0.41 points (95% CI −0.27 to 1.10) — a fraction of the 3-point difference considered the smallest that matters — and there were no differences in severity over the year, flare consultations, quality of life, or costs. Leave-on emollients remain standard; the bath additive adds nothing measurable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one large, pragmatic, decisive null.

cards.headline: BATHE: 483 children, 12 months — bath additives moved eczema scores by 0.41 POEM points against a 3-point minimum that matters
cards.summary: BATHE: 483 children, 12 months — bath additives moved eczema scores by 0.41 POEM points against a 3-point minimum that matters
cards.people: 483 children aged 1–11 years with atopic eczema in 96 general practices in Wales and western and southern England, randomised pragmatically (open label) to prescribed emollient bath additives plus standard care or standard care with no bath additives for 12 months; 482 analysed, with weekly POEM scores for the first 16 weeks as the primary outcome.
cards.result: Mean POEM over 16 weeks was 7.5 (SD 6.0) with bath additives versus 8.4 (6.0) without; after adjustment, scores in the no-additives group were 0.41 points higher (95% CI −0.27 to 1.10) — not significant and far below the 3-point minimal clinically important difference. No differences in year-long severity, exacerbation consultations, quality of life, resource use, or adverse effects. The trial tested bath additives as a class, prescribed by the children's usual teams; it does not tie the result to a single named product.
cards.watchOut: Open label by necessity (families know what is in the bath), with a patient-reported primary outcome — but a null this complete, across every secondary outcome and the economic analysis, is hard to argue with.
cards.source: Santer M et al.. Emollient bath additives for the treatment of childhood eczema (BATHE): multicentre pragmatic parallel group randomised controlled trial of clinical and cost effectiveness. The BMJ. 2018. PMID: 29724749. shelves.title: Glaucoma drops really do save sight: visual-field loss delayed (HR 0.44) in glaucoma, and onset cut from 9.5% to 4.4% in high eye pressure
shelves.question: In people with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension, do pressure-lowering eye drops preserve vision and prevent glaucoma compared with placebo or observation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Ophthalmic · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents/*administration & dosage · Female · Glaucoma, Open-Angle/*drug therapy/physiopathology · Humans · Intraocular Pressure/drug effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Latanoprost · Male · Middle Aged · Ophthalmic Solutions/administration & dosage · Prostaglandins F, Synthetic/*administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Visual Fields/drug effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Glaucoma drops are prescribed for decades on a chain of reasoning — drops lower eye pressure, pressure damages the optic nerve, so drops must save sight — that long rested on the pressure number alone. Two landmark trials closed the loop. UKGTS randomised 516 people with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma to latanoprost or placebo drops: pressure fell 3.8 versus 0.9 mmHg, and visual-field deterioration was delayed with a hazard ratio of 0.44 (0.28–0.69; p=0.0003) — the first placebo-controlled proof that a drop preserves visual function, strong enough that the safety committee stopped the trial early. OHTS asked the earlier question in 1,636 people with high eye pressure but no glaucoma: treatment cut the 5-year probability of developing glaucoma from 9.5% to 4.4% (HR 0.40, 0.27–0.59) — about five cases prevented per hundred people treated for five years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): sight itself, not just pressure, in two large randomised trials.

cards.headline: UKGTS: latanoprost delayed visual-field deterioration versus placebo (HR 0.44, 0.28–0.69) — the first placebo-controlled proof a drop preserves vision
cards.summary: UKGTS: latanoprost delayed visual-field deterioration versus placebo (HR 0.44, 0.28–0.69) — the first placebo-controlled proof a drop preserves vision
cards.people: 516 people with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma at ten UK centres, randomised triple-masked to latanoprost 0.005% drops or placebo drops once daily to both eyes; primary outcome time to visual-field deterioration within 24 months.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean pressure reduction was 3.8 mmHg on latanoprost versus 0.9 mmHg on placebo, and visual-field preservation was significantly longer on latanoprost: adjusted hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.69; p=0.0003). The data and safety monitoring committee recommended stopping early after an interim analysis. 18 serious adverse events occurred, none attributable to the study drug. Registry ID: ISRCTN96423140 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: Visual-field deterioration is the functional outcome that precedes disability — not a pressure surrogate. Early stopping can exaggerate effects, but the margin here is wide. Latanoprost is a defined drug; no product question arises.
cards.source: Garway-Heath DF et al.. Latanoprost for open-angle glaucoma (UKGTS): a randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25533656. Registry ID: ISRCTN96423140. cards.headline: OHTS: treating high eye pressure cut 5-year glaucoma onset from 9.5% to 4.4% (HR 0.40)
cards.summary: OHTS: treating high eye pressure cut 5-year glaucoma onset from 9.5% to 4.4% (HR 0.40)
cards.people: 1,636 people aged 40–80 with ocular hypertension (raised pressure, no glaucomatous damage) randomised to topical ocular hypotensive medication or observation, with a pressure goal of ≥20% reduction and ≤24 mmHg in the treated group.
cards.result: Mean pressure fell 22.5% on treatment versus 4.0% under observation. At 60 months the cumulative probability of developing primary open-angle glaucoma was 4.4% treated versus 9.5% observed (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.27–0.59; p<0.0001) — an absolute reduction of about 5 cases per 100 people over 5 years, with little evidence of increased systemic or ocular risk. The treated group used commercially available drops of several kinds, so the result belongs to pressure lowering as a strategy.
cards.watchOut: Treating everyone with high pressure means treating many who would never convert — about 19 of 20 observed patients stayed glaucoma-free for 5 years. Who to treat is a risk-stratification question layered on top of this shelf's efficacy answer.
cards.source: Kass MA et al.. The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study: a randomized trial determines that topical ocular hypotensive medication delays or prevents the onset of primary open-angle glaucoma. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2002. PMID: 12049574. shelves.title: Collagen peptides for skin: two small trials from one group show device-measured improvements — a maybe, not the marketing
shelves.question: In middle-aged women, do oral collagen peptide supplements improve skin wrinkles and elasticity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Collagen/administration & dosage/*pharmacology · Collagen Type I/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Elastin/metabolism · Female · Fibrillins · Humans · Microfilament Proteins/metabolism · Middle Aged · Peptides/administration & dosage/*pharmacology · Skin Aging/*drug effects · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Collagen drinks and powders are a large market built on a small evidence base: two little double-blind trials from one research group, both of the same kind of specific bioactive collagen peptides. In the wrinkle trial (114 women aged 45–65), 2.5 g/day of the named peptide product Verisol cut eye-wrinkle volume by about 20% relative to placebo after 8 weeks (p<0.05), with skin procollagen up 65% and elastin up 18% in a biopsy subgroup; the wrinkle effect persisted four weeks after stopping. In the elasticity trial (69 women aged 35–55), 2.5 g or 5 g of collagen peptides improved measured skin elasticity significantly against placebo over 8 weeks, while moisture and water-loss outcomes reached significance only in subgroups. Objective instruments, tiny samples, surrogate cosmetic endpoints, one group, one product family, and no independent replication: the profile of a weak-evidence stamp. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Proksch 2014 (wrinkles): Verisol peptides cut eye-wrinkle volume ~20% versus placebo at 8 weeks; procollagen up 65% in biopsies
cards.summary: Proksch 2014 (wrinkles): Verisol peptides cut eye-wrinkle volume ~20% versus placebo at 8 weeks; procollagen up 65% in biopsies
cards.people: 114 women aged 45–65 randomised double-blind to the specific bioactive collagen peptide product Verisol 2.5 g once daily (n=57) or placebo (n=57) for 8 weeks, with objective wrinkle measurement and a suction-blister biopsy subgroup; follow-up 4 weeks after the last dose.
cards.result: Eye-wrinkle volume fell significantly versus placebo after 4 and 8 weeks of intake (20% reduction at 8 weeks; p<0.05), and the effect persisted 4 weeks after stopping. In the biopsy subgroup, procollagen type I was 65% higher and elastin 18% higher than placebo after 8 weeks; fibrillin rose 6%, not significantly. The record names the tested product (Verisol bioactive collagen peptides); it does not name a manufacturer.
cards.watchOut: Cosmetic surrogate endpoints measured on instruments, in 114 women, by the group that developed this literature. A 20% change in a wrinkle-volume metric is not the same as looking visibly younger, and no blinded photographic or patient-rated primary outcome anchors the claim.
cards.source: Proksch E et al.. Oral intake of specific bioactive collagen peptides reduces skin wrinkles and increases dermal matrix synthesis. Skin Pharmacology and Physiology. 2014. cards.headline: Proksch 2014 (elasticity): collagen peptides improved skin elasticity at both 2.5 g and 5 g; moisture effects were subgroup-only
cards.summary: Proksch 2014 (elasticity): collagen peptides improved skin elasticity at both 2.5 g and 5 g; moisture effects were subgroup-only
cards.people: 69 women aged 35–55 randomised double-blind to collagen hydrolysate of specific peptides 2.5 g or 5.0 g once daily or placebo (23 per group) for 8 weeks, with objective measurement of elasticity, moisture, transepidermal water loss and roughness, plus a 4-week post-treatment follow-up.
cards.result: Skin elasticity improved significantly in both peptide groups versus placebo by 8 weeks, and remained significantly higher at the 4-week follow-up in the older women. Skin moisture and evaporation moved favourably only in subgroup analyses and did not reach overall significance. No side effects were noted. cards.watchOut: Twenty-three women per arm. Elasticity is a device measurement, not a clinical outcome, and with the wrinkle trial it forms a single-group, single-product evidence base.

shelves.title: Gargling to prevent and shorten colds and other upper respiratory infections
shelves.question: Does gargling — with plain water or with hypertonic saline — prevent upper respiratory tract infections, or shorten them once they start?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents, Local · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouthwashes · Povidone-Iodine · Respiratory Tract Infections · Water · Common Cold
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one 387-person randomised prevention trial found water gargling cut first upper respiratory infections by 36% in relative terms (absolute incidence 0.17 vs 0.26 episodes per 30 person-days), and one small open-label pilot found saline irrigation-plus-gargling shortened colds by about two days. Both trials are unblindable by nature and the treatment evidence is pilot-sized, which holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Gargling with plain water cut first colds by about a third in relative terms; povidone-iodine gargling did not
cards.summary: Gargling with plain water cut first colds by about a third in relative terms; povidone-iodine gargling did not
cards.people: 387 healthy volunteers aged 18–65 in Japan, followed for 60 days over one winter; water gargling, povidone-iodine gargling, or usual care
cards.result: First-URTI incidence was 0.26 episodes per 30 person-days on usual care, 0.17 with water gargling and 0.24 with povidone-iodine gargling. Against control, the incidence rate ratio was 0.64 (95% CI 0.41–0.99) for water — a 36% relative reduction — and 0.89 (95% CI 0.60–1.33) for povidone-iodine, which made no clear difference. When infections did occur, water gargling tended to soften bronchial symptoms (P = 0.055).
cards.watchOut: Gargling cannot be blinded and infections were self-recorded, so expectation could colour the result; one winter, one country, and no registry entry in the record.
cards.source: Satomura K et al.. Prevention of upper respiratory tract infections by gargling: a randomized trial. Am J Prev Med. 2005. PMID: 16242593. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hypertonic saline nasal irrigation plus gargling shortened colds by about two days in a small pilot (the ELVIS pilot)
cards.summary: Hypertonic saline nasal irrigation plus gargling shortened colds by about two days in a small pilot (the ELVIS pilot)
cards.people: 68 adults within 48 hours of cold onset in Edinburgh, UK; 61 analysed; hypertonic saline nasal irrigation and gargling vs standard care
cards.result: Illness lasted 1.9 fewer days in the intervention arm (P = 0.01); over-the-counter medicine use was 36% lower, transmission to household contacts 35% lower, and viral shedding fell faster (≥0.5 log10/day; P = 0.04). 87% found the routine acceptable and 93% felt it made a difference.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial — its primary outcome was recruitment, not efficacy. Open-label and small, and the gargle was combined with nasal irrigation, so the gargle's own share is unknown; nasal saline irrigation itself is shelved at #637.
cards.source: Ramalingam S et al.. A pilot, open labelled, randomised controlled trial of hypertonic saline nasal irrigation and gargling for the common cold. Sci Rep. 2019. PMID: 30705369. cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: Two randomised trials point the same way: plain-water gargling prevented some colds in the one prevention trial, and saline irrigation-plus-gargling shortened colds in one small pilot. The evidence is thin and cannot be blinded, but the intervention is free and safe — a reasonable habit with modest expectations.
cards.watchOut: No large confirmatory trial exists for either use; the treatment claim rests on a 61-person pilot.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.

shelves.title: Topical tretinoin for photoaged skin
shelves.question: Does topical tretinoin cream improve the wrinkling and pigmentation of photoaged (sun-damaged) skin?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adult · Aged · Aging · Biopsy · Dermatitis, Contact · Double-Blind Method · Drug Evaluation · Face · Forearm · Humans · Middle Aged · Random Allocation
shelves.balance: LIKELY — three double-blind vehicle-controlled studies agree: 0.05% tretinoin beat vehicle on global photoaging response (68% vs 43% improved, n = 296), with split-body and biopsy support in the first trial and durability shown to 48 weeks. Cosmetic-grade outcomes and irritation-driven unblinding keep it short of a Level A claim.

cards.headline: Tretinoin-treated skin improved in nearly every patient; vehicle-treated skin in none of the faces
cards.summary: Tretinoin-treated skin improved in nearly every patient; vehicle-treated skin in none of the faces
cards.people: 30 patients completing a 16-week randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled study; tretinoin to one forearm and vehicle to the other, and tretinoin or vehicle to the face
cards.result: All 30 patients showed significant improvement in photoaging on the tretinoin-treated forearm and not on the vehicle-treated forearm. On the face, 14 of 15 tretinoin patients improved vs 0 of 15 vehicle patients. Histological changes were significant only in tretinoin-treated skin. Side effects were limited to irritation of tretinoin-exposed skin.
cards.watchOut: A small 1988 study with a split-body design; skin irritation can unblind patients and assessors.
cards.source: Weiss JS et al.. Topical tretinoin improves photoaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled study. JAMA. 1988. PMID: 3336176. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tretinoin emollient cream 0.05% beat vehicle in 296 patients; lower strengths did not
cards.summary: Tretinoin emollient cream 0.05% beat vehicle in 296 patients; lower strengths did not
cards.people: 296 adults with photodamaged facial skin in a 24-week double-blind multicentre study; tretinoin emollient cream 0.05%, 0.01% or 0.001% vs vehicle
cards.result: Improvement at the end of therapy: 68% on 0.05% cream vs 43% on vehicle (P < 0.001); an excellent or good response in 26% vs 11%. Fine wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation and roughness each improved more on 0.05% than on vehicle (P < 0.05). The 0.01% and 0.001% strengths did not differ significantly from vehicle. Mild-to-moderate erythema, peeling and burning were the commonest side effects.
cards.watchOut: Vehicle alone improved 43% of patients — moisturiser, sun behaviour and expectation do real work; the drug's added gain is the 25-point gap over vehicle.
cards.source: Olsen EA et al.. Tretinoin emollient cream: a new therapy for photodamaged skin. J Am Acad Dermatol. 1992. PMID: 1552056. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Continuing the cream for a second 24 weeks maintained the improvement, with fewer skin reactions
cards.summary: Continuing the cream for a second 24 weeks maintained the improvement, with fewer skin reactions
cards.people: 298 patients who had completed 24 weeks on tretinoin emollient cream 0.05% (n = 149) or 0.01% (n = 149), continuing the same strength for 24 further weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Maintenance of improvement, or further reduction in signs of photodamage, was noted in both investigator and patient evaluations and confirmed by skin-replica analysis. Cutaneous side effects were less common during the extension than during the first 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same programme's patients rather than an independent trial — it shows durability, not new proof.

cards.result: Tretinoin 0.05% cream produces a real, moderate improvement in fine wrinkling and mottled pigmentation over about six months, at the price of irritation that usually settles with continued use. shelves.title: Dual-action antihistamine eye drops for allergic conjunctivitis
shelves.question: Do dual-action antihistamine eye drops (alcaftadine, olopatadine) relieve the itching of allergic conjunctivitis better than placebo drops?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzazepines · Cedrus · Conjunctivitis, Allergic · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Histamine H1 Antagonists · Humans · Imidazoles · Incidence · Japan
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two double-masked, placebo-controlled allergen-challenge trials show clear, consistent anti-itch effects (P < 0.001 at all measured time points), and a 30-trial Cochrane review supports the drug class over placebo in the short term; but the direct evidence measures itching minutes after a laboratory allergen dose rather than real-world seasonal use, which holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Both alcaftadine and olopatadine beat placebo on itching at every time point, 16 and 24 hours after dosing
cards.summary: Both alcaftadine and olopatadine beat placebo on itching at every time point, 16 and 24 hours after dosing
cards.people: 127 people with allergic conjunctivitis in a multicentre, double-masked, randomised trial using the conjunctival allergen challenge model; alcaftadine 0.25% vs olopatadine 0.2% vs placebo, dosed twice over about five weeks
cards.result: For the primary measure — ocular itching at 3, 5 and 7 minutes after challenge — both active drops were statistically superior to placebo at every time point at both the 16-hour and 24-hour post-dose challenges (P < 0.0001). Alcaftadine scored numerically lower itch than olopatadine at every time point (significantly so at 3 minutes at 16 hours, P = 0.026), gave significantly less lid swelling than placebo throughout, and was the only treatment to relieve chemosis significantly at every 24-hour time point. All treatments were generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH terms. This is a laboratory allergen-challenge model — itch scored minutes after a deliberate allergen dose — not a pollen season in real life.
cards.source: Ackerman S et al.. A multicenter evaluation of the efficacy and duration of action of alcaftadine 0.25% and olopatadine 0.2% in the conjunctival allergen challenge model. J Asthma Allergy. 2013. PMID: 24109191. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: the record carries no MeSH terms

cards.headline: In a Japanese cedar-pollen challenge, alcaftadine beat vehicle and matched olopatadine
cards.summary: In a Japanese cedar-pollen challenge, alcaftadine beat vehicle and matched olopatadine
cards.people: 240 Japanese subjects sensitive to cedar pollen; alcaftadine 0.25% (challenged 8 hours post-dose) vs olopatadine 0.1% (challenged 4 hours post-dose) vs vehicle, double-blind
cards.result: Alcaftadine was significantly more effective than vehicle at preventing itching and conjunctival hyperaemia (P < 0.001) and non-inferior to olopatadine. Conjunctival hyperaemia scores at 7 and 15 minutes after challenge were significantly lower with alcaftadine than with olopatadine (P ≤ 0.027). Both drops were well tolerated, with no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Again a challenge-model study with outcomes measured in minutes, and the two drops were deliberately challenged at different times after dosing (8 vs 4 hours).
cards.source: Nakatani H et al.. Alcaftadine 0.25% versus Olopatadine 0.1% in Preventing Cedar Pollen Allergic Conjunctivitis in Japan: A Randomized Study. Ocul Immunol Inflamm. 2019. PMID: 29543548. cards.headline: Cochrane review: topical antihistamines and mast-cell stabilisers reduce symptoms vs placebo in the short term
cards.summary: Cochrane review: topical antihistamines and mast-cell stabilisers reduce symptoms vs placebo in the short term
cards.people: 30 randomised trials, 4,344 participants, 17 different drugs or comparisons, in seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis; treatment durations one to eight weeks
cards.result: The review found some evidence that topical antihistamines and mast-cell stabilisers reduce symptoms and signs of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis compared with placebo, with no serious adverse events reported for these treatments. Reporting varied so much, however, that meta-analysis was possible for only one comparison (olopatadine vs ketotifen), and there are no long-term efficacy data.
cards.watchOut: Short-term evidence only, and the reviewers warn that head-to-head comparisons between different drops need cautious interpretation.

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: In controlled allergen challenges, alcaftadine and olopatadine clearly beat placebo drops for itching and redness, and the wider trial literature supports short-term symptom relief from this drug class. What is not well proven is how much they help across a real pollen season, or whether one drop beats another.
cards.watchOut: Industry-run challenge studies dominate the direct evidence; real-world comparative trials are thin.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.
