shelves.title: Oil pulling for gums and breath: matched chlorhexidine in two 20-person trials — but nothing was ever compared with doing nothing
shelves.question: Does oil pulling (swishing oil in the mouth) improve gum health or bad breath?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Infective Agents, Local · Bacteria, Aerobic · Chlorhexidine · Colony Count, Microbial · Dental Plaque · Dental Plaque Index · Double-Blind Method · Gingivitis · Humans · India · Male · Mouthwashes · Phytotherapy · Sesame Oil
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — in two small trials from one research group (20 adolescents each, 10–14 days), swishing sesame oil improved plaque and gum scores about as much as chlorhexidine mouthwash — but every participant received an active treatment, so the trials cannot show that oil pulling beats ordinary brushing, water swishing, or simply being in a study. There is no placebo or no-treatment arm anywhere in the randomised record.

cards.headline: Sesame oil pulling vs chlorhexidine: plaque and gingivitis scores fell in BOTH groups (P < 0.001) over 10 days
cards.summary: Sesame oil pulling vs chlorhexidine: plaque and gingivitis scores fell in BOTH groups (P < 0.001) over 10 days
cards.people: 20 adolescent boys with plaque-induced gingivitis, randomised to oil pulling with sesame oil (n = 10) or chlorhexidine mouthwash (n = 10) each morning before brushing, for 10 days
cards.result: Plaque index and modified gingival index scores fell significantly in both groups (P < 0.001 in both), and total aerobic colony counts in plaque fell in both groups. There was no untreated, placebo or brushing-only group.
cards.watchOut: Ten participants per arm and ten days; with both groups improving equally, the trial is consistent with oil pulling working — and equally consistent with study participation improving everyone's brushing.

cards.summary: Synthesis: not disproven — simply never tested against nothing
cards.people: 40 adolescents across the two randomised trials carded
cards.result: Oil pulling with sesame oil performed comparably to chlorhexidine mouthwash on short-term plaque, gum and breath measures in two very small trials, with no comparison against placebo, water or usual care alone. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Pseudoephedrine for a blocked nose: it does open the nose on objective testing — one positive trial, one missed endpoint, and about +1 mmHg and +3 beats/min as the average price
shelves.question: In adults with nasal congestion from the common cold, does oral pseudoephedrine relieve congestion versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Airway Resistance/drug effects · Chi-Square Distribution · Common Cold/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Ephedrine/administration & dosage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Nasal Obstruction/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Rhinomanometry · Sympathomimetics/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Pseudoephedrine is the decongestant that survived the phenylephrine reckoning (shelf #2461) — and unlike phenylephrine, it has objective evidence behind it, though less than its reputation suggests. In the cleanest trial (Eccles 2005, PMID: 15794071), 238 adults with cold-related congestion took 60 mg or placebo: nasal airway resistance area-under-curve was significantly lower on pseudoephedrine after a single dose (p = 0.006) and after 3 days of dosing (p < 0.001), with subjective congestion scores significantly better on day 1 but not on the day-3 visual analogue scores. The second repeated-dose trial was cooler: in 216 subjects taking 60 mg four times daily for 3 days, the prespecified primary outcome — day-1 nasal airway resistance AUC — was not significantly different from placebo, with only small objective gains (total nasal volume +5.5% relative, p = 0.031) and a non-significant 7.0% relative fall in congestion VAS (p = 0.072) (Latte 2007, PMID: 17882915). The physiological price is real but small at standard doses: across 24 randomised trials (1,285 patients), pseudoephedrine raised systolic blood pressure by a mean of 0.99 mmHg (95% CI 0.08 to 1.90) and heart rate by 2.83 beats/min (2.0 to 3.6), with no diastolic effect; higher and immediate-release doses raised pressure more (Salerno 2005, PMID: 16087815). A real decongestant effect on objective testing, inconsistently felt by patients, bought with a small pressor effect — that is the whole of it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: a symptom claim; the blood-pressure data are carded as context, not as a benefit claim).

cards.headline: Eccles 2005: pseudoephedrine 60 mg significantly lowered nasal airway resistance versus placebo after one dose and after 3 days — subjective scores agreed on day 1, not on day 3
cards.summary: Eccles 2005: pseudoephedrine 60 mg significantly lowered nasal airway resistance versus placebo after one dose and after 3 days — subjective scores agreed on day 1, not on day 3
cards.people: 238 patients (mean age 20 years) with nasal congestion from an acute upper respiratory tract infection, in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial over 3 days at a single centre. Nasal airway resistance was measured objectively by posterior rhinomanometry hourly for 4 hours after dosing on day 1 (single dose) and day 3 (after multiple doses); subjective congestion was scored on visual analogue scales and as an end-of-day summary score.
cards.result: After a single dose, pseudoephedrine gave a significantly lower nasal airway resistance AUC 0–3 h (primary variable, p = 0.006) and AUC 0–4 h (p = 0.001) than placebo. On day 3, after multiple doses, both resistance measures again favoured pseudoephedrine (p < 0.001). Subjective congestion scores were significantly lower on pseudoephedrine on day 1 (VAS AUC 0–3 h p = 0.029; 0–4 h p = 0.021) but not on day 3; the summary congestion/stuffiness score over the study did favour pseudoephedrine (p = 0.016). Heart rate averaged 2–4 beats/min higher on pseudoephedrine; five adverse events were reported in each group, all judged unrelated.
cards.watchOut: Young subjects (mean age 20) with laboratory-measured colds are not the older, hypertensive, prostatic population that actually worries about this drug. Objective resistance and felt congestion part company by day 3 — the nose measures opener than it feels — and the trial was run by investigators closely associated with the common-cold research unit that produced much of this literature.
cards.source: Eccles R et al. Efficacy and safety of single and multiple doses of pseudoephedrine in the treatment of nasal congestion associated with common cold. American Journal of Rhinology. 2005. PMID: 15794071. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Latte 2007: the primary outcome missed — 3 days of pseudoephedrine 60 mg four times daily did not significantly beat placebo on day-1 nasal airway resistance AUC
cards.summary: Latte 2007: the primary outcome missed — 3 days of pseudoephedrine 60 mg four times daily did not significantly beat placebo on day-1 nasal airway resistance AUC
cards.people: 216 subjects with the common cold in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of pseudoephedrine 60 mg four times daily or matching placebo for 3 days (southern hemisphere). Measurements: posterior rhinomanometry, acoustic rhinometry, and subjective congestion on categorical and visual analogue scales. The prespecified primary efficacy outcome was day-1 nasal airway resistance area under the curve.
cards.result: The primary outcome was not significantly different between groups. After the first dose, pseudoephedrine showed small improvements over placebo on objective measures, including a 5.5% relative increase in total nasal volume 0.5–3 hours after dosing (p = 0.031). Pooling days 1 and 3, congestion VAS fell by 7.0% relative on pseudoephedrine (p = 0.072, not significant). The authors' own conclusion: small but nonsignificant improvements in objective assessments after a single dose.
cards.watchOut: Carded in full because it is the necessary counterweight: the largest repeated-dose monotherapy trial missed its primary endpoint. Read together with Eccles 2005, the pattern is a small objective effect near the edge of detectability — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE and not LIKELY, and why claims that pseudoephedrine 'clearly works' overstate two trials that between them produced one clear positive and one miss.
cards.source: Latte J et al. Clinical trial of 3 days of treatment with oral pseudoephedrine for the common cold in the southern hemisphere. American Journal of Rhinology. 2007. PMID: 17882915. cards.headline: Salerno 2005: across 24 randomised trials, pseudoephedrine raised systolic pressure by about 1 mmHg and heart rate by about 3 beats/min — more at higher and immediate-release doses
cards.summary: Salerno 2005: across 24 randomised trials, pseudoephedrine raised systolic pressure by about 1 mmHg and heart rate by about 3 beats/min — more at higher and immediate-release doses
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 24 randomised placebo-controlled trials of oral pseudoephedrine in adults with extractable vital-sign data (45 treatment arms, 1,285 patients), including patients with controlled hypertension. Outcomes: systolic and diastolic blood pressure and heart rate, pooled as weighted mean differences.
cards.result: Pseudoephedrine increased systolic blood pressure by a mean of 0.99 mmHg (95% CI 0.08 to 1.90) and heart rate by 2.83 beats/min (95% CI 2.0 to 3.6), both statistically significant; diastolic pressure was unaffected (0.63 mmHg, 95% CI −0.10 to 1.35). In controlled hypertension the systolic rise was similar (1.20 mmHg, 0.56 to 1.84). Higher doses and immediate-release preparations produced larger increases; shorter studies showed larger blood-pressure effects than longer ones.
cards.watchOut: Averages conceal tails: a mean 1 mmHg rise is compatible with occasional individuals — uncontrolled hypertension, MAO-inhibitor use, high doses — having much larger responses, and the trials excluded the patients most at risk. This card quantifies the average pressor effect at ordinary doses; it is not a safety clearance for everyone who reaches for the packet.
cards.source: Salerno SM et al. Effect of oral pseudoephedrine on blood pressure and heart rate: a meta-analysis. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005. PMID: 16087815. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small objective decongestant effect that patients feel inconsistently, with a small measurable pressor cost — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small objective decongestant effect that patients feel inconsistently, with a small measurable pressor cost — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy trials in common-cold congestion (n = 238 and n = 216) and one meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (1,285 patients) for the blood-pressure and heart-rate effects.
cards.result: One trial found significant objective decongestion after single and repeated doses; the other missed its primary objective endpoint and found only small, mostly non-significant gains. Subjective relief was significant on day 1 in one trial and non-significant pooled in the other. The pressor cost at standard doses averaged +0.99 mmHg systolic and +2.83 beats/min. Set beside shelf #2461 — oral phenylephrine, which failed to beat placebo at all — pseudoephedrine is the only oral decongestant with any positive objective trial evidence, which is a statement about the field as much as about the drug.
cards.watchOut: Combination products (pseudoephedrine plus paracetamol, aspirin or antihistamines) have their own trial literature and are not evidence for the single drug; one such trial (Eccles 2006, PMID: 17257455) was deliberately not carded here. Nothing in this record addresses congestion in allergic rhinitis as a separate question, children, or use beyond a few days.

shelves.title: Antihistamines for the common cold: a small benefit on the first day or two in adults, nothing after that and nothing in children — paid for in sedation
shelves.question: In adults with the common cold, do oral antihistamines (first-generation, sedating) reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Common Cold/drug therapy · Histamine Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a small, brief benefit in adults, then nothing. The Cochrane synthesis (De Sutter 2015, PMID: 26615034) pooled 18 randomised trials with 4,342 participants: in adults, antihistamines improved overall symptom severity on day 1 or 2 — 45% had a beneficial effect versus 38% on placebo (odds ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.92) — but there was no difference from day 3 onward, and the statistically detectable gains on single symptoms (rhinorrhoea mean difference −0.23 and sneezing −0.35 on 4–5-point scales at day 3) were judged clinically non-significant; there was no clinically significant effect on nasal obstruction. The best individual trials show the same shape at symptom level: clemastine cut rhinorrhoea severity on day 3 (1.02 versus 1.39, P < .001) in 403 adults with natural colds, while sedation hit 14% versus 1.5% on placebo (Turner 1997, PMID: 9356796); in experimental rhinovirus colds, clemastine reduced sneeze scores by 50% relative and secretion weights by 35% relative (Gwaltney 1996, PMID: 8729205). In children the two trials conflict and Cochrane concludes there is no evidence of effectiveness. So the honest answer to 'do antihistamines help a cold?' is: in adults, slightly, for the first day or two, mostly by drying and sedating — and the sedation is not a side issue, since for many combination cold remedies it is most of what the buyer feels. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit on overall symptoms in adults on days 1–2 / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) from day 3 onward and for individual symptoms at any point; no evidence in children (not Tier C: symptom claims only). Children's cough-and-cold treatment, including the diphenhydramine comparison, is homed at shelf #1045.

cards.headline: De Sutter 2015 (Cochrane): 18 trials, 4,342 participants — adults felt better on days 1–2 (45% vs 38%), no difference after that, no clinically significant effect on any single symptom, no evidence in children
cards.summary: De Sutter 2015 (Cochrane): 18 trials, 4,342 participants — adults felt better on days 1–2 (45% vs 38%), no difference after that, no clinically significant effect on any single symptom, no evidence in children
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 RCTs (De Sutter 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: 18 randomised controlled trials (17 publications) of antihistamine monotherapy versus placebo for the common cold, naturally occurring or experimentally induced, totalling 4,342 participants of whom only 212 were children. Combination products and patients with an allergic component were excluded — this is the antihistamine alone, for the cold alone.
cards.result: In adults there was a short-term benefit on overall symptom severity: on day 1 or 2, 45% had a beneficial effect on antihistamines versus 38% on placebo (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.92). There was no difference in the mid term (days 3–4) or long term (days 6–10). Sedating antihistamines produced small statistically significant gains on individual symptoms — rhinorrhoea at day 3: mean difference −0.23 (95% CI −0.39 to −0.06); sneezing at day 3: −0.35 (−0.49 to −0.20) on 4–5-point scales — which the reviewers judged clinically non-significant, with no clinically significant effect on nasal obstruction. Sedation was reported more often with sedating antihistamines, though the pooled difference was not statistically significant. The two trials in children conflicted; the reviewers conclude there is no evidence of effectiveness in children. Most trials were at low risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: A 7-percentage-point absolute advantage (45% vs 38%) on a global 'beneficial effect' judgement in the first 48 hours is the strongest number this literature produces — everything after day 2, and every individual symptom that matters to patients, is null or trivial. Most included trials tested first-generation (sedating) antihistamines; the review does not license claims for the non-sedating second-generation drugs as cold treatment.
cards.source: De Sutter AI et al. Antihistamines for the common cold. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26615034. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Turner 1997: clemastine eased rhinorrhoea and sneezing in 403 adults with natural colds — and sedated 14% versus 1.5% on placebo
cards.summary: Turner 1997: clemastine eased rhinorrhoea and sneezing in 403 adults with natural colds — and sedated 14% versus 1.5% on placebo
cards.people: 403 subjects (202 clemastine fumarate, 201 placebo) with new-onset (under 24 hours) cold symptoms including rhinorrhoea or sneezing, treated for 4 days in a double-blind trial. Outcomes: daily rhinorrhoea and sneezing severity scores, and sedation.
cards.result: Rhinorrhoea severity did not differ on day 2 but did on day 3 — mean score 1.02 ± 0.07 on clemastine versus 1.39 ± 0.07 on placebo (P < .001) — and the effect persisted on day 4; sneezing was significantly improved on days 2–4. Sedation occurred in 14% of clemastine subjects versus 1.5% on placebo (P < .0001) — roughly one extra sedated patient for every eight treated, against symptom-score gains of about a third of a point.
cards.watchOut: Symptom scores, not illness duration: clemastine did not shorten the cold, it dried it slightly while it lasted. The sedation rate (14%) is the figure a purchaser of a 'non-drowsy' era product least expects from a first-generation antihistamine, and it arrived in a trial population of otherwise well adults — in older patients the same pharmacology buys falls and confusion.
cards.source: Turner RB et al. Effectiveness of clemastine fumarate for treatment of rhinorrhea and sneezing associated with the common cold. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1997. PMID: 9356796. cards.headline: Gwaltney 1996: in experimental rhinovirus colds, clemastine halved sneeze scores and cut nasal secretion weights by about a third relative — other cold symptoms were unaffected
cards.summary: Gwaltney 1996: in experimental rhinovirus colds, clemastine halved sneeze scores and cut nasal secretion weights by about a third relative — other cold symptoms were unaffected
cards.people: Volunteers challenged with rhinovirus in a double-blind randomised trial; infected evaluable subjects numbered 75 on clemastine fumarate 1.34 mg twice daily and 75 on placebo, treated for 4 days beginning 24–60 hours after challenge. Outcomes: sneeze severity scores and counts, rhinorrhoea scores, weighed nasal secretions, and other cold symptoms.
cards.result: Over 4 days, mean sneeze scores fell by 50% relative, sneeze counts by 57% relative, rhinorrhoea scores by 27% relative and nasal secretion weights by 35% relative versus placebo (all relative measures as reported by the authors; day-by-day differences reached significance on most illness days, e.g. secretion weight day 3: 3.6 g versus 6.3 g, P = .03). Other cold symptoms were unaffected. Excess adverse effects on clemastine: dry mouth 6%, dry nose 19%, dry throat 17%.
cards.watchOut: An experimental-challenge model in young volunteers with a single virus, dosed on a schedule no shopper follows: it proves the pharmacology (less secretion, less sneezing) under laboratory conditions, and its relative reductions sound larger than the same effects feel in a natural cold — Turner's natural-cold trial is the translation, and there the gains were fractions of a point on severity scales.
cards.source: Gwaltney JM et al. Randomized controlled trial of clemastine fumarate for treatment of experimental rhinovirus colds. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1996. PMID: 8729205. cards.headline: Synthesis: a drying, sedating, two-day effect in adults and nothing beyond it — SPLIT (POSSIBLE days 1–2 / no difference thereafter)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a drying, sedating, two-day effect in adults and nothing beyond it — SPLIT (POSSIBLE days 1–2 / no difference thereafter)
cards.people: One Cochrane synthesis of 18 monotherapy trials (4,342 participants, 212 children) and the two most informative individual trials — clemastine in natural colds (n = 403) and in experimental rhinovirus colds (n = 150 infected evaluable).
cards.result: Adults: 45% versus 38% report benefit on days 1–2 (OR 0.74, 0.60–0.92); no overall benefit from day 3; individual-symptom effects statistically real but clinically non-significant; nasal obstruction unaffected. Children: two conflicting trials, no established benefit. Harms: sedation 14% versus 1.5% in the natural-cold trial, dry mouth/nose/throat in the challenge trial. The antihistamine in a cold remedy is doing something for about 48 hours — and much of what it does is make the patient drowsy and dry, which many experience as the medicine 'working'.
cards.watchOut: Monotherapy evidence only: the review excluded combination products, so this shelf cannot be quoted either for or against the multi-ingredient cold remedies on the shelf — each ingredient must carry its own evidence (pseudoephedrine at #2569, phenylephrine at #2461, guaifenesin at #2463). Nor does it cover antihistamines for allergic rhinitis, a different question with a different answer.

shelves.title: Montelukast for allergic rhinitis: better than placebo by a whisker, no better than an antihistamine, clearly beaten by a steroid spray — and it carries a boxed warning
shelves.question: In adults with allergic rhinitis, does montelukast relieve symptoms as well as oral antihistamines or intranasal corticosteroids?
shelves.mesh: Acetates/therapeutic use · Administration, Intranasal · Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Cyclopropanes/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Histamine H1 Antagonists/administration & dosage · Humans · Leukotriene Antagonists/therapeutic use · Photoperiod · Quality of Life · Quinolines/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Rhinitis, Allergic/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfides/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Montelukast works, but by margins that struggle to justify its risk frame. The 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis by Krishnamoorthy (15 studies, 10,387 participants) found montelukast beat placebo on daytime nasal symptoms by a mean difference of −0.12 points on a symptom scale — statistically firm, clinically tiny (PMID: 32915441). Against the standard treatments it loses or ties: oral antihistamines were superior to montelukast for daytime nasal symptoms (mean difference 0.08 in the antihistamine's favour, p = 0.002), and intranasal fluticasone was superior by a wide margin (daytime symptoms mean difference 0.71, night-time 0.63, both p < 0.001). The big placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape: in Nayak 2002 (907 patients), montelukast and loratadine each beat placebo, but adding montelukast to loratadine — the primary comparison — was not significantly better than loratadine alone (PMID: 12086367); Meltzer 2000 (460 patients) found each drug alone gave only 'modest improvements', with the combination better than either (PMID: 10808172). Against this small benefit sits a harm no comparator carries: in 2020 the US FDA required a boxed warning on montelukast for serious neuropsychiatric events (including suicidal thoughts and actions) and advised reserving it in allergic rhinitis for patients who do not respond to or cannot tolerate alternatives. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit versus placebo) / LIKELY (less effective than intranasal corticosteroids, and no better than oral antihistamines) (not Tier C: 15-study meta-analysis plus two large RCTs). The combined intranasal azelastine–fluticasone spray question is homed at shelf #907.

cards.headline: Krishnamoorthy 2020: montelukast beat placebo by 0.12 symptom points, lost to antihistamines on daytime symptoms, and lost heavily to intranasal fluticasone
cards.summary: Krishnamoorthy 2020: montelukast beat placebo by 0.12 symptom points, lost to antihistamines on daytime symptoms, and lost heavily to intranasal fluticasone
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials with 10,387 participants comparing montelukast with placebo, oral antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, or combinations, in allergic rhinitis. Outcomes: daytime and night-time nasal symptom scores, composite symptom score, daytime eye symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality-of-life scores.
cards.result: Montelukast was more effective than placebo on daytime nasal symptoms (mean difference −0.12, 95% CI −0.15 to −0.08), night-time symptoms (−0.09, −0.13 to −0.05), composite score (−0.08, −0.11 to −0.06), eye symptoms (−0.17, −0.33 to −0.02) and quality of life (−0.34, −0.49 to −0.20) — all small absolute differences on multi-point scales. Oral antihistamine was superior to montelukast for daytime nasal symptoms (MD 0.08, 0.03 to 0.13; p = 0.002), with no significant difference on composite score, eye symptoms or quality of life; montelukast's nominal night-time advantage was not significant (MD −0.03, p = 0.330). Intranasal fluticasone was clearly superior to montelukast on daytime (MD 0.71, 0.44 to 0.99) and night-time (MD 0.63, 0.29 to 0.97) nasal symptoms. Combining montelukast with an antihistamine beat either drug alone on daytime symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Mean differences of 0.08–0.12 on symptom scores are fractions of the smallest difference patients can feel; the one comparison with a margin a patient would notice is the steroid spray's 0.6–0.7-point advantage. The review's combination findings (montelukast plus antihistamine beats either alone) describe a two-drug regimen competing against one-drug standards that already beat montelukast.
cards.source: Krishnamoorthy M et al. Efficacy of Montelukast in Allergic Rhinitis Treatment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Drugs. 2020. PMID: 32915441. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nayak 2002: in 907 patients, montelukast and loratadine each beat placebo — but montelukast added to loratadine was not significantly better than loratadine alone
cards.summary: Nayak 2002: in 907 patients, montelukast and loratadine each beat placebo — but montelukast added to loratadine was not significantly better than loratadine alone
cards.people: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 907 patients aged 15–82 with fall seasonal allergic rhinitis, randomised after a placebo run-in to montelukast 10 mg (n = 155), loratadine 10 mg (n = 301), the combination (n = 302) or placebo (n = 149), once daily at bedtime for 2 weeks. Primary endpoint: daytime nasal symptoms score (congestion, rhinorrhoea, pruritus, sneezing).
cards.result: Each active treatment differed significantly from placebo on the primary endpoint (p ≤ 0.001) and on most secondary endpoints including night-time symptoms, eye symptoms and rhinitis-specific quality of life. However, the primary comparison — combination therapy versus loratadine alone — was not significantly different: montelukast added nothing demonstrable to an antihistamine. All active treatments had a safety profile generally similar to placebo over the 2 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks in one pollen season, industry-run, with a placebo run-in that enriches for responders. Even on those favourable terms, the trial's own primary comparison — does montelukast add to an antihistamine? — came back negative.
cards.source: Nayak AS et al. Efficacy and tolerability of montelukast alone or in combination with loratadine in seasonal allergic rhinitis: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial performed in the fall. cards.headline: Meltzer 2000: montelukast alone and loratadine alone each gave only 'modest improvements' in 460 patients; the combination beat both
cards.summary: Meltzer 2000: montelukast alone and loratadine alone each gave only 'modest improvements' in 460 patients; the combination beat both
cards.people: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled 2-week trial in 460 patients aged 15–75 with spring seasonal allergic rhinitis, allocated to montelukast 10 mg or 20 mg, loratadine 10 mg, montelukast 10 mg plus loratadine 10 mg, or placebo, once daily in the evening. Primary endpoint: daytime nasal symptoms score.
cards.result: The combination of montelukast with loratadine improved the primary endpoint significantly (p < .001) compared with placebo and with each agent alone, and also improved eye symptoms, night-time symptoms, individual daytime symptoms, global evaluations and quality of life versus placebo. Montelukast alone and loratadine alone each caused only modest improvements in rhinitis endpoints. All treatments were similarly well tolerated over the 2 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The two big trials disagree on the combination: Meltzer found it beat each drug alone, Nayak (twice the size) found no significant addition to loratadine. Neither trial ran long enough, or was designed, to detect the neuropsychiatric harms that later drove the boxed warning — short-trial tolerability is not the relevant safety evidence for this drug.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but third-place drug — montelukast sits behind the steroid spray and level with (or behind) a cheap antihistamine, with a unique warning attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but third-place drug — montelukast sits behind the steroid spray and level with (or behind) a cheap antihistamine, with a unique warning attached
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 trials (10,387 participants) and the two largest placebo-controlled trials of montelukast in seasonal allergic rhinitis (Nayak 2002, n = 907; Meltzer 2000, n = 460).
cards.result: Versus placebo: a consistent, small benefit (daytime nasal symptoms −0.12 points). Versus oral antihistamine: no better overall, and worse on daytime symptoms (+0.08 in the antihistamine's favour). Versus intranasal fluticasone: clearly worse (0.71 points daytime, 0.63 night-time in the spray's favour). Versus its own combination with an antihistamine: the combination is somewhat better than montelukast alone, which is an argument about the antihistamine, not for montelukast. Since 2020 the drug carries an FDA boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, with rhinitis use reserved for patients who fail or cannot tolerate alternatives.
cards.watchOut: This shelf judges montelukast for rhinitis alone. It does not cover its asthma indications, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, or patients with combined asthma–rhinitis in whom a single drug treating both was the original pitch — and the boxed-warning context (an FDA regulatory action of March 2020) is a harm frame from outside the trial evidence, included because it changed the drug's recommended place in rhinitis care.
cards.source: Synthesis of Krishnamoorthy M et al. Drugs. 2020 (PMID: 32915441); Nayak AS et al. Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology. 2002 (PMID: 12086367); Meltzer EO et al. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2000 (PMID: 10808172).

shelves.title: Acute vertigo: a single dose of an antihistamine relieves vertigo more than a benzodiazepine at 2 hours (16 points on a 100-point scale) — and neither class beat placebo at a week
shelves.question: In acute vertigo in the emergency department, do antihistamines beat benzodiazepines for vertigo relief?
shelves.mesh: Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use · Histamine Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Vertigo/drug therapy
shelves.balance: For the first two hours, yes; beyond that, neither drug class earns its keep. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Hunter 2022, PMID: 35849408) pooled the randomised trials of vestibular suppressants in acute vertigo of ≤2 weeks' duration: 27 trials identified, 17 (1,586 participants) in the quantitative analysis. On the primary outcome — change in 100-point vertigo VAS at 2 hours, 7 trials, 802 participants — single-dose antihistamines improved scores by 16.1 points more than single-dose benzodiazepines (95% CI 7.2 to 25.0), but by only a non-significant 2.7 points more than other active comparators such as metoclopramide or droperidol. At 1 week and 1 month, neither daily benzodiazepines nor antihistamines were superior to placebo, and the reviewers found no outcome on which benzodiazepine use was associated with improvement at all. The slate for this shelf named a 'Gerlier randomised trial'; no such head-to-head trial exists in the record — the 2022 JAMA Neurology evidence is this meta-analysis, whose head-to-head stratum rests on three older trials — and the shelf is built on the record as fetched. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (antihistamine superiority at 2 hours) / LIKELY (no difference from placebo at 1 week or 1 month for either class); not Tier C. Vestibular rehabilitation for ongoing dizziness is a different question, homed at #636 and #1465.

cards.headline: Hunter 2022: single-dose antihistamines beat benzodiazepines by 16.1 points on a 100-point vertigo scale at 2 hours — but not other active drugs, and nothing beat placebo at 1 week
cards.summary: Hunter 2022: single-dose antihistamines beat benzodiazepines by 16.1 points on a 100-point vertigo scale at 2 hours — but not other active drugs, and nothing beat placebo at 1 week
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Hunter 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing an antihistamine or a benzodiazepine with another comparator, placebo or no intervention in patients with acute vertigo lasting ≤2 weeks, from any cause. 27 trials were identified; 17 contributed to the quantitative meta-analysis (1,586 participants). Antihistamines studied included dimenhydrinate, meclizine, promethazine, betahistine, cinnarizine and flunarizine; the only benzodiazepines studied were diazepam and lorazepam. Primary outcome: change in 10- or 100-point vertigo/dizziness VAS at 2 hours.
cards.result: Seven trials (802 participants) reported the primary outcome: single-dose antihistamines produced significantly more improvement on 100-point VAS than benzodiazepines (difference 16.1 points, 95% CI 7.2 to 25.0), but not more than other active comparators (difference 2.7, −6.1 to 11.5). At 1 week and 1 month, neither daily benzodiazepines nor antihistamines were reported superior to placebo, including for complete resolution of symptoms. The reviewers conclude there is moderately strong evidence for antihistamines over benzodiazepines at 2 hours, and that the available evidence did not support an association of benzodiazepine use with improvement in any outcome for acute vertigo. Immediate-outcome trials were generally at low risk of bias; the 1-week and 1-month trials were at high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: The head-to-head antihistamine-versus-benzodiazepine stratum is only three trials within the seven reporting 2-hour outcomes — the 16.1-point estimate is moderately strong, not definitive, and pools different drugs within each class. Most patients had peripheral or non-specific vertigo; this evidence must never delay the central-cause workup (stroke) in a patient whose vertigo might be posterior circulation.
cards.source: Hunter BR et al. Efficacy of Benzodiazepines or Antihistamines for Patients With Acute Vertigo: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Neurol. 2022. PMID: 35849408. cards.headline: Synthesis: in the emergency department, reach for the antihistamine for the first two hours; do not send either class home as a daily treatment expecting benefit at a week
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the emergency department, reach for the antihistamine for the first two hours; do not send either class home as a daily treatment expecting benefit at a week
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis: 27 trials identified, 17 meta-analysed, 1,586 participants; 7 trials (802 participants) for the 2-hour primary outcome.
cards.result: At 2 hours: antihistamines > benzodiazepines by 16.1 VAS points (7.2–25.0); antihistamines ≈ other active comparators (2.7 points, non-significant). At 1 week and 1 month: neither class superior to placebo on improvement or complete resolution. Benzodiazepines: no demonstrated benefit on any outcome. The practical reading is narrow and useful — a single antihistamine dose for acute relief, and no evidence base for continuing vestibular suppressants as daily therapy.
cards.watchOut: A single-review shelf: the synthesis card restates the one carded review rather than triangulating independent sources, because this meta-analysis is the evidence — the individual head-to-head trials are inside it, not separately carded. BPPV specifically is a repositioning-manoeuvre question (#900), and betahistine for Ménière's is homed at #633.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hunter BR et al. JAMA Neurol. 2022 (PMID: 35849408).

shelves.title: Lichen sclerosus: clobetasol beat pimecrolimus on inflammation and appearance in the one head-to-head trial — symptoms improved equally on both
shelves.question: In lichen sclerosus, does ultrapotent topical corticosteroid beat topical calcineurin inhibitors for disease control?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage* · Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans/drug therapy* · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage* · Lichen Sclerosus et Atrophicus/drug therapy* · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic* · Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus/drug therapy*
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for clobetasol over the calcineurin inhibitors, on the outcomes that distinguish them. The systematic review of all seven randomised trials in genital lichen sclerosus (249 participants) found clobetasol propionate 0.05% clearly better than placebo (participant-rated improvement/remission relative risk 2.85, 95% CI 1.45 to 5.61), while head-to-head there was no difference between pimecrolimus and clobetasol in relieving pruritus (standardised mean difference −0.33, −0.99 to 0.33) or burning/pain (0.03, −0.62 to 0.69) — but pimecrolimus was clearly less effective on investigator-rated global improvement (−1.64, −2.40 to −0.87) (Chi CC et al., PMID: 22483994). The one direct double-blind trial (38 women with biopsy-proven vulvar disease) found the same pattern: clobetasol was superior to pimecrolimus at reducing biopsy-measured inflammation (P = .015), while itch and burning/pain improved in both groups without a significant difference (Goldstein AT et al., PMID: 21353334). The review also found no evidence supporting topical androgens or progesterone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for ultrapotent steroid over calcineurin inhibitor on inflammation and appearance — Tier C: the whole randomised base is 249 patients, and the head-to-head trial has 38.

cards.headline: Chi 2012 (systematic review, 7 RCTs, 249 participants): clobetasol beat placebo (RR 2.85); against pimecrolimus it tied on symptoms but won on investigator-rated improvement
cards.summary: Chi 2012 (systematic review, 7 RCTs, 249 participants): clobetasol beat placebo (RR 2.85); against pimecrolimus it tied on symptoms but won on investigator-rated improvement
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials with 249 participants covering six topical treatments for genital lichen sclerosus in women and men, synthesised using Cochrane Collaboration methodology (the published version of the Cochrane review). Comparisons included clobetasol propionate 0.05% versus placebo, mometasone furoate 0.05%, pimecrolimus versus clobetasol, and topical androgens and progesterone.
cards.result: Clobetasol was better than placebo on participant-rated improvement/remission of symptoms (relative risk 2.85, 95% CI 1.45 to 5.61) and investigator-rated global improvement (standardised mean difference 5.74, 4.26 to 7.23); mometasone also beat its comparator on phimosis grade. Between pimecrolimus and clobetasol there was no difference in pruritus change (SMD −0.33, −0.99 to 0.33) or burning/pain (SMD 0.03, −0.62 to 0.69), but pimecrolimus was less effective on investigator-rated global degree of improvement (SMD −1.64, −2.40 to −0.87). No evidence supported topical androgens or progesterone. Most included studies were small.
cards.watchOut: Seven trials and 249 participants is the entire randomised evidence base for a chronic scarring disease usually treated for years; most trials lasted weeks. The placebo comparison for clobetasol rests on very small studies, and the huge standardised effect (SMD 5.74) is the kind of number small trials produce and larger ones shrink.
cards.source: Chi CC et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on topical interventions for genital lichen sclerosus. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2012. PMID: 22483994. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Goldstein 2011 (38 women, double-blind): clobetasol reduced biopsy inflammation more than pimecrolimus (P = .015); itch and pain improved equally
cards.summary: Goldstein 2011 (38 women, double-blind): clobetasol reduced biopsy inflammation more than pimecrolimus (P = .015); itch and pain improved equally
cards.people: 38 women with biopsy-proven vulvar lichen sclerosus in a double-blind randomised trial of clobetasol versus pimecrolimus over 12 weeks, after a 2-week screening period. The primary endpoint was change in inflammation on paired biopsy specimens scored by a dermatopathologist; secondary endpoints were patient-rated pruritus and burning/pain (visual analogue scale) and investigator global assessment.
cards.result: Clobetasol was superior to pimecrolimus in improving biopsy inflammation (P = .015). Pruritus and burning/pain improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P = .32 and P = .93). Both groups improved significantly on the investigator global assessment total score (P = .001) and all three subscales. Serum drug levels did not approach levels of concern, and no adverse events were reported. The authors conclude clobetasol should remain first-line therapy.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-eight women and 12 weeks: the trial can detect a difference in biopsy inflammation but cannot speak to long-term outcomes that matter in lichen sclerosus — scarring, anatomical change, or the small long-term cancer risk — nor to maintenance regimens. This trial is one of the seven included in the Chi review carded on this shelf; the two cards are the review and its most informative included trial, not independent bodies of evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: steroids first — the calcineurin inhibitors relieve symptoms but control inflammation less well — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroids first — the calcineurin inhibitors relieve symptoms but control inflammation less well — LIKELY
cards.people: Seven randomised trials (249 participants) of topical treatments for genital lichen sclerosus, including one 38-woman double-blind head-to-head trial of clobetasol versus pimecrolimus in biopsy-proven vulvar disease.
cards.result: Clobetasol beat placebo decisively on symptoms and appearance. Against pimecrolimus, clobetasol tied on itch and burning/pain relief but was superior on biopsy inflammation (P = .015) and investigator-rated global improvement (SMD −1.64 favouring clobetasol). Topical androgens and progesterone had no supporting evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for ultrapotent corticosteroid over calcineurin inhibitor — Tier C on a 249-patient evidence base.
cards.watchOut: Symptom relief — what patients feel — was equal between the drug classes in the head-to-head data; the steroid's advantage is on inflammation and appearance, which are proxies for the long-term scarring outcomes no trial has measured. A patient who cannot tolerate steroids is not untreated on a calcineurin inhibitor; she is on a symptomatically equal, probably less disease-controlling second choice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chi CC et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2012 (PMID: 22483994); Goldstein AT et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2011 (PMID: 21353334).

shelves.title: Efinaconazole for toenail fungus: complete cure 18% and 15% versus 3% and 5% on vehicle after 48 weeks — the strongest topical evidence there is, and still only one cure in six
shelves.question: In adults with toenail onychomycosis, does topical efinaconazole 10% solution achieve complete or mycological cure compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Foot Dermatoses/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Onychomycosis/drug therapy · Triazoles/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two identical phase 3 trials and a Cochrane review land in the same place, which is rare for topical nail treatments. In Elewski 2013 (PMID: 23177180), 1,655 patients with distal lateral subungual toenail onychomycosis (20–50% involvement) applied efinaconazole 10% solution or vehicle daily for 48 weeks: mycological cure was 55.2% and 53.4% in the two studies versus significantly lower vehicle rates (p < 0.001), and the primary endpoint, complete cure at week 52 (0% clinical involvement plus negative microscopy and culture), was 17.8% versus 3.3% and 15.2% versus 5.5% (both p < 0.001); adverse events were local site reactions in about 2%, clinically similar to vehicle. The Cochrane review of topical and device-based toenail treatments (Foley K et al., PMID: 31978269; 56 studies, 12,501 participants) found high-quality evidence that efinaconazole beats vehicle for complete cure (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.24 to 5.60; 3 studies, 1,716 participants) and clinical cure (RR 3.07, 95% CI 2.08 to 4.53), moderate-quality evidence for mycological cure (RR 2.31, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.94), and a slightly higher adverse-event risk (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.20), mainly dermatitis and vesicles. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the relative effects are large and consistent, but keep the absolutes in view — complete cure is roughly one patient in six after a year of daily application, versus roughly one in twenty on vehicle; it is the best-evidenced topical option for patients avoiding oral antifungals, not a match for simply wanting the nail cured.

cards.headline: Elewski 2013 (two phase 3 trials, 1,655 patients): complete cure 17.8% versus 3.3% and 15.2% versus 5.5% at week 52; mycological cure ~55% versus vehicle (p < 0.001)
cards.summary: Elewski 2013 (two phase 3 trials, 1,655 patients): complete cure 17.8% versus 3.3% and 15.2% versus 5.5% at week 52; mycological cure ~55% versus vehicle (p < 0.001)
cards.people: Two identical multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled studies in patients with toenail distal lateral subungual onychomycosis with 20–50% clinical involvement (study 1: n = 870; study 2: n = 785), randomised 3:1 to efinaconazole 10% solution or vehicle, once daily for 48 weeks with 4 weeks of post-treatment follow-up; no debridement. Primary endpoint: complete cure (0% clinical involvement, negative potassium hydroxide examination and negative fungal culture) at week 52.
cards.result: Mycological cure rates were significantly greater with efinaconazole (study 1: 55.2%; study 2: 53.4%) than vehicle (p < 0.001). Complete cure, the primary endpoint, was also significantly greater for efinaconazole (study 1: 17.8% versus 3.3%; study 2: 15.2% versus 5.5%; p < 0.001). Treatment success (affected target toenail 0% to ≤10%) ranged from 21.3% to 44.8% (study 1) and 17.9% to 40.2% (study 2) on efinaconazole, versus 5.6% to 16.8% and 7.0% to 15.4% on vehicle. Adverse events associated with efinaconazole were local site reactions (2%) and clinically similar to vehicle. The authors note 52 weeks may be too brief to evaluate clinical cure in onychomycosis.
cards.watchOut: The relative benefit is large; the absolute complete-cure rate (15–18%) is the number patients actually experience, after 48 weeks of daily application to nails with only 20–50% involvement — more extensive disease, matrix involvement, and diabetes were not this population. 'Treatment success' ranges are wide because they span different involvement thresholds.
cards.source: Elewski BE et al. Efinaconazole 10% solution in the treatment of toenail onychomycosis: Two phase III multicenter, randomized, double-blind studies. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2013. PMID: 23177180. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Foley 2020 (Cochrane, 56 studies): high-quality evidence efinaconazole beats vehicle for complete cure (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.24 to 5.60)
cards.summary: Foley 2020 (Cochrane, 56 studies): high-quality evidence efinaconazole beats vehicle for complete cure (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.24 to 5.60)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of topical and device-based therapies for toenail onychomycosis confirmed by culture, microscopy, or histology: 56 studies, 12,501 participants (average age 27–68), mainly mild-to-moderate onychomycosis without matrix involvement; most studies lasted 48–52 weeks.
cards.result: Efinaconazole 10% solution was more effective than vehicle in achieving complete cure (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.24 to 5.60; 3 studies, 1,716 participants) and clinical cure (RR 3.07, 95% CI 2.08 to 4.53; 2 studies, 1,655 participants), both high-quality evidence, and probably more effective for mycological cure (RR 2.31, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.94; 3 studies, 1,716 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Risk of adverse events (such as dermatitis and vesicles) was slightly higher with efinaconazole (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.20; 3 studies, 1,701 participants; high-quality evidence). The review's general conclusion: evidence supports topical treatments, but complete cure rates with topical treatments are relatively low.
cards.watchOut: The risk ratios are relative measures: RR 3.54 for complete cure sits on a vehicle complete-cure rate of about 3–5%, giving the absolute rates in the trial card (15–18%). The review's efinaconazole pool includes the two Elewski trials, so review and trials are not independent witnesses — the value added is the GRADE rating and the comparison against every other topical.
cards.source: Foley K et al. Topical and device-based treatments for fungal infections of the toenails. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 31978269. Registry ID: NCT01080079 (one of 19 registry IDs listed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: the best-evidenced topical for toenail fungus — roughly triple the complete cures of vehicle, which still means about one in six cured after a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: the best-evidenced topical for toenail fungus — roughly triple the complete cures of vehicle, which still means about one in six cured after a year
cards.people: Two phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials (1,655 patients) plus the Cochrane topical-treatments review (56 studies, 12,501 participants).
cards.result: Complete cure at 52 weeks: 17.8% versus 3.3% and 15.2% versus 5.5% (both p < 0.001); Cochrane pooled RR 3.54 (95% CI 2.24 to 5.60), high-quality evidence. Mycological cure: 55.2% and 53.4% on efinaconazole (p < 0.001 versus vehicle). Harms: local reactions ~2%, similar to vehicle in the trials; slight excess of dermatitis/vesicles in the review (RR 1.10). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not compare efinaconazole with oral terbinafine (shelf #1156 covers systemic therapy) — for a patient who can take oral treatment, that comparison, not vehicle, is the real decision. Relapse after week 52 is unmeasured here. Tier C is not set: two phase 3 trials plus high-quality Cochrane evidence is a strong base, short of Level-A certainty because complete cure remains uncommon and long-term relapse is unknown.
cards.source: Synthesis of Elewski BE et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2013 (PMID: 23177180); Foley K et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020 (PMID: 31978269).

shelves.title: Ear drops for wax: 22% cleared versus 5% with no treatment in the one direct study — but no drop beat water, saline, or any rival drop in Cochrane's ten trials
shelves.question: In adults and children with impacted ear wax, do ear drops (cerumenolytics, oil-based, or water-based preparations) remove wax or ease syringing compared with no treatment or each other?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antipyrine/therapeutic use · Benzocaine/therapeutic use · Carbamide Peroxide · Carbonates/therapeutic use · Cerumen* · Child · Chlorobutanol/therapeutic use · Choline/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Dioctyl Sulfosuccinic Acid/therapeutic use · Drug Combinations · Ear Canal* · Ethanolamines/therapeutic use · Humans · Hygiene* · Peroxides/therapeutic use · Pharmaceutical Solutions/therapeutic use · Plant Oils/therapeutic use · Potassium/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Salicylates/therapeutic use · Sodium Chloride/therapeutic use · Surface-Active Agents/therapeutic use · Urea/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Water
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest Cochrane answer is that drops probably help a little versus doing nothing, and no drop has earned preference over another — or over plain water. In Aaron 2018 (PMID: 30043448), 10 randomised studies (623 participants, 900 ears) of oil-based, water-based and other cerumenolytic drops found, on low-quality evidence: active treatment versus no treatment in the single study addressing it cleared wax completely in 22% of ears versus 5% after five days (RR 4.09, 95% CI 1.00 to 16.80; 117 ears; NNTB = 8); active treatment versus water or saline showed no evidence of a difference (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.75; 3 studies, 257 ears); water or saline versus no treatment likewise showed no evidence of a difference (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.91 to 17.62; 76 ears); and head-to-head studies found no evidence that any one active treatment beat another, or that oil-based beat non-oil-based preparations. Adverse effects (discomfort, irritation, pain) were mild, infrequent (fewer than 30 participants across seven studies), and not significantly different between drop types; no emergencies or serious adverse effects occurred. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): using some drops for a few days before review or syringing is reasonable and harmless, but the evidence cannot name a best drop, cannot separate proprietary cerumenolytics from water or saline, and rests on small, mostly old studies (nine of ten over 15 years old at review).

cards.headline: Aaron 2018 (Cochrane, 10 RCTs, 623 participants): drops beat no treatment in one study (22% versus 5% complete clearance, RR 4.09) — and nothing beat water, saline, or any other drop
cards.summary: Aaron 2018 (Cochrane, 10 RCTs, 623 participants): drops beat no treatment in one study (22% versus 5% complete clearance, RR 4.09) — and nothing beat water, saline, or any other drop
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of ear drops (cerumenolytics) versus no treatment, water or saline, or another liquid treatment in adults and children with obstructing or impacted ear wax: 10 studies, 623 participants, 900 ears. Interventions included oil-based treatments (triethanolamine polypeptide, almond oil, benzocaine, chlorobutanol), water-based treatments (docusate sodium, carbamide peroxide, phenazone, choline salicylate, urea peroxide, potassium carbonate), saline or water alone, and no treatment. Primary outcome: proportion of patients (or ears) with complete wax clearance.
cards.result: Active treatment versus no treatment (one study, 117 ears): complete clearance in 22% versus 5% after five days (RR 4.09, 95% CI 1.00 to 16.80; NNTB = 8; low-quality evidence). Active treatment versus water or saline (3 studies, 213 participants, 257 ears): no evidence of a difference (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.75; low-quality evidence), unchanged when a 15-minute-application study was excluded. Water or saline versus no treatment (one study, 76 ears): no evidence of a difference (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.91 to 17.62). Head-to-head comparisons of active treatments: no evidence any was superior to another; oil-based versus non-oil-based subgroup analysis likewise showed no evidence of a difference. Adverse effects were mild and reported in fewer than 30 participants across seven studies, with no significant differences between drop types and no serious adverse effects in any study.
cards.watchOut: Every key comparison rests on one to three small studies at low quality, and nine of the ten studies were more than 15 years old — the confidence interval for the headline comparison (RR 4.09) runs from 1.00 (no effect) to 16.80. 'No evidence of a difference' between drops is not proof drops are equal; it is proof the trials were too small to tell. The review also could not say much about symptom relief, need for further intervention, or cost.
cards.source: Aaron K et al. Ear drops for the removal of ear wax. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30043448. Registry ID: NCT02829294. cards.headline: Synthesis: some drops for five days probably beat nothing; which drops is a question the trials cannot answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: some drops for five days probably beat nothing; which drops is a question the trials cannot answer
cards.people: One Cochrane review covering the whole randomised literature: 10 trials, 623 participants, 900 ears, in adults and children with impacted ear wax.
cards.result: Complete clearance: active drops 22% versus 5% no treatment (RR 4.09, 95% CI 1.00 to 16.80; one study). Active versus water/saline: RR 1.47 (95% CI 0.79 to 2.75) — no demonstrated difference. Any drop versus any other drop, oil versus non-oil: no demonstrated differences. Harms: mild, rare, no serious events. Certainty: low quality throughout. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Practical reading: the cheapest, gentlest option (a few days of oil or water-based drops, or water itself) is as defensible as any branded cerumenolytic on this evidence, and persistent impaction still ends in mechanical removal or irrigation — drops are an adjunct, not a guarantee. Do not use drops with a known perforated eardrum or ear pain/discharge without assessment; that safety triage is outside this review. Tier C is not set — a full Cochrane review exists — but its own grading is low quality, which is why the stamp is MAYBE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aaron K et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30043448).

shelves.title: Drops for swimmer's ear: steroid-containing drops cured more patients by days 14–21 and halved recurrence versus acetic acid — and adding antibiotic to steroid added nothing
shelves.question: In adults with acute otitis externa in primary care, do topical acetic acid, antibiotic drops, or antibiotic–steroid drops differ in cure and pain relief?
shelves.mesh: Acetic Acid/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neomycin/therapeutic use · Otitis Externa/drug therapy · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone Acetonide/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for steroid-containing drops over acetic acid alone. The one large primary-care trial (van Balen FA et al., PMID: 14630756) randomised 213 adults with acute otitis externa in Dutch general practice to acetic acid drops, corticosteroid-plus-acetic-acid drops, or steroid-plus-antibiotic drops: median symptom duration was 8.0 days on acetic acid, 7.0 days on steroid–acetic acid, and 6.0 days on steroid–antibiotic; overall cure rates were 38% at day 7, 68% at day 14 and 75% at day 21, and compared with acetic acid both steroid-containing regimens cured significantly more patients by day 14 (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.3, and OR 3.5, 1.6 to 7.7) and day 21 (OR 5.3, 2.0 to 13.7, and OR 3.9, 1.7 to 9.1), with less recurrence between days 21 and 42 (29% overall recurred; OR 0.3, 0.1 to 0.7, and OR 0.4, 0.2 to 1.0, versus acetic acid) — while the two steroid-containing regimens were equally effective as each other. The Cochrane review (Kaushik V et al., PMID: 20091565; 19 RCTs, 3,382 participants, mostly low quality) found topical antimicrobial-plus-steroid drops significantly more effective than placebo (OR 11, 95% CI 2.00 to 60.57; one trial), no clinically meaningful differences among most topical interventions, and the same exception: acetic acid, comparable at week 1, was significantly less effective than antibiotic/steroid drops at weeks 2 and 3 (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.62, and OR 0.25, 0.11 to 0.58), with symptoms lasting about two days longer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): use a steroid-containing drop rather than acetic acid alone when treatment beyond a few days is likely; adding the antibiotic to the steroid bought nothing measurable in the primary-care trial.

cards.headline: van Balen 2003 (213 adults, primary care): symptoms lasted a median 8.0 days on acetic acid versus 7.0 and 6.0 days on steroid-containing drops, with cure odds 2.4–5.3 times higher by days 14–21
cards.summary: van Balen 2003 (213 adults, primary care): symptoms lasted a median 8.0 days on acetic acid versus 7.0 and 6.0 days on steroid-containing drops, with cure odds 2.4–5.3 times higher by days 14–21
cards.people: 213 adults with acute otitis externa in 79 Dutch general practices, randomised double-blind to ear drops containing acetic acid alone, corticosteroid plus acetic acid, or steroid plus antibiotic. Primary outcome: duration of symptoms (days) from patient diaries; secondary outcomes: GP-assessed cure and recurrence between days 21 and 42.
cards.result: Symptoms lasted a median of 8.0 days (95% CI 7.0 to 9.0) in the acetic acid group, 7.0 days (5.8 to 8.3) in the steroid and acetic acid group, and 6.0 days (5.1 to 6.9) in the steroid and antibiotic group. Overall cure rates at 7, 14 and 21 days were 38%, 68% and 75%. Compared with acetic acid, significantly more patients were cured in the steroid and acetic acid group and the steroid and antibiotic group at day 14 (OR 2.4, 1.1 to 5.3, and 3.5, 1.6 to 7.7) and day 21 (OR 5.3, 2.0 to 13.7, and OR 3.9, 1.7 to 9.1). Recurrence between days 21 and 42 occurred in 29% (50/172) of patients and was significantly less in the steroid and acetic acid group (OR 0.3, 0.1 to 0.7) and steroid and antibiotic group (OR 0.4, 0.2 to 1.0) than with acetic acid. The authors conclude corticosteroid-containing drops are more effective than acetic acid drops, and the two steroid-containing regimens are equally effective.
cards.watchOut: Day-7 cure did not separate the groups in the figures reported — the steroid advantage appears at days 14–21 and in recurrence, i.e. in the slower-resolving half of patients; for an ear that settles within a week, acetic acid performed comparably. Odds ratios overstate the risk difference when cure is common (68–75% overall); the absolute message is a 1–2 day shorter median symptom course plus better late cure.

cards.headline: Kaushik 2010 (Cochrane, 19 RCTs, 3,382 participants): topical beats placebo (OR 11) and most topicals tie — except acetic acid, which falls behind antibiotic/steroid drops after week 1
cards.summary: Kaushik 2010 (Cochrane, 19 RCTs, 3,382 participants): topical beats placebo (OR 11) and most topicals tie — except acetic acid, which falls behind antibiotic/steroid drops after week 1
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of interventions for acute otitis externa (ear cleaning, topical medication, systemic therapy): 19 RCTs, 3,382 participants; overall study quality low; only two trials were conducted in primary care and ear cleaning formed part of treatment in 11 of 19.
cards.result: Topical antimicrobials containing steroids were significantly more effective than placebo drops (OR 11, 95% CI 2.00 to 60.57; one trial). In general no clinically meaningful differences in clinical cure were noted between the various topical interventions; the notable exception was a high-quality trial showing acetic acid significantly less effective than antibiotic/steroid drops in cure rate at two weeks (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.62) and three weeks (OR 0.25, 0.11 to 0.58). A low-quality trial found no difference between quinolone and non-quinolone antibiotics. Evidence for steroid-only drops was very limited. The reviewers note acetic acid was effective and comparable at week 1 but less effective when treatment extended beyond that point, with symptoms lasting about two days longer than with antibiotic/steroid drops, and that patients prescribed antibiotic/steroid drops can expect symptoms for approximately six days after treatment begins.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled impressions rest on single trials with very wide confidence intervals (the placebo comparison's OR of 11 spans 2.00 to 60.57), and hospital-based trials with ear cleaning may not generalise to primary care — the van Balen trial carded here is one of only two primary-care trials and carries most of the practical weight.
cards.source: Kaushik V et al. Interventions for acute otitis externa. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010. PMID: 20091565. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: steroid-containing drops beat acetic acid alone on late cure and recurrence; steroid-plus-antibiotic and steroid-plus-acid tie with each other
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroid-containing drops beat acetic acid alone on late cure and recurrence; steroid-plus-antibiotic and steroid-plus-acid tie with each other
cards.people: One primary-care RCT (213 adults) plus a 19-RCT Cochrane review (3,382 participants) of acute otitis externa treatments.
cards.result: Median symptom duration: 8.0 days (acetic acid) versus 7.0 (steroid–acetic acid) versus 6.0 days (steroid–antibiotic). Cure advantage for steroid-containing drops at day 14 (OR 2.4 and 3.5) and day 21 (OR 5.3 and 3.9); recurrence 29% overall, lower with steroid-containing drops (OR 0.3 and 0.4). Cochrane: topical antimicrobial/steroid over placebo OR 11; acetic acid comparable at week 1, inferior at weeks 2–3 (OR 0.29, 0.25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for steroid-containing drops over acetic acid alone.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, fungal otitis externa, ears with perforation or grommets, or diabetes/immunocompromise — all were outside or excluded from this evidence and need different management. Ototoxicity risk, cost and local resistance patterns, which the Cochrane authors list as legitimate tie-breakers among near-equal topicals, are not quantified in these records. Tier C is not set: an RCT plus a Cochrane review agree.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Balen FA et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2003 (PMID: 14630756); Kaushik V et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010 (PMID: 20091565).

shelves.title: Numbing ear drops for children's otitis media (CEDAR): antibiotics used by 3% versus 29% — a big signal from a trial that recruited a fraction of its target and never settled the pain question
shelves.question: In children with acute otitis media, do anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops reduce ear pain and antibiotic consumption compared with placebo drops or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Anesthetics/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Cost-Benefit Analysis · England · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Male · Otitis Media/drug therapy · Pain/drug therapy · Wales
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a well-designed pragmatic trial that fell far short of its recruitment target, leaving a large-looking effect on antibiotic use and no answer at all on pain. In CEDAR (Hay AD et al., PMID: 31304912), children aged 1–10 with acute otitis media and ear pain, not requiring immediate antibiotics, were randomised to anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops or usual care (with a smaller blinded three-group comparison against placebo drops): in the combined analysis, 1 of 39 children (3%) in the active-drops group consumed antibiotics within 8 days versus 11 of 38 (29%) in the usual-care group (unadjusted OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.55, p = 0.009; adjusted for delayed prescribing OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.87, p = 0.035); in the tiny placebo comparison, antibiotic consumption was 43% (3/7) on placebo drops versus 0% (0/10) on active drops (p = 0.051). Ear pain at day 2, however, was not shown to improve — the adjusted difference versus placebo (0.67, 95% CI −1.44 to 2.79; p = 0.51) is consistent with chance, on 17 children — and NHS costs were £12.66 (active drops) versus £11.36 (usual care), an estimated £5.19 per antibiotic prescription avoided with a high degree of uncertainty. No adverse events were reported in children receiving active drops. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the antibiotic-sparing signal is intriguing and mechanistically plausible only if the drops relieve pain — the very outcome the trial was too small to test; the authors themselves say the effect requires replication in a larger study. No qualifying systematic review of anaesthetic–analgesic drops for otitis media pain was found, so no synthesis card is added.

cards.headline: Hay 2019 (CEDAR): antibiotic consumption 3% (1/39) with anaesthetic–analgesic drops versus 29% (11/38) with usual care (adjusted OR 0.15) — but the trial recruited only 106 children and pain was untested
cards.summary: Hay 2019 (CEDAR): antibiotic consumption 3% (1/39) with anaesthetic–analgesic drops versus 29% (11/38) with usual care (adjusted OR 0.15) — but the trial recruited only 106 children and pain was untested
cards.people: Children aged 1–10 years presenting in primary care in England and Wales within 1 week of suspected acute otitis media onset, with ear pain in the preceding 24 hours and not requiring immediate antibiotics. Because placebo-drop supply was delayed, most children entered the unblinded two-group comparison of anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops versus usual care (n = 74) rather than the blinded three-group comparison with placebo drops (n = 32). Primary outcome: parent-reported antibiotic consumption over 8 days.
cards.result: Comparing active drops with usual care across the combined two- and three-group studies, 1 of 39 children (3%) in the active-drops group and 11 of 38 (29%) in the usual-care group consumed antibiotics in the 8 days after enrolment (unadjusted OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.55; p = 0.009; adjusted for delayed prescribing OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.87; p = 0.035). In the three-group study, 43% (3/7) of the placebo-drops group consumed antibiotics by day 8 versus 0% (0/10) of the active-drops group (p = 0.051). Ear pain at day 2 in the placebo comparison (placebo n = 7, active n = 10) showed an adjusted difference in means of 0.67 (95% CI −1.44 to 2.79; p = 0.51), consistent with chance. NHS costs were £12.66 for active drops and £11.36 for usual care (estimated £5.19 per antibiotic prescription avoided, with a high degree of uncertainty). No adverse events were reported in children receiving active drops. The authors state the estimated effects are imprecise because the sample-size target was not met, and that the reduction in antibiotic consumption requires replication in a larger study.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison (drops versus usual care) was unblinded — parents who had been given drops to use may simply have felt treated and not cashed in a delayed prescription, an effect of receiving something rather than of anaesthesia. The blinded placebo comparison that could separate those explanations had 17 children for pain and 17 for consumption. It is also unclear whether some delayed prescriptions were written before randomisation. A 3% versus 29% effect this large, from a trial this far under target, should be read as a hypothesis.
cards.source: Hay AD et al. Anaesthetic-analgesic ear drops to reduce antibiotic consumption in children with acute otitis media: the CEDAR RCT. cards.summary: Synthesis: one under-recruited trial — a striking antibiotic-sparing signal with the pain mechanism unproven, so the finding is a maybe pending replication
cards.people: One multicentre pragmatic RCT (106 children randomised; 77 in the main combined consumption analysis; 17 in the blinded placebo pain comparison) in primary-care children aged 1–10 with acute otitis media. No qualifying systematic review of anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops for this question was found on searching.
cards.result: Antibiotic consumption by day 8: 3% (1/39) active drops versus 29% (11/38) usual care (adjusted OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.87); versus placebo drops 0% (0/10) versus 43% (3/7), p = 0.051. Ear pain at day 2 versus placebo: adjusted difference 0.67 (95% CI −1.44 to 2.79), p = 0.51 — not established. Cost: £5.19 per antibiotic prescription avoided, highly uncertain. Harms: none reported on active drops. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the antibiotic figures without the recruitment failure beside them: the trial's own authors call the estimates imprecise and ask for replication. Oral analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) remains the evidenced mainstay for AOM pain and is a different shelf question. Tier C is set because the base is a single trial that missed its sample-size target.

shelves.title: Antihistamine updosing for chronic hives: 41 of 80 difficult cases became symptom-free as the dose rose to fourfold — with a modest pooled advantage (RR 1.13) and a little more sleepiness
shelves.question: In adults with chronic spontaneous urticaria uncontrolled on standard-dose antihistamines, does updosing levocetirizine or desloratadine (up to four times the licensed dose) improve hive control compared with standard dosing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cetirizine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Chronic Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Histamine H1 Antagonists, Non-Sedating/administration & dosage · Humans · Loratadine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Urticaria/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the guideline's first escalation step has one neat dose-escalation trial and a supportive meta-analysis behind it. In Staevska 2010 (PMID: 20226302), 80 patients with difficult-to-treat chronic urticaria were randomised double-blind to levocetirizine or desloratadine starting at the conventional 5 mg daily, escalating weekly to 10 mg, then 20 mg, then 20 mg of the opposite drug if relief was incomplete: 13 patients became symptom-free at 5 mg (9 levocetirizine versus 4 desloratadine), and 28 more became symptom-free on the higher doses — at 10 mg (8 levocetirizine, 7 desloratadine) and at 20 mg (5 and 1); of 28 patients nonresponsive to 20 mg desloratadine, 7 became symptom-free on 20 mg levocetirizine, while none of 18 levocetirizine nonresponders benefited from 20 mg desloratadine. The authors summarise the responsiveness pattern as roughly 15% good responders, 10% nonresponders, and 75% responding to higher-than-conventional doses; increasing doses improved quality of life without increasing somnolence, and no serious or severe adverse effects occurred. The meta-analysis of Xiao X et al. (PMID: 37024900; 7 RCTs pooled) found high-dose second-generation antihistamines gave a significantly higher response rate than standard dose (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26; p = 0.02) — a modest relative gain — with significantly more somnolence (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.09) but no difference in overall adverse events or withdrawals, and the authors caution the pooled doses studied were mostly up to twice standard, with few trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): updosing converts a substantial share of standard-dose nonresponders in the escalation trial and a small average advantage in the pool — worth doing before biologics, with the honest caveats that the pooled effect is modest, somnolence rises with dose, and the full fourfold strategy rests mainly on the single trial.

cards.headline: Staevska 2010: of 80 difficult-to-treat urticaria patients, 13 became symptom-free at 5 mg and 28 more at 10–20 mg — about 75% ultimately responded to higher-than-conventional doses
cards.summary: Staevska 2010: of 80 difficult-to-treat urticaria patients, 13 became symptom-free at 5 mg and 28 more at 10–20 mg — about 75% ultimately responded to higher-than-conventional doses
cards.people: 80 tertiary-referral patients with chronic urticaria (age range 19–67 years), randomised double-blind to levocetirizine or desloratadine (40 per drug), starting at the conventional daily dose of 5 mg and increasing weekly to 10 mg, 20 mg, or 20 mg of the opposite drug if symptom relief was incomplete. Outcomes: wheal and pruritus scores, quality of life, patient discomfort, somnolence and safety.
cards.result: Thirteen patients became symptom-free at 5 mg (9 levocetirizine versus 4 desloratadine), compared with 28 subjects becoming symptom-free on the higher doses of 10 mg (8 levocetirizine, 7 desloratadine) and 20 mg (5 levocetirizine, 1 desloratadine). Of the 28 patients nonresponsive to 20 mg desloratadine, 7 became symptom-free with 20 mg levocetirizine; none of the 18 levocetirizine nonresponders benefited from 20 mg desloratadine. Increasing antihistamine doses improved quality of life but did not increase somnolence. The authors describe great individual heterogeneity: approximately 15% of patients were good responders, approximately 10% nonresponders, and approximately 75% responders to higher-than-conventional antihistamine doses. No serious or severe adverse effects warranting discontinuation occurred with either drug.

The levocetirizine-over-desloratadine asymmetry at crossover is interesting but rests on small numbers (7 of 28 versus 0 of 18).
