cards.headline: Xiao 2023 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs): high-dose antihistamines raised response rate modestly (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) with more somnolence (risk difference 0.05)
cards.summary: Xiao 2023 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs): high-dose antihistamines raised response rate modestly (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) with more somnolence (risk difference 0.05)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of double-blind randomised trials comparing multiple (high) doses with standard doses of second-generation H1-antihistamines in chronic spontaneous urticaria: 13 studies identified, 7 meeting eligibility for the meta-analysis. Outcomes: response rate, adverse events, somnolence, withdrawal due to adverse events.
cards.result: High-dose second-generation antihistamines were associated with a significantly higher response rate than standard dose (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26; p = 0.02) — a 13% relative increase in response. High doses were also associated with significantly higher somnolence rates (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.09; p = 0.02). There was no significant difference in overall adverse events or withdrawal due to adverse events between high-dose and standard-dose treatment. The authors note the high doses studied were up to two times the standard dose, that somnolence appeared dose-dependent in some studies, and that given the limited number of studies the results should be interpreted with caution.
cards.watchOut: The pooled relative gain (RR 1.13) is small and its interval nearly touches 1 — very different in feel from the escalation trial's 75% figure, because the designs answer different questions (parallel high-versus-standard dosing, mostly only double dose, versus within-patient escalation to fourfold). The registry ID printed is the one carried in the review's record. Fourfold dosing specifically is barely represented in the pool.
cards.source: Xiao X et al. The efficacy and safety of high-dose nonsedating antihistamines in chronic spontaneous urticaria: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. BMC pharmacology & toxicology. 2023. PMID: 37024900. Registry ID: NCT00536380. cards.headline: Synthesis: escalation rescues many standard-dose failures in the one trial; the pooled parallel-dose advantage is real but modest, and sleepiness is the price
cards.summary: Synthesis: escalation rescues many standard-dose failures in the one trial; the pooled parallel-dose advantage is real but modest, and sleepiness is the price
cards.people: One double-blind dose-escalation trial (80 patients, levocetirizine/desloratadine to fourfold dose) plus a 7-RCT meta-analysis of high- versus standard-dose second-generation antihistamines in chronic spontaneous urticaria.
cards.result: Symptom-free: 13/80 at 5 mg, 28 more at 10–20 mg (Staevska); authors' summary — ~75% respond to higher-than-conventional doses, ~10% to none. Pooled response: RR 1.13 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) for high versus standard dose. Harms: no excess somnolence with escalation in Staevska and no serious adverse effects; pooled somnolence risk difference +0.05 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.09), no difference in overall adverse events or withdrawals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Updosing is off-label above the licensed dose in many jurisdictions, which is a counselling point, not an evidence point. This shelf sits before the biologic shelves (omalizumab and successors) in the ladder: it supports exhausting the cheap step first, but a patient still uncontrolled at fourfold dose has, on this record, roughly a one-in-ten-profile chance the antihistamine route was never going to work — move on rather than escalating indefinitely. Tier C is set because the fourfold strategy itself rests on a single escalation trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Staevska M et al. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 2010 (PMID: 20226302); Xiao X et al. BMC pharmacology & toxicology. 2023 (PMID: 37024900).

shelves.title: Early aflibercept in severe diabetic retinopathy without macular oedema: complications fall by two-thirds (16–19% versus 50% in PANORAMA; HR 0.32 in Protocol W) — but vision itself is no better at two years
shelves.question: In severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular oedema, does early aflibercept prevent vision-threatening complications compared with sham and deferred treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus/drug therapy · Diabetic Retinopathy/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Intravitreal Injections · Macular Edema/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for preventing complications and retinopathy progression, with no demonstrated vision advantage yet. In PANORAMA (Brown DM et al., PMID: 34351414; 402 eyes with severe NPDR), a ≥2-step retinopathy improvement at one year occurred in 65.2% (every-16-week dosing) and 79.9% (every-8-week/PRN) versus 15.0% on sham, and through week 100 vision-threatening complications or centre-involved macular oedema developed in 16.3% and 18.7% versus 50.4% on sham. In Protocol W (Maturi RK et al., PMID: 33784735; 399 eyes), the two-year cumulative probability of proliferative disease or vision-losing macular oedema was 16.3% with aflibercept versus 43.5% with sham (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.50) — yet mean visual acuity change was −0.9 versus −2.0 letters, a non-significant 0.5-letter difference, because the sham group was treated promptly when complications appeared. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early injections prevent anatomical complications; whether patients see better for it is unproven against a watch-and-treat strategy.

cards.headline: PANORAMA: ≥2-step retinopathy improvement at 1 year in 65.2%/79.9% on aflibercept vs 15.0% sham; complications by week 100 in 16.3%/18.7% vs 50.4%
cards.summary: PANORAMA: ≥2-step retinopathy improvement at 1 year in 65.2%/79.9% on aflibercept vs 15.0% sham; complications by week 100 in 16.3%/18.7% vs 50.4%
cards.people: 402 adults with severe NPDR (DRSS level 47 or 53), no macular oedema and acuity 20/40 or better, randomised to aflibercept 2 mg every 16 weeks (after 3 monthly doses), aflibercept every 8 weeks then PRN from week 56 (after 5 monthly doses), or sham, for 100 weeks. NCT02718326.
cards.result: At 52 weeks, ≥2-step DRSS improvement occurred in 65.2% (every-16-week arm; adjusted difference 50.1 percentage points) and 79.9% (every-8-week/PRN arm; adjusted difference 64.8 points) versus 15.0% on sham (P<0.001 for both). Through week 100, vision-threatening complications and/or centre-involved macular oedema developed in 16.3% and 18.7% of aflibercept eyes versus 50.4% of sham eyes (P<0.001). No new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: The headline endpoint is a photographic severity grade — a surrogate. Eyes started with good vision (20/40 or better), so there was little vision to gain; the clinical question is whether preventing complications beats treating them on arrival, which the complication rates alone cannot settle.

cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Maturi 2021, DRCR Protocol W)
cards.people: 399 eyes of 328 adults with moderate-to-severe NPDR (severity levels 43–53) without centre-involved macular oedema at 64 US/Canadian sites, randomised to aflibercept 2 mg (baseline, months 1, 2, 4, then every 4 months to 2 years) or sham; both groups received aflibercept if high-risk proliferative disease or vision-losing macular oedema developed. NCT02634333.
cards.result: The 2-year cumulative probability of developing proliferative diabetic retinopathy or centre-involved macular oedema with vision loss was 16.3% with aflibercept versus 43.5% with sham (HR 0.32, 97.5% CI 0.21 to 0.50; P<0.001): proliferative disease 13.5% versus 33.2%, vision-losing macular oedema 4.1% versus 14.8%. Mean acuity change was −0.9 (SD 5.8) versus −2.0 (6.1) letters (adjusted difference 0.5 letters, 97.5% CI −1.0 to 1.9; P=.47) — no visual benefit from preventive treatment through 2 years.
cards.watchOut: The deferred-treatment design is the honest comparator: sham eyes were rescued on complication, which is exactly the real-world alternative. Four-year results were pending in this record; if early treatment's advantage is real, it should appear as complications in the deferred arm leave permanent damage.

cards.headline: Synthesis: anatomical prevention is large and consistent across two trials; patient-felt benefit against prompt deferred treatment is nil so far
cards.summary: Synthesis: anatomical prevention is large and consistent across two trials; patient-felt benefit against prompt deferred treatment is nil so far
cards.people: PANORAMA (402 eyes, severe NPDR) and Protocol W (399 eyes, moderate-to-severe NPDR), both double-masked/sham-controlled aflibercept trials.
cards.result: Complications: 16–19% vs 50% (PANORAMA, week 100); 16.3% vs 43.5%, HR 0.32 (Protocol W, 2 years). Vision: no significant difference (−0.9 vs −2.0 letters). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for complication prevention; not Tier C — two concordant randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled eyes with good baseline vision and no macular oedema; eyes with worse starting points, or patients unlikely to attend monitoring, may rationally weigh early treatment differently — that judgement is not in the trial data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brown DM et al. JAMA ophthalmology. 2021 (PMID: 34351414); Maturi RK et al. JAMA ophthalmology. 2021 (PMID: 33784735).

shelves.title: Aflibercept 8 mg every 12–16 weeks matches 2 mg every 8 weeks on vision in both wet AMD and diabetic macular oedema — the gain is fewer injections, not better sight
shelves.question: In neovascular age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular oedema, does aflibercept 8 mg dosed every 12–16 weeks match standard aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks on vision?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/adverse effects · DEAE-Dextran · Macular Degeneration/drug therapy · Receptors, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — benefit in the form of durability: equal vision with a third fewer visits is the whole claim, and both trials support it. In PULSAR (Lanzetta P et al., PMID: 38461841; 1,009 treated patients with neovascular AMD), vision gains at 48 weeks were +6.7 letters (8 mg every 12 weeks) and +6.2 letters (every 16 weeks) versus +7.6 letters on 2 mg every 8 weeks — differences of −0.97 and −1.14 letters, within the 4-letter non-inferiority margin. In PHOTON (Brown DM et al., PMID: 38461843; 658 treated patients with diabetic macular oedema), gains were +8.8 and +7.9 letters versus +9.2 letters, likewise non-inferior. Ocular adverse-event rates in PULSAR were near-identical across arms (~38–39%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): 8 mg buys interval, not acuity — patients trade nothing measurable in vision for fewer injections over the first year.

cards.headline: PULSAR (nAMD): 8 mg q12/q16 gained +6.7/+6.2 letters vs +7.6 on 2 mg q8 — non-inferior (margin 4 letters); ocular adverse events ~38–39% in all arms
cards.summary: PULSAR (nAMD): 8 mg q12/q16 gained +6.7/+6.2 letters vs +7.6 on 2 mg q8 — non-inferior (margin 4 letters); ocular adverse events ~38–39% in all arms
cards.type: Randomised double-masked phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Lanzetta 2024, PULSAR)
cards.people: 1,011 adults with neovascular age-related macular degeneration at 223 sites randomised 1:1:1 to aflibercept 8 mg every 12 weeks, 8 mg every 16 weeks, or 2 mg every 8 weeks after 3 initial monthly doses; intervals in the 8 mg arms could be shortened from week 16 if disease-activity criteria were met. 1,009 received treatment. NCT04423718.
cards.result: Mean BCVA change at week 48 was +6.7 letters (SD 12.6) for 8 mg every 12 weeks and +6.2 (11.7) for every 16 weeks versus +7.6 (12.2) for 2 mg every 8 weeks; least-squares differences were −0.97 (95% CI −2.87 to 0.92) and −1.14 (−2.97 to 0.69) letters, meeting the 4-letter non-inferiority margin. Ocular adverse events in the study eye occurred in 39%, 38% and 39% of the three groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight weeks is the first chapter of a chronic disease: the record is explicit that the trial (96 weeks) is ongoing, and interval-shortening rules mean not every 8 mg patient actually stayed at 12–16 weeks — the average injection burden saved is smaller than the headline interval suggests.

randomised double-masked phase 3 non-inferiority trial (lanzetta 2024, pulsar) 1,011 adults with neovascular age-related macular degeneration at 223 sites randomised 1:1:1 to aflibercept 8 mg every 12 weeks, 8 mg every 16 weeks, or 2 mg every 8 weeks after 3 initial monthly doses; intervals in the 8 mg arms could be shortened from week 16 if disease-activity criteria were met. 1,009 received treatment. nct04423718. mean bcva change at week 48 was +6.7 letters (sd 12.6) for 8 mg every 12 weeks and +6.2 (11.7) for every 16 weeks versus +7.6 (12.2) for 2 mg every 8 weeks; least-squares differences were −0.97 (95% ci −2.87 to 0.92) and −1.14 (−2.97 to 0.69) letters, meeting the 4-letter non-inferiority margin. ocular adverse events in the study eye occurred in 39%, 38% and 39% of the three groups. forty-eight weeks is the first chapter of a chronic disease: the record is explicit that the trial (96 weeks) is ongoing, and interval-shortening rules mean not every 8 mg patient actually stayed at 12–16 weeks — the average injection burden saved is smaller than the headline interval suggests. lanzetta p et al. intravitreal aflibercept 8 mg in neovascular age-related macular degeneration (pulsar): 48-week results from a randomised, double-masked, non-inferiority, phase 3 trial. lancet (london, england). 2024. pmid: 38461841. registry id: nct04423718. mesh: adult · humans · angiogenesis inhibitors/adverse effects · deae-dextran · macular degeneration/drug therapy · receptors, vascular endothelial growth factor/therapeutic use · recombinant fusion proteins/adverse effects · treatment outcome

cards.type: Randomised double-masked phase 2/3 non-inferiority trial (Brown 2024, PHOTON)
cards.people: 660 adults with type 1 or 2 diabetes and centre-involved diabetic macular oedema at 138 sites in 7 countries, randomised (1:2:1) to aflibercept 8 mg every 12 weeks (n=329), 8 mg every 16 weeks (n=164), or 2 mg every 8 weeks (n=167) after initial monthly dosing; 658 treated. cards.result: Mean BCVA change at week 48 was +8.8 letters (SD 9.0) in the 8 mg every-12-weeks group, +7.9 (8.4) in the every-16-weeks group and +9.2 (9.0) in the 2 mg every-8-weeks group, meeting the pre-specified 4-letter non-inferiority margin for both 8 mg regimens.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant non-inferiority trials in two diseases — the 8 mg formulation's value is scheduling, and both trials price it honestly
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant non-inferiority trials in two diseases — the 8 mg formulation's value is scheduling, and both trials price it honestly
cards.people: PULSAR (1,009 treated, neovascular AMD) and PHOTON (658 treated, diabetic macular oedema), both randomised, double-masked, 48-week primary endpoints with a 4-letter margin.
cards.result: Vision differences versus standard dosing: −0.97 and −1.14 letters (PULSAR); gains within ~1.3 letters (PHOTON). Safety comparable in PULSAR. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit); not Tier C — two large concordant phase 3 trials.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial shows better vision, better anatomy at equal visits, or lower cost; systems deciding on the 8 mg formulation are buying visit capacity, and the record supports exactly that purchase and no more.

shelves.title: Ranibizumab port implant refilled twice a year matches monthly injections on vision through two years — paid for with more ocular adverse events (23.8% versus 10.2%), including endophthalmitis in 1.6%
shelves.question: In neovascular age-related macular degeneration, does the ranibizumab port delivery system refilled every 24 weeks match monthly ranibizumab injections on vision?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Choroidal Neovascularization/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Drug Delivery Systems · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ranibizumab/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Vascular Access Devices · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A/antagonists & inhibitors · Visual Acuity/physiology · Vitreous Body/drug effects · Wet Macular Degeneration/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vision equivalence is real; so is the surgical harm ledger. In Archway (Holekamp NM et al., PMID: 34597713; 418 patients previously responsive to anti-VEGF), vision change averaged over weeks 36–40 was +0.2 letters with the port delivery system refilled every 24 weeks versus +0.5 letters with monthly injections (difference −0.3 letters, 95% CI −1.7 to 1.1) — both non-inferior and equivalent — and 98.4% of port patients needed no supplemental injection before their first refill. At two years (Regillo C et al., PMID: 36870451) non-inferiority held at every timepoint, but prespecified ocular adverse events of special interest had accumulated in 23.8% of port patients versus 10.2% on injections, including endophthalmitis in 1.6%, implant dislocation in 1.6% and conjunctival erosion in 4.0%. Tier C: a single trial programme carrying a device benefit claim with a material harm profile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the port trades injection burden for surgical risk, at equal vision.

cards.headline: Archway primary: vision +0.2 letters (port, q24-week refill) vs +0.5 (monthly injections), difference −0.3 — non-inferior and equivalent; 98.4% needed no extra injection
cards.summary: Archway primary: vision +0.2 letters (port, q24-week refill) vs +0.5 (monthly injections), difference −0.3 — non-inferior and equivalent; 98.4% needed no extra injection
cards.people: 418 patients with neovascular AMD diagnosed within 9 months of screening and previously responsive to anti-VEGF therapy, randomised 3:2 to the port delivery system with ranibizumab 100 mg/mL and fixed 24-week refill-exchanges (248 treated) or monthly intravitreal ranibizumab 0.5 mg injections (167 treated). Baseline acuity ~74–76 letters. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Adjusted mean BCVA change averaged over weeks 36 and 40 was +0.2 letters (SE 0.5) with the port versus +0.5 (SE 0.6) with monthly injections (difference −0.3 letters, 95% CI −1.7 to 1.1), meeting both the −4.5-letter non-inferiority and ±4.5-letter equivalence margins. Of 246 port patients assessed, 242 (98.4%) received no supplemental ranibizumab before the first refill-exchange. Prespecified ocular adverse events of special interest occurred in 19.0% (port) versus 6.0% (injections), including 4 endophthalmitis cases (1.6%), 2 retinal detachments (0.8%) and 13 vitreous haemorrhages (5.2%) in the port arm.
cards.watchOut: Enrolled patients were pre-selected anti-VEGF responders with recently diagnosed disease — the population most likely to do well on any delivery system. The trial was open-label (assessor-masked), and the safety gap was visible from the primary report, not a late surprise.
cards.source: Holekamp NM et al. Archway Randomized Phase 3 Trial of the Port Delivery System with Ranibizumab for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration. Ophthalmology. 2022. PMID: 34597713. cards.headline: Archway 2-year: non-inferiority held at weeks 44/48, 60/64 and 88/92 (differences −0.2, +0.4, −0.6 letters); adverse events of special interest 23.8% vs 10.2%
cards.summary: Archway 2-year: non-inferiority held at weeks 44/48, 60/64 and 88/92 (differences −0.2, +0.4, −0.6 letters); adverse events of special interest 23.8% vs 10.2%
cards.people: The Archway cohort followed through four complete 24-week refill-exchange intervals (~2 years): port delivery with ranibizumab versus monthly ranibizumab injections, with a −3.9-letter non-inferiority margin for the 2-year timepoints.
cards.result: Differences in adjusted mean BCVA change (port minus monthly) were −0.2 letters (95% CI −1.8 to +1.3) averaged over weeks 44/48, +0.4 (−1.4 to +2.1) over weeks 60/64 and −0.6 (−2.5 to +1.3) over weeks 88/92 — non-inferior at each point, with generally comparable anatomy. Across the four refill intervals, 94.6–98.4% of port patients needed no supplemental injection. Ocular adverse events of special interest reached 23.8% (port) versus 10.2% (monthly), including conjunctival erosions in 4.0%, conjunctival retractions 2.4%, endophthalmitis 1.6% (4 cases) and implant dislocations 1.6% (4 cases); cataract was the commonest event in both arms (8.9% versus 6.0%).
cards.watchOut: Two years in, the device arm's event burden is still accumulating with each refill cycle while the injection arm's stays flat — the trade-off worsens with time even as the vision equivalence holds. Surgical learning curves and device iterations after this trial are outside the record.
cards.source: Regillo C et al. Archway Phase 3 Trial of the Port Delivery System with Ranibizumab for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration 2-Year Results. Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 36870451. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal vision, fewer injections, more surgery-related harm — a preference-sensitive trade, demonstrated by one trial programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal vision, fewer injections, more surgery-related harm — a preference-sensitive trade, demonstrated by one trial programme
cards.people: Archway phase 3 trial: 418 randomised, reports at ~40 weeks and 2 years (4 refill cycles).
cards.result: Vision: differences within ±0.6 letters at every timepoint; 94.6–98.4% of port patients free of supplemental injections per interval. shelves.title: Dexamethasone implant in diabetic macular oedema: ≥15-letter gains in 22.2% versus 12.0% on sham over three years — with cataract adverse events in 67.9% of phakic eyes and pressure rises in 27.7%
shelves.question: In diabetic macular oedema, does the sustained-release dexamethasone intravitreal implant improve vision compared with sham, and at what cost in cataract and raised intraocular pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Area Under Curve · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Diabetic Retinopathy/drug therapy · Drug Implants · Female · Humans · Intravitreal Injections · Macular Edema/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real vision benefit with the steroid bill itemised. In the pooled MEAD trials (Boyer DS et al., PMID: 24907062; two identical phase 3 trials, 1,048 patients), ≥15-letter vision gains at study end occurred in 22.2% on the 0.7 mg dexamethasone implant and 18.4% on the 0.35 mg implant versus 12.0% on sham, with mean retinal-thickness reductions of −111.6 and −107.9 µm versus −41.9 µm. The costs: cataract-related adverse events in 67.9% and 64.1% of phakic eyes versus 20.4% on sham. The MEAD pressure analysis (Maturi RK et al., PMID: 26871523) found ≥10 mmHg pressure rises in 27.7% and 24.8% versus 3.7%, pressure-lowering medication use in 41.5% and 37.6% versus 9.1%, but filtering surgery in only 0.3% per implant group, and vision gains were preserved in eyes whose pressure rose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effective, with cataract near-expected in phakic eyes and pressure usually manageable medically.

cards.headline: MEAD pooled trials: ≥15-letter gain 22.2% (0.7 mg) and 18.4% (0.35 mg) vs 12.0% sham; cataract events in 67.9%/64.1% of phakic eyes vs 20.4%
cards.summary: MEAD pooled trials: ≥15-letter gain 22.2% (0.7 mg) and 18.4% (0.35 mg) vs 12.0% sham; cataract events in 67.9%/64.1% of phakic eyes vs 20.4%
cards.type: Two pooled randomised sham-controlled phase 3 trials (Boyer 2014, MEAD)
cards.people: 1,048 patients with diabetic macular oedema, acuity 20/50 to 20/200 and central retinal thickness ≥300 µm, randomised 1:1:1 to the dexamethasone intravitreal implant (Ozurdex, as named in the publication) 0.7 mg, 0.35 mg, or sham, with retreatment no more often than every 6 months over 3 years. Mean treatments received: 4.1, 4.4 and 3.3. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: The proportion gaining ≥15 letters at study end was 22.2% (0.7 mg) and 18.4% (0.35 mg) versus 12.0% on sham (P≤0.018). Mean average central retinal thickness reduction was −111.6 µm and −107.9 µm versus −41.9 µm (P<0.001). Cataract-related adverse events in phakic eyes occurred in 67.9%, 64.1% and 20.4% respectively. In the primary report, 0.6% of the 0.7 mg group required trabeculectomy for pressure.
cards.watchOut: A 10-point absolute gain in the ≥15-letter outcome over three years is modest, and the sham group's 12.0% gain rate shows how much fluctuation and cataract surgery in the natural course contribute. Phakic patients should read the cataract figure as the price of admission, not a side note.
cards.source: Boyer DS et al. Three-year, randomized, sham-controlled trial of dexamethasone intravitreal implant in patients with diabetic macular edema. Ophthalmology. 2014. PMID: 24907062. cards.headline: MEAD pressure analysis: ≥10 mmHg rises in 27.7%/24.8% vs 3.7%; drops used by 41.5%/37.6% vs 9.1%; filtering surgery 0.3% per implant group; vision gains preserved despite pressure rises
cards.summary: MEAD pressure analysis: ≥10 mmHg rises in 27.7%/24.8% vs 3.7%; drops used by 41.5%/37.6% vs 9.1%; filtering surgery 0.3% per implant group; vision gains preserved despite pressure rises
cards.people: The 1,048 MEAD participants, analysed for intraocular pressure occurrence, management and significance across up to seven implant treatments at ≥6-month intervals over 3 years.
cards.result: Increases of ≥10 mmHg from baseline occurred in 27.7% (0.7 mg), 24.8% (0.35 mg) and 3.7% (sham) of patients, with no increase in frequency across repeat injections. Intraocular-pressure-lowering medication was used by 41.5%, 37.6% and 9.1%. One patient (0.3%) in each implant group had filtering surgery for a steroid-induced pressure rise. Among 0.7 mg patients with and without a ≥10 mmHg rise, ≥15-letter gains were 21.9% and 22.4% respectively — pressure rises did not erase the vision benefit.
cards.watchOut: Pressure was managed inside a trial with scheduled monitoring; in less monitored practice, steroid responders can present late. The analysis also cannot exclude harm in the small subgroup with pre-existing glaucoma, who are under-represented in such trials.
cards.source: Maturi RK et al. INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE IN PATIENTS WITH DIABETIC MACULAR EDEMA TREATED WITH DEXAMETHASONE INTRAVITREAL IMPLANT IN THE 3-YEAR MEAD STUDY. Retina (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2016. shelves.title: PreserFlo MicroShunt is NOT trabeculectomy's equal on pressure: success 53.9% versus 72.7% and pressure 14.3 versus 11.1 mmHg at one year — its case is fewer interventions (40.8% versus 67.4%) and less hypotony
shelves.question: In open-angle glaucoma, is the PreserFlo MicroShunt non-inferior to trabeculectomy for lowering intraocular pressure, with fewer complications?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alkylating Agents/administration & dosage · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glaucoma Drainage Implants · Glaucoma, Open-Angle/drug therapy/physiopathology/surgery · Humans · Intraocular Pressure/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Mitomycin/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Prosthesis Implantation · Single-Blind Method · Tonometry, Ocular · Trabeculectomy · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity/physiology · Visual Fields/physiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the non-inferiority claim fails on efficacy and succeeds only on parts of safety. In the randomised trial (Baker ND et al., PMID: 34051211; 527 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma), one-year surgical success (≥20% pressure reduction without more medication) was 53.9% with the MicroShunt versus 72.7% with trabeculectomy (P<0.01), and mean pressure fell to 14.3 mmHg (−29.1%) versus 11.1 mmHg (−45.4%). Against that, postoperative interventions were fewer with the MicroShunt (40.8% versus 67.4%) and transient hypotony less common (28.9% versus 49.6%), with vision-threatening complications uncommon in both arms (~1.0% MicroShunt). The 2025 meta-analysis (Governatori L et al., PMID: 39394492; 10 studies, 1,833 eyes) agrees: trabeculectomy achieved lower pressure (mean difference ~1.6–2.5 mmHg in trabeculectomy's favour), while the MicroShunt carried lower hypotony-maculopathy risk (OR 0.30) but higher reintervention rates in several subgroups. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose trabeculectomy for maximum pressure lowering; the MicroShunt trades pressure for a quieter postoperative course.

cards.headline: Panarelli/Baker randomised trial: success 53.9% MicroShunt vs 72.7% trabeculectomy; pressure 14.3 vs 11.1 mmHg; interventions 40.8% vs 67.4%; hypotony 28.9% vs 49.6%
cards.summary: Panarelli/Baker randomised trial: success 53.9% MicroShunt vs 72.7% trabeculectomy; pressure 14.3 vs 11.1 mmHg; interventions 40.8% vs 67.4%; hypotony 28.9% vs 49.6%
cards.people: 527 patients aged 40–85 with primary open-angle glaucoma, pressure 15–40 mmHg inadequately controlled on maximum tolerated therapy, randomised 3:1 to stand-alone ab-externo MicroShunt implantation (395) or trabeculectomy (132), both with mitomycin C. Mean visual-field mean deviation −12.34 dB. NCT01881425.
cards.result: Probability of surgical success at year 1 (≥20% reduction in mean diurnal pressure without increased medication count) was 53.9% (MicroShunt) versus 72.7% (trabeculectomy) (P<0.01) — non-inferiority not shown. Mean pressure fell from 21.1 mmHg in both groups to 14.3 ± 4.3 (−29.1%) versus 11.1 ± 4.3 mmHg (−45.4%); medications fell to 0.6 versus 0.3 (from ~3.1). Postoperative interventions including laser suture lysis: 40.8% versus 67.4% (P<0.01). Transient hypotony: 28.9% versus 49.6% (P<0.01). Vision-threatening complications were uncommon (1.0% in the MicroShunt arm as reported).
cards.watchOut: One-year results of a 2-year study, with a 3:1 randomisation that leaves the trabeculectomy arm comparatively small (n=132). 'Success' is a composite that penalises added drops — a patient at 15 mmHg on one drop counts as failure here, which flatters neither arm's real-world usefulness equally.
cards.source: Baker ND et al. Ab-Externo MicroShunt versus Trabeculectomy in Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma: One-Year Results from a 2-Year Randomized, Multicenter Study. Ophthalmology. 2021. PMID: 34051211. Registry ID: NCT01881425. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2025 (10 studies, 1,833 eyes): trabeculectomy lowers pressure more (MD ~1.6–2.5 mmHg); MicroShunt has less hypotony maculopathy (OR 0.30) but more reintervention in key subgroups
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2025 (10 studies, 1,833 eyes): trabeculectomy lowers pressure more (MD ~1.6–2.5 mmHg); MicroShunt has less hypotony maculopathy (OR 0.30) but more reintervention in key subgroups
cards.people: 10 randomised and non-randomised studies (1,833 eyes; 57.4% MicroShunt) in moderate-to-advanced glaucoma (mean deviation worse than −6 dB), comparing PreserFlo MicroShunt with trabeculectomy on success, pressure, complications and reintervention, searched to January 2024.
cards.result: Qualified and complete success rates did not differ significantly overall. Trabeculectomy achieved better pressure outcomes (mean difference 1.59 mmHg, p=0.0004, and greater pressure reduction, MD −2.52 mmHg, p=0.0003). The MicroShunt showed less visual-field progression in the pooled estimate (MD −1.21, p=0.03) and lower hypotony-maculopathy risk (OR 0.30, p=0.03), but a higher reintervention rate in patients without prior glaucoma surgery (OR 1.74, p=0.02) and in primary open-angle glaucoma (OR 1.84, p=0.04).
cards.watchOut: Most included studies are non-randomised, so the pooled success-rate equivalence is weaker evidence than the single randomised trial's clear efficacy gap; the visual-field-progression signal (p=0.03 across many outcomes) should be read as hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Governatori L et al. PreserFlo MicroShunt versus trabeculectomy: an updated meta-analysis and systematic review. Graefe's archive for clinical and experimental ophthalmology = Albrecht von Graefes Archiv fur klinische und experimentelle Ophthalmologie. 2025. PMID: 39394492. shelves.title: Newer glaucoma drops versus timolol: latanoprostene bunod beat timolol at every timepoint (pressure ≤18 mmHg in 22.9% versus 11.3%) — netarsudil only matched it in eyes starting below 25 mmHg, with red eye in half of users
shelves.question: In open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, do the newer drops — netarsudil (a Rho-kinase inhibitor) and latanoprostene bunod (a nitric-oxide-donating prostaglandin) — lower pressure as well as timolol or latanoprost?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two 'newer drops' have opposite stories against timolol. Latanoprostene bunod 0.024% once nightly beat timolol 0.5% twice daily in APOLLO (Weinreb RN et al., PMID: 26875002): mean pressure was significantly lower at all 9 assessment timepoints (P≤0.002), with 22.9% versus 11.3% of subjects at ≤18 mmHg at every timepoint and 34.9% versus 19.5% achieving ≥25% reductions. Netarsudil 0.02% once daily, in the pooled ROCKET-1 and ROCKET-2 report (Serle JB et al., PMID: 29199013; 1,167 patients), was non-inferior to timolol only in the per-protocol population whose baseline pressure was below 25 mmHg — and conjunctival hyperaemia occurred in 50–59% on netarsudil versus 8–11% on timolol. Neither trial compared against latanoprost, the usual first-line prostaglandin, so the shelf cannot place either drug against it. PROPOSED SPLIT: latanoprostene bunod is timolol's superior on pressure; netarsudil is its conditional equal with a cosmetic cost.

cards.headline: ROCKET-1/2 pooled report: netarsudil once daily non-inferior to timolol only in the <25 mmHg baseline subgroup (per-protocol); hyperaemia 50–53% (once daily) and 59% (twice daily) vs 8–11%
cards.summary: ROCKET-1/2 pooled report: netarsudil once daily non-inferior to timolol only in the <25 mmHg baseline subgroup (per-protocol); hyperaemia 50–53% (once daily) and 59% (twice daily) vs 8–11%
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised double-masked trials (Serle 2018, ROCKET-1 and ROCKET-2)
cards.people: 1,167 patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension after washout of prior drops, randomised to netarsudil 0.02% once daily, timolol 0.5% twice daily, and (ROCKET-2 only) netarsudil twice daily; data through 3 months. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Netarsudil produced significant pressure reductions from baseline (P<0.001) and was non-inferior to timolol in the per-protocol population with maximum baseline pressure <25 mmHg in both studies (the primary population in ROCKET-2; post hoc in ROCKET-1); twice-daily netarsudil was also non-inferior in ROCKET-2. The commonest adverse event was conjunctival hyperaemia: 53% (108/203, ROCKET-1) and 50% (126/251, ROCKET-2) on once-daily netarsudil, 59% (149/253) on twice-daily, versus 8% (17/208) to 11% (27/251) on timolol (P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority that depends on excluding higher-pressure eyes and on per-protocol analysis is a qualified claim: in unselected glaucoma, netarsudil's pressure effect is the weakest of the drugs on this shelf, and a red eye in half of users is an adherence problem, not just a cosmetic one. Three months is short.
cards.source: Serle JB et al. Two Phase 3 Clinical Trials Comparing the Safety and Efficacy of Netarsudil to Timolol in Patients With Elevated Intraocular Pressure: Rho Kinase Elevated IOP Treatment Trial 1 and 2 (ROCKET-1 and ROCKET-2). American journal of ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 29199013. cards.headline: APOLLO: latanoprostene bunod beat timolol at all 9 timepoints (P≤0.002); ≤18 mmHg at every visit in 22.9% vs 11.3%; ≥25% reduction in 34.9% vs 19.5%
cards.summary: APOLLO: latanoprostene bunod beat timolol at all 9 timepoints (P≤0.002); ≤18 mmHg at every visit in 22.9% vs 11.3%; ≥25% reduction in 34.9% vs 19.5%
cards.people: 420 subjects aged ≥18 with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension randomised 2:1 to latanoprostene bunod 0.024% once nightly (264 completers analysed) or timolol maleate 0.5% twice daily (123 completers) for 3 months; pressure measured at 8 am, 12 pm and 4 pm at weeks 2, 6 and month 3 (9 timepoints). The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Mean pressure in the study eye was significantly lower on latanoprostene bunod than timolol at all 9 timepoints (P≤0.002). The proportion with mean pressure ≤18 mmHg at every timepoint was 22.9% versus 11.3% (P=0.005), and with ≥25% pressure reduction at every timepoint 34.9% versus 19.5% (P=0.001). Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Three months, and the comparator is timolol — a drug many guidelines already place behind prostaglandins. Beating timolol establishes latanoprostene bunod as a credible prostaglandin-class option, not as superior to latanoprost itself, which was not in this trial.
cards.source: Weinreb RN et al. Latanoprostene Bunod 0.024% versus Timolol Maleate 0.5% in Subjects with Open-Angle Glaucoma or Ocular Hypertension: The APOLLO Study. Ophthalmology. 2016. phase 3 randomised double-masked trial (weinreb 2016, apollo) 420 subjects aged ≥18 with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension randomised 2:1 to latanoprostene bunod 0.024% once nightly (264 completers analysed) or timolol maleate 0.5% twice daily (123 completers) for 3 months; pressure measured at 8 am, 12 pm and 4 pm at weeks 2, 6 and month 3 (9 timepoints). the record carries no registry id. mean pressure in the study eye was significantly lower on latanoprostene bunod than timolol at all 9 timepoints (p≤0.002). the proportion with mean pressure ≤18 mmhg at every timepoint was 22.9% versus 11.3% (p=0.005), and with ≥25% pressure reduction at every timepoint 34.9% versus 19.5% (p=0.001). adverse events were similar between groups. three months, and the comparator is timolol — a drug many guidelines already place behind prostaglandins. beating timolol establishes latanoprostene bunod as a credible prostaglandin-class option, not as superior to latanoprost itself, which was not in this trial. weinreb rn et al. latanoprostene bunod 0.024% versus timolol maleate 0.5% in subjects with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension: the apollo study. ophthalmology. 2016. pmid: 26875002. mesh: administration, topical · adrenergic beta-antagonists/therapeutic use · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antihypertensive agents/therapeutic use · circadian rhythm/drug effects · double-blind method · female · glaucoma, open-angle/drug therapy/physiopathology · humans · intraocular pressure/drug effects · male · middle aged · ocular hypertension/drug therapy/physiopathology · ophthalmic solutions · prostaglandins f, synthetic/therapeutic use · timolol/therapeutic use · tonometry, ocular · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: one drug out-lowered timolol outright; the other matched it only in lower-pressure eyes and reddens half the eyes it treats
cards.summary: Synthesis: one drug out-lowered timolol outright; the other matched it only in lower-pressure eyes and reddens half the eyes it treats
cards.people: ROCKET-1 and ROCKET-2 (1,167 patients, netarsudil) and APOLLO (420 patients, latanoprostene bunod), all 3-month phase 3 trials against timolol 0.5% twice daily.
cards.result: Latanoprostene bunod: superior at 9/9 timepoints; ≤18 mmHg consistently in 22.9% vs 11.3%. Netarsudil: non-inferior only below 25 mmHg baseline; hyperaemia 50–59% vs 8–11%. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped; not Tier C — three phase 3 randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: The question also asks about latanoprost: neither programme trialled against it, so any latanoprost comparison would be indirect and is deliberately not made on this shelf.

shelves.title: Multifocal and EDOF lenses after cataract surgery: spectacle dependence falls (RR 0.63) and near vision improves, distance vision is unchanged — and haloes are 3.6 times as likely
shelves.question: After cataract surgery, do multifocal or extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses improve spectacle independence compared with monofocal lenses, and at what cost in glare and contrast?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cataract Extraction/rehabilitation · Contrast Sensitivity/physiology · Humans · Lenses, Intraocular/psychology · Patient Satisfaction · Prosthesis Design · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vision, Ocular/physiology · Visual Acuity/physiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — spectacle independence is bought with optical phenomena, and the exchange rate is now quantified. The Cochrane review (de Silva SR et al., PMID: 27943250; 20 trials, 2,230 people) found distance acuity no different between multifocal and monofocal lenses (RR 0.96 for unaided acuity worse than 6/6), better near vision with multifocals (RR 0.20 for near acuity worse than J3/J4), less spectacle dependence (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.73), but more glare (RR 1.41) and haloes (RR 3.58, 95% CI 1.99 to 6.46). The 2022 network meta-analysis (Cho JY et al., PMID: 36136323; 27 trials, 2,605 patients) adds the modern lens types: trifocals gave the best near acuity (mean difference −0.32 logMAR versus monofocal), EDOF lenses the best intermediate acuity, distance acuity was comparable for all, and it found no statistical differences in contrast sensitivity, glare or haloes — a softer harm picture than Cochrane's, from indirect comparisons. PROPOSED SPLIT: patients who prize glasses-free near vision gain it; patients who prize clean night vision pay for it.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (20 trials): distance acuity equal (RR 0.96), near acuity better (RR 0.20), spectacle dependence lower (RR 0.63), glare RR 1.41, haloes RR 3.58
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (20 trials): distance acuity equal (RR 0.96), near acuity better (RR 0.20), spectacle dependence lower (RR 0.63), glare RR 1.41, haloes RR 3.58
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (de Silva 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: 20 randomised trials enrolling 2,230 people (data on 2,061 people, 3,194 eyes) comparing multifocal with monofocal intraocular lenses after cataract extraction, mostly in Europe; two trials compared multifocal lenses with monovision.
cards.result: Distance acuity did not differ (pooled RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.03 for unaided acuity worse than 6/6; moderate certainty). Multifocal recipients had better near vision (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.58 for unaided near acuity worse than J3/J4; low certainty) and were less likely to be spectacle dependent (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.73; low certainty). Adverse visual phenomena were more prevalent and more troublesome with multifocals: glare RR 1.41 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.93) and haloes RR 3.58 (95% CI 1.99 to 6.46).
cards.watchOut: Lens makes and models varied widely and masking was near-impossible, so several estimates are low certainty; the near-vision analysis had very high heterogeneity (I2=93%) even though every study favoured multifocals. The 2016 lens generation is not today's.
cards.source: de Silva SR et al. Multifocal versus monofocal intraocular lenses after cataract extraction. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27943250. cards.headline: Network meta-analysis 2022 (27 trials): trifocals best for near (−0.32 logMAR vs monofocal), EDOF best for intermediate, distance equal — no statistical difference in glare, haloes or contrast
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis 2022 (27 trials): trifocals best for near (−0.32 logMAR vs monofocal), EDOF best for intermediate, distance equal — no statistical difference in glare, haloes or contrast
cards.type: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis (Cho 2022)
cards.people: 27 randomised trials comprising 2,605 patients undergoing bilateral cataract extraction with accommodative, multifocal, extended-depth-of-focus (EDOF) or monofocal intraocular lenses, searched to May 2021.
cards.result: Uncorrected near acuity was better with trifocal lenses (mean difference −0.32 logMAR, 95% credible interval −0.46 to −0.19) and older bifocal diffractive lenses (−0.33) than with monofocals. EDOF lenses provided better uncorrected intermediate acuity than monofocals, with no pairwise difference between EDOF and trifocal diffractive lenses. All multifocal types were comparable to monofocals for distance acuity. There were no statistical differences between multifocal and monofocal lenses for contrast sensitivity, glare or halos in this analysis.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates lean on indirect comparisons across different lens generations and trial eras, and 'no statistical difference' in the network does not erase Cochrane's direct-comparison harm signals (haloes RR 3.58) — the two reviews disagree on harm, and the direct evidence is the more conservative read.
cards.source: Cho JY et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the benefit (glasses-free near and intermediate vision) is consistent across both reviews; the harm (haloes and glare) is certain in direct comparisons and diluted in indirect ones
cards.summary: Synthesis: the benefit (glasses-free near and intermediate vision) is consistent across both reviews; the harm (haloes and glare) is certain in direct comparisons and diluted in indirect ones
cards.people: Cochrane review of 20 trials (2,230 people) and a network meta-analysis of 27 trials (2,605 patients) including modern trifocal and EDOF designs.
cards.result: Spectacle dependence RR 0.63; near acuity clearly better; distance acuity equal in both reviews. Haloes RR 3.58 and glare RR 1.41 (Cochrane, direct); not statistically different in the network analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped; not Tier C — two large randomised-trial syntheses.
cards.watchOut: Neither review can tell an individual patient whether they will be among the bothered minority — preoperative counselling, not lens statistics, is where this trade is actually decided.

shelves.title: Preventing macular oedema after cataract surgery: in non-diabetics the bromfenac-plus-dexamethasone combination beat either drop alone (clinically significant oedema 1.5% versus 3.6% and 5.1%) — in diabetics, an added triamcinolone injection thinned the macula further
shelves.question: Does perioperative topical bromfenac, dexamethasone, or their combination prevent cystoid macular oedema after cataract surgery in patients with and without diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Benzophenones/administration & dosage · Bromobenzenes/administration & dosage · Cataract Extraction/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Macular Edema/diagnosis/etiology/prevention & control · Male · Ophthalmic Solutions/administration & dosage · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combination in non-diabetics, from one large multicentre trial. In PREMED report 1 (Wielders LHP et al., PMID: 29778106; 914 non-diabetic patients), six-week central macular thickness was 284.5 µm on combined bromfenac plus dexamethasone versus 288.3 µm on bromfenac alone and 296.0 µm on dexamethasone alone (overall P=.006), and clinically significant macular oedema within 12 weeks occurred in 1.5% versus 3.6% and 5.1% (overall P=.043). In diabetics (report 2, PMID: 30055692; 213 patients), everyone received the bromfenac-plus-dexamethasone base; adding a subconjunctival triamcinolone injection lowered macular thickness by a further 12.3 µm at 6 weeks and 9.7 µm at 12 weeks, with no macular oedema cases in the triamcinolone group, while intravitreal bevacizumab added nothing. Tier C: each population's claim rests on a single trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combination drops are the best-tested prophylaxis in non-diabetics; diabetics may gain from an added depot steroid injection.

cards.headline: PREMED report 1 (non-diabetics, n=914): combination drops — macular thickness 284.5 µm vs 288.3 (bromfenac) and 296.0 (dexamethasone); clinically significant oedema 1.5% vs 3.6% and 5.1%
cards.summary: PREMED report 1 (non-diabetics, n=914): combination drops — macular thickness 284.5 µm vs 288.3 (bromfenac) and 296.0 (dexamethasone); clinically significant oedema 1.5% vs 3.6% and 5.1%
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial (Wielders 2018, ESCRS PREMED report 1)
cards.people: 914 non-diabetic patients having uneventful cataract surgery at 12 European centres, randomised to topical bromfenac 0.09% twice daily for 2 weeks, dexamethasone 0.1% four times daily tapering weekly, or both. Primary outcome: central subfield mean macular thickness at 6 weeks. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Six-week macular thickness was 288.3 µm (bromfenac), 296.0 µm (dexamethasone) and 284.5 µm (combination) (overall P=.006). Clinically significant macular oedema within 12 weeks occurred in 3.6%, 5.1% and 1.5% respectively (overall P=.043). The combination group had the lowest risk of clinically significant oedema.
cards.watchOut: Absolute event rates are low in non-diabetics (a 2–3.6 percentage-point absolute difference), macular thickness is a surrogate, and the trial used uneventful surgery only — complicated cases, where prophylaxis matters most, were excluded.
cards.source: Wielders LHP et al. European multicenter trial of the prevention of cystoid macular edema after cataract surgery in nondiabetics: ESCRS PREMED study report 1. Journal of cataract and refractive surgery. 2018. PMID: 29778106. cards.headline: PREMED report 2 (diabetics, n=213): on top of combination drops, subconjunctival triamcinolone cut macular thickness by a further 12.3 µm at 6 weeks and no triamcinolone patient developed oedema; bevacizumab added nothing
cards.summary: PREMED report 2 (diabetics, n=213): on top of combination drops, subconjunctival triamcinolone cut macular thickness by a further 12.3 µm at 6 weeks and no triamcinolone patient developed oedema; bevacizumab added nothing
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial (Wielders 2018, ESCRS PREMED report 2)
cards.people: 213 diabetic patients having phacoemulsification cataract surgery at 12 European centres; all received topical bromfenac 0.09% plus dexamethasone 0.1%, and were randomised to no additional treatment, a subconjunctival injection of triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg, an intravitreal injection of bevacizumab 1.25 mg, or both. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Macular thickness at 6 and 12 weeks was 12.3 µm and 9.7 µm lower in patients who received subconjunctival triamcinolone than in those who did not (P=.007 and P=.014). No patient who received triamcinolone developed cystoid macular oedema. Intravitreal bevacizumab had no significant effect on macular thickness.
cards.watchOut: Small (213 patients across four arms) and the comparison is of add-ons, not of the base drops — this trial cannot say whether diabetics need the combination itself. A thickness difference of ~10–12 µm is statistically real but clinically modest; the zero-oedema count rests on few patients.
cards.source: Wielders LHP et al. Randomized controlled European multicenter trial on the prevention of cystoid macular edema after cataract surgery in diabetics: ESCRS PREMED Study Report 2. Journal of cataract and refractive surgery. 2018. PMID: 30055692. shelves.title: Same-day surgery on both eyes: no sign of extra harm in the Cochrane review — endophthalmitis in 1 of 14,076 same-day patients versus 55 of 556,246 delayed, vision and refraction the same, costs lower, but certainty only moderate to very low
shelves.question: Is immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery as safe and effective as delayed sequential surgery for people needing both eyes done?
shelves.mesh: Cataract · Cataract Extraction/adverse effects/methods · Endophthalmitis · Humans · Lens Implantation, Intraocular/methods · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — operating on both eyes on the same day looked as safe and as effective as operating on separate days, and cheaper. The Cochrane review (Dickman MM et al., PMID: 35467755) of 14 studies and 276,260 participants found endophthalmitis in 1 of 14,076 same-day participants versus 55 of 556,246 delayed-surgery participants, no difference in the share of eyes missing the refractive target (risk ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.26 in the randomised trials) and no difference in postoperative complications (risk ratio 1.33, 95% CI 0.52 to 3.40), with lower total costs per participant for same-day surgery. An earlier meta-analysis (Malvankar-Mehta MS et al., PMID: 26121673) likewise found no significant difference in best-corrected visual acuity between the two approaches (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.01). The honest catch is certainty: Cochrane graded the evidence moderate to very low, the randomised base is only two trials, and bilateral simultaneous endophthalmitis — the catastrophic event same-day surgery is feared for — is too rare for any of these data to exclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): same-day bilateral cataract surgery shows no measurable disadvantage on any outcome the evidence can actually measure, at lower cost; the unmeasurable rare bilateral disaster remains a judgement call, not a data point.

cards.headline: Dickman 2022 (Cochrane): endophthalmitis 1/14,076 same-day versus 55/556,246 delayed; refractive misses risk ratio 0.84 and complications 1.33 — no difference on any measured outcome, costs lower
cards.summary: Dickman 2022 (Cochrane): endophthalmitis 1/14,076 same-day versus 55/556,246 delayed; refractive misses risk ratio 0.84 and complications 1.33 — no difference on any measured outcome, costs lower
cards.people: 14 studies (2 randomised trials, 7 non-randomised studies, 6 economic evaluations) in 276,260 people with bilateral age-related cataract (7,384 same-day immediate sequential bilateral surgery; 268,876 delayed sequential surgery), from Canada, Europe, Iran, Korea, the UK and the USA.
cards.result: Endophthalmitis occurred in 1 of 14,076 same-day participants and 55 of 556,246 delayed participants; relative effects were estimated too imprecisely to be reliable, and the reviewers found no evidence of an increased risk with same-day surgery. Eyes not achieving refraction within 1.0 dioptre of target at 1–3 months did not differ (randomised trials: risk ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.26; non-randomised: 1.02, 0.60 to 1.75), nor did postoperative complications (randomised: 1.33, 0.52 to 3.40; non-randomised: 1.04, 0.47 to 2.29). Patient-reported outcomes did not differ (standardised mean difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.03). Total costs per participant were lower for same-day surgery, though study results could not be pooled.
cards.watchOut: Certainty was graded moderate to very low throughout, the randomised evidence is just two trials at high-to-some-concerns risk of bias, and the safety totals lean heavily on non-randomised data. The feared event — simultaneous bilateral endophthalmitis — is so rare that 'no evidence of increased risk' is not the same as proof of equal risk.
cards.source: Dickman MM et al. Immediate sequential bilateral surgery versus delayed sequential bilateral surgery for cataracts. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 35467755. cards.headline: Malvankar-Mehta 2015: visual acuity improved equally after both approaches (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.01 between groups)
cards.summary: Malvankar-Mehta 2015: visual acuity improved equally after both approaches (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.01 between groups)
cards.people: 11 articles with 3,657 subjects undergoing immediate or delayed sequential bilateral cataract surgery, comparing postoperative utility scores and best-corrected visual acuity.
cards.result: Best-corrected visual acuity improved significantly after both surgeries (standardised mean difference -1.79 for same-day and -1.53 for delayed), with a non-significant difference between them (-0.18, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.01). Utility scores by time-trade-off, EQ-5D, HUI3 and VF-7 instruments showed non-significant differences between approaches; the Catquest questionnaire favoured same-day surgery in one analysis, while the VF-14 analysis was highly heterogeneous (I² = 97.1%).
cards.watchOut: An older, smaller synthesis than the Cochrane review, dominated by non-randomised comparisons and very heterogeneous patient-reported measures; it corroborates the direction of the Cochrane findings but adds no power on rare harms.
cards.source: Malvankar-Mehta MS et al. Immediate versus Delayed Sequential Bilateral Cataract Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 26121673. cards.headline: Synthesis: every measurable outcome is a draw, the bill is smaller, and the one outcome that matters most cannot be measured
cards.summary: Synthesis: every measurable outcome is a draw, the bill is smaller, and the one outcome that matters most cannot be measured
cards.people: Cochrane review of 14 studies (276,260 participants) plus an earlier meta-analysis of 11 articles (3,657 subjects), comparing same-day with separate-day bilateral cataract surgery.
cards.result: Endophthalmitis: 1/14,076 versus 55/556,246. Refractive misses: risk ratio 0.84 (0.57 to 1.26). Complications: 1.33 (0.52 to 3.40). Visual acuity between groups: standardised mean difference -0.18 (-0.37 to 0.01). Costs: lower per participant for same-day surgery in the studies that reported them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Both syntheses rest substantially on non-randomised data for safety; a bilateral blinding infection occurring once in tens of thousands of cases would be invisible in these numbers, so the residual objection to same-day surgery is principled rather than statistical.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dickman MM et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022 (PMID: 35467755); Malvankar-Mehta MS et al. PloS one. 2015 (PMID: 26121673).

shelves.title: Clascoterone 1% cream: clear or almost clear in 18.4% and 20.3% versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle at 12 weeks in two phase 3 trials — a real but modest win, with mostly mild local redness
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe facial acne, does clascoterone 1% cream — a topical androgen-receptor inhibitor — clear lesions better than vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris/diagnosis/drug therapy · Adolescent · Adult · Androgen Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Child · Cortodoxone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Erythema/chemically induced/diagnosis · Face · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Propionates/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Severity of Illness Index · Skin Cream/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first topical androgen-receptor inhibitor beat vehicle in two identical phase 3 trials, by a modest margin. Treatment success (clear or almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement) at week 12 was 18.4% and 20.3% on clascoterone cream 1% twice daily versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle (Hebert A et al., PMID: 32320027), with inflammatory lesion counts falling by 19.3 and 20.0 versus 15.5 and 12.6 on vehicle. In the open-label extension (Eichenfield LF et al., PMID: 37556524), 18.1% of patients reported treatment-emergent adverse events over up to 9 further months, the commonest local reactions being erythema and scaling/dryness, and 48.9% of per-protocol completers had clear or almost-clear faces at study end. The catch is scale: roughly four of five treated patients did not reach clear/almost-clear at 12 weeks, and there is no comparison against any established acne treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clascoterone 1% cream is a genuinely effective, well-tolerated addition for moderate-to-severe facial acne — an incremental option, not a replacement for standard therapy.

cards.headline: Hebert 2020 (CB-03-01/25 and /26): treatment success 18.4% and 20.3% on clascoterone versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle at week 12 (both P<.001)
cards.summary: Hebert 2020 (CB-03-01/25 and /26): treatment success 18.4% and 20.3% on clascoterone versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle at week 12 (both P<.001)
cards.people: 1,440 males and nonpregnant females aged 9 years and older with moderate or severe facial acne (30–75 inflammatory and 30–100 noninflammatory lesions), randomised to clascoterone cream 1% or vehicle applied to the whole face twice daily for 12 weeks, in two identical multicentre studies (353 vs 355 and 369 vs 363 participants).
cards.result: Treatment success (Investigator's Global Assessment 0 or 1 with ≥2-grade improvement) at week 12: 18.4% versus 9.0% in trial 25 and 20.3% versus 6.5% in trial 26 (both P<.001). Absolute noninflammatory lesion change was -19.4 in both trials versus -13.0 and -10.8 on vehicle; inflammatory lesion change was -19.3 and -20.0 versus -15.5 and -12.6. Adverse event rates were low and mostly mild; the predominant local skin reaction was trace or mild erythema.
cards.watchOut: Absolute success rates are modest — about 80% of treated patients were not clear or almost clear at 12 weeks — and the comparator is vehicle, not benzoyl peroxide, a retinoid or an antibiotic, so clascoterone's place in the treatment order is untested. Industry-conducted trials in a selected trial population.
cards.source: Hebert A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Topical Clascoterone Cream, 1%, for Treatment in Patients With Facial Acne: Two Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA dermatology. 2020. PMID: 32320027. Registry ID: NCT02608450 and NCT02608476. cards.headline: Eichenfield 2023 (long-term extension): 18.1% reported treatment-emergent events over up to 9 months; 48.9% of completers clear or almost clear at study end
cards.summary: Eichenfield 2023 (long-term extension): 18.1% reported treatment-emergent events over up to 9 months; 48.9% of completers clear or almost clear at study end
cards.people: 600 patients aged 12 years and older from the phase 3 trials (311 originally clascoterone, 289 vehicle) applying clascoterone cream 1% twice daily to face (and trunk if desired) for up to 9 months; 343 completed.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 108 of 598 treated patients (18.1%), similar whether originally randomised to clascoterone (18.0%) or vehicle (18.1%). The commonest local skin reactions on the face were scaling/dryness (10.0% previous clascoterone, 7.3% previous vehicle) and erythema (8.0% and 7.7%). Among per-protocol completers, clear or almost-clear (IGA 0/1) was reached by 48.9% (156/319) for the face and 52.4% (65/124) for the trunk at study end.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no comparator and a completer analysis — the rising success percentages partly reflect who stayed in and the freedom to stop and restart treatment, so they describe durability and tolerability, not added efficacy.
cards.source: Eichenfield LF et al. Long-Term Safety and Efficacy of Twice-Daily Topical Clascoterone Cream 1% in Patients Greater Than or Equal to 12 Years of Age With Acne Vulgaris. Journal of drugs in dermatology : JDD. 2023. PMID: 37556524. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, modest vehicle-beating effect with a clean long-term safety record — and no head-to-head data at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, modest vehicle-beating effect with a clean long-term safety record — and no head-to-head data at all
cards.people: Two identical 12-week phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials (1,440 patients) plus a 9-month open-label extension (600 patients) of clascoterone cream 1% twice daily for moderate-to-severe facial acne.
cards.result: Treatment success at week 12: 18.4% and 20.3% versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle. Inflammatory lesion reductions: -19.3 and -20.0 versus -15.5 and -12.6. Long-term treatment-emergent adverse events: 18.1%, mostly mild local reactions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Every efficacy figure comes from vehicle comparisons; whether clascoterone adds anything on top of, or instead of, standard topical therapy is unknown from these records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hebert A et al. JAMA dermatology. 2020 (PMID: 32320027); Eichenfield LF et al. Journal of drugs in dermatology : JDD. 2023 (PMID: 37556524).

shelves.title: Trifarotene cream for face and trunk acne: both PERFECT phase 3 trials positive on every endpoint (all P<.001) — the abstracts report significance without success percentages; a 52-week open-label study reached 65.1% clear or almost clear on the face
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe acne of the face and trunk, does trifarotene 50 µg/g cream improve lesion counts and success rates compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris/drug therapy · Adolescent · Adult · Child · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Erythema/chemically induced · Facial Dermatoses/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Specificity · Retinoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Skin Cream/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Torso · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trifarotene, a retinoid selective for the skin-predominant RAR-γ receptor, beat vehicle on every primary and secondary endpoint in two phase 3 trials covering both face and trunk (Tan J et al., PMID: 30802558): facial success, truncal success, and inflammatory and noninflammatory lesion counts on both sites were all highly significant (P<.001) at week 12. The published abstract does not state the absolute success percentages, so the size of the win cannot be quoted from the record — a declared gap on this shelf. What can be sized is durability: in the 52-week open-label study (Blume-Peytavi U et al., PMID: 31306527), facial success rose from 26.6% at week 12 to 65.1% at week 52 and truncal success from 38.6% to 66.9%, with trifarotene-related treatment-emergent adverse events in 12.6% and local irritation concentrated in the first weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trifarotene works on face and trunk acne with the usual early retinoid irritation; the pivotal abstracts' missing percentages keep this at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

cards.headline: Tan 2019 (PERFECT 1 and 2): facial and truncal success and lesion counts all highly significant in favour of trifarotene at week 12 (P<.001) — percentages not stated in the record
cards.summary: Tan 2019 (PERFECT 1 and 2): facial and truncal success and lesion counts all highly significant in favour of trifarotene at week 12 (P<.001) — percentages not stated in the record
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials (Tan 2019, PERFECT 1 and 2)
cards.people: Subjects aged 9 years and older with moderate facial and truncal acne in two double-blind, randomised, vehicle-controlled 12-week studies of once-daily trifarotene 50 µg/g cream versus vehicle.
cards.result: At week 12, facial success (Investigator's Global Assessment clear or almost clear with ≥2-grade improvement), truncal success (Physician's Global Assessment), and absolute and percentage changes in inflammatory and noninflammatory lesion counts on both face and trunk were all highly significant in favour of trifarotene (P<.001 for each). The abstract reports the significance of these comparisons without the underlying success percentages or lesion-count values.
cards.watchOut: A p-value-only abstract: the treatment effect's size cannot be verified from the PubMed record, so this shelf deliberately quotes no pivotal-trial percentages. Adjunctive topical or systemic treatments were not studied.
cards.source: Tan J et al. Randomized phase 3 evaluation of trifarotene 50 μg/g cream treatment of moderate facial and truncal acne. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2019. PMID: 30802558. cards.headline: Blume-Peytavi 2020 (52-week open-label): facial success 26.6% at week 12 rising to 65.1% at week 52; related adverse events 12.6%, none serious
cards.summary: Blume-Peytavi 2020 (52-week open-label): facial success 26.6% at week 12 rising to 65.1% at week 52; related adverse events 12.6%, none serious
cards.people: 453 patients with moderate facial and truncal acne treated with trifarotene 50 µg/g cream once daily for 52 weeks; 342 (75.5%) completed.
cards.result: Investigator's Global Assessment (face) success was 26.6% at week 12 and 65.1% at week 52; Physician's Global Assessment (trunk) success was 38.6% and 66.9%; success on both sites in the same patient was 57.9% at week 52. Trifarotene-related treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 12.6% of patients, none serious, mostly cutaneous and in the first 3 months; severe local tolerability signs were reported by 2.2% to 7.1% (face) and 2.5% to 5.4% (trunk). shelves.title: Combined oral contraceptives for acne in women: all nine placebo-controlled trials in the Cochrane review favoured the pill — a drospirenone pill gave clear or almost-clear skin at about four times the placebo odds; which progestin is best stays unclear
shelves.question: In women with acne, do combined oral contraceptives improve lesion counts compared with placebo or other acne treatments?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris/drug therapy · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — combined oral contraceptives reduce facial acne lesions versus placebo, consistently. The Cochrane review (Arowojolu AO et al., PMID: 22786490) covered 31 trials with 12,579 participants; all nine placebo-controlled trials with analysable data showed combined pills reducing lesion counts, severity grades and self-assessed acne. A levonorgestrel pill cut total lesion counts by a mean 9.98 more than placebo; a drospirenone pill roughly tripled the odds of investigator-assessed clear or almost-clear skin (odds ratio 3.02, 95% CI 1.99 to 4.59). The largest single drospirenone trial (Koltun W et al., PMID: 18342647) put the odds of clear or almost-clear skin at 4.31 (95% CI 2.11 to 9.60) versus placebo over six cycles. What the evidence does not settle is ranking: differences between progestin types were inconsistent, and only one trial compared a pill with an antibiotic. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for women who also want contraception, a combined pill is a well-evidenced acne treatment; choosing between pills on acne grounds alone is not evidence-based.

cards.headline: Arowojolu 2012 (Cochrane): 31 trials, 12,579 women — all nine analysable placebo-controlled trials favoured the pill; drospirenone odds ratio 3.02 for clear or almost-clear skin
cards.summary: Arowojolu 2012 (Cochrane): 31 trials, 12,579 women — all nine analysable placebo-controlled trials favoured the pill; drospirenone odds ratio 3.02 for clear or almost-clear skin
cards.people: 31 randomised trials with 12,579 women with facial acne comparing a combined oral contraceptive (estrogen plus progestin) with placebo, another pill, or an antibiotic; 24 comparisons in total.
cards.result: All nine placebo-controlled trials with data showed combined pills reducing lesion counts, severity grades and self-assessed acne versus placebo. Levonorgestrel pill: total lesion counts lower by a mean difference of -9.98 (95% CI -16.51 to -3.45), with more clinician-assessed clear or almost-clear skin. Drospirenone pill (two trials combined): investigator assessment of clear or almost-clear skin favoured drospirenone (odds ratio 3.02, 95% CI 1.99 to 4.59), with a greater percentage change in total lesion count in one trial (mean difference 29.08, 95% CI 3.13 to 55.03). Pills containing chlormadinone acetate or cyproterone acetate improved acne better than levonorgestrel in the available comparisons, but head-to-head results between progestins were inconsistent, and only one trial compared a pill with an antibiotic.
cards.watchOut: Most comparisons rest on one or two trials each, acne assessment methods were not standardised across trials, and the review is from 2012. The benefit is for facial acne in women seeking contraception — it says nothing about acne in men or about pills started for acne alone, where contraceptive risks enter the balance.

cards.headline: Koltun 2008: drospirenone 3 mg/ethinylestradiol 20 mcg (24/4) — odds of clear or almost-clear skin 4.31 (95% CI 2.11 to 9.60) versus placebo over six cycles
cards.summary: Koltun 2008: drospirenone 3 mg/ethinylestradiol 20 mcg (24/4) — odds of clear or almost-clear skin 4.31 (95% CI 2.11 to 9.60) versus placebo over six cycles
cards.people: 534 healthy females aged 14–45 years with moderate facial acne, randomised to drospirenone 3 mg/ethinylestradiol 20 mcg in a 24/4 regimen (n=266) or placebo (n=268) for six 28-day cycles.
cards.result: The drospirenone pill produced greater reductions from baseline in inflammatory, noninflammatory and total lesion counts than placebo, and the odds of investigator-rated 'clear' or 'almost clear' skin at endpoint were about fourfold higher on the pill (odds ratio 4.31, 95% CI 2.11 to 9.60; p=.001). The pill was well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with low-dose combined oral contraceptive use.
cards.watchOut: A single formulation and a single trial; the abstract gives the odds ratio without the absolute clear/almost-clear percentages, and six cycles in trial volunteers may flatter adherence versus real-world use.
cards.source: Koltun W et al. shelves.title: Dapsone 5% gel: two identical 12-week trials (3,010 patients) beat vehicle on global assessment and every lesion count (all P<.001) — the report gives p-values, not percentages; a year of open-label use cut inflammatory lesions by 58.2%
shelves.question: In moderate acne, does dapsone 5% gel reduce inflammatory lesions compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris/drug therapy/pathology · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child · Dapsone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gels · Humans · Male · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dapsone 5% gel beat vehicle in two identically designed 12-week trials totalling 3,010 patients (Draelos ZD et al., PMID: 17208334): superior on the investigator's global assessment and on mean percentage reductions in inflammatory, noninflammatory and total lesion counts (all P<.001), with inflammatory-lesion separation apparent by 4 weeks. The pivotal report gives p-values without the actual percentages — a declared gap that caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The size signal comes from the 12-month open-label study (Lucky AW et al., PMID: 17966175): mean inflammatory lesion counts fell 30.6% by one month and 58.2% by 12 months, with application-site reactions in 8.2% and no significant haematology or blood-chemistry changes — including in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase-deficient patients in the controlled trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dapsone 5% gel is an effective, well-tolerated twice-daily option for acne, on trials whose published record proves direction more clearly than size.

cards.headline: Draelos 2007 (two identical trials): dapsone gel superior on global assessment and all lesion counts at week 12 (all P<.001) in 3,010 patients — percentages not reported in the record
cards.summary: Draelos 2007 (two identical trials): dapsone gel superior on global assessment and all lesion counts at week 12 (all P<.001) in 3,010 patients — percentages not reported in the record
cards.people: 3,010 patients aged 12 years and older with acne vulgaris in two identically designed 12-week, randomised, double-blind studies of twice-daily dapsone gel 5% versus vehicle gel monotherapy.
cards.result: Dapsone gel achieved superior results on the investigator's global acne assessment (P<.001) and on mean percentage reductions in inflammatory, noninflammatory and total lesion counts (all P<.001) at week 12. Reductions in inflammatory lesion counts favouring dapsone were apparent as early as 2 weeks and statistically significant by 4 weeks. No clinically significant laboratory changes, including haemoglobin, were observed — even among glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase-deficient patients. Adverse events were comparable between groups and rarely led to discontinuation. The abstract reports p-values only, without the lesion-count percentages or global-assessment rates.
cards.watchOut: P-value-only reporting in the pivotal record: effect size cannot be verified from PubMed. Monotherapy only — adjunctive topical treatments and their impact were not studied.
cards.source: Draelos ZD et al. Two randomized studies demonstrate the efficacy and safety of dapsone gel, 5% for the treatment of acne vulgaris. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2007. PMID: 17208334. cards.headline: Lucky 2007 (12-month open-label): inflammatory lesions down 30.6% at 1 month and 58.2% at 12 months; application-site reactions 8.2%
cards.summary: Lucky 2007 (12-month open-label): inflammatory lesions down 30.6% at 1 month and 58.2% at 12 months; application-site reactions 8.2%
cards.people: 486 patients aged at least 12 years with acne vulgaris applying dapsone gel 5% twice daily for up to 12 months.
cards.result: Mean reduction from baseline in inflammatory lesion counts was 30.6% at one month and 58.2% at 12 months; noninflammatory and total lesion reductions at 12 months were 19.5% and 49.0% (all P=.002 versus baseline). Application-site reactions related to treatment were reported in 8.2% of patients, mostly mild to moderate; common non-application events were headache (20%) and nasopharyngitis (15%). No significant changes in haematology or blood chemistry were observed.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and open-label — the 58.2% figure includes natural history, regression to the mean and completer effects, so it sizes long-term use experience rather than drug-attributable benefit.
