shelves.title: Oral minoxidil 5 mg versus topical 5%: no superiority on hair-density measures at 24 weeks in the only head-to-head trial — a photographic win on the vertex only, and unwanted hair growth in 49% of the oral group
shelves.question: In androgenetic alopecia, is low-dose oral minoxidil as effective as topical minoxidil for hair density, and how do their side effects compare?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Minoxidil/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Alopecia/drug therapy · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Administration, Oral · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Administration, Topical · Adolescent · Hair/drug effects · Brazil · Scalp
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the only randomised head-to-head trial, oral minoxidil 5 mg daily did not demonstrate superiority over topical minoxidil 5% twice daily on the prespecified hair-density outcomes (Penha MA et al., PMID: 38598226). At 24 weeks, between-group differences in terminal hair density were 3.1 hairs/cm² on the frontal scalp (95% CI -18.2 to 21.5; P=.27) and 23.4 hairs/cm² on the vertex (95% CI -0.3 to 43.0; P=.09); total hair density differences were likewise non-significant. Blinded photographic evaluation favoured oral minoxidil on the vertex (24%; 95% CI 0 to 48; P=.04) but not the frontal scalp. The price of the tablet was hypertrichosis in 22 of 45 men (49%) and headache in 6 of 45 (14%). A network meta-analysis of monotherapies (Gupta AK et al., PMID: 38725143) ranked dutasteride 0.5 mg most effective for hair density and found oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors more effective than oral minoxidil — context that oral minoxidil is not the strongest oral option either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on density measures the oral and topical routes performed alike in one small trial; the choice turns on convenience, scalp irritation and tolerance of body-wide hair growth, not proven efficacy.

cards.headline: Penha 2024: terminal hair density differences 3.1 hairs/cm² frontal (P=.27) and 23.4 hairs/cm² vertex (P=.09) — oral minoxidil did not demonstrate superiority; hypertrichosis 49%
cards.summary: Penha 2024: terminal hair density differences 3.1 hairs/cm² frontal (P=.27) and 23.4 hairs/cm² vertex (P=.09) — oral minoxidil did not demonstrate superiority; hypertrichosis 49%
cards.people: 90 men aged 18–55 years with androgenetic alopecia (Norwood-Hamilton 3V, 4V or 5V) at a single Brazilian clinic, randomised to oral minoxidil 5 mg daily plus topical placebo, or topical minoxidil 5% 1 mL twice daily plus oral placebo, for 24 weeks; 68 completed (33 oral, 35 topical).
cards.result: Frontal terminal hair density change differed between groups by 3.1 hairs/cm² (95% CI -18.2 to 21.5; P=.27) and total density by 2.6 hairs/cm² (-10.3 to 15.8; P=.32). Vertex terminal density differed by 23.4 hairs/cm² (-0.3 to 43.0; P=.09) and total density by 5.5 hairs/cm² (-12.5 to 23.5; P=.32). Photographic analysis favoured oral minoxidil on the vertex (24%; 95% CI 0 to 48; P=.04) but not the frontal scalp (12%; -12 to 36; P=.24). The commonest adverse effects on oral minoxidil were hypertrichosis (22 of 45, 49%) and headache (6 of 45, 14%).
cards.watchOut: One small single-centre trial with 68 completers and wide confidence intervals — the vertex difference (23.4 hairs/cm², CI just crossing zero) is compatible with a real oral advantage the trial was too small to confirm. Men only, 24 weeks only, and the 5 mg dose is higher than the low doses (1–2.5 mg) many clinicians use, so its 49% hypertrichosis rate may overstate low-dose experience.

cards.people: Bayesian network meta-analysis of monotherapies for male androgenetic alopecia in men aged 18 years and older, comparing 20 active treatments and placebo/vehicle on 6-month change in total and terminal hair density.
cards.result: Dutasteride 0.5 mg once daily for 24 weeks ranked most effective for 6-month change in total hair density (SUCRA 87%) and terminal hair density (SUCRA 98%). The authors concluded that oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are more effective than oral minoxidil and newer agents such as microneedling and photobiomodulation, and that effectiveness can be dose-dependent.
cards.watchOut: An indirect-comparison ranking, not a head-to-head trial: it places oral minoxidil within the monotherapy league table but cannot substitute for the missing direct oral-versus-topical minoxidil comparison, and SUCRA rankings exaggerate small differences.

shelves.title: Ciclosporin versus methotrexate for severe childhood eczema (TREAT): ciclosporin clearly ahead at 12 weeks (o-SCORAD difference -5.69), methotrexate ahead by week 60 — speed versus staying power, with similar harms
shelves.question: In children and young people with severe atopic dermatitis, how does ciclosporin compare with methotrexate for disease control, speed of response and tolerability?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Adolescent · Cyclosporine/adverse effects · Methotrexate/adverse effects · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Filaggrin Proteins · Odds Ratio · Treatment Outcome · Severity of Illness Index · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: SPLIT — ciclosporin works faster, methotrexate lasts longer. In the TREAT trial (Flohr C et al., PMID: 37722926), 103 children and young people aged 2–16 years with severe atopic dermatitis were randomised to ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily or methotrexate 0.4 mg/kg weekly for 36 weeks. Ciclosporin improved disease severity more by week 12 (mean o-SCORAD difference -5.69, 97.5% CI -10.81 to -0.57; P=0.01), with more children reaching o-SCORAD 50 (odds ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.23 to 5.49). After treatment stopped, the picture reversed: by week 60 methotrexate was superior (odds ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.85 for the ciclosporin comparison), and participant-reported flares after stopping were higher in the ciclosporin arm (odds ratio 3.22, 95% CI 0.42 to 6.01). Adverse events were comparably frequent; serious adverse events occurred in 10% on ciclosporin and 14% on methotrexate. A network meta-analysis of systemic eczema treatments (Chu AWL et al., PMID: 37678577) likewise rates the evidence for both drugs as less certain than for newer biologics. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose ciclosporin when speed matters, methotrexate when durable control after stopping matters — one trial, 103 children, decides it.

cards.headline: Flohr 2023 (TREAT): ciclosporin ahead at week 12 (o-SCORAD -5.69, P=0.01; o-SCORAD 50 odds ratio 2.60), methotrexate ahead at week 60 (odds ratio 0.33); serious events 10% versus 14%
cards.summary: Flohr 2023 (TREAT): ciclosporin ahead at week 12 (o-SCORAD -5.69, P=0.01; o-SCORAD 50 odds ratio 2.60), methotrexate ahead at week 60 (odds ratio 0.33); serious events 10% versus 14%
cards.people: 103 children and young people aged 2–16 years with severe atopic dermatitis unresponsive to potent topical treatment, at 13 UK and Irish centres, randomised to oral ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily (n=52) or methotrexate 0.4 mg/kg weekly (n=51) for 36 weeks, with 24 weeks of follow-up after treatment.
cards.result: At 12 weeks ciclosporin showed greater improvement in objective SCORAD (mean difference -5.69, 97.5% CI -10.81 to -0.57; P=0.01) and more o-SCORAD 50 responses (odds ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.23 to 5.49; P=0.01). By 60 weeks methotrexate was superior (odds ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.85; P=0.02), a trend also seen for o-SCORAD 75, EASI 50 and EASI 75, and participant-reported flares after treatment cessation were higher in the ciclosporin arm (odds ratio 3.22, 95% CI 0.42 to 6.01; P=0.02). Quality of life improved with both and was sustained after stopping. Adverse-event frequency was comparable; serious adverse events affected 5 (10%) on ciclosporin and 7 (14%) on methotrexate. Filaggrin status did not affect outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 103 children decides a question clinicians face weekly; it was assessor-blinded rather than double-blind, the flare odds ratio's confidence interval is very wide (0.42 to 6.01), and neither drug was compared with the biologics now entering paediatric practice.
cards.source: Flohr C et al. Efficacy and safety of ciclosporin versus methotrexate in the treatment of severe atopic dermatitis in children and young people (TREAT): a multicentre parallel group assessor-blinded clinical trial. The British journal of dermatology. 2023. PMID: 37722926. cards.headline: Chu 2023 (network meta-analysis, 149 trials): efficacy and safety of ciclosporin and methotrexate in atopic dermatitis rated less certain than for dupilumab and the JAK inhibitors
cards.summary: Chu 2023 (network meta-analysis, 149 trials): efficacy and safety of ciclosporin and methotrexate in atopic dermatitis rated less certain than for dupilumab and the JAK inhibitors
cards.people: 149 randomised trials (28,686 patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) evaluating 75 systemic interventions and phototherapy, prepared for the 2023 AAAAI/ACAAI atopic dermatitis guidelines.
cards.result: With high-certainty evidence, high-dose upadacitinib was among the most effective treatments but also among the most harmful; dupilumab, lebrikizumab and tralokinumab were of intermediate effectiveness and among the safest. The efficacy and safety of azathioprine, oral corticosteroids, cyclosporine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, phototherapy and many novel agents were rated less certain.
cards.watchOut: A mostly adult, mostly placebo-anchored network — it grades the certainty around the two TREAT drugs rather than comparing them in children, and its indirect estimates cannot overturn TREAT's direct head-to-head result.
cards.source: Chu AWL et al. Systemic treatments for atopic dermatitis (eczema): Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized trials. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 2023. PMID: 37678577. shelves.title: Nemolizumab plus topical therapy (ARCADIA 1 & 2): clear or almost-clear skin in 36% and 38% versus 25% and 26%, EASI-75 in 44% and 42% versus 29% and 30% at week 16 — itch relief from week 1, responses largely maintained to week 48
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, does nemolizumab with background topical therapy reduce itch and skin severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Administration, Topical · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Calcineurin Inhibitors/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Pruritus/drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nemolizumab, an interleukin-31 receptor blocker aimed at itch, improved both skin clearance and itch on top of topical therapy in two replicate phase 3 trials (Silverberg JI et al., PMID: 39067461). At week 16, Investigator's Global Assessment success was 36% versus 25% in ARCADIA 1 (adjusted difference 11.5%) and 38% versus 26% in ARCADIA 2 (adjusted difference 12.2%), and EASI-75 responses were 44% versus 29% and 42% versus 30%. Itch improved significantly from week 1 and sleep by week 16. In the maintenance phase (Wollenberg A et al., PMID: 42272192), week-16 responders rerandomised to nemolizumab every 4 or 8 weeks maintained IGA success at week 48 in 61.5% and 60.4% versus 49.7% after withdrawal to placebo. Adverse-event rates were similar to placebo in the initial period (50% and 41% versus 45% and 44%). The gains are real but incremental — about one extra clear/almost-clear patient for every eight or nine treated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nemolizumab adds a modest, itch-led benefit over topical therapy alone, maintained with continued dosing.

cards.headline: Silverberg 2024 (ARCADIA 1 & 2): IGA success 36% vs 25% and 38% vs 26%; EASI-75 44% vs 29% and 42% vs 30% at week 16 (all significant)
cards.summary: Silverberg 2024 (ARCADIA 1 & 2): IGA success 36% vs 25% and 38% vs 26%; EASI-75 44% vs 29% and 42% vs 30% at week 16 (all significant)
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials (Silverberg 2024, ARCADIA 1 and ARCADIA 2)
cards.people: 1,728 adolescents and adults (aged 12 years and older) with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, associated pruritus and inadequate response to topical steroids, at 281 centres in 22 countries, randomised 2:1 to nemolizumab 30 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (60 mg loading dose) or placebo, both with background topical corticosteroids with or without calcineurin inhibitors, for the 16-week initial period (1,142 nemolizumab, 586 placebo).
cards.result: Both trials met both coprimary endpoints at week 16. IGA success: ARCADIA 1, 221 (36%) of 620 versus 79 (25%) of 321, adjusted difference 11.5% (97.5% CI 4.7 to 18.3; p=0.0003); ARCADIA 2, 197 (38%) of 522 versus 69 (26%) of 265, adjusted difference 12.2% (4.6 to 19.8; p=0.0006). EASI-75: 270 (44%) versus 93 (29%), adjusted difference 14.9% (p<0.0001); and 220 (42%) versus 80 (30%), adjusted difference 12.5% (p=0.0006). All key secondary endpoints, including itch improvement from week 1 and sleep improvement at week 16, favoured nemolizumab. Treatment-emergent adverse events: 50% and 41% on nemolizumab versus 45% and 44% on placebo; serious events 1% and 3% versus 1% and 1%; no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gains over background topical therapy are about 11–15 percentage points — meaningful for itch-driven disease but far from clearance for most patients. Both trials were industry-run (Galderma), enrolled patients with pruritus prominent enough to suit the drug's mechanism, and compare against placebo, not against dupilumab or a JAK inhibitor.
cards.source: Silverberg JI et al. Nemolizumab with concomitant topical therapy in adolescents and adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (ARCADIA 1 and ARCADIA 2): results from two replicate, double-blind, randomised controlled phase 3 trials. Lancet (London, England). 2024. PMID: 39067461. Registry ID: NCT03985943 and NCT03989349. cards.headline: Wollenberg 2026 (ARCADIA maintenance): week-48 IGA success maintained in 61.5% (every 4 weeks) and 60.4% (every 8 weeks) versus 49.7% after withdrawal
cards.summary: Wollenberg 2026 (ARCADIA maintenance): week-48 IGA success maintained in 61.5% (every 4 weeks) and 60.4% (every 8 weeks) versus 49.7% after withdrawal
cards.type: Randomised maintenance phase of two phase 3 trials (Wollenberg 2026)
cards.people: 507 week-16 responders to nemolizumab in ARCADIA 1 and 2, rerandomised 1:1:1 to nemolizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks, every 8 weeks, or placebo (nemolizumab withdrawal), all with background topical therapy, from week 16 to week 48.
cards.result: At week 48, IGA success was maintained by 61.5% on every-4-week dosing (difference versus withdrawal 11.8%, 95% CI 1.3 to 22.3) and 60.4% on every-8-week dosing (difference 10.7%, 0.3 to 21.0), versus 49.7% in the withdrawal group; EASI-75 maintenance was 76.3% and 75.7% versus 63.9%. At least one adverse event was reported by 53.5% to 58.3% across groups, without notable differences between regimens.
cards.watchOut: A responder-enriched population — half of even the withdrawn group maintained response, so the maintenance advantage is modest and applies only to patients who already responded by week 16.
cards.source: Wollenberg A et al. shelves.title: Abrocitinib 200 mg versus dupilumab (JADE DARE): faster itch relief (48% versus 26% responding by week 2) and more EASI-90 at week 4 (29% versus 15%) — one trial, and more adverse events (74% versus 65%)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, is abrocitinib 200 mg more effective than dupilumab for early itch relief and skin clearance, and how do their harms compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Pyrimidines · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the early endpoints it was designed around, abrocitinib 200 mg beat dupilumab in the single head-to-head JADE DARE trial (Reich K et al., PMID: 35871814). A 4-point itch improvement by week 2 was reached by 172 (48%) of 357 on abrocitinib versus 93 (26%) of 364 on dupilumab (difference 22.6%), and EASI-90 at week 4 by 101 (29%) of 354 versus 53 (15%) of 364 (difference 14.1%; both p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent on abrocitinib (268 of 362, 74%, versus 239 of 365, 65%), and two non-treatment-related deaths occurred in the abrocitinib group. Supporting evidence that abrocitinib works even after dupilumab comes from JADE EXTEND (Shi VY et al., PMID: 35439608), where 12 weeks of abrocitinib produced EASI-75 in 80.0% of prior dupilumab nonresponders on 200 mg. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): abrocitinib 200 mg is the faster drug for itch and early clearance in this one trial — a speed advantage bought with more adverse events, in a comparison that says nothing about long-term control or rare JAK-inhibitor harms.

cards.headline: Reich 2022 (JADE DARE): itch response at week 2 in 48% versus 26% and EASI-90 at week 4 in 29% versus 15%, both favouring abrocitinib (p<0.0001); adverse events 74% versus 65%
cards.summary: Reich 2022 (JADE DARE): itch response at week 2 in 48% versus 26% and EASI-90 at week 4 in 29% versus 15%, both favouring abrocitinib (p<0.0001); adverse events 74% versus 65%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind head-to-head phase 3 trial (Reich 2022, JADE DARE)
cards.people: 727 adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis requiring systemic therapy or inadequately responding to topicals, at 151 sites in 15 countries, randomised to oral abrocitinib 200 mg daily (n=362) or subcutaneous dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks (n=365) for 26 weeks, both with background topical therapy.
cards.result: Primary endpoints both favoured abrocitinib: Peak Pruritus NRS improvement of ≥4 points at week 2 in 172 (48%) of 357 versus 93 (26%) of 364 (difference 22.6%, 95% CI 15.8 to 29.5; p<0.0001), and EASI-90 at week 4 in 101 (29%) of 354 versus 53 (15%) of 364 (difference 14.1%, 8.2 to 20.0; p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 268 (74%) of 362 on abrocitinib and 239 (65%) of 365 on dupilumab. Two non-treatment-related deaths occurred in the abrocitinib group.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoints are early (weeks 2 and 4) and chosen where a fast oral JAK inhibitor shines; the record does not show abrocitinib superior on later or longer-term outcomes, and 26 weeks cannot address the class-level cardiovascular and malignancy questions that hang over JAK inhibitors. One trial, industry-run (Pfizer).
cards.source: Reich K et al. Efficacy and safety of abrocitinib versus dupilumab in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: a randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35871814. Registry ID: NCT04345367. cards.headline: Shi 2022 (JADE EXTEND switch analysis): after dupilumab, 12 weeks of abrocitinib gave EASI-75 in 93.5% of prior responders and 80.0% of prior nonresponders (200 mg)
cards.summary: Shi 2022 (JADE EXTEND switch analysis): after dupilumab, 12 weeks of abrocitinib gave EASI-75 in 93.5% of prior responders and 80.0% of prior nonresponders (200 mg)
cards.type: Phase 3 extension switch analysis (Shi 2022, JADE EXTEND)
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis who received dupilumab in the double-blind JADE COMPARE trial, then abrocitinib 200 mg or 100 mg once daily for 12 weeks in the JADE EXTEND extension, analysed by prior dupilumab response.
cards.result: Among prior dupilumab responders, EASI-75 was achieved by 93.5% on abrocitinib 200 mg and 90.2% on 100 mg, with ≥4-point itch improvement in 89.7% and 81.6%. Among prior dupilumab nonresponders, EASI-75 was achieved by 80.0% (200 mg) and 67.7% (100 mg), with itch improvement in 77.3% and 37.8%. Common adverse events were nasopharyngitis, nausea, acne and headache; conjunctivitis occurred less frequently on abrocitinib than during prior dupilumab.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm and a 12-week horizon in patients selected by completing a prior trial — this shows abrocitinib can work after dupilumab, not that it outperforms dupilumab head-to-head; that claim rests on JADE DARE alone.
cards.source: Shi VY et al. Phase 3 efficacy and safety of abrocitinib in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis after switching from dupilumab (JADE EXTEND). Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2022. PMID: 35439608. shelves.title: Roflumilast 0.15% cream for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis: clear or almost clear in 32.0% and 28.9% versus 15.2% and 12.0% on vehicle at 4 weeks in two phase 3 trials — gentle on skin, and twice-weekly proactive use held clear skin a median 281 days
shelves.question: In mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis, does roflumilast cream 0.15% achieve clear or almost-clear skin compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Aminopyridines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Benzamides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Adult · Child · Cyclopropanes/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Skin Cream/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Severity of Illness Index · Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Canada · Poland · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — roflumilast cream 0.15%, a once-daily non-steroidal PDE4 inhibitor, beat vehicle in two phase 3 trials in mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis (Simpson EL et al., PMID: 39292443). Validated IGA success at week 4 was 32.0% versus 15.2% in INTEGUMENT-1 and 28.9% versus 12.0% in INTEGUMENT-2 (both P<.001), with EASI-75 in 43.2% versus 22.0% and 42.0% versus 19.7%. Tolerability was the standout: investigators saw no irritation at the application site in at least 95% of roflumilast-treated patients at each time point. In the open-label extension (PMID: 39792455), 657 patients treated for up to 52 weeks reported adverse events in 36.7% (4.7% treatment-related), and patients who cleared and switched to twice-weekly proactive application maintained clear or almost-clear skin for a median of 281 days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest-clearance, high-tolerability topical for mild-to-moderate disease, including in children from age 6 — with efficacy sized at 4 weeks and durability evidence uncontrolled.

cards.headline: Simpson 2024 (INTEGUMENT-1 & 2): IGA success 32.0% vs 15.2% and 28.9% vs 12.0% at week 4 (P<.001); EASI-75 43.2%/42.0% vs 22.0%/19.7%; no irritation in ≥95% at any visit
cards.summary: Simpson 2024 (INTEGUMENT-1 & 2): IGA success 32.0% vs 15.2% and 28.9% vs 12.0% at week 4 (P<.001); EASI-75 43.2%/42.0% vs 22.0%/19.7%; no irritation in ≥95% at any visit
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials (Simpson 2024, INTEGUMENT-1 and INTEGUMENT-2)
cards.people: 1,337 patients aged 6 years and older with mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis (654 in INTEGUMENT-1, 683 in INTEGUMENT-2; mean age 27.7 years; mean body surface area involved 13.6%) at sites in the US, Canada and Poland, randomised 2:1 to roflumilast cream 0.15% or vehicle once daily for 4 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, Validated IGA for Atopic Dermatitis success (score 0 or 1 with ≥2-grade improvement) at week 4, was achieved by 32.0% versus 15.2% in INTEGUMENT-1 and 28.9% versus 12.0% in INTEGUMENT-2 (both P<.001). EASI-75 at week 4: 43.2% versus 22.0% and 42.0% versus 19.7% (both P<.001). Roflumilast was well tolerated with low rates of treatment-emergent adverse events; investigators noted no signs of irritation at the application site in at least 95% of treated patients at each time point, and 90% reported no or mild sensation at the application site.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short for a chronic disease, the population is mild-to-moderate (results do not extend to severe eczema), and the comparator is vehicle rather than a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor, so relative place in therapy is untested.
cards.source: Simpson EL et al. Roflumilast Cream, 0.15%, for Atopic Dermatitis in Adults and Children: INTEGUMENT-1 and INTEGUMENT-2 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA dermatology. 2024. PMID: 39292443. Registry ID: NCT04773587 and NCT04773600. cards.summary: INTEGUMENT-OLE (open-label extension): adverse events in 36.7% over up to 52 weeks (4.7% treatment-related); twice-weekly proactive use maintained clear/almost-clear skin a median 281 days
cards.people: 657 patients aged 6 years and older who completed a 4-week INTEGUMENT trial, applying roflumilast cream 0.15% for up to 52 weeks; patients reaching clear skin (vIGA-AD 0) switched to twice-weekly proactive application to previously affected, now normal-appearing sites.
cards.result: Adverse events were reported by 36.7% of patients, 4.7% of them treatment-related; application-site pain was reported for 0.5% and stinging/burning causing definite discomfort for 0.4% to 2.1% at any visit. Patients who achieved clear skin and switched to twice-weekly proactive application maintained clear or almost-clear status for a median of 281 days (Kaplan-Meier estimate).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, in trial completers — the 281-day maintenance figure describes what happened on continued proactive treatment, not a randomised comparison against stopping or against reactive-only care.

shelves.title: Proactive twice-weekly treatment of eczema-prone skin: flares cut to a relative risk of 0.46 with fluticasone and 0.78 with tacrolimus versus vehicle in the meta-analysis — long-term safety unproven
shelves.question: In atopic eczema that keeps flaring, does twice-weekly proactive tacrolimus (or topical corticosteroid) applied to previously affected skin prevent flares compared with reactive treatment alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Age Factors · Androstadienes/therapeutic use · Calcineurin Inhibitors · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Dermatologic Agents/therapeutic use · Female · Fluticasone · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Methylprednisolone/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tacrolimus/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — treating previously affected skin on a twice-weekly schedule, before any flare, prevents flares better than vehicle in the randomised evidence. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Schmitt J et al., PMID: 20819086) pooled eight vehicle-controlled trials: the relative risk of experiencing at least one flare was 0.46 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.55) with proactive fluticasone propionate — a 54% relative reduction — and 0.78 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.00) with proactive tacrolimus, with methylprednisolone aceponate also efficacious in its single trial. In the largest tacrolimus paradigm trial (Paller AS et al., PMID: 19015204), children whose eczema had stabilised and who applied tacrolimus three times weekly to previously affected skin had significantly more disease-free days and a significantly longer time to first relapse than those on vehicle. The open questions are long-term: the trials were too short and too small to establish the safety of years of proactive anti-inflammatory use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): proactive maintenance is a proven flare-prevention strategy, strongest for topical corticosteroid, with its long-term safety still asserted rather than shown.

cards.headline: Schmitt 2011 (meta-analysis): flare relative risk 0.46 with proactive fluticasone and 0.78 with proactive tacrolimus versus vehicle across eight trials
cards.summary: Schmitt 2011 (meta-analysis): flare relative risk 0.46 with proactive fluticasone and 0.78 with proactive tacrolimus versus vehicle across eight trials
cards.people: Nine articles reporting eight vehicle-controlled randomised trials of proactive topical therapy for flare prevention in atopic eczema: three trials of tacrolimus, four of fluticasone propionate, one of methylprednisolone aceponate, applied intermittently to previously affected skin.
cards.result: Each agent prevented flares better than vehicle. Pooled relative risks of experiencing at least one flare were 0.46 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.55) for topical fluticasone propionate and 0.78 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.00) for topical tacrolimus — that is, a 54% and a 22% relative reduction in flare risk respectively. Meta-regression indicated the findings were robust, and proactive therapy was generally well tolerated, though the included trials did not allow firm conclusions about long-term safety.
cards.watchOut: The fluticasone-versus-tacrolimus contrast is indirect (each against vehicle, in different trials and populations), and the tacrolimus confidence interval touches 1.00. Follow-up was months, not the years over which proactive therapy would actually be used.
cards.source: Schmitt J et al. cards.headline: Paller 2008: three-times-weekly tacrolimus on previously affected skin gave significantly more disease-free days and longer time to first relapse than vehicle in stabilised children
cards.summary: Paller 2008: three-times-weekly tacrolimus on previously affected skin gave significantly more disease-free days and longer time to first relapse than vehicle in stabilised children
cards.people: Children aged 2–15 years with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; 105 whose disease stabilised during an initial treatment phase were randomised to tacrolimus ointment 0.03% (n=68) or vehicle (n=37) applied once daily, three times weekly, to clinically normal but previously affected skin for up to 40 weeks, with corticosteroids prohibited.
cards.result: Tacrolimus-treated patients had significantly more disease-free days, a significantly longer time to first relapse, and significantly fewer disease relapse days than vehicle-treated patients. Adverse events did not differ between tacrolimus and vehicle in this phase (nor between the initial-phase treatments). The abstract reports these outcomes as significant without giving their numerical values.
cards.watchOut: A stabilised, responder-selected population — the result applies to maintenance after control is achieved, not to inducing control. Significance without numbers in the record limits how precisely the benefit can be sized from this card.
cards.source: Paller AS et al. Three times weekly tacrolimus ointment reduces relapse in stabilized atopic dermatitis: a new paradigm for use. Pediatrics. 2008. PMID: 19015204. shelves.title: Emollients for eczema: fewer flares (relative risk 0.40) and a sixfold longer time to flare (median 180 versus 30 days), but the average severity gain (-2.42 SCORAD points) is far below the 8.7 points patients would notice — low-quality evidence throughout
shelves.question: In people with atopic eczema, do standard emollients and moisturisers improve severity and reduce flares compared with no moisturiser or vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Eczema/drug therapy · Emollients/chemistry/therapeutic use · Humans · Patient Satisfaction · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Severity of Illness Index · Symptom Flare Up
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — moisturisers probably help eczema a little, and the Cochrane review is honest about how little certainty there is. Across 77 studies with 6,603 participants (van Zuuren EJ et al., PMID: 28166390), the six studies comparing moisturiser with no moisturiser found lower SCORAD scores (mean difference -2.42, 95% CI -4.55 to -0.28, in three studies) — well short of the 8.7-point minimal important difference — alongside fewer flares (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.70, in two studies), a prolonged time to flare (median 180 versus 30 days), and less topical corticosteroid needed (mean difference -9.30 g). Evidence for these no-treatment comparisons was low quality; most individual moisturisers beat their vehicles on some measures, and the reviewers found no reliable evidence that one moisturiser is better than another. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): emollients are a reasonable, low-harm foundation of eczema care with a small average effect — flare prevention and steroid-sparing are their best-supported benefits, not severity transformation.

cards.headline: van Zuuren 2017 (Cochrane): moisturiser versus none — SCORAD mean difference -2.42, flare relative risk 0.40, time to flare 180 versus 30 days, corticosteroid use -9.30 g; low-quality evidence
cards.summary: van Zuuren 2017 (Cochrane): moisturiser versus none — SCORAD mean difference -2.42, flare relative risk 0.40, time to flare 180 versus 30 days, corticosteroid use -9.30 g; low-quality evidence
cards.people: 77 randomised studies with 6,603 participants with eczema (mean age 18.6 years, mean study duration 6.7 weeks) comparing moisturisers with no moisturiser, vehicle, or other moisturisers; six studies made the moisturiser-versus-no-moisturiser comparison. Thirty-six studies were at high risk of bias, 34 unclear, seven low.
cards.result: Versus no moisturiser: lower SCORAD (three studies, 276 participants; mean difference -2.42, 95% CI -4.55 to -0.28), but the minimal important difference of 8.7 was unmet; fewer flares (two studies, 87 participants; relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.70); prolonged time to flare (median 180 versus 30 days); and less topical corticosteroid used (two studies, 222 participants; mean difference -9.30 g, 95% CI -15.3 to -3.27). Adverse events did not differ significantly in the one reporting study. Across all comparisons, participants rated moisturisers more effective than control for eczema (relative risk 2.46) and itch, with fewer flares (relative risk 0.33) and no difference in adverse events (relative risk 1.03). The reviewers found no reliable evidence that one moisturiser is better than another.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison (versus no moisturiser) rests on a handful of small, low-quality studies — two studies and 87 participants for the flare result — and most of the 77 studies compared one branded moisturiser against its vehicle rather than testing whether moisturising itself works. Tier C: a single review with low-certainty key comparisons carries this shelf.
cards.source: van Zuuren EJ et al. Emollients and moisturisers for eczema. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28166390. shelves.title: Wet-wrap therapy for atopic dermatitis: the meta-analysis of six small trials (19–51 patients each) could not show it beats topical steroids alone — low-quality evidence, with an imprecise infection signal (relative risk 6.35, 95% CI 0.83 to 48.55)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis in children, does wet-wrap therapy added to topical treatment improve severity compared with topical treatment alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Bandages/adverse effects · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Humans · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Skin Diseases, Infectious/etiology · Steroids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — wet wraps are widely used as a crisis intervention for severe eczema, but the randomised evidence that they add anything to topical steroids is thin. The systematic review and meta-analysis (González-López G et al., PMID: 27861727) found six trials of 19 to 51 patients each; severity and quality-of-life results were reported incompletely and were too heterogeneous to pool, the overall quality of evidence was low, and there was a non-significant tendency to more mild skin infections with wet wraps (pooled relative risk 6.35, 95% CI 0.83 to 48.55). The best single trial (Janmohamed SR et al., PMID: 24698702) compared wet wraps with diluted corticosteroid against wet wraps with emollient in children with severe eczema and found the steroid version acted faster and was more efficacious on objective SCORAD at every measuring point — which shows the steroid under the wrap matters, not that the wrap itself adds benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): wet-wrap therapy remains a plausible short-term rescue on weak evidence; its added value over the topical treatment it delivers is unproven.

cards.headline: González-López 2017 (meta-analysis): six trials of 19–51 patients; results too heterogeneous to pool, evidence low quality; mild skin infections relative risk 6.35 (0.83 to 48.55), non-significant
cards.summary: González-López 2017 (meta-analysis): six trials of 19–51 patients; results too heterogeneous to pool, evidence low quality; mild skin infections relative risk 6.35 (0.83 to 48.55), non-significant
cards.people: Six randomised trials comparing wet-wrap therapy (topical steroids under wet bandages or garments) with topical steroids alone, in children or adults with atopic dermatitis; sample sizes ranged from 19 to 51 patients.
cards.result: Clinical severity and quality-of-life results were reported incompletely and proved heterogeneous across studies, so no pooled efficacy estimate was possible. A non-significant tendency to increased risk of mild skin infections was observed with wet wraps (pooled relative risk 6.35, 95% confidence interval 0.83 to 48.55). The overall grade of quality of evidence for efficacy and safety outcomes was low, and the reviewers concluded the evidence that wet wraps are more effective than conventional topical steroid treatment is of low quality.
cards.watchOut: The infection relative risk of 6.35 sounds alarming but its confidence interval runs from 0.83 to 48.55 — it is a handful of mild infections in tiny trials, a signal to watch rather than a measured harm. Equally, 'low quality' cuts both ways: benefit is unproven, not disproven.
cards.source: González-López G et al. Efficacy and safety of wet wrap therapy for patients with atopic dermatitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The British journal of dermatology. 2017. cards.headline: Janmohamed 2014: wet wraps with diluted corticosteroid acted faster and beat emollient wet wraps on objective SCORAD at every time point in children with severe eczema
cards.summary: Janmohamed 2014: wet wraps with diluted corticosteroid acted faster and beat emollient wet wraps on objective SCORAD at every time point in children with severe eczema
cards.people: Children aged 6 months to 10 years with severe atopic dermatitis (objective SCORAD at least 40 ± 5), randomised double-blind to proactive wet-wrap treatment with diluted corticosteroid (mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment diluted 1:3, and 1:19 for the face) or with emollient (petrolatum 20% in cetomacrogol cream) over 4 weeks with tapering frequency.
cards.result: Wet wraps with diluted corticosteroids acted faster and were more efficacious than wet wraps with emollients; the difference in objective SCORAD was significant at all measuring points, as was the difference in quality-of-life index. The best results were in the 6-to-9-year and 0-to-3-year age groups. The abstract reports significance without the SCORAD values or the study's sample size.
cards.watchOut: Both arms wore wet wraps — this trial compares what goes under the wrap, not wrap versus no wrap, so it cannot carry a claim for wet wrapping itself. The authors themselves note the study group was relatively small.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a standard rescue treatment resting on six tiny trials and one trial that answers a different question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a standard rescue treatment resting on six tiny trials and one trial that answers a different question
cards.people: Systematic review of six randomised trials (19–51 patients each) plus one double-blind trial of diluted-steroid versus emollient wet wraps in children with severe eczema.
cards.result: Added benefit of the wrap itself over topical steroids: unproven, low-quality evidence. Mild skin infection signal: relative risk 6.35 (0.83 to 48.55), non-significant. Diluted steroid under the wrap beats emollient under the wrap on SCORAD at all points over 4 weeks. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit). Tier C: the shelf rests on small, low-quality trials.
cards.watchOut: Clinical enthusiasm for wet wraps far outruns this evidence base; a properly powered trial of wrap versus the same topical regimen unwrapped is the missing study.
cards.source: Synthesis of González-López G et al. The British journal of dermatology. 2017 (PMID: 27861727); Janmohamed SR et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2014 (PMID: 24698702).

shelves.title: Alitretinoin for severe chronic hand eczema: clear or almost-clear hands in up to 48% versus 17% on placebo in the 1,032-patient BACH trial — dose-dependent headache, lipid and thyroid effects, and relapse a median 5.5–6.2 months after stopping
shelves.question: In severe chronic hand eczema that topical steroids cannot control, does oral alitretinoin clear the hands compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Alitretinoin · Chronic Disease · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Routes · Eczema/drug therapy · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Hand Dermatoses/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Tretinoin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral alitretinoin cleared severe, steroid-refractory chronic hand eczema in the large BACH trial (Ruzicka T et al., PMID: 18294310): responses (clear or almost-clear hands on the Physician Global Assessment) reached up to 48% on alitretinoin versus 17% on placebo (P<0.001), with up to a 75% median reduction in disease signs and symptoms. Benefit came with the retinoid price list — dose-dependent headache, mucocutaneous events, hyperlipidaemia, and decreased free thyroxine and thyroid-stimulating hormone — and it did not last: median time to relapse after stopping was 5.5–6.2 months. For patients who did not fully respond, an extended further course (Lynde C et al., PMID: 22731739) produced response rates of 39% to 51% depending on prior treatment, with no late-arising toxicities over up to 48 weeks of total exposure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alitretinoin is an effective oral option for severe hand eczema that topicals cannot control — Tier C because one pivotal trial carries it, and a maintenance commitment rather than a cure.

cards.headline: Ruzicka 2008 (BACH): response in up to 48% on alitretinoin versus 17% on placebo (P<.001) in 1,032 patients with severe refractory chronic hand eczema
cards.summary: Ruzicka 2008 (BACH): response in up to 48% on alitretinoin versus 17% on placebo (P<.001) in 1,032 patients with severe refractory chronic hand eczema
cards.people: 1,032 patients with severe chronic hand eczema refractory to topical corticosteroids, at 111 dermatology clinics in Europe and Canada, randomised 1:2:2 to placebo, alitretinoin 10 mg, or alitretinoin 30 mg once daily for up to 24 weeks, with responders observed for relapse for 24 weeks after treatment.
cards.result: Responses, defined as clear or almost-clear hands on the Physician Global Assessment, were achieved in up to 48% of alitretinoin-treated patients compared with 17% on placebo (P<0.001), with up to a 75% median reduction in disease signs and symptoms. Treatment was well tolerated overall, with dose-dependent adverse effects comprising headache, mucocutaneous events, hyperlipidaemia, and decreased free thyroxine and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Median time to relapse (recurrence of 75% of initial signs and symptoms) was 5.5–6.2 months without anti-eczema medication.
cards.watchOut: One pivotal trial, however large; 'up to 48%' is the 30 mg arm's figure, and the dose that works best carries the most adverse effects. Like all retinoids, alitretinoin is teratogenic — a constraint the abstract does not discuss but which governs its real-world use in women of childbearing age.
cards.source: Ruzicka T et al. Efficacy and safety of oral alitretinoin (9-cis retinoic acid) in patients with severe chronic hand eczema refractory to topical corticosteroids: results of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. The British journal of dermatology. 2008. PMID: 18294310. cards.headline: Lynde 2012 (extended treatment): a further course of alitretinoin 30 mg produced responses in 39–51% of BACH non-full-responders, with no late toxicities up to 48 weeks
cards.summary: Lynde 2012 (extended treatment): a further course of alitretinoin 30 mg produced responses in 39–51% of BACH non-full-responders, with no late toxicities up to 48 weeks
cards.people: 243 patients whose hand eczema was rated mild, moderate or severe at the end of BACH (i.e. not fully responded), treated open-label with alitretinoin 30 mg once daily for a further 12–24 weeks, irrespective of whether they had received alitretinoin 30 mg, 10 mg or placebo in BACH.
cards.result: By the end of the follow-on study, Physician's Global Assessment response rates to the further 30 mg course were 50% in patients previously on 10 mg, 39% in patients previously on 30 mg, and 51% in patients previously on placebo. Alitretinoin was well tolerated, with no significant late-arising toxicities, for overall treatment durations of up to 48 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled in a selected non-responder population — the response rates show a second course can still work, but without a comparator they cannot separate drug effect from time and natural fluctuation.
cards.source: Lynde C et al. Extended treatment with oral alitretinoin for patients with chronic hand eczema not fully responding to initial treatment. Clinical and experimental dermatology. 2012. PMID: 22731739. cards.headline: Synthesis: the only oral with a large positive trial in this disease — effective, retinoid-priced, and temporary
cards.summary: Synthesis: the only oral with a large positive trial in this disease — effective, retinoid-priced, and temporary
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial of 1,032 patients (BACH, up to 24 weeks) plus an open-label extended-treatment study of 243 non-full-responders.

shelves.title: Adalimumab versus methotrexate in children with severe plaque psoriasis: PASI-75 in 58% versus 32% at week 16 — but clear or minimal disease (61% versus 41%) was not significant, in the only head-to-head trial (114 children)
shelves.question: In children with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, is adalimumab more effective than methotrexate for skin clearance, and how do their safety profiles compare?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Chronic Disease · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Psoriasis/drug therapy/pathology · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg beat methotrexate on the first of two ranked primary endpoints in the only head-to-head trial in children with severe plaque psoriasis (Papp K et al., PMID: 28478975): PASI-75 at week 16 was achieved by 22 (58%) of 38 on adalimumab versus 12 (32%) of 37 on methotrexate (p=0.027), while the second endpoint, clear or minimal Physician Global Assessment, favoured adalimumab without reaching significance (61% versus 41%; p=0.083). Infections were the commonest adverse events in all groups (45% on adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg, 57% on methotrexate during initial treatment), and no new safety risks emerged. The 52-week extension (Thaçi D et al., PMID: 31017657) found efficacy maintained or improved with continued adalimumab — including in children switched from methotrexate, whose PASI-75 rates rose from 31% to 86% across the reported range — with no serious infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adalimumab clears more children's skin than methotrexate at 16 weeks, on one small trial whose second primary endpoint did not confirm the first. Tier C for that single-trial base.

cards.headline: Papp 2017: PASI-75 in 58% on adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg versus 32% on methotrexate (p=0.027); clear or minimal PGA 61% versus 41% (p=0.083); infections commonest in all groups
cards.summary: Papp 2017: PASI-75 in 58% on adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg versus 32% on methotrexate (p=0.027); clear or minimal PGA 61% versus 41% (p=0.083); infections commonest in all groups
cards.people: 114 patients aged 4 to under 18 years with severe plaque psoriasis not responding to topical therapy, at 38 clinics in 13 countries, randomised 1:1:1 to adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg (n=38) or 0.4 mg/kg (n=39) subcutaneously every other week, or oral methotrexate 0.1–0.4 mg/kg once weekly (n=37), for 16 weeks, followed by withdrawal and retreatment periods.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI-75 was achieved by 22 (58%) of 38 in the adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg group versus 12 (32%) of 37 in the methotrexate group (p=0.027); clear or minimal PGA by 23 (61%) of 38 versus 15 (41%) of 37 (p=0.083). In the adalimumab 0.4 mg/kg group, 17 (44%) of 39 achieved PASI-75 and 16 (41%) achieved clear or minimal PGA. The most frequent adverse events were infections: 17 (45%) of 38 in the 0.8 mg/kg group, 22 (56%) of 39 in the 0.4 mg/kg group, and 21 (57%) of 37 in the methotrexate group during initial treatment. Three serious adverse events, all in the 0.4 mg/kg group, were judged unrelated to study drug.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (37–39 per arm) in which the two ranked primary endpoints split — one significant, one not — and methotrexate dosing (0.1–0.4 mg/kg weekly, 16 weeks) may not reflect optimised, longer methotrexate use; methotrexate's slower onset is a known feature the 16-week horizon penalises.
cards.source: Papp K et al. Efficacy and safety of adalimumab every other week versus methotrexate once weekly in children and adolescents with severe chronic plaque psoriasis: a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28478975. Registry ID: NCT01251614. cards.headline: Thaçi 2019 (52-week extension): PASI-75 maintained or improved on continued adalimumab — 31–86% in children switched from methotrexate; no serious infections
cards.summary: Thaçi 2019 (52-week extension): PASI-75 maintained or improved on continued adalimumab — 31–86% in children switched from methotrexate; no serious infections
cards.type: Long-term extension of a randomised phase 3 trial (Thaçi 2019)
cards.people: 108 of the 114 randomised children entered the 52-week long-term extension, receiving adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg or 0.4 mg/kg (blinded or open-label) or remaining off treatment, analysed by initial-treatment and extension dose combinations; 93 received adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg.
cards.result: PASI-75 was maintained or improved from extension entry to its end: 31–86% of patients in the methotrexate(initial)/adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg(extension) group across the reported time points, 28–47% in the adalimumab 0.4 mg/kg groups, and 50–72% in the adalimumab 0.8/0.8 mg/kg group. No serious infections occurred in the extension, and no new safety risks were identified over 52 weeks of long-term adalimumab treatment.
cards.watchOut: An extension population of trial completers with multiple dose pathways and ranges rather than single clean percentages — it supports durability and switchability, not the size of adalimumab's advantage over methotrexate.
cards.source: Thaçi D et al. Sustained long-term efficacy and safety of adalimumab in paediatric patients with severe chronic plaque psoriasis from a randomized, double-blind, phase III study. The British journal of dermatology. 2019. PMID: 31017657. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial says adalimumab clears faster and more; the extension says the gains hold and transfers
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial says adalimumab clears faster and more; the extension says the gains hold and transfers
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (114 children, 16 weeks) plus its 52-week extension (108 children) comparing adalimumab with methotrexate in severe paediatric plaque psoriasis.
cards.result: Week 16: PASI-75 58% versus 32% (p=0.027); clear/minimal PGA 61% versus 41% (p=0.083). Infections: 45% (adalimumab 0.8) versus 57% (methotrexate). Extension: efficacy maintained or improved, including after switching from methotrexate; no serious infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: single-trial benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: With 114 children, this evidence cannot resolve rarer harms of either drug in children, nor compare adalimumab with the newer biologics now used in paediatric psoriasis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Papp K et al. Lancet (London, England). 2017 (PMID: 28478975); Thaçi D et al. The British journal of dermatology. 2019 (PMID: 31017657).

shelves.title: Home versus hospital UVB phototherapy for psoriasis (PLUTO): equally effective (SAPASI-50 in 82% versus 79%) and equally safe, with lower treatment burden and no higher costs (€800 versus €752 at end of therapy)
shelves.question: In plaque psoriasis needing ultraviolet B phototherapy, is home phototherapy as effective as outpatient phototherapy — and is it as safe?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Female · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Psoriasis/radiotherapy · Treatment Outcome · Ultraviolet Therapy/methods · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — where the treatment is delivered made no difference to what it achieved in the pragmatic PLUTO trial (Koek MB et al., PMID: 19423623): SAPASI-50 was reached by 82% of home-treated versus 79% of outpatient-treated patients (difference 2.8%, 95% CI -8.6 to 14.2), PASI-50 by 70% versus 73%, cumulative ultraviolet doses and short-term side effects were similar, and quality of life improved equally — while treatment burden was significantly lower at home and 42% of home patients rated the experience 'excellent' versus 23% of outpatients. The economic evaluation of the same trial (Koek MB et al., PMID: 20406865) found total costs of €800 for home versus €752 for outpatient treatment at end of therapy (difference €48, 95% CI -77 to 174) and near-identical QALY gains (0.296 versus 0.291). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): home UVB is as effective and safe as outpatient UVB for eligible patients, with less burden and no cost penalty — on one Dutch trial, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Koek 2009 (PLUTO): SAPASI-50 in 82% at home versus 79% outpatient (difference 2.8%, -8.6 to 14.2); PASI-50 70% versus 73%; side effects and cumulative dose similar; burden lower at home
cards.summary: Koek 2009 (PLUTO): SAPASI-50 in 82% at home versus 79% outpatient (difference 2.8%, -8.6 to 14.2); PASI-50 70% versus 73%; side effects and cumulative dose similar; burden lower at home
cards.people: 196 patients with mild-to-severe psoriasis clinically eligible for narrowband (TL-01) ultraviolet B phototherapy, at 14 Dutch hospitals, randomised to home phototherapy with a TL-01 unit or standard outpatient phototherapy, in routine-practice conditions; the first 105 were also followed for a year after therapy.
cards.result: SAPASI-50 was reached by 82% of home patients versus 79% of outpatients (difference 2.8%, 95% CI -8.6% to 14.2%) and PASI-50 by 70% versus 73% (-2.3%, -15.7 to 11.1%). Median SAPASI fell 82% at home (6.7 to 1.2) and 79% outpatient (7.0 to 1.4); median PASI fell 74% (8.4 to 2.2) and 70% (7.0 to 2.1). Total cumulative ultraviolet B doses were similar (51.5 versus 46.1 J/cm²), short-term side effects did not differ, and quality of life increased equally. Burden of treatment was significantly lower at home (all P≤0.001), and 42% (38/90) of home patients rated their experience 'excellent' versus 23% (20/88) of outpatients (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single-blind and single-country: patients knew their allocation (satisfaction and burden scores are vulnerable to that), home units and supervision were Dutch-practice standard, and long-term photocarcinogenesis cannot be assessed in a trial of this size and length. Tier C: one trial carries the equivalence claim.

cards.headline: Koek 2010 (PLUTO economic evaluation): total costs €800 home versus €752 outpatient at end of therapy; QALY gains 0.296 versus 0.291 — home treatment not more expensive
cards.summary: Koek 2010 (PLUTO economic evaluation): total costs €800 home versus €752 outpatient at end of therapy; QALY gains 0.296 versus 0.291 — home treatment not more expensive
cards.type: Economic evaluation alongside a randomised trial (Koek 2010)
cards.people: The 196 PLUTO participants, with costs, QALYs (EQ-5D) and days with a relevant treatment effect measured at end of phototherapy (mean 17.6 weeks) and, in 105 patients, one year after (mean 68.4 weeks), from a societal perspective in the Netherlands.
cards.result: Average total costs by end of phototherapy were €800 for home and €752 for outpatient treatment (incremental €48 per patient, 95% CI -77 to 174); by one year after therapy they were €1,272 and €1,148 (difference €124, -155 to 403). QALY gains were 0.296 versus 0.291 at end of therapy (difference 0.0052) and 1.153 versus 1.126 at one year (difference 0.0267); incremental costs per QALY were €9,276 and €4,646, both well below the €20,000 standard the authors cite. Days with a relevant treatment effect at one year were 216.5 versus 210.4.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, second publication — this is the cost side of PLUTO, not independent confirmation of its clinical result; Dutch 2009-era prices and reimbursement arrangements limit transfer to other systems.
cards.source: Koek MB et al. Cost effectiveness of home ultraviolet B phototherapy for psoriasis: economic evaluation of a randomised controlled trial (PLUTO study). shelves.title: Imiquimod versus surgery for low-risk basal cell carcinoma (SINS): success 84% versus 98% at 3 years and 82.5% versus 97.7% at 5 years — the cream works for most, but it is not a substitute for excision
shelves.question: For nodular and superficial basal cell carcinoma, is imiquimod 5% cream an acceptable substitute for surgical excision on tumour clearance at three and five years?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aminoquinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Basal Cell Carcinoma/drug therapy/surgery · Female · Humans · Imiquimod · Male · Middle Aged · Ointments · Skin Neoplasms/drug therapy/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT — imiquimod clears most low-risk basal cell carcinomas but is clearly inferior to surgery, so 'substitute' depends on what the patient is trading. In the SINS trial (Bath-Hextall F et al., PMID: 24332516), clinical success at 3 years was 178 (84%) of 213 on imiquimod versus 185 (98%) of 188 on surgical excision (relative risk 0.84, 98% CI 0.78 to 0.91), failing the prespecified non-inferiority margin. At 5 years (Williams HC et al., PMID: 27932240) success was 82.5% (170/206) versus 97.7% (173/177), with most imiquimod failures occurring in year 1 — lesions that respond early tend to stay clear. The Cochrane review of BCC interventions (Thomson J et al., PMID: 33202063) expresses the same gap as recurrence: 16.4% after imiquimod versus 1.6% after excision at 3 years (relative risk 10.30), while noting cosmetic outcomes can favour non-surgical treatment. Itching (211 versus 129 patients) and weeping (160 versus 81) were commoner with the cream. PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery remains the standard; imiquimod is a legitimate, knowingly less effective option for small low-risk lesions when surgery is declined, impractical, or cosmetically costly.

cards.headline: Bath-Hextall 2014 (SINS, 3 years): success 84% (178/213) on imiquimod versus 98% (185/188) on surgery — relative risk 0.84, non-inferiority not met
cards.summary: Bath-Hextall 2014 (SINS, 3 years): success 84% (178/213) on imiquimod versus 98% (185/188) on surgery — relative risk 0.84, non-inferiority not met
cards.people: 501 participants with histologically confirmed primary nodular or superficial basal-cell carcinoma at low-risk sites, at 12 UK centres, randomised to imiquimod 5% cream once daily (6 weeks for superficial, 12 weeks for nodular; n=254) or surgical excision with a 4 mm margin (n=247); 401 (80%) contributed to the 3-year modified intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: At 3 years, clinical success (no initial treatment failure or recurrence) was 178 (84%) of 213 on imiquimod versus 185 (98%) of 188 on surgery (relative risk 0.84, 98% CI 0.78 to 0.91; p<0.0001), against a prespecified non-inferiority margin of relative risk 0.87 — imiquimod was inferior by the trial's criterion. Patient-assessed cosmetic outcomes did not clearly differ. The commonest adverse events were itching (211 imiquimod versus 129 surgery patients) and weeping (160 versus 81); serious adverse events occurred in 99 (40%) versus 97 (42%), none judged treatment-related; 12 (5%) on imiquimod and 4 (2%) on surgery withdrew because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Low-risk sites and subtypes only — morphoeic, recurrent and Gorlin-syndrome patients were excluded, so the 84% figure flatters imiquimod relative to unselected practice. Participants could not be masked, and 20% of randomised patients did not contribute to the primary analysis.
cards.source: Bath-Hextall F et al. Surgical excision versus imiquimod 5% cream for nodular and superficial basal-cell carcinoma (SINS): a multicentre, non-inferiority, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2014. PMID: 24332516. Registry ID: NCT00066872 and ISRCTN48755084. cards.headline: Williams 2017 (SINS, 5 years): success 82.5% (170/206) on imiquimod versus 97.7% (173/177) on surgery — most imiquimod failures occurred in year 1
cards.summary: Williams 2017 (SINS, 5 years): success 82.5% (170/206) on imiquimod versus 97.7% (173/177) on surgery — most imiquimod failures occurred in year 1
cards.type: Five-year follow-up of a randomised trial (Williams 2017, SINS)
cards.people: The 501 SINS participants; 383 (96% of the 401 in the 3-year analysis) had 5-year data from dermatology review plus hospital, histopathology and general-practice records.
cards.result: Five-year success was 82.5% (170/206) for imiquimod versus 97.7% (173/177) for surgery (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.91; P<0.001), comparable to the 3-year rates of 83.6% (178/213) and 98.4% (185/188). Most imiquimod treatment failures occurred in year 1, so lesions responding early to the cream generally sustained their response.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, later report — durability data, not independent confirmation. Record-based recurrence ascertainment at 5 years can miss lesions treated outside the captured systems.
cards.source: Williams HC et al. Surgery Versus 5% Imiquimod for Nodular and Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma: 5-Year Results of the SINS Randomized Controlled Trial. The Journal of investigative dermatology. 2017. PMID: 27932240. Registry ID: NCT00066872 and ISRCTN48755084. cards.headline: Thomson 2020 (Cochrane): recurrence after imiquimod 16.4% versus 1.6% after excision at 3 years (relative risk 10.30); surgical treatments have the lowest recurrence rates overall
cards.summary: Thomson 2020 (Cochrane): recurrence after imiquimod 16.4% versus 1.6% after excision at 3 years (relative risk 10.30); surgical treatments have the lowest recurrence rates overall
cards.people: 52 randomised trials with 6,690 immunocompetent adults with histologically proven primary basal-cell carcinoma, comparing surgery, Mohs surgery, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, radiotherapy, cryotherapy and other interventions; most studies covered low-risk superficial and nodular subtypes.
cards.result: For imiquimod versus surgical excision in low-risk nodular or superficial BCC, imiquimod probably results in more recurrences at 3 years (16.4% versus 1.6%; relative risk 10.30, 95% CI 3.22 to 32.94; 1 study, 401 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and at 5 years (17.5% versus 2.3%; relative risk 7.73, 2.81 to 21.3; 383 participants). Observer-rated good or excellent cosmetic outcomes at 3 years favoured imiquimod (60.6% versus 35.6%; relative risk 1.70, 1.35 to 2.15; low-certainty evidence), while participant-rated cosmesis did not differ. Overall, surgical interventions had the lowest recurrence rates.
cards.watchOut: The imiquimod-versus-surgery numbers in this review are the SINS trial restated — the review's added value is the wider context (all other modalities also trail surgery on recurrence), not a second estimate of the same comparison.
cards.source: Thomson J et al. Interventions for basal cell carcinoma of the skin. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 33202063. shelves.title: Mohs surgery versus standard excision for facial basal cell carcinoma: no proven gain for primary tumours (10-year recurrence 4.4% versus 12.2%, p=0.10), a clear gain for recurrent ones (3.9% versus 13.5%, p=0.023) — at higher cost
shelves.question: For primary basal cell carcinoma of the face, does Mohs micrographic surgery reduce recurrence compared with standard surgical excision — for primary and for recurrent tumours?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Basal Cell Carcinoma/economics/surgery · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Facial Neoplasms/economics/surgery · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Care Costs · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mohs Surgery/economics · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/economics/surgery · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Skin Neoplasms/economics/surgery · Surgical Procedures, Operative/economics/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — Mohs micrographic surgery earns its extra cost and complexity for recurrent facial basal cell carcinoma, not demonstrably for primary tumours. In the Dutch randomised trial's 5-year report (Mosterd K et al., PMID: 19010733), recurrences among primary tumours were 4 (2.5%) after Mohs versus 7 (4.1%) after excision (p=0.397), while among recurrent tumours they were 2 (2.4%) after Mohs versus 10 (12.1%) after excision (p=0.015). At 10 years (van Loo E et al., PMID: 25262378) cumulative recurrence probabilities were 4.4% after Mohs versus 12.2% after excision for primary tumours (p=0.100) and 3.9% versus 13.5% for recurrent tumours (p=0.023) — the primary-tumour gap widened numerically without reaching significance. Treatment costs were higher for Mohs (€1,248 versus €990 for primary; €1,284 versus €1,043 for recurrent tumours), giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €23,454 for primary but €3,171 for recurrent disease. PROPOSED SPLIT: reserve Mohs for recurrent facial BCC (and judge primary cases on site and histology), because the trial proves a recurrence benefit only there. Tier C: a single trial, with substantial loss to follow-up.

cards.headline: Mosterd 2008 (5-year report): primary BCC recurrence 2.5% Mohs versus 4.1% excision (p=0.397); recurrent BCC 2.4% versus 12.1% (p=0.015); Mohs cost €1,248 versus €990 (primary) and €1,284 versus €1,043 (recurrent)
cards.summary: Mosterd 2008 (5-year report): primary BCC recurrence 2.5% Mohs versus 4.1% excision (p=0.397); recurrent BCC 2.4% versus 12.1% (p=0.015); Mohs cost €1,248 versus €990 (primary) and €1,284 versus €1,043 (recurrent)
cards.people: 408 primary and 204 recurrent facial basal-cell carcinomas, randomised separately to surgical excision or Mohs micrographic surgery at seven Dutch hospitals between 1999 and 2002, with 5 years of follow-up; 397 primary and 202 recurrent tumours were treated and analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Of 11 recurrences in primary BCC, seven (4.1%) followed excision and four (2.5%) followed Mohs (log-rank p=0.397). Of recurrences in recurrent BCC, ten (12.1%) followed excision and two (2.4%) followed Mohs (log-rank p=0.015). Total treatment costs were €1,248 for Mohs versus €990 for excision in primary BCC, and €1,284 versus €1,043 in recurrent BCC; incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were €23,454 (primary) and €3,171 (recurrent) per recurrence prevented. In recurrent BCC, aggressive histological subtype was a significant risk factor for recurrence.
cards.watchOut: Loss to follow-up was heavy — 127 of 397 treated primary tumours in 113 patients, and 56 of 202 recurrent tumours — so recurrence counts rest on incomplete observation, and the primary comparison was underpowered for the difference it eventually showed.
cards.source: Mosterd K et al. Surgical excision versus Mohs' micrographic surgery for primary and recurrent basal-cell carcinoma of the face: a prospective randomised controlled trial with 5-years' follow-up. The Lancet. randomised controlled trial (mosterd 2008) 408 primary and 204 recurrent facial basal-cell carcinomas, randomised separately to surgical excision or mohs micrographic surgery at seven dutch hospitals between 1999 and 2002, with 5 years of follow-up; 397 primary and 202 recurrent tumours were treated and analysed intention-to-treat. of 11 recurrences in primary bcc, seven (4.1%) followed excision and four (2.5%) followed mohs (log-rank p=0.397). of recurrences in recurrent bcc, ten (12.1%) followed excision and two (2.4%) followed mohs (log-rank p=0.015). total treatment costs were €1,248 for mohs versus €990 for excision in primary bcc, and €1,284 versus €1,043 in recurrent bcc; incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were €23,454 (primary) and €3,171 (recurrent) per recurrence prevented. in recurrent bcc, aggressive histological subtype was a significant risk factor for recurrence. loss to follow-up was heavy — 127 of 397 treated primary tumours in 113 patients, and 56 of 202 recurrent tumours — so recurrence counts rest on incomplete observation, and the primary comparison was underpowered for the difference it eventually showed. mosterd k et al. surgical excision versus mohs' micrographic surgery for primary and recurrent basal-cell carcinoma of the face: a prospective randomised controlled trial with 5-years' follow-up. the lancet. oncology. 2008. pmid: 19010733. registry id: isrctn65009900. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · basal cell carcinoma/economics/surgery · cost-benefit analysis · facial neoplasms/economics/surgery · female · follow-up studies · health care costs · humans · kaplan-meier estimate · male · middle aged · mohs surgery/economics · neoplasm recurrence, local/economics/surgery · proportional hazards models · prospective studies · skin neoplasms/economics/surgery · surgical procedures, operative/economics/methods · treatment outcome

cards.people: The same randomised cohort: 408 high-risk facial primary BCCs (diameter at least 1 cm, H-zone location, or aggressive histological subtype) and 204 facial recurrent BCCs allocated to excision or Mohs surgery, analysed by modified intention to treat at 10 years.
cards.result: Ten-year cumulative recurrence probabilities for primary BCC were 4.4% after Mohs and 12.2% after excision (log-rank p=0.100); for recurrent BCC, 3.9% after Mohs and 13.5% after excision (log-rank p=0.023). cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, two answers — Mohs is for the tumour that has already come back
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, two answers — Mohs is for the tumour that has already come back
cards.people: One randomised trial (612 facial basal-cell carcinomas) reported at 5 and 10 years, comparing Mohs micrographic surgery with standard surgical excision.
cards.result: Recurrent BCC: recurrence 2.4% versus 12.1% at 5 years (p=0.015); 3.9% versus 13.5% at 10 years (p=0.023). Primary BCC: 2.5% versus 4.1% (p=0.397); 4.4% versus 12.2% (p=0.100). Costs higher for Mohs in both strata. PROPOSED SPLIT. Tier C: single trial.

shelves.title: One course of fluorouracil 5% cream to prevent skin cancer in high-risk veterans: squamous cell carcinoma surgery cut from 4% to 1% in year 1 only — no effect on basal cell carcinoma and no overall benefit across the full trial
shelves.question: In veterans at high risk of keratinocyte carcinoma, does a single course of topical fluorouracil 5% cream prevent new squamous and basal cell carcinomas?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Basal Cell Carcinoma/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control/surgery · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control/surgery · Chemoprevention/methods · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mohs Surgery/methods/statistics & numerical data · Prognosis · Risk Assessment · Skin Cream/therapeutic use · Skin Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control/surgery · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — one short course of fluorouracil 5% cream bought exactly one year of protection against squamous cell carcinoma, and nothing else. In the Veterans Affairs trial (Weinstock MA et al., PMID: 29299592), 932 veterans with at least two prior keratinocyte carcinomas applied fluorouracil or vehicle to the face and ears twice daily for 2–4 weeks. In year 1, squamous cell carcinoma developed in 5 (1%) on fluorouracil versus 20 (4%) on control — a 75% relative reduction (95% CI 35% to 91%; P=.002) — while basal cell carcinoma was unaffected (45 [10%] versus 50 [11%], not significant). Over the whole study there was no difference in time to first keratinocyte, basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma. The economic analysis (Yoon J et al., PMID: 29505863) found the intervention arm's treatment and dermatology costs lower at 1 year ($2,106 versus $2,444) and $771 less per patient by 3 years. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but brief chemopreventive effect against squamous cell carcinoma in very-high-risk skin, with no basal-cell effect and no durable overall prevention. Tier C: a single trial carries the claim.

cards.headline: Weinstock 2018 (VAKCC): year-1 squamous cell carcinoma in 1% versus 4% (75% relative reduction, P=.002); basal cell carcinoma 10% versus 11%, not significant; no difference over the full study
cards.summary: Weinstock 2018 (VAKCC): year-1 squamous cell carcinoma in 1% versus 4% (75% relative reduction, P=.002); basal cell carcinoma 10% versus 11%, not significant; no difference over the full study
cards.people: 932 veterans (98% men, 99% white, median age 70 years) with a history of at least two keratinocyte carcinomas in the past 5 years, at 12 US Veterans Affairs centres, randomised to fluorouracil 5% cream (n=468) or vehicle (n=464) applied to face and ears twice daily for 2–4 weeks, followed for a median 2.8 years.
cards.result: Over the entire study there was no difference between groups in time to first keratinocyte, basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma: 299 participants developed a basal cell carcinoma endpoint and 108 a squamous cell carcinoma endpoint over 4 years. In the first year, however, 5 participants (1%) in the fluorouracil group developed a squamous cell carcinoma versus 20 (4%) in the control group — a 75% relative risk reduction (95% CI 35% to 91%; P=.002). The year-1 basal cell carcinoma reduction (45 [10%] versus 50 [11%]) was 11% relative and not statistically significant (95% CI 39% reduction to 31% increase). A reduction in keratinocyte carcinomas treated with Mohs surgery was also observed.
cards.watchOut: A single, almost entirely white male veteran population with exceptionally high baseline risk — the absolute year-1 squamous-cell gain (3 percentage points) will shrink in lower-risk skin. The headline effect is a first-year, secondary-timeframe finding; the trial's overall result across follow-up was null.
cards.source: Weinstock MA et al. Chemoprevention of Basal and Squamous Cell Carcinoma With a Single Course of Fluorouracil, 5%, Cream: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA dermatology. 2018. cards.summary: Yoon 2018 (VAKCC economic analysis): year-1 treatment and dermatology costs $2,106 on fluorouracil versus $2,444 on control; $771 less per patient by year 3
cards.type: Economic analysis of a randomised trial (Yoon 2018)
cards.people: The 932 VAKCC participants, with post-randomisation encounters and costs for keratinocyte carcinoma and actinic keratosis care measured from trial and Veterans Affairs administrative data over 3 years.
cards.result: At 1 year, the control arm had more squamous cell carcinoma treatment encounters (mean 0.04) than the intervention arm (0.01; P<.01), and the intervention arm had lower treatment and dermatologic costs: $2,106 (SD $2,079) versus $2,444 (SD $2,716; P=.02). After 3 years, the intervention arm had incurred $771 less cost per patient.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, second lens — cost savings inside one integrated payer (the VA), excluding care obtained outside it; they corroborate the year-1 squamous-cell effect rather than adding an independent result.
cards.source: Yoon J et al. Impact of topical fluorouracil cream on costs of treating keratinocyte carcinoma (nonmelanoma skin cancer) and actinic keratosis. cards.summary: Synthesis: chemoprevention with a one-year fuse — squamous yes, basal no, durable no, cheaper yes
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial (932 high-risk veterans) of a single 2–4-week course of fluorouracil 5% cream to face and ears, with its 3-year economic analysis.
