shelves.title: Low-dose minocycline (DFD-29, 40 mg) for papulopustular rosacea: IGA success beat placebo by 32.9 and 34.1 percentage points and doxycycline 40 mg by 18.0 and 28.3 points in two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In papulopustular rosacea, does once-daily low-dose minocycline (DFD-29) reduce inflammatory lesions better than doxycycline 40 mg and placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Rosacea/drug therapy/diagnosis · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Minocycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Adult · Doxycycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Severity of Illness Index · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DFD-29, a 40 mg low-dose modified-release minocycline formulation (the specific tested product in the MVOR trials), beat both placebo and the standard low-dose doxycycline 40 mg in two phase 3 trials (Bhatia N et al., PMID: 40042869). Investigator's Global Assessment success exceeded placebo by 32.9 percentage points in MVOR-1 and 34.1 points in MVOR-2, and exceeded doxycycline by 18.0 and 28.3 points (all significant). Inflammatory lesion reductions likewise favoured DFD-29 over placebo (least-squares mean differences -9.2 and -6.8 lesions) and over doxycycline (-4.7 and -3.5). Adverse events on DFD-29 were reported by 26.4% and 41.8% of participants, against 21.6% and 33.1% on doxycycline and 35.5% and 36.6% on placebo, with nasopharyngitis and COVID-19 the commonest events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the most effective oral agent yet tested head-to-head for papulopustular rosacea on these records — two industry trials of 16 weeks, with no data beyond that horizon and no comparison with topical standards.

cards.headline: Bhatia 2025 (MVOR-1 & MVOR-2): IGA success differences for DFD-29 of +32.9% and +34.1% versus placebo and +18.0% and +28.3% versus doxycycline; lesion reductions also superior on both comparisons
cards.summary: Bhatia 2025 (MVOR-1 & MVOR-2): IGA success differences for DFD-29 of +32.9% and +34.1% versus placebo and +18.0% and +28.3% versus doxycycline; lesion reductions also superior on both comparisons
cards.type: Two randomised phase 3 trials (Bhatia 2025, MVOR-1 and MVOR-2)
cards.people: 653 adults aged 18 years and older with moderate-to-severe papulopustular rosacea (323 in MVOR-1, 330 in MVOR-2; about three-quarters women; mean ages 47.2 and 51.6 years) at 61 centres in the US and Germany, randomised 3:3:2 to oral DFD-29 (minocycline hydrochloride) 40 mg, doxycycline 40 mg, or placebo once daily for 16 weeks.
cards.result: DFD-29 was superior to placebo on IGA success (treatment differences 32.9%, 95% CI 19.6 to 46.2, in MVOR-1 and 34.1%, 21.3 to 46.8, in MVOR-2; both P<.001) and superior to doxycycline (18.0%, 5.0 to 31.1; P=.01, and 28.3%, 17.4 to 39.3; P<.001). Least-squares mean inflammatory lesion reductions favoured DFD-29 over placebo (-9.2, -11.5 to -6.9; and -6.8, -8.9 to -4.8) and over doxycycline (-4.7, -6.7 to -2.8; and -3.5, -5.4 to -1.6; all P<.001). Adverse events: MVOR-1, 32 of 121 (26.4%) on DFD-29, 25 of 116 (21.6%) on doxycycline, 27 of 76 (35.5%) on placebo; MVOR-2, 51 of 122 (41.8%), 40 of 121 (33.1%) and 30 of 82 (36.6%). The commonest events were nasopharyngitis and COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports treatment differences without the absolute IGA success rates in each arm, so the differences cannot be re-based here. Sixteen weeks in moderate-to-severe disease, industry-run, and no comparison with metronidazole, ivermectin or azelaic acid topicals — the oral-versus-topical question stays open.
cards.source: Bhatia N et al. Efficacy, Safety, and Tolerability of Oral DFD-29, a Low-Dose Formulation of Minocycline, in Rosacea: Two Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA dermatology. 2025. PMID: 40042869. Registry ID: NCT05343455 and NCT05296629. shelves.title: Brimonidine 0.5% gel for rosacea redness: significantly more two-grade improvement than vehicle from 30 minutes to 12 hours on days 1, 15 and 29 in two pivotal trials (all P<.001) — a same-day effect, not a cure; the abstracts report no percentages
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe facial erythema of rosacea, does brimonidine tartrate gel 0.5% reduce redness on the day of application compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brimonidine Tartrate · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Facial Dermatoses/drug therapy/pathology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gels · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quinoxalines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Rosacea/drug therapy/pathology · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — brimonidine tartrate gel 0.5%, a vasoconstrictive alpha-2 agonist, reduces rosacea redness for the day it is applied. In the two pivotal randomised trials (Fowler J et al., PMID: 23839181), once-daily brimonidine was significantly more efficacious than vehicle throughout the 12 hours after application on days 1, 15 and 29, with a significant difference as early as 30 minutes after the first dose (all P<.001), and no tachyphylaxis, rebound or aggravation of other rosacea signs over 4 weeks. The earlier dose-finding programme (Fowler J et al., PMID: 22050040) showed a dose-dependent effect, with a single application of the 0.5% gel significantly reducing measured redness from 30 minutes to 12 hours, and the same two-grade success advantage on days 1, 15 and 29. Neither abstract reports the success percentages — a declared gap that caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a reliable same-day cosmetic pharmacology for persistent facial erythema — it treats the day, not the disease.

cards.headline: Fowler 2013 (two pivotal trials): brimonidine 0.5% gel significantly beat vehicle over 12 hours on days 1, 15 and 29, from 30 minutes after the first application (all P<.001); no tachyphylaxis or rebound
cards.summary: Fowler 2013 (two pivotal trials): brimonidine 0.5% gel significantly beat vehicle over 12 hours on days 1, 15 and 29, from 30 minutes after the first application (all P<.001); no tachyphylaxis or rebound
cards.people: Subjects with moderate-to-severe facial erythema of rosacea in two identically designed randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled studies, applying brimonidine tartrate gel 0.5% or vehicle once daily for 4 weeks, followed by a 4-week follow-up phase; erythema graded by Clinician's Erythema Assessment and Patient's Self-Assessment.
cards.result: Brimonidine gel 0.5% was significantly more efficacious than vehicle throughout the 12 hours after application on days 1, 15 and 29, with a significant difference as early as 30 minutes after the first application on day 1 (all P<.001). No tachyphylaxis, rebound or aggravation of other disease signs were observed. Adverse events were slightly more frequent on brimonidine than vehicle but were mostly dermatological, mild and transient. The abstract reports significance without the responder percentages or the trials' sample sizes.
cards.watchOut: P-value-only reporting in the pivotal record, and a 4-week horizon for a cosmetic endpoint: the trials prove the gel whitens skin for a day, repeatedly, but cannot speak to months of daily use, paradoxical erythema seen in later clinical experience, or any effect on rosacea progression.

cards.headline: Fowler 2012 (dose-finding studies A & B): a single 0.5% application cut measured redness from 30 minutes to 12 hours; two-grade success on both clinician and patient scales beat vehicle on days 1, 15 and 29 (all P<0.001)
cards.summary: Fowler 2012 (dose-finding studies A & B): a single 0.5% application cut measured redness from 30 minutes to 12 hours; two-grade success on both clinician and patient scales beat vehicle on days 1, 15 and 29 (all P<0.001)
cards.people: Study A: 122 subjects randomised to a single application of brimonidine gel 0.07%, 0.18%, 0.5% or vehicle. Study B: 269 subjects randomised over 4 weeks to brimonidine 0.5% once daily, 0.18% once daily, vehicle once daily, 0.18% twice daily, or vehicle twice daily, with 4 weeks of follow-up; redness measured by Clinician's Erythema Assessment, Patient's Self-Assessment and Chroma Meter.
cards.result: In study A, a single application reduced facial erythema dose-dependently; the difference between brimonidine 0.5% and vehicle in Chroma Meter redness was significant from 30 minutes to 12 hours after application. In study B, brimonidine 0.5% once daily had a statistically superior success profile — two-grade improvement on both clinician and patient assessments over 12 hours — versus vehicle once daily on days 1, 15 and 29 (all P<0.001). No tachyphylaxis, rebound of erythema or aggravation of telangiectasia or inflammatory lesions was observed; all regimens were safe and well tolerated with similarly low adverse-event incidence.
cards.watchOut: A dose-selection programme rather than confirmatory evidence, and again without responder percentages in the record; Chroma Meter redness is an instrument measure whose clinical meaningfulness rests on the parallel clinician/patient scales.

cards.result: Two-grade improvement on clinician and patient scales: significantly superior to vehicle at every measured point from 30 minutes to 12 hours, on days 1, 15 and 29 (all P<.001). shelves.title: Spesolimab for a generalised pustular psoriasis flare: pustules cleared in 54% versus 6% at one week in a 53-patient trial — infections in 47% by week 12 and systemic drug reactions keep this a specialist rescue treatment
shelves.question: In an acute flare of generalised pustular psoriasis, does a single intravenous dose of spesolimab clear pustules within a week compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Psoriasis/drug therapy · Receptors, Interleukin/antagonists & inhibitors · Severity of Illness Index · Symptom Flare Up
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single intravenous dose of spesolimab, an interleukin-36 receptor blocker, cleared pustules within a week in the Effisayil 1 trial (Bachelez H et al., PMID: 34936739): a pustulation subscore of 0 (no visible pustules) at week 1 was reached by 19 of 35 patients (54%) on spesolimab versus 1 of 18 (6%) on placebo (difference 49 percentage points, 95% CI 21 to 67; P<0.001), and a total score of 0 or 1 by 15 (43%) versus 2 (11%) (difference 32 points, 95% CI 2 to 53; P=0.02). The harms are not incidental: infections occurred in 6 of 35 (17%) through week 1 and in 24 of 51 patients (47%) who received spesolimab at any time by week 12; drug reactions occurred in 2 patients, one with concurrent drug-induced liver injury; and antidrug antibodies were detected in 23 of 50 (46%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a dramatic one-week effect in a rare, life-threatening flare — Tier C because a single 53-patient phase 2 trial, with an infection burden that demands specialist supervision, carries the whole claim.

cards.headline: Bachelez 2021 (Effisayil 1): pustulation subscore 0 at week 1 in 19/35 (54%) on spesolimab versus 1/18 (6%) on placebo (difference 49 points, P<0.001); infections 47% by week 12 among ever-treated
cards.summary: Bachelez 2021 (Effisayil 1): pustulation subscore 0 at week 1 in 19/35 (54%) on spesolimab versus 1/18 (6%) on placebo (difference 49 points, P<0.001); infections 47% by week 12 among ever-treated
cards.people: 53 patients with a generalised pustular psoriasis flare, randomised 2:1 to a single 900 mg intravenous dose of spesolimab (n=35) or placebo (n=18); both groups could receive open-label spesolimab on day 8 or as rescue after day 8, with follow-up to week 12. At baseline, 46% (spesolimab) and 39% (placebo) had a pustulation subscore of 3, and 37% and 33% a subscore of 4 (severe pustulation).
cards.result: At week 1, a Generalized Pustular Psoriasis Physician Global Assessment pustulation subscore of 0 was achieved by 19 of 35 (54%) on spesolimab versus 1 of 18 (6%) on placebo (difference 49 percentage points, 95% CI 21 to 67; P<0.001). A total GPPGA score of 0 or 1 was achieved by 15 (43%) versus 2 (11%) (difference 32 points, 95% CI 2 to 53; P=0.02). Infections occurred in 6 of 35 (17%) through the first week in the spesolimab group and in 24 of 51 (47%) of patients who received spesolimab at any time by week 12. Drug reactions were reported in 2 spesolimab patients, one concurrently with drug-induced hepatic injury. Antidrug antibodies were detected in 23 of 50 patients (46%) who received at least one dose.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-three patients with an ultra-rare disease, one week for the primary endpoint, and a design that let placebo patients cross to open-label spesolimab from day 8 — the week-12 infection figure (47%) pools all exposure and cannot be compared with a control rate. Longer and larger trials are needed, as the authors state.
cards.source: Bachelez H et al. Trial of Spesolimab for Generalized Pustular Psoriasis. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34936739. Registry ID: NCT03782792. shelves.title: Silicone gel sheeting for hypertrophic and keloid scars: the Cochrane review found fewer hypertrophic scars (relative risk 0.46) and thinner, better-coloured scars — but every trial was highly susceptible to bias, and a later randomised trial found no Vancouver Scar Scale difference between gel, sheet and pressure alone
shelves.question: For preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars, do silicone gel sheeting and silicone gel improve scar outcomes compared with no treatment or other dressings?
shelves.mesh: Cicatrix, Hypertrophic/prevention & control/therapy · Humans · Keloid/prevention & control/therapy · Occlusive Dressings · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Silicone Gels/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — silicone gel sheeting is a standard scar treatment resting on unusually weak trials. The Cochrane review (O'Brien L et al., PMID: 24030657) included 20 trials with 873 people: in prevention studies, silicone sheeting reduced hypertrophic scarring in people prone to scarring versus no treatment (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.98), and in treatment studies it reduced scar thickness (mean difference -2.00) and improved colour (relative risk 3.49, 95% CI 1.97 to 6.15) — but the reviewers stress these studies were highly susceptible to bias, so a great deal of uncertainty prevails. A later intraindividual randomised trial in hand-burn patients (Pruksapong C et al., PMID: 33173695) found no significant differences on any Vancouver Scar Scale parameter between silicone gel plus pressure garment, silicone sheet plus pressure garment, and pressure garment alone, though some patient-and-observer scale parameters favoured the silicone combinations and scar thickness improved earlier with gel. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): cheap, safe and plausibly helpful — and after four decades of use, still not properly proven.

cards.headline: O'Brien 2013 (Cochrane): prevention of hypertrophic scarring relative risk 0.46 (0.21 to 0.98); treatment scar thickness mean difference -2.00 and colour relative risk 3.49 — all from bias-prone trials
cards.summary: O'Brien 2013 (Cochrane): prevention of hypertrophic scarring relative risk 0.46 (0.21 to 0.98); treatment scar thickness mean difference -2.00 and colour relative risk 3.49 — all from bias-prone trials
cards.people: 20 randomised, quasi-randomised or controlled trials with 873 people aged 1.5 to 81 years, comparing adhesive silicone gel sheeting with no treatment, non-silicone dressings, other silicone products, laser therapy, triamcinolone injection, topical onion extract or pressure therapy, for preventing or treating hypertrophic and keloid scars.
cards.result: In prevention studies, silicone gel sheeting reduced the incidence of hypertrophic scarring in people prone to scarring versus no treatment (relative risk 0.46, 95% confidence interval 0.21 to 0.98). In treatment studies, sheeting produced a statistically significant reduction in scar thickness (mean difference -2.00, 95% CI -2.14 to -1.85) and colour amelioration (relative risk 3.49, 95% CI 1.97 to 6.15). The reviewers conclude there is weak evidence of benefit for prevention in high-risk individuals, but the poor quality of the research — studies highly susceptible to bias — means a great deal of uncertainty prevails.
cards.watchOut: The scar-thickness mean difference of -2.00 has an implausibly narrow confidence interval for this literature, a marker of the small, bias-prone trials underneath. Blinding a silicone sheet is near-impossible, which is part of why the evidence has stayed weak since 1981.
cards.source: O'Brien L et al. Silicone gel sheeting for preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 24030657. systematic review (cochrane, o'brien 2013) 20 randomised, quasi-randomised or controlled trials with 873 people aged 1.5 to 81 years, comparing adhesive silicone gel sheeting with no treatment, non-silicone dressings, other silicone products, laser therapy, triamcinolone injection, topical onion extract or pressure therapy, for preventing or treating hypertrophic and keloid scars. in prevention studies, silicone gel sheeting reduced the incidence of hypertrophic scarring in people prone to scarring versus no treatment (relative risk 0.46, 95% confidence interval 0.21 to 0.98). in treatment studies, sheeting produced a statistically significant reduction in scar thickness (mean difference -2.00, 95% ci -2.14 to -1.85) and colour amelioration (relative risk 3.49, 95% ci 1.97 to 6.15). the reviewers conclude there is weak evidence of benefit for prevention in high-risk individuals, but the poor quality of the research — studies highly susceptible to bias — means a great deal of uncertainty prevails. the scar-thickness mean difference of -2.00 has an implausibly narrow confidence interval for this literature, a marker of the small, bias-prone trials underneath. blinding a silicone sheet is near-impossible, which is part of why the evidence has stayed weak since 1981. o'brien l et al. silicone gel sheeting for preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. pmid: 24030657. mesh: cicatrix, hypertrophic/prevention & control/therapy · humans · keloid/prevention & control/therapy · occlusive dressings · randomized controlled trials as topic · silicone gels/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Pruksapong 2020: no significant Vancouver Scar Scale difference between silicone gel, silicone sheet (both with pressure garment) and pressure garment alone in hand burns; some patient/observer parameters favoured silicone
cards.summary: Pruksapong 2020: no significant Vancouver Scar Scale difference between silicone gel, silicone sheet (both with pressure garment) and pressure garment alone in hand burns; some patient/observer parameters favoured silicone
cards.type: Randomised intraindividual trial with systematic review (Pruksapong 2020)
cards.people: Patients with deep hand burns treated with skin grafts, in a prospective intraindividual randomised trial comparing silicone gel plus pressure garment, silicone gel sheet plus pressure garment, and pressure garment alone for hypertrophic scar prevention; the accompanying systematic review included only randomised trials of silicone materials in burned patients. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in any Vancouver Scar Scale parameter among the three groups. Three of six Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Score parameters differed significantly among groups (P<0.05): scar stiffness improved at 8 and 12 weeks in both silicone groups (with no difference between gel and sheet), scar thickness improved at 2, 4 and 8 weeks in the silicone gel group versus pressure alone, and scar irregularity improved at 2, 4, 8, 16 and 20 weeks in both silicone groups versus pressure alone.
cards.watchOut: Intraindividual design in a single burn population, with the abstract not stating the sample size; the split verdict between the two scar scales (observer scale null, patient/observer scale partly positive) is itself the finding — measurement choice drives the answer.
cards.source: Pruksapong C et al. shelves.title: Adding silver nitrate cautery to antiseptic nasal cream changed nothing: improvement in 89% versus 91% — and the children's review calls the whole field inconclusive
shelves.question: In children with recurrent anterior nosebleeds, does antiseptic nasal cream alone match silver nitrate cautery plus cream for stopping recurrences?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Administration, Topical · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/therapeutic use · Cautery/methods · Chlorhexidine/therapeutic use · Drug Combinations · Emulsions · Epistaxis/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Neomycin/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Silver Nitrate/therapeutic use · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — cautery added nothing measurable to antiseptic cream in the one randomised comparison. In Murthy 1999 (PMID: 10384851), 91% of patients on chlorhexidine–neomycin antiseptic cream alone improved versus 89% on cream plus silver nitrate cautery (P = 0.7569), with no difference between the under-16 and over-16 age groups (P = 1.000). The Cochrane review of interventions for recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children (Qureishi 2012, PMID: 22972071) found five small trials of 468 participants in total and concluded the results were inconclusive, with no statistically significant difference between any compared treatments; its one clear finding was procedural — 75% silver nitrate beat 95% silver nitrate at two weeks (88% versus 65% complete resolution, P = 0.01) and hurt less (mean pain score 1 versus 5, P = 0.001). So cream alone matching cautery-plus-cream is the best-supported reading, but it rests on one small mixed-age trial inside an inconclusive field. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no added benefit from cautery over antiseptic cream was shown, and the evidence base in children is thin.

cards.headline: Murthy 1999: improvement in 91% on antiseptic cream alone versus 89% on cream plus silver nitrate cautery (P = 0.7569)
cards.summary: Murthy 1999: improvement in 91% on antiseptic cream alone versus 89% on cream plus silver nitrate cautery (P = 0.7569)
cards.people: 64 consecutive outpatients with recurrent anterior epistaxis randomised to chlorhexidine–neomycin antiseptic nasal carrier cream alone or the same cream combined with silver nitrate cautery; results were available for 50 patients (22 cream alone, 28 combined). The trial mixed children and adults, analysing under-16 and over-16 age groups separately.
cards.result: Improvement in symptoms occurred in 20 of 22 patients (91%) on cream alone and 25 of 28 (89%) on cream plus cautery — no statistically significant difference (P = 0.7569). Comparing the under-16 and over-16 age groups across treatment arms likewise showed no significant difference (P = 1.000). The authors concluded silver nitrate cautery offers no added advantage in simple epistaxis in children or adults.
cards.watchOut: Only 50 of 64 randomised patients had results available, the population mixes children with adults (the child-specific estimate is an age-subgroup comparison), and follow-up and outcome definitions are those of a 1999 single-centre trial — this is a small, old null, not proof of exact equivalence.
cards.source: Murthy P et al. A randomised clinical trial of antiseptic nasal carrier cream and silver nitrate cautery in the treatment of recurrent anterior epistaxis. Clinical Otolaryngology and Allied Sciences. 1999. PMID: 10384851. cards.headline: Cochrane 2012 (children): five trials, 468 participants, no significant difference between any treatments — 75% silver nitrate beat 95% at two weeks and hurt less
cards.summary: Cochrane 2012 (children): five trials, 468 participants, no significant difference between any treatments — 75% silver nitrate beat 95% at two weeks and hurt less
cards.people: Five studies (four randomised trials and one quasi-randomised trial) involving 468 children up to age 16 with recurrent idiopathic epistaxis, comparing antiseptic (chlorhexidine–neomycin) cream versus no treatment, petroleum jelly versus no treatment, 75% versus 95% silver nitrate cautery, and cautery plus cream versus cream alone.
cards.result: Overall results were inconclusive, with no statistically significant difference found between the compared treatments on completion of the trials. The exception was concentration: 75% silver nitrate gave 88% complete resolution at two weeks versus 65% with 95% silver nitrate (P = 0.01), with lower pain scores (mean 1 versus 5, P = 0.001) despite local anaesthetic. No serious adverse effects were reported from any intervention, though cautery was reported as a painful experience by children.
cards.watchOut: No meta-analysis was possible because the trials were heterogeneous in treatments, procedures and quality; two trials were judged low risk of bias, two unclear and one high. The review's own conclusion is that the optimal management is unknown and high-quality trials with at least a year of follow-up are needed.
cards.source: Qureishi A et al. Interventions for recurrent idiopathic epistaxis (nosebleeds) in children. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22972071. cards.summary: Synthesis: cautery adds pain, not control — cream alone is a reasonable first step, on weak evidence
cards.people: One randomised trial of cream versus cream-plus-cautery (50 patients with results, children and adults) and one Cochrane review of five trials in 468 children with recurrent idiopathic epistaxis.

shelves.title: Intranasal steroids for acute sinusitis: 73% improved or resolved versus 66.4% on placebo — a real but modest edge, larger at higher doses
shelves.question: In acute rhinosinusitis, do intranasal corticosteroids added to antibiotics (or alone) speed symptom resolution compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Intranasal · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Adult · Child · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sinusitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest, dose-related gain in symptom resolution. The Cochrane review (Zalmanovici Trestioreanu 2013, PMID: 24293353) pooled four double-blind trials of 1,943 participants with acute sinusitis: resolution or improvement of symptoms occurred in 73% on intranasal corticosteroids versus 66.4% on placebo (risk ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.18). Higher doses worked better — for mometasone furoate, 400 µg gave a risk ratio of 1.10 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.18) versus 1.04 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.11) for 200 µg. No significant adverse events were reported and drop-out and recurrence rates did not differ. The trials tested the spray as monotherapy or as an adjunct to antibiotics over 15 or 21 days, so the shelf cannot separate the alone-versus-added question; what it supports is a small average benefit either way. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intranasal steroids raise the chance of improvement or resolution by about 7 percentage points over placebo in acute sinusitis.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2013: resolution or improvement in 73% on intranasal steroids versus 66.4% on placebo (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.18)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2013: resolution or improvement in 73% on intranasal steroids versus 66.4% on placebo (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.18)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane review, Zalmanovici Trestioreanu 2013)
cards.people: Four well-designed double-blind randomised trials involving 1,943 adults and children with acute sinusitis confirmed by radiological evidence or nasal endoscopy, comparing intranasal corticosteroids with placebo or no intervention for 15 or 21 days, as monotherapy or adjuvant to antibiotics. Loss to follow-up ranged from 7% to 41% across trials.
cards.result: Pooling the three trials in the meta-analysis, participants receiving intranasal corticosteroids were more likely to experience resolution or improvement of symptoms than those receiving placebo (73% versus 66.4%; risk ratio 1.11, 95% confidence interval 1.04 to 1.18). Higher doses had a stronger effect: mometasone furoate 400 µg gave RR 1.10 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.18) versus RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.11) for 200 µg. No significant adverse events were reported, and drop-out and recurrence rates did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain is about 7 percentage points and one trial lost 41% to follow-up; the evidence covers sinusitis confirmed by imaging or endoscopy, which is stricter than the clinical diagnosis most primary-care patients receive, and the pooled trials mix monotherapy with antibiotic-adjunct designs.
cards.source: Zalmanovici Trestioreanu A et al. Intranasal steroids for acute sinusitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24293353. shelves.title: Ciclosporin for antihistamine-resistant chronic urticaria: responders in both randomised trials — 8 of 19 versus 0 of 10 in the small one — with relapse the rule after stopping
shelves.question: In chronic spontaneous urticaria refractory to antihistamines, does ciclosporin induce remission compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Algorithms · Basophils/metabolism · Chronic Disease · Cyclosporine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dermatologic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Histamine Release/drug effects · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Urticaria/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials agree, both on background antihistamine. In Grattan 2000 (PMID: 10951147), patients with severe disease and a positive autologous serum skin test responded in 8 of 19 cases on ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily versus 0 of 10 on placebo at 4 weeks (P < 0.05), with mean weekly urticaria activity score falling by 12.7 points versus 2.3 on placebo (P = 0.005). In Vena 2006 (PMID: 17010756), therapeutic failures were fewer on 16 weeks of ciclosporin (3) than on placebo (11), with symptom scores significantly improved at 8 and 16 weeks. The catch is durability: six of Grattan's eight randomised responders relapsed within 6 weeks of stopping, and only five of 19 responders overall (26%) had not relapsed by study end — this is suppression while taking it, not remission after it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ciclosporin controls antihistamine-resistant urticaria while taken, at immunosuppressant cost, with relapse common on withdrawal.

cards.headline: Grattan 2000: response in 8 of 19 on ciclosporin versus 0 of 10 on placebo at 4 weeks; mean activity score fell 12.7 versus 2.3 points (P = 0.005)
cards.summary: Grattan 2000: response in 8 of 19 on ciclosporin versus 0 of 10 on placebo at 4 weeks; mean activity score fell 12.7 versus 2.3 points (P = 0.005)
cards.people: 30 patients with severe unremitting chronic urticaria responding poorly to antihistamines and with a positive autologous serum skin test, randomised to ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily (n = 20, as the Sandimmun formulation named in the record) or placebo (n = 10) for 4 weeks, all taking cetirizine 20 mg daily throughout; non-responders were offered open-label ciclosporin, and follow-up ran to 20 weeks or relapse.
cards.result: Eight of 19 patients completing active treatment responded at 4 weeks versus none on placebo (P < 0.05); three more met the response criterion at 2 weeks but not at 4. Mean reduction in weekly urticaria activity score between weeks 0 and 4 was 12.7 (95% CI 6.6 to 18.8) on ciclosporin versus 2.3 (95% CI −3.3 to 7.9) on placebo (P = 0.005). Of 17 non-responders who took open-label ciclosporin, 11 responded after 4 weeks; but six of the eight randomised responders relapsed within 6 weeks, and only five of 19 responders overall (26%) had not relapsed by the study end-point.
cards.watchOut: A very small trial in a selected subgroup (positive autologous serum skin test — an autoimmune-marker population), only 4 weeks of randomised treatment, and the relapse data show control rather than remission. Ciclosporin's renal and blood-pressure harms are not quantified in this record.
cards.source: Grattan CE et al. Randomized double-blind study of cyclosporin in chronic 'idiopathic' urticaria. British Journal of Dermatology. 2000. PMID: 10951147. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (grattan 2000) 30 patients with severe unremitting chronic urticaria responding poorly to antihistamines and with a positive autologous serum skin test, randomised to ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily (n = 20, as the sandimmun formulation named in the record) or placebo (n = 10) for 4 weeks, all taking cetirizine 20 mg daily throughout; non-responders were offered open-label ciclosporin, and follow-up ran to 20 weeks or relapse. eight of 19 patients completing active treatment responded at 4 weeks versus none on placebo (p < 0.05); three more met the response criterion at 2 weeks but not at 4. mean reduction in weekly urticaria activity score between weeks 0 and 4 was 12.7 (95% ci 6.6 to 18.8) on ciclosporin versus 2.3 (95% ci −3.3 to 7.9) on placebo (p = 0.005). of 17 non-responders who took open-label ciclosporin, 11 responded after 4 weeks; but six of the eight randomised responders relapsed within 6 weeks, and only five of 19 responders overall (26%) had not relapsed by the study end-point. a very small trial in a selected subgroup (positive autologous serum skin test — an autoimmune-marker population), only 4 weeks of randomised treatment, and the relapse data show control rather than remission. ciclosporin's renal and blood-pressure harms are not quantified in this record. grattan ce et al. randomized double-blind study of cyclosporin in chronic 'idiopathic' urticaria. british journal of dermatology. 2000. pmid: 10951147. mesh: adult · aged · algorithms · basophils/metabolism · chronic disease · cyclosporine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · dermatologic agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · double-blind method · female · follow-up studies · histamine release/drug effects · humans · immunosuppressive agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · male · middle aged · treatment outcome · urticaria/drug therapy

cards.headline: Vena 2006: therapeutic failures in 3 on 16-week ciclosporin versus 11 on placebo, symptom scores significantly better at 8 and 16 weeks
cards.summary: Vena 2006: therapeutic failures in 3 on 16-week ciclosporin versus 11 on placebo, symptom scores significantly better at 8 and 16 weeks
cards.people: 99 patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria in a three-arm double-blind study: 16 weeks of ciclosporin, 8 weeks of ciclosporin followed by 8 weeks of placebo, or 16 weeks of placebo; all patients received cetirizine throughout and were followed for a further 8 weeks. From day 28 the ciclosporin dose was 3 mg/kg daily.
cards.result: Fewer therapeutic failures occurred with 16-week ciclosporin (n = 3) than with placebo (n = 11) or 8-week ciclosporin (n = 8). After 8 and 16 weeks, symptom scores had significantly improved in both ciclosporin groups compared with placebo. Two patients discontinued because of hypertension.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports failure counts and significance without full score data, the dose was reduced to 3 mg/kg from day 28 (likely less effective but better tolerated than higher doses), and hypertension already appeared in this small sample — the class harms need monitoring the trials were too small to size.
cards.source: Vena GA et al. Cyclosporine in chronic idiopathic urticaria: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2006. PMID: 17010756. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — control while taking it, relapse when it stops
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one direction — control while taking it, relapse when it stops
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 129 patients with severe antihistamine-resistant chronic urticaria, ciclosporin for 4–16 weeks on background cetirizine.
cards.result: Response 8/19 versus 0/10 at 4 weeks (Grattan); therapeutic failures 3 versus 11 over 16 weeks (Vena). Durability is the weak point: six of eight randomised responders in Grattan relapsed within 6 weeks of stopping, and only 26% of all responders remained relapse-free at study end. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the relapse pattern and immunosuppressant harms on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for harms, populations were selected (severe, antihistamine-resistant, in Grattan autoantibody-positive), and no trial here compares ciclosporin with the anti-IgE and other options now used in this population. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised placebo-controlled trials carry the claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grattan CE et al. British Journal of Dermatology. 2000 (PMID: 10951147); Vena GA et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2006 (PMID: 17010756).

shelves.title: Peanut sublingual immunotherapy: 70% responders versus 15% on placebo at 44 weeks in the randomised trial — and a quarter of young children passed a 5,000 mg challenge after up to 5 years
shelves.question: In young children with peanut allergy, does sublingual immunotherapy raise the tolerated peanut dose and produce sustained unresponsiveness after stopping, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Allergens/immunology · Arachis/immunology · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Immune Tolerance · Immunization · Immunoglobulin E/metabolism · Infant · Male · Peanut Hypersensitivity/immunology/therapy · Sublingual Immunotherapy/methods · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — desensitisation is real; sustained unresponsiveness is shown in a minority, without a placebo arm. The randomised trial (Fleischer 2013, PMID: 23265698) found responders in 14 of 20 (70%) on peanut SLIT versus 3 of 20 (15%) on placebo after 44 weeks (P < .001), with median successfully consumed dose in responders rising from 3.5 mg to 496 mg. The long-term study in younger children (Kim 2019, PMID: 31493887) treated children aged 1 to 11 years with 2 mg/day for up to 5 years: 67% (32/48) consumed at least 750 mg at the final challenge and 25% (12/48) passed a 5,000 mg challenge, of whom 10 of 12 showed sustained unresponsiveness after 2 to 4 weeks off therapy. Side effects were mostly transient mouth itching (4.8% of doses in Kim; no epinephrine used). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): SLIT raises the tolerated dose in most treated children, but full sustained unresponsiveness after stopping was demonstrated in only about a fifth of the long-term cohort and never against placebo. Tier C is set: the young-child and sustained-unresponsiveness claims rest on a single uncontrolled long-term study.

cards.headline: Fleischer 2013: responders in 70% on peanut SLIT versus 15% on placebo after 44 weeks (P < .001)
cards.summary: Fleischer 2013: responders in 70% on peanut SLIT versus 15% on placebo after 44 weeks (P < .001)
cards.people: 40 subjects aged 12 to 37 years (median 15) with peanut allergy at five sites, randomised 1:1 to daily peanut or placebo sublingual immunotherapy after a baseline food challenge (median successfully consumed dose 46 mg); a 5 g challenge was performed after 44 weeks, after which placebo subjects crossed over to higher-dose SLIT.
cards.result: After 44 weeks, 14 of 20 (70%) on peanut SLIT were responders (consuming 5 g or at least tenfold their baseline threshold) versus 3 of 20 (15%) on placebo (P < .001). In responders, median successfully consumed dose rose from 3.5 mg to 496 mg, and to 996 mg after 68 weeks. Of 10,855 peanut doses through the week-44 challenges, 63.1% were symptom-free and, excluding mouth-and-throat symptoms, 95.2% were symptom-free.
cards.watchOut: These were adolescents and young adults, not the young children of the shelf question, the median tolerated dose achieved (about 0.5–1 g of peanut powder) is protection against accidental exposure rather than free eating, and the trial was not designed to test sustained unresponsiveness after stopping.
cards.source: Fleischer DM et al. Sublingual immunotherapy for peanut allergy: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial. Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2013. PMID: 23265698. Registry ID: NCT00580606. cards.headline: Kim 2019 (ages 1–11): 67% consumed ≥750 mg after up to 5 years of SLIT; 25% passed 5,000 mg and 10 of those 12 stayed unresponsive off therapy
cards.summary: Kim 2019 (ages 1–11): 67% consumed ≥750 mg after up to 5 years of SLIT; 25% passed 5,000 mg and 10 of those 12 stayed unresponsive off therapy
cards.people: 48 children aged 1 to 11 years with peanut allergy given peanut SLIT 2 mg/day for up to 5 years (37 completed 3 to 5 years); desensitisation was assessed by double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge up to 5,000 mg peanut protein after dosing ended, and sustained unresponsiveness by repeat challenge after 2 to 4 weeks without peanut exposure.
cards.result: 67% (32/48) successfully consumed 750 mg or more at the final challenge, and 25% (12/48) passed the 5,000 mg challenge without symptoms; 10 of these 12 demonstrated sustained unresponsiveness after 2 to 4 weeks off therapy. Side effects were reported with 4.8% of doses (transient mouth itching most common), 0.21% of doses needed antihistamine, and no epinephrine was administered. Peanut skin-test wheals and specific IgE fell significantly while specific IgG4 rose.
cards.watchOut: There is no placebo or control group in this long-term study — some children outgrow peanut allergy or improve naturally, so the sustained-unresponsiveness figure (10 of 48, about a fifth) cannot be credited to SLIT alone; 11 of 48 did not complete the programme.
cards.source: Kim EH et al. Long-term sublingual immunotherapy for peanut allergy in children: Clinical and immunologic evidence of desensitization. Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: desensitisation proven against placebo; lasting unresponsiveness plausible but unproven against control
cards.summary: Synthesis: desensitisation proven against placebo; lasting unresponsiveness plausible but unproven against control
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial (40 subjects aged 12–37) and one long-term open study (48 children aged 1–11, up to 5 years of treatment).
cards.result: Responders at 44 weeks: 70% versus 15% on placebo. After up to 5 years in young children: 67% tolerated ≥750 mg, 25% passed 5,000 mg, and 10 of 48 (about a fifth) showed sustained unresponsiveness 2–4 weeks after stopping. Safety across both: mostly transient mouth itching, no epinephrine in the long-term study. cards.watchOut: Mention-only discipline: earlier peanut SLIT reports from the same programme are discussed in the Kim record's background and are not carded here. Families should read the achieved doses as accident protection, not dietary freedom.

shelves.title: Tinea capitis: the fungus decides — terbinafine beats griseofulvin for Trichophyton (complete cure RR 1.47), griseofulvin beats terbinafine for Microsporum (RR 0.68)
shelves.question: In children with tinea capitis, does terbinafine clear infection faster and more completely than griseofulvin — and does the answer depend on whether the fungus is Trichophyton or Microsporum?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage · Child · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tinea Capitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by species. The Cochrane review (Chen 2017, PMID: 27816294; 25 randomised trials, 4,449 children) found terbinafine and griseofulvin similar for mixed infections (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.24), but terbinafine clearly better for Trichophyton tonsurans complete cure (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.77) and griseofulvin clearly better for Microsporum-only infections (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86). The largest trial programme (Elewski 2008, PMID: 18378354; 1,286 children in the efficacy population) matches: complete cure 45.1% on terbinafine versus 39.2% on griseofulvin overall, with terbinafine significantly better on every cure measure for T. tonsurans and griseofulvin significantly better for M. canis. Neither drug is 'the winner' — identifying the organism is what chooses the drug. PROPOSED SPLIT: terbinafine for Trichophyton, griseofulvin for Microsporum, either for mixed or unknown infections.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2017: mixed infections a draw (RR 1.08); Trichophyton favours terbinafine (RR 1.47); Microsporum favours griseofulvin (RR 0.68)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017: mixed infections a draw (RR 1.08); Trichophyton favours terbinafine (RR 1.47); Microsporum favours griseofulvin (RR 0.68)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (abridged Cochrane review, Chen 2017)
cards.people: 25 randomised controlled trials with 4,449 children with tinea capitis, comparing systemic antifungal drugs (terbinafine, griseofulvin, itraconazole, fluconazole) across Trichophyton and Microsporum infections.
cards.result: Terbinafine and griseofulvin had similar effects for children with mixed Trichophyton and Microsporum infections (risk ratio 1.08, 95% confidence interval 0.94 to 1.24). Terbinafine was better than griseofulvin for complete cure of T. tonsurans infections (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.77); griseofulvin was better than terbinafine for complete cure of infections caused solely by Microsporum species (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86). Against Trichophyton, itraconazole and fluconazole had effects similar to both main drugs.
cards.watchOut: All included studies were at unclear or high risk of bias with significant clinical heterogeneity, and the review graded its confidence down accordingly; species identification in routine practice is often unavailable, which is where the 'either drug' mixed-infection result does the work.
cards.source: Chen X et al. Systemic antifungal therapy for tinea capitis in children: An abridged Cochrane Review. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2017. PMID: 27816294. cards.headline: Elewski 2008 (two trials, 1,286 children): complete cure 45.1% terbinafine versus 39.2% griseofulvin — species subgroups split exactly as the review found
cards.summary: Elewski 2008 (two trials, 1,286 children): complete cure 45.1% terbinafine versus 39.2% griseofulvin — species subgroups split exactly as the review found
cards.people: Children aged 4–12 years with microscopy-confirmed tinea capitis randomised in two identical international trials to once-daily terbinafine oral granules (5–8 mg/kg; n = 1,040) or griseofulvin suspension at label doses (10–20 mg/kg; n = 509) for 6 weeks with 4 weeks of follow-up; the pooled efficacy population was 1,286 children with positive baseline cultures.
cards.result: Complete cure was 45.1% on terbinafine versus 39.2% on griseofulvin and mycologic cure 61.5% versus 55.5% (both P < .05); clinical cure favoured terbinafine but not significantly (P = .10). Subgroup analyses: terbinafine was significantly better than griseofulvin on all cure rates for Trichophyton tonsurans (P < .001), while for Microsporum canis mycologic and clinical cure were significantly better with griseofulvin (P < .05). About 50% of each group reported an adverse event, almost all mild or moderate, with no drug-related serious events.
cards.watchOut: The two component trials disagreed on complete cure (significant in trial 1, not trial 2) because the infecting species were distributed differently between them — which is itself the shelf's point. Griseofulvin was dosed per label, lower than some current practice, and adjuvant shampoos or topical agents were excluded.
cards.source: Elewski BE et al. Terbinafine hydrochloride oral granules versus oral griseofulvin suspension in children with tinea capitis: results of two randomized, investigator-blinded, multicenter, international, controlled trials. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2008. PMID: 18378354. cards.headline: Synthesis: no overall winner — culture (or local epidemiology) should pick the drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: no overall winner — culture (or local epidemiology) should pick the drug
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 25 trials (4,449 children) and the largest single trial programme within it (1,286 children in the efficacy analysis).
cards.result: Mixed infections: RR 1.08 (0.94–1.24). T. tonsurans: terbinafine better, RR 1.47 (1.22–1.77). Microsporum only: griseofulvin better, RR 0.68 (0.53–0.86) for terbinafine versus griseofulvin. Overall complete cure in the big trials: 45.1% versus 39.2%. PROPOSED SPLIT, by infecting species.
cards.watchOut: Complete cure rates under 50% in the largest trials are a reminder that both drugs fail often; non-response should prompt species identification and a switch across the split, not simply a longer course of the same drug. Tier C is not set: a 25-trial meta-analysis and concordant large trials carry the shelf.

shelves.title: Varenicline nasal spray for dry eye: Schirmer responders 47–49% versus 27.8% on vehicle in phase 3 — tear production clearly up, symptom relief less consistent
shelves.question: In dry eye disease, does varenicline solution nasal spray increase tear production and improve symptoms compared with vehicle?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Dry Eye Syndromes/diagnosis/drug therapy · Humans · Lubricant Eye Drops/therapeutic use · Nasal Sprays · Ophthalmic Solutions/therapeutic use · Tears · Treatment Outcome · Varenicline/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the sign is solid, the symptom is softer. In ONSET-2 (Wirta 2022, PMID: 34767866), a Schirmer improvement of at least 10 mm at week 4 was achieved by 47.3% on varenicline 0.03 mg and 49.2% on 0.06 mg versus 27.8% on vehicle (P < 0.0001 for both). In ONSET-1 (Wirta 2022, PMID: 36107843), the mean Schirmer advantage over vehicle was 7.7 mm (95% CI 3.8 to 11.7) at 0.03 mg and 7.5 mm (95% CI 3.4 to 11.6) at 0.06 mg (both P < 0.001). Symptoms split: eye dryness improved significantly at 0.03 mg in ONSET-1 (P = 0.021) but the ONSET-2 dryness difference was not significant in the controlled-environment chamber and only nominally significant in clinic. The price is nasal, not ocular: sneezing in 62–84% in ONSET-1 and at least one treatment-emergent event in 97–99% on active spray versus 57% on vehicle in ONSET-2, mostly mild sneezing, cough and throat irritation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): varenicline nasal spray reliably increases tear production over 4 weeks; how much patients feel it is less certain.

cards.headline: ONSET-2 (phase 3): Schirmer responders 47.3% (0.03 mg) and 49.2% (0.06 mg) versus 27.8% on vehicle (P < 0.0001)
cards.summary: ONSET-2 (phase 3): Schirmer responders 47.3% (0.03 mg) and 49.2% (0.06 mg) versus 27.8% on vehicle (P < 0.0001)
cards.people: 758 adults aged 22 or older with dry eye disease, an Ocular Surface Disease Index score of at least 23 and a Schirmer score of 10 mm or less, randomised 1:1:1 to twice-daily varenicline solution nasal spray 0.03 mg (n = 260), 0.06 mg (n = 246) or vehicle (n = 252) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: The primary end point (at least 10 mm improvement in Schirmer score at week 4) was met by 47.3% on 0.03 mg and 49.2% on 0.06 mg versus 27.8% on vehicle (P < 0.0001 for both doses), and change in Schirmer score was significantly greater on both doses (P < 0.0001). Eye dryness at week 4 improved versus vehicle but was not significant in the controlled adverse environment chamber and only nominally significant in the clinic. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 97.3% (0.03 mg), 99.2% (0.06 mg) and 57% (vehicle) — most mild and non-ocular (sneezing, cough, throat and instillation-site irritation).
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short for a chronic disease, the primary end point is a tear-production sign rather than how eyes feel, and the near-universal mild nasal events effectively unmask many participants — a real concern for the subjective symptom endpoints.

cards.summary: ONSET-1 (phase 2b): mean Schirmer advantage over vehicle of 7.7 mm at 0.03 mg and 7.5 mm at 0.06 mg (both P < 0.001); dryness significantly better only at 0.03 mg
cards.people: 182 patients aged 22 or older with a physician diagnosis of dry eye disease and previous artificial-tear use, randomised 1:1:1:1 to vehicle or varenicline nasal spray 0.006 mg, 0.03 mg or 0.06 mg twice daily; the primary end point was change in anaesthetised Schirmer score at day 28.
cards.result: After 28 days, the least-squares mean Schirmer difference versus vehicle was 7.7 mm (95% confidence interval 3.8 to 11.7; P < 0.001) at 0.03 mg and 7.5 mm (3.4 to 11.6; P < 0.001) at 0.06 mg. Eye dryness score fell significantly versus vehicle at 0.03 mg (P = 0.021) but not at 0.06 mg. Sneezing occurred in 62–84% and cough in 9–25%, transient and predominantly mild.
cards.watchOut: A small dose-ranging study (about 45 patients per arm) whose symptom result did not follow the dose — the 0.06 mg dose won on tears but not on dryness — foreshadowing the phase 3 symptom inconsistency.

shelves.title: Perfluorohexyloctane for evaporative dry eye: corneal staining and dryness both significantly better than saline in two phase 3 trials — differences of about 1 staining point and 8–10 dryness points
shelves.question: In evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction, does perfluorohexyloctane ophthalmic solution improve corneal staining and dryness compared with hypotonic saline control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Meibomian Gland Dysfunction · Fluorescein · Dry Eye Syndromes/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Ophthalmic Solutions · Tears · Meibomian Glands
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large phase 3 trials, both primary endpoints met in both. In GOBI (Tauber 2023, PMID: 36574848), the week-8 advantage over hypotonic saline was −0.97 points for total corneal fluorescein staining (95% CI −1.40 to −0.55) and −7.6 points for eye dryness on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −11.8 to −3.4), both P < 0.001. In MOJAVE (Sheppard 2023, PMID: 36948372), staining change was −2.3 versus −1.1 (difference −1.2, 95% CI −1.7 to −0.8) and dryness change −29.4 versus −19.2 (difference −10.2, 95% CI −14.4 to −6.1), both P < .001, with differences present from week 2. Ocular adverse events were similar to saline (12.9% versus 12.3% in MOJAVE) and no serious ocular events occurred in either trial. The effects are statistically robust but modest in size — about one staining point on a 15-point scale — and the trials run only 8 weeks. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): perfluorohexyloctane improves both the staining sign and the dryness symptom of meibomian-gland dry eye over 8 weeks, by a modest margin.

cards.headline: GOBI (phase 3): staining advantage −0.97 points and dryness advantage −7.6 points versus saline at week 8 (both P < 0.001)
cards.summary: GOBI (phase 3): staining advantage −0.97 points and dryness advantage −7.6 points versus saline at week 8 (both P < 0.001)
cards.people: 599 adults randomised (597 treated) with dry eye disease for at least 6 months associated with meibomian gland dysfunction — tear break-up time 5 seconds or less, Schirmer I at least 5 mm, meibomian gland score at least 3 and total corneal staining 4–11 — receiving perfluorohexyloctane (n = 303) or hypotonic 0.6% saline (n = 294) four times daily for 8 weeks.
cards.result: At week 8, improvement from baseline was significantly greater with perfluorohexyloctane than saline for total corneal fluorescein staining (least-squares mean treatment difference −0.97; 95% confidence interval −1.40 to −0.55) and eye dryness score (−7.6; −11.8 to −3.4), both P < 0.001. All key secondary endpoints also favoured treatment (P < 0.01), including dryness and staining at week 2 and burning/stinging at week 8 (−5.5). Most ocular adverse events were mild, no serious ocular events occurred, and one patient discontinued for eye irritation.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks only, in a selected population with demonstrable gland dysfunction and mid-range staining; the absolute staining gain is about 1 point on a 0–15 scale, so statistical strength should not be confused with a large clinical effect.
cards.source: Tauber J et al. NOV03 for Dry Eye Disease Associated with Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: Results of the Randomized Phase 3 GOBI Study. Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 36574848. cards.summary: MOJAVE (phase 3): staining −2.3 versus −1.1 and dryness −29.4 versus −19.2 at week 8 (both P < .001); ocular adverse events 12.9% versus 12.3%

shelves.title: After pterygium excision, conjunctival autograft halves 6-month recurrence versus amniotic membrane (RR 0.53) — and bare-sclera excision recurs in up to 80%
shelves.question: After pterygium excision, does conjunctival autograft reduce recurrence compared with amniotic membrane graft or bare sclera?
shelves.mesh: Amnion/transplantation · Autografts · Conjunctiva/transplantation · Humans · Pterygium/surgery · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Time Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for autograft over amniotic membrane; the bare-sclera comparison is historical, not randomised. The Cochrane review (Clearfield 2016, PMID: 26867004; 20 randomised trials, 1,947 eyes) found recurrence at 6 months ranging from 3.3% to 16.7% after conjunctival autograft versus 6.4% to 42.3% after amniotic membrane graft, a pooled risk ratio of 0.53 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.85) — a 47% relative reduction. For recurrent pterygia the advantage was larger (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.99). At 3 months there was no difference (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.77). Against bare sclera the review offers only background: recurrence with simple excision leaving bare sclera 'has been reported to be upwards of 80%', which is why grafting is standard — no randomised bare-sclera arm is pooled here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): conjunctival autograft is the better graft for preventing 6-month recurrence, especially for recurrent pterygium.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016: 6-month recurrence RR 0.53 (0.33–0.85) for autograft versus amniotic membrane; no difference at 3 months (RR 0.87)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016: 6-month recurrence RR 0.53 (0.33–0.85) for autograft versus amniotic membrane; no difference at 3 months (RR 0.87)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane review, Clearfield 2016)
cards.people: 20 randomised controlled trials analysing 1,947 eyes of 1,866 participants with primary or recurrent pterygium, conducted in eight countries, comparing conjunctival autograft with amniotic membrane transplant (each with or without adjunctive therapy); individual trials randomised 8 to 346 participants.
cards.result: Recurrence 6 months after surgery ranged from 3.3% to 16.7% in autograft groups and 6.4% to 42.3% in amniotic-membrane groups; the pooled risk ratio was 0.53 (95% confidence interval 0.33 to 0.85) — a 47% relative reduction. In recurrent pterygia the 6-month risk ratio was 0.45 (0.21 to 0.99). At 3 months the risk ratio was 0.87 (0.43 to 1.77), not significant. Excluding one thesis study without allocation concealment strengthened the 6-month estimate to RR 0.43 (0.30 to 0.62). Adverse events reported in more than one study were granuloma/pyogenic granuloma and raised intraocular pressure.
cards.watchOut: Overall risk of bias was unclear — many trials did not report randomisation or masking methods — and the bare-sclera arm of the shelf question has no pooled randomised comparison in this review: the 'upwards of 80%' bare-sclera recurrence figure is background reported in the review, not a meta-analytic result. Patient-reported outcomes and visual acuity were too sparse to analyse.

systematic review and meta-analysis (cochrane review, clearfield 2016) 20 randomised controlled trials analysing 1,947 eyes of 1,866 participants with primary or recurrent pterygium, conducted in eight countries, comparing conjunctival autograft with amniotic membrane transplant (each with or without adjunctive therapy); individual trials randomised 8 to 346 participants. recurrence 6 months after surgery ranged from 3.3% to 16.7% in autograft groups and 6.4% to 42.3% in amniotic-membrane groups; the pooled risk ratio was 0.53 (95% confidence interval 0.33 to 0.85) — a 47% relative reduction. in recurrent pterygia the 6-month risk ratio was 0.45 (0.21 to 0.99). at 3 months the risk ratio was 0.87 (0.43 to 1.77), not significant. excluding one thesis study without allocation concealment strengthened the 6-month estimate to rr 0.43 (0.30 to 0.62). adverse events reported in more than one study were granuloma/pyogenic granuloma and raised intraocular pressure. overall risk of bias was unclear — many trials did not report randomisation or masking methods — and the bare-sclera arm of the shelf question has no pooled randomised comparison in this review: the 'upwards of 80%' bare-sclera recurrence figure is background reported in the review, not a meta-analytic result. patient-reported outcomes and visual acuity were too sparse to analyse. clearfield e et al. conjunctival autograft for pterygium. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. pmid: 26867004. mesh: amnion/transplantation · autografts · conjunctiva/transplantation · humans · pterygium/surgery · randomized controlled trials as topic · recurrence · time factors

cards.headline: Cochrane summary (2017): autograft-treated eyes had half the recurrence of membrane-treated eyes, especially in recurrent pterygia
cards.summary: Cochrane summary (2017): autograft-treated eyes had half the recurrence of membrane-treated eyes, especially in recurrent pterygia
cards.type: Systematic review summary (Clearfield 2017, summarising the Cochrane review)
cards.people: The same 20 randomised trials, 1,866 participants (1,947 eyes) with primary or recurrent pterygium, conjunctival autograft versus amniotic membrane transplant; recurrence defined as regrowth of at least 1 mm onto the cornea at 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: The summary restates the pooled findings: a 47% lower relative risk of recurrence at 6 months with autograft (risk ratio 0.53, 95% confidence interval 0.33 to 0.85, from 1,021 eyes in 10 trials) and a 55% lower relative risk in recurrent pterygia (RR 0.45, 0.21 to 0.99, 96 eyes), with 3-month rates similar between grafts (538 eyes, 6 trials). It concludes autograft was more effective than amniotic membrane transplant for preventing recurrence by 6 months, especially in recurrent pterygia.
cards.watchOut: This card summarises the same Cochrane dataset as the first card — it is the review's own journal summary, not independent evidence, and it is carded to document the recurrence definition and the recurrent-pterygium subgroup, not to double the weight of evidence.
cards.source: Clearfield E et al. Conjunctival Autograft Versus Amniotic Membrane Transplantation for Treatment of Pterygium: Findings From a Cochrane Systematic Review. shelves.title: Blocked tear duct in infants: balloon dilation succeeded in 82% and intubation in 84% in prospective series — but no randomised trial has ever shown either beats simple probing
shelves.question: In infants and children with congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction that has not resolved, does balloon catheter dilation or nasolacrimal intubation beat simple probing for resolution?
shelves.mesh: Catheterization · Child, Preschool · Female · Fluorescein/pharmacokinetics · Fluorescent Dyes/pharmacokinetics · Humans · Infant · Lacrimal Apparatus Diseases/etiology · Lacrimal Duct Obstruction/complications/therapy · Male · Nasolacrimal Duct · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Tears/metabolism · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — not because the procedures fail, but because the head-to-head randomised evidence does not exist. In the PEDIG prospective series, primary balloon catheter dilation succeeded in 82% of eyes (95% CI 74% to 88%; Repka 2008, PMID: 18929305) — with no comparison group, so it cannot show superiority over probing. After a failed probing, balloon dilation and intubation performed alike: success in 77% of balloon eyes versus 84% (adjusted) of intubation eyes, risk ratio 1.08 (0.95 to 1.22) (Repka 2009, PMID: 19433712). And the one randomised trial in this area (Lee 2013, PMID: 23954210) compared timing, not technique: immediate office probing versus 6 months of observation then facility probing gave bilateral success in 66% versus 76% (difference −10%, 95% CI −35% to 14%), with 56% of observed infants resolving in both eyes without any surgery. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): balloon and intubation are reasonable escalations after failed probing, but 'beats probing' is unproven. Tier C is set: the technique comparison rests on non-randomised prospective cohorts.

cards.headline: PEDIG 2008: primary balloon dilation succeeded in 82% of eyes (95% CI 74–88%) — a single-arm series with no probing comparator
cards.summary: PEDIG 2008: primary balloon dilation succeeded in 82% of eyes (95% CI 74–88%) — a single-arm series with no probing comparator
cards.people: 102 children (151 eyes) aged 12 to under 48 months (mean 23 months) at 20 sites with congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction and no previous nasolacrimal surgery, all treated with balloon catheter dilation; success was absence of epiphora, increased tear lake and mucous discharge at the 1-month outcome visit.
cards.result: The proportion of eyes treated successfully was 82% (95% confidence interval 74% to 88%). The dye disappearance test at outcome was normal in 105 of 143 tested eyes (73%), indeterminate in 15 (10%) and abnormal in 23 (16%). The authors state plainly that without a randomised comparison they could not determine how this success rate compares with simple probing or intubation.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm data: an 82% success rate sounds strong until set against probing's own reported success and against spontaneous resolution; this study design cannot rank the techniques, and the outcome visit was only 1 month after surgery.
cards.source: Repka MX et al. Primary treatment of nasolacrimal duct obstruction with balloon catheter dilation in children younger than 4 years of age. Journal of AAPOS. 2008. PMID: 18929305. cards.headline: PEDIG 2009 (after failed probing): balloon success 77% versus intubation 84% adjusted — risk ratio 1.08 (0.95–1.22), no significant difference
cards.summary: PEDIG 2009 (after failed probing): balloon success 77% versus intubation 84% adjusted — risk ratio 1.08 (0.95–1.22), no significant difference
cards.people: 159 children aged 6 months to under 48 months with a history of a single failed nasolacrimal probing and at least one sign of obstruction; 199 eyes underwent either balloon catheter dilation or nasolacrimal duct intubation, with success assessed 6 months after surgery.
cards.result: Treatment success was reported in 65 of 84 eyes (77%; 95% confidence interval 65% to 85%) in the balloon group versus 72 of 88 eyes (84% after adjustment for intereye correlation; 74% to 91%) in the intubation group — risk ratio for success 1.08 (0.95 to 1.22) for intubation versus balloon. The authors concluded the two procedures alleviate signs in a similar percentage of patients.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen, not randomised, so case mix may differ between groups; and this is a post-failed-probing population — it says nothing about which procedure should be first-line.

cards.headline: PEDIG 2013 (randomised, timing not technique): immediate probing 66% bilateral success versus 76% with observation-then-probing; 56% resolved with no surgery at all
cards.summary: PEDIG 2013 (randomised, timing not technique): immediate probing 66% bilateral success versus 76% with observation-then-probing; 56% resolved with no surgery at all
cards.people: 57 infants aged 6 to under 10 months with bilateral congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, randomised to immediate office-based probing (n = 31) or 6 months of observation and non-surgical management followed by facility probing for unresolved cases (n = 26); success was absence of signs in both eyes at 18 months.
cards.result: In the observation group, obstruction resolved without surgery in both eyes for 14 participants (56%), in one eye for 5 (20%) and in neither for 6 (24%). Treatment success at 18 months in both eyes was 19 of 29 (66%) with immediate probing versus 19 of 25 (76%) with observation and deferred probing (difference −10%; 95% confidence interval −35% to 14%). Both approaches were judged successful and reasonable.
cards.watchOut: This trial randomised timing, not balloon or intubation versus probing — it is carded because it is the only randomised evidence in the area and because its 56% spontaneous-resolution rate is the benchmark any uncontrolled 'success rate' for balloon or intubation must beat to claim superiority.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three procedures, similar numbers, no randomised ranking — escalation after failed probing is practice, not proven superiority
cards.summary: Synthesis: three procedures, similar numbers, no randomised ranking — escalation after failed probing is practice, not proven superiority
cards.people: Two prospective PEDIG cohorts (151 eyes primary balloon; 199 eyes after failed probing) and one randomised PEDIG trial of probing timing (57 infants).
cards.result: Primary balloon dilation: 82% success, uncontrolled. After failed probing: balloon 77% versus intubation 84% adjusted (RR 1.08, 0.95–1.22). Spontaneous resolution without surgery: 56% of bilaterally affected infants over 6 months. No randomised trial compares balloon or intubation with probing head-to-head. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference), Tier C for the non-randomised technique evidence.
cards.watchOut: The null here is an absence-of-evidence null: balloon or intubation may genuinely help the individual child whose probing failed — the 2009 cohort supports using them then — but a shelf claim that they 'beat probing' would outrun every design on this page.

shelves.title: Bimodal neuromodulation for tinnitus (sound plus tongue stimulation, the Lenire device): symptoms fell in two large studies — but neither had a sham control, so how much is the device is unproven
shelves.question: In adults with chronic tinnitus — the phantom ringing a visitor simply asked about as 'what is tinnitus' — does bimodal neuromodulation (sound delivered to the ears paired with electrical stimulation of the tongue) reduce tinnitus symptom severity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Animals · Cohort Studies · Electric Stimulation · Humans · Research Design · Tinnitus/therapy · Tongue · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the symptom scores move, the control group is missing. In the randomised TENT-A1 study of 326 adults with chronic subjective tinnitus (Conlon B et al., PMID: 33028707), all three bimodal stimulation arms improved on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (effect sizes -0.87 to -0.92) and Tinnitus Functional Index (-0.77 to -0.87) over 12 weeks, with gains persisting to 12 months in some settings — but every arm received active stimulation, so there was no sham or untreated comparator. In the TENT-A3 pivotal study of 112 participants (Boedts M et al., PMID: 39160146), adding tongue stimulation after 6 weeks of sound-only stimulation raised the responder rate in moderate-to-severe tinnitus from 43.2% to 58.6% on the THI (p=0.022) — a within-person comparison, not a parallel control — and the difference was not seen in the full cohort. No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported in either study, and the device has FDA De Novo authorisation. This shelf exists because the visitor question 'what is tinnitus' is already answered live (Shelf #2298, and CBT at #634); bimodal neuromodulation is the cardable tinnitus intervention not already asked. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): symptom improvement is consistent and durable, but with no sham-controlled trial the specific effect of the device over sound therapy, attention and time is unmeasured.

cards.headline: Conlon 2020 (TENT-A1): 326 adults, all on active bimodal stimulation — THI effect sizes -0.87 to -0.92 at 12 weeks, some gains held at 12 months, no sham arm
cards.summary: Conlon 2020 (TENT-A1): 326 adults, all on active bimodal stimulation — THI effect sizes -0.87 to -0.92 at 12 weeks, some gains held at 12 months, no sham arm
cards.type: Randomised double-blind exploratory trial with three active arms (Conlon 2020, TENT-A1)
cards.people: 326 adults with chronic subjective tinnitus randomised to three parallel arms receiving different settings of bimodal neuromodulation (sound to the ears plus electrical stimulation to the tongue) for 12 weeks, with a 12-month post-treatment phase.
cards.result: Tinnitus symptom severity fell significantly in all arms at end of treatment: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory Cohen's d -0.87 to -0.92 (p<0.001) and Tinnitus Functional Index -0.77 to -0.87 (p<0.001). For specific stimulation settings, improvements continued for 12 months after treatment. Compliance and satisfaction were high and there were no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Randomised and double-blinded — but only between different active settings. With no sham, sound-only or waiting-list arm, the trial cannot separate the device's specific effect from placebo response, regression to the mean and the natural fluctuation of tinnitus, all of which are large for subjective tinnitus scores.

cards.headline: Boedts 2024 (TENT-A3): bimodal stage beat the sound-only stage in moderate-to-severe tinnitus (responders 58.6% vs 43.2%) — but not in the full cohort, and participants were their own controls
cards.summary: Boedts 2024 (TENT-A3): bimodal stage beat the sound-only stage in moderate-to-severe tinnitus (responders 58.6% vs 43.2%) — but not in the full cohort, and participants were their own controls
cards.type: Multi-site single-arm controlled pivotal trial (Boedts 2024, TENT-A3)
cards.people: 112 participants with tinnitus treated with the Lenire device: 6 weeks of sound-only stimulation (Stage 1) followed by 6 weeks of bimodal sound-plus-tongue stimulation (Stage 2), each participant serving as their own control. A responder was a >7-point improvement on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory.
cards.result: In participants with moderate or more severe tinnitus, the responder rate was 58.6% (95% CI 43.5% to 73.6%) in the bimodal stage versus 43.2% (95% CI 29.7% to 57.8%) in the sound-only stage (p=0.022); on the Tinnitus Functional Index the rates were 45.5% versus 29.6% (p=0.010). The superiority was not observed in the full cohort across all severity groups. There were no device-related serious adverse events. The results supported FDA De Novo approval of the Lenire device.
cards.watchOut: Stage 2 always followed Stage 1, so cumulative treatment time, expectation and dropout are entangled with the bimodal effect; the headline result is a subgroup (moderate-to-severe) finding, absent in the full cohort. The tested product is a specific commercial device — Lenire (Neuromod Devices) — named here because device identity is the intervention; results may not transfer to other bimodal devices or settings.
cards.source: Boedts M et al. Combining sound with tongue stimulation for the treatment of tinnitus: a multi-site single-arm controlled pivotal trial. Nature communications. 2024. PMID: 39160146. multi-site single-arm controlled pivotal trial (boedts 2024, tent-a3) 112 participants with tinnitus treated with the lenire device: 6 weeks of sound-only stimulation (stage 1) followed by 6 weeks of bimodal sound-plus-tongue stimulation (stage 2), each participant serving as their own control. a responder was a >7-point improvement on the tinnitus handicap inventory. in participants with moderate or more severe tinnitus, the responder rate was 58.6% (95% ci 43.5% to 73.6%) in the bimodal stage versus 43.2% (95% ci 29.7% to 57.8%) in the sound-only stage (p=0.022); on the tinnitus functional index the rates were 45.5% versus 29.6% (p=0.010). the superiority was not observed in the full cohort across all severity groups. there were no device-related serious adverse events. the results supported fda de novo approval of the lenire device. stage 2 always followed stage 1, so cumulative treatment time, expectation and dropout are entangled with the bimodal effect; the headline result is a subgroup (moderate-to-severe) finding, absent in the full cohort. the tested product is a specific commercial device — lenire (neuromod devices) — named here because device identity is the intervention; results may not transfer to other bimodal devices or settings. boedts m et al. combining sound with tongue stimulation for the treatment of tinnitus: a multi-site single-arm controlled pivotal trial. nature communications. 2024. pmid: 39160146. registry id: nct05227365. mesh: tinnitus/therapy · humans · female · male · middle aged · adult · tongue · treatment outcome · aged · electric stimulation therapy/methods/instrumentation · acoustic stimulation/methods · sound · combined modality therapy/methods

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent symptom improvement, no sham anywhere — the size of the true device effect is unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent symptom improvement, no sham anywhere — the size of the true device effect is unknown
cards.people: Two studies of the same bimodal device programme totalling 438 participants with chronic tinnitus: a 326-person randomised comparison of active settings (TENT-A1) and a 112-person single-arm staged pivotal study (TENT-A3).
cards.result: THI/TFI scores improved substantially in every treated group (effect sizes up to -0.92), the bimodal stage outperformed a preceding sound-only stage in moderate-to-severe tinnitus (58.6% vs 43.2% responders), and no treatment-related serious adverse events occurred. No study included a sham-stimulation or untreated control group. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single-device, sham-free evidence base.
cards.watchOut: Tinnitus trials are notoriously placebo-responsive, and both studies were run within the device developer's programme. A sham-controlled trial is the missing experiment; until it exists, patients should be told the improvement is real in the data but its cause is not isolated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Conlon B et al. Science Translational Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 33028707); Boedts M et al. Nature Communications. 2024 (PMID: 39160146).
