shelves.title: Trachoma mass treatment: community azithromycin beat tetracycline ointment (infection down 93% versus 77% in Egypt at one year) — but twice-yearly rounds added nothing over annual, and narrowing treatment to young children let infection creep back up
shelves.question: For trachoma control in endemic communities, does mass azithromycin distribution reduce ocular chlamydial infection better than community tetracycline treatment — and does giving it twice a year, or targeting it to young children, do better than annual whole-community rounds?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Azithromycin/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Directly Observed Therapy · Endemic Diseases · Ethiopia/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Hypersensitivity/complications · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis · Ointments · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/drug therapy · Tetracycline/administration & dosage · Trachoma/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — mass azithromycin works against the old standard; intensifying or narrowing it does not. In the three-country village trial (Schachter J et al., PMID: 10466664), community-wide oral azithromycin cleared infection in 866 (95%) of 924 initially positive people versus 482 (82%) of 587 on prolonged topical tetracycline, and at one year village infection rates had fallen further with azithromycin than tetracycline (relative reductions 93% versus 77% in Egypt, 78 versus 66% in The Gambia, 64 versus 55% in Tanzania). In hyperendemic Ethiopia (Gebre T et al., PMID: 22192488), however, twice-yearly distribution bought nothing over annual: after 42 months, infection prevalence in children was 3.2% in twice-yearly subdistricts versus 1.9% in annual ones, from baselines of 38.3% and 41.9% (pooled comparison p>0.99), though elimination may have been about 7.5 months faster with twice-yearly rounds (p=0.10). And after years of mass treatment, narrowing the target failed: in TANA II (Mahmud H et al., PMID: 37021692), communities randomised to treat only preschool children, or only households with an active case, saw childhood infection prevalence rise over 36 months (4.3% to 8.7% age-targeted; 2.8% to 6.3% household-targeted), with no difference between the two targeted strategies (adjusted difference 2.4 percentage points, 95% CI −4.8 to 9.6). PROPOSED SPLIT: annual whole-community azithromycin is the effective core; extra rounds add cost without prevalence benefit, and targeted rounds let transmission re-establish.

cards.headline: Schachter 1999 (Egypt, Gambia, Tanzania): community azithromycin cleared infection in 95% of positive people versus 82% on tetracycline; one-year village infection reductions 64–93% versus 55–77%
cards.summary: Schachter 1999 (Egypt, Gambia, Tanzania): community azithromycin cleared infection in 95% of positive people versus 82% on tetracycline; one-year village infection reductions 64–93% versus 55–77%
cards.people: Matched pairs of villages in trachoma-endemic areas of Egypt, The Gambia and Tanzania, randomised to community-wide oral azithromycin (three doses at weekly intervals) or 1% topical tetracycline daily for 6 weeks; infection measured by ligase chain reaction at baseline, 2–4.5 months and 12–14 months; baseline village-wide positivity ranged from 16.5% (Tanzania) to 43.6% (Egypt).
cards.result: Of participants initially LCR-positive, 866 (95%) of 924 who received at least one azithromycin dose were negative at follow-up, versus 482 (82%) of 587 who received 28 days or more of topical tetracycline. At 1 year, village-wide LCR positivity had fallen further with azithromycin than tetracycline in all three countries (reductions of 93% versus 77% in Egypt, 78 versus 66% in The Gambia, 64 versus 55% in Tanzania), and clinical activity also fell more after azithromycin. In multivariate analysis, not receiving azithromycin, age under 10 years, and baseline positivity predicted remaining positive at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: A village-pair design from the pre-elimination era, when the comparator was a 6-week ointment course with predictably poor real-world adherence — the trial measures azithromycin against the old programme as actually delivered, not against ointment perfectly applied. Infection, not blindness, is the outcome.
cards.source: Schachter J et al. Azithromycin in control of trachoma. Lancet. 1999. PMID: 10466664. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gebre 2012 (TANA, Ethiopia): annual versus twice-yearly mass azithromycin — infection in children 1.9% versus 3.2% at 42 months, no difference (p>0.99)
cards.summary: Gebre 2012 (TANA, Ethiopia): annual versus twice-yearly mass azithromycin — infection in children 1.9% versus 3.2% at 42 months, no difference (p>0.99)
cards.people: 24 subdistricts in hyperendemic northern Ethiopia randomised to annual or twice-yearly mass azithromycin for all residents of all ages (single directly observed oral dose; tetracycline ointment offered to infants under 12 months, pregnant women and those declining azithromycin); primary outcome prevalence of ocular chlamydial infection in children aged 0–9 years, measured every 6 months for 42 months; coverage in 1–9-year-olds exceeded 80% at every visit.
cards.result: Infection prevalence in children fell from a mean 41.9% (95% CI 31.5–52.2) at baseline to 1.9% (0.3–3.5) at 42 months with annual treatment, and from 38.3% (29.0–47.6) to 3.2% (0.0–6.5) with twice-yearly treatment; prevalence did not differ between arms at 18, 30 or 42 months (pooled regression p>0.99, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.06). Mean elimination time was 7.5 months earlier in the twice-yearly group (p=0.10), not significant.
cards.watchOut: Both arms improved enormously — the trial answers a programme-design question (is a second annual round worth it?) in a hyperendemic setting with high coverage; it does not test mass treatment against none, and its confidence interval cannot exclude a small speed advantage to twice-yearly rounds.
cards.source: Gebre T et al. Comparison of annual versus twice-yearly mass azithromycin treatment for hyperendemic trachoma in Ethiopia: a cluster-randomised trial. Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22192488. cards.headline: Mahmud 2023 (TANA II): after prior mass treatment, targeting azithromycin to preschool children or to case households let infection rise — 4.3% to 8.7% and 2.8% to 6.3% over 36 months
cards.summary: Mahmud 2023 (TANA II): after prior mass treatment, targeting azithromycin to preschool children or to case households let infection rise — 4.3% to 8.7% and 2.8% to 6.3% over 36 months
cards.people: 48 Ethiopian communities previously treated with annual mass azithromycin, randomised equally to annual distributions targeted to children aged 0–5 years, targeted to households containing a child with clinically active trachoma, continued whole-community annual distributions, or cessation; primary outcome community prevalence of ocular chlamydia infection in children aged 0–9 years at month 36, with laboratory staff masked.
cards.result: Infection prevalence among children rose from 4.3% (95% CI 0.9–8.6) at baseline to 8.7% (4.2–13.9) at month 36 in the age-targeted arm, and from 2.8% (0.8–5.3) to 6.3% (2.9–10.6) in the household-targeted arm. Adjusted for baseline, 36-month prevalence was 2.4 percentage points higher in the age-targeted than the household-targeted group (95% CI −4.8 to 9.6; p=0.50, the prespecified primary analysis). The authors concluded neither targeted approach reduced ocular chlamydia over the 3 years. No adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the two targeted arms in detail; the whole-community and cessation arms' trajectories are not in this record, so the card claims only what is shown — that targeting did not hold the line — not a quantified comparison against continued mass treatment.
cards.source: Mahmud H et al. Targeted Mass Azithromycin Distribution for Trachoma: A Community-Randomized Trial (TANA II). Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2023. PMID: 37021692. cards.headline: Synthesis: the antibiotic and the whole-community reach are what work — frequency beyond annual and clever targeting both fail their trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: the antibiotic and the whole-community reach are what work — frequency beyond annual and clever targeting both fail their trials
cards.people: Three cluster-randomised programmes: village pairs in three countries (azithromycin versus tetracycline), 24 Ethiopian subdistricts (annual versus twice-yearly), and 48 previously treated Ethiopian communities (targeted versus continued mass strategies).
cards.result: Versus tetracycline: infection clearance 95% versus 82% of positive individuals, with larger one-year village reductions in all three countries. Annual versus twice-yearly: 1.9% versus 3.2% prevalence at 42 months, no difference. Targeted after mass treatment: prevalence rose to 8.7% (age-targeted) and 6.3% (household-targeted) by 36 months. PROPOSED SPLIT, with the benefit carried by annual whole-community distribution.
cards.watchOut: All endpoints are ocular chlamydial infection or clinical activity, surrogates for the blindness trachoma programmes ultimately exist to prevent; and mass azithromycin's community effects beyond trachoma (including the child-mortality question) are housed on their own shelf in this library, not re-argued here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schachter J et al. Lancet. 1999 (PMID: 10466664); Gebre T et al. Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 22192488); Mahmud H et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2023 (PMID: 37021692).

shelves.title: Chlorhexidine mouthwash: plaque down by about a quarter and gingivitis measurably lower within weeks — a real effect on gum scores, paid for in tooth staining and altered taste
shelves.question: In people with gingivitis, does chlorhexidine mouthrinse used alongside brushing reduce plaque and gum inflammation compared with brushing alone or a placebo rinse — and at what cost in side effects?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Child · Chlorhexidine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dental Plaque/complications/drug therapy · Dental Plaque Index · Dental Prophylaxis · Female · Gingivitis/drug therapy/etiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouthwashes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Oral Hygiene · Publication Bias · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors · Tooth Discoloration/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for plaque and mild gingivitis scores, with staining as the certain price. The Cochrane review (James P et al., PMID: 28362061) included 51 studies analysing 5,345 participants: after 4-6 weeks, chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduced gingivitis by 0.21 on the 0-3 Gingival Index (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31; 10 trials, 805 participants with mild gingival inflammation; high-quality evidence) — an effect the reviewers note was not considered clinically relevant at that mild level — and reduced plaque by a large standardised amount (SMD 1.45 lower, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.90; 12 trials, 950 participants), with similar effects at 6 months. Extrinsic tooth staining increased by a large standardised amount at 4-6 weeks (SMD 1.07 higher, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.34; moderate-quality evidence), and taste disturbance, mucosal soreness/irritation and burning were commonly reported. A general-practice trial (Eaton KA et al., PMID: 9083904; 121 subjects, 98 completing) found 0.12% chlorhexidine reduced plaque accumulation by 28% and gingival inflammation by 25% over 12 weeks versus placebo rinse (plaque score 1.33 to 0.96 versus 1.31 to 1.13; p<0.001; gingival bleeding 0.56 to 0.42 versus unchanged 0.54-0.55). There were insufficient data for moderate or severe gingivitis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): chlorhexidine rinse does what the bottle claims on plaque and mild gum inflammation for as long as it is used — it is an adjunct to brushing, not a substitute, and it stains teeth.

cards.headline: James 2017 (Cochrane): 51 studies — gingivitis -0.21, plaque SMD -1.45, staining SMD +1.07; the gingivitis gain in mild disease 'not considered clinically relevant'
cards.summary: James 2017 (Cochrane): 51 studies — gingivitis -0.21, plaque SMD -1.45, staining SMD +1.07; the gingivitis gain in mild disease 'not considered clinically relevant'
cards.people: 51 randomised studies analysing 5,345 participants (children and adults with gingivitis or periodontitis, healthy participants, and some with medical conditions or special care needs), comparing chlorhexidine mouthrinse plus mechanical oral hygiene (brushing, with or without flossing or professional cleaning) against mechanical hygiene alone or with placebo/control rinse, for at least 4 weeks. Fifty studies were at high risk of bias, though the reviewers judged this did not affect the gingivitis and plaque quality assessments.
cards.result: Gingivitis at 4-6 weeks: mean reduction 0.21 on the 0-3 Gingival Index (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31; 10 trials, 805 participants with mild inflammation, mean score 1; high-quality evidence), with a similar effect at 6 months; insufficient data for mean scores of 1.1-3 (moderate/severe). Plaque at 4-6 weeks: SMD 1.45 lower (95% CI 1.00 to 1.90; 12 trials, 950 participants; high-quality evidence), similar at 6 months. Extrinsic tooth staining at 4-6 weeks: SMD 1.07 higher (95% CI 0.80 to 1.34; 8 trials, 415 participants; moderate-quality evidence), also increased at 7-12 weeks and 6 months. Calculus results were inconclusive; no concentration or rinsing-frequency advantage could be determined. Commonly reported adverse effects: taste disturbance/alteration (11 studies), mucosal soreness, irritation, mild desquamation or ulceration (13 studies), and burning sensation or burning tongue (9 studies).
cards.watchOut: The high-quality gingivitis estimate comes from people whose gums were only mildly inflamed to begin with, where a 0.21-point change is small; the review cannot say what chlorhexidine does for the moderate-to-severe gum disease people actually worry about. Plaque and staining are both large effects — the trade is intrinsic, not incidental.
cards.source: James P et al. Chlorhexidine mouthrinse as an adjunctive treatment for gingival health. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28362061. cards.headline: Eaton 1997: in ordinary dental practices, 0.12% chlorhexidine cut plaque by 28% and gingival inflammation by 25% over 12 weeks versus placebo rinse (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Eaton 1997: in ordinary dental practices, 0.12% chlorhexidine cut plaque by 28% and gingival inflammation by 25% over 12 weeks versus placebo rinse (p<0.001)
cards.people: 121 healthy subjects aged 18-65 (mean 35) in five general dental practices in the south of England, randomised to 0.12% chlorhexidine digluconate mouthrinse (60) or placebo rinse (61) for 12 weeks, with full-mouth plaque and gingival bleeding assessments at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks by calibrated examiners; 98 subjects (48 chlorhexidine, 50 placebo) completed the study. Baseline plaque and gingivitis levels were low.
cards.result: Whole-mouth plaque score at week 12: 0.96 in the chlorhexidine group (from 1.33 at baseline) versus 1.13 on placebo (from 1.31) — significantly lower (p<0.001). Gingival bleeding score fell from 0.56 to 0.42 with chlorhexidine and was unchanged on placebo (0.54 to 0.55). The authors summarise the effect as a 28% relative reduction in plaque accumulation and a 25% relative reduction in gingival inflammation over 12 weeks, with almost twice the reduction at proximal molar sites with heavy baseline plaque (50.6% versus 27.6%).
cards.watchOut: A feasibility-framed practice-based trial in people with low baseline disease, and 23 of 121 subjects did not complete; its percentages are relative reductions on index scores, not fewer cases of gum disease. It confirms the Cochrane direction in a real-world setting rather than extending it to sicker mouths.
cards.source: Eaton KA et al. The effects of a 0.12% chlorhexidine-digluconate-containing mouthrinse versus a placebo on plaque and gingival inflammation over a 3-month period. A multicentre study carried out in general dental practices. Journal of clinical periodontology. 1997. PMID: 9083904. cards.headline: Synthesis: the rare mouthwash claim the trials back — smaller plaque, calmer mild gums, browner teeth
cards.summary: Synthesis: the rare mouthwash claim the trials back — smaller plaque, calmer mild gums, browner teeth
cards.people: Cochrane review of 51 studies (5,345 participants) plus a 121-subject practice-based double-blind trial of 0.12% chlorhexidine rinse over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Gingivitis: -0.21 on a 0-3 index at 4-6 weeks in mild disease (high-quality evidence). Plaque: SMD 1.45 lower (Cochrane) and 28% relative reduction in the practice trial. Staining: SMD 1.07 higher, plus taste disturbance and mucosal irritation commonly reported. No proven advantage for any concentration or frequency, and no adequate data in moderate-to-severe gingivitis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as an adjunct to mechanical cleaning.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here shows chlorhexidine prevents periodontitis, tooth loss or the need for dental treatment — the outcomes are index scores over weeks to months. Tier C is not set: a 51-study Cochrane review carries the shelf.

shelves.title: Flurbiprofen throat lozenges: sore-throat relief significantly better than a plain demulcent lozenge from about 30 minutes, lasting 2-4 hours — in two industry-era double-blind trials totalling over 600 patients
shelves.question: In adults with sore throat from an upper respiratory infection, does a flurbiprofen 8.75 mg lozenge relieve throat pain better than a placebo (demulcent) lozenge, and how quickly and how long does it work?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Flurbiprofen/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Pharyngitis/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest symptomatic relief, measured in hours. In Watson N et al. (PMID: 11198725), 301 patients with subjective and objective signs of sore throat were randomised to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg lozenges (129), flurbiprofen 12.5 mg (43) or a demulcent placebo lozenge (129): the 8.75 mg lozenge was superior to placebo on a number of efficacy parameters, notably throat soreness, which was significantly reduced after 15 minutes (p<0.05) with effects sustained for at least 2 hours (p<0.05), and multiple dosing continued to provide effective relief over the 4-day treatment period; both treatments were well tolerated. In Benrimoj SI et al. (PMID: 27517548), 320 patients with sore throat from an upper respiratory tract infection were randomised to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg (128), 12.5 mg (64) or placebo lozenges (128): the 8.75 mg lozenge was significantly superior to placebo for total pain relief summed over 15-120 minutes and for throat soreness over 2 hours and swollen throat over 2 and 6 hours (all p<0.05); relief began within 15 minutes (attributed by the authors partly to the lozenge's demulcent effect), statistically significant differences from placebo were detected within 30 minutes and sustained over 4 hours, and there were no significant differences in adverse events once taste perversion reports were removed (p=0.776). The higher 12.5 mg dose was not significantly better than 8.75 mg in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a flurbiprofen lozenge is a reasonable purchase for a bad sore throat — expect a measurable edge over a plain lozenge for a few hours per lozenge, not a shorter illness.

cards.headline: Watson 2000: throat soreness significantly reduced from 15 minutes and sustained at least 2 hours versus placebo lozenge (p<0.05); relief maintained over 4 days of dosing
cards.summary: Watson 2000: throat soreness significantly reduced from 15 minutes and sustained at least 2 hours versus placebo lozenge (p<0.05); relief maintained over 4 days of dosing
cards.people: 301 patients with subjective and objective signs of sore throat, randomly assigned to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg lozenges (129), flurbiprofen 12.5 mg lozenges (43) or placebo — a demulcent lozenge without active drug (129). Efficacy was assessed on subjective rating scales primarily after a single dose and over a 4-day multiple-dose period.
cards.result: Flurbiprofen 8.75 mg was superior to placebo on a number of efficacy parameters, notably throat soreness: significantly reduced after 15 minutes (p<0.05), with effects sustained for at least 2 hours (p<0.05). Multiple dosing continued to provide effective symptomatic relief over the 4-day treatment period. Results for the 12.5 mg dose were variable — the authors attribute this to its small sample size (43) — but not inconsistent with previous trials. Both treatments were tolerated well. The record reports significance and time course rather than absolute score differences.
cards.watchOut: The placebo was itself a demulcent lozenge, so the trial isolates the drug's added effect over sucking a soothing lozenge — a fair and demanding comparator — but the abstract gives p-values without the size of the pain-score gap, so how much better it feels cannot be quantified from the record.
cards.source: Watson N et al. Relief of sore throat with the anti-inflammatory throat lozenge flurbiprofen 8.75 mg: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of efficacy and safety. International journal of clinical practice. 2000. PMID: 11198725. cards.headline: Benrimoj 2001: primary endpoint (total pain relief, 15-120 minutes) significantly better than placebo; swollen-throat relief significant at 2 and 6 hours; adverse events no different (p=0.776)
cards.summary: Benrimoj 2001: primary endpoint (total pain relief, 15-120 minutes) significantly better than placebo; swollen-throat relief significant at 2 and 6 hours; adverse events no different (p=0.776)
cards.people: 320 patients with objective and subjective evidence of sore throat due to upper respiratory tract infection, randomised to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg (128), flurbiprofen 12.5 mg (64) or demulcent placebo lozenges (128); single-dose efficacy was rated over 6 hours (pain relief, throat soreness, swollen throat) and tolerability was assessed over a 5-day multiple-dose regimen. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: Flurbiprofen 8.75 mg was significantly superior to placebo for the primary variable, total pain relief summed over 15-120 minutes (TOTPAR15-120min), and for reducing throat soreness over 2 hours and swollen throat over 2 and 6 hours (p<0.05). The 12.5 mg dose was not significantly better than 8.75 mg. Relief occurred within 15 minutes (attributed to demulcency), statistically significant active-versus-placebo differences were detected within 30 minutes and sustained over 4 hours. With taste perversion reports removed, adverse-event incidence did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.776).
cards.watchOut: Both flurbiprofen trials are from the product's launch era (2000-2001) and use the manufacturer's dose-ranging design; independent replication is absent. Sore throat is self-limiting — these trials measure comfort over hours, and no lozenge trial shows a shorter illness or fewer complications.
cards.source: Benrimoj SI et al. Efficacy and Tolerability of the Anti-inflammatory Throat Lozenge Flurbiprofen 8.75mg in the Treatment of Sore Throat : A Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study. Clinical drug investigation. 2001. PMID: 27517548. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine, short-lived edge over a plain lozenge — buy it for comfort, at the lower dose, with hours-long expectations
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine, short-lived edge over a plain lozenge — buy it for comfort, at the lower dose, with hours-long expectations
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials totalling 621 patients with sore throat (one in pharyngitis with objective signs, one in upper respiratory infection), each comparing flurbiprofen 8.75 mg and 12.5 mg lozenges with a demulcent placebo lozenge.
cards.result: Both trials: 8.75 mg significantly superior to placebo on summed pain relief and throat soreness (p<0.05), onset of significant separation within 15-30 minutes, duration at least 2 hours and up to 4-6 hours on some measures; 12.5 mg never significantly better than 8.75 mg; tolerability comparable to placebo apart from taste perversion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for symptomatic relief.
cards.watchOut: Neither record reports absolute pain-score differences, so the size of the benefit — as opposed to its existence and duration — is unquantified in the sources a buyer can check. Tier C is not set: two concordant double-blind trials carry the shelf.

shelves.title: Artificial tears for dry eye: symptoms improve in trials, but after 43 randomised comparisons Cochrane could not say any ordinary tear beats another — one polyacrylic-acid gel beat polyvinyl alcohol in two small trials
shelves.question: In adults with dry eye syndrome, do over-the-counter artificial tear drops relieve symptoms — and is any formulation demonstrably better than the others or than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acrylic Resins/administration & dosage · Dry Eye Syndromes/drug therapy · Humans · Lubricant Eye Drops/administration & dosage/chemistry · Nonprescription Drugs/administration & dosage/chemistry · Polyvinyl Alcohol/administration & dosage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — improvement is consistently reported, superiority is not. The Cochrane review (Pucker AD et al., PMID: 26905373) included 43 randomised trials with 3,497 participants with dry eye, almost all comparing one over-the-counter tear against another rather than against placebo: it found general uncertainty whether different tears provide similar relief of signs and symptoms compared with each other or placebo, with the single consistent result that 0.2% polyacrylic acid-based tears were more effective for dry eye symptoms than 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol-based tears in two trials (175 participants); all other comparisons produced contradictory results or no between-group differences. Evidence quality was low, and 18 further registered trials enrolling 2,079 participants had no published results — a high risk of publication bias. A modern head-to-head trial (Downie LE et al., PMID: 31734510; 242 subjects over 90 days) compared a nano-emulsion tear containing carboxymethylcellulose, glycerin, flaxseed and castor oils and osmoprotectants (named in the record as OM3) with a similar tear without trehalose and flaxseed oil (named in the record as Refresh Optive Advanced): both groups improved significantly on the Ocular Surface Disease Index, staining and tear breakup time, with small between-group differences favouring the nano-emulsion on combined staining at all timepoints and corneal staining at day 90 (p<0.05); treatment-related adverse events were 6.7% versus 9.8%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): tears are safe and symptoms do improve while using them — but the trial record gives no reason to pay a premium for one ordinary formulation over another. Prescription drops and omega-3 for dry eye are housed at live shelf #611.

cards.headline: Pucker 2016 (Cochrane): 43 trials, 3,497 participants — 'uncertainty' overall; only 0.2% polyacrylic acid over 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol was consistent (2 trials, 175 participants)
cards.summary: Pucker 2016 (Cochrane): 43 trials, 3,497 participants — 'uncertainty' overall; only 0.2% polyacrylic acid over 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol was consistent (2 trials, 175 participants)
cards.people: 43 randomised and quasi-randomised trials, 3,497 adults diagnosed with dry eye, comparing over-the-counter artificial tears with another class of tear, placebo or no treatment; heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria, formulations, comparisons and outcome measures limited meta-analysis, so most results were summarised narratively. Searches to December 2015.
cards.result: In general there was uncertainty whether different OTC artificial tears provide similar relief of signs and symptoms compared with each other or placebo. The exception: 0.2% polyacrylic acid-based tears were consistently more effective at treating dry eye symptoms than 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol-based tears in two trials (175 participants). All other included tears produced contradictory between-group results or no between-group differences. Tears may be generally safe but not without adverse events. Evidence quality was low (high risk of bias, poor outcome reporting), and 18 potentially eligible registered trials with 2,079 participants had no results available — a high risk of publication bias.
cards.watchOut: Almost none of this literature compares a tear against no treatment, so 'symptoms improve' inside trials cannot be separated from placebo effect, regression to the mean and the run-in care every participant receives. That is why this shelf is MAYBE despite 43 trials — quantity is not the problem; design is.
cards.source: Pucker AD et al. Over the counter (OTC) artificial tear drops for dry eye syndrome. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 26905373. cards.headline: Downie 2020: both tears improved symptoms significantly over 90 days; the flaxseed-oil nano-emulsion won only on staining measures (p<0.05), with fewer treatment-related adverse events (6.7% versus 9.8%)
cards.summary: Downie 2020: both tears improved symptoms significantly over 90 days; the flaxseed-oil nano-emulsion won only on staining measures (p<0.05), with fewer treatment-related adverse events (6.7% versus 9.8%)
cards.people: 242 subjects with dry eye disease, after a 7-day open-label run-in on carboxymethylcellulose 0.5% drops, randomised 1:1 for 90 days (at least twice daily) to a nano-emulsion tear containing carboxymethylcellulose, glycerin, flaxseed and castor oils and three osmoprotectants (120; named OM3 in the record) or a tear with the same ingredients except trehalose and flaxseed oil (122; named Refresh Optive Advanced in the record). Outcomes: Ocular Surface Disease Index (primary, change at day 90), tear breakup time and ocular staining.
cards.result: At day 90, significant improvements in OSDI, ocular staining and tear breakup time were evident in both treatment groups. Significant between-group differences (p<0.05) favouring the nano-emulsion were observed for combined ocular staining at all timepoints, corneal staining at day 90 and conjunctival staining at day 30 — not for the primary symptom endpoint as reported. Treatment-related adverse events: 6.7% (nano-emulsion) versus 9.8% (comparator); blurred vision was among the most common, at 0% versus 4.1%. The record reports directions and significance rather than the absolute OSDI changes.
cards.watchOut: A manufacturer-style formulation trial: both arms are active tears from the same product family, there is no placebo or no-treatment arm, and the wins are on staining (a sign) rather than the primary symptom score. It illustrates the Cochrane verdict — differences between tears, where found, are small and on surrogate measures.
cards.source: Downie LE et al. An artificial tear containing flaxseed oil for treating dry eye disease: A randomized controlled trial. The ocular surface. 2020. PMID: 31734510. randomised double-masked controlled trial (downie 2020) 242 subjects with dry eye disease, after a 7-day open-label run-in on carboxymethylcellulose 0.5% drops, randomised 1:1 for 90 days (at least twice daily) to a nano-emulsion tear containing carboxymethylcellulose, glycerin, flaxseed and castor oils and three osmoprotectants (120; named om3 in the record) or a tear with the same ingredients except trehalose and flaxseed oil (122; named refresh optive advanced in the record). outcomes: ocular surface disease index (primary, change at day 90), tear breakup time and ocular staining. at day 90, significant improvements in osdi, ocular staining and tear breakup time were evident in both treatment groups. significant between-group differences (p<0.05) favouring the nano-emulsion were observed for combined ocular staining at all timepoints, corneal staining at day 90 and conjunctival staining at day 30 — not for the primary symptom endpoint as reported. treatment-related adverse events: 6.7% (nano-emulsion) versus 9.8% (comparator); blurred vision was among the most common, at 0% versus 4.1%. the record reports directions and significance rather than the absolute osdi changes. a manufacturer-style formulation trial: both arms are active tears from the same product family, there is no placebo or no-treatment arm, and the wins are on staining (a sign) rather than the primary symptom score. it illustrates the cochrane verdict — differences between tears, where found, are small and on surrogate measures. downie le et al. an artificial tear containing flaxseed oil for treating dry eye disease: a randomized controlled trial. the ocular surface. 2020. pmid: 31734510. mesh: carboxymethylcellulose sodium · dry eye syndromes/drug therapy · humans · linseed oil · lubricant eye drops · ophthalmic solutions · tears

cards.headline: Synthesis: use tears for comfort — the evidence supports the category weakly and brand superiority barely at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: use tears for comfort — the evidence supports the category weakly and brand superiority barely at all
cards.people: Cochrane review of 43 trials (3,497 participants) plus a 242-subject double-masked formulation trial over 90 days, in adults with dry eye syndrome.
cards.result: Consistent findings: symptoms and signs improve during tear use in both arms of head-to-head trials; one formulation pair (polyacrylic acid over polyvinyl alcohol, 175 participants) and one staining advantage (nano-emulsion, p<0.05) are the only reproducible between-product differences; adverse events are uncommon (6.7-9.8% treatment-related in the modern trial). Eighteen registered trials (2,079 participants) remain unpublished. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Dry eye has strong placebo and Hawthorne effects and fluctuates with environment; patients whose symptoms persist despite tears need assessment for causes tears cannot fix. Tier C is not set: the shelf's caution comes from a Cochrane review, not a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pucker AD et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016 (PMID: 26905373); Downie LE et al. The ocular surface. 2020 (PMID: 31734510).

shelves.title: Ipratropium nasal spray for a cold: nasal discharge down 26% versus a salt-water spray and runny-nose severity down 31% — congestion untouched, nosebleeds and dryness up
shelves.question: In children and adults with the common cold, does intranasal ipratropium bromide spray reduce runny nose (rhinorrhoea) and nasal congestion compared with placebo spray or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Common Cold/drug therapy · Humans · Ipratropium/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Nasal Decongestants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Nasal Obstruction/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the dripping nose only; it does nothing for the blocked nose. The Cochrane review (AlBalawi ZH et al., PMID: 23784858) included seven trials with 2,144 participants: the four studies reporting subjective rhinorrhoea severity (1,959 participants) were consistent in finding statistically significant changes favouring ipratropium, two studies found better global improvement, but nasal congestion showed no significant change in any of the four studies reporting it; side effects were more frequent with ipratropium (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.40 to 3.11), mainly nasal dryness, blood-tinged mucus and nosebleeds, and overall risk of bias was moderate. The largest single trial (Hayden FG et al., PMID: 8678385; 411 healthy people aged 14-56 with colds of under 36 hours and at least moderate rhinorrhoea) measured the discharge itself: ipratropium 0.06% spray recipients had 26% less nasal discharge than the buffered-salt control spray (p=0.0024) and 34% less than untreated patients (p=0.0001), subjective rhinorrhoea severity was reduced by 31% relative versus control and 78% relative versus no treatment (p=0.0001 for both), and sneezing was reduced on days 2 and 4 (20% and 30% differences) — again with no reduction in nasal congestion. Blood-tinged mucus occurred in 16.8% on ipratropium versus 3.6% on control (p=0.01) and nasal dryness in 11.7% versus 3.6% (p=0.021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the one cold spray with a specific, measured anti-drip effect — useless for congestion, and it dries the nose it dries out.

cards.headline: AlBalawi 2013 (Cochrane): seven trials — rhinorrhoea significantly better in every reporting study, congestion unchanged in all four, side effects OR 2.09
cards.summary: AlBalawi 2013 (Cochrane): seven trials — rhinorrhoea significantly better in every reporting study, congestion unchanged in all four, side effects OR 2.09
cards.people: Seven randomised trials, 2,144 children and adults with the common cold, comparing intranasal ipratropium bromide with placebo spray or no treatment; primary outcomes were subjective rhinorrhoea severity, nasal congestion and overall improvement, with side effects (dry membranes, nosebleeds, systemic anticholinergic effects) secondary. Overall risk of bias was moderate.
cards.result: Four studies (1,959 participants) addressed subjective change in rhinorrhoea severity and were consistent in reporting statistically significant changes favouring ipratropium. Nasal congestion, reported in four studies, showed no significant change between groups. Two studies found a positive response for global assessment of overall improvement. Side effects were more frequent with ipratropium (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.40 to 3.11); commonly encountered were nasal dryness, blood-tinged mucus and epistaxis, appearing well tolerated and self-limiting. The authors conclude ipratropium is likely to be effective for rhinorrhoea, has no effect on congestion, and needs larger high-quality trials.
cards.watchOut: Subjective runny-nose scores in mostly moderate-bias trials are soft outcomes; the review could not pool a single headline number, which is why the objective discharge measurement in the Hayden trial below matters. Effects are for the days of a cold — nothing here supports use in allergic rhinitis, which is a different shelf's question.
cards.source: AlBalawi ZH et al. Intranasal ipratropium bromide for the common cold. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23784858. cards.headline: Hayden 1996: discharge weighed, not just rated — 26% less than control spray (p=0.0024), 34% less than no treatment (p=0.0001); blood-tinged mucus 16.8% versus 3.6%
cards.summary: Hayden 1996: discharge weighed, not just rated — 26% less than control spray (p=0.0024), 34% less than no treatment (p=0.0001); blood-tinged mucus 16.8% versus 3.6%
cards.people: 411 previously healthy people aged 14-56 at three university student health services, with cold symptoms for no more than 36 hours, at least moderate rhinorrhoea and documented nasal discharge of at least 1.5 g in one hour, randomised to ipratropium bromide 0.06% nasal spray (two 42-microgram sprays per nostril), buffered salt solution control spray, or no treatment, self-administered three to four times daily for 4 days; discharges were collected and weighed hourly during observation periods on days 1 and 2.
cards.result: Nasal discharge was 26% lower than control (p=0.0024) and 34% lower than no treatment (p=0.0001) in relative terms. Subjective rhinorrhoea severity was reduced by 31% relative versus control and 78% relative versus no treatment (p=0.0001 for both comparisons). Sneezing was reduced on day 2 (20% difference; p=0.03) and day 4 (30%; p=0.02), but nasal congestion was not reduced versus control spray. Blood-tinged mucus: 16.8% versus 3.6% (p=0.01); nasal dryness 11.7% versus 3.6% (p=0.021). Patients rated overall effectiveness more favourably for ipratropium on each day asked (p≤0.026 versus control; p≤0.002 versus no treatment).
cards.watchOut: Young healthy students with objectively heavy discharge are the best-case population for an anti-secretory drug; the 78% relative figure is against no treatment on a subjective scale and should not be quoted without its 26-31% blinded comparisons beside it. Four days of a cold is the whole horizon.
cards.source: Hayden FG et al. Effectiveness and safety of intranasal ipratropium bromide in common colds. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1996. PMID: 8678385. cards.headline: Synthesis: a narrow, honest win — the drip slows measurably, the blockage stays, and the nose pays in dryness and blood-tinged mucus
cards.summary: Synthesis: a narrow, honest win — the drip slows measurably, the blockage stays, and the nose pays in dryness and blood-tinged mucus
cards.people: Cochrane review of seven trials (2,144 participants) and its largest double-blind trial (411 participants with weighed nasal discharge), in common colds treated for up to four days.
cards.result: Rhinorrhoea: significant subjective improvement in all reporting trials; objectively 26% less discharge than control spray and 34% less than no treatment. Congestion: no effect in any study. Sneezing: modestly reduced. Harms: side effects OR 2.09 overall; blood-tinged mucus 16.8% versus 3.6% and dryness 11.7% versus 3.6% in the large trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), symptom-specific.
cards.watchOut: This is relief of one symptom of a self-limiting illness, not a cold treatment; people whose main misery is congestion should look to the decongestant shelves (#2461, #2569), whose records are separate. Tier C is not set: a Cochrane review plus a large concordant trial carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of AlBalawi ZH et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23784858); Hayden FG et al. Annals of internal medicine. 1996 (PMID: 8678385).

shelves.title: Salt-water nasal rinsing for colds: Cochrane says 'possibly' — the trials are small and biased, and the one big children's trial's symptom gains (about 0.3 points on a 4-point scale) may be too small to notice
shelves.question: In adults and children with acute upper respiratory infections (colds, rhinosinusitis), does saline nasal irrigation relieve symptoms compared with routine care or other sprays?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Child · Common Cold/therapy · Humans · Laryngitis/therapy · Nasal Lavage/adverse effects/methods · Pharyngitis/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Tract Infections/therapy · Rhinitis/therapy · Sinusitis/therapy · Sodium Chloride/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — cheap, safe, and supported by evidence its own reviewers call weak. The Cochrane review (King D et al., PMID: 25892369) found five randomised trials (544 children and 205 adults) comparing saline irrigation with routine care or other nose sprays — none against a placebo rinse: most results showed no difference between saline and control, and the trials were generally small and of low quality with unclear risk of bias. The one larger children's trial showed a significant reduction in nasal secretion score (mean difference -0.31, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.14) and nasal obstruction score (-0.33, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.19) — but the reviewers note a 0.33 difference on a four-point scale may have minimal clinical significance; that trial also found significantly less decongestant use in the saline group, and minor nasal discomfort or irritation was the only side effect reported, by a minority. That larger trial is Slapak I et al. (PMID: 18209140): 401 children aged 6-10 with uncomplicated cold or flu, randomised openly to standard medication alone or plus an isotonic seawater nasal wash (the tested product is named in the record as Physiomer), followed 12 weeks: at the second visit the saline group had better nasal secretion (mean 1.79 versus 2.10) and obstruction (1.25 versus 1.58) scores (p<0.05 for both), and by eight weeks fewer saline children were using antipyretics (9% versus 33%), decongestants (5% versus 47%), mucolytics (10% versus 37%) and systemic antiinfectives (6% versus 21%), with fewer reported illness days (31% versus 75%), school absences (17% versus 35%) and complications (8% versus 32%) (all p<0.05). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): rinsing may take a small edge off a cold and clearly substitutes for other medicines in one open trial — but that trial's very large prevention effects come from an unblinded design, and the blinded evidence base does not confirm them. Chronic rhinosinusitis irrigation is a different question, housed at live shelf #637.

cards.headline: King 2015 (Cochrane): five trials, most outcomes no different — secretion -0.31 and obstruction -0.33 in the one larger trial, 'may have minimal clinical significance'
cards.summary: King 2015 (Cochrane): five trials, most outcomes no different — secretion -0.31 and obstruction -0.33 in the one larger trial, 'may have minimal clinical significance'
cards.people: Five randomised trials in acute upper respiratory tract infections: 544 children (three studies) and 205 adults (two studies), comparing saline nasal irrigation with routine care or other nose sprays rather than placebo. Most trials were small and judged low quality, contributing to an unclear risk of bias; outcome measures varied so much that few could be pooled.
cards.result: Most results showed no difference between nasal saline treatment and control. The one larger children's trial showed significant reductions in nasal secretion score (mean difference -0.31, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.14) and nasal breathing (obstruction) score (MD -0.33, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.19) favouring saline, and a significant reduction in decongestant use in the saline group. Minor nasal discomfort and/or irritation was the only side effect reported, by a minority of participants. The authors conclude saline irrigation possibly has benefits for relieving acute URTI symptoms, but the small, high-bias trials reduce confidence in the evidence.
cards.watchOut: No trial used a sham rinse, so the ritual of rinsing is itself uncontrolled; and the review's positive numbers come entirely from one trial — the open-label Slapak study carded below — whose design the reviewers could not protect from bias.
cards.source: King D et al. Saline nasal irrigation for acute upper respiratory tract infections. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25892369. cards.headline: Slapak 2008: children on seawater wash used far fewer other medicines (decongestants 5% versus 47%) and reported fewer illness days (31% versus 75%) — in an open trial
cards.summary: Slapak 2008: children on seawater wash used far fewer other medicines (decongestants 5% versus 47%) and reported fewer illness days (31% versus 75%) — in an open trial
cards.people: 401 children aged 6-10 with uncomplicated cold or flu at eight Czech paediatric outpatient clinics, randomised to standard medication alone or standard medication plus nasal wash with a modified seawater solution (the tested product is named in the record as Physiomer), and observed for 12 weeks across an acute phase and a prevention phase. The comparison was open — families knew who was rinsing.
cards.result: At visit 2, the saline group had better scores on the 4-point symptom scale for nasal secretion (mean 1.79 versus 2.10) and obstruction (1.25 versus 1.58) (p<0.05 for both). At visit 3 (8 weeks), saline children had significantly lower scores for sore throat, cough, nasal obstruction and secretion (p<0.05 for all), and fewer were using antipyretics (9% versus 33%), nasal decongestants (5% versus 47%), mucolytics (10% versus 37%) or systemic antiinfectives (6% versus 21%) (p<0.05 for all). Illness days (31% versus 75%), school absences (17% versus 35%) and complications (8% versus 32%) were also significantly fewer (p<0.05 for all), with similar results at the final visit.
cards.watchOut: Effects of this size (a 44-percentage-point gap in illness days) from salt water, in a trial where parents knew the allocation and reported the outcomes, should be read as an upper bound inflated by expectation and reporting — the Cochrane reviewers, who include this trial, still land on 'possibly'. The tested product is a branded seawater preparation; plain saline was not separately trialled here.
cards.source: Slapak I et al. Efficacy of isotonic nasal wash (seawater) in the treatment and prevention of rhinitis in children. Archives of otolaryngology--head & neck surgery. 2008. PMID: 18209140. cards.headline: Synthesis: a harmless ritual with a small probable symptom edge and one unblinded trial claiming much more — believe the small claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: a harmless ritual with a small probable symptom edge and one unblinded trial claiming much more — believe the small claim
cards.people: Cochrane review of five randomised trials (544 children, 205 adults) in acute upper respiratory infections, dominated by one 401-child open-label trial of a branded seawater wash added to standard medication.
cards.result: Symptom scores: -0.31 (secretion) and -0.33 (obstruction) on 4-point scales in the large trial; most other pooled outcomes null. Medication use, illness days, absences and complications: all significantly lower in the open trial (for example decongestant use 5% versus 47%). Harms: minor nasal discomfort or irritation in a minority. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Families who rinse also tend to medicate less — whether the rinse replaces the medicines or the kind of family that rinses simply medicates less cannot be separated in an open trial. Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on a Cochrane review, with its weakness declared in the stamp itself.

shelves.title: Isotretinoin for acne: lesion counts fall by a clinically relevant amount in every trial — against antibiotics plus topicals the Cochrane pool found no lesion-count advantage (RR 1.01), with 67% more minor adverse effects
shelves.question: In people with acne vulgaris, does oral isotretinoin improve acne compared with placebo or oral antibiotics plus topical treatment — and what adverse effects accompany it?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Child · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Isotretinoin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — effective, on evidence weaker than its reputation, with frequent minor harms and unresolved serious-harm questions in the trial record. The Cochrane review (Costa CS et al., PMID: 30484286) included 31 randomised trials with 3,836 participants aged 12-55 with mild to severe acne: against oral antibiotics plus topical agents in moderate-to-severe acne, isotretinoin made no difference to investigator-assessed inflammatory lesion count (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06; three studies, 400 participants; very low-quality evidence), may slightly improve physician global assessment (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.32; 351 participants), and caused more less-serious adverse effects (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.98) such as dry lips and skin, cheilitis, vomiting and nausea; one serious adverse event (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) occurred in an isotretinoin group. Within isotretinoin dose comparisons, one trial reported 58%, 80% and 90% of participants achieving a 95% decrease in total inflammatory lesion count at 0.1, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg/day respectively. A second review (Vallerand IA et al., PMID: 28542914; 11 trials, 760 patients) found isotretinoin reduced lesion counts by a clinically relevant amount in all trials, always by more than control (placebo in two studies, oral antibiotics in seven), with statistically significant differences in two of three low-bias trials; adverse events were twice as frequent as control (751 versus 388 events), more than half dermatological dryness-related, and 12 participants withdrew for adverse events including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, cheilitis, acne flare, photophobia, raised liver enzymes and depressed mood. No included trial reported birth defects — trials exclude pregnancy, so the teratogenicity that dominates real-world isotretinoin governance is outside this trial record and is not quantified here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): isotretinoin works, including where the comparison is honest; what the trials cannot tell you is how much better than good antibiotic-plus-topical care it is, and its serious-harm management rests on regulation, not on these trials.

cards.headline: Costa 2018 (Cochrane): versus antibiotics plus topicals, lesion count RR 1.01 (very low quality), global assessment RR 1.15, minor adverse effects RR 1.67
cards.summary: Costa 2018 (Cochrane): versus antibiotics plus topicals, lesion count RR 1.01 (very low quality), global assessment RR 1.15, minor adverse effects RR 1.67
cards.people: 31 randomised trials, 3,836 participants aged 12-55 with mild to severe acne, mostly in Asia, Europe and North America; outcomes generally measured at 8-32 weeks (mean 19.7). Comparisons included isotretinoin versus placebo or other treatments (notably oral antibiotics plus topical agents) and isotretinoin dose/regimen comparisons. Pharmaceutical companies funded 12 trials; all but three studies had high risk of bias in at least one domain.
cards.result: Versus oral antibiotics plus topical agents (moderate-to-severe acne, 20-24 weeks): no difference in investigator-assessed inflammatory lesion count (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06; 3 studies, 400 participants; very low-quality evidence); physician global evaluation slightly favoured isotretinoin (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.32; 351 participants, 2 studies; low-quality); less serious adverse effects were more frequent (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.98) — dry lips/skin, cheilitis, vomiting, nausea. One serious adverse effect was found: Stevens-Johnson syndrome in the isotretinoin group (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.12 to 72.98). Dose data: at 20 weeks, 58%, 80% and 90% of participants achieved a 95% decrease in total inflammatory lesion count on 0.1, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg/day (150 participants, severe acne). Fourteen dose-comparison trials (906 participants) reported no serious adverse events; none of the included trials reported birth defects.
cards.watchOut: This is the uncomfortable card for isotretinoin's reputation: against a real comparator, on the hardest outcome, the pooled result is null — on very low-quality evidence, so it proves neither equivalence nor superiority. Most outcomes in this review are low or very low quality, with imprecision and attrition bias the stated reasons.
cards.source: Costa CS et al. Oral isotretinoin for acne. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30484286. cards.headline: Vallerand 2018: across 11 trials isotretinoin always beat control on lesion counts — and produced twice as many adverse events (751 versus 388)
cards.summary: Vallerand 2018: across 11 trials isotretinoin always beat control on lesion counts — and produced twice as many adverse events (751 versus 388)
cards.people: 11 randomised trials, 760 patients (mostly men; mean treatment ages 18 to 47.9 years), generally with moderate-to-severe acne, comparing isotretinoin with placebo (2 studies), oral antibiotics (7 studies) or other control (2 studies); results summarised descriptively. Registered with PROSPERO as CRD42015025080, as reported in the record.
cards.result: Across all trials, isotretinoin reduced acne lesion counts by a clinically relevant amount, and always by a greater amount than control; among trials at overall low risk of bias, two of three showed statistically significant differences favouring isotretinoin. Adverse events were twice as frequent with isotretinoin (751 events) as with control (388 events); more than half were dermatological and related to dryness. Twelve participants withdrew because of isotretinoin adverse events, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, cheilitis, xerosis, acne flare, photophobia, elevated liver enzymes, decreased appetite, headaches and depressed mood.
cards.watchOut: Seven hundred and sixty patients is a small total for a drug used by millions, follow-up is treatment-length, and event counting (751 versus 388) counts events, not patients — one patient can contribute several. Long-term remission after stopping, isotretinoin's main real-world claim, is not what these trials measured.
cards.source: Vallerand IA et al. Efficacy and adverse events of oral isotretinoin for acne: a systematic review. The British journal of dermatology. 2018. PMID: 28542914. cards.headline: Synthesis: it works — the open questions are 'how much better than the standard alternative?' and everything about long-term and serious harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: it works — the open questions are 'how much better than the standard alternative?' and everything about long-term and serious harm
cards.people: Two systematic reviews covering 31 trials (3,836 participants, Cochrane) and 11 trials (760 patients), in mild-to-severe acne treated for roughly 8-32 weeks.
cards.result: Lesion counts: always reduced more than control in the 11-trial review; no advantage over antibiotics plus topicals in the Cochrane head-to-head pool (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06, very low quality); physician global assessment RR 1.15. Dose response: 95% lesion-count reduction in 58%, 80% and 90% at 0.1, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg/day. Harms: minor adverse effects RR 1.67 versus standard care and twice the event count versus controls overall; one Stevens-Johnson case in each review's dataset; no birth defects reported in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), harms on the face.
cards.watchOut: Pregnancy is excluded from every trial here, so this shelf must never be read as quantifying isotretinoin's best-known serious risk; mood, lipid and liver effects are reported as events, not systematically measured outcomes. Tier C is not set under the written rule (the benefit claim rests on two multi-trial reviews), but the shelf is flagged in the wave summary for the coordinator's attention given the harm profile.

shelves.title: Triple-combination cream for melasma: complete clearing in 26.1% versus 4.6% for any two-ingredient version at 8 weeks — and 'none or mild' severity in 64.2% versus 39.4% against hydroquinone alone, at triple the irritation rate
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe facial melasma, does the fixed triple-combination cream (fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%, hydroquinone 4%, tretinoin 0.05%) clear pigmentation better than hydroquinone alone or dual-combination creams?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Dermatologic Agents/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Facial Dermatoses/diagnosis/drug therapy · Female · Fluocinolone Acetonide/therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hydroquinones/therapeutic use · Melanosis/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Ointments · Probability · Reference Values · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Tretinoin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clearly the strongest topical in its trials, over eight weeks, with irritation in about half of users. In two combined 8-week multicentre investigator-blind studies (Taylor SC et al., PMID: 12889718; 641 adults, predominantly female, with moderate-to-severe melasma and Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV), complete clearing at week 8 occurred in 26.1% on the triple combination versus 4.6% across the dual-combination groups (tretinoin+hydroquinone, tretinoin+fluocinolone, hydroquinone+fluocinolone, all at the same concentrations; p<.0001), and a 75% reduction in pigmentation was seen in more than 70% on triple therapy versus 30% on the dual agents; the commonest reactions in all groups were erythema, peeling, burning and stinging, mostly mild. In Asian patients with moderate-to-severe melasma (Chan R et al., PMID: 18616780; 242 randomised, 8 weeks), the triple cream (once nightly) beat hydroquinone 4% alone (twice daily) on the primary outcome: global severity 'none' or 'mild' at week 8 in 64.2% (77/120) versus 39.4% (48/122) (p<0.001), with patient satisfaction also favouring triple therapy (70.8% versus 49.6%; p=0.005) — but related adverse events occurred in 48.8% (63/129) versus 13.7% (18/131), none severe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for an eight-week course, the triple cream outperforms its own ingredients in pairs and hydroquinone alone by wide margins — the trials say nothing about staying clear after stopping, and melasma is a relapsing condition.

cards.headline: Taylor 2003: complete clearing 26.1% on triple therapy versus 4.6% on any dual combination at 8 weeks (p<.0001); 75% pigment reduction in over 70% versus 30%
cards.summary: Taylor 2003: complete clearing 26.1% on triple therapy versus 4.6% on any dual combination at 8 weeks (p<.0001); 75% pigment reduction in over 70% versus 30%
cards.type: Randomised investigator-blind trials (Taylor 2003, two combined studies)
cards.people: 641 adult patients, predominantly female, with moderate-to-severe facial melasma and Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV, randomised in two similarly designed 8-week multicentre studies to the triple combination (tretinoin 0.05%, hydroquinone 4.0%, fluocinolone acetonide 0.01% in a hydrophilic cream) or to one of three dual combinations at the same concentrations (tretinoin+hydroquinone, tretinoin+fluocinolone, hydroquinone+fluocinolone). Primary outcome: complete clearing by week 8 (intent-to-treat).
cards.result: Complete clearing at week 8: 26.1% with the triple combination versus 4.6% with the dual-combination groups (p<.0001). A 75% reduction in melasma/pigmentation at week 8 was observed in more than 70% of triple-therapy patients versus 30% on dual agents. The most common adverse reactions in all groups were erythema, skin peeling, burning and/or stinging; the majority of treatment-related events were mild.
cards.watchOut: Investigator-blind rather than double-blind, eight weeks only, and 'complete clearing' still happened for only about one patient in four — the honest headline is 'best available cream', not 'cure'. The dual comparators isolate the contribution of the third ingredient elegantly, but no arm tested sunscreen-plus-time, melasma's background therapy.
cards.source: Taylor SC et al. Efficacy and safety of a new triple-combination agent for the treatment of facial melasma. Cutis. 2003. PMID: 12889718. cards.headline: Chan 2008: in Asian patients, severity 'none or mild' in 64.2% versus 39.4% against hydroquinone 4% alone (p<0.001) — related adverse events 48.8% versus 13.7%
cards.summary: Chan 2008: in Asian patients, severity 'none or mild' in 64.2% versus 39.4% against hydroquinone 4% alone (p<0.001) — related adverse events 48.8% versus 13.7%
cards.people: East and South-East Asian patients aged 18 or older with moderate-to-severe facial melasma (242 in the primary efficacy analysis: 120 triple combination, 122 hydroquinone), treated for 8 weeks with the fixed triple cream (fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%, hydroquinone 4%, tretinoin 0.05%) once at bedtime or hydroquinone 4% cream twice daily; outcomes included global severity score, Melasma Area and Severity Index, global improvement and patient satisfaction.
cards.result: Primary outcome: global severity 'none' or 'mild' at week 8 in 77/120 (64.2%) on triple therapy versus 48/122 (39.4%) on hydroquinone (p<0.001); secondary efficacy variables confirmed the result. Patient satisfaction favoured triple therapy (90/127, 70.8%, versus 64/129, 49.6%; p=0.005). Related adverse events were more frequent on triple therapy (63/129, 48.8%) than on hydroquinone (18/131, 13.7%), but most were mild and none was severe.
cards.watchOut: One population (Asian skin), one season-length trial, and an irritation rate near one in two — the steroid component that helps short-term is also why this cream is not meant for indefinite use, a question an 8-week trial cannot address. Satisfaction was unblinded by design (patients knew their cream's feel), so treat the satisfaction gap cautiously.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the triple cream is the proven short-course winner for melasma — three ingredients beat two, and beat one, in over 880 randomised patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: the triple cream is the proven short-course winner for melasma — three ingredients beat two, and beat one, in over 880 randomised patients
cards.people: Two combined investigator-blind studies (641 patients, skin types I-IV) against dual combinations, and one investigator-blinded trial (242 analysed patients, Asian) against hydroquinone 4% alone; all treatments 8 weeks.
cards.result: Complete clearing: 26.1% versus 4.6% (versus duals). Severity none/mild: 64.2% versus 39.4% (versus hydroquinone). Satisfaction: 70.8% versus 49.6%. Harms: erythema, peeling, burning and stinging commonly; related adverse events 48.8% versus 13.7% against hydroquinone, none severe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for an 8-week course.
cards.watchOut: No trial here follows patients after the cream stops, and melasma characteristically recurs; long-term steroid and hydroquinone safety on the face is outside this record entirely. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised programmes carry the shelf.

shelves.title: Ketoconazole shampoo for tinea versicolor: healed with a negative tape test in 73% after three days of use — versus 5% on placebo shampoo; a single application did nearly as well (69%)
shelves.question: In people with tinea (pityriasis) versicolor, does ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied briefly to the skin clear the infection compared with placebo shampoo — and how does selenium sulfide shampoo compare?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hair Preparations · Humans · Ketoconazole/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Scalp Dermatoses/drug therapy · Tinea Versicolor/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a strikingly large effect in one large double-blind trial, for clearing an episode (this condition characteristically recurs, which the trial's 31 days cannot judge). In Lange DS et al. (PMID: 9843006), 312 patients with mycologically confirmed tinea versicolor were randomised to ketoconazole 2% shampoo as a single application, daily applications for three days, or placebo shampoo: clinical response at day 31 — defined as a global evaluation score of healed plus a negative cellophane tape test — was 73% in the 3-day group, 69% in the 1-day group and 5% on placebo (both ketoconazole regimens significantly more effective than placebo at p<.001 on clinical response, global scores and mycologic outcomes); the two ketoconazole regimens did not differ significantly from each other, and adverse events did not differ between groups, with no serious events and no withdrawals for adverse events. A smaller double-blind trial (Lusiana et al., PMID: 38021181) compared selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo (described in its abstract as SeS2) with ketoconazole 2% shampoo: mycological efficacy was 94% versus 86% in the order reported (ketoconazole versus selenium; p=0.182, not significant), with side effects in 22% versus 8% as reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a few applications of an antifungal shampoo clear most versicolor episodes within a month — expect the pale patches to fade more slowly than the fungus, and expect recurrence eventually, which no card here measures.

cards.headline: Lange 1998: clinical response at day 31 in 73% (3-day ketoconazole), 69% (1-day) and 5% (placebo) — p<.001, with no excess adverse events
cards.summary: Lange 1998: clinical response at day 31 in 73% (3-day ketoconazole), 69% (1-day) and 5% (placebo) — p<.001, with no excess adverse events
cards.people: 312 patients with mycologically confirmed tinea versicolor in a multicentre 31-day study, randomised to ketoconazole 2% shampoo as a single application (1 day), daily applications for 3 days, or placebo shampoo; efficacy required both a global evaluation score of 1 (healed) on a 5-point scale and a negative cellophane tape test at day 31, with tape tests also at baseline and days 3 and 10 and sign/symptom scoring (scaling, itching, erythema, hypo- and hyperpigmentation) on a 0-3 scale.
cards.result: Clinical response rates at day 31: 73% (3-day ketoconazole), 69% (1-day ketoconazole) and 5% (placebo). Both ketoconazole regimens were significantly more effective than placebo (p<.001) for clinical response, global evaluation scores and mycologic outcomes; the difference between the two ketoconazole regimens was not statistically significant. There were no significant differences between groups in the number of patients experiencing adverse events; no serious adverse events occurred and no patient withdrew prematurely because of an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one days is one episode: tinea versicolor is described in this very record as chronically recurring, and neither recurrence nor long-term pigment normalisation is measured. The 5% placebo response shows how little spontaneous clearing happens in a month — which makes the drug effect credible, but says nothing about next summer.

cards.headline: Lusiana 2022: selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo statistically indistinguishable from ketoconazole 2% — mycological efficacy 94% versus 86% as reported (p=0.182)
cards.summary: Lusiana 2022: selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo statistically indistinguishable from ketoconazole 2% — mycological efficacy 94% versus 86% as reported (p=0.182)
cards.people: Patients with pityriasis versicolor treated during September-December 2018 with selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo (described in the record's abstract as selenium disulfide, SeS2) or ketoconazole 2% shampoo, allocated by block randomisation and assessed by physical examination, scale provocation test, Wood's lamp and potassium hydroxide examination; analysis was by intention to treat. The record's abstract does not state the number of participants, and it carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: Mycological efficacy was not significantly different between the ketoconazole group and the selenium group — reported as 94% versus 86% in that order (p=0.182) — and side effects were reported in 22% versus 8% in the order given in the record, also described as not significantly different. The authors conclude selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo has the same mycological efficacy and side effects as ketoconazole 2% shampoo for pityriasis versicolor.
cards.watchOut: A small single-centre trial whose abstract omits its own sample size and reports percentages without the denominators; its role here is only to show the older selenium alternative was not beaten in a head-to-head test — not to establish equivalence, which a trial this size cannot do.

cards.people: One 312-patient multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial of ketoconazole 2% shampoo (1-day and 3-day regimens, 31 days) and one smaller double-blind head-to-head trial against selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo.

shelves.title: Amlexanox for mouth ulcers: pain and ulcer size significantly reduced by days 4-6 in two blinded trials — but neither record reports how much, and both come from one research group
shelves.question: In people with recurrent minor aphthous ulcers (canker sores), does topical amlexanox (adhesive tablets, pellicles or paste) reduce ulcer size and pain compared with a vehicle/placebo preparation?
shelves.mesh: Adhesives · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aminopyridines/therapeutic use · Anti-Allergic Agents/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Erythema/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy · Pharmaceutical Vehicles · Stomatitis, Aphthous/drug therapy · Tablets
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — significant p-values without published effect sizes, from a single research programme. In Liu J et al. (PMID: 16997114), 212 subjects with recurrent minor aphthous ulceration completed a double-blind vehicle-controlled multicentre trial of amlexanox oral adhesive tablets applied four times daily for five days (104 amlexanox, 108 vehicle): group differences favoured amlexanox for pain, ulcer size change and efficacy index at both day 4 and day 6 (all p<0.05), and for erythema and exudation at day 6; no systemic side effects were reported. In Meng W et al. (PMID: 19419555; Registry ID: NTR1727), 216 patients with minor recurrent aphthous ulcers were randomised to amlexanox adhesive pellicles or placebo pellicles four times daily for five days: ulcer size was significantly reduced (p=0.017 at day 4; p=0.038 at day 6) and ulcer pain significantly alleviated (p=0.021 at day 4; p=0.036 at day 6), with no significant difference in effectiveness between the pellicle and the tablet form studied previously by the same group. Neither record reports the actual size or pain differences, so how many hours or millimetres amlexanox buys cannot be stated from the sources. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): amlexanox probably speeds ulcer healing and pain relief a little over five days — the trials establish direction, not magnitude, and independent replication outside this one Chinese research programme is absent from the record.

cards.headline: Liu 2006: amlexanox tablets beat vehicle on pain, size and efficacy index at days 4 and 6 (all p<0.05) — magnitudes not reported; no systemic side effects
cards.summary: Liu 2006: amlexanox tablets beat vehicle on pain, size and efficacy index at days 4 and 6 (all p<0.05) — magnitudes not reported; no systemic side effects
cards.people: Subjects with recurrent minor aphthous ulceration in a Chinese multicentre trial, applying amlexanox oral adhesive tablets or vehicle tablets themselves four times a day for 5 days; 104 (amlexanox) and 108 (vehicle) subjects fulfilled the trial. Pain scale, ulcer size change, erythema and exudation degree, and an efficacy index were recorded at baseline and on the mornings of days 4 and 6.
cards.result: Group differences for all parameters except erythema and exudation at day 4 were statistically significant at both the day 4 and day 6 visits (p<0.05), favouring amlexanox; the authors conclude the tablets are effective and safe in reducing aphthous ulcer pain and lesion size, as well as erythema and exudation. No systemic side effects were reported. The record gives significance levels without the between-group differences in pain points or millimetres.
cards.watchOut: Aphthous ulcers heal by themselves in about a week, so a day-4-to-6 advantage is a claim about shaving the tail of a self-limiting lesion — worth having for a painful ulcer, but impossible to size from this record. 'Unparallel' in the record's own title appears to denote its non-crossover parallel design.

cards.headline: Meng 2009: pellicles reduce ulcer size (p=0.017 day 4; p=0.038 day 6) and pain (p=0.021; p=0.036) versus placebo — and match the group's earlier tablet results
cards.summary: Meng 2009: pellicles reduce ulcer size (p=0.017 day 4; p=0.038 day 6) and pain (p=0.021; p=0.036) versus placebo — and match the group's earlier tablet results
cards.people: 216 patients with minor recurrent aphthous ulcers in a Chinese multicentre study, randomised to amlexanox oral adhesive pellicles or placebo pellicles applied four times daily for five days, with ulcer size and pain measured on days 0, 4 and 6; results were then compared with the group's previous 104 cases treated with amlexanox tablets. Registry ID: NTR1727 (Netherlands Trial Register, as reported in the record). The formulation background in the record: amlexanox was developed as a 5% topical oral paste for recurrent aphthous stomatitis in most European countries.
cards.result: Amlexanox pellicles significantly reduced ulcer size (p=0.017 at day 4; p=0.038 at day 6) and alleviated ulcer pain (p=0.021 at day 4; p=0.036 at day 6) versus placebo. No significant difference in treatment effectiveness was observed between the pellicle and tablet forms; the authors report the pellicles seemed more comfortable to use and conclude they are as effective and safe as the tablets. As with the earlier trial, the record reports p-values rather than the size of the differences.
cards.watchOut: The p-values cluster just under 0.05 across multiple outcomes and days, the comparison with tablets is historical (the group's own earlier trial, not a randomised arm), and both amlexanox trials share senior authors — this is one programme's evidence, presented as two cards because two randomised comparisons exist.

cards.headline: Synthesis: direction consistent, magnitude unknown — a MAYBE earned by reporting gaps, not by negative data
cards.summary: Synthesis: direction consistent, magnitude unknown — a MAYBE earned by reporting gaps, not by negative data
cards.people: Two randomised blinded multicentre trials from one Chinese research programme: adhesive tablets versus vehicle (212 completers) and adhesive pellicles versus placebo (216 patients), each applied four times daily for five days in recurrent minor aphthous ulceration.
cards.result: Ulcer size: significantly reduced at days 4 and 6 in both trials (p=0.017-0.038 in the pellicle trial). Pain: significantly alleviated at days 4 and 6 in both (p=0.021-0.036 in the pellicle trial). Erythema/exudation: significantly better by day 6 in the tablet trial. Systemic side effects: none reported in the tablet trial. No effect sizes are reported in either record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses ulcer prevention, major aphthae, or comparison with topical corticosteroids — the other common canker-sore treatment — and amlexanox availability varies by country. Tier C is not set (two randomised blinded trials exist), but the single-programme origin is flagged in the wave summary for adjudication.
