shelves.title: Ciclopirox nail lacquer for toenail fungus: mycological cure 29% and 36% versus 11% and 9% on vehicle after 48 weeks — a year of daily painting for a one-in-three fungus cure in mild-to-moderate disease
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis, does ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer cure the fungus compared with vehicle lacquer or amorolfine lacquer?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage · Ciclopirox · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Foot Dermatoses/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Onychomycosis/drug therapy · Pharmaceutical Solutions/administration & dosage · Pyridones/administration & dosage · Reference Values · United States · World Health Organization
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but slow and partial cure, in carefully selected nails. The report of the two identically designed US pivotal trials (Gupta AK et al., PMID: 11051136) randomised 223 and 237 patients with mild-to-moderate dermatophyte toenail onychomycosis (20-65% of the target nail involved, no lunula involvement) to daily ciclopirox 8% lacquer or vehicle for 48 weeks: mycological cure (negative culture and negative microscopy) at the end of treatment was 29% versus 11% in study I and 36% versus 9% in study II; non-US studies reported mycological cure rates from 46.7% to 85.7% under more varied regimens. Causally related adverse effects were described as extremely uncommon in the review's summary, mostly transient local reactions such as erythema and application-site reaction, generally mild and clearing while patients continued use. A later formulation trial (Iorizzo M et al., PMID: 27171791; 120 evaluable patients with mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis, 48 weeks) compared a ciclopirox 8% HPCH lacquer (named P-3051 in the record) daily against amorolfine 5% lacquer twice weekly: treatment success was 58.3% versus 26.7% (p<0.001), complete cure 35.0% versus 11.7% (p<0.001), and mycological cure 100% versus 81.7% (p<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a patient who cannot or will not take oral terbinafine (live shelf #1156) and whose infection is mild-to-moderate without matrix involvement, a year of daily lacquer cures the fungus in roughly one in three — the newer efinaconazole record (pack #3048) shows complete cure in 15-18% on a stricter endpoint, and cross-trial comparisons between these lacquers are not randomised comparisons.

cards.headline: Gupta 2000 (pivotal US trials): mycological cure 29% versus 11% and 36% versus 9% after 48 weeks of daily lacquer — in nails with 20-65% involvement and no lunula disease
cards.summary: Gupta 2000 (pivotal US trials): mycological cure 29% versus 11% and 36% versus 9% after 48 weeks of daily lacquer — in nails with 20-65% involvement and no lunula disease
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled trials, reported together (Gupta 2000)
cards.people: Study I: 223 patients randomised (112 ciclopirox, 111 vehicle). Study II: 237 randomised (119 ciclopirox, 118 vehicle). All had mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes, with clinical features in at least one great toe, positive microscopy and positive dermatophyte culture, and 20-65% of the target nail involved at baseline. Lacquer was applied daily for 48 weeks to all toenails and affected fingernails; assessments every 4 weeks, mycology and photographic planimetry every 12 weeks. The record is a review-style report of these trials plus worldwide studies, not a single-trial paper.
cards.result: Mycological cure (negative culture and negative light microscopy) at the end of 48 weeks: study I, 29% on ciclopirox versus 11% on vehicle; study II, 36% versus 9% — described as significantly more effective than placebo, with efficacy against Trichophyton rubrum specified. Non-US studies reported mycological cure rates from 46.7% to 85.7%, under regimens that were sometimes less frequent and typically 6 months. Causally related treatment-emergent adverse effects were described as extremely safe in profile — most transient and localised (erythema, application-site reaction), generally mild and clearing while use continued.
cards.watchOut: Mycological cure is not a normal-looking nail: complete cure rates are lower, the trials excluded lunula (matrix) involvement and severe disease — exactly the nails patients most want fixed — and 48 weeks of daily application is an adherence marathon. The card's source is a narrative report of the trials rather than a primary trial publication, which is why its numbers are quoted as ranges across the two studies.
cards.source: Gupta AK et al. Ciclopirox nail lacquer topical solution 8% in the treatment of toenail onychomycosis. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2000. PMID: 11051136. cards.headline: Iorizzo 2016: ciclopirox HPCH lacquer beat amorolfine — treatment success 58.3% versus 26.7%, complete cure 35.0% versus 11.7%, mycological cure 100% versus 81.7% (all p<0.001)
cards.summary: Iorizzo 2016: ciclopirox HPCH lacquer beat amorolfine — treatment success 58.3% versus 26.7%, complete cure 35.0% versus 11.7%, mycological cure 100% versus 81.7% (all p<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded evaluator (Iorizzo 2016)
cards.people: 120 evaluable patients with mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis, homogeneous at baseline for race, pathogens, number of affected toenails and target-nail severity, treated for 48 weeks with the ciclopirox 8% HPCH lacquer named P-3051 in the record (60 patients, daily) or amorolfine 5% lacquer (60 patients, twice weekly). The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: At 48 weeks, statistical superiority for the ciclopirox HPCH lacquer versus amorolfine was reported on treatment success (58.3% versus 26.7%; p<0.001), complete cure (35.0% versus 11.7%; p<0.001) and mycological cure (100% versus 81.7%; p<0.001), with fungal eradication already statistically superior at week 24. The authors describe the formulation as a gold standard for topical treatment of mild-to-moderate onychomycosis, citing also a previous pivotal study against the insoluble ciclopirox formulation.
cards.watchOut: A 100% mycological cure rate in any onychomycosis trial should be read with suspicion — it exceeds the same drug's pivotal-trial results (29-36%) severalfold, in a 120-patient single trial of a proprietary formulation whose authors promote it as a gold standard. The direction (ciclopirox ≥ amorolfine) is plausible; the magnitudes are not corroborated.
cards.source: Iorizzo M et al. Ciclopirox 8% HPCH Nail Lacquer in the Treatment of Mild-to-Moderate Onychomycosis: A Randomized, Double-Blind Amorolfine Controlled Study Using a Blinded Evaluator. Skin appendage disorders. 2016. PMID: 27171791. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: lacquer works slowly on easy nails — roughly triple the vehicle's fungus cure, with complete cure in about a third at best after a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: lacquer works slowly on easy nails — roughly triple the vehicle's fungus cure, with complete cure in about a third at best after a year
cards.people: Two US pivotal vehicle-controlled trials (460 randomised patients, 48 weeks of daily ciclopirox 8%) and one 120-patient active-comparator trial of a newer ciclopirox formulation versus amorolfine, all in mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis without lunula involvement.
cards.result: Mycological cure versus vehicle: 29% versus 11% and 36% versus 9% at 48 weeks. Versus amorolfine: complete cure 35.0% versus 11.7% and treatment success 58.3% versus 26.7% for the HPCH formulation. Harms: local and mild in the pivotal programme. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), restricted to mild-to-moderate disease as trialled.
cards.watchOut: Oral terbinafine's cure rates (live shelf #1156) remain the benchmark this topical route does not approach; the lacquer's niche is patients who cannot take or decline oral therapy. The Iorizzo magnitudes are flagged on the card itself. Tier C is not set: two pivotal randomised trials carry the core claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gupta AK et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2000 (PMID: 11051136); Iorizzo M et al. Skin appendage disorders. 2016 (PMID: 27171791).

shelves.title: Uveitis first-line steroid-sparing therapy (FAST): mycophenolate did not beat methotrexate — success 57.1% versus 66.7% at 6 months, with a posterior-disease subgroup favouring methotrexate
shelves.question: In adults with noninfectious intermediate, posterior or pan-uveitis needing corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppression, is mycophenolate mofetil superior to methotrexate for achieving controlled inflammation on low-dose steroids?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Liver Function Tests · Male · Methotrexate/administration & dosage · Methotrexate/adverse effects · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Mycophenolic Acid/administration & dosage · Mycophenolic Acid/adverse effects · Mycophenolic Acid/therapeutic use · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Uveitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the superiority question asked. In the FAST trial, 216 adults with noninfectious uveitis needing steroid-sparing therapy were randomised to oral methotrexate 25 mg weekly or mycophenolate mofetil 3 g daily. Treatment success at 6 months — controlled inflammation in both eyes on no more than 7.5 mg prednisone daily and no more than 2 drops of prednisolone acetate, without failure for safety or intolerability — occurred in 66.7% on methotrexate versus 57.1% on mycophenolate (difference 9.5% [95% CI -5.3% to 21.8%]; odds ratio 1.50 [0.81 to 2.81]; P=0.20): mycophenolate was not superior. A prespecified anatomical split leaned the other way by site — posterior uveitis or panuveitis success 74.4% (methotrexate) versus 55.3% (mycophenolate), P=0.02, against 33.3% versus 63.6% in intermediate uveitis (P for interaction=0.004) — hypothesis-generating, not a verdict. Elevated liver enzymes were the commonest laboratory adverse event (13.0% methotrexate, 7.4% mycophenolate). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as first-line steroid-sparing therapy, mycophenolate is not superior to methotrexate; either drug controls about three in five patients by 6 months.

cards.headline: Rathinam 2019 (FAST): treatment success 66.7% on methotrexate versus 57.1% on mycophenolate at 6 months (P=0.20) — no superiority, opposite subgroup leans by uveitis site
cards.summary: Rathinam 2019 (FAST): treatment success 66.7% on methotrexate versus 57.1% on mycophenolate at 6 months (P=0.20) — no superiority, opposite subgroup leans by uveitis site
cards.people: 216 adults (median age 38 years; 62.5% women) with noninfectious intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis or panuveitis requiring corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppression, at 9 referral eye centres in India, the United States, Australia, Saudi Arabia and Mexico, randomised to oral methotrexate 25 mg weekly (n=107) or mycophenolate mofetil 3 g daily (n=109); 194 (89.8%) completed 6-month follow-up, with follow-up to 12 months.
cards.result: Treatment success at 6 months occurred in 64 (66.7%) patients on methotrexate versus 56 (57.1%) on mycophenolate (difference 9.5% [95% CI -5.3% to 21.8%]; odds ratio 1.50 [95% CI 0.81 to 2.81]; P=0.20). In posterior uveitis or panuveitis, success was 74.4% (methotrexate) versus 55.3% (mycophenolate) (difference 19.1% [3.6% to 30.6%]; P=0.02); in intermediate uveitis, 33.3% versus 63.6% (difference -30.3% [-51.6% to 1.1%]; P=0.07; P for interaction=0.004). Elevated liver enzymes occurred in 14 patients (13.0%) on methotrexate and 8 (7.4%) on mycophenolate.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, open to the anatomical-subgroup result being chance (the interaction cuts both ways and the intermediate-uveitis cells are small). Success is a composite that includes tolerability-driven failure, and both arms received background prednisolone tapering — the trial compares two active drugs, not either drug against none.
cards.source: Rathinam SR et al. Effect of Corticosteroid-Sparing Treatment With Mycophenolate Mofetil vs Methotrexate on Inflammation in Patients With Uveitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31503307. Registry ID: NCT01829295. cards.headline: Synthesis: one head-to-head trial, no winner overall — drug choice turns on the subgroup signal and on tolerability, not on proven superiority
cards.summary: Synthesis: one head-to-head trial, no winner overall — drug choice turns on the subgroup signal and on tolerability, not on proven superiority
cards.people: One randomised trial (FAST, 216 adults with noninfectious intermediate, posterior or pan-uveitis) comparing first-line methotrexate with mycophenolate mofetil as corticosteroid-sparing therapy over 6-12 months.
cards.result: Treatment success 66.7% (methotrexate) versus 57.1% (mycophenolate); difference 9.5% (95% CI -5.3% to 21.8%); P=0.20. Liver-enzyme elevations 13.0% versus 7.4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the superiority claim, Tier C because a single trial carries the comparison.

shelves.title: Cenegermin (nerve growth factor drops) for neurotrophic keratitis: corneal healing 55-75% versus 20-43% on vehicle across two randomised trials
shelves.question: In patients with moderate-to-severe neurotrophic keratitis (neurotrophic keratopathy), does topical cenegermin (recombinant human nerve growth factor) heal the corneal lesion compared with vehicle eye drops?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cornea/pathology · Cranial Nerve Diseases/diagnosis · Cranial Nerve Diseases/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Keratitis/diagnosis · Keratitis/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Nerve Growth Factor/administration & dosage · Ophthalmic Solutions/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Recombinant Proteins/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised vehicle-controlled trials of the same 8-week, six-drops-daily regimen point the same way. In the European REPARO phase 2 trial (156 patients), corneal healing at week 4 was 54.9% on cenegermin 10 µg/ml and 58.0% on 20 µg/ml versus 19.6% on vehicle (P<0.001 for both), rising at week 8 to 74.5% and 74.0% versus 43.1%. In the US NGF0214 trial (48 patients), healing by the conventional measure at week 8 was 69.6% on cenegermin 20 µg/ml versus 29.2% on vehicle (+40.4%; P=0.006), and by the conservative 0-mm-staining measure 65.2% versus 16.7% (P<0.001). More than 96% of healed REPARO patients stayed recurrence-free during follow-up. Adverse effects in both trials were mostly local, mild and transient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cenegermin roughly doubles corneal healing in neurotrophic keratitis over 8 weeks — a rare-disease evidence base of two small trials, one of them phase 2.

cards.headline: Bonini 2018 (REPARO): healing at week 4 in 54.9% (10 µg/ml) and 58.0% (20 µg/ml) versus 19.6% on vehicle (P<0.001); at week 8, 74.5% and 74.0% versus 43.1%
cards.summary: Bonini 2018 (REPARO): healing at week 4 in 54.9% (10 µg/ml) and 58.0% (20 µg/ml) versus 19.6% on vehicle (P<0.001); at week 8, 74.5% and 74.0% versus 43.1%
cards.people: 156 patients with stage 2 (moderate) or stage 3 (severe) neurotrophic keratitis in one eye, randomised 1:1:1 to recombinant human nerve growth factor 10 µg/ml, 20 µg/ml or vehicle, 6 drops daily for 8 weeks, then 48-56 weeks of follow-up; healing assessed by masked central readers.
cards.result: Corneal healing (<0.5-mm lesion staining) at week 4 (primary endpoint) was 19.6% on vehicle versus 54.9% on 10 µg/ml (+35.3%; 97.06% CI 15.88-54.71; P<0.001) and 58.0% on 20 µg/ml (+38.4%; 97.06% CI 18.96-57.83; P<0.001). At week 8, healing was 43.1% (vehicle) versus 74.5% (10 µg/ml; P=0.001) and 74.0% (20 µg/ml; P=0.002). A post hoc conservative measure (0-mm staining, no other persistent staining) maintained significant differences at weeks 4 and 8. More than 96% of patients who healed after cenegermin remained recurrence-free during follow-up. Adverse effects were mostly local, mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial with a high vehicle healing rate by week 8 (43.1%) — neurotrophic lesions can close with intensive standard care alone, so the attributable gain is the roughly 31-point difference, not the headline 74%. The conservative-healing analysis was post hoc.
cards.source: Bonini S et al. Phase II Randomized, Double-Masked, Vehicle-Controlled Trial of Recombinant Human Nerve Growth Factor for Neurotrophic Keratitis. Ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 29653858. randomised phase 2 trial (bonini 2018, reparo) 156 patients with stage 2 (moderate) or stage 3 (severe) neurotrophic keratitis in one eye, randomised 1:1:1 to recombinant human nerve growth factor 10 µg/ml, 20 µg/ml or vehicle, 6 drops daily for 8 weeks, then 48-56 weeks of follow-up; healing assessed by masked central readers. corneal healing (<0.5-mm lesion staining) at week 4 (primary endpoint) was 19.6% on vehicle versus 54.9% on 10 µg/ml (+35.3%; 97.06% ci 15.88-54.71; p<0.001) and 58.0% on 20 µg/ml (+38.4%; 97.06% ci 18.96-57.83; p<0.001). at week 8, healing was 43.1% (vehicle) versus 74.5% (10 µg/ml; p=0.001) and 74.0% (20 µg/ml; p=0.002). a post hoc conservative measure (0-mm staining, no other persistent staining) maintained significant differences at weeks 4 and 8. more than 96% of patients who healed after cenegermin remained recurrence-free during follow-up. adverse effects were mostly local, mild and transient. a phase 2 trial with a high vehicle healing rate by week 8 (43.1%) — neurotrophic lesions can close with intensive standard care alone, so the attributable gain is the roughly 31-point difference, not the headline 74%. the conservative-healing analysis was post hoc. bonini s et al. phase ii randomized, double-masked, vehicle-controlled trial of recombinant human nerve growth factor for neurotrophic keratitis. ophthalmology. 2018. pmid: 29653858. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · cornea/pathology · cranial nerve diseases/diagnosis · cranial nerve diseases/drug therapy · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · female · humans · keratitis/diagnosis · keratitis/drug therapy · male · middle aged · nerve growth factor/administration & dosage · ophthalmic solutions/administration & dosage · prospective studies · recombinant proteins/administration & dosage · treatment outcome · visual acuity · young adult

cards.headline: Pflugfelder 2020 (NGF0214): healing at week 8 in 69.6% versus 29.2% on vehicle by the conventional measure (+40.4%; P=0.006), 65.2% versus 16.7% by the conservative measure
cards.summary: Pflugfelder 2020 (NGF0214): healing at week 8 in 69.6% versus 29.2% on vehicle by the conventional measure (+40.4%; P=0.006), 65.2% versus 16.7% by the conservative measure
cards.people: 48 patients with neurotrophic keratopathy (persistent epithelial defect with or without stromal thinning) at 11 US sites, randomised 1:1 to cenegermin 20 µg/ml or vehicle eye drops, 6 drops daily for 8 weeks of masked treatment, with 24 weeks of follow-up; healing measured by masked central readers.
cards.result: Conventional healing (<0.5 mm lesion staining) at week 8 was achieved by 16 of 23 cenegermin patients (69.6%) versus 7 of 24 on vehicle (29.2%) (+40.4%; 95% CI 14.2%-66.6%; P=0.006). By the conservative measure (0-mm staining and no other residual staining), healing was 65.2% versus 16.7% (+48.6%; 95% CI 24.0%-73.1%; P<0.001). Cenegermin also showed significant reductions in lesion size and disease-progression rates; adverse effects were mostly local, mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: Only 48 patients — the pivotal US trial is smaller than the European phase 2 study, and its confidence interval for the healing advantage is wide (14.2 to 66.6 points). Vision and corneal-sensitivity outcomes are secondary and less decisive than the staining endpoint.
cards.source: Pflugfelder SC et al. Topical Recombinant Human Nerve Growth Factor (Cenegermin) for Neurotrophic Keratopathy: A Multicenter Randomized Vehicle-Controlled Pivotal Trial. Ophthalmology. 2020. PMID: 31585826. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one regimen, healing roughly doubled — in a rare disease where the trials are necessarily small
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one regimen, healing roughly doubled — in a rare disease where the trials are necessarily small
cards.people: Two randomised double-masked vehicle-controlled trials of cenegermin 20 µg/ml (and 10 µg/ml in REPARO), 6 drops daily for 8 weeks, in moderate-to-severe neurotrophic keratitis: REPARO (156 patients, Europe) and NGF0214 (48 patients, United States).
cards.result: Healing at week 8: 74.0-74.5% (REPARO) and 69.6% (NGF0214) on cenegermin versus 43.1% and 29.2% on vehicle. Conservative-measure healing (NGF0214): 65.2% versus 16.7%. Recurrence after healing: under 4% during REPARO follow-up. Adverse effects mostly local, mild, transient in both trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is lesion staining, a close surrogate for the outcomes patients fear (perforation, vision loss), which the trials were too small to measure. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials concur, though both come from the same development programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bonini S et al. Ophthalmology. 2018 (PMID: 29653858); Pflugfelder SC et al. Ophthalmology. 2020 (PMID: 31585826).

shelves.title: Idebenone for Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: the single randomised trial missed its primary endpoint — benefit appeared only in a post hoc subgroup with discordant vision between the eyes
shelves.question: In patients with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, does idebenone 900 mg/day improve visual acuity compared with placebo over 24 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antioxidants/pharmacology · Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Contrast Sensitivity/drug effects · DNA, Mitochondrial/genetics · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Optic Atrophy, Hereditary, Leber/drug therapy · Optic Atrophy, Hereditary, Leber/physiopathology · Placebos · Prospective Studies · Retina/ultrastructure · Ubiquinone/analogs & derivatives · Ubiquinone/pharmacology · Ubiquinone/therapeutic use · Visual Acuity/drug effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a possible benefit in a subgroup, from a trial that missed its primary endpoint. RHODOS randomised 85 patients with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (m.3460G>A, m.11778G>A or m.14484T>C mutations) to idebenone 900 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — best recovery in visual acuity — did not reach statistical significance in the intention-to-treat population, and the record reports no significant overall effect size. A post hoc interaction analysis found a different response in patients with discordant visual acuities between the eyes at baseline; in that subgroup, all secondary endpoints differed significantly between idebenone and placebo. Idebenone was safe and well tolerated. A post hoc subgroup inside a small, primary-negative trial is the weakest form of randomised evidence — it identifies who might benefit, it does not prove that anyone does. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): idebenone may help the subgroup of LHON patients whose two eyes differ in acuity, on post hoc evidence only.

cards.headline: Klopstock 2011 (RHODOS): primary endpoint (best visual-acuity recovery) not significant overall; all secondary endpoints favoured idebenone only in the post hoc discordant-acuity subgroup
cards.summary: Klopstock 2011 (RHODOS): primary endpoint (best visual-acuity recovery) not significant overall; all secondary endpoints favoured idebenone only in the post hoc discordant-acuity subgroup
cards.people: 85 patients with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy due to m.3460G>A, m.11778G>A or m.14484T>C mitochondrial DNA mutations, in a 24-week multicentre double-blind trial of idebenone 900 mg/day versus placebo; endpoints included best recovery and change in visual acuity, colour-contrast sensitivity and retinal nerve fibre layer thickness in subgroups.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, best recovery in visual acuity, did not reach statistical significance in the intention-to-treat population. Post hoc interaction analysis showed a different response to idebenone in patients with discordant visual acuities at baseline; in these patients, all secondary endpoints were significantly different between the idebenone and placebo groups. Idebenone was safe and well tolerated. The record reports no numerical effect sizes for the visual outcomes in its abstract.
cards.watchOut: The positive claim is entirely post hoc and subgroup-based in an 85-patient rare-disease trial — exactly the pattern most prone to false positives. The absence of reported effect sizes in the record means neither the size nor the precision of the subgroup benefit can be stated from the verified source.
cards.source: Klopstock T et al. A randomized placebo-controlled trial of idebenone in Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy. Brain : a journal of neurology. 2011. PMID: 21788663. cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial, a missed primary, a post hoc subgroup — the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RHODOS, 85 patients with genetically confirmed Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy) of idebenone 900 mg/day over 24 weeks.
cards.result: Primary endpoint: not statistically significant. Secondary endpoints: significant in favour of idebenone only within the post hoc subgroup with discordant baseline visual acuities. Safety: idebenone was safe and well tolerated in the trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C because a single trial with a post hoc subgroup carries the claim.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set. Any stronger stamp would require a confirmatory trial enrolling the discordant-acuity subgroup prospectively; none is carded here.

shelves.title: Five-grass pollen SLIT tablet: symptom scores cut by about a quarter to a third versus placebo in adults and in children — and the benefit was still there a season after three years of treatment stopped
shelves.question: In children and adults with grass-pollen allergic rhinitis, does five-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy reduce symptom-and-medication scores compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Sublingual · Adolescent · Adult · Antigens, Plant/adverse effects,immunology,therapeutic use · Conjunctivitis, Allergic/diagnosis,immunology,therapy · Desensitization, Immunologic/methods · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Poaceae/adverse effects,immunology · Pollen/adverse effects,immunology · Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal/diagnosis,immunology,therapy · Tablets
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised double-blind trials of the same five-grass pollen tablet, one in each age group, plus a post-treatment season. In 628 adults (Didier A et al., PMID: 17935764), mean Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score in the first pollen season was 3.58 on the 300-IR dose and 3.74 on the 500-IR dose versus 4.93 on placebo (P=.0001 and P=.0006), while the 100-IR dose (4.70) did not separate from placebo. In 278 children and adolescents aged 5–17 (Wahn U et al., PMID: 19046761), the 300-IR tablet improved the total symptom score versus placebo (P=.001), a mean relative improvement of 28.0% and a median relative improvement of 39.3%, with rescue-medication scores and days on rescue medication also lower (P=.0064 and P=.0146). After three consecutive pre- and co-seasonal years, benefit persisted into the untreated fourth season (Didier A et al., PMID: 23600548): adjusted symptom-score differences versus placebo of −1.14 and −1.43 points, relative differences of −22.9% and −28.5%, in 435 patients. Adverse events in the paediatric trial were generally mild or moderate and no serious side effects were reported in either first-season trial. The tested product is the five-grass pollen sublingual tablet (300 IR) of Stallergènes, Antony, France, named in the paediatric record — a different product from the single-grass tablet homed on Shelf #379. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the five-grass tablet reduces symptom and rescue-medication scores by roughly a quarter to a third relative to placebo across adults and children, with a post-treatment season of carry-over after three years of use.

cards.headline: Didier 2007 (adults): symptom score 3.58 at 300 IR and 3.74 at 500 IR versus 4.93 on placebo (P=.0001 / P=.0006) — the 100-IR dose did not separate
cards.summary: Didier 2007 (adults): symptom score 3.58 at 300 IR and 3.74 at 500 IR versus 4.93 on placebo (P=.0001 / P=.0006) — the 100-IR dose did not separate
cards.people: 628 adults with grass-pollen rhinoconjunctivitis (confirmed by positive skin prick test and serum-specific IgE) in a multinational trial, randomised to once-daily sublingual tablets of a standardised 5-grass pollen extract at 100, 300 or 500 index of reactivity (IR), or placebo, started 4 months before the estimated pollen season and continued through it; primary outcome was the Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score.
cards.result: Mean total symptom score was 3.58 ± 3.0 at 300 IR (P=.0001 versus placebo) and 3.74 ± 3.1 at 500 IR (P=.0006) versus 4.93 ± 3.2 on placebo, in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses; the 100-IR group scored 4.70 ± 3.1 and was not significantly different from placebo. All secondary variables (individual symptom scores, rescue medication use, quality of life) confirmed the efficacy of the 300-IR and 500-IR doses. No serious side effects were reported, and the authors judged the risk–benefit ratio to favour the 300-IR dose.
cards.watchOut: One pollen season only, and the endpoint is a symptom score: the absolute gain at 300 IR is about 1.35 points on the total symptom score against a placebo score of 4.93. The dose split matters — quoting this trial for 'grass tablets' without the dose hides that the 100-IR dose failed.
cards.source: Didier A et al. Optimal dose, efficacy, and safety of once-daily sublingual immunotherapy with a 5-grass pollen tablet for seasonal allergic rhinitis. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2007. PMID: 17935764. cards.headline: Wahn 2009 (children 5–17): 300-IR five-grass tablet beat placebo on total symptom score (P=.001) — 28.0% mean relative improvement — and cut rescue-medication use
cards.summary: Wahn 2009 (children 5–17): 300-IR five-grass tablet beat placebo on total symptom score (P=.001) — 28.0% mean relative improvement — and cut rescue-medication use
cards.people: 278 children and adolescents aged 5–17 years with grass pollen-related rhinoconjunctivitis (positive skin prick test and serum-specific IgE) in a multinational trial, randomised to once-daily 300-IR 5-grass-pollen SLIT tablets (Stallergènes, Antony, France, as named in the record) or placebo, started 4 months before the pollen season and continued through it; the intention-to-treat population was 266 children (mean age 10.9 ± 3.22 years). Primary outcome was the rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (6 symptoms).
cards.result: The total symptom score differed highly significantly between the 300-IR and placebo groups (P=.001): a mean relative improvement of 28.0% and a median relative improvement of 39.3% over placebo. Rescue medication score and the proportion of days using rescue medication during the pollen season were also significantly lower on the tablet (P=.0064 and P=.0146). Adverse events were generally mild or moderate in intensity and expected; no serious side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative improvements in scores, as the record states them — the record does not print the absolute group symptom scores, so the absolute size of the gain cannot be stated from this record. One season, in children whose hay fever may remit or change with age regardless of treatment.

cards.headline: Didier 2013: after three pre- and co-seasonal years, the untreated fourth season still favoured the tablet — adjusted symptom score −1.14 to −1.43 points versus placebo (relative −22.9% to −28.5%)
cards.summary: Didier 2013: after three pre- and co-seasonal years, the untreated fourth season still favoured the tablet — adjusted symptom score −1.14 to −1.43 points versus placebo (relative −22.9% to −28.5%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled long-term trial, post-treatment season report (Didier 2013)
cards.people: Adults aged 18–50 sensitised to grass pollen with more than two seasons of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and a retrospective total symptom score ≥12 (0–18 scale), randomised to a 300-IR 5-grass pollen tablet begun 4 months (4M) or 2 months (2M) before each pollen season, or placebo, for three consecutive years, then followed through a fourth, immunotherapy-free season; 435 patients contributed to the year-4 efficacy analyses. Primary post-treatment outcome was the Average Adjusted Symptom Score (symptom score adjusted for rescue medication use).
cards.result: In the fourth, untreated pollen season, least-squares mean differences in the adjusted symptom score versus placebo were −1.14 (95% CI −2.03 to −0.26, P=.0114) for the 4M group and −1.43 (95% CI −2.32 to −0.53, P=.0019) for the 2M group — relative differences of −22.9% and −28.5% versus placebo, labelled relative in the record. Total symptom score, rescue medication score and quality-of-life score also differed significantly in the active groups' favour. No safety risk was identified during the post-treatment period.
cards.watchOut: This is the follow-through report of one long-term trial programme, not an independent replication, and only 435 of the originally randomised patients contributed to the year-4 analysis — attrition over four years can flatter a carry-over estimate. One post-treatment season is shown; durability beyond that is not in this record.
cards.source: Didier A et al. Post-treatment efficacy of discontinuous treatment with 300IR 5-grass pollen sublingual tablet in adults with grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. cards.headline: Synthesis: one product, two age groups, one direction — symptom and medication scores down by roughly a quarter to a third relative to placebo, with a season of carry-over
cards.summary: Synthesis: one product, two age groups, one direction — symptom and medication scores down by roughly a quarter to a third relative to placebo, with a season of carry-over
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled first-season trials of the 300-IR five-grass pollen sublingual tablet (Stallergènes) — 628 adults (Didier 2007) and 278 children and adolescents aged 5–17 (Wahn 2009) — plus the three-year trial programme's untreated fourth-season report in 435 adults (Didier 2013).
cards.result: Adults: total symptom score 3.58 (300 IR) versus 4.93 on placebo. Children: total symptom score significantly better on the tablet (P=.001), a 28.0% mean relative improvement, with rescue-medication score and rescue-medication days also reduced. Post-treatment season after three years: adjusted symptom score −1.14 to −1.43 points versus placebo (relative −22.9% to −28.5%). No serious side effects were reported in the first-season trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Symptom scores are patient-felt but soft endpoints, pollen seasons vary in intensity between years and sites, and the carry-over card is a follow-through of the same programme rather than independent confirmation. This shelf covers the five-grass Stallergènes tablet only; the single-grass (timothy) tablet and its asthma-prevention question are homed separately on Shelf #379, and results should not be borrowed between the two products. Tier C per the 4,000–5,000 band rule.

shelves.title: Bimekizumab versus adalimumab in plaque psoriasis: clear or almost-clear skin in 85% versus 57% at week 16 in BE SURE — with oral candidiasis and diarrhoea as the price, and a 91% versus 1% placebo-controlled clearance rate behind it
shelves.question: In adults with plaque psoriasis, does bimekizumab achieve complete skin clearance more often than adalimumab?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Candidiasis, Oral/etiology · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-17/antagonists & inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Psoriasis/drug therapy · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one head-to-head trial against adalimumab, backed by one placebo-controlled trial of the same drug. In BE SURE (Warren RB et al., PMID: 33891379), 478 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomised to bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks (with or without a switch to every 8 weeks after week 16) or adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks: at week 16 a PASI 90 response (at least 90% improvement) occurred in 275 of 319 (86.2%) on bimekizumab versus 75 of 159 (47.2%) on adalimumab (adjusted risk difference 39.3 percentage points; P<0.001 for noninferiority and superiority), and an Investigator's Global Assessment score of 0 or 1 (clear or almost clear) in 272 of 319 (85.3%) versus 91 of 159 (57.2%). In BE READY (Gordon KB et al., PMID: 33549192), bimekizumab achieved PASI 90 in 317 of 349 (91%) versus 1 of 86 (1%) on placebo at week 16, with IGA 0 or 1 in 323 of 349 (93%) versus 1 of 86 (1%). The harm ledger is the IL-17 class signature: oral candidiasis and diarrhoea occurred more frequently with bimekizumab in BE SURE, and treatment-emergent adverse events in BE READY's first 16 weeks ran 61% on bimekizumab versus 41% on placebo. Neither record's abstract reports PASI 100 (literally complete clearance), so this shelf's claim is clear-or-almost-clear skin and PASI 90, not total clearance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): bimekizumab clears or nearly clears skin substantially more often than adalimumab at week 16 in a single head-to-head phase 3 trial, at the cost of more oral candidiasis and diarrhoea; Tier C because the adalimumab comparison rests on that one trial.

cards.headline: BE SURE (Warren 2021): PASI 90 in 86.2% on bimekizumab versus 47.2% on adalimumab at week 16, IGA 0/1 in 85.3% versus 57.2% — oral candidiasis and diarrhoea more frequent on bimekizumab
cards.summary: BE SURE (Warren 2021): PASI 90 in 86.2% on bimekizumab versus 47.2% on adalimumab at week 16, IGA 0/1 in 85.3% versus 57.2% — oral candidiasis and diarrhoea more frequent on bimekizumab
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (Warren 2021, BE SURE)
cards.people: 478 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (mean age 44.9 years, mean baseline PASI score 19.8) randomised 1:1:1 to subcutaneous bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks for 56 weeks (n=158), bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks for 16 weeks then every 8 weeks to week 56 (n=161), or adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks for 24 weeks followed by bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks to week 56 (n=159).
cards.result: At week 16, a PASI 90 response occurred in 275 of 319 patients (86.2%) who received bimekizumab (both dose groups combined) and 75 of 159 (47.2%) who received adalimumab (adjusted risk difference 39.3 percentage points; 95% CI 30.9 to 47.7; P<0.001 for noninferiority and superiority). An IGA score of 0 or 1 occurred in 272 of 319 (85.3%) on bimekizumab and 91 of 159 (57.2%) on adalimumab (adjusted risk difference 28.2 percentage points; 95% CI 19.7 to 36.7; P<0.001 for noninferiority and superiority). The most common adverse events with bimekizumab were upper respiratory tract infections, oral candidiasis (predominantly mild or moderate), hypertension, and diarrhoea, with oral candidiasis and diarrhoea more frequent than on adalimumab.
cards.watchOut: This is the only head-to-head trial against adalimumab, and its placebo-free design means the comparison is exactly as strong as this one trial. The abstract reports PASI 90 and IGA 0/1 — not PASI 100 — so 'complete clearance' in the strict sense is not a figure this record carries. After week 24 the adalimumab group switched to bimekizumab, so no randomised adalimumab comparison exists beyond that point.
cards.source: Warren RB et al. Bimekizumab versus Adalimumab in Plaque Psoriasis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33891379. Registry ID: NCT03412747. cards.headline: BE READY (Gordon 2021): PASI 90 in 91% on bimekizumab versus 1% on placebo at week 16, IGA 0/1 in 93% versus 1% — responses held to week 56 on either maintenance schedule
cards.summary: BE READY (Gordon 2021): PASI 90 in 91% on bimekizumab versus 1% on placebo at week 16, IGA 0/1 in 93% versus 1% — responses held to week 56 on either maintenance schedule
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Gordon 2021, BE READY)
cards.people: 435 adults aged 18 years or older with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis at 77 sites in nine countries, randomised 4:1 to bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks (n=349) or placebo every 4 weeks (n=86) for 16 weeks; week-16 PASI 90 responders on bimekizumab were then re-allocated to bimekizumab every 4 weeks, every 8 weeks, or placebo for weeks 16–56.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 90 was achieved by 317 (91%) of 349 patients on bimekizumab versus 1 (1%) of 86 on placebo (risk difference 89.8; 95% CI 86.1–93.4; p<0.0001), and an IGA score of 0 or 1 by 323 (93%) of 349 versus 1 (1%) of 86 (risk difference 91.5; 95% CI 88.0–94.9; p<0.0001). Responses were maintained through week 56 on both bimekizumab maintenance schedules. Treatment-emergent adverse events in the initial 16 weeks were reported in 213 (61%) of 349 on bimekizumab and 35 (41%) of 86 on placebo; from weeks 16 to 56 they were reported in 78 (74%) of 106 on every-4-week bimekizumab, 77 (77%) of 100 on every-8-week bimekizumab, and 72 (69%) of 105 on placebo (withdrawal).
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparator, not adalimumab — this card supports that bimekizumab's clearance rates are real and durable, not that they beat any specific rival. The withdrawal-phase adverse-event rates include the placebo (withdrawal) arm at 69%, so long-term tolerability differences are narrower than the week-16 split suggests.
cards.source: Gordon KB et al. Bimekizumab efficacy and safety in moderate to severe plaque psoriasis (BE READY): a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised withdrawal phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 33549192. Registry ID: NCT03410992. cards.headline: Synthesis: one head-to-head win over adalimumab plus one decisive placebo-controlled trial — clearance is large, candidiasis is the standing price
cards.summary: Synthesis: one head-to-head win over adalimumab plus one decisive placebo-controlled trial — clearance is large, candidiasis is the standing price
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind phase 3 trials totalling 913 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: BE SURE (n=478, versus adalimumab) and BE READY (n=435, versus placebo with a randomised withdrawal phase).
cards.result: Week-16 PASI 90: 86.2% on bimekizumab versus 47.2% on adalimumab (BE SURE) and 91% versus 1% against placebo (BE READY). Week-16 IGA 0/1: 85.3% versus 57.2% (BE SURE) and 93% versus 1% (BE READY). Harm: oral candidiasis and diarrhoea more frequent on bimekizumab in BE SURE; treatment-emergent adverse events 61% versus 41% over the first 16 weeks of BE READY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the adalimumab claim rests on a single head-to-head trial, and neither abstract reports PASI 100, so the shelf claims clear-or-almost-clear skin, not literal complete clearance.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial flag for the head-to-head question: BE SURE is the only randomised bimekizumab-versus-adalimumab trial carded here; BE READY is a placebo-controlled supporting trial, not a second adalimumab comparison. A sibling psoriasis shelf already cards BE VIVID (bimekizumab versus ustekinumab, PMID: 33549193) — that record is deliberately not re-carded here under the one-home rule.

shelves.title: Ocriplasmin injection: vitreomacular adhesion released in 26.5% versus 10.1% and macular holes closed without surgery in 40.6% versus 10.6% — but most eyes still need watching or surgery, and transient ocular side effects are common
shelves.question: In patients with symptomatic vitreomacular traction, does a single intravitreal ocriplasmin injection release the traction and close macular holes compared with placebo injection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Eye Diseases/drug therapy · Fibrinolysin/therapeutic use · Humans · Intravitreal Injections · Peptide Fragments/therapeutic use · Retina/pathology · Retinal Perforations/drug therapy · Visual Acuity · Vitreous Body/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials, a real but minority anatomical win. In the pooled MIVI-TRUST trials (Stalmans P et al., PMID: 22894573), vitreomacular adhesion resolved by day 28 in 26.5% of ocriplasmin eyes versus 10.1% on placebo (P<0.001), and macular holes closed without surgery in 40.6% versus 10.6% (P<0.001). The price is transient ocular adverse events in 68.4% versus 53.5% (floaters, photopsia, injection pain, conjunctival haemorrhage), with serious ocular events similar between groups. Three of four treated eyes did not achieve release, so this is an option that spares a minority an operation, not a replacement for vitrectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single ocriplasmin injection releases traction and closes holes in a substantial minority, best in younger, phakic eyes with focal adhesion and small holes.

cards.headline: Stalmans 2012 (MIVI-TRUST, two phase 3 trials): adhesion resolved in 26.5% versus 10.1% at day 28; holes closed in 40.6% versus 10.6%; ocular adverse events 68.4% versus 53.5%
cards.summary: Stalmans 2012 (MIVI-TRUST, two phase 3 trials): adhesion resolved in 26.5% versus 10.1% at day 28; holes closed in 40.6% versus 10.6%; ocular adverse events 68.4% versus 53.5%
cards.people: 652 eyes with symptomatic vitreomacular adhesion (464 ocriplasmin 125 µg single intravitreal injection, 188 placebo injection) in two multicentre trials; primary endpoint resolution of vitreomacular adhesion at day 28.
cards.result: Vitreomacular adhesion resolved in 26.5% of ocriplasmin eyes versus 10.1% of placebo eyes (P<0.001). Total posterior vitreous detachment: 13.4% versus 3.7% (P<0.001). Non-surgical macular-hole closure: 40.6% versus 10.6% (P<0.001). Best-corrected visual acuity was more likely to improve by at least three lines with ocriplasmin. Ocular adverse events occurred in 68.4% versus 53.5% (P<0.001); serious ocular adverse events were similar (P=0.26).
cards.watchOut: The endpoints are anatomical at 28 days: roughly three-quarters of treated eyes did not achieve release, and the trials do not show that injection-first reduces eventual vitrectomy rates or improves long-term vision for the average patient. Adverse events were mainly transient but were self-reported symptoms (floaters, photopsia) that matter to patients.
cards.source: Stalmans P et al. Enzymatic vitreolysis with ocriplasmin for vitreomacular traction and macular holes. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22894573. cards.headline: Haller 2015 (MIVI-TRUST subgroup analyses): benefit concentrated in younger patients, phakic eyes, focal adhesion ≤1500 µm, no epiretinal membrane, and holes ≤250 µm wide
cards.summary: Haller 2015 (MIVI-TRUST subgroup analyses): benefit concentrated in younger patients, phakic eyes, focal adhesion ≤1500 µm, no epiretinal membrane, and holes ≤250 µm wide
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analyses of two randomised trials (Haller 2015)
cards.people: The same 652 randomised patients (464 ocriplasmin, 188 placebo) from the two MIVI-TRUST trials, analysed across prespecified subpopulations over 6 months.
cards.result: Resolution of vitreomacular adhesion at day 28 occurred more often in patients under 65 years, eyes without epiretinal membrane, eyes with a macular hole, phakic eyes, and eyes with focal adhesion ≤1500 µm. Eyes with hole width ≤250 µm were more likely to achieve non-surgical closure. Treatment differences favoured ocriplasmin across each subgroup studied.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup analyses of the same two trials are not independent confirmation — they refine who benefits rather than adding a third trial. Eyes with epiretinal membrane or broad adhesion are precisely the ones least likely to respond, and they are common in clinic.
cards.source: Haller JA et al. Efficacy of intravitreal ocriplasmin for treatment of vitreomacular adhesion: subgroup analyses from two randomized trials. Ophthalmology. 2015. PMID: 25240630. cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine minority win, predictable in advance — patient selection is the whole game
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine minority win, predictable in advance — patient selection is the whole game
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind phase 3 trials, 652 eyes, single ocriplasmin 125 µg injection versus placebo injection, with prespecified subgroup analyses.
cards.result: Adhesion release 26.5% versus 10.1%; non-surgical hole closure 40.6% versus 10.6%; ocular adverse events 68.4% versus 53.5%, serious events similar. Benefit is largest in younger, phakic eyes with focal adhesion and small (≤250 µm) holes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Dexamethasone implant for macular oedema after retinal vein occlusion: vision improves faster and more often than sham in two identical trials — the gain peaks by day 90, and repeated implants bring cataract progression in 29.8% of phakic eyes
shelves.question: In macular oedema after retinal vein occlusion, does the dexamethasone intravitreal implant improve vision compared with sham — and at what cataract and pressure cost?
shelves.mesh: Absorbable Implants · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Implants · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Macular Edema/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Retinal Vein Occlusion/complications/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity/physiology · Vitreous Body
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster, more frequent visual improvement, paid for in pressure rises and, with repeat dosing, cataract. In the two identical GENEVA trials (Haller JA et al., PMID: 20417567), eyes on the dexamethasone implant reached a ≥15-letter gain significantly sooner than sham (P<0.001), with the advantage concentrated at days 30–90; intraocular pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60 and was back to sham levels by day 180. Over 12 months with a second implant (PMID: 21764136), ≥15-letter gains were seen in 30% and 32% of patients 60 days after the first and second implants, but cataract progression occurred in 29.8% of phakic eyes receiving two 0.7 mg implants versus 5.7% on sham. This shelf is a different drug and question from the ranibizumab shelf for the same condition (live #894). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real short-horizon visual gain with a steroid's predictable ocular price.

cards.headline: Haller 2010 (GENEVA, two identical trials): time to ≥15-letter gain significantly shorter on implant (P<0.001); pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60, equal to sham by day 180
cards.summary: Haller 2010 (GENEVA, two identical trials): time to ≥15-letter gain significantly shorter on implant (P<0.001); pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60, equal to sham by day 180
cards.people: 1,267 patients with vision loss from macular oedema due to branch (BRVO) or central (CRVO) retinal vein occlusion, randomised to a single dexamethasone implant 0.7 mg (n=427), 0.35 mg (n=414), or sham (n=426), followed 6 months.
cards.result: Time to achieve a ≥15-letter improvement in best-corrected visual acuity was significantly less in both implant groups than sham (P<0.001). The percentage of eyes with a ≥15-letter improvement was significantly higher on implant at days 30–90 (P<0.001), and ≥15-letter loss was significantly less frequent on the 0.7 mg implant at all visits (P≤0.036). Intraocular pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60 (both doses) and was not different from sham by day 180. No significant between-group difference in cataract or cataract surgery at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: The record reports the pooled primary outcome as time-to-event rather than a single absolute percentage gaining ≥15 letters, and the visual advantage is a peak effect around days 30–90 from a single implant — durability beyond one implant cycle is addressed only by the open-label extension below.
cards.source: Haller JA et al. Randomized, sham-controlled trial of dexamethasone intravitreal implant in patients with macular edema due to retinal vein occlusion. Ophthalmology. 2010. PMID: 20417567. cards.headline: Haller 2011 (12-month GENEVA extension): ≥15-letter gains in 30–32% after each implant, but cataract progression in 29.8% of phakic eyes given two 0.7 mg implants versus 5.7% on sham
cards.summary: Haller 2011 (12-month GENEVA extension): ≥15-letter gains in 30–32% after each implant, but cataract progression in 29.8% of phakic eyes given two 0.7 mg implants versus 5.7% on sham
cards.people: 1,256 patients from the GENEVA trials; at day 180, 997 patients received an open-label 0.7 mg implant if vision or retinal thickness criteria were met; safety was the primary outcome of the extension.
cards.result: A ≥15-letter improvement was achieved by 30% and 32% of patients 60 days after the first and second 0.7 mg implants respectively. Cataract progression occurred in 90 of 302 phakic eyes (29.8%) receiving two 0.7 mg implants versus 5 of 88 sham-treated phakic eyes (5.7%); cataract surgery in 1.3% versus 1.1%. A ≥10 mmHg pressure rise occurred in 12.6% after the first and 15.4% after the second implant, usually transient and controlled with medication or observation; an additional 10.3% of patients started pressure-lowering medication after the second implant.
cards.watchOut: The extension was open-label and re-treatment was conditional on still having poor vision or thick retina, so the 12-month efficacy figures describe a selected subgroup, not the original randomised comparison. The cataract signal, by contrast, is a randomised-phase comparison and is the honest long-term price.
cards.source: Haller JA et al. Dexamethasone intravitreal implant in patients with macular edema related to branch or central retinal vein occlusion twelve-month study results. Ophthalmology. 2011. cards.headline: Synthesis: a peak-effect steroid — vision sooner, cataract later
cards.summary: Synthesis: a peak-effect steroid — vision sooner, cataract later
cards.people: Two identical randomised sham-controlled trials (1,267 patients) plus their 12-month extension, in macular oedema after branch or central retinal vein occlusion.
cards.result: Implant eyes reached ≥15-letter gains significantly faster than sham, with 30–32% gaining ≥15 letters 60 days after an implant; pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% transiently; cataract progression after two implants was 29.8% versus 5.7% in phakic eyes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the cataract and pressure costs on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Anti-VEGF therapy (live #894, ranibizumab) is the competing standard for this condition and this shelf makes no head-to-head claim; the implant's niche is where injections burden, response, or patient factors favour a longer-acting steroid despite its ocular price.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haller JA et al. Ophthalmology. 2010 (PMID: 20417567); Haller JA et al. Ophthalmology. 2011 (PMID: 21764136).

shelves.title: Fluocinolone implant in diabetic macular oedema (FAME): ≥15-letter gains in 28.7% versus 18.9% on sham at three years — but the benefit lives in chronic oedema (34.0% versus 13.4%), is absent in newer oedema, and nearly every phakic eye develops cataract
shelves.question: In diabetic macular oedema, does the fluocinolone acetonide implant sustain vision compared with sham or laser in the FAME trials?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Cataract/etiology/therapy · Diabetic Retinopathy/diagnosis/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Implants · Fluocinolone Acetonide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Fluorescein Angiography · Follow-Up Studies · Glaucoma/etiology/surgery · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Macular Edema/diagnosis/drug therapy · Phacoemulsification · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Trabeculectomy · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity/physiology · Vitreous Body
shelves.balance: SPLIT — benefit in chronic oedema, none shown in non-chronic oedema, with a heavy steroid price either way. In the two FAME trials (Campochiaro PA et al., PMID: 22727177), ≥15-letter gains at month 36 were 28.7% (low-dose insert) and 27.8% (high-dose) versus 18.9% on sham (P=0.018). The preplanned duration analysis (Cunha-Vaz J et al., PMID: 24935282) splits the result: in oedema present ≥3 years, low-dose gains were 34.0% versus 13.4% on sham (P<0.001); in oedema under 3 years, 22.3% versus 27.8% (P=0.275) — no benefit. Almost all phakic patients on the insert developed cataract, and incisional glaucoma surgery by month 36 was needed in 4.8% (low dose) and 8.1% (high dose). This is a different implant from the dexamethasone implant shelf in diabetic macular oedema (pack #4021). PROPOSED SPLIT: reserve judgement for chronic, previously laser-treated oedema; the trials do not support it earlier in the disease.

cards.headline: Campochiaro 2012 (FAME, two trials): ≥15-letter gains at month 36 in 28.7% (low dose) and 27.8% (high dose) versus 18.9% on sham (P=0.018)
cards.summary: Campochiaro 2012 (FAME, two trials): ≥15-letter gains at month 36 in 28.7% (low dose) and 27.8% (high dose) versus 18.9% on sham (P=0.018)
cards.people: 953 patients with persistent diabetic macular oedema despite at least one macular laser treatment, randomised 1:2:2 to sham injection (n=185), low-dose fluocinolone insert 0.2 µg/day (n=375), or high-dose 0.5 µg/day (n=393), with rescue laser allowed after 6 weeks and re-treatment after 1 year, followed 36 months.
cards.result: At month 36 (last observation carried forward), ≥15-letter gains were 28.7% (low dose) and 27.8% (high dose) versus 18.9% on sham (P=0.018); among patients still in the trial, 33.0% and 31.9% versus 21.4% (P=0.030). A ≥2-step retinopathy improvement occurred in 13.7% and 10.1% versus 8.9%. Almost all phakic patients in the insert groups developed cataract, though post-cataract-surgery visual benefit matched pseudophakic patients. Incisional glaucoma surgery at month 36: 4.8% (low dose) and 8.1% (high dose).
cards.watchOut: Every patient had already failed to clear oedema with laser, and rescue laser plus re-treatment were allowed in all arms, so this is an implant-plus-usual-care effect in a chronic, treatment-experienced population — not evidence for first-line use. The cataract outcome is close to a certainty in phakic eyes, so the visual figures are inseparable from cataract surgery.
cards.source: Campochiaro PA et al. Sustained delivery fluocinolone acetonide vitreous inserts provide benefit for at least 3 years in patients with diabetic macular edema. Ophthalmology. 2012. PMID: 22727177. cards.headline: Cunha-Vaz 2014 (FAME chronicity analysis): low-dose benefit 34.0% versus 13.4% in chronic oedema (P<0.001), but 22.3% versus 27.8% in non-chronic oedema (P=0.275)
cards.summary: Cunha-Vaz 2014 (FAME chronicity analysis): low-dose benefit 34.0% versus 13.4% in chronic oedema (P<0.001), but 22.3% versus 27.8% in non-chronic oedema (P=0.275)
cards.type: Preplanned subgroup analysis of two randomised trials (Cunha-Vaz 2014)
cards.people: The same FAME population (sham n=185, low-dose n=375, high-dose n=393), split by oedema duration at baseline: chronic (≥3 years) versus non-chronic (<3 years).
cards.result: At month 36, the low-dose versus sham difference in ≥15-letter gains was significantly greater in chronic oedema (34.0% versus 13.4%; P<0.001) than in non-chronic oedema (22.3% versus 27.8%; P=0.275). The greater chronic-oedema response was not explained by baseline ocular characteristics, anatomical changes, re-treatment, or ancillary therapies. The ocular adverse-event profile of the low-dose insert was similar regardless of oedema duration.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup split — even a preplanned one — is weaker evidence than the overall trial result, and the non-chronic arm's sham rate (27.8%) exceeding the low-dose rate is a reminder that newer oedema often improves with standard care alone. The split justifies the SPLIT stamp, not two separate confident claims.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the implant earns its keep only where oedema has already proved stubborn — and cataract is part of the package
cards.summary: Synthesis: the implant earns its keep only where oedema has already proved stubborn — and cataract is part of the package
cards.people: Two randomised sham-controlled trials (FAME, 953 patients with laser-persistent diabetic macular oedema) and their preplanned chronicity analysis, 36 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Overall ≥15-letter gains: 28.7%/27.8% (inserts) versus 18.9% (sham). By duration: chronic oedema 34.0% versus 13.4%; non-chronic 22.3% versus 27.8% (no benefit). Harms: cataract in almost all phakic eyes; incisional glaucoma surgery 4.8% (low dose) and 8.1% (high dose). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) confined to chronic oedema.
cards.watchOut: FAME predates routine anti-VEGF therapy as the comparator, so the trials answer implant-versus-sham/laser, not implant-versus-modern-standard; positioning against anti-VEGF or the dexamethasone implant (pack #4021) is extrapolation beyond this record.

shelves.title: Steroid irrigations after sinus surgery: one small double-blind trial found better symptom and endoscopy scores with budesonide rinses, a Samter's-triad trial found no added benefit over saline — and neither measured relapse or revision surgery
shelves.question: After endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis, do high-volume corticosteroid irrigations reduce relapse and revision surgery compared with saline irrigation?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Budesonide/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Endoscopy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nasal Lavage/methods · Paranasal Sinuses/physiopathology/surgery · Postoperative Care/methods · Prospective Studies · Reference Values · Rhinitis/diagnosis/surgery · Risk Assessment · Sinusitis/diagnosis/surgery · Sodium Chloride/pharmacology · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two double-blind trials disagree, and the outcome the question asks about was never measured. In a general chronic rhinosinusitis population after surgery (Ahamed S et al., PMID: 38440477), budesonide irrigation (0.5 mg in 200 mL, twice daily) beat saline on 3-month symptom scores (SNOT-22 26.69 versus 30.54; p<0.0001) and endoscopy scores. In Samter's triad patients (Rotenberg BW et al., PMID: 21997904), adding budesonide — as spray or mixed into irrigation — gave no benefit over saline irrigation alone at 6 or 12 months. Neither trial reported relapse rates or revision surgery, so any claim about preventing re-operation is unsupported by this record. This shelf is distinct from live #905 (surgery versus clarithromycin in chronic rhinosinusitis). PROPOSED SPLIT: possible short-term symptom benefit in ordinary post-surgical rhinosinusitis; no shown benefit in Samter's triad; revision surgery unstudied.

cards.headline: Rotenberg 2011: in Samter's triad, saline alone, saline plus budesonide spray, and saline mixed with budesonide all improved — with no difference between groups at 6 or 12 months
cards.summary: Rotenberg 2011: in Samter's triad, saline alone, saline plus budesonide spray, and saline mixed with budesonide all improved — with no difference between groups at 6 or 12 months
cards.people: 60 patients with Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease) and chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery, randomised postoperatively to saline irrigation alone, saline irrigation plus separate budesonide nasal spray, or saline irrigation mixed with budesonide spray; outcomes at baseline, 6 months and 1 year.
cards.result: All groups improved significantly and clinically from baseline on Sino-Nasal Outcome Test scores, Lund-Mackay CT scores and Lund-Kennedy endoscopic scores, with improvement sustained but lessened at 1 year. No statistically or clinically significant differences were observed between the three regimens at any time point (P>0.05) — no treatment effect for adding budesonide. Safety measures (ACTH levels, intraocular pressure) showed no between-group signal in the record.
cards.watchOut: Samter's triad is the most steroid-responsive-looking phenotype, yet it is also the most relapsing; a null here may reflect ceiling effects of surgery plus any irrigation, or a genuinely steroid-resistant subgroup. Either way this trial does not generalise cleanly to ordinary rhinosinusitis — which is why the stamp splits rather than averages.
cards.source: Rotenberg BW et al. Postoperative care for Samter's triad patients undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery: a double-blinded, randomized controlled trial. The Laryngoscope. 2011. PMID: 21997904. cards.headline: Ahamed 2024: budesonide high-volume rinse beat saline at 3 months — SNOT-22 26.69 versus 30.54 (p<0.0001), endoscopy score 4.06 versus 4.50 (p=0.0031)
cards.summary: Ahamed 2024: budesonide high-volume rinse beat saline at 3 months — SNOT-22 26.69 versus 30.54 (p<0.0001), endoscopy score 4.06 versus 4.50 (p=0.0031)
cards.people: 88 post-surgical chronic rhinosinusitis patients (44 per group; chronic rhinosinusitis subset of 55 analysed) receiving normal saline or budesonide nasal irrigation 0.5 mg in 200 mL twice daily via a high-volume low-pressure device, assessed at 2 weeks and 3 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, patient-reported SNOT-22 was significantly better with budesonide irrigation (26.69 ± 2.92) than saline (30.54 ± 2.81; p<0.0001), and the Lund-Kennedy endoscopic score was better (4.06 ± 0.74 versus 4.50 ± 0.67; p=0.0031). The authors conclude budesonide irrigation gives better patient benefit and wound healing than saline alone.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 88 patients with 3-month follow-up and score differences of modest size; the record carries no MeSH terms and reports no relapse, polyp-recurrence or revision-surgery outcomes. Three months after surgery is wound-healing territory, not relapse territory.
cards.source: Ahamed S et al. Double Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Budesonide and Saline Nasal Rinses in the Post-operative Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis. Indian journal of otolaryngology and head and neck surgery : official publication of the Association of Otolaryngologists of India. 2024. PMID: 38440477. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Synthesis: symptom scores split by population; the surgical outcomes in the question are simply absent
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials of postoperative budesonide delivered with irrigation after endoscopic sinus surgery: 60 Samter's triad patients (12 months) and 88 general chronic rhinosinusitis patients (3 months).
cards.result: General population: SNOT-22 and endoscopy scores favour budesonide rinse at 3 months. Samter's triad: no added benefit over saline at 6–12 months. Relapse and revision surgery: reported in neither trial. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for short-term scores in ordinary post-surgical disease only.
cards.watchOut: Anyone citing this shelf for 'steroid rinses prevent revision surgery' is going beyond the record: the trials were neither long enough nor designed to count re-operations. A revision-surgery trial would need years of follow-up and hundreds of patients.

shelves.title: Articaine versus lidocaine for dental anaesthesia: success odds roughly doubled overall (OR 2.44) and nearly quadrupled for infiltration (OR 3.81) — the edge shrinks for nerve blocks and vanishes in symptomatic teeth; paraesthesia was not a randomised-trial finding
shelves.question: For dental extractions and oral surgery, is articaine more effective than lidocaine for successful local anaesthesia, and does it carry more paraesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anesthesia, Dental · Anesthesia, Local · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage · Carticaine/administration & dosage · Dental Pulp/drug effects · Humans · Injections · Lidocaine/administration & dosage · Mandibular Nerve · Nerve Block/methods · Probability · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for anaesthetic success, with the advantage depending on technique. Pooling the randomised trials (Brandt RG et al., PMID: 21531931), articaine's odds of successful pulpal anaesthesia were 2.44 times lidocaine's (95% CI 1.59–3.76), rising to an odds ratio of 3.81 (2.71–5.36) for infiltration but only 1.57 (1.12–2.21) for mandibular block, with no difference in symptomatic teeth. A second meta-analysis (Katyal V et al., PMID: 20006669) found a relative success risk of 1.31 (1.12–1.54) in the posterior first molar and no difference in post-injection adverse events (relative risk 1.05, 0.66–1.65). On paraesthesia: neither meta-analysis of the randomised trials reports a paraesthesia excess — that concern rests on observational reports outside this randomised record, and this shelf does not card it as a trial finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): choose articaine where infiltration success matters; do not expect a block advantage in hot, symptomatic teeth.

cards.headline: Brandt 2011 (meta-analysis of RCTs): success OR 2.44 overall, 3.81 for infiltration, 1.57 for mandibular block — and no difference in symptomatic teeth
cards.summary: Brandt 2011 (meta-analysis of RCTs): success OR 2.44 overall, 3.81 for infiltration, 1.57 for mandibular block — and no difference in symptomatic teeth
cards.people: Thirteen randomised trials in adults directly comparing articaine with lidocaine local anaesthetic solutions for pulpal anaesthesia, identified from MEDLINE and Embase, with subgroup analyses by infiltration versus mandibular inferior alveolar block technique. The 13 trials enrolled 1,022 participants in total (the participant total reported for this meta-analysis in Martin et al.'s 2021 overview of the articaine evidence, BDJ Open); nine of the 13 trials were crossover designs and four used independent samples.
cards.result: Articaine had a superior probability of achieving anaesthetic success, odds ratio 2.44 (95% CI 1.59–3.76; P<0.0001). For infiltration alone the odds ratio was 3.81 (2.71–5.36; P<0.00001); for mandibular block it was weaker at 1.57 (1.12–2.21; P=0.009); in symptomatic teeth there was no difference between the solutions.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios flatter the difference when success is common — the absolute gain is largest where lidocaine infiltration already works reasonably and smallest exactly where dentists struggle most (the symptomatic mandibular molar). 'Success' definitions varied across the pooled trials.
cards.source: Brandt RG et al. The pulpal anesthetic efficacy of articaine versus lidocaine in dentistry: a meta-analysis. Journal of the American Dental Association (1939). 2011. PMID: 21531931. cards.headline: Katyal 2010 (meta-analysis of RCTs): success relative risk 1.31 in the posterior first molar; post-injection adverse events RR 1.05 — no safety difference, slightly more post-injection pain with articaine
cards.summary: Katyal 2010 (meta-analysis of RCTs): success relative risk 1.31 in the posterior first molar; post-injection adverse events RR 1.05 — no safety difference, slightly more post-injection pain with articaine
cards.people: Nine randomised trials comparing 4% articaine (1:100,000 epinephrine) with 2% lignocaine (1:100,000 epinephrine) for maxillary and mandibular infiltration and block anaesthesia in routine dental treatment, from Cochrane Central, Medline, Embase and other sources including the manufacturer's Australian division. The review lists its nine trials individually (its Table 2) and reports no single pooled participant total.
cards.result: Articaine was more likely to achieve anaesthetic success in the posterior first molar area, relative risk 1.31 (95% CI 1.12–1.54; P=0.0009). Post-injection adverse events did not differ, relative risk 1.05 (0.66–1.65; P=0.85). Articaine injections scored higher on post-reversal pain (weighted mean difference 6.49 on a visual analogue scale, 0.02–12.96; P=0.05), falling to 1.10 by day three.
cards.watchOut: The paraesthesia question cannot be answered from these trials: prolonged numbness is rare and was not a reported outcome in the pooled randomised data, so this meta-analysis's 'no difference in adverse events' covers common events only. The paraesthesia literature is observational and is deliberately not carded here.
cards.source: Katyal V et al. The efficacy and safety of articaine versus lignocaine in dental treatments: a meta-analysis. Journal of dentistry. 2010. PMID: 20006669. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real technique-dependent edge on success; the paraesthesia fear is not in the randomised record
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real technique-dependent edge on success; the paraesthesia fear is not in the randomised record
cards.people: Two independent meta-analyses of randomised articaine-versus-lidocaine trials (Brandt 2011; Katyal 2010), covering infiltration and block techniques in routine dentistry.
cards.result: Success: OR 2.44 overall, 3.81 infiltration, 1.57 block, no difference in symptomatic teeth; molar success RR 1.31. Safety in trials: post-injection adverse events RR 1.05 (no difference); slightly higher short-lived post-injection pain with articaine. Paraesthesia: not reported as an outcome in the pooled randomised trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both meta-analyses pool small, older, often crossover trials with varying success definitions, and one searched with manufacturer assistance — the direction is consistent across both, which is why this reaches POSSIBLE, but the symptomatic-tooth null should temper chairside expectations.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone around third-molar surgery: pooled trials show less early pain (NNT 4) and less swelling (NNT 5) with submucosal injection — the trismus gain is under 5 mm and not clinically significant
shelves.question: In patients having surgical removal of impacted third molars, does pre- or peri-operative dexamethasone reduce swelling, trismus and pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Edema/drug therapy · Humans · Molar, Third/surgery · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tooth Extraction · Tooth, Impacted/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent across two meta-analyses for pain and swelling, weakest exactly where patients hope most (jaw opening). The larger pooled analysis (O'Hare PE et al., PMID: 31078366; 17 trials of submucosal dexamethasone) found the greatest clinical effects were early postoperative pain (number needed to treat 4) and early oedema (NNT 5), with moderate-quality evidence for late pain and early oedema reduction — but the trismus reduction was under 5 mm and not clinically significant. The earlier meta-analysis (Moraschini V et al., PMID: 26458538; 8 articles) agrees: oedema and pain reduced, no statistically significant difference for trismus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a peri-operative dexamethasone injection buys a modest, real reduction in pain and swelling over the first days; it does not meaningfully loosen a stiff jaw.

cards.headline: O'Hare 2019 (17 trials): early pain NNT 4, early oedema NNT 5 — but trismus reduction <5 mm, 'not clinically significant'
cards.summary: O'Hare 2019 (17 trials): early pain NNT 4, early oedema NNT 5 — but trismus reduction <5 mm, 'not clinically significant'
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (O'Hare 2019)
cards.people: 17 randomised and quasi-randomised trials of submucosal dexamethasone in adults undergoing impacted mandibular third-molar surgery, searched to June 2018, independently assessed for risk of bias. The review reports no single pooled participant total in its record — its meta-analyses pool each outcome separately.
cards.result: Low-quality evidence supported reductions in early postoperative pain, early and late trismus, and late oedema; moderate-quality evidence supported reduction of late postoperative pain and early oedema. The greatest clinical effects were early postoperative pain (number needed to treat = 4) and early postoperative oedema (NNT = 5). The reduction in trismus was not clinically significant (<5 mm).
cards.watchOut: Evidence quality was low to moderate, doses and timing varied across trials, and the record reports numbers-needed-to-treat rather than pooled millimetre or pain-score differences — so the size of the swelling benefit in millimetres cannot be quoted from this record. Harms of a single peri-operative steroid dose were not the review's focus.

cards.people: Eight articles on submucosal dexamethasone injection after impacted third-molar surgery, covering 476 patients in total (256 in the dexamethasone groups and 220 in the control groups), from PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Central and Web of Science to June 2015; intervention effects expressed as mean differences in millimetres for the swelling outcomes.
cards.result: The meta-analysis found submucosal dexamethasone reduced postoperative signs and symptoms of impacted third-molar surgery, especially oedema and pain. For trismus, there was no statistically significant difference between dexamethasone and the placebo solution.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports direction and significance without the pooled millimetre values, and eligibility admitted non-randomised alongside randomised trials — concordant with O'Hare 2019 on every outcome, but the weaker of the two records. Two meta-analyses agreeing is reassuring; both pool substantially the same small trial literature.
