shelves.title: Tranexamic acid mouthwash after dental extraction on anticoagulants: in the warfarin era it cut bleeding patients from 8 of 20 to 1 of 19 — in the modern NOAC trial the primary outcome was null (26.4% versus 28.6%), with fewer delayed bleeds only
shelves.question: In patients on oral anticoagulants having dental extractions, does tranexamic acid mouthwash reduce postoperative bleeding compared with placebo or standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · Clinical Trials as Topic · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouthwashes · Random Allocation · Surgery, Oral · Tooth Extraction · Tranexamic Acid/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by anticoagulant era and by bleeding timing. In 1989, in patients continuing warfarin-type anticoagulation (Sindet-Pedersen S et al., PMID: 2648144), tranexamic acid mouthwash (4.8% solution, four times daily for 7 days) left 1 of 19 patients with a postoperative bleed versus 8 of 20 patients (10 episodes) on placebo (P=0.01), with no systemic side effects. In the modern EXTRACT-NOAC trial (Ockerman A et al., PMID: 33939696), 10% tranexamic acid mouthwash did not reduce any post-extraction bleeding by day 7 (26.4% versus 28.6%; relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.60–1.42; P=0.72), though delayed bleeding (rate ratio 0.32, 0.12–0.89) and bleeding after multiple extractions (rate ratio 0.40, 0.20–0.78) were lower. PROPOSED SPLIT: a large benefit in the small older warfarin trial; in today's NOAC patients, no overall benefit, with a possible delayed-bleed advantage.

cards.headline: Sindet-Pedersen 1989: postoperative bleeding in 1 of 19 patients on tranexamic mouthwash versus 8 of 20 (10 episodes) on placebo (P=0.01), anticoagulation continued unchanged
cards.summary: Sindet-Pedersen 1989: postoperative bleeding in 1 of 19 patients on tranexamic mouthwash versus 8 of 20 (10 episodes) on placebo (P=0.01), anticoagulation continued unchanged
cards.people: 39 patients receiving anticoagulants for cardiac valvular stenosis, a prosthetic cardiac valve, or a vascular prosthesis, undergoing oral surgery with no change in anticoagulant therapy before or after surgery; the socket was irrigated with 10 mL of 4.8% tranexamic acid or placebo before suturing, then patients rinsed with 10 mL four times daily for 7 days (19 tranexamic acid, 20 placebo).
cards.result: Eight patients in the placebo group had a total of 10 postoperative bleeding episodes, whereas only 1 patient in the tranexamic acid group had a bleeding episode (P=0.01). Baseline variables including the level of anticoagulation did not differ between groups. There were no systemic side effects. The authors conclude local antifibrinolytic therapy prevents bleeding after oral surgery in anticoagulated patients.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine patients from the warfarin era, when anticoagulation intensity and extraction practice differed from today; an effect this large (roughly an 85% relative reduction in patients bleeding) in a sample this small is exactly the pattern that later, larger trials often shrink — which is what the second card shows.
cards.source: Sindet-Pedersen S et al. Hemostatic effect of tranexamic acid mouthwash in anticoagulant-treated patients undergoing oral surgery. The New England journal of medicine. 1989. PMID: 2648144. cards.headline: Ockerman 2021 (EXTRACT-NOAC): any bleeding 26.4% versus 28.6% (RR 0.92, P=0.72) — but delayed bleeding rate ratio 0.32 and multiple-extraction bleeding 0.40
cards.summary: Ockerman 2021 (EXTRACT-NOAC): any bleeding 26.4% versus 28.6% (RR 0.92, P=0.72) — but delayed bleeding rate ratio 0.32 and multiple-extraction bleeding 0.40
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Ockerman 2021, EXTRACT-NOAC)
cards.people: 218 patients on non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants undergoing dental extraction (106 tranexamic acid, 112 placebo; mean ages 74.8 and 72.7 years), using 10% tranexamic acid or placebo mouthwash once before extraction then three times daily for 3 days; primary outcome any post-extraction oral bleeding up to day 7.
cards.result: Post-extraction bleeding occurred in 28 of 106 patients (26.4%) on tranexamic acid and 32 of 112 (28.6%) on placebo (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.42; P=0.72). Total bleeds were 46 versus 85 (rate ratio 0.57, 0.31 to 1.05; P=0.07). Periprocedural and early bleeding did not differ; delayed bleeding (rate ratio 0.32, 0.12 to 0.89) and bleeding after multiple extractions (rate ratio 0.40, 0.20 to 0.78) were lower on tranexamic acid. One placebo patient had a transient ischaemic attack while interrupting NOAC therapy for the extraction.
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early after a futility analysis and compliance was self-reported, so the subgroup signals (delayed, multiple-extraction) are hypothesis-generating. Baseline bleeding rates on NOACs are far lower-stakes than in the warfarin-era trial — most bleeds here were minor oral oozing, not the events the 1989 regimen was preventing.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the mouthwash did not change — the anticoagulants and the bleeding risk did
cards.summary: Synthesis: the mouthwash did not change — the anticoagulants and the bleeding risk did
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials 32 years apart: 39 warfarin-era patients (1989) and 218 NOAC patients (2021), tranexamic acid mouthwash versus placebo after dental extraction with anticoagulation continued.
cards.result: Warfarin era: patients bleeding 1/19 versus 8/20 (P=0.01). NOAC era: any bleeding 26.4% versus 28.6% (relative risk 0.92, not significant); delayed bleeding rate ratio 0.32; multiple-extraction bleeding rate ratio 0.40. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit by era and bleeding timing, not a blanket yes or no.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial supports stopping the anticoagulant to solve the bleeding problem — both kept it running, and the one thrombotic event in EXTRACT-NOAC occurred in a patient who interrupted therapy. The practical reading is: tranexamic mouthwash is cheap insurance for delayed oozing, not a proven shield in NOAC patients overall.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sindet-Pedersen S et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1989 (PMID: 2648144); Ockerman A et al. PLoS medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33939696).

shelves.title: Socket preservation grafting: about 2 mm less horizontal and 1.7 mm less vertical ridge shrinkage across 22 randomised trials — whether that buys better implants later was not shown
shelves.question: In patients having a tooth extracted, does socket (ridge) preservation grafting reduce ridge resorption and improve later implant outcomes compared with unassisted healing?
shelves.mesh: Alveolar Bone Loss · Alveolar Process · Alveolar Ridge Augmentation · Animals · Bone Substitutes · Bone Transplantation · Cattle · Humans · Swine · Tooth Extraction · Tooth Socket
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ridge dimensions, a surrogate; the implant-outcome half of the question is unverified. Across 22 randomised trials (Avila-Ortiz G et al., PMID: 30623987), socket grafting (ridge preservation) versus extraction alone prevented horizontal resorption by a pooled 1.99 mm (95% CI 1.54–2.44; p<0.00001), vertical mid-buccal resorption by 1.72 mm (0.96–2.48) and vertical mid-lingual resorption by 1.16 mm (0.81–1.52) at 3–6 months, with the largest preservation where the buccal wall was thicker than 1.0 mm (3.2 mm versus 1.29 mm for thinner walls, allograft subgroup). No superior graft modality could be determined, and patient-reported outcomes were comparable in the two studies reporting them. Neither this record nor any card below demonstrates fewer failed implants, fewer later augmentations, or better prosthetic outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): grafting preserves roughly 1–2 mm of ridge that would otherwise be lost; whether that millimetre changes the implant story is asserted by practice, not shown by these trials.

cards.headline: Avila-Ortiz 2019 (22 RCTs): ridge preservation prevented 1.99 mm horizontal, 1.72 mm mid-buccal vertical and 1.16 mm mid-lingual vertical resorption versus extraction alone
cards.summary: Avila-Ortiz 2019 (22 RCTs): ridge preservation prevented 1.99 mm horizontal, 1.72 mm mid-buccal vertical and 1.16 mm mid-lingual vertical resorption versus extraction alone
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Avila-Ortiz 2019)
cards.people: 22 randomised clinical trials (25 articles), enrolling 730 participants in total (initial participant numbers summed from the review's Table 1), comparing alveolar ridge preservation modalities — bovine or porcine bone particles, allograft, alloplastics, blood-derived products, cell therapy, rhBMP-2, or socket sealing alone, most with socket sealing — against tooth extraction alone, with healing assessed at 3–6 months.
cards.result: Pooled socket grafting versus extraction alone prevented horizontal bone resorption by 1.99 mm (95% CI 1.54–2.44; p<0.00001), vertical mid-buccal resorption by 1.72 mm (0.96–2.48; p<0.00001) and vertical mid-lingual resorption by 1.16 mm (0.81–1.52; p<0.00001). Sites with buccal bone thickness >1.0 mm showed more favourable preservation (allograft-plus-sealing difference 3.2 mm) than thinner walls (1.29 mm). No superior preservation modality could be determined; xenogenic or allogenic particles covered with a collagen membrane or sponge were associated with the most favourable horizontal outcomes. Patient-reported outcomes were comparable between groups in the two studies reporting them.
cards.watchOut: Millimetres of ridge at 3–6 months are a surrogate: the record does not report implant survival, need for later augmentation, or prosthetic success, so the clinical value of the preserved 2 mm is inferred, not measured. Nine different modalities are pooled under one umbrella, and thin-walled sockets — the ones clinicians worry about most — gained least.

PMID: 30623987. cards.summary: Synthesis: the ridge shrinks less with a graft — full stop; the implant payoff is not in this record
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials of socket grafting versus unassisted healing after tooth extraction, outcomes at 3–6 months.
cards.result: Horizontal resorption reduced by 1.99 mm; vertical mid-buccal by 1.72 mm; vertical mid-lingual by 1.16 mm; patient-reported outcomes comparable. Later implant outcomes: not reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for dimensional preservation only.

Cost, graft-related complications and the no-graft pathway's later augmentation rates all sit outside the verified record.

shelves.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis at dental implant placement: older pooled trials suggested fewer failures (RR 0.40, NNT 33) — the largest modern placebo trial found failures of 2.5% versus 3.0% and no significant benefit
shelves.question: In patients receiving dental implants, does antibiotic prophylaxis reduce early implant failure and postoperative infection compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amoxicillin/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Antibiotic Prophylaxis/adverse effects · Dental Implantation, Endosseous/adverse effects · Dental Implants/adverse effects · Dental Restoration Failure · Humans
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by era and baseline risk. The Cochrane-based review (Esposito M et al., PMID: 20623035) pooled 4 randomised trials and found significantly more implant failures without antibiotics (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19–0.84, favouring prophylaxis), translating to a number needed to treat of 33 at a 5% control failure rate, with no significant difference in infections or adverse events. The largest single trial since (Momand P et al., PMID: 35075765; 474 patients, 2 g amoxicillin versus placebo, double-blind) found implant failures in 2.5% on antibiotics versus 3.0% on placebo and infections in 0.8% versus 2.1% — both non-significant — and its authors conclude prophylaxis is likely of small benefit and should be avoided in most cases. PROPOSED SPLIT: where baseline failure risk is low, routine prophylaxis buys little; the older pooled benefit was estimated at higher baseline risk.

cards.headline: Momand 2022 (474 patients, double-blind): implant failure 2.5% versus 3.0% and infection 0.8% versus 2.1% on amoxicillin versus placebo — neither significant
cards.summary: Momand 2022 (474 patients, double-blind): implant failure 2.5% versus 3.0% and infection 0.8% versus 2.1% on amoxicillin versus placebo — neither significant
cards.people: 474 healthy or relatively healthy patients receiving dental implants at seven clinics in southern Sweden, randomised to a single preoperative 2 g amoxicillin dose or identical placebo; primary outcome implant failure, secondary outcomes postoperative infection and adverse events, assessed at 7–14 days and 3–6 months (238 antibiotic, 235 placebo evaluated).
cards.result: Implant failures occurred in six patients (2.5%) on antibiotics and seven (3.0%) on placebo; postoperative infections in two patients (0.8%) versus five (2.1%). Between-group differences in both outcomes were non-significant, and no patient reported adverse events. The authors conclude antibiotic prophylaxis at implant placement is likely of small benefit and should be avoided in most cases, particularly given rising antimicrobial resistance.
cards.watchOut: With failure rates this low, even 474 patients cannot exclude a small absolute benefit — the trial's confidence story is 'no large effect', not 'exactly zero'. Patients needing bone augmentation or with complex surgery were outside this healthy-patient frame, and extrapolation to them is not licensed by this record.

cards.headline: Esposito 2010 (Cochrane review, 4 RCTs): failures significantly fewer with prophylaxis — RR 0.40 (0.19–0.84), NNT 33 at a 5% failure rate without antibiotics
cards.summary: Esposito 2010 (Cochrane review, 4 RCTs): failures significantly fewer with prophylaxis — RR 0.40 (0.19–0.84), NNT 33 at a 5% failure rate without antibiotics
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Esposito 2010)
cards.people: Four randomised trials with at least 3 months' follow-up comparing prophylactic antibiotics versus none/placebo at dental implant placement, searched to June 2010: three trials of 2 g preoperative amoxicillin versus placebo (927 patients) and one of 1 g amoxicillin plus 500 mg four times daily for 2 days versus no antibiotics (80 patients).
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed significantly more patients experiencing implant failures in the group not receiving antibiotics: risk ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.84) favouring antibiotics. The number needed to treat to prevent one patient having an implant failure was 33 (95% CI 17–100), based on a 5% patient failure rate without antibiotics. Prosthesis failures, postoperative infections and adverse events did not differ significantly; only two minor adverse events were recorded. The review's first author was also first author of two included trials but was not involved in their quality assessment.
cards.watchOut: The NNT of 33 is arithmetic on a 5% baseline failure rate; at the 3.0% placebo failure rate of the modern trial above, the same relative effect would imply an NNT near 55 — and the modern trial did not confirm even that relative effect. Small, older trials plus authorship overlap argue for reading the pooled RR as an upper bound.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the relative effect shrank as baseline failure rates fell — routine prophylaxis is hard to justify at modern rates
cards.summary: Synthesis: the relative effect shrank as baseline failure rates fell — routine prophylaxis is hard to justify at modern rates
cards.people: Four older randomised trials pooled by Cochrane (1,007 patients) and one modern double-blind multicentre trial (474 patients), all testing chiefly single-dose preoperative amoxicillin versus placebo/no antibiotic at implant placement.
cards.result: Pooled older trials: failure risk ratio 0.40 (0.19–0.84); NNT 33 at 5% baseline risk. Modern trial: failures 2.5% versus 3.0%, infections 0.8% versus 2.1%, both non-significant. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit plausible at higher baseline risk, unproven and likely tiny at contemporary low rates.
cards.watchOut: Neither record addresses prolonged postoperative courses, penicillin-allergic alternatives, or augmented/complex sites. The stewardship cost of treating ~33–55 patients to possibly prevent one failure belongs on the face of any decision drawn from this shelf.

shelves.title: Full-mouth disinfection within 24 hours versus quadrant-by-quadrant cleaning: across 20 randomised trials there was no benefit in pocket depth (MD 0.11 mm) or attachment at 6–8 months — one visit or four, the gums end up the same
shelves.question: In patients with chronic periodontitis, does full-mouth disinfection within 24 hours improve probing depth compared with quadrant-wise scaling and root planing over weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/therapeutic use · Chronic Periodontitis/drug therapy · Humans · Tooth Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-pooled null. The Cochrane review (Jervøe-Storm PM et al., PMID: 35763286) included 20 randomised trials with 944 participants: at 6–8 months, full-mouth disinfection versus conventional quadrant scaling and root planing showed no evidence of benefit for probing pocket depth (mean difference 0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.27; 6 trials, 224 participants; low-certainty) or clinical attachment gain (0.07 mm, −0.11 to 0.24), and full-mouth scaling without antiseptic was likewise null (pocket depth mean difference 0.03 mm, −0.14 to 0.20). The head-to-head trial of the three protocols (Swierkot K et al., PMID: 19236536) agrees: all improved, with no group differences by 8 months. This shelf answers the periodontal-outcome question only; live #462 homes the different question of periodontal treatment and HbA1c in diabetes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): compressing treatment into 24 hours, with or without antiseptic disinfection, does not deepen the result — choose the schedule on logistics and patient preference.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022 (20 RCTs, 944 participants): no benefit for full-mouth disinfection over quadrant treatment — pocket depth MD 0.11 mm (−0.04 to 0.27), attachment MD 0.07 mm at 6–8 months
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022 (20 RCTs, 944 participants): no benefit for full-mouth disinfection over quadrant treatment — pocket depth MD 0.11 mm (−0.04 to 0.27), attachment MD 0.07 mm at 6–8 months
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Jervøe-Storm 2022)
cards.people: 20 randomised trials (944 participants with periodontitis by the 1999 classification, follow-up at least 3 months) comparing full-mouth scaling within 24 hours, full-mouth disinfection (24-hour instrumentation plus adjunctive antiseptic), and conventional quadrant scaling and root planing over weekly visits; primary outcomes tooth loss and probing pocket depth change.
cards.result: No study assessed tooth loss. Full-mouth disinfection versus control at 6–8 months: probing depth mean difference 0.11 mm (95% CI −0.04 to 0.27; 6 trials, 224 participants; low-certainty) and attachment gain 0.07 mm (−0.11 to 0.24; low-certainty), with no evidence of benefit for bleeding on probing (very low-certainty). Full-mouth scaling without antiseptic versus control: probing depth mean difference 0.03 mm (−0.14 to 0.20; 5 trials, 148 participants). Full-mouth disinfection versus full-mouth scaling: probing depth mean difference −0.11 mm (−0.30 to 0.07; P=0.22).
cards.watchOut: Certainty was low to very low and several trials were at high or unclear risk of bias, so the honest statement is 'no evidence of benefit', with confidence intervals tight enough to exclude a large effect but not a small one. A tenth of a millimetre would not change a single clinical decision in any case.
cards.source: Jervøe-Storm PM et al. Full-mouth treatment modalities (within 24 hours) for periodontitis in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 35763286. cards.headline: Swierkot 2009 (three-arm RCT): all three protocols improved significantly; the only group differences were at 1–2 months and had vanished by 8 months
cards.summary: Swierkot 2009 (three-arm RCT): all three protocols improved significantly; the only group differences were at 1–2 months and had vanished by 8 months
cards.people: 28 patients with generalised chronic periodontitis randomised to quadrant scaling and root planing at 1-week intervals, one-stage full-mouth scaling within 24 hours, or one-stage full-mouth disinfection (24-hour scaling plus chlorhexidine); 25 completed, with clinical and microbiological measures at baseline and 1, 2, 4 and 8 months.
cards.result: All three modalities produced significant clinical improvement at every time point. Group differences appeared only at 1 and 2 months (the full-mouth scaling group showed greater early probing-depth and bleeding reductions than the other two); by 8 months there were no significant group differences. Bacterial counts fell in every group, significantly only for Prevotella intermedia in the disinfection group at 8 months.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five completers cannot detect small differences, and the transient early advantage for full-mouth scaling is the kind of finding that powered the original enthusiasm for one-stage treatment — the 8-month convergence, replicated across the Cochrane pool, is the durable message.
cards.source: Swierkot K et al. One-stage full-mouth disinfection versus quadrant and full-mouth root planing. Journal of clinical periodontology. 2009. PMID: 19236536. cards.headline: Synthesis: schedule is logistics, not therapy — 24-hour protocols match, but do not beat, quadrant treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: schedule is logistics, not therapy — 24-hour protocols match, but do not beat, quadrant treatment
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 20 randomised trials (944 participants) and one three-arm randomised trial (25 completers) comparing full-mouth scaling, full-mouth disinfection and quadrant-wise scaling and root planing in periodontitis.
cards.result: Probing depth differences at 6–8 months: 0.11 mm (disinfection versus quadrant) and 0.03 mm (full-mouth scaling versus quadrant), both non-significant with intervals excluding large effects; attachment differences likewise null; no tooth-loss data anywhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The one thing a 24-hour protocol plausibly changes — number of visits, patient burden, short-term bacteraemia exposure — was not this shelf's outcome set. Clinicians may still choose it for scheduling; they should not promise deeper pockets-healing for it.

shelves.title: Acute urticaria: adding a steroid to the antihistamine did nothing in both trials (itch gone at 2 days in 62% with prednisone versus 76% without) — and the H2 add-on has never been randomised at all
shelves.question: In adults with acute urticaria, does adding an H2 blocker or a corticosteroid to an H1 antihistamine improve symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Cetirizine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Histamine H1 Antagonists, Non-Sedating/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Urticaria/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adding a corticosteroid to an H1 antihistamine does not improve acute urticaria in either randomised trial. In the larger trial (Barniol C et al., PMID: 28476259), complete itch relief at 2 days occurred in 62% of patients given prednisone plus levocetirizine versus 76% given levocetirizine alone (difference 14%, 95% CI −31% to 4%), with relapses in 30% versus 24%. In the second trial (Palungwachira P et al., PMID: 32139204), adding intravenous dexamethasone to chlorpheniramine produced no significant difference in itch scores at 60 minutes, and patients also given oral prednisolone at discharge had more active urticaria at 1-week and 1-month follow-up. For the H2-blocker half of the question there is no add-on trial at all: the one randomised H2 study (Moscati RM et al., PMID: 2404434) compared cimetidine instead of an H1 blocker, not in addition to one, finding improvement in 87% on cimetidine versus 76% on diphenhydramine with less sedation on cimetidine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine steroid bursts on top of an antihistamine are an unproven habit for uncomplicated acute urticaria; the H2 add-on question remains untested in randomised trials.

cards.headline: Barniol 2018: itch completely gone at 2 days in 62% on prednisone plus levocetirizine versus 76% on levocetirizine alone — the steroid arm did numerically worse
cards.summary: Barniol 2018: itch completely gone at 2 days in 62% on prednisone plus levocetirizine versus 76% on levocetirizine alone — the steroid arm did numerically worse
cards.people: 100 emergency-department patients aged 18 or older with acute urticaria of no more than 24 hours' duration (anaphylaxis excluded), all given levocetirizine 5 mg orally for 5 days and randomised double-blind to prednisone 40 mg orally for 4 days or placebo; 50 patients per group.
cards.result: At 2-day follow-up, 62% of patients in the prednisone group had an itch score of 0 versus 76% of those in the placebo group (difference 14%, 95% CI −31% to 4%). Relapses were reported by 30% on prednisone and 24% on placebo. Mild adverse events were reported by 12% on prednisone and 14% on placebo. The authors conclude the addition of a prednisone burst did not improve the symptomatic and clinical response of acute urticaria to levocetirizine.
cards.watchOut: Patients with anaphylaxis or angioedema-driven presentations were outside this trial's frame — the null applies to uncomplicated acute urticaria, and the trial does not license withholding steroids where airway or angioedema concerns drive the decision.

cards.headline: Palungwachira 2021: adding intravenous dexamethasone to chlorpheniramine made no difference to itch at 60 minutes — and the group also sent home on prednisolone had more active urticaria later
cards.summary: Palungwachira 2021: adding intravenous dexamethasone to chlorpheniramine made no difference to itch at 60 minutes — and the group also sent home on prednisolone had more active urticaria later
cards.people: 75 adult emergency-department patients in Thailand with acute urticaria and a pruritus score above 5 on a visual analogue scale, randomised double-blind to intravenous chlorpheniramine alone, chlorpheniramine plus intravenous dexamethasone, or chlorpheniramine plus dexamethasone plus 5 days of oral prednisolone at discharge (25 patients per group).
cards.result: Itch scores fell in all groups, but there was no significant difference in scores at 60 minutes between the chlorpheniramine-only group (n = 25) and the pooled dexamethasone groups (n = 50). At 1-week and 1-month follow-up, active urticaria (urticaria activity score over 7 days) was more prevalent in the group also given oral prednisolone than in the control group. The authors found no evidence that adding intravenous dexamethasone improves severe pruritus from uncomplicated acute urticaria and discourage adjunctive corticosteroids.
cards.watchOut: Small (25 per arm) and single-centre, with a 60-minute primary window that cannot detect a late steroid effect — but its direction matches the larger Barniol trial, including the suggestion of rebound activity after a steroid course, so the two trials corroborate rather than merely repeat each other.

cards.headline: Moscati 1990: cimetidine alone relieved acute urticaria about as well as diphenhydramine alone (improvement in 87% versus 76%) — an H2-instead-of-H1 trial, because no H2 add-on trial exists
cards.summary: Moscati 1990: cimetidine alone relieved acute urticaria about as well as diphenhydramine alone (improvement in 87% versus 76%) — an H2-instead-of-H1 trial, because no H2 add-on trial exists
cards.people: 93 patients presenting to an emergency department with acute urticaria, randomised double-blind to a single intramuscular dose of diphenhydramine 50 mg (an H1 blocker) or cimetidine 300 mg (an H2 blocker), with itching, wheals, sedation and overall improvement scored before treatment and 30 minutes after.
cards.result: Each medication provided significant relief of itching and wheal intensity (P < .0001 for both). Overall improvement was reported by 87% of cimetidine patients and 76% of diphenhydramine patients. Sedation was caused by both drugs but was significantly greater with diphenhydramine (P = .0001).
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a different question from the one on the shelf: cimetidine as a substitute for, not an addition to, an H1 blocker, assessed at 30 minutes after a single intramuscular dose. It is carded to show the boundary honestly — the popular H1-plus-H2 combination has never been tested in a randomised trial this search could find.
cards.source: Moscati RM et al. Comparison of cimetidine and diphenhydramine in the treatment of acute urticaria. Annals of emergency medicine. 1990. PMID: 2404434. cards.headline: Synthesis: steroids on top of an antihistamine — two trials, no benefit; H2 add-on — no trial at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroids on top of an antihistamine — two trials, no benefit; H2 add-on — no trial at all
cards.people: Two randomised steroid add-on trials (100 and 75 emergency-department patients) and one 93-patient head-to-head trial of an H2 blocker versus an H1 blocker.
cards.result: Complete itch relief at 2 days: 62% with prednisone added versus 76% without (Barniol 2018). Itch at 60 minutes: no significant difference with dexamethasone added (Palungwachira 2021). H2 blocker instead of H1 blocker: improvement 87% versus 76%, less sedation (Moscati 1990). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: for uncomplicated acute urticaria, treat with the antihistamine; the steroid burst adds nothing measurable.
cards.watchOut: Adjuncts in anaphylaxis are a different question, homed at pack #3867 (where the randomised record is empty); nothing here should be read across to anaphylaxis or to urticaria with angioedema.

shelves.title: Corneal abrasion: the pressure patch heals nothing — pooled healing was identical by 48 hours and the biggest trial found unpatched eyes healed faster with less pain
shelves.question: In adults with corneal abrasion, does a pressure patch improve healing or pain compared with no patch?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Bandages · Cornea/physiology · Corneal Injuries · Eye Foreign Bodies/physiopathology/therapy · Eye Injuries, Penetrating/physiopathology/therapy · Female · Humans · Intraocular Pressure · Male · Middle Aged · Mydriatics/therapeutic use · Ointments · Postoperative Pain/physiopathology/therapy · Wound Healing/physiology · Wounds, Nonpenetrating/physiopathology/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — patching a corneal abrasion does not speed healing or relieve pain, and may slightly delay healing on the first day. The largest single trial (Kaiser PK et al., PMID: 9098299) randomised 223 patients with traumatic or foreign-body-removal abrasions to a pressure patch or no patch on top of antibiotic ointment and mydriatics: the no-patch patients healed significantly faster and had less pain in both the traumatic (120 patients) and foreign-body (81 patients) groups, with better compliance when unpatched. The Cochrane review (Lim CH et al., PMID: 27457359) pooled 12 trials (1,080 participants): patched eyes were less likely to be healed at 24 hours (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.00), with no difference at 48 hours (risk ratio 0.97, 0.91 to 1.02) or 72 hours (risk ratio 1.01, 0.97 to 1.05), a mean healing time 0.14 days longer with a patch (0 to 0.27 days), and pain ratings generally similar between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for simple, non-contact-lens-related abrasions, the patch is ritual, not treatment — antibiotics and time do the work.

cards.headline: Kaiser 1995: unpatched abrasions healed significantly faster with less pain — in both traumatic (120 patients) and foreign-body (81 patients) abrasions
cards.summary: Kaiser 1995: unpatched abrasions healed significantly faster with less pain — in both traumatic (120 patients) and foreign-body (81 patients) abrasions
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kaiser 1995, Corneal Abrasion Patching Study Group)
cards.people: 223 patients with noninfected, non-contact-lens-related traumatic corneal abrasions or abrasions after removal of a corneal foreign body, all given topical antibiotics and mydriatics and randomised to a pressure patch or no patch, followed daily; 22 patients were excluded from analysis, leaving 120 traumatic and 81 foreign-body-removal abrasions.
cards.result: Patients with traumatic corneal abrasions healed significantly faster, had less pain and had fewer reports of blurred vision when they were not wearing a patch; photophobia, tearing and foreign-body sensation were similar between groups. For abrasions after foreign-body removal, patients again healed significantly faster and had less pain unpatched, with no difference in photophobia, tearing, foreign-body sensation or blurred vision. Compliance was better in the no-patch group.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports the direction and significance of the differences but not their numerical size, so no effect estimate is quoted from this trial. The population explicitly excludes infected and contact-lens-related abrasions — patching (and everything else) in contact-lens wearers, who carry Pseudomonas risk, is a different question this trial does not answer.
cards.source: Kaiser PK et al. A comparison of pressure patching versus no patching for corneal abrasions due to trauma or foreign body removal. Corneal Abrasion Patching Study Group. Ophthalmology. 1995. PMID: 9098299. cards.headline: Lim 2016 (Cochrane): patched eyes were less likely healed at 24 hours (risk ratio 0.89), identical by 48–72 hours, and took 0.14 days longer to heal overall
cards.summary: Lim 2016 (Cochrane): patched eyes were less likely healed at 24 hours (risk ratio 0.89), identical by 48–72 hours, and took 0.14 days longer to heal overall
cards.people: 12 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (1,080 participants) comparing patching with no patching for simple corneal abrasions, conducted in the UK (4), USA (4), Canada (2), Brazil (1) and Switzerland (1); seven trials were at high risk of bias in one or more domains.
cards.result: People receiving a patch may be less likely to have a healed abrasion at 24 hours than those not receiving a patch (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.00; 7 trials, 531 participants; low-certainty evidence), with similar healing at 48 hours (risk ratio 0.97, 0.91 to 1.02; 6 trials, 497 participants) and 72 hours (risk ratio 1.01, 0.97 to 1.05; 4 trials, 430 participants). Participants receiving a patch took slightly longer to heal (mean difference 0.14 days longer, 95% CI 0 to 0.27 days; 6 trials, 642 participants). Pain scores, reported by ten trials, were generally similar between patch and no-patch groups.
cards.watchOut: Certainty is low to moderate and most included trials are small and old; the 24-hour risk ratio's interval just touches 1.00, so 'slightly slower on day one' is a suggestion, not a proof of harm — the solid finding is the absence of any benefit at every time point.
cards.source: Lim CH et al. Patching for corneal abrasion. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27457359. cards.headline: Synthesis: no healing benefit at 24, 48 or 72 hours, no pain benefit — drop the patch for simple abrasions
cards.summary: Synthesis: no healing benefit at 24, 48 or 72 hours, no pain benefit — drop the patch for simple abrasions

shelves.title: Shingles: valaciclovir ended the pain about two weeks sooner than aciclovir at the median (38 versus 51 days) — in the single head-to-head trial ever run
shelves.question: In adults with herpes zoster, does valaciclovir beat aciclovir for pain duration?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Herpes Zoster/complications/drug therapy/immunology · Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus/complications/drug therapy/immunology · Humans · Immunocompetence · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/drug therapy/etiology · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Quality of Life · Valacyclovir · Valine/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial: in the one large head-to-head trial (Beutner KR et al., PMID: 7492102), valaciclovir shortened herpes zoster pain compared with aciclovir in immunocompetent adults aged 50 and over. Median duration of zoster-associated pain was 38 days on valaciclovir 1,000 mg three times daily for 7 days and 44 days on the 14-day course, versus 51 days on aciclovir 800 mg five times daily (P = 0.001 and P = 0.03 respectively), and the proportion of patients with pain persisting at 6 months was 19.3% on valaciclovir versus 25.7% on aciclovir. Rash healing, pain intensity and quality-of-life measures did not differ between treatments, and adverse events were similar. Single-trial flag: this shelf rests on one randomised trial — no second head-to-head trial of valaciclovir against aciclovir for zoster was found — so the claim is exactly as strong as that one trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): valaciclovir resolves zoster pain about two weeks sooner at the median than aciclovir, with simpler three-times-daily dosing, on single-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Beutner 1995: median zoster pain lasted 38 days on valaciclovir (7-day course) versus 51 days on aciclovir, and pain at 6 months affected 19.3% versus 25.7%
cards.summary: Beutner 1995: median zoster pain lasted 38 days on valaciclovir (7-day course) versus 51 days on aciclovir, and pain at 6 months affected 19.3% versus 25.7%
cards.people: 1,141 immunocompetent adults aged 50 years or over with localised herpes zoster, randomised double-blind at multiple centres to oral valaciclovir 1,000 mg three times daily for 7 days, valaciclovir 1,000 mg three times daily for 14 days, or oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, and evaluated for 6 months (intent-to-treat analysis).
cards.result: Valaciclovir for 7 or 14 days significantly accelerated the resolution of herpes zoster-associated pain compared with aciclovir (P = 0.001 and P = 0.03 respectively); median pain durations were 38 days (7-day course) and 44 days (14-day course) versus 51 days for aciclovir. Valaciclovir also reduced the duration of postherpetic neuralgia and decreased the proportion of patients with pain persisting for 6 months (19.3% versus 25.7%). There were no differences between treatments in pain intensity or quality-of-life measures, cutaneous manifestations resolved at similar rates in all groups, and adverse events were similar in nature and prevalence, with no clinically important changes in haematology or clinical chemistry.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial evidence from 1995, in immunocompetent patients aged 50 and over only — it does not cover younger or immunocompromised patients, and the benefit is in how long pain lasts, not how bad it is: pain intensity scores were identical. The 14-day valaciclovir course was not better than the 7-day course (44 versus 38 days at the median), so longer is not better on this record.
cards.source: Beutner KR et al. Valaciclovir compared with acyclovir for improved therapy for herpes zoster in immunocompetent adults. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 1995. PMID: 7492102. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large trial, a real but narrow win — pain ends sooner, nothing else changes
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large trial, a real but narrow win — pain ends sooner, nothing else changes
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial, 1,141 immunocompetent adults aged 50 or over with herpes zoster, followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Median pain duration 38 days (valaciclovir 7 days) and 44 days (valaciclovir 14 days) versus 51 days (aciclovir); pain persisting at 6 months 19.3% versus 25.7%; rash healing, pain intensity, quality of life and adverse events not different. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C, single-trial flag declared on the face of the shelf: valaciclovir is the more convenient and modestly more effective oral option for shortening zoster pain in older immunocompetent adults.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf: under this band's relaxed intake a single randomised trial may carry a shelf, but the developer should note there is no confirmatory head-to-head trial, and famciclovir — the other modern comparator — is outside this question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Beutner KR et al. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 1995 (PMID: 7492102).

shelves.title: Deuruxolitinib for severe alopecia areata: SALT ≤20 at 24 weeks in 30–42% across two phase 3 trials versus 0.8% on placebo — a different JAK inhibitor from the baricitinib/ritlecitinib shelf
shelves.question: In patients with alopecia areata (adolescents/adults), does deuruxolitinib or another JAK inhibitor regrow hair?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Alopecia Areata/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Janus Kinase 1/antagonists & inhibitors · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects,administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Patient Satisfaction · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Pyrroles/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials of a drug not covered by the existing baricitinib/ritlecitinib shelf. In THRIVE-AA1 (King B et al., PMID: 39053611), a Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) score ≤20 at 24 weeks was achieved by 29.6% on deuruxolitinib 8 mg twice daily and 41.5% on 12 mg twice daily versus 0.8% on placebo. THRIVE-AA2 (Tsianakas A et al., PMID: 41317911; 517 randomised) replicated it: 33.0% (8 mg), 38.3% (12 mg) and 0.8% (placebo), p<0.0001 for both doses. Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate and consistent with other oral JAK inhibitors; neither trial assessed durability after stopping or long-term safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deuruxolitinib regrows hair in roughly a third of adults with severe alopecia areata over 24 weeks, with long-term and off-treatment durability unshown.

cards.people: Adults aged 18–65 years with alopecia areata and ≥50% hair loss, randomised to deuruxolitinib 8 mg twice daily, 12 mg twice daily, or placebo for 24 weeks (total randomised number not stated in the record's abstract).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — SALT score ≤20 at week 24 — was met by 29.6% on 8 mg and 41.5% on 12 mg versus 0.8% on placebo (significant for both doses). shelves.title: Upadacitinib beats dupilumab head-to-head in atopic dermatitis: EASI75 at week 16 in 71.0% versus 61.1% (Heads Up), and the combined EASI90-plus-itch endpoint in 19.9% versus 8.9% (Level Up) — faster itch relief, more infections and laboratory events
shelves.question: In patients with atopic dermatitis, does upadacitinib beat dupilumab for itch and clearance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects · Dermatitis, Atopic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Eczema · Female · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/adverse effects · Humans · Male · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two head-to-head randomised trials point the same way. In Heads Up (Blauvelt A et al., PMID: 34347860; 692 adults), EASI75 at week 16 was achieved by 71.0% on upadacitinib 30 mg daily versus 61.1% on dupilumab (p=0.006), EASI100 by 27.9% versus 7.6% (p<0.001), with itch improvement already separated at week 1 (31.4% versus 8.8% mean improvement; p<0.001). In Level Up (Silverberg JI et al., PMID: 39438067), the combined endpoint of EASI90 plus Worst Pruritus NRS 0/1 at week 16 was achieved by 19.9% on response-escalated upadacitinib versus 8.9% on dupilumab (p<0.001). The price in Heads Up: serious infection, eczema herpeticum, herpes zoster and laboratory adverse events were more frequent on upadacitinib; conjunctivitis and injection-site reactions were more frequent on dupilumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): upadacitinib clears skin faster and more completely than dupilumab, trading injection-site and eye effects for infection and laboratory effects.

cards.headline: Heads Up: EASI75 at week 16 in 71.0% on upadacitinib versus 61.1% on dupilumab (p=0.006); EASI100 27.9% versus 7.6%
cards.summary: Heads Up: EASI75 at week 16 in 71.0% on upadacitinib versus 61.1% on dupilumab (p=0.006); EASI100 27.9% versus 7.6%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3b head-to-head trial (Blauvelt 2021, Heads Up)
cards.people: 692 adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis who were candidates for systemic therapy (348 upadacitinib, 344 dupilumab), treated with oral upadacitinib 30 mg once daily or subcutaneous dupilumab 300 mg every other week in a 24-week double-blind, double-dummy trial at 129 centres.
cards.result: EASI75 at week 16 (primary): 71.0% upadacitinib versus 61.1% dupilumab (p=0.006). EASI100 at week 16: 27.9% versus 7.6% (p<0.001). EASI75 as early as week 2: 43.7% versus 17.4% (p<0.001). Worst Pruritus NRS improvement at week 1: 31.4% versus 8.8% (p<0.001). Serious infection, eczema herpeticum, herpes zoster and laboratory-related adverse events were higher with upadacitinib; conjunctivitis and injection-site reactions were higher with dupilumab.
cards.watchOut: Upadacitinib was used at 30 mg — the higher dose — throughout, so the comparison is against dupilumab at its standard dose but not at upadacitinib's lower 15 mg dose; 16–24 weeks cannot judge long-term JAK-inhibitor safety.
cards.source: Blauvelt A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Upadacitinib vs Dupilumab in Adults With Moderate-to-Severe Atopic Dermatitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA dermatology. 2021. PMID: 34347860. Registry ID: NCT03738397. cards.headline: Level Up: simultaneous EASI90 and itch 0/1 at week 16 in 19.9% on upadacitinib versus 8.9% on dupilumab (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Level Up: simultaneous EASI90 and itch 0/1 at week 16 in 19.9% on upadacitinib versus 8.9% on dupilumab (p<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3b/4 head-to-head trial (Silverberg 2024, Level Up)
cards.people: Adolescents and adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and inadequate response to systemic therapy (or where it was inadvisable), randomised to upadacitinib started at 15 mg and escalated to 30 mg on response criteria, or dupilumab per its label, for 16 weeks (period 1); open-label with blinded efficacy assessors.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — simultaneous EASI90 and Worst Pruritus NRS 0/1 at week 16 — was achieved by 19.9% on upadacitinib versus 8.9% on dupilumab (p<0.001). Upadacitinib was superior on all ranked secondary endpoints, with higher itch response rates as early as day 2 in post hoc analyses. No new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (assessors blinded, patients not) can inflate patient-reported itch differences, and the dose-escalation design means the upadacitinib arm is a strategy, not a fixed dose — the two head-to-head trials are concordant in direction but not identical in design.

shelves.title: Central retinal vein occlusion (LEAVO): aflibercept matched ranibizumab on vision at 100 weeks with about two fewer injections — bevacizumab non-inferiority was not shown (single-trial shelf)
shelves.question: In patients with retinal vein occlusion, does aflibercept beat ranibizumab head-to-head for vision?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — aflibercept non-inferior to ranibizumab / bevacizumab non-inferiority not shown. The live ranibizumab shelf (#894) answers ranibizumab versus sham; this shelf answers the head-to-head question in central retinal vein occlusion from the single LEAVO trial (Hykin P et al., PMID: 31465100; 463 patients). Mean visual-acuity gain at 100 weeks was 12.5 letters on ranibizumab, 15.1 letters on aflibercept and 9.8 letters on bevacizumab. Aflibercept was non-inferior to ranibizumab (adjusted difference 2.23 letters, 95% CI −2.17 to 6.63; p<0.001 for non-inferiority) with fewer mean injections (10.0 versus 11.8; difference −1.9, 95% CI −2.9 to −0.8). Bevacizumab was not shown non-inferior (difference −1.73 letters, 95% CI −6.12 to 2.67; p=0.07). PROPOSED SPLIT: aflibercept is a vision-equivalent alternative to ranibizumab with a slightly lighter injection load; bevacizumab's equivalence remains unproven in this trial.

cards.headline: LEAVO: aflibercept non-inferior to ranibizumab at 100 weeks (+2.23 letters, 95% CI −2.17 to 6.63); bevacizumab not non-inferior (−1.73 letters, 95% CI −6.12 to 2.67)
cards.summary: LEAVO: aflibercept non-inferior to ranibizumab at 100 weeks (+2.23 letters, 95% CI −2.17 to 6.63); bevacizumab not non-inferior (−1.73 letters, 95% CI −6.12 to 2.67)
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial (Hykin 2019, LEAVO) — single-trial shelf
cards.people: 463 adults (mean age 69.1 years, 57.2% male) with macular oedema from central retinal vein occlusion of <12 months and visual acuity 19–78 letters, randomised at 44 UK NHS departments to repeated intravitreal ranibizumab 0.5 mg (n=155), aflibercept 2.0 mg (n=154) or bevacizumab 1.25 mg (n=154) for 100 weeks.
cards.result: Mean gain in best-corrected visual acuity at 100 weeks: 12.5 letters (ranibizumab), 15.1 letters (aflibercept), 9.8 letters (bevacizumab). Aflibercept was non-inferior to ranibizumab in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses (lower CI bound above −5 letters). Bevacizumab did not meet non-inferiority. Mean injections: 10.0 (aflibercept) versus 11.8 (ranibizumab), difference −1.9 (95% CI −2.9 to −0.8).
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf — flagged as such. LEAVO covers central occlusion only, not the branch occlusion half of the live #894 question, and 'not shown non-inferior' for bevacizumab is inconclusive rather than proof of inferiority: the confidence interval includes both no difference and a clinically meaningful deficit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one large three-arm trial — aflibercept equals ranibizumab, bevacizumab unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large three-arm trial — aflibercept equals ranibizumab, bevacizumab unresolved
cards.people: One randomised double-masked non-inferiority trial (LEAVO, 463 patients with central retinal vein occlusion macular oedema, 100 weeks).
cards.result: Vision gain: 15.1 letters (aflibercept), 12.5 letters (ranibizumab), 9.8 letters (bevacizumab). Aflibercept non-inferior with 1.9 fewer injections on average; bevacizumab non-inferiority not established (p=0.07). PROPOSED SPLIT, single-trial.

shelves.title: Perioperative dexamethasone in adult tonsillectomy: less nausea, vomiting and pain in two small double-blind trials — a 62% relative fall in postoperative nausea and vomiting in the larger one
shelves.question: In patients having tonsillectomy, does perioperative dexamethasone reduce postoperative nausea and pain in adults?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anesthetics, Intravenous · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Antiemetics/administration & dosage · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Isoquinolines · Male · Middle Aged · Mivacurium · Neuromuscular Nondepolarizing Agents · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/etiology,prevention & control · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting/etiology,prevention & control · Propofol · Tonsillectomy/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind placebo-controlled trials in adults (the paediatric dexamethasone literature is a different population and is not carded here). McKean S et al. (PMID: 16441800; 72 adults) found a single 10 mg intravenous dose at induction produced a 62% relative decrease in postoperative nausea and vomiting (p=0.001), a 23% relative decrease in day-of-operation pain scores (p=0.016) and a 17.5% lower mean pain score over 7 days (p<0.001), with no adverse effects seen. Al-Shehri AM et al. (PMID: 15573850; 30 adults) found a 24-hour, three-dose dexamethasone course (6 mg per dose) gave significantly less pain, nausea and vomiting, better healing and less granulation over 2 weeks, with no side effects reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a cheap single intervention eases the first week for adults, on small-trial evidence.

cards.headline: McKean 2006: single 10 mg dexamethasone at induction — 62% relative decrease in nausea/vomiting (p=0.001), pain down 23% on day 0 and 17.5% over 7 days

cards.people: 72 adults aged 16–70 years (ASA 1) listed for elective tonsillectomy at a UK district general hospital, randomised to a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone 10 mg or saline 2 mL after induction with a consistent anaesthetic technique; data completion was 64% (46 of 72).
cards.result: Postoperative nausea and vomiting: statistically significant 62% relative decrease with dexamethasone (p=0.001) — a relative measure, reported by the record without the absolute rates. Pain: 23% relative decrease in day-of-operation scores (p=0.016) and 17.5% lower mean pain score across 7 postoperative days (p<0.001). Time to first food and drink was also recorded. No adverse effects were seen.
cards.watchOut: Only 46 of 72 patients completed the data — a 36% loss in a small trial can manufacture or erase effects of this size, and the headline nausea figure is relative-only in the record, so its absolute size cannot be stated from this source.

shelves.title: Ingrown toenail: adding phenol after nail avulsion cuts recurrence — relative risk 0.13 in the 2023 meta-analysis of 36 studies and 14% versus 41% in the one like-for-like trial — but the trial quality is rated very low and phenol raised post-operative infection in the earlier Cochrane review
shelves.question: 'How do I treat an ingrown toenail?' — In people with an ingrowing toenail, how do surgical treatments (especially partial nail avulsion with phenolisation of the matrix) compare with conservative care and with avulsion alone for recurrence, and what harms come with phenol?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Local · Female · Humans · Male · Nails/surgery · Nails, Ingrown/surgery · Phenol · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Toes/pathology · Toes/surgery
shelves.balance: The consistent finding across three successive syntheses is that destroying part of the nail matrix with phenol after avulsion lowers recurrence — but the underlying trials are poor. The 2005 Cochrane review found avulsion plus phenol beat surgical excision for symptomatic recurrence at 6 months or more (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80, relative) and beat avulsion alone by a wide relative margin (OR 0.07; 0.04–0.12), at the cost of more post-operative infection (OR 5.69; 1.93–16.77) (Rounding 2005, PMID: 15846620). The 2012 Cochrane update (24 RCTs, 2,826 participants) found surgery better than gutter treatment at preventing recurrence and probably better than orthonyxia (brace), and in the single like-for-like study — partial nail avulsion with matrix excision with or without phenol, 117 participants — recurrence was 14% with phenol versus 41% without (RR 0.34; 0.17–0.69, relative; an absolute difference of 27 percentage points) (Eekhof 2012, PMID: 22513901). The 2023 meta-analysis (36 studies, 3,756 participants) again found phenol plus avulsion far below avulsion alone for recurrence (RR 0.13; 0.06–0.27, relative) but rated that evidence very low quality and concluded the research in this area is poor (Exley 2023, PMID: 37301845). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: phenolisation probably reduces recurrence after avulsion — the direction is consistent across every synthesis — but certainty is capped by very-low-quality trials, and the older review's infection signal has not been cleanly resolved.

cards.headline: Rounding 2005 (Cochrane): avulsion plus phenol beat excision (OR 0.44) and avulsion alone (OR 0.07) for recurrence — but post-operative infection rose (OR 5.69)
cards.summary: Rounding 2005 (Cochrane): avulsion plus phenol beat excision (OR 0.44) and avulsion alone (OR 0.07) for recurrence — but post-operative infection rose (OR 5.69)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of surgical treatments for ingrowing toenails (Rounding 2005)
cards.people: People with ingrowing toenails in the randomised trials gathered by the Cochrane review of surgical treatments, comparing nail avulsion with phenol application against surgical excision techniques and against avulsion without phenol.
cards.result: Avulsion with phenol was significantly better than surgical excision at preventing symptomatic recurrence at 6 months or more (odds ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80 — a relative measure). Avulsion with phenol also significantly reduced recurrence compared with avulsion without phenol (OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.04–0.12, relative). The trade-off in the same comparison: post-operative infection was significantly increased with phenol (OR 5.69; 95% CI 1.93–16.77, relative).
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios exaggerate effects when events are common, and these pooled trials were small and old; the infection odds ratio of 5.69 has a wide interval (1.93–16.77). This review was superseded by the 2012 Cochrane update carded next, which did not reproduce a clear phenol–infection difference across its postoperative comparisons — the infection signal should be read as unresolved, not settled either way.
cards.source: Rounding C, Bloomfield S. Surgical treatments for ingrowing toenails. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2005. PMID: 15846620. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Eekhof 2012 (Cochrane update): 24 trials, 2,826 participants — surgery beat conservative gutter treatment for recurrence, and in the one like-for-like study phenol cut recurrence from 41% to 14%
cards.summary: Eekhof 2012 (Cochrane update): 24 trials, 2,826 participants — surgery beat conservative gutter treatment for recurrence, and in the one like-for-like study phenol cut recurrence from 41% to 14%
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of interventions for ingrowing toenails, 24 RCTs (Eekhof 2012)
cards.people: 2,826 participants across 24 randomised trials (5 of non-surgical interventions, 19 of surgical interventions); 16 of the studies reported recurrence outcomes, including one 117-participant study comparing the same operation — partial nail avulsion plus matrix excision — with and without phenol.
cards.result: Surgical interventions were better than gutter treatment (a conservative splinting method) at preventing recurrence, and probably better than orthonyxia (nail brace). In the single study comparing identical operations with and without phenol, recurrence was 14% with phenol versus 41% without (risk ratio 0.34; 95% CI 0.17–0.69 — relative; the absolute difference was 27 percentage points). Across postoperative interventions more broadly, there was no significant difference in infection rate, pain or healing time.
cards.watchOut: Only one of the 24 trials isolates phenol's contribution on top of the same operation, and it had 117 participants — the 14% versus 41% figures rest on that single study. 'Surgery beats gutter treatment' pools operations of quite different kinds; the review could not rank the operations against each other, and most included trials were at unclear or high risk of bias by modern standards.
cards.source: Eekhof JAH, Van Wijk B, Knuistingh Neven A, van der Wouden JC. Interventions for ingrowing toenails. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22513901. cards.headline: Exley 2023: phenol plus avulsion versus avulsion alone, recurrence risk ratio 0.13 — consistent benefit, but the evidence was rated very low quality
cards.summary: Exley 2023: phenol plus avulsion versus avulsion alone, recurrence risk ratio 0.13 — consistent benefit, but the evidence was rated very low quality
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs of surgical treatment for ingrown toenails (Exley 2023)
cards.people: 36 studies with 3,756 participants (62.7% male) in the systematic review of surgical treatments for ingrown toenails, 31 of them in the meta-analysis; this card covers part I of the review, on recurrence and relief of symptoms.
cards.result: Phenolisation with avulsion versus avulsion without phenol gave a recurrence risk ratio of 0.13 (95% CI 0.06–0.27; p<0.001 — a relative measure), but the reviewers rated this evidence very low quality. Chemical ablation and surgical excision each versus conservative management were not significant (RR 0.55; 0.19–1.61 and RR 0.72; 0.33–1.56), nor was chemical versus surgical treatment (RR 0.75; 0.46–1.21). The authors concluded that phenolisation appears to reduce recurrence, that around 1 minute of phenol application appears optimum (a less certain finding), and that the quality of research for ingrown toenail surgery is poor.
cards.watchOut: A risk ratio of 0.13 sounds decisive; the reviewers' own 'very low quality' rating is the honest headline — small trials, inconsistent technique (phenol strength and application time vary), and short follow-up. The non-significant comparisons against conservative care had wide intervals, so they show absence of proof, not proof that conservative care equals surgery for recurrent or severe cases.
cards.source: Exley V, Jones K, O'Carroll G, Watson J, Backhouse M. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials on surgical treatments for ingrown toenails part I: recurrence and relief of symptoms. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2023. cards.headline: Synthesis: phenol after avulsion is the one intervention that consistently lowers recurrence (14% versus 41% in the like-for-like trial) — certainty is limited by very-low-quality trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: phenol after avulsion is the one intervention that consistently lowers recurrence (14% versus 41% in the like-for-like trial) — certainty is limited by very-low-quality trials
cards.people: Three successive syntheses spanning 2005–2023: two Cochrane reviews (Rounding 2005; Eekhof 2012 — 24 RCTs, 2,826 participants) and a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (Exley 2023 — 36 studies, 3,756 participants).
cards.result: Every synthesis points the same way on recurrence: avulsion plus phenol beat avulsion alone (OR 0.07 in 2005; RR 0.13 in 2023, both relative), and the single like-for-like trial put absolute recurrence at 14% with phenol versus 41% without (RR 0.34). Surgery as a class beat conservative gutter treatment for preventing recurrence, and probably beat nail bracing. Harms: the 2005 review found more post-operative infection with phenol (OR 5.69), while the 2012 review found no significant infection difference across postoperative comparisons — unresolved. The 2023 reviewers rated the phenol evidence very low quality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: for a recurrent ingrown toenail, partial nail avulsion with phenolisation of the matrix probably reduces recurrence compared with avulsion alone; first-episode, milder cases can reasonably start with conservative care, for which the trial record is thinner rather than negative.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE by the evidence grading in the fetched records themselves (very low quality in the most recent synthesis), not by disagreement among them. This shelf addresses recurrence prevention and comparative treatment; it does not cover infected ingrown toenails needing antibiotics, toenails in diabetes or poor circulation (where phenol and surgery carry different risks), or total nail avulsion, none of which the fetched records isolate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rounding C, Bloomfield S. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2005 (PMID: 15846620); Eekhof JAH et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22513901); Exley V et al. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2023 (PMID: 37301845).

shelves.question: How is acanthosis nigricans treated — in people with insulin-resistance-associated acanthosis nigricans (the dark, velvety skin thickening of the neck and folds), do metformin, pioglitazone or other systemic treatments improve the skin, and how do they compare?
shelves.mesh: Acanthosis nigricans · Canthex · alpha-lipoic acid · insulin resistance · metformin (keywords as printed in the Sett 2019 record; the MeSH lists for this shelf's records did not render when fetched — see build flag in the part summary)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the evidence is three small randomised head-to-head trials with no placebo arm and no blinded skin assessment in the largest, so every positive finding is a within-group improvement. Metformin 500 mg twice daily and pioglitazone 7.5 mg twice daily both significantly improved lesion grading over 12 weeks with no significant difference between them (Jain 2026, PMID: 41449989; 65 patients), metformin producing the greater BMI and weight fall. Metformin and the branded fixed combination Canthex (alpha-lipoic acid, biotin, calcium pantothenate and zinc sulfate) likewise both significantly reduced neck lesion severity and texture with no intergroup difference at any follow-up (Sett 2019, PMID: 30983607; 33 patients analysed, double-blind). A second metformin-versus-pioglitazone report (Jain 2026, PMID: 40826852; 50 patients) found the same pattern — both improved, no significant between-group difference — with larger metabolic falls on pioglitazone (HOMA-IR −35.8% versus −28.56%). Because no trial compares any drug with placebo or with no treatment, spontaneous improvement, weight change and regression to the mean cannot be excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by design: treating the underlying insulin resistance is the consistent thread, and no agent has beaten another.

cards.headline: Jain 2026 (randomised, open-label, 65 patients): metformin and pioglitazone both significantly improved acanthosis nigricans by 12 weeks — no significant difference between them; metformin cut weight and BMI more
cards.summary: Jain 2026 (randomised, open-label, 65 patients): metformin and pioglitazone both significantly improved acanthosis nigricans by 12 weeks — no significant difference between them; metformin cut weight and BMI more
cards.type: Randomised open-label head-to-head trial, metformin versus pioglitazone (Jain 2026)
cards.people: 65 patients with acanthosis nigricans (mean age 35 years) randomised to metformin 500 mg twice daily or pioglitazone 7.5 mg twice daily for 3 months, with lesion grading, acanthosis nigricans severity index score, BMI and metabolic parameters assessed at baseline and follow-up.
cards.result: Both groups showed significant improvement in clinical grading by 12 weeks, with no significant difference between the groups. Metformin significantly reduced BMI (29.55 ± 3.51 to 28.92 ± 3.44 kg/m²) and body weight (76.58 ± 10.21 to 74.64 ± 10.30 kg), more than pioglitazone. The authors concluded both agents were effective in improving acanthosis nigricans, metformin showing greater benefit in weight and BMI reduction, and pioglitazone a favourable metabolic profile, and that acanthosis nigricans may serve as a clinical marker of metabolic dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo or untreated arm: 'both improved significantly' is a before-and-after statement in each arm, and unblinded grading of a visible skin sign is exactly where expectation bias bites. The between-group comparison — the part randomisation protects — was null for the skin outcomes.
cards.source: Jain R, Kumar P, Kumar M, et al. Acanthosis Nigricans and Metabolic Parameters: A Randomised Controlled Trial Comparing Metformin and Pioglitazone. Indian Dermatology Online Journal. 2026. PMID: 41449989. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not rendered in the record as fetched this session — see build flag in the part summary.

cards.headline: Sett 2019 (double-blind RCT, 33 patients analysed): metformin and the branded combination Canthex both cut neck lesion severity and texture (P < 0.001 within groups) — no intergroup difference at any follow-up
cards.summary: Sett 2019 (double-blind RCT, 33 patients analysed): metformin and the branded combination Canthex both cut neck lesion severity and texture (P < 0.001 within groups) — no intergroup difference at any follow-up
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial, metformin versus a branded antioxidant combination (Sett 2019)
cards.people: Patients with acanthosis nigricans enrolled in a double-blind randomised trial (registered CTRI/2017/02/007880) comparing metformin 500 mg twice daily with the fixed combination Canthex — alpha-lipoic acid plus biotin, calcium pantothenate and zinc sulfate — twice daily for 12 weeks; 33 patients analysed by modified intention-to-treat, graded on neck lesion severity and texture scales.
cards.result: A significant reduction in the severity and texture of neck lesions was observed in both the metformin and Canthex groups (P < 0.001) from the first follow-up visit; there was no intergroup difference at any follow-up visit. Weight, body mass index and waist circumference decreased significantly in both groups, and the insulin-resistance index (HOMA-IR) decreased significantly in the metformin group (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The comparator was an active branded combination, not a placebo (the trial was active-controlled) — and despite double-blinding, with 33 patients analysed the trial could miss a real difference between the two. The Canthex arm is carded under its tested product name, as this library's naming rule requires for combination products; results for this specific formulation do not transfer to alpha-lipoic acid or supplements generally.
cards.source: Sett A, Pradhan S, Sancheti K, Basu D, Datta A, Biswas L, Das S, Pal SK, Gupta N, Sil A, Das NK. Effectiveness and Safety of Metformin versus Canthex™ in Patients with Acanthosis Nigricans: A Randomized, Double-blind Controlled Trial. Indian Journal of Dermatology. 2019. PMID: 30983607. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/02/007880. MeSH: not rendered in the record as fetched this session — see build flag in the part summary.

cards.headline: Jain 2026, second report (50 patients): both drugs improved skin and metabolism, no significant between-group difference — pioglitazone cut HOMA-IR by 35.8% versus 28.56% on metformin
cards.summary: Jain 2026, second report (50 patients): both drugs improved skin and metabolism, no significant between-group difference — pioglitazone cut HOMA-IR by 35.8% versus 28.56% on metformin
cards.type: Prospective interventional comparison, metformin versus pioglitazone (Jain 2026)
cards.people: 50 patients with acanthosis nigricans allocated to metformin or pioglitazone, with skin scores and metabolic parameters (fasting insulin, glucose, triglycerides, HOMA-IR) measured before and after treatment.
cards.result: Both metformin and pioglitazone significantly improved acanthosis nigricans and metabolic parameters, with no statistically significant difference between the groups. Fasting insulin fell 19.9% on metformin and 20.86% on pioglitazone; fasting glucose fell 14.3% and 11%; triglycerides fell 9% and 10%; HOMA-IR fell 28.56% on metformin and 35.8% on pioglitazone. The authors concluded both agents are effective and that improvement in insulin sensitivity correlates with improvement in the skin lesions.
cards.watchOut: This record has no abstract in PubMed, so its numbers come from the journal's own page rather than the PubMed record this library normally requires — flagged in the part summary for desk verification before any serve. It appears to be a second report from the same centre and authors as the 65-patient trial on the first card; treat the two as one evidence stream, not two independent confirmations.
cards.source: Jain R, Kumar P, Kumar M, et al. Comparison of metformin and pioglitazone in metabolic and dermatological outcomes in patients with acanthosis nigricans: a single centre prospective interventional study. Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology. 2026. PMID: 40826852. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three small head-to-head trials, zero placebo arms — insulin-sensitising treatment improves the skin within groups, and nothing has beaten anything else
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small head-to-head trials, zero placebo arms — insulin-sensitising treatment improves the skin within groups, and nothing has beaten anything else
cards.people: Jain 2026 (65 patients, open-label randomised), Sett 2019 (33 patients analysed, double-blind randomised), Jain 2026 second report (50 patients, prospective).
cards.result: Metformin versus pioglitazone: significant within-group skin improvement in both arms at 12 weeks, no significant between-group difference in either report; metformin reduced weight/BMI more, pioglitazone reduced HOMA-IR more in one report (35.8% versus 28.56%). Metformin versus the Canthex combination: significant within-group improvement in both (P < 0.001), no intergroup difference. No placebo-controlled estimate of any treatment's effect on acanthosis nigricans exists in the records fetched. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the pattern is consistent with treating insulin resistance helping the skin, but every number is a within-group change in a small trial.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Topical retinoids, keratolytics and laser treatments are widely used for this condition but produced no trial records with extractable numbers in this session's fetch, so they are not carded; weight loss itself — the intervention most likely to change both the skin and the insulin resistance — has likewise never been isolated in a trial here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jain R et al. Indian Dermatology Online Journal. 2026 (PMID: 41449989); Sett A et al. Indian Journal of Dermatology. 2019 (PMID: 30983607); Jain R et al. Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology. 2026 (PMID: 40826852).
