shelves.title: Birch-bark gel (Oleogel-S10, Filsuvez) for epidermolysis bullosa wounds: complete target-wound closure by day 45 in 41.3% versus 28.9% on control gel in the phase III EASE trial
shelves.question: In people with epidermolysis bullosa, does the birch-bark extract gel Oleogel-S10 (Filsuvez) heal wounds faster and reduce wound burden compared with a control gel?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage · Epidermolysis Bullosa/drug therapy · Humans · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase III randomised trial programme (EASE) carries this shelf, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In the double-blind phase (Kern JS et al., PMID: 36689495; 223 patients with dystrophic or junctional EB, 109 Oleogel-S10 versus 114 control gel), first complete closure of the target wound within 45 days occurred in 41.3% on Oleogel-S10 versus 28.9% on control gel (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.05; P = 0.013) — a 44% relative increase, and a 12.4-percentage-point absolute difference; adverse events were near-identical (81.7% versus 80.7%, predominantly mild-to-moderate). In the 24-month open-label phase (Murrell DF et al., PMID: 39821055; 205 patients, all on Oleogel-S10), wound burden fell and stayed down in those treated throughout (body-surface-area percentage change −5.9% at 12 months and −3.7% at 24 months from double-blind baseline), with adverse events in 77.1% (severe 18.0%, serious 24.4% — in a population with severe disease), 7.8% withdrawing for adverse events, and nine deaths, none attributed to treatment. A post-hoc analysis in patients who began with daily dressing changes (Bruckner AL et al., PMID: 40908727) found fewer daily changes needed by day 90 in 35.6% versus 10.6% (P = 0.005). The tested product is named exactly as trialled: Oleogel-S10 (birch triterpenes / birch bark extract), marketed as Filsuvez, developed by Amryt (now Chiesi). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): faster closure of a chosen target wound, by a modest absolute margin, in the only randomised trial — meaningful in a disease with no other approved wound therapy, but one trial, industry-run, with a confidence interval whose lower bound (1.01) sits just above no effect.

cards.headline: Kern 2023 (EASE double-blind phase): first complete target-wound closure within 45 days in 41.3% on Oleogel-S10 versus 28.9% on control gel (RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.05; P = 0.013)
cards.summary: Kern 2023 (EASE double-blind phase): first complete target-wound closure within 45 days in 41.3% on Oleogel-S10 versus 28.9% on control gel (RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.05; P = 0.013)
cards.type: Phase III randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trial — EASE (Kern 2023)
cards.people: 223 patients with dystrophic or junctional epidermolysis bullosa enrolled and treated (109 Oleogel-S10, 114 control gel) in the EASE study; Oleogel-S10 is a topical gel of birch triterpenes (birch bark extract), marketed as Filsuvez, applied to partial-thickness EB wounds, with one target wound per patient for the primary endpoint. Primary endpoint: first complete closure of the target wound within 45 days.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: Oleogel-S10 resulted in 41.3% of patients with first complete target wound closure within 45 days, compared with 28.9% in the control gel arm (relative risk 1.44, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 2.05; P = 0.013). The absolute difference was 12.4 percentage points. Adverse events occurred with similar frequency on Oleogel-S10 (81.7%) and control gel (80.7%) and were predominantly of mild-to-moderate intensity (4.6% were severe). The authors conclude Oleogel-S10 is the first therapy to demonstrate accelerated wound healing in EB and was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one target wound per patient, and a relative-risk confidence interval (1.01 to 2.05) whose lower bound barely clears 1 — the true acceleration could be small. Complete closure of a single chosen wound within 45 days is not the same as overall disease improvement, wounds in EB characteristically reopen, and the trial was funded by the product's developer (Amryt Research Limited). The control gel itself is an active wound-care vehicle, which is why the control closure rate (28.9%) is substantial.
cards.source: Kern JS, Sprecher E, Fernandez MF, Schauer F, Bodemer C, Cunningham T, Löwe S, Davis C, Sumeray M, Bruckner AL, Murrell DF, EASE investigators. Efficacy and safety of Oleogel-S10 (birch triterpenes) for epidermolysis bullosa: results from the phase III randomized double-blind phase of the EASE study. British Journal of Dermatology. 2023. PMID: 36689495. Registry ID: NCT03068780. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Murrell 2025 (EASE 24-month open-label phase, n=205): wound burden stayed reduced (BSAP −5.9% at 12 months, −3.7% at 24 months in those treated throughout); adverse events in 77.1%, nine deaths — none attributed to treatment
cards.summary: Murrell 2025 (EASE 24-month open-label phase, n=205): wound burden stayed reduced (BSAP −5.9% at 12 months, −3.7% at 24 months in those treated throughout); adverse events in 77.1%, nine deaths — none attributed to treatment
cards.type: Open-label extension of the EASE phase III study (Murrell 2025)
cards.people: 205 patients from both double-blind arms entered the single-arm 24-month open-label phase and received Oleogel-S10 on all partial-thickness EB wounds; 72% were aged under 18 years and 86.8% had dystrophic EB (recessive dystrophic EB predominating, 78.0%). Mean treatment duration 584.7 (SD 246.1) days with adherence above 99%.
cards.result: In patients treated with Oleogel-S10 throughout, mean (SD) changes in body surface area percentage (BSAP) of wounds from double-blind baseline were −4.3% (8.1) at 3 months (P < 0.001), −5.9% (8.6) at 12 months (P < 0.001) and −3.7% (9.0) at 24 months (P = 0.003); EBDASI skin activity scores changed by −3.9, −5.1 and −3.0 at the same time points (all P ≤ 0.007). Adverse events were reported in 77.1% of patients, typically mild-to-moderate; severe adverse events in 18.0% and serious adverse events in 24.4%. Adverse events led to withdrawal in 7.8% (n=16), including three with treatment-related events. Target-wound infections were infrequent (n=7). Nine deaths were reported; none were attributable to the treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-arm: everyone is on the gel, there is no comparator, and patients who stay in a 24-month extension are those doing well enough to continue — so the sustained BSAP reductions cannot be credited to the gel alone, and the high adverse-event percentages largely reflect the severity of EB itself rather than drug harm. This card's job is durability and long-term tolerability, not efficacy proof; the blinded card above carries the efficacy claim.
cards.source: Murrell DF, Bodemer C, Bruckner AL, Cunningham T, Davis C, Fernández MF, Kiritsi D, Maher L, Sprecher E, Torres-Pradilla M, Kern JS. Long-term safety and efficacy of Oleogel-S10 (birch bark extract) in epidermolysis bullosa: 24-month results from the phase III EASE study. British Journal of Dermatology. 2025. PMID: 39821055. Registry ID: NCT03068780. cards.headline: Bruckner 2025 (EASE post-hoc, patients with daily dressing changes at baseline): fewer daily changes needed by day 90 in 35.6% on Oleogel-S10 versus 10.6% on control (P = 0.005); weekly changes fell by 1.36 versus 0.41
cards.summary: Bruckner 2025 (EASE post-hoc, patients with daily dressing changes at baseline): fewer daily changes needed by day 90 in 35.6% on Oleogel-S10 versus 10.6% on control (P = 0.005); weekly changes fell by 1.36 versus 0.41
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the EASE randomised phase (Bruckner 2025)
cards.people: EASE participants who required daily dressing changes at baseline (Oleogel-S10 n=47, control gel n=53), analysed for dressing-change frequency, time burden and estimated dressing costs over the study.
cards.result: By day 90, 35.6% of Oleogel-S10 patients required fewer daily dressing changes versus 10.6% of the control group (P = 0.005). Weekly dressing changes reduced by 1.36 ± 0.24 with Oleogel-S10 compared with 0.41 ± 0.23 for control (difference −0.95 ± 0.33; P = 0.005). Estimated time saved per week was 10.7 hours with Oleogel-S10 (6.4 hours patient, 4.3 hours caregiver) versus 4.0 hours with control (2.4 patient, 1.6 caregiver). Estimated dressing costs reduced by 59%, from $63.4k to $25.9k per patient over 27 months. The authors conclude Oleogel-S10 significantly reduced dressing frequency and time burden.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and restricted to the subgroup with daily dressing changes at baseline — the subgroup with the most room to improve — and the time and cost figures are modelled estimates built on the observed change counts, not measured savings. Dressing burden is the outcome families feel most, so the direction matters, but treat the dollar and hour figures as illustrative arithmetic on a subgroup, not as trial endpoints.

cards.headline: Synthesis: faster closure of a target wound by a modest absolute margin, sustained burden reduction open-label — from a single trial programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster closure of a target wound by a modest absolute margin, sustained burden reduction open-label — from a single trial programme
cards.people: The EASE phase III programme: double-blind phase (Kern 2023, 223 patients), 24-month open-label phase (Murrell 2025, 205 patients) and a dressing-burden post-hoc analysis (Bruckner 2025), all under NCT03068780.
cards.result: Blinded: first complete target-wound closure within 45 days 41.3% versus 28.9% (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.05; absolute difference 12.4 percentage points; P = 0.013); adverse events 81.7% versus 80.7%. Open-label to 24 months: wound body-surface-area percentage down 5.9% at 12 months and 3.7% at 24 months in those treated throughout; adverse events in 77.1%, withdrawals for adverse events 7.8%, nine deaths none attributed. Dressing burden: fewer daily changes by day 90 in 35.6% versus 10.6% (P = 0.005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is Oleogel-S10 (Filsuvez) for partial-thickness wounds in dystrophic and junctional EB — the populations EASE enrolled. It says nothing about EB simplex or Kindler EB wound care, about other dressings or wound products (no comparative trials were carded), or about the newer gene/cell therapies for dystrophic EB, which answer different questions. Other birch-bark or 'birch triterpene' products are not the tested preparation and cannot borrow this trial. Tier C.

shelves.title: Suppressive acyclovir for recurrent erythema multiforme: median attacks 0 versus 3 over 6 months in the one double-blind trial — of 20 patients
shelves.question: In people whose erythema multiforme keeps coming back, usually after herpes simplex, does taking acyclovir every day prevent further attacks compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/therapeutic use · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Erythema Multiforme/drug therapy · Female · Herpes Simplex/complications · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped exactly to the tested question: continuous suppressive acyclovir for recurrent (mostly herpes-simplex-associated) erythema multiforme. The entire randomised evidence is one small double-blind trial (Tatnall FM et al., PMID: 7888365): 20 patients with more than four attacks a year (15 herpes-precipitated) took acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 months; median attacks on treatment were 0 on acyclovir versus 3 on placebo (P < 0.0005), 7 of 11 acyclovir patients had no attacks at all, and two went into complete remission after treatment while every placebo patient continued to have attacks. The large referral series behind it (Schofield JK et al., PMID: 8504046; 65 patients, 71% herpes-precipitated) found 55% of patients derived benefit from acyclovir regimens (continuous, or a patient-initiated 5-day course at herpes onset), with the most resistant 11 patients achieving complete suppression on azathioprine. A systematic review of all EM interventions (de Risi-Pugliese T et al., PMID: 30680804) found, from 1,558 references, exactly one RCT and six case series in the whole field, and graded the acyclovir evidence low-level. A single 20-patient trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean its result. BOUNDARY: this shelf is prevention of recurrent EM only. Acute EM and EM major are managed supportively; no trial evidence for treating an acute attack was found, and steroids for acute EM are untested in RCTs.

cards.headline: Tatnall 1995 (the only double-blind trial): median EM attacks 0 on continuous acyclovir versus 3 on placebo over 6 months (P < 0.0005); 7 of 11 attack-free, 2 in complete remission afterwards
cards.summary: Tatnall 1995 (the only double-blind trial): median EM attacks 0 on continuous acyclovir versus 3 on placebo over 6 months (P < 0.0005); 7 of 11 attack-free, 2 in complete remission afterwards
cards.people: 20 patients with recurrent erythema multiforme suffering more than four attacks per year, enrolled in a 6-month double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of acyclovir 400 mg twice daily (11 patients) versus placebo (9 patients); in 15 patients the disease was precipitated by recurrent herpes simplex, and nine of the 11 acyclovir-group patients had herpes-precipitated disease.
cards.result: The median number of EM attacks during the treatment period was zero in the acyclovir-treated group, compared with three in the placebo-treated group (P < 0.0005, Wilcoxon rank sum test). Seven of the 11 patients treated with continuous acyclovir had no attacks while taking the drug, and one showed almost complete disease suppression. Following treatment, two acyclovir patients went into complete remission, whereas all individuals in the placebo group continued to have attacks. One of the two acyclovir patients with idiopathic (non-herpes) disease also showed complete suppression on treatment. The authors conclude continuous acyclovir therapy can completely suppress attacks of recurrent EM and in some cases may induce remission.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, from 1995, never replicated in a second randomised trial. The effect is large and the P value tiny, but a single small trial in a selected group (very frequent attacks, mostly herpes-linked) cannot say how well suppression works in milder or non-herpes recurrent EM, how long it must continue, or what happens on stopping beyond the two remissions reported. Valacyclovir and famciclovir are used in practice by extrapolation; they have no EM trial of their own.
cards.source: Tatnall FM, Schofield JK, Leigh IM. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of continuous acyclovir therapy in recurrent erythema multiforme. British Journal of Dermatology. 1995. PMID: 7888365. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Schofield 1993 (the 65-patient series behind the trial): 71% herpes-precipitated; 55% of patients benefited from acyclovir regimens; the 11 most resistant patients were all completely suppressed on azathioprine
cards.summary: Schofield 1993 (the 65-patient series behind the trial): 71% herpes-precipitated; 55% of patients benefited from acyclovir regimens; the 11 most resistant patients were all completely suppressed on azathioprine
cards.people: 65 patients with recurrent erythema multiforme reviewed at a specialist clinic: mean six attacks per year (range 2–24), mean disease duration 9.5 years (range 2–36), oral mucous membrane involvement in 69%; in 46 patients (71%) attacks were precipitated by a preceding herpes simplex virus infection.
cards.result: Acyclovir was the most useful first-line treatment, with 55% of patients deriving benefit from either continuous oral acyclovir or a patient-initiated 5-day oral course at the onset of herpes simplex virus infection. Of those failing to respond to acyclovir, a small proportion responded to dapsone. The most resistant patients (11) were treated with azathioprine, with complete disease suppression in all cases.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, retrospective and from a referral clinic whose patients are the severe end of the condition: '55% derived benefit' has no comparator, mixes two different acyclovir strategies (continuous and episodic), and cannot be read as an efficacy estimate. The azathioprine observation (11 of 11 suppressed) is hypothesis-grade only — no control, no randomisation, in patients chosen precisely because everything else had failed. This card documents the treatment ladder as practised; the trial card above is the evidence.
cards.source: Schofield JK, Tatnall FM, Leigh IM. Recurrent erythema multiforme: clinical features and treatment in a large series of patients. British Journal of Dermatology. 1993. PMID: 8504046. cards.headline: de Risi-Pugliese 2019 (systematic review of ALL erythema multiforme interventions): from 1,558 references, one RCT and six case series — 'low-level evidence' for continuous acyclovir, everything else retrospective series only
cards.summary: de Risi-Pugliese 2019 (systematic review of ALL erythema multiforme interventions): from 1,558 references, one RCT and six case series — 'low-level evidence' for continuous acyclovir, everything else retrospective series only
cards.people: Systematic review of any topical or systemic treatment for acute and chronic erythema multiforme in adults, searching MEDLINE, CENTRAL, EMBASE and LILACS to March 2018; randomised trials, observational studies and case series with n ≥ 10 were eligible (isolated mucosal EM excluded to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome contamination).
cards.result: From 1,558 references, one RCT and six case series were included. The RCT (n=20) showed a significant difference in complete remission of EM with continuous acyclovir versus placebo over 6 months. One case series found a mean reduction in flare duration with thalidomide for recurrent EM (5.1 versus 16.2 days; n=20). Adverse events were poorly or not reported in the included studies, and quality of life was never assessed. The reviewers conclude there is low-level evidence for continuous acyclovir treatment for recurrent EM (one RCT), evidence for other treatments rests only on retrospective case series, and safety data are insufficient. PROSPERO registration CRD42016053175.
cards.watchOut: A systematic review whose entire harvest is one 20-patient RCT and six series is a map of an evidence desert: it confirms the acyclovir trial is not hiding among better studies, and that nothing else in EM — steroids, dapsone, azathioprine, thalidomide — has ever been randomised. The thalidomide flare-duration figures come from a single uncontrolled series and are flagged by the reviewers as a prompt for research, not a finding to act on.
cards.source: de Risi-Pugliese T, Sbidian E, Ingen-Housz-Oro S, Le Cleach L. Interventions for erythema multiforme: a systematic review. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology. 2019. PMID: 30680804. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; PROSPERO CRD42016053175). cards.headline: Synthesis: one small, clean, unreplicated trial — suppression works in the patients it was tested in, and nothing else in recurrent EM has been tested at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small, clean, unreplicated trial — suppression works in the patients it was tested in, and nothing else in recurrent EM has been tested at all
cards.people: One double-blind RCT (Tatnall 1995, 20 patients), one 65-patient specialist series (Schofield 1993) and one systematic review of the whole EM treatment literature (de Risi-Pugliese 2019).
cards.result: Continuous acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for 6 months: median attacks 0 versus 3 on placebo (P < 0.0005); 7 of 11 attack-free on treatment; 2 remissions after treatment versus none on placebo. Practice-level corroboration: 55% of 65 series patients benefited from acyclovir regimens; 71% of recurrent EM was herpes-precipitated. Whole-literature check: one RCT and six case series exist for all EM treatments combined; acyclovir graded low-level evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small trial caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Recurrent EM prevention only. This shelf does not cover treatment of an acute EM attack, EM major, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (a different, drug-driven emergency), and it does not validate valacyclovir or famciclovir, which are extrapolations from acyclovir. Tier C.

shelves.title: Oral oxybutynin for excessive sweating: responders 60% versus 27% on placebo in the largest RCT — three small, short trials, with dry mouth in 43–100%
shelves.question: In people with hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) of the palms, armpits, feet or generalised, does oral oxybutynin reduce sweating compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Female · Humans · Hyperhidrosis/drug therapy · Male · Mandelic Acids/administration & dosage · Muscarinic Antagonists/administration & dosage · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Xerostomia/chemically induced · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small, short randomised placebo-controlled trials of oral oxybutynin, all positive, none longer than 6 weeks. The largest (Schollhammer M et al., PMID: 26114588; 62 patients with localised or generalised hyperhidrosis, oxybutynin titrated 2.5 to 7.5 mg/day) found 60% of oxybutynin patients improved at least one point on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS) at 6 weeks versus 27% on placebo (P = 0.009) — a 33-percentage-point absolute difference — with mean Dermatology Life Quality Index improvement of 6.9 versus 2.3 points, and dry mouth in 43% versus 11%. The first trial (Wolosker N et al., PMID: 22341836; 50 patients with palmar/axillary hyperhidrosis, titrated to 5 mg twice daily) reported improvement in over 70% of oxybutynin patients for palmar and axillary sweating and over 90% for plantar sweating at 6 weeks, with quality of life improved in 65.2% and dry mouth in 47.8%. In women with persistent plantar hyperhidrosis after sympathectomy (Costa Jr AS et al., PMID: 24519200; 32 patients, oxybutynin 10 mg/day, 30 days), quality-of-life scores improved on oxybutynin (40.4 to 17.5; P = 0.001) with objectively measured transepidermal water loss falling significantly (P = 0.001) versus no change on placebo (P = 0.95) — but dry mouth in 100% versus 43.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction across three trials, but small samples, 30-day to 6-week horizons, mostly subjective outcomes, and an anticholinergic side-effect burden that is part of the treatment, not an accident of it. BOUNDARY: botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium cloth for armpit sweating are homed on Shelf #2476 and are not re-carded here; iontophoresis has no cardable comparative trial data in this build (see summary flag).

cards.headline: Schollhammer 2015 (largest RCT): HDSS responders 60% on oxybutynin versus 27% on placebo (P = 0.009); DLQI improved 6.9 versus 2.3 points; dry mouth 43% versus 11%
cards.summary: Schollhammer 2015 (largest RCT): HDSS responders 60% on oxybutynin versus 27% on placebo (P = 0.009); DLQI improved 6.9 versus 2.3 points; dry mouth 43% versus 11%
cards.people: 62 patients with localised or generalised hyperhidrosis (83% generalised) enrolled in France from June 2013 to January 2014, randomised to oxybutynin — started at 2.5 mg per day and increased gradually to 7.5 mg per day — or placebo for 6 weeks. Primary outcome: improvement of at least one point on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS); Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and tolerance also reported.
cards.result: Oxybutynin was superior to placebo on the primary outcome: 60% of patients treated with oxybutynin, compared with 27% of patients treated with placebo, improved at least one point on the HDSS (P = 0.009) — a 33-percentage-point absolute difference in responder rates. The mean improvement in quality of life measured by DLQI was significantly better in the oxybutynin arm (6.9 points) than in the placebo arm (2.3 points). The most frequent side effect was dry mouth, observed in 43% of patients in the oxybutynin arm compared with 11% in the placebo arm. The authors conclude low-dose oxybutynin is effective in reducing symptoms of hyperhidrosis in generalised or localised forms, with frequent but minor side effects, mainly dry mouth.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-two patients and six weeks, with a one-point HDSS improvement as the responder definition — a real but modest bar on a four-point subjective scale, in a condition with a large placebo response (27% of placebo patients also 'responded'). Dry mouth at 43% partially unblinds an anticholinergic trial: patients who feel the drug's signature side effect know which arm they are likely on, which inflates subjective outcomes. Nothing here addresses use beyond six weeks.

cards.headline: Wolosker 2012 (first RCT, palmar/axillary): palmar and axillary sweating improved in over 70% of oxybutynin patients at 6 weeks, plantar in over 90%; quality of life improved in 65.2%; dry mouth 47.8%
cards.summary: Wolosker 2012 (first RCT, palmar/axillary): palmar and axillary sweating improved in over 70% of oxybutynin patients at 6 weeks, plantar in over 90%; quality of life improved in 65.2%; dry mouth 47.8%
cards.people: 50 consecutive patients with palmar hyperhidrosis (with axillary and plantar involvement assessed) treated at a São Paulo centre from December 2010 to February 2011 with oxybutynin or placebo; five patients (10.0%) were lost to follow-up, leaving 45 analysed. Oxybutynin was titrated: 2.5 mg once daily in week 1, 2.5 mg twice daily on days 8–21, then 5 mg twice daily to the end of week 6. Outcomes by clinical questionnaire and a quality-of-life protocol before and after treatment.
cards.result: Palmar and axillary hyperhidrosis improved in more than 70% of the oxybutynin patients, and 47.8% of those presented great improvement. Plantar hyperhidrosis improved in more than 90% of the patients. Most patients (65.2%) showed improvements in their quality of life. Side effects were minor, with dry mouth the most frequent (47.8%). The authors conclude that treatment of palmar and axillary hyperhidrosis with oxybutynin is a good initial alternative, given good results and improved quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The published abstract reports the oxybutynin-arm percentages without printing the placebo arm's corresponding rates, so no absolute between-group difference can be stated from the record — the card reports the figures exactly as the record gives them. Outcomes are unvalidated questionnaire scores over six weeks in a single centre whose group has published extensively on this treatment; read the percentages as 'most treated patients reported improvement', corroborated directionally by the Schollhammer trial's placebo-controlled responder gap.
cards.source: Wolosker N, de Campos JRM, Kauffman P, Puech-Leão P. A randomized placebo-controlled trial of oxybutynin for the initial treatment of palmar and axillary hyperhidrosis. cards.headline: Costa 2014 (plantar sweating persisting after sympathectomy): quality-of-life score 40.4 → 17.5 on oxybutynin (P = 0.001) and measured water loss fell (P = 0.001 versus P = 0.95 on placebo) — but dry mouth in 100% versus 43.8%
cards.summary: Costa 2014 (plantar sweating persisting after sympathectomy): quality-of-life score 40.4 → 17.5 on oxybutynin (P = 0.001) and measured water loss fell (P = 0.001 versus P = 0.95 on placebo) — but dry mouth in 100% versus 43.8%
cards.people: 32 women with persistent plantar hyperhidrosis (and compensatory sweating) after thoracoscopic sympathectomy for palmar-plantar hyperhidrosis, randomised 16 to oxybutynin 10 mg daily and 16 to placebo, assessed with a hyperhidrosis quality-of-life questionnaire and objective transepidermal water-loss measurement over the treatment period.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the groups before treatment. After oxybutynin treatment there was a decrease in symptoms and clinical improvement on the quality-of-life questionnaire (before treatment 40.4 versus after treatment 17.5; P = 0.001); the placebo group showed only modest improvement (P = 0.09). Transepidermal water-loss measurements showed no difference in the placebo group (P = 0.95), whereas the oxybutynin group showed a significant decrease (P = 0.001) — the one objective sweat measurement in this shelf's trials. The most common side effect was dry mouth (100% in the oxybutynin group versus 43.8% in the placebo group; P = 0.001). The authors conclude oxybutynin was effective for persistent plantar hyperhidrosis after sympathectomy, with better quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A narrow, specific population — women whose feet still sweat after chest sympathectomy — at the highest dose used in these trials (10 mg/day), where dry mouth was universal (100%): at that rate the side effect is effectively part of the treatment, and complete unblinding is likely. Thirty-two patients and a short treatment period; the objective water-loss result is the card's strength, the generalisability its limit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three small short trials, one direction — oxybutynin beats placebo on sweating and quality of life, and dry mouth comes with it
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small short trials, one direction — oxybutynin beats placebo on sweating and quality of life, and dry mouth comes with it
cards.people: Three randomised placebo-controlled trials: Schollhammer 2015 (62 patients, generalised/localised), Wolosker 2012 (50 patients, palmar/axillary) and Costa 2014 (32 women, plantar after sympathectomy).
cards.result: Responder/improvement rates favour oxybutynin in all three: HDSS ≥1-point responders 60% versus 27% (P = 0.009) with DLQI gains 6.9 versus 2.3 points; palmar/axillary improvement in over 70% of treated patients with quality of life improved in 65.2%; and quality-of-life score 40.4 → 17.5 (P = 0.001) with objectively reduced transepidermal water loss (P = 0.001 versus 0.95) in the post-sympathectomy trial. Dry mouth: 43% versus 11%, 47.8%, and 100% versus 43.8% respectively, rising with dose. All trials lasted 30 days to 6 weeks; no trial compared oxybutynin with any active treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is oral oxybutynin only. Botulinum toxin and the glycopyrronium tosylate cloth for axillary hyperhidrosis are homed on Shelf #2476; iontophoresis, topical anticholinergics, microwave thermolysis and sympathectomy are not covered here. Long-term anticholinergic burden (including cognitive concerns with chronic use, especially in older people) is outside these 6-week trials entirely and should weigh in any decision to continue the drug for years. Tier C.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schollhammer M et al. British Journal of Dermatology. 2015 (PMID: 26114588); Wolosker N et al. Journal of Vascular Surgery. 2012 (PMID: 22341836); Costa Jr AS et al. Clinics (São Paulo). 2014 (PMID: 24519200).

shelves.title: Granuloma annulare: no randomised trials exist — in the largest systematic review (689 patients, all uncontrolled reports), complete clearance ranged from 17.7% with topical steroids to about 83% in small JAK-inhibitor case collections
shelves.question: I have granuloma annulare (ring-shaped skin plaques) — what treatments have been reported to clear it, and how much can I trust the numbers?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Dermatologic Agents/therapeutic use · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Granuloma Annulare/drug therapy · Granuloma Annulare/epidemiology · Granuloma Annulare/therapy · Hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · PUVA Therapy · Retinoids/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there are no randomised trials of treatment for granuloma annulare; the entire quantitative record is uncontrolled case reports and series, pooled in one systematic review of generalised granuloma annulare (Bettolini 2025, PMID: 40586485; PROSPERO CRD42025632216): 689 patients (mean age 52.8 years, 72.6% female) and 754 recorded treatments. Complete-response rates in that pooled, uncontrolled record: topical corticosteroid monotherapy 17.7% (17 of 96) with 38.5% (37 of 96) showing no response; oral corticosteroids 85.7% (12 of 14 — a very small group, two of them also on topical steroids); intralesional corticosteroids 33.3% (3 of 9); PUVA phototherapy 49.4% (41 of 83); UVA1 34.2% (14 of 41); narrowband UVB 30.4% (17 of 56); hydroxychloroquine 44.2% (34 of 77) with 42.9% (33 of 77) not improving; dapsone 33.3% (17 of 51); methotrexate 28% (7 of 25); JAK inhibitors 82.8% (24 of 29); anti-TNF agents 84% (21 of 25). The review's authors themselves caution that outcomes from isolated case reports must be interpreted with care because spontaneous remission and placebo effects cannot be excluded, and that publication bias likely under-reports failures — the highest rates sit in the smallest, newest case collections (JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF), which is the classic signature of that bias. The review proposes a stepwise approach beginning with hydroxychloroquine and phototherapy, reserving anti-TNF and JAK inhibitors for refractory cases. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): treatments are reported to clear generalised granuloma annulare at the rates above, but with no control group anywhere in the record, no rate can be credited to the treatment rather than to the disease's own course.

cards.headline: Bettolini 2025 — corticosteroids: topical steroids alone cleared only 17.7% completely (17/96) with 38.5% not responding; oral steroids cleared 85.7% but in just 14 patients
cards.summary: Bettolini 2025 — corticosteroids: topical steroids alone cleared only 17.7% completely (17/96) with 38.5% not responding; oral steroids cleared 85.7% but in just 14 patients
cards.type: Systematic review of case reports and series — corticosteroid outcomes (Bettolini 2025)
cards.people: Patients with generalised granuloma annulare in the pooled case-report and case-series literature (689 patients overall in the review) who received corticosteroid monotherapy as their current treatment: topical corticosteroids 96 patients, oral corticosteroids 14, intralesional corticosteroids 9.
cards.result: Topical corticosteroid monotherapy: complete response 17.7% (17 of 96), partial response 43.8% (42 of 96), no response 38.5% (37 of 96). Oral corticosteroids: complete response 85.7% (12 of 14, including two patients also using topical steroids) and partial response 14.3% (2 of 14). Intralesional corticosteroids: complete response 33.3% (3 of 9), partial 55.6% (5 of 9), no response 11.1% (1 of 9). The review notes most patients had previously received steroids, with discontinuation plausibly due to lack of efficacy, relapse on withdrawal, or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Every figure in this card is an uncontrolled response proportion, not a treatment effect: generalised granuloma annulare waxes, wanes and sometimes remits spontaneously, and case reports preferentially publish successes. The oral-steroid figure (12 of 14) is the kind of small, selected denominator that inflates most; it should never be quoted without its n. The same review's data are split across this shelf's three evidence cards — they are one source, not three corroborating ones.
cards.source: Bettolini L, Maione V, Carugno A, et al. Management Strategies for Generalised Granuloma Annulare: A Systematic Review of Current and Emerging Therapies. cards.headline: Bettolini 2025 — phototherapy and hydroxychloroquine: PUVA complete response 49.4% (41/83), hydroxychloroquine 44.2% (34/77) with 42.9% not improving, dapsone 33.3% (17/51)
cards.summary: Bettolini 2025 — phototherapy and hydroxychloroquine: PUVA complete response 49.4% (41/83), hydroxychloroquine 44.2% (34/77) with 42.9% not improving, dapsone 33.3% (17/51)
cards.type: Systematic review of case reports and series — phototherapy, antimalarial and sulfone outcomes (Bettolini 2025)
cards.people: Patients with generalised granuloma annulare in the same pooled uncontrolled literature who received phototherapy (PUVA 83, UVA1 41, narrowband UVB 56), hydroxychloroquine (77) or dapsone (51) as current treatment.
cards.result: PUVA: complete response 49.4% (41 of 83), partial 37.6% (31 of 83), no response 13.3% (11 of 83). UVA1: complete 34.2% (14 of 41), partial 58.5% (24 of 41), no response 7.3% (3 of 41). Narrowband UVB: complete 30.4% (17 of 56), partial 37.5% (21 of 56), no response 32.6% (18 of 56; percentages as printed in the review, which sum to slightly over 100% on rounding). Hydroxychloroquine: complete 44.2% (34 of 77), partial 13% (10 of 77), no improvement 42.9% (33 of 77). Dapsone: complete remission 33.3% (17 of 51), partial 25.5% (13 of 51), no effect 41.2% (21 of 51). On these pooled figures the review places hydroxychloroquine and phototherapy (PUVA first) as its proposed first-line step.
cards.watchOut: These treatments were typically given to patients whose disease had already failed topical therapy, so their denominators are harder cases than the topical-steroid group — cross-treatment comparisons of these percentages are not like-for-like. Hydroxychloroquine's split (44% complete, 43% none) is the honest picture of a coin-flip literature: pooled case series cannot say which patients, if any, the drug itself cleared.
cards.source: Bettolini L, Maione V, Carugno A, et al. Management Strategies for Generalised Granuloma Annulare: A Systematic Review of Current and Emerging Therapies. cards.headline: Bettolini 2025 — JAK inhibitors and anti-TNF agents: complete responses of 82.8% (24/29) and 84% (21/25) in small refractory-case collections, against 28% (7/25) for methotrexate in the same review
cards.summary: Bettolini 2025 — JAK inhibitors and anti-TNF agents: complete responses of 82.8% (24/29) and 84% (21/25) in small refractory-case collections, against 28% (7/25) for methotrexate in the same review
cards.type: Systematic review of case reports and series — biologic and targeted-therapy outcomes (Bettolini 2025)
cards.people: Patients with generalised granuloma annulare, largely refractory to earlier treatments, reported in case reports and small series: JAK inhibitors 29 (tofacitinib 15, upadacitinib 10, baricitinib 3, abrocitinib 1); anti-TNF-α agents 25 (adalimumab 20, infliximab 3, certolizumab 1, golimumab 1); methotrexate 25 as a same-review comparator.
cards.result: JAK inhibitors: complete response 82.8% (24 of 29), partial improvement in the remaining 17.2% (5 of 29) — no non-responders were reported. Anti-TNF-α agents: complete response 84% (21 of 25), partial 12% (3 of 25). Methotrexate, by contrast, achieved complete response in 28% (7 of 25), partial in 28% (7 of 25) and no response in 44% (11 of 25). The review's authors recommend anti-TNF agents or JAK inhibitors only for refractory cases, and caution in their discussion that outcomes in isolated case reports should be interpreted with appropriate caution because spontaneous remission or placebo effects cannot be excluded, and that publication bias likely under-reports treatment failures.
cards.watchOut: A complete absence of reported non-responders (0 of 29 on JAK inhibitors) in a case-report literature is itself the warning sign: clinicians publish successes, not failures, and the review says so. These are also off-label, costly, immunosuppressive treatments being summarised from a few dozen selected patients — the numbers describe what has been published, not what a clinic should expect. This card exists so the figures are on record with their provenance attached, not as a recommendation.
cards.source: Bettolini L, Maione V, Carugno A, et al. Management Strategies for Generalised Granuloma Annulare: A Systematic Review of Current and Emerging Therapies. Australasian Journal of Dermatology. 2025. PMID: 40586485. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42025632216 (systematic review registration). cards.headline: Synthesis: a condition with many reported treatments and no controlled evidence — response rates from 18% to 84%, all uncontrolled, all vulnerable to publication bias
cards.summary: Synthesis: a condition with many reported treatments and no controlled evidence — response rates from 18% to 84%, all uncontrolled, all vulnerable to publication bias
cards.people: One systematic review (Bettolini 2025) pooling 689 patients with generalised granuloma annulare and 754 treatments from case reports, case series, cross-sectional and cohort studies — the designs the review states it included; no randomised or controlled trials exist in the record.
cards.result: Complete-response proportions by treatment: topical corticosteroids 17.7% (17/96); methotrexate 28% (7/25); narrowband UVB 30.4% (17/56); dapsone 33.3% (17/51); UVA1 34.2% (14/41); hydroxychloroquine 44.2% (34/77); PUVA 49.4% (41/83); oral corticosteroids 85.7% (12/14); JAK inhibitors 82.8% (24/29); anti-TNF agents 84% (21/25). The review proposes hydroxychloroquine and phototherapy first-line, sulfones or retinoids second-line, and anti-TNF or JAK inhibitors for refractory disease, while noting observation without active treatment may be reasonable in mild or asymptomatic cases. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — reported clearance happens on many treatments; attribution to any treatment is not possible on this record.
cards.watchOut: Scope is generalised granuloma annulare — the review's population. Localised granuloma annulare, the common form, frequently resolves without treatment and is not what these numbers describe. A single-source shelf: all three evidence cards draw on the same review, so the shelf's weight is one systematic review of uncontrolled reports, and its stamp is set accordingly. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bettolini L et al. Australasian Journal of Dermatology. 2025 (PMID: 40586485; full text via PMC12418146).

shelves.title: Laser hair removal clears shaving bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): Nd:YAG laser plus eflornithine cream cut hair by a median 99.5% in a blinded trial
shelves.question: What treatments work for ingrown hairs and shaving bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)?
shelves.mesh: Eflornithine / administration & dosage · Folliculitis · Hair Diseases / drug therapy · Hair Removal / methods · Laser Therapy · Lasers, Solid-State / therapeutic use · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: Three small randomised trials, all in men, all point the same way: removing the hair removes the bumps. In the double-blind paired trial of Xia 2012 (PMID 22226431), 27 men with pseudofolliculitis barbae had long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser to the whole bearded neck every 4 weeks for 16 weeks, with eflornithine cream on one side and placebo cream on the other: median hair reduction 99.5% (range 48.5-100.0%) on the eflornithine side vs 85.0% (range 50.5-94.5%) on the placebo side (P<.001), with significantly fewer inflammatory papules on the eflornithine side. Amer 2021 (PMID 33559240) randomised 20 men to Nd:YAG laser or chemical peeling (up to 5 sessions, 3 months' follow-up): the reduction in papules/pustules was statistically significantly greater with laser in the mandibular and neck regions, though the abstract reports no numeric effect sizes. Leheta 2009 (PMID 20101340) randomised 20 men in a split-face design to long-pulse alexandrite laser (GentleLase, Candela Corp.) on one half and intense pulsed light (Chromolite, Chromogenex Technologies Ltd.) on the other: the alexandrite side reached about 80% improvement in 7 sessions, the IPL side needed 10-12 sessions for about 50% improvement, with less recurrence over 1 year on the alexandrite side. Harms were mild: pain with laser, transient hyperpigmentation, mild erythema and burning with peeling. The evidence is small, short-term and all-male, so the stamp stays at: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Xia 2012: Nd:YAG laser plus eflornithine cream cut hair by a median 99.5% vs 85.0% with laser plus placebo cream
cards.summary: Xia 2012: Nd:YAG laser plus eflornithine cream cut hair by a median 99.5% vs 85.0% with laser plus placebo cream
cards.people: 27 men with pseudofolliculitis barbae; each man's bearded neck was split right/left between eflornithine and placebo cream, both over the same laser treatment
cards.result: Long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser (25-30 J/cm2, 20-30 ms pulse, 10-mm spot) every 4 weeks for 16 weeks. At 16 weeks median hair reduction was 99.5% (range 48.5-100.0%) on the eflornithine side vs 85.0% (range 50.5-94.5%) on the placebo side (P<.001); the eflornithine side also had a statistically significant decrease in inflammatory papules. No follow-up beyond 16 weeks.
cards.watchOut: 27 men only, all military, and no follow-up beyond 16 weeks - durability of the effect is unknown.
cards.source: Xia Y, Cho S, Howard RS, Maggio KL. Topical eflornithine hydrochloride improves the effectiveness of standard laser hair removal for treating pseudofolliculitis barbae: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2012. PMID: 22226431. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Amer 2021: in 20 men, Nd:YAG laser reduced papules and pustules significantly more than chemical peeling

cards.headline: Synthesis: laser hair removal is the treatment with the best evidence for shaving bumps; adding eflornithine cream helps further
cards.summary: Synthesis: laser hair removal is the treatment with the best evidence for shaving bumps; adding eflornithine cream helps further
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded randomised trials: 27 + 20 + 20 men
cards.result: Across the three trials, laser hair removal consistently reduced hair and bumps: median 99.5% hair reduction with laser plus eflornithine vs 85.0% with laser plus placebo (Xia 2012), laser significantly better than chemical peeling (Amer 2021), and alexandrite laser faster and more durable than IPL (Leheta 2009). No trial followed patients beyond a year, and no trial included women.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are small, all-male and short; the stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher.
cards.source: Synthesis of Xia 2012 (PMID 22226431), Amer 2021 (PMID 33559240) and Leheta 2009 (PMID 20101340).

shelves.title: Keratosis pilaris: 10% lactic acid cut lesions by 66% and 5% salicylic acid by 52% in a randomised trial; laser looks most supported in a review of 47 articles
shelves.question: What treatments help keratosis pilaris (the rough bumps on the upper arms and thighs)?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Multiple / therapy · Darier Disease / therapy · Humans · Low-Level Light Therapy
shelves.balance: The evidence is thin and uneven. Kootiratrakarn 2015 (PMID 25802513) randomised patients with keratosis pilaris to 10% lactic acid or 5% salicylic acid cream twice daily for 3 months: mean lesion reduction from baseline was 66% with lactic acid and 52% with salicylic acid, both statistically significant, with only mild local irritation - but the abstract gives no total number of patients, so the card prints 'N not documented'. McCormick 2024 (PMID 38206153) was a 4-week open-label, noncomparative study of a 20% urea moisturising cream in 30 participants aged 18-65: the percent change in skin smoothness/texture was significant at 1 week and 4 weeks (P<=0.001), most were satisfied at 4 weeks, and there were no significant adverse events - but without a control group the improvement cannot be separated from natural variation or expectation. Maghfour 2022 (PMID 32886029) systematically reviewed 47 articles from 1,150 screened and found laser therapy, particularly Q-switched Nd:YAG, the most supported treatment, with topicals (mineral oil-hydrophil petrolat, tacrolimus, azelaic acid, salicylic acid) also effective at least for appearance - but outcome measures varied between studies, so no pooled effect size exists. Nothing here is strong or controlled enough to go beyond: PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Kootiratrakarn 2015: 10% lactic acid cut keratosis pilaris lesions by 66% and 5% salicylic acid by 52% over 3 months
cards.summary: Kootiratrakarn 2015: 10% lactic acid cut keratosis pilaris lesions by 66% and 5% salicylic acid by 52% over 3 months
cards.people: Patients with keratosis pilaris randomised to 10% lactic acid or 5% salicylic acid cream twice daily for 3 months, assessed to 4 weeks after treatment; N not documented
cards.result: Mean reduction of lesions from baseline was 66% with 10% lactic acid and 52% with 5% salicylic acid, both statistically significant. Stratum-corneum conductance rose in both groups and the improvement was maintained to follow-up; no significant differences in transepidermal water loss. Adverse effects were limited to mild local skin irritation, with no systemic side effects.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives no total number of patients, so the card prints 'N not documented'; and the trial compared two active creams with no untreated control.
cards.source: Kootiratrakarn T, Kampirapap K, Chunhasewee C. Epidermal permeability barrier in the treatment of keratosis pilaris. Dermatol Res Pract. 2015. PMID: 25802513. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: McCormick 2024: a 20% urea cream improved skin smoothness in 30 people with keratosis pilaris, significant at 1 and 4 weeks (P<=0.001)
cards.summary: McCormick 2024: a 20% urea cream improved skin smoothness in 30 people with keratosis pilaris, significant at 1 and 4 weeks (P<=0.001)
cards.people: 30 participants aged 18-65 years with keratosis pilaris who completed a 4-week study of a 20% urea moisturising cream once daily
cards.result: The percent change in skin smoothness/texture from baseline was significant after 1 week and after 4 weeks of use (P<=0.001). cards.headline: Maghfour 2022: across 47 articles, laser therapy (especially Q-switched Nd:YAG) was the most supported treatment for keratosis pilaris
cards.summary: Maghfour 2022: across 47 articles, laser therapy (especially Q-switched Nd:YAG) was the most supported treatment for keratosis pilaris
cards.people: Systematic review of keratosis pilaris treatments: 1,150 non-duplicated articles screened, 47 included
cards.result: The most supported form of treatment was laser therapy, particularly the Q-switched Nd:YAG laser. Topical treatments including mineral oil-hydrophil petrolat, tacrolimus, azelaic acid and salicylic acid were also effective at least for improving the appearance of keratosis pilaris. Measured treatment outcomes varied among studies.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneous studies with varied outcome measures and no pooled effect size - the review ranks treatments but cannot say how much any one helps.

shelves.title: Perforated eardrum: acute traumatic perforations healed 94% overall with no advantage from paper patching in the randomised trial — patches only shortened healing time in large perforations, while office patching closed 59.8% of chronic small dry perforations
shelves.question: For a perforated eardrum (tympanic membrane perforation), does patching improve healing compared with watchful waiting — in acute traumatic perforations, and in chronic perforations?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Otologic Surgical Procedures / methods* · Prospective Studies · Tissue Adhesives / administration & dosage* · Tympanic Membrane Perforation / etiology · Tympanic Membrane Perforation / pathology · Tympanic Membrane Perforation / surgery* · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT. For acute traumatic perforations, two randomised trials agree that patching does not significantly raise the final closure rate: Lindeman 1987 (PMID: 3675893) found 94% healed by two months with no difference between paper patch and control, and Park 2011 (PMID: 21593464), in perforations over half the drum, found closure of 93.3% (Steri-Strips), 84.2% (paper patch) and 78.9% (observation), not statistically significant — though patching shortened healing time and reduced repeat procedures. For chronic, dry, small perforations the question is different: Yazdani 2026 (PMID: 41729596) reports 59.8% complete closure 8 weeks after office paper patching in an uncontrolled series of 204 perforations. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (acute traumatic: patching made no difference to final closure · chronic small dry: office patching POSSIBLE on uncontrolled evidence).

cards.headline: Lindeman 1987: paper patching made no difference — overall healing 94% at two months
cards.summary: Lindeman 1987: paper patching made no difference — overall healing 94% at two months
cards.people: 60 patients with acute traumatic tympanic membrane perforations, randomly allocated to a paper prosthesis (patch) group or a control group; 42 (70%) were seen within two days; all received oral antibiotics for ten days.
cards.result: Overall healing rate two months after trauma was 94% (37 of 39 patients with outcome data). No significant difference between the patched and control patients was observed. Intermittent secretion occurred in six patients and did not influence outcome. The authors conclude acute traumatic perforations do not need routine paper patching.
cards.watchOut: Small and old, with outcome data on 39 of 60 randomised patients, and everyone received antibiotics — it rules out a large closure benefit from patching, not a modest one, and says nothing about chronic perforations.
cards.source: Lindeman P, Edström S, Granström G, Jacobsson S, von Sydow C, Westin T, Aberg B. Acute traumatic tympanic membrane perforations. Cover or observe? Arch Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 1987. PMID: 3675893. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Park 2011: in large traumatic perforations, closure 93.3% (Steri-Strips) versus 84.2% (paper patch) versus 78.9% (observation) — not statistically significant; patching healed faster
cards.summary: Park 2011: in large traumatic perforations, closure 93.3% (Steri-Strips) versus 84.2% (paper patch) versus 78.9% (observation) — not statistically significant; patching healed faster
cards.people: 87 patients with traumatic tympanic membrane perforations larger than 50% of the drum, randomised prospectively to Steri-Strips patching, paper patching, or conservative observation (2009 to 2011, tertiary hospital).
cards.result: Closure rates: Steri-Strips 93.3%, paper patch 84.2%, observation 78.9% — no statistically significant difference between the three groups. Both patching groups had shorter healing times than observation, and Steri-Strips reduced the need for repeat procedures; otorrhea (ear discharge) was significantly more common with Steri-Strips than with observation (absolute rates not printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: Even in perforations over half the drum, the closure gap did not reach significance at n=87 — patching's demonstrated gain is speed of healing and fewer repeat procedures, bought with more discharge in the Steri-Strips arm.
cards.source: Park MK, Kim KH, Lee JD, Lee BD. Repair of large traumatic tympanic membrane perforation with a Steri-Strips patch. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2011. PMID: 21593464. cards.headline: Yazdani 2026: office paper patching closed 59.8% of chronic, dry, small perforations by 8 weeks (uncontrolled series)
cards.summary: Yazdani 2026: office paper patching closed 59.8% of chronic, dry, small perforations by 8 weeks (uncontrolled series)
cards.people: 161 patients with 204 chronic (over 6 months), dry, small (under 50%) tympanic membrane perforations treated in a tertiary neurotology clinic, 2016 to 2022; perforation edges freshened with trichloroacetic acid and a hook, then a sterile paper patch placed in the office.
cards.result: By 8 weeks: complete healing in 59.8% (122) and partial healing in 12.7% (26) of perforations. Healing was predicted by smaller perforation size (P = 0.001), anterior or superior location (P < 0.001) and younger age (P < 0.005). No complications were reported.
cards.watchOut: No control group — some chronic perforations close or shrink without intervention, so 59.8% is a description of what happened after patching in selected small, dry perforations, not proof of how many patching itself closed; formal surgical repair (myringoplasty/tympanoplasty) outcomes are outside this record.
cards.source: Yazdani Y et al. In-Office Paper Patch Placement for Tympanic Membrane Perforation. Otol Neurotol. 2026. PMID: 41729596. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: acute traumatic perforations mostly heal alone and patching does not raise final closure; chronic small dry perforations are a separate, weaker-evidence question
cards.summary: Synthesis: acute traumatic perforations mostly heal alone and patching does not raise final closure; chronic small dry perforations are a separate, weaker-evidence question
cards.people: Three sources: two randomised trials in acute traumatic perforation (Lindeman 1987, n=60; Park 2011, n=87) and one uncontrolled series in chronic perforation (Yazdani 2026, 204 perforations).
cards.result: Final closure, acute: 94% overall with no patch advantage (Lindeman 1987); 93.3% versus 84.2% versus 78.9% for Steri-Strips, paper patch and observation in large perforations, not significant, with faster healing when patched (Park 2011). Chronic small dry perforations: 59.8% completely healed 8 weeks after office paper patching, uncontrolled (Yazdani 2026). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Nothing carded here covers perforations with infection, cholesteatoma, ossicular damage or hearing-loss outcomes in detail — those change management entirely and need specialist assessment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lindeman 1987 (PMID: 3675893), Park 2011 (PMID: 21593464) and Yazdani 2026 (PMID: 41729596).

shelves.title: Pilonidal sinus: flap operations cut recurrence versus midline closure (relative odds ratio 0.31 across 50 trials, 5,762 people) and the Karydakis flap healed in a median 14 days versus 49 — though the one 11-year trial found recurrences equal
shelves.question: For chronic pilonidal sinus disease, how do flap operations (Karydakis, Limberg) compare with midline closure and with excision left to heal by secondary intention, for recurrence, infection and healing time?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Chronic Disease · Humans · Length of Stay / statistics & numerical data · Pilonidal Sinus* / surgery · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Surgical Flaps* · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for off-midline flap closure over midline closure. Two systematic reviews point the same way: Wiinblad 2025 (PMID: 39982788), across 50 RCTs and 5,762 participants, found flap operations had lower recurrence than primary midline closure (relative odds ratio 0.31) and lower infection (relative odds ratio 0.33), with secondary-intention healing always slowest; Alsalaumy 2026 (PMID: 41854814) found the Karydakis flap beat midline closure on recurrence (relative odds ratio 0.30) and returned patients to work 6.5 days sooner. The caution comes from the only long-follow-up head-to-head RCT, Hemmingsson 2022 (NCT00412659; PMID not captured this session): healing was far faster with the Karydakis flap (median 14 versus 49 days) but recurrences were five in each group at a median 11 years. Certainty in the reviews is very low to low. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Wiinblad 2025: flap operations beat midline closure on recurrence (relative odds ratio 0.31) and infection (relative odds ratio 0.33) across 50 trials
cards.summary: Wiinblad 2025: flap operations beat midline closure on recurrence (relative odds ratio 0.31) and infection (relative odds ratio 0.33) across 50 trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Wiinblad 2025)
cards.people: 5,762 participants in 50 randomised trials (2002 to 2024) comparing operations for chronic pilonidal sinus disease: secondary healing, primary midline closure, Bascom, Limberg and Karydakis procedures. Odds ratios are relative measures; pooled absolute recurrence rates are not printed in the record.
cards.result: Recurrence: flap operations versus primary midline closure odds ratio 0.31 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.51; p < 0.01); flap versus secondary healing odds ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.13; p = 0.08) — heterogeneous and not significant. Infection: flap versus primary closure odds ratio 0.33 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.48); flap versus secondary healing odds ratio 0.48 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.77). Recurrence was similar between Limberg and Karydakis operations. All trials found secondary healing had significantly longer healing times than any other operation. Certainty of evidence: very low to low.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials had high or medium risk of bias, small numbers and short follow-up — recurrence in pilonidal disease keeps accruing for years, so short trials flatter every technique; the review's own certainty rating is very low to low.
cards.source: Wiinblad IM, Ulrichsen J, Brandstrup B. Outcome After Surgical Treatment for Chronic Pilonidal Sinus Disease: A Systematic Review of Common Surgical Techniques. Dis Colon Rectum. 2025. PMID: 39982788. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Alsalaumy 2026: Karydakis flap versus midline closure — recurrence odds ratio 0.30 and back to work 6.5 days sooner
cards.summary: Alsalaumy 2026: Karydakis flap versus midline closure — recurrence odds ratio 0.30 and back to work 6.5 days sooner
cards.people: 3,108 patients in 15 randomised and comparative cohort studies: Karydakis flap 1,257, midline closure 1,593, excision with healing by secondary intention 258. Odds ratios are relative measures; absolute rates are not printed in the record.
cards.result: Recurrence: Karydakis flap versus midline closure odds ratio 0.30 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.59; p < 0.001); versus secondary-intention healing odds ratio 0.29 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.71; p = 0.006). Infection: Karydakis versus secondary-intention healing odds ratio 0.06 (95% CI 0.007 to 0.486; p = 0.008). Return to work was earlier with the Karydakis flap by 6.5 days versus midline closure and 18.9 days versus secondary-intention healing; hospital stay did not differ versus midline closure (mean difference -0.08 days).
cards.watchOut: A single-author review mixing randomised trials with comparative cohorts, and its infection advantage over midline closure in the full analysis was null (odds ratio 1.01 in the review's own table) — the consistent signal is recurrence and recovery speed, not infection versus midline closure.
cards.source: Alsalaumy AHA. Comparative study of the Karydakis flap versus conventional surgical techniques for pilonidal sinus disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Updates Surg. 2026. PMID: 41854814. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hemmingsson 2022: Karydakis flap healed in a median 14 days versus 49 days for midline suture — but recurrences were 5 versus 5 at 11 years
cards.summary: Hemmingsson 2022: Karydakis flap healed in a median 14 days versus 49 days for midline suture — but recurrences were 5 versus 5 at 11 years
cards.people: Patients with pilonidal sinus randomised at two Swedish hospitals (2006 to 2015) to excision with midline suture or Karydakis flap surgery; total randomised number not documented in the sources fetched this session (printed as not documented per house rule). Median follow-up 11 years.
cards.result: Median wound healing time: 14 days (95% CI 12 to 20) after Karydakis flap versus 49 days (95% CI 32 to 66) after midline closure (P < 0.001). Recurrences: five in each group (P = 0.753) — no difference at a median 11 years. Numbers taken from the trial report and the authors' published response fetched this session (PMC), not from the PubMed abstract (see flag in the part summary).
cards.watchOut: The one long-follow-up head-to-head trial tempers the meta-analyses: the healing-time advantage is large and real, but the pooled recurrence advantage of the flap did not appear in this trial at 11 years — midline closure's poor reputation rests substantially on shorter and weaker studies.
cards.source: Hemmingsson O, Binnermark F, Odensten C, Rutegård M, Franklin KA, Haapamäki MM. cards.headline: Synthesis: move the closure off the midline — flaps heal faster and probably recur less, but the recurrence claim is weaker than the pooled numbers suggest
cards.summary: Synthesis: move the closure off the midline — flaps heal faster and probably recur less, but the recurrence claim is weaker than the pooled numbers suggest
cards.people: Three sources: two systematic reviews (Wiinblad 2025, 50 RCTs, 5,762 participants; Alsalaumy 2026, 15 studies, 3,108 patients) and one long-term RCT (Hemmingsson 2022, NCT00412659).
cards.result: Recurrence, flaps versus midline closure: relative odds ratio 0.31 (Wiinblad 2025) and 0.30 for the Karydakis flap specifically (Alsalaumy 2026) — but 5 versus 5 recurrences at 11 years in the only long-follow-up RCT (Hemmingsson 2022). Healing: median 14 versus 49 days favouring the Karydakis flap (Hemmingsson 2022); secondary-intention healing was slowest in every comparison. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Minimally invasive options (pit-picking/Gips, laser, endoscopic approaches) and acute-abscess management are not covered by the carded comparisons, which concern elective surgery for chronic pilonidal disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wiinblad 2025 (PMID: 39982788), Alsalaumy 2026 (PMID: 41854814) and Hemmingsson 2022 (NCT00412659).

shelves.title: Pityriasis rosea: acyclovir probably improves the rash (relative risk 2.45 across 3 trials, 141 people; 86.66% vs 33.33% complete resolution in the double-blind trial) — but its effect on itch is unresolved
shelves.question: In pityriasis rosea, do acyclovir, macrolide antibiotics, steroids or other treatments improve the rash or the itch compared with placebo or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents / therapeutic use* · Anti-Inflammatory Agents / therapeutic use · Antiviral Agents / therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Dermatologic Agents / therapeutic use · Female · Histamine H1 Antagonists / therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phototherapy · Pityriasis Rosea / drug therapy* · Pruritus / drug therapy* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for oral acyclovir on rash improvement; the itch evidence is unsettled. Contreras-Ruiz 2019 (PMID: 31684696), the Cochrane review of 14 trials (761 participants), found acyclovir probably improves practitioner-rated rash (relative risk 2.45, 3 trials, 141 participants) while its itch results conflicted — one 21-patient trial found placebo better for itch resolution. Ciccarese 2024 (PMID: 39597810), a network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs, ranked acyclovir best for rash improvement (relative risk 2.55 versus placebo) and oral steroids best for itch. The primary trials bracket the plausible effect: Drago 2006 (PMID: 16384760), unblinded, found 79% versus 4% full regression by day 14; Ganguly 2014 (PMID: 24995231), double-blind, found complete resolution of 86.66% versus 33.33%. Macrolides other than erythromycin showed probably no difference from placebo. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Contreras-Ruiz 2019 (Cochrane): acyclovir improved practitioner-rated rash (relative risk 2.45, 3 trials, 141 people) but itch results conflicted; erythromycin's rash estimate was uninformative (relative risk 4.02, CI 0.28 to 56.61)
cards.summary: Contreras-Ruiz 2019 (Cochrane): acyclovir improved practitioner-rated rash (relative risk 2.45, 3 trials, 141 people) but itch results conflicted; erythromycin's rash estimate was uninformative (relative risk 4.02, CI 0.28 to 56.61)
cards.people: 761 participants in 14 randomised trials of treatments for pityriasis rosea (macrolides, acyclovir, phototherapy, steroids, antihistamines, Chinese medicine); all outcomes assessed within two weeks of treatment.
cards.result: Acyclovir versus placebo, vitamins or no treatment: practitioner-rated rash improvement relative risk 2.45 (95% CI 1.33 to 4.53; 3 studies, 141 participants; moderate-quality evidence) — a relative measure; absolute improvement rates are not printed in the record. Itch resolution in one 21-participant trial was higher with placebo than acyclovir (relative risk 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.94). Acyclovir added to standard care (calamine plus cetirizine) increased itch resolution (relative risk 4.50, 95% CI 1.22 to 16.62; 24 participants; low-quality). Erythromycin versus placebo: rash improvement relative risk 4.02 (95% CI 0.28 to 56.61; 2 studies, 86 participants; low-quality) — compatible with benefit either way; itch-score reduction was larger with erythromycin (mean difference 3.95, 95% CI 3.37 to 4.53; 34 participants). Clarithromycin and azithromycin showed probably no difference from placebo.
cards.watchOut: No trial measured the review's primary outcome (participant-rated good or excellent rash improvement), blinding and selective-reporting bias were common, and every pooled estimate rests on one to three small trials — 'probably' in Cochrane's wording is doing real work here.
cards.source: Contreras-Ruiz J, Peternel S, Jiménez Gutiérrez C, Culav-Koscak I, Reveiz L, Silbermann-Reynoso MDL. Interventions for pityriasis rosea. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. PMID: 31684696. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ciccarese 2024: network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs — acyclovir ranked best for rash improvement (relative risk 2.55 versus placebo); oral steroids ranked best for itch
cards.summary: Ciccarese 2024: network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs — acyclovir ranked best for rash improvement (relative risk 2.55 versus placebo); oral steroids ranked best for itch
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials of pharmacological treatments for pityriasis rosea, pooled in a network meta-analysis; total participant number not printed in the record. Risk ratios are relative measures; absolute rates are not printed in the record.
cards.result: Rash improvement versus placebo: acyclovir relative risk 2.55 (95% CI 1.81 to 3.58) and erythromycin relative risk 1.69 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.33) were the only significant results; acyclovir outperformed all other tested interventions (ranking score SUCRA 0.92). Itch resolution versus placebo: only oral steroids (relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.72; SUCRA 0.90) and oral steroids plus antihistamine (relative risk 0.47, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.99) were significantly superior — note the itch risk ratios below 1 reflect the review's outcome coding for unresolved itch. The authors position acyclovir for extensive, persistent lesions or systemic symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings (SUCRA) make small, heterogeneous trial sets look more decisive than they are — most comparisons are indirect, and the same trials feed the Cochrane review on this shelf, so the two reviews are not independent confirmations.
cards.source: Ciccarese G, Facciorusso A, Herzum A, Fidanzi C, Recalcati S, Foti C, Drago F. Comparative Efficacy of Different Pharmacological Treatments for Pityriasis Rosea: A Network Meta-Analysis. J Clin Med. 2024. PMID: 39597810. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Drago 2006: high-dose acyclovir — 79% fully regressed by day 14 versus 4% on placebo; lesions cleared in 18.5 versus 37.9 days (non-randomised, unblinded)
cards.summary: Drago 2006: high-dose acyclovir — 79% fully regressed by day 14 versus 4% on placebo; lesions cleared in 18.5 versus 37.9 days (non-randomised, unblinded)
cards.type: Controlled clinical trial, neither randomised nor double-blind (Drago 2006)
cards.people: 87 consecutive patients with pityriasis rosea treated for one week with oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily or placebo.
cards.result: Full regression by day 14: 79% of the acyclovir group versus 4% of the placebo group — an absolute difference of 75 percentage points. Time to lesion clearance: 18.5 days on acyclovir versus 37.9 days on placebo; clearance was faster when treatment began in the first week from onset (17.2 days) than later (19.7 days), with significantly fewer new lesions at day 7 in those treated early.
cards.watchOut: The authors state the limitation themselves: neither randomised nor double-blind — in a self-limiting rash, an unblinded comparison can manufacture exactly this kind of dramatic gap, which is why the blinded trial on this shelf matters more despite its smaller effect.
cards.source: Drago F, Vecchio F, Rebora A. Use of high-dose acyclovir in pityriasis rosea. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2006. PMID: 16384760. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ganguly 2014: the double-blind test — complete resolution 86.66% on acyclovir versus 33.33% on placebo at day 14
cards.summary: Ganguly 2014: the double-blind test — complete resolution 86.66% on acyclovir versus 33.33% on placebo at day 14
cards.people: 73 patients with pityriasis rosea randomised double-blind to high-dose oral acyclovir (38) or placebo (35); follow-up data were available for 60 and analysed.
cards.result: Complete resolution at day 7: 53.33% on acyclovir versus 10% on placebo; at day 14: 86.66% versus 33.33% — an absolute difference of about 53 percentage points at day 14. The differences were statistically significant (exact p values not printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, single-author trial with 13 of 73 randomised patients missing from the analysis and no printed confidence intervals — supportive of the Cochrane direction, but not strong enough to carry the claim alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: acyclovir probably speeds rash clearance; itch is a separate, unsettled question; the disease settles on its own in 2 to 12 weeks regardless
cards.summary: Synthesis: acyclovir probably speeds rash clearance; itch is a separate, unsettled question; the disease settles on its own in 2 to 12 weeks regardless
cards.people: Four sources: the Cochrane review (Contreras-Ruiz 2019, 14 trials, 761 participants), a network meta-analysis (Ciccarese 2024, 12 RCTs), one non-randomised controlled trial (Drago 2006, n=87) and one double-blind RCT (Ganguly 2014, n=73 randomised, 60 analysed).
cards.result: Rash improvement: relative risk 2.45 for acyclovir versus comparators in Cochrane pooling; complete resolution 86.66% versus 33.33% at day 14 in the blinded trial; 79% versus 4% full regression in the unblinded trial. Itch: conflicting — placebo beat acyclovir for itch resolution in one tiny trial, while oral steroids ranked best for itch in the network analysis. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Pityriasis rosea is self-limiting — treatment is for extensive, persistent or very itchy disease, and reassurance remains the default for typical cases; pregnancy and atypical presentations change the assessment and are outside this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Contreras-Ruiz 2019 (PMID: 31684696), Ciccarese 2024 (PMID: 39597810), Drago 2006 (PMID: 16384760) and Ganguly 2014 (PMID: 24995231).

shelves.title: Polymorphic light eruption: hydroxychloroquine beat placebo on rash in one small 1987 trial (13 vs 15 patients, P < 0.01) and edged chloroquine in 117 patients; calcipotriol cream cut provoked symptoms by 32% in 13 patients
shelves.question: In people with polymorphic light eruption, which treatments reduce or prevent the eruption, and how strong is the trial evidence?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antimalarials/administration & dosage · Antimalarials/adverse effects · Chloroquine/administration & dosage · Chloroquine/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Hydroxychloroquine/administration & dosage · Hydroxychloroquine/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Photosensitivity Disorders/drug therapy · Photosensitivity Disorders/etiology · Sunlight/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for antimalarials, on small old trials. The only placebo-controlled trial of hydroxychloroquine (Murphy 1987, PMID: 3552020; 13 patients on active treatment and 15 on placebo over June-August 1982) found moderate clinical improvement with a statistically significant improvement in skin rash (P less than 0.01). The larger head-to-head trial (Pareek 2008, PMID: 18187817; 117 patients) found hydroxychloroquine beat chloroquine on burning, itching and erythema severity scores (P < 0.05) but not scaling (P = 0.229), with good-to-excellent responses in 68.9% on hydroxychloroquine versus 63% on chloroquine and no placebo arm, so neither drug is proven against no treatment by this trial. A tiny intra-individual trial of calcipotriol cream (PMID: 21428979; NCT00871052; 13 patients, lesions provoked in 12) found pretreatment reduced the PLE test score by an average of 32% relative to placebo cream (95% CI 21-44%; P = 0.0022) after photoprovocation. No trial of topical or systemic corticosteroids or of desensitisation phototherapy was carded this session. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): hydroxychloroquine probably eases PLE, but the placebo-controlled evidence is one 28-patient trial from 1987.

cards.headline: Murphy 1987: hydroxychloroquine improved the PLE rash significantly versus placebo (P less than 0.01) in 13 treated versus 15 placebo patients
cards.summary: Murphy 1987: hydroxychloroquine improved the PLE rash significantly versus placebo (P less than 0.01) in 13 treated versus 15 placebo patients
cards.people: 13 patients with polymorphic light eruption on active hydroxychloroquine treatment and 15 on placebo, in a double-blind controlled trial run over June, July and August 1982 (n=28 in total).
cards.result: Moderate clinical improvement occurred on hydroxychloroquine, associated with a statistically significant improvement in skin rash (P less than 0.01). The abstract reports no response-rate percentages for either group.
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=28) and from 1982; the abstract gives a P value for rash but no absolute response rates, so the size of the benefit cannot be judged from the record.
