cards.headline: Pareek 2008: hydroxychloroquine beat chloroquine on burning, itching and erythema scores (P < 0.05), with good-to-excellent response in 68.9% versus 63% of 117 patients
cards.summary: Pareek 2008: hydroxychloroquine beat chloroquine on burning, itching and erythema scores (P < 0.05), with good-to-excellent response in 68.9% versus 63% of 117 patients
cards.people: 117 patients with polymorphic light eruption (68 men, 49 women, ages 18-73 years) at two Indian centres, randomised to hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily for one month then 200 mg once daily for one month (n=63) or chloroquine 250 mg twice daily then 250 mg once daily (n=54), treated for two months and assessed to 12 weeks.
cards.result: Severity scores for burning, itching and erythema fell significantly more with hydroxychloroquine than chloroquine (P < 0.05); scaling did not differ (P = 0.229). Good-to-excellent response was reported by 68.9% of hydroxychloroquine patients and 63% of chloroquine patients. Adverse events were mild to moderate; no serious adverse events and no ocular toxicity were reported. A published letter (Singh 2008) disputed the superiority claim, noting only a marginal difference.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm: both groups improving over a summer season cannot be separated from natural course or sun behaviour. Several authors were employees of the hydroxychloroquine manufacturer (IPCA Laboratories), and a published correspondence challenged the conclusion.
cards.source: Pareek A, Khopkar U, Sacchidanand S, Chandurkar N, Naik GS. Comparative study of efficacy and safety of hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine in polymorphic light eruption: a randomized, double-blind, multicentric study. cards.headline: Calcipotriol trial 2011: calcipotriol cream cut provoked PLE symptoms by an average of 32% relative to placebo cream (95% CI 21-44%; P = 0.0022) in 13 patients (n=13 printed on the face)
cards.summary: Calcipotriol trial 2011: calcipotriol cream cut provoked PLE symptoms by an average of 32% relative to placebo cream (95% CI 21-44%; P = 0.0022) in 13 patients (n=13 printed on the face)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, intra-individual half-body (calcipotriol PLE trial 2011)
cards.people: 13 patients with PLE (10 women, 3 men; mean age 37 years) who pretreated two symmetrical test fields with calcipotriol or placebo cream twice daily for 7 days before photoprovocation with solar-simulated UV radiation; lesions were provoked in 12 of 13 (92%).
cards.result: Compared with placebo, calcipotriol pretreatment reduced the PLE test score by an average of 32% (95% CI 21-44%; P = 0.0022, exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test) from 48 h to 144 h after first photoprovocation. Calcipotriol fields scored lower in 7 of 12 cases (58%) at 48 h, 9 (75%) at 72 h and 10 (83%) at 144 h; across all time points together, calcipotriol diminished the score in all 12 photoprovocable patients (P = 0.0005).
cards.watchOut: Only 13 patients (n printed on the face) and an artificial photoprovocation test-field outcome, not real-world eruptions over a season; a preventive effect on test fields may not translate into fewer clinical episodes.

cards.summary: Synthesis: antimalarials have the only placebo-controlled support, and it rests on one 28-patient trial from 1987
cards.people: Across the three carded studies: 28 patients in the placebo-controlled hydroxychloroquine trial, 117 in the hydroxychloroquine-versus-chloroquine trial, and 13 in the calcipotriol photoprovocation trial.
cards.result: Hydroxychloroquine improved rash versus placebo (P < 0.01; Murphy 1987) and edged chloroquine on symptom scores without a placebo control (Pareek 2008); calcipotriol cream reduced provoked test-field symptoms by 32% on average versus placebo cream in 13 patients. shelves.title: Pyoderma gangrenosum: ciclosporin and prednisolone heal identically (47% by 6 months on each in STOP GAP); infliximab beat placebo 46% vs 6% at week 2 in the one small placebo-controlled trial
shelves.question: In people with pyoderma gangrenosum, how do ciclosporin, prednisolone, infliximab and topical therapy compare for healing ulcers?
shelves.mesh: Cyclosporine/administration & dosage · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Pyoderma Gangrenosum/drug therapy · Pyoderma Gangrenosum/pathology · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Varicose Ulcer/drug therapy · Varicose Ulcer/pathology · Wound Healing/drug effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The two standard systemic drugs are equal: in STOP GAP (Ormerod 2015, PMID: 26071094; ISRCTN35898459; 112 analysed), healing speed at 6 weeks differed by 0.003 cm2/day (95% CI -0.20 to 0.21; P=0.97) between ciclosporin and prednisolone, and 47% of each group had healed by 6 months, with serious adverse reactions, especially infections, commoner on prednisolone. Infliximab beat placebo in the only placebo-controlled trial (Brooklyn 2006, PMID: 16188920; 30 patients): improvement at week 2 in 46% (6/13) versus 6% (1/17) (p=0.025). For smaller ulcers managed topically, the STOP GAP prospective cohort (Thomas 2016, PMID: 27502313; 66 patients, no comparator) saw 28 of 66 (43.8%) healed by 6 months on mainly clobetasol or tacrolimus. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose between ciclosporin and prednisolone on side-effect profile; infliximab has real but small-trial placebo-controlled support; topical therapy heals a similar share of milder disease without systemic toxicity.

cards.headline: Ormerod 2015 (STOP GAP): ciclosporin and prednisolone healed at the same speed (adjusted difference 0.003 cm2/day, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.21; P=0.97), with 47% healed by 6 months on each
cards.summary: Ormerod 2015 (STOP GAP): ciclosporin and prednisolone healed at the same speed (adjusted difference 0.003 cm2/day, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.21; P=0.97), with 47% healed by 6 months on each
cards.people: 121 patients (73 women, mean age 54 years) with clinician-diagnosed pyoderma gangrenosum at 39 UK hospitals; diagnosis revised in 9 after randomisation, leaving 112 in the analysis set (59 ciclosporin 4 mg/kg/day, max 400 mg/day; 53 prednisolone 0.75 mg/kg/day, max 75 mg/day).
cards.result: Mean (SD) speed of healing at 6 weeks was -0.21 (1.00) cm2/day on ciclosporin versus -0.14 (0.42) on prednisolone; adjusted mean difference 0.003 cm2/day (95% CI -0.20 to 0.21; P=0.97). By 6 months ulcers had healed in 28/59 (47%) on ciclosporin and 25/53 (47%) on prednisolone; recurrence after healing was 8 (30%) versus 7 (28%). Adverse reactions were similar (68% versus 66%) but serious adverse reactions, especially infections, were more common in the prednisolone group.
cards.watchOut: Observer-blind only — patients and treating clinicians knew the drug, and 9 of 121 randomised patients had their diagnosis revised after randomisation; fewer than half healed by 6 months on either drug, so 'equal' also means 'equally slow'.
cards.source: Ormerod AD, Thomas KS, Craig FE, Mitchell E, Greenlaw N, Norrie J, Mason JM, Walton S, Johnston GA, Williams HC; UK Dermatology Clinical Trials Network's STOP GAP Team. Comparison of the two most commonly used treatments for pyoderma gangrenosum: results of the STOP GAP randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2015. PMID: 26071094. Registry ID: ISRCTN35898459. cards.headline: Brooklyn 2006: infliximab improved 46% (6/13) versus 6% (1/17) on placebo at week 2 (p=0.025) in 30 patients
cards.summary: Brooklyn 2006: infliximab improved 46% (6/13) versus 6% (1/17) on placebo at week 2 (p=0.025) in 30 patients
cards.people: 30 patients aged 18 or older with a clinical diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum, randomised to a single infusion of infliximab 5 mg/kg (n=13) or placebo (n=17) at week 0; non-responders at week 2 were offered open-label infliximab.
cards.result: At week 2, significantly more infliximab patients had improved: 46% (6/13) versus 6% (1/17) on placebo (p=0.025) — an absolute difference of about 40 percentage points. Overall, 29 patients received infliximab and 69% (20/29) showed a beneficial clinical response; the remission rate at week 6 was 21% (6/29) and 31% (9/29) had no response.
cards.watchOut: Only 30 patients and a 2-week primary endpoint after a single infusion; the 69% overall response figure mixes randomised and open-label treatment, so only the week-2 contrast (6/13 vs 1/17) is controlled evidence.
cards.source: Brooklyn TN, Dunnill MGS, Shetty A, Bowden JJ, Williams JDL, Griffiths CEM, Forbes A, Greenwood R, Probert CS. Infliximab for the treatment of pyoderma gangrenosum: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial. Gut. 2006. PMID: 16188920. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Thomas 2016: on topical therapy alone, 28 of 66 ulcers (43.8%) healed by 6 months, median time to healing 145 days — with no randomised comparator
cards.summary: Thomas 2016: on topical therapy alone, 28 of 66 ulcers (43.8%) healed by 6 months, median time to healing 145 days — with no randomised comparator
cards.people: 66 UK secondary-care patients (ages 22-85 years) with clinically diagnosed pyoderma gangrenosum judged suitable for topical treatment (STOP GAP topical cohort, recruited July 2009 to June 2012), treated per normal practice, mainly with topical corticosteroids (classes I-III) or tacrolimus 0.03% or 0.1%; clobetasol propionate 0.05% was the most commonly prescribed.
cards.result: Overall, 28 of 66 ulcers (43.8%) healed by 6 months. The median time to healing was 145 days (95% CI 96 days to infinity). Four patients (15% of those healed, as reported in the journal text) had a recurrence. The primary outcome was speed of healing at 6 weeks. Numbers are taken from the journal article record (Glasgow eprint and publisher PDF) fetched this session; the PubMed page itself failed to load and was not retried.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled and in patients selected as suitable for topical treatment (smaller, milder ulcers): the 43.8% healing cannot be credited to the creams over natural history, and these patients are not comparable with the systemic-trial population.

shelves.title: Skin cysts: removing the whole cyst wall is what stops them coming back — punch incision matched elliptical excision on recurrence with a wound a third as long (0.73 vs 2.34 cm), and draining alone recurred more than excision across 1,303 patients
shelves.question: In people with a skin (epidermoid/epidermal inclusion) cyst, which removal technique — complete elliptical excision, punch or minimal incision, incision and drainage, or one-stage excision when inflamed — gives the lowest recurrence with the best cosmetic result?
shelves.mesh: Epidermal Cyst / surgery*
shelves.balance: Complete removal of the cyst wall is what prevents recurrence, and the carded evidence is consistent on that: a 2026 systematic review (Guru Naidu, PMID: 41769601; 5 studies, 1,303 patients) found complete surgical excision consistently associated with lower recurrence than incision and drainage. How the wall is reached matters for the scar, not the recurrence: in the randomised trial (Lee 2006, PMID: 16681659; 60 patients) punch incision left a 0.73 cm wound in 12.7 minutes versus 2.34 cm and 21.6 minutes for elliptical excision, with no significant recurrence difference. For inflamed cysts, one-stage excision (Jun 2010; 351 patients, retrospective) halved antibiotic exposure (5.1 vs 10.9 days) and cost about a third of the conventional drain-first approach, but wound infection was higher (6.0% vs 1.6%). PROPOSED: SPLIT (complete excision beats drainage alone for recurrence; small-incision techniques match elliptical excision on recurrence with smaller scars; one-stage excision of inflamed cysts trades fewer antibiotics for more wound infections).

cards.headline: Lee & Lee 2006: punch incision removed epidermal inclusion cysts through a 0.73 cm wound in 12.7 minutes versus 2.34 cm and 21.6 minutes for elliptical excision — with no significant difference in recurrence and no complications in the punch group
cards.summary: Lee & Lee 2006: punch incision removed epidermal inclusion cysts through a 0.73 cm wound in 12.7 minutes versus 2.34 cm and 21.6 minutes for elliptical excision — with no significant difference in recurrence and no complications in the punch group
cards.people: 60 patients with non-infected epidermal inclusion cysts, randomly treated with punch incision or elliptical excision over a 16-month period.
cards.result: Mean wound length was 0.73 cm in the punch incision group versus 2.34 cm in the elliptical excision group (p < .001). Mean operative time was 12.7 minutes versus 21.6 minutes (p < .001). No complication occurred in the punch incision group, and there was no significant difference in recurrence rate. The authors concluded punch incision gives a superior cosmetic result at a low recurrence rate, best for cysts of 1 to 2 cm on the face or in areas of cosmetic concern.
cards.watchOut: Author list and exact recurrence counts were not captured from the record this session — the card reports only what the fetched abstract states, including its unquantified 'no significant difference' for recurrence. Sixty patients with uninfected cysts only; nothing here covers inflamed or ruptured cysts.

cards.headline: Jun 2010: excising inflamed sebaceous cysts in one stage halved antibiotic exposure (5.1 vs 10.9 days) and cost about a third of the conventional drain-first approach, in 351 patients
cards.summary: Jun 2010: excising inflamed sebaceous cysts in one stage halved antibiotic exposure (5.1 vs 10.9 days) and cost about a third of the conventional drain-first approach, in 351 patients
cards.people: 351 patients with inflamed sebaceous cysts at Tongji Hospital, Shanghai (2005–2009): 166 underwent one-stage (primary) excision with 5 days of antibiotics; 185 underwent conventional treatment — incision and drainage plus antibiotics, then elective excision 1–2 months later. Retrospective comparison.
cards.result: Mean antibiotic exposure was 5.1 days with one-stage excision versus 10.9 days with conventional treatment. In the conventional group, abscess formation or spontaneous rupture occurred in 131 of 185 patients (70.8%); the remaining 54 (29.2%) healed and had elective excision after 1–3 months. Mean healing time in the one-stage group was 10.1 days, and conventional treatment cost on average 3.18 times as much as one-stage treatment. Postoperative wound infection was 6.0% in the one-stage group versus 1.6% in the conventional group (figures as reported in the fetched full text).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre: surgeons chose who got immediate excision, so the one-stage group may have had milder inflammation. The infection trade-off runs the other way (6.0% vs 1.6%), and recurrence — the outcome that matters most for cyst surgery — is not reported in the fetched text.
cards.source: Jun GB, et al. One-stage excision of inflamed sebaceous cyst versus the conventional method. South African Journal of Surgery. 2010. cards.headline: Guru Naidu 2026: across 5 studies and 1,303 patients, complete surgical excision was consistently associated with lower recurrence than incision and drainage, while minimally invasive and CO2 laser techniques gave favourable cosmetic outcomes
cards.summary: Guru Naidu 2026: across 5 studies and 1,303 patients, complete surgical excision was consistently associated with lower recurrence than incision and drainage, while minimally invasive and CO2 laser techniques gave favourable cosmetic outcomes
cards.people: Systematic review of 5 studies involving a total of 1,303 patients with epidermoid (sebaceous) cysts, comparing excision, incision and drainage, minimally invasive and CO2 laser-assisted techniques (search to December 2025).
cards.result: Complete surgical excision was consistently associated with lower recurrence rates compared with incision and drainage. Minimally invasive and CO2 laser-assisted techniques demonstrated favourable cosmetic outcomes with acceptable complication rates. The review concluded complete excision including removal of the entire cyst wall remains the preferred management to minimise recurrence, while calling for further prospective studies.
cards.watchOut: The review's abstract reports directions, not pooled numbers — no pooled recurrence rates are printed on this card because none were captured from the record. Its own study table gives a different total (1,402 patients) from its abstract (1,303); the abstract figure is the one carded, and the discrepancy is flagged rather than resolved.
cards.source: Guru Naidu S, Can Guru Naidu NC, Borgas P, Balasubramaniam D. Surgical Excision Versus Incision and Drainage for Epidermoid (Sebaceous) Cysts: A Systematic Review. Cureus. 2026. PMID: 41769601. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: remove the whole cyst wall — how big the hole is matters for the scar, not for recurrence; draining alone leaves the cyst to come back
cards.summary: Synthesis: remove the whole cyst wall — how big the hole is matters for the scar, not for recurrence; draining alone leaves the cyst to come back
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: one randomised trial (n = 60), one retrospective comparison (n = 351) and one systematic review (5 studies, 1,303 patients).
cards.result: Every carded comparison agrees the cyst wall is the point: complete excision recurs less than incision and drainage (Guru Naidu 2026), and small-opening techniques (punch incision; minimal excision in the wider literature) match elliptical excision on recurrence while leaving wounds a third of the length (0.73 vs 2.34 cm) and taking about half the time (Lee 2006). For inflamed cysts, one-stage excision halved antibiotic days and cost versus drain-first-then-excise, at a higher wound-infection rate (Jun 2010). PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (complete wall excision beats drainage for recurrence · small-incision techniques equal on recurrence, better on scar and speed · one-stage excision of inflamed cysts: fewer antibiotics, more wound infections).
cards.watchOut: An epidermoid cyst that is simply left alone also has an evidence-free natural history in this literature — no carded study compares excision with watchful waiting, so these results answer 'how to remove' for people who have already decided on removal, not 'whether to remove'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lee 2006 (PMID: 16681659), Jun 2010 (PMID not captured this session) and Guru Naidu 2026 (PMID: 41769601), carded above.

shelves.title: Skin tags: scissors beat laser head-to-head (85% vs 71% fully healed at 12 weeks across 1,257 tags), electrosurgery beat freezing on satisfaction, and home freezing pens cleared anywhere from 7% to 64% of tags depending on the device
shelves.question: In people who want skin tags (acrochordons) removed, how do scissor snip excision, laser, cryotherapy, electrosurgery and home cryogenic devices compare on clearance, healing, pain and satisfaction?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Three randomised comparisons, three different winners by setting. In the largest, a split-body trial (Haase 2025, PMID: 40347285; 68 patients, 1,257 tags), scissor snip excision beat non-ablative 532 nm laser on complete healing at 12 weeks (85% vs 71%), pain (2.6 vs 3.42) and patient preference (63% vs 19%). In an assessor-blind trial (PMID: 39512253), electrosurgery gave significantly higher patient and physician satisfaction than cryotherapy for skin tags, with cryotherapy leaving hypopigmentation in 3.1% and depigmentation in 6.3% of lesions (pooled across lesion types). For home treatment, device choice dominated: the Pixie cryogenic pen cleared 64.3% of tags completely versus 7.1% for a comparator pen (Antunes 2021, PMID: 34019230). No trial compares removal with leaving tags alone, and none reports recurrence. PROPOSED: SPLIT (clinic: scissors/electrosurgery ahead of laser/cryotherapy in head-to-head trials; home freezing: 7–64% clearance depending on device).

cards.headline: Haase 2025: scissors beat laser for skin tags — complete healing at 12 weeks in 85% versus 71% of 1,257 tags, with less pain (2.6 vs 3.42) and 63% of patients preferring scissors for future treatment
cards.summary: Haase 2025: scissors beat laser for skin tags — complete healing at 12 weeks in 85% versus 71% of 1,257 tags, with less pain (2.6 vs 3.42) and 63% of patients preferring scissors for future treatment
cards.people: 68 patients with a total of 1,257 skin tags (fibroma pendulans) on the neck or axillae; each patient received both treatments in a randomised split-body design — scissor snip excision on one side, non-ablative 532 nm LBO laser on the other — with outcomes at 4 and 12 weeks, observer-blinded.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, complete healing was 85% with scissor excision versus 71% with laser (p = 0.00001); the adjusted overall response rate was 92.64% versus 84.19%. Pain scores were lower for scissors (mean 2.6) than laser (mean 3.42). Patient preference favoured scissors: 63% would choose scissors again, 19% laser, 18% indifferent. Laser was 39% faster when dressing time was counted, but caused more redness and hyper- and hypopigmentation, and laser-treated tags could persist as necrotic remnants for up to three weeks.
cards.watchOut: One laser type (non-ablative 532 nm) and one anatomical region (neck/axillae): ablative CO2 laser, the device most clinics actually use for tags, was not tested. Tags within a patient are not independent observations, so the very small p-value overstates the precision of the 85% vs 71% contrast.
cards.source: Haase O, Winkelmann-Schirmer C, Mrowka P, Krengel S. Removal of skin tags: scissor excision versus non-ablative 532nm-LBO-laser in a randomized intraindividual controlled observer-blinded clinical trial: Laser is not always better. Archives of Dermatological Research. 2025. PMID: 40347285. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: 2024 blinded randomised trial: for skin tags, electrosurgery gave significantly higher patient and physician satisfaction than cryotherapy; cryotherapy left hypopigmentation in 3.1% and depigmentation in 6.3% of treated lesions (all lesion types pooled)
cards.summary: 2024 blinded randomised trial: for skin tags, electrosurgery gave significantly higher patient and physician satisfaction than cryotherapy; cryotherapy left hypopigmentation in 3.1% and depigmentation in 6.3% of treated lesions (all lesion types pooled)
cards.type: Assessor-blind randomised trial, four lesion types (2024)
cards.people: 128 lesions across four types (sebaceous hyperplasia, seborrheic keratosis, cherry angioma and skin tags), 32 lesions per type, each split between cryotherapy and electrosurgery by sealed envelope in an assessor-blind trial; the skin-tag subgroup was 16 lesions per treatment.
cards.result: For sebaceous hyperplasia, cherry angioma and skin tags, patient and physician satisfaction was significantly higher for electrosurgery than cryotherapy during follow-up (p < 0.05); seborrheic keratosis responded better to cryotherapy. Across all lesion types, hypopigmentation occurred in 2 (3.1%) and depigmentation in 4 (6.3%) of cryotherapy cases; in the electrosurgery group, hypopigmentation occurred in 4 (6.3%) and atrophic scars in 2 (3.1%). The authors concluded electrosurgery appears more effective for skin tags, while cryotherapy is more effective for seborrheic keratosis.
cards.watchOut: The skin-tag evidence inside this trial is 32 lesions and a satisfaction score — no tag-specific clearance or recurrence rates were captured. Satisfaction is a soft outcome in an assessor-blind (not patient-blind) comparison of a one-visit electrical treatment against freezing, whose result declares itself over days.
cards.source: Evaluation and Comparison of the Efficacy and Safety of Cryotherapy and Electrosurgery in the Treatment of Sebaceous Hyperplasia, Seborrheic Keratosis, Cherry Angioma, and Skin Tag: A Blinded Randomized Clinical Trial Study. Health Science Reports. 2024. PMID: 39512253. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session (Author names and skin-tag-specific response rates were not captured from the record this session; satisfaction is the outcome the abstract reports for skin tags.)

cards.headline: Antunes 2021: a home cryogenic pen (Pixie) cleared 64.3% of skin tags completely versus 7.1% for a comparator home device (Wortie) — device choice dominates home freezing results
cards.summary: Antunes 2021: a home cryogenic pen (Pixie) cleared 64.3% of skin tags completely versus 7.1% for a comparator home device (Wortie) — device choice dominates home freezing results
cards.type: Prospective single-blind randomised comparative device trial (Antunes 2021)
cards.people: 56 healthy volunteers aged 18–65 with skin tags of 2–5 mm on the neck, breast or under the arms, randomised to the Pixie Skin Tag cryogenic pen (−80 °C) or the Wortie skin tag remover (dimethyl-ether based); up to three treatments at 15-day intervals, investigator-blinded, single centre. The tested products are named because home freezing devices are not interchangeable and the publication names them.
cards.result: 64.3% of Pixie-treated tags disappeared completely during the study — half of them after one treatment — versus 7.1% with the comparator device (p < 0.001), a 57.1 percentage-point absolute difference in complete disappearance. Both devices were reported safe and painless; very good tolerability was reported by 64.3% of the Pixie group and 96.4% of the comparator group.
cards.watchOut: An industry-style device-versus-device trial with no untreated or clinic-treatment control: it shows one home pen beats another, not that home freezing beats doing nothing — and even the winning device left over a third of tags behind. Participants were unblinded (the devices look different), and skin types were I–III only.
cards.source: Antunes A, Rossel B, Adriaens E, et al. Efficacy Evaluation of the Pixie® Skin Tag Cryogenic Device on Skin Tags in a Prospective, Single-Blinded, Randomized, Comparative Clinical Trial. Dermatology and Therapy. 2021. PMID: 34019230. Registry ID: ANSL 2018-A01804-51 (registration as printed in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: in the clinic, cutting tags off beats freezing or lasering them in head-to-head trials; at home, which freezing pen you buy matters more than freezing itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the clinic, cutting tags off beats freezing or lasering them in head-to-head trials; at home, which freezing pen you buy matters more than freezing itself
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded randomised trials: split-body scissor-versus-laser (68 patients, 1,257 tags), assessor-blind cryotherapy-versus-electrosurgery (32 skin-tag lesions within a 128-lesion trial) and home cryo-pen versus comparator pen (56 volunteers).
cards.result: Clinic removal: scissor snip excision healed more tags than non-ablative laser (85% vs 71% at 12 weeks) with less pain, and electrosurgery satisfied patients and physicians more than cryotherapy. Home removal: complete clearance ranged from 64.3% down to 7.1% depending purely on which cryogenic pen was used. No trial compares any removal method with leaving tags alone, and none reports long-term recurrence. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (scissors and electrosurgery ahead in clinic comparisons · home cryo devices: 7–64% clearance by device).
cards.watchOut: Skin tags are benign and removal is cosmetic or for snagging/irritation; none of these trials enrolled tags that were atypical, pigmented or diagnostically uncertain — a tag that looks wrong needs excision and histology, not a freezing pen, and that clinical rule has no trial behind it either way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haase 2025 (PMID: 40347285), the 2024 cryotherapy-versus-electrosurgery trial (PMID: 39512253) and Antunes 2021 (PMID: 34019230), carded above.

shelves.title: Stretch marks: tretinoin cream improved early red marks (80% vs 8% much improved on placebo cream), while for white marks CO2 laser and microneedling helped equally — and neither has ever been tested against simply leaving them alone
shelves.question: In people with stretch marks (striae distensae), do topical tretinoin, fractional CO2 laser, microneedling or platelet-rich plasma improve the marks compared with vehicle, each other, or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: The evidence splits by the age of the marks. For early, red, active stretch marks, the one double-blind vehicle-controlled trial (Kang 1996, PMID: 8624148; 22 patients) found 0.1% tretinoin clearly better than vehicle: 80% versus 8% with definite or marked improvement at 6 months, and treated marks shrank 14% in length while vehicle marks grew 10%. For mature white marks (striae alba), a randomised split-body trial (Saki 2022, PMID: 34796595; 40 patients) found fractional CO2 laser and microneedling both shrank striae significantly with no difference between them — but with no untreated control, improvement over natural fading is unproven. Adding platelet-rich plasma to CO2 laser (Madegowda 2023, PMID: 38189063; 24 patients) raised 'excellent' responses from 16.6% to 33.3%, with hyperpigmentation in 19 of 24 patients resolving by 6 months. PROPOSED: SPLIT (tretinoin POSSIBLE for early red marks only; devices improve white marks versus baseline, unproven versus doing nothing).

cards.headline: Kang 1996: 0.1% tretinoin cream improved early stretch marks — 8 of 10 treated patients (80%) had definite or marked improvement at 6 months versus 1 of 12 (8%) on vehicle; marks shrank 14% in length while vehicle marks grew 10%
cards.summary: Kang 1996: 0.1% tretinoin cream improved early stretch marks — 8 of 10 treated patients (80%) had definite or marked improvement at 6 months versus 1 of 12 (8%) on vehicle; marks shrank 14% in length while vehicle marks grew 10%
cards.people: 22 patients with early, clinically active stretch marks, randomised double-blind to daily 0.1% tretinoin cream (n = 10) or vehicle (n = 12) for 6 months.
cards.result: After 2 months the tretinoin group had significantly better severity scores than vehicle (P < .05). After 6 months, 8 of 10 tretinoin patients (80%) had definite or marked improvement versus 1 of 12 vehicle patients (8%) (P = .002). Target marks on tretinoin decreased in mean length by 14% and width by 8%, while vehicle marks increased by 10% in length (P < .001) and 24% in width (P = .008). Biopsies showed no significant histological differences between groups.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two patients, and the trial deliberately enrolled only early, active (red) marks — it says nothing about the mature white marks most people actually present with. The clinical improvement without any histological change is unexplained, and tretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy, the setting of the commonest stretch marks of all.
cards.source: Kang S, Kim KJ, Griffiths CEM, et al. Topical tretinoin (retinoic acid) improves early stretch marks. Archives of Dermatology. 1996. PMID: 8624148. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Saki 2022: for white stretch marks (striae alba), fractional CO2 laser and microneedling both shrank the largest striae significantly (P < 0.001) with no significant difference between them over 10 months
cards.summary: Saki 2022: for white stretch marks (striae alba), fractional CO2 laser and microneedling both shrank the largest striae significantly (P < 0.001) with no significant difference between them over 10 months
cards.people: 40 patients (mean age 28.1 years) with striae alba; each patient's sides were randomly assigned to fractional CO2 laser or microneedling, four treatments at monthly intervals, followed for 10 months.
cards.result: The median cross-section of the largest striae decreased significantly in both groups (P < 0.001), with no statistically significant difference between the two groups before treatment or 6 months after. Visual analogue scores also improved significantly in both groups, with no significant between-treatment difference at any visit. No clinically significant adverse effects were observed. The authors concluded both treatments are efficient for striae distensae.
cards.watchOut: No untreated side and no sham: stretch marks fade and flatten with time on their own, so 'both improved significantly' cannot separate treatment effect from natural history — the trial can only support the narrower claim that the two methods did not differ from each other. Effect sizes (how much the striae shrank) were not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Madegowda 2023: adding platelet-rich plasma to fractional CO2 laser raised excellent responses from 16.6% to 33.3% of patients, with hyperpigmentation the commonest side effect (19 of 24 patients, resolving by 6 months)
cards.summary: Madegowda 2023: adding platelet-rich plasma to fractional CO2 laser raised excellent responses from 16.6% to 33.3% of patients, with hyperpigmentation the commonest side effect (19 of 24 patients, resolving by 6 months)
cards.people: 24 patients with bilateral striae of the abdomen, upper or lower limbs; both sides received fractional CO2 laser monthly for three sessions, with platelet-rich plasma (PRP) added on the left side only.
cards.result: All patients improved on both sides. On laser alone, responses were moderate in 6 patients (25%), good in 14 (56%) and excellent in 4 (16.6%). On laser plus PRP, responses were moderate in 5 (20.8%), good in 11 (45.8%) and excellent in 8 (33.3%). Hyperpigmentation was the most common side effect, seen in 19 patients on both sides, and resolved spontaneously by 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 24), unblinded grading categories ('moderate/good/excellent') assigned by the treating team, and PRP was always added to the same (left) side rather than randomised — side and treatment are confounded. The doubling of 'excellent' responses is a shift within a subjective scale, not a measured change in the marks.

cards.headline: Synthesis: early red marks respond to tretinoin in one small blinded trial; for white marks, laser and microneedling look alike and neither has beaten doing nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: early red marks respond to tretinoin in one small blinded trial; for white marks, laser and microneedling look alike and neither has beaten doing nothing
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: one double-blind vehicle-controlled trial (n = 22, early marks), one randomised split-body trial (n = 40, white marks) and one split-body comparative study (n = 24).
cards.result: The evidence splits cleanly by stage. For early, active marks, 0.1% tretinoin beat its vehicle clearly (80% vs 8% much improved) in the only placebo-controlled trial — a 1996 study of 22 people. For mature white marks, fractional CO2 laser and microneedling improved marks to a statistically indistinguishable degree, and adding PRP to laser shifted more patients into the 'excellent' category (33.3% vs 16.6%); neither device trial included an untreated control, so improvement over time alone is unmeasured. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (tretinoin: POSSIBLE benefit for early red marks only · devices for white marks: improvement shown, advantage over natural history unproven).
cards.watchOut: No carded study measures what patients usually ask — whether marks become invisible. Outcomes are severity scores, widths and grader categories; even in the positive tretinoin trial the marks shrank by only 14% in length. Pregnancy-related marks, the commonest kind, cannot be treated with tretinoin during pregnancy itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kang 1996 (PMID: 8624148), Saki 2022 (PMID: 34796595) and Madegowda 2023 (PMID: 38189063), carded above.

shelves.title: Hearing interventions in older adults — the economic evidence only: a 2026 systematic review of 27 studies generally found hearing aids and cochlear implants cost-effective, and two hearing-aid economic studies put the cost at about S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years (Singapore) with cost-effectiveness in China depending on the aid lasting over about 2.5 years
shelves.question: What do economic evaluations support for hearing interventions in older adults?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for economic value only — this is an economics shelf, not a clinical-effectiveness shelf. The 2026 systematic review (PMID: 42862436; 27 studies in 28 articles) found cost-effectiveness analyses generally judged cochlear implants and hearing aids cost-effective compared with no intervention, and cost-benefit analyses showed positive net monetary benefits, while flagging omitted downstream costs, limited carer and societal impacts and inconsistent outcome measurement. Two individual hearing-aid evaluations agree in direction: a Singapore delayed-start cost-utility study (PMID: 33261603; 427 older adults) estimated S$42,790 per QALY at 3 months, improving to S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years if use continued; and a Chinese randomised-trial-based analysis (PMID: 37306959; 385 adults) found hearing aids cost-effective with high probability provided the devices lasted, with a quality-adjusted life year gain of 0.017. The clinical question of hearing treatment and cognition is homed at live shelf #350 (the ACHIEVE trial) and is NOT re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), economics only.

cards.headline: Raichand 2026: across 27 economic evaluations, hearing aids and cochlear implants were generally cost-effective versus no intervention — with downstream costs, carer impacts and long-term care largely missing from the models
cards.summary: Raichand 2026: across 27 economic evaluations, hearing aids and cochlear implants were generally cost-effective versus no intervention — with downstream costs, carer impacts and long-term care largely missing from the models
cards.people: 27 studies in 28 articles meeting inclusion criteria (full economic evaluations of hearing interventions in adults aged 60 years and over, searched to August 2026 as printed in the record): 22 studies reported cost-effectiveness analyses, including 19 cost-utility analyses, and 6 reported cost-benefit analyses, with 1 study reporting both; costs were standardised to 2024 US dollars.
cards.result: Cost-effectiveness analyses generally found cochlear implants and hearing aids to be cost-effective compared with no intervention, and cochlear implants were often cost-effective compared with hearing aids in eligible populations. Post-hearing-aid counselling or rehabilitation, transcutaneous bone conduction devices and cochlear implant processor upgrades were generally cost-effective, and cost-benefit analyses indicated positive net monetary benefits. Health-related quality of life was most commonly measured with the Health Utilities Index Mark 3; key drivers were utility gains, intervention costs, age at intervention and device compliance. Limitations included omission of downstream costs, limited carer and societal impacts, inconsistent preference-based outcome measurement, insufficient model validation, limited equity analysis and no evaluations in institutional or long-term care settings.
cards.watchOut: A review of models and evaluations, not of patients: 'generally cost-effective' inherits every included model's assumptions, and the review itself lists what the models leave out — downstream savings, carers, and long-term care — any of which could move the answer either way.
cards.source: Raichand S et al. Economic Evaluations of Hearing Interventions in Older Adults: A Systematic Review of Evidence and Methods. Advances in Therapy. 2026. PMID: 42862436. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kaur 2020: fitting hearing aids in a Singapore delayed-start study cost S$42,790 per QALY at 3 months, improving to an estimated S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years if people kept using them
cards.summary: Kaur 2020: fitting hearing aids in a Singapore delayed-start study cost S$42,790 per QALY at 3 months, improving to an estimated S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years if people kept using them
cards.type: Cost-utility analysis within a randomised delayed-start study (Kaur 2020)
cards.people: 427 older adults screened in a community mobile hearing clinic (264 fitted with hearing aids immediately, 163 in a delayed-start not-fitted group), all with at least moderate hearing loss in at least one ear, no prior hearing-aid use and a Mini-Mental State Examination score of at least 18; costs and utility were measured at 3 months and projected to 5 years.
cards.result: At 3 months, hearing-aid fitting led to a mean utility increase of 0.12 and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of S$42,790 per QALY (95% CI S$32,793 to S$62,221 per QALY). At 5 years the ratio was estimated at S$11,964 per QALY (95% CI S$8,996 to S$17,080 per QALY), assuming 70% of participants continued using the hearing aid; as fewer individuals continued use, the ratio increased (that is, value worsened). The authors conclude long-term cost-effectiveness depends on continued usage.
cards.watchOut: The attractive 5-year figure is a projection built on a 3-month utility measurement and an assumed 70% continuation rate — real-world hearing-aid abandonment is exactly the variable the result is sensitive to.
cards.source: Kaur P et al. Cost-utility analysis of hearing aid device for older adults in the community: a delayed start study. BMC Health Services Research. 2020. PMID: 33261603. cards.headline: Ye 2023: in a Chinese randomised trial of 385 adults, hearing aids gained 0.017 QALYs and were cost-effective with high probability if the devices lasted — very cost-effective only if lifespan exceeded 6.87 years
cards.summary: Ye 2023: in a Chinese randomised trial of 385 adults, hearing aids gained 0.017 QALYs and were cost-effective with high probability if the devices lasted — very cost-effective only if lifespan exceeded 6.87 years
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis based on a randomised controlled trial (Ye 2023)
cards.people: 385 subjects aged 45 years and older with moderate or above hearing loss in rural China, randomly assigned to hearing aids (n = 150) or no intervention (n = 235); the analysis assumed an average hearing-aid lifespan of N years, with annual purchase cost of 10,000/N yuan and annual maintenance cost of 41.48 yuan.
cards.result: Wearing a hearing aid increased quality-adjusted life years by 0.017 and saved 243.34 yuan per year in healthcare costs. On the authors' calculations, if N is greater than 6.87 years the intervention is very cost-effective; if N is between 2.52 and 6.87 years the cost-effectiveness is acceptable; if N is under 2.52 years it is not cost-effective. Because the average lifespan of hearing aids is between 3 and 7 years, the authors conclude hearing-aid interventions can be considered cost-effective with high probability.
cards.watchOut: The entire conclusion turns on device lifespan, an assumption rather than a measured outcome, and the population starts at age 45 in rural China — costs, thresholds and lifespans do not transfer directly to other health systems.
cards.source: Ye X et al. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Hearing Aids for Middle-Aged and Older Adults in China: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Otology & Neurotology. 2023. PMID: 37306959. cards.headline: Synthesis: the economic literature generally finds hearing aids and cochlear implants in older adults to be good value versus no intervention — an economics conclusion, resting on models whose own reviewers list important omissions
cards.summary: Synthesis: the economic literature generally finds hearing aids and cochlear implants in older adults to be good value versus no intervention — an economics conclusion, resting on models whose own reviewers list important omissions
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of 27 economic evaluations, one cost-utility analysis inside a randomised delayed-start study (427 participants), and one cost-effectiveness analysis based on a randomised trial (385 participants). No clinical-effect trial is carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The review found hearing aids and cochlear implants generally cost-effective versus no intervention, with positive net monetary benefits in cost-benefit analyses (Raichand 2026). The individual studies agree for hearing aids: S$11,964 per QALY projected over 5 years in Singapore, conditional on continued use (Kaur 2020), and cost-effectiveness in China conditional on device lifespan above about 2.5 years (Ye 2023). Whether hearing treatment changes cognition is a different question, homed at live shelf #350 (ACHIEVE) and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — economic value only.
cards.watchOut: Cost-effectiveness thresholds differ by country and payer, and none of the carded evaluations were conducted in institutional or long-term care — the setting where hearing loss is most prevalent in old age.
cards.source: Synthesis of Raichand S et al. Advances in Therapy. 2026 (PMID: 42862436); Kaur P et al. BMC Health Services Research. 2020 (PMID: 33261603); Ye X et al. Otology & Neurotology. 2023 (PMID: 37306959).

shelves.title: Foam dressings for pressure ulcers: no proven advantage over simple dressings — healing comparisons against basic contact dressings and hydrocolloids are all non-significant on very low-certainty evidence
shelves.question: In adults with pressure ulcers, are advanced foam dressings better than simple dressings for healing?
shelves.mesh: Bandages, Hydrocolloid · Humans · Hydrogels · Middle Aged · Pressure Ulcer · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Silicones · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that superiority is unproven, stated plainly. The direct randomised comparisons of foam against simple dressings do not show better healing: versus basic wound contact dressings the pooled healing risk ratios were 1.33 (95% CI 0.62 to 2.88) short term and 1.17 (0.79 to 1.72) medium term, and versus hydrocolloid dressings 0.85 (0.54 to 1.34) — every interval crosses no-effect and the Cochrane reviewers graded the certainty very low (Walker 2017). Network meta-analyses lean favourable — foam versus saline gauze RR 1.52 (1.03 to 2.26) in Westby 2017 and foam versus hydroactive dressings RR 1.18 (0.95 to 1.48) in Furuya-Kanamori 2019 — but both sets of authors warn that the networks are sparse, the trials small and biased, and rankings unreliable. Where a comparison is null it is stated as such: on the direct evidence, foam made no proven difference to healing. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — foam dressings have not been shown to heal pressure ulcers better than simple dressings.

cards.headline: Walker 2017 (Cochrane): across nine trials (483 participants), it was uncertain whether foam dressings beat basic wound contact dressings — healing RR 1.33 (short term) and 1.17 (medium term), both non-significant, very low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Walker 2017 (Cochrane): across nine trials (483 participants), it was uncertain whether foam dressings beat basic wound contact dressings — healing RR 1.33 (short term) and 1.17 (medium term), both non-significant, very low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Walker 2017)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials with 483 participants, all adults aged 59 years or older with an existing pressure ulcer Category/Stage II or above, in any care setting; three trials (181 participants) compared foam with basic wound contact dressings, with follow-up from 8 weeks or less to 8–24 weeks.
cards.result: It was uncertain whether foam dressings affected the probability of healing compared with basic wound contact dressings in the short term (relative risk (RR) 1.33, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.88) or medium term (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.72) — neither is statistically significant, so on these data foam made no proven difference. One medium-term time-to-healing estimate favoured foam (mean difference −35.80 days, 95% CI −56.77 to −14.83) but the reviewers graded the certainty very low. Adverse events in the medium term: RR 0.58 (0.33 to 1.05). The reviewers conclude it is uncertain whether foam dressings are more clinically effective, acceptable, or cost effective than alternative dressings.
cards.watchOut: Nine small trials (median samples around 20 per comparison) with high risk of bias: the confidence intervals are wide enough to include both worthwhile benefit and harm, so 'no proven difference' is the finding — not proof of equivalence.

cards.headline: Walker 2017 (Cochrane), foam versus other advanced dressings: foam did not beat hydrocolloid dressings either (healing RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.54–1.34) in four trials with 230 participants
cards.summary: Walker 2017 (Cochrane), foam versus other advanced dressings: foam did not beat hydrocolloid dressings either (healing RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.54–1.34) in four trials with 230 participants
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, second comparison (Walker 2017)
cards.people: The same Cochrane review's foam-versus-hydrocolloid comparison: four trials with a median sample size of 20 participants (230 participants in total) comparing foam dressings with hydrocolloid dressings over eight weeks or less; three trials reported healing.
cards.result: It was uncertain whether foam dressings affected the probability of healing compared with hydrocolloid dressings over short follow-up (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.34 — not significant; the point estimate favours hydrocolloid). Risk of adverse events did not clearly differ (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.11). Evidence certainty was very low, downgraded for very serious study limitations and serious imprecision. A separate one-trial comparison of foam versus hydrogel (34 participants) likewise found no clear difference in healing (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.28).
cards.watchOut: This card and the first card report two comparisons from the same review (PMID 29025198) — they are two contrasts of one evidence base, not two independent confirmations, and the shelf's synthesis counts the review once.

cards.headline: Westby 2017 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): foam dressings versus saline gauze gave a healing RR of 1.52 (95% CI 1.03–2.26), but the network was sparse and the reviewers had no confidence in any ranking of dressings
cards.summary: Westby 2017 (Cochrane network meta-analysis): foam dressings versus saline gauze gave a healing RR of 1.52 (95% CI 1.03–2.26), but the network was sparse and the reviewers had no confidence in any ranking of dressings
cards.type: Cochrane network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Westby 2017)
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 51 randomised studies (2,947 participants) of dressings and topical agents for pressure ulcers Stage 2 or above; the healing network itself linked 39 studies in 2,127 participants, of whom 783 had completely healed wounds, across 21 interventions.
cards.result: Compared with saline gauze, foam dressings gave a risk ratio for complete healing of 1.52 (95% CI 1.03 to 2.26) — labelled low-certainty evidence by the reviewers, with high risk of bias and imprecision. The reviewers state plainly that the network is sparse, the vast majority of the evidence is low or very low certainty, and they have no confidence in the findings regarding the rank order of interventions; it is generally unclear whether the treatments examined are more effective than saline gauze.
cards.watchOut: A nominally significant network estimate built mostly from small, high-bias trials is exactly the kind of result the reviewers warn against acting on: the direct head-to-head evidence (previous cards) does not confirm it.

cards.headline: Furuya-Kanamori 2019 (network meta-analysis): foam ranked above hydroactive dressings (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95–1.48 — not significant), and every dressing group ranked above basic dressings, with substantial uncertainty throughout
cards.summary: Furuya-Kanamori 2019 (network meta-analysis): foam ranked above hydroactive dressings (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95–1.48 — not significant), and every dressing group ranked above basic dressings, with substantial uncertainty throughout
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 40 randomised trials (1,757 participants) comparing five dressing groups — basic, foam, active, hydroactive, and other — for pressure injury healing, using hydroactive dressings (the stated current standard) as the reference.
cards.result: All dressing groups ranked better than basic dressings (saline gauze or similar inert dressings). Against hydroactive dressings, foam gave a relative risk of complete healing of 1.18 (95% CI 0.95–1.48) and active dressings 1.16 (0.92–1.47) — neither statistically significant. The authors state there was substantial uncertainty around the point estimates, that the analysis supports replacing basic dressings with hydroactive dressings, and that foam and active dressings seem promising but need further high-quality investigation.
cards.watchOut: Rankings in a network meta-analysis can look decisive while every underlying interval crosses no-effect — as here, where the foam estimate (1.18, CI 0.95–1.48) is compatible with foam being slightly worse than the standard dressing.

cards.headline: Synthesis: advanced foam dressings are not proven better than simple dressings for healing pressure ulcers — direct comparisons are non-significant on very low-certainty evidence, and the favourable network estimates come with the reviewers' own warnings
cards.summary: Synthesis: advanced foam dressings are not proven better than simple dressings for healing pressure ulcers — direct comparisons are non-significant on very low-certainty evidence, and the favourable network estimates come with the reviewers' own warnings
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of nine foam trials (483 participants; counted once although two of its comparisons are carded), one Cochrane network meta-analysis (51 studies, 2,947 participants) and one further network meta-analysis (40 trials, 1,757 participants), with overlapping primary trials across the reviews. Total unique participants exceed 30 many times over, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the weakness is certainty, not size, and it is printed here.
cards.result: Direct evidence: foam versus basic wound contact dressings, healing RR 1.33 (0.62–2.88) short term and 1.17 (0.79–1.72) medium term; foam versus hydrocolloid, RR 0.85 (0.54–1.34) — all non-significant, all very low certainty (Walker 2017). Indirect evidence: foam versus saline gauze RR 1.52 (1.03–2.26), low certainty, within a network the reviewers say cannot support rankings (Westby 2017); foam versus hydroactive RR 1.18 (0.95–1.48), non-significant (Furuya-Kanamori 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): foam may help and is a reasonable dressing choice for exudate and comfort, but better healing than simple dressings is unproven.
cards.watchOut: The three reviews share primary trials, so their apparent agreement is partly the same small trials counted three ways; no large, low-bias head-to-head trial of foam versus a simple dressing is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.source: Synthesis of Walker RM et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 29025198); Westby MJ et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28639707); Furuya-Kanamori L et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2019 (PMID: 30471948).

shelves.title: Cryotherapy vs salicylic acid for plantar warts (PARTIAL): no — clearance was 13.6% vs 14.3% in the dedicated trial and cryotherapy costs more; the general-wart advantage on the home shelf does not extend to plantar warts
shelves.question: In adults with plantar warts, is cryotherapy more effective than salicylic acid?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cryotherapy/economics · Cryotherapy/standards · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Salicylic Acid/economics · Salicylic Acid/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Warts/drug therapy · Warts/surgery · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective (the treatment made no difference). PARTIAL completion of live shelf #622. That shelf covers cutaneous warts generally — its trial's plantar subgroup (n = 124) found no significant difference between cryotherapy, salicylic acid and waiting, and its Cochrane review reports a feet subgroup — and those records are NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: plantar warts specifically, from the plantar-only trials. In EVerT, the dedicated multicentre trial (240 patients aged 12 and over), complete clearance at 12 weeks was 13.6% on cryotherapy vs 14.3% on daily 50% salicylic acid (P = 0.89), with no difference in time to clearance or 6-month clearance (Cockayne 2011). In VRAIE, in plantar warts that had already failed a salicylic-acid course, second-line complete remission at day 90 was 11% on liquid nitrogen vs 20% on salicylic acid, in an under-enrolled trial (Chanal 2025). A 26-patient study found a salicylic-acid-containing combination cream (cantharidin–podophylotoxin–salicylic acid — not salicylic acid alone, labelled on its card) cleared more patients than cryotherapy (Kaçar 2012). Absolute clearance is low on both treatments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid for plantar warts (the treatment made no difference in the two direct randomised trials).

cards.headline: EVerT 2011: in 240 patients with plantar warts, cryotherapy did not beat daily 50% salicylic acid — complete clearance at 12 weeks was 13.6% on cryotherapy vs 14.3% on salicylic acid (P = 0.89) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: EVerT 2011: in 240 patients with plantar warts, cryotherapy did not beat daily 50% salicylic acid — complete clearance at 12 weeks was 13.6% on cryotherapy vs 14.3% on salicylic acid (P = 0.89) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Multicentre pragmatic randomised controlled trial, EVerT (Cockayne 2011)
cards.people: 240 eligible patients aged 12 years and over presenting with a verruca (plantar wart) suitable for both treatments, recruited in podiatry clinics, university podiatry schools and primary care in England, Scotland and Ireland, randomised to cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen delivered by a health-care professional (117 allocated) or daily patient self-treatment with 50% salicylic acid for a maximum of 8 weeks (123 allocated); the primary outcome was complete clearance of all verrucae at 12 weeks. The trial enrolled adolescents as well as adults — the record does not print a mean age or an adults-only subgroup, printed on the face.
cards.result: There was no evidence of a difference in clearance rates for the primary outcome: 15/110 (13.6%) in the cryotherapy group vs 17/119 (14.3%) in the salicylic acid group (P = 0.89 — absolute proportions as printed; the treatment made no difference). Results did not change when controlled for age, previous treatment or wart type, or when patient preferences were explored. There was no evidence of a difference in time to clearance (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.51 to 1.25; P = 0.33) or in clearance at 6 months (33.7% cryotherapy vs 30.5% salicylic acid), or in the number of verrucae at 12 weeks (incidence rate ratio 1.08; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.43; P = 0.62). Nineteen participants reported 28 adverse events, 14 in each group. Cryotherapy was associated with higher mean costs per additional healed patient (£101.17, as printed, with the confidence interval truncated in the record).
cards.watchOut: The definitive plantar-wart trial is a null with low absolute clearance in both arms (about 1 in 7 at 12 weeks) — the clinical message is not that salicylic acid is good, but that cryotherapy's extra cost, pain and clinic visits buy no extra clearance for plantar warts.
cards.source: Cockayne S et al. EVerT: cryotherapy versus salicylic acid for the treatment of verrucae--a randomised controlled trial. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2011. cards.headline: VRAIE 2025: in previously treated plantar warts, second-line cryotherapy again did not beat salicylic acid — complete remission at day 90 in 11% on liquid nitrogen vs 20% on 50% salicylic acid, in a trial that enrolled only 174 of its planned 660 patients
cards.summary: VRAIE 2025: in previously treated plantar warts, second-line cryotherapy again did not beat salicylic acid — complete remission at day 90 in 11% on liquid nitrogen vs 20% on 50% salicylic acid, in a trial that enrolled only 174 of its planned 660 patients
cards.type: Multicentre pragmatic randomised controlled trial, VRAIE (Chanal 2025)
cards.people: Patients with plantar warts who had failed an initial 5-week regimen of salicylic acid (of 358 patients enrolled in the pre-inclusion period, 140 achieved complete remission on that first-line course and 174 non-responders were randomised) to one of four second-line treatments: 50% salicylic acid ointment under occlusion (41 assigned), liquid nitrogen cryotherapy (36), 5% fluorouracil cream (33) or 5% imiquimod cream (42), with a duct-tape arm (22) withdrawn during the study; the primary outcome was complete remission at day 90. Myrmecia warts were 83.9% of cases.
cards.result: On day 90, complete remission was achieved by 6 (20%) patients in the salicylic acid group, 3 (11%) in the cryotherapy group, 1 (3.5%) in the fluorouracil group and 2 (6.6%) in the imiquimod group — the percentages are as printed in the record and are based on the patients assessed at day 90, which are fewer than the numbers assigned. The trial enrolled 54% of its target and the authors conclude that no treatment had a substantial positive effect as second-line treatment of plantar warts. The record prints no P values for the cryotherapy-versus-salicylic-acid contrast.
cards.watchOut: A second-line population (everyone had already failed salicylic acid, which biases the re-test of salicylic acid downward and cryotherapy's showing is still worse numerically), and a badly under-enrolled trial: its value is directional corroboration of EVerT, not independent precision.
cards.source: Chanal J et al. cards.headline: Kaçar 2012: in 26 patients with plantar warts, a salicylic-acid-containing combination cream (cantharidin–podophylotoxin–salicylic acid) cleared more patients than cryotherapy (14 of the CPS group vs 5 of 12 (41.7%) on cryotherapy; P = 0.001) — a combination product, not salicylic acid alone, in a very small trial (N = 26 on the face)
cards.summary: Kaçar 2012: in 26 patients with plantar warts, a salicylic-acid-containing combination cream (cantharidin–podophylotoxin–salicylic acid) cleared more patients than cryotherapy (14 of the CPS group vs 5 of 12 (41.7%) on cryotherapy; P = 0.001) — a combination product, not salicylic acid alone, in a very small trial (N = 26 on the face)
cards.people: 26 patients with a total of 134 plantar warts, treated consecutively with either cryotherapy or topical CPS — a proprietary formulation of 1% cantharidin, 5% podophylotoxin and 30% salicylic acid — every 2 weeks for up to five sessions; patients without complete clearance could switch to the other treatment. N = 26 printed on the face.
cards.result: Fourteen patients were completely cleared of their warts with topical CPS, whereas only 5 of 12 patients (41.7%) were completely cleared with cryotherapy (P = 0.001 — the record prints no total denominator for the CPS group in the abstract beyond the 26 included patients). In seven patients without complete clearance, therapy was switched to CPS; of the three who completed follow-up after switching, two were cleared and one was not. The authors conclude topical CPS is more effective than cryotherapy in the treatment of plantar warts.
cards.watchOut: This card does not test salicylic acid alone — CPS is a three-drug proprietary combination in which salicylic acid is the minority ingredient — and with 26 patients it is the weakest card on the shelf; it is included, labelled, because it is a plantar-specific randomised comparison of cryotherapy against a salicylic-acid-containing topical, and it points the same way as the two larger trials: cryotherapy is not the better treatment.
cards.source: Kaçar N et al. Cantharidin-podophylotoxin-salicylic acid versus cryotherapy in the treatment of plantar warts: a randomized prospective study. cards.headline: Synthesis: for plantar warts, cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid — the two direct randomised trials found no difference (13.6% vs 14.3% cleared; second-line 11% vs 20%), and absolute clearance is low on both
cards.summary: Synthesis: for plantar warts, cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid — the two direct randomised trials found no difference (13.6% vs 14.3% cleared; second-line 11% vs 20%), and absolute clearance is low on both
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre pragmatic trial of first-line treatment (240 patients aged 12 and over), one multicentre pragmatic trial of second-line treatment after salicylic-acid failure (174 randomised), and one very small randomised study of a salicylic-acid-containing combination cream (26 patients). Total randomised participants are 440 across the three reports, so no small-N stamp labelling applies to the shelf; the smallest study's N is printed on its card face.
cards.result: EVerT found complete clearance at 12 weeks in 13.6% on cryotherapy vs 14.3% on daily 50% salicylic acid (P = 0.89), with no difference in time to clearance or in 6-month clearance (33.7% vs 30.5%; Cockayne 2011). VRAIE, in warts that had already failed salicylic acid, found day-90 remission in 11% on cryotherapy vs 20% on salicylic acid, with no treatment showing a substantial effect (Chanal 2025). A salicylic-acid-containing combination cream beat cryotherapy in a 26-patient study (Kaçar 2012). The plantar subgroup of the general cutaneous-wart trial on home shelf #622 pointed the same way and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid for plantar warts (the treatment made no difference in the direct trials).
cards.watchOut: Low clearance in every arm (roughly 1 in 7 first-line at 12 weeks) means 'no difference' should not be read as 'both work well' — for plantar warts the choice between these two is about cost, pain and convenience, not efficacy, and watchful waiting remains a defensible option as the home shelf notes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cockayne S et al. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2011 (PMID: 21899812); Chanal J et al. Annales de dermatologie et de venereologie. 2025 (PMID: 40743833); Kaçar N et al. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV. 2012 (PMID: 21790794).

shelves.title: Moderate acne: benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid ranks above a topical antibiotic alone in network meta-analyses — an indirect, low-confidence advantage, clearest for noninflammatory lesions
shelves.question: For moderate acne, is topical benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid better than a topical antibiotic alone?
shelves.mesh: Acne Vulgaris · Adapalene · Benzoyl Peroxide · Dermatologic Agents · Drug Combinations · Gels · Humans · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #619, which covers the fixed adapalene–benzoyl peroxide gel against its own components (and oral spironolactone in adult women); this shelf covers the comparison #619 does not make — the benzoyl peroxide–retinoid combination against a topical antibiotic used alone — and does not re-card #619's trials. No large head-to-head trial of the combination against antibiotic monotherapy was found in the records fetched; the answer rests on network meta-analyses that rank all topical options on a common scale. In the mild-to-moderate acne network (Stuart 2021; 40 trials, 18,089 participants), benzoyl peroxide with adapalene was ranked the most effective topical treatment for self-reported improvement, ahead of benzoyl peroxide alone and of monotherapies, with slightly more withdrawals (2.5%) than adapalene alone (1.0%). In the all-severity pharmacological network (Huang 2023; 221 trials, 65,601 patients), combination regimens containing a retinoid and benzoyl peroxide ranked just below oral isotretinoin and the triple combination, while topical antibiotic monotherapy was comparable to other monotherapies for inflammatory lesions and weaker for noninflammatory lesions — the lesion type retinoids treat. The Cochrane benzoyl peroxide review (Yang 2020) adds the caution that benzoyl peroxide alone was essentially indistinguishable from clindamycin alone on participant-reported improvement (relative risk 0.95), so the combination's edge over an antibiotic alone comes from adding the retinoid, not from benzoyl peroxide itself, and overall confidence in the network evidence was rated low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for moderate acne, benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid is probably more effective than a topical antibiotic alone, particularly for noninflammatory lesions, at the cost of slightly more local irritation and withdrawal.

cards.headline: Stuart 2021: in mild-to-moderate acne, adapalene combined with benzoyl peroxide was ranked the most effective topical treatment in a network of 40 trials — ahead of every monotherapy, including topical antibiotics
cards.summary: Stuart 2021: in mild-to-moderate acne, adapalene combined with benzoyl peroxide was ranked the most effective topical treatment in a network of 40 trials — ahead of every monotherapy, including topical antibiotics
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 40 randomised trials with 18,089 participants with mild-to-moderate acne (searches to June 2020); 11 trials reported the primary outcome of patient global assessment of improvement. Confidence in the overall evidence was assessed as low.
cards.result: Compared with vehicle, benzoyl peroxide was effective for self-reported improvement (35% versus 26%), and the combinations of benzoyl peroxide with adapalene (54% versus 35%) or with clindamycin (49% versus 35%) were ranked more effective than benzoyl peroxide alone; the authors conclude adapalene in combination with benzoyl peroxide may be the most effective treatment for acne. Withdrawal due to adverse events was low for all treatments but slightly higher for benzoyl peroxide with adapalene (2.5%) or with clindamycin (2.7%) than for benzoyl peroxide (1.6%) or adapalene alone (1.0%). Inconsistent reporting precluded firmer conclusions.
cards.watchOut: The ranking is largely indirect — built by comparing each treatment against common comparators rather than against antibiotic monotherapy head-to-head — and the review itself rates confidence as low, which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE and not LIKELY.
cards.source: Stuart B et al. Topical preparations for the treatment of mild-to-moderate acne vulgaris: systematic review and network meta-analysis. The British Journal of Dermatology. 2021. cards.headline: Huang 2023: across 221 acne trials, retinoid–benzoyl peroxide combination therapy ranked near the top for lesion reduction, while topical antibiotics alone matched other monotherapies only for inflammatory lesions and lagged on noninflammatory lesions
cards.summary: Huang 2023: across 221 acne trials, retinoid–benzoyl peroxide combination therapy ranked near the top for lesion reduction, while topical antibiotics alone matched other monotherapies only for inflammatory lesions and lagged on noninflammatory lesions
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 210 articles describing 221 randomised trials and 37 interventions, with 65,601 patients in the primary analysis of percentage reduction in total lesion count; mean age 20.4 years, median treatment duration 12 weeks, median baseline counts 72 total, 27 inflammatory and 44 noninflammatory lesions.
cards.result: The most effective treatment was oral isotretinoin (mean difference 48.41 in percentage reduction of total lesions), followed by triple therapy containing a topical antibiotic, a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide (mean difference 38.15) and triple therapy with an oral antibiotic, a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide (mean difference 34.83). For monotherapies, oral or topical antibiotics or topical retinoids had comparable efficacy for inflammatory lesions, while oral or topical antibiotics had less effect on noninflammatory lesions. The record reports rankings and mean differences against the network reference rather than a single direct combination-versus-antibiotic contrast.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings reward combinations that were tested in more severe populations and say nothing about antibiotic resistance, the stewardship reason guidelines already discourage antibiotic monotherapy; the efficacy gap is clearest for noninflammatory (comedonal) lesions.
cards.source: Huang CY et al. Comparative Efficacy of Pharmacological Treatments for Acne Vulgaris: A Network Meta-Analysis of 221 Randomized Controlled Trials. Annals of Family Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37487721. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yang 2020 (Cochrane): benzoyl peroxide alone was no better than clindamycin alone on participant-reported improvement (relative risk 0.95) — so any advantage of the combination over an antibiotic alone rests on the added retinoid
cards.summary: Yang 2020 (Cochrane): benzoyl peroxide alone was no better than clindamycin alone on participant-reported improvement (relative risk 0.95) — so any advantage of the combination over an antibiotic alone rests on the added retinoid
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 120 randomised trials (29,592 participants randomised in 116 trials) of topical benzoyl peroxide for acne; where reported, 72 trials included mild-to-moderate acne and 26 severe acne, with mean ages 18 to 30 years. Risk of performance, detection and attrition bias was commonly high or unclear.
cards.result: Benzoyl peroxide may be more effective than placebo or no treatment for participant-reported improvement (relative risk 1.27; 95% CI 1.12 to 1.45; 3 trials, 2,234 participants; low-certainty evidence; relative measure). There may be little to no difference between benzoyl peroxide and adapalene (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.10; 5 trials, 1,472 participants) or between benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin (relative risk 0.95; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.34; 1 trial, 240 participants; treatment for 10 weeks). Withdrawal due to adverse events may be higher with benzoyl peroxide than with placebo (relative risk 2.13; 95% CI 1.55 to 2.93), and the risk of mild-to-moderate adverse events may be higher with benzoyl peroxide than with clindamycin (relative risk 1.24; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.58; moderate-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: This review compares benzoyl peroxide monotherapy and add-on use, not the fixed retinoid combination against an antibiotic; it is carded to keep the shelf honest about which ingredient does the work.
cards.source: Yang Z et al. Topical benzoyl peroxide for acne. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32175593. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: network evidence ranks benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid above topical antibiotic monotherapy for moderate acne — most clearly for noninflammatory lesions — but the comparison is indirect and rated low-confidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: network evidence ranks benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid above topical antibiotic monotherapy for moderate acne — most clearly for noninflammatory lesions — but the comparison is indirect and rated low-confidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: two network meta-analyses (40 trials, 18,089 participants with mild-to-moderate acne; 221 trials, 65,601 patients across severities) and one Cochrane review (120 trials, 29,592 participants). The syntheses overlap in their included trials by design, so their participant counts must not be summed as independent patients. No carded trial compares the combination directly against a topical antibiotic alone.
cards.result: Adapalene with benzoyl peroxide was ranked the most effective topical treatment for mild-to-moderate acne (Stuart 2021), and retinoid–benzoyl peroxide combinations ranked just below isotretinoin and triple therapy for total lesion reduction, with topical antibiotics weaker on noninflammatory lesions (Huang 2023). Benzoyl peroxide alone did not differ from clindamycin alone (relative risk 0.95; Yang 2020). Withdrawals were slightly higher on the combination (2.5%) than on monotherapy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: If a direct, adequately powered trial of the fixed combination against clindamycin or erythromycin alone exists outside these syntheses' searches, it should replace the indirect ranking as this shelf's anchor.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stuart B et al. The British Journal of Dermatology. 2021 (PMID: 33825196); Huang CY et al. Annals of Family Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37487721); Yang Z et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32175593).
