shelves.title: Biologics versus methotrexate for plaque psoriasis (PARTIAL completion of live #377): far greater clearance on biologics — PASI 75 79.6% vs 35.5% in the direct trial
shelves.question: For chronic plaque psoriasis, how do biologic therapies compare with methotrexate for skin clearance?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Psoriasis · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — biologics clear skin substantially more completely than methotrexate. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #377 already answers how completely each modern biologic class clears skin against placebo and older biologics; this shelf asks the comparison #377 does not make — biologics against methotrexate, the conventional first systemic. The one large direct randomised comparison, CHAMPION, found PASI 75 at 16 weeks in 79.6% on adalimumab versus 35.5% on methotrexate and 18.9% on placebo, with complete clearance in 16.7% versus 7.3%; its benefit–risk analysis counted about four times as many adverse-event-free response days on adalimumab (36.9 vs 8.3 days), while methotrexate had the most discontinuations, chiefly hepatic. The Cochrane network meta-analysis of all systemic treatments ranks the biologic classes far above the conventional agents for PASI 90 and places methotrexate down with the non-biologics — finding no significant difference between methotrexate and the small molecules apremilast or tofacitinib — while cautioning that methotrexate itself rests on few trials in the network. The paediatric head-to-head (adalimumab versus methotrexate in children) is homed on live pack #4040 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for skin clearance, biologic therapies beat methotrexate — shown directly for adalimumab and consistently across classes in network evidence.

cards.headline: CHAMPION 2008: the direct comparison — PASI 75 at 16 weeks in 79.6% on adalimumab versus 35.5% on methotrexate and 18.9% on placebo; complete clearance 16.7% vs 7.3% vs 1.9%
cards.summary: CHAMPION 2008: the direct comparison — PASI 75 at 16 weeks in 79.6% on adalimumab versus 35.5% on methotrexate and 18.9% on placebo; complete clearance 16.7% vs 7.3% vs 1.9%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, three arms (CHAMPION; Saurat 2008)
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis randomised double-blind for 16 weeks to adalimumab (80 mg at week 0, then 40 mg every other week; n = 108), oral methotrexate (7.5 mg weekly, increased as needed and tolerated to 25 mg; n = 110), or placebo (n = 53). Primary endpoint was PASI 75 at week 16.
cards.result: PASI 75 was achieved by 79.6% of adalimumab patients versus 35.5% on methotrexate (P < 0.001) and 18.9% on placebo (P < 0.001); complete clearance was achieved by 16.7% versus 7.3% versus 1.9%. Response to adalimumab was rapid (57% mean PASI improvement by week 4). Adverse events were similar across groups overall, but adverse events leading to discontinuation were greatest in the methotrexate group, primarily because of hepatic-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks is induction only, methotrexate was titrated over the trial so its full effect may lag the fixed biologic schedule, and one biologic (adalimumab, a TNF inhibitor) carries the direct evidence — the newer IL-17/IL-23 classes have never been trialled head-to-head against methotrexate.

cards.headline: CHAMPION benefit–risk analysis 2010: adalimumab gave about four times as many adverse-event-free response days as methotrexate (36.9 vs 8.3 days over 16 weeks)
cards.summary: CHAMPION benefit–risk analysis 2010: adalimumab gave about four times as many adverse-event-free response days as methotrexate (36.9 vs 8.3 days over 16 weeks)
cards.type: Benefit–risk secondary analysis of a randomised trial (CHAMPION; Reich 2010)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the CHAMPION trial population (adalimumab n = 107, methotrexate n = 110, placebo n = 53 analysed), followed for 16 weeks; response was defined as ≥75% improvement in PASI, combined with days free of adverse events of graded severity.
cards.result: Adalimumab was associated with substantially more days of response free of any adverse events than methotrexate or placebo (36.9 [SD 31.1] vs 8.3 [15.9] vs 6.7 [18.1] days), and likewise for days free of moderate-to-severe adverse events (43.8 vs 11.1 vs 7.9), infection-related adverse events (48.5 vs 12.4 vs 9.2) and study-drug-related adverse events (44.6 vs 11.8 vs 10.0) — all P < .0001 for adalimumab versus methotrexate or placebo. The authors conclude adalimumab showed a superior benefit–risk profile, with four times as many adverse-event-free response days.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial as the first card re-analysed, not independent evidence; a 16-week window cannot capture the uncommon long-term harms of either drug, and the composite 'AE-free response days' measure is the investigators' construction, favourable by design to the arm with more responders.
cards.source: Reich K et al. Benefit-risk analysis of adalimumab versus methotrexate and placebo in the treatment of moderate to severe psoriasis: comparison of adverse event-free response days in the CHAMPION trial. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2010. PMID: 20933301. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane network meta-analysis 2021: across all systemic treatments, the biologic classes rank far above methotrexate for PASI 90 — and methotrexate itself was evaluated in few trials
cards.summary: Cochrane network meta-analysis 2021: across all systemic treatments, the biologic classes rank far above methotrexate for PASI 90 — and methotrexate itself was evaluated in few trials
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane; Sbidian 2021)
cards.people: Living Cochrane network meta-analysis of randomised trials of systemic treatments (non-biologic agents, small molecules and biologics) in adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, updated to September 2020; primary outcomes were PASI 90 and serious adverse events at induction (8–24 weeks).
cards.result: For PASI 90 versus placebo, the most effective treatments were biologics — infliximab (relative risk 50.29, 95% CI 20.96–120.67; high-certainty evidence), ixekizumab (RR 32.48, 95% CI 27.13–38.87), risankizumab (RR 28.76, 95% CI 23.96–34.54), bimekizumab (RR 58.64), secukinumab (RR 25.79), guselkumab (RR 25.52) and brodalumab (RR 23.55), all relative measures against placebo response rates that are near zero. There was no significant difference between tofacitinib or apremilast and the three non-biological drugs — fumaric acid esters, ciclosporin and methotrexate — and the reviewers urge a conservative interpretation for methotrexate and several other agents because they were evaluated in few trials in the network. No intervention differed significantly from placebo for serious adverse events, on low-to-moderate certainty evidence.
cards.watchOut: The biologic-versus-methotrexate contrast here is indirect (through placebo), the placebo-anchored relative risks look enormous because placebo PASI 90 is near zero, and the network's methotrexate node is thin — the direct trial on the first card remains the anchor for the comparison.
cards.source: Sbidian E et al. Systemic pharmacological treatments for chronic plaque psoriasis: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33871055. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: directly and indirectly, biologics clear skin far more completely than methotrexate — PASI 75 roughly 80% versus 36% in the one head-to-head trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: directly and indirectly, biologics clear skin far more completely than methotrexate — PASI 75 roughly 80% versus 36% in the one head-to-head trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one three-arm randomised head-to-head trial (CHAMPION, 271 patients) with its benefit–risk re-analysis, and one Cochrane network meta-analysis spanning the randomised systemic-treatment literature to September 2020. Total carded participants exceed 270 in the direct trial alone, with the network covering the class literature, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Adalimumab beat methotrexate head-to-head on PASI 75 (79.6% vs 35.5%) and complete clearance (16.7% vs 7.3%) at 16 weeks, with more adverse-event-free response days (36.9 vs 8.3); the network analysis ranks every leading biologic class above the conventional agents for PASI 90 and groups methotrexate with the least effective systemics. How completely each biologic class clears skin against placebo and older biologics is homed on live shelf #377, and the paediatric adalimumab-versus-methotrexate trial on live pack #4040; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): biologic therapies achieve substantially greater skin clearance than methotrexate in chronic plaque psoriasis.
cards.watchOut: Clearance is not the whole decision: methotrexate is oral, inexpensive and long-characterised, biologics are injectable immunosuppressants needing screening and monitoring, and the carded comparison covers 16–24-week induction — long-term comparative safety comes from registries, not these records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Saurat JH et al. The British journal of dermatology. 2008 (PMID: 18047523); Reich K et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2010 (PMID: 20933301); Sbidian E et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021 (PMID: 33871055).

shelves.title: Apremilast as the primary question (PARTIAL completion of live #1155): effective versus placebo in three trials — the oral option when biologics cannot be taken, with partial rather than complete clearance
shelves.question: In adults with psoriasis, is apremilast effective for those who cannot take biologics?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors · Psoriasis · Severity of Illness Index · Thalidomide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo — with the population caveat printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: on live shelf #1155 apremilast appears only as the comparator arm inside the deucravacitinib POETYK trials; this shelf makes apremilast the question. No trial has enrolled only patients who cannot take biologics — that population is defined by exclusion in practice, not by a trial — but three placebo-controlled phase III trials in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, the setting in which an oral non-biologic option is chosen, agree: PASI 75 at week 16 in 33.1% (ESTEEM 1, 844 patients) and 28.8% (ESTEEM 2, 411 patients) on apremilast 30 mg twice daily versus 5.3% and 5.8% on placebo, and 39.8% versus 11.9% in the biologic-naive LIBERATE population, with responses maintained to week 52 and a mild-to-moderate adverse-event profile (nausea, diarrhoea, nasopharyngitis, headache) and no biologic-style immunosuppression monitoring in the trial reports. Clearance is partial, not complete — roughly a third reach PASI 75, far below biologic rates on live shelf #377 — which is exactly the trade a biologic-ineligible patient is making. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): apremilast is effective versus placebo for adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, the evidence base for its use when biologics cannot be taken, though that specific population has not been trialled as such.

cards.headline: ESTEEM 1 2015: apremilast PASI 75 at week 16 in 33.1% versus 5.3% on placebo (844 patients), with response maintained through the withdrawal phase
cards.summary: ESTEEM 1 2015: apremilast PASI 75 at week 16 in 33.1% versus 5.3% on placebo (844 patients), with response maintained through the withdrawal phase
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase III (ESTEEM 1; Papp 2015)
cards.people: 844 adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised 2:1 to apremilast 30 mg twice daily (n = 562) or placebo (n = 282) in a phase III double-blind trial; at week 16 the placebo group switched to apremilast, followed by a randomised withdrawal phase to week 52.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 75 was achieved by 33.1% on apremilast versus 5.3% on placebo (P < .0001; primary endpoint). Among patients rerandomised at week 32, 61.0% of those kept on apremilast achieved PASI 75 at week 52 versus 11.7% rerandomised to placebo. During the placebo-controlled period, at least one adverse event occurred in 69.3% on apremilast and 55.7% on placebo, most mild or moderate, and no new significant adverse events emerged with continued exposure; data were limited to 52 weeks.
cards.watchOut: ESTEEM enrolled moderate-to-severe patients generally, not patients selected for biologic ineligibility, and a 33.1% PASI 75 rate is partial clearance — this trial proves apremilast works, not that it replaces a biologic for someone who could take one.
cards.source: Papp K et al. Apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor, in patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis: Results of a phase III, randomized, controlled trial (Efficacy and Safety Trial Evaluating the Effects of Apremilast in Psoriasis [ESTEEM] 1). cards.headline: ESTEEM 2 2015: the replicate trial agrees — PASI 75 in 28.8% versus 5.8% on placebo at week 16, PASI 50 in 55.5% versus 19.7%
cards.summary: ESTEEM 2 2015: the replicate trial agrees — PASI 75 in 28.8% versus 5.8% on placebo at week 16, PASI 50 in 55.5% versus 19.7%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase III (ESTEEM 2; Paul 2015)
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised 2:1 to apremilast 30 mg twice daily or placebo; the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 274 apremilast and 137 placebo patients. Placebo patients switched to apremilast at week 16, and week-32 responders were rerandomised to continue or withdraw.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 75 was achieved by 28.8% on apremilast versus 5.8% on placebo, PASI 50 by 55.5% versus 19.7%, and a static Physician's Global Assessment of 0 or 1 by 20.4% versus 4.4% (all P < 0.001). Most patients rerandomised to continue apremilast at week 32 retained PASI 50 at week 52 (80%). Quality of life and pruritus improved significantly versus placebo; the most common adverse events were nausea, diarrhoea, nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infection, and exposure-adjusted adverse-event incidence did not rise over 52 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Same caveat as ESTEEM 1 — a general moderate-to-severe population, not a biologic-ineligible one — and only about one patient in five reached clear or almost-clear skin (sPGA 0/1, 20.4%), so expectations should be set at meaningful improvement, not clearance.
cards.source: Paul C et al. Efficacy and safety of apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor, in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis over 52 weeks: a phase III, randomized controlled trial (ESTEEM 2). The British journal of dermatology. 2015. PMID: 26357944. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LIBERATE 2017: in biologic-naive patients, apremilast PASI 75 was 39.8% versus 11.9% on placebo at week 16 — and switching from etanercept to apremilast kept responses to week 52
cards.summary: LIBERATE 2017: in biologic-naive patients, apremilast PASI 75 was 39.8% versus 11.9% on placebo at week 16 — and switching from etanercept to apremilast kept responses to week 52
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase IIIb (LIBERATE; Reich 2017)
cards.people: 250 biologic-naive patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised double-blind to placebo (n = 84), apremilast 30 mg twice daily (n = 83), or etanercept 50 mg weekly (n = 83) for 16 weeks, after which all patients continued or switched to apremilast through week 104; outcomes are reported to week 52. The trial was not designed for an apremilast-versus-etanercept comparison.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 75 was achieved by 39.8% on apremilast versus 11.9% on placebo (P < 0.0001); etanercept achieved 48.2% (P < 0.0001 vs placebo), a figure the record presents without a designed head-to-head test against apremilast. At week 52, PASI 75 was maintained in 47.3% of the apremilast/apremilast group, 49.4% of the etanercept-to-apremilast switch group and 47.9% of the placebo-to-apremilast group. Common adverse events (nausea, diarrhoea, upper respiratory infection, nasopharyngitis, headache) were mostly mild or moderate, with diarrhoea and nausea generally resolving in the first month, and no new safety issues on switching from etanercept.
cards.watchOut: Biologic-naive is not biologic-ineligible: LIBERATE's patients could have taken a biologic and one arm did. The etanercept arm is context for the switch question, and the record is explicit that apremilast-versus-etanercept efficacy was not a designed comparison.
cards.source: Reich K et al. The efficacy and safety of apremilast, etanercept and placebo in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: 52-week results from a phase IIIb, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (LIBERATE). etanercept achieved 48.2% (p < 0.0001 vs placebo), a figure the record presents without a designed head-to-head test against apremilast. at week 52, pasi 75 was maintained in 47.3% of the apremilast/apremilast group, 49.4% of the etanercept-to-apremilast switch group and 47.9% of the placebo-to-apremilast group. common adverse events (nausea, diarrhoea, upper respiratory infection, nasopharyngitis, headache) were mostly mild or moderate, with diarrhoea and nausea generally resolving in the first month, and no new safety issues on switching from etanercept. biologic-naive is not biologic-ineligible: liberate's patients could have taken a biologic and one arm did. the etanercept arm is context for the switch question, and the record is explicit that apremilast-versus-etanercept efficacy was not a designed comparison. reich k et al. the efficacy and safety of apremilast, etanercept and placebo in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: 52-week results from a phase iiib, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (liberate). journal of the european academy of dermatology and venereology : jeadv. 2017. pmid: 27768242. registry id: nct01690299. mesh: adult · anti-inflammatory agents, non-steroidal · diarrhea · double-blind method · etanercept · female · headache · humans · male · middle aged · nasopharyngitis · nausea · pain · phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitors · pruritus · psoriasis · respiratory tract infections · severity of illness index · symptom assessment · tension-type headache · thalidomide

cards.headline: Synthesis: three placebo-controlled trials agree apremilast works — about a third reach PASI 75 — which is the evidence behind choosing it when a biologic is not an option
cards.summary: Synthesis: three placebo-controlled trials agree apremilast works — about a third reach PASI 75 — which is the evidence behind choosing it when a biologic is not an option
cards.people: The carded evidence: two phase III randomised trials (ESTEEM 1, 844 patients; ESTEEM 2, 411 patients) and one phase IIIb trial in biologic-naive patients (LIBERATE, 250 patients), all of apremilast 30 mg twice daily versus placebo in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Total carded participants are 1,505, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: PASI 75 at week 16 was 33.1% vs 5.3%, 28.8% vs 5.8% and 39.8% vs 11.9% (apremilast vs placebo) across the three trials, with responses maintained to week 52 and mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal and respiratory adverse events. Apremilast as the comparator inside the deucravacitinib trials is homed on live shelf #1155 and is not re-carded here. No carded trial enrolled only biologic-ineligible patients, and the shelf does not pretend otherwise. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): apremilast is effective versus placebo in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis — the trial basis for its use in adults who cannot take biologics.
cards.watchOut: Effectiveness here means improvement, not clearance: roughly two-thirds of patients do not reach PASI 75, and anyone weighing apremilast against a biologic they could actually take should compare these rates with the biologic rates on live shelf #377.
cards.source: Synthesis of Papp K et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2015 (PMID: 26089047); Paul C et al. The British journal of dermatology. 2015 (PMID: 26357944); Reich K et al. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV. 2017 (PMID: 27768242).

shelves.title: Oral finasteride versus topical minoxidil, head-to-head in men (PARTIAL completion of live #623): finasteride ahead in three open comparative trials
shelves.question: For male pattern hair loss, is oral finasteride more effective than topical minoxidil?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Administration, Topical · Adolescent · Adult · Alopecia · Analysis of Variance · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Finasteride · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Minoxidil · Patient Satisfaction · Probability · Reference Values · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in the head-to-head trials, oral finasteride 1 mg beat topical minoxidil on clinician-rated improvement (80% vs 52% in Arca 2004; 80.5% vs 59% in Hu 2015), and finasteride-containing regimens beat minoxidil alone in Khandpur 2002 — but every direct comparison is open-label with largely subjective endpoints, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #623 already answers finasteride versus placebo and minoxidil versus placebo separately; this shelf answers only the direct comparison, and neither homed placebo trial is re-carded here. The combination of both drugs beat either alone in two of the three trials (94.1% improved in Hu 2015), so 'which single drug' is not the same question as 'what works best overall'.

cards.headline: Arca 2004: oral finasteride beat 5% topical minoxidil head-to-head — clinical cure in 80% (32/40) versus 52% (13/25) at 12 months
cards.summary: Arca 2004: oral finasteride beat 5% topical minoxidil head-to-head — clinical cure in 80% (32/40) versus 52% (13/25) at 12 months
cards.people: 65 men with mild to severe androgenetic alopecia in an open, randomised comparative study: 40 assigned to oral finasteride 1 mg/day and 25 to 5% topical minoxidil solution twice daily, each for 12 months.
cards.result: Clinical cure rates (increased hair intensity on clinical evaluation) were 80% (32/40) on oral finasteride versus 52% (13/25) on topical minoxidil, and the authors concluded oral finasteride was more effective (P < 0.05). Side effects were mild: on finasteride, 6 men reported loss of libido and 1 increased body hair; on minoxidil, 1 man had scalp irritation; all resolved on stopping.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a clinician-judged 'cure' endpoint and unequal group sizes (40 vs 25); expectation effects cannot be excluded, and the trial predates standardised hair-count reporting.
cards.source: Arca E et al. An open, randomized, comparative study of oral finasteride and 5% topical minoxidil in male androgenetic alopecia. Dermatology (Basel, Switzerland). 2004. PMID: 15316165. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hu 2015: in 428 Chinese men evaluated at 12 months, improvement in 80.5% on finasteride versus 59% on 5% minoxidil — and 94.1% on the combination
cards.summary: Hu 2015: in 428 Chinese men evaluated at 12 months, improvement in 80.5% on finasteride versus 59% on 5% minoxidil — and 94.1% on the combination
cards.people: 450 Chinese men with male androgenetic alopecia randomised to oral finasteride 1 mg/day (n = 160), 5% topical minoxidil (n = 130), or both combined (n = 160) for 12 months; efficacy was evaluated in 428 men (154, 122 and 152 respectively).
cards.result: At 12 months, 80.5% of the finasteride group, 59% of the minoxidil group and 94.1% of the combination group showed improvement; the authors concluded finasteride is superior to 5% minoxidil and the combined medication showed the best efficacy. Adverse reactions were uncommon (finasteride 1.8%; minoxidil 6.1%) and disappeared after drug withdrawal.
cards.watchOut: The record does not describe blinding, and 'improvement' is a global clinical judgement rather than a counted hair-density endpoint; 22 of 450 randomised men were not evaluated at treatment end.
cards.source: Hu R et al. Combined treatment with oral finasteride and topical minoxidil in male androgenetic alopecia: a randomized and comparative study in Chinese patients. Dermatologic therapy. 2015. PMID: 26031764. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Khandpur 2002: finasteride-containing regimens improved significantly more than minoxidil 2% alone (P < 0.05) over one year
cards.summary: Khandpur 2002: finasteride-containing regimens improved significantly more than minoxidil 2% alone (P < 0.05) over one year
cards.type: Open-label randomised comparative trial, four arms (Khandpur 2002)
cards.people: 100 men with androgenetic alopecia (Hamilton grades II–IV) in an open, randomised, parallel-group study of oral finasteride 1 mg/day alone (30 men), finasteride plus topical 2% minoxidil (36), topical 2% minoxidil alone (24), and finasteride plus topical 2% ketoconazole shampoo (10), assessed over one year by patient and physician scores and global photographic review.
cards.result: Hair growth was observed in all groups, best with finasteride plus minoxidil, then finasteride plus ketoconazole, then finasteride alone, then minoxidil alone; men receiving finasteride alone or in combination showed statistically significant improvement (P < 0.05) over minoxidil-only recipients. No significant drug-related side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The minoxidil arm used the weaker 2% solution (not the 5% tested in the other two trials), groups were small and unequal, and outcomes were score-based rather than hair counts — this trial supports the direction of the other two, not a precise effect size.
cards.source: Khandpur S et al. Comparative efficacy of various treatment regimens for androgenetic alopecia in men. The Journal of dermatology. 2002. PMID: 12227482. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three open comparative trials agree finasteride beats topical minoxidil head-to-head — but none was blinded, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: three open comparative trials agree finasteride beats topical minoxidil head-to-head — but none was blinded, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised head-to-head comparisons in men (Arca 2004, n = 65; Hu 2015, n = 428 evaluated; Khandpur 2002, n = 100). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Improvement rates favoured oral finasteride 1 mg over topical minoxidil in every direct comparison (80% vs 52%; 80.5% vs 59%; finasteride regimens significantly better than minoxidil alone, P < 0.05), and combining the two drugs beat either alone where tested (94.1% in Hu 2015). The separate placebo-controlled evidence for each drug is homed on live shelf #623 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral finasteride is more effective than topical minoxidil in direct comparisons, on open-label, largely subjective evidence.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are open-label and two rely on global improvement judgements; a blinded head-to-head trial with counted hair density does not exist in the carded record, which is why this shelf cannot rise above POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Arca E et al. Dermatology (Basel, Switzerland). 2004 (PMID: 15316165); Hu R et al. Dermatologic therapy. 2015 (PMID: 26031764); Khandpur S et al. The Journal of dermatology. 2002 (PMID: 12227482).

shelves.title: Topical minoxidil versus placebo in women with hair loss (PARTIAL completion of live #4031): more hair per cm² in two double-blind trials and the Cochrane pooling
shelves.question: In women with hair loss, does topical minoxidil improve hair density?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adolescent · Adult · Alopecia · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hair · Humans · Middle Aged · Minoxidil · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: LIKELY — topical minoxidil improves hair density in women with female pattern hair loss: two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Lucky 2004, 381 women; Tsuboi 2007, 280 women) and the Cochrane pooling (relative risk 1.93 for participant-rated moderate-to-marked regrowth; +13.18 hairs/cm² versus placebo) all point the same way, across 1%, 2% and 5% formulations. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #4031 covers oral versus topical minoxidil in men; the topical-versus-placebo question in women is answered here, and no card from #4031 is re-used. The gains are real but modest in absolute terms — roughly 6–13 extra hairs per cm² over placebo — and the 5% strength buys a small patient-rated edge over 2% at the cost of more itching, irritation and unwanted facial hair growth.

cards.headline: Lucky 2004: in 381 women, 5% topical minoxidil beat placebo on all three primary endpoints at 48 weeks; 2% beat placebo on hair count and investigator assessment
cards.summary: Lucky 2004: in 381 women, 5% topical minoxidil beat placebo on all three primary endpoints at 48 weeks; 2% beat placebo on hair count and investigator assessment
cards.people: 381 women aged 18–49 with female pattern hair loss in a 48-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial, applying 5% topical minoxidil solution (n = 153), 2% topical minoxidil solution (n = 154), or placebo vehicle (n = 74) twice daily.
cards.result: After 48 weeks, 5% minoxidil was superior to placebo for change in nonvellus hair count and for patient and investigator assessments of hair growth/scalp coverage; 2% minoxidil was superior to placebo for hair count and investigator assessment, but not for the patient assessment of hair growth. The 5% group rated treatment benefit higher than the 2% group (statistically superior at week 48). Pruritus, local irritation and hypertrichosis were more frequent with 5% than with 2% or placebo; neither strength showed systemic adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The record reports superiority on the primary endpoints without printing the absolute hair-count changes, so the size of the gain has to come from the Tsuboi trial and the Cochrane pooling on the next cards; the placebo group (n = 74) was half the size of each active group.
cards.source: Lucky AW et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 5% and 2% topical minoxidil solutions in the treatment of female pattern hair loss. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2004. PMID: 15034503. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tsuboi 2007: 1% topical minoxidil raised nonvellus hair count by 8.15/cm² versus 2.03/cm² on placebo in 280 Japanese women (difference 6.12, P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Tsuboi 2007: 1% topical minoxidil raised nonvellus hair count by 8.15/cm² versus 2.03/cm² on placebo in 280 Japanese women (difference 6.12, P < 0.001)
cards.people: 280 Japanese women aged 20 or older with androgenetic alopecia in a double-blind trial of 1% topical minoxidil (n = 140) or placebo (n = 140) for 24 weeks; the primary variable was mean change from baseline in non-vellus hair count per cm².
cards.result: Mean change in non-vellus hair count was 8.15/cm² on 1% minoxidil versus 2.03/cm² on placebo (difference 6.12, 95% CI 3.29–8.96; P < 0.001). Investigators rated moderate-or-better improvement in 29.2% (40/137) on minoxidil versus 11.8% (16/136) on placebo (P < 0.001), and patients rated themselves improved-or-better in 36.5% versus 23.5% (P = 0.019). Treatment was well tolerated without significant adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: This trial used the 1% strength in Japanese women over 24 weeks — it proves the class effect at low strength, but its absolute gains should not be quoted as the expected effect of the 5% products used elsewhere.
cards.source: Tsuboi R et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 1% topical minoxidil solution in the treatment of androgenetic alopecia in Japanese women. European journal of dermatology : EJD. 2007. PMID: 17324826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (female pattern hair loss): pooled minoxidil beat placebo — regrowth relative risk 1.93 and +13.18 hairs/cm²
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (female pattern hair loss): pooled minoxidil beat placebo — regrowth relative risk 1.93 and +13.18 hairs/cm²
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Cochrane (van Zuuren 2016)
cards.people: The 2016 Cochrane review of interventions for female pattern hair loss included 47 trials with 5,290 participants; the minoxidil-versus-placebo pooling drew on six studies for participant-rated regrowth (593 minoxidil, 555 placebo), seven studies (1,181 participants) for investigator ratings, and eight studies (1,242 participants) for total hair count.
cards.result: A greater proportion of minoxidil-treated participants reported moderate-to-marked regrowth than on placebo (157/593 versus 77/555; relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.51–2.47; moderate-quality evidence), investigator ratings agreed (relative risk 2.35, 95% CI 1.68–3.28), and total hair count rose by an extra 13.18 hairs/cm² over placebo (95% CI 10.92–15.44; low-quality evidence). Adverse events did not differ significantly between twice-daily minoxidil 2% and placebo (40/407 versus 28/320; relative risk 1.24, 95% CI 0.82–1.87).
cards.watchOut: Only five of the review's 47 trials were at low risk of bias (26 unclear, 16 high), and the pooled hair-count estimate is graded low quality — the direction is consistent across every analysis, but the exact size of the benefit is less certain than the pooled figure looks.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in women, topical minoxidil improves hair density versus placebo across strengths and populations — LIKELY, with modest absolute gains
cards.summary: Synthesis: in women, topical minoxidil improves hair density versus placebo across strengths and populations — LIKELY, with modest absolute gains
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Lucky 2004, 381 women; Tsuboi 2007, 280 women) and the Cochrane meta-analysis of the female pattern hair loss trial literature (van Zuuren 2016). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Every carded analysis favours minoxidil: 5% and 2% beat placebo on hair count at 48 weeks (Lucky), 1% beat placebo by 6.12 hairs/cm² at 24 weeks (Tsuboi), and pooling gives a relative risk of 1.93 for participant-rated moderate-to-marked regrowth and +13.18 hairs/cm² versus placebo (Cochrane). The oral-versus-topical comparison in men is homed on live shelf #4031 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY: topical minoxidil improves hair density in women with female pattern hair loss, by a modest absolute amount.
cards.watchOut: Benefit is measured over 24–48 weeks of twice-daily use and is lost on stopping in the underlying literature; none of the carded records tests once-daily 5% foam against placebo directly in women.

shelves.title: Ketoconazole versus selenium sulfide shampoo, head-to-head (PARTIAL completion of live #2494): no efficacy winner in three randomised trials
shelves.question: For seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, is ketoconazole shampoo more effective than selenium sulfide?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Child, Preschool · Dermatitis, Seborrheic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hair Preparations · Humans · Ketoconazole · Male · Middle Aged · Scalp Dermatoses · Selenium Compounds · Severity of Illness Index · Soaps · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference between the two shampoos) — across three head-to-head randomised trials spanning 1993–2026, ketoconazole shampoo was not more effective than selenium sulfide/disulfide shampoo on symptom and scale scores: the one early advantage (Danby 1993, superiority at day 8 only) did not persist, and the two modern double-blind trials found no significant between-group difference at any time point. The differences that do appear are in tolerability and cosmesis — all nine adverse experiences in Danby 1993 occurred on selenium sulfide, while the modern selenium disulfide formulations were rated better for hair softness and acceptability. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2494 covers ketoconazole shampoo versus placebo; the direct comparison with selenium sulfide is answered here. Note the modern trials tested specific formulated selenium disulfide shampoos (1% and 0.6% micronized); where the fetched record does not name the brand or company, the card says so plainly.

cards.headline: Danby 1993: ketoconazole 2% and selenium sulfide 2.5% both beat placebo for moderate-to-severe dandruff; ketoconazole was ahead only at day 8 — and all 9 adverse experiences were on selenium sulfide
cards.summary: Danby 1993: ketoconazole 2% and selenium sulfide 2.5% both beat placebo for moderate-to-severe dandruff; ketoconazole was ahead only at day 8 — and all 9 adverse experiences were on selenium sulfide
cards.people: 246 patients with moderate to severe dandruff in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ketoconazole 2% shampoo versus selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo versus placebo shampoo, assessed on adherent and loose dandruff scores, irritation, itching, yeast cells and investigator global improvement.
cards.result: Mean total adherent dandruff scores fell with both medicated shampoos, each significantly better than placebo at all visits; ketoconazole was statistically superior to selenium sulfide at day 8 only (P = 0.0026). Both medicated shampoos beat placebo for irritation and itching. Of the nine adverse experiences reported during treatment, all involved patients treated with selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo; the authors concluded both shampoos are effective, with ketoconazole appearing better tolerated. The record does not name the brand or company of either shampoo.
cards.watchOut: A 1993 trial in dandruff (the scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis spectrum) with score-based endpoints; the single day-8 difference is one time point among many and did not persist, so it should not be quoted as overall superiority.
cards.source: Danby FW et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of ketoconazole 2% shampoo versus selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo in the treatment of moderate to severe dandruff. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 1993. PMID: 8245236. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Barbosa 2024: selenium disulfide 1% shampoo matched ketoconazole 2% over 4 weeks in 64 adults with moderate-to-severe scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis (severity score −71% vs −69%)
cards.summary: Barbosa 2024: selenium disulfide 1% shampoo matched ketoconazole 2% over 4 weeks in 64 adults with moderate-to-severe scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis (severity score −71% vs −69%)
cards.people: 64 adult subjects with moderate to severe scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis (severity score > 6) in a multicentre, double-blind, randomised 4-week study of a 1% selenium disulfide-based shampoo versus a 2% ketoconazole shampoo, applied per product indications, with clinical examinations on days 3, 7, 14 and 28. The fetched record does not name the brand or company of either tested shampoo.
cards.result: The seborrhoeic dermatitis severity score improved significantly in both groups from day 3 (P < 0.001), reaching −71% on selenium disulfide and −69% on ketoconazole at day 28; total scale scores fell −75% versus −68%, all subjects' severity had decreased to mild by day 28, and signs and symptoms improved significantly in both groups. Quality of life improved earlier with the selenium disulfide shampoo and its cosmetic acceptability was higher; both shampoos were very well tolerated. The authors conclude the selenium disulfide shampoo is a reliable alternative to ketoconazole shampoo.
cards.watchOut: The percentages are within-group improvements; the record reports no significant between-group efficacy difference, and with 64 subjects the trial cannot exclude modest differences. The tested selenium product is a specific formulated shampoo — the record does not name its brand or company, and other selenium shampoos may differ.
cards.source: Barbosa V et al. A Comparative Randomized Clinical Study Assessing the Efficacy of a 1% Selenium Disulfide-Based Shampoo versus 2% Ketoconazole Shampoo in Subjects with Moderate to Severe Scalp Seborrheic Dermatitis. cards.headline: Farris 2026: 0.6% micronized selenium disulfide matched 2% ketoconazole over 6 weeks (scale score −77.9% vs −69.5%) with no significant difference at any time point — and better-rated hair cosmesis
cards.summary: Farris 2026: 0.6% micronized selenium disulfide matched 2% ketoconazole over 6 weeks (scale score −77.9% vs −69.5%) with no significant difference at any time point — and better-rated hair cosmesis
cards.people: 87 men and women with moderate to severe dandruff/scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis in a single-centre, 6-week, randomised, double-blind study comparing a 0.6% micronized selenium disulfide shampoo with a 2% ketoconazole shampoo. The fetched record does not name the brand or company of either tested shampoo.
cards.result: After 6 weeks, total scale score fell 77.9% on selenium disulfide versus 69.5% on ketoconazole, the seborrhoeic dermatitis symptom scale fell 74.5% versus 68.0%, and pruritus severity fell 75.9% versus 76.2% (all within-group P < 0.001); there was no significant difference between the two groups for these outcomes at any time point. Tolerability was excellent for both. On cosmesis, subjects across curl types significantly favoured the selenium disulfide shampoo for leaving hair soft, supple, glossy and natural-appearing (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and cosmesis-focused; 'matches' is the authors' framing of non-significant differences in an 87-subject study not powered as a formal non-inferiority trial, and the tested selenium shampoo is one specific micronized formulation whose brand/company the record does not name.
cards.source: Farris PK et al. Beyond Efficacy: 0.6% Selenium Disulfide Shampoo Matches 2% Ketoconazole for Seborrheic Dermatitis with Superior Cosmesis. Journal of drugs in dermatology : JDD. 2026. PMID: 41931685. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ketoconazole is not more effective than selenium sulfide/disulfide shampoo in any head-to-head trial — the choice turns on tolerability and hair feel
cards.summary: Synthesis: ketoconazole is not more effective than selenium sulfide/disulfide shampoo in any head-to-head trial — the choice turns on tolerability and hair feel
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised head-to-head trials (Danby 1993, n = 246; Barbosa 2024, n = 64; Farris 2026, n = 87). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Ketoconazole beat selenium sulfide at one early time point in 1993 (day 8, P = 0.0026) and not thereafter; the 2024 and 2026 double-blind trials found near-identical score reductions (severity −71% vs −69%; scale score −77.9% vs −69.5%) with no significant between-group difference at any time point. Ketoconazole versus placebo is homed on live shelf #2494 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): neither shampoo is more effective; selenium products caused all the adverse experiences in the oldest trial and won on cosmesis in the newest.
cards.watchOut: The selenium side of this comparison changed across 33 years (2.5% sulfide suspension to formulated 1% and 0.6% micronized disulfide shampoos); equivalence shown for the modern formulations does not automatically transfer to every selenium shampoo on the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Danby FW et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 1993 (PMID: 8245236); Barbosa V et al. Skin appendage disorders. 2024 (PMID: 39659649); Farris PK et al. Journal of drugs in dermatology : JDD. 2026 (PMID: 41931685).

shelves.title: Antihistamine eye drops versus oral antihistamines for allergic eye symptoms (PARTIAL completion of live #2518): drops win on itching in three direct comparisons
shelves.question: For allergic eye symptoms, are antihistamine eye drops more effective than oral antihistamines?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Allergens · Anti-Allergic Agents · Child · Conjunctivitis, Allergic · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Histamine H1 Antagonists · Humans · Ketotifen · Loratadine · Male · Middle Aged · Ophthalmic Solutions · Rhinitis, Allergic, Seasonal · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in direct comparisons, antihistamine eye drops relieved ocular itching better than an oral antihistamine alone: ketotifen drops beat oral desloratadine at every measured time point in an allergen-challenge trial (Crampton 2003), adding olopatadine drops to loratadine beat loratadine alone within 20 minutes of the first dose (Lanier 2001), and topical levocabastine beat oral terfenadine on ocular itching in a small 8-week seasonal trial (Bahmer 1994). The stamp stays at POSSIBLE because the trials are small, two rest on laboratory allergen challenge or adjunctive designs, and the oldest comparator (terfenadine) has since been withdrawn for cardiac toxicity. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2518 covers antihistamine eye drops versus placebo; the head-to-head against oral antihistamines is answered here, and no #2518 card is re-used. Eye drops treat the eye only — the oral drug remains the one that also treats the nose.

cards.headline: Crampton 2003: ketotifen eye drops beat oral desloratadine on ocular itching at every time point after allergen challenge — alone or combined
cards.summary: Crampton 2003: ketotifen eye drops beat oral desloratadine on ocular itching at every time point after allergen challenge — alone or combined
cards.people: 82 subjects (55 women, 27 men; mean age 42.8 years) with seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in a randomised, double-masked, placebo- and active-controlled conjunctival allergen challenge trial: ketotifen 0.025% ophthalmic solution plus placebo tablet (n = 27), desloratadine 5 mg tablet plus placebo eyedrop (n = 27), or both active treatments (n = 26), used for about 4 weeks before a final bilateral allergen challenge 2 hours after dosing.
cards.result: Mean ocular itching scores were significantly lower in the ketotifen-alone and ketotifen-plus-desloratadine groups than in the desloratadine-alone group at all time points (3, 5 and 7 minutes after challenge; P ≤ 0.05), and total ocular redness was significantly lower with ketotifen than in the other groups at most time points. The proportion requesting relief drops after challenge was significantly lower in both ketotifen groups than with desloratadine alone (P = 0.004). Nasal symptoms were attenuated by all treatments without significant between-group differences, except at 50 minutes (combination better than ketotifen alone).
cards.watchOut: A laboratory allergen-challenge model measures itching minutes after a controlled dose — it ranks the routes cleanly but is not real-world seasonal exposure, and the groups were small (26–27 subjects each).
cards.source: Crampton HJ. Comparison of ketotifen fumarate ophthalmic solution alone, desloratadine alone, and their combination for inhibition of the signs and symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in the conjunctival allergen challenge model: a double-masked, placebo- and active-controlled trial. cards.headline: Lanier 2001: adding olopatadine eye drops to loratadine relieved ocular itching and redness better than loratadine alone — significantly within 20 minutes of the first dose
cards.summary: Lanier 2001: adding olopatadine eye drops to loratadine relieved ocular itching and redness better than loratadine alone — significantly within 20 minutes of the first dose
cards.people: 94 patients aged 7–74 with active seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in a three-centre, observer-masked, randomised parallel-group study: olopatadine 0.1% ophthalmic solution twice daily adjunctive to loratadine 10 mg once daily, versus loratadine alone, for 7 days.
cards.result: Patients receiving olopatadine plus loratadine had less ocular itching than those on loratadine alone (P = 0.0436) and rated their ocular condition as more improved (P < 0.0022); twenty minutes after initial dosing, the combination relieved ocular itching and redness significantly better than loratadine alone (P = 0.001). Rhinoconjunctivitis quality-of-life scores improved in both groups, with overall and most domain scores significantly better on the combination at day 7 (P < 0.05). Both regimens were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This is an adjunctive design — drops added to the oral drug versus the oral drug alone — so it shows the drop adds ocular benefit on top of an oral antihistamine rather than testing drops as a complete substitute; the trial lasted only 7 days and included children as young as 7.
cards.source: Lanier BQ et al. Olopatadine ophthalmic solution adjunctive to loratadine compared with loratadine alone in patients with active seasonal allergic conjunctivitis symptoms. Annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the American College of Allergy, Asthma, & Immunology. 2001. PMID: 11428736. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised, observer-masked, treatment-controlled trial (lanier 2001) 94 patients aged 7–74 with active seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in a three-centre, observer-masked, randomised parallel-group study: olopatadine 0.1% ophthalmic solution twice daily adjunctive to loratadine 10 mg once daily, versus loratadine alone, for 7 days. patients receiving olopatadine plus loratadine had less ocular itching than those on loratadine alone (p = 0.0436) and rated their ocular condition as more improved (p < 0.0022); twenty minutes after initial dosing, the combination relieved ocular itching and redness significantly better than loratadine alone (p = 0.001). rhinoconjunctivitis quality-of-life scores improved in both groups, with overall and most domain scores significantly better on the combination at day 7 (p < 0.05). both regimens were well tolerated. this is an adjunctive design — drops added to the oral drug versus the oral drug alone — so it shows the drop adds ocular benefit on top of an oral antihistamine rather than testing drops as a complete substitute; the trial lasted only 7 days and included children as young as 7. lanier bq et al. olopatadine ophthalmic solution adjunctive to loratadine compared with loratadine alone in patients with active seasonal allergic conjunctivitis symptoms. annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the american college of allergy, asthma, & immunology. 2001. pmid: 11428736. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · asthenia · child · conjunctivitis, allergic · dibenzoxepins · drug therapy, combination · dyspepsia · female · humans · loratadine · male · middle aged · olopatadine hydrochloride · xerostomia

cards.headline: Bahmer 1994: topical levocabastine beat oral terfenadine on ocular itching (P = .02) over 8 weeks of pollen season in 27 patients
cards.summary: Bahmer 1994: topical levocabastine beat oral terfenadine on ocular itching (P = .02) over 8 weeks of pollen season in 27 patients
cards.people: 27 patients with seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in a double-blind, parallel-group study over 8 weeks comparing topical levocabastine (eye drops plus nasal spray, the spray used only as required — 46% usage) with oral terfenadine 60 mg twice daily (nasal spray available as required — 56% usage); therapeutic efficacy was a secondary objective, the main aim being ocular tolerability of the drops.
cards.result: Levocabastine was significantly more effective than terfenadine in relieving ocular itching (P = .02), investigator symptom-severity ratings consistently favoured levocabastine, and 88% of levocabastine-treated patients rated the effect on ocular symptoms excellent or good versus 75% on terfenadine; nasal-symptom satisfaction was 75% in each group. Adverse reactions occurred in 31% on levocabastine versus 43% on terfenadine, and the drops were well tolerated on ophthalmologic examination.
cards.watchOut: Only 27 patients, and the levocabastine arm combined eye drops with an as-needed nasal spray, so the ocular comparison is not drops-alone in the strictest sense; terfenadine was later withdrawn worldwide over cardiac arrhythmia risk, so this trial ranks routes, not today's drugs.
cards.source: Bahmer FA et al. Safety and efficacy of topical levocabastine compared with oral terfenadine. Annals of allergy. 1994. PMID: 7909999. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: eye drops beat an oral antihistamine for eye symptoms in every direct comparison — POSSIBLE, on small and partly laboratory evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: eye drops beat an oral antihistamine for eye symptoms in every direct comparison — POSSIBLE, on small and partly laboratory evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: one allergen-challenge trial (Crampton 2003, n = 82), one adjunctive randomised trial (Lanier 2001, n = 94), and one small double-blind seasonal trial (Bahmer 1994, n = 27). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Topical treatment won on ocular itching in all three designs: ketotifen drops significantly below oral desloratadine at every post-challenge time point; olopatadine added to loratadine significantly better than loratadine alone from 20 minutes after the first dose; levocabastine significantly better than oral terfenadine on itching (P = .02). Eye drops versus placebo is homed on live shelf #2518 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: for allergic eye symptoms specifically, antihistamine eye drops are more effective than oral antihistamines; nasal symptoms are a different question, where the drops showed no advantage.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial compares a modern dual-action drop alone against a modern oral antihistamine alone through a full pollen season in a large sample; the direction is consistent, the precision is not.

shelves.title: Nasal steroid spray versus oral antihistamine, head-to-head in allergic rhinitis (PARTIAL completion of live #2666): the spray wins on nasal symptoms
shelves.question: In adults with allergic rhinitis, is a nasal steroid spray more effective than an oral antihistamine?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Female · Humans · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Receptors, Histamine H1 · Rhinitis, Allergic, Perennial · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for nasal symptoms, a nasal steroid spray is more effective than an oral antihistamine: the meta-analysis of 16 head-to-head randomised trials (Weiner 1998, 2,267 subjects) found significantly greater relief of blockage, discharge, sneezing, itch and total nasal symptoms with intranasal corticosteroids, and the largest single trial (Ratner 1998, 600 patients) found fluticasone spray significantly better than loratadine, which itself did not separate from placebo on symptom scores. The one place the spray does not win is eye symptoms, where Weiner found no significant difference. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: on live shelf #2666 the steroid spray and the oral antihistamine appear only as comparators to montelukast; the direct head-to-head is answered here, and no #2666 card is re-used. Adding the antihistamine tablet to the spray added little or nothing in the carded trials.

cards.headline: Weiner 1998 meta-analysis (16 head-to-head trials, 2,267 subjects): intranasal corticosteroids beat oral antihistamines on every nasal symptom — but not on eye symptoms
cards.summary: Weiner 1998 meta-analysis (16 head-to-head trials, 2,267 subjects): intranasal corticosteroids beat oral antihistamines on every nasal symptom — but not on eye symptoms
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Weiner 1998)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised controlled trials (2,267 subjects with allergic rhinitis, published 1966–1997) directly comparing intranasal corticosteroids with oral H1 antihistamines, pooling standardised mean differences for nasal and eye symptoms.
cards.result: Intranasal corticosteroids produced significantly greater relief than oral antihistamines of nasal blockage (standardised mean difference −0.63, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.53), nasal discharge (−0.5, 95% CI −0.6 to −0.4), sneezing (−0.49, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.39), nasal itch (−0.38, 95% CI −0.49 to −0.21), postnasal drip (−0.24, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.06) and total nasal symptoms (−0.42, 95% CI −0.53 to −0.32), and global ratings favoured the spray (odds ratio for deterioration of symptoms 0.26, 95% CI 0.08–0.8). There were no significant differences between treatments for nasal discomfort, nasal resistance, or eye symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are from 1966–1997, so several used first-generation or early second-generation antihistamines and older steroid sprays; effects on sneezing, total nasal symptoms and eye symptoms were significantly heterogeneous between studies, though the direction for nasal outcomes was consistent.
cards.source: Weiner JM et al. Intranasal corticosteroids versus oral H1 receptor antagonists in allergic rhinitis: systematic review of randomised controlled trials. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1998. PMID: 9848901. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ratner 1998: in 600 patients, fluticasone nasal spray beat loratadine on symptom scores and quality of life (P < .001) — and loratadine did not separate from placebo
cards.summary: Ratner 1998: in 600 patients, fluticasone nasal spray beat loratadine on symptom scores and quality of life (P < .001) — and loratadine did not separate from placebo
cards.people: 600 patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis (mountain cedar season, south central Texas) in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial of fluticasone propionate aqueous nasal spray 200 µg once daily, loratadine 10 mg once daily, both combined, or placebo (spray plus tablet), for 2 weeks.
cards.result: Clinician- and patient-rated total and individual nasal symptom scores and overall evaluations were significantly lower (better) in the fluticasone and fluticasone-plus-loratadine groups than in the loratadine-only and placebo groups (P < .001); loratadine was not statistically different from placebo on clinician or patient symptom scores or overall evaluations. Quality-of-life scores (Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire) improved significantly more with fluticasone than with loratadine alone or placebo (P < .001), and adding loratadine to fluticasone gave no significant benefit over fluticasone alone. No serious or unusual drug-related adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A single 2-week season in one pollen region, with loratadine — among the weaker oral antihistamines — as the comparator; the trial answers spray-versus-loratadine decisively but should not be read as the margin against every oral antihistamine.
cards.source: Ratner PH et al. A comparison of the efficacy of fluticasone propionate aqueous nasal spray and loratadine, alone and in combination, for the treatment of seasonal allergic rhinitis. The Journal of family practice. 1998. PMID: 9722799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Di Lorenzo 2004: fluticasone spray alone beat cetirizine plus montelukast combined on total symptom score (P = 0.009) and congestion (P < 0.001) in 100 patients
cards.summary: Di Lorenzo 2004: fluticasone spray alone beat cetirizine plus montelukast combined on total symptom score (P = 0.009) and congestion (P < 0.001) in 100 patients
cards.people: 100 patients aged 12–50 with moderate-to-severe Parietaria pollen seasonal allergic rhinitis in a randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled parallel-group trial: fluticasone propionate nasal spray 200 µg once daily alone (n = 20), fluticasone plus cetirizine (n = 20), fluticasone plus montelukast (n = 20), cetirizine plus montelukast (n = 20), or placebo (n = 20), through a pollen season.
cards.result: All active treatments beat placebo on total symptom, rhinorrhea, sneezing and nasal itching scores (P < 0.001), but only the fluticasone-containing groups separated from placebo on nasal congestion. Fluticasone alone was significantly better than cetirizine plus montelukast — a two-drug oral combination — on total symptom score (P = 0.009), nasal congestion on waking (P < 0.001) and daily congestion (P < 0.001); adding cetirizine or montelukast to fluticasone offered no substantial advantage over fluticasone monotherapy. Nasal lavage eosinophils and eosinophil cationic protein also favoured the fluticasone groups (P < 0.001 versus the cetirizine-plus-montelukast group).
cards.watchOut: There is no cetirizine-alone arm — the oral comparator is cetirizine combined with montelukast, which makes the spray's win more striking but indirect as a test of spray versus a single antihistamine tablet; arms were small (20 patients each) and the allergen was a single regional pollen.

cards.headline: Synthesis: nasal steroid spray beats oral antihistamine for nasal symptoms across the pooled trials and the largest single trial — LIKELY; eye symptoms are the exception
cards.summary: Synthesis: nasal steroid spray beats oral antihistamine for nasal symptoms across the pooled trials and the largest single trial — LIKELY; eye symptoms are the exception
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 16 head-to-head randomised trials (Weiner 1998, 2,267 subjects) and two double-blind double-dummy trials (Ratner 1998, n = 600; Di Lorenzo 2004, n = 100). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Intranasal corticosteroids gave significantly greater relief than oral antihistamines on blockage, discharge, sneezing, itch and total nasal symptoms in the pooled analysis (standardised mean differences −0.24 to −0.63); fluticasone spray beat loratadine on symptoms and quality of life at P < .001 in the 600-patient trial; and fluticasone alone beat an oral cetirizine-plus-montelukast combination in the five-arm trial. No carded analysis found an oral antihistamine advantage for any nasal outcome; eye symptoms showed no significant difference (Weiner 1998). The montelukast comparison that frames both drugs on live shelf #2666 is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY: a nasal steroid spray is more effective than an oral antihistamine for the nasal symptoms of allergic rhinitis.
cards.watchOut: The evidence base is concentrated in seasonal allergic rhinitis and older drug generations; it does not address combination spray products (steroid-plus-antihistamine in one device), which are a separate question.

Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2004 (PMID: 14987306).

shelves.title: Multilayer compression versus no compression for venous leg ulcers (PARTIAL completion of live #1221): four-layer bandaging healed ulcers faster than usual care in both pragmatic trials, and all eight direct randomised comparisons favoured compression
shelves.question: For venous leg ulcers, does multilayer compression bandaging heal ulcers faster than no compression?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Ambulatory Care · Ambulatory Care Facilities · Bandages · Community Health Services · Cost-Benefit Analysis · England · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Home Care Services · Humans · Leg Ulcer · Male · Patient Satisfaction · Recurrence · Rural Health Services · Treatment Outcome · Urban Health Services
shelves.balance: LIKELY — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1221, which compares compression systems against each other (VenUS I, IV and 6); the slice built here is the prior question #1221 assumes: multilayer compression against no systematic compression at all. Two pragmatic randomised trials compared organised four-layer bandaging with the usual care of their era, in which compression was inconsistent or absent: healing was faster with four-layer bandaging in both (healing rate ratio 1.45 in Morrell 1998; 54% vs 34% healed at 3 months in O'Brien 2003). The Cochrane review of all compression trials found 8 randomised trials directly comparing compression with no compression, every one favouring compression on healing outcomes, and concluded compression increases ulcer healing rates compared with no compression (O'Meara 2012). PROPOSED LIKELY: multilayer compression heals venous leg ulcers faster than no compression — the remaining argument, homed on #1221, is only about which system delivers it best.

cards.headline: Morrell 1998: community clinics using four-layer bandaging healed venous ulcers faster than district-nurse usual care (healing rate 1.45; 34% vs 24% healed at 12 weeks)
cards.summary: Morrell 1998: community clinics using four-layer bandaging healed venous ulcers faster than district-nurse usual care (healing rate 1.45; 34% vs 24% healed at 12 weeks)
cards.people: 233 patients with venous leg ulcers in four Trent trusts, randomised to weekly four-layer compression bandaging in community leg ulcer clinics (120 patients) or usual care at home from the district nursing service (113 patients), followed for 1 year.
cards.result: Ulcers in the clinic group healed sooner over the 12-month follow-up (log rank P = 0.03); at 12 weeks, 34% of clinic-group patients were healed compared with 24% of controls, and the crude initial healing rate ratio was 1.45 (95% CI 1.04 to 2.03). Health status did not differ between groups, and mean total NHS costs were similar (£878.06 per year clinic vs £859.34 control; P = 0.89).
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles the bandage with the clinic: trained nurses, weekly review and a clinic setting all travelled with the four-layer system, and 'usual care' in 1990s district nursing was variable rather than a protocol of no compression — the trial shows the organised compression service beat what patients were actually getting.
cards.source: Morrell CJ et al. Cost effectiveness of community leg ulcer clinics: randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1998. PMID: 9582132. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: O'Brien 2003: four-layer bandaging healed 54% of venous ulcers by 3 months versus 34% on usual care (P = 0.006)
cards.summary: O'Brien 2003: four-layer bandaging healed 54% of venous ulcers by 3 months versus 34% on usual care (P = 0.006)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with economic analysis (community)
cards.people: 200 patients with a venous leg ulcer in a community setting, randomised to four-layer compression bandaging (100 patients) or to continue their usual system of care (100 patients), followed for 12 weeks; analysis by intention to treat.
cards.result: The Kaplan–Meier estimate of healing at 3 months was 54% with four-layer bandaging and 34% in the control group, and four-layer bandaging healed ulcers significantly earlier throughout the 3 months (P = 0.006). Median cost per leg healed was lower with four-layer bandaging (€210 vs €234; P = 0.040). The authors conclude four-layer bandaging was the most effective method of treating venous leg ulcers in a community setting.
cards.watchOut: As in Morrell, the control was each patient's pre-existing usual care rather than a defined no-compression protocol, so the trial measures four-layer bandaging against the real-world alternative of its time — which is the comparison the question asks, but not a placebo-style contrast.
cards.source: O'Brien JF et al. Randomized clinical trial and economic analysis of four-layer compression bandaging for venous ulcers. The British journal of surgery. 2003. PMID: 12854102. cards.headline: Cochrane review 2012: 8 randomised trials directly compared compression with no compression — healing outcomes were better with compression in every one
cards.summary: Cochrane review 2012: 8 randomised trials directly compared compression with no compression — healing outcomes were better with compression in every one
cards.people: Systematic review of 48 randomised controlled trials (4,321 participants) of compression bandages and stockings for venous leg ulcers, including trials whose comparator was no compression (primary dressing alone or a non-compressive bandage).
cards.result: There was evidence from eight randomised trials (reported unpooled) that healing outcomes, including time to healing, are better when patients receive compression compared with no compression. The review also found multi-component systems more effective than single-component systems for complete healing, and concluded: compression increases ulcer healing rates compared with no compression, and multi-component systems containing an elastic bandage appear more effective than mainly inelastic systems.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials were small and at unclear or high risk of bias, and the compression-versus-none trials could not be pooled — the consistency of direction across all eight, plus the two larger pragmatic trials carded above, is what carries the stamp.
cards.source: O'Meara S et al. Compression for venous leg ulcers. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 23152202. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two pragmatic trials and eight direct randomised comparisons all point the same way — multilayer compression heals venous ulcers faster than no compression — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two pragmatic trials and eight direct randomised comparisons all point the same way — multilayer compression heals venous ulcers faster than no compression — LIKELY
cards.people: The carded evidence: two pragmatic randomised trials of four-layer bandaging versus usual care (233 and 200 patients) and one Cochrane review of 48 randomised trials (4,321 participants) including 8 direct compression-versus-no-compression trials. Total carded participants exceed 4,700, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Four-layer bandaging beat usual care on healing in both trials (rate ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.03; and 54% vs 34% healed at 3 months, P = 0.006), and every one of the eight direct randomised comparisons in the Cochrane review favoured compression. PROPOSED LIKELY: multilayer compression bandaging heals venous leg ulcers faster than no compression. Which compression system to use is a separate question, homed on live shelf #1221, and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: 'No compression' in practice means usual care without systematic compression, not a blinded placebo bandage — such a trial cannot be blinded, and none exists; the claim is about real-world care, which is where the question is asked.
cards.source: Synthesis of Morrell CJ et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1998 (PMID: 9582132); O'Brien JF et al. The British journal of surgery. 2003 (PMID: 12854102); O'Meara S et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012 (PMID: 23152202).

shelves.title: Cellulitis route: oral therapy matched intravenous therapy for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate disease — one blinded trial, one route analysis, one Cochrane comparison (duration is live #506)
shelves.question: In adults with uncomplicated cellulitis, is oral antibiotic therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Pharmaceutic · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Canada · Cefazolin · Cephalexin · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Probenecid · Prospective Studies · Soft Tissue Infections
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — for uncomplicated, mild-to-moderate cellulitis, oral therapy performed as well as intravenous therapy in the small route literature; severe cellulitis is not answered here. Live shelf #506 answers the neighbouring duration question (how many days), not route, and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The one double-blind route trial (Dalen 2018) randomised 206 emergency-department patients with uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection to oral cephalexin or intravenous cefazolin plus oral probenecid: failure at 72 hours was 4.2% versus 6.1% and clinical cure at 7 days 100% versus 97.7%. A route analysis extracted from a multicentre cellulitis trial (Williams & Brindle 2020, 323 patients) found route was chosen by severity in practice, yet patients given only oral therapy were more likely to have improved by day 5 and were as likely to be back to normal activities at days 10 and 30. The older Cochrane review of cellulitis interventions (Kilburn 2010, 25 studies, 2,488 participants) found, in the two studies comparing an oral macrolide with intravenous penicillin, that oral therapy could be more effective than intravenous therapy (relative risk 0.85 for the symptom outcome). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral is a reasonable route for uncomplicated cellulitis that is mild to moderate and improving; the evidence base is one modest blinded trial in mixed skin infections, one non-randomised route analysis, and an old heterogeneous review — hence the cap.

cards.headline: Dalen 2018: oral cephalexin was non-inferior to intravenous cefazolin plus probenecid — failure at 72 hours 4.2% versus 6.1%, cure at 7 days 100% versus 97.7%
cards.summary: Dalen 2018: oral cephalexin was non-inferior to intravenous cefazolin plus probenecid — failure at 72 hours 4.2% versus 6.1%, cure at 7 days 100% versus 97.7%
cards.people: 206 patients presenting to two Canadian emergency departments with uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection, randomised double-dummy double-blind 1:1 to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily (104 patients) or intravenous cefazolin 2 g daily plus oral probenecid 1 g daily (102 patients), for up to 7 days.
cards.result: Failure of therapy at 72 hours occurred in 4.2% of the oral cephalexin group and 6.1% of the intravenous cefazolin group (risk difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.7% to 7.6%), meeting the non-inferiority comparison. Clinical cure at 7 days was 100% on cephalexin and 97.7% on cefazolin (risk difference −2.3%, 95% CI −6.7% to 0.8%). The authors conclude cephalexin at appropriate doses is a safe and effective alternative to outpatient parenteral cefazolin for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection.
cards.watchOut: The enrolled population was uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection presenting to an emergency department — predominantly cellulitis-type infection but recorded as skin and soft-tissue infection, not cellulitis alone — and the intravenous regimen was once-daily cefazolin enabled by probenecid, an outpatient-parenteral model rather than inpatient intravenous care.
cards.source: Dalen D et al. Intravenous cefazolin plus oral probenecid versus oral cephalexin for the treatment of skin and soft tissue infections: a double-blind, non-inferiority, randomised controlled trial. Emergency medicine journal : EMJ. 2018. PMID: 29914924. Registry ID: NCT01029782. cards.headline: Williams & Brindle 2020: in 323 cellulitis patients from a multicentre trial, oral-only therapy was at least as good as any intravenous therapy — improvement at day 5 was commoner on oral therapy alone
cards.summary: Williams & Brindle 2020: in 323 cellulitis patients from a multicentre trial, oral-only therapy was at least as good as any intravenous therapy — improvement at day 5 was commoner on oral therapy alone
cards.type: Route analysis extracted from a multicentre trial — route not randomised (Williams & Brindle 2020)
cards.people: 323 patients with antibiotic data extracted from a multicentre clinical trial of antibiotic therapy for cellulitis (NCT01876628); 114 received some intravenous therapy and the remainder oral therapy only. Intravenous therapy was preferred in patients who had received antibiotics before trial entry and in those characterised as more severe (C-reactive protein above 100 mg/L, affected area above 5% of skin surface, or systemic inflammatory response score at least 1).
cards.result: Patients given only oral therapy were more likely to have improved at day 5 than those given at least a single dose of intravenous therapy (P = 0.015), and were as likely to be back to their normal activities at day 10 (P = 0.90) and day 30 (P = 0.86). The authors conclude recovery was not associated with the route of administration for patients with cellulitis of similar severity.
cards.watchOut: Route was chosen by clinicians, not randomised, and sicker patients were channelled to intravenous therapy; that the oral group still did at least as well is reassuring, but this is an observational comparison inside trial data, not a randomised route test.
cards.source: Williams OM, Brindle R. Antibiotic route and duration of therapy for cellulitis: data extracted from a multi-center clinical trial. International journal of antimicrobial agents. 2020. PMID: 32629112. Registry ID: NCT01876628 (the trial from which the data were extracted). cards.headline: Kilburn 2010 Cochrane review: in the two studies comparing an oral macrolide with intravenous penicillin, oral therapy could be more effective than intravenous therapy (relative risk 0.85)
cards.summary: Kilburn 2010 Cochrane review: in the two studies comparing an oral macrolide with intravenous penicillin, oral therapy could be more effective than intravenous therapy (relative risk 0.85)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Kilburn 2010)
cards.people: Cochrane review of 25 randomised studies with 2,488 participants comparing interventions for non-surgically-acquired cellulitis and erysipelas; three trials with 419 people compared macrolides or streptogramins with penicillin antibiotics, two of them using an oral macrolide against intravenous penicillin.
cards.result: Macrolides/streptogramins were more effective than penicillin antibiotics on the primary symptom outcome (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.73–0.97), and in the two studies using oral macrolide against intravenous penicillin, oral therapies could be more effective than intravenous therapies (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.98). The reviewers cautioned that no two trials examined the same drugs, that most recommendations rest on single trials, and that only two studies investigated severe cellulitis.
cards.watchOut: A 2010 review of small, drug-heterogeneous trials: the oral-versus-intravenous signal comes from two studies with particular drugs (oral macrolide versus intravenous penicillin), so it supports the route conclusion generally rather than for any specific antibiotic pair.
cards.source: Kilburn SA et al. Interventions for cellulitis and erysipelas. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010. PMID: 20556757. Registry ID: none in the record.
