cards.headline: Synthesis: for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate cellulitis, oral therapy matched intravenous therapy wherever the route was compared — a thin, older evidence base
cards.summary: Synthesis: for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate cellulitis, oral therapy matched intravenous therapy wherever the route was compared — a thin, older evidence base
cards.people: The carded evidence: one double-blind non-inferiority route trial in uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection (Dalen, 206 patients), one non-randomised route analysis in trial-enrolled cellulitis patients (Williams & Brindle, 323 patients), and one Cochrane review of cellulitis interventions (Kilburn, 25 studies, 2,488 participants).
cards.result: Failure and cure rates on oral therapy were at least as good as on intravenous therapy in the blinded trial (failure 4.2% versus 6.1%; cure 100% versus 97.7%); the route analysis found no recovery advantage for intravenous therapy at days 5, 10 or 30 despite intravenous patients being more severe at baseline; and the Cochrane subgroup comparison favoured oral over intravenous therapy (relative risk 0.85). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral therapy is as effective as intravenous therapy for uncomplicated cellulitis of mild-to-moderate severity. Duration — a different question — is homed on live shelf #506 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here tests severe, necrotising, periorbital or rapidly progressing cellulitis, or patients who cannot absorb oral drugs; the route answer applies to the uncomplicated population the question names.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dalen D et al. Emergency medicine journal. 2018 (PMID: 29914924); Williams OM, Brindle R. International journal of antimicrobial agents. 2020 (PMID: 32629112); Kilburn SA et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010 (PMID: 20556757).

shelves.title: Linezolid vs vancomycin for MRSA complicated skin infection (PARTIAL completion of live #504): equivalent overall, superior in proven MRSA
shelves.question: In adults with complicated skin infection due to MRSA, is linezolid more effective than vancomycin for clinical cure?
shelves.mesh: Acetamides · Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents · Female · Humans · Internationality · Linezolid · Male · Methicillin Resistance · Middle Aged · Oxazolidinones · Skin Diseases, Bacterial · Soft Tissue Infections · Staphylococcal Infections · Staphylococcus aureus · Treatment Outcome · Vancomycin
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #504 already answers linezolid versus vancomycin in MRSA pneumonia; this shelf answers the skin-infection population only, and no pneumonia study is re-carded here. In complicated skin and soft-tissue infection, the two randomised trials point the same way: linezolid is at least as effective as vancomycin overall, and in the patients with proven MRSA in the largest trial it was clearly more effective (clinical cure 88.6% vs 66.9% at test of cure). The second, MRSA-proven trial found similar per-protocol success, with linezolid ahead in the modified intention-to-treat population and on microbiological success at end of treatment, plus shorter hospital stay and intravenous therapy. The pooled analysis of three trials (1,056 patients) found the same pattern — comparable success in diabetic patients, higher success with linezolid in non-diabetic patients, and shorter stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: linezolid is at least as effective as vancomycin for clinical cure of MRSA complicated skin infection, with superiority shown in the proven-MRSA population of the largest trial — held at POSSIBLE because the dedicated MRSA trial's per-protocol analysis was not significant and the clearest superiority figure comes from a pathogen-confirmed subset.

cards.headline: Weigelt 2005: in proven MRSA complicated skin infection, linezolid cured 88.6% vs 66.9% with vancomycin (P<0.001); overall cure was equivalent (92.2% vs 88.5%)
cards.summary: Weigelt 2005: in proven MRSA complicated skin infection, linezolid cured 88.6% vs 66.9% with vancomycin (P<0.001); overall cure was equivalent (92.2% vs 88.5%)
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with complicated skin and soft-tissue infections due to suspected or proven methicillin-resistant gram-positive pathogens (cellulitis, abscesses, infected ulcers, burns <10% body surface), randomised open-label 1:1 to linezolid 600 mg every 12 h intravenously or orally, or vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 h; the proven-MRSA analysis set was 140 linezolid and 145 vancomycin patients.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population, clinical cure at test of cure was 92.2% with linezolid and 88.5% with vancomycin (P=0.057) — equivalent overall. In patients with MRSA infections, linezolid was superior: 124/140 (88.6%) cured versus 97/145 (66.9%) with vancomycin (P<0.001). Drug-related adverse events were reported in similar numbers in both arms.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial, and the superiority figure comes from the pathogen-confirmed MRSA subset rather than the whole randomised population, where the drugs were equivalent — the subset is, however, exactly the population this shelf's question asks about.

randomised controlled trial (weigelt 2005) hospitalised adults with complicated skin and soft-tissue infections due to suspected or proven methicillin-resistant gram-positive pathogens (cellulitis, abscesses, infected ulcers, burns <10% body surface), randomised open-label 1:1 to linezolid 600 mg every 12 h intravenously or orally, or vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 h; the proven-mrsa analysis set was 140 linezolid and 145 vancomycin patients. in the intention-to-treat population, clinical cure at test of cure was 92.2% with linezolid and 88.5% with vancomycin (p=0.057) — equivalent overall. in patients with mrsa infections, linezolid was superior: 124/140 (88.6%) cured versus 97/145 (66.9%) with vancomycin (p<0.001). drug-related adverse events were reported in similar numbers in both arms. open-label trial, and the superiority figure comes from the pathogen-confirmed mrsa subset rather than the whole randomised population, where the drugs were equivalent — the subset is, however, exactly the population this shelf's question asks about. weigelt j et al. linezolid versus vancomycin in treatment of complicated skin and soft tissue infections. antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2005. pmid: 15917519. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acetamides · adult · aged · anti-infective agents · female · humans · internationality · linezolid · male · methicillin resistance · middle aged · oxazolidinones · skin diseases, bacterial · soft tissue infections · staphylococcal infections · staphylococcus aureus · treatment outcome · vancomycin

cards.headline: Itani 2010: in proven MRSA complicated skin infection, per-protocol success was similar, but linezolid was ahead in the modified intention-to-treat population and on end-of-treatment microbiological success
cards.summary: Itani 2010: in proven MRSA complicated skin infection, per-protocol success was similar, but linezolid was ahead in the modified intention-to-treat population and on end-of-treatment microbiological success
cards.people: Adults with proven MRSA complicated skin and soft-tissue infection randomised open-label to oral or intravenous linezolid or intravenous vancomycin (total enrolment is not printed in the record — N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Clinical success was similar in the per-protocol population (P=.249), significantly higher with linezolid in the modified intent-to-treat population (P=.048), and microbiological success was higher for linezolid at end of treatment (P<.001) and similar at end of study (P=.127). Linezolid patients had a significantly shorter length of stay and duration of intravenous therapy. Both agents were well tolerated, with adverse events matching each drug's established profile.
cards.watchOut: The per-protocol analysis — usually the more conservative test in a non-inferiority-style comparison — was not significant; the linezolid advantage rests on the modified intention-to-treat and end-of-treatment microbiological analyses, and the abstract reports P values without the underlying success percentages.

cards.headline: Lipsky 2011 (pooled, 1,056 patients): clinical success comparable in diabetic patients (74% vs 71%) but higher with linezolid in non-diabetic patients (90% vs 81%), with shorter stay on linezolid
cards.summary: Lipsky 2011 (pooled, 1,056 patients): clinical success comparable in diabetic patients (74% vs 71%) but higher with linezolid in non-diabetic patients (90% vs 81%), with shorter stay on linezolid
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised trials (Lipsky 2011)
cards.people: Pooled data from three prospective randomised trials in which 1,056 patients with MRSA complicated skin and skin-structure infection were randomised to linezolid (intravenous or oral) or vancomycin (intravenous) every 12 h for 7–28 days; 349 patients had diabetes and 707 did not.
cards.result: Among diabetic patients, clinical success was comparable (74% linezolid vs 71% vancomycin) and microbiological success similar (60% vs 54%). Among non-diabetic patients, clinical success (90% vs 81%) and microbiological success (78% vs 65%) were higher with linezolid. Adjusted mean length of stay was shorter with linezolid in both diabetic (9.5 vs 11.7 days; p=0.03) and non-diabetic (7.6 vs 8.9 days; p=0.02) patients; drug-related adverse-event rates were comparable.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-analysis of trials that include the two trials carded above, so it is corroboration rather than a fully independent third trial; its distinctive contribution is the diabetes split, where the linezolid advantage disappears.

cards.headline: Synthesis: linezolid is at least vancomycin's equal for MRSA skin infection, and better in the proven-MRSA analysis of the largest trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: linezolid is at least vancomycin's equal for MRSA skin infection, and better in the proven-MRSA analysis of the largest trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials in complicated skin and soft-tissue infection (Weigelt 2005; Itani 2010) and a pooled analysis of three trials totalling 1,056 randomised patients (Lipsky 2011). The MRSA pneumonia question is homed on live shelf #504 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Overall cure was equivalent in Weigelt (92.2% vs 88.5%), but in proven MRSA infection linezolid cured 88.6% vs 66.9% (P<0.001). Itani found similar per-protocol success with linezolid ahead on modified intention-to-treat success (P=.048) and end-of-treatment microbiological success (P<.001), with shorter stay and intravenous duration. The pooled analysis found comparable success in diabetic patients (74% vs 71%) and higher success with linezolid in non-diabetic patients (90% vs 81%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): more effective in proven-MRSA analyses, at least as effective overall.
cards.watchOut: Both trials were open-label, and vancomycin dosing in the 2005 trial was a fixed 1 g twice daily rather than modern weight- and level-guided dosing — part of the measured gap may belong to the comparator's dosing, not the drugs.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weigelt J et al. Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2005 (PMID: 15917519); Itani KM et al. American journal of surgery. 2010 (PMID: 20227056); Lipsky BA et al. International journal of infectious diseases. 2011 (PMID: 21134775).

shelves.title: Risankizumab for plaque psoriasis: PASI 90 in 77% versus 40% on ustekinumab in the phase 2 head-to-head, superiority over adalimumab (IMMvent) and secukinumab (IMMerge) in phase 3 — the UltIMMa trials versus ustekinumab and placebo are carded at live shelf #377
shelves.question: In adults with plaque psoriasis, does risankizumab clear skin better than ustekinumab or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dermatologic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Interleukin-12/antagonists & inhibitors · Interleukin-23/antagonists & inhibitors · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Psoriasis/classification,drug therapy · Scalp/pathology · Severity of Illness Index · Ustekinumab/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). FLAG — precedent (b) build, stated prominently: the anchor UltIMMa-1/UltIMMa-2 report (Gordon 2018, PMID 30097359) is already carded as Card 1 of live shelf #377, the class-efficacy shelf for plaque-psoriasis biologics, whose question is class-wide (how completely modern biologics clear skin, and at what safety cost). This pack's question is the narrower drug-specific head-to-head — does risankizumab beat ustekinumab or placebo — and at least three free (ungated) reports answer it, so the pack is built on those free reports with the UltIMMa home cross-pointed and PMID 30097359 kept out of every card source line; no UltIMMa figures are re-printed here. On the free reports: the direct ustekinumab comparison is Papp 2017 (phase 2, 166 patients): PASI 90 at week 12 in 77% on pooled 90/180 mg risankizumab versus 40% on ustekinumab, and complete clearance (PASI 100) in 45% versus 18%. Two further phase 3 head-to-heads against other proven biologics point the same way: IMMvent versus adalimumab (PASI 90 72% vs 47% at week 16; switching adalimumab intermediate responders to risankizumab beat continuing adalimumab at week 44, 66% vs 21%) and IMMerge versus secukinumab (PASI 90 noninferior at week 16 and superior at week 52, 86.6% vs 57.1%). Adverse-event frequencies were similar across arms in each trial. Risankizumab's other homes are different diseases and are not this question: Crohn's disease (live #771 and pack #5885), ulcerative colitis (pack #3576) and psoriatic arthritis (pack #5450). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent superiority over active comparators across three randomised head-to-head programmes, with the placebo contrast housed at live #377.

cards.headline: Papp 2017 (phase 2 head-to-head): PASI 90 at week 12 in 77% on risankizumab (90/180 mg pooled) versus 40% on ustekinumab; PASI 100 in 45% versus 18%
cards.summary: Papp 2017 (phase 2 head-to-head): PASI 90 at week 12 in 77% on risankizumab (90/180 mg pooled) versus 40% on ustekinumab; PASI 100 in 45% versus 18%
cards.people: 166 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised double-blind to risankizumab (a single 18 mg dose, or 90 mg or 180 mg at weeks 0, 4 and 16) or ustekinumab (45 or 90 mg by weight at weeks 0, 4 and 16). The primary endpoint was PASI 90 at week 12.
cards.result: PASI 90 was achieved by 77% (64 of 83) in the pooled 90 mg and 180 mg risankizumab groups versus 40% (16 of 40) on ustekinumab (P < 0.001); PASI 100 was achieved by 45% versus 18%. Efficacy was generally maintained up to 20 weeks after the final 90/180 mg dose. Serious adverse events occurred in 12% (18 mg group), 15% (90 mg group) and 8% (ustekinumab group), with none in the 180 mg group; the authors note the trial was not large or long enough for safety conclusions.
cards.watchOut: A dose-ranging phase 2 trial (166 patients) using 90/180 mg regimens, not the licensed 150 mg dose; the phase 3 ustekinumab comparison at the licensed dose is the UltIMMa pair, carded at live shelf #377 and cross-pointed in this pack's balance rather than re-carded.
cards.source: Papp KA et al. Risankizumab versus Ustekinumab for Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28423301. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02054481. cards.headline: Reich 2019 (IMMvent): PASI 90 at week 16 in 72% on risankizumab versus 47% on adalimumab; switching adalimumab intermediate responders to risankizumab beat staying on adalimumab (66% vs 21% at week 44)
cards.summary: Reich 2019 (IMMvent): PASI 90 at week 16 in 72% on risankizumab versus 47% on adalimumab; switching adalimumab intermediate responders to risankizumab beat staying on adalimumab (66% vs 21% at week 44)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3, active-comparator (IMMvent; Reich 2019)
cards.people: 605 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised 1:1 double-blind to risankizumab 150 mg (weeks 0 and 4) or adalimumab (80 mg then 40 mg every other week) for 16 weeks; adalimumab intermediate responders were then re-randomised to continue adalimumab or switch to risankizumab for weeks 16–44.
cards.result: At week 16, PASI 90 was achieved by 218 of 301 patients (72%) on risankizumab versus 144 of 304 (47%) on adalimumab (adjusted absolute difference 24.9 percentage points, 95% CI 17.5 to 32.4; p < 0.0001), and sPGA 0 or 1 by 84% versus 60% (the record prints 252 patients in the risankizumab group for this endpoint). In part B, PASI 90 at week 44 was achieved by 35 of 53 (66%) switched to risankizumab versus 12 of 56 (21%) continuing adalimumab (adjusted difference 45.0 points; p < 0.0001). Adverse events in part A: 56% on risankizumab versus 57% on adalimumab.
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is adalimumab, not ustekinumab or placebo — it corroborates risankizumab's relative skin-clearance strength against a second proven biologic. Part B's switch comparison rests on 109 re-randomised intermediate responders.
cards.source: Reich K et al. Risankizumab compared with adalimumab in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (IMMvent): a randomised, double-blind, active-comparator-controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 31280967. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02694523. cards.headline: Warren 2021 (IMMerge): risankizumab noninferior to secukinumab at week 16 and superior at week 52 — PASI 90 in 86.6% versus 57.1%
cards.summary: Warren 2021 (IMMerge): risankizumab noninferior to secukinumab at week 16 and superior at week 52 — PASI 90 in 86.6% versus 57.1%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3, open-label with blinded efficacy assessment (IMMerge; Warren 2021)
cards.people: 327 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis randomised 1:1 in an open-label, efficacy-assessor-blinded phase 3 trial to risankizumab 150 mg (n = 164) or secukinumab 300 mg (n = 163) over 52 weeks.
cards.result: PASI 90 at week 16: 73.8% on risankizumab versus 65.6% on secukinumab (difference 8.2 points, 96.25% CI −2.2 to 18.6), meeting the 12% noninferiority margin. PASI 90 at week 52: 86.6% versus 57.1% (difference 29.8 points, 95% CI 20.8 to 38.8; P < 0.001), meeting the superiority endpoint; all week-52 secondary endpoints (PASI 100, sPGA 0 or 1, PASI 75) also favoured risankizumab (P < 0.001). No new safety concerns were identified, with less frequent dosing on risankizumab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (assessors blinded), and again the comparator is a third biologic (secukinumab), not ustekinumab or placebo. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields, so none is printed.
cards.source: Warren RB et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: risankizumab clears skin better than every active comparator it has faced head-to-head — LIKELY (benefit); the placebo and phase 3 ustekinumab data home at live #377
cards.summary: Synthesis: risankizumab clears skin better than every active comparator it has faced head-to-head — LIKELY (benefit); the placebo and phase 3 ustekinumab data home at live #377
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis across the phase 2 ustekinumab trial (166 patients), IMMvent (605) and IMMerge (327), with the UltIMMa replicate pair carded at live shelf #377.
cards.result: Three randomised head-to-head programmes, three wins on PASI 90 — against ustekinumab (phase 2), adalimumab and secukinumab (phase 3) — with adverse-event rates similar to comparators. The stamp grades skin clearance only; these trials make no mortality or long-term safety claims.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF in diabetic macular oedema: no vision advantage — similar gains, far fewer injections, more cataract and raised pressure
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic macular oedema, does a dexamethasone implant improve vision compared with anti-VEGF therapy (rather than sham)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Bevacizumab · Delayed-Action Preparations/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Diabetic Retinopathy/drug therapy,physiopathology · Drug Implants · Female · Humans · Intravitreal Injections · Macula Lutea/pathology · Macular Edema/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Regression Analysis · Surveys and Questionnaires · Visual Acuity/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. The head-to-head answer is no vision advantage. BEVORDEX (Gillies 2014; 88 eyes) found 10-or-more-letter gains in 41% of implant eyes versus 40% of bevacizumab eyes (P = 0.83), with 11% of implant eyes losing 10 or more letters (mostly cataract) versus none on bevacizumab; the implant thinned the macula more (−187 vs −122 µm) with a third of the injections (2.7 vs 8.6). DRCR Protocol U (Maturi 2018) found adding the implant to ranibizumab in persistent oedema made no difference to vision at 24 weeks (the treatment made no difference; −0.5 letters) despite greater thinning, with pressure rises in 29% versus 0%. Cochrane (Rittiphairoj 2020; 2 trials, 451 eyes) found slightly less acuity improvement with the implant than anti-VEGF therapy and more than 4-fold relative increases in cataract progression and pressure-lowering treatment. Implant and company are named exactly as published (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc.) under the clarification exception. Implant versus sham is home pack #4021; this shelf is the anti-VEGF comparison it does not cover.

cards.headline: BEVORDEX (Gillies 2014): dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc.) matched bevacizumab on vision gains at 12 months — 41% versus 40% of eyes gained 10 or more letters — with fewer injections but more vision loss, mainly from cataract
cards.summary: BEVORDEX (Gillies 2014): dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc.) matched bevacizumab on vision gains at 12 months — 41% versus 40% of eyes gained 10 or more letters — with fewer injections but more vision loss, mainly from cataract
cards.type: Randomised head-to-head trial, BEVORDEX 12-month report (Gillies 2014) — 88 eyes of 61 patients; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01298076
cards.people: 88 eyes of 61 patients with centre-involving diabetic macular oedema in a phase 2, multicentre, randomised, single-masked head-to-head trial: 42 eyes received bevacizumab (Avastin; Genentech) every 4 weeks and 46 eyes received the dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc., Irvine, CA) every 16 weeks, both as needed. Primary outcome: proportion of eyes improving by 10 or more letters at 12 months. Product and company names are given exactly as published, under the clarification exception for a named implant product.
cards.result: Improvement of 10 or more letters occurred in 19 of 46 dexamethasone-implant eyes (41%) versus 17 of 42 bevacizumab eyes (40%; P = 0.83) — the implant made no difference to the chance of a 10-letter gain. No bevacizumab eye lost 10 or more letters, whereas 5 of 46 implant eyes (11%) did, mostly because of cataract. Mean central macular thickness fell more with the implant (−187 µm vs −122 µm; P = 0.015), and implant eyes needed far fewer injections (mean 2.7 vs 8.6). Vision-related quality-of-life scores improved in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 2 trial of 88 eyes, single-masked, with both eyes of some patients enrolled: it can show the two treatments are in the same range, not that they are equivalent, and its cataract signal accrues with time — the 24-month and 5-year BEVORDEX follow-ups exist and are not carded here.
cards.source: Gillies MC et al. A randomized clinical trial of intravitreal bevacizumab versus intravitreal dexamethasone for diabetic macular edema: the BEVORDEX study. Ophthalmology. 2014. PMID: 25155371. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01298076. cards.headline: DRCR Retina Network Protocol U (Maturi 2018): adding a dexamethasone implant to continued ranibizumab in persistent diabetic macular oedema made no difference to vision at 24 weeks (the treatment made no difference) — while thinning the retina more and raising eye pressure
cards.summary: DRCR Retina Network Protocol U (Maturi 2018): adding a dexamethasone implant to continued ranibizumab in persistent diabetic macular oedema made no difference to vision at 24 weeks (the treatment made no difference) — while thinning the retina more and raising eye pressure
cards.type: Randomised trial, DRCR Retina Network Protocol U (Maturi 2018) — 129 eyes of 116 patients; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01945866
cards.people: 129 eyes from 116 adults with persistent diabetic macular oedema despite anti-VEGF therapy, in a phase 2 multicentre randomised trial at 40 US sites: after a run-in of 3 monthly ranibizumab injections, eyes were randomised to continued ranibizumab plus a 700 µg dexamethasone implant (65 eyes) or continued ranibizumab plus sham (64 eyes). Primary outcome: change in visual-acuity letter score at 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean visual-acuity improvement was 2.7 letters with the added implant versus 3.0 letters with ranibizumab alone (adjusted difference −0.5 letters, 95% CI −3.6 to 2.5; P = .73) — the treatment made no difference to vision. Retinal thickness fell more with the implant (central subfield thickness −110 µm vs −62 µm; adjusted difference −52 µm, P < .001), but 19 eyes (29%) in the combination group had raised intraocular pressure or started pressure-lowering drops, versus 0 in the ranibizumab-only group (P < .001).
cards.watchOut: This is an add-on question in anti-VEGF–persistent oedema, not a first-line head-to-head: it shows steroid anatomy gains do not convert into vision gains in this refractory population, and 24 weeks is short for cataract — the implant's main long-term cost — to declare itself.
cards.source: Maturi RK et al. Effect of Adding Dexamethasone to Continued Ranibizumab Treatment in Patients With Persistent Diabetic Macular Edema: A DRCR Network Phase 2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 29127949. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01945866. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Rittiphairoj 2020): across 2 trials (451 eyes), vision improved slightly less with the dexamethasone implant than with anti-VEGF therapy, and cataract progression and pressure-lowering treatment were each more than 4 times as common with the implant (relative figures)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Rittiphairoj 2020): across 2 trials (451 eyes), vision improved slightly less with the dexamethasone implant than with anti-VEGF therapy, and cataract progression and pressure-lowering treatment were each more than 4 times as common with the implant (relative figures)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane, Rittiphairoj 2020) — dexamethasone-vs-anti-VEGF stratum: 2 trials, 451 eyes
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of intravitreal steroids for diabetic macular oedema: 10 trials, 4,348 participants, 4,505 eyes. The dexamethasone-implant-versus-anti-VEGF comparison rests on 2 trials (451 eyes) comparing the 0.7 mg implant with bevacizumab or ranibizumab.
cards.result: At 12 months, visual acuity improved slightly less with dexamethasone than with anti-VEGF therapy (mean difference 0.07 logMAR, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.09; moderate-certainty evidence) — a relative-scale difference of roughly 3–4 letters. The chance of gaining 3 or more lines was inconsistent between the two trials (relative risk 0.99 against bevacizumab in the 88-eye trial; 0.50 against ranibizumab in the 432-participant trial; low certainty). Cataract progression and the need for intraocular-pressure–lowering medication each rose more than 4-fold with the implant compared with anti-VEGF therapy (relative risks; moderate-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: The pooled 'slightly less vision' estimate leans on one larger ranibizumab trial that is not separately carded here; most trials in the review carried unclear or high risk of bias, and steroid-versus-sham results elsewhere in the review (home pack #4021's question) must not be read as evidence against anti-VEGF therapy.
cards.source: Rittiphairoj T et al. Intravitreal steroids for macular edema in diabetes. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 33206392. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01298076, NCT01492400, NCT00367133, NCT00344968, NCT00682539, NCT00168337, NCT00168389, NCT00167518. cards.headline: Synthesis: against anti-VEGF therapy the implant does not improve vision more — gains are similar or slightly smaller, injections are far fewer, and cataract and raised pressure are the price
cards.summary: Synthesis: against anti-VEGF therapy the implant does not improve vision more — gains are similar or slightly smaller, injections are far fewer, and cataract and raised pressure are the price
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct head-to-head trial (BEVORDEX, 88 eyes), one add-on trial in persistent oedema (DRCR Protocol U, 129 eyes), and the Cochrane synthesis of the 2 head-to-head trials (451 eyes).
cards.result: No carded source shows a vision advantage for the dexamethasone implant over anti-VEGF therapy: BEVORDEX found identical 10-letter gain rates (41% vs 40%), Protocol U found adding the implant made no difference to vision (the treatment made no difference; −0.5 letters, CI spanning zero), and Cochrane found slightly less acuity improvement with the implant at 12 months. The implant consistently wins on anatomy (greater thickness reduction) and treatment burden (2.7 vs 8.6 injections in BEVORDEX) and consistently loses on cataract and intraocular pressure. Home pack #4021 covers implant versus sham; this shelf is the anti-VEGF head-to-head slice it does not cover.
cards.watchOut: The head-to-head base is one small phase 2 trial plus one larger trial visible only through the Cochrane pool; pseudophakic eyes (no lens left to cataract) may reasonably read this balance differently, and no carded trial was powered for rare harms such as endophthalmitis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gillies MC et al. Ophthalmology. 2014 (PMID: 25155371); Maturi RK et al. JAMA ophthalmology. 2018 (PMID: 29127949); Rittiphairoj T et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020 (PMID: 33206392). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Tezepelumab for nasal polyps (WAYPOINT): polyp score down 2.07 points and congestion down 1.03 versus placebo at 52 weeks — one strongly positive phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, does tezepelumab improve polyp size and nasal symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Injections, Subcutaneous · Nasal Polyps/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy,surgery · Rhinosinusitis/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy,surgery · Severity of Illness Index · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Otorhinolaryngologic Surgical Procedures/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome · Olfaction Disorders/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology,surgery · Endoscopy/statistics & numerical data · Sino-Nasal Outcome Test
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme. WAYPOINT (Lipworth 2025; 408 adults with severe, uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps) found tezepelumab 210 mg every 4 weeks beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints at 52 weeks: total nasal-polyp score −2.07 (95% CI −2.39 to −1.74) and nasal-congestion score −1.03 (95% CI −1.20 to −0.86), with significant gains in smell, SNOT-22 (−27.26), Lund-Mackay score (−5.72) and total symptom score, and far fewer indications for polyp surgery (0.5% vs 22.1%) or systemic glucocorticoids (5.2% vs 18.3%). The NAVIGATOR asthma trial's polyp subgroup (Laidlaw 2023) showed concordant SNOT-22 improvement (−10.58 at week 52). A 2025 review confirms WAYPOINT is the only dedicated trial and the drug was not yet approved for this indication. Home live shelf #375 is the biologics class shelf (dupilumab largest, omalizumab named); tezepelumab is not in its question and WAYPOINT postdates it.

cards.headline: WAYPOINT (Lipworth 2025): tezepelumab cut the nasal-polyp score by 2.07 points more than placebo at 52 weeks and nasal congestion by 1.03 points — with polyp surgery indicated in 0.5% versus 22.1%
cards.summary: WAYPOINT (Lipworth 2025): tezepelumab cut the nasal-polyp score by 2.07 points more than placebo at 52 weeks and nasal congestion by 1.03 points — with polyp surgery indicated in 0.5% versus 22.1%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, WAYPOINT (Lipworth 2025) — N = 408; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04851964
cards.people: 408 adults with physician-diagnosed, symptomatic, severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps were randomised to standard care plus tezepelumab 210 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (203 patients) or placebo (205 patients) for 52 weeks. Coprimary endpoints: change in total nasal-polyp score (0–8 across both nostrils) and mean nasal-congestion score (0–3) at week 52. This is the WAYPOINT phase 3 trial, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04851964.
cards.result: At week 52, tezepelumab improved the total nasal-polyp score by a mean difference of −2.07 versus placebo (95% CI −2.39 to −1.74) and the nasal-congestion score by −1.03 (95% CI −1.20 to −0.86; P < 0.001 for both). Loss-of-smell score (−1.00), SNOT-22 total score (−27.26), Lund-Mackay CT score (−5.72) and total symptom score (−6.89) all improved significantly (P < 0.001 for all). Surgery for nasal polyps was indicated in 0.5% on tezepelumab versus 22.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.02, a relative figure), and systemic glucocorticoid use was 5.2% versus 18.3% (hazard ratio 0.12, a relative figure).
cards.watchOut: One trial, one programme: every number on this card comes from a single sponsor-run phase 3 study in severe, uncontrolled disease on background standard care — the effects cannot be read across to milder polyps, and there is no head-to-head against the established biologics on home shelf #375.
cards.source: Lipworth BJ et al. Tezepelumab in Adults with Severe Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40106374. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04851964. p < 0.001 for both). loss-of-smell score (−1.00), snot-22 total score (−27.26), lund-mackay ct score (−5.72) and total symptom score (−6.89) all improved significantly (p < 0.001 for all). surgery for nasal polyps was indicated in 0.5% on tezepelumab versus 22.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.02, a relative figure), and systemic glucocorticoid use was 5.2% versus 18.3% (hazard ratio 0.12, a relative figure). one trial, one programme: every number on this card comes from a single sponsor-run phase 3 study in severe, uncontrolled disease on background standard care — the effects cannot be read across to milder polyps, and there is no head-to-head against the established biologics on home shelf #375. lipworth bj et al. tezepelumab in adults with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. the new england journal of medicine. 2025. pmid: 40106374. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct04851964. mesh: adult · female · humans · male · middle aged · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · chronic disease/drug therapy · double-blind method · injections, subcutaneous · nasal polyps/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy,surgery · rhinosinusitis/complications,diagnosis,drug therapy,surgery · severity of illness index · glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · otorhinolaryngologic surgical procedures/statistics & numerical data · treatment outcome · olfaction disorders/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology,surgery · endoscopy/statistics & numerical data · sino-nasal outcome test

cards.headline: NAVIGATOR sinonasal analysis (Laidlaw 2023): in severe asthma patients who also had nasal polyps, tezepelumab improved SNOT-22 scores by about 10.6 points more than placebo at 52 weeks
cards.summary: NAVIGATOR sinonasal analysis (Laidlaw 2023): in severe asthma patients who also had nasal polyps, tezepelumab improved SNOT-22 scores by about 10.6 points more than placebo at 52 weeks
cards.type: Prespecified exploratory subgroup analysis of a randomised asthma trial, NAVIGATOR (Laidlaw 2023) — polyp subgroup n = 118 of 1,059
cards.people: Prespecified exploratory analysis of the phase 3 NAVIGATOR asthma trial (1,059 patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma randomised to tezepelumab 210 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks), examining the subgroup with nasal polyps in the 2 years before randomisation (118 patients) for sinonasal outcomes, including the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22).
cards.result: In patients with nasal polyps, tezepelumab reduced SNOT-22 total scores versus placebo by a least-squares mean difference of −12.57 points at week 28 (95% CI −19.40 to −5.73) and −10.58 points at week 52 (95% CI −17.75 to −3.41). Asthma exacerbation rates fell by 85% (relative figure) in the polyp subgroup. The authors describe clinically meaningful improvements in sino-nasal symptoms in severe asthma with comorbid polyps.
cards.watchOut: An asthma trial's polyp subgroup, not a rhinosinusitis trial: polyp size was not an endpoint, entry required severe asthma rather than severe sinus disease, and the record for this report carries no MeSH list (see source line) — supportive context for WAYPOINT, not independent confirmation of polyp shrinkage. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Review (Priessnitz 2025): tezepelumab is a promising but still investigational agent for nasal polyps — WAYPOINT is its only dedicated trial, and it was not approved for this indication at the time of the review
cards.summary: Review (Priessnitz 2025): tezepelumab is a promising but still investigational agent for nasal polyps — WAYPOINT is its only dedicated trial, and it was not approved for this indication at the time of the review
cards.people: Narrative review of the efficacy and safety of tezepelumab in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, covering the phase 3 WAYPOINT trial, post hoc NAVIGATOR sinonasal analyses, and the drug's type 2 inflammation biomarker effects.
cards.result: The review reports WAYPOINT's polyp-score reduction (−2.07), congestion reduction (−1.03) and SNOT-22 improvement, and a 98% relative reduction in the need for endoscopic sinus surgery versus placebo, alongside NAVIGATOR post hoc SNOT-22 improvements. It notes a favourable safety profile without increased serious infection or hypersensitivity, states plainly that tezepelumab was not approved for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps at the time of writing, and identifies ongoing trials (including ESSENCE) as needed to clarify long-term efficacy, safety and positioning relative to existing monoclonal antibodies.
cards.watchOut: A review adds interpretation, not patients: its numbers are WAYPOINT's and NAVIGATOR's restated, so this shelf's entire primary evidence remains the single WAYPOINT trial — which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Priessnitz J et al. Evaluating the efficacy and safety of tezepelumab in the treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Immunotherapy. 2025. PMID: 41084787. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large, strongly positive phase 3 trial (WAYPOINT) — tezepelumab shrinks polyps and relieves congestion versus placebo in severe disease; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large, strongly positive phase 3 trial (WAYPOINT) — tezepelumab shrinks polyps and relieves congestion versus placebo in severe disease; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: the WAYPOINT randomised trial (408 patients), a supportive sinonasal subgroup analysis from the NAVIGATOR asthma trial (118 patients with polyps), and a 2025 narrative review confirming no second dedicated trial exists yet.
cards.result: WAYPOINT met both coprimary endpoints decisively at 52 weeks (polyp score −2.07 and congestion −1.03 versus placebo, both P < 0.001), with parallel gains in smell, SNOT-22, CT score and symptom score, and far fewer decisions to operate (0.5% vs 22.1%) or to use systemic steroids (5.2% vs 18.3%). NAVIGATOR's polyp subgroup moved in the same direction on symptoms. Home live shelf #375 covers the biologics class (dupilumab largest, omalizumab named); tezepelumab is not in its question and WAYPOINT (2025) postdates it — this shelf is that uncovered slice, with no cross-trial ranking against dupilumab implied.
cards.watchOut: Single-programme evidence: replication, long-term safety in sinus disease, and any comparison with established biologics are all still missing; relative hazard ratios for surgery and steroid use describe large relative effects on outcomes whose absolute rates are printed on the card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lipworth BJ et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40106374); Laidlaw TM et al. Journal of asthma and allergy. 2023 (PMID: 37692126); Priessnitz J et al. Immunotherapy. 2025 (PMID: 41084787). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty after the first treatment wears off: pressure falls again in cohort studies — observational evidence only, no randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma whose first selective laser trabeculoplasty worked and then wore off, does repeating the laser lower pressure again?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Exfoliation Syndrome/physiopathology,surgery · Female · Glaucoma, Open-Angle/physiopathology,surgery · Humans · Intraocular Pressure/physiology · Laser Therapy · Male · Reoperation · Retrospective Studies · Tonometry, Ocular · Trabeculectomy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only. Four retrospective cohorts agree that repeating 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) after a first successful treatment has worn off lowers intraocular pressure again: Hong 2009 (44 eyes) found a smaller reduction than the first treatment at 1–3 months (−2.9 vs −5.0 mm Hg) but no significant difference at other time points or in success rates; Avery 2013 (42 eyes) found no significant difference in reduction or success and significantly longer benefit from the repeat; Khouri 2014 found significant reductions sustained to 24 months (29% of eyes over 20% at 2 years). No randomised trial exists, retreatment was chosen clinically in every cohort, and concurrent drops were not controlled — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the evidence is labelled observational on every card. Live shelf #609 asks laser-first versus drops (LiGHT) — a different question; repeat treatment is not its question.

cards.headline: Hong 2009: repeat 360-degree SLT lowered pressure again after a first successful treatment wore off — by less than the first treatment at 1–3 months (−2.9 vs −5.0 mm Hg), with no significant difference at the other time points
cards.summary: Hong 2009: repeat 360-degree SLT lowered pressure again after a first successful treatment wore off — by less than the first treatment at 1–3 months (−2.9 vs −5.0 mm Hg), with no significant difference at the other time points
cards.people: Retrospective chart review (observational): 44 eyes of 35 patients aged 18 or over with open-angle glaucoma (primary open-angle, pseudoexfoliation or pigmentary), uncontrolled on maximum tolerable medical therapy, whose initial 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT1) was successful for at least 6 months, then lost efficacy and was followed by repeat 360-degree SLT (SLT2). Prior argon laser trabeculoplasty or glaucoma surgery excluded.
cards.result: Intraocular pressure fell after both treatments. The reduction was significantly smaller after repeat treatment at 1–3 months (average −2.9 mm Hg after SLT2 vs −5.0 mm Hg after SLT1, P=0.01), with no statistically significant difference at 1–4 weeks or 5–8 months. Using success as at least a 20% reduction from peak pressure, success rates for SLT1 and SLT2 were not significantly different, and timing of the repeat (6–12 months vs 12 months or more after SLT1) made no significant difference. The authors conclude repeat 360-degree SLT may be safe and effective after an initially successful treatment has failed, from as early as 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and uncontrolled: eyes were selected for retreatment clinically, concurrent drops were not controlled, and regression to the mean cannot be excluded — hence the observational cap on the stamp.
cards.source: Observational cohort (retrospective chart review) | Hong BK et al. Repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty. J Glaucoma. 2009. PMID: 19295367. Registry ID: none in the record (observational, pre-registration era practice). cards.headline: Avery 2013: repeat primary SLT matched the first treatment on pressure reduction, success rate — and lasted significantly longer
cards.summary: Avery 2013: repeat primary SLT matched the first treatment on pressure reduction, success rate — and lasted significantly longer
cards.people: Retrospective study (observational): 42 eyes of 42 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma. All had primary SLT (40–50 shots over 360 degrees); SLT was repeated in all patients after failure to maintain target intraocular pressure. Success was a pressure reduction of at least 20% and below an individually determined target.
cards.result: No significant difference between initial and repeat treatments was found for mean reduction in intraocular pressure, success rate, or (on the primary comparison) duration of success; survival analysis found significantly longer benefit for repeat treatment compared with initial treatment (P<0.01). The authors conclude repeat SLT has similar efficacy to primary SLT for pressure reduction and success rates, with a longer duration of treatment success.
cards.watchOut: A single retrospective series; 'no significant difference' in a 42-eye cohort is not proof of equivalence, and the longer repeat benefit comes from one survival analysis.
cards.source: Observational cohort (retrospective) | Avery N et al. Repeatability of primary selective laser trabeculoplasty in patients with primary open-angle glaucoma. Int Ophthalmol. 2013. PMID: 23371484. Registry ID: none in the record (observational). cards.headline: Khouri 2014 (long-term cohort): repeat SLT kept pressure significantly below baseline out to 24 months, with 29% of eyes achieving over 20% reduction at 2 years
cards.summary: Khouri 2014 (long-term cohort): repeat SLT kept pressure significantly below baseline out to 24 months, with 29% of eyes achieving over 20% reduction at 2 years
cards.people: Single-centre retrospective review (observational): 45 eyes of 25 subjects (mean age 73 ± 9 years) with open-angle glaucoma undergoing repeat SLT, at a mean interval of 28.3 ± 12.7 months after the initial treatment. Eyes with prior argon laser trabeculoplasty or incisional surgery excluded.
cards.result: Mean intraocular pressure reductions after repeat SLT were statistically significant versus baseline at 1, 4, 8, 12, 18 and 24 months. Reductions after first and repeat SLT were comparable at most time points except 4, 8 and 12 months, when the initial treatment had yielded significantly greater reductions. At 24 months, 29% of eyes achieved a reduction over 20% and 39% at least 15% after repeat SLT, versus 36% and 54% after initial treatment (P>0.05).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single centre, 25 subjects contributing 45 eyes (eyes are not independent); the record for this paper carries no MeSH list — see the fallback note on the source line.
cards.source: Observational cohort (retrospective) | Khouri AS et al. Long term efficacy of repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty. J Ophthalmic Vis Res. 2014. PMID: 25709769. Registry ID: none in the record (observational). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Khouri 2014 (modest-response cohort): eyes that responded only modestly to a first SLT succeeded after repeat SLT about as often as initial strong responders (37% vs 52%, not significant)
cards.summary: Khouri 2014 (modest-response cohort): eyes that responded only modestly to a first SLT succeeded after repeat SLT about as often as initial strong responders (37% vs 52%, not significant)
cards.people: Retrospective chart review (observational): 51 eyes receiving initial 360-degree SLT (SLT1) and subsequent SLT (SLT2), 2003–2011, at a large academic ophthalmology practice. Successful response was a 12-month mean pressure reduction of at least 20%; modest response was under 20%.
cards.result: Pressure fell significantly from baseline after both SLT1 and SLT2. The proportion succeeding after repeat treatment did not differ significantly between eyes whose initial response was modest and those whose initial response was successful (36.67% vs 52.38%, P=0.26), and log-rank analysis found no difference in repeat success by initial response class (P=0.41). The authors raise the possibility that repeat SLT should not be excluded after only a modest initial response. Note this cohort answers a neighbouring question — repeat after a modest first response — rather than repeat after a successful-then-worn-off first treatment.
cards.watchOut: This cohort's first responses were modest, not successful-then-worn-off — it supports repeat SLT generally but is one step removed from this shelf's exact question, and it is retrospective.

cards.headline: Synthesis: repeat SLT lowers pressure again in every carded cohort — but all of the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: repeat SLT lowers pressure again in every carded cohort — but all of the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded observational cohorts (Hong 2009; Avery 2013; Khouri 2014 long-term; Khouri 2014 modest-response). No randomised trial of repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty was found in the fetched records.
cards.result: Across cohorts, repeat 360-degree SLT after a first treatment has worn off lowers intraocular pressure again, typically by somewhat less than the first treatment at some time points (Hong: −2.9 vs −5.0 mm Hg at 1–3 months) and by a comparable amount at others, with roughly three in ten eyes still achieving over 20% reduction at 24 months (Khouri long-term) and with repeat benefit lasting at least as long as the first in the one survival analysis (Avery). Because every carded report is a retrospective, uncontrolled cohort, regression to the mean, concurrent medication changes and selection of eyes for retreatment cannot be excluded — the evidence is observational throughout and the stamp is capped accordingly. First-line laser versus drops is a different question, homed on live shelf #609 (the LiGHT trial); this shelf is only about repeating a treatment that worked and then wore off.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis of observational cohorts only; a randomised trial of repeat SLT would be needed to lift the stamp above POSSIBLE.

J Ophthalmic Vis Res. 2014 (PMID: 25709769); Khouri AS et al. Middle East Afr J Ophthalmol. 2014 (PMID: 25100902). Registry IDs: none in the records (all observational).
cards.search: synthesis: repeat slt lowers pressure again in every carded cohort — but all of the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at possible synthesis: repeat slt lowers pressure again in every carded cohort — but all of the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at possible in adults with open-angle glaucoma whose first selective laser trabeculoplasty worked and then wore off, does repeating the laser lower pressure again? synthesis synthesis of the four carded observational cohorts (hong 2009; avery 2013; khouri 2014 long-term; khouri 2014 modest-response). no randomised trial of repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty was found in the fetched records. across cohorts, repeat 360-degree slt after a first treatment has worn off lowers intraocular pressure again, typically by somewhat less than the first treatment at some time points (hong: −2.9 vs −5.0 mm hg at 1–3 months) and by a comparable amount at others, with roughly three in ten eyes still achieving over 20% reduction at 24 months (khouri long-term) and with repeat benefit lasting at least as long as the first in the one survival analysis (avery). because every carded report is a retrospective, uncontrolled cohort, regression to the mean, concurrent medication changes and selection of eyes for retreatment cannot be excluded — the evidence is observational throughout and the stamp is capped accordingly. first-line laser versus drops is a different question, homed on live shelf #609 (the light trial); this shelf is only about repeating a treatment that worked and then wore off. synthesis of observational cohorts only; a randomised trial of repeat slt would be needed to lift the stamp above possible. synthesis of hong bk et al. j glaucoma. 2009 (pmid: 19295367); avery n et al. int ophthalmol. 2013 (pmid: 23371484); khouri as et al. j ophthalmic vis res. 2014 (pmid: 25709769); khouri as et al. middle east afr j ophthalmol. 2014 (pmid: 25100902). registry ids: none in the records (all observational).

shelves.title: Early clear-lens extraction versus laser peripheral iridotomy in primary angle-closure disease (EAGLE): pressure 1.18 mm Hg lower, drop-free control 66% versus 18%, ICER £14,284 per QALY
shelves.question: In adults with primary angle-closure disease, is early clear-lens extraction more effective and safer than laser peripheral iridotomy for intraocular pressure and glaucoma progression? (EAGLE.)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large randomised programme (EAGLE). In EAGLE (Azuara-Blanco 2016, PMID: 27707497), 419 patients aged 50 or older with newly diagnosed primary angle closure (intraocular pressure 30 mm Hg or greater) or primary angle-closure glaucoma were randomised to clear-lens extraction or standard care (laser peripheral iridotomy plus topical treatment): at 36 months health status was 0.052 higher and mean intraocular pressure 1.18 mm Hg lower with lens extraction, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was £14,284 per quality-adjusted life-year. The secondary analysis found 90% versus 67% met a good-response criterion and 66% versus 18% were drop-free with good control after lens extraction versus iridotomy (Mitchell 2023, PMID: 35387778), and the within-trial economic evaluation found lens extraction might become cost saving by 10 years (Javanbakht 2017, PMID: 28087548). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one trial programme caps the stamp, however clean its result; the comparison is against iridotomy plus medical therapy, not iridotomy alone forever, and lens extraction is irreversible intraocular surgery.

cards.headline: Azuara-Blanco 2016 (EAGLE RCT, 419 patients): clear-lens extraction beat standard care on health status (+0.052) and intraocular pressure (1.18 mm Hg lower) at 36 months; ICER £14,284 per QALY
cards.summary: Azuara-Blanco 2016 (EAGLE RCT, 419 patients): clear-lens extraction beat standard care on health status (+0.052) and intraocular pressure (1.18 mm Hg lower) at 36 months; ICER £14,284 per QALY
cards.people: 419 patients aged 50 years or older without cataract, with newly diagnosed primary angle closure with intraocular pressure 30 mm Hg or greater (155 patients) or primary angle-closure glaucoma (263 patients), enrolled at 30 hospital eye services in five countries and randomised to clear-lens extraction (n=208) or standard care with laser peripheral iridotomy and topical medical treatment (n=211).
cards.result: At 36 months, mean health status (European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions) was 0.87 (SD 0.12) after lens extraction, 0.052 higher than standard care (95% CI 0.015-0.088; p=0.005), and mean intraocular pressure was 16.6 (SD 3.5) mm Hg, 1.18 mm Hg lower than standard care (95% CI -1.99 to -0.38; p=0.004). The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was £14,284 per quality-adjusted life-year gained. Irreversible loss of vision occurred in one participant after lens extraction and three after standard care; no patients had serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One trial programme, and the comparator was iridotomy followed by medical therapy and surgery as needed — not iridotomy as a one-off. Participants had no cataract, so lens extraction traded a clear natural lens for an implant; long-term implant-related risks sit outside the 36-month window.
cards.source: Azuara-Blanco A et al. Effectiveness of early lens extraction for the treatment of primary angle-closure glaucoma (EAGLE): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27707497. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cataract Extraction; Glaucoma, Angle-Closure; Humans; Intraocular Pressure; Lens, Crystalline; Quality of Life

cards.headline: Mitchell 2023 (EAGLE secondary analysis, 369 completers): good intraocular-pressure response in 90% after lens extraction versus 67% after iridotomy; drop-free optimal response 66% versus 18%
cards.summary: Mitchell 2023 (EAGLE secondary analysis, 369 completers): good intraocular-pressure response in 90% after lens extraction versus 67% after iridotomy; drop-free optimal response 66% versus 18%
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial (EAGLE, Mitchell 2023)
cards.people: 369 EAGLE participants (182 clear-lens extraction, 187 laser peripheral iridotomy) who completed the 36-month follow-up examination; response definitions were pre-specified for this analysis: good response = intraocular pressure <21 mm Hg without additional surgery; optimal response = good response and medication-free.
cards.result: After clear-lens extraction, 90% met the good-response criterion compared with 67% after laser peripheral iridotomy, and 66% met the optimal-response criterion compared with 18%, with significantly longer drops/surgery-free survival (p<0.05 for all). In multivariable analysis, randomisation to lens extraction (OR 10.1, 95% CI 6.1-16.8), Chinese ethnicity (OR 2.3) and no prior glaucoma drops (OR 2.8) predicted maintaining an optimal response; higher baseline intraocular pressure predicted a worse response.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same single trial — it sharpens who responds, it is not independent confirmation. Response definitions were constructed for this analysis, and 50 of the 419 randomised patients did not complete the 36-month examination.
cards.source: Mitchell WG et al. Predictors of long-term intraocular pressure control after lens extraction in primary angle closure glaucoma: results from the EAGLE trial. British Journal of Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 35387778. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Javanbakht 2017 (EAGLE economic evaluation): lens extraction cost £2,467 versus £1,486 over 3 years with 2.602 versus 2.533 QALYs; modelled to possibly become cost saving by 10 years
cards.summary: Javanbakht 2017 (EAGLE economic evaluation): lens extraction cost £2,467 versus £1,486 over 3 years with 2.602 versus 2.533 QALYs; modelled to possibly become cost saving by 10 years
cards.people: EAGLE participants followed for 36 months at 22 UK hospital eye services (mean age 67.5 years, 57.5% women, 35.4% primary angle closure and the remainder primary angle-closure glaucoma), with a Markov model extrapolating to 5 and 10 years from a UK NHS perspective.
cards.result: Mean health service costs were higher with lens extraction (£2,467 versus £1,486) and mean adjusted quality-adjusted life-years were also higher (2.602 versus 2.533), giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £14,284 per QALY gained at 3 years. Modelling suggested the ratio falls to £7,090 per QALY by 5 years and that lens extraction may be cost saving by 10 years, with a 67-89% probability of being cost-effective at 3 years.
cards.watchOut: UK NHS costs and a modelled 10-year horizon: the cost-saving claim is an extrapolation, not observed data, and transfer to other health systems is uncertain.
cards.source: Javanbakht M et al. Early lens extraction with intraocular lens implantation for the treatment of primary angle closure glaucoma: an economic evaluation based on data from the EAGLE trial. BMJ Open. 2017. PMID: 28087548. Registry ID: ISRCTN44464607. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme favours early clear-lens extraction over iridotomy-based standard care on pressure, drop burden, quality of life and cost-effectiveness — POSSIBLE on a single programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme favours early clear-lens extraction over iridotomy-based standard care on pressure, drop burden, quality of life and cost-effectiveness — POSSIBLE on a single programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above, all from the single EAGLE randomised programme (419 randomised; 369 with 36-month examinations).
cards.result: Every EAGLE output points the same way: lower intraocular pressure, far more patients controlled without drops (66% versus 18% optimal response), slightly better health status, and an acceptable cost per QALY that improves with time horizon. There is no second randomised programme to confirm it, and the intervention is irreversible surgery on a clear lens, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit) despite the trial's size and quality.
cards.watchOut: All three cards are one trial. A confirmatory trial in a different population — EAGLE enrolled few patients of Asian ethnicity (1.4% in the UK economic cohort), the group at highest angle-closure risk — would be needed before this could be stamped higher.
cards.source: Synthesis of Azuara-Blanco A et al. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27707497; Mitchell WG et al. British Journal of Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 35387778; Javanbakht M et al. BMJ Open. 2017. PMID: 28087548. Registry ID ISRCTN44464607 as on the Javanbakht card above.

shelves.title: XEN gel stent versus trabeculectomy in open-angle glaucoma: trabeculectomy lowers pressure ~2 mm Hg further with higher success; XEN needs more needling but fewer visits and less vision loss; hypotony not clearly different
shelves.question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma, does a subconjunctival gel stent (XEN) lower intraocular pressure as durably as trabeculectomy, with fewer hypotony complications?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two operations trade places by outcome, on an observational base (labelled). Trabeculectomy lowers intraocular pressure further and succeeds more often: across 11 comparative studies (1,260 eyes) the pooled pressure reduction favoured trabeculectomy by a mean 2.16 mm Hg, with higher qualified and complete success (Bhatti 2026, PMID: 42539846), and the 24-month cohort found final pressure 12.5 versus 14.6 mm Hg (Wanichwecharungruang 2021, PMID: 34411152). The XEN 45 gel stent (XEN Gel Stent, Allergan/AbbVie, as named in the publications) gave the gentler course: fewer early postoperative visits, less vision loss and less surgically induced astigmatism, at the price of more bleb needling/transconjunctival needle revision (Schlenker 2018, PMID: 32672652). On the question's hypotony point, the pooled analysis found no statistically significant difference in hypotony rates (with substantial heterogeneity, I²=76%), and the 24-month cohort reported a lower rate of numerical hypotony with XEN. PROPOSED SPLIT: trabeculectomy wins on pressure and success; XEN wins on postoperative burden; hypotony is not clearly different. All comparative evidence here is observational, which caps confidence.

cards.headline: Schlenker 2018 (retrospective multicentre cohort, 354 eyes): gelatin stent eyes needed more needle revisions (42.2% versus 32.5%) but had fewer first-month visits, less >2-line vision loss (12.4% versus 21.9% adjusted) and faster visual recovery than trabeculectomy
cards.summary: Schlenker 2018 (retrospective multicentre cohort, 354 eyes): gelatin stent eyes needed more needle revisions (42.2% versus 32.5%) but had fewer first-month visits, less >2-line vision loss (12.4% versus 21.9% adjusted) and faster visual recovery than trabeculectomy
cards.people: 354 eyes of 293 patients with uncontrolled glaucoma at four academic centres (Toronto, Frankfurt, Salzburg, Leuven) undergoing standalone ab interno gelatin microstent (XEN) implantation with mitomycin C (185 eyes) or trabeculectomy with mitomycin C (169 eyes), 2011-2015.
cards.result: An in-clinic intervention by last follow-up occurred in 51.4% of microstent eyes and 62.1% of trabeculectomy eyes (log-rank P=0.0004); the commonest intervention was transconjunctival needle revision (TCNR), received by 42.2% of microstent versus 32.5% of trabeculectomy eyes (adjusted HR 1.73, 95% CI 1.10-2.71). Microstent eyes averaged 1.00 fewer visits in the first month (P<0.001), had less >2-line vision loss at last follow-up (12.4% versus 21.9% adjusted, P=0.0383), regained baseline visual acuity more often (adjusted HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.10-2.00) and had less surgically induced astigmatism (>0.5 D in 25.3% versus 40.7% adjusted).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: surgeons chose the operation, so case-mix differences can explain part of the contrast. This report covers the postoperative course, not long-term pressure durability.
cards.source: Schlenker MB et al. Standalone Ab Interno Gelatin Stent versus Trabeculectomy: Postoperative Interventions, Visual Outcomes, and Visits. Ophthalmology Glaucoma. 2018. PMID: 32672652. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wanichwecharungruang 2021 (retrospective cohort, 114 eyes, 24 months): success comparable (overall 71.4% XEN versus 73.3% trabeculectomy) but final pressure higher after XEN (14.6 versus 12.5 mm Hg); XEN had a lower rate of numerical hypotony
cards.summary: Wanichwecharungruang 2021 (retrospective cohort, 114 eyes, 24 months): success comparable (overall 71.4% XEN versus 73.3% trabeculectomy) but final pressure higher after XEN (14.6 versus 12.5 mm Hg); XEN had a lower rate of numerical hypotony
cards.people: 114 eyes with mild-to-moderate primary glaucoma and medically uncontrolled intraocular pressure (preoperative 16-33 mm Hg) at a tertiary eye centre: 57 eyes received a XEN45 gel implant and 57 underwent trabeculectomy, both with adjunctive mitomycin C.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean intraocular pressure fell from 21.6 (SD 4.0) to 14.6 (SD 3.5) mm Hg with XEN (a 32.4% relative reduction) and from 22.5 (SD 5.8) to 12.5 (SD 4.1) mm Hg with trabeculectomy (a 44.4% relative reduction); final pressure was significantly higher after XEN (p=0.008). Mean medication count fell from 2.2 to 0.5 (XEN) and from 2.4 to 0.8 (trabeculectomy), not significantly different at the end (p=0.225). Overall success was 71.4% versus 73.3% (p=0.850) and complete success 62.9% versus 62.2% (p=0.954). XEN had a lower rate of numerical hypotony than trabeculectomy, and no serious complication occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, retrospective, 57 eyes per arm, and 'numerical hypotony' is a pressure reading, not necessarily a clinical hypotony complication; 24 months is mid-term, not lifetime durability.
cards.source: Wanichwecharungruang B et al. 24-month outcomes of XEN45 gel implant versus trabeculectomy in primary glaucoma. PLoS One. 2021. PMID: 34411152. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bhatti 2026 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 11 studies, 1,260 eyes): trabeculectomy achieved greater pressure reduction (mean difference 2.16 mm Hg) and higher success; hypotony rates did not differ significantly; XEN had less bleb leakage but more needling
cards.summary: Bhatti 2026 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 11 studies, 1,260 eyes): trabeculectomy achieved greater pressure reduction (mean difference 2.16 mm Hg) and higher success; hypotony rates did not differ significantly; XEN had less bleb leakage but more needling
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies (Bhatti 2026)
cards.people: 11 comparative studies of ab-interno XEN 45 gel implantation versus trabeculectomy in glaucoma, comprising 1,260 eyes (645 XEN, 615 trabeculectomy), pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: Trabeculectomy achieved significantly greater intraocular pressure reduction (mean difference -2.16 mm Hg, 95% CI -2.88 to -1.44; I²=43%) and higher qualified success (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.18-2.14) and complete success (OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.16-2.56). The number of antiglaucoma medications did not differ (mean difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.18). Rates of hyphema, choroidal detachment, hypotony, flat anterior chamber, bleb revision and reoperation showed no statistically significant differences, though heterogeneity was substantial for hypotony (I²=76%). XEN had significantly lower risks of bleb leakage and endophthalmitis but higher rates of bleb needling.
cards.watchOut: The pooled base is predominantly non-randomised, and the hypotony comparison carries I²=76% heterogeneity — 'no significant difference' here means the studies disagree, not that equivalence is proven.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — trabeculectomy lowers pressure further and succeeds more often; the XEN gel stent costs more needling but a lighter postoperative course; hypotony is not clearly different (observational base)
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — trabeculectomy lowers pressure further and succeeds more often; the XEN gel stent costs more needling but a lighter postoperative course; hypotony is not clearly different (observational base)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: two retrospective cohorts (354 and 114 eyes) and one meta-analysis of 11 comparative studies (1,260 eyes). No randomised head-to-head trial is among the fetched records.
cards.result: The pattern is consistent across reports: expect roughly 2 mm Hg less pressure reduction and lower complete success with the XEN gel stent, balanced by fewer early visits, less vision loss and less astigmatism, with the maintenance burden shifted to bleb needling. On hypotony — the complication the stent is often chosen to avoid — neither the cohort nor the pooled analysis shows a clear advantage. Choice therefore turns on the target pressure: low target pressures favour trabeculectomy; a gentler course at a mid-teen target favours the stent.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence throughout: selection by surgeon preference is the standing confounder, and a randomised comparison could move either the pressure gap or the complication rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schlenker MB et al. Ophthalmology Glaucoma. 2018. PMID: 32672652; Wanichwecharungruang B et al. PLoS One. 2021. PMID: 34411152; Bhatti MI et al. Therapeutic Advances in Ophthalmology. 2026. PMID: 42539846. Registry IDs as on the cards above.

shelves.title: DMEK versus DSAEK/DSEK for corneal endothelial failure (DETECT): 1.8 lines better acuity at 6 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months, with more rebubbling as the trade
shelves.question: In adults with corneal endothelial failure, does Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) give faster and better visual recovery than Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK/DSEK)? (DETECT.)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial plus concordant observational syntheses. The DETECT randomised trial (Chamberlain 2019, PMID: 29945801) found Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) gave 1.5 lines better best spectacle-corrected visual acuity at 3 months, 1.8 lines at 6 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months than ultrathin Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (UT-DSAEK), with similar complication rates and endothelial cell counts. The meta-analysis of retrospective comparisons found the same direction — 12-month acuity 0.16 versus 0.30 logMAR, fewer rejections with DMEK but more rebubbling (Marques 2019, PMID: 29661044) — and the Cochrane review, written before DETECT, found low-certainty evidence of better acuity with DMEK at the cost of more graft dislocations (Stuart 2018, PMID: 29940078). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): DETECT randomised only 38 patients, and the supporting base is retrospective, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite concordance.

cards.headline: Chamberlain 2019 (DETECT RCT, 50 eyes of 38 patients): DMEK gave 1.8 lines better acuity than ultrathin DSAEK at 6 months (P<0.001), 1.5 lines at 3 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months; complications similar
cards.summary: Chamberlain 2019 (DETECT RCT, 50 eyes of 38 patients): DMEK gave 1.8 lines better acuity than ultrathin DSAEK at 6 months (P<0.001), 1.5 lines at 3 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months; complications similar
cards.people: 50 eyes of 38 patients with corneal endothelial dysfunction from Fuchs endothelial dystrophy or pseudophakic bullous keratopathy, considered good candidates for either operation, randomised by the eye bank to ultrathin DSAEK (UT-DSAEK) or DMEK 1-2 days before surgery by two surgeons at two US centres; patients and outcome assessors were masked.
cards.result: After correcting for baseline acuity, DMEK gave better best spectacle-corrected visual acuity than UT-DSAEK by 1.5 lines at 3 months (95% CI 0.6-2.5 lines better; P=0.002), 1.8 lines at 6 months (95% CI 1.0-2.8; P<0.001, the primary outcome) and 1.4 lines at 12 months (95% CI 0.7-2.2; P<0.001). Mean endothelial cell counts were 1963 versus 2113 cells/mm² at 6 months (P=0.17) and 1855 versus 2070 cells/mm² at 12 months (P=0.051). Intraoperative and postoperative complication rates were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 38 patients at two expert centres, and the comparator was ultrathin DSAEK — the best version of the older operation. Results from two experienced DMEK surgeons may not transfer to a surgeon's early DMEK learning curve.

cards.headline: Marques 2019 (meta-analysis, 10 retrospective studies, 947 eyes): acuity better with DMEK at every time point (0.16 versus 0.30 logMAR at 12 months); rejection 60% relatively lower, rebubbling more frequent (RR 2.48)
cards.summary: Marques 2019 (meta-analysis, 10 retrospective studies, 947 eyes): acuity better with DMEK at every time point (0.16 versus 0.30 logMAR at 12 months); rejection 60% relatively lower, rebubbling more frequent (RR 2.48)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of retrospective comparative studies (Marques 2019) — observational base
cards.people: 947 eyes with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy in 10 retrospective comparative studies of DMEK (646 eyes) versus DSAEK, searched to August 2017.
cards.result: Best-corrected visual acuity was better with DMEK at 3, 6 and 12 months (0.16 logMAR with DMEK versus 0.30 logMAR with DSAEK at 12 months; p<0.001). DMEK had a 60% lower rejection rate in relative terms (risk ratio 0.4, 95% CI 0.24-0.67; p=0.0005) but required more rebubbling (risk ratio 2.48, 95% CI 1.32-4.64; p=0.005). Primary graft failure and endothelial cell density loss did not differ significantly. Patient satisfaction was higher after DMEK (odds ratio 10.29, 95% CI 3.55-29.80).
cards.watchOut: All ten studies were retrospective and of moderate methodological quality, in Fuchs dystrophy only; surgeon selection of easier eyes for DMEK can inflate its advantage. The rejection figure is a relative measure; the record gives no absolute rates beside it.
cards.source: Marques RE et al. DMEK versus DSAEK for Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy: A meta-analysis. European Journal of Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 29661044. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stuart 2018 (Cochrane review, 4 non-randomised paired-eye studies, 144 eyes): low-certainty evidence of better 1-year acuity with DMEK (mean difference -0.14 logMAR), with more graft dislocations (RR 5.40)
cards.summary: Stuart 2018 (Cochrane review, 4 non-randomised paired-eye studies, 144 eyes): low-certainty evidence of better 1-year acuity with DMEK (mean difference -0.14 logMAR), with more graft dislocations (RR 5.40)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of non-randomised studies (Stuart 2018)
cards.people: 72 participants (144 eyes) with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and endothelial failure in four non-randomised contralateral-eye studies in which DSAEK was performed in the first eye and DMEK in the fellow eye; the review (search to August 2017) found no randomised trials at that date.
cards.result: At one year, DMEK may give better best-corrected visual acuity than DSAEK (mean difference -0.14 logMAR, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.10; 4 studies, 140 eyes; low-certainty evidence). No participant had severe visual loss. Endothelial cell count data were inconclusive. No primary graft failure and only one graft rejection were recorded across 144 eyes. Graft dislocation was more common with DMEK (risk ratio 5.40, 95% CI 1.51-19.3; very low-certainty evidence), recorded in one or two per 100 DSAEK participants and more often with DMEK.
cards.watchOut: Pre-DETECT and rated high risk of bias: DSAEK always preceded DMEK in the same patients, so era and learning effects run through every comparison. Its dislocation signal is the caution the randomised trial was too small to settle.
cards.source: Stuart AJ et al. Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) versus Descemet's stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK) for corneal endothelial failure. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29940078. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: DMEK recovers vision faster and to a better level than DSAEK/DSEK — about 1.5-1.8 lines in the one randomised trial — at the cost of more rebubbling/dislocation; POSSIBLE on a small randomised base
cards.summary: Synthesis: DMEK recovers vision faster and to a better level than DSAEK/DSEK — about 1.5-1.8 lines in the one randomised trial — at the cost of more rebubbling/dislocation; POSSIBLE on a small randomised base
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: one randomised trial (50 eyes of 38 patients), one meta-analysis of 10 retrospective studies (947 eyes) and one Cochrane review of 4 paired-eye studies (144 eyes).
cards.result: All three sources agree on direction: better and faster acuity with DMEK, no clear endothelial-cell penalty, fewer rejections, and a consistent counter-signal of more graft dislocation/rebubbling with DMEK. The randomised evidence is a single 38-patient trial, so the benefit stamp is POSSIBLE; the rebubbling cost is the part of the trade a patient should hear before choosing.
cards.watchOut: DETECT compared DMEK with ultrathin DSAEK specifically; older standard-thickness DSAEK/DSEK would likely fare worse, so this shelf's gap is a conservative estimate of the DMEK advantage.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chamberlain W et al. Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 29945801; Marques RE et al. European Journal of Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 29661044; Stuart AJ et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29940078. Registry IDs as on the cards above.
