shelves.title: PARTIAL (home #625 for established field therapies): tirbanibulin 1% ointment 5-day for actinic keratosis — complete clearance 44% and 54% versus 5% and 13% on vehicle, 47% recurrence at 1 year, no head-to-head versus established therapies
shelves.question: In adults with actinic keratosis, does tirbanibulin 1% ointment (5-day course) clear lesions versus vehicle, and how does its clearance compare with the established field therapies?
shelves.balance: PARTIAL SHELF — flagged prominently: the established field therapies for actinic keratosis (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate) are already homed at Shelf #625, whose head-to-head trial found 5-fluorouracil the most durable of those four at 12 months. This shelf covers only the slice #625 does not: tirbanibulin 1% ointment (Klisyri, Athenex — the tested product as published), the newest field agent, which has never been randomised head-to-head against any of the #625 therapies. Against vehicle, the two identically designed phase 3 trials (Blauvelt 2021, PMID: 33567191) found complete clearance at day 57 in 44% and 54% on tirbanibulin versus 5% and 13% on vehicle, with recurrence in an estimated 47% of complete responders by 1 year. Phase 2 data set the 5-day course (Kempers 2020, PMID: 33196758), and a single-arm phase 3 study supports tolerability over a 100 cm² field (Bhatia 2024, PMID: 39268198). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clear superiority over vehicle on a 5-day course, but no comparative claim against fluorouracil or the other established therapies can be made from this evidence, and 1-year recurrence is substantial. Cross-point: see Shelf #625 for the established-therapy comparison.

cards.headline: Blauvelt 2021 (two phase 3 RCTs, 702 patients): complete clearance at day 57 in 44% and 54% on tirbanibulin 1% (5 days) versus 5% and 13% on vehicle; 47% of complete responders recurred by 1 year
cards.summary: Blauvelt 2021 (two phase 3 RCTs, 702 patients): complete clearance at day 57 in 44% and 54% on tirbanibulin 1% (5 days) versus 5% and 13% on vehicle; 47% of complete responders recurred by 1 year
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials (KX01 programme, Blauvelt 2021)
cards.people: 702 adults with actinic keratoses on the face or scalp (351 per trial), randomised 1:1 double-blind to tirbanibulin 1% ointment or vehicle ointment, self-applied once daily for 5 consecutive days to a 25 cm² area containing four to eight lesions.
cards.result: Complete (100%) lesion clearance at day 57 occurred in trial 1 in 44% on tirbanibulin (77 of 175) versus 5% on vehicle (8 of 176) — a difference of 40 percentage points (95% CI 32-47; P<0.001) — and in trial 2 in 54% (97 of 178) versus 13% (22 of 173), a difference of 42 percentage points (95% CI 33-51; P<0.001). Partial (≥75%) clearance was also significantly higher with tirbanibulin. At 1 year, the estimated percentage of patients with recurrent lesions was 47% among those who had had a complete response to tirbanibulin. Local reactions were erythema in 91% and flaking/scaling in 82%; application-site pain occurred in 10% and pruritus in 9%, all resolving.
cards.watchOut: Vehicle-controlled only: these trials say nothing about how tirbanibulin compares with 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod or photodynamic therapy (that comparison lives at Shelf #625 for the older agents, and tirbanibulin is not in it). Clearance is judged at day 57 and nearly half of complete responders recurred within a year.
cards.source: Blauvelt A et al. Phase 3 Trials of Tirbanibulin Ointment for Actinic Keratosis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33567191. Registry ID: NCT03285477; NCT03285490. cards.headline: Kempers 2020 (phase 1/2 programme): 5-day tirbanibulin gave 43% complete clearance of face/scalp lesions at day 57 versus 32% for 3 days — the basis for the 5-day phase 3 regimen
cards.summary: Kempers 2020 (phase 1/2 programme): 5-day tirbanibulin gave 43% complete clearance of face/scalp lesions at day 57 versus 32% for 3 days — the basis for the 5-day phase 3 regimen
cards.people: Phase 1: 30 patients with forearm actinic keratoses in four cohorts (25 or 100 cm², 3 or 5 days). Phase 2: 168 patients with face or scalp lesions in two cohorts receiving tirbanibulin ointment 1% once daily for 3 or 5 days over 25 cm², evaluated to day 57.
cards.result: Forearm lesions were reduced by day 45 in all phase 1 cohorts. In phase 2, complete clearance at day 57 was 43% in the 5-day cohort and 32% in the 3-day cohort. Adverse reactions were mainly transient mild local erythema and flaking/scaling, pruritus and pain, and plasma concentrations were low or undetectable. On this activity and tolerability, the 5-day regimen was selected for phase 3 development.
cards.watchOut: Open regimen-finding cohorts without a vehicle control in the phase 2 face/scalp study; its role is to explain where the 5-day course came from, not to add independent proof of efficacy.

cards.type: Phase 3 open-label single-arm safety study (Bhatia 2024) — no comparator
cards.people: 105 adults with a treatment field of approximately 100 cm² on the face or balding scalp containing 4-12 actinic keratoses, treated open-label with tirbanibulin once daily for 5 consecutive days over the whole field — four times the licensed 25 cm² area.
cards.result: Erythema (96.1%) and flaking/scaling (84.4%) were the commonest local tolerability signs, mostly mild-to-moderate and resolved or near baseline by day 29; severe erythema occurred in 5.8% and severe flaking/scaling in 8.7%. cards.result: Tirbanibulin's proven claim is narrow and solid: complete clearance in 44-54% versus 5-13% on vehicle at day 57, with transient local reactions and a 47% estimated 1-year recurrence among complete responders. shelves.title: Aqueous humour dynamics (physiology): fluorophotometry measures formation at about 2.75 µL/min by day, falling to about half during sleep, and normal intraocular pressure varies by no more than about 5 mmHg across 24 hours
shelves.question: In healthy humans, at what rate is aqueous humour formed and drained, and how large is the normal diurnal swing in intraocular pressure?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Aqueous Humor/physiology · Circadian Rhythm · Intraocular Pressure · Fluorometry/methods · Anterior Chamber · Ciliary Body
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): aqueous humour is secreted by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil, and drains through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal, with intraocular pressure set by the balance of formation and outflow resistance. The carded primary human studies quantify that system by fluorophotometry, the Brubaker programme's method: aqueous flow in normal subjects averages 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min during office hours (95% range 1.8 to 4.3 µL/min), follows a circadian rhythm — highest in the morning, slightly lower in the afternoon, and about half the morning rate during sleep — and declines about 3.2% per decade after age 10 (Brubaker 1991, the Friedenwald Lecture synthesising the programme's clinical experiments). The companion fluorophotometry studies print the method's working values in untreated normal eyes (for example 2.4 µL/min in placebo-treated fellow eyes in the clonidine study, Lee 1984, where a 21% flow reduction accompanied a 2 mmHg pressure fall). For the pressure side, the carded 24-hour study of 25 normal subjects found that normal individuals did not show diurnal intraocular-pressure variation greater than 5 mmHg across six measurements in 24 hours — in contrast to pseudoexfoliation patients, over half of whom exceeded 5 mmHg (Altintaş 2004). Drainage rate equals formation rate at steady state by definition; no carded record prints a separate directly-measured drainage number, so none is claimed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Brubaker 1991 (Friedenwald Lecture): aqueous flow averages 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min by day, with sleep rates about half the morning rate
cards.summary: Brubaker 1991 (Friedenwald Lecture): aqueous flow averages 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min by day, with sleep rates about half the morning rate
cards.type: Primary-programme synthesis lecture (human fluorophotometry experiments, Brubaker programme)
cards.people: Normal human subjects measured by fluorophotometry across the Brubaker programme's clinical experiments (measurements averaged during normal office hours for the headline rate; circadian studies measured morning, afternoon and sleep rates in the same subjects).
cards.result: The rate of aqueous flow is 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min in normal subjects, with a normal (95%) range of 1.8 to 4.3 µL/min. Flow follows a circadian rhythm: highest during morning hours, slightly lower during afternoon hours, and during sleep approximately one half of the morning rate; the rhythm persists in both eyes of persons with unilateral Horner's syndrome, so it is not driven by sympathetic tone to one eye. Flow declines slightly after age 10, by 3.2% per decade, with no significant difference between men and women. Flow is insensitive to moderate changes in intraocular pressure. Among drugs, beta-adrenergic antagonists, carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-2 agonists suppress flow usefully — timolol suppresses daytime flow but has no effect on the flow of sleeping subjects, whereas acetazolamide and apraclonidine can reduce sleep flow.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme leader's lecture synthesising many fluorophotometry experiments rather than one trial with one protocol, and its MeSH record includes an Animals heading from the lecture's scope — every value carded here is from the human clinical experiments the lecture reports, and the underlying single-study values appear on the companion cards.
cards.source: Brubaker RF. Flow of aqueous humor in humans [The Friedenwald Lecture]. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science. 1991. PMID: 1748546. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lee, Topper & Brubaker 1984: untreated normal eyes flowed at 2.4 µL/min by fluorophotometry, and a 21% flow reduction came with a 2 mmHg pressure fall
cards.summary: Lee, Topper & Brubaker 1984: untreated normal eyes flowed at 2.4 µL/min by fluorophotometry, and a 21% flow reduction came with a 2 mmHg pressure fall
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised double-blind fluorophotometry, normal volunteers)
cards.people: 24 normal human subjects in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled fluorophotometry study: one eye received topical 0.125% clonidine and the fellow eye placebo, with aqueous flow, intraocular pressure, anterior chamber volume, pupil size, pulse and blood pressure measured.
cards.result: Aqueous humour flow was 21% lower in clonidine-treated eyes than in fellow placebo-treated eyes — 1.9 µL/min compared with 2.4 µL/min — the placebo-eye value giving a single-study untreated flow rate consistent with the programme average. Clonidine-treated eyes had a statistically significant 2 mmHg decrease in intraocular pressure; fellow placebo eyes also fell slightly, and the between-eye pressure difference was not significant. No significant difference was found in anterior chamber volume, blood-aqueous barrier diffusion constant or apparent resistance between the eyes.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its untreated fellow-eye flow value (2.4 µL/min) and the flow–pressure pairing; the drug effect itself (an alpha-2 agonist) belongs to glaucoma pharmacology, and a 21% flow change producing only a 2 mmHg pressure change illustrates why flow and pressure cannot be interconverted without outflow resistance.
cards.source: Lee DA, Topper JE, Brubaker RF. Effect of clonidine on aqueous humor flow in normal human eyes. Experimental Eye Research. 1984. PMID: 6373331. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lee, Brubaker & Nagataki 1981: fluorophotometry in 25 normal subjects — the method's baseline precision, with a 12% (non-significant) flow difference as its noise scale
cards.summary: Lee, Brubaker & Nagataki 1981: fluorophotometry in 25 normal subjects — the method's baseline precision, with a 12% (non-significant) flow difference as its noise scale
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised double-blind fluorophotometry methods study, normal volunteers)
cards.people: 25 normal human subjects in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled fluorophotometry study of 0.5% topical thymoxamine (an alpha-adrenergic antagonist) versus placebo, with aqueous formation rate, intraocular pressure, anterior chamber volume and blood-aqueous barrier permeability measured; 4 subjects were used for the permeability substudy.
cards.result: Thymoxamine-treated eyes had 12% greater aqueous humour flow than placebo-treated eyes, but the difference was not statistically significant, and no statistically significant difference was found in the rate of aqueous formation, intraocular pressure, anterior chamber volume or blood-aqueous barrier permeability between treated and placebo eyes — the treatment made no difference on any measured variable. For this shelf the study's value is methodological: in 25 normal subjects, fluorophotometry's between-eye comparisons carry a noise scale of roughly a tenth of the flow rate, which is the precision context for the 2.75 µL/min programme average.
cards.watchOut: A null drug study carded as a methods/precision anchor, not as evidence about alpha-blockade: its authors list four rival explanations for the null (dose, receptors, tone, or no role for the receptor system), and the shelf adopts none of them.

cards.headline: Altintaş 2004: across six measurements in 24 hours, normal subjects never varied intraocular pressure by more than 5 mmHg
cards.summary: Altintaş 2004: across six measurements in 24 hours, normal subjects never varied intraocular pressure by more than 5 mmHg
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour diurnal pressure curves, normal controls with disease contrast group)
cards.people: 25 age- and sex-matched normal subjects (one eye each) prospectively admitted for diurnal intraocular-pressure testing — six measurements over 24 hours — alongside 29 eyes of 19 patients with pseudoexfoliation syndrome studied for contrast.
cards.result: Normal individuals did not show diurnal variation greater than 5 mmHg. The pseudoexfoliation patients differed on every summary measure (mean, maximum, minimum and range of pressure, each p < 0.05 versus controls): 55.6% of them showed diurnal variation greater than 5 mmHg and 10% had variations of 10 mmHg or more. The normal diurnal swing carded here is therefore a ceiling statement from this study — within about 5 mmHg across the day in healthy eyes — rather than a single mean amplitude, which the fetched abstract does not print for the control group.
cards.watchOut: Measurements were daytime-clinic tonometry at six time points in admitted patients, not continuous or nocturnal/supine monitoring — the true night-time peak, when aqueous flow is halved but posture raises episcleral venous pressure, is not captured by this study's swing estimate.
cards.source: Altintaş O et al. Diurnal intraocular pressure variation in pseudoexfoliation syndrome. European Journal of Ophthalmology. 2004. PMID: 15638098. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: about 2.75 µL/min formed (and therefore drained) by day, about half that in sleep, and a normal pressure swing contained within about 5 mmHg
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 2.75 µL/min formed (and therefore drained) by day, about half that in sleep, and a normal pressure swing contained within about 5 mmHg
cards.people: Synthesis across Brubaker 1991 (programme fluorophotometry), Lee 1984 and Lee 1981 (single-study fluorophotometry in 24–25 normal subjects) and Altintaş 2004 (24-hour pressures in 25 normal subjects).
cards.result: Formation and drainage balance at about 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min during the day (single-study untreated values 2.4 µL/min), flow halves during sleep while pressure stays comparatively contained, and the normal 24-hour intraocular-pressure excursion stays within about 5 mmHg. The system's slack is visible in the clonidine pairing: a 21% flow reduction moved pressure by only about 2 mmHg, because outflow resistance, not flow alone, sets pressure.
cards.watchOut: The flow numbers all descend from one method (fluorophotometry) and largely one programme, and the diurnal-swing ceiling comes from a single control group measured sitting in clinic hours — posture and night-time values rest on the textbook's account.

shelves.title: Mepolizumab for nasal polyps (SYNAPSE): polyp score and obstruction improved, and fewer patients went on to sinus surgery
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps inadequately controlled on intranasal steroids, does mepolizumab reduce polyp size, nasal obstruction and need for surgery versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Nasal Polyps · Synapses · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 programme only, so the stamp is capped. In SYNAPSE (407 adults with recurrent, refractory severe bilateral polyps, all previously operated and eligible for repeat surgery), mepolizumab 100 mg every 4 weeks for 52 weeks improved the total endoscopic polyp score by an adjusted median difference of -0.73 and nasal obstruction by -3.14 points versus placebo, and a prespecified surgery analysis found fewer patients were put on a waiting list for sinus surgery (13.9% vs 28.5% by week 52). This shelf is the mepolizumab slice only: the class home, live shelf #375, cards dupilumab and omalizumab and does not card SYNAPSE. Effects are real but modest next to the dupilumab gradient on #375 — a cross-trial reading, not a head-to-head trial.

cards.headline: SYNAPSE (Han 2021): mepolizumab improved polyp score (-0.73) and nasal obstruction (-3.14) versus placebo at 52 weeks
cards.summary: SYNAPSE (Han 2021): mepolizumab improved polyp score (-0.73) and nasal obstruction (-3.14) versus placebo at 52 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (SYNAPSE), 52 weeks.
cards.people: 407 adults (206 mepolizumab, 201 placebo) at 93 centres in 11 countries, all with recurrent, refractory, severe bilateral nasal polyps despite standard care, at least one nasal surgery in the past 10 years, and eligibility for repeat surgery; mepolizumab 100 mg subcutaneously or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks on top of intranasal mometasone and standard care.
cards.result: Total endoscopic nasal polyp score improved versus placebo (adjusted difference in medians -0.73, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.34; p<0.0001) and mean nasal obstruction visual analogue score during weeks 49-52 improved by -3.14 (95% CI -4.09 to -2.18; p<0.0001). Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 15% on mepolizumab and 9% on placebo; on-treatment serious adverse events occurred in 6% in each group, none considered treatment-related on mepolizumab.
cards.watchOut: A single programme caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The polyp-score gain (-0.73) is smaller than the dupilumab effect carded on live shelf #375 (about -2 points) — but that is a cross-trial comparison in differently selected patients, not a randomised head-to-head, and must not be read as proof mepolizumab is the weaker drug for an individual patient.
cards.source: Han JK et al. Mepolizumab for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (SYNAPSE): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2021;9:1141-1153. PMID: 33872587 · NCT03085797 (registry ID stated in the record). cards.headline: SYNAPSE surgery analysis (Fokkens 2023): mepolizumab roughly halved the risk of going on a sinus-surgery waiting list (13.9% vs 28.5%)
cards.summary: SYNAPSE surgery analysis (Fokkens 2023): mepolizumab roughly halved the risk of going on a sinus-surgery waiting list (13.9% vs 28.5%)
cards.type: Prespecified in-depth analysis of surgery endpoints within the SYNAPSE phase 3 trial.
cards.people: The same 407 SYNAPSE patients (206 mepolizumab, 201 placebo), all eligible for repeat sinus surgery at entry; time to first inclusion on a surgery waiting list and time to first actual sinus surgery were assessed to week 52.
cards.result: By week 52 the Kaplan-Meier probability of being included on a waiting list for sinus surgery was 13.9% (95% CI 9.8% to 19.5%) on mepolizumab versus 28.5% (22.7% to 35.4%) on placebo. The reduction in actual sinus surgery held irrespective of time since the last surgery before screening (hazard ratio 0.28 [0.09 to 0.84] for <3 years and 0.50 [0.26 to 0.98] for 3 years or more) and of baseline blood eosinophil count.
cards.watchOut: Surgery endpoints are secondary analyses of the same single trial, not independent confirmation — they deepen SYNAPSE rather than widen the evidence base, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Fokkens WJ et al. Mepolizumab for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (SYNAPSE): In-depth sinus surgery analysis. Allergy. 2023;78:812-821. PMID: 35822924 · NCT03085797 (registry ID stated in the record). MeSH: Adult · Humans · Nasal Polyps · Sinusitis · Chronic Disease · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Rhinitis

cards.headline: SYNAPSE corticosteroid analysis (Chupp 2023): fewer patients needed systemic steroids for polyps on mepolizumab (25.4% vs 37.5% by week 52)
cards.summary: SYNAPSE corticosteroid analysis (Chupp 2023): fewer patients needed systemic steroids for polyps on mepolizumab (25.4% vs 37.5% by week 52)
cards.type: Prespecified and post hoc secondary analyses of the SYNAPSE phase 3 trial.
cards.people: The same SYNAPSE population (407 adults with severe CRSwNP eligible for repeat surgery); this analysis assessed time to first systemic corticosteroid course for nasal polyps and total prednisolone-equivalent oral dose among patients who needed at least one course.
cards.result: By week 52, the Kaplan-Meier probability of requiring systemic corticosteroids for nasal polyps was 25.4% (95% CI 20.0 to 32.1) on mepolizumab versus 37.5% (31.1 to 44.6) on placebo. Among patients who did require steroids, mean total prednisolone-equivalent dose was lower on mepolizumab (438.9 mg/year, SD 350.4) than placebo (505.2 mg/year, SD 455). Mepolizumab's improvements in polyp score, obstruction and quality-of-life scores held irrespective of how many steroid courses patients had needed before the trial.
cards.watchOut: Still the same single trial — this card adds an outcome dimension (steroid sparing, a real harm-reduction benefit given steroid toxicity), not independent confirmation.
cards.source: Chupp G et al. Mepolizumab Reduces Systemic Corticosteroid Use in Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps. J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract. 2023. PMID: 37586475 · NCT03085797 (registry ID stated in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: mepolizumab helps severe, previously operated CRSwNP — polyp, obstruction and surgery endpoints move together in one trial programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: mepolizumab helps severe, previously operated CRSwNP — polyp, obstruction and surgery endpoints move together in one trial programme
cards.people: The carded evidence is one phase 3 trial (SYNAPSE, 407 patients) and two analyses of it (surgery endpoints; corticosteroid sparing). Live shelf #375 homes dupilumab and omalizumab for the same condition and does not card mepolizumab.
cards.result: Polyp score, nasal obstruction and the need for further surgery all favoured mepolizumab over placebo at 52 weeks, with serious adverse events balanced between groups (6% each). The honest claim is a single-programme POSSIBLE: benefit is demonstrated, but there is no second confirmatory trial and no randomised comparison against dupilumab or omalizumab.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise beyond the trial fence: recurrent, refractory, severe bilateral disease in patients who had already had surgery and were candidates for more — not ordinary sinusitis with incidental polyps.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1-2. No new data.

shelves.title: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (single trial, 1995): immediate vitrectomy benefited only eyes with light-perception-only vision (20/40 or better in 33% vs 11%) — no benefit at hand-motions or better, and none from intravenous antibiotics
shelves.question: In adults with acute postoperative endophthalmitis after cataract surgery, does immediate pars plana vitrectomy improve final vision versus vitreous tap/biopsy with intravitreal antibiotics — and does the answer depend on presenting vision (light perception only versus hand motions or better)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amikacin/therapeutic use* · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage, therapeutic use* · Cataract Extraction/adverse effects · Ceftazidime/therapeutic use* · Cephalosporins/administration & dosage, therapeutic use* · Endophthalmitis/microbiology, therapy* · Eye Infections, Bacterial/etiology, therapy* · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Lenses, Intraocular/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vision, Ocular · Visual Acuity · Vitrectomy*
shelves.balance: SINGLE-TRIAL SHELF, labelled as such on its face. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (420 patients, reported 1995) is old and pre-dates modern small-gauge vitrectomy; a 2022 Cochrane review searched to May 2022 and found it is still the only randomised trial of early vitrectomy versus tap and inject, grading the evidence very low to low certainty. Its conclusion is driven by one subgroup: with light perception-only vision at presentation, immediate vitrectomy gave 20/40 or better acuity in 33% versus 11% and severe visual loss in 20% versus 47% versus tap/biopsy; with hand-motions vision or better there was no difference, and intravenous antibiotics made no difference to acuity or media clarity in any group. Modern retrospective series (Far 2021, 1,355 eyes) find tap and inject noninferior overall (relative risk 1.04 for ≥2-line improvement), but they are confounded by indication and do not test the light-perception subgroup. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the light-perception-only presentation only.

cards.headline: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study 1995 (single RCT, 420 patients): immediate vitrectomy helped only the light-perception-only subgroup — 20/40 or better in 33% versus 11%, severe visual loss in 20% versus 47%; no benefit with hand-motions or better vision, and no benefit from intravenous antibiotics
cards.summary: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study 1995 (single RCT, 420 patients): immediate vitrectomy helped only the light-perception-only subgroup — 20/40 or better in 33% versus 11%, severe visual loss in 20% versus 47%; no benefit with hand-motions or better vision, and no benefit from intravenous antibiotics
cards.type: Randomised factorial trial — the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS Group 1995)
cards.people: 420 patients with clinical evidence of bacterial endophthalmitis within 6 weeks after cataract surgery or secondary intraocular lens implantation, randomised at multiple centres in a 2 × 2 factorial design to immediate pars plana vitrectomy (VIT) or vitreous tap/biopsy (TAP), and to systemic antibiotics (ceftazidime and amikacin) or none; visual acuity and media clarity assessed at 9 months with an Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study chart.
cards.result: There was no difference in final visual acuity or media clarity with or without systemic antibiotics. In patients whose initial visual acuity was hand motions or better, there was no difference in visual outcome whether or not immediate vitrectomy was performed. In the subgroup with light perception-only vision, vitrectomy produced a threefold increase in achieving 20/40 or better acuity (33% vs 11%), approximately a twofold chance of achieving 20/100 or better (56% vs 30%), and a 50% relative decrease in the frequency of severe visual loss (20% vs 47% — absolute rates printed here) over tap/biopsy; the difference was statistically significant (P < .001, log rank test for cumulative visual acuity scores) over the entire range of vision.
cards.watchOut: SINGLE-TRIAL SHELF, and an old one: this 1995 trial pre-dates modern small-gauge (23/25/27-gauge) vitrectomy, modern intravitreal practice and current organism patterns, and it studied endophthalmitis after cataract surgery or secondary lens implantation only — not post-injection, traumatic or endogenous endophthalmitis. The entire vitrectomy conclusion rests on the light-perception-only subgroup; applying it to patients presenting with better vision misreads the trial.
cards.source: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study Group. Results of the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study. A randomized trial of immediate vitrectomy and of intravenous antibiotics for the treatment of postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis. Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study Group. Archives of ophthalmology (Chicago, Ill. : 1960). 1995. PMID: 7487614. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Muqit 2022 (Cochrane review): the EVS remains the single RCT meeting criteria for early vitrectomy versus tap and inject — certainty rated very low to low, 24 of 420 participants without final follow-up
cards.summary: Muqit 2022 (Cochrane review): the EVS remains the single RCT meeting criteria for early vitrectomy versus tap and inject — certainty rated very low to low, 24 of 420 participants without final follow-up
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (searched to 5 May 2022) of randomised trials comparing pars plana vitrectomy plus intravitreal antibiotics versus intravitreal antibiotics alone (tap and inject) for immediate management of exogenous endophthalmitis, with GRADE certainty assessment.
cards.result: A single RCT met the inclusion criteria — the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study, 420 participants, of whom 24 did not have final follow-up (12 died, 5 withdrew consent, 7 were unwilling to return). At three months, 41% of all participants achieved 20/40 or better acuity and 69% had 20/100 or better. The study authors reported no statistically significant difference in visual acuity between treatment groups overall (very low-certainty evidence), and there was low-certainty evidence of a similar requirement for additional surgical procedures (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.21). Adverse effects included dislocated intraocular lens (n = 2) and macular infarction (n = 1) in the vitrectomy group and expulsive haemorrhage (n = 1) in the tap group.
cards.watchOut: A Cochrane review whose entire content is one 1995 trial cannot add independent certainty — it confirms the evidence base is a single trial and grades it very low to low certainty overall. The review's predefined acuity outcomes were not reported by the trial in the form the review sought.
cards.source: Muqit MM et al. Early vitrectomy for exogenous endophthalmitis following surgery. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 36398614. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Far 2021 (meta-analysis of 15 retrospective series, 1,355 eyes): in the modern era, tap and inject was noninferior to vitrectomy — relative risk of improving ≥2 lines 1.04 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.23)
cards.summary: Far 2021 (meta-analysis of 15 retrospective series, 1,355 eyes): in the modern era, tap and inject was noninferior to vitrectomy — relative risk of improving ≥2 lines 1.04 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.23)
cards.people: Fifteen retrospective case series (1,355 eyes) published 2010–2020 comparing prompt pars plana vitrectomy with tap biopsy and intravitreal antimicrobial injection for postinjection and postsurgery endophthalmitis; 739 eyes (55%) received intravitreal injection and 616 (45%) vitrectomy as initial treatment. Methodological quality assessed with the Cochrane ROBINS-I tool.
cards.result: The overall relative risk of improving 2 or more lines with vitrectomy compared with intravitreal injection was 1.04 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.23; P = 0.61; I² = 0%), with a mean logMAR difference in improvement of 0.04 (95% CI −0.18 to 0.27; P = 0.69). Results were robust in subgroup analyses by causative procedure. The authors conclude intravitreal antimicrobial injection is noninferior to vitrectomy for postcataract, postinjection and post-vitrectomy endophthalmitis in these series.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective series carry severe confounding by indication — eyes sent straight to vitrectomy are usually the worst eyes — so 'noninferior' here means the modern observational record does not reproduce an EVS-style vitrectomy advantage outside the light-perception subgroup; it does not prove equivalence, and it does not overturn the EVS subgroup result on its own terms.
cards.source: Far PM et al. TAP AND INJECT VERSUS PARS PLANA VITRECTOMY FOR POSTPROCEDURAL ENDOPHTHALMITIS: A Meta-analysis. Retina (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2021. PMID: 34009185. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a single-trial shelf — the EVS (1995) supports immediate vitrectomy only for light-perception-only presentations, and no later randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single-trial shelf — the EVS (1995) supports immediate vitrectomy only for light-perception-only presentations, and no later randomised trial exists
cards.people: One randomised trial (420 patients, 1995), a Cochrane review that found that same single trial and nothing else, and a meta-analysis of 15 modern retrospective series (1,355 eyes).
cards.result: EVS: no vitrectomy benefit at hand-motions or better vision; in light-perception-only eyes, 20/40 or better in 33% vs 11% and severe visual loss in 20% vs 47% versus tap. No benefit from intravenous antibiotics on any outcome. Modern series: relative risk 1.04 for ≥2-line improvement, vitrectomy versus tap and inject. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), stamped as a single-trial shelf.
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf must be read with its three qualifiers: one trial, from 1995, pre-dating modern small-gauge vitrectomy — and its conclusion is driven by the light-perception-only subgroup. For a patient presenting with hand-motions vision or better, the trial itself found no benefit from immediate vitrectomy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study Group. Archives of Ophthalmology. 1995 (PMID: 7487614); Muqit MMK et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022 (PMID: 36398614); Far PM et al. Retina. 2021 (PMID: 34009185).

shelves.title: Face-down posturing after macular-hole vitrectomy: SPLIT by hole size — small holes close either way; for holes ≥400 μm a closure advantage is suggested but unproven (95.5% vs 85.6%, P = .08 in the largest trial), with better acuity face-down
shelves.question: In adults having vitrectomy for full-thickness macular hole, does strict face-down posturing improve hole closure and vision versus face-forward or no positioning, and does hole size change the answer?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Fluorocarbons/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Postoperative Care/methods · Prone Position* · Prospective Studies · Retinal Perforations/diagnosis, surgery* · Sulfur Hexafluoride/administration & dosage · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity · Vitrectomy*
shelves.balance: SPLIT, with hole size as the effect modifier. For holes under 400 μm every source agrees positioning does not matter: closure was 100 versus 96 per 100 eyes in the Cochrane subgroup analysis, and Guillaubey's post hoc analysis found no positional influence. For holes of 400 μm or more the sources divide: Guillaubey (150 eyes) found overall closure of 97.4% face-down versus 87.5% seated (P = .027) and recommended face-down for large holes; the PIMS trial (Pasu 2020, 185 patients, all holes ≥400 μm) found closure of 95.5% versus 85.6% face-forward — not significant (P = .08) — but significantly better acuity improvement face-down (about 3 versus 1 Snellen lines, P = .01); Alberti & la Cour's noninferiority trial found closure identical at 97.1% in both arms, including large holes; and the Cochrane review (Cundy 2023, 8 RCTs, 709 eyes, low certainty) pooled a closure relative risk of 1.05 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.12) overall and 1.08 (0.93 to 1.26) in large holes. PROPOSED SPLIT (by hole size).

cards.headline: Guillaubey 2008 (RCT, 150 eyes): face-down versus seated positioning — closure 97.4% versus 87.5% overall, but no difference for holes smaller than 400 μm (post hoc)
cards.summary: Guillaubey 2008 (RCT, 150 eyes): face-down versus seated positioning — closure 97.4% versus 87.5% overall, but no difference for holes smaller than 400 μm (post hoc)
cards.people: 144 patients (150 eyes) with idiopathic macular hole at two French university hospitals, randomised after complete vitrectomy with fluid–air exchange and intraocular gas tamponade to keep a seated position (72 eyes) or a face-down position (78 eyes) for five days; acuity, fundus examination and optical coherence tomography before and six months after surgery. Registered as ISRCTN21076960.
cards.result: The overall anatomic success rate was 92.7%: holes sealed in 63 of 72 seated eyes (87.5%) and 76 of 78 face-down eyes (97.4%) (P = .027). Mean visual acuity increased from 0.86 to 0.61 logMAR overall, similarly in both groups (0.88 to 0.61 seated; 0.84 to 0.60 face-down). In a post hoc analysis by hole size, the success rate in holes smaller than 400 μm was not influenced by postoperative position (P = .47). The authors recommend face-down positioning in holes larger than 400 μm and identify hole size as an important factor affecting outcome.
cards.watchOut: The hole-size interaction — the finding this shelf turns on — comes from a post hoc analysis, and the seated group is not a 'no positioning' group: both arms postured, differing in direction. Five days of positioning, gas tamponade without the internal limiting membrane peel detail modern series assume.

cards.headline: Alberti & la Cour 2016 (noninferiority RCT, 81 enrolled, 68 analysed): nonsupine positioning was noninferior — closure 97.1% in both groups, including the ≥400 μm subgroup (93.8% face-down vs 100% nonsupine)
cards.summary: Alberti & la Cour 2016 (noninferiority RCT, 81 enrolled, 68 analysed): nonsupine positioning was noninferior — closure 97.1% in both groups, including the ≥400 μm subgroup (93.8% face-down vs 100% nonsupine)
cards.people: 81 pseudophakic participants at a single centre undergoing pars plana vitrectomy, internal limiting membrane peeling and perfluoropropane gas tamponade for full-thickness macular hole, randomised open-label to face-down positioning or nonsupine positioning; primary outcome was hole closure, with a −15% noninferiority margin for nonsupine positioning assuming a 95% closure rate; final analysis included 68 participants.
cards.result: Closure rates were equal in both positioning groups: 33 of 34 (97.1%; 95% CI 84.7 to 99.9) in each. In the ≥400 μm subgroup, closure was 93.8% with face-down and 100.0% with nonsupine positioning (P = 0.43). Final visual acuity did not differ significantly between groups (P = 0.60). Median gas fill on day 4 was 78% (range 57–86) face-down and 76% (56–85) nonsupine (P = 0.51), and gas fill was significantly higher in closed than unclosed holes (P = 0.02). The authors conclude nonsupine positioning is noninferior to face-down positioning.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen of 81 enrolled participants are not in the final analysis, the noninferiority margin was wide (−15%), and the trial was open-label — but it is the one trial designed to test whether posture can be relaxed, and it found closure rates identical to the decimal point, including in large holes.

cards.headline: Pasu 2020 — PIMS (multicentre RCT, 185 patients, all holes ≥400 μm): closure 95.5% face-down versus 85.6% face-forward did not reach significance (P = .08), but visual acuity improvement was better face-down (3 versus 1 Snellen lines, P = .01)
cards.summary: Pasu 2020 — PIMS (multicentre RCT, 185 patients, all holes ≥400 μm): closure 95.5% face-down versus 85.6% face-forward did not reach significance (P = .08), but visual acuity improvement was better face-down (3 versus 1 Snellen lines, P = .01)
cards.people: 185 participants with idiopathic full-thickness macular hole of at least 400 μm minimum linear diameter and duration under 12 months, at 9 UK sites, all undergoing vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling and 14% perfluoropropane gas, randomised to advice to position face-down or face forward for 8 hours daily for 5 days, with masked optical coherence tomography assessment at 3 months. Registered as ISRCTN12410596, as reported in the record.
cards.result: Macular hole closure was observed in 95.5% of the face-down group and 85.6% of the face-forward group (adjusted odds ratio 3.15, 95% CI 0.87 to 11.41; P = .08) — a 9.9 percentage point absolute difference that did not reach significance. Mean improvement in best-corrected visual acuity at 3 months was 0.57 (SD 0.42) logMAR (about 3 Snellen lines) face-down versus 0.34 (0.69) logMAR (about 1 line) face-forward (adjusted mean difference 0.22, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.38; P = .01). Quality-of-life scores (NEI VFQ-25) did not differ (P = .41). The authors conclude the results do not prove face-down positioning closes large holes more often, but support the possibility of superior visual acuity outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial, restricted to the large holes where face-down posturing is supposed to matter most, missed significance on its primary outcome — the confidence interval (OR 0.87 to 11.41) is wide enough to include both no effect and a large one. The acuity advantage is a secondary outcome at only 3 months.

cards.headline: Cundy 2023 (Cochrane review, 8 RCTs, 709 eyes): closure 95 versus 85 per 100 eyes (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.12; low certainty) — and no significant advantage in either hole-size subgroup
cards.summary: Cundy 2023 (Cochrane review, 8 RCTs, 709 eyes): closure 95 versus 85 per 100 eyes (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.12; low certainty) — and no significant advantage in either hole-size subgroup
cards.people: Eight randomised trials allocating 709 eyes (699 participants) comparing postoperative face-down positioning with no face-down positioning after macular hole surgery, with positioning durations of 3 days (two studies), 5 days (two) and 10 days (three), varying control postures and surgical procedures; primary outcome was anatomical hole closure at one to six months. Certainty assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Successful closure was reported in 95 of every 100 eyes advised to position face-down and 85 of every 100 eyes not so advised (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.12; 709 eyes, 8 studies; I² = 44%). In holes of at least 400 μm (327 eyes, 5 studies), closure was 94 versus 84 per 100 (relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.26; I² = 62%). In holes under 400 μm (129 eyes, 4 studies), closure was 100 versus 96 per 100 (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.11; I² = 0%). The certainty of evidence was low, downgraded for imprecision and study-design limitations; all studies were at high or unclear risk of bias for unmeasured adherence to the prescribed positioning.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate sits in tension with the individual positive trials: heterogeneity in duration (3–10 days), control posture and surgery, plus universally unmeasured adherence, means the review's low-certainty near-null average and Guillaubey's significant result can both be faithful to their data. Neither should be quoted alone.
cards.source: Cundy O et al. Face-down positioning or posturing after macular hole surgery. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2023. PMID: 37987517. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by hole size and by outcome — small holes close either way; for large holes the closure advantage is suggested but unproven, with a possible acuity advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by hole size and by outcome — small holes close either way; for large holes the closure advantage is suggested but unproven, with a possible acuity advantage
cards.people: Four randomised trials and a Cochrane review of eight (709 eyes): Guillaubey (150 eyes), Alberti & la Cour (68 analysed), PIMS in large holes only (185 patients), and the pooled Cochrane estimate.
cards.result: Small holes (<400 μm): closure is high regardless of posture in every source (Cochrane: 100 vs 96 per 100). Large holes (≥400 μm): Guillaubey's post hoc analysis and the Lange pilot favoured face-down, Alberti found nonsupine noninferior with equal closure, PIMS found 95.5% vs 85.6% (P = .08) with significantly better acuity face-down, and the Cochrane large-hole subgroup pooled a relative risk of 1.08 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.26). PROPOSED SPLIT (by hole size).
cards.watchOut: Hole size is the effect modifier every source points to, but the large-hole closure benefit remains a suggestion distributed across one post hoc analysis, one pilot and one near-significant large trial — against one noninferiority trial and a null pooled subgroup. The Lange pilot RCT (PMID: 21941361, 30 patients; large-hole closure 91% vs 40%) is cited here in the synthesis only, not carded, because its numbers are already inside the Cochrane pool.
cards.source: Synthesis of Guillaubey A et al. American Journal of Ophthalmology. 2008 (PMID: 18440484); Alberti M & la Cour M. Retina. 2016 (PMID: 27046458); Pasu S et al. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2020 (PMID: 32379288); Cundy O et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 37987517).

shelves.title: Repeated low-level red-light therapy for progressing childhood myopia: axial elongation 0.13 mm versus 0.38 mm at 1 year in the pivotal Chinese randomised trial — but the base is short-term, from one country's programmes, and a retinal-damage case report has appeared
shelves.question: In children with progressing myopia, does repeated low-level red-light therapy slow axial elongation and refractive progression versus single-vision spectacles, and what retinal safety signals have appeared?
shelves.mesh: Child · Disease Progression · Eyeglasses · Humans · Myopia · Phototherapy · Refraction, Ocular · Single-Blind Method · Axial Length, Eye · Follow-Up Studies · Atropine/therapeutic use · Mydriatics/therapeutic use · Myopia/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Retinal Diseases/diagnosis,etiology · Retinal Detachment · Eye Injuries/diagnosis,etiology · Lasers
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with an open retinal-safety question. In the pivotal multicentre randomised trial (Jiang Y et al., PMID: 34863776), 264 Chinese children aged 8–13 were randomised to repeated low-level red-light (RLRL) therapy plus single-vision spectacles versus spectacles alone for 12 months: adjusted axial elongation was 0.13 mm versus 0.38 mm and refractive progression −0.20 D versus −0.79 D (between-group differences 0.26 mm and −0.59 D), with no severe adverse events, no functional visual loss and no structural damage on OCT in the trial. A meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials with 1,031 children (Wang F et al., PMID: 37565498) found the same direction (axial length mean difference −0.25 mm; spherical equivalent +0.60 D). In the 2-year post-trial follow-up (Xiong R et al., PMID: 36054314; 114 children analysed), children who continued RLRL had the least 2-year elongation (0.16 mm) and stopping treatment produced a modest rebound. Against this, a published case report (Liu H et al., PMID: 37227712) describes retinal damage after RLRL exposure in a 12-year-old girl — a single case, but in a therapy given to healthy children's eyes. The fetched trial records describe the device only by specification — a home-use desktop device emitting 650-nm red light, 3 minutes twice daily, 5 days per week — and do not name a brand or maker in the record; current marketed devices may differ. The randomised base is short-term and concentrated in Chinese trial programmes. The atropine slice is homed on live Shelf #614 and the multifocal-lens slice on live Shelf #618; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): RLRL slows axial elongation and refractive progression over 1 year in the trials done so far, but long-term and independent replication are lacking and retinal-safety case reports mean the harm side is not closed.

cards.headline: Jiang 2022 (pivotal RCT): 12-month axial elongation 0.13 mm on red-light therapy versus 0.38 mm on spectacles alone; refraction −0.20 D versus −0.79 D; no structural damage on OCT in-trial
cards.summary: Jiang 2022 (pivotal RCT): 12-month axial elongation 0.13 mm on red-light therapy versus 0.38 mm on spectacles alone; refraction −0.20 D versus −0.79 D; no structural damage on OCT in-trial
cards.people: 264 children aged 8–13 years in China with myopia of −1.00 to −5.00 D, randomised to RLRL plus single-vision spectacles or spectacles alone; RLRL was a home desktop device emitting 650-nm red light (about 1600 lux; 0.29 mW for a 4-mm pupil), 3 minutes per session, twice daily, 5 days per week, under parental supervision; 246 children (93.2%) were analysed.
cards.result: Adjusted 12-month axial elongation was 0.13 mm (95% CI 0.09 to 0.17) on RLRL versus 0.38 mm (0.34 to 0.42) on spectacles; spherical-equivalent progression was −0.20 D (−0.29 to −0.11) versus −0.79 D (−0.88 to −0.69). Between-group differences were 0.26 mm (0.20 to 0.31) and −0.59 D (−0.72 to −0.46). No severe adverse events (sudden vision loss of 2 or more lines, or scotoma), no functional visual loss on acuity testing, and no structural damage on OCT scans were observed.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (children and parents could tell who had the device), 12 months only, and run within one country's programme — the effect size is large for a myopia-control intervention and awaits independent replication elsewhere. The record describes the device by specification only; it does not name a brand or maker.

multicentre randomised single-blind controlled trial (jiang 2022) 264 children aged 8–13 years in china with myopia of −1.00 to −5.00 d, randomised to rlrl plus single-vision spectacles or spectacles alone; rlrl was a home desktop device emitting 650-nm red light (about 1600 lux; 0.29 mw for a 4-mm pupil), 3 minutes per session, twice daily, 5 days per week, under parental supervision; 246 children (93.2%) were analysed. adjusted 12-month axial elongation was 0.13 mm (95% ci 0.09 to 0.17) on rlrl versus 0.38 mm (0.34 to 0.42) on spectacles; spherical-equivalent progression was −0.20 d (−0.29 to −0.11) versus −0.79 d (−0.88 to −0.69). between-group differences were 0.26 mm (0.20 to 0.31) and −0.59 d (−0.72 to −0.46). no severe adverse events (sudden vision loss of 2 or more lines, or scotoma), no functional visual loss on acuity testing, and no structural damage on oct scans were observed. single-blind (children and parents could tell who had the device), 12 months only, and run within one country's programme — the effect size is large for a myopia-control intervention and awaits independent replication elsewhere. the record describes the device by specification only; it does not name a brand or maker. jiang y et al. effect of repeated low-level red-light therapy for myopia control in children: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. ophthalmology. 2022. pmid: 34863776. registry id: none in the record. mesh: child · disease progression · eyeglasses · humans · myopia · phototherapy · refraction, ocular · single-blind method

cards.headline: Wang 2023 (meta-analysis of 7 RCTs, 1,031 children): axial length −0.25 mm and spherical equivalent +0.60 D favouring red-light therapy
cards.summary: Wang 2023 (meta-analysis of 7 RCTs, 1,031 children): axial length −0.25 mm and spherical equivalent +0.60 D favouring red-light therapy
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Wang 2023)
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials with 1,031 children with myopia aged 6–16 years, comparing RLRL therapy against no-RLRL controls (single-vision lenses, orthokeratology or low-dose atropine in subgroup analyses), with 6- and 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: RLRL was associated with less axial elongation (mean difference −0.25 mm, 95% CI −0.32 to −0.17, P<0.001; I²=13%) and better (less negative) cycloplegic spherical equivalent (mean difference +0.60 D, 0.44 to 0.76, P<0.001; I²=20%). Subgroup results were consistent against single-vision lenses and against active comparators, and at both 6 and 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are short (6–12 months) and geographically concentrated, so the meta-analysis inherits the pivotal programme's limitations rather than independently confirming it; the review searched Chinese databases (Wanfang, CNKI) alongside PubMed, Embase and Cochrane, reflecting where this literature sits.
cards.source: Wang F et al. Repeated Low-Level Red Light Therapy for the Control of Myopia in Children: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Eye & contact lens. 2023. PMID: 37565498. cards.headline: Xiong 2022 (2-year post-trial follow-up, 114 analysed): continuing red-light therapy gave the least 2-year elongation (0.16 mm); stopping produced a modest rebound (second-year elongation 0.42 mm)
cards.summary: Xiong 2022 (2-year post-trial follow-up, 114 analysed): continuing red-light therapy gave the least 2-year elongation (0.16 mm); stopping produced a modest rebound (second-year elongation 0.42 mm)
cards.type: Post-trial follow-up of a randomised trial cohort (Xiong 2022)
cards.people: Children from the pivotal 1-year trial who were eligible for a second year (199 eligible; 138 attended; 114 analysed), grouped by whether they continued RLRL, stopped it, started it, or never had it (RLRL-RLRL n=11; RLRL-SVS n=52; SVS-RLRL n=10; SVS-SVS n=41).
cards.result: Second-year axial elongation was 0.12 mm in continuers versus 0.42 mm in those who stopped RLRL, 0.05 mm in those who started it, and 0.28 mm in never-treated children (P<0.001). Over 2 years, elongation was smallest in continuers (0.16 mm) and largest in never-treated children (0.64 mm); spherical-equivalent change ordered the same way (−0.31 D versus −1.24 D). No self-reported adverse events or functional or structural damage were noted.
cards.watchOut: This is a post-trial observational follow-up, not a re-randomisation: families chose whether to continue, the continuer group is only 11 children, and 43% of eligible children were not analysed — the rebound estimate is therefore fragile.
cards.source: Xiong R et al. Sustained and rebound effect of repeated low-level red-light therapy on myopia control: A 2-year post-trial follow-up study. Clinical & experimental ophthalmology. 2022. cards.headline: Liu 2023 (case report, N=1): retinal damage in a 12-year-old girl after repeated low-level red-light exposure
cards.summary: Liu 2023 (case report, N=1): retinal damage in a 12-year-old girl after repeated low-level red-light exposure
cards.type: Case report (Liu 2023) — safety signal, N=1, printed plainly
cards.people: A single case: a 12-year-old girl with myopia who sustained retinal damage after repeated low-level red-light laser exposure, reported in JAMA Ophthalmology.
cards.result: The report documents retinal damage following RLRL exposure in one child. A single case cannot estimate how often this happens, and the pivotal trial (264 children, OCT-monitored) found no structural damage — but the case shows the harm is possible in real-world use, outside trial monitoring.
cards.watchOut: Carded as a safety signal, not as an efficacy study, and labelled N=1 on its face. Device settings, exposure history and susceptibility in this case cannot be generalised from the abstract-level record; the point for the shelf is that retinal-safety reports exist and must sit beside the efficacy trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: strong 1-year efficacy in one country's trials, a rebound on stopping, and an unclosed retinal-safety file
cards.summary: Synthesis: strong 1-year efficacy in one country's trials, a rebound on stopping, and an unclosed retinal-safety file
cards.people: One pivotal multicentre RCT (264 children), its 2-year post-trial follow-up (114 analysed), a 7-trial meta-analysis (1,031 children) and one retinal-damage case report, all fetched from PubMed this session.
cards.result: Axial elongation at 1 year: 0.13 mm on RLRL versus 0.38 mm on spectacles alone; meta-analysis mean difference −0.25 mm. Benefit persists while treatment continues and partly rebounds on stopping. No harm was seen inside the monitored trial; retinal damage has been reported in a single case outside it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: efficacy is concordant but short-term and single-geography, and the safety question is open.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as covering myopia control generally: atropine is live Shelf #614 and multifocal/dual-focus lenses are live Shelf #618. The fetched records do not name the tested device's brand or maker; marketed devices may differ in output from the trial device specification (650 nm, about 1600 lux).
cards.source: Synthesis of Jiang Y et al. Ophthalmology. 2022 (PMID: 34863776); Xiong R et al. Clinical & experimental ophthalmology. 2022 (PMID: 36054314); Wang F et al. Eye & contact lens. 2023 (PMID: 37565498); Liu H et al. JAMA ophthalmology. 2023 (PMID: 37227712).

shelves.title: Intense pulsed light for evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction: tear-film measures and symptoms improve versus sham in small masked trials, and a 15-trial meta-analysis agrees — but the trials are small and short
shelves.question: In adults with evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction, does intense pulsed light therapy improve symptoms and tear-film measures versus sham light treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Double-Blind Method · Dry Eye Syndromes/therapy · Eyelid Diseases/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Meibomian Glands/radiation effects · Middle Aged · Phototherapy/methods · Prospective Studies · Young Adult · Corynebacterium · France · Intense Pulsed Light Therapy · Meibomian Gland Dysfunction · Meibomian Glands · Tears · Treatment Outcome · Dry Eye Syndromes/etiology,metabolism,therapy · Fluorescein/metabolism · Intense Pulsed Light Therapy/methods · Lipids · Lubricant Eye Drops · Meibomian Gland Dysfunction/complications,therapy · Meibomian Glands/metabolism · Tears/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant sources, all small or pooled from small trials. In a double-masked paired-eye placebo-controlled trial (Craig JP et al., PMID: 25678687), 28 participants had one eye treated with intense pulsed light (IPL) and the partner eye sham-treated: lipid layer grade and non-invasive tear break-up time improved only in treated eyes (break-up time 14.1 versus 8.6 seconds at day 45), and 86% reported fewer symptoms in the treated eye. In a parallel-group double-masked placebo-controlled trial of 87 participants (Xue AL et al., PMID: 32007523) using the E-Eye Intense Regulated Pulsed Light device (E-Swin, France) — the device class named as published in that trial — symptom scores (OSDI, SPEED, SANDE), lipid layer thickness and gland capping improved, with the five-flash regimen separating earlier and more fully than four flashes. A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials with 1,142 patients (Miao S et al., PMID: 36044829) found IPL better than sham on symptom scores and tear break-up time, and IPL plus gland expression better than expression alone on several measures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IPL improves tear-film quality and symptoms in MGD over weeks to a few months; durability beyond a treatment course, optimal regimens, and any effect on gland structure long-term are not settled by this base.

cards.headline: Craig 2015 (paired-eye, double-masked, N=28): lipid layer grade and tear break-up time improved only in the IPL-treated eye (14.1 vs 8.6 seconds at day 45); 86% reported fewer symptoms in the treated eye
cards.summary: Craig 2015 (paired-eye, double-masked, N=28): lipid layer grade and tear break-up time improved only in the IPL-treated eye (14.1 vs 8.6 seconds at day 45); 86% reported fewer symptoms in the treated eye
cards.people: 28 participants with meibomian gland dysfunction; homogeneously sequenced IPL pulses were delivered to one eye and placebo treatment to the partner eye on days 1, 15 and 45, so each participant was their own control.
cards.result: Lipid layer grade improved significantly in treated eyes (P<0.001) but not control eyes (P=0.714), with 82% of treated eyes improving by at least one grade. Non-invasive tear break-up time improved in treated eyes (P<0.001) and at day 45 was 14.1 ± 9.8 seconds versus 8.6 ± 8.2 seconds in control eyes (P<0.001). Tear evaporation rate and meniscus height did not differ. Symptom scores improved in the treated eye (P=0.015) but not the control eye (P=0.245).
cards.watchOut: A paired-eye design controls between-person variation beautifully but cannot capture whole-person symptom relief, and 28 participants is small; the abstract does not name the IPL device used. Follow-up ends at day 45.
cards.source: Craig JP et al. Prospective trial of intense pulsed light for the treatment of meibomian gland dysfunction. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 2015. PMID: 25678687. Registry ID: ACTRN12614000162617. cards.headline: Xue 2020 (parallel-group RCT, N=87): IPL with the E-Eye device (E-Swin, France) improved OSDI/SPEED/SANDE scores, lipid layer thickness and gland capping; five flashes beat four
cards.summary: Xue 2020 (parallel-group RCT, N=87): IPL with the E-Eye device (E-Swin, France) improved OSDI/SPEED/SANDE scores, lipid layer thickness and gland capping; five flashes beat four
cards.people: 87 symptomatic participants (mean age 53 years) with clinical signs of MGD, randomised to four or five homogeneously sequenced light pulses or placebo to both eyes, using the E-Eye Intense Regulated Pulsed Light device (E-Swin, France) as named in the record; assessed to day 105.
cards.result: Both IPL regimens produced significant decreases in OSDI, SPEED and SANDE symptom scores and in meibomian gland capping, with increased tear-film lipid layer thickness (all P<0.05). Sustained improvements were present from day 75 in both groups, but earlier changes (from day 45) in lipid layer quality, capping, OSDI and SANDE were limited to the five-flash group, leading the authors to suggest an initial course of at least four treatments before judging efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports within-group improvements and the five-versus-four-flash contrast more fully than the IPL-versus-placebo contrast; it is a single-centre-style programme with day-105 horizons. Device named as published for this trial; other IPL devices are not interchangeable by assumption.
cards.source: Xue AL et al. Randomised double-masked placebo-controlled trial of the cumulative treatment efficacy profile of intense pulsed light therapy for meibomian gland dysfunction. The ocular surface. 2020. PMID: 32007523. Registry ID: ACTRN12616000667415. cards.headline: Miao 2022 (meta-analysis, 15 RCTs, 1,142 patients): IPL beat sham on OSDI, SPEED and tear break-up time; IPL plus expression beat expression alone on several measures
cards.summary: Miao 2022 (meta-analysis, 15 RCTs, 1,142 patients): IPL beat sham on OSDI, SPEED and tear break-up time; IPL plus expression beat expression alone on several measures
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Miao 2022)
cards.people: 15 randomised controlled trials with 1,142 patients (2,284 eyes) with dry eye disease caused by MGD, comparing IPL alone, IPL plus meibomian gland expression, expression alone, and sham, in literature to November 2021.
cards.result: Versus sham, IPL significantly improved OSDI, SPEED, artificial-tear use, tear-film lipid layer, gland quality and expression scores, corneal staining, tear break-up time and non-invasive break-up time. Versus expression alone, IPL plus expression improved SPEED, corneal staining and break-up time; some comparisons (IPL plus expression versus expression on OSDI and gland scores; IPL versus expression on OSDI/SPEED) showed no significant difference.
cards.watchOut: Pooling 15 mostly small trials does not remove their shared limits — varied devices, pulse regimens and comparators, and short follow-up. The mixed null comparisons against active expression therapy are part of the picture, not noise to discard.
cards.source: Miao S et al. Effect of Intense Pulsed Light Therapy in Dry Eye Disease Caused by Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Eye & contact lens. 2022. PMID: 36044829. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, modest, short-horizon benefit on tear film and symptoms — regimen and durability unsettled
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, modest, short-horizon benefit on tear film and symptoms — regimen and durability unsettled
cards.people: Two masked placebo/sham-controlled trials (28 paired-eye; 87 parallel-group) and a 15-trial meta-analysis (1,142 patients) in MGD-related evaporative dry eye.
cards.result: Treated eyes/patients improve on lipid layer, break-up time and symptom scores versus sham; the pooled estimate agrees. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: concordant randomised evidence, capped by small trials, heterogeneous devices and follow-up measured in weeks to months.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about IPL for MGD only — the library's dry-eye drop and spray shelves ask different questions. Symptom scores are subjective and sham light treatment is hard to mask perfectly; that is why this is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

shelves.title: Tonsillectomy for PFAPA syndrome: complete resolution in 63% versus 5% (Garavello) and all operated children symptom-free at 6 months versus half unoperated (Renko) — two small concordant randomised trials, 67 children in total
shelves.question: In children with PFAPA syndrome (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis), does tonsillectomy resolve or markedly reduce fever episodes versus watchful waiting or medical management?
shelves.mesh: Child, Preschool · Familial Mediterranean Fever/complications,surgery · Female · Humans · Lymphadenitis/complications,surgery · Male · Pharyngitis/complications,surgery · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Stomatitis, Aphthous/complications,surgery · Syndrome · Tonsillectomy · Adenoidectomy · Adolescent · Child · Fever of Unknown Origin/surgery · Lymphadenitis/surgery · Pharyngitis/surgery · Severity of Illness Index · Stomatitis, Aphthous/surgery · Treatment Outcome · Adenoidectomy/methods · Fever/surgery · Infant · Periodicity · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tonsillectomy/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on a small base that must be printed: two randomised trials, 67 children randomised in total (65 analysed in the Cochrane synthesis). In Renko M et al. (PMID: 17719940), 26 children were randomised to tonsillectomy or follow-up alone; at 6 months all 14 operated children and 6 of 12 control children (50%) were symptom-free (difference 50%, 95% CI 23% to 75%, P<.001) — half the control group resolved spontaneously. In Garavello W et al. (PMID: 19464029), 39 children were randomised to adenotonsillectomy or expectant management for 18 months: complete resolution in 63% versus 5% (P<.001), and mean episodes 0.7 versus 8.1 (P<.001). The Cochrane review (Burton MJ et al., PMID: 31886897) judged both trials at low risk of bias and concluded children with PFAPA likely experience less fever and less severe episodes after surgery (moderate-certainty evidence; resolution risk ratio 4.38, 95% CI 0.64 to 30.11 — a wide interval). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): surgery resolves or markedly reduces attacks in most operated children, with the honest caveats that the total randomised base is 67 children, PFAPA often remits on its own (half of Renko's controls by 6 months), and surgery carries its own risks, which these small trials were not sized to measure.

cards.headline: Renko 2007 (RCT, N=26): at 6 months all 14 tonsillectomy children were symptom-free versus 6 of 12 controls (50%) — difference 50% (95% CI 23% to 75%)
cards.summary: Renko 2007 (RCT, N=26): at 6 months all 14 tonsillectomy children were symptom-free versus 6 of 12 controls (50%) — difference 50% (95% CI 23% to 75%)
cards.people: 26 consecutive children (mean age 4.1 years) with at least 5 PFAPA attacks, recruited at 3 tertiary paediatric hospitals in Finland (1999–2003), randomised to tonsillectomy or follow-up alone, with symptom diaries for 12 months; control children could cross to tonsillectomy after 6 months if attacks recurred.
cards.result: Six months after randomisation, all 14 children in the tonsillectomy group and 6 of 12 (50%) in the control group were free of symptoms (difference 50%, 95% CI 23% to 75%, P<.001). Five of the 6 still-symptomatic control children then had tonsillectomy; the remaining child kept having (milder) recurrences.
cards.watchOut: Very small trial, and its own control arm is the caution: half of unoperated children resolved within 6 months anyway, so some operated 'cures' would have happened without surgery. Crossover after 6 months ends the randomised contrast.
cards.source: Renko M et al. A randomized, controlled trial of tonsillectomy in periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis syndrome. The Journal of pediatrics. 2007. PMID: 17719940. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Garavello 2009 (RCT, N=39): complete resolution 63% on adenotonsillectomy versus 5% on expectant management over 18 months; mean episodes 0.7 versus 8.1
cards.summary: Garavello 2009 (RCT, N=39): complete resolution 63% on adenotonsillectomy versus 5% on expectant management over 18 months; mean episodes 0.7 versus 8.1
cards.people: 39 children with PFAPA syndrome diagnosed by standard criteria, randomised to adenotonsillectomy (n=19) or expectant management (n=20), recording all episodes prospectively with clinical review every 3 months for 18 months.
cards.result: Complete resolution occurred in 63% of the surgery group versus 5% of controls (P<.001). The mean number of episodes during the study was 0.7 ± 1.2 with surgery versus 8.1 ± 3.9 with expectant management (P<.001), and episodes that did occur were less severe in the surgery group.
cards.watchOut: Still a small single trial (39 children), unblinded by necessity — episode recording by families who know whether surgery happened can inflate contrasts. It used adenotonsillectomy, so its result is not purely a tonsillectomy result.
cards.source: Garavello W et al. Effectiveness of adenotonsillectomy in PFAPA syndrome: a randomized study. The Journal of pediatrics. 2009. PMID: 19464029. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Burton 2019 (Cochrane): 2 trials, 67 children randomised (65 analysed), both low risk of bias — surgery likely reduces fever episodes; resolution risk ratio 4.38 with a wide interval (0.64 to 30.11), moderate certainty
cards.summary: Burton 2019 (Cochrane): 2 trials, 67 children randomised (65 analysed), both low risk of bias — surgery likely reduces fever episodes; resolution risk ratio 4.38 with a wide interval (0.64 to 30.11), moderate certainty
cards.people: The two randomised trials above (Garavello's 39 children with rigid diagnostic criteria, 18 months; Renko's smaller trial, reported by Cochrane as 28 children with less stringent criteria, 6 months), comparing tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy against non-surgical treatment in children with PFAPA.
cards.result: Combining the trials, children with PFAPA likely experience less fever and less severe episodes after surgery than with no surgery (moderate-certainty evidence). The risk ratio for immediate resolution persisting to end of follow-up was 4.38 (95% CI 0.64 to 30.11), with a number needed to treat to benefit of 2 on the review's assumed untreated resolution rate of 156 per 1,000. Both trials reported no surgical complications in the review's summary of harm outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Note a counting wrinkle the shelf keeps visible: Cochrane describes the smaller trial as 28 children while the trial report itself randomised 26 — the review's total is 67 randomised, 65 analysed. 'No complications reported' in 65 children cannot exclude uncommon surgical harms such as post-tonsillectomy bleeding.
cards.source: Burton MJ et al. Tonsillectomy for periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis syndrome (PFAPA). The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: operate and most children's attacks stop or shrink — on 67 randomised children, against a syndrome that often remits by itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: operate and most children's attacks stop or shrink — on 67 randomised children, against a syndrome that often remits by itself
cards.people: Two randomised trials (26 and 39 children) and their Cochrane synthesis (67 randomised, 65 analysed) in childhood PFAPA.
cards.result: Resolution: 63% versus 5% (18 months, adenotonsillectomy) and 100% versus 50% symptom-free (6 months, tonsillectomy). Episode burden: 0.7 versus 8.1 mean episodes in the longer trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: two concordant low-bias-risk trials plus moderate-certainty Cochrane grading, with total N printed because the base is small.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is PFAPA only — tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection and for childhood sleep apnoea are different questions homed elsewhere. Spontaneous remission (50% of Renko's controls at 6 months) means watchful waiting remains a defensible choice for milder cases.

shelves.title: Posterior nasal nerve ablation for chronic rhinitis: responders 73% versus 37% on sham (cryoablation) and 68% versus 41% on sham (radiofrequency) at 3 months — real effects over a substantial sham response, in industry device trials; durability data are post-crossover extensions
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinitis inadequately controlled by medical therapy, does posterior nasal nerve ablation — cryoablation or temperature-controlled radiofrequency — improve nasal symptom scores versus a sham procedure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cryotherapy · Humans · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Rhinitis/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Rhinitis · Temperature · Nose · Rhinorrhea · Rhinitis/surgery,therapy · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Chronic Disease · Radiofrequency Ablation · Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two sham-controlled device trials agree, and both carry a large sham response that must stay on the face. Cryoablation of the posterior nasal nerve (the ClariFix device programme; Del Signore AG et al., PMID: 34355872): in 133 enrolled adults (127 analysed), responders at 90 days (≥30% fall in reflective Total Nasal Symptom Score) were 73.4% on active treatment versus 36.5% on sham (P<0.001). Temperature-controlled radiofrequency neurolysis (the RhinAer device programme; Stolovitzky JP et al., PMID: 34527852): in 116 randomised adults, responders at 3 months were 67.5% versus 41.0% on sham (P=.009), with mean symptom-score falls of −3.6 versus −2.2 (P=.013). Both pivotal trials are industry device trials; roughly 4 in 10 sham patients met the responder definition, so the procedure-specific gain is the roughly 27–37 percentage-point difference, not the headline responder rate. Longer-term figures come from extensions after the sham arm crossed over to active treatment (12-month responder rate 80.6% in the radiofrequency programme, PMID: 35714267; 2-year responder rate 87.3% in the combined treated group, PMID: 38266636) — those are uncontrolled follow-ups, labelled as such, not randomised durability evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): both ablation modalities beat sham at 3 months by a similar margin; how much is device, how much is procedure ritual, and how long benefit lasts without a control group, remain open.

cards.headline: Del Signore 2022 (cryoablation sham RCT, 127 analysed): responders at 90 days 73.4% active versus 36.5% sham (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Del Signore 2022 (cryoablation sham RCT, 127 analysed): responders at 90 days 73.4% active versus 36.5% sham (P<0.001)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised sham-controlled patient-blinded trial (Del Signore 2022) — ClariFix cryotherapy programme
cards.people: 133 adults enrolled at 12 US centres with moderate-to-severe chronic rhinitis (reflective Total Nasal Symptom Score at least 4, with rhinorrhea at least 2 and congestion at least 1) who were candidates for posterior nasal nerve cryotherapy under local anaesthesia; 127 (64 active, 63 sham) contributed 90-day results.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — responders, defined as a 30% or greater reduction in rTNSS at 90 days — was met by 73.4% (47 of 64) on cryotherapy versus 36.5% (23 of 63) on sham (P<0.001). Improvements in rTNSS, quality-of-life (RQLQ(S)) and NOSE scores were also greater on active treatment (P<0.001). One serious procedure-related adverse event (an anxiety/panic attack) was reported.
cards.watchOut: The sham responder rate of 36.5% is substantial: the treatment-attributable gain is about 37 percentage points, not 73%. This is an industry device trial with a 90-day primary endpoint; the fetched record describes the intervention as cryotherapy and does not itself print the ClariFix brand name — the device name is as published for this programme in the trial's full report.
cards.source: Del Signore AG et al. Cryotherapy for treatment of chronic rhinitis: 3-month outcomes of a randomized, sham-controlled trial. International forum of allergy & rhinology. 2022. PMID: 34355872. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Cryotherapy · Humans · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Rhinitis/therapy · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Stolovitzky 2021 (radiofrequency sham RCT, N=116): responders at 3 months 67.5% active versus 41.0% sham (P=.009); mean rTNSS fall −3.6 versus −2.2
cards.summary: Stolovitzky 2021 (radiofrequency sham RCT, N=116): responders at 3 months 67.5% active versus 41.0% sham (P=.009); mean rTNSS fall −3.6 versus −2.2
cards.type: Multicentre randomised sham-controlled single-blinded trial (Stolovitzky 2021) — RhinAer temperature-controlled radiofrequency programme
cards.people: Adults at 16 US otolaryngology centres with chronic rhinitis and 24-hour rTNSS of at least 6 (moderate-to-severe rhinorrhea, mild-to-severe congestion), randomised 2:1 to temperature-controlled radiofrequency neurolysis of the posterior nasal nerve area (n=77) or a sham procedure with no energy delivery (n=39).
cards.result: At 3 months the responder rate (≥30% rTNSS improvement) was 67.5% (95% CI 55.9% to 77.8%) on active treatment versus 41.0% (25.6% to 57.9%) on sham (P=.009). Mean rTNSS change was −3.6 (−4.2 to −3.0) versus −2.2 (−3.2 to −1.3) (P=.013). Three device/procedure-related adverse events were reported, all resolved.
cards.watchOut: Again a large sham response (41.0% responders) — the incremental gain is about 27 percentage points. Industry device trial; single-blinded. The fetched record's MeSH was not captured this session (see summary debt note), and the record describes a temperature-controlled RF device without printing the RhinAer brand name, which is as published for this programme in the full report.
