cards.headline: Takashima 2023 (radiofrequency 12-month extension): responder rate 80.6% at 12 months in the original active arm — after unblinding, with sham patients crossed over, so uncontrolled
cards.summary: Takashima 2023 (radiofrequency 12-month extension): responder rate 80.6% at 12 months in the original active arm — after unblinding, with sham patients crossed over, so uncontrolled
cards.type: Post-crossover extension of a randomised trial (Takashima 2023) — labelled uncontrolled follow-up
cards.people: The index active-treatment arm of the Stolovitzky trial (n=77 at baseline; 67 assessed at 12 months), unblinded at 3 months and followed to 12 months; sham-arm patients were invited to cross over to active treatment at 3 months, and their early course is reported alongside.
cards.result: At 12 months the responder rate in the index active arm was 80.6% (95% CI 69.1% to 89.2%), with mean rTNSS change −4.8 (−5.5 to −4.1), a 57.8% improvement from baseline. No serious adverse events were reported; 8 device/procedure-related adverse events had been reported in the trial to date.
cards.watchOut: Labelled plainly: after the 3-month primary endpoint there is no concurrent control group — crossover and unblinding mean these figures show persistence in treated patients, not proof that benefit exceeds what sham or natural history would have shown at 12 months.

cards.type: Two-year post-crossover extension (Takashima 2024) — labelled uncontrolled follow-up
cards.people: The combined group of index active-arm and crossed-over sham-arm patients treated with temperature-controlled radiofrequency ablation (N=104 treated; N=79 assessed at 2 years) from the same multicentre trial programme.
cards.result: At 2 years, mean rTNSS change was −5.3 (95% CI −5.8 to −4.8; 64.6% improvement) and the responder rate was 87.3% (78.0% to 93.8%). All four symptom components improved, most for rhinorrhea and congestion; 44.6% of the 56 baseline medication users had stopped or reduced at least one medication class. No serious device/procedure-related adverse events were reported over 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled extension with about a quarter of treated patients not assessed at 2 years; the authors' own sensitivity handling (last-observation imputation for losses, imputation for patients who had further nasal procedures) signals how fragile long-term percentages are. Durability is suggestive, not randomised evidence.

cards.people: Two sham-controlled randomised device trials (cryoablation, 127 analysed; radiofrequency, 116 randomised) plus their post-crossover extensions to 12 months and 2 years in chronic rhinitis.
cards.result: Responder rates at 3 months: 73.4% versus 36.5% (cryoablation) and 67.5% versus 41.0% (radiofrequency). Extensions report maintained improvement to 2 years without controls. shelves.title: House-dust-mite SLIT tablet for allergic rhinitis: symptom-and-medication scores about 17–22% lower (relative) than placebo across three large trials of two different tablets — benefit maintained a year after a 1-year course stopped (Bergmann)
shelves.question: In children and adults with house-dust-mite allergic rhinitis, does a house-dust-mite sublingual immunotherapy tablet reduce symptom-and-medication scores versus placebo, including after treatment stops?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Sublingual · Adult · Animals · Antigens, Dermatophagoides/administration & dosage,immunology · Desensitization, Immunologic/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin E/blood,immunology · Immunoglobulin G/blood,immunology · Male · Pyroglyphidae/immunology · Rhinitis, Allergic · Rhinitis, Allergic, Perennial/immunology,therapy · Skin Tests · Tablets · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Adolescent · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antigens, Dermatophagoides/immunology,therapeutic use · Asthma/immunology,therapy · Child · Conjunctivitis, Allergic/immunology,therapy · Middle Aged · Placebo Effect · Rhinitis, Allergic/immunology,therapy · Sublingual Immunotherapy/methods · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, two different products, consistent relative gains of about a fifth. Bergmann KC et al. (PMID: 24388010) randomised 509 adults to the Stallergenes house-dust-mite sublingual tablet at 500 IR or 300 IR or placebo for 1 year: Average Adjusted Symptom Scores were reduced by 20.2% and 17.9% relative to placebo (P=.0066 and P=.0150), and efficacy was maintained through a subsequent treatment-free year — the after-stopping evidence in this base. Nolte H et al. (PMID: 27521719) randomised 1,482 North American adolescents and adults to the SQ HDM SLIT-tablet (MK-8237; Merck & Co, Kenilworth, NJ / ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark, as named in the record) at 12 SQ-HDM or placebo for about 52 weeks: the total combined rhinitis score improved by 17% relative to placebo (95% CI 10% to 25%). Schuster A et al. (PMID: 39678704) randomised 1,460 children aged 5–11 to the same SQ tablet or placebo for about a year: total combined rhinitis score was 1.0 point lower in absolute terms, a 22.0% relative reduction (95% CI 12.0 to 31.1, P<.0001). Adverse events were mainly application-site reactions; no anaphylaxis was reported in Bergmann, and one non-serious systemic allergic reaction treated with epinephrine occurred at first supervised administration in Nolte. All percentage gains here are relative reductions, stated as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest relative improvement in symptom-and-medication scores, with one trial showing carry-over a year after stopping. The grass-pollen SLIT tablet is homed on pack #4283 and dust-mite avoidance for asthma on pack #4148; neither is re-carded here, and the gated Demoly and Virchow records already homed elsewhere are not used.

cards.headline: Bergmann 2014 (RCT, N=509 adults): symptom scores 20.2% (500 IR) and 17.9% (300 IR) lower relative to placebo after 1 year — and efficacy maintained through the treatment-free year that followed
cards.summary: Bergmann 2014 (RCT, N=509 adults): symptom scores 20.2% (500 IR) and 17.9% (300 IR) lower relative to placebo after 1 year — and efficacy maintained through the treatment-free year that followed
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with treatment-free follow-up year (Bergmann 2014)
cards.people: 509 adults with house-dust-mite-associated allergic rhinitis, randomised to once-daily sublingual tablets of house dust mite allergen extracts (the Stallergenes HDM tablet programme) at 500 IR or 300 IR, or placebo, for 1 year; 427 continued into the subsequent immunotherapy-free year.
cards.result: Mean Average Adjusted Symptom Scores over the primary period were reduced versus placebo by 20.2% at 500 IR (P=.0066) and 17.9% at 300 IR (P=.0150) — relative reductions, as reported. Efficacy of both doses was maintained during the treatment-free follow-up year. Onset of action was at 4 months. Adverse events were generally application-site reactions; no anaphylaxis was reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative to placebo scores, not absolute score falls, and the abstract does not print the absolute scores. The record names the doses in IR units and the extract type; the product's brand name does not appear in the fetched record, so this card names the programme and maker lineage only as far as the record goes (Stallergenes HDM tablet; the 300 IR tablet is the Actair programme as described in the companion drug-profile literature, not in this record).

cards.headline: Nolte 2016 (RCT, N=1,482, North America): total combined rhinitis score improved 17% relative to placebo (95% CI 10% to 25%) on the 12 SQ-HDM tablet (MK-8237)
cards.summary: Nolte 2016 (RCT, N=1,482, North America): total combined rhinitis score improved 17% relative to placebo (95% CI 10% to 25%) on the 12 SQ-HDM tablet (MK-8237)
cards.people: 1,482 adolescents and adults (aged 12 and over) in North America with house-dust-mite-induced allergic rhinitis with or without conjunctivitis (some with asthma), randomised to a daily SQ HDM SLIT-tablet at 12 SQ-HDM (MK-8237; Merck & Co, Kenilworth, NJ / ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark, as named in the record) or placebo for up to about 52 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — average total combined rhinitis score (symptom plus medication scores) over the last 8 treatment weeks — improved by 17% relative to placebo (95% CI 10% to 25%). Secondary endpoints improved by 16–18% relative to placebo (all nominal P<.001 except the rhinitis medication score, P=.15). No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported; one non-serious systemic allergic reaction at first supervised administration was treated with epinephrine.
cards.watchOut: A 17% relative improvement on a combined score is modest in absolute terms, and the medication-score component alone did not reach significance (P=.15). This is a different product (SQ-standardised, ALK/Merck) from Bergmann's IR-dosed Stallergenes tablet — the shelf treats them as two tested products for the same question, not as interchangeable doses.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two products, three large trials, one consistent story — about a fifth better than placebo in relative terms, with one trial's post-treatment year holding up
cards.summary: Synthesis: two products, three large trials, one consistent story — about a fifth better than placebo in relative terms, with one trial's post-treatment year holding up
cards.people: Three double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 3,451 randomised participants (509 adults; 1,482 adolescents/adults; 1,460 children aged 5–11) of two distinct HDM SLIT tablets.
cards.result: Relative reductions in symptom-and-medication scores versus placebo: 17.9–20.2% (Bergmann), 17% (Nolte), 22.0% (Schuster, = 1.0 point absolute). Only Bergmann measured the after-stopping question: benefit persisted through a treatment-free year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: large concordant trials, capped at POSSIBLE because absolute gains are modest and the two products' results are pooled here only at the level of the shared question.
cards.watchOut: PARTIAL-slice discipline: the grass-pollen SLIT tablet (pack #4283) and HDM avoidance measures for asthma (pack #4148) are different questions and are not re-carded. The Demoly JACI phase III record (PMID: 26292778) and the Virchow JAMA asthma record (PMID: 27115376) were gate-checked and found already carded elsewhere, so they are deliberately excluded from this pack's source lines.

shelves.title: Intralesional therapy for keloid scars: combined triamcinolone + 5-fluorouracil beats either drug alone in the syntheses (odds ratios 3.45 and 4.17 for a good response) — but the trials underneath are small, heterogeneous and often unblinded; total randomised evidence is thin
shelves.question: In patients with established keloid scars, do intralesional therapies — corticosteroid alone, 5-fluorouracil alone, or the combination (with or without excision) — flatten scars and prevent recurrence better than each other or no injection treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Child, Preschool · Cicatrix, Hypertrophic/drug therapy,pathology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Intralesional · Keloid/drug therapy,pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Pruritus/drug therapy · Triamcinolone/administration & dosage · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Keloid/diagnosis,drug therapy · Skin/drug effects,pathology · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone Acetonide/administration & dosage · Cicatrix, Hypertrophic/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Keloid/drug therapy · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Keloid/pathology · Pharmaceutical Preparations · Triamcinolone Acetonide/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the syntheses point one way and say plainly how weak the ground is. The most direct synthesis (Mavilakandy AK et al., PMID: 37337341) pooled 13 studies (12 randomised) of keloids and hypertrophic scars: combined intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (TAC) + 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) gave superior objective treatment efficacy versus TAC alone (odds ratio 3.45, 95% CI 2.22 to 5.35) and versus 5-FU alone (odds ratio 4.17, 2.21 to 7.87), with less telangiectasia than TAC alone (odds ratio 0.24, 0.11 to 0.52). The earlier 5-FU systematic review (Bijlard E et al., PMID: 25805099) covered 18 papers and 482 patients: 5-FU was reported effective in 45–96% of patients, only the TAC:5-FU combination may perform better than TAC alone, and the reviewers state the level of evidence is poor. A network meta-analysis (Sun P et al., PMID: 31853608; 23 studies, 1,513 patients with pathological scars) ranked combination injections highest and found corticosteroid + 5-FU better than corticosteroid alone or verapamil alone, with no significant difference from 5-FU alone. The one double-blind head-to-head trial carded directly (Darougheh A et al., PMID: 19018794; 40 patients) found good-to-excellent improvement in 55% on TAC + 5-FU versus 20% on TAC alone by patient report (P=.02). Total evidence base: the syntheses overlap and cannot simply be added; the unique-patient total across the reviews is in the low thousands at most, built from many small heterogeneous trials with variable recurrence windows. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination is probably the better injection, on evidence that would not support a stronger word. Silicone gel/sheeting is homed on pack #4049 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Darougheh 2009 (double-blind RCT, N=40): good-to-excellent improvement in 55% on triamcinolone + 5-FU versus 20% on triamcinolone alone (patient-reported, P=.02)
cards.summary: Darougheh 2009 (double-blind RCT, N=40): good-to-excellent improvement in 55% on triamcinolone + 5-FU versus 20% on triamcinolone alone (patient-reported, P=.02)
cards.people: 40 patients with keloid and hypertrophic scars, randomised to weekly intralesional injections for 8 weeks of triamcinolone acetonide alone or triamcinolone plus 5-fluorouracil; 33 completed the 12-week study (4 and 3 dropouts by group).
cards.result: Both groups improved on nearly all lesion parameters (erythema, pruritus, pliability, height, length, width), more significantly in the combination group (P<.05 for all except pruritus measures). Good-to-excellent (>50%) improvement was reported by 20% of the TAC-alone group versus 55% of the combination group by patients (P=.02), and by 15% versus 40% by trained observers (P=.08, not significant).
cards.watchOut: One small 12-week trial mixing keloids with hypertrophic scars, with no recurrence follow-up beyond 12 weeks — keloid recurrence is the outcome that matters most and the one this design cannot see. The observer-rated contrast did not reach significance.
cards.source: Darougheh A et al. Intralesional triamcinolone alone or in combination with 5-fluorouracil for the treatment of keloid and hypertrophic scars. cards.summary: Bijlard 2015 (systematic review, 18 papers, 482 patients): 5-FU reported effective in 45–96% of patients; only TAC:5-FU may beat TAC alone — and the reviewers call the evidence level poor
cards.people: 18 papers reporting intralesional 5-fluorouracil alone, or 5-FU combined with triamcinolone or with excision, in keloid treatment, totalling 482 patients, from searches of 8 databases to September 2014.
cards.result: 5-FU treatment was reported effective in 45–96% of patients across the included reports — a range so wide it signals heterogeneity rather than a usable estimate. The reviewers conclude that only the TAC:5-FU combination may perform better than TAC alone, and that the poor level of evidence means superiority of repeated combination injections over TAC alone, across doses and schedules, remains to be established.
cards.watchOut: Carded as the honesty anchor of this shelf: much of the underlying literature is uncontrolled or small, 'effective' is defined differently across papers, and recurrence windows vary. Total N (482 patients) is printed here as the task requires for this row.

cards.headline: Mavilakandy 2024 (meta-analysis, 13 studies): combination TAC + 5-FU superior to TAC alone (OR 3.45, 2.22 to 5.35) and to 5-FU alone (OR 4.17, 2.21 to 7.87) for 51–100% improvement
cards.summary: Mavilakandy 2024 (meta-analysis, 13 studies): combination TAC + 5-FU superior to TAC alone (OR 3.45, 2.22 to 5.35) and to 5-FU alone (OR 4.17, 2.21 to 7.87) for 51–100% improvement
cards.people: 13 studies (12 randomised controlled trials and 1 non-randomised study) comparing combined intralesional triamcinolone + 5-fluorouracil against monotherapy TAC or monotherapy 5-FU for keloids and hypertrophic scars, from Embase, MEDLINE and CENTRAL searches.
cards.result: The combined group showed superior objective treatment efficacy (51–100% improvement) versus monotherapy TAC (odds ratio 3.45, 95% CI 2.22 to 5.35; I²=0%; P<.00001) and versus monotherapy 5-FU (odds ratio 4.17, 2.21 to 7.87; I²=0%; P<.0001). Telangiectasia was less frequent with combination therapy than with TAC alone (odds ratio 0.24, 0.11 to 0.52). The authors note the evidence base is limited and call for patient-reported outcomes in future trials.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios on a dichotomised '51–100% improvement' endpoint flatter small trials, and I²=0% across clinically heterogeneous regimens is not the same as consistency of dose, schedule or scar type. Keloids and hypertrophic scars are pooled, as in most of this literature.

cards.summary: Sun 2021 (network meta-analysis, 23 studies, 1,513 patients): combination injections ranked highest; corticosteroid + 5-FU better than corticosteroid alone or verapamil alone, not significantly different from 5-FU alone
cards.people: 23 studies with 1,513 patients with pathological scars (hypertrophic scars and keloids), comparing injected botulinum toxin type A, corticosteroids, verapamil, 5-fluorouracil and their combinations, drawn from Chinese and international databases (Wanfang, VIP, CNKI, PubMed, Cochrane, Embase).
cards.result: Botulinum toxin A combined with corticosteroid ranked best by SUCRA, followed by corticosteroid combined with 5-FU; there was no significant difference among botulinum toxin A, corticosteroid + 5-FU, verapamil and 5-FU in the network estimates, while corticosteroid + 5-FU was better than corticosteroid alone and verapamil alone but not significantly different from 5-FU alone. No publication bias was detected on the funnel plot.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings (SUCRA) are the least stable output of a sparse network — the 'best' ranking rests substantially on indirect comparisons among small trials, several from regional databases with variable quality control. Read the direct-comparison syntheses (cards above) as primary; this card shows the wider injection landscape.

cards.people: One double-blind head-to-head RCT (40 patients), a 5-FU systematic review (18 papers, 482 patients), a combination-therapy meta-analysis (13 studies) and a network meta-analysis (23 studies, 1,513 patients) — overlapping literatures, not additive totals.

shelves.title: Beremagene geperpavec (Vyjuvek, Krystal Biotech) for dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa: complete wound healing 67% versus 22% on placebo at 6 months in the GEM-3 intra-patient trial — total randomised N=31 patients, printed on the face by rare-disease necessity
shelves.question: In people with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, does topical beremagene geperpavec close wounds versus placebo gel applied to matched wounds in the same patient?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Collagen Type VII/genetics,metabolism · Epidermolysis Bullosa Dystrophica/genetics,metabolism,therapy · Genetic Therapy · Humans · Keratinocytes/metabolism · Mice · Skin/metabolism · Administration, Topical · Collagen Type VII/administration & dosage,adverse effects,genetics,metabolism · Epidermolysis Bullosa Dystrophica/drug therapy,genetics,metabolism · Pruritus/chemically induced · Wound Healing/drug effects,genetics · Genetic Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Epidermolysis Bullosa Dystrophica/therapy,genetics · Male · Female · Adult · Quality of Life · Genetic Therapy/methods,adverse effects · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Collagen Type VII/genetics · Wound Healing/genetics · Genetic Vectors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Herpesvirus 1, Human/genetics · Adolescent · Patient Satisfaction/statistics & numerical data · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Child · Skin/pathology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive phase 3 trial whose total randomised base is 31 patients, printed here and in the stamp line as required. In GEM-3 (Guide SV et al., PMID: 36516090), 31 patients aged 6 months or older with genetically confirmed dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa each contributed a matched primary wound pair; one wound received weekly beremagene geperpavec (B-VEC) and the other placebo for 26 weeks. Complete wound healing at 6 months occurred in 67% of B-VEC wounds versus 22% of placebo wounds (difference 46 percentage points, 95% CI 24 to 68; P=0.002), and at 3 months in 71% versus 20% (difference 51 points, 29 to 73; P<0.001). Pain on dressing change improved slightly more with B-VEC (adjusted difference −0.61 on a 0–10 scale at week 22); adverse events included pruritus and chills. The earlier GEM-1/2 randomised phase 1/2 trial (Gurevich I et al., PMID: 35347281) treated matched wounds in 9 patients (N printed plainly — below the usual 10-person floor, carded because it is the programme's first-in-human randomised evidence in a rare disease) and met its C7-expression, anchoring-fibril and wound-area objectives with no grade 2 or above treatment-related adverse events. The open-label extension (Marinkovich MP et al., PMID: 40220208) followed 47 subjects for up to 112 weeks with no new safety signals and maintained closure in rollover wounds (61.1–89.5%). The product is beremagene geperpavec (Vyjuvek), the HSV-1-based COL7A1 gene-therapy gel of Krystal Biotech, named exactly as published. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intra-patient design makes 31 patients more informative than 31 patients in a parallel trial, but a single small phase 3 programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind intra-patient randomised placebo-controlled trial (Guide 2022, GEM-3)
cards.people: 31 patients aged 6 months or older with genetically confirmed dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa; for each patient a matched primary wound pair (matched by size, region and appearance) was selected, and the two wounds were randomised 1:1 to weekly beremagene geperpavec or placebo gel for 26 weeks — each patient is their own control.
cards.result: Complete wound healing at 6 months: 67% of B-VEC wounds versus 22% of placebo wounds (difference 46 percentage points, 95% CI 24 to 68; P=0.002). At 3 months: 71% versus 20% (difference 51 points, 29 to 73; P<0.001). Pain severity during dressing changes fell slightly more with B-VEC (adjusted least-squares mean difference −0.61, 95% CI −1.10 to −0.13, at week 22, on a 0–10 scale). Adverse events with B-VEC and placebo included pruritus and chills.
cards.watchOut: Total randomised N=31 patients is printed on the face by rare-disease necessity — the intra-patient wound-pair design removes between-patient variation, which is why a trial this small can still be informative, but it remains a single phase 3 trial from one development programme. The pain difference (−0.61 of 10) is small.

cards.headline: Gurevich 2022, GEM-1/2 (phase 1/2 randomised trial, N=9 patients — printed plainly, below the usual floor): matched wounds treated repeatedly over 12 weeks; C7 expression and anchoring fibrils restored; no grade ≥2 treatment-related adverse events
cards.summary: Gurevich 2022, GEM-1/2 (phase 1/2 randomised trial, N=9 patients — printed plainly, below the usual floor): matched wounds treated repeatedly over 12 weeks; C7 expression and anchoring fibrils restored; no grade ≥2 treatment-related adverse events
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled phase 1 and 2 trial (Gurevich 2022, GEM-1/2)
cards.people: 9 patients with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa whose matched wounds received topical B-VEC or placebo repeatedly over 12 weeks, after laboratory work showing B-VEC restored type VII collagen expression in patient keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
cards.result: Primary and secondary objectives — C7 expression, anchoring fibril assembly, wound surface area reduction, duration of wound closure and time to wound closure — were met following B-VEC treatment. No grade 2 or above B-VEC-related adverse events, vector shedding or tissue-bound skin immunoreactants were noted; HSV-1 and C7 antibodies sometimes increased after treatment without apparent impact on safety or efficacy. A patient-reported pain outcome was not assessed because only a small proportion of wounds was treated.
cards.watchOut: N=9 patients is below the library's usual 10-person evidence floor; it is carded, with its N printed, because it is the randomised first-in-human step of the same programme that GEM-3 completed, in a rare disease — not as standalone proof of benefit. The abstract reports objectives 'met' without wound-level percentages, so none are claimed here.

cards.headline: Marinkovich 2025 (open-label extension, 47 subjects, up to 112 weeks): no new safety signals; phase 3 rollover wounds maintained closure rates of 61.1–89.5% to month 12
cards.summary: Marinkovich 2025 (open-label extension, 47 subjects, up to 112 weeks): no new safety signals; phase 3 rollover wounds maintained closure rates of 61.1–89.5% to month 12
cards.people: 47 subjects with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (24 rolled over from phase 3; 23 treatment-naive) receiving weekly B-VEC to target wounds for up to 112 weeks (median 81 weeks).
cards.result: Thirty-five subjects (74.5%) reported one or more adverse events, mostly mild or moderate; 17 serious adverse events occurred in 14 subjects and none was considered treatment-related; no adverse event led to discontinuation. Treatment satisfaction was high; quality-of-life results were inconclusive. Among rollover subjects, wounds treated with B-VEC in phase 3 maintained closure rates of 61.1–89.5% from baseline to month 12 of the extension.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with variable follow-up and no comparator — this card answers 'does longer use reveal new harm or obvious loss of effect?', not 'does it still beat placebo?'. Serious events in this population reflect the underlying disease burden, and attribution was by the investigators.

cards.people: GEM-3 phase 3 intra-patient RCT (31 patients), GEM-1/2 phase 1/2 randomised trial (9 patients) and an open-label extension (47 subjects) of beremagene geperpavec (Vyjuvek, Krystal Biotech) in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
cards.result: Complete healing 67% versus 22% at 6 months and 71% versus 20% at 3 months (GEM-3); mechanistic objectives met in phase 1/2; no new safety signals over up to 112 weeks of extension treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C, with the total randomised N printed in the stamp line as required for a base under ~30–31 patients.
cards.watchOut: The birch-bark gel shelf (pack #5349) is a different product with a different mechanism for the same disease family and is not duplicated here. shelves.title: Dark adaptation: threshold falls in two steps — a fast cone step, then a slow rod step whose time course is rhodopsin regeneration (first-order, ~400-second time constant in the classic densitometry), reaching a final rod threshold that is reached progressively later with age
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the time course of dark adaptation — the rod–cone break, the rate of rhodopsin regeneration after a bleach, and the final rod threshold — measured by psychophysics and fundus reflectometry?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Dark Adaptation · Dark Adaptation/physiology · Densitometry · Humans · Kinetics · Light · Photolysis · Photoreceptor Cells/metabolism,physiology · Regeneration · Retinal Pigments/metabolism · Retinal Rod Photoreceptor Cells/physiology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: after a bleach, sensitivity recovers in two limbs — cones first (fast, limited range), then rods (slow, several log units) with the rod–cone break between them — and the rod limb's time course is the regeneration of rhodopsin from its bleached state, ending at the final rod threshold. The carded human studies supply each piece from primary measurement: the two-step psychophysical curve (Hecht 1935); densitometric regeneration kinetics and the shared ~400-second threshold/regeneration time constant (Alpern 1971, using Rushton's reflectometry method); fast cone pigment–threshold tracking (Hollins & Alpern 1973); and the quantified slowing with age in 94 adults (Jackson 1999). Lamb & Pugh's 2004 synthesis (PMID 15177205, fetched this session) frames the modern mechanism — recovery rate-limited by 11-cis retinal delivery — and is cited as framing, not carded as primary evidence. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Hecht 1935: dark adaptation proceeds in two steps — a rapid, small first part (cones) and a slow, prolonged, large second part (rods)
cards.summary: Hecht 1935: dark adaptation proceeds in two steps — a rapid, small first part (cones) and a slow, prolonged, large second part (rods)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (classic psychophysics of dark adaptation) — N not documented in the fetched record
cards.people: Human observers dark-adapting with retinal fields of different size and location, including small foveal fields, large central fields, an annulus at 20 degrees, and a 2-degree field at varying eccentricity. (Number of observers not stated in the fetched record.)
cards.result: Threshold fell in two steps: the first rapid, short and small in extent; the second slow, prolonged and large — attributed in the record to cone and rod function respectively. With small foveal fields the first part dominated and only traces of the second appeared; as field area increased the first part changed little while the second covered an increasing intensity range and appeared sooner. A peripheral annulus behaved like a whole field reaching the same eccentricity — the shape of the curve is set by where the field sits on the centre-to-periphery sensitivity gradient, the origin of the classic rod–cone break.
cards.watchOut: Classic 1935 study: N is not documented in the fetched record and is printed as such, per the labelling rule. The record carries no MeSH terms, so the source line uses the standing fallback rather than invented terms.

cards.headline: Alpern 1971: rhodopsin regenerated at a rate proportional to the amount still bleached (constant ~0.0025/s), and rod threshold recovery shared a ~400-second time constant with regeneration
cards.summary: Alpern 1971: rhodopsin regenerated at a rate proportional to the amount still bleached (constant ~0.0025/s), and rod threshold recovery shared a ~400-second time constant with regeneration
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (fundus densitometry and threshold kinetics) — densitometry in human subjects; threshold–regeneration relation from one rod monochromat, labelled on the face
cards.people: Human eye studied by Rushton's reflexion (fundus) densitometry at a retinal region 18 degrees temporal to the fovea, with bleaching and steady-light equilibrium protocols; the threshold relation was measured in the peripheral retina of a rod monochromat, where there are few cones.
cards.result: During a 10-second bleach no regeneration occurred and bleaching rate was proportional to quantum catch (constant about 10⁻⁷ (td·sec)⁻¹). At equilibrium under a steady light, photolysis matched regeneration, and the regeneration rate was proportional to the amount of pigment still bleached, with a proportionality constant of about 0.0025 sec⁻¹ — the same in light or dark, so regeneration proceeds independently of bleaching. In the rod monochromat's peripheral retina, dark adaptation followed a simple exponential over nearly 7 log₁₀ units; rhodopsin regeneration and log threshold shared a time constant of about 400 seconds, each log-unit fall in threshold accompanied by a 0.835% increase in rhodopsin.
cards.watchOut: The ~400-second time constant and the 0.835%-per-log-unit relation rest on a single rod-monochromat retina, as the record states — an n-of-1 classic, printed plainly. The record also warns the kinetics differ after very short bright flashes (blue-absorbing intermediates), so the equation applies to the longer bleaches studied.
cards.source: Alpern M. Rhodopsin kinetics in the human eye. The Journal of physiology. 1971. PMID: 5097608. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hollins & Alpern 1973: cone pigment regeneration and foveal threshold recovery are much faster than rod recovery, and log threshold tracked the fraction of unregenerated cone pigment
cards.summary: Hollins & Alpern 1973: cone pigment regeneration and foveal threshold recovery are much faster than rod recovery, and log threshold tracked the fraction of unregenerated cone pigment
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (cone densitometry and foveal thresholds) — N not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Normal human subjects studied at the fovea after a wide range of bleaches, with red–green cone pigment regeneration measured in the dark alongside threshold elevation, testing the Dowling–Rushton relation (direct proportionality between log threshold elevation and fraction of unregenerated pigment). (Number of subjects not stated in the fetched record.)
cards.result: Cone pigment regeneration and threshold recovery were much faster after short bleaches than a simple monomolecular reaction predicts, and recovery after a fixed short bleach was faster the weaker the bleach. Except for the first 30 seconds after relatively weak bleaches, and the entire recovery after a very brief (<0.001 s) saturating flash bleaching a little over 50%, the Dowling–Rushton relation fitted the results over the whole range tested with a single proportionality constant — cone threshold in the dark is, to that approximation, a readout of how much cone pigment remains bleached.
cards.watchOut: N is not documented in the fetched abstract and is printed as such. This is the cone limb of the curve — fast and foveal — and should not be read as the time course of the rod limb, which the Alpern and Jackson cards carry.
cards.source: Hollins M et al. Dark adaptation and visual pigment regeneration in human cones. The Journal of general physiology. 1973. PMID: 4755849. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jackson 1999: in 94 adults, rod-mediated dark adaptation slowed with age — the rhodopsin-regeneration time constant lengthened by 8.4 seconds per decade after a 98% bleach
cards.summary: Jackson 1999: in 94 adults, rod-mediated dark adaptation slowed with age — the rhodopsin-regeneration time constant lengthened by 8.4 seconds per decade after a 98% bleach
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-cohort dark adaptation after near-total bleach) — N = 94
cards.people: 94 adults from their 20s to their 80s, dark adaptation measured as rod-mediated sensitivity recovery after a 98% bleach; macular health graded from fundus photography in subjects over 49, thresholds corrected for individual lens density, pupil diameter controlled.
cards.result: Rod-mediated recovery slowed dramatically with age, attributable to delayed rhodopsin regeneration rather than to optical changes (pupillary miosis and lens density could not account for it and were controlled). During the second component of the rod phase, the rate of sensitivity recovery fell by 0.02 log unit/min per decade, the time constant of rhodopsin regeneration increased by 8.4 s per decade, and the time to come within 0.3 log units of baseline scotopic sensitivity increased by 2.76 minutes per decade.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional age comparison, not longitudinal follow-up; the per-decade figures are regression slopes across the cohort, as the record reports them.
cards.source: Jackson GR et al. Aging and dark adaptation. Vision research. 1999. PMID: 10748929. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/physiology · Dark Adaptation/physiology · Humans · Middle Aged · Retinal Rod Photoreceptor Cells/physiology

cards.headline: Synthesis: the dark-adaptation curve is two recoveries — fast cone pigment regeneration, then slow rhodopsin regeneration whose kinetics set the rod limb and the final threshold
cards.summary: Synthesis: the dark-adaptation curve is two recoveries — fast cone pigment regeneration, then slow rhodopsin regeneration whose kinetics set the rod limb and the final threshold
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (special senses chapters), with Lamb & Pugh 2004 (PMID 15177205) as the field's synthesis that recovery after large bleaches is rate-limited by delivery of 11-cis retinal to opsin. No new data.
cards.result: The biphasic curve — a rapid small cone step and a slow large rod step, separated by the rod–cone break — was mapped psychophysically in 1935 (PMID 19872930). Densitometry tied the rod limb to pigment: regeneration is first-order in the amount still bleached (~0.0025/s), and log threshold and regeneration share a ~400-second time constant (PMID 5097608); cone pigment and foveal threshold recover far faster, again tracking unregenerated pigment (PMID 4755849). Ageing slows the rod limb measurably — time constant +8.4 s per decade, ~2.76 minutes per decade longer to near-baseline sensitivity (PMID 10748929). Rushton's own densitometry papers were the method source for the carded Alpern work; the specific Rushton records located by author search this session could not be verified with usable abstracts and are not separately carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: normal human dark adaptation and pigment regeneration. Dark adaptation as a diagnostic test in macular disease is a clinical question, not this physiology shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 19872930, 5097608, 4755849, 10748929), framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Inverted ILM flap for large macular holes: closure 98% versus 88% in the originating randomised trial, with flat-open holes almost abolished (2% vs 19%) and better 12-month vision; a four-trial meta-analysis gives odds ratio 4.89 for anatomic success
shelves.question: In adults with large full-thickness macular holes (>400 µm), does vitrectomy with an inverted internal-limiting-membrane flap improve hole closure and vision versus conventional ILM peeling?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for closure of large holes. This pack is the PARTIAL slice the library lacked: pack #4614 asks about ocriplasmin injection and pack #6621 asks about face-down posturing after macular-hole vitrectomy — neither asks the flap-versus-peel technique question, and no homed report is carded here. The originating randomised trial (Michalewska 2010; 101 eyes with holes >400 µm) found closure in 98% with the inverted flap versus 88% with standard peeling, flat-open holes (closed but with bare pigment epithelium and poor vision) in 2% versus 19%, and better mean 12-month acuity (0.28 versus 0.17; P=0.001). A second randomised trial in still larger holes (Kannan 2018; 60 patients, holes 600-1500 µm) found anatomical success 90.0% versus 70.0% — the same direction, not statistically significant on its own (P=0.125). The meta-analysis of the four randomised trials (Chen 2020; 276 eyes) pooled an odds ratio of 4.89 (95% CI 2.09-11.47) for anatomic success and 5.23 (95% CI 2.83-9.66) for type 1 closure in favour of the flap, with better postoperative acuity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for anatomical closure; the visual advantage is smaller and less certain than the closure advantage.

cards.headline: Michalewska 2010 (prospective randomised trial, 101 eyes, holes >400 µm): inverted flap versus standard vitrectomy with ILM peeling — closure 98% versus 88%, flat-open 2% versus 19%, 12-month acuity 0.28 versus 0.17 (P=0.001)
cards.summary: Michalewska 2010 (prospective randomised trial, 101 eyes, holes >400 µm): inverted flap versus standard vitrectomy with ILM peeling — closure 98% versus 88%, flat-open 2% versus 19%, 12-month acuity 0.28 versus 0.17 (P=0.001)
cards.people: Patients with macular holes larger than 400 µm: group 1, 51 eyes of 40 patients, underwent standard three-port pars plana vitrectomy with complete ILM removal and air; group 2, 50 eyes of 46 patients, underwent the inverted ILM flap technique, in which a stained ILM remnant left attached to the hole margins is inverted to cover the hole; spectral optical coherence tomography and examination were performed to 12 months.
cards.result: Macular hole closure was observed in 88% of group 1 and 98% of group 2. A flat-open appearance (flat hole roof with bare retinal pigment epithelium) occurred in 19% of group 1 versus 2% of group 2. Mean (or median) postoperative visual acuity at 12 months was 0.17 (range 0.1-0.6) in group 1 versus 0.28 (range 0.02-0.8) in group 2 (P=0.001), from preoperative means of 0.12 and 0.078 respectively. The authors conclude the flap technique prevents the flat-open appearance and improves anatomic and functional outcomes for holes over 400 µm.
cards.watchOut: The originating centre's trial, with the technique's inventors as operators — the closure gap (98% vs 88%) is modest in absolute terms and the headline benefit is as much about the quality of closure (flat-open abolition) as about closure itself. Acuity is reported as decimal means/medians with wide, overlapping ranges.
cards.source: Michalewska Z et al. Inverted internal limiting membrane flap technique for large macular holes. Ophthalmology. 2010. PMID: 20541263. prospective randomised clinical trial (michalewska 2010) patients with macular holes larger than 400 µm: group 1, 51 eyes of 40 patients, underwent standard three-port pars plana vitrectomy with complete ilm removal and air; group 2, 50 eyes of 46 patients, underwent the inverted ilm flap technique, in which a stained ilm remnant left attached to the hole margins is inverted to cover the hole; spectral optical coherence tomography and examination were performed to 12 months. macular hole closure was observed in 88% of group 1 and 98% of group 2. a flat-open appearance (flat hole roof with bare retinal pigment epithelium) occurred in 19% of group 1 versus 2% of group 2. mean (or median) postoperative visual acuity at 12 months was 0.17 (range 0.1-0.6) in group 1 versus 0.28 (range 0.02-0.8) in group 2 (p=0.001), from preoperative means of 0.12 and 0.078 respectively. the authors conclude the flap technique prevents the flat-open appearance and improves anatomic and functional outcomes for holes over 400 µm. the originating centre's trial, with the technique's inventors as operators — the closure gap (98% vs 88%) is modest in absolute terms and the headline benefit is as much about the quality of closure (flat-open abolition) as about closure itself. acuity is reported as decimal means/medians with wide, overlapping ranges. michalewska z et al. inverted internal limiting membrane flap technique for large macular holes. ophthalmology. 2010. pmid: 20541263. registry id: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). mesh: aged · basement membrane/surgery · female · fluorescein angiography · humans · male · ophthalmologic surgical procedures · prospective studies · retinal perforations/diagnosis/physiopathology/surgery · retinal pigment epithelium/pathology · surgical flaps · tomography, optical coherence · visual acuity/physiology · vitrectomy

cards.headline: Kannan 2018 (randomised trial, 60 patients, holes 600-1500 µm): inverted flap versus peeling — anatomical success 90.0% versus 70.0% (P=0.125, not significant), acuity modestly better with the flap (also not significant)
cards.summary: Kannan 2018 (randomised trial, 60 patients, holes 600-1500 µm): inverted flap versus peeling — anatomical success 90.0% versus 70.0% (P=0.125, not significant), acuity modestly better with the flap (also not significant)
cards.people: 60 patients with idiopathic large full-thickness macular holes (minimum diameter 600-1500 µm; mean minimum diameter about 760 µm in the peeling group and 803 µm in the flap group), randomised to ILM peeling (group A, 30 patients) or inverted ILM flap (group B, 30 patients), with anatomical and visual outcomes at 6 months; anatomical success required flattening of the hole with neurosensory retina completely covering the fovea.
cards.result: Anatomical success was 70.0% in group A versus 90.0% in group B (P=0.125). Mean best-corrected acuity at 6 months was logMAR 0.65 (Snellen equivalent 20/89) versus logMAR 0.53 (20/68) (P=0.060); mean improvement was 1.4 versus 2.1 lines (P=0.353), and acuity of 20/60 or better was achieved by 13.3% versus 20.0% (P=0.766). The authors conclude the outcomes are statistically similar between the techniques in this sample.
cards.watchOut: The honest counterweight card: in the largest holes, an independent centre found a 20-point closure advantage that its 60-patient sample could not confirm statistically. Direction agrees with Michalewska; precision does not. Registered with the Clinical Trials Registry - India as CTRI/2017/11/010474, as reported in the record.
cards.source: Kannan NB et al. Comparative study of inverted internal limiting membrane (ILM) flap and ILM peeling technique in large macular holes: a randomized-control trial. BMC ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 30029621. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/11/010474 (Clinical Trials Registry - India, as reported in the record). cards.headline: Chen 2020 (meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials, 276 eyes): anatomic success odds ratio 4.89 and type 1 closure odds ratio 5.23 in favour of the inverted flap, with better postoperative acuity
cards.summary: Chen 2020 (meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials, 276 eyes): anatomic success odds ratio 4.89 and type 1 closure odds ratio 5.23 in favour of the inverted flap, with better postoperative acuity
cards.people: Four randomised trials (276 eyes: 135 inverted flap, 141 conventional peeling) in idiopathic large macular holes, all using gas tamponade, with follow-up of 3 months in two studies, 6 months in one and 12 months in one; outcomes were anatomic success, type 1 closure (neurosensory retina present over the hole), postoperative best-corrected acuity and change in acuity.
cards.result: Anatomic success favoured the inverted flap (odds ratio 4.89; 95% CI 2.09-11.47; P=0.0003), as did type 1 closure (odds ratio 5.23; 95% CI 2.83-9.66; P<0.00001). Postoperative logMAR acuity and mean change in acuity also favoured the flap (weighted mean differences 0.17, 95% CI 0.11-0.24, and 0.08, 95% CI 0.01-0.16, respectively). Odds ratios are relative measures: with closure already near 88-90% on peeling, an odds ratio near 5 corresponds to a much smaller absolute gain, of the order of the 98% versus 88% seen in the originating trial.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials, two of them carded above — the pooled estimate inherits their single-centre and inventor-centre features, and follow-up is as short as 3 months in half the base. The acuity advantage (0.08-0.17 logMAR) is about one line or less.
cards.source: Chen G et al. Inverted ILM flap technique versus conventional ILM peeling for idiopathic large macular holes: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PloS one. 2020. PMID: 32706833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: LIKELY (benefit) for closure — the flap's clearest win is converting flat-open failures into true closures
cards.summary: Synthesis: LIKELY (benefit) for closure — the flap's clearest win is converting flat-open failures into true closures
cards.people: Two individually carded randomised trials (101 and 60 eyes) within a four-trial, 276-eye meta-analysis, all in holes over 400 µm. Cross-points: pack #4614 (ocriplasmin injection) and pack #6621 (face-down posturing) cover neighbouring macular-hole questions; none of their reports is carded here.
cards.result: Closure 98% vs 88% and flat-open 2% vs 19% (Michalewska); 90.0% vs 70.0% closure, not significant alone (Kannan); pooled odds ratio 4.89 for anatomic success and 5.23 for type 1 closure, with a small acuity advantage. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for anatomical closure in large holes.
cards.watchOut: Evidence is confined to idiopathic large holes in surgical series; it does not address small holes (where peeling already closes nearly all), traumatic or secondary holes, or surgeon learning curves with the flap technique.

shelves.title: Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna, Spark Therapeutics) for RPE65 retinal dystrophy: functional vision improved in the phase 3 trial (mobility-test change 1.8 vs 0.2 light levels; 65% passed at the lowest light level vs none) — a single programme with a pivotal N of 31
shelves.question: In people with biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated inherited retinal dystrophy, does subretinal voretigene neparvovec (the AAV2 gene therapy tested in the licensing programme — name the product and maker as published) improve functional vision (multi-luminance mobility testing) and visual fields versus no gene therapy?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single development programme, capped at POSSIBLE, with a small pivotal N stated plainly. A premise correction to the build brief: the pivotal evidence is NOT single-arm or externally controlled. The phase 3 trial (Russell 2017) was randomised and controlled — 31 participants assigned 2:1 to bilateral subretinal voretigene neparvovec (1.5×10^11 vector genomes per eye) or to a concurrent no-treatment control group, with outcome graders masked; controls crossed over to treatment after the one-year primary endpoint, so controlled comparison exists only for year 1. At one year the mean bilateral multi-luminance mobility test change was 1.8 (SD 1.1) light levels in the intervention group versus 0.2 (1.0) in controls (difference 1.6, 95% CI 0.72-2.41; P=0.0013), and 65% of treated participants passed the mobility course at the lowest luminance tested (1 lux) versus no controls. The product is voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna), developed by Spark Therapeutics, named as published in the trial record. Durability comes only from within-programme follow-on reports: the phase 1 contralateral-eye study (Bennett 2016; 11 participants) and the combined phase 1/3 durability report (Maguire 2019; 40 treated subjects) found mobility and light-sensitivity gains maintained to 4 years in the phase 1 cohort and 2 years in phase 3, with a safety profile consistent with vitrectomy and subretinal injection and no product-related serious adverse events or deleterious immune responses in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme; pivotal trial N = 31.

cards.headline: Russell 2017 — phase 3 (randomised controlled trial, 31 enrolled, 29 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis): bilateral voretigene neparvovec versus no-treatment control — mobility-test change 1.8 versus 0.2 light levels (difference 1.6, 95% CI 0.72-2.41; P=0.0013)
cards.summary: Russell 2017 — phase 3 (randomised controlled trial, 31 enrolled, 29 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis): bilateral voretigene neparvovec versus no-treatment control — mobility-test change 1.8 versus 0.2 light levels (difference 1.6, 95% CI 0.72-2.41; P=0.0013)
cards.people: 31 individuals aged 3 years or older at two US sites with confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations, acuity 20/60 or worse or visual field under 20 degrees in each eye, sufficient viable retina and ability to perform multi-luminance mobility testing (MLMT); randomised 2:1 to bilateral subretinal injection of 1.5×10^11 vector genomes of voretigene neparvovec in 0.3 mL per eye (n=21) or control (n=10), with one withdrawal from each group before intervention (modified intention-to-treat: 20 intervention, 9 control). The control construction is stated plainly: a concurrent randomised group receiving no gene therapy during the first year, with masked outcome graders; the record's funding line names Spark Therapeutics, the maker of the product (Luxturna).
cards.result: At 1 year, mean bilateral MLMT change score was 1.8 (SD 1.1) light levels in the intervention group versus 0.2 (1.0) in the control group (difference 1.6, 95% CI 0.72-2.41; P=0.0013). Thirteen of 20 intervention participants (65%), but no control participants, passed the MLMT at the lowest luminance level tested (1 lux) — the maximum possible improvement. No product-related serious adverse events or deleterious immune responses occurred; two intervention participants had serious adverse events unrelated to participation (a pre-existing seizure disorder and oral-surgery complications), and most ocular events were mild.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment (participants knew whether they had been injected) with a performance-based primary endpoint — masked grading mitigates but cannot remove expectancy effects on a mobility course. The controlled period is one year only, because controls were then offered treatment; everything beyond year 1 is uncontrolled follow-on. N = 31 is small by necessity in a rare disease, and the stamp carries it.
cards.source: Russell S et al. Efficacy and safety of voretigene neparvovec (AAV2-hRPE65v2) in patients with RPE65-mediated inherited retinal dystrophy: a randomised, controlled, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28712537. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00999609. cards.headline: Bennett 2016 — phase 1 follow-on (11 participants): second-eye (contralateral) AAV2-hRPE65v2 administration was safe, with mobility and light-sensitivity gains in the newly treated eye persisting to 3 years
cards.summary: Bennett 2016 — phase 1 follow-on (11 participants): second-eye (contralateral) AAV2-hRPE65v2 administration was safe, with mobility and light-sensitivity gains in the newly treated eye persisting to 3 years
cards.people: 11 children and adults (aged 11-46 at second administration) with RPE65 mutation-associated inherited retinal dystrophy who had received a unilateral subretinal injection in the earlier phase 1 study, now receiving one dose of AAV2-hRPE65v2 (1.5×10^11 vector genomes in 300 µL) into the contralateral, previously uninjected eye, 1.71-4.58 years after the first injection, with follow-up to 3 years.
cards.result: No adverse events related to the vector were reported; procedure-related events were mostly mild (dellen formation in three patients, cataracts in two), and one patient developed bacterial endophthalmitis and was excluded from analyses. In pooled analysis of ten participants, mean mobility and full-field light sensitivity in the second eye improved by day 30 and persisted to year 3 (mobility P=0.0003; white-light full-field sensitivity P<0.0001), with no significant change in the previously injected eyes over the same period and no significant pooled change in visual acuity in either eye (P>0.49). No significant immunogenicity was noted.
cards.watchOut: Eleven participants, no control group, and one excluded for endophthalmitis — a serious procedural harm that belongs in any counselling. This study answers the second-eye safety question; it is not independent confirmation of efficacy, being the same programme and largely the same investigator group as the phase 3 trial.
cards.source: Bennett J et al. Safety and durability of effect of contralateral-eye administration of AAV2 gene therapy in patients with childhood-onset blindness caused by RPE65 mutations: a follow-on phase 1 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27375040. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01208389. cards.headline: Maguire 2019 — durability report (40 treated subjects across the phase 1 follow-on and phase 3 trials): mobility gains essentially maintained (phase 1: 2.4 light levels at year 4 versus 2.6 at year 1; phase 3: 1.9 at year 2), light sensitivity improved by more than 2 log units
cards.summary: Maguire 2019 — durability report (40 treated subjects across the phase 1 follow-on and phase 3 trials): mobility gains essentially maintained (phase 1: 2.4 light levels at year 4 versus 2.6 at year 1; phase 3: 1.9 at year 2), light sensitivity improved by more than 2 log units
cards.type: Durability report of the phase 1 follow-on and phase 3 trials (Maguire 2019)
cards.people: 40 subjects who received 1.5×10^11 vector genomes of voretigene neparvovec-rzyl per eye in at least one eye across the programme: 11 phase 1 follow-on subjects and 29 phase 3 subjects (20 original intervention and 9 control/intervention, the latter treated after crossing over). Common endpoints were MLMT change, full-field light sensitivity threshold (FST) and best-corrected visual acuity.
cards.result: Mean MLMT lux score change was 2.4 (SD 1.3) at 4 years versus 2.6 (1.6) at 1 year in phase 1 follow-on subjects (n=8 with data), 1.9 (1.1) at 2 years and 1.9 (1.0) at 1 year in original-intervention phase 3 subjects (n=20), and 2.1 (1.6) at 1 year after administration in control/intervention subjects (n=9). All three groups maintained an average FST improvement of more than 2 log10(cd.s/m2) at 1 year and subsequent available visits. The safety profile was consistent with vitrectomy and the subretinal injection procedure, with no deleterious immune responses; the authors conclude the effect is nearly maximal by 30 days and durable for 4 years, with observation ongoing.
cards.watchOut: These are the same patients as the two cards above, re-reported at later time points — durability evidence, not new patients. After crossover there is no untreated comparison, so 'maintained gain' cannot be separated from test familiarity or natural history within this report; and the year-4 phase 1 figure rests on 8 subjects.
cards.source: Maguire AM et al. Efficacy, Safety, and Durability of Voretigene Neparvovec-rzyl in RPE65 Mutation-Associated Inherited Retinal Dystrophy: Results of Phase 1 and 3 Trials. Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 31443789. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, one randomised year, consistent functional gains that persist in follow-on
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, one randomised year, consistent functional gains that persist in follow-on
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (31 enrolled), one phase 1 contralateral-eye follow-on (11 participants) and a combined durability report (40 treated subjects, overlapping populations).
cards.result: Year-1 controlled result: MLMT change 1.8 versus 0.2 light levels (P=0.0013); 65% versus 0% passing at 1 lux. Follow-on: gains maintained to 4 years (phase 1) and 2 years (phase 3), light sensitivity improved by over 2 log units, no product-related serious adverse events in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme cap, pivotal N = 31 printed on the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Everything carded here comes from one sponsor programme (Spark Therapeutics) at a small number of US sites; independent replication does not exist for a first-in-class gene therapy. The build brief's description of the pivotal evidence as single-arm/externally controlled was corrected at build: the phase 3 trial was randomised against a concurrent no-treatment control for its first year, as its fetched record shows.
cards.source: Synthesis of Russell S et al. Lancet (London, England). 2017 (PMID: 28712537); Bennett J et al. Lancet (London, England). 2016 (PMID: 27375040); Maguire AM et al. Ophthalmology. 2019 (PMID: 31443789).

shelves.title: Tube shunt versus trabeculectomy as the FIRST glaucoma operation (PTVT): failure rates did not differ significantly at 3 or 5 years (33% vs 28%; 42% vs 35%) — trabeculectomy gave lower pressure on fewer drops, tube surgery fewer serious early complications
shelves.question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma and no prior incisional surgery, is a tube shunt non-inferior to trabeculectomy with mitomycin as the first operation for pressure control, failure and complications?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no difference) — a single trial programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE, and all four cards below are explicitly labelled reports of the one Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (PTVT) Study (242 patients, no prior incisional surgery, 350-mm² Baerveldt implant versus trabeculectomy with mitomycin C). This is the PARTIAL slice the library lacked: live shelf #617 asks the tube-versus-trabeculectomy question only in eyes with prior surgery or high failure risk (the TVT population), and none of its reports is carded here. In PTVT, trabeculectomy was ahead at 1 year (failure 7.9% versus 17.3%; P=0.01), but the gap closed: failure at 3 years was 28% versus 33% (P=0.17) and at 5 years 35% versus 42% (P=0.21) — no significant difference at either later point. Pressure told a steadier story in trabeculectomy's favour early (12.1 versus 14.0 mmHg at 3 years) and converged by 5 years (13.0 versus 13.4 mmHg; P=0.52), while medication burden stayed lower after trabeculectomy throughout (1.3 versus 2.2 drops at 5 years; P<0.001). Serious complications requiring reoperation or costing ≥2 lines of vision were fewer with the tube at 1 year (1% versus 7%; P=0.03) and similar by 3 years (2% versus 8%; P=0.11). Visual fields declined at statistically indistinguishable rates (-0.47 versus -0.32 dB/year; P=0.23). On the trial's own primary outcome at its longest follow-up, the treatment made no significant difference — but PTVT was a superiority trial, not a formal noninferiority trial, so 'non-inferior' is a description of the result, not a tested claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference).

cards.headline: PTVT report 1 of the single trial — 1 year (Gedde 2018): failure 17.3% tube versus 7.9% trabeculectomy (P=0.01; hazard ratio 2.59); pressure 13.8 versus 12.4 mmHg; medications 2.1 versus 0.9; serious complications 1% versus 7% (P=0.03)
cards.summary: PTVT report 1 of the single trial — 1 year (Gedde 2018): failure 17.3% tube versus 7.9% trabeculectomy (P=0.01; hazard ratio 2.59); pressure 13.8 versus 12.4 mmHg; medications 2.1 versus 0.9; serious complications 1% versus 7% (P=0.03)
cards.people: 242 eyes of 242 patients with medically uncontrolled glaucoma and no previous incisional ocular surgery at 16 centres, randomised to a tube shunt (350-mm² Baerveldt glaucoma implant; n=125) or trabeculectomy with mitomycin C (0.4 mg/ml for 2 minutes; n=117). Failure was defined as pressure over 21 mmHg or reduced less than 20% from baseline, pressure of 5 mmHg or less, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception. This card is the 1-year report of the single PTVT trial; the 3-year, 5-year and visual-field cards below are later reports of the same trial, not separate trials.
cards.result: Cumulative failure during the first year was 17.3% in the tube group versus 7.9% in the trabeculectomy group (P=0.01; hazard ratio 2.59, 95% CI 1.20-5.60). Mean pressure at 1 year was 13.8 (SD 4.1) mmHg tube versus 12.4 (4.4) mmHg trabeculectomy (P=0.01), on 2.1 (1.4) versus 0.9 (1.4) glaucoma medications (P<0.001). Postoperative complications occurred in 29% (tube) versus 41% (trabeculectomy) of patients (P=0.06); serious complications requiring reoperation or producing a loss of 2 or more Snellen lines occurred in 1 patient (1%) versus 8 patients (7%) (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: The 1-year snapshot is the least favourable to the tube of any PTVT report — tube shunts characteristically take longer to reach their pressure plateau. Judging the comparison on this report alone would misstate the trial; the 3- and 5-year reports below supersede it for the failure outcome.
cards.source: Gedde SJ et al. Treatment Outcomes in the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy Study after 1 Year of Follow-up. Ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 29477688. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PTVT report 2 of the single trial — 3 years (Gedde 2020): failure 33% tube versus 28% trabeculectomy (P=0.17, not significant); pressure 14.0 versus 12.1 mmHg (P=0.008); medications 2.1 versus 1.2
cards.summary: PTVT report 2 of the single trial — 3 years (Gedde 2020): failure 33% tube versus 28% trabeculectomy (P=0.17, not significant); pressure 14.0 versus 12.1 mmHg (P=0.008); medications 2.1 versus 1.2
cards.people: The same 242 PTVT patients (125 tube, 117 trabeculectomy with mitomycin C), unmasked multicentre randomised trial, with failure defined as pressure over 21 mmHg or reduced less than 20% from baseline, pressure of 5 mmHg or less, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception; secondary outcomes included pressure, medications, acuity and complications. A later report of the same trial as the 1-year card above.
cards.result: Cumulative probability of failure at 3 years was 33% in the tube group versus 28% in the trabeculectomy group (P=0.17; hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.9-2.2) — not statistically significant. Mean pressure was 14.0 (SD 4.2) mmHg versus 12.1 (4.8) mmHg (P=0.008), on 2.1 (1.4) versus 1.2 (1.5) medications (P<0.001). Serious complications requiring reoperation or producing loss of 2 or more Snellen lines developed in 3 patients (2%) tube versus 9 patients (8%) trabeculectomy (P=0.11).
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval on the failure hazard ratio (0.9-2.2) still includes a doubling of failure risk with the tube — 'not significant' here means unresolved at this horizon, not proven equal; the trial was not designed or analysed as a noninferiority study.
cards.source: Gedde SJ et al. Treatment Outcomes in the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy Study after 3 Years of Follow-up. Ophthalmology. 2020. PMID: 31727428. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PTVT report 3 of the single trial — 5 years (Gedde 2022): failure 42% tube versus 35% trabeculectomy (P=0.21, not significant); pressure essentially equal (13.4 versus 13.0 mmHg; P=0.52); medications 2.2 versus 1.3 (P<0.001)
cards.summary: PTVT report 3 of the single trial — 5 years (Gedde 2022): failure 42% tube versus 35% trabeculectomy (P=0.21, not significant); pressure essentially equal (13.4 versus 13.0 mmHg; P=0.52); medications 2.2 versus 1.3 (P<0.001)
cards.people: The same 242 PTVT patients (125 tube, 117 trabeculectomy with mitomycin C 0.4 mg/ml for 2 minutes) at 16 clinical centres, followed for 5 years; primary outcome the rate of surgical failure (pressure over 21 mmHg or reduced less than 20% from baseline, pressure of 5 mmHg or less, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception). The longest report of the single PTVT trial.
cards.result: Cumulative probability of failure at 5 years was 42% in the tube group versus 35% in the trabeculectomy group (P=0.21; hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 0.86-2.01) — no significant difference. Mean pressure at 5 years was 13.4 (SD 3.5) mmHg tube versus 13.0 (5.2) mmHg trabeculectomy (P=0.52), on 2.2 (1.3) versus 1.3 (1.4) glaucoma medications (P<0.001). The authors conclude the two operations produced similar pressures at 5 years, with fewer medications required after trabeculectomy.
cards.watchOut: Failure accumulated in both arms — by 5 years roughly two in five tube eyes and one in three trabeculectomy eyes had met the failure definition, a reminder that 'no difference' is not 'both work well'. The medication gap (about one extra drop after tube surgery) is the most durable practical difference in the trial.
cards.source: Gedde SJ et al. Treatment Outcomes in the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy Study after 5 Years of Follow-up. Ophthalmology. 2022. PMID: 35835337. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PTVT report 4 of the single trial — visual fields (Swaminathan 2024): field loss -0.47 dB/year tube versus -0.32 dB/year trabeculectomy (P=0.23, not significant); worse pressure control, not operation type, predicted faster loss
cards.summary: PTVT report 4 of the single trial — visual fields (Swaminathan 2024): field loss -0.47 dB/year tube versus -0.32 dB/year trabeculectomy (P=0.23, not significant); worse pressure control, not operation type, predicted faster loss
cards.type: Randomised trial report — PTVT, visual-field analysis (Swaminathan 2024)
cards.people: 155 eyes (155 subjects) from the PTVT trial with reliable standard automated perimetry (84 tube, 71 trabeculectomy), from 730 evaluated visual-field tests (average 4.7 per eye) over baseline and annual testing for 5 years; baseline mean deviation was -12.8 (SD 8.3) dB tube versus -12.0 (8.4) dB trabeculectomy (P=0.57). A secondary-outcome report of the same single trial as the three cards above.
cards.result: Mean rate of change in visual-field mean deviation was -0.47 (SD 0.43) dB/year in the tube group versus -0.32 (0.39) dB/year in the trabeculectomy group (P=0.23) — no statistically significant difference. Eyes with mean pressure 14-17.5 mmHg lost field faster than eyes with mean pressure under 14 mmHg (-0.59 versus -0.27 dB/year; P=0.012), and multivariable analysis identified older age and worse pressure control — not the operation — as risk factors for faster progression.
cards.watchOut: Only 155 of the 242 randomised eyes contributed reliable fields, so this is a subset analysis of the trial, with the usual attrition caveats; a 0.15 dB/year difference, if real, would take many years to become clinically visible, and the trial cannot resolve differences of that size.
cards.source: Swaminathan SS et al. Visual Field Outcomes in the Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy Study. Ophthalmology. 2024. PMID: 38582154. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (no difference) — one trial, four reports; the operations converge on failure and pressure, and differ on drops and early serious complications
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (no difference) — one trial, four reports; the operations converge on failure and pressure, and differ on drops and early serious complications
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial (PTVT, 242 patients with no prior incisional surgery), reported at 1, 3 and 5 years plus a visual-field analysis. Cross-point: live shelf #617 covers tube versus trabeculectomy in eyes with prior surgery or high failure risk (TVT) — a different population; none of its reports is carded here.
cards.result: Failure: 17.3% vs 7.9% at 1 year (P=0.01), 33% vs 28% at 3 years (P=0.17), 42% vs 35% at 5 years (P=0.21). Pressure equal by 5 years; medications persistently fewer after trabeculectomy (1.3 vs 2.2); serious early complications fewer with the tube (1% vs 7% at 1 year); visual-field loss rates not significantly different. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference) — single-programme cap.
cards.watchOut: PTVT tested one tube (350-mm² Baerveldt implant) and one trabeculectomy protocol (mitomycin C 0.4 mg/ml for 2 minutes) in medically uncontrolled glaucoma without prior incisional surgery; results do not automatically transfer to other implants, to eyes with prior cataract surgery only, or to formal noninferiority claims.

shelves.title: Submacular haemorrhage in wet AMD: no randomised trial has tested pneumatic displacement against anti-VEGF alone — the one randomised trial (STAR, 90 patients) found surgery no better than pneumatic displacement (+16.8 vs +16.4 letters), and the comparative cohorts are size-dependent and confounded
shelves.question: In adults with submacular haemorrhage secondary to neovascular age-related macular degeneration, does pneumatic displacement with subretinal or intravitreal tissue plasminogen activator (± anti-VEGF) improve vision versus anti-VEGF therapy alone?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — graded GAP-E, and the evidence map matters more than any single number. No randomised trial has compared pneumatic displacement (± tissue plasminogen activator) against anti-VEGF therapy alone, which is the question as asked. The one randomised trial in the field, STAR (Gabrielle 2023; 90 patients, haemorrhage within 14 days, over 2 disc areas), compared the two active displacement strategies against each other — vitrectomy with subretinal tPA and gas versus pneumatic displacement with intravitreal tPA and gas, both with ranibizumab — and found no superiority for surgery: acuity change at 3 months was +16.8 letters with surgery versus +16.4 letters with pneumatic displacement (adjusted difference 1.9 letters, 95% CI -11.0 to 14.9; P=0.767), with similar outcomes at 6 months and no unexpected safety concerns; the authors note the trial cannot establish equivalence either. The only direct evidence on displacement versus anti-VEGF alone is a retrospective three-way comparison (Jeong 2020; 77 eyes, treatment chosen by the surgeon): for medium-sized haemorrhages, displacement rates were 67% (pneumatic displacement) and 83% (surgery) versus 33% with anti-VEGF alone, with better acuity in the displacement groups; for large haemorrhages surgery displaced more than pneumatic displacement (86% versus 25%); for small haemorrhages all three strategies improved acuity similarly. A 2026 network meta-analysis (150 studies reviewed, 38 in the network, 2,125 eyes) found non-vitrectomy therapies had better acuity outcomes and fewer complications than vitrectomy-based treatment, but concluded there is no consensus standard and large randomised trials are still needed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for displacement over anti-VEGF alone in medium-to-large haemorrhages — cohort-grade only.

cards.headline: STAR 2023 (randomised trial, 90 patients): vitrectomy + subretinal tPA + gas versus pneumatic displacement (intravitreal tPA + gas), both with ranibizumab — acuity gain +16.8 versus +16.4 letters at 3 months (P=0.767); surgery not superior
cards.summary: STAR 2023 (randomised trial, 90 patients): vitrectomy + subretinal tPA + gas versus pneumatic displacement (intravitreal tPA + gas), both with ranibizumab — acuity gain +16.8 versus +16.4 letters at 3 months (P=0.767); surgery not superior
cards.people: 90 patients aged 50 or over with neovascular AMD and recent submacular haemorrhage (within 14 days, more than 2 optic disc areas, predominantly overlying the retinal pigment epithelium), randomised at multiple centres to surgery (pars plana vitrectomy, subretinal tPA up to 0.5 ml/50 µg, 20% sulfur hexafluoride tamponade) or pneumatic displacement (0.05 ml intravitreal tPA 50 µg plus 0.3 ml pure sulfur hexafluoride); both groups received intravitreal ranibizumab 0.5 mg at the intervention and months 1 and 2, then as needed, over 6 months; 78 patients (86.7%) completed the 3-month primary-endpoint visit.
cards.result: Mean best-corrected visual acuity change at month 3 was +16.8 letters (95% CI 8.7-24.9) in the surgery group versus +16.4 letters (95% CI 7.1-25.7) with pneumatic displacement (adjusted difference 1.9 letters, 95% CI -11.0 to 14.9; P=0.767) — surgery was not superior. Secondary outcomes at month 6 were similar, and no unexpected ocular safety concerns were observed in either group. The authors state the design and results cannot be used to establish equivalence between the treatments.
cards.watchOut: STAR does not answer this shelf's headline question: both arms displaced the haemorrhage and both received anti-VEGF, so there is no anti-VEGF-alone arm. Its null is also wide — the confidence interval (-11.0 to +14.9 letters) spans more than two lines of vision in either direction. The record's MeSH erroneously includes 'Infant, Newborn'; the population was adults aged 50 or over, as the abstract states.
cards.source: Gabrielle PH et al. cards.headline: Jeong 2020 (retrospective comparison, 77 eyes, surgeon-chosen treatment): for medium haemorrhages, displacement 67% (pneumatic) and 83% (surgery) versus 33% (anti-VEGF alone); for large haemorrhages, surgery 86% versus pneumatic 25%; small haemorrhages did well on all three
cards.summary: Jeong 2020 (retrospective comparison, 77 eyes, surgeon-chosen treatment): for medium haemorrhages, displacement 67% (pneumatic) and 83% (surgery) versus 33% (anti-VEGF alone); for large haemorrhages, surgery 86% versus pneumatic 25%; small haemorrhages did well on all three
cards.people: 77 patients with submacular haemorrhage secondary to exudative AMD, grouped by haemorrhage size (small: 45 eyes, 1 to under 4 disc diameters; medium: 21 eyes, 4 or more disc diameters within the temporal arcade; large: 11 eyes, 4 or more disc diameters extending beyond the arcade) and treated at the surgeon's discretion with anti-VEGF monotherapy, pneumatic displacement with anti-VEGF, or vitrectomy with subretinal tPA and gas tamponade.
cards.result: In small haemorrhages, all three modalities showed gradual acuity improvement with haemorrhage regression or displacement rates over 75%. In medium haemorrhages, pneumatic displacement and surgery were associated with better acuity and more displacement than anti-VEGF monotherapy (displacement 67% and 83% respectively versus 33%). In large haemorrhages, surgery showed better visual improvement and a higher displacement rate than pneumatic displacement (86% versus 25%). The authors conclude that in larger haemorrhages, invasive techniques including pneumatic displacement or surgery were more advantageous than anti-VEGF monotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by indication in both directions: surgeons chose the treatment, plausibly reserving invasive options for worse or better-prognosis eyes, and the size strata are small (21 and 11 eyes in the strata where the claimed advantage sits). This is the only carded source that directly compares displacement against anti-VEGF alone, and it is the weakest design on the shelf — hence the MAYBE stamp. The record carries no MeSH list.
cards.source: Jeong S et al. Management of a Submacular Hemorrhage Secondary to Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Comparison of Three Treatment Modalities. Journal of clinical medicine. 2020. PMID: 32987903. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
