cards.headline: Pastor-Idoate 2026 (systematic review and network meta-analysis; 150 studies reviewed, 38 in the network, 2,125 eyes): non-vitrectomy strategies ranked better for acuity with fewer complications — but 'no consensus on a standard evidence-based treatment'
cards.summary: Pastor-Idoate 2026 (systematic review and network meta-analysis; 150 studies reviewed, 38 in the network, 2,125 eyes): non-vitrectomy strategies ranked better for acuity with fewer complications — but 'no consensus on a standard evidence-based treatment'
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (Pastor-Idoate 2026, Spanish Vitreo-Retinal Society)
cards.people: 150 studies of interventions for submacular haemorrhage (randomised trials, cohort studies and case series), of which 38 entered the network meta-analysis; the acuity analysis covered 26 studies, 20 interventions and 2,125 eyes, with moderate heterogeneity (I²=28.9%).
cards.result: Non-vitrectomy therapies showed better best-corrected acuity outcomes and fewer complications (such as retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage) than vitrectomy-based treatments, which achieved better anatomical results. By P-score ranking, 'Observation' had the highest probability of being most effective for acuity (P-score 0.8051), followed by anti-VEGF monotherapy and non-vitrectomy combinations — but the authors caution that the observation group rested on only two studies (26 eyes) with clinical heterogeneity. No publication bias was detected (Egger's test P=0.582). The review concludes there is no consensus on a standard evidence-based treatment and that further large-scale randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: A network built largely from case series and cohorts inherits all their confounding — the top ranking of 'Observation' on 26 eyes is the clearest warning against reading the rankings literally. The review's value here is its map of the field (20 interventions, no standard), not a verdict for any one of them.
cards.source: Pastor-Idoate S et al. Interventions for submacular haemorrhage: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of controversies-On behalf of the Spanish Vitreo-Retinal Society (SERV). Acta ophthalmologica. 2026. PMID: 40772916. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) — displacement probably helps larger haemorrhages, but the decisive trial has not been done
cards.summary: Synthesis: MAYBE (weak evidence) — displacement probably helps larger haemorrhages, but the decisive trial has not been done
cards.people: One randomised trial of surgery versus pneumatic displacement (90 patients, both arms with anti-VEGF), one retrospective three-way cohort (77 eyes) and one network meta-analysis (2,125 eyes across 26 studies).
cards.result: Surgery versus pneumatic displacement: no difference (+16.8 vs +16.4 letters, P=0.767). Displacement versus anti-VEGF alone: better displacement and acuity for medium haemorrhages in one retrospective cohort (67-83% vs 33% displacement); small haemorrhages did well on any strategy. Field-wide synthesis: no consensus standard. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for displacement in medium-to-large haemorrhages, GAP-E grade.
cards.watchOut: A large pan-European randomised trial (TIGER, vitrectomy with subretinal tPA versus aflibercept) exists as a published protocol only (PMID 35101110, a protocol record with no results) and is therefore not carded as evidence; if it reports, this shelf's stamp should be revisited. Timing (days since bleed) and haemorrhage size dominate prognosis and differ across every source here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gabrielle PH et al. Ophthalmology. 2023 (PMID: 37088447); Jeong S et al. Journal of clinical medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32987903); Pastor-Idoate S et al. Acta ophthalmologica. 2026 (PMID: 40772916).

shelves.title: Dropless cataract surgery: injected antibiotic–steroid regimens match drops on inflammation — the depot needed rescue drops in over half, and no trial was powered for endophthalmitis
shelves.question: In adults having routine cataract surgery, does a "dropless" regimen (intracameral or transzonular antibiotic–steroid, as tested in the programmes) prevent endophthalmitis and postoperative inflammation as well as conventional topical drops, and does it reduce drop-burden problems?
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence says dropless regimens control postoperative inflammation and macular thickening about as well as drops — with one sharp exception: in the Danish five-arm trial the sub-Tenon dexamethasone depot arm needed additional anti-inflammatory treatment in 56.6% of patients, and early aqueous flare was higher with the depot than with combination drops. The intracameral dexamethasone suspension IBI-10090 (named Dexycu in the record; the publication record names no company) cleared anterior-chamber cells at the same rate as prednisolone drops by day 8. The antibiotic-containing regimens (transzonular triamcinolone–moxifloxacin; intravitreal triamcinolone–moxifloxacin–vancomycin) rest on a single-arm series and a retrospective comparison, not randomisation. On endophthalmitis — the outcome patients most fear — no carded study reports a powered comparison: the infection claim for dropless surgery is cohort-grade at best, exactly as the slate flagged. Patient preference, where measured, strongly favours not using drops.

cards.headline: The Danish RCT: sub-Tenon depot (the dropless arm) matched drops on macular thickness and vision — but 56.6% needed extra anti-inflammatory treatment
cards.summary: The Danish RCT: sub-Tenon depot (the dropless arm) matched drops on macular thickness and vision — but 56.6% needed extra anti-inflammatory treatment
cards.people: 470 low-risk patients (mean age 72.2 years; 61.7% women) undergoing phacoemulsification for age-related cataract, randomised to five prophylactic regimens (94 per group), including a sub-Tenon depot of dexamethasone phosphate as the dropless arm versus prednisolone-plus-ketorolac drops.
cards.result: At 3 months, mean central subfield thickness was 255.2 µm in the sub-Tenon group versus 250.7 µm in the preoperative prednisolone-plus-NSAID control group, with no significant differences in thickness or visual acuity between any regimen and control — but 47 of 83 participants (56.6%) in the sub-Tenon group needed additional anti-inflammatory treatment. Starting drops 3 days preoperatively was not superior to starting on the day of surgery.
cards.watchOut: The dropless arm here was a steroid depot only — no antibiotic component — and 'no difference on thickness' coexisted with most depot patients ending up on rescue drops anyway, which is the opposite of the dropless promise.
cards.source: Randomised clinical trial (Erichsen/Holm programme, Rigshospitalet Glostrup). Erichsen JH et al.. Prednisolone and Ketorolac vs Ketorolac Monotherapy or Sub-Tenon Prophylaxis for Macular Thickening in Cataract Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA ophthalmology. 2021. PMID: 34383010. Registry ID: NCT03383328. cards.headline: IBI-10090 (Dexycu) intracameral dexamethasone: cell clearing 51.6% versus 50.9% on prednisolone drops at day 8
cards.summary: IBI-10090 (Dexycu) intracameral dexamethasone: cell clearing 51.6% versus 50.9% on prednisolone drops at day 8
cards.people: 181 patients in a phase 3 multicentre US trial (126 receiving IBI-10090, 55 prednisolone acetate 1.0% drops in the safety analysis), randomised 2:1 after cataract surgery, followed 90 days. The tested product is named in the record as IBI-10090, an anterior-chamber dexamethasone drug-delivery suspension (Dexycu); the record names no company.
cards.result: By 8 days postoperatively, 51.6% of IBI-10090 eyes and 50.9% of prednisolone eyes had anterior chamber cell clearing; over 98% of eyes in both groups had clearing at 90 days. The most common adverse events in the IBI-10090 group were increased intraocular pressure (11.1%) and iritis (6.3%); the fall in endothelial cell density did not differ between groups. Of IBI-10090 patients, 68.7% strongly agreed that not having to use eyedrops was very convenient.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the product replaces only the steroid drop — it carries no antibiotic, so this trial says nothing about endophthalmitis prophylaxis. Industry-formulation trial of a single named product; results do not transfer to compounded mixtures.
cards.source: Phase 3 randomised multicentre trial (Donnenfeld et al.). Donnenfeld ED et al.. Safety of IBI-10090 for inflammation associated with cataract surgery: Phase 3 multicenter study. Journal of cataract and refractive surgery. 2018. PMID: 30139638. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Transzonular triamcinolone–moxifloxacin: 96% reached 6/9 or better at 3 months in a single-arm series of 200 eyes — no comparator, no infection outcome reported
cards.summary: Transzonular triamcinolone–moxifloxacin: 96% reached 6/9 or better at 3 months in a single-arm series of 200 eyes — no comparator, no infection outcome reported
cards.people: 200 eyes in a prospective, non-randomised, single-arm interventional study of phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation; 0.1 ml each of moxifloxacin and triamcinolone acetonide injected transzonularly after lens implantation. The record names the drugs generically and names no branded product or company. Patients with glaucoma or known steroid response were excluded.
cards.result: Uncorrected visual acuity better than 6/9 was achieved in 96% of patients at 3 months; mean intraocular pressure stayed normal at every visit; 20 patients reported floaters on day 1, falling to zero by day 60; no patient needed any eye drop during the entire postoperative period.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and self-selected (patients consented after being told the pros and cons): with no drops group beside it, 'safe and advantageous' is the authors' framing, not a comparison. Endophthalmitis is not reported as an outcome in the record.

cards.headline: Retrospective 1,058-eye comparison: intravitreal triamcinolone–moxifloxacin–vancomycin had less persistent inflammation than drops — but higher adjusted odds of macular oedema (OR 3.21, relative)
cards.summary: Retrospective 1,058-eye comparison: intravitreal triamcinolone–moxifloxacin–vancomycin had less persistent inflammation than drops — but higher adjusted odds of macular oedema (OR 3.21, relative)
cards.people: 1,058 eyes in a retrospective comparative case series (571 receiving an intraoperative pars plana intravitreal antibiotic–steroid injection of triamcinolone, moxifloxacin and vancomycin; 487 receiving a standard postoperative topical regimen), follow-up 1–6 months. Observational — treatment was not randomised.
cards.result: Best-corrected acuity of 20/25 or better was reached by 87.4% of injected eyes versus 78.8% of controls. Persistent anterior chamber inflammation occurred in 2.6% versus 8.0% and rebound inflammation in 2.6% versus 6.4%, but cystoid macular oedema occurred in 4.7% versus 3.9%, and the adjusted odds ratio for macular oedema with the injection was 3.21 (95% CI 1.42 to 7.23, a relative measure). IOP spikes (≥10 mm Hg) occurred in 1.9% versus 0.4%.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by surgeon/era choice of regimen; the adjusted macular-oedema signal (OR 3.21) cuts against the inflammation benefit, and a 1–6-month window in ~1,000 eyes cannot settle a complication as rare as endophthalmitis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: dropless ≈ drops for inflammation and vision; the infection question is unanswered by design
cards.summary: Synthesis: dropless ≈ drops for inflammation and vision; the infection question is unanswered by design
cards.people: Four reports: one 470-patient randomised trial with a steroid-depot dropless arm, one 181-patient phase 3 trial of a named intracameral dexamethasone suspension, one 200-eye single-arm transzonular series, and one 1,058-eye retrospective comparison.
cards.result: Inflammation and visual outcomes were broadly equivalent between dropless regimens and drops, but the depot arm needed rescue treatment in 56.6%, the retrospective injection series carried higher adjusted macular-oedema odds, and no carded study was powered for — or even reported — endophthalmitis as a comparative outcome. The stamp is POSSIBLE: equivalence on surrogates, silence on the rare harm that matters most.
cards.watchOut: Named products are given exactly as the publications give them; where a record names no brand or company (the transzonular series), the card says so plainly.

shelves.title: Oral tranexamic acid for melasma: pigmentation falls by about half in small placebo-controlled trials — off-label, with thrombosis screening part of the deal
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe melasma, does oral tranexamic acid improve pigmentation (MASI) versus placebo or topical therapy alone, and at what thrombotic-safety cost in screened patients?
shelves.balance: This shelf is the oral-tranexamic-acid slice the library was missing: pack #4222 homes the topical triple-combination cream question and does not card oral tranexamic acid. Four small randomised trials point the same way — modified MASI falls by about half on oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily over 3 months, against ~11–19% on placebo or hydroquinone alone, and much of the gain persists 3 months after stopping. The safety side must be read honestly: these were screened patients, the samples are far too small to detect a rare thrombotic event, and 'no serious adverse events' in ~230 trial patients is not proof of thrombotic safety. Oral tranexamic acid for melasma is off-label; a personal or family history of thrombosis is the screening question the trials applied and any real-world use must apply. Cross-point: pack #4222 (topical triple-combination cream versus hydroquinone).

cards.headline: Del Rosario 2018: mMASI fell 49% on oral tranexamic acid versus 18% on placebo at 3 months
cards.summary: Del Rosario 2018: mMASI fell 49% on oral tranexamic acid versus 18% on placebo at 3 months
cards.people: 44 patients with moderate-to-severe melasma enrolled (39 completed), predominantly Hispanic women at a single centre; tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months, both with sunscreen, then 3 months of sunscreen only.
cards.result: At 3 months the modified MASI score had fallen 49% in the tranexamic acid group versus 18% in the control group; patients with severe melasma improved more than those with moderate melasma. Three months after treatment stopped, scores remained 26% below baseline on tranexamic acid versus 19% on placebo. No serious adverse events were noted in either group.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, 39 completers, and a largely Hispanic female sample — generalisability is narrow, and a trial this size cannot see a rare clot. Participants were screened; the result does not license unscreened use.

cards.headline: Shihab 2020: adding oral tranexamic acid to hydroquinone cut mMASI 55% versus 10.9% for hydroquinone alone
cards.summary: Shihab 2020: adding oral tranexamic acid to hydroquinone cut mMASI 55% versus 10.9% for hydroquinone alone
cards.people: 50 subjects with moderate-to-severe melasma, all completing the study: hydroquinone 4% cream plus sunscreen with either oral tranexamic acid or placebo capsules for 3 months, then 3 months on sunscreen alone.
cards.result: Modified MASI fell 55% (mean 8.96 to 4.0) in the tranexamic-acid group versus 10.9% (8.53 to 7.6) with hydroquinone alone at 3 months. Three months after stopping, scores were still 42% below baseline versus 4.7%. Melanin index by mexameter moved in the same direction. No serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: This tests tranexamic acid as an add-on to hydroquinone, not as monotherapy — the comparison on this card is the combination against topical therapy alone. Fifty patients, one centre.

cards.headline: Colferai 2019: melasma improved by all four assessment methods in 50% on tranexamic acid versus 5.9% on placebo
cards.summary: Colferai 2019: melasma improved by all four assessment methods in 50% on tranexamic acid versus 5.9% on placebo
cards.people: 47 patients with facial melasma selected at a single philanthropic dermatology clinic (37 completed: 20 tranexamic acid, 17 placebo; 36 women, 1 man; mean age 43.97 years); tranexamic acid 250 mg orally twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks, all using tinted SPF 50 sunscreen.
cards.result: Melasma improved by all four evaluation methods (photographs, colorimetry, MELASQoL and MASI) in 50% of the tranexamic-acid group versus 5.9% of the placebo group (P < 0.005). No patient had severe side effects.
cards.watchOut: Ten of 47 selected patients did not complete, and the endpoint is a composite 'improved by all methods' judgment rather than a single prespecified score — a softer outcome than the MASI cards beside it.

cards.headline: Prathyoosha 2024: MASI fell 65.91% on oral tranexamic acid versus 17.22% on placebo cream — but the trial was not blinded
cards.summary: Prathyoosha 2024: MASI fell 65.91% on oral tranexamic acid versus 17.22% on placebo cream — but the trial was not blinded
cards.people: 90 patients with melasma (30 per group): oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily, nightly modified Kligman's formula cream, or nightly placebo cream, for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean MASI reduction at 12 weeks was 9.94 points (65.91%) on oral tranexamic acid, 6.12 (54.78%) on the modified Kligman's formula and 2.07 (17.22%) on placebo cream; oral tranexamic acid beat placebo significantly, and did not differ significantly from the topical formula (P = 0.29). Adverse effects in all groups were mild and self-limiting.
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves flag the limited sample, non-blinded design and absent follow-up — expectation effects on a visible pigment endpoint cannot be excluded, so this card supports, but cannot carry, the shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent ~50% pigment reduction across four small trials — POSSIBLE, off-label, screening-dependent
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent ~50% pigment reduction across four small trials — POSSIBLE, off-label, screening-dependent
cards.people: Four randomised trials totalling 231 enrolled patients (44 + 50 + 47 + 90), all using tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily for about 3 months in screened patients with moderate-to-severe melasma.
cards.result: Every trial favours oral tranexamic acid: mMASI reductions of 49–66% against 11–19% in control arms, with partial persistence after stopping. No serious adverse events were reported, but the combined base is far too small to exclude a rare thrombotic harm — the trials' screening, not their event counts, is the safety evidence. Stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Off-label use. The thrombotic-safety question is answered by screening (thrombosis history), not by these trials' zero-event counts; do not read 'no serious adverse events' as a clean bill.

shelves.title: Low-dose oral minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia: head-to-head trials find it about equal to topical minoxidil — with more unwanted hair growth
shelves.question: In adults with androgenetic alopecia, does low-dose oral minoxidil improve hair density versus placebo — and how does it compare with topical minoxidil — at what cost in hypertrichosis, oedema and cardiovascular effects?
shelves.balance: The library's homes ask the neighbouring questions — pack #6008 (oral finasteride versus topical minoxidil) and pack #6009 (topical minoxidil in women) — and neither cards the oral route; this shelf builds only on the oral-minoxidil reports those homes do not contain. Three randomised head-to-head trials, carded per dose as the slate required and never pooled, converge on equivalence rather than superiority: oral 2.5 mg (men) / 1.25 mg (women) matched topical on photographic improvement (67% versus 73%); oral 1 mg matched 5% topical on hair diameter; and a three-arm trial found one-grade improvement in 25% on oral versus 10% on topical, a non-significant difference. The cost side is consistent: hypertrichosis in 30% versus 9% in the double-dummy trial, plus headache (20%), dizziness (15%) and pedal oedema (5%) in the three-arm trial's oral group. No placebo-controlled oral-minoxidil trial is carded here, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE; the use is off-label at every dose carded.

cards.headline: Chaudhry 2026 (double-blind, double-dummy): photographic improvement 67% on oral versus 73% on topical — hypertrichosis 30% versus 9%
cards.summary: Chaudhry 2026 (double-blind, double-dummy): photographic improvement 67% on oral versus 73% on topical — hypertrichosis 30% versus 9%
cards.people: 100 patients aged 18–50 years with androgenetic alopecia randomised to oral minoxidil once daily (2.5 mg in males, 1.25 mg in females) plus placebo spray, or topical minoxidil twice daily (5% in males, 2% in females) plus placebo tablet, for 6 months; 90 completed 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mild-to-excellent photographic improvement (≥+1 on a 7-point scale) occurred in 67% of the oral group and 73% of the topical group (p = 0.652); patient satisfaction was 80.4% versus 70.5% (p = 0.332). Hypertrichosis was significantly more frequent on oral minoxidil (30% vs 9%, p = 0.011); contact dermatitis occurred only with topical (11% vs 0%, p = 0.025). No serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: The authors state plainly the study was not powered to establish non-inferiority or equivalence — 'no significant difference' here is absence of evidence of a difference, not proof the routes are equal.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oral ≈ topical in every head-to-head — equivalence claimed, never proven; hypertrichosis is the consistent price
cards.summary: Synthesis: oral ≈ topical in every head-to-head — equivalence claimed, never proven; hypertrichosis is the consistent price
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 240 patients (100 + 65 + 75), carded per dose (2.5/1.25 mg, 1 mg, and one dose not documented in its record) and not pooled.
cards.result: No trial found oral minoxidil superior to topical, and none was powered to prove equivalence; satisfaction trends favour the tablet, hypertrichosis (30% vs 9%) and systemic symptoms (headache, dizziness, oedema) go the other way. With no placebo-controlled card on this shelf, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) for an off-label use. The dose-comparison trial of 0.25 mg versus 1 mg in women (Nascimento e Silva 2022, PMID: 35077777) was NOT carded: its PubMed record carries no abstract, so its content could not be verified from the fetched record this session.
cards.watchOut: Off-label at all carded doses. Doses differ across cards by design — do not pool them into a single 'oral minoxidil effect'. Cross-points: packs #6008 and #6009 (topical-route homes).

shelves.title: Sofpironium gel for axillary hyperhidrosis: two phase 3 programmes beat vehicle on severity and sweat weight
shelves.question: In adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, does sofpironium bromide gel (the topical anticholinergic tested in the CARDIGAN programme) reduce sweat production and severity scores versus vehicle?
shelves.balance: Pack #2476 homes botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium tosylate cloth for this condition; sofpironium gel — a different product and formulation — appears nowhere in it, and this shelf cards only the sofpironium reports. The evidence is unusually tidy for a dermatology shelf: the pooled CARDIGAN I and II phase 3 trials of sofpironium topical gel 12.45% (701 patients) met both co-primary endpoints against vehicle; the Japanese phase 3 trial of the 5% gel (BBI-4000; 281 patients) met its combined severity-plus-sweat-weight endpoint 53.9% versus 36.4%; a phase 2 dose-ranging trial found all three concentrations superior to vehicle on severity scores; and a 52-week open-label extension held the response at ~58%. Harms are the expected local and anticholinergic ones — application-site dermatitis and erythema, with adverse-drug-reaction rates of 16.3% versus 5.0% in the Japanese trial — and no serious treatment-related events were reported. Where a publication record names no manufacturer, the card says so plainly, per the product-naming rule.

cards.headline: CARDIGAN I/II pooled (2025): sofpironium gel 12.45% beat vehicle on both co-primary endpoints (P < .0001 and P = .0002)
cards.summary: CARDIGAN I/II pooled (2025): sofpironium gel 12.45% beat vehicle on both co-primary endpoints (P < .0001 and P = .0002)
cards.people: 701 patients aged 9 years and older with primary axillary hyperhidrosis in two replicate double-blind phase 3 trials (353 sofpironium topical gel 12.45%, 348 vehicle), applied once daily to the axillae for 6 weeks. The record names the product as sofpironium topical gel, 12.45%; it names no manufacturer.
cards.result: For the co-primary endpoint of ≥2-point improvement on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Measure-Axillary-7, pooled results significantly favoured sofpironium over vehicle (P < .0001); for the co-primary gravimetric sweat-production endpoint, the treatment group had a greater reduction (P = .0002). Secondary endpoints also significantly favoured the gel, and treatment was well tolerated. The record reports P values rather than responder percentages for the pooled primaries, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A pooled report of two trials carded as one programme — the two CARDIGAN trials are not counted twice on this shelf. Six weeks of treatment only; durability comes from the Japanese extension card, a different concentration.

cards.headline: Japanese phase 3 (2021): combined severity-and-sweat endpoint met by 53.9% on 5% sofpironium gel versus 36.4% on vehicle
cards.summary: Japanese phase 3 (2021): combined severity-and-sweat endpoint met by 53.9% on 5% sofpironium gel versus 36.4% on vehicle
cards.people: 281 Japanese patients with primary axillary hyperhidrosis randomised to 5% sofpironium bromide (BBI-4000) gel (141) or vehicle (140) for 6 weeks; 70.1% female, median age 35.0 years. The record names the product as 5% sofpironium bromide (BBI-4000) gel; it names no manufacturer.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (HDSS of 1 or 2 plus ≥50% reduction in gravimetric sweat weight) was achieved by 53.9% on sofpironium versus 36.4% on vehicle — an absolute difference of 17.5% (95% CI 6.02 to 28.93; P = 0.003). cards.watchOut: A 5% concentration — not the 12.45% CARDIGAN formulation — in a single-country population; the two phase 3 programmes agree in direction but are not the same product strength, and the cards are not pooled.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 programmes, one direction — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 programmes, one direction — LIKELY
cards.people: Four reports: pooled CARDIGAN I/II (701 patients, 12.45% gel), the Japanese phase 3 trial (281 patients, 5% gel), a phase 2 dose-ranging trial (N not documented in its record), and a 52-week open-label extension (185 patients).
cards.result: Both pivotal programmes beat vehicle on prespecified primary endpoints combining patient-rated severity and gravimetric sweat weight; phase 2 shows the effect across concentrations, and the extension shows it persisting to a year. cards.watchOut: Concentrations differ between programmes (12.45% versus 5%) and are carded separately, never pooled; manufacturer names appear only where a publication record gives one — none of the four records names one.

shelves.title: Accommodation across the lifespan: objective amplitude is far below the push-up numbers, holds to about age 20, then collapses to zero by the 50s — while the ciliary muscle keeps contracting
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does the amplitude of eye accommodation decline across the lifespan — what did the classic subjective (push-up, minus-lens) and objective (dynamic retinoscopy / open-field autorefraction) measurements show, and how much of presbyopia is lenticular stiffening versus ciliary/zonular failure on human lens-stretching and imaging studies?
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong, optics and accommodation): the Helmholtz mechanism — ciliary contraction releases zonular tension and the elastic lens rounds up. The human measurement literature separates the two candidate failures cleanly. Objective autorefraction (Anderson programme) shows true amplitude is far below the classic subjective push-up figures — which overestimate, especially in young children — plateaus until about age 20, then declines sigmoidally to zero beyond 50. Human MRI (Strenk programme) shows the ciliary muscle contracting in every subject into the ninth decade, with an accommodative diameter change undiminished by age: the muscle works; the ageing, thickening lens stops answering. The lens-stiffening side of the mechanism rests partly on ex vivo human donor-lens work (the Fisher spinning-lens lineage and later donor-lens stretching studies) — that is labelled here as ex vivo/textbook prose, not carded as in-vivo human evidence, and primate lens-stretching data are not carded at all.

cards.headline: Anderson 2014: push-up overestimates hugely in young children — 16.00 D subjective versus 7.94 D objective at age 3–5 (N = 236)
cards.summary: Anderson 2014: push-up overestimates hugely in young children — 16.00 D subjective versus 7.94 D objective at age 3–5 (N = 236)
cards.people: 236 subjects aged 3 to 64 years; monocular amplitude measured three ways in random order — subjective push-up, objective minus-lens-stimulated and objective proximal-stimulated autorefraction (Grand Seiko), using a 1.5-mm letter target.
cards.result: Objective amplitudes were lower than subjective push-up at all ages, most dramatically at age 3–5 (push-up 16.00 ± 4.98 D versus objective proximal 7.94 ± 2.37 D and objective lens-stimulated 6.20 ± 1.99 D). Objective amplitudes were largest at age 6–10 (8.81 ± 1.24 D proximal; 8.05 ± 1.82 D lens-stimulated), then decreased gradually until a rapid decline to presbyopia in the fourth decade. The two objective techniques tracked each other closely (R² = 0.85), proximal reading 0.55 D higher on average.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional, not longitudinal — the 'lifespan curve' is stitched across people, not followed within them; autorefraction measures refractive response, which is the functional quantity but not lens shape itself.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (subjective versus objective accommodative amplitude, preschool to presbyopia). Anderson HA et al.. cards.headline: Anderson 2008: objective amplitude is flat to ~age 20, then falls sigmoidally — rapid decline 20–50, tapering to 0 beyond 50 (N = 140)
cards.summary: Anderson 2008: objective amplitude is flat to ~age 20, then falls sigmoidally — rapid decline 20–50, tapering to 0 beyond 50 (N = 140)
cards.people: 140 subjects aged 3 to 40 years; accommodative responses measured with a Grand Seiko autorefractor viewing a target at 33 cm through minus lenses of increasing power until the response saturated.
cards.result: Maximum amplitude fitted a curvilinear function of age (y = 7.33 − 0.0035(age − 3)², P < 0.001); tangent analysis showed amplitude relatively stable until age 20. Pooled with earlier objective adult data to age 70, a sigmoidal fit showed stable amplitudes below 20, a rapid linear decline between 20 and 50, and a taper to 0 beyond 50 years.
cards.watchOut: The beyond-40 portion of the sigmoid is borrowed from previously published adult datasets pooled by the authors — the card reports the pooled fit as the authors present it, and the study's own subjects stop at 40.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (minus-lens-stimulated objective amplitude versus age). Anderson HA et al.. cards.headline: Strenk 1999 (MRI): the ciliary muscle contracts at every age from 22 to 83 — it is the lens that stops responding (N = 25)
cards.summary: Strenk 1999 (MRI): the ciliary muscle contracts at every age from 22 to 83 — it is the lens that stops responding (N = 25)
cards.people: 25 subjects aged 22 through 83 years imaged with a 1.5-T MRI and custom eye coil at relaxed accommodation (0.1 D) and strong accommodative effort (8.0 D); ciliary ring diameter, lens equatorial diameter and lens thickness measured from the images.
cards.result: Muscle contraction was present in all subjects and reduced only slightly with advancing age. The unaccommodated ciliary ring diameter decreased with age, and unaccommodated lens thickness increased with age, while lens thickness under accommodative effort was only modestly age-dependent — in-vivo human evidence that presbyopia is not primarily a ciliary muscle failure.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five subjects spread across six decades — a few per decade; MRI spatial resolution limits the smallest diameter changes, and effort at 8.0 D is a stimulus, not a guarantee of equal neural drive at every age.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (MRI of ciliary muscle and lens with age). Strenk SA et al.. Age-related changes in human ciliary muscle and lens: a magnetic resonance imaging study. cards.headline: Strenk 2006 (MRI): accommodative ciliary-ring change averaged 0.64 mm and was undiminished by age or by lens replacement (48 eyes of 40 people)
cards.summary: Strenk 2006 (MRI): accommodative ciliary-ring change averaged 0.64 mm and was undiminished by age or by lens replacement (48 eyes of 40 people)
cards.people: 48 eyes of 40 people aged 22 to 91 years (32 phakic volunteers, one eye each; 8 patients with a monocular intraocular lens, both eyes), imaged during physiological accommodation and at rest; ciliary muscle ring diameter measured.
cards.result: The ciliary muscle remained active throughout life: the accommodative change in its diameter (mean 0.64 mm, P < .00001) was undiminished by age or by intraocular-lens implantation, and preliminary data showed the change statistically identical in phakic and pseudophakic eyes. Phakic ciliary diameter itself decreased markedly with age in both accommodative states.
cards.watchOut: Includes pseudophakic eyes — a patient-adjacent subgroup carded for the muscle question only; the muscle's preserved movement says nothing about how much force reaches a stiffened natural lens, which is the ex vivo part of the story told in the balance, not on a card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the amplitude curve is objective, sigmoidal and complete by the 50s — and the muscle is innocent
cards.summary: Synthesis: the amplitude curve is objective, sigmoidal and complete by the 50s — and the muscle is innocent
cards.people: Four primary human studies (N = 236, 140, 25, and 40 people/48 eyes): two objective-autorefraction lifespan studies and two in-vivo MRI studies of the ciliary muscle and lens.
cards.result: Objective amplitude peaks in childhood at ~8–9 D (not the ~16 D of push-up lore), holds to about age 20, falls steeply from 20 to 50 and reaches ~0 beyond 50. At every age the ciliary muscle still contracts; the unaccommodated lens thickens with age and its accommodative shape change fades. The lenticular-stiffening mechanism itself leans on ex vivo donor-lens mechanics (Fisher lineage), presented in the balance as textbook/ex vivo framing and deliberately not carded as in-vivo evidence. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Duane's classic subjective curves are described, not carded: the original reports predate PubMed indexing and carry no fetchable record, so no card rests on them — the objective studies carded here are the verifiable replacement, and they exist precisely to correct the subjective numbers.

shelves.title: The post-illumination pupil response: the pupil stays constricted ~1.5 mm after bright blue light is switched off — a melanopsin signal that shrinks in glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the post-illumination pupil response — how long does the pupil stay constricted after a bright (especially short-wavelength) light is switched off, how is the response isolated as melanopsin/ipRGC-driven, and how does it fail in outer-retinal disease while the afferent light reflex survives?
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, retinal phototransduction): a small population of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin signals irradiance directly, with slow, sustained kinetics unlike the transient rod/cone response. The human pupillometry literature isolates that signal by colour and timing: the constriction that persists after a bright short-wavelength stimulus is switched off — the post-illumination pupil response (PIPR) — matches melanopsin's spectral tuning, is present in all healthy subjects, and survives as a measurable inner-retinal signal even when outer-retinal disease has degraded the rod/cone-driven components. The disease cards (glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa) are carded as physiology-in-disease contrasts, the standard way this response is characterised, not as treatment evidence.

cards.headline: Gamlin 2007: the sustained post-offset pupil response in humans carries melanopsin's spectral tuning and slow kinetics
cards.summary: Gamlin 2007: the sustained post-offset pupil response in humans carries melanopsin's spectral tuning and slow kinetics
cards.people: Human subjects (with parallel macaque experiments) studied with sustained pupil responses during continuous light and after light offset, including pharmacological blockade of conventional photoreceptor signals in the primate work. The human N is not documented in the fetched record and is printed that way.
cards.result: In humans, the sustained pupil response after light offset documented the contribution of intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells to the pupillary response: the responses display the unique spectral tuning, slow kinetics and irradiance coding of melanopsin-derived ganglion-cell photoresponses, persisting during continuous light and after offset when rod/cone-driven responses have decayed.
cards.watchOut: A mixed human–primate report: the pharmacological-isolation experiments are macaque, and only the human post-offset observations are carded here; the record does not document the human N, so no N is claimed.

cards.headline: Kankipati 2010: PIPR present in all 37 healthy subjects — 1.5 mm after blue light, net 1.4 mm over red (N = 37)
cards.summary: Kankipati 2010: PIPR present in all 37 healthy subjects — 1.5 mm after blue light, net 1.4 mm over red (N = 37)
cards.people: 37 subjects without ocular disease (mean age 48.6 years); a 60°, 10-second light stimulus (470 nm blue or 623 nm red) presented to one dilated eye, with the consensual response of the fellow eye recorded by infrared pupillometry for 50 seconds after light cessation.
cards.result: A positive PIPR was seen in all subjects. The population-average PIPR for 470-nm light was 1.5 mm (SEM 0.10), and the net PIPR (blue minus red) was 1.4 mm (SEM 0.09, P < 0.0001) — the blue–red subtraction is what isolates the melanopsin component from the generic post-stimulus response.
cards.watchOut: One laboratory's stimulus geometry (60°, 10 s, specified irradiance); absolute millimetre values travel with the protocol, so cross-study comparisons should use the net (blue-minus-red) figure.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (post-illumination pupil response in subjects without ocular disease). Kankipati L et al.. cards.headline: Kankipati 2011: net PIPR halved in glaucoma — 0.6 mm versus 1.3 mm in age-matched controls (N = 16 + 19)
cards.summary: Kankipati 2011: net PIPR halved in glaucoma — 0.6 mm versus 1.3 mm in age-matched controls (N = 16 + 19)
cards.people: 16 glaucoma patients (mean age 63.7 years) and 19 age-matched controls (mean age 59 years), tested with the same 10-second blue (470 nm) and red (623 nm) stimuli, consensual pupil recorded for 50 seconds after offset.
cards.result: The net PIPR was 0.6 mm (SEM 0.12) in glaucoma patients versus 1.3 mm (SEM 0.16) in controls — significantly smaller (P < 0.001) — showing the melanopsin-driven sustained response is itself damaged in glaucoma, a ganglion-cell disease, rather than merely reflecting outer-retinal input loss.
cards.watchOut: Small groups and a clinic population; a physiological contrast (disease versus health), carded as characterisation of the response, not as a diagnostic-accuracy claim.

cards.headline: Kardon 2011: in retinitis pigmentosa the rod/cone-weighted pupil responses fall while bright-blue sustained responses remain recordable (N = 32 + 43)
cards.summary: Kardon 2011: in retinitis pigmentosa the rod/cone-weighted pupil responses fall while bright-blue sustained responses remain recordable (N = 32 + 43)
cards.people: 32 patients with retinitis pigmentosa and visual loss and 43 normal subjects, tested with a chromatic pupillometer using red and blue lights at 1, 10 and 100 cd/m²; pupil responses compared with visual field and electroretinography results.
cards.result: Pupil responses differed significantly between RP patients and normals in conditions emphasising rod (1 cd/m² blue) or cone (100 cd/m² red) contribution (P < 0.001), and patients with a non-recordable scotopic ERG had significantly reduced responses to low-intensity blue light — yet responses remained recordable in all but one patient, who responded only to bright blue light, the melanopsin-weighted stimulus: the inner-retinal sustained pathway outlasts the failing outer retina.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic-technology evaluation in a disease cohort; severity varied across patients, so the card reports the group contrast and the recordable-response observation, not a per-patient rule.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (chromatic pupillometry in retinitis pigmentosa). Kardon R et al.. Chromatic pupillometry in patients with retinitis pigmentosa. Ophthalmology. 2011. cards.headline: Synthesis: a colour- and time-isolated melanopsin signal — universal in health, diminished in ganglion-cell and outer-retinal disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: a colour- and time-isolated melanopsin signal — universal in health, diminished in ganglion-cell and outer-retinal disease
cards.people: Four primary human studies: the Gamlin characterisation (human N not documented in its record), 37 healthy subjects, 16 glaucoma patients with 19 controls, and 32 RP patients with 43 controls.
cards.result: After bright blue light is switched off, the healthy pupil stays constricted by ~1.5 mm, with a net blue-over-red PIPR of ~1.4 mm isolating the melanopsin/ipRGC component (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep framing). The net response halves in glaucoma and the rod/cone-weighted components fail in RP while bright-blue responses persist — the dissociation the question asks about. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Absolute PIPR millimetres are protocol-bound (stimulus size, duration, irradiance differ between laboratories); the net blue-minus-red measure is the portable quantity.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gamlin PD et al. Vision research. 2007 (PMID: 17320141); Kankipati L et al. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 2010 (PMID: 20007832); Kankipati L et al. shelves.title: Transepidermal water loss (physiology): healthy skin leaks 2–44 g/m²/h depending on the body site — lowest on the breast, highest in the axilla and palm — and after tape-stripping the barrier recovers ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours in light skin, faster in dark skin
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how leaky is the skin barrier at rest — what are normal transepidermal water-loss rates by body site, how fast does the barrier recover after tape-stripping disruption, and how do age and humidity change both?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing here is thinner than for other physiology rows — Boron & Boulpaep and Ganong treat the skin as a barrier organ only briefly — and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as the row itself directs. Measurement was standardised by the European Society of Contact Dermatitis group (Pinnagoda 1990, cited in prose as the methods anchor, not carded as an evidence study). The pooled reference literature (212 studies, 86 skin areas) puts healthy adult TEWL between 2.3 g/m²/h on breast skin and 44.0 g/m²/h in the axilla — site dominates every other variable (Akdeniz 2018). A modern four-site primary study agrees in pattern: forearm lowest at 11 g/m²/h, palm highest at 41 g/m²/h (John 2023; N = 15). A 500-volunteer normative cohort found the forehead the highest-TEWL facial/trunk site tested and lower TEWL in middle and older age groups (Mehta 2018) — consistent with the pooled finding that TEWL in elderly skin is similar to or lower than in younger adults, which corrects the intuitive 'older skin leaks more' assumption: basal leak does not rise with age, even though aged barrier recovery is slower (the recovery-age literature is partly murine and is not carded). Recovery after tape-stripping is quantified in humans: light skin types recovered ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours, dark skin types ~43% and ~72% (Reed 1995), and psychological stress delayed recovery by 10% at 2 hours in a randomised laboratory study (Robles 2007; N = 85). Humidity effects named in the row question are handled by the standardisation literature (measurements are made under controlled temperature/humidity) rather than by a carded dose-response study, and no humidity number is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Akdeniz 2018 (systematic review and meta-analysis of primary studies): healthy adult TEWL ran from 2.3 g/m²/h (breast) to 44.0 g/m²/h (axilla) across 86 skin areas in 212 studies
cards.summary: Akdeniz 2018 (systematic review and meta-analysis of primary studies): healthy adult TEWL ran from 2.3 g/m²/h (breast) to 44.0 g/m²/h (axilla) across 86 skin areas in 212 studies
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of primary human measurement studies (reference values)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis update pooling primary empirical observational and interventional studies in healthy adults that reported quantitative TEWL with spread and clear skin area and age; 45 studies were added in this update, giving TEWL estimates for 86 skin areas in 212 studies, with per-area sample sizes from 4 to 4,013 (mid volar right forearm).
cards.result: The lowest pooled TEWL was 2.3 g/m²/h (95% CI 1.9–2.7) for breast skin and the highest 44.0 g/m²/h (95% CI 39.8–48.2) for the axilla — a roughly 19-fold site range in healthy skin. Differences between measurement devices seemed clinically minimal. TEWL in elderly people was either similar to or lower than in younger groups, though the evidence was limited. Right-left symmetry between measuring sites was supported. The authors' central point is the shelf's: TEWL is highly dependent on skin area, and mean and spread should always be reported.
cards.watchOut: A pooled reference synthesis, carded as the normative anchor alongside the primary studies on this shelf; individual primary values (next cards) sit inside its ranges, and per-area samples as small as 4 mean the extreme sites rest on thinner data than the forearm.
cards.source: Akdeniz M et al. Transepidermal water loss in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis update. The British journal of dermatology. 2018. PMID: 30022486. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: John 2023: TEWL was lowest on the forearm (11 g/m²/h) and highest on the palm (41 g/m²/h) in the same 15 healthy volunteers
cards.summary: John 2023: TEWL was lowest on the forearm (11 g/m²/h) and highest on the palm (41 g/m²/h) in the same 15 healthy volunteers
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multi-site TEWL mapping)
cards.people: 15 healthy volunteers measured at four anatomical regions — palm, forearm, sole and lower lumbar (L3) — with four CE-marked non-invasive techniques in a repeated-measures design by the same operator on separate days. Small study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: TEWL values were lowest on the forearm, averaging 11 g/m²/h, and highest on the palm, averaging 41 g/m²/h. Skin hydration was similar at three of four sites (the sole averaged 13 arbitrary units), erythema showed high inter-subject variation with no significant site or side differences, and TEWL between-day reliability ranged from good to poor (intra-class correlation 0.74–0.4) depending on site — site differences are real and large, and repeatability is site-dependent.
cards.watchOut: N = 15: the forearm-to-palm ordering matches the 212-study pooled literature, which is what carries the numbers; the study's own reliability range is a warning against over-reading any single-session TEWL value.
cards.source: John AJUK et al. An evaluation of mechanical and biophysical skin parameters at different body locations. Skin research and technology. 2023. PMID: 36823505. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mehta 2018: in 500 healthy volunteers the forehead showed the highest TEWL of the sites tested, and TEWL was lower in middle and older age groups (N = 500)
cards.summary: Mehta 2018: in 500 healthy volunteers the forehead showed the highest TEWL of the sites tested, and TEWL was lower in middle and older age groups (N = 500)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative biophysical cohort)
cards.people: 500 healthy Indian volunteers aged 5–70 years, with TEWL, hydration, elasticity and sebum measured on four pre-selected body sites with a Dermalab instrument and skin pH by probe, analysed across age groups and sex.
cards.result: The forehead showed higher median TEWL and hydration than the other sites. All parameters were higher in males than in females except sebum content, which was equal. TEWL and hydration were lower in the middle and older age groups, skin pH did not differ significantly with age, and sebum content was higher in the middle and older groups. The record prints these as group comparisons without absolute TEWL values, so none are claimed here — the card carries the site and age pattern from the largest single normative cohort on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Published as a Letter and confined to one geographical area without seasonal variation; its age direction (lower TEWL in older groups) agrees with the pooled literature, but absolute values cannot be extracted from its record.
cards.source: Mehta HH et al. A cross-sectional study of variations in the biophysical parameters of skin among healthy volunteers. Indian journal of dermatology, venereology and leprology. 2018. PMID: 29491191. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reed 1995: after tape-stripping, light skin (types II/III) recovered ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours; dark skin (types V/VI) needed more than twice as many strippings to disrupt and recovered faster — 43% by 6 hours, 72% by 48 hours
cards.summary: Reed 1995: after tape-stripping, light skin (types II/III) recovered ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours; dark skin (types V/VI) needed more than twice as many strippings to disrupt and recovered faster — 43% by 6 hours, 72% by 48 hours
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (tape-stripping disruption and barrier recovery)
cards.people: Healthy human subjects aged 22–38 years in three comparisons: white (n = 8) versus Asian (n = 6); male (n = 7) versus female (n = 7); and skin type II/III (n = 14) versus skin type V/VI (n = 7). Basal TEWL was measured by evaporimetry at three volar-forearm sites; barrier integrity was the number of tape strippings needed to reach TEWL ≥ 20 g/m²/h, and recovery was tracked at 6, 24 and 48 hours and 1 week. Small groups — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Neither the strippings required to perturb the barrier nor recovery rates differed between white and Asian subjects or between women and men. Skin type divided the results: types II/III required only 29.6 ± 2.4 strippings to perturb the barrier versus 66.7 ± 6.9 for types V/VI, and recovery in types II/III was approximately 20% by 6 hours and 55% by 48 hours, versus 43% and 72% at the same times in types V/VI — darkly pigmented skin, independent of race as grouped here, had both a more resistant barrier and a faster-recovering one, with stripping removing the same weight of stratum corneum in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Groups of 6–14 young adults at one body site: the recovery percentages are the classic human tape-stripping kinetics, but they describe young forearm skin, and the skin-type grouping is the record's own 1995 classification, printed as published.
cards.source: Reed JT et al. Skin type, but neither race nor gender, influence epidermal permeability barrier function. Archives of dermatology. 1995. PMID: 7574829. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Robles 2007: a laboratory stressor delayed skin-barrier recovery by 10% at 2 hours after tape-stripping; social support beforehand did not prevent it (N = 85)
cards.summary: Robles 2007: a laboratory stressor delayed skin-barrier recovery by 10% at 2 hours after tape-stripping; social support beforehand did not prevent it (N = 85)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised stress manipulation, tape-stripping recovery)
cards.people: 85 healthy participants (mean age 22.9 ± 4.4 years) randomised to No Stress (reading task), Stress (Trier Social Stress Test) or Stress + Social Support (support from a confederate before the stressor), with barrier recovery followed by TEWL for up to 2 hours after tape-stripping disruption.
cards.result: Compared with No Stress, the stressor delayed skin-barrier recovery by 10% at 2 hours after disruption (effect size r = 0.29) and increased anxiety, negative affect and cardiovascular activity. Social support did not influence psychological or physiological responses or barrier recovery. Larger systolic blood-pressure responses predicted faster, not slower, recovery (r = 0.26). The card shows recovery kinetics are not purely local: the same barrier, in the same person, recovers measurably slower under acute psychological stress.
cards.watchOut: Recovery was followed for only 2 hours, so this card measures the early phase of the Reed card's 48-hour curve; the 10% figure is a relative delay at that time point, printed as the record gives it.
cards.source: Robles TF et al. Stress, social support, and delayed skin barrier recovery. Psychosomatic medicine. 2007. PMID: 17942836. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: resting TEWL is a site property first (2–44 g/m²/h across the body), age lowers rather than raises basal leak, and a stripped barrier recovers over hours-to-days at a rate set by skin type and state — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: resting TEWL is a site property first (2–44 g/m²/h across the body), age lowers rather than raises basal leak, and a stripped barrier recovers over hours-to-days at a rate set by skin type and state — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: a 212-study pooled reference synthesis, primary cohorts of 15 and 500 volunteers, tape-stripping studies with groups of 6–14, and an 85-person randomised stress study.
cards.result: Healthy skin is not uniformly leaky: the pooled reference range runs from 2.3 g/m²/h (breast) to 44.0 g/m²/h (axilla), with forearm ~11 and palm ~41 g/m²/h in a single four-site study — any TEWL number without its site is meaningless. Basal TEWL does not rise with age (lower in middle/older groups in the 500-person cohort; similar or lower in the pooled elderly data). After tape-stripping, recovery is ~20% at 6 hours and ~55% at 48 hours in light skin types and materially faster in dark skin types, and acute psychological stress delays early recovery by 10% (a relative delay). The classic Grubauer 1989 'TEWL as the signal for barrier recovery' paper was NOT carded — its fetched record is a hairless-mouse study, and animal data are not evidence cards on this shelf; the human recovery kinetics stand on Reed 1995 and Robles 2007. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

shelves.title: Lenadogene nolparvovec for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy: all three phase 3 trials missed their primary endpoints — treated and sham/placebo eyes improved together, and the bilateral-benefit claim rests on post hoc interpretation, not on any randomised contrast
shelves.question: In patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (chiefly m.11778G>A) treated within a year of vision loss, does intravitreal lenadogene nolparvovec improve visual acuity versus sham injection?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a missed-primary programme, presented as published. Lenadogene nolparvovec (the rAAV2/2-ND4 allotopic gene therapy, designated GS010 in the REVERSE report; the fetched records name the vector and the GS010 designation but do not name a company, so none is printed) was tested in three phase 3 sham- or placebo-controlled trials in m.11778G>A LHON, each using the fellow eye as the control. RESCUE (treated ≤6 months from onset; 38 subjects in the efficacy analysis): the week-48 primary endpoint — difference in BCVA change between treated and sham eyes — was −0.01 logMAR (P = 0.89) against a −0.3 logMAR target; not met. REVERSE (treated 6–12 months from onset; 37 subjects): the same primary contrast was not met (P = 0.894), because sham eyes improved almost as much as treated eyes by week 96 (+13 vs +15 ETDRS letters) — the unexpected bilateral improvement the programme attributes, post hoc and with nonhuman-primate vector-transfer data, to contralateral spread. REFLECT (bilateral versus unilateral treatment; 98 patients): the primary endpoint in second-affected/not-yet-affected eyes was again not statistically different between lenadogene and placebo at 1.5 years, though within-group improvements from baseline were reported and intraocular inflammation occurred in 70.7% of treated versus 10.2% of placebo eyes. Three trials, three missed primaries, and improvement in control eyes in all of them: the randomised evidence does not separate the product from sham on any prespecified primary contrast, and claims of benefit rest on within-group change, comparison with natural history, and a post hoc bilateral-effect mechanism. The product is not approved in the US/EU (per the row's flag). The other LHON treatment shelf is pack #4253 (idebenone) — a different intervention, cross-pointed here; none of its references is carded on this shelf. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), with the null primary contrasts printed on the face.

cards.headline: RESCUE (phase 3, ≤6 months from onset): primary endpoint not met — week-48 BCVA difference between lenadogene and sham eyes was −0.01 logMAR (P = 0.89) against a −0.3 logMAR target
cards.summary: RESCUE (phase 3, ≤6 months from onset): primary endpoint not met — week-48 BCVA difference between lenadogene and sham eyes was −0.01 logMAR (P = 0.89) against a −0.3 logMAR target
cards.people: Subjects with the m.11778G>A mutation and vision loss ≤6 months from onset in 1 or both eyes; each subject's right eye was randomised 1:1 to a single intravitreal injection of rAAV2/2-ND4 (9 × 10¹⁰ viral genomes in 90 µl) or sham, and the left eye received the treatment not allocated to the right. The efficacy analysis included 38 subjects; mean age 36.8 years, 82% male; mean duration of vision loss at treatment 3.6 months (treated eyes) and 3.9 months (sham eyes); baseline logMAR BCVA 1.31 (0.52) and 1.26 (0.62). Follow-up extended to week 96.
cards.result: At week 48, the difference in change from baseline in BCVA between rAAV2/2-ND4-treated and sham-treated eyes was −0.01 logMAR (P = 0.89); the primary endpoint of a −0.3 logMAR (15-letter) difference was not met. Mean BCVA in both groups deteriorated over the initial weeks to a worst point at week 24, plateaued to week 48, then improved by +10 (treated) and +9 (sham) ETDRS letters equivalent from the plateau — the recovery phase occurred in sham eyes too. At 96 weeks, visual outcomes in injected and uninjected eyes were comparable, as the record states.
cards.watchOut: The fellow-eye design means the 'control' eye belongs to a treated patient — if the bilateral-effect hypothesis is true, the design dilutes its own contrast; if it is false, the sham-eye recovery is natural history. Either way, the prespecified primary contrast is the randomised evidence, and it was null.

cards.headline: REVERSE (phase 3, 6–12 months from onset): primary endpoint not met (P = 0.894) — by week 96 treated eyes had gained +15 ETDRS letters and sham eyes +13, the bilateral improvement on which the programme's claim rests
cards.summary: REVERSE (phase 3, 6–12 months from onset): primary endpoint not met (P = 0.894) — by week 96 treated eyes had gained +15 ETDRS letters and sham eyes +13, the bilateral improvement on which the programme's claim rests
cards.people: 37 subjects carrying the m.11778G>A (MT-ND4) mutation with duration of vision loss between 6 and 12 months; each subject's right eye was randomised 1:1 to a single intravitreal injection of rAAV2/2-ND4 (GS010) or sham, the left eye receiving the other allocation, with 96-week follow-up.
cards.result: Sustained visual improvement was observed in both eyes over 96 weeks. At week 96, treated eyes showed a mean BCVA improvement of −0.308 logMAR (+15 ETDRS letters) and sham-treated eyes −0.259 logMAR (+13 ETDRS letters). Consequently the primary endpoint — the difference in BCVA change from baseline to week 48 between the treatment groups — was not met (P = 0.894). At week 96, 25 subjects (68%) had a clinically relevant recovery in at least one eye and 29 (78%) had improvement in both eyes. A nonhuman primate study found viral vector DNA in the contralateral non-injected eye's anterior segment, retina and optic nerve, offered as a plausible mechanism for the bilateral improvement; that primate work is mechanistic support reported inside this paper, not a human efficacy result, and the bilateral interpretation of the human data is post hoc relative to the missed primary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Within-group gains of +13 to +15 letters sound large, but they occurred in sham eyes at nearly the same size, in a disease whose natural history includes partial spontaneous recovery — without a separated randomised contrast or a concurrent untreated control, the gains cannot be attributed to the product from this trial alone.

cards.headline: REFLECT (phase 3, bilateral vs unilateral): primary endpoint again not statistically different at 1.5 years; within-group BCVA improvements reported, and intraocular inflammation occurred in 70.7% of treated versus 10.2% of placebo eyes (N = 98)
cards.summary: REFLECT (phase 3, bilateral vs unilateral): primary endpoint again not statistically different at 1.5 years; within-group BCVA improvements reported, and intraocular inflammation occurred in 70.7% of treated versus 10.2% of placebo eyes (N = 98)
cards.people: 98 patients with a confirmed m.11778G>A mutation in a randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial of bilateral intravitreal lenadogene nolparvovec (rAAV2/2-ND4): 48 patients treated bilaterally and 50 unilaterally — in all patients the first-affected eye received gene therapy, and the fellow eye was randomised to gene therapy or placebo. The primary endpoint was the difference in BCVA change from baseline in second-affected/not-yet-affected eyes, lenadogene versus placebo, at 1.5 years.
cards.result: The change from baseline in BCVA at 1.5 years was not statistically different between second-affected/not-yet-affected eyes receiving lenadogene nolparvovec and placebo — the primary endpoint was not met. Statistically significant improvements from baseline were reported in treated eyes (−0.23 logMAR in first-affected eyes of bilaterally treated patients, P < 0.01; −0.15 logMAR in second-affected/not-yet-affected eyes of bilaterally treated patients and first-affected eyes of unilaterally treated patients, P < 0.05), and improvement from nadir was similar in placebo-treated second eyes (−0.26 logMAR) to treated ones. The proportion with one or both eyes on-chart at 1.5 years was 85.4% (bilateral) and 72.0% (unilateral). The therapy was well tolerated systemically; intraocular inflammation, mostly mild and controlled with topical corticosteroids, occurred in 70.7% of lenadogene-treated eyes versus 10.2% of placebo-treated eyes.
cards.watchOut: REFLECT's design assumes the bilateral effect it was built to exploit: with first-affected eyes always treated, the placebo second eyes are fellow eyes of treated patients, so the trial cannot cleanly separate product effect from contralateral transfer or natural history — and its prespecified primary contrast was still null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials, three missed primary endpoints, control-eye improvement in every trial — the randomised programme does not separate lenadogene nolparvovec from sham, and the benefit claim is post hoc
cards.summary: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials, three missed primary endpoints, control-eye improvement in every trial — the randomised programme does not separate lenadogene nolparvovec from sham, and the benefit claim is post hoc
cards.people: 173 patients in total across the carded phase 3 programme: RESCUE 38 (treated ≤6 months from onset), REVERSE 37 (6–12 months), REFLECT 98 (bilateral versus unilateral) — all with the m.11778G>A MT-ND4 mutation.
cards.result: Primary endpoints: RESCUE −0.01 logMAR difference at week 48 (P = 0.89; target −0.3) — not met. REVERSE between-group difference at week 48 — not met (P = 0.894), with week-96 gains of +15 letters (treated) and +13 letters (sham). REFLECT second-eye contrast at 1.5 years — not statistically different; not met. In every trial the control eyes improved substantially, which is simultaneously the programme's proposed mechanism (contralateral vector transfer, supported by primate data reported within the REVERSE paper) and the reason no randomised contrast separates the product from sham: the two readings cannot be distinguished by these designs. Safety: no systemic issues in REFLECT; intraocular inflammation in 70.7% of treated versus 10.2% of placebo eyes, mostly mild and steroid-controlled. Benefit claims beyond the trials rest on within-group change and indirect comparison with natural history — post hoc evidence, labelled as such. The idebenone shelf for the same disease is pack #4253 (its PMIDs are not carded here). PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the treatment made no difference on any phase 3 primary endpoint; a bilateral benefit remains possible but unproven by a randomised contrast.
cards.watchOut: A regulatory or natural-history comparison may yet change the picture, and the 5-year follow-up literature exists but is not carded here; on the carded randomised evidence alone, no stronger stamp is defensible, and the missed primaries — not the post hoc bilateral narrative — are the programme's headline result.

shelves.title: Depemokimab in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2): twice-yearly dosing improved polyp score by 0.7 and 0.6 points vs placebo — a real but modest effect, the smallest in its class in indirect comparison
shelves.question: In adults with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps inadequately controlled on intranasal corticosteroids, does depemokimab (ultra-long-acting anti-IL-5) versus placebo improve nasal polyp score and nasal obstruction?
mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. This shelf asks the depemokimab-specific question that live shelf #375 (biologics in CRSwNP) does not: #375 cards dupilumab (SINUS-24/52) and omalizumab (POLYP 1/2) only, and is cross-pointed here rather than duplicated — none of its references is carded on this shelf. Depemokimab in asthma is a separate, already-homed question (pack #6210). ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2 are two replicate phase 3 trials reported in ONE Lancet publication; under the library convention (the PROMIS precedent) that publication counts as one report, with both trials explicitly labelled on its card. Together they randomised 540 patients with inadequately controlled CRSwNP (polyp score ≥5, prior surgery or systemic corticosteroids) to depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks: polyp-score differences vs placebo were −0.7 (ANCHOR-1; p<0.001) and −0.6 (ANCHOR-2; p=0.004), and nasal-obstruction differences −0.23 (p=0.047) and −0.25 (p=0.025) on a 0–3 scale — statistically significant but modest absolute effects. A pooled safety analysis of SWIFT-1/-2 and ANCHOR-1/-2 (1,290 patients) found adverse events in 73% on depemokimab vs 78% on placebo and serious adverse events in 5% vs 10%, with no fatal or treatment-related serious events. A 2026 network meta-analysis of 15 CRSwNP biologic trials (3,642 patients) placed depemokimab behind dupilumab (and, at later time-points, tezepelumab) on polyp and congestion scores — an indirect comparison, labelled as such. The twice-yearly dosing is the practical distinction; the effect size is the smallest in its class in that indirect ranking. The slate records FDA approval for CRSwNP on Dec 16, 2025.

cards.headline: ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2 (replicate phase 3, one publication — counted as one report, both trials labelled): polyp-score differences −0.7 (p<0.001) and −0.6 (p=0.004); nasal-obstruction differences −0.23 (p=0.047) and −0.25 (p=0.025) vs placebo
cards.summary: ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2 (replicate phase 3, one publication — counted as one report, both trials labelled): polyp-score differences −0.7 (p<0.001) and −0.6 (p=0.004); nasal-obstruction differences −0.23 (p=0.047) and −0.25 (p=0.025) vs placebo
cards.type: Two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2), reported in one publication and counted as one report
cards.people: 540 individuals randomised across the two replicate trials at 190 centres in 16 countries (full analysis set 528: depemokimab n=272, placebo n=256); adults with inadequately controlled CRSwNP, endoscopic bilateral nasal polyp score ≥5, previous CRSwNP surgery or previous treatment with / intolerance to systemic corticosteroids, and severe symptoms; depemokimab 100 mg subcutaneously or placebo every 26 weeks with standard of care, stratified by previous surgery. Coprimary endpoints: change in total endoscopic nasal polyp score (0–8) at week 52 and mean nasal obstruction score (0–3) over weeks 49–52.
cards.result: Depemokimab improved both coprimary endpoints vs placebo in both trials: total nasal polyp score treatment difference −0.7 (95% CI −1.1 to −0.3; p<0.001) in ANCHOR-1 and −0.6 (−1.0 to −0.2; p=0.004) in ANCHOR-2 (integrated −0.7; −0.9 to −0.4); mean nasal obstruction score difference −0.23 (−0.46 to 0.00; p=0.047) in ANCHOR-1 and −0.25 (−0.46 to −0.03; p=0.025) in ANCHOR-2 (integrated −0.24; −0.39 to −0.08). Adverse events were similar between groups: 74% (depemokimab) vs 79% (placebo) in ANCHOR-1 and 76% vs 80% in ANCHOR-2.
cards.watchOut: Convention card: the two replicate trials share one publication and are counted as a single report on this shelf (the PROMIS precedent), exactly as live #375 counts SINUS-24/52 as one reference. cards.headline: Pooled safety of twice-yearly depemokimab across SWIFT-1/-2 (asthma) and ANCHOR-1/-2 (CRSwNP), 1,290 patients: adverse events 73% vs 78% on placebo; serious adverse events 5% vs 10%; no fatal or treatment-related serious events
cards.summary: Pooled safety of twice-yearly depemokimab across SWIFT-1/-2 (asthma) and ANCHOR-1/-2 (CRSwNP), 1,290 patients: adverse events 73% vs 78% on placebo; serious adverse events 5% vs 10%; no fatal or treatment-related serious events
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of four phase 3 trials
cards.people: 1,290 patients in the pooled safety population of the four phase 3 trials (depemokimab n=773, placebo n=517), receiving subcutaneous depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks for 52 weeks; adverse-event frequency, severity, time to onset, duration and relative risk were evaluated, together with immunogenicity.
cards.result: On-treatment adverse events were reported by 73% of depemokimab and 78% of placebo patients, mostly mild or moderate and transient, with similar durations between groups. Serious adverse events occurred in 5% vs 10% and discontinuations for adverse events in <1% vs 1%. No fatal adverse events or treatment-related serious adverse events (per investigator assessment) were reported. Relative risks vs placebo were similar for all common adverse events except asthma and back pain, which were less frequent on depemokimab. Antidrug and neutralising antibodies were infrequent, with no association between antidrug-antibody status and efficacy identified.
cards.watchOut: Pools asthma with CRSwNP populations and re-uses the ANCHOR patients from Card 1: it is a distinct report about safety, not an independent efficacy population.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis of CRSwNP biologics (15 randomised trials, 3,642 patients): dupilumab produced greater polyp and congestion reductions than depemokimab at 20–24 weeks, and dupilumab and tezepelumab did so at 48–56 weeks — indirect comparisons only
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis of CRSwNP biologics (15 randomised trials, 3,642 patients): dupilumab produced greater polyp and congestion reductions than depemokimab at 20–24 weeks, and dupilumab and tezepelumab did so at 48–56 weeks — indirect comparisons only
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 15 randomised trials of seven biologic agents (dupilumab, omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, depemokimab, tezepelumab, stapokibart) in severe CRSwNP, identified from PubMed and EMBASE; primary outcomes were change in nasal polyp score and nasal congestion score at 20–24 and 48–56 weeks.
cards.result: At 20–24 weeks, dupilumab and stapokibart produced greater reductions in nasal polyp and congestion scores than depemokimab, omalizumab and benralizumab, with no significant difference between dupilumab and stapokibart (polyp-score mean difference 0.29; 95% CI −0.97 to 0.40). At 48–56 weeks, dupilumab and tezepelumab produced greater reductions than depemokimab, mepolizumab or benralizumab, with no significant difference between dupilumab and tezepelumab (0.32; −0.17 to 0.81). Dupilumab, tezepelumab (48–56 weeks) and stapokibart (20–24 weeks) also showed superior secondary-endpoint results. Safety profiles were comparable across agents. The authors state that indirect comparisons did not demonstrate superiority of stapokibart or tezepelumab over dupilumab and that direct comparative trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: Every cross-drug ranking here is indirect — no head-to-head trial of depemokimab against dupilumab exists in this analysis; the ranking contextualises ANCHOR's modest absolute effects (and is consistent with live #375's gradient, where dupilumab's effect was largest) but proves nothing on its own.

cards.headline: Synthesis: real, replicated, modest — twice-yearly depemokimab beats placebo on polyps and obstruction; POSSIBLE under the one-publication convention
cards.summary: Synthesis: real, replicated, modest — twice-yearly depemokimab beats placebo on polyps and obstruction; POSSIBLE under the one-publication convention
cards.people: Adults with severe CRSwNP inadequately controlled on intranasal corticosteroids, most with prior surgery or systemic corticosteroids.
cards.result: Two replicate trials in one publication (one report by convention) show concordant, statistically significant but small absolute benefits (−0.6 to −0.7 polyp points; about −0.24 obstruction points) with a clean pooled safety profile; indirect comparison places the effect below dupilumab's. Live shelf #375 remains the home for dupilumab and omalizumab in CRSwNP and pack #6210 for depemokimab in asthma; this shelf homes only the depemokimab-in-CRSwNP question.

shelves.title: Avapritinib for indolent systemic mastocytosis (PIONEER)
shelves.question: In adults with indolent systemic mastocytosis and moderate-to-severe symptoms despite supportive care, does avapritinib 25 mg daily, versus placebo, improve total symptom score?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Mastocytosis, Systemic/drug therapy · Avapritinib · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-kit/antagonists & inhibitors · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Triazines/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme (one randomised trial, PIONEER, reported three ways) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In the placebo-controlled part, avapritinib 25 mg daily reduced the total symptom score by 15.6 points versus 9.2 points on placebo at 24 weeks — note the large placebo response: the drug's advantage over placebo is the 6.4-point difference, not the full 15.6. Objective markers moved far more decisively (54% versus 0% achieved at least a 50% reduction in serum tryptase), cutaneous outcomes improved in the trial's skin report, and symptom improvement was sustained at about 3 years in the open-label extension (mean change −19.39 points among those still assessed). The primary endpoint is patient-reported and subjective, which is why concordant objective markers matter. Harms at the 25 mg dose were dominated by oedema, with few discontinuations. This shelf is the mastocytosis question only: avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour is a different question, homed at pack #6709, and none of that record is carded here.

cards.headline: PIONEER randomised part (Gotlib 2023): total symptom score fell 15.6 points on avapritinib versus 9.2 on placebo at 24 weeks (p<0.003); at least 50% tryptase reduction in 54% versus 0%
cards.summary: PIONEER randomised part (Gotlib 2023): total symptom score fell 15.6 points on avapritinib versus 9.2 on placebo at 24 weeks (p<0.003); at least 50% tryptase reduction in 54% versus 0%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, part 2 (Gotlib 2023, PIONEER)
cards.people: 212 adults with indolent systemic mastocytosis and moderate-to-severe symptoms (total symptom score at least 28 on a 0–110 scale) despite best supportive care, randomised 2:1 to avapritinib 25 mg once daily (141) or placebo (71), both with best supportive care, for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean change in total symptom score was −15.6 points (95% CI −18.6 to −12.6) on avapritinib versus −9.2 points (−13.1 to −5.2) on placebo (p<0.003). A reduction of at least 50% in serum tryptase was achieved by 76 of 141 (54%) on avapritinib versus 0 of 71 on placebo (p<0.001). Oedema and increases in alkaline phosphatase were more common with avapritinib; few patients discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a patient-reported symptom score and the placebo group improved by 9.2 points — expectation, supportive care and regression to the mean are all in that number. The tryptase result (54% vs 0%) is the objective anchor that the symptom difference is pharmacological, not only perceptual.
