cards.headline: PIONEER cutaneous report (Siebenhaar 2026) — second report of the same trial: skin lesion area fell 36.6% on avapritinib versus 1.8% on placebo, and skin mast-cell burden fell 22.1% versus a 10.1% rise
cards.summary: PIONEER cutaneous report (Siebenhaar 2026) — second report of the same trial: skin lesion area fell 36.6% on avapritinib versus 1.8% on placebo, and skin mast-cell burden fell 22.1% versus a 10.1% rise
cards.type: Randomised trial report — cutaneous outcomes of PIONEER part 2 (Siebenhaar 2026)
cards.people: The same PIONEER part 2 population (141 avapritinib, 71 placebo) assessed for skin outcomes at week 24; photography was optional, so the lesion-area and colour analysis population (111 patients) was smaller than the full study population. This is a second labelled report of the one PIONEER trial, not a new trial.
cards.result: Mean percent reduction in lesional surface area in the most affected area was −36.6% with avapritinib versus −1.8% with placebo; 86% versus 0% had improved skin lesion colour. Mean percent change in skin mast-cell burden was −22.1% versus +10.1%. The skin symptom domain score improved more on avapritinib (mean change −7.2 vs −2.8; p<0.0001), including itching, flushing and spots. Avapritinib was well tolerated in this report.
cards.watchOut: Optional photography shrank the lesion analysis set to 111 of 212 patients, so the skin-area figures come from a self-selected subset. Skin colour improvement (86% vs 0%) is a striking contrast but rests on that same subset.

cards.headline: PIONEER 3-year open-label extension (Akin 2026): symptom improvement was sustained (mean total symptom score change −19.39) over a median of about 3 years on avapritinib, with oedema the most frequent treatment-related event
cards.summary: PIONEER 3-year open-label extension (Akin 2026): symptom improvement was sustained (mean total symptom score change −19.39) over a median of about 3 years on avapritinib, with oedema the most frequent treatment-related event
cards.type: Open-label extension report of the PIONEER trial — no comparator (Akin 2026)
cards.people: 226 patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis who initiated avapritinib 25 mg once daily plus best supportive care in PIONEER parts 1, 2 or 3 and continued into the open-label part 3 (dose increase to 50 mg permitted at investigator discretion); median treatment duration 40.0 months as of the February 2025 cutoff. Open-label, no comparator — labelled as such.
cards.result: Mean change in total symptom score was −19.39 points among the 127 patients assessed at about 3 years. Most treatment-related adverse events were grade 1–2; oedema events were the most frequent. Serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in 3 patients (1%), and 7 patients (3%) discontinued because of treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label follow-up of patients who stayed on treatment: the −19.39 figure describes the 127 patients still assessed at 3 years out of 226 who started, so it is a completer picture that naturally flatters durability. It supports tolerability over years; it cannot re-prove efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: avapritinib improves symptoms and mast-cell burden in indolent systemic mastocytosis — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: avapritinib improves symptoms and mast-cell burden in indolent systemic mastocytosis — POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports, all from the single PIONEER programme: the randomised placebo-controlled part (212 patients), its cutaneous-outcomes report, and its 3-year open-label extension (226 patients started).
cards.result: Against placebo, avapritinib improved the symptom score by an additional 6.4 points at 24 weeks, with far larger effects on objective burden markers (tryptase, skin mast-cell burden), and benefit and tolerability persisted in open-label follow-up. Because there is one trial from one programme and the primary endpoint is subjective with a large placebo response, the stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit). The gastrointestinal stromal tumour record for this drug is a different question, homed at pack #6709, and is not evidence for this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Long-term safety beyond about 3 years, and any effect on anaphylaxis frequency, progression to advanced disease or survival, are not established by the carded reports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gotlib J et al. NEJM evidence. 2023 (PMID: 38320129); Siebenhaar F et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2026 (PMID: 41690487); Akin C et al. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 2026 (PMID: 41985569), all carded above.

shelves.title: Extracapsular dissection for benign parotid tumours: less temporary facial weakness and Frey syndrome, no recurrence penalty — in selected tumours
shelves.question: In adults with benign parotid tumours, does extracapsular dissection reduce facial-nerve injury, Frey syndrome and recurrence versus superficial (or partial superficial) parotidectomy?
shelves.mesh: Cohort Studies · Disease-Free Survival · Dissection/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Neoplasm Invasiveness/pathology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/mortality,pathology,surgery · Neoplasm Staging · Parotid Gland/surgery · Parotid Neoplasms/mortality,pathology,surgery · Retrospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Surgical Procedures, Operative/methods · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The unresolved build-time floor check for this row is resolved on the face: at least three comparative reports were required and four verify (a 9-study meta-analysis of 1,882 patients, and comparative cohorts of 182, 89 and 55 patients), so the shelf is built — but the base is entirely observational, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE and is labelled on every card. The central bias is stated plainly, per the slate flag: extracapsular series select smaller, mobile tumours (explicitly so in the smallest cohort), so part of the lower complication rate is case selection. Within that fence, the findings are consistent: less transient facial paresis and Frey syndrome, no difference in permanent paralysis, and no recurrence difference even at a mean 13 years of follow-up. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational.

cards.headline: Albergotti 2012 (meta-analysis, 9 studies, 1,882 patients): extracapsular dissection halved-plus transient facial paresis (8.0% vs 20.4%) and cut Frey syndrome (4.5% vs 26.1%), with no difference in recurrence or permanent paralysis
cards.summary: Albergotti 2012 (meta-analysis, 9 studies, 1,882 patients): extracapsular dissection halved-plus transient facial paresis (8.0% vs 20.4%) and cut Frey syndrome (4.5% vs 26.1%), with no difference in recurrence or permanent paralysis
cards.type: Meta-analysis of comparative cohort studies (Albergotti 2012) — observational
cards.people: Nine comparative studies (1,882 patients) of extracapsular dissection (ECD) versus superficial parotidectomy (SP) for solitary benign parotid tumours. Comparative cohort evidence, pooled — no randomised trials in the base.
cards.result: Recurrence did not differ between ECD and SP (odds ratio 0.557, 95% CI 0.271 to 1.147). Transient facial nerve paresis was significantly lower after ECD (59 of 741, 8.0%) than SP (81 of 397, 20.4%) (OR 0.256, 95% CI 0.174 to 0.377), and Frey syndrome was less frequent after ECD (27 of 602, 4.5%) than SP (75 of 287, 26.1%) (OR 0.117, 95% CI 0.071 to 0.191) — relative measures, with the absolute rates printed beside them. Permanent facial paralysis did not differ (OR 0.878, 95% CI 0.282 to 2.730) — the treatment made no difference on that outcome.
cards.watchOut: Tumour-size selection is the central bias of this whole literature: ECD series select smaller, mobile, solitary tumours, so lower complication rates partly reflect easier tumours, not only gentler surgery.
cards.source: Albergotti WG et al. Extracapsular dissection for benign parotid tumors: a meta-analysis. The Laryngoscope. 2012. PMID: 22753318. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Schapher 2021 (comparative cohort, 182 patients, mean 13-year follow-up): recurrence was 2% overall with no difference by technique, while facial nerve paresis was significantly lower after extracapsular dissection
cards.summary: Schapher 2021 (comparative cohort, 182 patients, mean 13-year follow-up): recurrence was 2% overall with no difference by technique, while facial nerve paresis was significantly lower after extracapsular dissection
cards.people: 182 patients treated exclusively for parotid pleomorphic adenomas at a tertiary centre (2000–2004), 29.7% by extracapsular dissection and 70.3% by other surgical modalities including facial nerve dissection, with thorough follow-up examinations over a mean 13 years in 98 patients. Retrospective comparative evidence.
cards.result: After long-term follow-up, 98% of patients (96 of 98) were recurrence-free, with no significant difference in recurrence between techniques (P < .331 as reported). Extracapsular dissection resulted in significantly lower facial nerve paresis rates than the other modalities (P < .001). Paresis rates rose significantly with tumour size and location category.
cards.watchOut: Only 53.8% of the original cohort had the thorough long-term follow-up, and technique was chosen by the surgeons — larger/deeper tumours went to the more extensive operations.
cards.source: Schapher M et al. Extracapsular Dissection in Pleomorphic Adenomas of the Parotid Gland: Results After 13 Years of Follow-up. The Laryngoscope. 2021. PMID: 32396221. cards.headline: Liu 2023 (comparative cohort, 89 patients, parotid-tail tumours): temporary facial paralysis was 5% after extracapsular dissection versus 26.5% after partial superficial parotidectomy, and sialocele 10% versus 36.7%
cards.summary: Liu 2023 (comparative cohort, 89 patients, parotid-tail tumours): temporary facial paralysis was 5% after extracapsular dissection versus 26.5% after partial superficial parotidectomy, and sialocele 10% versus 36.7%
cards.people: 89 patients with benign tumours in the tail of the parotid gland at one centre: 40 treated by extracapsular dissection with a transparotid facial-nerve-dissection approach and 49 by partial superficial parotidectomy with a retrograde approach. Retrospective comparative evidence.
cards.result: Temporary facial paralysis occurred in 2 of 40 patients (5%) after extracapsular dissection versus 13 of 49 (26.5%) after partial superficial parotidectomy (P = 0.007), and sialocele in 4 (10%) versus 18 (36.7%) (P = 0.002). Mean surgical time did not differ significantly (59 vs 64 minutes, P = 0.302).
cards.watchOut: Tail-of-gland tumours only, and the comparison bundles two differences at once (dissection extent and nerve-approach), so the benefit cannot be assigned to extracapsular dissection alone.
cards.source: Liu Z et al. cards.headline: Elmarghani 2025 (comparative cohort, 55 patients, single surgeon): temporary facial palsy was 15% after extracapsular dissection versus 35% after superficial parotidectomy, with no recurrences in any group over a mean 4.8 years
cards.summary: Elmarghani 2025 (comparative cohort, 55 patients, single surgeon): temporary facial palsy was 15% after extracapsular dissection versus 35% after superficial parotidectomy, with no recurrences in any group over a mean 4.8 years
cards.people: 55 patients treated by a single surgeon in Scotland (2015–2022): 34 extracapsular dissection, 17 superficial parotidectomy and 4 total parotidectomy, followed for a mean 4.8 years. Retrospective comparative evidence.
cards.result: Temporary facial nerve palsy was 15% after extracapsular dissection, 35% after superficial and 75% after total parotidectomy; the one persistent palsy occurred in the extracapsular group. Seromas were more frequent after extracapsular dissection (18%). No haematomas or recurrences occurred in any cohort, capsule integrity and tumour-free margins exceeded 88% in all groups, and same-day discharge was achieved in 82% of extracapsular cases versus 6% of superficial cases (p < .00001). The extracapsular group had smaller average tumour size.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-surgeon and explicitly confounded by tumour size (smaller tumours in the extracapsular group) — the authors state this did not affect outcomes, but the design cannot prove that. The record carried no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.source: Elmarghani M et al. Extracapsular Dissection Versus Superficial and Total Parotidectomy for Benign Parotid Tumours: A Retrospective Single-Centre Study. Cureus. 2025. PMID: 41209900. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: across at least four comparative reports, extracapsular dissection consistently shows less temporary nerve injury and Frey syndrome with no recurrence penalty — but every report is observational and selection favours the dissection group
cards.summary: Synthesis: across at least four comparative reports, extracapsular dissection consistently shows less temporary nerve injury and Frey syndrome with no recurrence penalty — but every report is observational and selection favours the dissection group
cards.people: A build-time floor check was run for this shelf: at least three comparative reports were required, and four verify — a 9-study meta-analysis (1,882 patients) and comparative cohorts of 182, 89 and 55 patients. All are observational; no randomised trial is in the base.
cards.result: Transient facial paresis is lower after extracapsular dissection in every comparative report (8.0% vs 20.4% pooled; 5% vs 26.5%; 15% vs 35%), Frey syndrome is lower where reported (4.5% vs 26.1%), and recurrence does not differ, including at a mean 13 years. Permanent paralysis does not differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, capped at POSSIBLE, with tumour-size selection carried on the face.
cards.watchOut: If a tumour is large, deep-lobe or fixed, it was largely not in these extracapsular series at all — the shelf's conclusion applies to the smaller, mobile, superficial tumours the technique was used for.
cards.source: Synthesis of Albergotti WG et al. The Laryngoscope. 2012; Schapher M et al. The Laryngoscope. 2021; Liu Z et al. International Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. 2023; Elmarghani M et al. Cureus. 2025.

shelves.title: Coblation tonsillectomy: a little less pain for the first days, no difference by day 7, and a possible increase in secondary bleeding
shelves.question: In children and adults having tonsillectomy (± adenoidectomy), does coblation reduce postoperative pain, haemorrhage and time to normal diet versus cold-steel dissection with bipolar haemostasis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects,methods · Child · Humans · Hypertrophy/surgery · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control · Palatine Tonsil/pathology,surgery · Postoperative Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sodium Chloride/therapeutic use · Tonsillectomy/adverse effects,instrumentation,methods · Tonsillitis/surgery
shelves.balance: The trial and synthesis data split exactly as the slate flag predicted, and both sides are presented. For pain: within-patient randomised trials found the coblation side significantly less painful for the first 1–3 days and no differently thereafter, and the Cochrane review (29 trials, 2,561 participants) found the same shape — a day-1 advantage shrinking to nothing by day 7 — on very low to low quality evidence. For bleeding: primary haemorrhage was similar, but secondary haemorrhage was higher with coblation in the Cochrane absolute risks (5% vs 3.6%) and in the largest single trial (1,004 patients), which otherwise favoured coblation on time, blood loss and recovery. The tested coblation system is not named by brand in the carded records, so no brand claim is made. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Pynnonen 2017 (Cochrane review, 29 RCTs, 2,561 participants): coblation may reduce pain on day 1 only, with little or no difference by day 7, similar primary bleeding, and a possible small increase in secondary bleeding (absolute 5% vs 3.6%)
cards.summary: Pynnonen 2017 (Cochrane review, 29 RCTs, 2,561 participants): coblation may reduce pain on day 1 only, with little or no difference by day 7, similar primary bleeding, and a possible small increase in secondary bleeding (absolute 5% vs 3.6%)
cards.people: 29 randomised trials (2,561 participants — 7 adult-only, 16 child-only, 6 mixed) of extracapsular coblation tonsillectomy versus other surgical techniques for chronic tonsillitis or tonsillar hypertrophy; all studies were at moderate or high risk of bias.
cards.result: Pain at day 1 favoured coblation (standardised mean difference −0.79, 95% CI −1.38 to −0.19; 538 participants; very low-quality evidence), shrinking by day 3 (−0.44, 95% CI −0.97 to 0.09) and absent by day 7 (−0.01; low-quality evidence). Primary bleeding was similar (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.05). Secondary bleeding risk was higher with coblation (RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.95), corresponding to an absolute risk of 5% versus 3.6% — a difference of 1.3 percentage points (95% CI 0.2 points lower to 3.5 points higher). Data did not permit pooled conclusions on time to normal diet or activity, or on operating duration.
cards.watchOut: Very low to low quality evidence throughout, and most trials did not report data in a form that could be pooled — the review's own conclusion is that it is uncertain whether coblation has any advantage.
cards.source: Pynnonen M et al. Coblation versus other surgical techniques for tonsillectomy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28828761. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Polites 2006 (within-patient RCT, N = 20 adults): the coblation side hurt significantly less on days 1–3, and no differently on days 4–10
cards.summary: Polites 2006 (within-patient RCT, N = 20 adults): the coblation side hurt significantly less on days 1–3, and no differently on days 4–10
cards.people: 20 adult patients having tonsillectomy for recurrent/chronic tonsillitis, each having one tonsil randomly removed by coblation and the other by standard dissection, rating pain per side daily for 10 days on a visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Coblation was significantly less painful than dissection on day 1 (P < 0.001), day 2 (P = 0.003) and day 3 (P = 0.018). For all subsequent days (4–10) there was no significant difference in pain between the techniques. The authors conclude the early benefit makes coblation potentially attractive for day-case tonsillectomy in adults.
cards.watchOut: Only 20 patients, and side-specific pain rating after bilateral surgery is inherently hard for patients to separate — a design that can exaggerate a technique difference.
cards.source: Polites N et al. Postoperative pain following coblation tonsillectomy: randomized clinical trial. ANZ journal of surgery. 2006. PMID: 16681537. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/etiology,prevention & control · Tonsillectomy/methods

cards.headline: Rakesh 2012 (within-patient RCT, N = 60 adults): coblation sides had less blood loss (11 vs 34 mL) and less pain for the first 72 hours; no haemorrhage on either side; healing was slower on the coblation side
cards.summary: Rakesh 2012 (within-patient RCT, N = 60 adults): coblation sides had less blood loss (11 vs 34 mL) and less pain for the first 72 hours; no haemorrhage on either side; healing was slower on the coblation side
cards.people: 60 adult patients having tonsillectomy for benign indications, each randomised to have one tonsil removed by coblation (subcapsular radiofrequency ablation) and the other by conventional dissection, assessed to day 20 for pain, bleeding and fossa healing.
cards.result: Operative blood loss was 11 mL on the coblation side versus 34 mL on the conventional side (P = 0.009); coblation took longer (15 vs 11 minutes, P > 0.05). 77% of patients said the coblation side was less painful over the 20-day recovery, with significant pain-score differences at 6, 12, 24, 48 and 72 hours but not beyond. There was no reactionary or secondary haemorrhage on either side, and healing took longer on the coblation side.
cards.watchOut: Zero haemorrhages in 60 patients cannot test the secondary-haemorrhage question at all — that needs the large parallel-group and audit data, which point the other way (next card and Cochrane card).
cards.source: Rakesh S et al. A Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind Study of Coblation versus Dissection Tonsillectomy in Adult Patients. Indian journal of otolaryngology and head and neck surgery. 2012. PMID: 23998038. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: El-Taher 2019 (parallel-group RCT, N = 1,004, ages 4–35): coblation was faster with less blood loss and earlier return to diet/activity — but was associated with a higher incidence of secondary haemorrhage
cards.summary: El-Taher 2019 (parallel-group RCT, N = 1,004, ages 4–35): coblation was faster with less blood loss and earlier return to diet/activity — but was associated with a higher incidence of secondary haemorrhage
cards.people: 1,004 patients (mean age 10.4 years, range 4–35) randomised to coblation tonsillectomy (507) or conventional tonsillectomy (497) in a prospective double-blind randomised study, comparing operative time, blood loss, return to normal activity and diet, and primary and secondary haemorrhage.
cards.result: The authors report coblation offered significant advantages over the dissection method — less operative time, decreased intraoperative blood loss, and earlier restoration of daily activities and normal diet. However, coblation tonsillectomy was associated with a higher incidence of secondary haemorrhage. (The record's abstract states these directions without the underlying percentages, so no rates are printed here.)
cards.watchOut: The largest single trial carded, but its abstract reports directions without numbers for its key outcomes — including the haemorrhage excess — so the size of both its benefits and its harm cannot be verified from the record.
cards.source: El-Taher M et al. Coblation Versus Conventional Tonsillectomy: A Double Blind Randomized Controlled Trial. The Journal of craniofacial surgery. 2019. PMID: 31741955. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: early pain is probably a little less with coblation; by a week there is no difference; and the secondary-haemorrhage signal points against it in the largest data
cards.summary: Synthesis: early pain is probably a little less with coblation; by a week there is no difference; and the secondary-haemorrhage signal points against it in the largest data
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 29 RCTs (2,561 participants), two small within-patient randomised trials (20 and 60 adults) and one large parallel-group trial (1,004 patients).
cards.result: Pain: less on days 1–3 in the within-patient trials and in the Cochrane day-1 pooling, none by day 7. Blood loss at operation: less with coblation where measured. Haemorrhage: primary bleeding similar (Cochrane RR 0.99); secondary bleeding possibly higher with coblation (Cochrane absolute 5% vs 3.6%; the 1,004-patient trial also found a higher secondary-haemorrhage incidence). PROPOSED SPLIT — a small early-pain benefit against a possible late-bleeding cost, on low-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: Trials and audits disagree on haemorrhage precisely because trials are too small for a ~4–5% event and audits are uncontrolled — this shelf presents both, per the slate flag, and does not resolve them into one number.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pynnonen M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017; Polites N et al. ANZ Journal of Surgery. 2006; Rakesh S et al. Indian Journal of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery. 2012; El-Taher M et al. Journal of Craniofacial Surgery. 2019.

shelves.title: Ahmed valve versus Baerveldt implant: Baerveldt controlled pressure better in both randomised trials, with more hypotony-type failures
shelves.question: In adults with advanced glaucoma inadequately controlled on drops or after failed trabeculectomy, how do the two valved/non-valved tube shunts compare — Ahmed valve versus Baerveldt implant — on pressure control, failure, hypotony and reoperation (the ABC and AVB randomised trials)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Device Removal · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glaucoma/physiopathology,surgery · Glaucoma Drainage Implants · Humans · Intraocular Pressure/physiology · Intraoperative Complications · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Prospective Studies · Prosthesis Implantation · Reoperation · Tonometry, Ocular · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two independent randomised trials of exactly the devices named in the question — the tested products are named as published, per the clarification exception: the Ahmed FP7 Glaucoma Valve (New World Medical) versus the Baerveldt 101-350 / Baerveldt-350 Glaucoma Implant (Abbott Medical Optics). Both trials agree on direction: Baerveldt eyes ran about 2–3 mmHg lower, failure was significantly lower with Baerveldt in the AVB trial at 1 and 5 years and non-significantly lower in the ABC trial, and the failure modes flipped — Ahmed failures were mostly uncontrolled pressure, Baerveldt failures disproportionately hypotony, explantation or lost light perception, with more early postoperative complications in ABC's Baerveldt arm. The trials' failure definitions differ (21 vs 18 mmHg ceilings), so rates are compared within trials only. This shelf is device-versus-device only — it does not duplicate the tube-versus-trabeculectomy comparison shelved elsewhere. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Budenz 2011 — ABC Study, 1 year (RCT, N = 276): Baerveldt eyes had lower pressure (13.2 vs 15.4 mmHg) with similar failure (14.0% vs 16.4%) and more early postoperative complications
cards.summary: Budenz 2011 — ABC Study, 1 year (RCT, N = 276): Baerveldt eyes had lower pressure (13.2 vs 15.4 mmHg) with similar failure (14.0% vs 16.4%) and more early postoperative complications
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial — ABC Study (Budenz 2011)
cards.people: 276 patients (143 Ahmed, 133 Baerveldt), aged 18–85, with refractory glaucoma and intraocular pressure (IOP) ≥ 18 mmHg in whom an aqueous shunt was planned, randomised to the Ahmed Glaucoma Valve model FP7 (New World Medical, Rancho Cucamonga, CA) or the Baerveldt Glaucoma Implant model 101-350 (Abbott Medical Optics, Abbott Park, IL). Failure was IOP > 21 mmHg or not reduced by 20%, IOP ≤ 5 mmHg, reoperation/removal, or loss of light perception.
cards.result: Preoperative IOP was 31.2 ± 11.2 mmHg (Ahmed) and 31.8 ± 12.5 mmHg (Baerveldt). At 1 year, mean IOP was 15.4 ± 5.5 mmHg with Ahmed versus 13.2 ± 6.8 mmHg with Baerveldt (P = 0.007), on 1.8 ± 1.3 versus 1.5 ± 1.4 glaucoma medications (P = 0.071). Cumulative failure was 16.4% (Ahmed) versus 14.0% (Baerveldt) (P = 0.52 — the treatment made no significant difference to failure at 1 year). More patients in the Baerveldt group experienced early postoperative complications.
cards.watchOut: A refractory-glaucoma population with previous intraocular surgery — not primary-surgery patients; the tube-versus-trabeculectomy question is a different shelf and is not duplicated here.
cards.source: Budenz DL et al. Treatment outcomes in the Ahmed Baerveldt Comparison Study after 1 year of follow-up. Ophthalmology. 2011. PMID: 20932583. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Budenz 2015 — ABC Study, 5 years (RCT, N = 276): Baerveldt kept pressure lower (12.7 vs 14.7 mmHg); total failure still did not differ (39.4% vs 44.7%), but the reasons flipped — Ahmed failed by high pressure, Baerveldt by hypotony and explantation
cards.summary: Budenz 2015 — ABC Study, 5 years (RCT, N = 276): Baerveldt kept pressure lower (12.7 vs 14.7 mmHg); total failure still did not differ (39.4% vs 44.7%), but the reasons flipped — Ahmed failed by high pressure, Baerveldt by hypotony and explantation
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial — ABC Study 5-year report (Budenz 2015)
cards.people: The same 276 ABC Study patients (143 Ahmed FP7, 133 Baerveldt 101-350) followed to 5 years, with failure, IOP, visual acuity, glaucoma medications and complications as outcomes.
cards.result: At 5 years, IOP was 14.7 ± 4.4 mmHg (Ahmed) versus 12.7 ± 4.5 mmHg (Baerveldt) (P = 0.015), on 2.2 ± 1.4 versus 1.8 ± 1.5 medications (P = 0.28). Cumulative failure was 44.7% versus 39.4% (P = 0.65, not significant). Of the failures, inadequate pressure control or reoperation accounted for 46 Ahmed eyes (80% of Ahmed failures) versus 25 Baerveldt eyes (53%), while persistent hypotony, explantation or loss of light perception accounted for 11 Ahmed eyes (20%) versus 22 Baerveldt eyes (47%).
cards.watchOut: Five-year attrition in a refractory-glaucoma cohort is substantial; the failure-reason breakdown is among failures, not all randomised eyes — the percentages are printed on that basis.
cards.source: Budenz DL et al. Five-year treatment outcomes in the Ahmed Baerveldt comparison study. Ophthalmology. 2015. PMID: 25439606. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Christakis 2011 — AVB Study, 1 year (RCT, N = 238): failure was significantly lower with Baerveldt (28% vs 43%), and pressure lower (13.6 vs 16.5 mmHg)
cards.summary: Christakis 2011 — AVB Study, 1 year (RCT, N = 238): failure was significantly lower with Baerveldt (28% vs 43%), and pressure lower (13.6 vs 16.5 mmHg)
cards.people: 238 patients (124 Ahmed, 114 Baerveldt), aged 18 or older, with uncontrolled glaucoma refractory to medical, laser and surgical therapy, randomised to the Ahmed-FP7 valve (New World Medical, Inc., Rancho Cucamonga, CA) or the Baerveldt-350 implant (Abbott Medical Optics, Inc., Santa Ana, CA). Failure was IOP outside 5–18 mmHg or reduced < 20% for two consecutive visits after 3 months, vision-threatening complications, additional glaucoma procedures, or loss of light perception.
cards.result: Mean preoperative IOP was 31.4 ± 10.8 mmHg on 3.1 ± 1.0 medications. At 1 year, cumulative failure was 43% with Ahmed versus 28% with Baerveldt (P = 0.02), and mean IOP was 16.5 ± 5.3 mmHg versus 13.6 ± 4.8 mmHg (P < 0.001), favouring the non-valved Baerveldt device on both measures.
cards.watchOut: The AVB failure definition (target ceiling 18 mmHg) is stricter than ABC's (21 mmHg), which is why AVB failure rates are higher overall — compare devices within each trial, not failure rates across trials.
cards.source: Christakis PG et al. The Ahmed Versus Baerveldt study: one-year treatment outcomes. Ophthalmology. 2011. PMID: 21889801. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Christakis 2016 — AVB Study, 5 years (RCT, N = 238): failure remained lower with Baerveldt (40% vs 53%, P = 0.04); hypotony caused failure only in Baerveldt eyes (4%)
cards.summary: Christakis 2016 — AVB Study, 5 years (RCT, N = 238): failure remained lower with Baerveldt (40% vs 53%, P = 0.04); hypotony caused failure only in Baerveldt eyes (4%)
cards.type: International multicentre randomised trial — AVB Study 5-year report (Christakis 2016)
cards.people: The same 238 AVB Study patients (124 Ahmed-FP7, 114 Baerveldt-350) followed to 5 years; most had failed, or were at high risk of failing, trabeculectomy. Outcomes were failure, IOP, medication use, visual acuity, complications and interventions.
cards.result: At 5 years, cumulative failure was 53% with Ahmed versus 40% with Baerveldt (P = 0.04), the main reason in both groups being high IOP. De novo glaucoma reoperation was 18% versus 11% (P = 0.22, not significant). Hypotony resulted in failure in 5 Baerveldt patients (4%) compared with none in the Ahmed group — the valved device's protection against early over-drainage showing up, at 5 years, as a failure-mode difference rather than a total-failure difference.
cards.watchOut: Two trials, two failure definitions and two eras of recruitment — the device ordering is consistent, but the absolute failure percentages (ABC 39–45%, AVB 40–53%) must not be merged.
cards.source: Christakis PG et al. The Ahmed Versus Baerveldt Study: Five-Year Treatment Outcomes. Ophthalmology. 2016. PMID: 27544023. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in both randomised trials the non-valved Baerveldt implant controlled pressure better and failed less or equally — and failed differently, by hypotony rather than high pressure
cards.summary: Synthesis: in both randomised trials the non-valved Baerveldt implant controlled pressure better and failed less or equally — and failed differently, by hypotony rather than high pressure
cards.people: Two independent multicentre randomised trials of the same device pair: ABC (276 patients) and AVB (238 patients), each reported at 1 and 5 years — 514 randomised patients in total.
cards.result: Baerveldt eyes ran 2–3 mmHg lower pressure in both trials at both timepoints. Failure favoured Baerveldt significantly in AVB (28% vs 43% at 1 year; 40% vs 53% at 5 years) and non-significantly in ABC (14.0% vs 16.4%; 39.4% vs 44.7%). The consistent counterweight: hypotony-type failures clustered in Baerveldt eyes, and early postoperative complications were more frequent with Baerveldt in ABC. PROPOSED LIKELY — the direction is concordant across two independent trials, with the hypotony trade-off on the face.
cards.watchOut: These are refractory/advanced glaucomas, many after failed trabeculectomy — the comparison does not extend to primary tube surgery in milder disease, and it does not re-ask the tube-versus-trabeculectomy question shelved elsewhere.
cards.source: Synthesis of Budenz DL et al. Ophthalmology. 2011 and 2015 (ABC Study); Christakis PG et al. Ophthalmology. 2011 and 2016 (AVB Study).

shelves.title: Trifocal and extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses versus monofocal lenses in bilateral cataract surgery: better intermediate/near vision and spectacle independence, at a cost in contrast sensitivity and halos
shelves.question: In adults having cataract surgery in both eyes, do trifocal or extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses improve spectacle independence and intermediate/near vision versus monofocal lenses, at what cost in dysphotopsia and contrast sensitivity?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised EDOF trials and a non-randomised trifocal comparison agree that presbyopia-correcting lenses improve intermediate and near vision and spectacle independence over monofocal lenses, with distance vision preserved; the costs are reduced contrast sensitivity and more halos. Industry sponsorship is near-universal in this base, and the trifocal limb rests on a non-randomised comparison, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. Tested lenses are named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: TECNIS Symfony ZXR00 and AT LARA 829MP (EDOF), CT ASPHINA 409MP and TECNIS 1-piece ZCB00 (monofocal controls); the trifocal report does not name a single branded lens in its record.

cards.headline: Chang 2022 (Symfony pivotal RCT, 299 patients): EDOF lens matched monofocal on distance vision and beat it on intermediate and near vision (both P<.0001); spectacle-free most of the time in 85.0% versus 59.9%
cards.summary: Chang 2022 (Symfony pivotal RCT, 299 patients): EDOF lens matched monofocal on distance vision and beat it on intermediate and near vision (both P<.0001); spectacle-free most of the time in 85.0% versus 59.9%
cards.people: 299 patients at 15 US sites randomised to bilateral implantation with the TECNIS Symfony extended-depth-of-focus IOL (ZXR00, n=148) or the TECNIS 1-piece monofocal IOL (ZCB00, n=151); patient- and evaluator-masked; outcomes at 6 months.
cards.result: Mean binocular uncorrected distance acuity was comparable between groups (P=.1011). The Symfony group had significantly better binocular uncorrected intermediate and near acuity and better distance-corrected intermediate and near acuity (all P<.0001). More Symfony recipients reported wearing spectacles none or a little of the time for overall vision (85.0% vs 59.9%, P<.0001). Dysphotopsia rates with Symfony were low: mild-to-moderate night glare 2.7%, halo 13.6% mild-to-moderate and 2.7% severe, starbursts 7.5% mild-to-moderate and 1.4% severe.
cards.watchOut: A single manufacturer's pivotal trial comparing its own EDOF lens with its own monofocal lens; 6-month follow-up only, and halo/glare were self-reported symptoms rather than measured contrast thresholds.
cards.source: Chang DH et al. Visual outcomes and safety of an extended depth-of-focus intraocular lens: results of a pivotal clinical trial. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2022. PMID: 34269326. Registry ID: NCT02203721. cards.headline: Reinhard 2021 (multicentre RCT, 211 patients): both EDOF lenses beat the monofocal lens on binocular depth of focus and on intermediate/near acuity (P<.0001); contrast sensitivity was higher with the monofocal lens
cards.summary: Reinhard 2021 (multicentre RCT, 211 patients): both EDOF lenses beat the monofocal lens on binocular depth of focus and on intermediate/near acuity (P<.0001); contrast sensitivity was higher with the monofocal lens
cards.people: 211 cataract patients aged 50-80 randomised to bilateral implantation with the AT LARA 829MP EDOF lens, the TECNIS Symfony EDOF lens, or the CT ASPHINA 409MP monofocal lens; follow-up to 4-6 months.
cards.result: Distance acuity was similar for all lenses at 6 months; intermediate and near acuity were significantly better for both EDOF lenses than for the monofocal lens (p<0.0001). Both EDOF lenses were significantly better than the monofocal lens at all levels for binocular depth of focus (AT LARA all p<0.0001; Symfony all p=0.002). Contrast sensitivity was higher with the monofocal CT ASPHINA 409MP, but both EDOF lenses had a better spectacle independence rate. No lens tilt or general safety issues occurred.
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance levels without absolute acuity differences for most endpoints, so the size of the intermediate/near gain cannot be quantified from this record alone; lens makers' involvement is typical of this literature.
cards.source: Reinhard T et al. Comparison of two extended depth of focus intraocular lenses with a monofocal lens: a multi-centre randomised trial. Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2021. PMID: 32915276. Registry ID: NCT03172351. cards.headline: Zhang 2023 (non-randomised controlled trial, 91 patients, 138 eyes): trifocal lenses gave better uncorrected vision at all distances and better spectacle independence and satisfaction; monofocal lenses gave better mesopic contrast sensitivity at specific frequencies
cards.summary: Zhang 2023 (non-randomised controlled trial, 91 patients, 138 eyes): trifocal lenses gave better uncorrected vision at all distances and better spectacle independence and satisfaction; monofocal lenses gave better mesopic contrast sensitivity at specific frequencies
cards.people: 91 patients (138 eyes) implanted with a trifocal IOL or a monofocal IOL after phacoemulsification at a tertiary hospital in Wuhan, China, June-December 2020; non-randomised controlled design; monocular testing and questionnaires at 3 months. The record does not name the specific trifocal product tested.
cards.result: Uncorrected acuity was statistically better with trifocal IOLs at distance, intermediate and near. Monofocal IOLs had statistically better mesopic contrast sensitivity at specific spatial frequencies. Defocus curves, spectacle independence and surgical satisfaction were statistically worse with monofocal lenses, and trifocal patients scored better on subjective quality-of-vision and quality-of-life questionnaires; objective optical quality measures (modulation transfer function, Strehl ratio) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised: patients who chose or were chosen for trifocal lenses may differ systematically (motivation, willingness to pay), which can inflate satisfaction and spectacle-independence differences. Three months is early follow-up.
cards.source: Zhang W et al. Comparison of postoperative visual performance between trifocal intraocular lens and monofocal intraocular lens. Saudi Medical Journal. 2023. PMID: 37182920. cards.headline: Liu 2019 (meta-analysis, 9 comparative studies, 1,336 eyes): EDOF lenses beat monofocal lenses on intermediate acuity (weighted mean difference -0.17 logMAR) and near acuity (-0.17), with spectacle independence relative risk 2.81 — but reduced contrast sensitivity and more halos
cards.summary: Liu 2019 (meta-analysis, 9 comparative studies, 1,336 eyes): EDOF lenses beat monofocal lenses on intermediate acuity (weighted mean difference -0.17 logMAR) and near acuity (-0.17), with spectacle independence relative risk 2.81 — but reduced contrast sensitivity and more halos
cards.people: Nine comparative clinical trials of bilateral EDOF IOL implantation in cataract patients, totalling 1,336 eyes, pooled with random-effects models; subgroups by control-lens type (monofocal or trifocal).
cards.result: Versus monofocal IOLs, EDOF IOLs produced better uncorrected intermediate visual acuity (weighted mean difference -0.17, 95% CI -0.26 to -0.08, P=0.0001) and uncorrected near acuity (weighted mean difference -0.17, 95% CI -0.21 to -0.12, P<0.00001), with higher spectacle independence (relative risk 2.81, 95% CI 1.06 to 7.46, P=0.04), but reduced contrast sensitivity and more frequent halos. Versus trifocal IOLs, EDOF lenses had worse near acuity (mean difference 0.10 logMAR, P<0.0001) but better contrast sensitivity. Serious postoperative complications were rare.
cards.watchOut: The spectacle-independence relative risk (2.81) is a relative measure with a wide confidence interval (1.06-7.46); the pooled trials are largely industry-supported, and halo/contrast outcomes were reported inconsistently across the nine studies.
cards.source: Liu J et al. Efficacy and safety of extended depth of focus intraocular lenses in cataract surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 31477053. cards.headline: Synthesis: presbyopia-correcting lenses buy intermediate/near vision and spectacle independence at a contrast and halo cost — POSSIBLE on a concordant but industry-run base
cards.summary: Synthesis: presbyopia-correcting lenses buy intermediate/near vision and spectacle independence at a contrast and halo cost — POSSIBLE on a concordant but industry-run base
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: two randomised EDOF-versus-monofocal trials (299 and 211 patients), one non-randomised trifocal-versus-monofocal comparison (91 patients) and one meta-analysis of 9 studies (1,336 eyes).
cards.result: Every comparison favours EDOF/trifocal lenses for intermediate and near vision and spectacle independence (85.0% vs 59.9% largely spectacle-free in the pivotal trial; pooled spectacle-independence relative risk 2.81), with distance vision preserved. Every comparison also shows the same trade: lower contrast sensitivity and more halos with the presbyopia-correcting lenses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent, but the base is manufacturer-run and the trifocal limb is non-randomised.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial follows patients beyond 6 months, and none compares a trifocal lens head-to-head with an EDOF lens in a randomised design; the choice between trifocal and EDOF rests on the meta-analytic subgroup contrast, not a direct trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chang DH et al. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2022 (PMID: 34269326); Reinhard T et al. Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2021 (PMID: 32915276); Zhang W et al. Saudi Medical Journal. 2023 (PMID: 37182920); Liu J et al. BMC Ophthalmology. 2019 (PMID: 31477053).

shelves.title: Descemet stripping only (DSO) for Fuchs dystrophy without stromal scarring: corneas clear in most selected patients in cohort reports, but no completed randomised comparison with DMEK exists yet
shelves.question: In adults with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and no stromal scarring, does Descemet stripping only (DSO/DWEK, with or without topical rho-kinase inhibitor) clear the cornea and restore vision versus Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the DSO limb rests entirely on observational reports: a prospective 23-eye series with adjunctive ripasudil (clearance in 22 of 23 eyes), a retrospective long-term series (12 of 13 eyes cleared; 10 of 13 maintained clearance at 5 years) and an individual-patient meta-analysis of 68 cases (85% clearance). No completed randomised DSO-versus-DMEK result exists: the DETECT II randomised trial (DMEK versus DSO with ripasudil, 60 patients planned, NCT05275972) has published a protocol only. The DMEK comparator evidence is homed on shelf #6427 (the DETECT trial of DMEK versus ultrathin DSAEK) and is not re-carded here. Patient selection is the whole question: every DSO report required central-only guttae with a healthy peripheral endothelial reserve. Build-time floor check (item U2): the free DSO base is exactly three cardable reports at or above the 10-human floor — a fourth 5-patient series falls below the floor and was not carded.

cards.headline: Moloney 2021 (Sydney Eye Hospital, prospective pre-post trial, 23 eyes): DSO plus topical ripasudil cleared 22 of 23 corneas at a mean 4.1 weeks; 39% relapsed when ripasudil stopped and re-cleared on restarting
cards.summary: Moloney 2021 (Sydney Eye Hospital, prospective pre-post trial, 23 eyes): DSO plus topical ripasudil cleared 22 of 23 corneas at a mean 4.1 weeks; 39% relapsed when ripasudil stopped and re-cleared on restarting
cards.type: Prospective pre-post clinical trial with historical controls (Moloney 2021) — observational-grade
cards.people: 23 eyes of 23 patients with symptomatic Fuchs endothelial dystrophy from central guttae, all with superior endothelial cell count above 1,000 cells/mm², treated with Descemet stripping only (peeling technique, no other intervention) plus ripasudil 0.4% drops six times daily from day 1 until corneal clearance; historical control group for healing-time and cell-count comparisons; data safety monitoring board oversight.
cards.result: Twenty-two of 23 eyes achieved corneal clearance at a mean of 4.1 weeks, and every patient achieving clearance improved in vision: mean uncorrected acuity improved by 0.20 logMAR and best spectacle-corrected acuity by 0.156 logMAR. One patient failed to clear and underwent DMEK at week 12. Twenty-one of 22 patients who cleared were satisfied. Thirty-nine percent relapsed with oedema after stopping ripasudil and cleared again on recommencing at a lower dose. Commonest adverse effects were ocular irritation (43%) locally and gastrointestinal upset (24%) systemically; no serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: No concurrent DMEK control arm: the comparison is with historical healing times, and entry required a strong peripheral endothelial reserve (superior count above 1,000 cells/mm²), so these clearance rates apply only to carefully selected Fuchs patients. The 39% relapse rate on stopping ripasudil means the drug limb is doing real work.
cards.source: Moloney G et al. Descemet Stripping Only Supplemented With Topical Ripasudil for Fuchs Endothelial Dystrophy: 12-Month Outcomes of the Sydney Eye Hospital Study. Cornea. 2021. PMID: 32740006. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hakim 2024 (retrospective series, 13 eyes of 11 patients): 12 of 13 eyes cleared after DSO; 10 of 13 (77%) kept clear corneas for at least 5 years, and failed eyes were rescued by later keratoplasty
cards.summary: Hakim 2024 (retrospective series, 13 eyes of 11 patients): 12 of 13 eyes cleared after DSO; 10 of 13 (77%) kept clear corneas for at least 5 years, and failed eyes were rescued by later keratoplasty
cards.people: 11 patients (13 eyes) with Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy who underwent Descemet stripping only at a single institution in 2016-2017, reviewed retrospectively for 5- and 6-year outcomes.
cards.result: Twelve of 13 eyes achieved corneal clearance. Two eyes developed corneal decompensation requiring subsequent endothelial keratoplasty, after which clearance and good vision were achieved. Of the 10 eyes maintaining clear corneas, 9 had best-corrected acuity of at least 20/30 at 5 years (mean 0.18 ± 0.16 logMAR); at 6 years, 7 of 8 eyes had acuity better than 20/40 (mean 0.17 ± 0.04 logMAR). Ten of 13 eyes (77%) responded and maintained clear central corneas for at least 5 years.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen eyes from one institution with no comparator; eyes that failed were counted as successes of the rescue pathway, not of DSO itself. Long-term durability beyond 6 years is still unreported.
cards.source: Hakim FE et al. Descemet Stripping Only: Long-Term Outcomes. Cornea. 2024. PMID: 37921677. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Din 2022 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 68 DSO cases): corneal clearance in 85%; clearance faster with rho-kinase inhibitors (4.9 versus 10.1 weeks) and central cell counts higher
cards.summary: Din 2022 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 68 DSO cases): corneal clearance in 85%; clearance faster with rho-kinase inhibitors (4.9 versus 10.1 weeks) and central cell counts higher
cards.type: Individual-patient meta-analysis of case series (Din 2022) — observational base
cards.people: 68 cases from published DSO case series (including combined phacoemulsification-DSO and rho-kinase-inhibitor series) identified in MEDLINE, Embase and Cochrane CENTRAL; mean follow-up 12.4 months.
cards.result: DSO achieved corneal clearance in 85% (58/68). Mean time to clearance was 4.9 weeks with rho-kinase inhibitors versus 10.1 weeks with observation (P<0.0001). Mean postoperative central endothelial cell count was higher with rho-kinase inhibitors (1,151 ± 245 versus 765 ± 169 cells/mm², P<0.018). Best-corrected acuity improved in 61 eyes (90%), with mean final acuity 0.17 logMAR. Success factors were a 4-mm descemetorhexis, a clear peripheral endothelium without guttae or decompensation, and low central corneal thickness. The commonest complication was deep stromal scarring at the descemetorhexis edge (9 cases); no intraoperative complications were reported.
cards.watchOut: A pooling of case series is still case-series evidence: publication bias favours successful DSO reports, series overlap with the other carded reports is likely, and there is no DMEK arm anywhere in the pooled data.
cards.source: Din N et al. Surgical Management of Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy: A Treatment Algorithm and Individual Patient Meta-Analysis of Descemet Stripping Only. Cornea. 2022. cards.headline: Synthesis: DSO works in selected Fuchs eyes on observational evidence alone — MAYBE (weak evidence), with the randomised answer still pending
cards.summary: Synthesis: DSO works in selected Fuchs eyes on observational evidence alone — MAYBE (weak evidence), with the randomised answer still pending
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: one prospective 23-eye ripasudil-adjunct series, one retrospective 13-eye long-term series and one 68-case individual-patient meta-analysis. A 5-patient 5-year series exists but falls below the 10-human evidence floor and was not carded.
cards.result: Clearance rates cluster at 77-96% in selected eyes (central guttae only, preserved peripheral endothelium), vision improves by roughly 0.16-0.20 logMAR where reported, rho-kinase inhibition roughly halves time to clearance (4.9 vs 10.1 weeks), and failed DSO can be rescued by later keratoplasty. Nothing here compares DSO with DMEK in the same patients: that comparison is the DETECT II randomised trial (NCT05275972), published as a protocol only. The DMEK evidence itself is homed on shelf #6427 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Selection is destiny in this literature: quoting an 85% clearance rate to an unselected Fuchs patient would mislead. Until DETECT II reports, DSO-versus-DMEK is a judgement call, not an evidence-based ranking.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moloney G et al. Cornea. 2021 (PMID: 32740006); Hakim FE et al. Cornea. 2024 (PMID: 37921677); Din N et al. Cornea. 2022 (PMID: 35942547).

shelves.title: Varenicline nasal spray for dry eye disease: tear production and symptoms improve across severity, menopausal and fellow-eye analyses of the ONSET programme
shelves.question: In adults with dry eye disease, does varenicline nasal spray improve tear production (Schirmer) and dry-eye symptoms versus vehicle spray?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme (the ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 vehicle-controlled trials) supports varenicline solution nasal spray 0.03 mg: the integrated analyses carded here show Schirmer gains of about 5.5-6.7 mm over vehicle and roughly 2.3-3.4 times the odds (relative measure) of a 10-mm Schirmer improvement, consistent across disease severity, menopausal status and study/fellow eyes. The primary ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 trial reports are carded on another shelf in this library and are not re-carded here; this shelf cards the programme's integrated and post-hoc analyses, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. The tested product as published is OC-01 (varenicline solution) nasal spray. Sneezing is the signature adverse effect (82-84% in the autoimmune subgroup report, graded mild by 98%). The Schirmer endpoint is a sign, not a symptom — symptom (eye dryness score) differences were smaller and not significant in every subgroup.

cards.headline: Sheppard 2023 (integrated ONSET analysis, 602 patients): varenicline spray raised the odds of a ≥10-mm Schirmer improvement 2.3-3.4-fold (relative measure) across severity subgroups, with no severity interaction
cards.summary: Sheppard 2023 (integrated ONSET analysis, 602 patients): varenicline spray raised the odds of a ≥10-mm Schirmer improvement 2.3-3.4-fold (relative measure) across severity subgroups, with no severity interaction
cards.type: Integrated analysis of two randomised trials (Sheppard 2023)
cards.people: Integrated data from the ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 randomised trials: adults 22 or older with dry eye disease (Ocular Surface Disease Index ≥23, corneal staining ≥2 in at least one region, Schirmer ≤10 mm) randomised to varenicline solution nasal spray 0.03 mg (n=308) or vehicle control (n=294); pre-specified subgroups by baseline Schirmer (≤5 vs >5 mm) and eye dryness score (<60 vs ≥60).
cards.result: No treatment-by-subgroup interaction was observed for any endpoint (P>.05). The odds of achieving a ≥10-mm Schirmer improvement on varenicline versus vehicle were 3.4 (95% CI 2.0-5.6) for baseline Schirmer ≤5 and 2.3 (1.3-4.0) for >5; by eye dryness score, 3.4 (1.9-6.1) for <60 and 2.5 (1.5-4.0) for ≥60 — all relative (odds) measures. Least-squares mean eye-dryness-score differences versus vehicle were -7.4 (95% CI -12.5 to -2.4) for Schirmer ≤5 and -2.8 (-8.7 to 3.1) for >5; -2.9 (-8.3 to 2.5) for dryness <60 and -8.1 (-13.6 to -2.6) for ≥60, so symptom differences were not significant in every subgroup.
cards.watchOut: This is a subgroup analysis of the same two trials, not independent replication: it shows the effect does not shrink in severe disease, but it cannot add certainty beyond the parent programme. Two of the four symptom confidence intervals cross zero.
cards.source: Sheppard JD et al. Does Dry Eye Disease Severity Impact Efficacy of Varenicline Solution Nasal Spray on Sign and Symptom Treatment Outcomes? Optometry and Vision Science. 2023. PMID: 36728653. Registry ID: NCT03636061 (programme registration as given in the record). cards.headline: Katz 2022 (post-hoc bilateral analysis, 891 patients): Schirmer improved in fellow eyes almost as much as study eyes (8.7-8.8 mm versus 10.4-10.5 mm on active spray, versus 2.7-4.9 mm on vehicle)
cards.summary: Katz 2022 (post-hoc bilateral analysis, 891 patients): Schirmer improved in fellow eyes almost as much as study eyes (8.7-8.8 mm versus 10.4-10.5 mm on active spray, versus 2.7-4.9 mm on vehicle)
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of two randomised trials (Katz 2022)
cards.people: All 891 patients randomised in the ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 trials to OC-01 (varenicline solution) nasal spray 0.03 mg, 0.06 mg, or vehicle in each nostril twice daily for 28 days; one eye was designated the study eye and the other the fellow eye; post-hoc analysis.
cards.result: Mean Schirmer improvement from baseline to day 28 in study eyes was 10.4 mm (0.03 mg), 10.5 mm (0.06 mg) and 4.9 mm (vehicle); in fellow eyes the corresponding values were 8.7 mm, 8.8 mm and 2.7 mm. The proportions achieving a ≥10-mm Schirmer improvement were 48.1%, 48.4% and 25.9% in study eyes and 42.9%, 43.9% and 19.7% in fellow eyes. No significant treatment-by-subgroup interactions were seen by baseline eye dryness score (<40 vs ≥40).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and within-programme: the bilateral finding is mechanistically reassuring (a nasal spray should act on both lacrimal glands) but adds no new randomised comparison. Vehicle Schirmer gains of 2.7-4.9 mm show a large vehicle/placebo component in the sign endpoint.
cards.source: Katz J et al. Bilateral Effect of OC-01 (Varenicline Solution) Nasal Spray for Treatment of Signs and Symptoms in Individuals with Mild, Moderate, and Severe Dry Eye Disease. cards.summary: Nijm 2023 (post-hoc menopausal analysis, 449 women): Schirmer treatment difference 6.7 mm in premenopausal and 5.5 mm in postmenopausal women; dryness-score differences -5.5 and -4.1 — no menopause interaction

cards.people: 449 women from the ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 trials randomised to OC-01 (varenicline solution) nasal spray 0.03 mg or vehicle, with known self-reported menopausal status (postmenopausal versus not).
cards.result: Treatment-by-menopausal-status interaction terms were not statistically significant for Schirmer score or eye dryness score (p>0.05). cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, consistent sign benefit, smaller symptom benefit — POSSIBLE, with the primary reports homed elsewhere
cards.summary: Synthesis: one programme, consistent sign benefit, smaller symptom benefit — POSSIBLE, with the primary reports homed elsewhere
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: integrated and post-hoc analyses covering 602-891 randomised patients from the single ONSET-1/ONSET-2 programme of varenicline solution nasal spray versus vehicle over 28 days.
cards.result: Tear production improves consistently: Schirmer treatment differences of about 5.5-6.7 mm, ≥10-mm responder proportions of about 48% on active spray versus 26% on vehicle in study eyes, and effects that hold across severity, menopausal status, autoimmune history and fellow eyes. Symptom (eye dryness) differences are smaller (-3 to -8 points on a 100-point scale) and not significant in every subgroup. The primary ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 reports are carded on another shelf in this library and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single sponsor programme, however internally consistent, caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: All carded evidence derives from 28-day trials; durability, adherence to a twice-daily nasal spray, and comparison with topical ciclosporin or lifitegrast are outside this record entirely.

shelves.title: Fluticasone by exhalation delivery system (EDS-FLU, XHANCE) for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: polyp grade, congestion and quality of life improve in two replicate randomised trials
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, does fluticasone delivered by an exhalation delivery system (EDS-FLU) reduce polyp grade, congestion and exacerbations versus placebo delivery system — including in patients who would otherwise be surgical candidates?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate 323-patient randomised trials (NAVIGATE I and II) of the exhalation delivery system with fluticasone (EDS-FLU; XHANCE, OptiNose — named exactly as published, per the clarification exception) beat the placebo delivery system on both co-primary endpoints (congestion and polyp grade, P<.05 to P<.001), improved Sino-Nasal Outcome Test scores by about 10 points more than placebo, eliminated polyps on at least one side in about 25% versus 8.7%, and cut the number of patients meeting surgical-indication criteria by 62-67% in NAVIGATE II. The later ReOpen trials extend the finding to chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps and show 56-66% fewer exacerbations (relative measure) — carded here as a third limb with its broader population stated. This shelf does not answer device-versus-conventional-spray: every comparator was the same device delivering placebo.

cards.headline: Sindwani 2019 (NAVIGATE I RCT, 323 patients): all EDS-FLU doses improved both co-primary endpoints (congestion and polyp grade, P<.05) and SNOT-22 (P≤.005); about 65% reported being much or very much improved
cards.summary: Sindwani 2019 (NAVIGATE I RCT, 323 patients): all EDS-FLU doses improved both co-primary endpoints (congestion and polyp grade, P<.05) and SNOT-22 (P≤.005); about 65% reported being much or very much improved
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-device-controlled trial (NAVIGATE I, Sindwani 2019)
cards.people: 323 subjects with nasal polyps and moderate-to-severe congestion/obstruction, 94.4% with prior corticosteroid use and 60.4% with prior surgery, randomised to EDS-FLU 93, 186 or 372 µg or EDS-placebo twice daily for 24 weeks (16 double-blind plus 8-week extension).
cards.result: All EDS-FLU doses produced significant improvement in both co-primary endpoints (change in nasal congestion and polyp grade, P<.05) and in SNOT-22 total score (P≤.005), and significantly improved all four cardinal symptoms (P<.05). Approximately 80% of subjects reported improvement with EDS-FLU, with 65% reporting 'much' or 'very much' improvement by week 16. Adverse events were generally local, most commonly epistaxis, and similar to other intranasal steroids.
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance without absolute congestion or polyp-grade changes for the co-primaries, so effect sizes here lean on NAVIGATE II and the patient-global figures. The comparator is the device without drug — this trial cannot say the device beats a standard spray delivering the same steroid.
cards.source: Sindwani R et al. NAVIGATE I: Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blind Trial of the Exhalation Delivery System With Fluticasone for Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps. American Journal of Rhinology & Allergy. 2019. PMID: 30477309. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Leopold 2019 (NAVIGATE II RCT, 323 patients): EDS-FLU superior on both co-primaries (P<.001); polyps eliminated on at least one side in about 25% versus 8.7%; surgical eligibility fell 62-67%
cards.summary: Leopold 2019 (NAVIGATE II RCT, 323 patients): EDS-FLU superior on both co-primaries (P<.001); polyps eliminated on at least one side in about 25% versus 8.7%; surgical eligibility fell 62-67%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-device-controlled trial (NAVIGATE II, Leopold 2019)
cards.people: 323 patients aged 18 or older with moderate-to-severe congestion and nasal polyps, randomised to twice-daily EDS-FLU (93, 186 or 372 µg) or EDS-placebo for 24 weeks (16 double-blind plus 8 open-label).
cards.result: EDS-FLU was superior on both co-primary endpoints (congestion at 4 weeks and summed bilateral polyp grade at 16 weeks, P<.001 versus EDS-placebo at all doses). Sino-Nasal Outcome Test scores improved by -21.1 to -21.4 versus -11.7 at week 16 (P<.05, all doses). Polyps were eliminated on at least one side in approximately 25% of patients at week 24 versus 8.7% with EDS-placebo (P≤.014). Sixty-eight percent of EDS-FLU patients reported 'much' or 'very much' improvement, and the number eligible for surgery decreased by 62%-67%. Safety was similar to conventional corticosteroid nasal sprays.
cards.watchOut: 'Eligible for surgery decreased by 62-67%' is a criteria-based endpoint, not a count of operations avoided; the open-label final 8 weeks (all patients on 372 µg) cannot support dose comparisons at week 24.
cards.source: Leopold DA et al. NAVIGATE II: Randomized, double-blind trial of the exhalation delivery system with fluticasone for nasal polyposis. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2019. PMID: 29928924. Registry ID: NCT01624662. cards.headline: Palmer 2024 (ReOpen1 and ReOpen2 RCTs, 555 patients): symptom scores improved about 1 point more than placebo-device (P≤.011), sinus opacification improved, and exacerbations fell 56-66% (relative measure)
cards.summary: Palmer 2024 (ReOpen1 and ReOpen2 RCTs, 555 patients): symptom scores improved about 1 point more than placebo-device (P≤.011), sinus opacification improved, and exacerbations fell 56-66% (relative measure)
cards.people: Two randomised EDS-placebo-controlled trials at 120 sites in 13 countries in adults with chronic rhinosinusitis irrespective of polyps (ReOpen1, N=332) or exclusively without polyps (ReOpen2, N=223), receiving EDS-FLU 1 or 2 sprays per nostril or EDS-placebo twice daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Composite symptom score least-squares mean change versus EDS-placebo: ReOpen1 -1.58 and -1.60 versus -0.62 (P<.001, P<.001); ReOpen2 -1.54 and -1.74 versus -0.81 (P=.011, P=.001). Ethmoid/maxillary sinus opacification improved significantly versus placebo in both trials. Acute exacerbations were reduced by 56% to 66% in relative terms with EDS-FLU versus EDS-placebo (P=.001). Symptom reductions were similar in patients who had been using standard-delivery nasal steroids just before entry. Adverse events were similar to standard-delivery intranasal steroids.
cards.watchOut: ReOpen enrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps — a broader population than this shelf's polyp question — so its exacerbation result supports the device in CRS generally, not polyp shrinkage specifically. The exacerbation reduction is relative; the record gives no absolute exacerbation rates beside it.
cards.source: Palmer JN et al. Efficacy of EDS-FLU for Chronic Rhinosinusitis: Two Randomized Controlled Trials (ReOpen1 and ReOpen2). The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice. 2024. PMID: 38244014. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult; Humans; Chronic Disease; Fluticasone; Nasal Polyps; Rhinitis; Rhinosinusitis; Sinusitis; Steroids

cards.headline: Synthesis: replicate randomised evidence that EDS-FLU beats its own placebo device on symptoms, polyp grade and quality of life — LIKELY, within that comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: replicate randomised evidence that EDS-FLU beats its own placebo device on symptoms, polyp grade and quality of life — LIKELY, within that comparator
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: NAVIGATE I (323 patients with polyps), NAVIGATE II (323 patients with polyps) and ReOpen1/2 (555 patients with CRS with or without polyps).
cards.result: Both polyp trials met both co-primary endpoints at every dose; SNOT-22 improved about 10 points beyond placebo-device; about a quarter of treated patients lost polyps on at least one side versus 8.7% on placebo-device; exacerbations fell 56-66% in relative terms in the broader CRS trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo delivery system. Nothing here compares EDS-FLU with a conventional steroid spray or with biologics.
cards.watchOut: All trials are the device manufacturer's programme (EDS-FLU is XHANCE, OptiNose, as published); independent replication and any head-to-head against conventional sprays remain absent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sindwani R et al. American Journal of Rhinology & Allergy. 2019 (PMID: 30477309); Leopold DA et al. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2019 (PMID: 29928924); Palmer JN et al. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice. 2024 (PMID: 38244014).

shelves.title: Steroid-eluting sinus implants after sinus surgery: fewer postoperative interventions and less polyposis in intrapatient randomised trials; in-office implants also help recurrent polyposis
shelves.question: In adults having endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis, does a steroid-eluting sinus implant placed at surgery reduce postoperative interventions, oral-steroid need and polyp recurrence versus no implant (or a non-eluting spacer)?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised programmes of mometasone-furoate-eluting bioabsorbable implants (the PROPEL family, Intersect ENT — named as published, per the clarification exception) point the same way: ADVANCE II (105 patients, intrapatient control) found a 29.0% relative reduction in postoperative interventions and a 44.9% relative reduction in frank polyposis on drug-eluting versus non-eluting sides; the frontal-ostia trial (80 patients, intrapatient control) found postoperative intervention needed in 11.5% versus 32.8% of sides at day 30 (absolute difference -21.3%); and RESOLVE (100 patients, in-office placement for recurrent polyposis — a different population, carded as its own limb) improved obstruction scores and polyp grade versus sham at 6 months. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE: two of three trials use within-patient side comparisons with short horizons, and the base is one manufacturer's programme.

cards.headline: Marple 2012 (ADVANCE II RCT, 105 patients, intrapatient control): drug-eluting implant gave a 29.0% relative reduction in postoperative interventions and 44.9% relative reduction in frank polyposis versus the non-eluting side
cards.summary: Marple 2012 (ADVANCE II RCT, 105 patients, intrapatient control): drug-eluting implant gave a 29.0% relative reduction in postoperative interventions and 44.9% relative reduction in frank polyposis versus the non-eluting side
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, intrapatient control, double-blind grading (ADVANCE II, Marple 2012)
cards.people: 105 patients with chronic rhinosinusitis undergoing bilateral ethmoidectomy at academic and private US centres, randomised within-patient: one ethmoid sinus received the mometasone-furoate-releasing bioabsorbable implant and the other a non-drug-releasing implant; outcomes graded from randomised video-endoscopies by three blinded sinus surgeons.
cards.result: Implants were deployed in all 210 ethmoid sinuses. Compared with control sinuses, drug-releasing implants produced a 29.0% relative reduction in postoperative interventions (P=.028), a 52% relative decrease in lysis of adhesions (P=.005) and a 44.9% relative reduction in frank polyposis (P=.002). No clinically significant changes in intraocular pressure or cataracts were observed. All reductions are relative measures; the record does not print absolute intervention rates beside them.
cards.watchOut: Intrapatient design halves the effective independence of the comparison and systemic/postoperative care is shared between sides; headline figures are relative reductions without absolute rates in the record, so the absolute benefit per patient is smaller than 29% sounds.
cards.source: Marple BF et al. Advance II: a prospective, randomized study assessing safety and efficacy of bioabsorbable steroid-releasing sinus implants. Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. 2012. PMID: 22301107. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Luong 2018 (frontal-ostia RCT, 80 patients, intrapatient control): intervention needed at day 30 in 11.5% of implant sides versus 32.8% of surgery-only sides (difference -21.3%)
cards.summary: Luong 2018 (frontal-ostia RCT, 80 patients, intrapatient control): intervention needed at day 30 in 11.5% of implant sides versus 32.8% of surgery-only sides (difference -21.3%)
cards.people: 80 adults (mean age 49.5 years; 66% men) at 12 US centres undergoing bilateral frontal sinusotomies, with one frontal sinus ostium randomised to the hourglass-shaped bioabsorbable steroid-releasing implant (370 µg mometasone furoate) and the other to surgery alone; standardised postoperative care; grading by an independent blinded surgeon.
cards.result: At day 30, need for postoperative intervention was 11.5% on implant sides versus 32.8% on surgery-only sides (mean difference -21.3%, 95% CI -35.1% to -7.6%). Restenosis/occlusion was also reduced (difference -22.7%, 95% CI -33.5% to -11.9%), and benefits persisted at day 90 (intervention difference -11.7%; restenosis difference -17.4%). No implant-related adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: No other immediate postoperative corticosteroids were given, so the trial compares implant-plus-no-steroid against neither — centres that already use postoperative steroid irrigations may see a smaller increment. Ninety days is the outer horizon.
cards.source: Luong A et al. Safety and Effectiveness of a Bioabsorbable Steroid-Releasing Implant for the Paranasal Sinus Ostia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery. 2018. PMID: 29098299. Registry ID: NCT02266810. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Forwith 2016 (RESOLVE RCT, 100 patients, in-office limb): implant for recurrent polyposis improved ethmoid obstruction (P<.001) and polyp grade (P=.018) versus sham at 6 months; controls were 3.6 times likelier to still be surgical candidates
cards.summary: Forwith 2016 (RESOLVE RCT, 100 patients, in-office limb): implant for recurrent polyposis improved ethmoid obstruction (P<.001) and polyp grade (P=.018) versus sham at 6 months; controls were 3.6 times likelier to still be surgical candidates
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, blinded trial — in-office recurrent-disease limb (RESOLVE, Forwith 2016)
cards.people: 100 patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps who had failed medical treatment after prior endoscopic sinus surgery and were candidates for revision surgery, randomised to in-office placement of the mometasone-eluting implant (n=57) or a sham procedure (n=43); blinded endoscopic grading with independent video review.
cards.result: At 6 months, treated patients had significant improvement in Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation score (p=0.021), ethmoid sinus obstruction (p<0.001) and bilateral polyp grade (p=0.018) versus controls; mean obstruction/congestion score change was -1.06 versus -0.44 (p=0.124). Control patients were at 3.6 times higher risk (relative measure) of remaining indicated for revision surgery than treated patients.
cards.watchOut: This is the recurrent-polyposis, in-office population — not the at-surgery population of the other two cards — and one symptom endpoint (obstruction/congestion score) did not reach significance (p=0.124). Do not pool its results with the at-surgery trials.
cards.source: Forwith KD et al. RESOLVE: bioabsorbable steroid-eluting sinus implants for in-office treatment of recurrent sinonasal polyposis after sinus surgery: 6-month outcomes from a randomized, controlled, blinded study. International Forum of Allergy & Rhinology. 2016. PMID: 26992115. Registry ID: NCT01732536. cards.headline: Synthesis: implants reduce early postoperative intervention and polyposis in both settings — POSSIBLE on short-horizon intrapatient evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: implants reduce early postoperative intervention and polyposis in both settings — POSSIBLE on short-horizon intrapatient evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: ADVANCE II (105 patients, at-surgery ethmoid), the frontal-ostia trial (80 patients, at-surgery frontal), and RESOLVE (100 patients, in-office recurrent polyposis).
cards.result: At-surgery implants cut the need for postoperative intervention (29.0% relative reduction; 11.5% vs 32.8% of frontal ostia in absolute terms) and roughly halved polyposis/adhesion outcomes in relative terms; in-office implants improved obstruction and polyp grade at 6 months in recurrent disease. No ocular safety signal appeared. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction, but one manufacturer's programme, within-patient designs and 30-180-day horizons cap the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Long-term recurrence, cost-effectiveness and comparison with postoperative steroid irrigations are outside the carded record; the at-surgery and in-office limbs answer different clinical questions and are kept separate on this shelf.
