shelves.title: Botulinum toxin for adductor spasmodic dysphonia: voice improves for weeks in two small double-blind trials, with breathiness in up to three-quarters and benefit fading across each injection cycle
shelves.question: In adults with adductor spasmodic dysphonia, do botulinum toxin injections into the thyroarytenoid muscles improve voice quality and fluency versus sham or no injection, how long does benefit last, and what is the breathiness cost?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised limb verifies (so this shelf is built as a treatment shelf, not demoted): a 13-patient double-blind placebo-controlled study found marked acoustic improvement and patient-rated benefit, and a 24-patient multicentre double-blind trial found aberrant phoneme counts fell by 7.0 versus 0.2 at 4 weeks (p=0.0148), with benefit persisting 12 weeks. The cost is breathiness: breathy hoarseness in 77.3% and aspiration when drinking in 40.9% in the multicentre trial, resolving within about 4 weeks. A prospective 22-patient cycle study shows the lived pattern: quality-of-life scores peak at 30% of each ~26-week cycle and exceed 75/100 for only 14% of the cycle. The tested product in the multicentre trial is named as published (Botox); dosing is individualised in practice. Outcomes are perceptual/acoustic scales, presented as such.

cards.headline: Troung 1991 (double-blind placebo-controlled study, 13 patients): botulinum toxin A markedly reduced voice perturbation and improved spectrographic voice characteristics versus saline; patients rated significant improvement
cards.summary: Troung 1991 (double-blind placebo-controlled study, 13 patients): botulinum toxin A markedly reduced voice perturbation and improved spectrographic voice characteristics versus saline; patients rated significant improvement
cards.people: 13 patients with adductor spasmodic dysphonia, diagnosed independently by speech pathologists, an otolaryngologist and a neurologist, receiving botulinum toxin A or saline injected into each thyroarytenoid muscle under electromyographic and laryngoscopic guidance in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design.
cards.result: Botulinum toxin A markedly reduced perturbation, decreased fundamental frequency range and improved spectrographic characteristics of the voice; fundamental frequency and phonation time were unchanged. Patients injected with toxin noticed significant improvement in their voices compared with the placebo group. Excessive breathiness occurred in two patients and mild bleeding in one in the toxin group; saline injection caused vocal-cord oedema in one patient. The authors concluded toxin A was an effective and safe treatment.
cards.watchOut: Only 13 patients from the founding era of this treatment, with acoustic endpoints and no modern patient-reported voice scale; the record gives no per-group numerical effect sizes, so 'markedly reduced' is the authors' wording, not a quantified effect.
cards.source: Troung DD et al. Double-blind controlled study of botulinum toxin in adductor spasmodic dysphonia. The Laryngoscope. 1991. PMID: 2041443. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hyodo 2021 (multicentre double-blind RCT, 24 patients): aberrant phonemes fell by 7.0 versus 0.2 at 4 weeks (p=0.0148) and improvement persisted 12 weeks — but breathy hoarseness hit 77.3% and aspiration on drinking 40.9%
cards.summary: Hyodo 2021 (multicentre double-blind RCT, 24 patients): aberrant phonemes fell by 7.0 versus 0.2 at 4 weeks (p=0.0148) and improvement persisted 12 weeks — but breathy hoarseness hit 77.3% and aspiration on drinking 40.9%
cards.people: 24 patients (22 with adductor and 2 with abductor spasmodic dysphonia) at multiple Japanese centres in a placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial (with open-label extension) of botulinum toxin (Botox, as published) injected into the intrinsic laryngeal muscles; primary endpoint was change in aberrant morae (phonemes) at 4 weeks.
cards.result: In the adductor group, aberrant morae at 4 weeks fell by 7.0 ± 2.30 (mean ± SE) on botulinum toxin versus 0.2 ± 0.46 on placebo (p=0.0148), and improvement persisted for 12 weeks. The GRBAS strain element fell significantly at 2 weeks, and Voice Handicap Index and visual analogue scores also improved. One of the two abductor patients responded. Adverse events were breathy hoarseness (77.3%) and aspiration when drinking (40.9%), all mild and resolved within 4 weeks. The trial supported regulatory approval of the treatment in Japan.
cards.watchOut: The adductor result rests on 22 patients and a phoneme-count endpoint specific to Japanese speech (morae); breathiness in over three-quarters of patients is the expected early effect of the treatment, not a rare complication — patients must be counselled that the first weeks trade strain for breathiness.
cards.source: Hyodo M et al. cards.headline: Paniello 2008 (prospective cycle series, 22 patients): voice quality of life peaked at 77.4/100 at 30% of each 25.9-week cycle and exceeded 75 for only 14% of the cycle — benefit is real but part-time
cards.summary: Paniello 2008 (prospective cycle series, 22 patients): voice quality of life peaked at 77.4/100 at 30% of each 25.9-week cycle and exceeded 75 for only 14% of the cycle — benefit is real but part-time
cards.people: 22 patients with adductor spasmodic dysphonia on stable-dose botulinum toxin injections, followed prospectively with voice-related quality of life (VRQOL) collected every 4 weeks through one to three full injection cycles; mean age 59.8 years; 11 patients completed three cycles.
cards.result: The average injection cycle was 25.9 weeks. Total VRQOL peaked at 77.4 (of 100) at 30% of the cycle, then gradually declined; scores exceeded 75 during only 14% of the cycle (54.6% of the cycle if the threshold is lowered to 70), and averaged 52.8 at the beginning and end of each cycle. Social-emotional subscores were significantly better than physical subscores (P<.05). Results were similar across three cycles in the 11 patients completing all three.
cards.watchOut: No untreated comparator — this card measures the shape of benefit within treated cycles, not efficacy. It is carded because duration-of-benefit is half of this shelf's question and the randomised trials report only 4-12-week windows.

cards.headline: Synthesis: injections work for weeks, not months, and breathiness is the price — POSSIBLE on two very small blinded trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: injections work for weeks, not months, and breathiness is the price — POSSIBLE on two very small blinded trials
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (13 and 24 patients) and one prospective 22-patient injection-cycle series.
cards.result: Blinded evidence shows improved acoustic/phoneme measures and patient-rated voice at 4 weeks (aberrant morae -7.0 vs -0.2, p=0.0148), persisting to 12 weeks; the cycle series shows quality of life peaking mid-cycle and spending most of each ~26-week cycle below peak. Breathiness (up to 77.3%) and transient aspiration (40.9%) are the consistent costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction is consistent and blinded, but the total randomised base is 37 patients with perceptual endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Dosing is individualised and product-specific in practice, and no carded trial compares injection strategies, doses or muscles; abductor dysphonia evidence here is two patients and should not be quoted as established.

shelves.title: Platelet-rich plasma for androgenetic alopecia: hair density rises versus placebo in pooled randomised trials, but diameter gains are inconsistent and publication bias is documented — a SPLIT base
shelves.question: In adults with androgenetic alopecia, does platelet-rich plasma injection improve hair density and diameter versus saline placebo — and how does it compare with topical minoxidil?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the density limb favours platelet-rich plasma (PRP): the 2024 meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (431 patients) found +27.55 hairs/cm² versus placebo, and the two carded primary trials are positive. But the split is real: hair diameter did not significantly beat placebo in the 2023 pooling (and the 2024 diameter estimate's confidence interval crosses zero), heterogeneity is extreme (I² about 96%), the 2024 reviewers document evident publication bias and grade the evidence low quality, and one carded trial's clinical limb is a half-head design whose record mixes human efficacy with a mouse mechanistic experiment. Preparation protocols (activation, centrifugation, session spacing) are heterogeneous and not interchangeable — protocols are stated per report as published, per the clarification exception. The neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere and not re-carded here: shelf #6008 asks oral finasteride versus topical minoxidil head-to-head, and shelf #6009 asks topical minoxidil versus placebo in women; no carded trial here compares PRP directly with minoxidil, so that half of the question remains unanswered by direct evidence.

cards.headline: Gentile 2015 (randomised placebo-controlled half-head trial, 20 men analysed): PRP side gained a mean 45.9 hairs/cm² in total density versus baseline after three monthly treatments; no side effects
cards.summary: Gentile 2015 (randomised placebo-controlled half-head trial, 20 men analysed): PRP side gained a mean 45.9 hairs/cm² in total density versus baseline after three monthly treatments; no side effects
cards.people: 23 men with pattern hair loss enrolled (20 analysed) in a randomised, evaluator-blinded, placebo-controlled half-head study: autologous PRP injected into half the scalp and placebo into the other half, three treatments at 30-day intervals, with computerised trichograms and 2-year follow-up.
cards.result: After three treatment cycles, mean hair number rose by 33.6 hairs in the target area and total hair density by a mean 45.9 hairs/cm² versus baseline values. Microscopy showed increased epidermal thickness and hair-follicle numbers two weeks after the last treatment (p<.05), with more Ki67-positive keratinocytes and small vessels around follicles. No side effects were noted during treatment. Relapse appeared in 4 patients by 12-16 months after the last treatment, and those patients were re-treated.
cards.watchOut: Twenty analysed men, within-person half-head design, and the headline density figure is change versus baseline on the treated side rather than a printed treated-versus-placebo difference — read it as supportive, not definitive. Three of 23 enrolled patients were excluded without the record detailing why.
cards.source: Gentile P et al. The Effect of Platelet-Rich Plasma in Hair Regrowth: A Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial. Stem Cells Translational Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26400925. cards.summary: Qu 2021 (randomised double-blind half-head study, 52 patients): hair count, density, diameter and anagen ratio all improved significantly on the PRP side at 6 months versus the control side
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled half-head study — human limb only (Qu 2021)
cards.people: 52 patients with androgenetic alopecia in China in a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind half-head study of PRP versus control, assessed at 6 months for mean hair count, density, diameter and anagen hair ratio. (The same publication reports a mouse-model mechanistic experiment; only the human clinical limb is carded here — no animal data are used as evidence on this shelf.)
cards.result: Mean hair count, density, diameter and anagen hair ratio in the PRP group showed significant improvement at 6 months compared with the control side. The authors concluded the study proved the therapeutic efficacy and safety of PRP in Chinese patients with androgenetic alopecia.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance without absolute effect sizes for the human outcomes, and the half-head design means 'control' is the patient's other scalp side. The publication's mouse experiments are mechanistic background only and are not evidence for this shelf.

cards.headline: Kieling 2024 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs, 431 patients): density +27.55 hairs/cm² versus placebo (95% CI 14.04-41.06) — but I² 96%, low-quality evidence and evident publication bias; diameter +2.02 µm with CI crossing zero
cards.summary: Kieling 2024 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs, 431 patients): density +27.55 hairs/cm² versus placebo (95% CI 14.04-41.06) — but I² 96%, low-quality evidence and evident publication bias; diameter +2.02 µm with CI crossing zero
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Kieling 2024)
cards.people: Fourteen randomised clinical trials involving 431 patients aged 15-63 with androgenetic alopecia (Norwood I-VII, Ludwig I-III) comparing PRP with placebo for hair density; 13 trials entered the meta-analysis; protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023407334); risk of bias by RoB-2 and certainty by GRADE.
cards.result: Hair density favoured PRP: mean difference 27.55 hairs/cm² (95% CI 14.04-41.06, p<.05) with very high heterogeneity (I²=95.99%). Hair diameter did not clearly favour PRP: mean difference 2.02 µm (95% CI -0.85 to 4.88, I²=77.11%). The authors state the studies were highly heterogeneous and low quality with evident publication bias, grade the evidence low quality, and recommend further high-quality randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's caution card: with I² near 96% and documented publication bias, the pooled +27.55 hairs/cm² is best read as an upper-bound average across incompatible protocols, not an expected result for any single PRP preparation.
cards.source: Kieling L et al. Is autologous platelet-rich plasma capable of increasing hair density in patients with androgenic alopecia? cards.headline: Zhang 2023 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 238 patients): density significantly higher than placebo at 3 and 6 months, but hair count and diameter versus placebo were not significant — the SPLIT in one review
cards.summary: Zhang 2023 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 238 patients): density significantly higher than placebo at 3 and 6 months, but hair count and diameter versus placebo were not significant — the SPLIT in one review
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Zhang 2023)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials involving 238 patients with androgenetic alopecia comparing PRP with placebo for hair density, hair count and hair diameter, searched to March 2022; review registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022362432).
cards.result: PRP increased hair density at 3 and 6 months with statistically significant differences versus placebo (P<.05). PRP increased hair count and hair diameter versus baseline, but there was no significant difference versus placebo for those outcomes (P>.05). Two of seven studies reporting harms described adverse reactions; no serious adverse reactions were found.
cards.watchOut: Smaller and earlier than the 2024 synthesis, with overlapping included trials — the two meta-analyses are not independent confirmations. Its null diameter/count-versus-placebo findings are the reason this shelf is stamped SPLIT rather than POSSIBLE.

cards.summary: Synthesis: density yes, diameter unproven, protocols incomparable — SPLIT, and the minoxidil comparison is still untested head-to-head
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: two small randomised half-head trials (20 and 52 patients) and two meta-analyses (14 trials/431 patients; 9 trials/238 patients, overlapping).
cards.result: Hair density favours PRP over placebo in both primary trials and both poolings (+27.55 hairs/cm² in the largest); hair count and diameter versus placebo are null in one pooling and confidence-interval-crossing in the other; heterogeneity (I² about 96%) and documented publication bias cap confidence. No carded trial compares PRP with topical minoxidil directly — that comparison lives only in combination-therapy reports outside this shelf, while the finasteride-versus-minoxidil and minoxidil-in-women questions are homed on shelves #6008 and #6009. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: PRP is a preparation, not a product: activation, spin protocol and session spacing differ across every carded trial, so a negative or positive result for one protocol does not transfer to another clinic's protocol.

shelves.title: Cysteamine 5% and thiamidol for melasma: both lighten pigmentation about as much as hydroquinone 4% in small randomised trials, with more early irritation from cysteamine
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe melasma, do cysteamine 5% cream or thiamidol-containing regimens improve pigmentation (MASI) versus hydroquinone or vehicle, and how do irritation and relapse compare?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, as hydroquinone alternatives) — both limbs verify with at least three reports each in total across the shelf: cysteamine 5% cream lightened melasma in two randomised comparisons with hydroquinone 4% (mMASI reductions 21-38% on cysteamine versus 32-53% on hydroquinone — hydroquinone numerically ahead on the index, differences significant in the larger trial), and thiamidol 0.2% matched hydroquinone in one randomised trial (mMASI -43% versus -33%, no significant difference) and beat vehicle over 24 weeks in another, with pigmentation regressing toward baseline after stopping. Tested products as published, per the clarification exception: cysteamine 5% cream (the records do not name a brand or maker); thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol) 0.2% in the hydroquinone comparison, and a thiamidol Dual Serum/Day Care SPF30/Night Care regimen in the vehicle trial (maker not named in either record). This shelf is a PARTIAL completion: shelf #4222 asks the triple-combination cream versus hydroquinone question and is not re-carded here; the oral tranexamic acid slice is a separate shelf again. Irritation: cysteamine caused more early local effects (erythema, burning) than hydroquinone; thiamidol's effects were mild, with allergic contact dermatitis in 2 of about 25 hydroquinone users in the comparison trial record as published.

cards.headline: Lima 2020 (multicentre evaluator-blinded trial, 40 women): mMASI fell 38% on cysteamine 5% versus 53% on hydroquinone 4% at 120 days (P=0.017) — effective, but hydroquinone ahead on the index
cards.summary: Lima 2020 (multicentre evaluator-blinded trial, 40 women): mMASI fell 38% on cysteamine 5% versus 53% on hydroquinone 4% at 120 days (P=0.017) — effective, but hydroquinone ahead on the index
cards.people: 40 women with facial melasma in a quasi-randomised, multicentre, evaluator-blinded trial of nightly 5% cysteamine cream or 4% hydroquinone cream for 120 days, both groups using tinted sunscreen (SPF 50); assessed by modified MASI, MELASQoL, colourimetry and standardised photographs at 60 and 120 days. The record does not name a brand or maker for the cysteamine cream.
cards.result: Mean mMASI reduction was 24% on cysteamine versus 41% on hydroquinone at 60 days (P=0.015) and 38% versus 53% at 120 days (P=0.017). Photographic evaluation showed up to 74% improvement in both groups without a significant between-group difference (P=0.087), and colourimetry showed progressive depigmentation in both groups (P>0.160 between groups). Quality of life (MELASQoL) fell progressively in both groups, more on hydroquinone at 120 days (P=0.018). No severe adverse effects occurred; erythema and burning were the main local effects with cysteamine, at frequencies not significantly different from hydroquinone (P>0.170).
cards.watchOut: Quasi-randomised and only 40 women; the honest reading is 'cysteamine works, hydroquinone works a bit more on the index' — this card does not support claiming equivalence, and photographic/global ratings (which showed no difference) are softer endpoints than mMASI.
cards.source: Lima PB et al. A comparative study of topical 5% cysteamine versus 4% hydroquinone in the treatment of facial melasma in women. International Journal of Dermatology. 2020. PMID: 32864760. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cysteamine; Female; Humans; Hydroquinones; Hyperpigmentation; Melanosis; Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Nguyen 2021 (double-blind RCT, 20 recruited, 14 completing): mMASI fell 21.3% on cysteamine versus 32% on hydroquinone at 16 weeks — difference not significant (P=0.3); cysteamine less well tolerated
cards.summary: Nguyen 2021 (double-blind RCT, 20 recruited, 14 completing): mMASI fell 21.3% on cysteamine versus 32% on hydroquinone at 16 weeks — difference not significant (P=0.3); cysteamine less well tolerated
cards.people: 20 participants in Victoria, Australia, randomised double-blind to cysteamine cream or hydroquinone cream for 16 weeks; 14 completed (5 cysteamine, 9 hydroquinone); primary outcome change in modified MASI, analysed intention-to-treat. The record does not name a brand or maker for either cream.
cards.result: At week 16, mMASI fell by 1.52 ± 0.69 points (21.3%) on cysteamine and 2.96 ± 1.15 points (32%) on hydroquinone; the between-group difference was not statistically significant (P=0.3). Hydroquinone was generally better tolerated; cysteamine side effects were more common but mild and reversible. The authors concluded cysteamine may have comparable efficacy and offers an alternative for patients wishing to avoid or rotate off hydroquinone, while calling for larger trials.
cards.watchOut: Very small and leaky: 6 of 20 participants did not complete, asymmetrically (the cysteamine arm finished with 5). A non-significant difference in a 20-person trial is absence of evidence, not evidence of equivalence.

cards.headline: Lima 2021 (evaluator-blinded RCT, 50 women): thiamidol 0.2% cut mMASI by 43% versus 33% on hydroquinone 4% at 90 days — no significant difference between groups (P≥0.09); only mild effects on thiamidol
cards.summary: Lima 2021 (evaluator-blinded RCT, 50 women): thiamidol 0.2% cut mMASI by 43% versus 33% on hydroquinone 4% at 90 days — no significant difference between groups (P≥0.09); only mild effects on thiamidol
cards.people: 50 women with facial melasma (mean age 43 years; 86% phototypes III-IV) randomised to a double layer of 0.2% thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol) twice daily or 4% hydroquinone cream at bedtime for 90 days, both with tinted sunscreen (SPF 60); one hydroquinone participant did not complete. The record does not name the thiamidol product's brand or maker.
cards.result: Both groups reduced mMASI, MELASQoL and colour-contrast scores (P<0.01 within groups). Mean mMASI reduction was 43% (95% CI 35-50%) on thiamidol versus 33% (23-42%) on hydroquinone, with no significant between-group difference in mMASI, quality of life, colourimetry or global improvement (P≥0.09). Global improvement was rated in 84% on thiamidol versus 74% on hydroquinone. Adverse effects on thiamidol were only mild; allergic contact dermatitis occurred in two participants (8%) in the hydroquinone group as reported.
cards.watchOut: Ninety days in one centre, run September-November (falling UV season in the study hemisphere context matters for melasma); 'no significant difference' in 50 patients leaves room for a real difference in either direction.

cards.headline: Roggenkamp 2021 (double-blind vehicle-controlled RCT, 48 women): thiamidol regimen beat vehicle on MASI at every time point over 24 weeks (P<0.001-0.043) — and the advantage had washed out 13-20 weeks after stopping
cards.summary: Roggenkamp 2021 (double-blind vehicle-controlled RCT, 48 women): thiamidol regimen beat vehicle on MASI at every time point over 24 weeks (P<0.001-0.043) — and the advantage had washed out 13-20 weeks after stopping
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trial with regression phase (Roggenkamp 2021)
cards.people: 48 women with moderate-to-severe melasma (phototypes III-V) randomised to a thiamidol regimen (Dual Serum daily, plus Day Care SPF30 in the morning or Night Care in the evening, all containing thiamidol; n=23) or the same routine with vehicle formulations (n=25) for 24 weeks, with a follow-up visit 13-20 weeks after treatment ended. The record does not name the regimen's brand or maker.
cards.result: Clinical photography and MASI improved on thiamidol significantly versus baseline (p<0.001) and versus vehicle (p<0.001-0.043) at all time points to treatment end. At follow-up after stopping, MASI was still significantly lower than baseline but no longer differed between thiamidol and vehicle groups. Skin lightness and quality of life improved versus baseline without significant between-group differences. Thiamidol was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The regression phase is the key honesty check: gains fade after stopping, as with hydroquinone — thiamidol is maintenance therapy, not a cure. The multi-product regimen (serum plus day/night creams) also means the tested intervention is a routine, not a single cream.
cards.source: Roggenkamp D et al. Thiamidol in moderate-to-severe melasma: 24-week, randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled clinical study with subsequent regression phase. cards.headline: Synthesis: two credible non-hydroquinone options, neither shown better than hydroquinone — POSSIBLE as alternatives, with relapse on stopping
cards.summary: Synthesis: two credible non-hydroquinone options, neither shown better than hydroquinone — POSSIBLE as alternatives, with relapse on stopping
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: cysteamine versus hydroquinone in 40 and 20 women; thiamidol versus hydroquinone in 50 women and versus vehicle in 48 women. The triple-combination question is homed on shelf #4222 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Cysteamine 5% lightens melasma (mMASI -21% to -38%) but trailed hydroquinone numerically in both trials, significantly in the larger one (-38% vs -53%). Thiamidol matched hydroquinone (-43% vs -33%, not significant) and beat vehicle over 24 weeks, with the advantage gone 13-20 weeks after stopping. Irritation is early and mild-to-moderate, worse with cysteamine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit as hydroquinone alternatives): real lightening in every trial, but small samples, short horizons and no superiority over hydroquinone anywhere.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial exceeds 120 days of treatment or 50 participants per comparison, none tests cysteamine against thiamidol, and brand/maker information for the tested creams is absent from the records — current retail products may differ from what was trialled.

shelves.title: Daylight versus conventional photodynamic therapy for actinic keratoses: clearance is similar for thin lesions and lower when thick lesions are included — with far less pain
shelves.question: In adults with facial actinic keratoses, is daylight photodynamic therapy as effective as conventional (lamp) photodynamic therapy for lesion clearance, with less pain?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is by lesion grade. Pooled across six randomised trials (369 patients, 5,556 lesions, methyl aminolevulinate with red light as the conventional arm), complete response did not differ significantly overall (relative risk 0.93, p=0.07); daylight therapy was non-inferior where trials included only grade I-II lesions (relative risk 0.97) but less effective where grade III (thick) lesions were included (relative risk 0.87, p<0.001). The pain limb is not split: daylight therapy's maximal pain score was 4.51 points lower (pooled mean difference) and adverse events fewer (relative risk 0.70), and the founding split-face trial found lesion reductions of 79% (daylight) versus 71% (lamp). Tested photosensitiser as published: methyl aminolevulinate (MAL) cream in the pooled and founding trials; the Chinese trial used photodynamic therapy as practised locally (record names aminolevulinic-acid class agents). Daylight dose depends on latitude and season — the founding trials are Danish, the confirmatory trial is from Shanghai, China.

cards.headline: Mei 2019 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 369 patients, 5,556 lesions): complete response relative risk 0.93 overall (p=0.07) — non-inferior in grade I-II-only studies (0.97), inferior where grade III lesions were included (0.87, p<0.001); pain -4.51 points
cards.summary: Mei 2019 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 369 patients, 5,556 lesions): complete response relative risk 0.93 overall (p=0.07) — non-inferior in grade I-II-only studies (0.97), inferior where grade III lesions were included (0.87, p<0.001); pain -4.51 points
cards.people: Six randomised trials with 369 patients and 5,556 actinic keratosis lesions comparing daylight photodynamic therapy with conventional photodynamic therapy (red light, methyl aminolevulinate), searched in PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library.
cards.result: Overall complete response did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.93, p=0.07). In subgroup analysis, daylight therapy was non-inferior for complete response in studies including only grade I-II lesions (relative risk 0.97, p=0.41) but less effective in studies that also included grade III lesions (relative risk 0.87, p<0.001). Daylight therapy had a significantly lower maximal pain score (mean difference -4.51, p<0.001) and a lower risk of adverse events (relative risk 0.70, p<0.001). All relative risks are relative measures; the record does not print pooled absolute clearance rates beside them.
cards.watchOut: The grade-III subgroup contrast is between studies, not within them, so it may partly reflect study-level differences (geography, protocols) rather than lesion grade alone. Lesion-level pooling (5,556 lesions in 369 patients) overstates statistical independence.
cards.source: Mei X et al. Daylight versus conventional photodynamic therapy for the treatment of actinic keratosis: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Photodiagnosis and Photodynamic Therapy. 2019. PMID: 30412779. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wiegell 2008 (randomised split-face trial, 29 patients, Denmark): lesion reduction 79% with daylight versus 71% with red-LED conventional PDT (P=0.13) — and LED illumination was significantly more painful (P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Wiegell 2008 (randomised split-face trial, 29 patients, Denmark): lesion reduction 79% with daylight versus 71% with red-LED conventional PDT (P=0.13) — and LED illumination was significantly more painful (P<0.0001)
cards.people: 29 patients with actinic keratoses of the face and scalp treated with methyl aminolevulinate PDT in two symmetrical areas: one side illuminated by red LED light (37 J/cm²) after 3 hours' occlusive incubation, the other exposed to daylight for 2.5 hours after 30 minutes' occlusion.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in treatment effect (P=0.13): actinic keratosis lesions fell by 79% in the daylight area versus 71% in the LED area. Response in the daylight area did not depend on daylight intensity. Illumination with LED was more painful than daylight (P<0.0001). Erythema and crusting occurred after both treatments and were similar between areas.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine patients at Danish latitude — daylight dose there is not daylight dose in Arizona or Queensland, and winter treatment was not tested. A P=0.13 in 29 patients cannot exclude a moderate efficacy difference.
cards.source: Wiegell SR et al. cards.headline: Zhu 2018 (randomised trial, 60 patients, Shanghai): lesion clearance 95.5% with daylight PDT versus 96.8% with conventional PDT after three sessions — pain scores 1.7 versus 5.2, adverse events 36.7% versus 63.3%
cards.summary: Zhu 2018 (randomised trial, 60 patients, Shanghai): lesion clearance 95.5% with daylight PDT versus 96.8% with conventional PDT after three sessions — pain scores 1.7 versus 5.2, adverse events 36.7% versus 63.3%
cards.people: 60 patients with actinic keratoses (grades I-III) in Shanghai, China, randomised to daylight or conventional photodynamic therapy, one session every two weeks for three sessions; 55 patients completed the study; endpoints were lesion response, pain scores and adverse events one month after the third session.
cards.result: Overall lesion clearance was 95.5% with daylight PDT versus 96.8% with conventional PDT. In some sites (eyebrow and sideburns), conventional PDT cured more lesions. Pain was nearly absent with daylight therapy: scores 1.7 ± 0.9 versus 5.2 ± 1.7 with conventional therapy. Fewer daylight patients had related adverse events (36.7% vs 63.3%).
cards.watchOut: Three treatment sessions (the European daylight protocol is usually one or two), lesion-level clearance percentages without a printed significance test in the record, and grades I-III pooled — the grade-specific split from the meta-analysis cannot be checked in this trial's record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: choose daylight for thin lesions and pain-averse patients; keep the lamp for thick lesions — SPLIT by grade
cards.summary: Synthesis: choose daylight for thin lesions and pain-averse patients; keep the lamp for thick lesions — SPLIT by grade
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: a 6-trial meta-analysis (369 patients, 5,556 lesions), a 29-patient Danish split-face trial and a 60-patient Shanghai randomised trial.
cards.result: Clearance: statistically indistinguishable overall (relative risk 0.93; 79% vs 71% lesion reduction split-face; 95.5% vs 96.8% after three sessions), with the pooled subgroup signal that daylight loses ground when grade III lesions are in the mix (relative risk 0.87). Pain and adverse events favour daylight everywhere (pain -4.51 pooled points; 1.7 vs 5.2 in Shanghai; adverse-event relative risk 0.70). PROPOSED SPLIT: efficacy splits by lesion grade, tolerability does not split at all.
cards.watchOut: All carded daylight evidence is northern-temperate or Shanghai latitude with treatment in usable daylight; equatorial, high-UV and winter protocols are untested in this record, and sunscreen/aftercare details differ between protocols.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mei X et al. Photodiagnosis and Photodynamic Therapy. 2019 (PMID: 30412779); Wiegell SR et al. The British Journal of Dermatology. 2008 (PMID: 18294318); Zhu L et al. Photodiagnosis and Photodynamic Therapy. 2018 (PMID: 30336290).

shelves.title: Autologous skin cell suspension (RECELL) for burns: healing matches conventional grafting with about a third less donor skin in the pivotal trial, and re-epithelialisation is about 1.7 days faster in pooled trials
shelves.question: In patients with deep partial- or full-thickness burns, does autologous skin cell suspension sprayed over widely meshed autograft (the RECELL programme) reduce donor-skin requirements and match healing/graft take versus conventional autografting?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the tested system is named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: the RECELL System / RECELL Autologous Cell Harvesting Device (AVITA Medical, as published). In the pivotal within-subject randomised trial (30 patients, mixed-depth burns), cell suspension over widely meshed graft healed 92% versus 85% of control areas at 8 weeks (non-inferiority met) while using 32% less donor skin (relative measure, P<.001). In the deep partial-thickness trial, healing at 4 weeks was 98% versus 100% for conventional grafting, while donor areas were about 40 times smaller and donor sites healed faster with less pain — that record does not state its patient number, so it is printed as N not documented. The 2025 meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (358 patients) found re-epithelialisation 1.71 days faster, but (the treatment made no difference) to complete healing by week 4, pain, scar scores, infection or further-intervention rates. Donor-site and healing endpoints are reported separately throughout, not composited.

cards.headline: Holmes 2019 (pivotal within-subject RCT, 30 patients): 92% versus 85% healed at 8 weeks (non-inferior) with 32% less donor skin used (P<.001) for mixed-depth burns
cards.summary: Holmes 2019 (pivotal within-subject RCT, 30 patients): 92% versus 85% healed at 8 weeks (non-inferior) with 32% less donor skin used (P<.001) for mixed-depth burns
cards.people: 30 subjects with mixed-depth burns (including full-thickness) without confluent dermis at multiple centres; each subject had one area treated with standard meshed split-thickness graft (control) and one area treated with the RECELL System combined with a more widely meshed graft, randomised by area; outcomes included closure, donor skin use, satisfaction and scarring to one year. The system prepares a suspension of the patient's own skin cells at the point of care, using 1 cm² of skin to treat up to 80 cm² of burn, as published.
cards.result: At 8 weeks, 85% of control-treated wounds and 92% of RECELL-treated wounds were healed, establishing non-inferiority for wound healing. Treatment areas were similar in mean size, but mean donor skin use was significantly reduced by 32% (relative measure) with RECELL (p<.001), establishing superiority for donor-skin reduction. Secondary effectiveness and safety outcomes were similar between treatments.
cards.watchOut: Thirty subjects and a within-subject design: the 32% donor saving is relative, and non-inferiority at 8 weeks in mixed-depth burns does not by itself prove equivalence for large full-thickness burns, where the widely meshed graft underneath is doing much of the work.
cards.source: Holmes JH 4th et al. Demonstration of the safety and effectiveness of the RECELL System combined with split-thickness meshed autografts for the reduction of donor skin to treat mixed-depth burn injuries. Burns. 2019. PMID: 30578048. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Holmes 2018 (prospective randomised comparative study, N not documented in the record): 98% versus 100% healed at 4 weeks in deep partial-thickness burns — donor area about 40 times smaller, donor sites healed faster with less pain
cards.summary: Holmes 2018 (prospective randomised comparative study, N not documented in the record): 98% versus 100% healed at 4 weeks in deep partial-thickness burns — donor area about 40 times smaller, donor sites healed faster with less pain
cards.people: Patients with deep partial-thickness burns treated prospectively at multiple centres with the ReCell Autologous Cell Harvesting Device (autologous skin cell suspension) versus meshed split-thickness skin graft (control), with treatment and donor sites followed to one year for healing, scarring and pain. N not documented in the record fetched this session.
cards.result: At 4 weeks, 98% of cell-suspension-treated sites were healed versus 100% of controls; pain and scarring assessments at treatment sites were similar between groups. The mean ReCell donor area was approximately 40 times smaller than the control donor area (P<.0001), significantly more ReCell donor sites were healed at one week (P=.04), and patients reported significantly less donor-site pain over the first 16 weeks (P≤.05 at each time point) and higher long-term satisfaction with donor-site outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The record does not state how many patients were studied, so this card's weight cannot be judged precisely — treat its donor-site findings as supportive of the pivotal trial rather than independent proof. Treatment-site pain and scarring (the treatment made no difference) between groups.

cards.headline: Obeid 2025 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 358 patients): re-epithelialisation 1.71 days faster with cell suspension (P=0.001) — but (the treatment made no difference) to complete healing by week 4, pain, scar scores or infection
cards.summary: Obeid 2025 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 358 patients): re-epithelialisation 1.71 days faster with cell suspension (P=0.001) — but (the treatment made no difference) to complete healing by week 4, pain, scar scores or infection
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Obeid 2025)
cards.people: Nine randomised studies (358 patients) of autologous skin cell suspensions (such as ReCell) versus standard treatment for burn injuries, searched to November 2024 across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and CENTRAL; risk of bias assessed with RoB-2.
cards.result: Time to re-epithelialisation was significantly shorter with cell suspension (mean difference -1.71 days, 95% CI -2.73 to -0.70, p=0.001; moderate heterogeneity, I²=58%). Secondary outcomes showed no significant differences: postoperative pain (p=0.42), POSAS scar scores (p=0.69), Vancouver Scar Scale (p=0.48), complete healing by week 4 (relative risk 0.98, 95% CI 0.94-1.02, p=0.24), infection (relative risk 0.85, p=0.78) and need for further interventions (relative risk 0.15, p=0.07) — that is, on those outcomes the treatment made no difference versus standard care.
cards.watchOut: The pooled suspension trials are not all the RECELL-over-meshed-graft protocol of the pivotal trial, and 1.71 days faster re-epithelialisation did not translate into more complete healing by week 4 — speed of surface closure and finished healing are different endpoints.
cards.source: Obeid FM et al. Effect of Autologous Skin Cell Suspensions Versus Standard Treatment on Re-Epithelialization in Burn Injuries: A Meta-Analysis of RCTs. cards.headline: Synthesis: same healing, less donor skin — the benefit is at the donor site, not the burn — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: same healing, less donor skin — the benefit is at the donor site, not the burn — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: the pivotal 30-patient within-subject trial, the deep partial-thickness comparative trial (N not documented in its record) and a 9-trial, 358-patient meta-analysis.
cards.result: Healing matches conventional grafting (92% vs 85% at 8 weeks; 98% vs 100% at 4 weeks; pooled complete-healing relative risk 0.98 — the treatment made no difference to finished healing), while donor skin use falls (32% relative reduction in the pivotal trial; donor areas about 40 times smaller in the comparative trial) and re-epithelialisation is 1.71 days faster in pooled data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real donor-site advantage on one manufacturer's small randomised base, with no demonstrated advantage in scar quality or pain at the burn itself.
cards.watchOut: Cost, learning curve and performance in very large total-body-surface-area burns are outside the carded record; the donor-skin saving matters most exactly where evidence is thinnest (massive burns with scarce donor sites).

shelves.title: Microwave thermolysis for armpit sweating: beats sham at 30 days, and about 7 in 10 treated patients were still responders at 12 months
shelves.question: In adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, does microwave thermolysis of the sweat glands reduce sweat production and severity durably (12 months or more) versus sham treatment?
shelves.mesh: Hyperhidrosis · Microwaves · Axilla · Sweating · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: One randomised, sham-controlled, blinded trial anchors this slice. In Glaser 2012, 89% (72/81) of microwave-treated adults were responders (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale score 1 or 2) at 30 days versus 54% (21/39) on sham, and the active group's responder rate was 69% when follow-up ended at 12 months. Later reports are smaller and uncontrolled or within-patient: an energy-level comparison in 20 adults found high energy slightly better than medium at 3 months; a telephone survey (18 of 24 patients, mean follow-up 38 months) found a mean HDSS fall of 1.6 points and self-reported sweat reduction of 61-70%; and a 103-patient clinic cohort with 45 survey responders at 3 years found median HDSS improved from 3 to 2. Adverse events were generally mild and transient (swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, nodules), all resolved in the survey cohort within 12 weeks. The tested device is the miraDry microwave system (Miramar Labs) programme device; the sham trial's record describes it as a proprietary microwave energy device. This shelf is the microwave slice of the hyperhidrosis family: the home shelf #2476 covers botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium cloth, and a separate slice covers sofpironium gel - neither is duplicated here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single sham-controlled trial with a large early margin, with durability beyond the trial resting on small cohorts and surveys.

cards.headline: Glaser 2012 (sham-controlled trial): responders 89% on microwave versus 54% on sham at 30 days; 69% still responders at 12 months
cards.summary: Glaser 2012 (sham-controlled trial): responders 89% on microwave versus 54% on sham at 30 days; 69% still responders at 12 months
cards.people: 120 adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale score 3 or 4 and baseline sweat production greater than 50 mg/5 min), randomised to active microwave treatment (81) or sham (39) in a blinded study. The record describes the treatment as a proprietary microwave energy device that isolates and heats target tissue - the miraDry microwave system programme device (Miramar Labs).
cards.result: Thirty days after treatment, the active group had a responder rate (HDSS score of 1 or 2) of 89% (72/81) and the sham group 54% (21/39) (P < .001). Treatment efficacy was stable from 3 months (74%) to 12 months (69%), when follow-up ended; the sham group was followed for 6 months and the active group for 12 months. Adverse events were generally mild, and all but one resolved over time.
cards.watchOut: A single investigational-device trial, and the sham responder rate was high (54%), so the patient-reported HDSS margin is smaller than the headline rates suggest. The 12-month figure has no sham comparator - the sham group was only followed for 6 months.
cards.source: Glaser DA et al.. A randomized, blinded clinical evaluation of a novel microwave device for treating axillary hyperhidrosis: the dermatologic reduction in underarm perspiration study.. Dermatologic surgery : official publication for American Society for Dermatologic Surgery [et al.]. 2012. PMID: 22289389. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Grove 2023: high-energy microwave beat medium-energy slightly at 3 months in a 20-patient within-patient comparison
cards.summary: Grove 2023: high-energy microwave beat medium-energy slightly at 3 months in a 20-patient within-patient comparison
cards.type: Prospective randomised within-patient controlled study (energy-level comparison)
cards.people: 20 adults with axillary hyperhidrosis and osmidrosis in a prospective, randomised, patient-blinded, intraindividually controlled study: one axilla received microwave thermolysis at medium energy (level 3) and the other at high energy (level 5), with 3 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Overall Dermatology Life Quality Index fell from a median of 10 to 4 (median reduction 6.5 points, p = 0.0002). HDSS fell from a median of 4 to 2 on both sides, with a median reduction of 1 point for medium energy and 2 points for high energy (p = 0.014). Odor scores fell from a median of 8 to 3 on both sides. Local skin reactions were mild and transient, but slightly more pronounced after high-energy treatment.
cards.watchOut: No untreated or sham control - both axillae were treated, so this card speaks to energy setting, not to whether microwave works. Small (20 patients) and short (3 months).
cards.source: Grove GL et al.. Impact of microwave thermolysis energy levels on patient-reported outcomes for axillary hyperhidrosis and osmidrosis.. Lasers in surgery and medicine. 2023. PMID: 36229952. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lin 2021 (long-term survey): HDSS down 1.6 points and sweat down 61-70% at a mean of 38 months, in 18 respondents
cards.summary: Lin 2021 (long-term survey): HDSS down 1.6 points and sweat down 61-70% at a mean of 38 months, in 18 respondents
cards.type: Long-term follow-up survey of a treated cohort (no control group)
cards.people: 24 patients treated with a microwave energy device for bilateral axillary hyperhidrosis between 2014 and 2018, of whom 18 completed a standardised telephone survey; mean follow-up 38 months (range 12-52).
cards.result: Mean HDSS was reduced by 1.6 points (95% CI 1.2-2.0, p < .01) and mean sweat reduction was 61-70%. Sixty-seven percent reported reduced odor and 54% no longer required deodorant. Adverse effects included bruising (67%), pain (56%), swelling (44%), numbness (28%) and nodules (22%); 66% of side effects resolved within 2 weeks and all resolved within 12 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Only 18 of 24 patients responded, outcomes are self-reported years later with no control group, and recall and responder bias are likely - this is durability colouring, not proof.
cards.source: Lin MJ et al.. A survey of long-term results with microwave energy device for treating axillary hyperhidrosis.. Journal of cosmetic and laser therapy : official publication of the European Society for Laser Dermatology. 2021. PMID: 34409892. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Micu 2026 (3-year clinic cohort): HDSS median 3 to 2 and quality-of-life score median 26 to 6 among 45 responders
cards.summary: Micu 2026 (3-year clinic cohort): HDSS median 3 to 2 and quality-of-life score median 26 to 6 among 45 responders
cards.type: Single-centre cohort with 3-year postal survey follow-up (no control group)
cards.people: 103 patients with severe primary axillary hyperhidrosis who received one or two microwave (Miradry) treatments at a Swedish dermatology clinic between 2020 and 2022; 87 were contacted at 3 years and 45 returned the survey (response rate 51.7%).
cards.result: At 3 years, statistically significant improvement was observed in both HDSS (median 3 at inclusion to median 2 at 3 years) and the Hyperhidrosis Quality of Life index (median 26 at baseline to median 6 at 3 years) among responders.
cards.watchOut: Barely half of contacted patients responded, so satisfied patients are likely over-represented; there is no comparator and no objective sweat measurement at 3 years.
cards.source: Micu E et al.. Three-Year Results Following Microwave Therapy in Patients with Severe Primary Axillary Hyperhidrosis.. Aesthetic plastic surgery. 2026. PMID: 41326743. cards.headline: Synthesis: one sham-controlled trial plus small cohorts - POSSIBLE (benefit), durability graded separately
cards.summary: Synthesis: one sham-controlled trial plus small cohorts - POSSIBLE (benefit), durability graded separately
cards.people: Adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis across one 120-patient sham-controlled trial, one 20-patient within-patient energy study, and two uncontrolled follow-up reports (24 treated / 18 surveyed; 103 treated / 45 surveyed).
cards.result: Microwave thermolysis beat sham at 30 days (89% versus 54% responders) and held a 69% responder rate at 12 months in the trial; cohort and survey reports remain favourable out to about 3 years but have no controls and substantial non-response. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Durability past 12 months rests entirely on uncontrolled surveys and cohorts. The home shelf #2476 (botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium cloth for the same condition) is cross-pointed, not duplicated; no head-to-head trial of microwave versus those treatments was carded here.

shelves.title: Fractional laser for hypertrophic burn scars: split - one within-scar trial clearly positive, one mixed, one donor-site trial found no difference
shelves.question: In patients with hypertrophic burn scars, does fractional laser treatment (ablative carbon dioxide or non-ablative, as tested) improve scar pliability, thickness and symptoms versus untreated or conventionally treated control scars?
shelves.mesh: Burns · Cicatrix, Hypertrophic · Lasers, Gas · Laser Therapy · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: The randomised base is small and it points in different directions - a genuine split. A paediatric split-scar trial (23 enrolled, 20 completed) found total Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS) scores of 44.95 on low-energy fractional carbon dioxide laser sites versus 64.85 on untreated control sites at 6 months. The ELIPSE trial (15 adults, each patient their own control, three ablative fractional CO2 treatments) found no significant difference in Vancouver Scar Scale (VSS), erythema or pigmentation, although patient POSAS thickness and texture improved and blinded photo raters scored treated scars better. A donor-site scar trial (20 patients) found laser-treated and standard-care-only sites were not different on any measure over time (the treatment made no difference). A three-arm trial of pulsed dye laser, ablative fractional CO2, or both found improvement in all arms with the largest (non-significant) gains for combination treatment, mainly in immature scars; its record does not state the patient number. Laser-assisted drug delivery is a separate question and is not carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit is shown against untreated within-scar controls in one small trial, mixed in a second, and absent in a third - scar type (early burn scar versus donor-site scar) and control choice appear to decide the result.

cards.headline: Won 2022 (paediatric split-scar trial): POSAS total 44.95 on laser sites versus 64.85 on control sites at 6 months
cards.summary: Won 2022 (paediatric split-scar trial): POSAS total 44.95 on laser sites versus 64.85 on control sites at 6 months
cards.people: 23 patients aged under 12 years with hypertrophic scars enrolled (20 completed) in a prospective, randomised, split-scar study; each scar was divided, with the two ends randomly assigned to low-energy carbon dioxide fractional laser or control and the centre excluded as a transition zone. Three laser treatments were given at 1-month intervals.
cards.result: At 6 months after the final treatment, total POSAS score was significantly lower (better) for the treated site (44.95) than the control site (64.85, p < 0.0001); patient scores were 19.95 versus 29.95 and observer scores 26.00 versus 34.90 (both p < 0.0001). Pain, pruritus, color, stiffness and thickness scores all favoured the treated site; irregularity did not differ. Average treatment-pain score was 3.5 of 10.
cards.watchOut: Children only, early-stage scars, and a within-scar untreated control - this shows laser beats no treatment on the same scar, not that it beats conventional scar care. Small: 20 completers.
cards.source: Won T et al.. The efficacy and safety of low-energy carbon dioxide fractional laser use in the treatment of early-stage pediatric hypertrophic scars: A prospective, randomized, split-scar study.. Lasers in surgery and medicine. 2022. PMID: 34487566. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ELIPSE 2023: no difference on Vancouver scores, but patient-rated thickness and texture improved and blinded raters preferred treated scars
cards.summary: ELIPSE 2023: no difference on Vancouver scores, but patient-rated thickness and texture improved and blinded raters preferred treated scars
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial (ELIPSE; within-patient control)
cards.people: 15 adult patients with a burn-related scar about 3 months after injury, each with two comparable non-contiguous scar areas of 1% total body surface area; areas were randomised to three ablative fractional carbon dioxide laser treatments at 6-week intervals or control, each patient acting as their own control, with follow-up to 12 months.
cards.result: No significant difference was found in Vancouver Scar Scale, scar erythema, or pigmentation. Patient POSAS improved in scar thickness and texture following laser. All elements of the Brisbane Burn Scar Impact Profile improved in both control and laser groups. Blinded raters scored laser-treated scars better than controls on photo assessment. Gene-expression analysis showed sustained changes in fibroblasts from treated scars.
cards.watchOut: Only 15 patients, and the scar-impact profile improved just as much in control scars - early burn scars improve on their own, which is exactly what a control arm is for. The positive signals are patient-rated texture/thickness and photo ratings, not the blinded VSS.
cards.source: Lewis CJ et al.. Carbon dioxide laser treatment of burn-related scarring: Results of the ELIPSE (Early Laser Intervention Promotes Scar Evolution) prospective randomized controlled trial.. Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS. 2023. PMID: 37393760. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: D'Orio 2025 (donor-site scars): laser and standard care were not different on any measure (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: D'Orio 2025 (donor-site scars): laser and standard care were not different on any measure (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 20 burn patients whose split-thickness skin-graft donor-site scars were randomised to six ablative fractional CO2 laser treatments plus standard care or standard care only, with serial biopsies and scar scales (POSAS, Vancouver Scar Scale, and an institutional comparison scale).
cards.result: Over time, donor-site control and donor-site treated sites were not different in transepidermal water loss, elasticity, erythema, melanin index, cellularity, rete ridge ratio, epidermal thickness, POSAS-observer, POSAS-patient, VSS, or comparison-scale scores. Patient-perceived scores improved in all sites, including controls, over the study course.
cards.watchOut: Donor-site scars are not hypertrophic burn scars proper - they are the trial's deliberate substitute site, chosen because withholding laser from grafted hypertrophic scars troubled clinicians. The null may not transfer to true hypertrophic scars, but it is the only carded trial with a standard-care control.

cards.headline: Kivi 2024: all laser arms improved; combination pulsed dye plus fractional CO2 improved most, but not significantly
cards.summary: Kivi 2024: all laser arms improved; combination pulsed dye plus fractional CO2 improved most, but not significantly
cards.type: Single-blinded randomised controlled trial (three laser arms, no untreated control)
cards.people: Patients with hypertrophic or keloid burn scars randomised in a single-blinded trial to pulsed dye laser alone, ablative fractional carbon dioxide laser alone, or the combination; scars were assessed before treatment and 40 days after the last session. The record does not state the number of patients - N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In all groups, Vancouver Scar Scale score, scar color, vascularity, height and pliability improved significantly; improvement was greatest in the combination group, particularly for vascularity and pliability, although the superiority of the combined group was not statistically significant. The advantage of combination over pulsed dye alone appeared in immature scars (under 1 year) but not mature scars.
cards.watchOut: No untreated or conventional-care arm, so improvement over time cannot be separated from natural scar maturation; a 2026 published letter questioned the trial's scar-count and Vancouver-score reporting, so treat its numbers as unsettled. N not documented in the record.

shelves.title: Picosecond versus nanosecond lasers for tattoo removal: split - faster clearance in three head-to-head studies, no clearance advantage in two
shelves.question: In adults seeking tattoo removal, do picosecond-domain lasers clear pigment faster (fewer sessions to 75% or greater clearance) than nanosecond Q-switched lasers, by ink colour, and at what cost in blistering and dyspigmentation?
shelves.mesh: Tattooing · Laser Therapy · Lasers, Solid-State · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Five head-to-head comparisons, and they split. The 1998 intratattoo trial (16 patients, black tattoos, all parameters held constant except pulse duration) found picosecond pulses lightened significantly more than nanosecond pulses in 12 of 16 tattoos. The largest randomised split-tattoo study (49 patients) reached 75% or greater clearance in 33% of picosecond halves versus 14% of nanosecond halves (P = 0.008), driven by black/blue tattoos (34% versus 9%); only 1 of 5 polychromic tattoos cleared that well on either laser. The newest randomised split-tattoo trial (30 subjects, 755-nm alexandrite both arms) found higher clearance scores and satisfactory clearance in 73.3% versus 23.3%. Against that, a randomised split-study of 1064-nm Nd:YAG (21 patients, 30 black tattoos, two sessions) found no difference in clearance at all (P = 1.00), though picosecond hurt less (pain 3.8 versus 7.9 of 10), and a retrospective eyeliner-tattoo comparison (40 versus 32 patients) found no difference after one session. Harms: blistering and crusting were less frequent with picosecond in the alexandrite trial, but hyperpigmentation was more frequent (21.33% versus 12%). Several programmes are industry-supported and device-specific; tested devices are named per card as published, and where the record names no commercial device that is stated. PROPOSED SPLIT: picosecond clears black/blue ink faster in most comparisons, but the advantage disappears in the 1064-nm two-session trial and in eyeliner tattoos, and it does not extend to polychromic ink.

cards.headline: Ross 1998: picosecond pulses lightened black tattoos significantly more than nanosecond pulses in 12 of 16 tattoos
cards.summary: Ross 1998: picosecond pulses lightened black tattoos significantly more than nanosecond pulses in 12 of 16 tattoos
cards.type: Intratattoo controlled comparison trial (single-blind photographic assessment)
cards.people: 16 consecutive patients with black tattoos, all completing the study, in an intratattoo comparison: designated parts of the same tattoo were treated with 35-picosecond or 10-nanosecond pulses from two Nd:YAG lasers, four treatments at 4-week intervals, with every parameter except pulse duration held constant (0.65 J/cm2). The record names no commercial device.
cards.result: On completion, blinded dermatologists rating photographs found significant lightening in the picosecond-treated areas compared with nanosecond-treated areas in 12 of 16 tattoos. Mean depth of pigment alteration was greater for picosecond pulses but not significantly; biopsy and in-vitro ink findings were similar for both pulse durations.
cards.watchOut: Black ink only, a laboratory prototype comparison from 1998, and only four treatments - it establishes the pulse-duration principle, not modern commercial-device performance.
cards.source: Ross V et al.. Comparison of responses of tattoos to picosecond and nanosecond Q-switched neodymium: YAG lasers.. Archives of dermatology. 1998. PMID: 9487208. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lorgeou 2018 (49 patients): clearance of 75% or more in 33% of picosecond halves versus 14% of nanosecond halves
cards.summary: Lorgeou 2018 (49 patients): clearance of 75% or more in 33% of picosecond halves versus 14% of nanosecond halves
cards.people: 49 adults with all types of tattoos (85.7% professional, 8.2% permanent make-up, 6.1% non-professional; mostly black or blue, 10.2% polychromatic) in a prospective randomised split-tattoo study: one half treated with a picosecond laser, the other with a nanosecond laser, assessed on standardised pictures 2 months after the last session by two blinded physicians. The record does not name the commercial devices.
cards.result: A reduction of 75% or more in colour intensity was obtained for 33% of tattoos treated with the picosecond lasers compared with 14% with the nanosecond laser (P = 0.008). For monochrome black or blue tattoos, improvement over 75% was 34% versus 9%. Only one of the five polychromic tattoos achieved more than 75% improvement with either laser type. Side-effect differences were minimal, with a tendency for picosecond treatment to be less painful.
cards.watchOut: Two different picosecond lasers were pooled against one nanosecond laser, and absolute clearance remained modest - even on picosecond, two-thirds of tattoos did not reach 75% clearance.
cards.source: Lorgeou A et al.. Comparison of two picosecond lasers to a nanosecond laser for treating tattoos: a prospective randomized study on 49 patients.. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV. 2018. PMID: 28758261. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pinto 2017: no clearance difference between picosecond and nanosecond 1064-nm Nd:YAG after two sessions (P = 1.00) - but picosecond hurt much less
cards.summary: Pinto 2017: no clearance difference between picosecond and nanosecond 1064-nm Nd:YAG after two sessions (P = 1.00) - but picosecond hurt much less
cards.people: 21 patients with 30 black tattoos treated with a picosecond laser and a nanosecond laser (both Nd:YAG, 1064 nm) in a split-study design, two sessions at 6-week intervals, with blinded observers rating randomised digital photographs. The record does not name the commercial devices.
cards.result: Average clearance showed no statistical difference between nanosecond and picosecond treatment (P = 1.00). Pain on a 0-10 scale was 3.8 (SD 1.0) for picosecond versus 7.9 (SD 1.1) for nanosecond (P < 0.001). Transient side-effects and hypo- and hyperpigmentation occurred with no significant difference between the lasers.
cards.watchOut: Only two treatment sessions - a speed advantage for picosecond, if any at this wavelength, may need more sessions to appear; equally, the trial is the cleanest same-wavelength comparison and it found none.
cards.source: Pinto F et al.. cards.headline: Ma 2026 (755-nm alexandrite, split-tattoo): satisfactory clearance 73.3% with picosecond versus 23.3% with nanosecond
cards.summary: Ma 2026 (755-nm alexandrite, split-tattoo): satisfactory clearance 73.3% with picosecond versus 23.3% with nanosecond
cards.people: 30 subjects with professional (53.3%), amateur (33.3%) or cosmetic (13.3%) black/blue tattoos in a prospective randomised split-tattoo trial: one half treated with a 755-nm picosecond alexandrite laser, the other with a 755-nm nanosecond alexandrite laser, at 3-month intervals for five sessions, with 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: Picosecond achieved higher clearance scores (median 8, IQR 6-9, versus 5, IQR 2.75-6.25; p < 0.0001) and more satisfactory clearance (score 7 or more: 73.3% versus 23.3%; p = 0.0003). Complete clearance occurred in 10% of picosecond sites versus none with nanosecond. Pain was lower with picosecond. Bleeding (2% versus 8%), blistering (7.33% versus 15.33%) and crusting (7.33% versus 15.33%) were less frequent with picosecond, but hyperpigmentation was more frequent (21.33% versus 12%; p = 0.043).
cards.watchOut: Black/blue tattoos only, a single-centre 2026 trial, and the hyperpigmentation excess runs against picosecond - the clearance win is not cost-free, especially in skin prone to pigment change.
cards.source: Ma G et al.. 755-nm Picosecond vs. Nanosecond Alexandrite Lasers for Tattoo Removal: A Randomized, Split-Tattoo Clinical Trial.. Plastic and reconstructive surgery. 2026. PMID: 41729109. Registry ID: ChiCTR2300069281 (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, stated in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Zhang 2018 (retrospective, eyeliner tattoos): no difference between picosecond alexandrite and nanosecond Nd:YAG
cards.summary: Zhang 2018 (retrospective, eyeliner tattoos): no difference between picosecond alexandrite and nanosecond Nd:YAG
cards.people: 72 patients with blue-black Chinese eyeliner tattoos present for over 10 years, reviewed retrospectively: 40 treated with an alexandrite picosecond laser (750 ps) and 32 with an Nd:YAG nanosecond laser, all completing at least one treatment and follow-up.
cards.result: The median number of treatments was 1 (range 1-4). After a single session, no difference was found between the two lasers for eyeliner removal (p > 0.05), and among patients achieving an excellent clearance response there was still no difference (p > 0.05). Transient side-effects occurred in both groups with no significant adverse reactions in either.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and observational, and the comparison confounds pulse duration with laser type and wavelength (alexandrite picosecond versus Nd:YAG nanosecond) - it cannot isolate the pulse-duration effect. Most patients had only one session.
cards.source: Zhang M et al.. Comparison of treatment with an Alexandrite picosecond laser and Nd:YAG nanosecond laser for removing blue-black Chinese eyeliner tattoos.. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT - picosecond faster for black/blue ink in three comparisons, no advantage in two, and no help for polychromic ink
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT - picosecond faster for black/blue ink in three comparisons, no advantage in two, and no help for polychromic ink
cards.people: Adults seeking tattoo removal across five head-to-head reports (16, 49, 21, 30 and 72 patients; total 188), four prospective split-tattoo designs and one retrospective comparison.
cards.result: Picosecond cleared more in the 1998 intratattoo trial (12 of 16), the 49-patient randomised study (33% versus 14% reaching 75% clearance) and the 755-nm alexandrite trial (satisfactory clearance 73.3% versus 23.3%); it cleared no more in the 1064-nm two-session trial (P = 1.00) or the eyeliner comparison. Pain consistently favoured picosecond; hyperpigmentation was higher with picosecond in the alexandrite trial. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Results are colour-, wavelength- and session-count-specific and must not be pooled into a single 'picosecond is better' claim; several device programmes are industry-supported, and commercial device names are absent from most records.

shelves.title: Sebum excretion rates (physiology): low in childhood, rising at puberty, steady in men to age 80, and falling gradually in women after the menopause
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast is sebum excreted - sebum excretion rates and casual levels by site, sex and age (the post-pubertal peak and the post-menopausal fall), measured by absorbent-tape and solvent-extraction methods?
shelves.mesh: Sebum · Sebaceous Glands · Aging · Sex Factors · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing here is thin (Boron & Boulpaep; Ganong cover skin appendages briefly), and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as stated plainly. Two quantities are measured: the casual level (surface lipid on unprepared skin) and the sebum excretion rate (SER, surface lipid flow from a previously cleaned area, by absorbent-paper gravimetry in the Strauss-Pochi tradition and by photometric tape/sebumeter methods since). The age pattern is concordant: Pochi, Strauss and Downing (1979) found secretion low in children, rising from mid-to-late childhood under androgen influence into the late teens, then essentially unchanged in men until age 80, while in women secretion falls gradually after the menopause with no further change after the seventh decade - attributed to falling endogenous androgen production, with glands paradoxically enlarging as cellular turnover slows. Modern measurement cohorts add scale and variability: casual level and SER run 1.6-2.1 times higher in self-described oily than dry skin (62 Thai women), forehead SER measured twice 7 days apart in 40 healthy adults varied with sleep timing, free testosterone and 5-alpha-reductase type 1 expression in women, and parallel trials in 100 Japanese and 30 Caucasian volunteers formalised the SER-versus-casual-level distinction across populations. This is gland output, a different quantity from transepidermal water loss (barrier leak), which is shelved separately. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Pochi, Strauss & Downing 1979: sebum low in childhood, rises at puberty, holds in men to age 80, falls in women after the menopause
cards.summary: Pochi, Strauss & Downing 1979: sebum low in childhood, rises at puberty, holds in men to age 80, falls in women after the menopause
cards.people: Humans across the lifespan examined in the Pochi-Strauss sebum-production programme by quantitative and qualitative examination of sebum; the record does not state the number of subjects - N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Sebaceous secretion is low in children and begins to increase in mid- to late childhood under the influence of androgens, continuing until the late teens, after which no further significant change takes place until late in life. In elderly men, sebum levels remain essentially unchanged from younger adults until age 80. In women, secretion decreases gradually after menopause and shows no significant change after the seventh decade. Surface lipid levels fall with age while the glands become larger, attributed to decreased cellular turnover; glands retained the capacity to respond to administered androgen (fluoxymesterone).
cards.watchOut: A 1979 programme summary whose record gives the pattern without subject numbers or rate values - carded for the lifespan pattern, which every later cohort reproduces; do not quote a numeric rate from this card.
cards.source: Pochi PE et al.. Age-related changes in sebaceous gland activity.. The Journal of investigative dermatology. 1979. PMID: 448169. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thadanipon 2020: casual sebum and excretion rate 1.6-2.1 times higher in oily-skinned than dry-skinned women (62 volunteers)
cards.summary: Thadanipon 2020: casual sebum and excretion rate 1.6-2.1 times higher in oily-skinned than dry-skinned women (62 volunteers)
cards.people: 62 healthy Thai women with self-described oily or dry skin; casual sebum level (CSL), sebum excretion rate (SER), pore size and stratum corneum hydration measured at several facial sites.
cards.result: Casual sebum level and sebum excretion rate were significantly higher in the oily-skinned than the dry-skinned group, by 1.6-2.1 times. Mean pore area and clinical pore size did not differ between groups and did not correlate with CSL or SER. Corneometry (hydration) was significantly higher in the dry-skinned group and correlated negatively with CSL. Subjective skin type tracked the amount of sebum, not pore size.
cards.watchOut: Women only, facial sites only, and groups defined by self-described skin type - it calibrates the oily-dry contrast, not a population reference range.

cards.headline: Bissonnette 2015: forehead sebum excretion measured a week apart in 40 adults varied with sleep timing, free testosterone and enzyme expression in women
cards.summary: Bissonnette 2015: forehead sebum excretion measured a week apart in 40 adults varied with sleep timing, free testosterone and enzyme expression in women
cards.people: 40 healthy subjects whose forehead sebum excretion rate was measured twice, 7 days apart, alongside serum androgens, 5-alpha-reductase type 1 gene expression, forehead temperature, sleep habits, diet, washing routine and ultraviolet exposure.
cards.result: The time subjects fell asleep correlated positively with the change in SER on the left (P = 0.010; R = 0.402) and right (P = 0.002; R = 0.467) forehead. SER correlated inversely with 5-alpha-reductase type 1 expression, and free testosterone correlated inversely with that expression; in sex-specific analyses these correlations were significant only in women. The authors conclude that sleep patterns, free testosterone and enzyme activity contribute to visit-to-visit SER variability.
cards.watchOut: This card is about measurement variability, not a normative rate: a single SER reading carries substantial within-person noise, which is why the classic literature repeats measurements.

cards.headline: Draelos 2006: parallel trials in 100 Japanese and 30 Caucasian volunteers separated the excretion rate from the casual level
cards.summary: Draelos 2006: parallel trials in 100 Japanese and 30 Caucasian volunteers separated the excretion rate from the casual level
cards.type: Randomised measurement trials (intervention trial carded for its sebum-measurement design)
cards.people: 100 Japanese subjects in a double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel trial (50 active, 50 placebo) with sebum excretion rate measured at baseline, week 2 and week 4, and 30 Caucasian subjects in a randomised split-face study over 6 weeks with SER and casual sebum levels (CSL) measured at baseline, week 3 and week 6; the intervention tested was topical 2% niacinamide moisturiser.
cards.result: Baseline SER did not differ between groups in the Japanese trial. After treatment, the niacinamide group showed significantly lowered SER at 2 and 4 weeks in Japanese subjects; in Caucasian subjects, CSL was significantly reduced after 6 weeks but SER was not. The two measurement quantities therefore behaved differently in the two populations.
cards.watchOut: Carded as measurement physiology - the SER/CSL distinction and its population difference - not as a recommendation for niacinamide, which is a cosmetic intervention question outside this shelf.
