shelves.title: Epidermal turnover time (physiology): about 39-48 days for the whole epidermis by autoradiographic kinetics, about 19 days across the stratum corneum by dansyl chloride
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how long does the epidermis take to renew - stratum-corneum transit time and total epidermal turnover time measured by dansyl-chloride fluorescence decay, autoradiography and modern fluorescence methods, and how do age and body site change them?
shelves.mesh: Epidermis · Epidermal Cells · Cell Division · Time Factors · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Boron & Boulpaep, epithelial renewal): the epidermis renews continuously, with keratinocytes born in the basal layer transiting the viable layers and the stratum corneum before shedding. The carded human measurements agree on a weeks-scale total but differ by method, and that method-dependence is core content. Weinstein's tritiated-thymidine autoradiography programme (1984) built the compartment model - proliferative, viable differentiated and stratum corneum compartments turning over at very similar rates (1246, 1417 and 1490 cells/day/mm2) - and put the mean total epidermal turnover time at 39 days, with a germinative cell cycle of 311 hours. Iizuka's 1994 re-computation from Weinstein's own compartment data put the total at 47-48 days instead of 39, and Bergstresser and Taylor's desquamation-based model (1977) independently derived 45 days for volar forearm. For the stratum corneum alone, dansyl-chloride staining in 18 healthy women gave a turnover time of 19.3 days on untreated skin, roughly halving to 10.9 days under subclinical irritant exposure - a stimulus limb, labelled as such. The classic dansyl-chloride transit report by Baker and Kligman (1967) was checked this session: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is refused as an evidence card and named here only as the historical anchor of the method. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED (total turnover in the 39-48 day range, method-dependent; stratum-corneum transit about 19 days at rest).

cards.headline: Weinstein 1984 (autoradiography): mean total epidermal turnover 39 days; germinative cell cycle 311 hours
cards.summary: Weinstein 1984 (autoradiography): mean total epidermal turnover 39 days; germinative cell cycle 311 hours
cards.type: Autoradiographic cell-kinetics study in human volunteers
cards.people: Normal human epidermis studied with tritiated-thymidine autoradiography in the Weinstein programme; the duration of DNA synthesis was obtained from a composite fraction-of-labelled-mitoses curve from 11 normal subjects, and the growth fraction (60%) was estimated from the literature and human skin xenografts.
cards.result: The germinative labelling index was 2.7% (SD 1.2) and DNA synthesis duration 14 hours, giving a proliferative cell cycle duration of 311 hours. Turnover rates in the three compartments were very similar (proliferative 1246, viable differentiated 1417, stratum corneum 1490 cells/day/mm2), confirming kinetic homeostasis. The mean epidermal turnover time of the entire tissue was 39 days. Normal-appearing epidermis from psoriasis patients had a labelling index of 4.2% (SD 0.9), about 50% higher.
cards.watchOut: The 39-day figure is model-derived from compartment rates, not a directly timed transit, and one input (growth fraction) came partly from xenograft and literature estimates - which is why the re-computation on the next card lands higher.
cards.source: Weinstein GD et al.. Cell proliferation in normal epidermis.. The Journal of investigative dermatology. 1984. PMID: 6725985. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Iizuka 1994: re-computing Weinstein's compartment data gives a total turnover of 47-48 days, not 39
cards.summary: Iizuka 1994: re-computing Weinstein's compartment data gives a total turnover of 47-48 days, not 39
cards.type: Kinetic re-analysis (modelling) of published human volunteer data
cards.people: A kinetic re-analysis of Weinstein's published normal-human epidermal data (Journal of Investigative Dermatology 1984), subdividing turnover into proliferative, differentiated and stratum-corneum compartments and summing them.
cards.result: Epidermal turnover time is the time taken for the epidermis to replace itself, and the total is the sum of the compartment turnover times. Calculated that way from Weinstein's data, the epidermal turnover time was 47-48 days instead of 39 days.
cards.watchOut: Not a new measurement - the same underlying data yield 39 or 47-48 days depending on how compartment times are summed. Quote total turnover as a range, never a single day-count.
cards.source: Iizuka H et al.. Epidermal turnover time.. Journal of dermatological science. 1994. PMID: 7865480. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bergstresser & Taylor 1977: desquamation-based model derives a total turnover of 45 days for volar forearm
cards.summary: Bergstresser & Taylor 1977: desquamation-based model derives a total turnover of 45 days for volar forearm
cards.people: Human volar forearm epidermis modelled from stratum-corneum desquamation rates and the consequent obligatory turnover of the keratinocyte layer; the record does not state a subject number - N not documented in the record.
cards.result: A total epidermal turnover time of 45 days was derived from the model for the human volar forearms - independently close to the autoradiographic estimates, by an entirely different (shedding-rate) route.
cards.watchOut: A derived model value for one body site (volar forearm), not a timed measurement, and site-specific - turnover at other sites cannot be read off it.

cards.headline: Wilhelm 1990 (dansyl chloride): stratum-corneum turnover 19.3 days on untreated skin in 18 women; irritant exposure cut it to 10.9 days
cards.summary: Wilhelm 1990 (dansyl chloride): stratum-corneum turnover 19.3 days on untreated skin in 18 women; irritant exposure cut it to 10.9 days
cards.type: Dansyl-chloride fluorescence-decay measurement study (with irritant-stimulus limb)
cards.people: 18 healthy female volunteers in whom stratum-corneum turnover time was measured by the dansyl-chloride staining method on untreated skin, water-treated control skin, and skin exposed daily to the irritant sodium lauryl sulphate (7.5%, 20 minutes, 5 days a week for 3 weeks).
cards.result: Stratum-corneum turnover time of untreated skin was 19.3 days (SEM 0.8) and was unchanged by water treatment (19.3, SEM 2.0) but was significantly reduced by sodium lauryl sulphate to 10.9 days (SEM 0.6; P <= 0.0001 versus controls), while transepidermal water loss rose up to 3.3-fold. Baseline water loss correlated with the intensity of irritation.
cards.watchOut: This card measures the stratum corneum only, not whole-epidermis turnover, and its irritant limb is physiology under a controlled stimulus, not resting physiology - the resting value is the 19.3 days.
cards.source: Wilhelm KP et al.. Increased stratum corneum turnover induced by subclinical irritant dermatitis.. The British journal of dermatology. 1990. PMID: 2369560. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: whole-epidermis renewal about 39-48 days by kinetics, stratum corneum about 19 days by dansyl chloride - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: whole-epidermis renewal about 39-48 days by kinetics, stratum corneum about 19 days by dansyl chloride - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers across the autoradiographic programme (11 subjects for the synthesis-duration curve), a compartment re-analysis, a desquamation model, and 18 women in the dansyl-chloride study.
cards.result: Total epidermal turnover computes to 39 days (Weinstein), 47-48 days on re-computation of the same data, and 45 days by an independent desquamation model; stratum-corneum transit alone measured 19.3 days at rest. The classic Baker and Kligman dansyl-chloride transit report (1967) was refused as an evidence card because its fetched record carries an empty abstract; it is named in the balance as the method's historical anchor only. Framing per Boron & Boulpaep epithelial renewal. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Never quote one day-count: the honest statement is a method-dependent range (about 39-48 days total; about 19 days for stratum corneum), and irritant or diseased skin turns over much faster.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weinstein GD et al.. Cell proliferation in normal epidermis.. The Journal of investigative dermatology. 1984. PMID: 6725985. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Nail growth rates (physiology): fingernails about 0.10 mm a day, slowing by about half across the lifespan; the classic record is one man's 35-year thumbnail
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast do nails grow - fingernail versus toenail linear growth rates, the digit gradient, and the slowing with age - measured by marked-nail and photographic methods?
shelves.mesh: Nails · Aging · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for skin appendages is thin (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep), and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, stated plainly. The classic anchor is Bean's single-subject longitudinal record (N = 1, labelled on its face): his left thumbnail grew 0.123 mm/day at age 32 and 0.095 mm/day at age 67, over 35 years of self-measurement. Orentreich's ageing programme generalised the pattern - linear nail growth falls by about 50% over the lifespan, with circadian and roughly 7-year rhythms superimposed. The modern normative cohort (50 young adults, all 500 fingernails measured) puts average fingernail growth at 0.103 mm/day, with a digit gradient (left index fastest at 0.13 mm/day in that cohort, little fingers slowest) and no sex or hand-dominance correlation; a thumb-measurement study found 0.09 mm/day in controls and 0.10 mm/day in pregnancy (no significant difference). On toenails: the carded records quantify fingernails and the thumbnail; the slower toenail rate given in textbooks (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) is presented here as the textbook's account, because no carded record in this session confirms a toenail value. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Bean 1980 (N = 1, 35 years): his left thumbnail slowed from 0.123 mm/day at age 32 to 0.095 mm/day at age 67
cards.summary: Bean 1980 (N = 1, 35 years): his left thumbnail slowed from 0.123 mm/day at age 32 to 0.095 mm/day at age 67
cards.people: A single subject - the author himself (N = 1) - who measured the growth of his own nails for 35 years; this card reports the left thumbnail series. A single-subject classic, carded with its N printed plainly, as this physiology stream allows.
cards.result: The average daily growth of the left thumbnail varied from 0.123 mm a day during the first part of the study, when he was 32 years of age, to 0.095 mm a day at the age of 67 - a slowing of roughly a quarter over 35 years in this one nail.
cards.watchOut: N = 1: one man's thumbnail cannot set a population rate. Its value is the within-person ageing slope measured the same way for 35 years - the longest such record in the literature.
cards.source: Bean WB et al.. Nail growth. Thirty-five years of observation.. Archives of internal medicine. 1980. PMID: 7352807. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Orentreich 1979: linear nail growth falls by about 50% over the lifespan, with circadian and roughly 7-year rhythms
cards.summary: Orentreich 1979: linear nail growth falls by about 50% over the lifespan, with circadian and roughly 7-year rhythms
cards.people: Humans (and beagle dogs, as a lifespan comparison) in the Orentreich ageing programme, using linear nail growth measured over a year as a noninvasive ageing marker; the record does not state the human subject number - N not documented in the record. Only the human findings are carded here; the dog data are comparative prose in the original report, not a carded result.
cards.result: The rate of linear nail growth decreases 50% over the life spans of both dogs and humans; in the beagle, whose lifespan is 20% of man's, the rate of decrease was 5 times faster. There are circadian and multiple-year biorhythms: approximately 7-year periods of slow decline alternate with 7-year periods of more rapid decline. A one-year measurement, with known influencing factors controlled, gives data that are both age-related and age-caused.
cards.watchOut: The 50% figure spans the whole lifespan and mixes cross-sectional and longitudinal elements; the record prints no subject number, and many endogenous and exogenous factors influence the rate, as the authors themselves warn.
cards.source: Orentreich N et al.. The effect of aging on the rate of linear nail growth.. The Journal of investigative dermatology. 1979. PMID: 448171. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Babu 2024: average fingernail growth 0.103 mm/day across 500 fingernails in 50 young adults; little fingers slowest
cards.summary: Babu 2024: average fingernail growth 0.103 mm/day across 500 fingernails in 50 young adults; little fingers slowest
cards.people: 50 young adults aged 18-40 years in India; all 500 fingernails were painted with three coats of nail polish by a standardised protocol and growth was measured with a digital Vernier caliper from the nail fold every 10 days for 1 month.
cards.result: Average fingernail growth was 0.103 mm/day. There was no correlation with sex or hand dominance. Growth was greatest in the left index finger (0.13 mm/day) and left thumb, and least in the little fingers (0.101 mm/day). The growth rate reduced as the days of the study progressed.
cards.watchOut: One month of measurement in 18-40-year-olds only - it cannot speak to the age slowing, and its digit gradient (index fastest) is this cohort's finding, measured by the polish-displacement method.
cards.source: Babu V et al.. The Normal Growth Rate of Human Fingernails in Indian Population.. Indian journal of plastic surgery : official publication of the Association of Plastic Surgeons of India. 2024. PMID: 39345670. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Altan 2018: thumbnail growth 0.09 mm/day in controls and 0.10 mm/day in pregnancy - no significant difference; thickness did differ
cards.summary: Altan 2018: thumbnail growth 0.09 mm/day in controls and 0.10 mm/day in pregnancy - no significant difference; thickness did differ
cards.people: Pregnant women and a control group of healthy female volunteers; thumb nail-plate growth was measured by digital calipers from the lunula to the free edge at repeated visits, and nail-plate thickness at the free edge. The record does not state the group sizes - N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Mean nail-plate growth was 0.1 (SD 0.05) mm/day in pregnant women and 0.09 (SD 0.05) mm/day in controls, with no statistically significant difference (P = 0.438). Nail-plate thickness did differ: 0.87 (SD 0.19) mm in pregnancy versus 0.75 (SD 0.17) mm in controls (P < 0.001). Dermatological examination found no significant differences in nail findings.
cards.watchOut: Thumbnail only, women only, and group sizes are not in the record - carded because its control rate (0.09 mm/day) independently corroborates the roughly 0.10 mm/day fingernail figure.
cards.source: Altan Ferhatoğlu Z et al.. Morphology, growth rate, and thickness of the nail plate during the pregnancy.. International journal of dermatology. 2018. PMID: 30035300. cards.headline: Synthesis: fingernails about 0.10 mm/day in young adults, slowing with age - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: fingernails about 0.10 mm/day in young adults, slowing with age - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Healthy humans across a 35-year single-subject series (N = 1, labelled), an ageing programme (N not documented), a 50-adult normative cohort, and a thumb case-control study (N not documented).
cards.result: Fingernail growth measures about 0.10 mm/day in young adults (0.103 mm/day across 500 nails; 0.09 mm/day for control thumbnails), varies by digit, and slows with age - by about a quarter over 35 years in Bean's thumbnail and by about half across the lifespan in Orentreich's programme. No carded record confirms a toenail rate; the slower toenail growth in the balance is the textbook account (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep), not a carded measurement. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Rates are method- and digit-specific (marked-nail, polish-displacement and caliper methods), and the two oldest anchors carry N = 1 and N not documented respectively - both are labelled on their faces.

shelves.title: Saccadic eye movements (physiology): the main sequence - peak velocity rises with amplitude (about 213 degrees/s at 5 degrees to 455 degrees/s at 30 degrees horizontally) at every age
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast do saccadic eye movements run - the main-sequence relationship between saccade amplitude, peak velocity and duration, latency distributions, and how fatigue and age change them, measured by infrared oculography?
shelves.mesh: Saccades · Eye Movements · Reaction Time · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, oculomotor control): saccades are the rapid conjugate eye movements that refixate the visual target, and their amplitude, peak velocity and duration are so tightly coupled - the 'main sequence' - that a saccade's size predicts its speed. The carded normative cohorts quantify it with infrared/video oculography. Hopf 2018 (100 healthy participants aged 6-76) gives the cleanest main sequence: mean horizontal peak velocity 213 degrees/s for 5-degree, 352 for 15-degree and 455 for 30-degree target steps (vertical values lower: 208, 303 and 391 degrees/s), with the velocity-amplitude association present at every age and no relevant age effect on peak velocity, gain or latency in adults - latency shortens through childhood and adolescence and trends slightly up in the elderly. Two larger cohorts put more weight on ageing: Seferlis 2015 (250 subjects in five age bands of 50) found significant age differences in saccade latency, velocity and accuracy, with elderly subjects deteriorating on all parameters, and Bonnet 2013 (145 subjects aged 19-82) found latency of pro- and antisaccades increased with age and upward prosaccade velocity fell. The classic Bahill main-sequence characterisations were checked this session: their fetched records carry empty abstracts or describe computer simulation rather than human measurement, so they are refused as evidence cards and named here only as the historical anchor of the term. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED (main sequence concordant in all cohorts; the size of the ageing effect on velocity is the one point of disagreement, stated on the face).

cards.headline: Hopf 2018: main sequence quantified in 100 healthy people - peak velocity 213, 352 and 455 degrees/s for 5, 15 and 30-degree horizontal saccades
cards.summary: Hopf 2018: main sequence quantified in 100 healthy people - peak velocity 213, 352 and 455 degrees/s for 5, 15 and 30-degree horizontal saccades
cards.people: 100 healthy participants aged 6-76 years undergoing ophthalmologic examination and saccadometry with an infrared video-oculography device sampling at 220 Hz; reflexive saccades were evoked in four directions at three target displacements each (5/15/30 degrees horizontal; 5/10/20 degrees vertical), measuring peak velocity, gain and latency.
cards.result: Mean peak velocity was 213 (SD 29) degrees/s at 5 degrees, 352 (SD 50) at 15 degrees and 455 (SD 67) at 30 degrees horizontally, and 208 (SD 36), 303 (SD 50) and 391 (SD 71) degrees/s vertically. The peak velocity-eccentricity association was present at any age in all directions. A linear mixed model found no relevant effect of age on peak velocity, gain or latency; latency shortens during childhood and adolescence, is relatively stable in adulthood, and trends slightly upward in the elderly. Saccades were more precise for small target displacements.
cards.watchOut: Reflexive saccades only, on one 220 Hz video-oculography device - its means serve that set-up; voluntary and memory-guided saccades have different metrics.
cards.source: Hopf S et al.. Age dependent normative data of vertical and horizontal reflexive saccades.. PloS one. 2018. PMID: 30226877. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Seferlis 2015: 250 healthy subjects in five age bands - ageing significantly changed saccade latency, velocity and accuracy
cards.summary: Seferlis 2015: 250 healthy subjects in five age bands - ageing significantly changed saccade latency, velocity and accuracy
cards.people: 250 healthy subjects aged 18-70 years in five groups of 50 (18-30, 31-40, 41-50, 51-60, 61-70 years), tested prospectively by video-oculography for smooth pursuit, saccades (latency, velocity, accuracy) and optokinetic movements.
cards.result: A statistically significant difference between age groups was found in all parameters analysed for the smooth pursuit, saccade and optokinetic tests. Elderly healthy subjects showed deterioration of performance in all eye-tracking parameters tested, leading the authors to conclude that age must be taken into account when interpreting eye-tracking tests.
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance, not the per-band saccade values, so this card establishes that age effects exist across 18-70 years without quantifying them - and its conclusion sits in tension with Hopf's finding of no relevant adult age effect on peak velocity; both are reported as published.

cards.headline: Bonnet 2013: 145 healthy subjects - antisaccade and prosaccade latency rose with age, upward prosaccade velocity fell, and direction mattered
cards.summary: Bonnet 2013: 145 healthy subjects - antisaccade and prosaccade latency rose with age, upward prosaccade velocity fell, and direction mattered
cards.people: 145 healthy subjects aged 19-82 years whose horizontal and vertical prosaccades, antisaccades and smooth pursuit were recorded with video-oculography; gender and education did not influence the metrics.
cards.result: With age, the latency of leftward and vertical pro- and antisaccades increased (p < 0.001), velocity of upward prosaccades decreased (p < 0.001), gain of rightward and upward prosaccades diminished (p < 0.001), and antisaccade error rate increased (p < 0.001). Pro- and antisaccades showed right/left and up/down asymmetries. The skewness of the saccade velocity profile was stable across the lifespan.
cards.watchOut: Age effects here are direction-specific (upward velocity, leftward and vertical latency) - pooling all directions, as some normative sets do, hides them; metrics must be separated by direction, per the authors.
cards.source: Bonnet C et al.. Horizontal and vertical eye movement metrics: what is important?. cards.headline: Synthesis: the main sequence holds at every age; latency lengthens with age - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: the main sequence holds at every age; latency lengthens with age - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Healthy volunteers across three video-oculography normative cohorts (100 aged 6-76; 250 aged 18-70; 145 aged 19-82; total 495).
cards.result: Peak velocity scales tightly with amplitude (horizontally about 213 degrees/s at 5 degrees to 455 degrees/s at 30 degrees) in all cohorts - the main sequence. Latency shortens through childhood and lengthens in older adults; whether adult peak velocity itself falls with age is disputed between the carded cohorts (no relevant effect in Hopf; significant group differences in Seferlis; direction-specific falls in Bonnet) and is stated as disputed. The classic Bahill characterisations were refused as evidence cards because their fetched records carry empty abstracts or report simulation, not human measurement. Framing per Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep oculomotor control. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Normative values are device- and paradigm-bound (reflexive versus voluntary saccades; sampling rate), and fatigue effects named in the question were not quantified by any carded record - no fatigue claim is made.

shelves.title: Taste thresholds (physiology): salt and bitter detection thresholds rise modestly with age, sweet and sour do not - and the method decides the answer
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are taste thresholds - detection and recognition thresholds for sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami by whole-mouth and regional (filter-paper and electrogustometry) methods, and how much do they rise with age and smoking?
shelves.mesh: Taste Threshold · Taste · Aging · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, chemical senses): taste buds transduce sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami, and thresholds are measured either chemically (whole-mouth solutions, filter-paper discs, taste strips) or electrically (electrogustometry). The methods are not interchangeable, so this shelf cards per method. The classic whole-mouth ageing cohort (Weiffenbach 1982, 81 adults aged 23-88) found quality-specific change: sodium chloride detection thresholds rose a small but significant amount with age, quinine (bitter) thresholds rose more weakly, and sucrose and citric acid thresholds were not significantly related to age. Electrogustometry in a normal population (Grant 1987) likewise found detection thresholds significantly elevated with age - and with smoking - with no sex difference. Regional chemical testing in 203 healthy participants (Cavazzana 2019) found front-of-tongue thresholds lower than back-of-tongue for quinine, PTC and PROP taste strips, and confirmed that genetic non-tasting is common for PTC/PROP but rare for quinine. The PROP programme (Lucchina 1998) formalised the inherited bitter phenotype - nontasters, medium tasters and supertasters - which dominates bitter thresholds more than age does. No carded record quantifies umami thresholds, and none is claimed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Weiffenbach 1982: in 81 adults aged 23-88, salt thresholds rose significantly with age, bitter weakly, sweet and sour not at all
cards.summary: Weiffenbach 1982: in 81 adults aged 23-88, salt thresholds rose significantly with age, bitter weakly, sweet and sour not at all
cards.people: 81 adults between 23 and 88 years of age whose whole-mouth detection thresholds were obtained for each of the four basic taste qualities (sodium chloride, quinine sulfate, sucrose, citric acid), with procedures controlling for age-related changes in response criterion and salivary sodium.
cards.result: Sodium chloride thresholds showed a small but significant increase with age. Quinine sulfate thresholds displayed a similar but weaker relation to age. Sucrose and citric acid thresholds were not significantly related to age. Citric acid alone showed a sex effect. Detection thresholds for the four taste qualities undergo different changes with age.
cards.watchOut: Detection thresholds only (recognition thresholds run higher and were not the measure here), and the age rise for salt is small - this refutes any blanket 'taste fades with age' claim rather than supporting one.
cards.source: Weiffenbach JM et al.. Taste thresholds: quality specific variation with human aging.. Journal of gerontology. 1982. PMID: 7069164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Grant 1987 (electrogustometry): detection thresholds significantly elevated with age and with smoking; no sex difference
cards.summary: Grant 1987 (electrogustometry): detection thresholds significantly elevated with age and with smoking; no sex difference
cards.people: Normal subjects in whom an electrogustometer was evaluated for taste-threshold measurement, with electrogustometric values also determined in patients before and after trigeminal-nerve surgery and in trigeminal sensory neuropathy (patient findings are context, not carded results). The record does not state the normal-subject number - N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In normal subjects, no sex difference in taste threshold was noted; however, there was a significant elevation in detection threshold with age and with smoking. Many patients with trigeminal nerve disorders had abnormal electrogustometric thresholds. The authors conclude electrogustometry is a convenient method for clinically assessing taste.
cards.watchOut: Electrical thresholds are not chemical taste thresholds - electrogustometry measures response to current at the tongue, and its age/smoking elevation cannot be converted into solution-concentration terms.

cards.headline: Cavazzana 2019: 203 volunteers on taste strips - front of tongue more sensitive than back; quinine perceived even by PROP/PTC non-tasters
cards.summary: Cavazzana 2019: 203 volunteers on taste strips - front of tongue more sensitive than back; quinine perceived even by PROP/PTC non-tasters
cards.type: Regional (taste-strip) threshold study in healthy volunteers
cards.people: 203 healthy participants (56% female, mean age 28 years) whose detection thresholds for quinine, phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) and 6-n-propylthiouracil (PROP) were measured with taste strips at seven concentrations, applied to the front and back parts of the tongue.
cards.result: The inability to perceive quinine was less frequent than the inability to perceive PTC and PROP: people can perceive quinine's bitterness even if they are non-tasters for PROP/PTC. Strong correlations between PTC and PROP thresholds were observed, and correlations between quinine and PTC/PROP thresholds also emerged. Detection thresholds were lower (more sensitive) at the front of the tongue than the back for all three bitter stimuli.
cards.watchOut: Young volunteers (mean age 28) and bitter stimuli only - this card calibrates regional and genetic variation, not ageing, and strip thresholds are method-specific.

cards.headline: Lucchina 1998 (PROP programme): bitter phenotype is inherited - nontasters, medium tasters and supertasters - and more women are supertasters
cards.summary: Lucchina 1998 (PROP programme): bitter phenotype is inherited - nontasters, medium tasters and supertasters - and more women are supertasters
cards.people: Reportedly healthy volunteers aged 21-62 years in three psychophysical studies (S1: n = 163; S2: n = 152; S3: n = 136) rating PROP-impregnated paper and PROP solutions against sucrose on labelled magnitude and category scales, analysed by TAS2R38-era taster classification (genotype framing as published).
cards.result: The ability to taste PROP is genetically determined: PROP tastes moderately bitter to medium tasters, intensely bitter to supertasters, and tasteless to nontasters. In S1 and S2, higher PROP perception tracked higher perceived sucrose intensity (r = 0.32, p < 0.001; r = 0.25, p < 0.01). A higher frequency of females than males were supertasters, and the PROP effect on sweet perception was most evident in female supertasters.
cards.watchOut: PROP status is a phenotype of one bitter receptor pathway - it must not be generalised to 'bitter taste' as a whole, as the quinine card shows; suprathreshold intensity ratings are not detection thresholds.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ageing raises salt (and weakly bitter) chemical thresholds, electrogustometric thresholds rise with age and smoking, genetics dominates PROP - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: ageing raises salt (and weakly bitter) chemical thresholds, electrogustometric thresholds rise with age and smoking, genetics dominates PROP - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Healthy humans across a whole-mouth ageing cohort (81 adults), an electrogustometry normative study (N not documented), a taste-strip regional study (203 volunteers), and the PROP phenotyping programme (163, 152 and 136 volunteers).
cards.result: Taste ageing is quality-specific, not global: salt detection thresholds rise modestly with age, bitter weakly, sweet and sour not significantly; electrogustometric thresholds rise with age and smoking with no sex difference; regional thresholds are lower at the tongue's front; and inherited PROP phenotype splits bitter perception into nontasters, medium tasters and supertasters. No carded record quantifies umami thresholds. Framing per Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep chemical senses. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Whole-mouth, filter-paper/strip and electrogustometric thresholds are three different measurements and are carded separately throughout - never convert or pool them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weiffenbach JM et al.. Taste thresholds: quality specific variation with human aging.. Journal of gerontology. 1982. PMID: 7069164. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Smell thresholds across the lifespan (physiology): identification peaks in the third to fifth decades, falls markedly after the seventh, and women outperform men at every age
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how do smell detection thresholds and odour identification scores change across the lifespan - at what age does decline accelerate, how large is the sex difference, and what fraction of older adults are functionally anosmic on standardised testing (UPSIT and Sniffin' Sticks)?
shelves.mesh: Smell · Sensory Thresholds · Aging · Sex Factors · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, olfaction): olfactory receptor neurons project to the olfactory bulb, and function is tested by detection thresholds (weakest perceived odour) and by suprathreshold identification and discrimination - related but distinct measures, carded as such. The lifespan curve is concordant across the two great normative programmes. Doty's University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) programme (1984; 1,955 persons aged 5-99) found women outperforming men at all ages, nonsmokers outperforming smokers, peak performance in the third through fifth decades, and decline markedly after the seventh: more than half of 65-80-year-olds and more than three-quarters of those over 80 evidenced major olfactory impairment. The Sniffin' Sticks programme agrees and adds thresholds: in 3,282 subjects (Hummel 2007) the composite TDI score's 10th percentile fell from 30.3 at ages 16-35 to 19.6 over age 55, with odor thresholds declining most dramatically of the three subtests; the extended norms (9,139 subjects, Oleszkiewicz 2019) found the steepest score fall between ages 60 and 71 and hyposmia defined at TDI under 30.75. The population check (Beaver Dam Offspring Study, 2,838 adults) found measured olfactory impairment in 3.8% overall, rising from 0.6% under 35 to 13.9% at 65 or older, more common in men. Identification tests are culture- and language-loaded, and each programme's norms describe its own population - stated on the face, per this row's flag. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Doty 1984 (UPSIT): 1,955 people aged 5-99 - peak identification in the third to fifth decades; major impairment in over half of 65-80-year-olds and over three-quarters past 80
cards.summary: Doty 1984 (UPSIT): 1,955 people aged 5-99 - peak identification in the third to fifth decades; major impairment in over half of 65-80-year-olds and over three-quarters past 80
cards.people: 1,955 persons ranging in age from 5 to 99 years whose smell identification ability was measured with the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) programme in the Doty laboratory.
cards.result: On average, women outperformed men at all ages, and nonsmokers outperformed smokers. Peak performance occurred in the third through fifth decades and declined markedly after the seventh. More than half of those 65 to 80 years old evidenced major olfactory impairment; after 80 years, more than three-quarters evidenced major impairment.
cards.watchOut: Identification is a suprathreshold, culture- and language-loaded task (recognising named odours), not a detection threshold - 'major impairment' here means identification failure against young-adult norms in a US test population.
cards.source: Doty RL et al.. Smell identification ability: changes with age.. Science (New York, N.Y.). 1984. PMID: 6505700. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hummel 2007 (Sniffin' Sticks): 3,282 subjects - TDI 10th percentile falls from 30.3 at 16-35 years to 19.6 past 55; thresholds decline most
cards.summary: Hummel 2007 (Sniffin' Sticks): 3,282 subjects - TDI 10th percentile falls from 30.3 at 16-35 years to 19.6 past 55; thresholds decline most
cards.type: Normative cohort (threshold, discrimination and identification battery)
cards.people: 3,282 subjects tested with the Sniffin' Sticks battery - odor threshold, discrimination and identification summed as the TDI score - extending earlier norms that had rested on only 30 healthy subjects over 55.
cards.result: The TDI score at the 10th percentile (the hyposmia cut-off) was 24.9 under 15 years, 30.3 at ages 16-35, 27.3 at 36-55, and 19.6 over 55 years. Women outperformed men on all three subtests. Age changed the subtests unequally: odor thresholds declined most dramatically with age, compared with discrimination and identification.
cards.watchOut: German test population and odour set; the 10th-percentile convention defines hyposmia statistically against the reference group, so the same raw score classifies differently at different ages by design.

cards.headline: Oleszkiewicz 2019 (extended Sniffin' Sticks norms): 9,139 subjects aged 5-96 - scores halve outside the 20-30 peak; steepest fall at 60-71 years
cards.summary: Oleszkiewicz 2019 (extended Sniffin' Sticks norms): 9,139 subjects aged 5-96 - scores halve outside the 20-30 peak; steepest fall at 60-71 years
cards.people: 9,139 healthy subjects (4,928 females aged 5-96 years; 4,211 males aged 5-91 years) tested with the standard Sniffin' Sticks battery (threshold, discrimination, identification; TDI sum score), providing norms in narrow age groups.
cards.result: Age-related changes were found in each domain, most pronounced for thresholds. Individuals aged 20-30 years performed best, whereas children under 10 and adults over 71 scored only half as well. Sex differences favoured women. The most pronounced score increase ran from age 5 through 20 years, with a dramatic decrease at age 60 through 71 years. Hyposmia was set at a TDI score below 30.75.
cards.watchOut: Pooled healthy-volunteer normative data assembled across centres and years - ideal for age-band reference, but 'healthy subject' selection means population impairment rates must come from population cohorts (next card), not from these norms.

cards.headline: Schubert 2012 (Beaver Dam Offspring Study): measured olfactory impairment 3.8% overall, 0.6% under 35, 13.9% at 65 or older, in 2,838 adults
cards.summary: Schubert 2012 (Beaver Dam Offspring Study): measured olfactory impairment 3.8% overall, 0.6% under 35, 13.9% at 65 or older, in 2,838 adults
cards.people: 2,838 participants aged 21-84 years (mean 49) in the Beaver Dam Offspring Study (Wisconsin, USA), whose odor identification was measured as part of a population cohort examination, with risk factors, dietary choices and quality of life also assessed.
cards.result: Overall prevalence of olfactory impairment was 3.8%, rising with age from 0.6% in those under 35 years to 13.9% among those 65 or older, and it was more common in men than women. Each 5-year age increase carried an odds ratio of 1.48 (95% CI 1.33-1.64) for impairment; nasal polyps or deviated septum (OR 2.69) and low ankle-brachial index (OR 3.62) were also associated. Impaired participants were less likely to report that food tasted as good as it used to, but impairment showed no association with general health-related quality of life or depressive symptoms.
cards.watchOut: A largely middle-aged US population cohort using an identification screen - its 13.9% at 65+ is not comparable with Doty's 'major impairment' fractions, which used a fuller identification battery against young norms; the two definitions measure different depths of loss, and both are reported as published.
cards.source: Schubert CR et al.. Olfactory impairment in an adult population: the Beaver Dam Offspring Study.. Chemical senses. 2012. PMID: 22045704. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: smell peaks at 20-50, thresholds fall fastest, decline accelerates after 60 - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED

shelves.title: Pure-tone hearing thresholds with age: the ISO 7029 curves climb fastest at high frequencies and faster in men — and longitudinal decline starts earlier than cross-sectional curves suggest
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what do pure-tone hearing thresholds do with age — the ISO 7029 median threshold-versus-age curves by frequency and sex, and what did the longitudinal (Baltimore) measurements show about within-person decline rates versus cross-sectional estimates?
shelves.mesh: Audiometry, Pure-Tone · Auditory Threshold · Presbycusis · Sex Factors · Longitudinal Studies · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the age course of pure-tone thresholds as standardised in ISO 7029 and measured in the carded human cohorts, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep (audition). Three concordant limbs: (1) the cross-sectional shape — thresholds rise with age, steepest at high frequencies, men poorer than women (Framingham, N = 1,662; the Robinson unscreened-population companion analysis, which found the 'pathological overlay' of an unscreened population equivalent to accelerated ageing); (2) the longitudinal correction — in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (681 men, 416 women, screened), within-person decline was detectable in men by age 30 and ran more than twice as fast in men as in women, while learning effects bias cross-sectional and short-term estimates, so cross-sectional curves and true within-person decline are different quantities; (3) the standard's own limits — a Norwegian validation (232 sampled, 60 otologically normal) found the ISO female low-frequency coefficient may be set too low and the otologically-normal screen inconsistent after age 60. Exact decibel cells of the ISO 7029 tables are the standard's account, not re-derived from the fetched records, and the shelf says so on its Synthesis card. This shelf is about normative thresholds; the hearing treatment and device shelves ask different questions.

cards.headline: Pearson 1995 (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging): within-person hearing decline is detectable in men by age 30, runs more than twice as fast in men as in women, and is highly variable even in a screened, low-noise group (681 men, 416 women)
cards.summary: Pearson 1995 (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging): within-person hearing decline is detectable in men by age 30, runs more than twice as fast in men as in women, and is highly variable even in a screened, low-noise group (681 men, 416 women)
cards.type: Human longitudinal cohort study (pure-tone audiometry, BLSA), J Acoust Soc Am 1995
cards.people: 681 men and 416 women in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, screened to exclude otological disease, unilateral loss and noise-induced loss, followed since 1965 with pulsed-tone tracking thresholds from 500 to 8000 Hz; longitudinal patterns estimated with mixed-effects regression models.
cards.result: Hearing sensitivity declined more than twice as fast in men as in women at most ages and frequencies. Longitudinal decline was detectable at all frequencies among men by age 30; in women the age of onset was later and varied by frequency. Women were more sensitive than men above 1000 Hz, men more sensitive at lower frequencies. Learning effects biased cross-sectional and short-term longitudinal estimates, and levels and rates of change were highly variable even in this selected group — age-associated loss occurs even with relatively low-noise occupations and no evidence of noise-induced loss.
cards.watchOut: A screened, relatively low-noise volunteer cohort — its rates are a cleaner ageing signal than population rates, not a prediction for an unscreened individual.
cards.source: Pearson JD, Morrell CH, Gordon-Salant S, Brant LJ, et al. Gender differences in a longitudinal study of age-associated hearing loss. cards.headline: Gates 1990 (Framingham): in 1,662 people in their 60s–90s, pure-tone thresholds rose with age and men had poorer sensitivity than women, while middle-ear measures did not change with age or sex
cards.summary: Gates 1990 (Framingham): in 1,662 people in their 60s–90s, pure-tone thresholds rose with age and men had poorer sensitivity than women, while middle-ear measures did not change with age or sex
cards.type: Human population cohort study (audiometry, Framingham), Ear Hear 1990
cards.people: 1,662 men and women of the Framingham cohort in their 60th through 90th decades, tested at biennial exam 18 (1983–1985) with a hearing questionnaire, pure-tone sensitivity, acoustic compliance measures and word-recognition testing.
cards.result: Pure-tone thresholds increased with age; the rate of change with age did not differ by gender even though men had poorer threshold sensitivity. Maximum word recognition declined with age more rapidly in men and was poorer in men at all ages. Acoustic compliance and middle-ear pressure did not vary with gender or age, pointing to a sensorineural rather than conductive basis for the age gradient. Hearing aids were being used by only 10% of subjects likely to benefit from amplification.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional within one exam cycle: cohort and era effects (including past noise exposure) are folded into its age gradient — the contrast with the longitudinal Baltimore card is the point of this shelf.
cards.source: Gates GA, Cooper JC, Kannel WB, Miller NJ. Hearing in the elderly: the Framingham cohort, 1983-1985. Part I. Basic audiometric test results. Ear and Hearing. 1990. PMID: 2210098. cards.headline: Robinson 1988: the unscreened-population companion to ISO 7029 — typical thresholds converge with the otologically-normal standard at the extremes, and the 'pathological overlay' behaves like accelerated ageing
cards.summary: Robinson 1988: the unscreened-population companion to ISO 7029 — typical thresholds converge with the otologically-normal standard at the extremes, and the 'pathological overlay' behaves like accelerated ageing
cards.type: Human normative-data synthesis (audiometric reference values), Br J Audiol 1988
cards.people: A critical analysis of published threshold-versus-age material for the typical unscreened population, presented in companion form to ISO 7029, whose screened ('otologically normal') curves rest on Robinson and Sutton (1978). No single new cohort N is printed in the record — it is a normative-data synthesis of published studies.
cards.result: The unscreened-population distributions converged closely to ISO 7029 at the extremity of the distributions, and showed striking uniformity of form among apparently discordant studies. The adventitious hearing loss carried by an unscreened population — the so-called 'pathological overlay' — was essentially equivalent to accelerated ageing. The practical consequence the record draws: comparing a noise-exposed worker against an age-matched otologically-normal baseline attributes that overlay to noise, which is why the unscreened companion curves exist.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of published datasets, not a primary cohort — carded as the documentary basis of the ISO 7029 framework this shelf is about, and labelled as such.
cards.source: Robinson DW. Threshold of hearing as a function of age and sex for the typical unscreened population. British Journal of Audiology. 1988. PMID: 3365524. cards.headline: Stenklev & Laukli 2004: tested against ISO 7029, the standard's female coefficient may be set too low at low frequencies, and its 'otologically normal' screening separates inconsistently after age 60 (232 sampled, 60 otologically normal)
cards.summary: Stenklev & Laukli 2004: tested against ISO 7029, the standard's female coefficient may be set too low at low frequencies, and its 'otologically normal' screening separates inconsistently after age 60 (232 sampled, 60 otologically normal)
cards.type: Human audiometric study (normative-standard validation), Int J Audiol 2004
cards.people: A random sample of 232 elderly Norwegian subjects given a battery including pure-tone audiometry in the conventional and extended high-frequency ranges, compared against the ISO 7029 normative distributions; 60 otologically normal (ON) subjects were selected for comparative analysis.
cards.result: After mathematical transformation of the threshold data, the ISO 7029 normative alpha coefficient in females appeared set too low compared with this sample at the lower frequencies, leading to an underestimation of hearing thresholds in ON females. In the ON sample, thresholds deteriorated with age in the extended high-frequency range; no gender threshold differences were found there, although unmeasurable responses were more prevalent in males at some frequencies. Threshold differences between ON and unscreened subjects were not consistent at any frequency, so the ON screening criteria in ISO 7029 may be unreliable in subjects over 60 years.
cards.watchOut: One national sample measured against the standard — it qualifies ISO 7029 at the edges (older ages, female low frequencies) rather than overturning the curves.
cards.source: Stenklev NC, Laukli E. Presbyacusis-hearing thresholds and the ISO 7029. International Journal of Audiology. 2004. PMID: 15357413. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: thresholds climb with age, fastest at high frequencies and faster in men — and the cross-sectional curves and the longitudinal record tell measurably different stories
cards.summary: Synthesis: thresholds climb with age, fastest at high frequencies and faster in men — and the cross-sectional curves and the longitudinal record tell measurably different stories
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded records above (the Baltimore longitudinal programme, the Framingham cohort, the Robinson unscreened-population companion analysis, and the Norwegian ISO 7029 validation), framed by the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep account of audition.
cards.result: The settled shape, as the textbook (Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep) presents it and the carded human data support: pure-tone thresholds rise progressively with age, the rise is steepest at the highest frequencies, and men carry poorer thresholds than women through most of adult life. The longitudinal Baltimore record adds what cross-sectional curves cannot: within-person decline in men is already detectable by age 30, proceeds more than twice as fast as in women, and cross-sectional estimates are distorted by learning effects and cohort noise history — so a median ISO 7029 curve for a decade is a population reference, not an individual's trajectory. The standard itself is not beyond measurement criticism: its female low-frequency coefficient may run low, and its otologically-normal screening separates inconsistently after 60. Exact decibel values for each decade, frequency and sex are the ISO 7029 standard's own published tables — presented here as the standard's account, since the fetched records confirm the shape, the sex difference and the longitudinal rates rather than reprinting every cell of the table.
cards.watchOut: Population, era and screening definition move these curves materially; the shelf's numbers are reference distributions for otologically defined groups, not diagnostic cut-offs for a single patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 7876442, 2210098, 3365524, 15357413), with Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: The scalp hair cycle: years-long anagen that ageing and balding shorten, a distinct shedding (exogen) phase — measured by following the same hairs for over a decade
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the hair cycle at the scalp — anagen duration and fraction, daily shedding counts, and linear hair growth rate — measured by phototrichogram and unit-area trichogram, and how do site, sex and age change them?
shelves.mesh: Hair · Hair Follicle · Scalp · Aging · Alopecia · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the phase sequence (anagen → catagen → telogen → exogen) is textbook-settled (Boron & Boulpaep framing on skin appendages is thin here, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), but the quantitative human base is small and the classic anchor unverifiable: Kligman's 1959 characterisation was refused as a card because its record fetched this session has no abstract (refusal reported on the Synthesis card). What the carded human studies do show, concordantly: phototrichogram follow-up of the same scalps for 8–15 years (two series of 10 men, ~10,000 cycles counted) finds ageing and balding shorten anagen in a growing share of follicles, thin the shaft and lengthen the empty latency before regrowth; contrast-enhanced phototrichogram is validated against biopsy for staging every phase; linear growth rate tracks shaft thickness and is slower in pattern loss than in equally thick control hair (13 healthy controls); and shedding is a distinct exogen phase, normally under 7 hairs/cm² at sampling. The familiar absolute figures (anagen ~2–6 years, ~85–90% in anagen, growth ~0.3–0.4 mm/day, shedding ~50–100/day) are carried explicitly as the textbook's account, not as values a carded record measured. The alopecia treatment shelves (finasteride/minoxidil, PRP) ask different questions.

cards.headline: Courtois 1995: following the same scalps monthly for 8–14 years, ageing shortened hair growth, thinned the thickest shafts and lengthened the empty interval before a replacement hair emerged (10 men)
cards.summary: Courtois 1995: following the same scalps monthly for 8–14 years, ageing shortened hair growth, thinned the thickest shafts and lengthened the empty interval before a replacement hair emerged (10 men)
cards.type: Human longitudinal phototrichogram study (scalp hair cycle and ageing), Br J Dermatol 1995
cards.people: Ten male subjects, balding and non-balding, studied by phototrichogram — repeated identification of each individual hair on the same precise scalp area, with its growth phase established — at monthly intervals over 8–14 years. Small longitudinal series: N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: Ageing was characterised by a reduction in the duration of hair growth and in the diameter of hair shafts, most evident in the thickest hairs, and a prolongation of the interval separating the loss of a hair in telogen and the emergence of a replacement hair in anagen. Together these changes progressively impoverish scalp hair with age; they resemble the changes of male-pattern balding, though less marked.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 men, followed exceptionally long — the design trades breadth for duration; women, other sites and other ancestries are not in this record.
cards.source: Courtois M, Loussouarn G, Hourseau C, Grollier JF. Ageing and hair cycles. The British Journal of Dermatology. 1995. PMID: 7756156. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Aging · Alopecia · Hair · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Photography

cards.headline: Courtois 1994: almost 10,000 hair cycles counted over 15 years — balding is anagen shortening in a growing share of follicles, plus longer latency after a hair falls (10 men)
cards.summary: Courtois 1994: almost 10,000 hair cycles counted over 15 years — balding is anagen shortening in a growing share of follicles, plus longer latency after a hair falls (10 men)
cards.type: Human longitudinal phototrichogram study (hair-cycle dynamics in alopecia), Skin Pharmacol 1994
cards.people: Ten male subjects, with or without alopecia, followed by phototrichogram over 15 years; almost 10,000 individual hair cycles accounted for. Small series: N = 10 printed on the face.
cards.result: Male-pattern alopecia emerged as profound modification of the duration, succession and frequency of hair cycles: (1) a decrease in anagen duration for a proportion of hairs that grows as alopecia advances, so more hairs pass prematurely into telogen and the rate of hair loss rises; (2) a parallel decline in hair diameter; (3) longer latency between the fall of a hair and the onset of regrowth, so fewer hairs are present on the scalp surface at any time — the shorter, finer hairs being absent more often and for longer.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is within a 10-man series spanning balding and non-balding scalps; the cycle-count is large, the person-count is not — both are printed on the face.
cards.source: Courtois M, Loussouarn G, Hourseau C, Grollier JF. Hair cycle and alopecia. Skin Pharmacology. 1994. PMID: 8003330. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Aging · Alopecia · Hair · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Photography · Scalp

cards.headline: Van Neste 2001: contrast-enhanced phototrichogram can stage every phase — anagen, catagen, telogen and the empty follicle — and matches biopsy counts for thick hair
cards.summary: Van Neste 2001: contrast-enhanced phototrichogram can stage every phase — anagen, catagen, telogen and the empty follicle — and matches biopsy counts for thick hair
cards.type: Human methods validation study (phototrichogram versus histology), Eur J Dermatol 2001
cards.people: Balding scalp of male subjects with androgenetic alopecia analysed with the standard phototrichogram and with contrast-enhanced phototrichogram (CE-PTG), followed by scalp biopsy with transverse sectioning and light microscopy as the reference. The record does not print the subject number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Compared with standard phototrichogram, CE-PTG significantly improved detection of thin as well as thick hair; equal numbers of thick hair (diameter > 40 micrometres in the record's units as printed) were detected by CE-PTG and by histology, and CE-PTG detected severely miniaturised fibres down to 8 micrometres, comparable to biopsy analysis. All growth stages — anagen, catagen and telogen — and the empty follicle stage could be clearly observed, although staging of the most severely affected follicles was not always possible by either method. This is the measurement validation on which quantitative hair-cycle claims in humans rest.
cards.watchOut: A methods record in alopecia scalp: it validates the instrument, it does not itself supply healthy-scalp normative fractions. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Van Neste DJ. cards.headline: Van Neste 2014: linear hair growth rate tracks shaft thickness, and is slower in pattern hair loss than in equally thick hair from healthy controls (13 healthy men, 87 with pattern loss)
cards.summary: Van Neste 2014: linear hair growth rate tracks shaft thickness, and is slower in pattern hair loss than in equally thick hair from healthy controls (13 healthy men, 87 with pattern loss)
cards.type: Human imaging study (linear hair growth rate, controls versus pattern loss), Eur J Dermatol 2014
cards.people: 179 paired images from contrast-enhanced phototrichogram with exogen collection in 13 healthy male controls and 87 men with male pattern hair loss, analysed by in-vivo imaging and computer-assisted image analysis after manual processing.
cards.result: There was a global positive correlation between hair thickness and linear growth rate (P < 0.0001), and growth rate was significantly slower in pattern hair loss than in equally thick hairs from controls (P < 0.0005); growth in the more severe patterns was significantly reduced compared with equally thick hair from less severely affected men or controls (P ≤ 0.001). Reduced growth rate, together with thinning and shortening of anagen, contributes to the impression of decreased hair volume. The record reports the comparisons and their significance, not a single pooled mm/day figure — none is printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: The healthy-control limb is 13 men; growth-rate values are comparative in this record, so the shelf's absolute growth-rate figure is carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card, not as this study's result.
cards.source: Van Neste D. Why care about linear hair growth rates (LHGR)? a study using in vivo imaging and computer assisted image analysis after manual processing (CAIAMP) in unaffected male controls and men with male pattern hair loss (MPHL). European Journal of Dermatology. 2014. PMID: 25445091. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Van Neste 2007: shedding is its own phase — exogen hairs are passively retained, can be sampled specifically, and normally number fewer than 7 per cm² of scalp
cards.summary: Van Neste 2007: shedding is its own phase — exogen hairs are passively retained, can be sampled specifically, and normally number fewer than 7 per cm² of scalp
cards.type: Human scalp study (exogen phase characterisation), Skin Res Technol 2007
cards.people: Human scalp studied with non-invasive exogen entrapment in silicon-based polymers, calibrated-dynamometer extraction of growing and non-growing hairs, histochemical staining and scanning electron microscopy of root ends, and documentation of all cycle stages by contrast-enhanced phototrichogram; men and women, adolescents to middle age (record's MeSH age bands). The record does not print a single total subject N in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Anagen and telogen hairs are firmly anchored to the follicle, with cohesion forces correlated with hair thickness; exogen hairs, by contrast, are passively retained. Telogen clubs retain cellular elements of the outer root sheath that exogen roots lack, and the exogen collection method left anagen, catagen and telogen follicles unaffected. Under the study's conditions, casual levels of exogen hair in normal individuals were usually less than 7 hairs per cm² — a measured anchor for what 'daily shedding' looks like at the scalp surface.
cards.watchOut: Exogen counts are method- and condition-specific ('under the present experimental conditions', in the record's words); they are not a universal daily-shed constant.
cards.source: Van Neste D, Leroy T, Conil S. Exogen hair characterization in human scalp. Skin Research and Technology. 2007. PMID: 17908196. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the scalp cycle is years of anagen, weeks of catagen, months of telogen — a textbook-settled sequence whose human quantification still rests on very small, very long series
cards.summary: Synthesis: the scalp cycle is years of anagen, weeks of catagen, months of telogen — a textbook-settled sequence whose human quantification still rests on very small, very long series
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human records above (the two Courtois longitudinal phototrichogram series, the two Van Neste measurement studies and the exogen characterisation), framed by Boron & Boulpaep on skin appendages — thin textbook framing, as the slate for this row states: the row rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature.
cards.result: What the carded human data establish: individual scalp hairs can be followed for years by phototrichogram; ageing and balding both shorten anagen in a growing share of follicles, thin the shaft and lengthen the empty latency before regrowth (10 men, ~10,000 cycles, 8–15 years of follow-up); the measurement itself is validated against biopsy; growth rate rises with shaft thickness and is slower in pattern loss than in healthy controls; and shedding is a distinct, measurable exogen phase, normally under 7 hairs per cm² at sampling. The familiar absolute figures — anagen lasting roughly 2–6 years with about 85–90% of scalp follicles in anagen at any time, catagen of a few weeks, telogen of a few months, linear growth of roughly 0.3–0.4 mm/day and shedding of roughly 50–100 hairs a day — are presented as the textbook's account (Boron & Boulpaep / Ganong framing): they are consistent with the carded records but are not numbers any single fetched record on this shelf measured, and the shelf does not dress them as such. REFUSAL, reported as required: Kligman's 1959 'The human hair cycle', the classic anchor named for this row, was refused as a card because its PubMed record fetched this session carries no abstract, so its content could not be verified from the record — it is named here, not carded. The stamp is EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED for exactly that reason: the phase sequence is textbook-settled, but the quantitative human base carded here is small-N and the classic anchor is unverifiable from its record.
cards.watchOut: Almost everything carded here is men, scalp only, and small-N by person even when large by hair count; site, sex and age gradients beyond ageing in men are thin in the fetched records.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 7756156, 8003330, 11399539, 25445091, 17908196), with Boron & Boulpaep textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: The tear film in health: basal turnover ~15%/min by fluorophotometry, break-up at ~11–12 seconds, osmolarity just under 300 mOsm/L
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what does the tear film do — tear turnover rate by fluorophotometry, break-up time distributions, tear osmolarity ranges, and basal versus reflex secretion rates?
shelves.mesh: Tears · Fluorophotometry · Osmolar Concentration · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the healthy tear film's measured behaviour, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep (lacrimal apparatus — thin framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs). Turnover is the concordant limb: basal tear turnover by fluorophotometry was 15.6 ± 5.4%/min in 41 healthy controls (Kuppens & van Best) and 13.1–17.5%/min across three European centres under one standardised protocol — roughly a sixth of the film per minute. Break-up time in health centres at ~11 s by automated non-invasive measurement (N = 237) and ~12 s by fluorescein (N = 30), carded per method, never pooled. Osmolarity centres just under 300 mOsm/L (289.0 ± 5.8 in the large cohort; 299.06 ± 7.65 in young adults), with no age or sex effect on break-up time or osmolarity in the large cohort. REFUSAL: the classic Mishima 1966 tear-volume/tear-flow anchor was refused as a card — its record fetched this session has no abstract (reported on the Synthesis card). The dry-eye treatment shelves ask different questions.

cards.headline: Kuppens & van Best 1992: basal tear turnover in healthy eyes is 15.6 ± 5.4%/min by fluorophotometry — lower in glaucoma, and lower still on timolol (41 healthy controls)
cards.summary: Kuppens & van Best 1992: basal tear turnover in healthy eyes is 15.6 ± 5.4%/min by fluorophotometry — lower in glaucoma, and lower still on timolol (41 healthy controls)
cards.type: Human fluorophotometry study (basal tear turnover), Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 1992
cards.people: 41 healthy control subjects, 13 open-angle glaucoma patients using no ophthalmic medication and 24 glaucoma patients using daily timolol; basal tear turnover (turnover at the lowest reflex lacrimation achievable under physiologic conditions) measured by fluorophotometry from the decay of tear fluorescence after 1 microlitre of 2% fluorescein, discarding the first 5 minutes.
cards.result: Basal tear turnover was 15.6 ± 5.4%/min in healthy controls, significantly higher than in untreated glaucoma patients (12.3 ± 4.1%/min) and in timolol-treated patients (10.1 ± 3.2%/min) (P < 0.02); the timolol group was also significantly below the untreated glaucoma group (P = 0.03). Tear-film break-up time in the timolol group was significantly shorter than in the other two groups. Health, then, is a turnover of roughly a sixth of the tear film per minute at basal (minimal-reflex) conditions.
cards.watchOut: Basal turnover is a deliberately minimised-reflex measurement; it is not the higher turnover seen with reflex tearing, and the glaucoma/timolol limbs are disease/drug contrasts, not health values.
cards.source: Kuppens EV, Stolwijk TR, de Keizer RJ, van Best JA. Basal tear turnover and topical timolol in glaucoma patients and healthy controls by fluorophotometry. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science. 1992. PMID: 1428718. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Administration, Topical · Fluorophotometry · Glaucoma · Humans · Intraocular Pressure · Reference Values · Reproducibility of Results · Tears · Timolol

cards.headline: van Best 1995 (European concerted action): with one standardised protocol, healthy basal tear turnover was 13.1–17.5%/min across three European cities — the method travels
cards.summary: van Best 1995 (European concerted action): with one standardised protocol, healthy basal tear turnover was 13.1–17.5%/min across three European cities — the method travels
cards.type: Human multicentre methods study (standardised basal tear turnover), Graefes Arch Clin Exp Ophthalmol 1995
cards.people: Healthy volunteers aged 20–70 years in three European cities (Clermont-Ferrand n = 4, Leiden n = 24, Madrid n = 20), measured with identical commercial fluorophotometers under a standardised protocol: 1-microlitre fluorescein drop, mono-exponential decay taken as basal tear flow. One centre contributed only 4 volunteers — printed on the face.
cards.result: Mean basal tear turnover was 13.1 ± 4.6%/min (Clermont-Ferrand), 16.0 ± 5.2%/min (Leiden) and 17.5 ± 3.4%/min (Madrid); the differences between cities were not significant (P > 0.09). Under one protocol, then, healthy basal turnover sits in the mid-teens percent per minute wherever it is measured — the cross-centre concordance that makes the Kuppens healthy value (15.6%/min) a reference rather than a local artefact.
cards.watchOut: Centre Ns are uneven (4, 24, 20); the claim is concordance of means under a shared protocol, not precision at the smallest centre.
cards.source: van Best JA, Benitez del Castillo JM, Coulangeon LM. Measurement of basal tear turnover using a standardized protocol. European concerted action on ocular fluorometry. Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 1995. PMID: 7721117. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Singh 2022: in 237 healthy people, non-invasive break-up time averaged 10.95 ± 2.02 s, tear meniscus height 0.34 ± 0.07 mm and osmolarity 289.0 ± 5.8 mOsm/L — with no age or sex effect on break-up time or osmolarity
cards.summary: Singh 2022: in 237 healthy people, non-invasive break-up time averaged 10.95 ± 2.02 s, tear meniscus height 0.34 ± 0.07 mm and osmolarity 289.0 ± 5.8 mOsm/L — with no age or sex effect on break-up time or osmolarity
cards.type: Human normative study (automated tear-film assessment in health), Front Med 2022
cards.people: 237 healthy subjects (474 eyes; 150 males; mean age 40 ± 17 years, range 10–78) with no ocular disease, assessed automatically with the Keratograph 5M (OCULUS GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany — device named as published) for tear meniscus height and non-invasive tear break-up time (NIBUT), and the TearLab Osmolarity System (TearLab Corporation, California, USA — named as published) for osmolarity.
cards.result: Mean tear meniscus height was 0.34 ± 0.07 mm, mean NIBUT 10.95 ± 2.02 s and mean tear osmolarity 289.0 ± 5.8 mOsm/L. Age had a small positive relationship with meniscus height (0.002 mm/year, P < 0.0001) but no effect on NIBUT (P = 0.26) or osmolarity (P = 0.27); there were no sex differences in any parameter, and meniscus height, NIBUT and osmolarity were not significantly associated with each other. In health these three quantities are therefore near-independent descriptors, not interchangeable proxies.
cards.watchOut: One population (Indian) and one device pair; NIBUT by automated keratograph is not the same measurement as fluorescein break-up time — compare the Masmali card's fluorescein TBUT of ~12 s as a neighbouring, not identical, quantity.
cards.source: Singh S, Srivastav S, Mohamed A, Basu S. Non-invasive Tear Film Assessment in Normal Population: Effect of Age, Sex, and Interparametric Relationship. Frontiers in Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35721069. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Masmali 2014: tear osmolarity in 30 healthy young adults averaged 299.06 ± 7.65 mOsm/L on the TearLab system, with fluorescein break-up time ~12 s and good repeatability
cards.summary: Masmali 2014: tear osmolarity in 30 healthy young adults averaged 299.06 ± 7.65 mOsm/L on the TearLab system, with fluorescein break-up time ~12 s and good repeatability
cards.type: Human normative study (tear osmolarity repeatability in health), Eye Contact Lens 2014
cards.people: 30 healthy young adults (13 men, 17 women; age 20–40 years, mean 28.57 ± 5.58) in Saudi Arabia with no dry-eye symptoms or ocular disease, screened with slit-lamp examination, phenol red thread, tear break-up time (TBUT) and the McMonnies questionnaire; three osmolarity measurements in one eye at 5-minute intervals with the TearLab osmometer (named as published).
cards.result: Overall mean tear osmolarity was 299.06 ± 7.65 mOsm/L — 50% of subjects read 299–312 mOsm/L, 40% read 288–299 and 10% read 277–288 — within the published reference range the record cites (298.0–301.9 mOsm/L). Repeated readings did not differ significantly (P = 0.945), showing good precision. Mean TBUT was 12 ± 1.7 s (right) and 12.5 ± 1.6 s (left), and phenol red thread wetting 22 ± 7.7 mm and 21.5 ± 6.6 mm; osmolarity correlated negatively with TBUT. cards.headline: Synthesis: the healthy tear film turns over at roughly a sixth of its volume a minute, breaks up at about 11–12 seconds, and sits just under 300 mOsm/L
cards.summary: Synthesis: the healthy tear film turns over at roughly a sixth of its volume a minute, breaks up at about 11–12 seconds, and sits just under 300 mOsm/L
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (the two fluorophotometry turnover programmes and the two modern normative device cohorts), framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep on the lacrimal apparatus — thin textbook framing, as this row's slate states: the shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature.
cards.result: Turnover: basal tear turnover by fluorophotometry is 15.6 ± 5.4%/min in healthy controls in one laboratory and 13.1–17.5%/min across three European centres under one standardised protocol — a concordant mid-teens percent per minute, i.e. the basal tear film replaces roughly a sixth of itself each minute; glaucoma and timolol lower it. Stability: break-up time in health is ~11 s non-invasively (automated keratograph, N = 237) and ~12 s by fluorescein (N = 30) — neighbouring methods, similar centre. Composition: osmolarity centres at 289–299 mOsm/L depending on cohort and device, with no age or sex effect in the large cohort. REFUSAL, reported as required: Mishima and colleagues' 1966 'Determination of tear volume and tear flow', the classic fluorophotometric-era anchor named for this row, was refused as a card because its PubMed record fetched this session carries no abstract, so its values could not be verified from the record — it is named here, not carded, and no tear-volume figure from it is printed on this shelf. Basal versus reflex secretion rates beyond the basal-turnover definition itself are presented only as the textbook's account: the carded records measure the basal state by design, and reflex rates are not quantified in any fetched record here.
cards.watchOut: Every quantity here is method-bound (fluorophotometry vs automated NIBUT vs lab-on-chip osmolarity); the shelf cards per method and never pools devices into one number.

shelves.title: Mepolizumab in hypereosinophilic syndrome: flares 28% versus 56% in one phase 3 trial — fewer flares, some steroid-sparing
shelves.question: In adults with hypereosinophilic syndrome, does mepolizumab, compared with placebo plus standard care, reduce disease flares and spare glucocorticoids?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Child · Double-Blind Method · Eosinophils/metabolism · Humans · Hypereosinophilic Syndrome/blood,drug therapy · Leukocyte Count · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the single phase 3 trial (108 patients with FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome and recent flares), mepolizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks halved the proportion with one or more flares over 32 weeks (28% vs 56%; odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.64). The effect was consistent across baseline eosinophil subgroups, and the open-label extension showed continued flare control with at least 50% oral corticosteroid dose reductions in 28% of steroid-treated patients. A single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Mepolizumab in EGPA is a different question, homed on pack #1653, and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 3 primary trial (Roufosse 2020): flares in 28% on mepolizumab versus 56% on placebo over 32 weeks (odds ratio 0.28; P=0.003)
cards.summary: Phase 3 primary trial (Roufosse 2020): flares in 28% on mepolizumab versus 56% on placebo over 32 weeks (odds ratio 0.28; P=0.003)
cards.people: 108 patients with FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome, two or more flares in the previous 12 months and a screening blood eosinophil count of at least 1,000 cells/µL, at 39 centres in 13 countries, randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous mepolizumab 300 mg (n=54) or placebo (n=54) every 4 weeks for 32 weeks, plus existing HES therapy. Primary outcome: one or more flares (or early withdrawal, counted as a flare) during the study.
cards.result: One or more flares occurred in 15 of 54 patients (28%) on mepolizumab versus 30 of 54 (56%) on placebo — a 50% lower proportion (P=0.002); logistic regression gave an odds ratio of 0.28 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.64; P=0.003). On-treatment adverse events were similar (89% vs 87%). The authors conclude mepolizumab significantly reduced flares with no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 3 trial in a selected population — FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative disease with recent flares and eosinophils ≥1,000 cells/µL. It does not cover myeloid-variant HES, and early withdrawal counted as a flare, which is conservative but blends tolerability into the efficacy endpoint.
cards.source: Roufosse F et al. Efficacy and safety of mepolizumab in hypereosinophilic syndrome: A phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2020. PMID: 32956756. Registry ID: NCT02836496.
