cards.headline: Flare analysis by baseline eosinophil count (Rothenberg 2022): mepolizumab cut the proportion with flares by 63% to 90% across every baseline eosinophil subgroup
cards.summary: Flare analysis by baseline eosinophil count (Rothenberg 2022): mepolizumab cut the proportion with flares by 63% to 90% across every baseline eosinophil subgroup
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Rothenberg 2022)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the same phase 3 trial (108 patients, NCT02836496): patients aged 12 or older with HES for at least 6 months, two or more flares in the previous year and screening eosinophils ≥1,000 cells/µL, randomised to mepolizumab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks plus baseline HES therapy. Outcomes were examined by baseline blood eosinophil count (<1,500; 1,500 to <2,500; ≥2,500 cells/µL) and serum interleukin-5 level.
cards.result: Across eosinophil subgroups, mepolizumab reduced the proportion of patients with one or more flares by 63% to 90% and the flare rate by 58% to 84%, with no significant treatment-by-eosinophil interaction (P=0.76 and P=0.90). Fatigue (Brief Fatigue Inventory item 3) improved more with mepolizumab in every subgroup (for example 61% vs 0% improved at eosinophils ≥2,500 cells/µL). Most patients had undetectable baseline interleukin-5; in that group mepolizumab reduced the proportion with flares by 77% and the flare rate by 67%.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc analysis of the same single trial — it shows the effect is not confined to the highest-eosinophil patients, but subgroup percentages (one is 61% vs 0%) rest on very small numbers and add no independent replication.
cards.source: Rothenberg ME et al. Mepolizumab Reduces Hypereosinophilic Syndrome Flares Irrespective of Blood Eosinophil Count and Interleukin-5. J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract. 2022. PMID: 35568330. cards.headline: Open-label extension (Gleich 2021): flare rates stayed low for 20 more weeks and 28% of steroid-treated patients halved their oral corticosteroid dose
cards.summary: Open-label extension (Gleich 2021): flare rates stayed low for 20 more weeks and 28% of steroid-treated patients halved their oral corticosteroid dose
cards.people: 102 of the 104 patients who completed the phase 3 trial (52 previously on placebo, 50 previously on mepolizumab) entered a 20-week open-label extension on mepolizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks plus background therapy. Primary endpoints were safety-based; flare rates, oral corticosteroid dose and blood eosinophil count were also assessed.
cards.result: Adverse events were reported by 65% of patients, treatment-related events by 15% and serious events by 9%; none were fatal. Annualised flare rates were 0.37 events/year (95% CI 0.16 to 0.86) in the previous-placebo group and 0.14 (0.04 to 0.49) in the previous-mepolizumab group. Of 72 patients receiving oral corticosteroids in weeks 0–4, 20 (28%) achieved reductions of at least 50% in mean daily dose during weeks 16–20. Blood eosinophil count fell by 89% at week 20 in previous-placebo patients and stayed reduced in previous-mepolizumab patients.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, in trial completers — the steroid-sparing figure (28% halving dose) is the clinically useful signal, but without a comparator it cannot separate drug effect from protocol-driven tapering.
cards.source: Gleich GJ et al. Safety and Efficacy of Mepolizumab in Hypereosinophilic Syndrome: An Open-Label Extension Study. J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract. 2021. PMID: 34389506. Registry ID: NCT03306043 (extension; parent trial NCT02836496). cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme, consistently fewer flares and some steroid-sparing — benefit is probable but rests on a single trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme, consistently fewer flares and some steroid-sparing — benefit is probable but rests on a single trial
cards.people: One phase 3 programme reported three times: the primary trial (108 patients), a post-hoc flare analysis of the same trial, and its 20-week open-label extension (102 patients).
cards.result: Flares: 28% versus 56% over 32 weeks (odds ratio 0.28), consistent across baseline eosinophil counts and interleukin-5 levels, with low flare rates maintained in the extension and at least halving of oral corticosteroid dose in 28% of steroid-treated patients. Harms were similar to placebo in the blinded phase. Mepolizumab in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis — a different disease question — is homed on pack #1653 and is not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Everything rests on one trial programme in FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative, flare-prone HES; there is no second trial, no mortality or organ-damage endpoint, and no evidence here for myeloid or lymphocytic-variant disease.

shelves.title: Balloon sinuplasty versus functional endoscopic sinus surgery
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis (without polyps, or with limited disease) who are candidates for sinus surgery, does standalone balloon catheter dilation of the sinus ostia achieve symptom relief and patency comparable to functional endoscopic sinus surgery, with what recovery and revision-surgery trade-offs?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Sinusitis/surgery · Rhinitis/surgery · Catheterization/methods · Endoscopy/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised programme plus one small independent trial point the same way, which caps the stamp. In REMODEL, standalone balloon dilation was noninferior to FESS for symptom improvement at 6 months (SNOT-20 improvement 1.67 vs 1.60) and at 1 year (−1.64 vs −1.65), with ostial patency 96.7% versus 98.7%, revision surgery 2% in each arm, and clear recovery advantages (debridements 0.1 vs 1.2 per patient; shorter pain-medication use and recovery time). The full-cohort/meta-analysis report (135 randomised patients; 358 pooled dilation patients) found comparability out to 24 months. An independent Finnish randomised trial against uncinectomy in isolated maxillary disease also found equal symptom improvement and less synechia with balloon treatment. The population fence is strict: uncomplicated maxillary, with or without anterior ethmoid, disease in patients who already met criteria for surgery. The tested dilation system is not named in the REMODEL record's abstract, so no brand claim is made here.

cards.headline: REMODEL 2013: standalone balloon dilation was noninferior to FESS for symptom improvement at 6 months, with far fewer postoperative debridements
cards.summary: REMODEL 2013: standalone balloon dilation was noninferior to FESS for symptom improvement at 6 months, with far fewer postoperative debridements
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised controlled trial (REMODEL primary report)
cards.people: 92 adults with uncomplicated chronic rhinosinusitis of the maxillary sinuses, with or without anterior ethmoid disease, who met criteria for medically necessary FESS, randomised 1:1 to office balloon dilation (50) or FESS (42) and followed 6 months. The record does not name the dilation system or its maker.
cards.result: Mean SNOT-20 improvement was 1.67 ± 1.10 after balloon dilation versus 1.60 ± 0.96 after FESS — clinically meaningful and significant in both arms (p<0.0001), with balloon dilation noninferior (p<0.001). Debridements per patient were 0.1 ± 0.6 versus 1.2 ± 1.0 (balloon superior, p<0.0001); nasal bleeding, duration of prescription pain-medication use, recovery time and short-term symptom improvement all favoured balloon dilation. No complications occurred in either group; one revision surgery was reported in each arm.
cards.watchOut: REMODEL enrolled only uncomplicated maxillary ± anterior ethmoid disease in patients already judged surgical candidates — the result does not extend to frontal/sphenoid disease, polyps or complicated sinusitis, and the trial was industry-era device research whose funder is not stated in the record.
cards.source: Cutler J et al. Standalone balloon dilation versus sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis: a prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled trial. Am J Rhinol Allergy. 2013. PMID: 23920419. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: REMODEL 1-year follow-up: symptom gains held in both arms (SNOT-20 change −1.64 balloon versus −1.65 FESS), ostial patency ~97–99%, revision 2% in each arm
cards.summary: REMODEL 1-year follow-up: symptom gains held in both arms (SNOT-20 change −1.64 balloon versus −1.65 FESS), ostial patency ~97–99%, revision 2% in each arm
cards.type: Randomised trial 1-year follow-up report — same REMODEL programme, not an independent trial
cards.people: The 92 REMODEL patients (50 balloon dilation, 42 FESS); 89 (96.7%) completed 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: Both groups kept clinically meaningful, significant improvement in overall SNOT-20 and all four subscales; the 1-year mean change after balloon dilation (−1.64) was noninferior to FESS (−1.65; p<0.001). Ostial patency was 96.7% after balloon dilation and 98.7% after FESS, rhinosinusitis episodes fell significantly in both groups (mean decrease 4.2 vs 3.5), and work productivity and activity impairment improved in both. No complications; revision surgery rate 2% in each arm through 1 year.
cards.watchOut: A follow-on report of the same 92 patients — it adds durability, not independent confirmation; attrition was low but the population remains the narrow REMODEL one.

cards.headline: REMODEL full cohort and meta-analysis 2016: outcomes comparable between FESS and balloon dilation out to 24 months; pooled standalone dilation technical success 97.5%
cards.summary: REMODEL full cohort and meta-analysis 2016: outcomes comparable between FESS and balloon dilation out to 24 months; pooled standalone dilation technical success 97.5%
cards.type: Randomised trial full-cohort report plus meta-analysis of standalone balloon dilation studies — REMODEL programme
cards.people: REMODEL full-study cohort of 135 patients treated with FESS or in-office balloon dilation (130 with 12-month data, 66 at 18 months, 25 at 24 months), plus a meta-analysis of six standalone balloon dilation studies including 358 patients. The record does not name the dilation system or its maker.
cards.result: REMODEL outcomes at 18–24 months were consistent with the 6- and 12-month results. In the meta-analysis, technical success was 97.5% and mean SNOT scores were significantly and clinically improved at all time points (P<.0001), with significant reductions in work/school days missed, homebound days, physician/nurse visits, acute infections and antibiotic prescriptions; mean recovery time was 1.4 days. Twelve-month symptom improvement and revision rates did not differ between the REMODEL FESS arm (59), the REMODEL balloon arm (71) and pooled single-arm dilation studies (243).
cards.watchOut: Only 25 REMODEL patients reached 24 months, and most of the pooled dilation evidence is single-arm — the comparison at long horizons rests heavily on the randomised arms' early data. Hybrid balloon-plus-FESS procedures are a different question and are not pooled here.
cards.source: Chandra RK et al. REMODEL larger cohort with long-term outcomes and meta-analysis of standalone balloon dilation studies. Laryngoscope. 2016. PMID: 26228589. cards.headline: Bizaki 2016: balloon sinuplasty and uncinectomy improved symptoms equally in isolated maxillary sinusitis, with less synechia after balloon treatment
cards.summary: Bizaki 2016: balloon sinuplasty and uncinectomy improved symptoms equally in isolated maxillary sinusitis, with less synechia after balloon treatment
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, non-blinded controlled trial (independent of REMODEL)
cards.people: Adults with symptomatic isolated chronic or recurrent rhinosinusitis of the maxillary sinus without severe CT findings, at Tampere University Hospital, Finland, randomised to uncinectomy or balloon sinuplasty and assessed at 3 and 6 months. N not documented in the record's abstract — the number of patients is not stated there.
cards.result: Both balloon sinuplasty and uncinectomy significantly improved almost all SNOT-22 parameters (P<0.05), with no significant difference between the groups (P>0.05); nasal airway resistance fell after treatment on rhinomanometry. Balloon sinuplasty was associated with a significantly lesser risk of synechia. The authors note the smaller synechia risk and promising efficiency only partly compensate for the balloon's high material cost.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the abstract, non-blinded, and the comparator is uncinectomy alone rather than full FESS — a narrower, milder-disease comparison than REMODEL's.
cards.source: Bizaki AJ et al. Decrease of nasal airway resistance and alleviations of symptoms after balloon sinuplasty in patients with isolated chronic rhinosinusitis: a prospective, randomised clinical study. cards.headline: Synthesis: standalone balloon dilation matches FESS for symptoms in limited maxillary disease, with faster recovery — within a narrow, mostly single-programme base
cards.summary: Synthesis: standalone balloon dilation matches FESS for symptoms in limited maxillary disease, with faster recovery — within a narrow, mostly single-programme base
cards.people: One randomised programme (REMODEL: 92 patients in the primary report, 135 in the full cohort) plus one independent Finnish randomised comparison against uncinectomy (N not documented in its record).
cards.result: Symptom improvement, ostial patency (~97–99% at 1 year) and revision rates (~2% per arm at 1 year) were comparable between standalone balloon dilation and FESS, while recovery, pain-medication duration and debridement burden favoured balloon dilation. The independent trial points the same way against a lesser operation (uncinectomy).
cards.watchOut: The evidence covers uncomplicated maxillary ± anterior ethmoid disease in surgical candidates only. It does not cover polyp disease, frontal or sphenoid disease, or hybrid balloon-plus-FESS surgery, and the randomised base is essentially one programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Inferior turbinate reduction techniques for nasal obstruction
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinitis / inferior turbinate hypertrophy and nasal obstruction despite medical therapy, does inferior turbinate reduction (radiofrequency ablation or the tested surgical techniques) improve nasal obstruction versus sham, medical therapy or alternative techniques?
shelves.mesh: Turbinates/surgery · Nasal Obstruction/surgery · Radiofrequency Ablation/methods · Rhinitis/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the sham-controlled limb rests on a single trial, which caps the stamp. In that trial (98 patients), radiofrequency ablation, diode laser and microdebrider-assisted turbinoplasty each reduced nasal-obstruction scores significantly more than a placebo procedure at 3 months (P=.03, .02 and .04 respectively) — while the placebo procedure itself also improved symptoms significantly, so the increment over sham is real but modest. Technique-comparison evidence is separate: temperature-controlled versus bipolar radiofrequency were equivalent on symptoms and objective measures to 1 year (84 patients; bipolar much faster to perform), and a split-side study (60 patients) ranked ultrasound reduction above radiofrequency above submucosal cauterisation. No record names a device brand or maker, so techniques are named generically here, exactly as published.

cards.headline: Harju 2018: radiofrequency ablation, diode laser and microdebrider turbinoplasty each beat a placebo procedure for nasal obstruction — but the placebo procedure itself improved symptoms significantly
cards.summary: Harju 2018: radiofrequency ablation, diode laser and microdebrider turbinoplasty each beat a placebo procedure for nasal obstruction — but the placebo procedure itself improved symptoms significantly
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, single-blinded, placebo-controlled trial (four arms)
cards.people: 98 consecutive patients with enlarged inferior turbinates from persistent year-round rhinitis, randomised 1:2:2:2 to a placebo procedure, radiofrequency ablation, diode laser or microdebrider-assisted inferior turbinoplasty, all under local anaesthesia with eyes covered; assessed at 3 months. The record names the techniques generically and gives no device brand or maker.
cards.result: Nasal-obstruction visual analogue scores fell significantly in ALL groups, including placebo. Each active technique reduced obstruction significantly more than placebo: radiofrequency ablation P=.03, diode laser P=.02, microdebrider-assisted turbinoplasty P=.04. The authors stress the placebo effect had a large role in the overall improvement.
cards.watchOut: The only sham-controlled study in this pack, and it is a single 98-patient trial at 3 months: the honest reading is a real but modest increment over a large placebo response, with no durability data.
cards.source: Harju T et al. A prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled study of inferior turbinate surgery. Laryngoscope. 2018. PMID: 29392727. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Banhiran 2015: temperature-controlled and bipolar radiofrequency gave similar outcomes for turbinate reduction, with much shorter operating time for bipolar
cards.summary: Banhiran 2015: temperature-controlled and bipolar radiofrequency gave similar outcomes for turbinate reduction, with much shorter operating time for bipolar
cards.type: Prospective, randomised non-inferiority trial (technique comparison, no sham arm)
cards.people: 84 adults with chronic rhinitis refractory to medication, randomised to temperature-controlled radiofrequency (42) or bipolar radiofrequency (42); outcomes at 4 weeks and 1 year, objective measures by blinded assessors. Registry: NCT01054521. The record names the techniques generically and gives no device brand or maker.
cards.result: No significant difference between techniques in subjective (obstruction, discharge, sneezing, hyposmia, postnasal drip visual analogue scores) or objective outcomes at 4 weeks — 95% CIs of mean differences lay within the pre-set −1.5 to 1.5 margin except for nasal discharge — and still no difference at 1 year. Operating time was far longer for temperature-controlled treatment (481.5 ± 36.2 vs 37.1 ± 3.0 seconds; p<0.001); bipolar treatment left slightly more crusting (p=0.04). Pain was minimal and bleeding minor in both, with no serious adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: A technique-versus-technique trial cannot show either technique beats doing nothing — that evidence comes only from the Harju sham-controlled card; non-inferiority margins were generous (±1.5 on a 0–10 scale).
cards.source: Banhiran W et al. A randomized study of temperature-controlled versus bipolar radiofrequency for inferior turbinate reduction. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2015. PMID: 25432641. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01054521 , from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Gindros 2010: ultrasound turbinate reduction ranked best, then radiofrequency, then submucosal cauterisation — all improved obstruction within patients' own two sides
cards.summary: Gindros 2010: ultrasound turbinate reduction ranked best, then radiofrequency, then submucosal cauterisation — all improved obstruction within patients' own two sides
cards.people: 60 patients with chronic hypertrophic rhinitis of non-allergic aetiology unresponsive to conservative treatment: in 30, ultrasound reduction on the left side and monopolar diathermy on the right; in 30, radiofrequency coblation on the left and ultrasound on the right. Assessed before surgery and at 1, 3 and 6 months by visual analogue scales, active anterior rhinomanometry and acoustic rhinometry.
cards.result: Subjective and objective evaluation showed significant postoperative improvement in all cases. The best results were obtained with the ultrasound procedure, second with radiofrequency, and least with electrocautery, although electrocautery did not differ significantly from radiofrequency. The authors conclude ultrasound reduction is effective and safe in medically refractory hypertrophic rhinitis.
cards.watchOut: Split-side designs measure each side's airflow, but the patient experiences one nose — subjective scores cannot be cleanly attributed to a side, and there is no sham or untreated control; rankings rest on modest between-technique differences.
cards.source: Gindros G et al. Comparison of ultrasound turbinate reduction, radiofrequency tissue ablation and submucosal cauterization in inferior turbinate hypertrophy. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2010. PMID: 20432043. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: active turbinate reduction beats sham by a modest margin; between techniques, differences are small and inconsistently ranked
cards.summary: Synthesis: active turbinate reduction beats sham by a modest margin; between techniques, differences are small and inconsistently ranked
cards.people: Three randomised studies totalling 242 patients: one four-arm sham-controlled trial (98), one radiofrequency-versus-radiofrequency non-inferiority trial (84) and one split-side three-technique comparison (60).
cards.result: Sham-controlled evidence (one trial) shows radiofrequency ablation, diode laser and microdebrider turbinoplasty each reduce obstruction significantly more than a placebo procedure at 3 months, against a large placebo response. shelves.title: Punctal plugs for dry eye disease
shelves.question: In adults with dry eye disease, does punctal occlusion (punctal plugs, the types tested) improve symptoms, tear-film measures and corneal staining versus no occlusion / sham, and how do plug types compare on retention and complications (epiphora, canaliculitis, extrusion)?
shelves.mesh: Dry Eye Syndromes/therapy · Punctal Plugs · Lacrimal Apparatus/surgery · Prostheses and Implants · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled evidence does not establish a symptom benefit. The Cochrane review (18 trials, 711 participants) found little or no improvement in symptom scores with punctal plugs versus no plugs (very low-certainty evidence), with only small favourable differences in fluorescein staining (mean difference −1.50 points in one trial) and tear-film stability (+1.93 seconds in one trial), and fewer artificial-tear applications in one trial. Small individual trials report within-group improvements in symptoms, break-up time and staining (SmartPlug vs silicone, 36 eyes; post-LASIK plugs vs no plugs, 18 patients — the one direct comparison favouring plugs on signs and symptoms), but most lack an untreated control. Where plug types were compared head-to-head, efficacy was similar and retention was the real difference: Parasol plugs (Odyssey Medical / Beaver Visitec, as published) were retained in 68% versus 32% for Super Flex plugs (Eagle Vision / Oasis Medical, as published) at 6 months, and one trial lost 33% of silicone plugs spontaneously. Harms are mostly epiphora, itching and displacement, with inflammatory complications such as dacryocystitis less common. Symptoms and signs are kept separate throughout, as they frequently disagree in this literature.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2017: across 18 trials (711 participants), whether punctal plugs improve dry-eye symptoms versus no plugs was inconclusive — very low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017: across 18 trials (711 participants), whether punctal plugs improve dry-eye symptoms versus no plugs was inconclusive — very low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials
cards.people: 18 trials, 711 participants (1249 eyes) from 10 countries, of collagen or silicone punctal plugs in symptomatic aqueous tear deficiency or dry eye syndrome; evidence last updated 8 December 2016.
cards.result: Five trials compared plugs with no plugs: the three reporting symptoms used different scales and all showed little or no improvement in symptom scores with plugs. Fluorescein staining was slightly less with plugs in one trial (mean difference −1.50 points, 95% CI −1.88 to −1.12; 61 eyes, low-certainty) and tear-film stability slightly better (mean difference 1.93 seconds more, 95% CI 0.67 to 3.20; 28 eyes, low-certainty); artificial-tear applications were fewer with plugs in one trial (mean difference −2.70, 95% CI −3.11 to −2.29; 61 eyes). Against artificial tears, staining and tear production showed little or no difference. Adverse events in plug groups included epiphora, itching, lid tenderness/swelling with mucous discharge, and plug displacement; dacryocystitis is the less common inflammatory risk the review names.
cards.watchOut: The review's own verdict is inconclusiveness: trials were poorly reported, at unclear risk of bias, and heterogeneous in plug type, dry-eye severity and methods — individual trial authors' positive conclusions do not survive pooling.
cards.source: Ervin AM et al. Punctal occlusion for dry eye syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017. PMID: 28649802. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cochrane systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials 18 trials, 711 participants (1249 eyes) from 10 countries, of collagen or silicone punctal plugs in symptomatic aqueous tear deficiency or dry eye syndrome; evidence last updated 8 december 2016. five trials compared plugs with no plugs: the three reporting symptoms used different scales and all showed little or no improvement in symptom scores with plugs. fluorescein staining was slightly less with plugs in one trial (mean difference −1.50 points, 95% ci −1.88 to −1.12; 61 eyes, low-certainty) and tear-film stability slightly better (mean difference 1.93 seconds more, 95% ci 0.67 to 3.20; 28 eyes, low-certainty); artificial-tear applications were fewer with plugs in one trial (mean difference −2.70, 95% ci −3.11 to −2.29; 61 eyes). against artificial tears, staining and tear production showed little or no difference. adverse events in plug groups included epiphora, itching, lid tenderness/swelling with mucous discharge, and plug displacement; dacryocystitis is the less common inflammatory risk the review names. the review's own verdict is inconclusiveness: trials were poorly reported, at unclear risk of bias, and heterogeneous in plug type, dry-eye severity and methods — individual trial authors' positive conclusions do not survive pooling. ervin am et al. punctal occlusion for dry eye syndrome. cochrane database syst rev. 2017. pmid: 28649802. registry id: none in the record's databank fields. mesh: dry eye syndromes/therapy · female · humans · lacrimal apparatus · male · punctal plugs · randomized controlled trials as topic · tears · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Brissette 2015: Parasol plugs were retained far better than Super Flex plugs at 6 months (68% versus 32%), and signs improved within both plug groups
cards.summary: Brissette 2015: Parasol plugs were retained far better than Super Flex plugs at 6 months (68% versus 32%), and signs improved within both plug groups
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, controlled trial of plug types (retention primary outcome)
cards.people: 50 eyes of patients with moderate-to-severe dry eye at a Canadian university hospital, each eye separately randomised to a Super Flex plug (Eagle Vision, Memphis, Tennessee, USA; Softplug — Oasis Medical Inc, Glendora, California, USA) or a Parasol plug (Odyssey Medical, Memphis, Tennessee, USA; Beaver Visitec International, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA), as named in the publication.
cards.result: Plug retention at 6 months differed significantly (P=.011): 68% of Parasol plugs retained versus 32% of Super Flex plugs. Parasol eyes needed artificial tears less frequently at 6 months (P=.024). All secondary measures (Schirmer I, tear meniscus height, tear break-up time, fluorescein corneal staining) improved significantly within plug groups at 6 months except conjunctival staining; no other between-group differences and no plug complications were reported.
cards.watchOut: An eye-level randomised comparison of two products, not of plugs versus no treatment: within-group sign improvements have no untreated control, and retention — the decisive difference — is a device property, not proof of symptom benefit.
cards.source: Brissette AR et al. Punctal Plug Retention Rates for the Treatment of Moderate to Severe Dry Eye: A Randomized, Double-Masked, Controlled Clinical Trial. Am J Ophthalmol. 2015. PMID: 25998003. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Burgess 2008: SmartPlug and silicone plugs improved symptoms, tear break-up time and staining equally over ~11 weeks; a third of silicone plugs were lost spontaneously
cards.summary: Burgess 2008: SmartPlug and silicone plugs improved symptoms, tear break-up time and staining equally over ~11 weeks; a third of silicone plugs were lost spontaneously
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial of plug types
cards.people: 36 eyes with dry-eye symptoms, tear break-up time under 5 seconds and ocular surface damage on staining, randomised to silicone plug or SmartPlug inferior punctal occlusion (products named as published; the record gives no maker for either). Mean follow-up 11.2 weeks.
cards.result: Both plug types significantly improved symptom scores (silicone P=0.002; SmartPlug P=0.005), tear break-up time (P=0.035 and P=0.009) and fluorescein and rose Bengal staining, with no significant difference between plugs on these measures; SmartPlug eyes also improved tear meniscus height (P=0.037). Artificial-tear use fell in 10 of 18 silicone eyes (55.6%) and 11 of 18 SmartPlug eyes (61.1%). Minor insertion complications occurred in 4 silicone eyes (22%) and 2 SmartPlug eyes (11%); spontaneous loss occurred with 6 silicone plugs (33%).
cards.watchOut: 36 eyes, no untreated or sham arm, ~11 weeks: within-group improvements cannot be separated from natural fluctuation and co-treatment, which is exactly the gap the Cochrane review exposes.
cards.source: Burgess PI et al. SmartPlug versus silicone punctal plug therapy for dry eye: a prospective randomized trial. Cornea. 2008. PMID: 18434839. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Yung 2012: in post-LASIK dry eye unresponsive to artificial tears, punctal plugs beat no plugs on staining, tear break-up time and functional visual acuity at 3 months
cards.summary: Yung 2012: in post-LASIK dry eye unresponsive to artificial tears, punctal plugs beat no plugs on staining, tear break-up time and functional visual acuity at 3 months
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled study (plugs versus no plugs)
cards.people: 25 eyes of 18 patients after LASIK who met Japanese dry-eye criteria and had not responded to artificial tears by 1 month after surgery, randomly divided into a plug group (plugs in superior and inferior puncta) and a non-plug group; compared at 1 and 3 months after surgery.
cards.result: At 3 months, surface regularity index, fluorescein staining and tear break-up time were significantly better in the plug group. Changes from 1 to 3 months in uncorrected and functional visual acuity, staining, tear break-up time and symptoms improved significantly in the plug group compared with the non-plug group. The authors conclude punctal occlusion of both puncta is effective for post-LASIK dry eye uncontrolled by artificial tears alone.
cards.watchOut: The smallest and most specific card here: 18 patients in a self-limiting post-surgical condition, where part of the gain may be the natural post-LASIK recovery the randomisation only partly controls for at this size.
cards.source: Yung YH et al. Punctal plugs for treatment of post-LASIK dry eye. Jpn J Ophthalmol. 2012. PMID: 22358586. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Altan-Yaycioglu 2005: collagen and silicone plugs performed alike in the short term — both raised tear volume and tear-film retention on scintigraphy
cards.summary: Altan-Yaycioglu 2005: collagen and silicone plugs performed alike in the short term — both raised tear volume and tear-film retention on scintigraphy
cards.type: Prospective randomised clinical trial of plug types, with lacrimal scintigraphy
cards.people: 24 dry-eye patients: group I 22 eyes received collagen plugs, group II 26 eyes received silicone plugs; normal control subjects contributed 22 eyes. Schirmer I, tear break-up time, rose Bengal staining and scintigraphic tear half-life (T½) and retention index were measured before and after occlusion.
cards.result: In both patient groups Schirmer I, tear break-up time and rose Bengal staining improved significantly after plug insertion; mean T½ and retention index rose significantly in both groups (P<.0001 for both), with no significant difference between collagen and silicone groups (P>.05) and post-insertion values similar between the plug types.
cards.watchOut: Short-term, 24 patients, no untreated dry-eye control arm: it compares two plug materials on tear-retention physiology, not plugs against no treatment for symptoms.
cards.source: Altan-Yaycioglu R et al. Silicone versus collagen plugs for treating dry eye: results of a prospective randomized trial including lacrimal scintigraphy. Am J Ophthalmol. 2005. PMID: 15939391. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: signs and tear retention improve in small trials, but the pooled symptom verdict is inconclusive — plug choice is mainly a retention question
cards.summary: Synthesis: signs and tear retention improve in small trials, but the pooled symptom verdict is inconclusive — plug choice is mainly a retention question
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 18 trials (711 participants) plus four small randomised comparisons carded here (50 eyes, 36 eyes, 25 eyes of 18 patients, and 24 patients).
cards.result: Symptoms: little or no improvement versus no plugs in the pooled Cochrane analysis (very low-certainty). Signs: small favourable differences in staining and tear-film stability, and consistent within-trial improvements. Between plug types, efficacy looks similar (SmartPlug vs silicone; collagen vs silicone), while retention differs sharply by design (Parasol 68% vs Super Flex 32% at 6 months; 33% spontaneous loss of silicone plugs in one trial). Harms are usually minor — epiphora, itching, displacement — with dacryocystitis the less common inflammatory complication.
cards.watchOut: Symptom and sign endpoints disagree across this literature, so they are reported separately here and never composited. Most positive findings come from trials without an untreated control arm.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Autologous serum eye drops for dry eye disease
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe dry eye disease (including Sjögren-related and post-LASIK), do autologous serum eye drops improve symptoms, corneal staining and tear-film measures versus artificial tears / conventional lubricant therapy?
shelves.mesh: Dry Eye Syndromes/drug therapy · Serum · Ophthalmic Solutions/administration & dosage · Tears/physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — several small randomised trials agree on tear-film signs, while symptom effects are less consistent, which caps the stamp. Against artificial tears, 20% autologous serum (the commonest concentration where a record states one) prolonged tear break-up time in the severe-dry-eye crossover (20 patients; OSDI fell 55.18% on serum versus 19.50% on artificial tears, P<0.001, with no staining difference), improved nearly all clinical parameters in a 144-patient Hansen's-disease trial, and prolonged break-up time with lower rose Bengal staining after LASIK (27 patients) without a symptom difference. A pilot crossover found allogeneic serum comparable to autologous, with neither significantly improving OSDI. Preparation protocols vary between trials and one record does not state its concentration; where a publication does not document a standardised product, current preparations may differ in composition and effect. Sjögren-specific randomised evidence was not separately verified, so the shelf makes no Sjögren-specific claim.

cards.headline: Celebi 2014: 20% autologous serum beat preservative-free artificial tears on symptoms and tear stability in severe dry eye (OSDI fell 55% versus 20%)
cards.summary: Celebi 2014: 20% autologous serum beat preservative-free artificial tears on symptoms and tear stability in severe dry eye (OSDI fell 55% versus 20%)
cards.people: 20 consecutive patients (40 eyes; 18 female, 2 male) with severe dry eye syndrome refractory to conventional treatment, crossing over between 20% autologous serum eye drops and preservative-free artificial tears, 1 month per period.
cards.result: After 1 month, tear break-up time was significantly higher with serum (P<0.001) and the OSDI symptom score fell more (55.18% decrease with serum versus 19.50% with artificial tears; P<0.001). Schirmer test and Oxford conjunctival/corneal staining grades did not differ significantly between treatments (P>0.05).
cards.watchOut: 20 patients, 1-month periods, and the wins are symptoms and break-up time while staining — the sign clinicians watch — did not differ; crossover carry-over is possible with a biological tear substitute.
cards.source: Celebi AR et al. The efficacy of autologous serum eye drops for severe dry eye syndrome: a randomized double-blind crossover study. Graefes Arch Clin Exp Ophthalmol. 2014. PMID: 24566903. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Mukhopadhyay 2015: in Hansen's-disease dry eye, 20% autologous serum improved nearly all clinical parameters at 6 weeks versus artificial tears, in a 144-patient three-arm trial
cards.summary: Mukhopadhyay 2015: in Hansen's-disease dry eye, 20% autologous serum improved nearly all clinical parameters at 6 weeks versus artificial tears, in a 144-patient three-arm trial
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind three-arm trial (cord blood serum vs autologous serum vs artificial tears)
cards.people: 144 consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe dry eye in Hansen's disease, randomly divided into three groups receiving 20% cord blood serum, 20% autologous serum or preservative-free artificial tears, six times daily for 6 weeks, with reassessment 12 weeks after stopping treatment (registry CTRI/2013/07/003802, as printed in the record).
cards.result: In the autologous serum group all clinical parameters except Schirmer I improved significantly at the first post-treatment analysis, sustained at the second analysis except tear break-up time and conjunctival impression cytology grading. In the artificial-tears group, improvements were non-significant except break-up time at the first analysis and largely absent later. Tear lysozyme and lactoferrin rose in both serum groups (statistically insignificant); total tear protein rose in the serum groups and fell on artificial tears.
cards.watchOut: A specific population (Hansen's-disease dry eye) and a three-arm design in which the headline comparisons are within-group changes; the cord-blood arm is a different product and is not evidence for autologous serum.
cards.source: Mukhopadhyay S et al. Comparative role of 20% cord blood serum and 20% autologous serum in dry eye associated with Hansen's disease: a tear proteomic study. Br J Ophthalmol. 2015. PMID: 25138758. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Noda-Tsuruya 2006: after LASIK, autologous serum prolonged tear break-up time and lowered rose Bengal staining versus artificial tears — but dryness symptoms did not differ
cards.summary: Noda-Tsuruya 2006: after LASIK, autologous serum prolonged tear break-up time and lowered rose Bengal staining versus artificial tears — but dryness symptoms did not differ
cards.people: 54 eyes of 27 male patients who underwent LASIK, divided into autologous serum eye drops versus artificial tears postoperatively; Schirmer test with anaesthesia, break-up time and rose Bengal and fluorescein staining compared to 6 months. The record does not state the serum concentration used.
cards.result: Tear break-up time was greater with serum than artificial tears at 6 months, and rose Bengal score was lower at 1 and 3 months. Schirmer values and fluorescein scores did not differ between groups, and subjective dryness scores did not differ between groups. Within the serum group, break-up time rose and staining fell versus preoperative values; within the artificial-tears group no measure changed.
cards.watchOut: All-male, post-surgical, self-limiting dry eye in 27 patients: sign benefits without a symptom difference is the recurring pattern of this literature, and the concentration/protocol is not stated in the record.
cards.source: Noda-Tsuruya T et al. Autologous serum eye drops for dry eye after LASIK. J Refract Surg. 2006. PMID: 16447938. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: van der Meer 2021: allogeneic serum drops matched autologous drops in severe dry eye — and neither significantly improved the primary symptom score in this pilot
cards.summary: van der Meer 2021: allogeneic serum drops matched autologous drops in severe dry eye — and neither significantly improved the primary symptom score in this pilot
cards.type: Pilot, double-blind, randomised crossover trial (allogeneic versus autologous serum)
cards.people: 19 patients enrolled with severe dry eyes (15 completed), randomised to autologous serum for 1 month then, after 1-month washout, allogeneic serum for 1 month, or the reverse order. OSDI was the primary endpoint.
cards.result: OSDI improved from 62 ± 19 to 57 ± 18 on autologous serum and from 59 ± 20 to 56 ± 23 on allogeneic serum; estimated mean differences were −4.2 (95% CI −9.5 to 1.2) and −4.5 (−9.8 to 0.9) respectively — neither statistically significant. Adverse events were mild and resolved completely. The authors conclude the two preparations have comparable efficacy and tolerability, with allogeneic drops an alternative for patients unable to donate blood.
cards.watchOut: A 15-completer pilot cannot establish equivalence, and its non-significant primary endpoint tempers the larger symptom claims elsewhere; it is carded as the adjacent allogeneic limb, not as proof autologous serum beats conventional tears.
cards.source: van der Meer PF et al. Allogeneic and autologous serum eye drops: a pilot double-blind randomized crossover trial. Acta Ophthalmol. 2021. PMID: 33590715. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: serum drops improve tear stability and some staining scores, with symptom benefit clearest in one small crossover trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: serum drops improve tear stability and some staining scores, with symptom benefit clearest in one small crossover trial
cards.people: Four randomised reports: two crossover trials in severe dry eye (20 patients; 19 enrolled/15 completing), a 144-patient three-arm trial in Hansen's-disease dry eye, and a 27-patient post-LASIK trial. Systematic reviews of this literature exist and are consistent with the sign-level benefits, but the cards here are the primary trials.
cards.result: Against artificial tears, 20% autologous serum improved tear break-up time in every comparative trial and rose Bengal staining after LASIK; the largest symptom advantage (OSDI −55% vs −20%) comes from the 20-patient crossover. Schirmer values and fluorescein/Oxford staining often did not differ. Allogeneic serum performed comparably to autologous in a small pilot whose primary endpoint was not significant for either preparation.
cards.watchOut: Preparations vary — 20% is the commonest concentration where stated, protocols differ, and one carded trial does not state its concentration. Current manufactured or blood-service products may differ from the trial preparations. Sjögren-specific randomised evidence was not separately verified this session, so no Sjögren-specific claim is made.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Thermal pulsation (LipiFlow) for meibomian gland dysfunction
shelves.question: In adults with meibomian gland dysfunction and evaporative dry eye, does a single vectored thermal pulsation treatment (the tested LipiFlow programme) improve gland function, tear break-up and symptoms versus warm-compress / sham / alternative thermal pulsation systems, and how long does benefit last?
shelves.mesh: Meibomian Gland Dysfunction/therapy · Dry Eye Syndromes/therapy · Hyperthermia, Induced/methods · Meibomian Glands · Tears
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the gland-function and symptom-superiority questions answer differently. Named as published, per the clarification exception: the tested system is LipiFlow® (vectored thermal pulsation). A single 12-minute treatment improved gland secretion number, secretion score and lipid layer thickness for at least 3 months versus warm compress with lid massage (50 subjects), and a second system, SYSTANE iLux, was noninferior to LipiFlow on gland score, break-up time and symptom bother at every visit out to 12 months (236 subjects). A 10-trial meta-analysis (761 patients) found LipiFlow superior to lid hygiene on OSDI (mean difference −7.4) and SPEED scores — but the Cochrane review (13 trials, 1155 participants) found conflicting symptom evidence versus warm compresses, no difference in gland expression or break-up time in that comparison, and low/very low certainty throughout, with thermostatic devices actually ahead on OSDI at 4 weeks in pooled data. Industry sponsorship is common in this base. No vision-threatening adverse events were reported in any carded trial.

cards.headline: Meng 2023: a single LipiFlow treatment improved gland secretion and symptoms for at least 3 months versus warm compress with lid massage
cards.summary: Meng 2023: a single LipiFlow treatment improved gland secretion and symptoms for at least 3 months versus warm compress with lid massage
cards.type: Randomised controlled clinical trial (single treatment versus home regimen)
cards.people: 50 subjects (100 eyes) with meibomian gland dysfunction in China, randomised to a single 12-minute LipiFlow® thermal pulsation treatment (50 eyes) or warm compress daily for 2 weeks after an initial manual lid massage (50 eyes); followed 3 months. The device is named as published in the record by its registered product name, LipiFlow®; the record does not state its maker on its face.
cards.result: SPEED symptom scores and tear break-up time improved in both groups from baseline to 3 months. Meibomian glands yielding lipid secretion number, gland secretion score and lipid layer thickness improved in the LipiFlow group and were maintained without significant regression at 3 months. Corneal fluorescein staining improved more in the warm-compress group at 1 month. Lipid layer thickness correlated positively with break-up time and gland secretion measures.
cards.watchOut: 50 subjects with eyes as the unit in places, 3 months only, and an active comparator that itself improved symptoms — the trial shows durability of gland-function gains, not superiority on symptoms; sponsorship is not stated in the record.
cards.source: Meng Z et al. Efficacy and Safety evaluation of a single thermal pulsation system treatment (Lipiflow®) on meibomian gland dysfunction: a randomized controlled clinical trial. Int Ophthalmol. 2023. PMID: 36112256. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Wesley 2022: SYSTANE iLux was noninferior to LipiFlow at every visit out to 12 months after a single treatment (236 subjects)
cards.summary: Wesley 2022: SYSTANE iLux was noninferior to LipiFlow at every visit out to 12 months after a single treatment (236 subjects)
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre, assessor-masked non-inferiority (equivalence) trial — two thermal pulsation systems
cards.people: 236 subjects aged 18 or over with meibomian gland dysfunction and evaporative dry eye (lower-lid meibomian gland score ≤12, non-invasive break-up time <10 seconds, symptom-bother score >16), randomised 1:1 to a single SYSTANE iLux treatment (119) or a single LipiFlow treatment (117), as the two systems are named in the publication; 227 completed the study (mean age 57.3 ± 13.8 years). Registry: NCT03956225.
cards.result: At 12 months, least-squares mean change in meibomian gland score was 17.4 ± 1.97 with iLux versus 17.8 ± 1.98 with LipiFlow. Non-inferiority of iLux to LipiFlow was achieved at all post-treatment visits for gland score (lower 95% confidence limit of the difference >−5), non-invasive break-up time (>−2.5 seconds) and symptom-bother score (upper limit <12). No other serious ocular or device-related adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A device-versus-device equivalence trial: it shows the two systems perform alike for a year, not that either beats sham or home care. Industry sponsorship is common in this literature and the record's support line does not name a funder on its face.
cards.source: Wesley G et al. Comparison of Two Thermal Pulsation Systems in the Treatment of Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: A Randomized, Multicenter Study. Optom Vis Sci. 2022. PMID: 35383732. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03956225 , from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Hu 2022 meta-analysis: across 10 RCTs (761 patients), LipiFlow beat lid hygiene on symptoms and gland function, with no excess adverse events
cards.summary: Hu 2022 meta-analysis: across 10 RCTs (761 patients), LipiFlow beat lid hygiene on symptoms and gland function, with no excess adverse events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 10 randomised trials incorporating 761 patients with meibomian gland dysfunction, comparing the LipiFlow® vectored thermal pulsation system with lid hygiene or no treatment (literature to 4 January 2021).
cards.result: Versus lid hygiene, LipiFlow improved corneal fluorescein staining (mean difference −0.42, 95% CI −0.75 to −0.1), OSDI score (mean difference −7.4, 95% CI −11.06 to −3.74), SPEED score (mean difference −2.7, 95% CI −3.95 to −1.45), glands yielding liquid secretion (mean difference 1.3, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.82) and gland secretion score (mean difference 4.09, 95% CI 1.18 to 6.99) in the main subgroup; versus no treatment, OSDI, SPEED and gland measures also improved significantly. Adverse events were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves flag improper units of randomisation/analysis as the leading source of heterogeneity — several underlying trials randomised eyes, not people — so pooled symptom differences should be read as approximate.
cards.source: Hu J et al. Efficacy and safety of a vectored thermal pulsation system (Lipiflow®) in the treatment of meibomian gland dysfunction: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Graefes Arch Clin Exp Ophthalmol. 2022. PMID: 34374808. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Cochrane 2024: across 13 trials (1155 participants), LipiFlow performed similarly to other dry-eye treatments — conflicting symptom evidence versus warm compresses, low/very low certainty throughout
cards.summary: Cochrane 2024: across 13 trials (1155 participants), LipiFlow performed similarly to other dry-eye treatments — conflicting symptom evidence versus warm compresses, low/very low certainty throughout
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials
cards.people: 13 trials randomising 1155 participants (66% female, ages 19–86) comparing the LipiFlow Thermal Pulsation System with warm compresses (5 trials), thermostatic devices (5), an oral intervention (1), topical medication (1), or eyelid hygiene with/without LipiFlow (1); searches to 24 October 2022.
cards.result: Against basic warm compresses, symptom-score results at 4 weeks conflicted between questionnaires, with no evidence of difference in gland expression, meibum quality or break-up time. Thermostatic devices reduced OSDI more than LipiFlow at 4 weeks (mean difference 4.59, 95% CI 1.23 to 7.95; 553 participants; very low-certainty). LipiFlow beat oral doxycycline on SPEED at 3 months in one 24-participant trial (mean difference −4.00, 95% CI −7.33 to −0.67; very low-certainty) and lifitegrast 5% may beat LipiFlow on gland expression in one 50-participant trial. No trial reported an intervention-related vision-threatening adverse event. The reviewers judged the best evidence at high risk of bias, low or very low certainty.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane verdict deliberately tempers the positive meta-analysis card: masking is hard with devices, methods were unstandardised, and most comparisons rest on single small trials.
cards.source: Pucker AD et al. LipiFlow for the treatment of dry eye disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024. PMID: 38314898. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: gland-function gains are consistent, symptom superiority over good home care is not — and a second system matches LipiFlow for a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: gland-function gains are consistent, symptom superiority over good home care is not — and a second system matches LipiFlow for a year
cards.people: Randomised evidence totalling over 1000 participants across the carded trials and reviews: a 50-subject single-treatment RCT, a 236-subject two-device equivalence trial, a 10-trial meta-analysis (761 patients) and a 13-trial Cochrane review (1155 participants).
cards.result: LipiFlow (the tested vectored thermal pulsation system, named as published) improves meibomian gland secretion measures and lipid layer thickness for at least 3 months after one treatment, and SYSTANE iLux was noninferior to it out to 12 months. Symptom scores improve, but whether they improve more than warm compresses/lid hygiene is contested between the positive meta-analysis and the Cochrane review. No vision-threatening device adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Durability beyond 3 months for LipiFlow versus home care rests on the device-versus-device trial and cohorts, not on sham-controlled data; industry sponsorship is common in this base. Timepoints are graded separately on each card for that reason.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Systemic antibiotics for chronic rhinosinusitis: doxycycline in polyps and long-term macrolides
shelves.question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis, do systemic antibiotics — oral doxycycline in CRSwNP, and long-term low-dose macrolide in CRS (chiefly without polyps) — improve symptoms, endoscopy and polyp size versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Sinusitis/drug therapy · Nasal Polyps/drug therapy · Doxycycline/therapeutic use · Macrolides/therapeutic use · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — each limb is internally mixed, and the limbs are never pooled. Doxycycline in CRSwNP (3 randomised reports, 196 patients): polyp size fell significantly versus placebo with an effect present at 12 weeks in a 47-patient three-arm trial, and SNOT-22 and smell improved versus placebo in a 100-patient trial (P=.037 and P=.048) — but adding doxycycline to a 20-day oral steroid course made no difference in a 49-patient trial that lost ~53% of participants. Long-term low-dose macrolide in CRS (3 randomised reports, 190 patients): roxithromycin 150 mg daily for 3 months improved SNOT-20, endoscopy and saccharine transit time versus placebo (64 patients, benefit correlating with low IgE), and postoperative azithromycin improved SNOT-22 statistically without proven clinical significance (66 patients) — but the MACS trial of weekly azithromycin in recalcitrant disease (60 patients) found no benefit on any symptom, endoscopic, flow, smell or microbiology outcome (the treatment made no difference). Antimicrobial resistance and, for macrolides, QT prolongation are the standing harms of long courses and are not measured by these small trials.

cards.headline: Van Zele 2010 (doxycycline limb): 20 days of doxycycline shrank nasal polyps versus placebo for 12 weeks — a moderate effect, smaller and longer than methylprednisolone's
cards.summary: Van Zele 2010 (doxycycline limb): 20 days of doxycycline shrank nasal polyps versus placebo for 12 weeks — a moderate effect, smaller and longer than methylprednisolone's
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (three arms)
cards.people: 47 participants with bilateral nasal polyps and chronic rhinosinusitis, randomly assigned to methylprednisolone in decreasing doses (32–8 mg daily), doxycycline (200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg daily) or placebo for 20 days, followed 12 weeks; nasal peak inspiratory flow, symptoms, endoscopy and inflammatory markers in nasal secretions and blood were measured.
cards.result: Methylprednisolone and doxycycline each significantly decreased nasal polyp size compared with placebo. The steroid effect was maximal at week 3 and lasted to week 8; the doxycycline effect was moderate but present for 12 weeks. Doxycycline significantly reduced myeloperoxidase, eosinophilic cationic protein and matrix metalloproteinase 9 in nasal secretions; methylprednisolone reduced a different (eosinophil-side) marker set.
cards.watchOut: 47 patients across three arms — roughly 15–16 per arm — so the doxycycline contrast is a small single trial; polyp size is an endoscopic sign, and the symptom outcomes are secondary in the record.

cards.headline: Nabavi 2023 (doxycycline limb): 6 weeks of doxycycline improved SNOT-22 quality of life and sense of smell versus placebo in 100 patients (both P<.05)
cards.summary: Nabavi 2023 (doxycycline limb): 6 weeks of doxycycline improved SNOT-22 quality of life and sense of smell versus placebo in 100 patients (both P<.05)
cards.people: 100 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, randomly assigned to doxycycline (200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg daily) or placebo for 6 weeks, all receiving fluticasone, montelukast and nasal irrigation; primary outcome SNOT-22 quality of life, with peak nasal inspiratory flow, symptom visual analogue scales and CT Lund-Mackay scores (registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials as IRCT20210403050817N1, as printed in the record).
cards.result: Doxycycline significantly improved SNOT-22 (P=.037) and sense of smell (P=.048) versus placebo. Baseline SNOT-22 did not modify the effect, and response did not differ by nasal eosinophilia, nor correlate with serum IgE (P=.220) or blood eosinophil count (P=.190). The authors describe the smell benefit as temporary.
cards.watchOut: P-values of .037 and .048 sit close to the significance threshold with several outcomes measured, and all patients received three background therapies — the estimate is for doxycycline as an add-on, not alone.
cards.source: Nabavi M et al. Doxycycline Improves Quality of Life and Anosmia in Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyposis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Am J Rhinol Allergy. 2023. cards.headline: Parasher 2019 (doxycycline limb): adding doxycycline to a 20-day oral steroid course made no difference to SNOT-22, polyp or symptom scores — in a trial half the patients left
cards.summary: Parasher 2019 (doxycycline limb): adding doxycycline to a 20-day oral steroid course made no difference to SNOT-22, polyp or symptom scores — in a trial half the patients left
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (add-on design, high dropout)
cards.people: 49 patients with moderate or severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps at a tertiary centre, randomised to a 20-day course of oral corticosteroids plus doxycycline (24) or plus placebo (25); SNOT-22, nasal polyp scores and visual analogue scores at baseline and 3, 8 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in SNOT-22, polyp scores or visual analogue scores between the arms. Twelve patients dropped out of the treatment group and 14 of the placebo group — most commonly for severe CRS and asthma exacerbations — leaving the trial underpowered, as the authors state; they suggest the dropout pattern itself may show this severe population is not optimally managed with medical therapy alone.
cards.watchOut: With ~53% dropout the null is weak evidence of no effect — but it is the only card testing doxycycline added to systemic steroids, the commonest real-world pairing, and it cannot be waved away.
cards.source: Parasher AK et al. The role of doxycycline in the management of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Am J Otolaryngol. 2019. PMID: 31126631. cards.headline: Wallwork 2006 (macrolide limb): 3 months of low-dose roxithromycin improved SNOT-20, endoscopy and saccharine transit time versus placebo, chiefly in patients with low IgE
cards.summary: Wallwork 2006 (macrolide limb): 3 months of low-dose roxithromycin improved SNOT-20, endoscopy and saccharine transit time versus placebo, chiefly in patients with low IgE
cards.people: 64 patients with chronic rhinosinusitis randomised to roxithromycin 150 mg daily for 3 months or placebo; outcomes SNOT-20, peak nasal inspiratory flow, saccharine transit time, olfactory function, nasal endoscopy and lavage interleukin-8, fucose and α2-macroglobulin.
cards.result: Statistically significant improvements in the macrolide group in SNOT-20 score, nasal endoscopy, saccharine transit time and lavage interleukin-8 (P<.05), correlating with low IgE levels; no significant improvement in olfactory function, peak flow or lavage fucose/α2-macroglobulin, and no improvement in any outcome on placebo. The authors conclude macrolides may benefit chronic rhinosinusitis, particularly with low IgE.
cards.watchOut: The first placebo-controlled macrolide trial and still a single 64-patient study; the low-IgE responder pattern is a subgroup correlation, and roxithromycin is not the macrolide most formularies stock.
cards.source: Wallwork B et al. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of macrolide in the treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis. Laryngoscope. 2006. PMID: 16467702. cards.headline: Videler 2011 / MACS (macrolide limb): long-term low-dose azithromycin made no difference on any outcome in recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Videler 2011 / MACS (macrolide limb): long-term low-dose azithromycin made no difference on any outcome in recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 60 patients (median age 49 years) with recalcitrant chronic rhinosinusitis with and without polyps, unresponsive to optimal medical therapy and, in 92%, to surgery; 50% had asthma and 58% had had revision surgery. Azithromycin was given 500 mg daily for 3 days, then 500 mg weekly for 11 weeks, versus placebo, with monitoring to 3 months after treatment.
cards.result: No significant difference between azithromycin and placebo on SNOT-22, patient response rating, visual analogue scores or SF-36, and no relevant significant differences in endoscopy, peak nasal inspiratory flow, smell tests or microbiology. The authors discuss disease severity, possible under-dosage and under-powering as explanations, and call for more research.
cards.watchOut: The null comes from the most treatment-resistant population in this pack — it does not directly refute Wallwork's less refractory population, but it is the largest placebo-controlled macrolide trial here and it is flatly negative.
cards.source: Videler WJ et al. Lack of efficacy of long-term, low-dose azithromycin in chronic rhinosinusitis: a randomized controlled trial. Allergy. 2011. PMID: 21884529. cards.headline: Amali 2015 (macrolide limb): post-surgical low-dose azithromycin improved SNOT-22 statistically versus conventional care alone, without sufficient evidence of clinical significance
cards.summary: Amali 2015 (macrolide limb): post-surgical low-dose azithromycin improved SNOT-22 statistically versus conventional care alone, without sufficient evidence of clinical significance
cards.people: 66 patients with chronic rhinosinusitis after functional endoscopic sinus surgery, randomised to conventional treatment (fluticasone nasal spray plus saline irrigation) or conventional treatment plus azithromycin 250 mg daily for 3 months; SNOT-22 measured before surgery and 3 months after.
cards.result: The azithromycin group showed a statistically significant improvement in SNOT-22 and a higher percentage change at 3 months than controls. Smoking correlated with percentage change in the placebo group; Lund-Mackay score, age and symptom duration did not. The authors state there was not sufficient evidence to support clinical significance at this dose and call for larger trials with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A post-surgical add-on population, an unblinded-sounding control of conventional care alone, and an author-declared gap between statistical and clinical significance — the weakest of the three macrolide cards.
cards.source: Amali A et al. Long-term postoperative azithromycin in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis: A randomized clinical trial. Am J Rhinol Allergy. 2015. PMID: 26637580. cards.headline: Synthesis: both antibiotic limbs are genuinely mixed — small positive trials against a flat null in the largest macrolide trial and a broken null in the steroid add-on trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: both antibiotic limbs are genuinely mixed — small positive trials against a flat null in the largest macrolide trial and a broken null in the steroid add-on trial
cards.people: Doxycycline limb: three randomised reports in CRSwNP totalling 196 patients (47, 100 and 49). Macrolide limb: three randomised reports in CRS totalling 190 patients (64, 60 and 66). The limbs are synthesised separately and never pooled into a class claim.
cards.result: Doxycycline: polyp size fell versus placebo for 12 weeks in the three-arm trial and SNOT-22/smell improved in the 100-patient trial, but adding doxycycline to oral steroids showed no difference in a trial with ~53% dropout. Macrolides: roxithromycin improved symptoms and endoscopy (low-IgE patients most), postoperative azithromycin improved SNOT-22 statistically without proven clinical significance, and the MACS azithromycin trial in recalcitrant disease found no benefit on any outcome. Long-term macrolide use also carries antimicrobial-resistance and QT-prolongation concerns that belong in any prescribing decision, though the carded trials were too small and short to measure them.
cards.watchOut: Populations differ by limb and by trial — polyp versus non-polyp disease, pre- versus post-surgical, refractory versus ordinary — so a positive in one population does not rescue a null in another. No card here supports antibiotics as a substitute for intranasal steroids or surgery.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: The nasal cycle: present in every subject on 48-hour rhinometry, mostly as a mixed pattern when awake and a classic reciprocal pattern in sleep, with a mean phase of about 3–4 hours that lengthens during sleep
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the nasal cycle — the spontaneous alternating congestion/decongestion of the two nasal passages: its period, the fraction of people who show a classic reciprocal pattern on long-term rhinometry, and how do posture and sleep stage affect it?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Adult · Rhinomanometry · Middle Aged · Time Factors · Young Adult · Nasal Cavity · Sleep
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for the nasal cycle is thin — Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep treat nasal vasculature briefly (textbook framing, not evidence) — so, as the slate row directs, this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Four primary human studies are carded: the posture experiments of Cole & Haight 1986; a 6-person, 7-hour rhinomanometry study (Preece & Eccles 1994, N printed on its face per the labelling rule); a 20-person 24-hour rhinoflowmetry study with simultaneous polysomnography (Kimura 2013); and the first continuous 48-hour long-term rhinoflowmetry study (Lindemann 2024, N=30). Together they settle the existence and rough period of the cycle (mean phase about 3–4 hours, with very wide between- and within-person variation), and they correct the single-measurement picture: on continuous recording every subject shows a cycle, but the textbook 'classic' reciprocal pattern is only one component — awake recordings are dominated by a mixed pattern, while sleep recordings are dominated by the classic pattern. Posture modulates amplitude without abolishing the cycle, and phase reversals cluster in REM sleep and with postural change, never in slow-wave sleep.

cards.headline: Cole & Haight 1986: the nasal cycle persists standing, supine and laterally recumbent and across 24 hours — recumbency augments its amplitude while combined nasal resistance stays near 2–3 cmH2O/L/s
cards.summary: Cole & Haight 1986: the nasal cycle persists standing, supine and laterally recumbent and across 24 hours — recumbency augments its amplitude while combined nasal resistance stays near 2–3 cmH2O/L/s
cards.people: Healthy young adults with normal noses, studied seated, standing, supine and laterally recumbent, including 24-hour periods of unrestricted light activity, rest and recumbency (the fetched record does not state the number of subjects).
cards.result: The spontaneous nasal cycle of airflow resistance, alternating between the two cavities in seated subjects, persisted in every posture tested and throughout 24-hour recordings. Recumbency augmented the amplitude of the cycle, yet resistance of the combined nasal cavities changed little with daytime activity or nocturnal sleeping postures, remaining similar to upright values in the range of 2 to 3 cmH2O/L/s in normal noses. By contrast, noses with fixed unilateral obstruction showed high cyclical combined resistances — the cycle is benign physiology only when total resistance stays low.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record does not state the sample size, so no N is printed beyond the population description — treat this as the classic qualitative programme anchor for posture, with quantification coming from the later continuous-recording studies.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (classic) | Cole P, Haight JS. Posture and the nasal cycle. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 1986. PMID: 3717848. cards.headline: Lindemann 2024: on the first continuous 48-hour recording, 100% of 30 healthy subjects showed a nasal cycle — mixed type commonest overall (97%), classic type dominant in sleep (97%), mean phase 206 ± 83 minutes
cards.summary: Lindemann 2024: on the first continuous 48-hour recording, 100% of 30 healthy subjects showed a nasal cycle — mixed type commonest overall (97%), classic type dominant in sleep (97%), mean phase 206 ± 83 minutes
cards.people: 30 rhinologically healthy subjects (20 women, 10 men) wearing long-term rhinoflowmetry continuously for 48 hours under everyday conditions; cycle types classified as classic, in concert, one-sided, no-cycle and mixed.
cards.result: A nasal cycle was detected in 100% of subjects over 48 hours, and classical cycle components were detected at least once in every subject; the no-cycle type was never observed. The mixed type — a combination of classical and in-concert components — was the commonest pattern overall (97% of subjects). Awake recordings were dominated by the mixed type (80%), while sleep recordings were dominated by the classical reciprocal type (97%). Mean phase duration was 206 ± 83 minutes. The authors note long-term rhinoflowmetry is the only method allowing continuous measurement during daily routine, and that results of earlier single-stage examinations should be questioned.
cards.watchOut: Thirty subjects from one centre with one proprietary long-term rhinoflowmetry method — the 100% detection figure is method-bound: shorter or single-time-point methods detect the cycle in fewer people, as the 1994 card below shows.

cards.headline: Preece & Eccles 1994 (N=6, printed on the face): only 3 of 6 healthy subjects showed a classic reciprocal cycle over 7 hours — and skin temperature moved in parallel on both sides, with no reciprocal relation to nasal resistance
cards.summary: Preece & Eccles 1994 (N=6, printed on the face): only 3 of 6 healthy subjects showed a classic reciprocal cycle over 7 hours — and skin temperature moved in parallel on both sides, with no reciprocal relation to nasal resistance
cards.people: 6 healthy subjects aged 22–25 years (N=6 — a classic small study, labelled plainly per the reference-floor rule), with right and left nasal airway resistance by active posterior rhinomanometry and skin temperature at cheek, nose and forearm measured every 30 minutes over 7 hours.
cards.result: Three of the six subjects exhibited a nasal cycle with spontaneous reciprocal changes in nasal airway resistance (right–left resistance correlation r=0.64 to −0.78 in those subjects). Right and left skin temperatures, in contrast, correlated positively and strongly (r=0.74 to 0.93) — both sides changed in parallel with no reciprocal relationship. The authors conclude there is no relationship between nasal airway resistance and skin temperature in healthy subjects despite both being under sympathetic vasoconstrictor control — a small-study caution against assuming every sympathetically controlled variable cycles reciprocally.
cards.watchOut: N=6 over a single 7-hour window — the 3-of-6 detection rate reflects a short observation window as much as biology; the 48-hour study above detected a cycle in every subject. Do not read this card as 'half of people have no nasal cycle'.

cards.headline: Kimura 2013: 19 of 20 healthy subjects showed a detectable cycle over 24 hours; mean duration 234 minutes, significantly longer in sleep than wakefulness, with phase reversals tending to occur in REM sleep (68.8%) and never in slow-wave sleep
cards.summary: Kimura 2013: 19 of 20 healthy subjects showed a detectable cycle over 24 hours; mean duration 234 minutes, significantly longer in sleep than wakefulness, with phase reversals tending to occur in REM sleep (68.8%) and never in slow-wave sleep
cards.people: 20 healthy subjects aged 20–56 years without nasal pathology or medical, psychiatric or sleep disorders, measured with a portable rhinoflowmeter recording airflow through each nostril independently over 24 hours, with simultaneous nocturnal polysomnography.
cards.result: Nineteen of 20 subjects showed a detectable nasal cycle, and 16 of the 19 changed cyclic phase during sleep. Mean cycle duration was 234.2 ± 282.4 minutes (median 164.1 minutes) with considerable variation, and mean duration during sleep was significantly longer than during wakefulness (P<0.005). Reversal of cyclic phase during sleep tended to be associated with REM sleep (68.8%) and with postural changes (18.8%), and never occurred in slow-wave sleep. Phase changes may be absent in subjects with severe nasal septal deviation.
cards.watchOut: The standard deviation (282 minutes) exceeds the mean cycle duration — the period is a loose central tendency, not a clock; individual phases vary widely within the same person.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (24-hour rhinoflowmetry with polysomnography) | Kimura A, Chiba S, Capasso R, Yagi T et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the nasal cycle is universal on long enough recording, runs at roughly 3–4 hours per phase, and is a pattern mixture — mixed when awake, classic in sleep — modulated by posture and sleep stage
cards.summary: Synthesis: the nasal cycle is universal on long enough recording, runs at roughly 3–4 hours per phase, and is a pattern mixture — mixed when awake, classic in sleep — modulated by posture and sleep stage
cards.people: Synthesis of Cole & Haight 1986, Preece & Eccles 1994 (N=6), Kimura 2013 (N=20) and Lindemann 2024 (N=30), with Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep named as thin textbook framing (not evidence cards).
cards.result: The measurement literature, read whole, gives a coherent picture. Alternating congestion and decongestion of the two nasal passages is normal physiology: detected in 19 of 20 subjects over 24 hours and in 30 of 30 over 48 hours, whereas a single 7-hour window caught a classic reciprocal pattern in only 3 of 6 — detection is a function of observation length and method. The mean phase is about 3–4 hours (206 ± 83 minutes over 48 hours; median 164 minutes in the 24-hour study) with very large variability. The 'classic' reciprocal textbook pattern is real but is only one component: awake life is dominated by a mixed pattern (classical plus in-concert components), while sleep is dominated by the classic pattern (97% of sleep recordings in the 48-hour study) and cycle phases lengthen in sleep. Posture augments amplitude in recumbency without abolishing the cycle and without raising total nasal resistance in normal noses (about 2–3 cmH2O/L/s combined); phase reversals cluster around REM sleep and postural change and never occur in slow-wave sleep. Skin temperature does not cycle reciprocally with the nose (the N=6 study), so the cycle is a specifically nasal vasomotor phenomenon, not a whole-body sided rhythm.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: textbook framing is thin for this topic and the shelf rests on four primary measurement studies (total carded N=56 plus the unnumbered 1986 cohort) using three different recording methods — the pattern conclusions are concordant across methods, but any single percentage is method-bound.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cole P, Haight JS. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 1986 (PMID: 3717848); Preece M, Eccles R. Rhinology. 1994 (PMID: 8029619); Kimura A et al. Laryngoscope. 2013 (PMID: 23576311); Lindemann J et al. Rhinology. 2024 (PMID: 38088419). Registry IDs: none in the records.
