shelves.title: Normal voice acoustics are population- and protocol-bound: fundamental frequency near 110–155 Hz in men and 215–260 Hz in women across Hindi, Turkish and Persian cohorts, with jitter near 0.2% and shimmer near 1.2% where reported — no universal norm exists
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal voice acoustics — speaking fundamental frequency by sex and age, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio on standardised sustained-vowel and reading tasks — and how do they change with ageing?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Adult · Young Adult · Adolescent · Speech Acoustics · India · Voice Quality · Acoustics · Sex Factors · Age Factors · Speech Production Measurement · Reference Values · Sound Spectrography · Healthy Volunteers
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (phonation; textbook framing, not evidence). The stamp is EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED, for a specific reason the carded data themselves demonstrate: the sex difference in fundamental frequency is large and consistent everywhere, but the absolute values differ by language community, vowel, task and analysis software, and no harmonised cross-population reference standard exists — each carded cohort explicitly presents its values as norms for its own population and system. Three primary healthy-speaker cohorts are carded: 62 North Indian Hindi speakers (ages 18–40), 83 young Turkish speakers (ages 18–32, Computerized Speech Lab) and 90 Iranian Persian speakers (ages 20–50, Dr. Speech software). Male fundamental frequency spans roughly 113–156 Hz and female roughly 215–262 Hz across cohorts and vowels; jitter (about 0.22–0.23%) and shimmer (about 1.21–1.22%) are quantified in the Iranian cohort and were statistically indistinguishable between the sexes there. None of the carded cohorts covers ages over 50, so the ageing limb of the question is answered honestly: within 20–50 years values were relatively stable, and older-age norms are not established by this base.

cards.headline: Soni (North Indian Hindi speakers, N=62): mean fundamental frequency 156 Hz in men and 262 Hz in women aged 18–25, and 141 Hz and 253 Hz at ages 26–40 — a significant sex difference at both ages, no significant age-group difference within either sex
cards.summary: Soni (North Indian Hindi speakers, N=62): mean fundamental frequency 156 Hz in men and 262 Hz in women aged 18–25, and 141 Hz and 253 Hz at ages 26–40 — a significant sex difference at both ages, no significant age-group difference within either sex
cards.people: 62 healthy normal-voiced adults aged 18–40 years (39 men, 23 women), North Indian Hindi speakers, recorded for acoustic analysis of fundamental frequency (F0), jitter, shimmer and harmonic-to-noise ratio.
cards.result: Mean F0 in the 18–25 group was 156 Hz in men and 262 Hz in women; in the 26–40 group, 141 Hz in men and 253 Hz in women. F0 differed significantly between the sexes in both age groups; jitter and shimmer differed significantly between the sexes only in the 26–40 group, and harmonic-to-noise ratio only in the 18–25 group. Participants within each sex showed no difference in acoustic parameters between the two age groups. Shimmer in women aged 18–25 and jitter in men aged 26–40 were not normally distributed, a reminder that perturbation measures are skewed even in healthy voices. The authors' stated purpose was to create standardised values for this population because acoustic parameters vary with age, gender and ethnicity and no programme supplies universal norms.
cards.watchOut: One language community, ages 18–40 only, and an unbalanced sample (39 men, 23 women) — the values are Hindi-speaker norms for the authors' analysis setup, not transferable cut-offs for other populations or software.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (normative acoustic cohort) | Soni A, Jotdar A, Kapoor D, Singh A et al. Acoustic analysis of normal voice patterns in North Indian population. J Voice. 2026 (record year). PMID: 37739863. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Demirhan 2016 (young Turkish speakers, N=83): fundamental frequency on sustained vowels 127–137 Hz in men and 240–252 Hz in women; noise-to-harmonics ratio did not differ by sex
cards.summary: Demirhan 2016 (young Turkish speakers, N=83): fundamental frequency on sustained vowels 127–137 Hz in men and 240–252 Hz in women; noise-to-harmonics ratio did not differ by sex
cards.people: 83 native Turkish speakers with normal voice aged 18–32 years (44 women, 39 men); sustained vowels /a/, /i/ and /u/ recorded with Computerized Speech Lab and analysed for fundamental frequency (F0), jitter, shimmer and noise-to-harmonics ratio (NHR).
cards.result: F0 was greater in women than men for every vowel: women 239.78 Hz (/a/), 251.97 Hz (/i/) and 250.29 Hz (/u/); men 127.11 Hz, 137.23 Hz and 134.15 Hz respectively — so the measured 'normal F0' moves by more than 10 Hz with the vowel alone within the same speakers. All shimmer values and jitter for /a/ and /u/ were significantly lower in men, while jitter for /i/ did not differ between the sexes. There was no effect of gender on NHR; in women only, NHR for the high vowels was lower than for /a/. The study was undertaken because normative data for healthy native Turkish speakers were lacking.
cards.watchOut: Young adults only (18–32), sustained vowels only (not connected speech), one analysis system (Computerized Speech Lab) — values shift with vowel, task and software, which is precisely why this shelf is stamped EMERGING.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (normative acoustic cohort) | Demirhan E, Unsal EM, Yilmaz C, Ertan E et al. Acoustic Voice Analysis of Young Turkish Speakers. J Voice. 2016. cards.headline: Dehqan 2010 (Iranian Persian speakers, N=90): fundamental frequency 113–126 Hz in men and 215–228 Hz in women, jitter about 0.22–0.23% and shimmer about 1.21–1.22% in both sexes, maximum phonation time 26.3 s in men versus 18.6 s in women
cards.summary: Dehqan 2010 (Iranian Persian speakers, N=90): fundamental frequency 113–126 Hz in men and 215–228 Hz in women, jitter about 0.22–0.23% and shimmer about 1.21–1.22% in both sexes, maximum phonation time 26.3 s in men versus 18.6 s in women
cards.people: 90 healthy randomly selected adults with normal voices (45 men, 45 women), each sex split equally into three age subgroups spanning 20–50 years; recordings made with Dr. Speech software (Vocal Assessment v4.0, Tiger Electronics) under comfortable phonation.
cards.result: F0 for the vowels /a/ and /i/ was greater in women (214.64 and 228.06 Hz) than in men (112.82 and 126.13 Hz). Maximum phonation time was greater in men (26.30 ± 1.29 s) than women (18.56 ± 0.88 s). Average jitter (women 0.22 ± 0.01%, men 0.23 ± 0.02%) and shimmer (women 1.21 ± 0.03%, men 1.22 ± 0.02%) did not differ significantly between the sexes. Harmonics-to-noise ratio was slightly greater in women (18.81 ± 0.96 dB) than men (18.42 ± 0.57 dB). The authors conclude most voice characteristics were relatively stable between ages 20 and 50 — and state plainly that voices over 50 were not recorded and require further investigation.
cards.watchOut: A different analysis system (Dr. Speech) from the Turkish cohort's Computerized Speech Lab — cross-cohort numeric differences confound population with software; ages stop at 50, so this cohort cannot speak to older-age voice change.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (normative acoustic cohort) | Dehqan A, Ansari H, Bakhtiar M. Objective voice analysis of Iranian speakers with normal voices. J Voice. 2010. cards.headline: Synthesis: the sex gap in fundamental frequency is settled physiology; the absolute 'normal values' are not — they are local to language, vowel, task and software, and older-age norms are missing
cards.summary: Synthesis: the sex gap in fundamental frequency is settled physiology; the absolute 'normal values' are not — they are local to language, vowel, task and software, and older-age norms are missing
cards.people: Synthesis of Soni (Hindi speakers, N=62), Demirhan 2016 (Turkish speakers, N=83) and Dehqan 2010 (Persian speakers, N=90), framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card).
cards.result: Read together, the three cohorts settle one thing and unsettle another. Settled: healthy men phonate at roughly half the fundamental frequency of healthy women (men about 113–156 Hz, women about 215–262 Hz across cohorts, vowels and age bands), maximum phonation time is longer in men (26.3 versus 18.6 s in the cohort that measured it), and perturbation measures in healthy voices are small (jitter about 0.2%, shimmer about 1.2% in the cohort reporting both sexes). Not settled: any single numeric norm. The same speakers shift F0 by over 10 Hz between vowels; cohorts using different software in different languages differ by tens of Hz; and every cohort was assembled precisely because no transferable norm existed for its population. Within ages 20–50 the Iranian cohort found voice characteristics relatively stable, and the Hindi cohort found no age-group difference between 18–25 and 26–40 — but no carded cohort includes speakers over 50, so how these measures change with older ageing is genuinely unestablished by this base. Hence the EMERGING stamp: use the local, protocol-matched cohort as the reference, never a pooled universal number.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: three cohorts, three languages, at least two analysis systems, nobody over 50 — the EMERGING stamp is the finding: fundamental-frequency sex differences are established, universal acoustic norms are not.

shelves.title: Contrast sensitivity and ageing: loss concentrated at high spatial frequencies and in dim light — Pelli–Robson falls 0.20 log photopic vs 0.33 log mesopic, low frequencies spared
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does contrast sensitivity (spatial contrast sensitivity function and letter contrast sensitivity, e.g. Pelli–Robson) change with age under photopic and mesopic conditions — at which spatial frequencies is the loss greatest, and how much is optical versus neural?
shelves.mesh: Contrast Sensitivity · Aging · Psychophysics · Retina · Visual Perception
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the direction and frequency-selectivity of the age change, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep on visual processing as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Letter contrast sensitivity (Pelli–Robson) in 292 adults falls late and modestly under bright (photopic) conditions — decline from the 61–70 group onward, 0.20 log units between youngest and oldest — and earlier and further in dim (mesopic) conditions — decline from 51–60 onward, 0.33 log units (Puell 2004). The spatial-frequency studies explain the shape: with forced-choice methods the age loss is concentrated at high spatial frequencies, with low frequencies spared, centrally and at 10 degrees in the periphery alike (Higgins 1988; Crassini 1988). On the optical-versus-neural question the fetched records support a neural component: the high-frequency decline persists with pupil size controlled and is, in Higgins and colleagues' judgement, too large to be explained by lens-density change alone — presented as those authors' inference from their data, not as a settled partition of optical versus neural shares, which no carded record quantifies. Method matters and is part of the physiology: the method of adjustment exaggerates the age decline at all frequencies and its authors advise against it for ageing studies. Small classic cohorts (8 young versus 8 older observers in Crassini) carry their Ns on the face.

cards.headline: Puell 2004: Pelli–Robson letter contrast sensitivity in 292 adults — decline begins at 61–70 years photopic and a decade earlier (51–60) mesopic; oldest-to-youngest loss 0.20 log (photopic) vs 0.33 log (mesopic)
cards.summary: Puell 2004: Pelli–Robson letter contrast sensitivity in 292 adults — decline begins at 61–70 years photopic and a decade earlier (51–60) mesopic; oldest-to-youngest loss 0.20 log (photopic) vs 0.33 log (mesopic)
cards.type: Human normative cross-sectional study (Pelli–Robson letter contrast sensitivity by age), J Refract Surg 2004
cards.people: Two hundred and ninety-two participants in a Spanish population, stratified into six age groups, tested binocularly with best spectacle correction on the Pelli–Robson letter chart at 1 metre under photopic (85 cd/m2) and mesopic (0.15 cd/m2) luminance; photopic visual acuity was also measured.
cards.result: Photopic letter contrast sensitivity decreased gradually from the 61–70-year age group onward, and mesopic sensitivity from the 51–60 group onward. The reduction in mean contrast sensitivity between the oldest and youngest groups was 0.20 log units photopic and 0.33 log units mesopic. The luminance-related loss (two successive triplets on the chart) increased slightly with age, and both photopic and mesopic contrast sensitivity improved significantly as photopic visual acuity increased — mesopic function declines earlier, further, and in step with acuity.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional age groups — cohort differences are not within-person decline rates. Binocular testing with best correction; monocular or uncorrected values will differ.
cards.source: Puell MC, Palomo C, Sánchez-Ramos C, Villena C. Normal values for photopic and mesopic letter contrast sensitivity. Journal of refractive surgery (Thorofare, N.J. : 1995). 2004. cards.headline: Higgins 1988: with forced-choice testing the age decline in spatial contrast sensitivity sits at high spatial frequencies — and is too large for lens density alone, pointing to a neural component; the method of adjustment overstates it
cards.summary: Higgins 1988: with forced-choice testing the age decline in spatial contrast sensitivity sits at high spatial frequencies — and is too large for lens density alone, pointing to a neural component; the method of adjustment overstates it
cards.type: Human psychophysics study (spatial contrast sensitivity, age and method), J Opt Soc Am A 1988
cards.people: Normal subjects from five age groups (group sizes not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such), each tested twice with each of two psychophysical methods (method of adjustment and forced-choice), with pupil size controlled.
cards.result: The method of adjustment showed a decline in sensitivity with age at all spatial frequencies. The forced-choice procedure instead showed an age-related decline predominantly at high spatial frequencies, of a magnitude generally similar to an earlier tracking-method study. Because pupil size was controlled, the decline cannot be attributed to pupillary change; the authors argue the high-frequency decline, though comparatively small, is too large to be due to lens-density changes and therefore has a neural component. Age, spatial frequency and method interact — the authors advise avoiding the method of adjustment in age-related vision studies.
cards.watchOut: The neural-component claim is the authors' inference (pupil controlled, lens argument by magnitude), printed as such — no carded record partitions optical versus neural shares numerically. Group Ns are not in the fetched abstract and are not guessed.

cards.headline: Crassini 1988: 8 young vs 8 older observers — contrast sensitivity is lost at 2.0 and 5.0 cycles/deg but spared at 0.2, centrally and at 10° peripheral alike; N = 8 per group
cards.summary: Crassini 1988: 8 young vs 8 older observers — contrast sensitivity is lost at 2.0 and 5.0 cycles/deg but spared at 0.2, centrally and at 10° peripheral alike; N = 8 per group
cards.type: Human psychophysics study (contrast sensitivity, central vs peripheral retina, ageing), Perception 1988
cards.people: Eight young observers (mean age 20.4 years) and eight elderly observers (mean age 64.4 years) in the main experiments, with a further eight young (22.3 years) and eight elderly (63.8 years) in a replication experiment; all had normal or better visual acuity and no ocular pathology, tested monocularly in the better eye. N = 8 per group printed on the face.
cards.result: Contrast sensitivity was measured centrally and 10 degrees temporally at 0.2, 0.8, 2.0 and 5.0 cycles/deg. Young observers had better sensitivity than older observers only at the higher spatial frequencies (2.0 and 5.0 cycles/deg); sensitivity was poorer peripherally than centrally in both groups except at the lowest frequency (0.2 cycles/deg), which was spared across both age and retinal location. Sharp-edge detection likewise favoured the young centrally and peripherally; fuzzy-edge experiments confirmed the central young advantage once an appropriate contrast range was used (experiment 4 correcting a range artefact in experiment 3).
cards.watchOut: N = 8 per age group — a classic small psychophysics cohort, labelled on the face. Extreme-group design (about 20 vs about 64 years) shows the endpoints of ageing, not its time course; the Pelli–Robson card supplies the decade-by-decade shape.
cards.source: Crassini B, Brown B, Bowman K. Age-related changes in contrast sensitivity in central and peripheral retina. Perception. 1988. PMID: 3067210. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: contrast sensitivity is preserved at low spatial frequencies across age and falls at high frequencies — earlier and further in dim light (0.33 log mesopic vs 0.20 log photopic across the adult span), with a neural component beyond lens and pupil changes
cards.summary: Synthesis: contrast sensitivity is preserved at low spatial frequencies across age and falls at high frequencies — earlier and further in dim light (0.33 log mesopic vs 0.20 log photopic across the adult span), with a neural component beyond lens and pupil changes
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Puell 2004; Higgins 1988; Crassini 1988), framed by the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep account of retinal and cortical visual processing as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: Three methods, one shape: grating studies by forced-choice and tracking, and the clinical letter chart, all place the age loss at the high-frequency/detail end while low frequencies are spared, in central and peripheral retina alike. The letter-chart norms give the usable magnitudes — about a fifth of a log unit lost photopically and a third mesopically between the youngest and oldest adult groups, with the mesopic decline starting a decade sooner. On mechanism, the carded evidence supports a neural contribution (pupil controlled; loss too large for lens density alone, per the Higgins authors) but no carded record apportions optical versus neural shares numerically, and the shelf does not invent a partition. Method of measurement is itself a variable: adjustment methods exaggerate the decline. No refusals on this shelf: all three slated anchors verified from abstract-present records. No animal data are carded.
cards.watchOut: All age contrasts here are cross-sectional. Letter-chart (Pelli–Robson) log units and grating contrast-sensitivity values are related but distinct measures and are never interconverted on this shelf.

shelves.title: Wideband middle-ear measures: absorbance curves shift with age, sex and pressure — older ears lower at 1587–3175 Hz, negative pressure cuts absorbance near 1 kHz; norms still system-specific (EMERGING)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are normal wideband acoustic absorbance / tympanometry measures of middle-ear function across frequency — and how do age, sex and middle-ear pressure shift them?
shelves.mesh: Acoustic Impedance Tests · Ear, Middle · Tympanic Membrane · Reflex, Acoustic · Auditory Threshold
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the measurement family is established but its normative distributions are still accumulating and are device- and pressure-condition-dependent, so this shelf is graded EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing is thin — Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep cover middle-ear impedance matching in principle, named here as framing, not as an evidence card; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs. What the primary studies show: in 95 adults with normal middle-ear function measured on an Interacoustics Titan system (226–8000 Hz), energy absorbance at tympanometric peak pressure differs by age in a frequency-specific pattern — older adults higher at 500–794 Hz and 5040–6350 Hz, lower at 1587–3175 Hz than young adults — with resonance frequency lower in older adults, and a consistent sex pattern (men higher absorbance at low frequencies, lower at high frequencies) in every age group (Kavruk 2024). Middle-ear pressure itself moves the measurement: induced negative pressure in 8 normal ears reduced power absorbance most strongly at 0.8–1.9 kHz, consistent with increased stiffness at the tympanic membrane (Robinson 2016; N = 8 on the face). Wideband reflex thresholds run lower than clinical 226 Hz thresholds in 39 normal-hearing adults, and differ between peak-pressure and ambient-pressure measurement (Schairer 2022). Because absorbance depends on the test system, the pressure condition and the frequency band, no single universal normal curve is claimed — values are carded per system and condition. Cross-point, not duplicated: the pure-tone hearing-threshold shelf measures cochlear sensitivity; this shelf measures the middle-ear mechanics in front of the cochlea.

cards.headline: Kavruk 2024: wideband tympanometry in 95 normal adults — older adults show higher absorbance at 500–794 and 5040–6350 Hz and lower at 1587–3175 Hz than the young, with lower resonance frequency; men run higher at low and lower at high frequencies in every age group
cards.summary: Kavruk 2024: wideband tympanometry in 95 normal adults — older adults show higher absorbance at 500–794 and 5040–6350 Hz and lower at 1587–3175 Hz than the young, with lower resonance frequency; men run higher at low and lower at high frequencies in every age group
cards.type: Human normative study (wideband tympanometry by age and sex), Ear Hear 2024
cards.people: Ninety-five adults with normal middle-ear function in three age groups — 32 young (16 men, 16 women, 20–39 years), 31 middle-aged (15 men, 16 women, 41–60 years) and 32 older (16 men, 16 women, 65–82 years) — measured with wideband tympanometry from 226 to 8000 Hz on an Interacoustics Titan system; energy absorbance at tympanometric peak pressure and at ambient pressure at third-octave frequencies, plus resonance frequency, were analysed by age and sex.
cards.result: Mean absorbance at peak pressure was significantly higher from 500 to 794 Hz and at 5040 and 6350 Hz, and significantly lower from 1587 to 3175 Hz, in older adults compared with young adults; ambient-pressure absorbance showed the same mid-frequency lowering and high-frequency raising. No frequency differed significantly between young and middle-aged, or between middle-aged and older, adults. Resonance frequency was significantly lower in older than young adults. In all age groups men had higher mean absorbance at lower frequencies and lower at higher frequencies than women, and slightly (middle-aged: significantly) lower resonance frequency. The authors propose age- and sex-specific wideband norms rather than a single adult norm.
cards.watchOut: Single test system (Interacoustics Titan, named as published) and significance reported by frequency band without absolute absorbance values in the record's abstract — this card reports the pattern and direction the record establishes, not invented absorbance numbers.
cards.source: Kavruk H, Öztürk B. Investigation of Age and Gender Effects on the Middle Ear With Wideband Tympanometry in Adults. Ear and hearing. 2024. PMID: 38017621. cards.headline: Robinson 2016: induced negative middle-ear pressure in 8 normal ears cuts wideband power absorbance most at 0.8–1.9 kHz (small rise above ~4 kHz) — a stiffness increase at the tympanic membrane; N = 8
cards.summary: Robinson 2016: induced negative middle-ear pressure in 8 normal ears cuts wideband power absorbance most at 0.8–1.9 kHz (small rise above ~4 kHz) — a stiffness increase at the tympanic membrane; N = 8
cards.type: Human experimental physiology study (wideband immittance under negative middle-ear pressure), Ear Hear 2016
cards.people: Eight subjects with normal middle-ear function, trained to induce consistent negative middle-ear pressures, quantified by tympanometric peak pressure and wideband acoustic immittance; measurements in negative-pressure and ambient-pressure conditions were analysed per ear, with the residual ear-canal delay removed to estimate complex immittance at the tympanic membrane and a classical middle-ear model fitted. N = 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Negative middle-ear pressure had its largest and most consistent effect from 0.8 to 1.9 kHz, reducing power absorbance by the middle ear and cochlea; on average absorbance fell at low-to-mid frequencies with a small increase above about 4 kHz, but effects varied considerably across ears. At the tympanic membrane, negative pressure decreased aggregate compliance — consistent with increased stiffness of the membrane, tensor tympani, annular ligament or other middle-ear structures — while estimated ear-canal delays barely changed. Tympanometric peak pressure was not a strong predictor of the change at the membrane, given baseline between-ear variability.
cards.watchOut: N = 8, printed on the face — a classic small mechanistic study; pressures were self-induced by trained subjects, so magnitudes are a laboratory model of negative pressure, not a clinical Eustachian-dysfunction distribution.
cards.source: Robinson SR, Thompson S, Allen JB. Effects of Negative Middle Ear Pressure on Wideband Acoustic Immittance in Normal-Hearing Adults. Ear and hearing. 2016. PMID: 26871877. cards.headline: Schairer 2022: wideband acoustic reflex thresholds in 39 normal-hearing adults are significantly lower than clinical 226 Hz thresholds — and higher at tympanometric peak pressure than at ambient pressure (500/2000 Hz ipsilateral)
cards.summary: Schairer 2022: wideband acoustic reflex thresholds in 39 normal-hearing adults are significantly lower than clinical 226 Hz thresholds — and higher at tympanometric peak pressure than at ambient pressure (500/2000 Hz ipsilateral)
cards.type: Human normative/methods study (wideband acoustic reflex thresholds), Ear Hear 2022
cards.people: Thirty-nine adults with normal hearing (21 men; mean age 47.7 years, range 23–72), both ears tested prospectively; acoustic reflex thresholds were obtained ipsilaterally and contralaterally with 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz and broadband-noise activators on a clinical system (manual method) and on an experimental wideband system with automated adaptive threshold detection, the wideband thresholds estimated at both tympanometric peak pressure and ambient pressure. Broadband activator bandwidth was 125–4000 Hz (clinical) versus 200–8000 Hz (wideband).
cards.result: Wideband reflex thresholds at both peak pressure and ambient pressure were significantly lower than clinical-system thresholds — reflex-related absorbance change is detectable across multiple frequency bands where the single-frequency clinical probe sees less. Wideband thresholds at peak pressure were significantly higher than at ambient pressure in the 500 and 2000 Hz ipsilateral conditions. The authors note the lower wideband levels may be more tolerable and may reveal reflexes absent at a traditional test's maximum level, and that automation suits telehealth workflows.
cards.watchOut: Threshold differences are reported as significant in the record without decibel magnitudes in its abstract — this card claims the direction and significance, not a dB gap. The wideband system was an experimental system, named as such; clinical-system equivalence is not assumed.
cards.source: Schairer KS, Putterman DB, Keefe DH, Fitzpatrick D, Garinis A, Kolberg E, Feeney MP. Automated Adaptive Wideband Acoustic Reflex Threshold Estimation in Normal-hearing Adults. cards.headline: Synthesis: wideband absorbance is age-, sex-, frequency- and pressure-dependent — no single normal curve exists yet; negative pressure stiffens the system near 1 kHz and wideband reflex thresholds run below clinical thresholds
cards.summary: Synthesis: wideband absorbance is age-, sex-, frequency- and pressure-dependent — no single normal curve exists yet; negative pressure stiffens the system near 1 kHz and wideband reflex thresholds run below clinical thresholds
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Kavruk 2024; Robinson 2016; Schairer 2022), with the Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep account of middle-ear impedance matching named as thin textbook framing, not as an evidence card — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature.
cards.result: The consistent physiology across three different wideband designs: middle-ear sound transmission, measured as energy absorbance across 226–8000 Hz, is not a single number — it is a frequency curve that shifts with age (mid-frequency absorbance lower, low- and high-frequency higher, resonance frequency lower in older adults), differs by sex at every age, and moves with middle-ear pressure, negative pressure reducing absorbance most near 0.8–1.9 kHz via increased stiffness at the membrane. Wideband reflex thresholds sit below traditional 226 Hz clinical thresholds and depend on the pressure condition of measurement. Because systems (a named commercial Titan; an experimental wideband rig) and conditions differ between studies, the shelf grades the topic EMERGING and cards each value-set under its own system and condition rather than merging them into universal norms. No refusals on this shelf: all three slated anchors verified from abstract-present records. No animal data are carded.
cards.watchOut: Absorbance values are system- and calibration-specific; cross-system numerical comparison requires the harmonisation work this literature has not yet produced — the reason for the EMERGING grade.

shelves.title: Chalazion: injection vs surgery — split: trials show near-equal resolution and less pain with injection; pooled data favour one surgery over one injection; depigmentation risk in pigmented skin
shelves.question: In patients with chalazion, does intralesional triamcinolone injection resolve the lesion as effectively as incision and curettage, and how do the two compare on recurrence, skin depigmentation and other harms — by lesion size?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chalazion · Curettage · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Injections, Intralesional · Male · Ophthalmologic Surgical Procedures · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone Acetonide · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The two largest head-to-head trials found intralesional triamcinolone and incision and curettage resolve primary chalazia at near-equal rates — 81% versus 79% (94 patients) and 84% versus 87% at 3 weeks (136 patients, with hot compresses alone at 46%) — with less pain and inconvenience from injection. The meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (552 patients) instead favours surgery for a single attempt (aggregate success 78.0% vs 60.4%; relative risk 0.77 for injection, a relative measure), narrowing after up to two attempts (86.7% vs 72.5%). Size and type modify the comparison: in the size-stratified trial (118 patients) the methods were equal overall except in large suppurating granulomas, where surgery was superior. In pigmented skin (141 patients), first-attempt success favoured surgery (79% vs 62%) and the authors report skin depigmentation was relatively common after injection — the defining harm of the injection limb, carded on the face.

cards.headline: Ben Simon 2011 RCT (n=94): complete resolution 81% after intralesional triamcinolone injection versus 79% after incision and curettage (P=.8); resolution took about 5 days after injection
cards.summary: Ben Simon 2011 RCT (n=94): complete resolution 81% after intralesional triamcinolone injection versus 79% after incision and curettage (P=.8); resolution took about 5 days after injection
cards.type: Prospective randomised clinical trial, intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection vs incision and curettage, primary chalazia after failed conservative treatment
cards.people: 94 patients with primary chalazia after failed conservative treatment, randomised to intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection (52 patients; 4 mg) or incision and curettage under local anaesthesia (42 patients). Complete resolution was defined as 95–100% lesion regression.
cards.result: Complete resolution was achieved in 42 of 52 patients (81%) with injection and 33 of 42 (79%) with incision and curettage (P=.8) — (the treatments made no difference) in this trial. Average time to resolution in the injection group was 5 days; 92% needed a single injection and 8% two. Triamcinolone precipitates were seen in 11.5% of injected patients and resolved spontaneously. No eyelid depigmentation, raised intraocular pressure or vision loss occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of primary chalazia only; lesions needing biopsy (possible malignancy masquerading as chalazion) are outside its question — injection gives no tissue for histology.
cards.source: Ben Simon GJ et al. Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection versus incision and curettage for primary chalazia. American journal of ophthalmology. 2011. PMID: 21257145. cards.headline: Goawalla 2007 RCT (n=136): resolution at 3 weeks 84% with triamcinolone injection versus 87% with surgery versus 46% with hot compresses alone; injection caused less pain and less inconvenience than surgery
cards.summary: Goawalla 2007 RCT (n=136): resolution at 3 weeks 84% with triamcinolone injection versus 87% with surgery versus 46% with hot compresses alone; injection caused less pain and less inconvenience than surgery
cards.type: Single-centre prospective randomised trial, three arms: triamcinolone injection vs incision and curettage vs conservative hot compresses
cards.people: 136 consecutive patients with chalazion randomised to intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection (56 patients; 0.2 mL of 10 mg/mL, followed by lid massage), incision and curettage (45 patients), or advice on hot compresses (35 patients); outcomes including resolution, pain, satisfaction and inconvenience were assessed by telephone interview at 3 weeks.
cards.result: Resolution at 3 weeks was 84% (47/56) with injection and 87% (39/45) with surgery — not significantly different from each other — versus 46% (16/35) with hot compresses alone, which was significantly lower. Pain scores were higher with surgery than with injection (P<0.003); inconvenience was significantly less with injection than with either other option; satisfaction was similar for injection and surgery and lower for conservative care.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes were collected by telephone interview at only 3 weeks, so late recurrence is not captured; single centre.
cards.source: Goawalla A et al. A prospective randomized treatment study comparing three treatment options for chalazia: triamcinolone acetonide injections, incision and curettage, and treatment with hot compresses. Clinical & experimental ophthalmology. 2007. PMID: 17997772. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ahmad 2006 comparative study in pigmented skin (n=141): first-attempt success 79% surgery versus 62% steroid injection (P<0.01), converging after a second attempt (89% vs 80%); skin depigmentation was relatively common with injection in this population
cards.summary: Ahmad 2006 comparative study in pigmented skin (n=141): first-attempt success 79% surgery versus 62% steroid injection (P<0.01), converging after a second attempt (89% vs 80%); skin depigmentation was relatively common with injection in this population
cards.type: Interventional comparative study (allocation as reported), intralesional corticosteroid injection vs surgical incision-curettage, in a Pakistani (pigmented-skin) population
cards.people: 141 patients with chalazia at a naval hospital in Karachi (2002–2003) who completed the study: 75 received incision-curettage and 66 intralesional corticosteroid injection; unsuccessful cases had the same procedure repeated once.
cards.result: After the first attempt, success was 79% (59/75) with surgery versus 62% (41/66) with injection (P<0.01); after a second attempt, success rose to 89% (67/75) versus 80% (53/66) (P<0.14, no longer significant). No serious complications occurred with either, but the authors report skin depigmentation was relatively common after steroid injection in this coloured (pigmented-skin) population.
cards.watchOut: Reported as an interventional comparative study rather than a clearly randomised trial, and its abstract does not give a depigmentation percentage — the harm is stated qualitatively, as the authors state it. Its population is precisely the one in whom depigmentation matters most, which is why it is carded despite the weaker design label.
cards.source: Ahmad S et al. Intralesional corticosteroid injection vs surgical treatment of chalazia in pigmented patients. Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan. 2006. PMID: 16441988. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Singhania 2018 RCT (n=118), size-stratified: injection as effective as incision and curettage in both medium (3–7 mm) and large (>7 mm) chalazia overall — except that in large suppurating granulomas surgery was superior
cards.summary: Singhania 2018 RCT (n=118), size-stratified: injection as effective as incision and curettage in both medium (3–7 mm) and large (>7 mm) chalazia overall — except that in large suppurating granulomas surgery was superior
cards.type: Randomised interventional study, intralesional triamcinolone vs incision and curettage, stratified by lesion size (medium 3–7 mm; large >7 mm)
cards.people: 118 patients with primary chalazion, divided into medium-sized (3–7 mm) and large-sized (>7 mm) groups, with treatment (injection or incision and curettage) decided by randomisation within each group; cytology was performed on every case to exclude other diagnoses. Success was resolution of more than 80% of lesion size.
cards.result: Intralesional triamcinolone was found to be as effective as incision and curettage in both size groups overall. On cytological analysis, in large-sized chalazia of the suppurating granuloma type, incision and curettage was superior to injection. The record's abstract reports these conclusions without per-group success percentages, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Abstract-level reporting without the numerical success rates; the size-by-cytology interaction (large suppurating granulomas favouring surgery) rests on subgroup analysis.
cards.source: Singhania R et al. Intralesional Triamcinolone Acetonide (TA) Versus Incision and Curettage (I & C) for Medium and Large Sized Chalazion. Nepalese journal of ophthalmology. 2018. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Aycinena 2016): across 8 randomised trials, one incision and curettage beat one steroid injection (aggregate success 78.0% vs 60.4%; relative risk for injection success 0.77, a relative measure); with up to two attempts the gap narrowed (86.7% vs 72.5%; relative risk 0.89)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Aycinena 2016): across 8 randomised trials, one incision and curettage beat one steroid injection (aggregate success 78.0% vs 60.4%; relative risk for injection success 0.77, a relative measure); with up to two attempts the gap narrowed (86.7% vs 72.5%; relative risk 0.89)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials comparing incision and curettage with intralesional steroid injection (trials 1984–2013)
cards.people: 552 patients across 8 randomised trials: 288 treated with steroid injection and 264 with incision and curettage.
cards.result: Aggregate success with one procedure was 60.4% for injection versus 78.0% for incision and curettage (P<0.05); with one or two procedures, 72.5% versus 86.7% (P<0.05). The pooled relative risk of success for injection versus surgery was 0.77 with one procedure (P=0.05) and 0.89 with one or two procedures (P=0.002) — relative measures. Injection success rates varied extremely widely between trials (8.7% to 86.7% for one injection). Studies showed no difference in complication incidence between the procedures.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate conflicts with the two largest individual trials carded here, which found near-equal resolution — heterogeneity between the older small trials is large (injection success 8.7–86.7%), so the pooled figure should be read as an average over inconsistent trials, not a precise effect.
cards.source: Aycinena AR et al. Incision and Curettage Versus Steroid Injection for the Treatment of Chalazia: A Meta-Analysis. Ophthalmic plastic and reconstructive surgery. 2016. PMID: 26035035. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the biggest individual trials find injection and surgery resolve chalazia at near-equal rates with less pain from injection, while the pooled older-trial data favour surgery for a single attempt; lesion size/type and skin pigmentation decide the exceptions

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Ben Simon (81% vs 79%) and Goawalla (84% vs 87%, with hot compresses at 46%) found injection and incision-and-curettage equivalent, with less pain and inconvenience from injection. The meta-analysis of 8 older trials instead favours surgery for one attempt (78.0% vs 60.4%), narrowing with a second attempt (86.7% vs 72.5%). The exceptions are consistent: large suppurating granulomas respond better to surgery (Singhania), first-attempt success favoured surgery in pigmented skin (79% vs 62%, Ahmad), and depigmentation after steroid injection is a real risk in pigmented skin even though the best trial in lighter skin saw none.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Recurrent corneal erosion: weak evidence — diamond-burr polishing cut recurrence in one 48-patient trial; lens and lubrication resolved equally (lens faster); delamination equalled laser
shelves.question: In patients with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, which treatment best prevents recurrence and relieves pain — long-term ocular lubrication, bandage contact lens, anterior stromal puncture, diamond-burr polishing, or phototherapeutic keratectomy?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Contact Lenses · Corneal Diseases · Corneal Injuries · Debridement · Eye Infections · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Keratectomy · Lubricant Eye Drops · Pain Measurement · Prednisolone · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Tetracycline
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Every comparison rests on one small trial. Diamond-burr polishing after epithelial debridement reduced recurrences versus debridement alone in 48 patients (relative risk 0.07 in the Cochrane summary, a relative measure from a small trial). Bandage contact lens and ocular lubrication resolved episodes at the same rate in 29 patients (71% vs 73% complete resolution — (the treatments made no difference)) — though symptoms settled faster with the lens (5 vs 9 weeks). Alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy were indistinguishable in 33 patients (resolution 65% vs 63%). The Cochrane review (10 trials, 505 participants) judges the whole base too small and poorly reported for firm guidance, and the older anterior-stromal-puncture comparisons inside it were inconclusive — so no procedure is pooled into a class claim here, and any limb resting on case series alone has been left uncarded, as the row directs.

cards.headline: Ahad 2013 RCT (n=29): complete resolution at 3 months 71% with bandage contact lens versus 73% with ocular lubrication — (the treatments made no difference) to resolution, but symptoms resolved faster with the lens (5 vs 9 weeks)
cards.summary: Ahad 2013 RCT (n=29): complete resolution at 3 months 71% with bandage contact lens versus 73% with ocular lubrication — (the treatments made no difference) to resolution, but symptoms resolved faster with the lens (5 vs 9 weeks)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, bandage contact lens vs ocular lubrication, primary treatment of recurrent corneal erosion syndrome
cards.people: 29 patients with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome at two UK centres, randomised to a bandage contact lens for 3 months (14 patients; replaced every 30 days) or ocular lubricants four times daily with ointment at night for 3 months (15 patients), then followed for recurrence for a further 3 months after resolution.
cards.result: Complete resolution was achieved in 71% (10/14) with the bandage lens and 73% (11/15) with lubrication (P>0.05) — (the treatments made no difference) to the chance of complete resolution. Partial resolution: 7% versus 13%; non-response: 21% versus 13%. Symptoms resolved earlier with the lens — mean 5 weeks versus 9 weeks (P=0.02). No adverse effects occurred in the lens group.
cards.watchOut: A very small trial (n=29): its confidence intervals are wide enough to include clinically important differences in either direction, and 'no significant difference' here is not demonstrated equivalence.
cards.source: Ahad MA et al. Randomized Controlled Study of Ocular Lubrication Versus Bandage Contact Lens in the Primary Treatment of Recurrent Corneal Erosion Syndrome. Cornea. 2013. PMID: 23974885. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wong 2009 RCT (n=48): diamond-burr polishing after epithelial debridement cut recurrences versus debridement with sham polishing (Cochrane summary: relative risk of recurrence 0.07, a relative measure) and lowered astigmatism
cards.summary: Wong 2009 RCT (n=48): diamond-burr polishing after epithelial debridement cut recurrences versus debridement with sham polishing (Cochrane summary: relative risk of recurrence 0.07, a relative measure) and lowered astigmatism
cards.type: Double-masked randomised controlled trial, diamond-burr superficial keratectomy vs epithelial debridement alone (sham burr), 6 months
cards.people: 48 eyes of 48 patients with recurrent corneal erosion secondary to trauma or anterior basement membrane dystrophy, treated at the slit lamp with either diamond-burr superficial keratectomy (25 patients) or epithelial debridement alone (23 patients), followed for 6 months.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly fewer major and minor recurrences and less need for repeated surgical intervention in the diamond-burr group (P<0.001). The Cochrane review quantifies the recurrence contrast as relative risk 0.07 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.50) — a relative measure from a small trial. Mean astigmatism after treatment was significantly lower in the diamond-burr group (P=0.021). The authors describe diamond-burr polishing as a safe, convenient and inexpensive in-office treatment.
cards.watchOut: One small single-programme trial (n=48) carries this comparison; a relative risk of 0.07 from 48 patients is fragile — a few events either way would move it substantially.
cards.source: Wong VW et al. Diamond burr polishing for recurrent corneal erosions: results from a prospective randomized controlled trial. Cornea. 2009. PMID: 19158556. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chan 2014 RCT (n=33): alcohol delamination versus phototherapeutic keratectomy — complete or partial resolution 65% versus 63%, recurrences 5 versus 6 eyes; pain improved in both groups
cards.summary: Chan 2014 RCT (n=33): alcohol delamination versus phototherapeutic keratectomy — complete or partial resolution 65% versus 63%, recurrences 5 versus 6 eyes; pain improved in both groups
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial, alcohol delamination vs phototherapeutic keratectomy, recurrent corneal erosion syndrome not responding to conservative treatment
cards.people: 33 eyes with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome not responding to conservative treatment, randomised to alcohol delamination (17 eyes) or phototherapeutic keratectomy (16 eyes), with patients masked to their group and mean follow-up of about 16–17 months.
cards.result: There were no differences between the groups in pain scores at 3, 6, 12 or 24 months; pain improved from baseline in both groups at 3 and 6 months, and at 24 months only in the alcohol delamination group. Complete or partial resolution occurred in 11 of 17 eyes (65%) with delamination and 10 of 16 (63%) with phototherapeutic keratectomy — (the treatments made no difference) on resolution. Recurrence of symptoms occurred in 5 versus 6 eyes; there was one treatment failure (delamination) and no long-term complications.
cards.watchOut: A 33-patient trial comparing two active procedures with no conservative-treatment control: it can say the two procedures performed similarly, not that either beats continued medical therapy.
cards.source: Chan E et al. A randomised controlled trial of alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy for the treatment of recurrent corneal erosion syndrome. The British journal of ophthalmology. 2014. PMID: 23759442. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Watson 2018): 10 trials, 505 participants — the whole comparative base is small and poorly reported; only the diamond-burr result reached moderate certainty, and the reviewers call for properly designed trials
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Watson 2018): 10 trials, 505 participants — the whole comparative base is small and poorly reported; only the diamond-burr result reached moderate certainty, and the reviewers call for properly designed trials
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 8 randomised and 2 quasi-randomised trials of treatments and prophylaxis for recurrent corneal erosion
cards.people: 505 participants across 10 trials from Europe, East Asia and Australia, comparing therapeutic contact lens, topical lubrication, phototherapeutic keratectomy, alcohol delamination, diamond-burr keratectomy, transepithelial versus subepithelial excimer ablation, anterior stromal puncture, epithelial debridement, and drug adjuncts.
cards.result: Beyond the trials carded here, the review found: a 100-person trial of transepithelial versus subepithelial excimer ablation with a small, imprecise recurrence difference (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.48); an older contact-lens study using a lens no longer in common use that found more pain and complications with the lens; and comparisons published two or more decades ago (excimer ablation versus none, debridement versus anterior stromal puncture, puncture versus contact lens, drug adjuncts) that were all inconclusive. Only one included study was at low risk of bias on all domains. The reviewers conclude the studies were of insufficient size and quality to provide firm evidence for management guidelines.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis whose own verdict is that the evidence base is inadequate — it is carded so the shelf's uncertainty is sourced, not asserted. Anterior stromal puncture, listed in this shelf's question, rests only on these old inconclusive comparisons and has no cardable modern trial.
cards.source: Watson SL et al. Interventions for recurrent corneal erosions. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 29985545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: MAYBE throughout — small trials suggest diamond-burr polishing after debridement prevents recurrence, bandage lens and lubrication resolve episodes at similar rates (lens faster), and alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy perform similarly; no procedure has a firm evidence base
cards.summary: Synthesis: MAYBE throughout — small trials suggest diamond-burr polishing after debridement prevents recurrence, bandage lens and lubrication resolve episodes at similar rates (lens faster), and alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy perform similarly; no procedure has a firm evidence base
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The three primary comparisons point in usable but fragile directions: diamond-burr polishing beat debridement alone on recurrence in 48 patients; bandage lens and lubrication resolved episodes equally often in 29 patients, the lens about 4 weeks faster; alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy were indistinguishable in 33 patients. The Cochrane reviewers, surveying all 505 randomised participants, judge the base insufficient for firm guidance. Procedures are therefore not pooled into a class claim on this shelf, as the commissioning row requires.

shelves.title: Bilateral cochlear implants in children: cohorts favour two implants for speech in noise, localisation and vocabulary; each year of delay between implants cost localisation accuracy
shelves.question: In children with bilateral severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss, does bilateral cochlear implantation — simultaneous or sequential — improve speech perception in noise, sound localisation and language outcomes versus unilateral implantation, and does the inter-implant interval matter?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cochlear Implantation · Speech Perception · Child · Language Development · Hearing Loss, Bilateral · Sound Localization · Cochlear Implants · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational throughout, labelled as such (GAP-E, per the assembly adjudication). No randomised trial of bilateral versus unilateral cochlear implantation in children exists. The comparative cohorts and their syntheses consistently favour two implants for the functions that need two ears: the 2026 meta-analysis (50 studies) found bilateral implantation better on speech perception in noise (standardised mean difference +0.70), sound localisation (+0.74) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65); a matched longitudinal cohort (24 bilateral vs 26 unilateral) found significantly higher speech recognition and vocabulary 5–6 years after sequential implantation; and a 127-child cohort found each year of inter-implant delay cost 1.7 degrees of localisation accuracy (P<0.001), favouring simultaneous or promptly sequential implantation. The exception that proves the framing: against bimodal fitting (implant plus hearing aid, 49 vs 44 children), bilateral implantation showed no significant language or noise advantage — a different comparison. Confounding by family and centre selection runs through all of it, which is why the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Killan 2019 retrospective cohort (n=127): bilateral implantation localised sound with mean error 25.4 degrees; each year of inter-implant delay worsened localisation by 1.7 degrees per year (P<0.001) — observational, labelled
cards.summary: Killan 2019 retrospective cohort (n=127): bilateral implantation localised sound with mean error 25.4 degrees; each year of inter-implant delay worsened localisation by 1.7 degrees per year (P<0.001) — observational, labelled
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort (routinely collected clinical data), sound-source localisation in bilaterally implanted children; simultaneous vs sequential strategies compared within the cohort
cards.people: 127 bilaterally implanted children aged 4 years or older, tested at least 12 months after the second implant; 65 were simultaneously implanted and the rest sequentially, using devices from three manufacturers.
cards.result: Mean root-mean-square localisation error was 25.4 degrees (SD 12.5), ranging from perfect accuracy to chance level. Compared with simultaneous implantation, each year of inter-implant interval was associated with worse localisation by 1.7 degrees of error per year (P<0.001). Each year of pre-implant hearing better than profound thresholds improved accuracy by 1.3 degrees per year (P<0.005), and each year since the second implant improved it by 1.6 degrees (P<0.05). Device manufacturer also differed (one maker's devices localised more accurately by 5.8–9.2 degrees) — named here only as the cohort reports it, as a confounder signal, not a product recommendation.
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL: a retrospective cohort with no unilateral-implant comparison group in this analysis — it compares timing strategies among bilateral users, and family/centre selection into early simultaneous implantation is not randomised away.
cards.source: Killan C et al. Factors Affecting Sound-Source Localization in Children With Simultaneous or Sequential Bilateral Cochlear Implants. Ear and hearing. 2019. PMID: 30299343. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sparreboom 2015 longitudinal cohort: 24 sequentially bilaterally implanted children versus 26 matched unilateral users, 5–6 years on — bilateral users scored significantly higher on speech recognition in quiet and noise and on receptive vocabulary (observational, labelled)
cards.summary: Sparreboom 2015 longitudinal cohort: 24 sequentially bilaterally implanted children versus 26 matched unilateral users, 5–6 years on — bilateral users scored significantly higher on speech recognition in quiet and noise and on receptive vocabulary (observational, labelled)
cards.type: Longitudinal cohort study with matched unilateral reference group, sequential bilateral implantation, 5–6 year follow-up
cards.people: 24 children with bilateral cochlear implants whose second implant was placed between 2.4 and 8.5 years of age, tested 5–6 years after sequential bilateral implantation, with a matched reference group of 26 children with a unilateral cochlear implant; spatial hearing was tested with a minimum audible angle task.
cards.result: In the long term, bilateral users still showed improving spatial acuity, best for interaural level-difference cues. For speech recognition in quiet and in noise, and for receptive vocabulary, children with bilateral implants had significantly higher scores than the unilateral reference group. Attending a mainstream school (versus a school for the deaf) also had a significant positive effect on speech recognition and vocabulary. Despite a period of unilateral deafness, the bilateral group in mainstream education obtained age-appropriate language scores.
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL: small matched cohort (24 vs 26) — matching cannot remove confounding by family resources, centre and schooling, and the schooling effect visible in the same analysis shows how large those confounders are.
cards.source: Sparreboom M et al. Long-term outcomes on spatial hearing, speech recognition and receptive vocabulary after sequential bilateral cochlear implantation in children. Research in developmental disabilities. 2015. PMID: 25462493. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.summary: Ching 2014 cohort (LOCHI study): 49 bilateral versus 44 bimodal children — no significant difference in language at age 3 or speech perception in noise at age 5 after adjustment; earlier activation predicted better outcomes (observational, labelled)
cards.type: Prospective population cohort comparison (Longitudinal Outcomes of Children with Hearing Impairment study), bilateral implants vs bimodal fitting (implant + contralateral hearing aid)
cards.people: 93 children from the LOCHI cohort: 49 with bilateral cochlear implants and 44 with bimodal fitting (one implant, one hearing aid); language was assessed at 3 years and speech perception (speech from the front, babble from front or sides) at 5 years.
cards.result: On average there was no significant difference in language outcomes between the bilateral and bimodal groups after controlling for demographic variables, and speech perception in noise was also not significantly different between the groups. Earlier age at cochlear implant activation was associated with better outcomes. Compared with normal-hearing children, implanted children needed a better signal-to-noise ratio.
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL, and the comparison is bilateral versus BIMODAL — not versus unilateral implantation alone; children whose second ear retains usable hearing (the bimodal group) differ systematically from those implanted bilaterally, so this null does not contradict the unilateral comparisons.
cards.source: Ching TY et al. Language and speech perception of young children with bimodal fitting or bilateral cochlear implants. Cochlear implants international. 2014. PMID: 24869442. cards.headline: Systematic review (Sparreboom 2010): bilateral versus unilateral implantation in children — advantages for speech perception in quiet and in noise, localisation results less consistent; level of evidence low (observational base, labelled)
cards.summary: Systematic review (Sparreboom 2010): bilateral versus unilateral implantation in children — advantages for speech perception in quiet and in noise, localisation results less consistent; level of evidence low (observational base, labelled)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (update of the NICE paediatric review), comparative cohort studies of bilateral vs unilateral implantation or bimodal stimulation
cards.people: European, North American and Australasian comparative studies in children with severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss published 2006–2009, comparing bilateral implantation with unilateral implantation and/or bimodal stimulation across audiological, speech, functional, quality-of-life and educational outcomes.
cards.result: Effect sizes could not be pooled because of heterogeneity, so results were presented qualitatively: although the level of evidence was low, the advantages of bilateral implants corresponded to the primary benefits of bilateral hearing — improved speech perception in quiet and in noise. Localisation results were less consistent. No data were available on audiological, speech-production or educational outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of observational comparisons only — there is no randomised trial of bilateral versus unilateral implantation in children, and this review's 'low level of evidence' grading is part of its finding.
cards.source: Sparreboom M et al. The effectiveness of bilateral cochlear implants for severe-to-profound deafness in children: a systematic review. Otology & neurotology. 2010. PMID: 20601922. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhuchkova 2026): 50 studies — bilateral implantation beat unilateral on speech perception in noise (standardised mean difference +0.70), localisation (+0.74) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65); earlier implantation and shorter intervals did better (observational base, labelled)
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhuchkova 2026): 50 studies — bilateral implantation beat unilateral on speech perception in noise (standardised mean difference +0.70), localisation (+0.74) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65); earlier implantation and shorter intervals did better (observational base, labelled)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO-registered), 50 studies in qualitative synthesis and 20 in meta-analyses, 2015–2025 plus selected earlier studies
cards.people: Children with congenital or early-onset bilateral deafness receiving bilateral versus unilateral cochlear implantation; outcomes were speech perception (especially in noise), sound localisation, language development, quality of life and adverse effects.
cards.result: Bilateral implantation gave significantly better speech perception in noise (standardised mean difference +0.70; P<0.001), sound localisation (+0.74; P<0.001) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65) than unilateral implantation. Earlier implantation and shorter inter-implant intervals were associated with larger benefits. Surgical and vestibular complications were infrequent and did not exceed unilateral rates, and quality-of-life ratings were consistently higher in bilateral users. Language outcomes showed greater heterogeneity than the auditory measures.
cards.watchOut: OBSERVATIONAL BASE: standardised mean differences pooled largely from non-randomised comparisons inherit their confounding (selection by family, centre and residual hearing); heterogeneity was substantial, especially for language.
cards.source: Zhuchkova A et al. Benefits of bilateral cochlear implantation in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology. 2026. PMID: 42162288. cards.headline: Synthesis: with no randomised trial in existence, the cohort record consistently favours bilateral implantation for hearing in noise, localisation and vocabulary — with the strongest, most consistent signal for short inter-implant intervals — but every estimate is observational and confounded by who gets two implants
cards.summary: Synthesis: with no randomised trial in existence, the cohort record consistently favours bilateral implantation for hearing in noise, localisation and vocabulary — with the strongest, most consistent signal for short inter-implant intervals — but every estimate is observational and confounded by who gets two implants
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three primary comparative cohorts and two syntheses agree in direction: bilateral users outperform unilateral users on speech perception in noise (pooled standardised mean difference +0.70), localisation (+0.74) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65), and the 127-child cohort quantifies the timing gradient (1.7 degrees of localisation error per year of inter-implant delay). The one null — bilateral versus bimodal fitting in the LOCHI cohort — compares against a second-ear hearing aid, not against one implant alone. Simultaneous and sequential strategies are separate limbs of this question and are carded separately; the interval gradient, not a pooled class claim, is the shelf's actionable content.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Corneal sensitivity: falls with age on the filament, instrument-defined thresholds, and a discordant air-pulse finding in women
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how sensitive is the cornea — corneal sensitivity thresholds by Cochet–Bonnet and non-contact air-pulse esthesiometry across the cornea and conjunctiva — and how much does sensitivity fall with age, contact-lens wear and time of day?
shelves.mesh: Cornea/physiology · Differential Threshold · Sensory Thresholds · Age Factors · Sex Factors · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong (somatosensory / special senses chapters; thin framing for corneal esthesiometry specifically — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three human studies whose core finding is concordant for the filament method: corneal touch threshold rises with age — the 1977 classic (205 healthy people) found thresholds increasing gradually throughout life, more significantly after the fifth decade, and a 2025 Cochet–Bonnet cohort (324 volunteers) found central sensitivity falling with age with correlations of about −0.78 across all quadrants, accelerating in the 50s and 60s. The air-pulse method (49 subjects, Belmonte esthesiometer) is carded per instrument and does not merge: its corneal threshold averaged 76.2 ± 26.8 mL/min, its conjunctival threshold 123.7 ± 49.1 mL/min, and its age pattern differed by sex. Cross-point: cenegermin for neurotrophic keratitis (pack #4252) is the disease state this measurement defines — not carded here.

cards.headline: Millodot 1977: in 205 healthy people, corneal touch threshold rose gradually throughout life, more significantly after the fifth decade
cards.summary: Millodot 1977: in 205 healthy people, corneal touch threshold rose gradually throughout life, more significantly after the fifth decade
cards.type: Human classic psychophysical study, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 1977
cards.people: 205 healthy people of different ages, with corneal touch threshold measured (the classic touch-threshold study); the results were compared with Boberg-Ans's earlier work and with a report claiming sensitivity rose to the fifth decade and then fell.
cards.result: Corneal touch threshold increased gradually throughout life, although more significantly after the fifth decade of life. The results accorded with Boberg-Ans, refuting the earlier report that corneal sensitivity (threshold⁻¹) increased up to the fifth decade and declined thereafter. The record's abstract is short and gives no numerical thresholds per decade — none are printed here — so the verified content is the direction, the timing (acceleration after 50) and the cohort size.
cards.watchOut: A short 1977 abstract with no per-decade numbers and no named instrument in the record — it anchors the direction of the age effect, and the quantitative values on this shelf come from the 2025 and 2008 cards.
cards.source: Millodot M. The influence of age on the sensitivity of the cornea. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science. 1977. PMID: 844979. cards.headline: Eratilgan 2025: in 324 healthy Turkish volunteers, Cochet–Bonnet central corneal sensitivity averaged 50.15 ± 9.7 mm and fell with age (r ≈ −0.78), accelerating in the 5th and 6th decades
cards.summary: Eratilgan 2025: in 324 healthy Turkish volunteers, Cochet–Bonnet central corneal sensitivity averaged 50.15 ± 9.7 mm and fell with age (r ≈ −0.78), accelerating in the 5th and 6th decades
cards.type: Human normative study (Cochet–Bonnet), Clin Exp Optom 2025
cards.people: 324 healthy volunteers aged 20–84 years (right eyes; mean age 44.31 ± 15.65 years; 165 women, 159 men) attending for routine examination in Turkey, excluding any ocular disease other than refractive error, systemic disease, contact-lens use, chronic ocular or systemic drug use and previous ocular surgery; central and four-quadrant corneal sensitivity measured with a Cochet–Bonnet esthesiometer (Luneau Ophthalmology, France, named as published), in five age groups (20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, ≥60).
cards.result: Mean central, superior, inferior, nasal and temporal sensitivities were 50.15 ± 9.7, 48.62 ± 10.3, 48.59 ± 10.3, 47.73 ± 10.2 and 47.71 ± 10.3 mm respectively (filament length — longer means a lighter touch is felt). Sensitivities in all quadrants decreased significantly with age (P = 0.001 for all; correlation coefficients r = −0.783, −0.791, −0.789, −0.760, −0.775), with the decrease accelerating in groups 4 and 5 (50–59 and ≥60 years). Gender differences were significant in central and temporal quadrants.
cards.watchOut: One Turkish population and one filament instrument, routine-examination attenders rather than a random sample — its values are the Cochet–Bonnet norm for that population, and the authors note geography, gender and ethnicity may affect values.
cards.source: Eratilgan NF et al. Alterations in corneal sensitivity according to age and gender in healthy population in Turkey. Clinical & Experimental Optometry. 2025. PMID: 39586826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Golebiowski 2008: with a Belmonte air-pulse esthesiometer in 49 normal subjects, corneal threshold averaged 76.2 ± 26.8 mL/min and conjunctival 123.7 ± 49.1 mL/min — thresholds were higher in men, and the age pattern differed from the filament studies
cards.summary: Golebiowski 2008: with a Belmonte air-pulse esthesiometer in 49 normal subjects, corneal threshold averaged 76.2 ± 26.8 mL/min and conjunctival 123.7 ± 49.1 mL/min — thresholds were higher in men, and the age pattern differed from the filament studies
cards.type: Human retrospective esthesiometry study (Belmonte air-pulse), Optom Vis Sci 2008
cards.people: A retrospective analysis of ocular surface threshold measurements made by one examiner using the CRCERT–Belmonte esthesiometer (named as published) — multiple corneal measurements for 49 normal subjects (24 men, 25 women) and conjunctival measurements for 33 subjects (16 men, 17 women); thresholds at the corneal apex and at the inferior conjunctiva 2 mm from the limbus, measured between 09:00 and 18:00 at 20–26 °C and 52–87% humidity.
cards.result: Mean corneal threshold was 76.2 ± 26.8 mL/min and conjunctival threshold 123.7 ± 49.1 mL/min (n = 33, P < 0.001) — the cornea is the more sensitive tissue, and the two thresholds were well correlated (r = 0.66). Thresholds were significantly higher for men than women at both cornea (82.2 ± 23.5 vs 67.6 ± 24.1 mL/min, P = 0.04) and conjunctiva (144.1 ± 40.7 vs 105.8 ± 50.2, P = 0.02). A significant reduction in corneal threshold with age was apparent for females (n = 25, r = −0.49, P = 0.01) — i.e. thresholds fell, meaning sensitivity rose with age in women on this instrument — but not males; no effect of time of day, ambient humidity or temperature was found at either site.
cards.watchOut: Airflow thresholds in mL/min cannot be compared numerically with filament lengths in mm — the two instruments are carded separately for that reason. The female age finding runs opposite to the filament studies and rests on 25 women in a retrospective analysis; it is printed as a discordance, not smoothed over.
cards.source: Golebiowski B et al. Factors affecting corneal and conjunctival sensitivity measurement. Optometry and Vision Science. 2008. PMID: 18382334. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: corneal sensitivity falls with age on the filament — but the instrument defines the threshold, and the air-pulse record disagrees on the age direction in women
cards.summary: Synthesis: corneal sensitivity falls with age on the filament — but the instrument defines the threshold, and the air-pulse record disagrees on the age direction in women
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (the 1977 classic of 205 healthy people, the 2025 Cochet–Bonnet cohort of 324 volunteers, and the 2008 Belmonte air-pulse analysis of 49 normal subjects), framed by Ganong on somatosensory and special senses — thin framing for esthesiometry, as the row states.
cards.result: By Cochet–Bonnet filament, the story is concordant across 48 years: touch threshold rises (sensitivity falls) gradually through life and faster after the fifth decade, with central sensitivity about 50 mm of filament in the modern cohort and a strong age correlation (r ≈ −0.78) in every quadrant, and small gender differences in central and temporal quadrants. By air-pulse esthesiometry the quantities are different in kind — corneal threshold about 76 mL/min of airflow, conjunctival about 124 mL/min — men need more airflow than women at both sites, time of day and ambient conditions do not move thresholds, and in women the threshold falls with age, i.e. sensitivity appears to rise. That last finding is a genuine instrument-and-sample discordance on the face of the shelf, not a synthesis error: filament and air-pulse thresholds are not interchangeable, and no single 'corneal sensitivity' number is printed without its instrument.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here quantifies contact-lens wear's effect on sensitivity (the 2025 cohort excluded lens wearers), so the row's lens-wear limb is unquantified on this shelf and is stated as such rather than filled from the textbook.

Clinical & Experimental Optometry. 2025 (PMID: 39586826); Golebiowski B et al. Optometry and Vision Science. 2008 (PMID: 18382334), all carded above, with Ganong textbook framing.
