synthesis synthesis of the three carded human records (the 1977 classic of 205 healthy people, the 2025 cochet–bonnet cohort of 324 volunteers, and the 2008 belmonte air-pulse analysis of 49 normal subjects), framed by ganong on somatosensory and special senses — thin framing for esthesiometry, as the row states. by cochet–bonnet filament, the story is concordant across 48 years: touch threshold rises (sensitivity falls) gradually through life and faster after the fifth decade, with central sensitivity about 50 mm of filament in the modern cohort and a strong age correlation (r ≈ −0.78) in every quadrant, and small gender differences in central and temporal quadrants. by air-pulse esthesiometry the quantities are different in kind — corneal threshold about 76 ml/min of airflow, conjunctival about 124 ml/min — men need more airflow than women at both sites, time of day and ambient conditions do not move thresholds, and in women the threshold falls with age, i.e. sensitivity appears to rise. that last finding is a genuine instrument-and-sample discordance on the face of the shelf, not a synthesis error: filament and air-pulse thresholds are not interchangeable, and no single 'corneal sensitivity' number is printed without its instrument. no carded record here quantifies contact-lens wear's effect on sensitivity (the 2025 cohort excluded lens wearers), so the row's lens-wear limb is unquantified on this shelf and is stated as such rather than filled from the textbook. synthesis of millodot m. investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 1977 (pmid: 844979); eratilgan nf et al. clinical & experimental optometry. 2025 (pmid: 39586826); golebiowski b et al. optometry and vision science. 2008 (pmid: 18382334), all carded above, with ganong textbook framing. registry id: none in the record. mesh: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Spontaneous blink rate: ~17/min at rest, 4.5/min reading, 26/min in conversation — the task sets the rate
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the spontaneous eye blink rate at rest, during reading and during conversation — its mean and wide between-person spread — and how do gaze position, lighting and age change it?
shelves.mesh: Blinking/physiology · Reading · Speech · Fixation, Ocular/physiology · Cluster Analysis
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong and Guyton & Hall on eyelid and lacrimal physiology (thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three human video studies that agree on the shape and the scale: at rest, spontaneous blink rate is roughly 12–17 blinks/min; reading collapses it to about 4.5/min (a 55.08% relative fall from rest in the 150-person study, with the absolute values 17 → 4.5/min printed beside it); conversation raises it to about 26/min (a 99.70% relative rise from rest, 17 → 26/min); and the spread between healthy people is wide and skewed, with a distinct 'frequent blinker' cluster above 20/min. Cross-point: the tear-film physiology shelf (pack #6952 — tear turnover and osmolarity) describes what blinking pumps; this shelf measures the blink itself.

cards.headline: Bentivoglio 1997: in 150 healthy volunteers, blink rate was 17/min at rest, 26/min in conversation and 4.5/min while reading — a 55.08% relative fall reading, a 99.70% relative rise talking (absolutes printed beside)
cards.summary: Bentivoglio 1997: in 150 healthy volunteers, blink rate was 17/min at rest, 26/min in conversation and 4.5/min while reading — a 55.08% relative fall reading, a 99.70% relative rise talking (absolutes printed beside)
cards.type: Human videotaped blink-rate study (rest / reading / conversation), Mov Disord 1997
cards.people: 150 healthy volunteers (70 men, 80 women; mean age 35.9 ± 17.9 years, range 5–87 years), videotaped in a standard setting while performing three tasks: resting quietly, reading a short passage, and talking freely; mean blink rate computed during each task.
cards.result: Mean blink rate at rest was 17 blinks/min, during conversation it increased to 26, and it was as low as 4.5 while reading. Compared with rest, blink rate decreased by 55.08% relative while reading (P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁵) and increased by 99.70% relative during conversation (P < 1 × 10⁻⁹); compared with reading, it increased during conversation by 577.8% relative (P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁷) — relative changes, with the absolute rates (17, 26 and 4.5/min) printed beside them. The most common pattern was conversation > rest > reading (101 subjects, 67.3%); 34 subjects (22.7%) showed rest > conversation > reading and 12 (8.0%) conversation > reading > rest. Eye colour and wearing glasses did not influence rate; women had higher rates than men only while reading; no age-related differences were found. The distribution curves were highly reproducible in each task and best fitted by a log-normal distribution.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative changes between tasks, not absolute rates — that is why the absolute 17/26/4.5 per minute are printed with them; and a short reading passage in a laboratory is not a day of screen reading, so the reading figure is a task value, not a daily average.
cards.source: Bentivoglio AR et al. Analysis of blink rate patterns in normal subjects. Movement Disorders. 1997. PMID: 9399231. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Doughty 2006: in 100 men, spontaneous blink rate in silence averaged 13.8 ± 9.7/min (range 2.8–48) — a skewed distribution that cluster analysis split into 'normal' and 'frequent' blinkers above 20/min
cards.summary: Doughty 2006: in 100 men, spontaneous blink rate in silence averaged 13.8 ± 9.7/min (range 2.8–48) — a skewed distribution that cluster analysis split into 'normal' and 'frequent' blinkers above 20/min
cards.type: Human videotaped blink-rate study (cluster analysis), Eye Contact Lens 2006
cards.people: 100 men aged 23–57 years with no significant eye disease, questioned on ocular symptoms, with 5-minute video recordings of the eyes in primary gaze and in silence between 11:00 and 17:00; spontaneous eye blink rate and palpebral aperture assessed from video, and central corneal threshold touch sensitivity then measured with a Cochet–Bonnet aesthesiometer.
cards.result: Average spontaneous eye blink rate was 13.8 ± 9.7 blinks/min (range 2.8–48 blinks/min), with a heterogeneous distribution skewed to higher values. It was not obviously dependent on time of day, number of mild symptoms, or central corneal sensitivity (P ≥ 0.6), and showed no correlation with palpebral aperture height (P = 0.546) and only a possible weak association with age (P = 0.082, r = 0.175). A hierarchical cluster analysis resolved the distribution into two distinct groups (P < 0.001, F ratio = 222): 'normal' blinkers and 'frequent' blinkers, the latter defined as a rate above 20 blinks/min in primary gaze and silence.
cards.watchOut: Men only, aged 23–57, in silence and primary gaze — the 13.8/min mean and the 20/min 'frequent' line describe that condition, not blinking in general; the cluster split is a statistical grouping of one distribution, not a disease category.
cards.source: Doughty MJ et al. Further analysis of the human spontaneous eye blink rate by a cluster analysis-based approach to categorize individuals with 'normal' versus 'frequent' eye blink activity. Eye & Contact Lens. 2006. PMID: 17099391. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Blinking/physiology · Cluster Analysis · Cornea/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged

cards.headline: Doughty 2014: in 32 young adults, blink rate was 11.7 ± 0.9/min in primary gaze — rising with upward gaze (13.0) and with glare (14.4), and further with upward gaze plus glare (15.0)
cards.summary: Doughty 2014: in 32 young adults, blink rate was 11.7 ± 0.9/min in primary gaze — rising with upward gaze (13.0) and with glare (14.4), and further with upward gaze plus glare (15.0)
cards.type: Human videotaped blink-rate study (gaze and glare), Graefes Arch Clin Exp Ophthalmol 2014
cards.people: 32 subjects aged 18–24 years, with separate 5-minute video recordings in different gaze directions (horizontal, slightly upwards, slightly downwards) under normal lighting or a distant lighting glare source.
cards.result: Spontaneous eyeblink rate in primary eye gaze under normal lighting was 11.7 ± 0.9 eyeblinks/min with a coefficient of variation of 20.5%. A non-significant decrease was noted with downward gaze, but a slight significant increase with upward gaze (to 13.0 ± 1.1/min, coefficient of variation 26.1%). In the presence of glare, the rate in primary gaze increased significantly (P < 0.001) to 14.4 ± 1.3/min, with a progressive increase over time; on upward gaze with glare it rose further (average 15.0 ± 2.4/min, P < 0.001; coefficient of variation 29.2%).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two subjects aged 18–24 — a narrow, young sample — and the glare effect grows over the recording, so the 14.4/min figure is a mean over a changing response, not a steady state.
cards.source: Doughty MJ. Spontaneous eyeblink activity under different conditions of gaze (eye position) and visual glare. Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2014. cards.headline: Synthesis: the blink is a task signal, not a vital sign — ~12–17/min at rest, ~4.5/min reading, ~26/min in conversation, with a wide, skewed spread between healthy people
cards.summary: Synthesis: the blink is a task signal, not a vital sign — ~12–17/min at rest, ~4.5/min reading, ~26/min in conversation, with a wide, skewed spread between healthy people
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (150 volunteers across the three tasks; 100 men in silence in primary gaze; 32 young adults under gaze and glare conditions), framed by Ganong / Guyton & Hall on eyelid and lacrimal physiology — thin framing, as the row states.
cards.result: Spontaneous blink rate is set by what the eyes are doing, not by age or eye colour: in the 150-person study, rest was 17/min, conversation 26/min and reading 4.5/min, with the task order conversation > rest > reading in two-thirds of people; in silence and primary gaze the other cohorts read 13.8 ± 9.7/min (100 men, range 2.8–48) and 11.7 ± 0.9/min (32 young adults). The between-person spread is wide and skewed — a distinct 'frequent blinker' cluster sits above 20/min in silence — and it is not explained by age, mild symptoms, corneal sensitivity or palpebral aperture. Gaze and glare move it modestly: upward gaze to 13.0/min, glare to 14.4/min, upward gaze plus glare to 15.0/min. A single 'normal blink rate' without a stated task is therefore meaningless; the task is part of the value.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here quantifies a lighting effect beyond the glare experiment, and the age limb is a null — the large study found no age-related differences and the 100-man study found only a weak, non-significant trend — so no age gradient is printed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bentivoglio AR et al. Movement Disorders. 1997 (PMID: 9399231); Doughty MJ et al. Eye & Contact Lens. 2006 (PMID: 17099391); Doughty MJ. Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2014 (PMID: 24872023), all carded above, with Ganong / Guyton & Hall textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Peripapillary RNFL thickness on SD-OCT: ~87–105 μm by cohort and device, thinning 0.38 μm/year
shelves.question: In healthy eyes, what is peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer thickness on spectral-domain OCT — its mean and 1st/5th-percentile limits by age, sex, ethnicity and optic-disc size — and how fast does it thin with normal ageing?
shelves.mesh: Nerve Fibers/pathology · Tomography, Optical Coherence/methods · Optic Disk/pathology · Reference Values · Retinal Ganglion Cells/pathology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong on vision / retinal structure (thin framing for OCT biometry — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three primary SD-OCT records plus a 617-subject interocular-symmetry cohort: across the European Eye Epidemiology consortium's eight cohorts (16,084 adults), mean peripapillary RNFL thickness ranged from 86.8 ± 21.4 μm (Rotterdam Study I) to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm (Rotterdam Study III), thinning with age at −0.38 μm per year; the Cirrus-versus-Stratus comparison (97 healthy subjects) shows device values are not interchangeable (proportional bias, and Cirrus intervisit reproducibility 4.31–22.01 μm); and in 103 healthy myopic participants the RNFL bundle pattern itself shifts with axial length, changing how maps must be read. Percentile limits are device-normative-database constructs, not biological constants. Cross-point in prose: the companion macular-thickness question (slate row S9-4-39) is the sibling OCT metric and is carded separately — it is not merged into this shelf.

cards.headline: Mauschitz 2018 (E3): in 16,084 European adults across 8 cohorts, mean peripapillary RNFL thickness ranged from 86.8 ± 21.4 μm to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm, thinning by 0.38 μm per year of age
cards.summary: Mauschitz 2018 (E3): in 16,084 European adults across 8 cohorts, mean peripapillary RNFL thickness ranged from 86.8 ± 21.4 μm to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm, thinning by 0.38 μm per year of age
cards.type: Human cross-sectional meta-analysis (E3 consortium, SD-OCT), Ophthalmology 2018
cards.people: 16,084 European adults from 8 cohort studies of the European Eye Epidemiology (E3) consortium (mean age range across cohorts 56.9 ± 12.3 to 82.1 ± 4.2 years), in a cross-sectional meta-analysis of peripapillary RNFL thickness measured by spectral-domain OCT, with associations examined by multivariable linear regression per study and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: Mean peripapillary RNFL thickness ranged from 86.8 ± 21.4 μm in the Rotterdam Study I to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm in the Rotterdam Study III. Reduced thickness was associated with older age (β = −0.38 μm/year; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.18), higher intraocular pressure (β = −0.36 μm/mmHg), visual impairment (β = −5.50 μm), and history of systemic hypertension (β = −0.54 μm) and stroke (β = −1.94 μm). Higher thickness was associated with more hyperopic spherical equivalent (β = 1.39 μm/diopter) and with current smoking (β = 1.53 μm versus never-smokers). The age slope implies about 3.8 μm of thinning per decade — arithmetic on the reported β, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: Older European adults (mean cohort ages 57–82) with a mix of platforms across cohorts — the 86.8–104.7 μm range is a between-cohort range, not a single population's reference interval, and the smoking association (thicker RNFL in smokers) is an observational association, not a protective effect.
cards.source: Mauschitz MM et al. Systemic and Ocular Determinants of Peripapillary Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer Thickness Measurements in the European Eye Epidemiology (E3) Population. Ophthalmology. 2018. PMID: 29716786. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Leung 2009: Cirrus HD-OCT versus Stratus OCT in 97 healthy subjects — Cirrus intravisit repeatability 5.12–15.02 μm, intervisit 4.31–22.01 μm, with proportional bias between devices
cards.summary: Leung 2009: Cirrus HD-OCT versus Stratus OCT in 97 healthy subjects — Cirrus intravisit repeatability 5.12–15.02 μm, intervisit 4.31–22.01 μm, with proportional bias between devices
cards.type: Human device-comparison study (Cirrus SD-OCT vs Stratus TD-OCT), Ophthalmology 2009
cards.people: 97 normal subjects and 83 glaucoma patients in a prospective cross-sectional study, one eye each imaged with a spectral-domain OCT device (Cirrus HD-OCT; Carl Zeiss Meditec, named as published) and a time-domain OCT device (Stratus OCT; Carl Zeiss Meditec, named as published); 16 and 31 normal eyes were selected randomly to evaluate intravisit repeatability and intervisit reproducibility respectively, with agreement by Bland–Altman plots and diagnostic performance by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.
cards.result: Intravisit repeatability of Cirrus HD-OCT ranged between 5.12 and 15.02 μm, and intervisit reproducibility between 4.31 and 22.01 μm. Intervisit variabilities of sectoral and average RNFL thicknesses were lower for Cirrus than Stratus, significantly so at 1, 3, 4 and 8–11 o'clock (P ≤ 0.021). There were proportional biases between the two devices: the difference in RNFL thicknesses increased with the means. Diagnostic performance was comparable (average RNFL area under the curve 0.962 for Cirrus, 0.956 for Stratus) and the structure–function association comparable (R² = 0.580 vs 0.623).
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports variability and diagnostic performance, not a mean healthy RNFL thickness — none is printed from this card; its role is the device lesson, and the glaucoma patients (83) are the diagnostic-performance contrast, not healthy norms.
cards.source: Leung CK et al. Retinal nerve fiber layer imaging with spectral-domain optical coherence tomography: a variability and diagnostic performance study. Ophthalmology. 2009. PMID: 19464061. cards.headline: Leung 2012: in 103 healthy myopic participants (189 eyes), the RNFL bundles converge temporally with axial length — and the area of abnormal RNFL measurement grows with it
cards.summary: Leung 2012: in 103 healthy myopic participants (189 eyes), the RNFL bundles converge temporally with axial length — and the area of abnormal RNFL measurement grows with it
cards.type: Human SD-OCT study (healthy myopic eyes), Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2012
cards.people: 189 myopic eyes from 103 normal healthy myopic participants, imaged by spectral-domain OCT; the angle between the long axes of the superotemporal and inferotemporal RNFL bundles (the RNFL distribution angle) and the abnormal area in the RNFL thickness deviation map were measured, with associations analysed by linear mixed models.
cards.result: The RNFL distribution angle decreased with axial length (P < 0.011). In univariate analysis the area of abnormal RNFL measurement was positively associated with axial length (P = 0.001) and negatively associated with the RNFL distribution angle (P < 0.001), average RNFL thickness (P < 0.001), optic disc area (P ≤ 0.001) and signal strength (P = 0.026); in multivariate analysis it was negatively associated with the RNFL distribution angle independent of the other covariates. The superotemporal and inferotemporal bundles converge temporally with increasing myopia, which was associated with an increase in the area of abnormal RNFL measurement — so interpreting an RNFL map in a myopic eye requires accounting for the bundle distribution pattern.
cards.watchOut: Myopic eyes only, retrospective, one device family: 'abnormal area' here means area flagged against the device's normative database in healthy myopes — a false-positive signal, not disease — and no mean RNFL thickness is printed from this record.
cards.source: Leung CK et al. Retinal nerve fiber layer imaging with spectral-domain optical coherence tomography: interpreting the RNFL maps in healthy myopic eyes. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science. 2012. PMID: 22997288. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hwang 2014: in 617 healthy subjects (1,234 eyes) on Cirrus SD-OCT, the normal interocular difference limit (2.5th–97.5th percentile) was 9.5 μm globally — a percentile construct, not a biological constant
cards.summary: Hwang 2014: in 617 healthy subjects (1,234 eyes) on Cirrus SD-OCT, the normal interocular difference limit (2.5th–97.5th percentile) was 9.5 μm globally — a percentile construct, not a biological constant
cards.type: Human normative study (interocular symmetry, Cirrus SD-OCT), Clin Exp Optom 2014
cards.people: 1,234 healthy eyes from 617 subjects (mean age 36.4 ± 19.8 years, range 5–80; mean refractive error −2.67 ± 2.91 D, range −14.13 to +5.75 D), with peripapillary RNFL thickness measured by Cirrus high-definition spectral-domain OCT (named as published); interocular differences (right minus left) in global and quadrant thicknesses were measured, with effects of age and refractive error examined.
cards.result: Cut-off limits for normal interocular RNFL thickness differences (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of normative data) in the global area and in the superior, nasal, inferior and temporal quadrants were 9.5, 23.0, 15.6, 20.0 and 22.6 μm respectively. Mean interocular differences were 0.7 (P < 0.001), −3.9 (P < 0.001), 2.6 (P < 0.001), 1.1 (P = 0.007) and 3.0 μm (P < 0.001) in the global, superior, nasal, inferior and temporal areas. Interocular differences were not significantly correlated with age or refractive error.
cards.watchOut: One device (Cirrus), one population, wide refractive range — the 9.5 μm global limit is that device's normative-database percentile cut-off for that population, and the quadrant limits are far wider (up to 23.0 μm superiorly), so a global limit must not be applied quadrant by quadrant.
cards.source: Hwang YH et al. Interocular symmetry of retinal nerve fibre layer thickness in healthy eyes: a spectral-domain optical coherence tomographic study. Clinical & Experimental Optometry. 2014. PMID: 25331078. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: peripapillary RNFL thickness centres at roughly 87–105 μm depending on cohort and device, thins about 0.38 μm per year, and is a device-relative measurement — read the map against the right normative database
cards.summary: Synthesis: peripapillary RNFL thickness centres at roughly 87–105 μm depending on cohort and device, thins about 0.38 μm per year, and is a device-relative measurement — read the map against the right normative database
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records (the 16,084-adult E3 meta-analysis; the 97-healthy-subject Cirrus-vs-Stratus comparison; the 103 healthy myopic participants; and the 617-subject interocular-symmetry cohort), framed by Ganong on vision / retinal structure — thin framing for OCT biometry, as the row states.
cards.result: Mean peripapillary RNFL thickness on spectral-domain OCT sits in the high-80s to mid-100s of micrometres (86.8 ± 21.4 to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm across E3 cohorts), with the cohort and the device doing much of the moving: Cirrus and Stratus values show proportional bias and are not interchangeable, and Cirrus sectoral reproducibility alone spans 4.31–22.01 μm between visits. Age thins the layer at −0.38 μm/year (about 3.8 μm per decade, arithmetic on the reported slope), higher intraocular pressure and vascular history thin it further, and hyperopia thickens it. In myopic eyes the bundle geometry itself changes — bundles converge temporally with axial length, and the area flagged 'abnormal' against a normative database grows — so a map must be read with refraction and disc size in mind. The percentile limits printed here (e.g. a 9.5 μm normal interocular difference globally on Cirrus) are constructs of a device's normative database, not biological constants. The companion macular-thickness question (slate row S9-4-39) is a separate OCT metric, carded separately, not merged here.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here gives 1st/5th-percentile RNFL limits by sex and ethnicity as a single table, and the E3 cohorts are European adults with mean ages 57–82 — the shelf therefore gives the age slope and the cohort range, the device lesson, and one device's percentile construction, rather than a universal centile table that no fetched record supports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mauschitz MM et al. Ophthalmology. 2018 (PMID: 29716786); Leung CK et al. Ophthalmology. 2009 (PMID: 19464061); Leung CK et al. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science. 2012 (PMID: 22997288); Hwang YH et al. Clinical & Experimental Optometry. 2014 (PMID: 25331078), all carded above, with Ganong textbook framing. shelves.title: Macular thickness in health is a device number: Spectralis central subfield ~270 µm (ceiling 315 µm), swept-source ~228 µm in the same population, Cirrus ~241 µm in children — conversion equations exist because raw values differ
shelves.question: In healthy eyes, what is macular thickness on spectral-domain OCT — central subfield and ETDRS-sector means by age, sex and ethnicity — and how reproducible are the measurements?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/physiology · Body Weights and Measures · Female · Fourier Analysis · Humans · Intraocular Pressure/physiology · Macula Lutea/anatomy & histology · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Reference Values · Tomography, Optical Coherence/methods · Visual Acuity/physiology · Young Adult · Cross-Sectional Studies · Diabetic Retinopathy/diagnosis · Healthy Volunteers · Macula Lutea/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Organ Size · Adolescent · Nerve Fibers · Retinal Ganglion Cells · Multiple Sclerosis/diagnostic imaging · Child · Optic Disk/diagnostic imaging · Retrospective Studies · Saudi Arabia
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, vision/retinal structure) is thin for OCT biometry, as the slate row states — the primary measurement literature carries this shelf. Healthy macular thickness is a device-relative quantity. On Spectralis spectral-domain OCT, 50 healthy adults gave a central subfield (CSF) mean of 270.2 µm (SD 22.5) and central point thickness of 227.3 µm, with a proposed normal CSF ceiling of 315 µm and no significant age or sex effect (Grover 2009). The same retinas measure differently on other platforms: in 290 normal Chinese eyes, swept-source OCT read CSF at 227.8 µm where spectral-domain read 260.0 µm (Xiong 2021), and an 11-site international cohort of 546 healthy controls derived explicit Spectralis-to-Cirrus conversion equations for retinal layer thicknesses, with layer thinning after age 40 of 2.4 µm per decade (peripapillary RNFL) and 1.4 µm per decade (macular GCIPL) (Kenney 2022). Cirrus norms in healthy children give CSF 240.6 µm (Raffa 2023). The companion peripapillary RNFL thickness question is homed on the sibling shelf (slate row S9-4-38) and is cross-pointed here in prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Spectralis normative macular thickness (N = 50 healthy adults): central point 227.3 µm, central subfield 270.2 µm — proposed normal central-subfield ceiling 315 µm (Grover 2009)
cards.summary: Spectralis normative macular thickness (N = 50 healthy adults): central point 227.3 µm, central subfield 270.2 µm — proposed normal central-subfield ceiling 315 µm (Grover 2009)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative Spectralis SD-OCT macular thickness)
cards.people: 50 subjects aged 20-84 years with no known retinal disease, best-corrected acuity 20/20 and normal intraocular pressure, in three age groups (20-40, 41-60, 61+ years); Spectralis high-definition spectral-domain OCT (Heidelberg Engineering), single operator, right eyes analysed by default.
cards.result: Mean central point thickness was 227.3 µm (SD 23.2) and mean central subfield (CSF) thickness 270.2 µm (SD 22.5). Of the nine ETDRS subfields the outer nasal quadrant was thickest at 339.5 µm (SD 16.9). Retinal thickness did not differ significantly with age (P = .62) or gender (P = .1); a difference between Black and White subjects was suggested (P = .007). The authors propose 315 µm as the guideline upper value for normal CSF thickness on this device.
cards.watchOut: Single-device, single-centre norms from 50 subjects: the 315 µm ceiling is a Spectralis construct — Cirrus, Topcon and swept-source values for the same retina differ systematically (see the device-comparison cards).
cards.source: Grover S et al. American journal of ophthalmology. 2009. PMID: 19427616. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Same eyes, two machines, ~32 µm apart: swept-source CSF 227.8 µm vs spectral-domain 260.0 µm in 290 normal Chinese eyes — with a derived conversion equation (Xiong 2021)
cards.summary: Same eyes, two machines, ~32 µm apart: swept-source CSF 227.8 µm vs spectral-domain 260.0 µm in 290 normal Chinese eyes — with a derived conversion equation (Xiong 2021)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (paired SS-OCT vs SD-OCT macular thickness in healthy and diabetic eyes)
cards.people: 290 normal eyes (plus diabetic eyes without and with retinopathy) from community residents aged 30-80 years in Guangzhou, China; macular thickness measured on both swept-source OCT (Triton DRI OCT, Topcon) and spectral-domain OCT (Heidelberg Engineering). Devices named as published. Only the normal-eye limb is carded here.
cards.result: In normal eyes, mean central subfield thickness was 227.8 µm (SD 19.4) by swept-source OCT versus 260.0 µm (SD 19.7) by spectral-domain OCT (p < .0001) — swept-source values were significantly thinner in every subfield, yet agreement was excellent (all intraclass correlations > 0.9). CSF was thicker in men than women on swept-source (237.2 vs 222.0 µm, p < .0001). Conversion equations relating CSF, central point thickness and macular volume between the devices were derived, with over 95% of predicted values within 10% of actual in the diabetic groups. The authors propose swept-source CSF thresholds of 275 µm (men) and 260 µm (women) as minimum criteria for macular oedema in this population.
cards.watchOut: The ~32 µm CSF gap between platforms on identical eyes is the core lesson: a 'macular thickness' number without its device is uninterpretable, and oedema cut-offs must be device- and sex-specific as the authors set them.
cards.source: Xiong K et al. Current eye research. 2021. PMID: 33879001. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: International healthy cohort (N = 546, 11 sites): Spectralis-to-Cirrus conversion equations for retinal layer thickness, and thinning of about 2.4 µm per decade after age 40 (Kenney 2022)
cards.summary: International healthy cohort (N = 546, 11 sites): Spectralis-to-Cirrus conversion equations for retinal layer thickness, and thinning of about 2.4 µm per decade after age 40 (Kenney 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (international normative SD-OCT cohort and cross-device conversion)
cards.people: 546 healthy controls aged 18-87 years (mean 39.3, SD 14.6; 54% male) at 11 international sites (IMSVISUAL consortium), scanned on Spectralis or Cirrus spectral-domain OCT; a single-site subset was scanned on both devices the same day (346 for the nerve-fibre equation, 228 for the ganglion-cell equation).
cards.result: The conversion equations were: Cirrus peripapillary RNFL = -5.0 + (1.0 × Spectralis global value), and Cirrus macular ganglion cell + inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) = -4.5 + (0.9 × Spectralis global value) (standard error 0.02 for both). After age 40, peripapillary RNFL declined by 2.4 µm per decade and GCIPL by 1.4 µm per decade (both P < 0.001, adjusted for sex, race and country). Women had slightly thicker RNFL (2.6 µm, P = 0.003); neither measure was associated with race/ethnicity.
cards.watchOut: This cohort's macular measure is the GCIPL layer, not total central-subfield thickness — it is carded for the conversion equations and the age-decline rates, and must not be read as a source of CSF values; individual measurements remain non-interchangeable between devices, which is why the equations exist.
cards.source: Kenney R et al. Journal of neuro-ophthalmology : the official journal of the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society. 2022. PMID: 36049213. Registry ID: none in the record. primary human physiology study (international normative sd-oct cohort and cross-device conversion) 546 healthy controls aged 18-87 years (mean 39.3, sd 14.6; 54% male) at 11 international sites (imsvisual consortium), scanned on spectralis or cirrus spectral-domain oct; a single-site subset was scanned on both devices the same day (346 for the nerve-fibre equation, 228 for the ganglion-cell equation). the conversion equations were: cirrus peripapillary rnfl = -5.0 + (1.0 × spectralis global value), and cirrus macular ganglion cell + inner plexiform layer (gcipl) = -4.5 + (0.9 × spectralis global value) (standard error 0.02 for both). after age 40, peripapillary rnfl declined by 2.4 µm per decade and gcipl by 1.4 µm per decade (both p < 0.001, adjusted for sex, race and country). women had slightly thicker rnfl (2.6 µm, p = 0.003); neither measure was associated with race/ethnicity. this cohort's macular measure is the gcipl layer, not total central-subfield thickness — it is carded for the conversion equations and the age-decline rates, and must not be read as a source of csf values; individual measurements remain non-interchangeable between devices, which is why the equations exist. kenney r et al. journal of neuro-ophthalmology : the official journal of the north american neuro-ophthalmology society. 2022. pmid: 36049213. registry id: none in the record. mesh: male · female · humans · adolescent · young adult · adult · middle aged · aged · aged, 80 and over · tomography, optical coherence/methods · nerve fibers · retinal ganglion cells · cross-sectional studies · multiple sclerosis/diagnostic imaging

cards.headline: Cirrus norms in 135 healthy Saudi children: central subfield 240.6 µm, mean macular thickness 275.9 µm — boys' central macula thicker than girls' (Raffa 2023)
cards.summary: Cirrus norms in 135 healthy Saudi children: central subfield 240.6 µm, mean macular thickness 275.9 µm — boys' central macula thicker than girls' (Raffa 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative Cirrus OCT in healthy children)
cards.people: 135 full-term healthy Saudi children aged 4-18 years at a university hospital ophthalmology clinic; Cirrus high-definition OCT normative data for macula, retinal nerve fibre layer and optic nerve head (retrospective).
cards.result: Mean central subfield thickness was 240.6 µm, mean macular thickness 275.9 µm and mean macular volume 9.9 mm3. Macular values showed no significant association with age except in the superior inner macula; boys had a significantly thicker central macula than girls. Mean RNFL thickness was 93.9 µm (the companion nerve-fibre metric — see the sibling shelf on peripapillary RNFL thickness, row S9-4-38).
cards.watchOut: Paediatric, single-ethnicity Cirrus norms: useful as the second-platform limb, but children's values and this device's segmentation must not be carried into adult Spectralis practice.
cards.source: Raffa L et al. Saudi medical journal. 2023. PMID: 38016746. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy central subfield thickness is roughly 228-270 µm depending on the machine — Spectralis ~270 µm, Cirrus (children) ~241 µm, swept-source ~228 µm against 260 µm on spectral-domain in the same eyes
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy central subfield thickness is roughly 228-270 µm depending on the machine — Spectralis ~270 µm, Cirrus (children) ~241 µm, swept-source ~228 µm against 260 µm on spectral-domain in the same eyes
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong's account of retinal structure — thin textbook framing for OCT biometry, as the slate row states; the primary measurement literature carries this shelf. The convergent picture: on Spectralis, healthy central subfield thickness averages 270.2 µm (SD 22.5; N = 50) with a proposed normal ceiling of 315 µm, and no significant age or sex effect on total retinal thickness (Grover 2009). Paired same-eye measurement shows the number belongs to the device: swept-source read 227.8 µm where spectral-domain read 260.0 µm (Xiong 2021), and formal Spectralis-to-Cirrus conversion equations exist for layer thicknesses in a 546-person international cohort, which also sizes healthy ageing at -2.4 µm per decade (nerve fibre layer) and -1.4 µm per decade (ganglion cell layer) after age 40 (Kenney 2022). Cirrus paediatric norms (CSF 240.6 µm; Raffa 2023) complete the second-platform limb. The companion peripapillary RNFL shelf (slate row S9-4-38) homes the nerve-fibre metric; this shelf homes macular thickness only. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Cross-platform conversion equations reduce but do not abolish device differences; percentile limits are normative-database constructs of each platform, not biological constants.

shelves.title: Normal cornea ~535 µm on average (SD ~31 µm): population means run 511 µm (South India) to 556 µm (Tehran), thinning a few µm per decade, and shifting applanation IOP ~2 mmHg per 100 µm
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is central corneal thickness — its population mean and spread by ethnicity, age and sex — and by how much does a thick or thin cornea bias applanation intraocular-pressure readings?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Ganong, vision/aqueous dynamics) is brief; the population measurement literature carries this shelf, and the related pressure-dynamics physiology lives on the aqueous humour/diurnal IOP shelf (pack #6436). The pooled literature normal for central corneal thickness (CCT) is 0.534-0.536 mm with a standard deviation of about 0.031 mm (Doughty & Zaman 2000, labelled meta-analysis of ~600 datasets). Primary population studies bracket that pooled value: Tehran 555.6 µm (SD 39.9; N = 410, Orbscan), healthy Italians 532.2 µm (N = 400), and South India 511.4 µm (SD 33.5; N = 6,754, ultrasound) — a spread to which both ancestry and pachymetry method contribute. Age thins the cornea by roughly 2.4-4.3 µm per decade in the Chennai data; sex differences are small and inconsistent. The clinical stake is applanation tonometry: about 2.0-2.5 mmHg of measured IOP per 100 µm of CCT in Chennai, versus ~1.1 mmHg per 10% CCT difference in healthy eyes in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Tehran Eye Study (410 people, population-based): mean central corneal thickness 555.6 µm (SD 39.9) — thicker than most ethnic groups, falling with age (Hashemi 2009)
cards.summary: Tehran Eye Study (410 people, population-based): mean central corneal thickness 555.6 µm (SD 39.9) — thicker than most ethnic groups, falling with age (Hashemi 2009)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based corneal thickness, Orbscan II)
cards.people: 410 people aged 14 years and older (800 eyes) selected by stratified random cluster sampling in Tehran, Iran; corneal thickness at central, thinnest and four peripheral points by Orbscan II; results reported for right eyes, standardised for age and sex.
cards.result: Mean central corneal thickness was 555.6 µm (SD 39.9) and mean thinnest-point thickness 550.7 µm (SD 40.6); corneal thickness was below 500 µm at its minimum in 9.6% of participants. The superior cornea was thickest and the thinnest point was usually inferotemporal. Sex showed no significant relationship with thickness; participants under 20 had significantly thicker corneas than older participants (P = 0.001 centrally), and in multiple regression age and anterior chamber depth were inversely correlated with CCT. The authors note this population's mean is relatively high compared with other ethnic groups.
cards.watchOut: Orbscan optical pachymetry reads differently from ultrasound — compare the Chennai ultrasound mean (511 µm) with method in mind, not as a pure ethnicity effect.
cards.source: Hashemi H et al. Cornea. 2009. PMID: 19411957. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chennai Glaucoma Study (6,754 analysed, population-based): mean CCT 511.4 µm (SD 33.5) — thinner in women and rural residents, thinning 2.4-4.3 µm per decade (Vijaya 2010)
cards.summary: Chennai Glaucoma Study (6,754 analysed, population-based): mean CCT 511.4 µm (SD 33.5) — thinner in women and rural residents, thinning 2.4-4.3 µm per decade (Vijaya 2010)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based CCT by ultrasound pachymetry)
cards.people: 6,754 bilaterally phakic adults aged 40 years and older (from 7,774 examined) in rural and urban South Indian populations; central corneal thickness by ultrasonic pachymetry with applanation tonometry.
cards.result: Mean CCT was 511.4 µm (SD 33.5); men (515.6 µm, SD 33.8) were significantly thicker than women (508.0 µm, SD 32.8; P = 0.0001), and the urban population averaged 18 µm thicker than the rural. CCT decreased with age in both sexes (P < 0.0001): by 4.34 µm per decade (95% CI 3.24-5.44) rurally and 2.41 µm per decade (95% CI 1.25-3.53) in the urban population. Each 100 µm of extra CCT was associated with 1.96 mmHg higher measured intraocular pressure in the rural population and 2.45 mmHg in the urban population.
cards.watchOut: A glaucoma-study sampling frame in adults 40+: the age slope and the IOP-association are population estimates for South Indians and travel with the ultrasound method used.
cards.source: Vijaya L et al. Ophthalmology. 2010. PMID: 20079536. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Healthy Italian cohort (N = 400): mean CCT 532.2 µm alongside corneal biomechanics — hysteresis falls with age while CCT tracks it (Strobbe 2014)
cards.summary: Healthy Italian cohort (N = 400): mean CCT 532.2 µm alongside corneal biomechanics — hysteresis falls with age while CCT tracks it (Strobbe 2014)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (CCT and corneal biomechanics in healthy adults)
cards.people: 400 healthy Italian subjects (168 men, 232 women; mean age 58.8, SD 17.2 years) in five age subgroups; corneal hysteresis, resistance factor and central corneal thickness by Ocular Response Analyzer with integrated handheld pachymeter.
cards.result: Mean central corneal thickness was 532.2 µm; mean corneal hysteresis was 10.0 mmHg (SD 1.6) and resistance factor 10.5 mmHg (SD 1.7). Women had lower hysteresis (9.9 vs 10.2 mmHg, P = 0.04) and resistance factor (10.3 vs 10.8 mmHg, P = 0.03) than men. Hysteresis was highest in the youngest subgroup (11.2, SD 1.5 mmHg) and lowest in the oldest (9.0, SD 1.1 mmHg); hysteresis and resistance factor correlated with each other (r = 0.58) and both correlated positively with CCT (r = 0.27 and 0.57).
cards.watchOut: The study's primary quantities are biomechanical (hysteresis/resistance), with CCT as a covariate from a handheld pachymeter — its 532 µm mean sits between the Chennai and Tehran population means, as method and population both differ.
cards.source: Strobbe E et al. Cornea. 2014. PMID: 25014149. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of ~600 datasets (labelled synthesis): 'normal' CCT averages 0.534-0.536 mm with SD ~0.031 mm — and a 10% thicker cornea reads ~1.1 mmHg higher IOP in healthy eyes (Doughty & Zaman 2000)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of ~600 datasets (labelled synthesis): 'normal' CCT averages 0.534-0.536 mm with SD ~0.031 mm — and a 10% thicker cornea reads ~1.1 mmHg higher IOP in healthy eyes (Doughty & Zaman 2000)
cards.type: Synthesis — review and meta-analysis of published human CCT datasets (labelled)
cards.people: Review and meta-analysis of some 600 published central-corneal-thickness datasets (1968 to mid-1999), 300 from eyes designated normal and 134 including intraocular pressure measures. Labelled synthesis of prior human data — not a new cohort.
cards.result: Across 300 normal-eye datasets the group-averaged CCT was 0.534 mm; across 230 datasets reporting variance it was 0.536 mm (median 0.536; average SD 0.031 mm; coefficient of variation 5.8%). Slit-lamp pachymetry averaged slightly lower (0.530 mm) than ultrasound (0.544 mm). Age had no obvious effect in white populations, though an age-related decline appeared in non-white datasets. Meta-analysing CCT against applanation IOP: a 10% difference in CCT corresponded to a 3.4 mmHg (SD 0.9) IOP difference overall, but only 1.1 mmHg (SD 0.6) in eyes designated healthy — the authors conclude the tonometry impact in healthy eyes is unlikely to be clinically significant, while pachometry matters in chronic eye disease. Normal white-adult CCT is expected within ±11.6% of 0.535 mm (0.473-0.597 mm).
cards.watchOut: A 1968-1999 literature synthesis: its pooled mean anchors the field, but individual population studies since (Tehran 556 µm; Chennai 511 µm) show real between-population spread the single pooled number conceals.
cards.source: Doughty MJ et al. Survey of ophthalmology. 2000. PMID: 10734239. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy central corneal thickness centres near 535 µm with a ~31 µm standard deviation — Tehran 556 µm, Italy 532 µm, South India 511 µm — and biases applanation IOP by roughly 2 mmHg per 100 µm
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy central corneal thickness centres near 535 µm with a ~31 µm standard deviation — Tehran 556 µm, Italy 532 µm, South India 511 µm — and biases applanation IOP by roughly 2 mmHg per 100 µm
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary population studies and the one labelled meta-analysis above.
cards.result: Framed briefly by Ganong (vision/aqueous dynamics); the pressure-dynamics physiology itself is homed on the aqueous humour/diurnal IOP shelf (pack #6436), cross-pointed here in prose. The primary populations span 511-556 µm mean CCT — Chennai 511.4 µm (SD 33.5; N = 6,754, ultrasound), Italy 532.2 µm (N = 400), Tehran 555.6 µm (SD 39.9; N = 410, Orbscan) — bracketing the Doughty & Zaman pooled normal of 534-536 µm (SD ~31 µm). Age thins the cornea modestly where measured by decade (2.4-4.3 µm per decade in Chennai; under-20s thickest in Tehran), sex differences are small and inconsistent (men +7.6 µm in Chennai; none in Tehran), and the practical consequence is tonometric: about 2.0-2.5 mmHg of measured IOP per 100 µm of CCT in the Chennai data, and ~1.1 mmHg per 10% CCT in healthy eyes in the meta-analysis. Method (ultrasound vs optical) contributes to the spread and is named on each card. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Population means must travel with their pachymetry method and sampling frame; no single 'normal CCT' licenses correcting an individual IOP reading by a fixed formula.

shelves.title: The normal pupil: ~5.4 mm in darkness, ~2.8 mm at 250 lux, shrinking 0.015-0.043 mm per year of age depending on light — with anisocoria growing 0.03 mm per decade
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large is the pupil — light-adapted and dark-adapted pupil diameter by age and luminance — and how much anisocoria is normal?
shelves.mesh: Accommodation, Ocular/physiology · Adaptation, Ocular/physiology · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/physiology · Eye Color/physiology · Female · Humans · Light · Male · Middle Aged · Pupil/physiology · Refractive Errors/physiopathology · Sex Factors · Autonomic Nervous System/physiology · Dark Adaptation/physiology · Geriatric Assessment · Pulse/physiology · Reaction Time/physiology · Reference Values · Reflex, Pupillary/physiology · Child · Cross-Sectional Studies · Healthy Volunteers · Mesopic Vision/physiology · Night Vision/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 51 (pupillary reflexes/autonomic control of the eye); Ganong (vision). The healthy pupil is a moving quantity set by luminance and age. In 245 normal subjects, mean diameter ran from 5.39 mm (SD 1.04) in darkness (0 lux) to 2.84 mm (SD 0.50) at 250 lux, and normal anisocoria grew by 0.03 mm per decade, larger in scotopic/mesopic light (Rickmann 2017). Age shrinks the pupil at every illuminance: light-adapted diameter fell linearly by 0.043 mm/year at low illuminance and 0.015 mm/year at high illuminance in 91 healthy subjects, independent of sex, refractive error and iris colour (Winn 1994); an independent normative sample found resting diameter correlating r = -0.63 with age (Tekin 2018), and a young-vs-old comparison (N = 12 + 14) confirmed smaller resting diameters and blunted darkness reflexes in the elderly (Bitsios 1996). This shelf covers resting pupil SIZE; the melanopsin post-illumination response is homed separately (pack #6796). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Light-adapted pupil size in 91 healthy subjects: diameter falls linearly with age at every illuminance — 0.043 mm/year at low light, 0.015 mm/year at high light (Winn 1994)
cards.summary: Light-adapted pupil size in 91 healthy subjects: diameter falls linearly with age at every illuminance — 0.043 mm/year at low light, 0.015 mm/year at high light (Winn 1994)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (light-adapted pupil diameter by age and illuminance)
cards.people: 91 subjects aged 17-83 years with normal healthy eyes; pupil diameter by objective infrared continuous recording at five photopic ocular illuminance levels (2.15 to 1050 lumens/m2) with accommodation held constant.
cards.result: Pupil size decreased linearly with age at all illuminance levels, and the age effect persisted even at the highest illuminance. The rate of shrinkage with age fell from 0.043 mm per year at the lowest illuminance to 0.015 mm per year at the highest. Between-subject variability at a given age roughly halved as luminance rose across the range studied. Pupil size was independent of gender, refractive error and iris colour (P > 0.1) — of the factors tested, only chronological age mattered (senile miosis).
cards.watchOut: Light-adapted (photopic) conditions only, with accommodation experimentally fixed: free-viewing and dark-adapted diameters are the other cards' territory.
cards.source: Winn B et al. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 1994. PMID: 8125724. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Digital pupillometry in 245 normal subjects (490 eyes): 5.39 mm in darkness, 2.84 mm at 250 lux — and anisocoria grows 0.03 mm per decade (Rickmann 2017)
cards.summary: Digital pupillometry in 245 normal subjects (490 eyes): 5.39 mm in darkness, 2.84 mm at 250 lux — and anisocoria grows 0.03 mm per decade (Rickmann 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (static pupil diameter and anisocoria across illumination)
cards.people: 245 healthy subjects (490 eyes; mean age 51.9, SD 18.3 years; range 6-87) measured with an infrared-video PupilX pupillometer (MEye Tech GmbH, named as published) at five illumination levels: 0, 0.5, 4, 32 and 250 lux; 90 images per 3-second measurement.
cards.result: Mean pupil diameter fell steadily with illumination: 5.39 mm (SD 1.04) at 0 lux, 5.20 mm (SD 1.00) at 0.5 lux, 4.70 mm (SD 0.97) at 4 lux, 3.74 mm (SD 0.78) at 32 lux and 2.84 mm (SD 0.50) at 250 lux. Anisocoria increased by 0.03 mm per life decade at all illumination levels (R2 = 0.43) and was larger under scotopic and mesopic conditions than in bright light.
cards.watchOut: One device and one centre's 'normal subjects' (including children from age 6): the millimetre values are this pupillometer's norms, and the anisocoria slope is a population average, not an individual limit.
cards.source: Rickmann A et al. Neuro-ophthalmology (Aeolus Press). 2017. PMID: 28228832. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Young vs old pupillary kinetics (12 young + 14 elderly, Ns printed): resting diameter smaller in the elderly in darkness and light, darkness-reflex amplitude and velocity reduced (Bitsios 1996)
cards.summary: Young vs old pupillary kinetics (12 young + 14 elderly, Ns printed): resting diameter smaller in the elderly in darkness and light, darkness-reflex amplitude and velocity reduced (Bitsios 1996)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (young vs elderly resting pupil size and reflex kinetics)
cards.people: 12 young healthy subjects (median age 19.5 years) and 14 elderly healthy subjects (median age 69 years); resting pupil diameter in light (16 and 32 Cd/m2) and darkness, plus darkness and light reflexes, by infrared television pupillometer. Small classic comparison — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Resting pupil diameter was smaller in the elderly group at all three illumination levels (p = 0.001). The amplitude and maximum dilatation velocity of the darkness reflex were smaller in the elderly (p = 0.001); light-reflex amplitude at the three highest intensities and constriction velocity at all intensities were smaller (p = 0.002), 75% recovery time was longer (p = 0.02), and light-reflex latency did not differ. The authors read the pattern — smaller resting size, diminished darkness reflex, prolonged recovery — as consistent with a sympathetic deficit in old age, with the light-reflex reductions largely secondary to the smaller pupil.
cards.watchOut: Two small extreme-age groups (N = 12 and N = 14) with significance levels but no millimetre means in the fetched record: this card anchors the direction and mechanism of the age effect, not numeric norms.
cards.source: Bitsios P et al. Age and ageing. 1996. PMID: 9003878. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Static and dynamic pupillometry norms in 155 healthy people: scotopic-to-photopic diameters all shrink with age — resting diameter correlates r = -0.63 with age (Tekin 2018)
cards.summary: Static and dynamic pupillometry norms in 155 healthy people: scotopic-to-photopic diameters all shrink with age — resting diameter correlates r = -0.63 with age (Tekin 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative static/dynamic pupillometry by age)
cards.people: 155 healthy participants (69 men, 86 women; mean age 29.7, SD 17.8 years) measured with an automatic quantitative pupillometry system: static scotopic, mesopic, low-photopic and high-photopic diameters, plus dynamic contraction/dilation parameters.
cards.result: Neither static nor dynamic measures differed significantly between males and females. Age correlated inversely and moderately with every static diameter (p < 0.05). Among dynamic measures, resting diameter (r = -0.63, p < 0.001), velocity of pupil contraction (r = -0.47) and velocity of dilation (r = -0.34) fell with age, while latency of pupil contraction rose with age (r = 0.29, p = 0.002). The authors present the dataset as population-specific normative pupillometry by age group.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record reports correlations and significance, not the per-age-group millimetre table (in the full text): the numeric diameter norms on this shelf come from the Winn and Rickmann cards.
cards.source: Tekin K et al. Clinical & experimental optometry. 2018. PMID: 29356077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the healthy pupil spans ~5.4 mm in darkness to ~2.8 mm in bright light, shrinks steadily with age at every luminance, and normally differs between eyes by an amount that grows ~0.03 mm per decade
cards.summary: Synthesis: the healthy pupil spans ~5.4 mm in darkness to ~2.8 mm in bright light, shrinks steadily with age at every luminance, and normally differs between eyes by an amount that grows ~0.03 mm per decade
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (ch. 51, pupillary reflexes and autonomic control of the eye) and Ganong (vision). The size distribution: mean diameter 5.39 mm at 0 lux falling through 4.70 mm at 4 lux to 2.84 mm at 250 lux in 245 normal subjects (Rickmann 2017). The age law is the most consistent finding in the field: light-adapted diameter falls linearly with age at every illuminance — fastest in dim light at 0.043 mm/year, slowest in bright light at 0.015 mm/year (Winn 1994, N = 91) — with resting diameter correlating r = -0.63 with age in an independent normative sample (Tekin 2018, N = 155), and young-vs-old comparison showing smaller resting size and blunted darkness reflexes in the elderly (Bitsios 1996). Sex, refractive error and iris colour do not move light-adapted size (Winn). Normal anisocoria is small, larger in the dark, and grows about 0.03 mm per decade (Rickmann). The melanopsin post-illumination pupil response is a different quantity, homed on pack #6796 and cross-pointed here in prose only. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Absolute millimetre norms are device- and protocol-bound (illumination in lux vs retinal illuminance are not interchangeable); the age slope and the light response are the portable findings.
cards.source: Synthesis of Winn B et al. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 1994 (PMID: 8125724); Rickmann A et al. shelves.title: Colour discrimination peaks at 20-29 years, then 100-hue errors climb steadily — gathering on the blue-yellow axis, with lens yellowing carrying part of the rise
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does colour discrimination change with age — Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue total error scores by decade and the emergence of blue–yellow (tritan-like) errors — in people with no eye disease?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Child · Color Perception/physiology · Color Perception Tests · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Retinal Cone Photoreceptor Cells/physiology · Aged, 80 and over · Child, Preschool · North America · Reproducibility of Results · Retinal Diseases/physiopathology · Visual Acuity · Age Factors · Color Perception · Color Perception Tests/methods
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (colour vision); Guyton & Hall, ch. 50 (retinal colour mechanisms). In disease-free eyes, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue performance follows a shallow U across life, replicated on three continents: total error scores are lowest at 20-29 years (Huang 1993, N = 120), discrimination is best between 20 and 50 years (Roy 1991, N = 115, North America — norms comparable with Verriest's European data), and total scores as published rise from ~7.4-7.6 in youth to ~10.1-10.2 in the 60s, correlating significantly with age in both eyes (Mantyjarvi 2001, N = 160, Macbeth lamp at 1000 lux). The added errors concentrate on the blue-yellow (tritan) axis (Huang), and lens changes are significantly associated with higher scores alongside age (Roy) — so part of 'ageing' colour loss is lenticular. Sex and eye side do not matter. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: FM 100-hue norms in 160 healthy people aged 10-69: mean total scores rise from ~7.4-7.6 to ~10.1-10.2 across the age span (Mantyjarvi 2001)
cards.summary: FM 100-hue norms in 160 healthy people aged 10-69: mean total scores rise from ~7.4-7.6 to ~10.1-10.2 across the age span (Mantyjarvi 2001)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (FM 100-hue normative scores by age)
cards.people: 160 persons aged 10-69 years (106 women, 54 men) with healthy eyes, tested with the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue test under a Macbeth Easel lamp at 1000 lux, right eye first; results in six age groups (10-19 through 60-69 years).
cards.result: Mean total scores in the right eye ranged from 7.44 (SD 2.46) to 10.07 (SD 2.03) across the six age groups, and in the left eye from 7.56 (SD 2.36) to 10.16 (SD 2.68) — scores as published by the author. Total score correlated significantly with age in both eyes (right R = 0.308, P = 0.0001; left R = 0.246, P = 0.0021). The author provides the age-group means and individual box scores as the reference for judging a patient's result normal or abnormal.
cards.watchOut: Scores are as published by the author (mean totals ~7.4-10.2, a different scale from the raw total error scores reported by some laboratories) — do not compare them directly with raw-score norms from other laboratories; illumination (Macbeth lamp, 1000 lux) is part of the norm.
cards.source: Mantyjarvi M et al. Documenta ophthalmologica. Advances in ophthalmology. 2001. PMID: 11475367. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: North American norms (N = 115, ages 5-81): colour discrimination is best at 20-50 years, and 100-hue errors rise with age and with lens changes (Roy 1991)
cards.summary: North American norms (N = 115, ages 5-81): colour discrimination is best at 20-50 years, and 100-hue errors rise with age and with lens changes (Roy 1991)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-specific FM 100-hue and D-15 norms)
cards.people: 115 normal North American subjects aged 5-81 years given the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue test and the Lanthony Desaturated Panel D-15, to obtain age-specific norms for both procedures.
cards.result: For each test, colour discrimination was best between the ages of 20 and 50 years. Both increasing age and the occurrence of lens changes were significantly associated with increasing 100-hue error scores. The age-specific 100-hue norms were comparable with Verriest's European norms; norms for the desaturated D-15 were judged problematic because that test showed somewhat greater variability than the 100-hue.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record gives the age pattern and the lens-change association without a numeric error-score table: the quantitative by-decade values on this shelf come from the Mantyjarvi and Huang cards.

cards.headline: FM 100-hue in 120 normal subjects (240 eyes): total error score lowest at 20-29 years and rising gradually thereafter — partial errors grow around the tritan axis with age (Huang 1993)
cards.summary: FM 100-hue in 120 normal subjects (240 eyes): total error score lowest at 20-29 years and rising gradually thereafter — partial errors grow around the tritan axis with age (Huang 1993)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (FM 100-hue total and partial error scores by age group)
cards.people: 120 normal subjects aged 10-69 years (240 eyes), divided into six age groups, tested with the FM 100-hue test; total and partial error scores analysed by age, sex and eye.
cards.result: Total error score did not differ significantly between males and females or between right and left eyes, but rose with age: it was lowest in the 20-29-year group and increased gradually with aging. Partial error scores showed the same pattern, with the larger partial errors appearing around the tritan axis as age increased — the blue-yellow axis along which age-related errors concentrate.
cards.watchOut: A 1993 single-centre normative series reported in a regional journal: its value is the independent replication of the U-shaped age curve and the tritan-axis concentration, concordant with the Finnish and North American datasets.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FM 100-hue performance peaks in the third decade, worsens gradually thereafter, and the extra errors gather on the blue-yellow (tritan) axis — lens changes account for part of the rise
cards.summary: Synthesis: FM 100-hue performance peaks in the third decade, worsens gradually thereafter, and the extra errors gather on the blue-yellow (tritan) axis — lens changes account for part of the rise
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (colour vision) and Guyton & Hall (ch. 50, retinal colour mechanisms). Three independent normative datasets on three continents agree on the shape of ageing colour discrimination in disease-free eyes: error scores are lowest in the 20-29-year group (Huang 1993, N = 120), discrimination is best between 20 and 50 (Roy 1991, N = 115), and total scores as published climb from ~7.4-7.6 in youth to ~10.1-10.2 by the 60s with a significant age correlation in both eyes (Mantyjarvi 2001, N = 160). The errors are not random: partial error scores grow around the tritan (blue-yellow) axis with age (Huang), and lens changes are significantly associated with higher error scores alongside age itself (Roy) — the record supports separating a lenticular contribution from any neural one only to that extent. Sex and eye side do not matter (Huang; Mantyjarvi). Test illumination belongs on the face of any norm (Mantyjarvi used a Macbeth lamp at 1000 lux). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Raw and author-transformed total error scores are both in circulation and are not interchangeable; a clinic's norms are valid only under comparable illumination and scoring.

shelves.title: Normal field sensitivity is flat to age 40, then falls — 5.5 dB peripherally by age 75 — while a healthy person's first-ever field runs ~4 dB low from learning alone
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does automated static perimetry sensitivity fall with age — differential light sensitivity by eccentricity and decade (Octopus/Humphrey normative studies) — and how large is the learning effect between a first and second visual field?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Models, Biological · Reference Values · Sensory Thresholds/physiology · Visual Field Tests/instrumentation,standards · Visual Fields/physiology · Aged, 80 and over · Contrast Sensitivity/physiology · Glaucoma/diagnosis,physiopathology · Prognosis · Visual Field Tests · Absorption · Light · Ocular Physiological Phenomena · Visual Field Tests/methods,statistics & numerical data · False Positive Reactions · Learning · Reproducibility of Results · Sensory Thresholds · Visual Field Tests/methods
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (vision/visual pathways); Guyton & Hall, ch. 51. Automated static perimetry sensitivity is age-shaped and platform-bound. The Octopus 101 normative model (81 healthy subjects, 10-79 years) shows differential luminance sensitivity nearly constant from 10-40 years, then declining ever more steeply, the loss growing with eccentricity — 5.5 dB at 25° superiorly between ages 10 and 75 — with total random SD 1.75 dB (Hermann 2008). Across six field tests in 100 normal subjects, standard automated perimetry had the least ageing effect, practice effect and variability, and short-wavelength perimetry the most (Gardiner 2006); SWAP variability is 2.7× white-on-white and shrinks toward 1.9× after correcting for lens media absorption, which also flattens its age slope by ~25% (Wild 1998). The learning effect is large: naive healthy adults improved mean deviation from -7.40 to -3.29 dB over three FDT sessions, with 50-64% of first fields falsely classifying as abnormal (Pierre-Filho 2010). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Octopus 101 normative model (81 healthy subjects, 10-79 years): sensitivity is flat from 10-40, then declines ever more steeply — 5.5 dB lost at 25° superiorly between ages 10 and 75 (Hermann 2008)
cards.summary: Octopus 101 normative model (81 healthy subjects, 10-79 years): sensitivity is flat from 10-40, then declines ever more steeply — 5.5 dB lost at 25° superiorly between ages 10 and 75 (Hermann 2008)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-dependent Octopus normative DLS model)
cards.people: 81 eyes of 81 ophthalmologically healthy subjects (11-12 per decade, aged 10-79 years); automated static perimetry of the central 30° on the Octopus 101 (background 10 cd/m2), 68-point grid, 4-2-2 staircase; a smooth mathematical model was fitted to the differential luminance sensitivity (DLS) thresholds.
cards.result: The model fitted well (r2 = 0.74) with total random standard deviation 1.75 dB (1.5 dB centrally, below 1.25 dB in a ring around the centre, higher at the border). Average DLS varied quadratically with age: close to constant for ages 10-40 and declining ever more steeply thereafter. The age effect grew with eccentricity; the greatest drop was in the peripheral superior hemifield, where DLS at 25° eccentricity was estimated 5.5 dB higher in 10-year-olds than in 75-year-olds. The model predicts age-related normal thresholds for any location in the central 30°.
cards.watchOut: Octopus 101 values with this staircase strategy: Humphrey decibel values are not numerically interchangeable, since background, stimulus and algorithm differ by platform.
cards.source: Hermann A et al. Acta ophthalmologica. 2008. PMID: 18070224. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Six visual-field tests in 100 normal subjects (20-85 years): standard automated perimetry shows the least ageing effect, practice effect and variability; short-wavelength the most (Gardiner 2006)
cards.summary: Six visual-field tests in 100 normal subjects (20-85 years): standard automated perimetry shows the least ageing effect, practice effect and variability; short-wavelength the most (Gardiner 2006)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age, practice and variability across six perimetric tests)
cards.people: 100 normal subjects aged 20-85 years tested with six procedures: standard automated perimetry (SAP), short-wavelength automated perimetry (SWAP), temporal modulation perimetry, frequency-doubling technology perimetry (FDT), detection acuity and resolution acuity perimetry; each test's results were normalised by its estimated dynamic range for direct comparison.
cards.result: Of the three clinically common tests, SWAP exhibited the greatest aging and practice effects and test-retest variability, followed by FDT, with SAP exhibiting the least of all three. Resolution acuity perimetry was the most variable test overall, followed by temporal modulation perimetry. The authors conclude these differences must be taken into account when evaluating glaucomatous loss with different functional tests and when comparing their speed of detection.
cards.watchOut: A comparative-methods study: it ranks the tests against each other rather than publishing a normative threshold table — the absolute Octopus norms come from the Hermann card.
cards.source: Gardiner SK et al. Optometry and vision science : official publication of the American Academy of Optometry. 2006. PMID: 16840869. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Normal SWAP variability on the Humphrey (51 experienced normal subjects): interindividual variation 2.7× white-on-white — falling to 1.9× after correcting for ocular media absorption (Wild 1998)
cards.summary: Normal SWAP variability on the Humphrey (51 experienced normal subjects): interindividual variation 2.7× white-on-white — falling to 1.9× after correcting for ocular media absorption (Wild 1998)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normal variability and media effects in SWAP vs white-on-white perimetry)
cards.people: 51 normal subjects stratified by decade (mean age 55.5; range 24-83 years), experienced in both white-on-white (W-W) and short-wavelength automated perimetry (SWAP); one eye examined on three occasions with Humphrey Field Analyzer Program 30-2, Full Threshold and FASTPAC strategies; ocular media absorption (OMA) measured from scotopic sensitivity at 410 vs 560 nm.
cards.result: SWAP examinations took 15.0% (Full Threshold) and 16.8% (FASTPAC) longer than W-W. The gradient of age-decline in mean sensitivity for SWAP was about 25% less steep after correction for ocular media absorption than before — part of the apparent age loss is lens absorption, not neural loss. Interindividual normal variability (coefficient of variation) for SWAP was 2.7 times that of W-W perimetry uncorrected (range 2.0-3.9) and 1.9 times (range 1.4-2.9) after OMA correction, so a proportionately larger sensitivity drop is required before a SWAP field counts as abnormal.
cards.watchOut: Experienced observers only, and a blue-on-yellow paradigm whose variability is intrinsically high: first-test SWAP fields in naive patients will vary more than these norms suggest.
cards.source: Wild JM et al. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 1998. PMID: 9430545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Learning effect on Humphrey Matrix FDT (28 perimetry-naive healthy adults): mean deviation improves from -7.40 dB to -3.29 dB over three sessions — and half of first fields look 'abnormal' (Pierre-Filho 2010)
cards.summary: Learning effect on Humphrey Matrix FDT (28 perimetry-naive healthy adults): mean deviation improves from -7.40 dB to -3.29 dB over three sessions — and half of first fields look 'abnormal' (Pierre-Filho 2010)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (perimetric learning effect in naive healthy subjects)
cards.people: 28 healthy adults with no history of visual field testing; one eye tested three times with the Humphrey Matrix frequency-doubling perimeter, 24-2 programme, full-threshold strategy; sessions compared for duration, indices and abnormal-point counts against Anderson's criteria.
cards.result: Mean deviation improved from -7.40 dB (SD 1.49) at the first session to -4.64 dB (SD 0.97) at the second and -3.29 dB (SD 0.93) at the third; pattern standard deviation fell significantly with repetition (P < 0.01), as did test duration, fixation losses, false negatives and abnormal-point counts (P < 0.05). False-positive 'abnormal' classifications ranged 50-64% at the first session, 29-54% at the second and 18-32% at the third. The authors conclude the learning effect must be considered in normal individuals with no perimetric experience.
cards.watchOut: FDT Matrix values, not standard white-on-white thresholds — but the lesson generalises: a first-ever field in a healthy person is systematically depressed and often flags abnormal, so normative comparisons assume a practised observer.
cards.source: Pierre-Filho Pde T et al. Eye (London, England). 2010. PMID: 19680272. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: normal perimetric sensitivity holds to ~40 years, then falls — fastest peripherally (5.5 dB by age 75 at 25° superiorly) — and a first field in a naive healthy eye is depressed by ~4 dB of pure learning
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal perimetric sensitivity holds to ~40 years, then falls — fastest peripherally (5.5 dB by age 75 at 25° superiorly) — and a first field in a naive healthy eye is depressed by ~4 dB of pure learning
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (vision/visual pathways) and Guyton & Hall (ch. 51). The Octopus normative model (N = 81) sets the shape: differential light sensitivity is nearly constant from 10-40 years, then declines with accelerating slope, the loss growing with eccentricity to 5.5 dB at 25° in the superior field between ages 10 and 75, with total random SD 1.75 dB (Hermann 2008). Platform matters: among six tests in 100 normal subjects, standard automated perimetry showed the least ageing, practice effect and variability, and short-wavelength perimetry the most (Gardiner 2006); SWAP's interindividual variability is 2.7× white-on-white, and correcting for ocular media absorption flattens its apparent age slope by ~25% — part of 'ageing' field loss is lens (Wild 1998). Superimposed on all of it is learning: naive healthy subjects improved mean deviation by ~4.1 dB over three FDT sessions while false-positive abnormal classifications fell from 50-64% to 18-32% (Pierre-Filho 2010). Values are platform- and strategy-specific and are carded as such. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Normative databases assume experienced, reliable observers and a specified platform/strategy; applying Octopus norms to Humphrey fields, or either to a patient's first-ever field, manufactures 'defects' out of learning and lens.

shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are vestibular-evoked myogenic potential norms — cervical VEMP p13–n23 latency, amplitude and threshold, and galvanic/ocular VEMP values, by age — and how steeply do amplitudes fall and response rates drop after age 60?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (hearing and equilibrium — vestibular apparatus); Guyton & Hall, ch. 49 (vestibular sensations). PARTIAL slice, per assembly adjudication: the vestibular-test battery shelf (pack #7071) reports VEMP age-trend directions inside a test-battery card and holds no normative values; this shelf builds only the quantitative-norms slice and cross-points #7071 in prose. The dedicated datasets converge on a post-50 inflection: in 280 healthy volunteers aged 10-85, cervical VEMP response rate and amplitude declined beyond the fifth decade while p13/n23 latencies prolonged and thresholds worsened (Singh 2014); an age-group study with manometer-controlled sternocleidomastoid contraction likewise found amplitude falling and thresholds rising in older adults, with latencies and asymmetry ratios unchanged in that protocol (Tourtillott 2010). Absolute values come from galvanic VEMP in 100 healthy adults: P1 latency 7.82 ms (SD 3.29), N1 22.06 ms (SD 3.95), P1-N1 amplitude 66.64 µV (SD 24.5), asymmetry 16.29% (SD 11.99), with significant age-group differences (Avci 2022). Stimulus (air/bone-conducted vs galvanic) and EMG normalisation dominate comparability — values are carded per protocol. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Cervical VEMP across seven age groups (N = 280 healthy volunteers, 10-85 years): response rate and amplitude hold to ~50, then decline as p13/n23 latencies prolong and thresholds worsen (Singh 2014)
cards.summary: Cervical VEMP across seven age groups (N = 280 healthy volunteers, 10-85 years): response rate and amplitude hold to ~50, then decline as p13/n23 latencies prolong and thresholds worsen (Singh 2014)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-stratified cervical VEMP normative parameters)
cards.people: 280 healthy volunteers aged 10-85 years in seven age groups (10-20 through above 70 years); cervical vestibular evoked myogenic potentials (sacculocollic response) with latency, amplitude, interaural asymmetry ratio, threshold and response rate compared across groups.
cards.result: Response rate and amplitude declined steadily with advancing age beyond the fifth decade (50-60 years). The latencies of P13 and N23 were prolonged and thresholds worsened with increasing age, also after 50 years. The authors conclude age-matched norms must be used when interpreting cVEMP, especially in individuals above 50 years of age.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record reports the directions and the post-50 inflection, not the per-group numeric latency/amplitude table (in the full text): the absolute galvanic-VEMP numbers on this shelf come from the Avci card, a different stimulus modality, carded separately.

cards.headline: Age groups compared with manometer-controlled neck contraction: VEMP amplitude falls and threshold rises in older adults, while p1/n1 latencies and asymmetry ratios do not change (Tourtillott 2010)
cards.summary: Age groups compared with manometer-controlled neck contraction: VEMP amplitude falls and threshold rises in older adults, while p1/n1 latencies and asymmetry ratios do not change (Tourtillott 2010)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-related cVEMP parameters with manometer EMG control)
cards.people: Healthy adults aged 23-84 years with no history of dizziness, neuromuscular pathology or cervical complaints, assigned to three age groups; cervical VEMPs at 130 dB SPL with sternocleidomastoid contraction monitored by a modified blood-pressure manometer feedback method (the record's abstract does not state the total N).
cards.result: Peak-to-peak amplitude and threshold differed significantly among age groups, with post hoc differences between the young group and both older groups — amplitude declined and thresholds rose with age. No significant differences were found in P1 and N1 latencies or in interaural amplitude-difference (asymmetry) ratios. The authors conclude normative age-related data may be necessary to interpret VEMP recordings in aging populations, and that the manometer method is a workable alternative for controlling SCM contraction when EMG equipment is unavailable.
cards.watchOut: Amplitude here is contraction-dependent even with manometer feedback — uncorrected amplitudes are not comparable with EMG-normalised amplitudes from other laboratories; and the latency null in this study contrasts with the prolongation Singh found, a protocol difference to keep on the face.
cards.source: Tourtillott BM et al. American journal of audiology. 2010. PMID: 20966352. Registry ID: none in the record.
