cards.headline: Galvanic VEMP normative data (N = 100 healthy adults, 200 ears): p1 latency 7.82 ms, n1 22.06 ms, amplitude 66.64 µV, asymmetry 16.29% — latencies lengthen and amplitude falls across five age groups (Avci 2022)
cards.summary: Galvanic VEMP normative data (N = 100 healthy adults, 200 ears): p1 latency 7.82 ms, n1 22.06 ms, amplitude 66.64 µV, asymmetry 16.29% — latencies lengthen and amplitude falls across five age groups (Avci 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (galvanic VEMP normative values and age effects)
cards.people: 100 healthy participants aged 18-65 years (mean 39.7, SD 13.9) in five age groups; galvanic vestibular evoked myogenic potentials (3 mA, 1 ms current) recorded from the sternocleidomastoid on both ears (200 ears).
cards.result: Responses were elicited from all participants. Mean P1 latency was 7.82 ms (SD 3.29) and N1 latency 22.06 ms (SD 3.95); mean P1-N1 amplitude was 66.64 µV (SD 24.5) and mean vestibular asymmetry 16.29% (SD 11.99). P1 and N1 latencies and P1-N1 amplitude differed significantly among age groups (p < 0.01): as age increased, latencies were prolonged and amplitudes gradually decreased. The authors offer the dataset as clinical norms aiding diagnosis of retrolabyrinthine lesions.
cards.watchOut: Galvanic stimulation bypasses the middle ear and end-organ mechanics of air/bone-conducted cVEMP — its latencies (notably the short P1) and amplitudes are a separate normative family and must not be pooled with acoustic cVEMP values.
cards.source: Avcı NB et al. Brazilian journal of otorhinolaryngology. 2022. PMID: 33012701. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: VEMP amplitudes and response rates are age-stable to about 50, then fall as thresholds rise — the quantitative norms (galvanic p1 7.8 ms, n1 22.1 ms, amplitude ~67 µV, asymmetry ~16%) must be read age-matched and protocol-matched
cards.summary: Synthesis: VEMP amplitudes and response rates are age-stable to about 50, then fall as thresholds rise — the quantitative norms (galvanic p1 7.8 ms, n1 22.1 ms, amplitude ~67 µV, asymmetry ~16%) must be read age-matched and protocol-matched
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (hearing and equilibrium) and Guyton & Hall (ch. 49, vestibular sensations). This shelf homes only the quantitative VEMP-norms slice: the neighbouring vestibular-test shelf (pack #7071, vHIT gain and caloric responses) reports VEMP age-trend directions inside a multi-test battery card and gives no normative values; it is cross-pointed here in prose only and its battery report is not re-carded. The dedicated VEMP datasets agree on the age law: in 280 healthy volunteers, cVEMP response rate and amplitude declined and p13/n23 latencies prolonged beyond the fifth decade (Singh 2014); an independent age-group study with manometer-controlled contraction confirmed falling amplitude and rising thresholds in older adults, with asymmetry ratios unchanged (Tourtillott 2010); and galvanic VEMP in 100 adults supplies absolute values — P1 7.82 ms, N1 22.06 ms, amplitude 66.64 µV, asymmetry 16.29% — with significant age-group differences in latencies and amplitude (Avci 2022). Stimulus modality (acoustic vs galvanic) and amplitude normalisation dominate comparability and are named on each card. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: No universal VEMP cut-off exists: an 'absent' response after 60 may be ageing, technique or disease, and only age-matched, protocol-matched norms can separate them.

shelves.title: Normal ears need only about -3 to -4 dB SNR with noise ahead and -11 dB with noise at the side — HINT norms that each language version must earn from its own listeners
shelves.question: In normal-hearing adults, what are speech reception thresholds in noise — Hearing in Noise Test (HINT) sentence thresholds in quiet and in noise — and how do they vary across language versions and noise direction?
shelves.mesh: Acoustic Stimulation · Adolescent · Adult · Auditory Threshold · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Noise · Phonetics · Reproducibility of Results · Speech Acoustics · Speech Intelligibility · Speech Perception · Speech Reception Threshold Test/standards · Asian People · Cochlear Implants · Language · Speech Discrimination Tests · Acoustic Stimulation/instrumentation,methods,standards · Audiometry, Speech/instrumentation,methods,standards · Diagnosis, Computer-Assisted · Pilot Projects · Software · Tape Recording
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (hearing) — speech-audiometry framing is brief, as the slate row states; the primary test-norming literature carries this shelf. In normal-hearing adults, the English Hearing in Noise Test gives a sentence reception threshold of 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and -2.92 dB signal-to-noise ratio in 72 dB(A) noise, with 95% measurement confidence intervals of about ±2.4-3.0 dB (Nilsson 1994). The Mandarin HINT (226 normal-hearing subjects across two dialect versions) gives quiet thresholds of 14.7 and 19.4 dB(A), noise-front thresholds of -4.3/-4.0 dB SNR and noise-side thresholds near -11 dB SNR (Wong 2007); the Cantonese HINT (142 subjects) gives 19.4 dB(A) in quiet, -3.9 dB front and about -10.5 dB at the side (Wong & Soli 2005). The consistent physiology: a ~7 dB spatial release from masking when noise moves to the side, and speech-in-noise thresholds that are a separate measurement from pure-tone thresholds (whose physiology shelf is homed separately). Norms are language-, dialect- and materials-specific. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: The original English HINT (Nilsson 1994): sentence reception threshold 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and -2.92 dB signal-to-noise in 72 dB(A) noise, with ±2.4-3.0 dB measurement confidence intervals
cards.summary: The original English HINT (Nilsson 1994): sentence reception threshold 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and -2.92 dB signal-to-noise in 72 dB(A) noise, with ±2.4-3.0 dB measurement confidence intervals
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (development and normative calibration of the English HINT)
cards.people: Normal-hearing listeners used to develop and calibrate the Hearing in Noise Test: 25 phonemically balanced lists of ten sentences, equated for intelligibility in spectrally matched noise, for adaptive measurement of sentence speech reception thresholds (sSRTs).
cards.result: Average sSRT was 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and 69.08 dB(A) in 72 dB(A) noise — a signal-to-noise ratio of -2.92 dB. The 95% confidence interval of a measurement was ±2.98 dB in quiet and ±2.41 dB in noise. Low-pass filtering raised sSRTs slightly when the 4- and 8-kHz bands were removed, but much larger increases occurred once the 2-kHz band was eliminated and bandwidth fell below 2.5 kHz; reliability held until bandwidth dropped below 2.5 kHz.
cards.watchOut: 1994 English sentence materials calibrated on normal-hearing listeners: these are the reference norms other language versions compare against, not thresholds for older or hearing-impaired listeners.
cards.source: Nilsson M et al. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. 1994. PMID: 8132902. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mandarin HINT norms (137 mainland + 89 Taiwan normal-hearing subjects): quiet threshold 14.7 vs 19.4 dB(A) by dialect version; noise-front -4.3/-4.0 dB SNR, noise-side about -11 dB SNR (Wong 2007)
cards.summary: Mandarin HINT norms (137 mainland + 89 Taiwan normal-hearing subjects): quiet threshold 14.7 vs 19.4 dB(A) by dialect version; noise-front -4.3/-4.0 dB SNR, noise-side about -11 dB SNR (Wong 2007)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Mandarin HINT development and normative thresholds)
cards.people: 137 native Mandarin (Putonghua) speakers in Mainland China and 89 in Taiwan, all with hearing thresholds of 25 dB HL or better; two test versions (MHINT-M and MHINT-T), each 24 lists of 20 sentences; reception thresholds for sentences (RTS) in quiet and in 65 dBA noise from the front, right and left, speech always from the front.
cards.result: Mean quiet RTS was 14.7 dBA with the mainland version and 19.4 dBA with the Taiwan version. In noise (mainland version): -4.3 dB SNR with noise front, -11.7 dB SNR with noise right and -11.7 dB SNR with noise left; the Taiwan version gave -4.0, -10.7 and -11.0 dB SNR respectively — slightly better than the English HINT norms. Within-list variability was low and inter-list reliability high. The ~7 dB advantage of side noise over front noise is the spatial release from masking, present in both versions.
cards.watchOut: Two dialect versions of the 'same' language differ by 4.7 dB in quiet — norms are materials-specific down to dialect, and none of these values transfer to English materials or vice versa.
cards.source: Wong LL et al. Ear and hearing. 2007. PMID: 17496652. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Asian People · Cochlear Implants · Female · Humans · Language · Male · Noise · Phonetics · Speech Discrimination Tests · Speech Perception

cards.headline: Cantonese HINT norms (142 normal-hearing subjects across the development studies): quiet 19.4 dB(A), noise-front -3.9 dB, noise-side -10.6/-10.5 dB (Wong & Soli 2005)
cards.summary: Cantonese HINT norms (142 normal-hearing subjects across the development studies): quiet 19.4 dB(A), noise-front -3.9 dB, noise-side -10.6/-10.5 dB (Wong & Soli 2005)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (Cantonese HINT development and normative thresholds)
cards.people: 142 subjects with normal hearing thresholds across five development studies; Cantonese Hearing In Noise Test built to the English HINT design (240 ten-syllable sentences; 24 lists of 10 or 12 lists of 20); thresholds under headphones in quiet and in 65 dBA noise simulated from the front, right (90°) and left (270°), speech from the front.
cards.result: With the 10-sentence lists, mean threshold in quiet was 19.4 dBA and reception thresholds were -3.9 dB (noise front), -10.6 dB (noise right) and -10.5 dB (noise left); the 20-sentence lists gave near-identical values (19.4, -4.0, -10.9 and -11.0 dB). Within-list variability was low and inter-list reliability high. The authors note the Cantonese norms are comparable to the English HINT norms, by design.
cards.watchOut: Headphone simulation of spatial noise, not free-field loudspeakers: absolute SNRs differ by presentation mode, and the norms describe young normal-hearing Cantonese listeners only.
cards.source: Wong LL et al. Ear and hearing. 2005. PMID: 15937409. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: normal-hearing adults understand sentences at about -3 to -4 dB SNR with noise in front and about -11 dB with noise at the side — in English, Mandarin and Cantonese alike, because each version was normed on its own listeners
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal-hearing adults understand sentences at about -3 to -4 dB SNR with noise in front and about -11 dB with noise at the side — in English, Mandarin and Cantonese alike, because each version was normed on its own listeners
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed briefly by Ganong (hearing) — the framing is thin, as the slate row states, and the test-norming literature carries this shelf. The English HINT reference values are 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and -2.92 dB SNR in noise (Nilsson 1994). The Mandarin versions give quiet thresholds of 14.7 (mainland) and 19.4 (Taiwan) dBA, noise-front thresholds of -4.3/-4.0 dB SNR and noise-side thresholds near -11 dB SNR (Wong 2007); the Cantonese version gives 19.4 dBA in quiet, -3.9 dB front and about -10.5 dB at the side (Wong & Soli 2005). Two portable facts emerge: speech-in-noise performance dissociates from the pure-tone audiogram (all these listeners had normal thresholds, yet need only a few dB of SNR — the quantity the pure-tone hearing-threshold physiology shelf, built from Slate 7, does not measure), and the ~7 dB spatial release when noise moves from front to side is consistent across languages. Absolute quiet thresholds vary by materials and dialect (14.7-23.9 dB(A)) and must never be quoted across versions. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Every HINT number belongs to its language version, list set and presentation mode; a patient tested on English materials is judged against English norms only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nilsson M et al. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. 1994 (PMID: 8132902); Wong LL et al. Ear and hearing. 2007 (PMID: 17496652); Wong LL et al. Ear and hearing. 2005 (PMID: 15937409). Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (hearing).

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing (cochlear mechanics) — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary test-norming literature, and says so. Three adult normative datasets span three device generations, carded PER DEVICE / PROTOCOL as the measurement demands: the 1996 ILO92 database (101 normal ears), a 2007 research protocol deriving an emission-threshold reference standard in 20 excellent-hearing young adults (optimal at f2/f1 = 1.21, 1-6 kHz, 95% within ±13 dB), and a 2024 head-to-head of Titan vs Eclipse in 63 normal-hearing adults (amplitudes agree; noise and SNR differ; both pass ≥6 dB SNR across frequencies, with unreliable responses at the edge frequencies). DPOAE dissociates from the pure-tone audiogram — that dissociation, against the built pure-tone threshold shelf, is core content; the TEOAE companion is shelf #7250. The stamp is graded down because the total adult base is small and every number is device-bound. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: First normative database on the ILO92 analyser: DP-grams and DP-growth functions from 101 normal ears of 101 healthy young adults (Vinck 1996)
cards.summary: First normative database on the ILO92 analyser: DP-grams and DP-growth functions from 101 normal ears of 101 healthy young adults (Vinck 1996)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (DPOAE normative database, ILO92 analyser)
cards.people: 101 normal ears of 101 healthy young adults; distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (2f1-f2) measured automatically on the commercially available Otodynamics ILO92 analyser using two data-collection protocols, in the form of DP-grams and DP-growth (input/output) functions, statistically processed into a normative database.
cards.result: The study's product is the normative database itself: at the time, the ILO92 let centres perform DPOAE measurements in different populations but with no relationship to normative data, and these 101-ear data were assembled to serve as the basis for research on DPOAE testing in ear pathology. The fetched record states the database's construction and scope; it does not print numeric DP-gram levels, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Device- and protocol-bound by construction: ILO92 DP-gram norms from 1996 are the first-generation reference, not a universal DPOAE limit — later cards use different stimulus rules and devices.
cards.source: Vinck BM et al. Distortion product otoacoustic emissions: a normative study. Audiology : official organ of the International Society of Audiology. 1996. PMID: 8937656. cards.headline: Emission-threshold reference standard (20 young adults, 40 ears): the optimal diagnostic measure is the DPOAE threshold at f2/f1 = 1.21 for f2 1-6 kHz, 95% within ±13 dB of the mean (Mills 2007)
cards.summary: Emission-threshold reference standard (20 young adults, 40 ears): the optimal diagnostic measure is the DPOAE threshold at f2/f1 = 1.21 for f2 1-6 kHz, 95% within ±13 dB of the mean (Mills 2007)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative DPOAE emission thresholds, research protocol)
cards.people: 20 young adults aged 18-24 years (40 ears; equal men and women) with excellent hearing — thresholds of 10 dB HL or better at 0.5-8 kHz and tympanometric peak within ±30 daPa of ambient in both ears. Two primary tones varied in 5-dB steps with L1 always 10 dB above L2; emission isoresponse threshold defined as the stimulus level giving an emission amplitude of -10 dB SPL; f2 at audiometric frequencies 1-8 kHz at ratios f2/f1 = 1.21 and 1.28.
cards.result: Reference standards for emission threshold level (an HL-like scale for emissions) were derived. For diagnosis, the optimal measure was the emission threshold at ratio 1.21 for f2 frequencies 1-6 kHz; the 8 kHz emission had a relatively high mean threshold and seemed less useful. Variability was adequately small: 95% of emission thresholds fell within ±13 dB of the mean at each frequency. Even within the 10 dB HL inclusion limit, emission thresholds rose slightly with auditory threshold — importantly only at 8 kHz, strongest in men.
cards.watchOut: A deliberately super-normal reference group (≤10 dB HL) of only 20 subjects: the ±13 dB band describes excellent ears under this exact L1/L2 rule, and the authors state the specific numerical results for distinguishing cochlear disorders remain to be firmly established.
cards.source: Mills DM et al. Evaluation of cochlear hearing disorders: normative distortion product otoacoustic emission measurements. Ear and hearing. 2007. PMID: 17982366. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Two current clinical devices compared head-to-head (63 normal-hearing adults): Titan and Eclipse give the same DPOAE amplitudes but different noise and SNR — both pass the ≥6 dB SNR criterion across frequencies (Cañete 2024)
cards.summary: Two current clinical devices compared head-to-head (63 normal-hearing adults): Titan and Eclipse give the same DPOAE amplitudes but different noise and SNR — both pass the ≥6 dB SNR criterion across frequencies (Cañete 2024)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (per-device DPOAE normative comparison, Titan vs Eclipse)
cards.people: 63 participants with normal hearing (mean age 23.2, SD 2.0 years); DPOAEs measured on two commercial Interacoustics clinical devices, Titan and Eclipse, at 31 frequencies from 500 to 10,000 Hz; signal and noise amplitudes and signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) analysed. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: DPOAE amplitude differed across frequencies, with a high number of unreliable responses at the edge frequencies (<828 Hz and >6,072 Hz). There were no significant differences between the two devices in DPOAE amplitudes, but recorded noise levels differed significantly, and SNRs — frequency-dependent, larger at higher frequencies — differed significantly between devices. Despite this, OAEs from both devices met the pass criterion (SNR ≥ 6 dB) consistently across frequencies, so the differences do not compromise test outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The device lesson is in the noise floor, not the signal: SNR-based pass/fail is device-dependent even when amplitudes agree, and edge frequencies (<828 Hz, >6,072 Hz) yield many unreliable responses in normal ears.
cards.source: Cañete OM et al. Comparison of Two Clinical Devices for the Measurement of Distortion Product Otoacoustic Emissions in Normal-Hearing Adults. Journal of audiology & otology. 2024. PMID: 38382519. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: DPOAE norms are real but device- and protocol-specific — three adult datasets across three device generations agree on the DP-gram's shape and a ≥6 dB SNR pass, on a small total base (101 ears; 20 adults; 63 adults)
cards.summary: Synthesis: DPOAE norms are real but device- and protocol-specific — three adult datasets across three device generations agree on the DP-gram's shape and a ≥6 dB SNR pass, on a small total base (101 ears; 20 adults; 63 adults)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (hearing — cochlear mechanics; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary test-norming literature). The first-generation ILO92 normative database covers 101 normal ears (Vinck 1996); the research-protocol reference standard defines an emission threshold (the level giving -10 dB SPL) in 20 excellent-hearing young adults, optimal at f2/f1 = 1.21 for 1-6 kHz with 95% of thresholds within ±13 dB of the mean (Mills 2007); and the current-device comparison in 63 adults shows Titan and Eclipse agree on amplitude but differ on noise and SNR while both meet the ≥6 dB SNR pass across frequencies (Cañete 2024). DPOAE is an objective cochlear measure that dissociates from the audiogram — the built pure-tone hearing-threshold physiology shelf is the cross-point, not re-carded here; the transient-evoked companion shelf is #7250. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the adult normative base is thin (no dataset exceeds 101 ears) and every value is bound to its device and primary-tone protocol, as printed on each card.
cards.watchOut: Never present one device's DP-gram limits as universal: primary-tone levels (L1/L2) and ratio dominate the numbers, and 8 kHz emissions behave differently from the 1-6 kHz range.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: TEOAE norms in young adults: larger in women and in Chinese ears, absent in 5 of 186 otologically normal ears, and linear protocols give better SNR than non-linear
shelves.question: In normal-hearing young adults, what are transient-evoked otoacoustic emission (TEOAE) amplitudes, whole-response reproducibility and signal-to-noise ratios — by sex, ear and ethnic group — and in what fraction of otologically normal ears is no response recordable despite normal hearing?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing (cochlear mechanics) — thin framing, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary test-norming literature, and says so. Three adult datasets: a representative population sample aged 18-25 (345 adults; norms from 186 otologically normal ears, including the distributional fact that 5 normal ears had no recordable response despite thresholds better than 20 dB), a sex-and-ethnic-group comparison (81 Caucasian + 81 Chinese young adults; amplitude higher in women and in Chinese ears at equal hearing sensitivity), and a protocol study (42 adults; post-processed linear recordings superior on noise, SNR and reproducibility, with tolerance-interval scoring criteria). TEOAE is kept separate from DPOAE (shelf #7249): a click-evoked whole-cochlea response is not a frequency-specific DP-gram. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Population sample aged 18-25 (345 adults, 688 ears): TEOAE norms from 186 otologically normal ears — and 5 normal ears with no recordable response despite thresholds better than 20 dB (Ferguson 2000)
cards.summary: Population sample aged 18-25 (345 adults, 688 ears): TEOAE norms from 186 otologically normal ears — and 5 normal ears with no recordable response despite thresholds better than 20 dB (Ferguson 2000)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population TEOAE normative sample, ILO88 non-linear mode)
cards.people: Representative population sample of 345 young adults aged 18-25 years (688 ears); transient-evoked otoacoustic emissions obtained with the Otodynamics ILO88 in standard non-linear mode; normative data presented for the 186 otologically normal (ON) ears.
cards.result: In 5 ON ears there was no recordable TEOAE response despite hearing threshold levels better than 20 dB — an absent TEOAE is a distributional fact in normal ears, not proof of pathology. The main factors affecting TEOAE level were: (1) gender — females had larger responses on average than males; (2) tympanometric measures — ears with entirely normal tympanometry had larger responses than ears with minor tympanometric abnormalities; (3) click stimulus intensity in the ear canal, correlating positively with TEOAE level; and (4) hearing threshold at 0.5 kHz, correlating negatively with amplitude. Social noise exposure had a small effect at 2 kHz (lower response in the exposed).
cards.watchOut: Norms are for the ILO88 non-linear click protocol in 18-25-year-olds: TEOAE level is partly a middle-ear and stimulus-level measurement (tympanometry, in-canal click intensity), not a pure cochlear number.
cards.source: Ferguson MA et al. Transient-evoked otoacoustic emissions in a representative population sample aged 18 to 25 years. Audiology : official organ of the International Society of Audiology. 2000. PMID: 10905398. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: TEOAE amplitude is higher in women than men and in Chinese than Caucasian young adults (81 + 81 normal-hearing adults) — with no racial difference in hearing sensitivity (Shahnaz 2008)
cards.summary: TEOAE amplitude is higher in women than men and in Chinese than Caucasian young adults (81 + 81 normal-hearing adults) — with no racial difference in hearing sensitivity (Shahnaz 2008)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TEOAE by sex and ethnic group, normal-hearing young adults)
cards.people: 81 Caucasian (mean age 27.8 years) and 81 Chinese (mean age 24.7 years) young adults with normal hearing; TEOAE amplitude, noise levels and hearing thresholds compared by race and gender in a single-author normative study.
cards.result: TEOAE amplitude was significantly higher in females than in males and significantly higher in the Chinese group than the Caucasian group. Females had better hearing sensitivity than males, consistent with the TEOAE results; hearing sensitivity did not differ statistically between the racial groups, although the race-by-threshold interaction was significant. Noise levels did not differ between racial groups, so the author attributes the amplitude differences most likely to middle-ear transmission properties or cochlear mechanisms.
cards.watchOut: Group mean differences are not individual diagnostic limits: a lower TEOAE in a Caucasian man may be entirely normal for his group — norms must be read against sex- and population-matched references.

cards.headline: Linear vs non-linear TEOAE protocols (normative database, 42 adults): post-processed linear recordings give lower noise, superior SNR and higher reproducibility — with normative scoring criteria at 2 and 3 kHz (Hatzopoulos 2003)
cards.summary: Linear vs non-linear TEOAE protocols (normative database, 42 adults): post-processed linear recordings give lower noise, superior SNR and higher reproducibility — with normative scoring criteria at 2 and 3 kHz (Hatzopoulos 2003)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TEOAE recording-protocol normative database)
cards.people: 42 adult subjects serving as a normative database; TEOAE responses elicited by clicks at average intensities of 72 dB p.e. SPL (linear protocol) and 84 dB p.e. SPL (non-linear protocol); stimulus artefact in linear recordings suppressed by a window function (3.8-13.8 ms) and a high-pass filter at 830 Hz; repeated-measures comparison of response, noise, correlation and SNR at 1.0-5.0 kHz.
cards.result: Unprocessed early segments (3.2-5.2 ms) of linear and non-linear responses had highly similar contours with no statistically significant mean differences. After post-processing, linear recordings showed significantly lower noise levels (and thus superior SNRs) and higher reproducibility values than non-linear recordings. Normative adult scoring criteria were calculated from free-distribution tolerance intervals for the TEOAE correlation and the SNRs at 2.0 and 3.0 kHz.
cards.watchOut: Protocol is destiny: linear and non-linear clicks at different intensities (72 vs 84 dB p.e. SPL) yield different noise and SNR norms — a clinic's pass criteria belong to the protocol that generated them.
cards.source: Hatzopoulos S et al. TEOAE recording protocols revised: data from adult subjects. International journal of audiology. 2003. PMID: 14570242. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in young adults TEOAEs are larger in women and in Chinese than Caucasian ears, absent in a small fraction of otologically normal ears (5 of 186), and protocol-dependent — linear recordings beat non-linear on noise, SNR and reproducibility
cards.summary: Synthesis: in young adults TEOAEs are larger in women and in Chinese than Caucasian ears, absent in a small fraction of otologically normal ears (5 of 186), and protocol-dependent — linear recordings beat non-linear on noise, SNR and reproducibility
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (hearing — cochlear mechanics; brief framing, the primary test-norming literature carries this shelf). The population anchor is the representative 18-25 sample: norms from 186 otologically normal ears, with 5 normal ears showing no recordable response despite thresholds better than 20 dB, and level driven by sex, tympanometry, in-canal click intensity and 0.5 kHz threshold (Ferguson 2000). Sex and population shift the distribution itself — amplitude higher in women and in Chinese than Caucasian adults at equal hearing sensitivity (Shahnaz 2008, 81 + 81). Protocol shifts it too: post-processed linear recordings give lower noise, superior SNR and higher reproducibility than the standard non-linear mode, with tolerance-interval scoring criteria at 2 and 3 kHz (Hatzopoulos 2003, N = 42). TEOAE (click-evoked, whole-cochlea) is a different measurement from the frequency-specific DPOAE DP-gram on companion shelf #7249 — carded separately. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: An absent TEOAE in a normal-hearing young adult is uncommon but documented (5 of 186 otologically normal ears): absence alone, with a normal audiogram and tympanogram, is a finding to repeat under the same protocol, not a diagnosis.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: ABR norms are a protocol, not a number: latencies adult by age 3, wave V shifts ~350 µs with electrode site and lengthens with click rate, BIC peaks at 6.06 ms (click) vs 9.47 ms (tone burst)
shelves.question: In normal-hearing humans, what are auditory brainstem response (ABR) norms — absolute latencies of waves I, III and V and the I-III, III-V and I-V interpeak intervals by age and sex, at standard click rates — and how do stimulus rate, intensity and binaural interaction change them?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing / auditory pathways; Guyton & Hall, hearing chapters — brief framing for evoked-potential norming; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary literature, and says so. Latencies are carded PER PROTOCOL, with the developmental limb kept separate from the adult norms: maturation from birth (adult equivalence by 9 months-3 years; I-III shortening 22% from 1 month to age 4-6; total N not documented in that record), isochronic mapping in 20 young adults (electrode site alone moves wave V by ~350 µs), a modern CLAD rate dataset in 42 healthy adults (waves I, III and V lengthen and shrink from 7.1 to 507.81 clicks/s; SP/AP ratio the stable measure), and the binaural interaction component in 18 adults (click peak 6.06 ms; 500 Hz tone-burst peak 9.47 ms). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Developmental limb: BAER latencies and interpeak intervals reach adult equivalence between 9 months and 3 years — I-III shortens 22%, III-V 15% and I-V 19% from 1 month to age 4-6 (Jiang 1991)
cards.summary: Developmental limb: BAER latencies and interpeak intervals reach adult equivalence between 9 months and 3 years — I-III shortens 22%, III-V 15% and I-V 19% from 1 month to age 4-6 (Jiang 1991)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (developmental BAER normative data, birth to adulthood)
cards.people: Brainstem auditory evoked responses (BAER) examined from birth to adulthood across age groups (1-month-old group through adults); wave latencies, interpeak intervals (IPIs), the III-V/I-III interval ratio and the wave V latency-intensity (L-I) function slope. The fetched record does not state the total number of subjects — N not documented in the record, printed here as the standing labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Adult equivalence was reached for most wave latencies and IPIs between the ages of 9 months and 3 years. From the 1-month group to the 4-6-year group, the I-III IPI shortened by 22%, the III-V IPI by 15% and the I-V IPI by 19% — the III-V/I-III ratio suggesting the I-III interval decreases more than III-V after term. The wave V L-I slope was slightly steeper in younger groups (40 microseconds/dB at 1 month vs 32 microseconds/dB in adults). The authors conclude age-dependent norms should be used when evaluating the L-I function. Normative data for the various BAER measures at different ages are presented in the paper.
cards.watchOut: This is the maturation limb, not the adult norm: applying adult latency limits to an infant would mislabel normal development as delay — and the record's unstated N is a limit on how far its percentile tables can be audited from the abstract.
cards.source: Jiang ZD et al. Brainstem auditory evoked responses from birth to adulthood: normative data of latency and interval. Hearing research. 1991. PMID: 1917718. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Isochronic mapping in 20 normally hearing young adults (10 men, 10 women): wave V appears up to ~350 µs earlier at some scalp sites than at the ipsilateral mastoid — electrode site is part of the 'latency' (Phillips 1995)
cards.summary: Isochronic mapping in 20 normally hearing young adults (10 men, 10 women): wave V appears up to ~350 µs earlier at some scalp sites than at the ipsilateral mastoid — electrode site is part of the 'latency' (Phillips 1995)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative isochronic ABR mapping, young adults)
cards.people: 10 male and 10 female normally hearing young adults; auditory brainstem responses recorded from 20 electrode sites for left, right and binaural stimulation of each ear, with peak-latency contours (isochronic maps) plotted for waves II, III and V; stimulus intensity, polarity and rate varied.
cards.result: Stimulus intensity, polarity and rate had no significant effect on the maps. On monaural stimulation, wave V was recorded first at the contralateral mastoid and ipsilaterally frontally, and last at the ipsilateral mastoid some 350 µs later; binaural stimulation gave a symmetrical map (wave V first frontally, last at the occiput). Wave III was recorded first ipsilaterally and frontally and last at the contralateral mastoid; wave II first at the rear of the contralateral mastoid and last forward of the ipsilateral mastoid. The wave V and III patterns agree with human physiological studies; the wave II pattern does not support the VIIth nerve alone as its generator.
cards.watchOut: A latency is a latency at an electrode: a ~350 µs site difference is the size of a clinically meaningful interpeak shift, so normative latency tables presuppose the standard electrode montage used to build them.
cards.source: Phillips AJ et al. Isochronic mapping of the auditory brainstem response: normative results. British journal of audiology. 1995. PMID: 8861409. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Audiometry, Pure-Tone · Evoked Potentials, Auditory, Brain Stem · Female · Functional Laterality · Humans · Male

cards.headline: Rate limb by CLAD deconvolution (42 healthy adults): waves I, III and V grow later and smaller as click rate rises from 7.1 to 507.81 clicks/s — the SP/AP ratio stays the stable measure (Kaf 2017)
cards.summary: Rate limb by CLAD deconvolution (42 healthy adults): waves I, III and V grow later and smaller as click rate rises from 7.1 to 507.81 clicks/s — the SP/AP ratio stays the stable measure (Kaf 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative ABR/ECochG stimulus-rate dataset, CLAD technique)
cards.people: 42 healthy individuals; extratympanic click electrocochleography (ECochG) and ABR recorded simultaneously (tympanic-membrane electrode; surface electrodes on forehead and mastoid) at seven stimulus rates using continuous loop averaging deconvolution (CLAD), from the standard 7.1 clicks/s up to 507.81 clicks/s.
cards.result: The ECochG compound action potential (AP) and ABR waves I, III and V decreased in amplitude and increased in latency as stimulus rate increased, with a sharp reduction in AP amplitude at 97.66 clicks/s and an asymptote at 292.97 clicks/s. The ECochG summating potential (SP) stayed relatively stable, so SP/AP ratios rose with rate; the SP/AP amplitude ratio showed more stability than AP amplitude and is recommended for evaluating cochlear and neural response. The dataset is presented as the normative neural-adaptation reference for CLAD ECochG/ABR.
cards.watchOut: Rates far above the clinical standard are the point of the study, not a clinical protocol: latency norms from 7.1 clicks/s must never be applied to a fast-rate recording, and CLAD-derived values belong to the CLAD technique.
cards.source: Kaf WA et al. Fast Click Rate Electrocochleography and Auditory Brainstem Response in Normal-Hearing Adults Using Continuous Loop Averaging Deconvolution. Ear and hearing. 2017. PMID: 27861251. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Binaural interaction component (18 normal-hearing young adults): the reliable click ABR-BIC peak sits at mean latency 6.06 ms (SD 0.354); the 500 Hz tone-burst BIC at 9.47 ms (SD 0.678), with larger amplitudes (Van Yper 2015)
cards.summary: Binaural interaction component (18 normal-hearing young adults): the reliable click ABR-BIC peak sits at mean latency 6.06 ms (SD 0.354); the 500 Hz tone-burst BIC at 9.47 ms (SD 0.678), with larger amplitudes (Van Yper 2015)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative ABR binaural interaction component)
cards.people: 18 normal-hearing young adults (8 women, 10 men); ABRs recorded to clicks and to 500 Hz tone bursts, monaurally and binaurally; the binaural interaction component (BIC) derived by subtracting the binaural response from the sum of the two monaural responses; inter-rater reliability investigated. Classic small normative study — its N is printed here on the face.
cards.result: Good inter-rater reliability was obtained for both click and 500 Hz tone-burst ABR-BICs. The most reliable click BIC peak — on the downslope of wave V — occurred at a mean latency of 6.06 ms (SD 0.354 ms). Reliable 500 Hz tone-burst BICs showed a broad positivity at the level of wave V with mean latency 9.47 ms (SD 0.678 ms), and amplitudes were larger for tone bursts than for clicks. The authors propose 500 Hz tone-burst BIC as a suitable technique for populations with low-frequency residual hearing (e.g. bimodal cochlear-implant users).
cards.watchOut: N = 18 and a derived difference waveform: BIC latencies are properties of the subtraction method and stimulus (click vs 500 Hz tone burst gives ~3.4 ms different peak latencies) — not interchangeable with ordinary wave I/III/V latencies.
cards.source: Van Yper LN et al. Binaural interaction in the auditory brainstem response: a normative study. Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology. 2015. PMID: 25240247. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ABR norms are protocol-bound — latencies mature by age 3, shift with electrode site (~350 µs) and stimulus rate, and the binaural interaction peak sits at 6.06 ms for clicks and 9.47 ms for 500 Hz tone bursts
cards.summary: Synthesis: ABR norms are protocol-bound — latencies mature by age 3, shift with electrode site (~350 µs) and stimulus rate, and the binaural interaction peak sits at 6.06 ms for clicks and 9.47 ms for 500 Hz tone bursts
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (hearing / auditory pathways) and Guyton & Hall (hearing chapters) — brief framing for evoked-potential norming; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary literature. The developmental limb: most latencies and interpeak intervals reach adult equivalence between 9 months and 3 years, with I-III shortening 22%, III-V 15% and I-V 19% from 1 month to age 4-6, and the wave V latency-intensity slope flattening from 40 to 32 µs/dB (Jiang 1991; total N not documented in the record). Adult limbs: scalp site alone moves wave V by ~350 µs in 20 young adults, with stimulus intensity, polarity and rate not significantly changing the maps (Phillips 1995); stimulus rate systematically lengthens waves I, III and V and shrinks their amplitudes across 7.1-507.81 clicks/s in 42 adults by CLAD, leaving the SP/AP ratio the stable measure (Kaf 2017); and the binaural interaction component peaks at 6.06 ms (clicks) and 9.47 ms (500 Hz tone bursts) in 18 adults (Van Yper 2015). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the standard-rate adult latency framework these datasets jointly document; every non-standard rate, stimulus or derivation is carded as its own limb.
cards.watchOut: Interpeak intervals travel better across laboratories than absolute latencies, but neither travels across stimulus rates, montages or derivations — a norm is a protocol, stated in full.

shelves.title: Axial length centres at 23.3–23.5 mm in older populations on two continents — men ~0.5 mm longer, with deeper chambers and flatter corneas
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are ocular axial length, anterior chamber depth and corneal curvature — population means, spreads and percentiles by age, sex and ethnicity — and how do the distributions differ between European and East Asian population eye studies?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Asian People · China · Eye/anatomy & histology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Ocular Physiological Phenomena · Aging/physiology · Anterior Chamber/anatomy & histology · Biometry · Body Weights and Measures · Cornea/anatomy & histology · Cross-Sectional Studies · Interferometry · Lasers · Reference Values · Refraction, Ocular/physiology · Sex Factors · White People · Age Factors · Axial Length, Eye/anatomy & histology · Corneal Topography · Tomography, Optical Coherence
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / ocular anatomy — thin framing for biometry; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three population eye studies on two continents put mean axial length within a third of a millimetre of each other: 23.25 ± 1.14 mm in older Beijing adults (optical low-coherence reflectometry; Yin 2012, 3,159 measured), 23.44 mm in older white Australians (IOL Master; Fotedar 2010, 1,335 right phakic eyes), and 23.48 mm in aged South China adults (IOL Master; Chen 2016, 1,015 right eyes). Men run longer, deeper and flatter than women in every study that reports sex splits. Device is named per study and right-eye conventions are carded as published. Myopia prevalence differences between populations are the context, not the content: this shelf reports distributions, not myopia-control treatment (homed at live #614). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Beijing Eye Study 2011 (3,159 measured of 3,468, ages 50–93): mean axial length 23.25 ± 1.14 mm (range 18.96–30.88) by optical low-coherence reflectometry (Yin 2012)
cards.summary: Beijing Eye Study 2011 (3,159 measured of 3,468, ages 50–93): mean axial length 23.25 ± 1.14 mm (range 18.96–30.88) by optical low-coherence reflectometry (Yin 2012)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population ocular axial length, Beijing Eye Study)
cards.people: Population-based cross-sectional study in Greater Beijing: 3,468 individuals (56.6% women), mean age 64.6 ± 9.8 years (range 50–93); axial length measured by optical low-coherence reflectometry and available in 3,159 (91.1%).
cards.result: Mean axial length was 23.25 ± 1.14 mm (range 18.96–30.88 mm) — similar to other urban populations and higher than a rural Central Indian population, as the authors report. In multivariate analysis longer axial length was significantly associated with higher age, greater body height, higher education and urban habitation, and with thicker central cornea, larger corneal curvature radius, deeper anterior chamber, thicker lens, more myopic refraction, larger pupil and better best-corrected acuity; in highly myopic eyes the education association reversed. The authors note the age association may be a survival artefact.
cards.watchOut: Both-eyes population measurement by low-coherence reflectometry in adults 50+: the mean is an older-urban-Chinese mean, and the positive age association is cross-sectional — the authors themselves raise survival artefact, so do not read it as eyes lengthening with age.
cards.source: Yin G et al. Ocular axial length and its associations in Chinese: the Beijing Eye Study. PloS one. 2012. PMID: 22927949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Blue Mountains Eye Study (1,335 right phakic eyes, age 59+): mean axial length 23.44 mm by IOL Master — men 23.76 vs women 23.19 mm; anterior chamber depth 3.10 mm, corneal curvature 43.42 D (Fotedar 2010)
cards.summary: Blue Mountains Eye Study (1,335 right phakic eyes, age 59+): mean axial length 23.44 mm by IOL Master — men 23.76 vs women 23.19 mm; anterior chamber depth 3.10 mm, corneal curvature 43.42 D (Fotedar 2010)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population ocular biometry by IOL Master, older white population)
cards.people: Cross-sectional analysis of the Blue Mountains Eye Study 10-year examinations (2002–2004): biometry in 1,952 persons aged 59 years or older; only right phakic eyes with biometry data (n = 1,335) included. Measurements by partial coherence laser interferometry (Zeiss IOL Master, named as published): axial length, corneal curvature (K1), anterior chamber depth and corneal diameter (white-to-white).
cards.result: Mean axial length was 23.44 mm (95% CI 23.38–23.50), greater in men (23.76 mm, CI 23.68–23.84) than women (23.19 mm, CI 23.11–23.27). Mean K1 was 43.42 D, anterior chamber depth 3.10 mm and white-to-white 12.06 mm. The axial length and anterior chamber depth distributions were positively skewed and peaked; white-to-white and K1 were near normal. From age 59, mean axial length fell with age (P for trend = 0.005), by 0.12 mm per decade in women (P = 0.0176) but only 0.02 mm per decade in men (P = 0.6319). Mean spherical equivalent was +0.58 D and correlated negatively with axial length and anterior chamber depth, not with K1 or white-to-white.
cards.watchOut: Right phakic eyes only, age 59+: cataract-surgery-era biometry in an older white population — the falling-with-age slope is a cross-sectional cohort pattern in survivors, not a within-eye change.
cards.source: Fotedar R et al. Distribution of axial length and ocular biometry measured using partial coherence laser interferometry (IOL Master) in an older white population. Ophthalmology. 2010. PMID: 20031227. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Guangzhou aged population (1,015 phakic right eyes, age 50+): axial length 23.48 mm, anterior chamber depth 3.03 mm, corneal curvature 44.20 (as printed) by IOL Master — men longer, deeper and flatter (Chen 2016)
cards.summary: Guangzhou aged population (1,015 phakic right eyes, age 50+): axial length 23.48 mm, anterior chamber depth 3.03 mm, corneal curvature 44.20 (as printed) by IOL Master — men longer, deeper and flatter (Chen 2016)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population axial length, anterior chamber depth and corneal curvature, South China)
cards.people: Cross-sectional study of inhabitants aged 50 years or older in Guangzhou, China (2013–2014): 1,117 participants recruited, data from 1,015 phakic right eyes analysed; axial length, anterior chamber depth and corneal curvature measured with an IOL Master (named as published).
cards.result: Mean axial length was 23.48 mm (95% CI 23.40–23.55), anterior chamber depth 3.03 mm (CI 3.01–3.05) and corneal curvature 44.20 (CI 44.11–44.29; printed in mm in the record's abstract, with sex-specific values printed in dioptres). Men had significantly longer axial length (23.68 vs 23.23 mm), deeper anterior chamber (3.13 vs 2.95 mm) and flatter cornea (43.85 D vs 44.50 D) than women (all P < 0.001). Anterior chamber depth fell with age in men (P = 0.002) but not women (P = 0.558). Longer eyes had flatter corneas (r = −0.437) and deeper chambers (r = 0.652). The authors place this cohort's axial length above Singaporean Chinese and below Malaysian and Caucasian values, with a shallower chamber than some other racial groups.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract prints the overall corneal curvature in mm and the sex-specific values in dioptres — carded exactly as published; do not silently convert or merge the two. Right eyes only, age 50+.
cards.source: Chen H et al. Distribution of axial length, anterior chamber depth, and corneal curvature in an aged population in South China. BMC ophthalmology. 2016. PMID: 27138378. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: mean axial length is 23.3–23.5 mm in every older population measured — men ~0.5 mm longer than women — with anterior chamber ~3.0–3.1 mm and corneal curvature ~43.4–44.2 D
cards.summary: Synthesis: mean axial length is 23.3–23.5 mm in every older population measured — men ~0.5 mm longer than women — with anterior chamber ~3.0–3.1 mm and corneal curvature ~43.4–44.2 D
cards.people: Synthesis of the three population biometry datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (vision / ocular anatomy) as thin framing; the shelf rests on the primary population literature. Beijing (23.25 ± 1.14 mm, low-coherence reflectometry, ages 50–93), older white Australians (23.44 mm, IOL Master, right phakic eyes, age 59+) and Guangzhou (23.48 mm, IOL Master, right eyes, age 50+) agree within 0.23 mm despite different devices and continents — the whole-globe length those posterior-segment shelves' refraction context needs. Sex is the most consistent split: men longer by ~0.45–0.57 mm, with deeper chambers and flatter corneas (Chen 2016; Fotedar 2010). Anterior chamber depth centres at 3.03–3.10 mm and shallows with age in men in the Guangzhou data. Cross-sectional age slopes disagree in direction between Beijing (positive, possibly survival artefact) and Blue Mountains (negative) — reported as published, not reconciled. Cross-point: structural OCT thickness shelves (RNFL, macular, corneal thickness) measure segments of this globe; myopia-control treatment is homed at live #614 and is not this shelf's content. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All three anchors are age-50+ populations and two are right-eye-only: these are older-adult distributions. Device (optical biometry vs ultrasound) changes values and is named per card; ultrasound biometry norms are not interchangeable with these.

shelves.title: OCTA norms are protocol-bound: superficial density ~44% at 6×6 mm vs ~53% at 3×3 mm, falling with age after 50 — and FAZ has no agreed abnormal cut-off
shelves.question: In healthy eyes, what are OCT-angiography vessel density (superficial and deep capillary plexuses, radial peripapillary capillaries) and foveal avascular zone area — normative values by age, sex and ethnicity — and how fast does vessel density fall with normal ageing?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Tomography, Optical Coherence/methods · Aged · Male · Female · Retinal Vessels/diagnostic imaging · Middle Aged · Aged, 80 and over · China/epidemiology · Fluorescein Angiography/methods · Reference Values · Urban Population · Macula Lutea/diagnostic imaging,blood supply · Healthy Volunteers · Fundus Oculi · Microvascular Density · East Asian People · Adult · Aging · Capillaries/diagnostic imaging · Follow-Up Studies · Macula Lutea/diagnostic imaging · ROC Curve · Reproducibility of Results · Retrospective Studies · Young Adult · Optic Disk/blood supply,diagnostic imaging · Photochemotherapy/methods · Retinal Vessels/diagnostic imaging,pathology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / retinal circulation — thin framing for OCT-angiography; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. The normative values are real but protocol-bound: a large Chinese elderly cohort on 6×6-mm scans reports superficial plexus density 43.9% and deep plexus 44.3% (Xu 2024, N = 1,461), while a 3×3-mm study reports 52.58% and 57.87% for the same plexuses (Coscas 2016, 135 eyes) — scan size, segmentation slab and device move the numbers systematically, so values are carded per-protocol and never pooled. Foveal avascular zone area has a wide normal spread and no agreed abnormal cut-off, stated plainly on the face. Ageing lowers vessel density in every dataset that tests it, most prominently after 50. Because the base is device-bound and the between-study spread is wide, the stamp is graded down. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Beichen Eye Study (1,461 healthy elderly of 5,840 examined, 6×6-mm OCTA): superficial density 43.9%, deep 44.3%, outer 21.9%, choriocapillaris 52.1% — every plexus falls with age (Xu 2024)
cards.summary: Beichen Eye Study (1,461 healthy elderly of 5,840 examined, 6×6-mm OCTA): superficial density 43.9%, deep 44.3%, outer 21.9%, choriocapillaris 52.1% — every plexus falls with age (Xu 2024)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population OCTA vessel-density norms, 6×6-mm, Chinese elderly)
cards.people: Observational population study in Beichen district, Tianjin, China: 5,840 healthy elderly participants examined; 1,461 healthy elderly citizens (30.4% men, median age 60.0 years, range 50–87) included in the normative analysis. OCTA 6×6-mm scan centred on the macula, built-in software quantifying vessel density by plexus; 90% medical reference ranges reported in the study.
cards.result: Vessel densities as reported: superficial capillary plexus 43.9% (3.2%), deep capillary plexus 44.3% (2.8%), outer capillary plexus 21.9% (5.9%) and choriocapillaris 52.1% (1.4%). Age was correlated with the vessel density of every capillary plexus. Sex was correlated with deep and outer plexus density, both higher in women (deep P < 0.001; outer P = 0.015). After age and sex adjustment, choroidal thickness correlated positively with superficial and deep density, ganglion-cell-layer thickness with outer plexus density, and best-corrected acuity with choriocapillaris density. This is the shelf's largest normative dataset, and its values belong to its 6×6-mm protocol.
cards.watchOut: Elderly urban Chinese population on one device's built-in software at 6×6 mm: do not apply these percentages to 3×3-mm scans or other devices — the Coscas card shows the same plexuses reading ~9–14 points higher at 3×3 mm.
cards.source: Xu S et al. Normative data and correlation parameters for vessel density measured by 6 × 6-mm optical coherence tomography angiography in a large chinese urban healthy elderly population: date from the Beichen eye study. BMC ophthalmology. 2024. PMID: 39030533. Registry ID: ChiCTR2000032280. cards.headline: Normative 3×3-mm OCTA (135 eyes of 70 healthy subjects, mean age 48.3): superficial density 52.58 ± 3.22% with FAZ 0.28 ± 0.10 mm²; deep density 57.87 ± 2.82% with FAZ 0.37 ± 0.12 mm² (Coscas 2016)
cards.summary: Normative 3×3-mm OCTA (135 eyes of 70 healthy subjects, mean age 48.3): superficial density 52.58 ± 3.22% with FAZ 0.28 ± 0.10 mm²; deep density 57.87 ± 2.82% with FAZ 0.37 ± 0.12 mm² (Coscas 2016)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative OCTA vessel density and FAZ, 3×3-mm)
cards.people: Retrospective chart review of healthy patients imaged with OCT angiography: 135 eyes of 70 subjects (51% male), mean age 48.3 ± 17.5 years, in three age groups (20–39, 40–59, 60+). A 3×3-mm fovea-centred area was scanned; automated segmentation separated superficial and deep plexuses; vessel density and FAZ computed, with inter- and intra-observer reproducibility assessed.
cards.result: At the superficial plexus, mean vessel density was 52.58 ± 3.22% and mean FAZ 0.28 ± 0.1 mm²; at the deep plexus, 57.87 ± 2.82% and 0.37 ± 0.12 mm². Density was significantly higher in the deep than the superficial plexus in all ETDRS sectors and age groups (P < 0.05), and higher in women than men after age 60 (P < 0.01). Mean FAZ area was lower in the 60+ group (P < 0.05). Reproducibility was good (interobserver 0.78–0.99 superficial, 0.67–0.92 deep). These are 3×3-mm prototype-software values — the protocol, not a universal norm.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, 70 subjects, prototype software: the FAZ shrinking with age in this dataset runs against the (non-significant) widening in the Abay card — FAZ age direction is unsettled, which is part of why this shelf is EMERGING.

primary human physiology study (normative octa vessel density and faz, 3×3-mm) retrospective chart review of healthy patients imaged with oct angiography: 135 eyes of 70 subjects (51% male), mean age 48.3 ± 17.5 years, in three age groups (20–39, 40–59, 60+). a 3×3-mm fovea-centred area was scanned; automated segmentation separated superficial and deep plexuses; vessel density and faz computed, with inter- and intra-observer reproducibility assessed. at the superficial plexus, mean vessel density was 52.58 ± 3.22% and mean faz 0.28 ± 0.1 mm²; at the deep plexus, 57.87 ± 2.82% and 0.37 ± 0.12 mm². density was significantly higher in the deep than the superficial plexus in all etdrs sectors and age groups (p < 0.05), and higher in women than men after age 60 (p < 0.01). mean faz area was lower in the 60+ group (p < 0.05). reproducibility was good (interobserver 0.78–0.99 superficial, 0.67–0.92 deep). these are 3×3-mm prototype-software values — the protocol, not a universal norm. retrospective, 70 subjects, prototype software: the faz shrinking with age in this dataset runs against the (non-significant) widening in the abay card — faz age direction is unsettled, which is part of why this shelf is emerging. coscas f et al. normative data for vascular density in superficial and deep capillary plexuses of healthy adults assessed by optical coherence tomography angiography. investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 2016. pmid: 27409475. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · aging · capillaries/diagnostic imaging · female · fluorescein angiography/methods · follow-up studies · fundus oculi · humans · macula lutea/diagnostic imaging · male · middle aged · roc curve · reference values · reproducibility of results · retinal vessels/diagnostic imaging · retrospective studies · tomography, optical coherence/methods · young adult

cards.headline: Healthy Nepalese eyes (210 subjects, 420 eyes, ages 10–70): superficial FAZ 459.96 ± 124.75 and deep FAZ 589.0 ± 141.39 (units as printed); superficial density 54.03 ± 9.34%, deep 25.91% (as printed) (Shyangbo 2022)
cards.summary: Healthy Nepalese eyes (210 subjects, 420 eyes, ages 10–70): superficial FAZ 459.96 ± 124.75 and deep FAZ 589.0 ± 141.39 (units as printed); superficial density 54.03 ± 9.34%, deep 25.91% (as printed) (Shyangbo 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative OCTA FAZ and vessel density, Nepalese population)
cards.people: Prospective cross-sectional population-based study of 210 healthy Nepalese subjects (420 eyes), aged 10–70 years, imaged with spectral-domain OCT angiography and enhanced depth imaging; FAZ area, superficial and deep vessel density and subfoveal choroidal thickness measured, with ocular and systemic associations modelled.
cards.result: Mean superficial FAZ area was 459.96 ± 124.75 μm (95% CI 443.08–476.83) and deep FAZ area 589.0 ± 141.39 μm (CI 570.77–609.02) — units exactly as printed in the record, where other studies report FAZ in mm². Superficial plexus vessel density was 54.03 ± 9.34% and deep plexus density 25.91 ± 38% as printed — a deep-plexus value far below the other datasets on this shelf, illustrating slab/device dependence rather than a population truth. Mean subfoveal choroidal thickness was 308.89 ± 68.87 μm. There was no significant inter-eye difference in FAZ parameters; myopic eyes had smaller FAZ, lower vessel density and thinner choroid. Superficial FAZ area associated with systolic and deep FAZ area with diastolic blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: Carded exactly as published, including the record's FAZ units and the deep-plexus density whose printed spread (±38%) exceeds its mean — treat the absolute deep-plexus figure as protocol-specific and internally odd, not as a norm to apply. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Shyangbo R et al. Normative Vascular Features on OCT Angiography in Healthy Nepalese Eyes. Clinical ophthalmology (Auckland, N.Z.). 2022. PMID: 36348748. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Age-gradient study (153 healthy eyes, ages 20–80): superficial and deep macular density significantly lower in older groups, prominently after 50; FAZ widening not significant; choriocapillaris flow falls with age (Abay 2022)
cards.summary: Age-gradient study (153 healthy eyes, ages 20–80): superficial and deep macular density significantly lower in older groups, prominently after 50; FAZ widening not significant; choriocapillaris flow falls with age (Abay 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-related OCTA vessel-density change, healthy eyes)
cards.people: Retrospective study of 153 eyes of 153 individuals aged 20–80 years with no systemic disease or optic-disc/retinal pathology, in five age groups. Retinal OCTA at 6×6 mm and optic-disc OCTA at 4.5×4.5 mm: superficial, deep and radial peripapillary plexus density, FAZ area and choriocapillaris flow area compared across age groups.
cards.result: Superficial plexus density was significantly associated with age for the whole image (P = 0.001), parafovea (P = 0.038) and perifovea (P = 0.001); deep plexus density likewise (whole image P = 0.004, parafovea P = 0.001, perifovea P = 0.002). Both plexuses' densities were significantly lower in older age groups, more prominently after 50 years. FAZ area increased with age but not significantly (P = 0.660). Choriocapillaris flow area decreased with age (P = 0.002), and radial peripapillary density inside the disc decreased with age (P = 0.038). The record reports significance and direction, not per-group density values, and this card claims no numeric rate of fall per decade.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective single-centre age contrast: it establishes that density falls with age and roughly when (after 50), not a per-decade rate — no dataset on this shelf supports quoting a '% per year' figure.
cards.source: Abay RN et al. Normative data assessment of age-related changes in macular and optic nerve head vessel density using optical coherence tomography angiography. Photodiagnosis and photodynamic therapy. 2022. PMID: 34775064. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: OCTA norms exist but travel with their protocol — 6×6-mm superficial density ~44% vs 3×3-mm ~53% — density falls with age after 50, and FAZ has a wide normal spread with no agreed abnormal cut-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: OCTA norms exist but travel with their protocol — 6×6-mm superficial density ~44% vs 3×3-mm ~53% — density falls with age after 50, and FAZ has a wide normal spread with no agreed abnormal cut-off
cards.people: Synthesis of the four normative datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (vision / retinal circulation) as thin framing; the shelf rests on the primary measurement literature. The consistent findings: vessel density is measurable with good reproducibility (Coscas 2016), is higher in the deep than superficial plexus within a given protocol, falls with age in every dataset (Xu 2024; Abay 2022 — prominently after 50), and runs higher in women in the older groups. The inconsistent findings are the absolute values: superficial density 43.9% at 6×6 mm in 1,461 elderly Chinese adults vs 52.58% at 3×3 mm in 70 mostly younger subjects, and a deep-plexus figure of 25.91% as printed in the Nepalese dataset vs 57.87% in the 3×3-mm dataset — scan size, slab and device, not biology, explain most of that spread. FAZ area centres around 0.28 mm² (superficial) and 0.37 mm² (deep) in the mm²-reporting study, with wide spread, an unsettled age direction, and no agreed abnormal cut-off — say so plainly rather than implying a threshold. Distinct from the structural OCT thickness shelves: OCTA measures flow signal, not thickness. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Never quote an OCTA density without its scan size, slab and device: a value that is normal on one protocol is 'abnormal' on another, and FAZ area alone does not separate health from disease at any agreed cut-off.

shelves.title: Stapedial reflex thresholds depend on component, probe tone and stimulus — absent in 4% of normal values at 226 Hz — and 1,565 older adults support no separate older range (PARTIAL slice of #7090)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are acoustic (stapedial) reflex thresholds — by stimulus frequency, probe tone and age — and what fraction of normal ears have absent reflexes at the highest stimulus levels?
shelves.mesh: Acoustic Stimulation/methods · Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Differential Threshold · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Reflex, Acoustic/physiology · Stapedius/physiology · Acoustic Impedance Tests · Acoustics · Audiometry · Cochlea/physiology · Ear, Middle/physiology · Prospective Studies · Reflex/physiology · Reproducibility of Results · Tympanic Membrane/physiology · Young Adult · Acoustic Impedance Tests/standards · Acoustic Stimulation · Aged, 80 and over · Auditory Threshold · Functional Laterality · Presbycusis/diagnosis,physiopathology · Pressure · Sex Factors · Stapedius/innervation,physiology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing — middle-ear reflex framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #7090: #7090 asks normal wideband absorbance / tympanometry across frequency (and includes one wideband reflex-estimation methods study); it does not ask the conventional acoustic stapedial reflex threshold distribution — by stimulus frequency, probe tone and age, with the fraction of normal ears whose reflexes are absent — which is this shelf's question alone. The conventional data: thresholds depend on the immittance component read, the probe tone and the stimulus (lowest for admittance at a 226-Hz probe with a 1,000-Hz stimulus), with 4% missing values at 226 Hz in 100 healthy adults (Ferekidou 2008); the wideband ipsilateral broadband-noise threshold runs 12 dB below the clinical threshold in 33 normal-hearing adults (Feeney 2017); and in 1,565 older adults the age effect on reflex thresholds is inconsistent and not clinically significant once hearing loss is allowed for (Golding 2007). Because the age question is unsettled and thresholds are component- and probe-specific, the stamp is graded down. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Conventional reflex thresholds in 100 healthy adults across five age decades: lowest for admittance (Y) at a 226-Hz probe with a 1,000-Hz stimulus — and 4% of values missing at 226 Hz (Ferekidou 2008)
cards.summary: Conventional reflex thresholds in 100 healthy adults across five age decades: lowest for admittance (Y) at a 226-Hz probe with a 1,000-Hz stimulus — and 4% of values missing at 226 Hz (Ferekidou 2008)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (conventional acoustic stapedial reflex thresholds by component, probe tone and age)
cards.people: 100 healthy persons in five age groups of 20 each (20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59 and 60–69 years). Acoustic reflex threshold determined for admittance (Y) and its components susceptance (B) and conductance (G) at 226-, 678- and 1,000-Hz probe tones, using 500-, 1,000-, 2,000- and 4,000-Hz stimuli.
cards.result: Statistically significant differences in acoustic reflex thresholds were found between components, stimuli and probe tones. The lowest threshold level was recorded for Y at the 226-Hz probe tone using the 1,000-Hz stimulus. Four percent of values were missing at 226 Hz — reflex absence at the tested levels in a small fraction of normal ears, a distributional fact of this measurement, not an error. Subjects in different age groups had different reflex thresholds. The authors conclude that reading B and G as well as Y gives more detailed middle-ear information than Y alone. The fetched record reports the pattern and the missing-value fraction, not a table of decibel thresholds, and this card claims no dB values.
cards.watchOut: N = 100 with 20 per decade: the age-group differences are real in this dataset but rest on small cells, and the record's abstract gives no numeric thresholds — any dB figure for a named frequency/probe combination would need the full text, and none is claimed here.
cards.source: Ferekidou E et al. Acoustic stapedial reflex in normal adults: biological behavior and determination of threshold levels. ORL; journal for oto-rhino-laryngology and its related specialties. 2008. PMID: 18391577. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wideband vs clinical reflex threshold in 33 normal-hearing adults: the wideband ipsilateral broadband-noise threshold averages 12 dB below the clinical threshold, with poorer test–retest reliability (Feeney 2017)
cards.summary: Wideband vs clinical reflex threshold in 33 normal-hearing adults: the wideband ipsilateral broadband-noise threshold averages 12 dB below the clinical threshold, with poorer test–retest reliability (Feeney 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative wideband immittance and acoustic stapedius reflex threshold, longitudinal test–retest)
cards.people: 33 normal-hearing adults (13 men, 20 women; mean age 26 years) with normal audiometry and clinical immittance, tested prospectively on two visits about 1 month apart. Wideband acoustic immittance battery (reflectance, equivalent admittance at the tympanic membrane) plus wideband and clinical acoustic stapedius reflex thresholds; wideband thresholds measured at tympanometric peak pressure.
cards.result: The mean wideband acoustic stapedius reflex threshold for an ipsilateral broadband-noise activator was 12 dB lower than the clinical ASRT, but had poorer reliability — the wideband method detects the reflex earlier, less repeatably. For the wider battery, test–retest reliability of absorbance was better at tympanometric peak pressure (downswept) than at ambient pressure around 1.0–1.26 kHz, and equivalent-admittance reliability ranged from 1–3 dB below 1.0 kHz to 8–9 dB at higher frequencies. This card is the bridge to home pack #7090: the wideband battery's norms live there; the clinical-threshold comparison — the conventional measurement's calibration against its wideband successor — is this shelf's slice.
cards.watchOut: Young adults (mean age 26) and N = 33, printed on the face: the 12 dB wideband–clinical gap is a young-normal-ear figure, and the poorer wideband reliability is part of the finding, not a footnote.
cards.source: Feeney MP et al. Normative Wideband Reflectance, Equivalent Admittance at the Tympanic Membrane, and Acoustic Stapedius Reflex Threshold in Adults. Ear and hearing. 2017. PMID: 28045835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Blue Mountains Hearing Study (1,565 older adults): after allowing for hearing loss, age effects on reflex thresholds are inconsistent — contralateral rises at selected frequencies only, not clinically significant (Golding 2007)
cards.summary: Blue Mountains Hearing Study (1,565 older adults): after allowing for hearing loss, age effects on reflex thresholds are inconsistent — contralateral rises at selected frequencies only, not clinically significant (Golding 2007)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (tympanometric and acoustic stapedius reflex measures in older adults, population sample)
cards.people: Representative sample of 1,565 older Australians in the Blue Mountains Hearing Study. Tympanometric peak pressure, peak compensated static acoustic admittance (peak Ytm) and acoustic stapedius reflex thresholds obtained; age and sex effects examined, with hearing loss allowed for in the reflex analysis.
cards.result: No significant age or sex effect was found for tympanometric peak pressure. Peak Ytm decreased with age in the left ear only and was consistently higher in men than women. For reflex thresholds, after allowing for hearing loss the effect of age was inconsistent: an increase with age appeared at selected frequencies only when measured contralaterally, and those changes were not clinically significant. The authors conclude current peak-Ytm normative data are too restricted for the older population, but there is insufficient evidence to warrant alternative normative data for the ASR threshold range in this same population — that is, older ears keep the standard reflex-threshold range, on this large dataset's evidence.
cards.watchOut: Older population with prevalent hearing loss: the 'no new norms needed' conclusion is conditional on allowing for hearing loss — raw thresholds in an older clinic sample will run higher for cochlear reasons, which is exactly the confound this analysis removes.
cards.source: Golding M et al. Tympanometric and acoustic stapedius reflex measures in older adults: the Blue Mountains Hearing Study. Journal of the American Academy of Audiology. 2007. PMID: 17715649. Registry ID: none in the record. primary human physiology study (tympanometric and acoustic stapedius reflex measures in older adults, population sample) representative sample of 1,565 older australians in the blue mountains hearing study. tympanometric peak pressure, peak compensated static acoustic admittance (peak ytm) and acoustic stapedius reflex thresholds obtained; age and sex effects examined, with hearing loss allowed for in the reflex analysis. no significant age or sex effect was found for tympanometric peak pressure. peak ytm decreased with age in the left ear only and was consistently higher in men than women. for reflex thresholds, after allowing for hearing loss the effect of age was inconsistent: an increase with age appeared at selected frequencies only when measured contralaterally, and those changes were not clinically significant. the authors conclude current peak-ytm normative data are too restricted for the older population, but there is insufficient evidence to warrant alternative normative data for the asr threshold range in this same population — that is, older ears keep the standard reflex-threshold range, on this large dataset's evidence. older population with prevalent hearing loss: the 'no new norms needed' conclusion is conditional on allowing for hearing loss — raw thresholds in an older clinic sample will run higher for cochlear reasons, which is exactly the confound this analysis removes. golding m et al. tympanometric and acoustic stapedius reflex measures in older adults: the blue mountains hearing study. journal of the american academy of audiology. 2007. pmid: 17715649. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acoustic impedance tests/standards · acoustic stimulation · aged · aged, 80 and over · aging/physiology · auditory threshold · ear, middle/physiology · female · functional laterality · humans · male · middle aged · presbycusis/diagnosis,physiopathology · pressure · reflex/physiology · sex factors · stapedius/innervation,physiology

cards.headline: Synthesis: conventional stapedial reflex thresholds are component-, probe- and stimulus-specific — lowest for admittance at 226 Hz with a 1,000-Hz stimulus, absent in ~4% of normal values at 226 Hz — and large older-adult data do not support a separate older reflex range
cards.summary: Synthesis: conventional stapedial reflex thresholds are component-, probe- and stimulus-specific — lowest for admittance at 226 Hz with a 1,000-Hz stimulus, absent in ~4% of normal values at 226 Hz — and large older-adult data do not support a separate older reflex range
cards.people: Synthesis of the three datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (hearing) briefly; the shelf rests on the primary measurement literature. PARTIAL slice of home pack #7090 (wideband absorbance / tympanometry norms): #7090's question is the wideband absorbance distribution and its one reflex card is a wideband estimation-methods study; the conventional threshold distribution carded here is not its question, and no study is shared between the packs. What the conventional data show: threshold is not one number — it moves with the immittance component read (Y vs B vs G), the probe tone (226 vs 678 vs 1,000 Hz) and the stimulus frequency, with the lowest thresholds for Y at 226 Hz with a 1,000-Hz stimulus and 4% missing values at 226 Hz in healthy adults (Ferekidou 2008, N = 100). The wideband successor method reads the same reflex 12 dB lower on a broadband-noise activator, with poorer reliability (Feeney 2017, N = 33). On age the datasets disagree in weight: small-cell decade differences in Ferekidou vs no clinically significant age effect, after hearing-loss adjustment, in 1,565 older adults (Golding 2007) — the larger dataset governs, and reflex absence in a normal ear remains a distributional fact to report, not smooth away. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: Ipsilateral vs contralateral stimulation changes thresholds (the Golding age signal was contralateral only): never pool the two routes, and never pool wideband with clinical 226-Hz thresholds — they differ by ~12 dB on the same ears.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
