shelves.title: Voice therapy for functional dysphonia: small RCTs favour named programmes (semi-occluded tract, stretch-and-flow) over vocal hygiene alone; biofeedback adds no voice benefit over placebo
shelves.question: In adults with functional (muscle-tension / behavioural) dysphonia, does structured voice therapy — semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises, stretch-and-flow, vocal function exercises, with or without electromyographic biofeedback — improve voice handicap, acoustic measures and laryngeal appearance versus vocal hygiene alone, sham or waitlist, and do the protocols differ?
shelves.mesh: Dysphonia · Humans · Phonation · Treatment Outcome · Voice Quality · Voice Training
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, protocol by protocol — never pooled. The randomised base is four small trials, each testing a NAMED programme against a weak comparator: a semi-occluded vocal-tract exercise programme plus vocal hygiene beat vocal hygiene alone (n=34); stretch-and-flow beat vocal hygiene alone (N not documented in the record) with large effect sizes in a preliminary trial; semi-occluded-tract therapy with EMG biofeedback equalled the same therapy with placebo biofeedback for voice, with added muscle-activity effects (n=22 women); and flow-resistant-tube therapy was noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises (n=20). A 2008 systematic review of six treatment RCTs found combined direct-plus-indirect therapy improved self-reported, observer-rated and instrumental functioning versus no intervention, while warning the real effects are probably smaller (publication bias). Samples are small (Ns printed on each card's face), blinding of a behavioural therapy is inherently partial, and no trial compares these programmes against each other adequately — the shelf answers each protocol family separately.

cards.headline: Semi-occluded vocal-tract programme RCT (Guzman 2020): physiologic voice therapy plus vocal hygiene improved handicap, symptoms and phonatory effort measures versus vocal hygiene alone (n=34)
cards.summary: Semi-occluded vocal-tract programme RCT (Guzman 2020): physiologic voice therapy plus vocal hygiene improved handicap, symptoms and phonatory effort measures versus vocal hygiene alone (n=34)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, physiologic voice therapy programme based on semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises + vocal hygiene vs vocal hygiene alone
cards.people: 34 participants with behavioural dysphonia randomised to physiologic voice therapy based on semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises plus a vocal hygiene programme (n=20) or vocal hygiene alone (n=14). Treatment was eight sessions; the experimental programme used seven phonatory tasks across four different semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises. All participants had laryngoscopic, aerodynamic, electroglottographic and acoustic assessment before and after.
cards.result: The experimental group improved significantly on the Voice Handicap Index, Voice Symptom Scale and Vocal Tract Discomfort Scale (decreases) and on self-perceived resonant voice quality (increase), with significant decreases in subglottic pressure, phonation threshold pressure and glottal airflow across tasks. The authors concluded most change should be expected in physical and functional variables, and that subglottic and phonation threshold pressures were the most change-sensitive measures, reflecting reduced phonatory effort.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=34, unevenly split 20/14), unblinded behavioural therapy against a minimal comparator (vocal hygiene alone), with many outcome measures and no effect sizes in the record — improvement over vocal hygiene alone is a low bar.
cards.source: Guzman M et al. Effectiveness of a physiologic voice therapy program based on different semioccluded vocal tract exercises in subjects with behavioral dysphonia: A randomized controlled trial. Journal of Communication Disorders. 2020. PMID: 32659480. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Dysphonia · Humans · Phonation · Treatment Outcome · Voice Quality · Voice Training

cards.headline: Stretch-and-flow RCT (Watts 2015): greater improvement in voice handicap, maximum phonation time and cepstral measures versus vocal hygiene education alone (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Stretch-and-flow RCT (Watts 2015): greater improvement in voice handicap, maximum phonation time and cepstral measures versus vocal hygiene education alone (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, stretch-and-flow voice therapy vs vocal hygiene education alone
cards.people: Participants with primary muscle tension dysphonia randomised to vocal hygiene education followed by 6 weeks of stretch-and-flow voice therapy, or vocal hygiene education only. Outcomes (Voice Handicap Index, maximum phonation time, s/z ratio, acoustic measures) were taken at baseline and within 2 weeks after treatment or the control period. The record does not state the number of participants — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Pre-to-post changes differed significantly between groups for Voice Handicap Index (P=0.003), maximum phonation time (P=0.013) and cepstral peak prominence in connected speech (P=0.025) and vowels (P=0.017), with large effect sizes favouring stretch-and-flow (Cohen's d 1.6 for VHI reduction, 1.2 for maximum phonation time, 1.2 and 1.1 for cepstral peak prominence). The authors describe the trial as preliminary and small, needing larger samples to confirm.
cards.watchOut: The sample size is not documented in the PubMed record (printed here as such), the authors themselves call it a preliminary small-sample trial, and the comparator is education alone — large effect sizes from small behavioural trials usually shrink in larger replications.
cards.source: Watts CR et al. A randomized controlled trial of stretch-and-flow voice therapy for muscle tension dysphonia. The Laryngoscope. 2015. PMID: 25641591. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EMG-biofeedback RCT (Ribeiro 2019): voice therapy with real EMG biofeedback equalled placebo-biofeedback therapy for voice, with added effects on muscle electrical activity (22 women)
cards.summary: EMG-biofeedback RCT (Ribeiro 2019): voice therapy with real EMG biofeedback equalled placebo-biofeedback therapy for voice, with added effects on muscle electrical activity (22 women)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled double-blind trial, voice therapy + EMG biofeedback vs voice therapy + placebo biofeedback
cards.people: 22 adult women with behavioural dysphonia randomised to vocal therapy with electromyographic biofeedback (n=11) or vocal therapy with placebo electromyographic biofeedback (n=11), in a randomised placebo-controlled double-blind trial. Both groups had eight 30-minute sessions, twice weekly, of semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises (trill, humming, fricative), with assessments before, after, and at one and three months.
cards.result: The vocal therapy promoted positive results in vocal quality and muscle electrical activity at rest in BOTH groups. Electromyographic biofeedback added positive results for muscle electrical activity during phonatory tasks, and those effects remained longer, but efficacy for the voice itself was equivalent to the placebo-biofeedback therapy. In short: the therapy helped; the biofeedback's added value was on muscle activity measures, not on voice outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Very small (11 per group) and women only; unusually for this shelf it does have a placebo control and blinding — and under that stricter design the added intervention (biofeedback) showed no extra voice benefit.
cards.source: Ribeiro VV et al. Effectiveness of Voice Therapy Associated With Electromyographic Biofeedback in Women With Behavioral Dysphonia: Randomized Placebo-Controlled Double-Blind Clinical Trial. Journal of Voice. 2019. cards.headline: Two-protocol RCT (Kapsner-Smith 2015): flow-resistant-tube therapy was noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises for voice handicap (n=20)
cards.summary: Two-protocol RCT (Kapsner-Smith 2015): flow-resistant-tube therapy was noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises for voice handicap (n=20)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, flow-resistant-tube therapy vs Vocal Function Exercises, with delayed-treatment control
cards.people: 20 subjects (16 women, 4 men) with dysphonia and/or vocal fatigue randomised to one of four conditions: immediate flow-resistant-tube therapy, immediate Vocal Function Exercises therapy, or delayed therapy with either programme (the delayed groups serving as a no-treatment control).
cards.result: Voice Handicap Index scores improved significantly for both treatment groups relative to the no-treatment group, and comparison of effect sizes suggests flow-resistant-tube therapy is noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises for reducing Voice Handicap Index scores. Significant reductions in roughness (Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice) were found for the flow-resistant-tube subjects, with no other significant voice-quality findings. The authors conclude either programme may improve voice quality of life in some individuals with dysphonia.
cards.watchOut: Only 20 subjects across four conditions — the noninferiority suggestion rests on effect-size comparison in a very small sample, and the delayed-treatment control period is short.
cards.source: Kapsner-Smith MR et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Two Semi-Occluded Vocal Tract Voice Therapy Protocols. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. 2015. PMID: 25675335. cards.headline: Systematic review (Ruotsalainen 2008): combined direct + indirect voice therapy improved functioning versus no intervention in functional dysphonia — with a publication-bias warning
cards.summary: Systematic review (Ruotsalainen 2008): combined direct + indirect voice therapy improved functioning versus no intervention in functional dysphonia — with a publication-bias warning
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, voice therapy for functional dysphonia / prevention of voice disorders
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of interventions for treating functional/nonorganic dysphonia or preventing voice disorders in adults, searching to 2006: six treatment RCTs and two prevention RCTs were identified.
cards.result: A combination of direct and indirect voice therapy, compared with no intervention, improved self-reported vocal functioning (standardised mean difference −1.07; 95% CI −1.94 to −0.19), observer-rated functioning (weighted mean difference −13.00; 95% CI −17.92 to −8.08) and instrumentally assessed functioning (WMD −1.20; 95% CI −2.37 to −0.03), with effects reported to remain for at least 14 weeks; effects were similar in patients and in screened teachers/student teachers. Two studies did not show voice training prevents voice disorders. Assessment of publication bias indicated the real effect sizes are probably smaller than reported.
cards.watchOut: Searches end in 2006, so this review predates three of the four trials carded above; its pooled comparison is against no intervention, and its own publication-bias assessment says the true effects are probably smaller.
cards.source: Ruotsalainen J et al. Systematic review of the treatment of functional dysphonia and prevention of voice disorders. Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. 2008. PMID: 18439458. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Voice Disorders · Voice Training

cards.headline: Synthesis: small randomised trials support structured voice therapy over vocal hygiene alone or no treatment for functional dysphonia — each named programme separately, with no adequate head-to-head hierarchy
cards.summary: Synthesis: small randomised trials support structured voice therapy over vocal hygiene alone or no treatment for functional dysphonia — each named programme separately, with no adequate head-to-head hierarchy
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Four small RCTs (n=34; N not documented; n=22; n=20) each found their named programme — semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises, stretch-and-flow, semi-occluded-tract therapy with or without EMG biofeedback, and flow-resistant-tube therapy versus Vocal Function Exercises — better than vocal hygiene alone, placebo biofeedback (for muscle measures only) or no treatment, and a 2008 systematic review of six RCTs found combined direct-plus-indirect therapy effective versus no intervention while warning of publication bias. No pooled 'voice therapy works' claim is made: comparators are weak, samples are small, and blinding is largely impossible. Prevention of voice disorders was not supported.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Retinal calibre: MESA means 144.1 ± 14.4 µm arteriolar and 214.0 ± 22.2 µm venular in 5,979 adults; in healthy Asians arterioles run 158.94 µm (Indian), 138.31 µm (Malay), 131.20 µm (Chinese) — ethnicity moves the mean by ~28 µm
shelves.question: In general-population adults, what are retinal arteriolar and venular calibres — central retinal arteriolar and venular equivalents (CRAE / CRVE) and the arteriole-to-venule ratio — their means, spreads and percentiles by age, sex, ethnicity and blood pressure, measured from standardised fundus photography?
shelves.mesh: Arterioles · Atherosclerosis · Blood Pressure · C-Reactive Protein · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cross-Sectional Studies · Ethnicity · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Male · Middle Aged · Retinal Vessels · Risk Factors · Venules · Reference Values · Fundus Oculi
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / retinal circulation (thin framing for a population-measurement row — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so). These are general-population samples, not disease-free cohorts (except the Asian study, which is disease-free by design) — each card states its sampling frame. MESA (5,979 people aged 45–84, four ethnic groups) sets the scale: mean arteriolar calibre 144.1 ± 14.4 µm and venular 214.0 ± 22.2 µm, narrower arterioles with higher blood pressure, and larger calibres in Black and Hispanic participants than in White and Chinese participants. The disease-free Asian study sharpens the ethnic gradient (arterioles: Indians 158.94 µm, Malays 138.31 µm, Chinese 131.20 µm). Grading software and photograph field change values — values are carded per protocol population, and blood-pressure associations are context, not treatment claims. cards.headline: MESA (Wong 2006): 5,979 people aged 45–84 of four ethnic groups — mean retinal arteriolar calibre 144.1 ± 14.4 µm and venular calibre 214.0 ± 22.2 µm from digital retinal photographs; Black and Hispanic participants had larger arteriolar and venular calibres than White and Chinese participants
cards.summary: MESA (Wong 2006): 5,979 people aged 45–84 of four ethnic groups — mean retinal arteriolar calibre 144.1 ± 14.4 µm and venular calibre 214.0 ± 22.2 µm from digital retinal photographs; Black and Hispanic participants had larger arteriolar and venular calibres than White and Chinese participants
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (retinal vascular calibre, MESA, general population)
cards.people: 5,979 persons aged 45–84 years residing in six US communities in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (white, black, Hispanic and Chinese participants) — a general-population sample, not a disease-free cohort; retinal vascular calibre measured and summarised from digital retinal photographs, with standard cardiovascular risk factors and inflammatory biomarkers assessed.
cards.result: Mean retinal arteriolar caliber was 144.1 ± 14.4 (SD) µm, and venular caliber 214.0 ± 22.2 µm. In models controlling for age, gender, race-ethnicity and centre, smaller arteriolar caliber was related to higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure, hypertension status, current alcohol consumption, greater body mass index and higher total homocysteine; larger venular caliber was related to diabetes, current smoking, greater body mass index and waist-hip ratio, higher glucose, triglyceride, LDL-cholesterol and inflammatory markers (hsCRP, fibrinogen, IL-6, sICAM-1, PAI-1) and lower HDL-cholesterol. In multivariate analyses, blacks and Hispanics had larger retinal arteriolar and venular calibers than whites and Chinese.
cards.watchOut: A risk-factor-laden general population aged 45–84: its means are population means, not healthy-eye norms — the disease-free Asian card below is the contrast, and the blood-pressure association is context, not a treatment claim.
cards.source: Wong TY et al. Retinal vascular caliber, cardiovascular risk factors, and inflammation: the multi-ethnic study of atherosclerosis (MESA). cards.headline: Beaver Dam Eye Study (Klein 2006): standardised calibre measurement in a random sample of 396 people aged 50–86 — the fetched record prints associations, not mean calibres, and this card claims none: wider venules tracked higher hsCRP, IL-6 and amyloid A; narrower arterioles tracked higher amyloid A and lower albumin and folate
cards.summary: Beaver Dam Eye Study (Klein 2006): standardised calibre measurement in a random sample of 396 people aged 50–86 — the fetched record prints associations, not mean calibres, and this card claims none: wider venules tracked higher hsCRP, IL-6 and amyloid A; narrower arterioles tracked higher amyloid A and lower albumin and folate
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (retinal vessel calibre and inflammatory markers, Beaver Dam random sample)
cards.people: A random sample of 396 persons aged 50–86 years from the Beaver Dam Eye Study who underwent baseline examination from 1988 to 1990; standardised protocols for blood collection and marker measurement, with arteriole and venule diameters measured from digitised photographs.
cards.result: While controlling for age, smoking status, diabetes status, serum HDL-cholesterol and hematocrit, wider retinal venular diameters were associated with higher serum high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin 6 and amyloid A levels. While controlling for age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, smoking, HDL-cholesterol and gout, smaller arteriolar diameters were associated with higher serum amyloid A and lower serum albumin and folate levels, but not with hsCRP or IL-6. Markers of endothelial dysfunction (soluble ICAM-1, soluble E-selectin) were not associated with either diameter. The authors interpret wider venular calibre as a possible marker of systemic inflammation.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional associations in 396 people: calibre differences here track inflammatory markers at a single time point — they establish covariation in a population sample, not that inflammation widens venules or that calibre predicts events.
cards.source: Klein R et al. Are inflammatory factors related to retinal vessel caliber? The Beaver Dam Eye Study. Archives of ophthalmology (Chicago, Ill. : 1960). 2006. PMID: 16401789. cards.headline: Healthy multiethnic Asians (Li 2013): in people free of clinical disease, Indians had the largest calibres (arterioles 158.94 µm, venules 228.26 µm), then Malays (138.31 µm, 204.26 µm), then Chinese (131.20 µm, 195.09 µm) — after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose
cards.summary: Healthy multiethnic Asians (Li 2013): in people free of clinical disease, Indians had the largest calibres (arterioles 158.94 µm, venules 228.26 µm), then Malays (138.31 µm, 204.26 µm), then Chinese (131.20 µm, 195.09 µm) — after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (retinal vessel geometric characteristics, healthy multiethnic Asian population)
cards.people: Healthy Chinese, Malay and Indian participants in a multiethnic Asian study, defined as nonsmokers without diabetes mellitus, uncontrolled hypertension, obesity, stroke, heart disease, glaucoma or retinopathy; retinal vascular parameters measured from retinal photographs with a computer-assisted program under a standardised protocol. The fetched record does not print the total N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: There were significant differences in retinal vascular caliber, tortuosity and fractal dimension among the three ethnic groups. In multiple linear regression controlling for age, sex, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose, Indians had the largest arteriolar and venular calibers (arterioles [SE]: 158.94 µm [1.00]; venules: 228.26 µm [1.53]), followed by Malays (arterioles: 138.31 µm [0.74]; venules: 204.26 µm [1.13]), then Chinese (arterioles: 131.20 µm [0.84]; venules: 195.09 µm [1.28]). Chinese had the largest arteriolar and venular tortuosity and venular fractal dimension (1.244 [0.003]). The authors note unmeasured environmental, lifestyle and genetic factors may also contribute.
cards.watchOut: The ethnic ordering is large — a 27.7 µm arteriolar gap between Indian and Chinese healthy participants exceeds many disease associations in this literature — so a calibre value without its population is uninterpretable; the absent total N in the fetched record is printed on this card, not filled in.
cards.source: Li X et al. Racial differences in retinal vessel geometric characteristics: a multiethnic study in healthy Asians. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 2013. PMID: 23652487. cards.headline: Synthesis: retinal calibre centres near 144 µm (arteriolar) and 214 µm (venular) in a US multiethnic population, but ethnicity alone moves the healthy mean by ~28 µm — calibre is a population measurement, graded from standardised fundus photographs
cards.summary: Synthesis: retinal calibre centres near 144 µm (arteriolar) and 214 µm (venular) in a US multiethnic population, but ethnicity alone moves the healthy mean by ~28 µm — calibre is a population measurement, graded from standardised fundus photographs
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Ganong (vision / retinal circulation; thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). MESA (Wong 2006; 5,979 general-population adults) gives arteriolar 144.1 ± 14.4 µm and venular 214.0 ± 22.2 µm, with narrower arterioles at higher blood pressure and larger calibres in Black and Hispanic than White and Chinese participants. Beaver Dam (Klein 2006; random sample of 396) adds the inflammatory covariation without printing means. The disease-free Asian study (Li 2013) isolates the ethnic gradient in healthy eyes: arterioles 158.94 µm (Indian), 138.31 µm (Malay), 131.20 µm (Chinese), adjusted. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the measurement, its scale and its population gradients are consistently documented across three standardised-photography programmes; no value is portable across populations or grading protocols. This shelf is distinct from the OCT thickness shelves and OCT-angiography pack #7258 — calibre in micrometres from fundus photographs is a different measurement.
cards.watchOut: Sampling frame first: MESA's means include hypertension and diabetes, Beaver Dam is a random older sample, and the Asian study excludes clinical disease — quoting any one as 'the normal calibre' without its frame repeats the error this shelf exists to correct.

shelves.title: Piclidenoson (CF101) in plaque psoriasis: COMFORT-1 PASI 75 was 9.7% vs 2.6% on placebo, and the phase II/III trial missed its primary endpoint — modest effects, placebo-like safety
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, does the oral A3 adenosine-receptor agonist piclidenoson (CF101), compared with placebo (or apremilast in the phase 2/3 lineage), improve psoriasis severity (PASI response)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Psoriasis · Male · Double-Blind Method · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Thalidomide · Severity of Illness Index · Adenosine
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Piclidenoson (CF101, Can-Fite — the specific tested product, named under the clarification exception because the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved for psoriasis) is an oral A3 adenosine-receptor agonist developed over a long, slow programme (2012–2024). The responses are modest throughout: the exploratory phase 2 trial's best dose (2 mg) achieved PASI 50 in 35.3%; the phase II/III trial MISSED its primary endpoint (PASI 75 at week 12: 8.5% vs 6.9% on placebo, P=0.621); and the phase 3 COMFORT-1 trial met its primary endpoint only at the 3 mg dose with a PASI 75 rate of 9.7% versus 2.6% on placebo (P=0.037) — far below the response rates of the biologic-era psoriasis treatments homed on their own shelves (cross-pointed in prose, not re-carded). Safety was consistently placebo-like and is the programme's strongest feature.

cards.headline: Exploratory phase 2 RCT (David 2012): CF101 2 mg twice daily improved PASI versus placebo at weeks 8 and 12; 35.3% achieved PASI 50 and 23.5% a physician global assessment of 0 or 1
cards.summary: Exploratory phase 2 RCT (David 2012): CF101 2 mg twice daily improved PASI versus placebo at weeks 8 and 12; 35.3% achieved PASI 50 and 23.5% a physician global assessment of 0 or 1
cards.type: Exploratory phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind dose-ranging placebo-controlled trial, oral CF101 (piclidenoson) vs placebo, 12 weeks
cards.people: 75 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque-type psoriasis were enrolled and randomised to oral CF101 1, 2 or 4 mg or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks in this multicentre dose-ranging phase 2 study.
cards.result: In the 2 mg group, mean PASI change from baseline improved progressively versus placebo, significantly at week 8 (P=0.047) and week 12 (P=0.031); 35.3% of 2 mg patients achieved a PASI ≥50 response and 23.5% achieved a physician's global assessment score of 0 or 1. CF101 was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory dose-ranging trial with 75 patients across four arms: the positive read rests on the single 2 mg arm's PASI change scores, and the headline response measure is PASI 50, a lower bar than the PASI 75 primary endpoints used later.
cards.source: David M et al. Treatment of plaque-type psoriasis with oral CF101: data from an exploratory randomized phase 2 clinical trial. cards.headline: Phase II/III RCT (David 2016): CF101 MISSED its primary endpoint — PASI 75 at week 12 was 8.5% on 2 mg versus 6.9% on placebo (P=0.621); later week-32 figures are uncontrolled after placebo crossover
cards.summary: Phase II/III RCT (David 2016): CF101 MISSED its primary endpoint — PASI 75 at week 12 was 8.5% on 2 mg versus 6.9% on placebo (P=0.621); later week-32 figures are uncontrolled after placebo crossover
cards.type: Phase II/III multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, oral CF101 (piclidenoson) vs placebo, with open-label crossover after week 12/16
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomised to CF101 1 or 2 mg or placebo twice daily in this multicentre double-blind 2-segment placebo-controlled study (total N not documented in the fetched record); at week 12 or 16 the placebo group crossed over to open-label CF101 to week 32, and the 1 mg group was discontinued for futility at the week-12 interim analysis.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: PASI 75 at week 12 was 8.5% (CF101 2 mg) versus 6.9% (placebo), P=0.621. At week 32 — after crossover, with no concurrent placebo arm — mean PASI improvement from baseline on CF101 2 mg was 57% (P<0.001 versus baseline), with PASI 50 in 63.5%, PASI 75 in 35.5%, PASI 90 in 24.7% and PASI 100 in 10.6%. Safety was similar to placebo; the most common adverse events were infections and gastrointestinal events, with no cumulative intolerance over 32 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial on its primary endpoint: the week-32 response percentages are within-group changes after the placebo arm crossed over to CF101, so they carry no comparative weight; the control arm is printed exactly as published (placebo twice daily, crossing over at week 12 or 16 by segment), and the fetched record does not document the total randomised N.
cards.source: David M et al. Treatment of Plaque-Type Psoriasis With Oral CF101: Data from a Phase II/III Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial. Journal of drugs in dermatology : JDD. 2016. cards.headline: COMFORT-1 phase 3 RCT (Papp 2024): piclidenoson 3 mg twice daily met the primary endpoint — PASI 75 at week 16 in 9.7% versus 2.6% on placebo (P=0.037); the 2 mg dose showed similar efficacy
cards.summary: COMFORT-1 phase 3 RCT (Papp 2024): piclidenoson 3 mg twice daily met the primary endpoint — PASI 75 at week 16 in 9.7% versus 2.6% on placebo (P=0.037); the 2 mg dose showed similar efficacy
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial (COMFORT-1), piclidenoson vs apremilast vs placebo, primary endpoint at week 16
cards.people: 529 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomised (3:3:3:2) to piclidenoson 2 mg twice daily, piclidenoson 3 mg twice daily, apremilast 30 mg twice daily or placebo and received at least one dose; the primary-endpoint efficacy population was 426 (piclidenoson 2 mg 127, piclidenoson 3 mg 103, apremilast 118, placebo 78). At week 16 the placebo arm was re-randomised to active treatment.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (PASI 75 at week 16 versus placebo) was met with the 3 mg dose: 9.7% versus 2.6% (P=0.037); piclidenoson 2 mg and 3 mg showed similar efficacy, and PASI responses continued to increase over time. At week 32, in the per-protocol population, Psoriasis Disability Index improvement was achieved by 58.0% (51/88) on piclidenoson 3 mg versus 55.1% (59/108) on apremilast, with the non-inferiority test trending towards significance (P=0.072). The safety and tolerability profile of piclidenoson was described as excellent and superior to apremilast.
cards.watchOut: Statistically positive but clinically modest: a 9.7% PASI 75 rate is far below biologic-era responses, the primary-endpoint population (426) is smaller than the randomised safety population (529), and the apremilast comparison at week 32 is a per-protocol disability-index read whose non-inferiority test did not reach significance (P=0.072).

Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV. 2024. PMID: 38279575. Registry ID: NCT03168256. phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial (comfort-1), piclidenoson vs apremilast vs placebo, primary endpoint at week 16 529 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomised (3:3:3:2) to piclidenoson 2 mg twice daily, piclidenoson 3 mg twice daily, apremilast 30 mg twice daily or placebo and received at least one dose; the primary-endpoint efficacy population was 426 (piclidenoson 2 mg 127, piclidenoson 3 mg 103, apremilast 118, placebo 78). at week 16 the placebo arm was re-randomised to active treatment. the primary endpoint (pasi 75 at week 16 versus placebo) was met with the 3 mg dose: 9.7% versus 2.6% (p=0.037); piclidenoson 2 mg and 3 mg showed similar efficacy, and pasi responses continued to increase over time. at week 32, in the per-protocol population, psoriasis disability index improvement was achieved by 58.0% (51/88) on piclidenoson 3 mg versus 55.1% (59/108) on apremilast, with the non-inferiority test trending towards significance (p=0.072). the safety and tolerability profile of piclidenoson was described as excellent and superior to apremilast. statistically positive but clinically modest: a 9.7% pasi 75 rate is far below biologic-era responses, the primary-endpoint population (426) is smaller than the randomised safety population (529), and the apremilast comparison at week 32 is a per-protocol disability-index read whose non-inferiority test did not reach significance (p=0.072). papp ka et al. efficacy and safety of piclidenoson in plaque psoriasis: results from a randomized phase 3 clinical trial (comfort-1). journal of the european academy of dermatology and venereology : jeadv. 2024. pmid: 38279575. registry id: nct03168256. mesh: humans · psoriasis · male · double-blind method · female · middle aged · adult · thalidomide · severity of illness index · adenosine

cards.result: Three randomised reports make up the programme: an exploratory phase 2 trial (n=75) with a PASI signal at 2 mg, a phase II/III trial that missed its PASI 75 primary endpoint at week 12 (its week-32 figures are uncontrolled after crossover), and the phase 3 COMFORT-1 trial (529 randomised), which met its primary endpoint at 3 mg twice daily with a PASI 75 rate of 9.7% versus 2.6%. The tested product is CF101/piclidenoson (Can-Fite), named under the clarification exception; the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved for psoriasis. Effect sizes are modest against the larger responses of biologic-era psoriasis treatments, which stay homed on their own shelves and are cross-pointed here in prose only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Peak nasal inspiratory flow norms: bilateral charts by age, height and sex, unilateral charts by height alone (pilot), and a Turkish control mean of 137.8 L/min — a flow, not the SNIP pressure of pack #7155
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is peak nasal inspiratory flow — bilateral and unilateral normal ranges in litres per minute by age, sex and height — and how reproducible is the measurement for serial and home use?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Body Height · Female · Humans · Inhalation · Male · Middle Aged · Nasal Cavity/physiology · Nasal Obstruction/diagnosis · Pulmonary Ventilation · Reference Values · Rhinomanometry · Sex Characteristics · Manometry · Nose/physiology · Pilot Projects · Young Adult · Inhalation/physiology · Nasal Obstruction/diagnosis,surgery · Nasal Septum/surgery · Nose Deformities, Acquired/surgery · Patient Care Planning · Pulmonary Ventilation/physiology · Rhinoplasty/methods · Visual Analog Scale
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, respiratory mechanics / nasal airflow sections, and Guyton & Hall, respiration chapters (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so). PNIF is a FLOW (L/min) reflecting nasal patency — distinct from sniff nasal inspiratory PRESSURE (SNIP, cmH2O, diaphragm strength), homed at pack #7155 and not re-carded here; the nasal cycle (pack territory S8-4-42) is a pattern question, not a flow range. The normative base is three datasets: bilateral PNIF charts against age, height and sex from 137 fulfilling volunteers (Ottaviano 2006 — the fetched record prints the chart construction, not numeric L/min values, and this shelf claims none from it); unilateral PNIF charts against height alone, the only correlating variable, in 97 fulfilling volunteers, explicitly a pilot (Ottaviano 2012); and a Turkish dataset giving the one printed mean — 137.8 L/min in 219 healthy controls (Ozkul 2013). Considerable between-person variability was unexplained by age, height or sex in the largest charting study. The stamp is EMERGING because two of three datasets print no numeric range in their records and the unilateral data are a pilot.

cards.headline: Bilateral PNIF normative charts (170 volunteers, 137 fulfilling criteria): PNIF related to age, height and sex, with no sex-by-age or sex-by-height interaction — and considerable unexplained between-person variability (Ottaviano 2006)
cards.summary: Bilateral PNIF normative charts (170 volunteers, 137 fulfilling criteria): PNIF related to age, height and sex, with no sex-by-age or sex-by-height interaction — and considerable unexplained between-person variability (Ottaviano 2006)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (bilateral PNIF, healthy adult volunteers)
cards.people: Repeated PNIF measurements in 170 volunteers; 137 fulfilled the study criteria — all non-smokers, non-asthmatic, without nose or paranasal sinus problems, aged 16–84 years. Tables were produced relating PNIF to age, sex and height in a Caucasian population.
cards.result: There was no interaction of sex with age or height. There was considerable residual variability of PNIF between individuals not explained by any of the variables studied. The authors conclude PNIF is a cheap, simple method to assess nasal patency in primary and secondary care, and the study provides normative chart data for a Caucasian population. The fetched record does not print numeric PNIF values in L/min, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Chart data without printed means in the record: the shelf uses this study for the structure of the norms (age/height/sex relations, large residual variability), never for a quoted L/min cut-off.
cards.source: Ottaviano G et al. Peak nasal inspiratory flow; normal range in adult population. Rhinology. 2006. PMID: 16550947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (unilateral PNIF, pilot)
cards.people: Repeated bilateral and unilateral PNIF measurements in 109 volunteers; 97 fulfilled the criteria — non-smokers, non-asthmatic, without nose or paranasal sinus problems, aged 13–80 years. The study is described by its authors as a pilot study.
cards.result: Tables relating unilateral PNIF to height were produced, height being the only studied variable that correlated statistically with unilateral PNIF. The authors conclude unilateral PNIF could, if confirmed in a larger series, help assess single-nostril patency — for example the functional effect of unilateral septal deviation or suspected unilateral occlusion. The fetched record prints no numeric L/min values, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A pilot with 97 fulfilling volunteers: unilateral and bilateral PNIF are different measurements and their values must never be merged — a single-nostril flow is not half a bilateral flow by assumption.

cards.headline: Turkish normative PNIF (219 healthy controls): mean PNIF 137.8 L/min — and control values matched post-septoplasty values in 50 patients while exceeding their preoperative values (Ozkul 2013)
cards.summary: Turkish normative PNIF (219 healthy controls): mean PNIF 137.8 L/min — and control values matched post-septoplasty values in 50 patients while exceeding their preoperative values (Ozkul 2013)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (healthy Turkish controls, with a septoplasty comparison group)
cards.people: 269 participants in total: 219 healthy control subjects providing the normative measurements, and 50 patients undergoing septoplasty whose preoperative and postoperative PNIF, nasal septal indices and visual analogue scale (VAS) scores were recorded.
cards.result: Mean PNIF in control subjects was 137.8 L/min. Postoperative PNIF, VAS and nasal septal index data in the surgical group were significantly higher than their preoperative data, and control-group PNIF, VAS and septal indices were consistent with the postoperative data and higher than the preoperative data. The authors identified this as a normal PNIF range for the healthy Turkish population, compatible with VAS scores.
cards.watchOut: One printed mean (137.8 L/min) from one population and device protocol: PNIF is effort- and technique-dependent (mask seal, maximal sniff instruction), so this mean is a population anchor, not a universal normal limit.
cards.source: Ozkul HM et al. Normal range of peak nasal inspiratory flow and its role in nasal septal surgery. The Journal of craniofacial surgery. 2013. PMID: 23714906. cards.result: Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (nasal airflow) and Guyton & Hall (respiration) — framing brief; the shelf rests on the measurement literature. Ottaviano 2006 supplies the bilateral chart structure, Ottaviano 2012 the unilateral (height-only) pilot, and Ozkul 2013 the one numeric anchor (mean 137.8 L/min in 219 healthy Turkish controls, matching post-septoplasty values). PNIF is a flow reflecting nasal patency; it is not SNIP (a pressure reflecting diaphragm strength, pack #7155), and the two are cross-pointed, never merged. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the datasets are small, two print no numeric range in their records, and reproducibility for serial/home use — part of this shelf's question — is asserted by the authors as the method's purpose rather than quantified in the fetched records.
cards.watchOut: Technique dominates this measurement: mask seal and the maximal-sniff instruction must match the normative protocol before any patient's value is compared with these charts.

shelves.title: Brivudine in herpes zoster: equivalent to famciclovir (PHN 11.3% vs 9.6%, n=2,027); PHN advantage over aciclovir is a survey-design result — and the fluoropyrimidine interaction can be lethal
shelves.question: In immunocompetent adults with herpes zoster, does once-daily oral brivudine versus aciclovir — or versus famciclovir — improve acute disease outcomes and reduce postherpetic neuralgia?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents · Bromodeoxyuridine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Herpes Zoster · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with two load-bearing cautions printed on the face. First, design: the favourable postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) result against aciclovir (PHN incidence 32.7% vs 43.5%, P=0.006) comes from a SURVEY follow-up of two randomised trials — former participants aged ≥50 interviewed 8–17 months later — not from a primary-endpoint RCT analysis, and the abstract itself notes the design's methodological disadvantages. Against famciclovir, in a true double-blind randomised trial of 2,027 patients, brivudine was only equivalent (PHN prevalence at 3 months 11.3% vs 9.6%). A 2024 meta-analysis of seven RCTs (2,095 brivudine, 2,076 control patients) found brivudine superior on efficacy and PHN incidence with no significant difference in adverse reactions, while concluding the safety evidence is insufficient. Second, safety: brivudine's interaction with fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and its prodrugs) is potentially lethal and belongs on the face of any brivudine record. Brivudine is licensed in parts of Europe, not in the US — regulatory status on the face.

cards.headline: Survey follow-up of two RCTs (Wassilew 2003) — DESIGN LABELLED: PHN incidence 32.7% on brivudin vs 43.5% on aciclovir (P=0.006) in a post-trial survey, not a primary-endpoint RCT result
cards.summary: Survey follow-up of two RCTs (Wassilew 2003) — DESIGN LABELLED: PHN incidence 32.7% on brivudin vs 43.5% on aciclovir (P=0.006) in a post-trial survey, not a primary-endpoint RCT result
cards.type: Survey follow-up study of two randomised double-blind trials (labelled survey design — not a primary-endpoint RCT analysis), brivudin vs aciclovir
cards.people: 608 herpes zoster patients treated in two prospective randomised double-blind trials with brivudin 125 mg once daily (n=309) or aciclovir 800 mg five times daily (n=299), each for 7 days; former participants aged ≥50 were interviewed during follow-up ranging from 8 to 17 months after treatment started, with neither investigators nor patients aware of the original treatment.
cards.result: The incidence of postherpetic neuralgia, defined as zoster-associated pain occurring or persisting after rash healing, was significantly lower in brivudin recipients (32.7%) than aciclovir recipients (43.5%; P=0.006). Mean duration of PHN was similar (173 vs 164 days; P=0.270). The authors describe this as the first evidence that brivudin favourably affects PHN incidence in immunocompetent elderly zoster patients, while explicitly noting the methodological disadvantages common to this type of survey study.
cards.watchOut: Survey design: PHN was ascertained by interviewing former trial participants 8–17 months later, so recall and follow-up-selection effects apply; do not present the 32.7% vs 43.5% contrast as a primary randomised endpoint.
cards.source: Wassilew SW et al. Oral brivudin in comparison with acyclovir for herpes zoster: a survey study on postherpetic neuralgia. Antiviral Research. 2003. PMID: 12834861. cards.headline: Multinational double-blind RCT (Wassilew 2005): brivudin EQUIVALENT to famciclovir — PHN prevalence at 3 months 11.3% vs 9.6% in 2,027 patients
cards.summary: Multinational double-blind RCT (Wassilew 2005): brivudin EQUIVALENT to famciclovir — PHN prevalence at 3 months 11.3% vs 9.6% in 2,027 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind multinational trial, brivudin vs famciclovir
cards.people: 2,027 immunocompetent herpes zoster patients aged ≥50 with zoster-related pain at presentation, randomised double-blind to brivudin 125 mg once daily or famciclovir 250 mg three times daily, each orally for 7 days.
cards.result: The prevalence of postherpetic neuralgia (at least moderate pain 3 months after treatment initiation) was 11.3% on brivudin versus 9.6% on famciclovir in the per-protocol population, and equivalence of the two drugs was demonstrated (P=0.01, per-protocol and intention-to-treat). Median PHN duration was 46.5 vs 58 days (P=0.54). Prevalence and duration of zoster-associated pain did not differ significantly, and the drugs were equivalent in stopping vesicle formation and accelerating lesion healing. Adverse events were similar in nature and prevalence. In patients ≥65, PHN prevalence was 16.4% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The largest brivudine trial is an equivalence result against an active comparator, not a superiority result — brivudin's advantage over famciclovir is the once-daily schedule, not better outcomes.
cards.source: Wassilew S et al. Brivudin compared with famciclovir in the treatment of herpes zoster: effects in acute disease and chronic pain in immunocompetent patients. A randomized, double-blind, multinational study. Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV. 2005. PMID: 15649191. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised double-blind multinational trial, brivudin vs famciclovir 2,027 immunocompetent herpes zoster patients aged ≥50 with zoster-related pain at presentation, randomised double-blind to brivudin 125 mg once daily or famciclovir 250 mg three times daily, each orally for 7 days. the prevalence of postherpetic neuralgia (at least moderate pain 3 months after treatment initiation) was 11.3% on brivudin versus 9.6% on famciclovir in the per-protocol population, and equivalence of the two drugs was demonstrated (p=0.01, per-protocol and intention-to-treat). median phn duration was 46.5 vs 58 days (p=0.54). prevalence and duration of zoster-associated pain did not differ significantly, and the drugs were equivalent in stopping vesicle formation and accelerating lesion healing. adverse events were similar in nature and prevalence. in patients ≥65, phn prevalence was 16.4% in both groups. the largest brivudine trial is an equivalence result against an active comparator, not a superiority result — brivudin's advantage over famciclovir is the once-daily schedule, not better outcomes. wassilew s et al. brivudin compared with famciclovir in the treatment of herpes zoster: effects in acute disease and chronic pain in immunocompetent patients. a randomized, double-blind, multinational study. journal of the european academy of dermatology and venereology : jeadv. 2005. pmid: 15649191. registry id: none in the record. mesh: 2-aminopurine · acute disease · administration, oral · aged · antiviral agents · bromodeoxyuridine · chronic disease · double-blind method · europe · famciclovir · female · herpes zoster · humans · male · middle aged · pain · pain measurement · prospective studies · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Chen 2024): seven RCTs (2,095 brivudine vs 2,076 control) — brivudine superior on efficacy (P=.0002) and PHN incidence (P=.04), adverse reactions not significantly different, safety evidence judged insufficient
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Chen 2024): seven RCTs (2,095 brivudine vs 2,076 control) — brivudine superior on efficacy (P=.0002) and PHN incidence (P=.04), adverse reactions not significantly different, safety evidence judged insufficient
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, brivudine vs control treatments
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials in herpes zoster, with 2,095 patients in the brivudine (experimental) groups and 2,076 in control groups, drawn from English- and Chinese-language databases to September 2022.
cards.result: The brivudine group was superior to control on efficacy (P=.0002) and on incidence of postherpetic neuralgia (P=.04). The incidence of adverse reactions did not differ significantly between groups (P=.22), and subgroup analyses of adverse events likewise showed no significant differences. The authors conclude brivudine is effective for herpes zoster but that the evidence on its safety is insufficient.
cards.watchOut: The pooled PHN advantage rests partly on the survey-design aciclovir comparison carded above, and the review itself flags the safety evidence as insufficient — trial adverse-event counts do not capture the fluoropyrimidine interaction risk, which arises in clinical co-prescribing, not inside these trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: equivalent to famciclovir in the large RCT, a survey-design PHN advantage over aciclovir, a positive meta-analysis — and a potentially lethal fluoropyrimidine interaction that leads the safety record
cards.summary: Synthesis: equivalent to famciclovir in the large RCT, a survey-design PHN advantage over aciclovir, a positive meta-analysis — and a potentially lethal fluoropyrimidine interaction that leads the safety record
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Brivudine once daily for 7 days is an effective zoster antiviral on this record: equivalent to famciclovir in the 2,027-patient double-blind trial (PHN at 3 months 11.3% vs 9.6%), superior on PHN incidence in the survey follow-up of the aciclovir trials (32.7% vs 43.5% — a survey result, labelled as such), and favoured in the seven-trial meta-analysis for efficacy and PHN with no significant excess of trial adverse reactions. SAFETY FLAG (load-bearing): brivudine interacts with fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and prodrugs such as capecitabine) — the interaction can be lethal, and brivudine must not be combined with them; this risk is not visible in the carded trials' adverse-event counts. Brivudine is licensed in parts of Europe and is not licensed in the US.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. The fluoropyrimidine warning is a standing pharmacological fact about the drug, flagged on the face as the commissioning row directs; it is not a result of the carded trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Population IOP distribution (PARTIAL beside pack #6436): means of 14.2-14.5 mmHg in Tehran, Yazd and Karachi — and 3.5-3.7% of healthy Pakistanis above the conventional 21 mmHg limit
shelves.question: In healthy general populations, what is the distribution of intraocular pressure measured by applanation tonometry — mean, spread and upper percentiles by age, sex and ethnicity — and how far do population means sit from the conventional 21 mmHg upper limit?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Intraocular Pressure · Iran/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Sex Distribution · Pakistan · Ocular Hypertension/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Ganong, ocular physiology sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population eye-study literature, and says so. This is the between-person DISTRIBUTION slice only: pack #6436 homes aqueous-humour formation/drainage rates and the within-person DIURNAL SWING of intraocular pressure, a different question, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Three independent population studies (Tehran, n=3,834 glaucoma-free participants aged 10 and over; Yazd, 2,098 healthy participants aged 40-80; Karachi, 7,201 healthy subjects) agree closely on the centre of the distribution — mean IOP 14.5, 14.2 and about 14.3-14.8 mmHg by applanation tonometry — while the conventional 21 mmHg upper limit sits in the tail: in Karachi 3.5% of men and 3.7% of women exceeded 21 mmHg despite being healthy. Ancestry breadth is limited — two of the three datasets are Iranian and the third is Pakistani — and that limit is on the face, not generalised past. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Tehran Eye Study (Hashemi 2005): mean IOP 14.5 (SD 2.6) mmHg by applanation tonometry in 3,834 glaucoma-free participants; 15.1 (2.9) mmHg at age 40 and over
cards.summary: Tehran Eye Study (Hashemi 2005): mean IOP 14.5 (SD 2.6) mmHg by applanation tonometry in 3,834 glaucoma-free participants; 15.1 (2.9) mmHg at age 40 and over
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based IOP distribution, applanation tonometry)
cards.people: 3,834 participants aged 10 years and older, free of glaucoma diagnosis or suspicion, from 4,565 Tehran citizens studied in the population-based cross-sectional Tehran Eye Study; all underwent applanation tonometry, fundus examination and interview under a standardised protocol.
cards.result: Mean (SD) intraocular pressure was 14.5 (2.6) mmHg overall — 14.4 (2.7) in men and 14.5 (2.5) in women — and 15.1 (2.9) mmHg in people aged 40 years and over. IOP increased significantly with age and with cup:disc ratio, except for a fall in old age; it increased with darker eye pigmentation except for blue/grey eyes, and non-linearly from emmetropic to highly myopic eyes. Age, iris colour and cup:disc ratio were related to IOP, but sex was not. The authors concluded the distribution differed from other geographical regions and advised a geographical approach to interpreting normal IOP.
cards.watchOut: Glaucoma diagnosis or suspicion was an exclusion, so the upper tail is a screened-healthy tail, not the raw population tail; the cohort includes participants from age 10, and the age-40-and-over mean (15.1 mmHg) is the adult-comparable figure.
cards.source: Hashemi H et al. Distribution of intraocular pressure in healthy Iranian individuals: the Tehran Eye Study. The British journal of ophthalmology. 2005. PMID: 15923494. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yazd Eye Study (Pakravan 2017): mean IOP 14.2 ± 2.5 mmHg by Goldmann applanation in healthy Iranians aged 40-80; IOP rose 0.02 mmHg per year of age and 0.02 mmHg per micron of corneal thickness
cards.summary: Yazd Eye Study (Pakravan 2017): mean IOP 14.2 ± 2.5 mmHg by Goldmann applanation in healthy Iranians aged 40-80; IOP rose 0.02 mmHg per year of age and 0.02 mmHg per micron of corneal thickness
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based IOP distribution, Goldmann applanation tonometry)
cards.people: 2,098 healthy Iranian participants aged 40-80 years (response rate 90.4% of 2,320 eligible), selected by cluster random sampling in Yazd, Iran, 2010-2011; examination included Goldmann applanation tonometry, ultrasonic pachymetry and visual field testing; the analysis used randomly selected normal eyes (2,262 normal eyes from 1,159 subjects, as published).
cards.result: Mean IOP was 14.2 ± 2.5 mmHg, mean central corneal thickness 543 ± 37 µm and mean vertical cup-to-disc ratio 0.32 ± 0.14. On multiple regression, IOP correlated significantly with age (regression coefficient 0.02 per year, p=0.015), central corneal thickness (0.02 per micron, p<0.001), spherical equivalent (-0.15 per dioptre, p=0.024) and smoking (0.89 mmHg higher in smokers, p=0.009). The authors concluded these values differ from other ethnicities and that ethnicity should be considered when interpreting an individual's measurements.
cards.watchOut: A second Iranian dataset — it confirms the Tehran centre of the distribution in an older age band but does not widen the ancestry base; corneal thickness moves the applanation reading itself (0.02 mmHg per micron), so part of the spread is measurement, not pressure.
cards.source: Pakravan M et al. Distribution of intraocular pressure, central corneal thickness and vertical cup-to-disc ratio in a healthy Iranian population: the Yazd Eye Study. Acta ophthalmologica. 2017. PMID: 27778447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Karachi population study (Qureshi 1996): in 7,201 healthy Pakistanis, 83-85% sat between 11 and 18 mmHg, but 3.5% of men and 3.7% of women exceeded 21 mmHg; IOP rose 0.3-0.5 mmHg per decade
cards.summary: Karachi population study (Qureshi 1996): in 7,201 healthy Pakistanis, 83-85% sat between 11 and 18 mmHg, but 3.5% of men and 3.7% of women exceeded 21 mmHg; IOP rose 0.3-0.5 mmHg per decade
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population frequency distribution of IOP)
cards.people: 7,201 healthy subjects of both sexes in Karachi, Pakistan, studied after controlling for factors that can affect IOP, as published; right- and left-eye pressures are reported separately by sex.
cards.result: The distribution was slightly skewed towards higher values. In men and women respectively, 85.1% and 82.2% ranged from 11 to 18 mmHg, 4.3% and 3.2% from 8 to 10 mmHg, and 7.1% and 11.2% from 19 to 21 mmHg; ocular hypertension (IOP above 21 mmHg) was found in 3.5% of men and 3.7% of women. Mean right/left IOP was 14.3 ± 0.17 / 14.4 ± 0.12 mmHg in men and 14.6 ± 0.14 / 14.8 ± 0.15 mmHg in women. IOP increased with age in both eyes and both sexes, by an average of 0.3 mmHg per decade in men and 0.5 mmHg per decade in women; women averaged 0.4 mmHg higher than men, significant only from the 31-40 age group onward.
cards.watchOut: The oldest of the three datasets (1996) and the only one printing the full frequency bands — its above-21 mmHg fraction (about 1 in 28 healthy people) is the card's key number, and it comes from a screened-healthy sample, not a glaucoma clinic.
cards.source: Qureshi IA et al. Distribution of intraocular pressure among healthy Pakistani. The Chinese journal of physiology. 1996. PMID: 8955565. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Synthesis of the three population datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong ocular physiology (framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). Tehran (n=3,834): mean 14.5 (SD 2.6) mmHg, 15.1 (2.9) at age 40 and over. Yazd (n=2,098, ages 40-80): mean 14.2 ± 2.5 mmHg by Goldmann applanation, rising with age and corneal thickness. Karachi (n=7,201): means about 14.3-14.8 mmHg, 83-85% of healthy people between 11 and 18 mmHg, and 3.5% of men / 3.7% of women above the conventional 21 mmHg upper limit. The within-person diurnal swing and aqueous-humour dynamics are homed at pack #6436 and are not re-carded here; ocular biometry is a different measurement. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the populations studied; ancestry breadth is limited (two Iranian datasets, one Pakistani) and the ranges must not be generalised past that without further population data.
cards.watchOut: Tonometry method and glaucoma-exclusion rules differ by study and are printed per card; a single IOP reading also carries the diurnal swing homed at pack #6436.

shelves.title: IOPI tongue strength and endurance norms: anterior maximum 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa and posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa in Taiwan adults; Korean strength falls from 46.7 kPa (young men) to 35.2 kPa over 60; Belgian strength lower after 70
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are maximum tongue strength and endurance — anterior and posterior, measured with the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (IOPI) — by age and sex, and how much do bulb position, visual feedback and testing order move the values used to judge lingual weakness in dysphagia assessment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength/physiology · Pressure · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Tongue/physiology · Young Adult · Taiwan
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep, gastrointestinal and swallowing sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three independent populations, ONE instrument (the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument, IOPI) — the values are instrument-specific and must not be generalised to other tongue-pressure devices. Belgian lifespan data (420 healthy adults): strength falls after age 70, endurance stays stable through most of life, anterior tongue exceeds posterior on both. Taiwan data (150 healthy adults) print the numbers: anterior maximum isometric pressure 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa, posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa, anterior endurance 13.86 ± 7.08 s, posterior 10.06 ± 5.40 s, with 33 kPa proposed in that study as a demarcation of weak tongue strength. Korean data (120 healthy adults, 40 per age band): young men averaged 46.7 ± 10.2 kPa maximal tongue strength vs 32.1 ± 7.9 kPa in young women, falling to 35.2 ± 9.0 and 34.5 ± 6.9 kPa in the over-60s. Strength and endurance are different measures and are carded separately. The stamp is graded down: one dataset's record prints no numeric pressures, and the Korean age-band Ns are modest (120 total across six age-by-sex cells). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

cards.headline: Belgian lifespan norms (Vanderwegen 2013): 420 healthy adults — tongue strength significantly lower after age 70 at both bulb positions, endurance stable through most of life; anterior tongue stronger and longer-enduring than posterior
cards.summary: Belgian lifespan norms (Vanderwegen 2013): 420 healthy adults — tongue strength significantly lower after age 70 at both bulb positions, endurance stable through most of life; anterior tongue stronger and longer-enduring than posterior
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (IOPI tongue strength and endurance norms, Belgian lifespan cohort)
cards.people: 420 healthy Belgian adults across the adult lifespan, measured with the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (IOPI) for maximum anterior and posterior tongue strength and endurance, with age, sex, bulb position, visual feedback and order of testing examined as influences.
cards.result: Older participants (over 70 years) demonstrated significantly lower strength than younger persons at the anterior and posterior tongue. Endurance remains stable throughout the major part of life. Sex influence remains significant but minor throughout life, with men showing higher pressures and longer endurance. The anterior part of the tongue has both higher strength and longer endurance than the posterior part. Mean maximum tongue pressures in this European population seem to be lower than American values and closer to Asian results, as published. The fetched record states these patterns without printing the numeric pressure values, and this card claims none.

cards.headline: Taiwan norms (Wu 2020): 150 healthy adults — anterior tongue maximum isometric pressure 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa, posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa; endurance 13.86 ± 7.08 s anterior, 10.06 ± 5.40 s posterior; 33 kPa proposed as the weak-strength demarcation
cards.summary: Taiwan norms (Wu 2020): 150 healthy adults — anterior tongue maximum isometric pressure 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa, posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa; endurance 13.86 ± 7.08 s anterior, 10.06 ± 5.40 s posterior; 33 kPa proposed as the weak-strength demarcation
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (IOPI labial and lingual strength norms, Taiwan)
cards.people: 150 healthy Chinese adults in Taiwan; 11 labial and lingual parameters measured with the IOPI, each three times, with the maximal value of three trials taken as the pressure for each parameter; tasks included maximum isometric pressure and saliva and water swallowing pressures.
cards.result: Mean (± SD) maximum isometric pressures were 24.81 ± 5.64 kPa for the lips, 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa for the anterior tongue and 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa for the posterior tongue — posterior tongue strength about 5% below anterior. Swallowing pressures were 85% (saliva) and 80% (water) of maximum for the anterior tongue, and 90% and 81% for the posterior tongue. Average endurance was 13.86 ± 7.08 s (anterior) and 10.06 ± 5.40 s (posterior). Maximum isometric pressures exceeded both swallowing pressures, and saliva swallowing pressures exceeded water. A value of 33 kPa in maximum isometric pressure could serve as a demarcation of weak tongue strength for healthy Chinese adults, as published. No statistically significant differences were found across the repeated trials for any parameter.
cards.watchOut: The 33 kPa demarcation is this study's proposal for healthy Chinese adults, not a validated dysphagia cut-off; swallowing pressures are percentages of maximum, so a weak maximum compresses the whole scale.

cards.headline: Korean norms (Jeong 2017): 120 healthy adults in three age bands — maximal tongue strength 46.7 ± 10.2 kPa in young men and 32.1 ± 7.9 kPa in young women, falling to 35.2 ± 9.0 and 34.5 ± 6.9 kPa over 60; tongue endurance fell from 28.8 s (young men) to 15.8 s
cards.summary: Korean norms (Jeong 2017): 120 healthy adults in three age bands — maximal tongue strength 46.7 ± 10.2 kPa in young men and 32.1 ± 7.9 kPa in young women, falling to 35.2 ± 9.0 and 34.5 ± 6.9 kPa over 60; tongue endurance fell from 28.8 s (young men) to 15.8 s
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (IOPI tongue, lip and cheek norms, Korean age bands)
cards.people: 120 healthy Korean subjects divided into three age groups (young 20-39, middle-aged 40-59, older over 60) and by sex — about 20 per age-by-sex cell, as published — measured with the IOPI for maximal strength and endurance of tongue, lip and cheek.
cards.result: Mean maximal tongue strength: young men 46.7 ± 10.2 kPa and women 32.1 ± 7.9 kPa; middle-aged men 40.9 ± 9.3 and women 36.9 ± 8.6 kPa; older men 35.2 ± 9.0 and women 34.5 ± 6.9 kPa. Mean tongue endurance: young men 28.8 ± 12.6 s and women 20.8 ± 13.5 s; middle-aged men 17.0 ± 8.5 and women 15.3 ± 5.2 s; older men 15.8 ± 6.7 and women 17.9 ± 8.1 s. Lip and cheek strength and endurance values are reported in the same record; the tongue values are the ones carded here.
cards.watchOut: Modest age-band Ns (120 total across six age-by-sex cells) are printed on the face; the record carries no MeSH terms (see source line). The young sex gap (men about 15 kPa higher) largely closes by the over-60 band — a pattern the Belgian card's 'minor sex influence' summary does not show, and the two are printed side by side rather than averaged.

cards.headline: Synthesis: IOPI tongue norms from three populations agree that anterior exceeds posterior, strength falls with age (after 70 in Belgium; band by band in Korea) and endurance is the more fragile measure in the Korean data — all values are IOPI-specific
cards.summary: Synthesis: IOPI tongue norms from three populations agree that anterior exceeds posterior, strength falls with age (after 70 in Belgium; band by band in Korea) and endurance is the more fragile measure in the Korean data — all values are IOPI-specific
cards.people: Synthesis of the three population datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep (gastrointestinal / swallowing sections; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature). Taiwan prints the reference numbers (anterior maximum 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa, posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa; endurance 13.86 and 10.06 s). Korea prints the age-by-sex gradient (young men 46.7 kPa falling to 35.2 kPa over 60; endurance roughly halving). Belgium (420 adults) supplies the lifespan pattern — strength lower after 70, endurance stable through most of life — without numeric pressures in its record. High-resolution pharyngeal manometry is a different measurement and is not carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: three genuine datasets on one instrument, but one prints no numbers in its record, the Korean cells are modest, and no value transfers to a non-IOPI device.
cards.watchOut: Strength and endurance are different measures, carded separately throughout; bulb position (anterior vs posterior) is part of every value.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Normal optic nerve sheath diameter: healthy means span 3.68 mm to 6.3 mm by ultrasound (CT 5.28 mm; pooled 4.78 mm) — the disagreement is the finding
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the normal optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) — mean and upper range in millimetres, measured 3 mm behind the globe — by measurement method (transorbital ultrasound vs computed tomography), sex and eyeball size, and how wide is the disagreement between published "normal" values that the raised-intracranial-pressure thresholds are built on?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Body Weight · Female · Healthy Volunteers · Humans · Intracranial Pressure · Male · Middle Aged · Optic Nerve · Regression Analysis · Sex Factors · Ultrasonography · Young Adult · Cross-Sectional Studies · Iran · Reference Values · Asian People · China · Retrospective Studies · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Algorithms
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cerebrospinal-fluid / intracranial-pressure sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary sonographic reference literature, and says so. The between-study spread IS the finding: published healthy mean optic nerve sheath diameters span 3.68 mm (ultrasound, 120 volunteers) to 6.3 mm (ultrasound, 100 South Iranian adults) — a 2.6 mm gap, wider than the distance between 'normal' and most raised-intracranial-pressure cut-offs in clinical use. A CT dataset (360 Chinese adults) sits between them at 5.28 mm measured 3 mm behind the globe and 4.34 mm at 10 mm, so measurement position is part of the number. The meta-analytic pooled transorbital-sonography mean across 39 studies and 2,927 volunteers is 4.78 mm (95% CI 4.63 to 4.94) with substantial heterogeneity (I² 50.6%), attributed by its authors in part to differing measurement methods. No single normal value may be printed without its method and population; ultrasound and CT values are carded per method and never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the datasets are real and independent, but they do not converge on a transferable normal value, which is precisely the shelf's content.

cards.headline: Ultrasound, 120 healthy volunteers (Goeres 2016): mean ONSD 3.68 mm (95% CI 2.85 to 4.40) — men 3.78 mm vs women 3.60 mm; no relationship with age, weight or height
cards.summary: Ultrasound, 120 healthy volunteers (Goeres 2016): mean ONSD 3.68 mm (95% CI 2.85 to 4.40) — men 3.78 mm vs women 3.60 mm; no relationship with age, weight or height
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transorbital ultrasound ONSD, healthy volunteers)
cards.people: 120 healthy adult volunteers (age 18–65, mean 29.3 years; 55 men, 65 women); optic nerve sheath diameter measured by ultrasound, with regression analysis against sex, age, height and weight.
cards.result: Mean ONSD was 3.68 mm (95% CI 2.85 to 4.40). On regression analysis, mean ONSD did not vary with age, weight or height but did vary with sex: men 3.78 mm (95% CI 3.23 to 4.48) versus women 3.60 mm (95% CI 2.83 to 4.11) — the authors suggested separate reference ranges for men and women may be needed. This is the lowest healthy mean on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A young volunteer sample (mean age 29.3) measured by one ultrasound protocol: its 3.68 mm mean sits 2.6 mm below the 2025 Iranian ultrasound mean on this shelf — the two cannot both be a universal normal, and neither is printed as one.
cards.source: Goeres P et al. Ultrasound assessment of optic nerve sheath diameter in healthy volunteers. Journal of critical care. 2016. PMID: 26596508. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ultrasound, 100 healthy South Iranian adults (Mohammadi 2025): mean ONSD 6.3 ± 0.42 mm measured 3 mm behind the globe — roughly 2.6 mm above the 2016 ultrasound mean, with no demographic or anthropometric correlation
cards.summary: Ultrasound, 100 healthy South Iranian adults (Mohammadi 2025): mean ONSD 6.3 ± 0.42 mm measured 3 mm behind the globe — roughly 2.6 mm above the 2016 ultrasound mean, with no demographic or anthropometric correlation
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transorbital ultrasound ONSD, healthy adults, South Iran)
cards.people: 100 healthy South Iranian adults (mean age 38.7 ± 9.8 years; 60 women); the left optic nerve sheath measured by ultrasound 3 mm behind the globe in two planes and averaged; mean axial (eyeball) length 23.53 ± 0.94 mm.
cards.result: The mean ONSD was 6.3 mm (SD ± 0.42) — reported by the authors as a mean in their results (their abstract also phrases 6.3 mm in upper-limit language; this card cards the value as a mean, as the results state). No significant correlation was found between ONSD and demographic or anthropometric factors (P = 0.236). This is the highest healthy mean on this shelf, from the same measurement family (transorbital ultrasound) as the lowest.
cards.watchOut: A single-eye (left), single-centre dataset whose mean exceeds many published raised-pressure thresholds: it demonstrates that technique and population dominate this measurement, and it must not be read as evidence that 6.3 mm is a transferable normal mean.
cards.source: Mohammadi A et al. Optic nerve sheath diameter measurement in healthy South Iranian adults from a cross-sectional ultrasonographic study. Scientific reports. 2025. PMID: 40389493. cards.headline: CT, 360 healthy Chinese adults (Han 2025): mean ONSD 5.28 mm at 3 mm behind the globe vs 4.34 mm at 10 mm — sex and eyeball transverse diameter were the influencing factors
cards.summary: CT, 360 healthy Chinese adults (Han 2025): mean ONSD 5.28 mm at 3 mm behind the globe vs 4.34 mm at 10 mm — sex and eyeball transverse diameter were the influencing factors
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (CT ONSD at 3 mm and 10 mm, healthy adults, China)
cards.people: 360 healthy Chinese adults (180 men, 180 women; median age 48.5 years) who underwent head CT at one hospital, March 2022 to May 2023 (retrospective study); eyeball transverse diameter (ETD) and ONSD at 3 mm and 10 mm behind the eyeball measured in both eyes.
cards.result: Mean ONSD was 5.28 mm (95% CI 5.23 to 5.32) at 3 mm behind the globe and 4.34 mm (95% CI 4.30 to 4.37) at 10 mm — the same heads give values almost 1 mm apart by measurement position alone. Mean ETD was 22.47 mm (95% CI 22.38 to 22.56); the ONSD/ETD ratio averaged 0.24 at 3 mm and 0.19 at 10 mm. Sex and ETD were influencing factors in univariate and multivariate regression (all parameters larger in men, P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: CT values are carded as CT values: they sit between the two ultrasound means on this shelf, but method, position (3 mm vs 10 mm) and population all move together here, so this dataset cannot arbitrate between the ultrasound studies.
cards.source: Han L et al. Related studies on measuring the normal values of optic nerve sheath diameter in healthy Chinese adults based on CT scans. Scientific reports. 2025. PMID: 39905072. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of transorbital sonography (Schroeder 2020): pooled healthy ONSD 4.78 mm (95% CI 4.63 to 4.94) across 39 studies and 2,927 volunteers — with substantial heterogeneity (I² 50.6%) attributed in part to differing measurement methods
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of transorbital sonography (Schroeder 2020): pooled healthy ONSD 4.78 mm (95% CI 4.63 to 4.94) across 39 studies and 2,927 volunteers — with substantial heterogeneity (I² 50.6%) attributed in part to differing measurement methods
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (transorbital sonography ONSD/OND reference values)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of transorbital sonography studies in adults without elevated intracranial pressure: 39 studies, 2,927 healthy volunteers (mean age 36.1 years, 44.4% women), 5,854 eyes; 34 studies contributed ONSD means and 13 optic nerve diameter means.
cards.result: The pooled mean ONSD was 4.78 mm (95% CI 4.63 to 4.94), with substantial heterogeneity between studies (I² = 50.6%); the pooled optic nerve diameter was 3.08 mm (95% CI 2.9 to 3.25, I² = 12.7%). Subgroup analyses found no significant differences by geographic continent (P = 0.139), age (P = 0.824) or sex (P = 0.093). The authors note that different measuring methods of ONSD result in higher heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: A pooled mean over heterogeneous methods is a description of the literature, not a clinical cut-off: with I² of 50.6% and primary means on this shelf spanning 3.68 to 6.3 mm, the pooled 4.78 mm must always travel with its spread.
cards.source: Schroeder C et al. Quantification of Optic Nerve and Sheath Diameter by Transorbital Sonography: A Systematic Review and Metanalysis. cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy ONSD means span 3.68 to 6.3 mm by ultrasound alone, with CT at 5.28 mm (3 mm position) and a pooled sonographic mean of 4.78 mm — there is no method-free 'normal ONSD', and raised-pressure thresholds inherit this disagreement

cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (cerebrospinal-fluid / intracranial-pressure sections; the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary sonographic reference literature). The primary datasets disagree by more than the clinical margin the measurement is asked to resolve: ultrasound means of 3.68 mm (Goeres 2016, 120 volunteers) and 6.3 mm (Mohammadi 2025, 100 adults); CT means of 5.28 mm at 3 mm and 4.34 mm at 10 mm behind the globe (Han 2025, 360 adults); and a 39-study pooled sonographic mean of 4.78 mm with substantial heterogeneity (Schroeder 2020). Sex and eyeball size shift values in the larger datasets. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the normative literature is real but non-convergent — any ONSD number used clinically must carry its method, its measurement position and its population, as printed on each card.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a raised-intracranial-pressure ONSD threshold without the normal-value method it was built against: the healthy means on this shelf differ by up to 2.6 mm within a single method family.
