shelves.title: Topical paromomycin for cutaneous leishmaniasis: ulcerative lesions respond (vs vehicle in two trials), non-ulcerative disease does not — and Panama had no vehicle arm
shelves.question: In patients with cutaneous leishmaniasis, does topical 15% paromomycin — alone, with gentamicin, or in an aquaphilic base — versus vehicle/placebo (or versus an intralesional active control) cure lesions, and does the answer differ between ulcerative and non-ulcerative disease?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gentamicins · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Leishmaniasis, Cutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Ointments · Paromomycin · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — lesion type and species decide the answer, and the trials are never pooled. For ulcerative lesions, topical 15% paromomycin beat vehicle in Tunisia (cure 81-82% versus 58%) and in Bolivia (77.5% versus 10%) — note how much natural history varies by species and setting (vehicle cure 58% versus 10%), so the absolute benefit is setting-dependent and is printed per trial, not averaged. The Panama trial compared the two active creams with each other (79% versus 78%) and has NO vehicle arm, so its cure rates cannot by themselves establish efficacy over natural healing. The one trial in non-ulcerative disease was negative. The tested formulations differ (WR 279,396 paromomycin-gentamicin cream; paromomycin in aquaphilic base; paromomycin with urea in white paraffin) and are named as the publications give them, under the clarification exception; other preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. No trial measures mucosal-leishmaniasis prevention or scarring — lesion cure only.

cards.headline: Tunisian phase 3 RCT (Ben Salah 2013): topical paromomycin cured ulcerative L. major lesions in 81-82% versus 58% on vehicle (P<0.001 for each active cream)
cards.summary: Tunisian phase 3 RCT (Ben Salah 2013): topical paromomycin cured ulcerative L. major lesions in 81-82% versus 58% on vehicle (P<0.001 for each active cream)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised vehicle-controlled trial, topical paromomycin +/- gentamicin (WR 279,396) vs vehicle, ulcerative L. major cutaneous leishmaniasis
cards.people: 375 patients with one to five ulcerative lesions from cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania major in Tunisia, randomised to a cream containing 15% paromomycin plus 0.5% gentamicin (called WR 279,396), 15% paromomycin alone, or vehicle control (the same base with neither drug); each lesion was treated once daily for 20 days, and any withdrawal counted as treatment failure.
cards.result: Cure of the index lesion — at least 50% size reduction by day 42, complete re-epithelialisation by day 98 and no relapse by day 168 — was 81% (95% CI 73 to 87) for paromomycin-gentamicin, 82% (95% CI 74 to 87) for paromomycin alone, and 58% (95% CI 50 to 67) for vehicle (P<0.001 for each active cream versus vehicle). Cure of the index lesion was accompanied by cure of all other lesions except in five patients. Mild-to-moderate application-site reactions were more frequent in the paromomycin groups than on vehicle.
cards.watchOut: The vehicle arm itself cured 58% — natural healing is high in this species and setting, so the absolute benefit here (about 23-24 percentage points) is setting-specific and must not be averaged with the Bolivian trial's very different vehicle rate.
cards.source: Ben Salah A et al. Topical paromomycin with or without gentamicin for cutaneous leishmaniasis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23388004. Registry ID: NCT00606580. cards.headline: Panamanian phase 3 RCT (Sosa 2019): paromomycin-gentamicin cured 79% versus 78% for paromomycin alone (P=0.84) — NO vehicle arm, labelled as such
cards.summary: Panamanian phase 3 RCT (Sosa 2019): paromomycin-gentamicin cured 79% versus 78% for paromomycin alone (P=0.84) — NO vehicle arm, labelled as such
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial, topical paromomycin-gentamicin vs paromomycin alone, New World cutaneous leishmaniasis (predominantly L. panamensis) — no vehicle arm
cards.people: 399 patients with one to ten cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions, primarily caused by Leishmania panamensis, in a randomised double-blind phase 3 trial in Panama; both creams were applied once daily for 20 days, and the primary endpoint was clinical cure of an index lesion confirmed to contain Leishmania, with no relapse.
cards.result: Clinical cure of the index lesion was 79% (95% CI 72 to 84) on paromomycin-gentamicin and 78% (95% CI 74 to 87) on paromomycin alone (P=0.84) — superiority of the combination cream was not demonstrated. The most common related adverse events were mild-to-moderate dermatitis, pain and pruritus. The authors note the roughly 80% cure rates for both creams were similar to those in Tunisia and to previously reported parenteral antimonial results.
cards.watchOut: No vehicle or placebo comparator: this trial compares two active creams and cannot by itself establish efficacy over natural healing. Its ~79% cure rates must never be quoted as efficacy over placebo. (The record's MeSH includes Leishmania major and Tunisia from the programme's earlier trial; the Panama population was predominantly L. panamensis, as the abstract states.)
cards.source: Sosa N et al. Topical paromomycin for New World cutaneous leishmaniasis. PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 2019. PMID: 31048871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bolivian RCT (Soto 2019): paromomycin-aquaphilic cured 77.5% versus 10% on vehicle (P<0.0001) in L. braziliensis disease, comparable to the intralesional-pentamidine positive control (70%)
cards.summary: Bolivian RCT (Soto 2019): paromomycin-aquaphilic cured 77.5% versus 10% on vehicle (P<0.0001) in L. braziliensis disease, comparable to the intralesional-pentamidine positive control (70%)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, topical paromomycin-aquaphilic vs vehicle vs intralesional pentamidine, L. braziliensis cutaneous leishmaniasis
cards.people: 80 patients with cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania braziliensis in Bolivia, randomised to 15% paromomycin in aquaphilic base (40 patients), aquaphilic vehicle (20 patients), or a positive control of intralesional pentamidine (20 patients), with cure assessed after 6 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Cure rates were 31/40 (77.5%, 95% CI 62.5 to 88) on paromomycin-aquaphilic, 2/20 (10%, 95% CI 3 to 30) on vehicle (P<0.0001 versus paromomycin-aquaphilic), and 14/20 (70%, 95% CI 48 to 85.5) on intralesional pentamidine. Both paromomycin-aquaphilic and the vehicle were very well tolerated, with only grade 1 adverse reactions in 5-10% of patients.
cards.watchOut: The vehicle cure rate here is 10% — the mirror image of Tunisia's 58%. The same cream's absolute benefit therefore depends entirely on species and setting; per-trial printing is mandatory and pooling is not done on this shelf.
cards.source: Soto J et al. Topical 15% Paromomycin-Aquaphilic for Bolivian Leishmania braziliensis Cutaneous Leishmaniasis: A Randomized, Placebo-controlled Trial. cards.headline: Honduran non-ulcerative RCT (Neva 1997): topical paromomycin was NOT effective in non-ulcerating cutaneous leishmaniasis — the programme's negative limb, in a different lesion type
cards.summary: Honduran non-ulcerative RCT (Neva 1997): topical paromomycin was NOT effective in non-ulcerating cutaneous leishmaniasis — the programme's negative limb, in a different lesion type
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, topical paromomycin + urea vs placebo, non-ulcerative cutaneous leishmaniasis (n=53) — negative limb
cards.people: 53 patients with non-ulcerating cutaneous leishmaniasis in Honduras, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of topical 15% paromomycin (aminosidine) with 10% urea in white paraffin versus placebo, at two study sites.
cards.result: The treatment was not effective — the fetched record reports no cure-rate advantage for topical paromomycin in this non-ulcerating disease, and prints no cure rates. Two unexpected findings emerged: Leishmania mexicana was found to be the cause of many lesions at one site (the first documented report of L. mexicana in Honduras), and those lesions were clinically indistinguishable from lesions caused by L. chagasi, the agent previously found for this form of leishmaniasis.
cards.watchOut: A different lesion type (non-ulcerative) and different species mix from the ulcerative trials — its negative result limits the indication, it does not cancel the ulcerative results, and the ulcerative results do not rescue it. The record prints no cure rates and none are claimed.
cards.source: Neva FA et al. Non-ulcerative cutaneous leishmaniasis in Honduras fails to respond to topical paromomycin. Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 1997. shelves.title: Braden scale: AUC 0.82 in general hospital studies, but specificity 0.28 in ICU and sensitivity 0.42 in surgical patients — one scale, three different tests
shelves.question: In hospitalised and critically ill adults, how well does the Braden scale (sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction / shear) predict who will develop a pressure injury — what are its pooled sensitivity, specificity and discrimination at the usual cut-offs, what cut-off performs best, and how badly does its performance fall in surgical and intensive-care populations?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Crush Injuries · Humans · Middle Aged · Pressure Ulcer · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Critical Care · Incidence · Intensive Care Units · Predictive Value of Tests · Surgical Procedures, Operative
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate overall, and sharply setting-dependent. Across 60 general hospital studies (49,326 individuals) the Braden scale pools at sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72 and AUC 0.82, with 18 the optimal cut-off in that one analysis. The same scale in ICU (11 studies, 10,044 patients) over-flags — sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.28, AUC 0.78 — and in surgical patients (3 studies, 609 patients) under-detects — sensitivity 0.42, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.69, with the authors concluding it cannot be used alone there. No pooled figure stands without its setting, and no card implies scoring or score-allocated prevention reduces injuries.

cards.headline: General-hospital meta-analysis (60 studies, 49,326 individuals): pooled sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72, AUC 0.82 — with 18 the optimal cut-off, and higher AUCs in prospective, hospital and younger-mean-age subgroups
cards.summary: General-hospital meta-analysis (60 studies, 49,326 individuals): pooled sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72, AUC 0.82 — with 18 the optimal cut-off, and higher AUCs in prospective, hospital and younger-mean-age subgroups
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of Braden scale predictive validity (60 studies, 49,326 individuals)
cards.people: 60 studies involving 49,326 individuals, published 1973–2020 and indexed in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, with two reviewers selecting studies independently and heterogeneity acknowledged across differing cut-offs.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.82), specificity 0.72 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.78), positive likelihood ratio 2.80, negative likelihood ratio 0.30, diagnostic odds ratio 9.00 and AUC 0.82 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.85). Subgroup AUCs were higher for prospective design (0.84), mean age under 60 years (0.87), hospital setting (0.82) and Caucasian populations (0.86); 18 was found to be the optimal cut-off value. The authors conclude the Braden scale has moderate predictive validity, with significant heterogeneity from differing cut-offs.
cards.watchOut: Cut-off 18 is a pooled optimum from this one meta-analysis, not a universal rule, and prints as such; the pooled pair averages over studies that themselves used different cut-offs, which is the stated source of heterogeneity.
cards.source: Huang C et al. Predictive validity of the braden scale for pressure injury risk assessment in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Nursing open. 2021. PMID: 33630407. cards.headline: ICU meta-analysis (11 studies, 10,044 patients, 1,058 with pressure ulcers): pooled sensitivity 0.89 but specificity only 0.28, AUC 0.78
cards.summary: ICU meta-analysis (11 studies, 10,044 patients, 1,058 with pressure ulcers): pooled sensitivity 0.89 but specificity only 0.28, AUC 0.78
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of Braden scale predictive validity in critical care (11 studies, 10,044 patients)
cards.people: 11 full-text studies of adult ICU patients (10,044 patients, comprising 1,058 patients with pressure ulcers), from English and Chinese databases and grey literature, quality scored with QUADAS-2, with meta-regression on blinding, study design and cut-off value.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity of the Braden scale for predicting pressure-ulcer risk in ICU adults was 0.89 (95% CI 0.87 to 0.91) but pooled specificity only 0.28 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.29), with a pooled diagnostic odds ratio of 6.29 (95% CI 4.09 to 9.68) and overall weighted AUC 0.7812 (95% CI 0.7163 to 0.8461). Heterogeneity was significant; meta-regression found no heterogeneity explained by blinding (P = 0.074), study design (P = 0.679) or cut-off value (P = 0.821). The authors conclude the scale has moderate predictive validity in ICU patients — good sensitivity, low specificity — and that modification or a new tool is warranted for ICU use.
cards.watchOut: In ICU the scale flags almost everyone: specificity of 0.28 means most patients it labels at-risk will not develop an ulcer, so an ICU pooled figure must never be printed without its setting — the same scale reads very differently on the general-hospital card above.
cards.source: Wei M et al. Predictive Validity of the Braden Scale for Pressure Ulcer Risk in Critical Care: A Meta-Analysis. Nursing in critical care. 2020. PMID: 31985893. cards.headline: Surgical-patient meta-analysis (3 studies, 609 patients): pooled sensitivity 0.42 and specificity 0.84, AUC 0.69 — the authors conclude the scale cannot be used alone in surgical patients
cards.summary: Surgical-patient meta-analysis (3 studies, 609 patients): pooled sensitivity 0.42 and specificity 0.84, AUC 0.69 — the authors conclude the scale cannot be used alone in surgical patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of Braden scale predictive validity in surgical patients (3 studies, 609 patients)
cards.people: 3 clinical studies (609 surgical patients) meeting inclusion criteria (sensitivity / specificity reported or calculable), found in PubMed and Web of Science through July 2011, with study quality assessed using the 14-item QUADAS instrument and two-by-two tables constructed from each article.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.42 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.47) and pooled specificity 0.84 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.85), with a combined diagnostic odds ratio of 4.40 (95% CI 2.98 to 6.50), area under the ROC curve 0.6921 and Q* 0.6466. Heterogeneity was significant. The authors conclude the Braden scale has low predictive validity for pressure-ulcer risk in surgical patients, cannot be used alone there, and that a new scale for surgical patients should be developed and tested.
cards.watchOut: The smallest base on this shelf (3 studies, 609 patients) and the mirror image of the ICU result — here the scale misses most cases (sensitivity 0.42) rather than over-flagging them; setting, not the scale alone, determines which failure mode appears.
cards.source: He W et al. ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿The Braden Scale cannot be used alone for assessing pressure ulcer risk in surgical patients: a meta-analysis. Ostomy/wound management. 2012. PMID: 22316631. cards.headline: Synthesis: one scale, three settings, three different tests — AUC 0.82 (sensitivity 0.78 / specificity 0.72) in general hospital studies, sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.28 in ICU, and sensitivity 0.42 / specificity 0.84 (AUC 0.69) in surgical patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: one scale, three settings, three different tests — AUC 0.82 (sensitivity 0.78 / specificity 0.72) in general hospital studies, sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.28 in ICU, and sensitivity 0.42 / specificity 0.84 (AUC 0.69) in surgical patients
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The setting gradient is the content. Across 60 general studies (49,326 individuals) the Braden scale pools at sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72 and AUC 0.82, with 18 the optimal cut-off in that analysis. In ICU (11 studies, 10,044 patients) it over-flags: sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.28, AUC 0.78. In surgical patients (3 studies, 609 patients) it under-detects: sensitivity 0.42, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.69, with the authors concluding it cannot be used alone there. No pooled figure may be printed without its setting. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf about risk prediction only: it proposes no prevention intervention and no card shows that scoring, or any prevention allocated by score, reduces pressure injuries.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each meta-analysis's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ruboxistaurin (never marketed): visual loss 5.5% vs 9.1% in PKC-DRS2, but PKC-DMES missed its macular-edema primary endpoint
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic retinopathy or diabetic macular edema, does the oral protein kinase C-β inhibitor ruboxistaurin, compared with placebo, reduce sustained moderate visual loss and delay progression to sight-threatening macular edema (the PKC-DRS / PKC-DMES programme)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Diabetic Retinopathy/drug therapy · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Indoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Macular Edema/drug therapy,physiopathology · Male · Maleimides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Protein Kinase C/antagonists & inhibitors · Protein Kinase C beta · Vision Disorders/prevention & control · Visual Acuity/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/complications · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetic Retinopathy/drug therapy,physiopathology,surgery · Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Indoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Laser Coagulation · Macular Edema/drug therapy,physiopathology,surgery · Maleimides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity · Macular Edema/complications · Vision Disorders/etiology,physiopathology · Visual Acuity/physiology · Young Adult · Diabetic Retinopathy/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology · Macular Edema/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology · Sickness Impact Profile · Surveys and Questionnaires · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Vision Disorders/diagnosis,drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sustained moderate visual loss only, on one never-marketed programme. Ruboxistaurin was never marketed: it was refused / left unapproved after regulatory review despite the visual-loss signal, and that flag leads. PKC-DRS2 (685 randomised) found sustained moderate visual loss in 5.5% on ruboxistaurin vs 9.1% on placebo (P = 0.034) — a 40% relative risk reduction but only 3.6 percentage points absolute. The one trial with a macular-edema primary endpoint, PKC-DMES (686 randomised), MISSED that primary endpoint (P = 0.14; adjusted HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.0). Two of the four reports are combined analyses overlapping the individual trials (6.1% vs 10.2%; 2.3% vs 4.4%, not significant) — the base is one programme, never four independent trials. All trials predate anti-VEGF therapy.

cards.headline: PKC-DRS2 (Aiello 2006): sustained moderate visual loss in 5.5% on ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day vs 9.1% on placebo over 36 months (P = 0.034) — a 40% relative risk reduction, 3.6 percentage points absolute
cards.summary: PKC-DRS2 (Aiello 2006): sustained moderate visual loss in 5.5% on ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day vs 9.1% on placebo over 36 months (P = 0.034) — a 40% relative risk reduction, 3.6 percentage points absolute
cards.type: Randomised double-masked placebo-controlled trial (PKC-DRS2), ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day vs placebo, 36 months
cards.people: 685 patients randomised at 70 clinical sites with moderately severe to very severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (ETDRS level ≥47A to ≤53E), best-corrected acuity ≥45 letters and no prior panretinal photocoagulation in at least one eye; oral ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day vs placebo for 36 months.
cards.result: Sustained moderate visual loss (≥15-letter ETDRS loss maintained ≥6 months) occurred in 5.5% of ruboxistaurin-treated patients vs 9.1% on placebo (P = 0.034) — the abstract's '40% risk reduction' is a relative measure; the absolute difference is 3.6 percentage points. ≥15-letter worsening was less frequent (6.7% vs 9.9%) and ≥15-letter improvement more frequent (4.9% vs 2.4%) on ruboxistaurin (P = 0.005 for the combined comparison). When baseline macular edema was >100 µm from the macular centre, ruboxistaurin was associated with less progression of edema to within 100 µm, and initial laser treatment for macular edema was 26% relatively less frequent (P = 0.008).
cards.watchOut: The programme's one clearly positive primary-outcome trial — but event rates are low (5.5–9.1%), the drug was never marketed, and the trial predates anti-VEGF therapy entirely; no comparison with any current standard exists.
cards.source: Aiello LP et al. Effect of ruboxistaurin on visual loss in patients with diabetic retinopathy. Ophthalmology. 2006. PMID: 16989901. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PKC-DMES (PKC-DMES Study Group 2007): the macular-edema primary outcome was NOT significantly delayed — progression to sight-threatening edema or photocoagulation, P = 0.14 unadjusted; adjusted HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.0), P = 0.06
cards.summary: PKC-DMES (PKC-DMES Study Group 2007): the macular-edema primary outcome was NOT significantly delayed — progression to sight-threatening edema or photocoagulation, P = 0.14 unadjusted; adjusted HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.0), P = 0.06
cards.type: Randomised double-masked placebo-controlled trial (PKC-DMES), ruboxistaurin vs placebo, 30 months — primary outcome missed
cards.people: 686 patients with diabetic macular edema farther than 300 µm from the macular centre, ETDRS retinopathy level 20 to 47A without prior photocoagulation and acuity ≥75 letters; oral ruboxistaurin 4, 16 or 32 mg/day vs placebo for 30 months.
cards.result: The primary outcome — progression to sight-threatening macular edema or application of focal/grid photocoagulation — was NOT significantly delayed by 32 mg ruboxistaurin vs placebo (P = 0.14 unadjusted; covariate-adjusted hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.0, P = 0.06; a hazard ratio is a relative measure). A secondary analysis of progression to sight-threatening edema alone favoured 32 mg (adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93, P = 0.02), and application of photocoagulation before progression varied by site. Ruboxistaurin was well tolerated. The authors conclude only that daily oral ruboxistaurin may delay progression of edema to a sight-threatening stage.
cards.watchOut: This is the one trial in the programme with a macular-edema primary endpoint, and it missed it: the secondary sight-threatening-edema analysis (HR 0.66) must never be printed as the trial's result without the missed primary beside it.
cards.source: PKC-DMES Study Group et al. Effect of ruboxistaurin in patients with diabetic macular edema: thirty-month results of the randomized PKC-DMES clinical trial. cards.headline: Combined analysis of PKC-DRS and PKC-DRS2 (Aiello 2011) — a combined analysis of two trials, not an independent trial: sustained moderate visual loss 6.1% on ruboxistaurin vs 10.2% on placebo (P = 0.011) in 813 patients (1,392 eyes)
cards.summary: Combined analysis of PKC-DRS and PKC-DRS2 (Aiello 2011) — a combined analysis of two trials, not an independent trial: sustained moderate visual loss 6.1% on ruboxistaurin vs 10.2% on placebo (P = 0.011) in 813 patients (1,392 eyes)
cards.type: Combined analysis of the PKC-DRS and PKC-DRS2 randomised trials (same programme — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 813 patients (412 ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day, 401 placebo; 1,392 eyes) with moderately severe to very severe nonproliferative retinopathy pooled from the two 3-year PKC-DRS programme trials. Labelled on its face as a combined analysis — it adds no new randomised patients beyond the programme's retinopathy trials.
cards.result: In the combined data, sustained moderate visual loss occurred in 6.1% of ruboxistaurin-treated patients vs 10.2% on placebo (P = 0.011) — an absolute difference of 4.1 percentage points. A ≥15-letter gain occurred in 4.7% vs 2.4% of eyes (P = 0.021) and a ≥15-letter loss in 7.4% vs 11.4% (P = 0.012). Among eyes without baseline focal/grid photocoagulation, fewer ruboxistaurin eyes required initial photocoagulation (26.7% vs 35.6%; P = 0.008). Diabetic macular edema was the probable primary cause of vision loss, and no safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Pooling two similar trials sharpens the visual-loss estimate but cannot create a second confirmation: the independent-trial base of this shelf is the retinopathy trials plus PKC-DMES, counted as one programme.

cards.headline: Prospectively defined combined analysis of MBDL/MBCU (Sheetz 2013) — also a combined analysis, labelled as such: sustained moderate visual loss 2.3% on ruboxistaurin vs 4.4% on placebo (P = 0.069), significant only in the ≥2-year subset (2.1% vs 4.4%, P = 0.045)
cards.summary: Prospectively defined combined analysis of MBDL/MBCU (Sheetz 2013) — also a combined analysis, labelled as such: sustained moderate visual loss 2.3% on ruboxistaurin vs 4.4% on placebo (P = 0.069), significant only in the ≥2-year subset (2.1% vs 4.4%, P = 0.045)
cards.type: Prospectively defined combined analysis of two phase 3 trials (MBDL/MBCU, same programme — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 1,028 patients (520 ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day, 508 placebo) from two phase 3 trials in milder retinopathy (ETDRS level 20 to 47D / 35B to 53E), baseline acuity ≥75 letters, no prior panretinal or focal photocoagulation in at least one eye; follow-up 3 years (MBDL) or 18–48 months (MBCU).
cards.result: Sustained moderate visual loss occurred in 2.3% on ruboxistaurin vs 4.4% on placebo (P = 0.069 — not significant); in patients with at least 2 years of follow-up (N = 825) it was 2.1% vs 4.4% (P = 0.045). Other acuity-related measures trended toward or reached significance for ruboxistaurin, but diabetic-macular-edema morphology measures (centre involvement, OCT centre thickness, focal photocoagulation) showed no consistent trend in either direction. Event rates were low and the authors note statistical significance was not achieved for the primary combined comparison.
cards.watchOut: In milder retinopathy the event rate halved (4.4% to 2.3%) yet the headline comparison missed significance — relative effects on a 2-percentage-point absolute base; the ≥2-year subset result is a subset, printed as such.
cards.source: Sheetz MJ et al. The effect of the oral PKC β inhibitor ruboxistaurin on vision loss in two phase 3 studies. Investigative ophthalmology & visual science. 2013. PMID: 23404115. cards.headline: Synthesis: a visual-loss signal across one programme — PKC-DRS2 positive (5.5% vs 9.1%), two combined analyses in the same direction (6.1% vs 10.2%; 2.3% vs 4.4%, NS) — while the one macular-edema-primary trial (PKC-DMES) missed its primary endpoint, and the drug was never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a visual-loss signal across one programme — PKC-DRS2 positive (5.5% vs 9.1%), two combined analyses in the same direction (6.1% vs 10.2%; 2.3% vs 4.4%, NS) — while the one macular-edema-primary trial (PKC-DMES) missed its primary endpoint, and the drug was never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Never marketed — the flag leads: ruboxistaurin was refused / left unapproved after regulatory review despite the visual-loss signal. The independent-trial base is one programme, not four trials: PKC-DRS2 (685 randomised) met its visual-loss outcome (sustained moderate visual loss 5.5% vs 9.1%, P = 0.034; 3.6 percentage points absolute); PKC-DMES (686 randomised) missed its macular-edema primary endpoint (P = 0.14; adjusted HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.0); and the two remaining reports are combined analyses overlapping those trials (PKC-DRS + DRS2: 6.1% vs 10.2%, P = 0.011; MBDL/MBCU: 2.3% vs 4.4%, P = 0.069). Absolute differences are 2–4 percentage points against the larger relative figures the abstracts headline. All trials predate anti-VEGF therapy; no comparison with any current standard exists, and the diabetic-neuropathy and albuminuria ruboxistaurin reports are different questions, not carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: combined analyses are labelled as combined analyses wherever they appear, and PKC-DMES's missed primary prints on the face of this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Cysteamine eye drops for corneal cystinosis: standard drops clear crystals and viscous 0.55% drops clear them faster — on small samples of 29, 16 and 31 patients
shelves.question: In patients with nephropathic cystinosis, do cysteamine eye drops, compared with placebo (fellow eye) or with a standard cysteamine formulation, clear corneal cystine crystals and reduce photophobia? (GAP-T: small-N formulation-comparison base — Ns 29 / 16 / 31 printed on the face; the only placebo-controlled evidence is the 1990 paired-eye trial.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Corneal Diseases/etiology,prevention & control · Crystallization · Cysteamine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cystinosis/complications,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Ophthalmic Solutions · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: GAP-T — small-N formulation-comparison base, labelled: the three reports enrol 29, 16 (efficacy study) and 31 patients, and the counts lead. The only placebo-controlled evidence is the 1990 paired-eye trial (10 clear responders of 29 entered); the other two reports compare formulations against each other, so this base shows standard cysteamine drops clear corneal crystals and a viscous formulation clears them faster — it does not contain a modern parallel-group placebo trial. Corneal crystal density is a surrogate for the visual outcomes patients care about; photophobia, improved in the viscous trial, is the only patient-felt endpoint in the base. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested formulations are named as the publications give them, for clarification not promotion: standard cysteamine hydrochloride 0.10% drops and viscous cysteamine hydrochloride 0.55% drops. Cross-point only: topical cysteamine cream in melasma (pack #6937) is a different condition, formulation and question and shares no anchor. The systemic cysteamine formulation question has exactly one randomised report and is not rowed here.

cards.headline: Report 1 of 3 — paired-eye placebo-controlled trial (1990, N = 29 entered): 10 patients showed marked clearing of corneal crystals in one eye versus the fellow eye, and on unmasking all 10 improved eyes were the cysteamine-treated eyes
cards.summary: Report 1 of 3 — paired-eye placebo-controlled trial (1990, N = 29 entered): 10 patients showed marked clearing of corneal crystals in one eye versus the fellow eye, and on unmasking all 10 improved eyes were the cysteamine-treated eyes
cards.type: Primary report — double-masked randomised placebo-controlled paired-eye trial
cards.people: 29 patients with nephropathic cystinosis entered a double-masked randomised placebo-controlled trial of topical cysteamine eye drops (18 younger than 42 months; 11 aged 4 to 31 years), one eye treated and the fellow eye as control, between November 1985 and September 1989.
cards.result: 8 of the younger and 2 of the older patients showed marked clearing in one eye; all 10 improved eyes proved to be the cysteamine-treated eyes. In 15 patients no marked difference was noted (8 judged to have been in the protocol too briefly, several poorly compliant); 4 were unavailable for follow-up.
cards.watchOut: This is the base's only placebo-controlled report, and it is a paired-eye design from 1990 with 10 clear responders of 29 entered — not a modern parallel-group placebo trial. Several non-responders were poorly compliant or briefly treated, as the report itself states.
cards.source: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. A randomized placebo-controlled trial of cysteamine eye drops in nephropathic cystinosis. Archives of ophthalmology (Chicago, Ill. : 1960). 1990. PMID: 2185723. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Report 2 of 3 — formulation trial (2003): a new room-temperature-stable cysteamine formulation was LESS effective than the standard formulation — a ≥1.00-unit fall in corneal cystine crystal score occurred in 47% of eyes on standard vs 7% on the new formulation (p = 0.04); no serious adverse reactions in either formulation (safety study N = 20; efficacy study N = 16)
cards.summary: Report 2 of 3 — formulation trial (2003): a new room-temperature-stable cysteamine formulation was LESS effective than the standard formulation — a ≥1.00-unit fall in corneal cystine crystal score occurred in 47% of eyes on standard vs 7% on the new formulation (p = 0.04); no serious adverse reactions in either formulation (safety study N = 20; efficacy study N = 16)
cards.type: Primary report — multicentre randomised double-masked formulation-comparison trial
cards.people: 20 subjects in the randomised double-blind safety study and 16 in the efficacy study, comparing a new room-temperature-stable topical cysteamine formulation with the standard formulation; the efficacy primary outcome was a reduction of corneal cystine crystal score by 1.00 or more units on reading-centre-graded photographs.
cards.result: No subject developed any serious adverse reaction with either formulation over 6 months. In the efficacy study, 47% of eyes on the standard formulation achieved a ≥1.00-unit score reduction after 1 year versus 7% on the new formulation (p = 0.04). The authors concluded the new formulation, although safe, was not as effective as the standard formulation.
cards.watchOut: A formulation comparison, not a placebo trial: it shows the standard formulation beats this particular new formulation, in an efficacy study of only 16 subjects. Do not read it as evidence about cysteamine versus no treatment.
cards.source: Tsilou et al. A multicentre randomised double masked clinical trial of a new formulation of topical cysteamine for the treatment of corneal cystine crystals in cystinosis. The British journal of ophthalmology. 2003. PMID: 12488257. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Report 3 of 3 — viscous-formulation phase 3 trial (2017, N = 31): mean change in confocal-microscopy total crystal score was −4.6 ± 3.1 on viscous cysteamine hydrochloride 0.55% vs −0.46 ± 3.38 on standard 0.10% (P < 0.0001) over 90 days, with photophobia also significantly more improved on viscous drops
cards.summary: Report 3 of 3 — viscous-formulation phase 3 trial (2017, N = 31): mean change in confocal-microscopy total crystal score was −4.6 ± 3.1 on viscous cysteamine hydrochloride 0.55% vs −0.46 ± 3.38 on standard 0.10% (P < 0.0001) over 90 days, with photophobia also significantly more improved on viscous drops
cards.type: Primary report — open-label randomised comparative phase 3 formulation trial
cards.people: 31 patients with cystinosis aged ≥2 years randomised 1:1 (15 viscous cysteamine hydrochloride 0.55%; 16 standard cysteamine hydrochloride 0.10%), four times daily for 90 days in both eyes, in an open-label randomised comparative phase 3 trial at two centres in France.
cards.result: The mean absolute change in in-vivo confocal-microscopy total score at day 90 was −4.6 ± 3.1 on viscous versus −0.46 ± 3.38 on standard drops (P < 0.0001). Photophobia, corneal cystine crystal scores and crystal depth were also significantly more improved on viscous drops. The most frequent local adverse drug reactions in both groups were stinging, burning, redness and blurred vision.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and small (N = 31): the crystal-density endpoint is a surrogate, and the comparison is against standard drops, not placebo. Photophobia is the one patient-felt endpoint in this base and it favoured the viscous formulation.
cards.source: Liang et al. A New Viscous Cysteamine Eye Drops Treatment for Ophthalmic Cystinosis: An Open-Label Randomized Comparative Phase III Pivotal Study. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the 1990 paired-eye placebo-controlled trial (N = 29 entered), the 2003 formulation trial (safety N = 20; efficacy N = 16) and the 2017 viscous-formulation phase 3 trial (N = 31).

shelves.title: Centor score for streptococcal pharyngitis in primary care: well calibrated, with a specificity of 0.82 at the antibiotic-consideration threshold of ≥3 — but in low-prevalence settings most score-positive patients do not have streptococcal pharyngitis (post-test probability 12–40% at 5–20% prevalence)
shelves.question: In adults presenting with sore throat in primary care, how accurately does the Centor score (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough — with the McIsaac age adjustment) predict group A streptococcal pharyngitis against throat culture — what pooled specificity does the score achieve at the antibiotic-consideration threshold of ≥3, what probability of streptococcal infection did the 206,870-patient validation find at each score from 0 to 4, and how did the score perform in a low-prevalence Malaysian primary-care cohort?

shelves.balance: This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not an antibiotic-prescribing shelf. The synthesis (21 studies, 4,839 adults) found individual signs and symptoms weak — positive likelihood ratios of only 1.45–2.33, labelled as likelihood ratios — while the Centor score as a decision rule at ≥3 achieved specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88) and was well calibrated (no significant difference between predicted and observed case counts across strata). The base-rate warning is part of every figure: at prior prevalences of 5–20%, a score of ≥3 yields a post-test probability of streptococcal pharyngitis of only 12–40% — in low-prevalence settings most score-positive patients do not have streptococcal pharyngitis. The large-scale validation (206,870 patients aged ≥3 at a US retail health chain; rapid-test/culture pathway — its setting prints with its figures) found, among patients ≥15, positivity rising by Centor score: 7% at 0, 12% at 1, 21% at 2, 38% at 3 and 57% at 4 (overall positivity 23% in that age group). The Malaysian primary-care cohort (215 adults, throat-swab culture) shows the low-prevalence extreme: only 6 isolates (2.4%) were group A streptococcus, so its sensitivities at scores 3 and 4 (each 50% — i.e. 3 of 6 cases; specificities 97.6% and 100%) rest on a very small positive count that prints on the face, and no card headlines them.

cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2011, 21 studies, 4,839 adults): individual signs and symptoms shifted probability only slightly (positive likelihood ratios 1.45–2.33, labelled as such); as a decision rule at ≥3 the Centor score had specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88), with post-test probability of streptococcal pharyngitis 12–40% at prior prevalences of 5–20%
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2011, 21 studies, 4,839 adults): individual signs and symptoms shifted probability only slightly (positive likelihood ratios 1.45–2.33, labelled as such); as a decision rule at ≥3 the Centor score had specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88), with post-test probability of streptococcal pharyngitis 12–40% at prior prevalences of 5–20%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — Centor score accuracy and calibration in adults
cards.people: Adults (>14 years) presenting with sore throat in primary care; studies assessing signs/symptoms and/or validating the Centor score against culture-based reference standards, pooled with a bivariate random-effects model; calibration assessed across score strata.
cards.result: Individual signs and symptoms generated only small shifts in post-test probability (positive likelihood ratios 1.45–2.33; negative likelihood ratios 0.54–0.72, labelled as such). At the antibiotic-consideration threshold (score ≥3), the Centor score's specificity was 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88). Pooled calibration showed no significant difference between predicted and observed group A streptococcal case counts across strata (risk ratios 0.72 for scores 0–1, 0.93 for 2–3, 1.14 for 4). The reviewers conclude the score is a well-calibrated prediction rule that can enhance appropriate antibiotic prescribing but should be used with caution in low-prevalence settings.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the base-rate warning (post-test probability 12–40% at 5–20% prevalence) prints with the ≥3 specificity wherever it is used. Accuracy only — this review does not test prescribing outcomes.
cards.source: Aalbers J et al. Predicting streptococcal pharyngitis in adults in primary care: a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of symptoms and signs and validation of the Centor score. BMC medicine. 2011. PMID: 21631919. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Large-scale validation (2012): among 206,870 patients at a US retail health chain, the proportion testing positive for group A streptococcus rose by Centor score from 7% at score 0 to 12% (1), 21% (2), 38% (3) and 57% (4) in patients aged ≥15 (overall positivity 23%)
cards.summary: Large-scale validation (2012): among 206,870 patients at a US retail health chain, the proportion testing positive for group A streptococcus rose by Centor score from 7% at score 0 to 12% (1), 21% (2), 38% (3) and 57% (4) in patients aged ≥15 (overall positivity 23%)
cards.type: Large-scale validation cohort — Centor/McIsaac stratum probabilities (US retail health chain)
cards.people: Retrospective analysis of 206,870 patients aged ≥3 years presenting with painful throat to a US national retail health chain (2006–2008), scored with the Centor and McIsaac scores (both 0–4) against the chain's rapid-test/culture pathway. The retail-clinic setting prints with these figures.
cards.result: For patients 15 years or older, 23% tested positive overall, by Centor score: 7% (score 0), 12% (1), 21% (2), 38% (3) and 57% (4). For patients 3 years or older, 27% tested positive overall, with McIsaac-score strata of 8%, 14%, 23%, 37% and 55% for scores 0–4. The confidence intervals overlapped with those of prior (much smaller) derivation reports, and the authors conclude the study validates both scores with more precise risk classification.
cards.watchOut: Stratum probabilities are prevalences within a US retail-clinic population using its testing pathway — they are not transportable post-test probabilities for other settings or prevalences. Even at score 4, 43% of patients ≥15 tested negative.
cards.source: Fine AM et al. Large-scale validation of the Centor and McIsaac scores to predict group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Archives of internal medicine. 2012. PMID: 22566485. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Low-prevalence validation (Malaysia, 2022): only 6 isolates (2.4%) of 215 adults were group A streptococcus — Centor scores 3 and 4 each had sensitivity 50% (3 of 6 cases) with specificities of 97.6% and 100%; the very small positive count prints on this shelf's face
cards.summary: Low-prevalence validation (Malaysia, 2022): only 6 isolates (2.4%) of 215 adults were group A streptococcus — Centor scores 3 and 4 each had sensitivity 50% (3 of 6 cases) with specificities of 97.6% and 100%; the very small positive count prints on this shelf's face
cards.type: Cross-sectional validation — Centor score vs throat culture (Malaysian primary care, very low prevalence)
cards.people: Cross-sectional validation in 215 adults presenting with sore throat to three public primary-care clinics in Sepang, Malaysia (convenience sampling), comparing Centor criteria against gold-standard throat-swab culture. Pharyngitis was diagnosed in 130 participants (60.5%). This report's PubMed record carries no MeSH terms ('none in the record' in its source line).
cards.result: Six isolates (2.4%) were identified as group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Both Centor scores 3 and 4 had a sensitivity of 50% and specificities of 97.6% and 100% respectively. The authors conclude a Centor score below 3 is favourable for excluding group A streptococcal pharyngitis, while scores of 3 and 4 require further examination to confirm the diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the positive count is 6 — the 50% sensitivities rest on 3 of 6 cases and no card may headline them. The report's usable content is the exclusion direction at scores <3 and the demonstration of base-rate collapse at 2.4% prevalence.
cards.source: Muthanna A et al. Diagnostic Accuracy of Centor Score for Diagnosis of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis among Adults in Primary Care Clinics in Malaysia. The Malaysian journal of medical sciences : MJMS. 2022. PMID: 36101529. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Centor score is a calibrated probability gradient, not a strep test — 7% to 57% across scores 0–4 in a large US cohort, specificity 0.82 at the ≥3 threshold, and post-test probabilities that stay below half at ordinary primary-care prevalences
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Centor score is a calibrated probability gradient, not a strep test — 7% to 57% across scores 0–4 in a large US cohort, specificity 0.82 at the ≥3 threshold, and post-test probabilities that stay below half at ordinary primary-care prevalences
cards.people: Three reports: a 21-study meta-analysis (4,839 adults), a 206,870-patient retail-clinic validation, and a 215-patient Malaysian culture validation with only 6 group A isolates (count printed).
cards.result: Individual signs are weak (positive LRs 1.45–2.33); the score's calibration is good and its ≥3 specificity is 0.82, but at 5–20% prevalence a positive score still means a 12–40% probability of streptococcal pharyngitis. The Malaysian cohort shows the same rule at 2.4% prevalence, where its sensitivity estimate rests on 3 cases.
cards.watchOut: Diagnostic accuracy only — no prescribing-outcome claim. Stratum probabilities always carry their setting and prevalence.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Whispered voice test for hearing impairment: adult sensitivity 90–100% in the systematic review, phrase-dependent AUCs 0.900–0.918 in older adults, and tuning-fork tests not supported for screening
shelves.question: At the bedside, how accurately does the whispered voice test (examiner whispers a letter / number combination or short phrases at arm's length behind the patient, masking the other ear) detect hearing impairment against pure-tone audiometry — what sensitivity and specificity ranges did the systematic review find in adults, what accuracy and inter-examiner reproducibility do standardised phrases achieve in older adults, and what summary likelihood ratios does the Rational Clinical Examination assign to the whispered voice and to the Rinne and Weber tuning-fork tests?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Hearing Disorders/diagnosis · Hearing Tests/methods,standards · Humans · Middle Aged · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: Technique is unstandardised across the primary literature (six techniques in the 2003 systematic review; phrase choice moves the AUC in the older-adult study) and prints on this shelf. The adult sensitivity headline (90–100%) comes from four studies inside the 2003 review and prints as a range from a synthesis, not as a pooled estimate. The Rational Clinical Examination gives the whispered voice a summary positive likelihood ratio of 6.1 and negative likelihood ratio of 0.03 (both labelled as such), while the tuning-fork limb is a negative result — Weber likelihood ratio 1.6, near 1 — and prints as such, not as an endorsement of Rinne / Weber screening. This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf.

cards.headline: Whispered voice systematic review (Pirozzo 2003, BMJ — 8 studies using six different techniques): in the four adult studies sensitivity was 90% or 100% and specificity 70–87%; in the four childhood studies sensitivity ranged 80–96% and specificity 90–98%, against pure-tone audiometry
cards.summary: Whispered voice systematic review (Pirozzo 2003, BMJ — 8 studies using six different techniques): in the four adult studies sensitivity was 90% or 100% and specificity 70–87%; in the four childhood studies sensitivity ranged 80–96% and specificity 90–98%, against pure-tone audiometry
cards.type: Systematic review of test accuracy (8 studies, six techniques)
cards.people: Cross-sectional accuracy studies of the whispered voice test with audiometry performed on at least 80% of participants; 8 studies, six different techniques — 4 in adults, 4 in children.
cards.result: Adult studies: sensitivity 90% or 100%, specificity 70% to 87%. Childhood studies: sensitivity 80% to 96%, specificity 90% to 98%. The reviewers call the test simple and accurate for detecting hearing impairment, with concern about lower sensitivity in children and overall reproducibility, particularly in primary care, and call for standardisation studies in primary care.
cards.watchOut: The adult 90–100% sensitivity is a range across four studies using different techniques, not a pooled estimate — no card may present it as one.
cards.source: Pirozzo S et al. Whispered voice test for screening for hearing impairment in adults and children: systematic review. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2003. PMID: 14576249. cards.headline: Standardised whispered phrases in older adults (Labanca 2017 — 210 adults aged 60–97 against audiometry): the best-performing phrases reached AUCs of 0.900–0.918 with inter-examiner reproducibility 0.81–0.877
cards.summary: Standardised whispered phrases in older adults (Labanca 2017 — 210 adults aged 60–97 against audiometry): the best-performing phrases reached AUCs of 0.900–0.918 with inter-examiner reproducibility 0.81–0.877
cards.type: Cross-sectional accuracy and reproducibility study in older adults (N = 210)
cards.people: 210 older adults aged 60–97 years; whispered voice test employing ten different phrases, audiometry as reference; the test was repeated on 20% of ears by a second examiner for inter-examiner reproducibility.
cards.result: The words and phrases with the highest AUC and reproducibility were 'shoe' (AUC 0.918; reproducibility 0.877), 'window' (AUC 0.917; 0.869), 'it looks like it's going to rain' (AUC 0.911; 0.810) and 'the bus is late' (AUC 0.900; 0.810). The authors conclude the whispered voice test is a useful screening tool in older people and propose these phrases be incorporated into the protocol.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the Brazilian Journal of Otorhinolaryngology; the PubMed record fetched this session gives Ciencia & saude coletiva — the record governs the source line. Phrase choice is part of the result: accuracy is phrase-dependent, not a property of whispering in general.
cards.source: Labanca L et al. Screening of hearing in elderly people: assessment of accuracy and reproducibility of the whispered voice test. Ciencia & saude coletiva. 2017. PMID: 29211164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rational Clinical Examination on bedside hearing manoeuvres (Bagai 2006, JAMA — 24 studies): inability to perceive a whispered voice had a summary positive likelihood ratio of 6.1 (95% CI 4.5 to 8.4) and normal perception a negative likelihood ratio of 0.03 (0 to 0.24), both labelled as such; an abnormal Weber test had a likelihood ratio of only 1.6 (1.0 to 2.3) and Rinne results varied too widely to summarise simply (positive likelihood ratios 2.7 to 62)
cards.summary: Rational Clinical Examination on bedside hearing manoeuvres (Bagai 2006, JAMA — 24 studies): inability to perceive a whispered voice had a summary positive likelihood ratio of 6.1 (95% CI 4.5 to 8.4) and normal perception a negative likelihood ratio of 0.03 (0 to 0.24), both labelled as such; an abnormal Weber test had a likelihood ratio of only 1.6 (1.0 to 2.3) and Rinne results varied too widely to summarise simply (positive likelihood ratios 2.7 to 62)
cards.type: Rational Clinical Examination systematic review (24 studies)
cards.people: Original studies of the accuracy or precision of screening questions and bedside tests for hearing impairment, 1966 to April 2005; 24 included studies, each assigned a methodological grade.
cards.result: Whispered voice: positive likelihood ratio 6.1 (95% CI 4.5 to 8.4) for inability to perceive, negative likelihood ratio 0.03 (0 to 0.24) for normal perception. Weber: abnormal response likelihood ratio 1.6 (1.0 to 2.3), normal 0.70 (0.48 to 1.0). Rinne: abnormal response likelihood ratios ranged 2.7 to 62, normal 0.01 to 0.85. The reviewers advise that people who perceive the whispered voice need no further testing, those who cannot require audiometry, and that the Weber and Rinne tests should not be used for general screening.
cards.watchOut: The tuning-fork limb is negative for screening (Weber likelihood ratio near 1) and prints as such. The whispered-voice likelihood ratios are summary values from a synthesis, labelled as such, not a single cohort's result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the whispered voice test is a sensitive bedside screen in adults (90–100% sensitivity across four studies in the 2003 review; summary negative likelihood ratio 0.03 in the Rational Clinical Examination), with phrase-dependent accuracy in older adults — while Rinne / Weber tuning-fork tests are not supported for general screening. Refusal recorded: the 1985 primary study of the test (PMID 3989786) has no abstract in its PubMed record and was therefore NOT carded as an anchor on this shelf

shelves.title: EAT-10 for dysphagia: pooled AUC 0.903 at cut-off ≥3 against instrumental evaluation — but 38% of penetration / aspiration missed in Parkinson's disease
shelves.question: In adults with suspected dysphagia, how accurately does the EAT-10 (Eating Assessment Tool — a ten-item self-administered symptom questionnaire, each item 0–4, abnormal at ≥3) detect dysphagia and aspiration against instrumental evaluation — what did its derivation study establish as the normal score distribution, what pooled accuracy does the meta-analysis find at cut-offs 2 and 3, and how badly does the questionnaire miss instrumentally proven penetration and aspiration in Parkinson's disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis · Esophageal Diseases/complications · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux/complications · Head and Neck Neoplasms/complications · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reproducibility of Results · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Voice Disorders/complications
shelves.balance: The EAT-10 measures symptoms, and its failure mode is silent or minimally symptomatic aspiration: the Parkinson's result (38% of patients with penetration or aspiration missed, AUC 0.65) prints beside the pooled figures on this shelf. The derivation study's validity is criterion / construct validity against diagnoses and treatment response, not aspiration accuracy, and prints as such. Cut-off choice trades sensitivity for specificity (0.89 / 0.59 at ≥2 vs 0.85 / 0.82 at ≥3), and no figure prints without its cut-off. Cross-point: a different EAT-10 report (postoperative, anterior cervical surgery) is carded on the postoperative swallow-screening shelf — this shelf asks the instrument's general accuracy. This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf.

cards.headline: EAT-10 derivation and validation (Belafsky 2008 — 482 patients, 629 surveys, plus a healthy community cohort; originators' report): internal consistency α 0.960; the normal cohort's mean score was 0.40 ± 1.01, supporting ≥3 as abnormal, while patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia averaged 23.10 ± 12.22
cards.summary: EAT-10 derivation and validation (Belafsky 2008 — 482 patients, 629 surveys, plus a healthy community cohort; originators' report): internal consistency α 0.960; the normal cohort's mean score was 0.40 ± 1.01, supporting ≥3 as abnormal, while patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia averaged 23.10 ± 12.22
cards.people: 482 patients (629 surveys) with a wide array of swallowing, voice, reflux and head-and-neck conditions, plus a community cohort of healthy volunteers for normative data. Programme-labelled: the originators' own report.
cards.result: Internal consistency (Cronbach alpha) 0.960; test-retest intra-item correlations 0.72 to 0.91. Mean EAT-10 scores: normal cohort 0.40 ± 1.01; oropharyngeal dysphagia 23.10 ± 12.22; oesophageal dysphagia 23.58 ± 13.18; head and neck cancer 22.42 ± 14.06; reflux 11.71 ± 9.61; voice disorders 9.19 ± 12.60. Mean score in treated dysphagia patients improved from 19.87 ± 10.5 to 5.2 ± 7.4 after treatment (P < 0.001). Normative data suggest a score of 3 or higher is abnormal.
cards.watchOut: This report establishes score distribution, reliability and construct / criterion validity against diagnoses and treatment response — it is not an aspiration-accuracy study against instrumental evaluation, and must not be quoted as one.

cards.headline: EAT-10 meta-analysis (Zhang 2023, Dysphagia — 7 studies, 1,064 subjects against FEES or videofluoroscopy): at cut-off 2 pooled sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.93) and specificity 0.59 (0.39 to 0.77), and at cut-off 3 sensitivity was 0.85 (0.68 to 0.94) and specificity 0.82 (0.65 to 0.92), with AUC 0.903 at cut-off 3 (likelihood ratios and diagnostic odds ratios labelled as such in the source)
cards.summary: EAT-10 meta-analysis (Zhang 2023, Dysphagia — 7 studies, 1,064 subjects against FEES or videofluoroscopy): at cut-off 2 pooled sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.93) and specificity 0.59 (0.39 to 0.77), and at cut-off 3 sensitivity was 0.85 (0.68 to 0.94) and specificity 0.82 (0.65 to 0.92), with AUC 0.903 at cut-off 3 (likelihood ratios and diagnostic odds ratios labelled as such in the source)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (7 studies, 1,064 subjects)
cards.people: 7 studies, 1,064 subjects from 7 countries, against flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing or videofluoroscopic swallowing study; 2 studies rated high quality, 5 medium quality.
cards.result: At cut-off 2: pooled sensitivity 0.89 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.93), specificity 0.59 (0.39 to 0.77), positive likelihood ratio 2.17, negative likelihood ratio 0.19, diagnostic odds ratio 11.49 (all labelled as such). At cut-off 3: sensitivity 0.85 (0.68 to 0.94), specificity 0.82 (0.65 to 0.92), positive likelihood ratio 4.84, negative likelihood ratio 0.18, diagnostic odds ratio 26.24. Areas under the curve were 0.873 (cut-off 2) and 0.903 (cut-off 3). The authors recommend cut-off 3 for better diagnostic accuracy.
cards.watchOut: Cut-off is part of every figure: ≥2 buys sensitivity at the cost of specificity (0.59); ≥3 reverses the trade. The wide intervals at cut-off 3 (sensitivity CI 0.68 to 0.94) print with the point estimates.

cards.headline: EAT-10 in Parkinson's disease (Schlickewei 2021 — prospective cross-sectional study, 50 patients against FEES): EAT-10 scores did not correlate significantly with Penetration-Aspiration Scale ratings, 19 of 50 patients (38%) with penetration or aspiration were not detected, and accuracy was only sufficient (AUC 0.65; at the optimal cut-off ≥6, sensitivity 58% and specificity 82%)
cards.summary: EAT-10 in Parkinson's disease (Schlickewei 2021 — prospective cross-sectional study, 50 patients against FEES): EAT-10 scores did not correlate significantly with Penetration-Aspiration Scale ratings, 19 of 50 patients (38%) with penetration or aspiration were not detected, and accuracy was only sufficient (AUC 0.65; at the optimal cut-off ≥6, sensitivity 58% and specificity 82%)
cards.type: Prospective cross-sectional accuracy study in Parkinson's disease (N = 50)
cards.people: 50 patients with Parkinson's disease who completed the EAT-10 and then underwent flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES), with Penetration-Aspiration Scale (PAS) ratings analysed retrospectively.
cards.result: PAS and EAT-10 did not correlate significantly, and selected EAT-10 items could not predict aspiration or residues. 19 of 50 patients (38%) with either penetration or aspiration were not detected by the EAT-10. Diagnostic accuracy was only sufficient (AUC 0.65); at the optimal cut-off of ≥6, sensitivity was 58% and specificity 82%. The authors conclude the EAT-10 is not suited to detecting penetration and aspiration in Parkinson's disease.

shelves.title: Waterlow scale for pressure-injury risk: AUC 0.623 and PPV 2.07% in 5,874 ICU patients, low sensitivity in the risk-scale meta-analysis — insufficient as a screening tool
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the Waterlow scale (body build, skin type, sex / age, continence, mobility, appetite and special-risk items; high risk conventionally at ≥15–20) predict who will develop a pressure injury — what discrimination did it achieve in a 5,874-patient multicentre intensive-care cohort and at what cut-off, how did it perform in a smaller hospital cohort scored serially alongside the Braden scale, and what does the meta-analysis of pressure-ulcer risk scales conclude about its sensitivity relative to the Braden and Norton scales?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Risk Assessment · Cohort Studies · Pressure Ulcer/diagnosis · Reproducibility of Results · Risk Factors · Intensive Care Units · ROC Curve
shelves.balance: The performance gradient is the content of this shelf: near-chance discrimination in the large ICU cohort (AUC 0.623, positive predictive value 2.07% at the derived cut-off of 19 — driven by that cohort's very low event rate, which prints with it) against moderate summary performance (summary AUC over 0.7) in the meta-analysis, whose authors still judge the Waterlow's sensitivity low and the scale insufficient as a screening tool. Cut-offs are not interchangeable across reports (17 vs 19 vs the conventional 15 / 20 bands) and print with their figures. The small cohort (N = 98) was pre-selected as elevated-risk on both scales, which prints. Distinct from the Braden shelf (different instrument); the meta-analysis carded here was also seen in the Norton audit and is carded here for its Waterlow limb, stated openly. This is a prediction-accuracy shelf, not a prevention shelf: no card implies Waterlow-guided prevention improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Waterlow in intensive care (Han 2024, Journal of Clinical Nursing — multicentre cohort, 72 ICUs in 38 hospitals; 5,874 critically ill adults screened on admission, 5,125 assessed regularly): AUC was 0.623 (95% CI 0.574 to 0.690); at the best-balance cut-off of 19, sensitivity was 62.7%, specificity 57.4%, PPV 2.07% and NPV 99.08%; test-retest reliability was 0.447 — the authors conclude the scale shows insufficient predictive validity and reliability in critical care
cards.summary: Waterlow in intensive care (Han 2024, Journal of Clinical Nursing — multicentre cohort, 72 ICUs in 38 hospitals; 5,874 critically ill adults screened on admission, 5,125 assessed regularly): AUC was 0.623 (95% CI 0.574 to 0.690); at the best-balance cut-off of 19, sensitivity was 62.7%, specificity 57.4%, PPV 2.07% and NPV 99.08%; test-retest reliability was 0.447 — the authors conclude the scale shows insufficient predictive validity and reliability in critical care
cards.type: Multicentre cohort study in intensive care (N = 5,874)
cards.people: 5,874 critical adult patients admitted to 72 ICUs in 38 tertiary hospitals (Gansu Province, China) for ≥24 hours without pressure injury on admission, screened with the Waterlow scale on admission, during stay and at discharge (April 2021 to February 2023); 5,125 assessed regularly.
cards.result: Area under the ROC curve 0.623 (95% CI 0.574 to 0.690). At cut-off 19 (best balance by Youden's index): sensitivity 62.7%, specificity 57.4%, positive predictive value 2.07%, negative predictive value 99.08%. Test-retest reliability between first and regular assessment was 0.447. The authors conclude the Waterlow scale shows insufficient predictive validity and reliability in discriminating critical adults at risk of pressure-injury development.
cards.watchOut: The PPV of 2.07% is driven by this ICU cohort's very low event rate and prints with it — it is not a property of the scale alone. Cut-off 19 here is a locally derived optimum, not the conventional 15 / 20 band.

cards.headline: Waterlow scored serially in hospital (Serpa 2009 — 98 hospitalised patients pre-selected as elevated-risk, scored on alternate days alongside the Braden scale): at the first assessment's cut-off of 17, sensitivity was 71.4% and specificity 67.0% (AUC 0.64, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93), with accuracy deteriorating at later assessments (cut-offs 20 / 20; sensitivity 85.7% / 85.7%, specificity 40.7% / 32.9%)
cards.summary: Waterlow scored serially in hospital (Serpa 2009 — 98 hospitalised patients pre-selected as elevated-risk, scored on alternate days alongside the Braden scale): at the first assessment's cut-off of 17, sensitivity was 71.4% and specificity 67.0% (AUC 0.64, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93), with accuracy deteriorating at later assessments (cut-offs 20 / 20; sensitivity 85.7% / 85.7%, specificity 40.7% / 32.9%)
cards.type: Predictive-validity study with serial scoring (N = 98, pre-selected elevated-risk)
cards.people: 98 adult hospitalised patients at a 220-bed private general hospital, pre-selected with Braden score ≤18 and Waterlow score ≥16 (mean age 71.1 years); skin assessment and both scales completed on alternate days, at least 3 times per patient.
cards.result: Cut-off scores were 17, 20 and 20 at the first, second and third assessments. Sensitivity was 71.4%, 85.7% and 85.7%; specificity 67.0%, 40.7% and 32.9%. Only the first assessment at cut-off 17 showed the reported accuracy (AUC 0.64, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.93). Probabilities of pressure-ulcer development were 14%, 10% and 9% when the test was positive (positive likelihood ratio) and 3% when negative, across assessments (likelihood ratios labelled as such in the source).
cards.watchOut: This cohort was pre-selected as elevated-risk on both scales, which inflates apparent performance and prints wherever its figures appear. The AUC interval (0.35 to 0.93) spans chance — the point estimate must not be quoted without it.
cards.source: Serpa LF et al. Predictive validity of Waterlow Scale for pressure ulcer development risk in hospitalized patients. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of pressure-ulcer risk scales (Park 2016 — 17 diagnostic studies, 5,185 patients): the Braden, Norton and Waterlow scales all showed summary AUCs over 0.7 (moderate predictive validity), but the Waterlow scale's sensitivity was low compared with the other scales and the authors judge it insufficient as a screening tool
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of pressure-ulcer risk scales (Park 2016 — 17 diagnostic studies, 5,185 patients): the Braden, Norton and Waterlow scales all showed summary AUCs over 0.7 (moderate predictive validity), but the Waterlow scale's sensitivity was low compared with the other scales and the authors judge it insufficient as a screening tool
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pressure-ulcer risk scales (17 studies, 5,185 patients)
cards.people: 17 diagnostic studies with high methodological quality involving 5,185 patients, covering the Cubbin & Jackson, modified Braden, Norton and Waterlow scales; quality assessed with QUADAS-II. Carded here for its Waterlow limb (the same synthesis was seen in the Norton audit — stated openly). This record carries no MeSH terms (source line reads 'MeSH: none in the record').
cards.result: Summary ROC areas under the curve for the Braden, Norton and Waterlow scales were all over 0.7, showing moderate predictive validity, with limited interpretation due to significant differences between studies. The Waterlow scale was insufficient as a screening tool owing to low sensitivity compared with the other scales. The authors conclude contemporary pressure-ulcer risk scales are not suitable for uniform practice under standardised criteria.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the Journal of Clinical Nursing; the PubMed record fetched this session gives Iranian journal of public health — the record governs the source line. A summary AUC over 0.7 beside a 'insufficient as a screening tool' verdict is the authors' own pairing — do not quote the AUC without the verdict.

shelves.title: Choroidal thickness in healthy eyes (PHYS, 4 Asian datasets): standardised subfoveal thickness 291.2 µm (N = 9,850), thinning ≈2.0 µm/year (N = 27,965), vascularity index far stabler than thickness — absolute values do not transport across populations
shelves.question: What is the thickness of the choroid (the vascular layer beneath the retina, measured by enhanced-depth-imaging OCT) in healthy eyes — what population-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness do the large Asian cohorts report, how fast does it thin with age, and how much less variable is the choroidal vascularity index than thickness itself? (PHYSIOLOGY: platform, segmentation method and axial-length confounding print with each value.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging · Choroid/blood supply · Choroid Diseases/diagnosis/pathology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Adolescent · Adult · Choroid/blood supply/diagnostic imaging · Cross-Sectional Studies · Fovea Centralis/diagnostic imaging · Healthy Volunteers · India · Retinal Vessels/diagnostic imaging · Tomography, Optical Coherence/methods · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four datasets, all Asian populations, with imaging platform and segmentation method printed beside each value (Nidek RS-3000 Advance EDI-OCT in Nagahama; Heidelberg Spectralis EDI in the Indian dataset — specific devices named where the publication gives them, per the standing product rule; the KNHANES and Beijing records' platforms are as published). The age- and sex-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness in 9,850 Nagahama participants was 291.2 µm, with axial length, age and sex the dominant determinants — axial length is the dominant confounder (highly myopic eyes thin the choroid) and prints beside every population mean. In 27,965 KNHANES participants (a general health-survey sample, not an eye-screened healthy cohort — printed as such) thickness declined at β −2.00 µm/year (right eye), with sex differences at ages 30–49 diminishing later. The choroidal vascularity index in 345 healthy Beijing eyes averaged 65.61 ± 2.33% with a coefficient of variation of 3.55% against 40.30% for thickness itself. The Indian dataset is small (43 individuals, 73 eyes; mean thickness 331.6 ± 63.9 µm) and its N prints on the face. Ethnic composition differs across all four datasets and no value transports across them. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age decline and the vascularity-index stability; EMERGING for any single population's absolute thickness as a cross-population norm.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 4 (Mori 2021, Ophthalmology Science — Nagahama population-based cohort, 9,850 participants with enhanced-depth-imaging OCT on the Nidek RS-3000 Advance): the age- and sex-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness was 291.2 µm, with axial length, age and sex the dominant determinants; standardised choroidal vascularity index was 66.88%
cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 4 (Mori 2021, Ophthalmology Science — Nagahama population-based cohort, 9,850 participants with enhanced-depth-imaging OCT on the Nidek RS-3000 Advance): the age- and sex-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness was 291.2 µm, with axial length, age and sex the dominant determinants; standardised choroidal vascularity index was 66.88%
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — subfoveal choroidal thickness, Nagahama cohort, Nidek RS-3000 EDI-OCT (dataset 1 of 4)
cards.people: 9,850 participants in the first follow-up (2013–2016) of the Nagahama Prospective Cohort, Japan, undergoing standardised ophthalmic examination including OCT with enhanced depth imaging (EDI; RS-3000 Advance, Nidek — the named device prints, per the standing product rule), with manual segmentation of the choroidoscleral interface. A general-population cohort, not an eye-screened healthy cohort in the strict sense — printed as such.
cards.result: Age-sex standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT), normalised choroidal intensity and choroidal vascularity index (CVI) were 291.2 μm, 0.653 and 66.88% respectively. In both men and women SFCT was associated negatively with age (P < 0.001). SFCT did not differ significantly between men and women overall (P = 0.87), but among younger participants (35–50 years) men showed significantly greater SFCT (P < 0.001). In multivariable analysis SFCT was associated significantly with age, sex, axial length, spherical equivalent and the age-by-sex interaction (all P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: This record carries no MeSH in PubMed — its source line says so, and the shelf's top-level MeSH is taken from the other datasets. Axial length is a dominant determinant: highly myopic eyes thin the choroid, and no population mean on this shelf may be read without that confounder beside it.

cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 4 (Kim 2026, Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology — Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2017–2021, normative sample 27,965 participants): subfoveal choroidal thickness declined with age (β −2.00 µm per year, right eye; −1.84 µm per year, left eye) and differed by sex at ages 30–49, the difference diminishing in older age groups
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 4 (Kim 2026, Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology — Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2017–2021, normative sample 27,965 participants): subfoveal choroidal thickness declined with age (β −2.00 µm per year, right eye; −1.84 µm per year, left eye) and differed by sex at ages 30–49, the difference diminishing in older age groups
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — subfoveal choroidal thickness by age and sex, KNHANES (dataset 2 of 4)
cards.people: 27,965 participants in KNHANES 2017–2021 who underwent comprehensive ophthalmic examinations including SFCT measurement, analysed with survey-weighted multivariable regression. A general health-survey sample, not an eye-screened healthy cohort — printed as such, per the row's flag.
cards.result: SFCT showed a significant linear decrease with advancing age in both eyes (right eye: β = −2.00, SE 0.12, P < 0.001; left eye: β = −1.84, SE 0.15, P < 0.001). Significant sex differences were observed at ages 30–39 (right eye difference −31.8 μm, 95% CI −48.6 to −15.0; left eye −33.1 μm, −51.1 to −15.1) and 40–49 (right −27.8 μm, −33.6 to −22.1; left −28.6 μm, −34.8 to −22.4), diminishing in older age groups. The authors present the dataset as a nationally representative normative reference framework for Korean eyes.
cards.watchOut: This record also carries no MeSH in PubMed — stated on its source line. A health-survey sample: ocular-disease exclusion is not the sampling frame, so its values are population values, not screened-healthy values, and do not transport to the Japanese or Indian datasets.

cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 4 (Agrawal 2016, Scientific Reports — Beijing Eye Study, 345 healthy eyes): the choroidal vascularity index (luminal / total choroidal area) averaged 65.61 ± 2.33%, with a coefficient of variation of 3.55% against 40.30% for subfoveal thickness itself
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 4 (Agrawal 2016, Scientific Reports — Beijing Eye Study, 345 healthy eyes): the choroidal vascularity index (luminal / total choroidal area) averaged 65.61 ± 2.33%, with a coefficient of variation of 3.55% against 40.30% for subfoveal thickness itself
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — choroidal vascularity index normative values (dataset 3 of 4)
cards.people: 345 healthy eyes in a population-based study (Beijing Eye Study), with enhanced-depth-imaging OCT scans segmented by a modified image-binarisation technique into luminal and stromal areas; the denominator is eyes, as published — the number of individuals is not separately documented in the abstract and prints as such.
cards.result: Subfoveal CVI ranged from 60.07 to 71.27% with a mean of 65.61 ± 2.33%. CVI was less variable than subfoveal choroidal thickness (coefficient of variation 3.55 vs 40.30 for SFCT). Higher CVI was associated with thicker SFCT but not with most physiological variables; CVI was a significant determinant of SFCT, and the authors propose CVI as a more robust marker of choroidal vascular status than thickness alone.
cards.watchOut: Eyes, not individuals, are the unit (345 eyes). CVI's stability is a within-this-study comparison of coefficients of variation — it does not make any single population's thickness value transportable across ethnic groups or platforms.
cards.source: Agrawal R et al. Choroidal vascularity index as a measure of vascular status of the choroid: Measurements in healthy eyes from a population-based study. Scientific reports. 2016. cards.people: 43 healthy Indian individuals (73 eyes; mean age 28.23 ± 15.29 years, range 14–59 — a young sample including adolescents, flagged here) imaged with the enhanced-depth-imaging feature of Spectralis OCT (the named platform prints), with choroidal and sublayer thickness measured by two observers. Small N = 43 individuals — printed on the face, per the row.
cards.result: Overall mean subfoveal choroidal thickness was 331.6 ± 63.9 μm. Mean large choroidal vessel layer (Haller's) thickness was 227.08 ± 51.24 μm and medium vessel layer (Sattler's) thickness 95.65 ± 23.62 μm. Choroidal thickness was maximum subfoveally, reducing gradually with distance from the fovea. This is the first study describing choroidal sublayer thickness in a healthy Indian population, as published.
cards.watchOut: Small N (43 individuals, 73 eyes) and a young age range (14–59, including adolescents): its higher mean thickness (331.6 µm) sits beside the Nagahama standardised 291.2 µm without either transporting to the other's population, platform or age structure.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in healthy eyes the choroid thins with age (β −2.00 µm/year in 27,965 Koreans; negative age association in 9,850 Japanese, standardised subfoveal thickness 291.2 µm), absolute thickness is population-, age- and axial-length-bound (331.6 µm in a small young Indian sample, N = 43), and the choroidal vascularity index is far less variable than thickness itself (mean 65.61%, coefficient of variation 3.55% vs 40.30% for thickness, in 345 healthy eyes) — ESTABLISHED for the age decline and the vascularity index's stability, EMERGING for any single population's absolute thickness as a cross-population norm

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: Mori 2021 (Nagahama, N = 9,850), Kim 2026 (KNHANES, N = 27,965), Agrawal 2016 (Beijing, 345 eyes) and Roy 2018 (India, 43 individuals / 73 eyes). Distinct from the built retinal-layer normative shelves (RNFL, macular thickness, corneal thickness, axial length) — the choroid is a different structure with different measurement physics.
cards.result: PHYSIOLOGY framing only — no intervention stamp applies. Imaging platform and segmentation method print with each value (Nidek RS-3000, Heidelberg Spectralis and equivalent EDI protocols are not interchangeable), and axial length — the dominant confounder — prints beside every population mean.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
